en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Path of Discrimination in the Minor Collection (Khuddakanikāya)
(First Part) Introduction to the Composition:
He who surpasses all worlds and possesses all splendor—
Endowed with all virtues that should be practiced,
and freed from all faults along with their latent tendencies,
he is liberated and the giver of supreme liberation.
With a mind ever cool with the sandalwood of compassion,
illuminating all those to be trained with the radiance of wisdom—
he who has become the supreme among all beings.
Having bowed my head to the Lord of Reality—
who, like the Sage, was supreme among all beings, and who, among the infinite sons of the Conqueror,
emulated the Teacher’s grace in his compassion, wisdom, and virtues for the welfare of living beings.
Having bowed down to that Sāriputta, the son of the Sage-King, the Elder who delights in many steadfast virtues,
whose beautiful fame has risen through the power of wisdom, and who is of most peaceful conduct— to him,
the disciple who is the General of the True Dharma and the one who sets in motion the Wheel of the True Dharma.
In the discourses spoken by the Tathāgata— who has attained the realization of the true meaning—
that which was uttered by him, who is skilled in speech and the leader who kindles the lamp of the Dhamma,
is the distinguished reading of the *Paṭisambhidā*; it is further specified by that name as "the Path."
Enveloped by the method of manifold mental diversity, always plunged into by those of profound wisdom,
and dedicated to their own welfare and the welfare of the world, it should be constantly cultivated by the virtuous.
It brings about the differentiation of knowledge and is frequented by many yogis.
Explaining the meaning that has not been heard before, following the sequence of both the Suttas and the logical arguments (yutti),
not deviating from his own established tenets, and not contradicting the tenets of others;
he brings together the method of the ancient commentaries and instructions in a manner that is appropriate.
"I shall speak this commentary for the benefit of people, for the sake of the long endurance of the True Dhamma.
Listen well and bear it in mind, O virtuous ones, for it clearly elucidates the True Dhamma.
In that context, because it is stated that "the path to the analytical knowledges" is specified by that particular name, it refers to the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.
The Path of Discrimination (Paṭisambhidāmagga) must now be explained. There are four discriminations:

discrimination of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā), discrimination of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā), discrimination of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā), and discrimination of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā). The "Path of Discrimination" is the path—the means of attainment—of these discriminations;
what is meant is that it is the cause for the acquisition of the discriminations. How is this their path?
If it is asked, "How so?"—it is because the teaching, when taught according to its various divisions, brings about the knowledge of the analytical powers (*paṭisambhidāñāṇa*).

For a teaching that is divided into various categories gives rise to the various manifestations of the knowledge of the analytical powers among noble individuals who hear it, and it serves as a condition for the future manifestation of the knowledge of the analytical powers among worldlings (*puthujjana*). And it has been said:
“For, by way of its divisions, the teaching brings about the analytical knowledge (*paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa*) that discerns the compact mass.
And this teaching is divided into various categories; therefore, its status as the path to the analytical knowledges is established.

In this context, “four” is the delimitation by number. “Analytical knowledges” (*paṭisambhidā*) refers to the specific types. “Knowledge regarding the meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).”
Because it is said: "Knowledge of the Dhamma is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma; therein, knowledge of the expression of the language of the Dhamma is the analytical knowledge of language;
and knowledge regarding knowledges is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity," these are not divisions of anything else, but rather divisions of knowledge itself.
Therefore, the meaning of "the four analytical knowledges" (catasso paṭisambhidā) is "four divisions of knowledge. Regarding the division of meaning...
The analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) is the knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding meanings, capable of discerning, analyzing, and defining them.
The analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*) is the knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding phenomena, capable of discerning, analyzing, and defining them.
[The analytical knowledge of language] is capable of discerning, analyzing, and defining the differentiation of etymological explanations (*nirutti*).
The knowledge that has reached the analysis of language (*nirutti*) regarding the expression of language is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).

The knowledge that has reached the analysis of ingenuity (*paṭibhāna*) regarding the capacity to discern, clarify, and define the various types of ingenuity is the analytical knowledge of ingenuity (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*).
In this context, "meaning" (*attha*) is, in brief, cause and fruit; for it is through following the cause that it is sought after and attained.

Because it is reached, it is called "meaning" (*attha*). In terms of its classification, however, these five phenomena should be understood as "meaning": whatever is produced by conditions, Nibbāna, the meaning of what has been spoken, fruition (*vipāka*), and functional (*kiriya*) consciousness.
For one who reflects upon that meaning, the knowledge that has penetrated the distinctions within that meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).
"Dhamma" is, in brief, condition. For it is called "dhamma" because it ordains, causes to proceed, and brings about this or that state;

therefore it is called dhamma. In detail, however, any cause whatsoever that produces a fruit—namely, the Noble Path, speech, the wholesome, and the unwholesome—these five things should be understood as "dhamma. For one who reflects upon that dhamma...
Knowledge that has reached analysis regarding that Dhamma is the discrimination of Dhamma (dhammapaṭisambhidā). For this very meaning is stated in the Abhidhamma:
"Knowledge regarding suffering is the discrimination of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā); knowledge regarding the origin of suffering is the discrimination of Dhamma;
knowledge regarding the cessation of suffering is the discrimination of meaning; knowledge regarding the way leading to the cessation of suffering is the discrimination of Dhamma."

Knowledge regarding the cause is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*); knowledge regarding the fruit of the cause is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*attha-paṭisambhidā*).
“Knowledge regarding those phenomena that have been born, become, produced, brought forth, fully manifested, and made manifest—this is the analytical knowledge of meaning;
[knowledge regarding] from which phenomena those phenomena have been born, become, produced, brought forth, and fully manifested...”
When these states have become manifest, the knowledge regarding them is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*).
“Knowledge regarding aging and death is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*attha-paṭisambhidā*); knowledge regarding the origin of aging and death is the analytical knowledge of phenomena;

knowledge regarding the cessation of aging and death is the analytical knowledge of meaning; knowledge regarding the practice leading to the cessation of aging and death is the analytical knowledge of phenomena.”

“Knowledge of birth … [and so on] … knowledge of existence … knowledge of clinging … knowledge of craving … knowledge of feeling … knowledge of contact … knowledge of the six sense bases … knowledge of name-and-form … knowledge of consciousness … knowledge of volitional formations is the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā). Knowledge of the arising of volitional formations is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā). Knowledge of the cessation of volitional formations …”

Knowledge of the meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*); knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of formations is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*).

“In this case, a bhikkhu knows the Dhamma: the discourses (*sutta*), mixed prose and verse (*geyya*), expositions (*veyyākaraṇa*), verses (*gāthā*), inspired utterances (*udāna*), ‘Thus it was said’ (*itivuttaka*), birth stories (*jātaka*), marvelous qualities (*abbhutadhamma*), and questions-and-answers (*vedalla*). This is called the analytical knowledge of phenomena. He [knows] each of those...”
One knows the meaning of what has been said: "This is the meaning of this statement; this is the meaning of that statement.
This is called the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).
"What are wholesome states? At whatever time a wholesome consciousness belonging to the sense sphere arises, accompanied by joy..."
“Associated with knowledge, having either visible form as its object... pe... or mental phenomena as its object, or whatever else it may be directed toward—at that time there is contact...
pe... there is non-distraction. These states are wholesome. Knowledge regarding these states is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā);
knowledge regarding their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā). Thus it is shown by way of repeated analysis.
Regarding "knowledge of the expression of the language of the Dhamma": this refers to the natural language and unerring terminology concerning both that meaning and those phenomena.
When one speaks, utters, or articulates that expression—the speaking, uttering, or articulation of it—one takes that articulated sound of natural language as an object and reflects upon it.
Regarding that expression of natural language, one understands: "This is natural language..."

"This is not the natural language. Thus, the knowledge that has reached the analysis of that natural language—known as the "linguistic expression" (dhammaniruttisaññitā) of the Māgadhī tongue, which is the root language of all beings—is the analytical insight into language (niruttipaṭisambhidā).

In this way, this analytical insight into language is said to have sound as its object, not conceptual designation (paññatti) as its object. Why? Because, having heard a sound, one thinks: "This is the natural language..."
He knows: "This is not the conventional designation of its own-nature. For one who has attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), when "contact" (phasso) is said, he knows:
"This is the conventional designation of its own-nature"; but when "contacts" (phassā) or "contact" (phassaṃ) is said, he knows: "This is not the conventional designation of its own-nature.
The same method applies to feeling (vedanā) and the other aggregates. Furthermore, he knows other sounds consisting of nouns, verbs, prefixes, particles, and phonemes.
“Does he not know? Insofar as, having heard a sound, one knows, “This is a natural language;
this is not a natural language,” by that same extent one will know that [language] as well.

However, having rejected the claim that this is the function of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), it was said, “Beings learn speech,” and this was stated: for parents, when [their] children are young...
Having laid them down on a couch or a chair, while conversing and performing various tasks, they establish for the children their respective speech forms, saying, "This was said by this person;
that was said by that person. As time passes, they come to know every form of speech.
The mother was a Tamil woman, and the father was an Andhaka. Their newborn child—
If he first hears his mother’s speech, he will speak the Tamil language; if he first hears his father’s speech, he will speak the Andhaka language;
but if he hears neither of their speeches, he will speak the Māgadhī language.
Even one who is reborn in a great forest where there is no village and no one else to speak with, by his own natural disposition—

When uttering speech, he will speak only in the Māgadhī language. In hell, in the animal realm, in the sphere of hungry ghosts, in the human world, and in the world of the gods—in all these places, the Māgadhī language alone is predominant.
Therein, other languages such as Oṭṭa, Kirāta, Andhaka, Yonaka, and Damila undergo transformation.
This alone is the single Māgadhī language, which is designated as the "speech of Brahmā according to reality" (yathābhūta-brahmavohāra) and the "noble speech" (ariyavohāra).
It does not change. Even the Fully Enlightened One, when committing the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Piṭakas to the oral tradition (*tanti*), committed it to the Māgadhī language alone.
Why? Because in this way, it is easy to convey the meaning.

Indeed, for those who have attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), the mere coming within the range of hearing of the word of the Buddha committed to the oral tradition in the Māgadhī language is itself a sufficient elaboration (*papañca*). In the ear...
However, as soon as it is struck [by the mind], the meaning manifests through hundreds and thousands of methods.

But that which has been committed to the textual tradition must be learned by striking [the palm] again and again with another language. Even after learning much, there is no such thing as the attainment of analytical knowledge for a worldling;
likewise, there is no such thing as a noble disciple who has not attained analytical knowledge.

"Knowledge regarding knowledges" refers to the analytical knowledge (*pabhedagata-ñāṇa*) directed toward that knowledge when one reviews it by taking all-encompassing knowledge (*sabbatthaka-ñāṇa*) as its object;

or, it is the detailed knowledge (*vitthāragata-ñāṇa*) regarding those three aforementioned knowledges by way of their respective spheres, functions, and so forth—this is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*).
Furthermore, these four analytical knowledges reach their differentiation in two places by means of five causes.
It should be understood that they become clear. In which two stages do they undergo differentiation?

In the stage of the trainee (*śaikṣa*) and in the stage of the non-trainee (*aśaikṣa*). Therein, [the wisdom] of the eighty great elders, such as the Elder Sāriputta, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, the Elder Mahākassapa, the Elder Mahākaccāyana, and the Elder Mahākoṭṭhita—[is differentiated].

The analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) have reached their full development in the stage of those beyond training (asekkhabhūmi), as in the case of the Elder Ānanda, the householder Citta, the lay follower Dhammika, the householder Upāli, and the female lay follower Khujjuttarā;
and they have also reached their full development in the stage of those in training (sekkhabhūmi). Thus, these analytical knowledges reach their full development within these two stages.
By what five causes are they clear? By attainment, by mastery of the scriptures, by hearing, by inquiry, and by previous application.
In this context, "attainment" refers to the realization of Arahantship. For one who has attained Arahantship, the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) become clear.
"Mastery of the scriptures" refers to the word of the Buddha. For one who masters that, the analytical knowledges become clear.

[They] exist. "Hearing" means hearing the true Dhamma (*saddhamma*). For one who hears the Dhamma with respect and making it their core concern, the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) become clear.

"Inquiry" (*paripucchā*) means discussion regarding the resolution of difficult points (*gaṇṭhipada*) and the meaning of words within the Canon (*pāḷi*), the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), and so forth.
For one who inquires into the meaning of the Canon and other texts they have mastered, the analytical knowledges become clear. "Prior application" (*pubbayoga*)...

"By name," it refers to the practice of insight meditation—attained through the state of being a practitioner (*yogāvacara*) in the dispensation of previous Buddhas by means of the "going and returning"—up to the vicinity of the "conformity" and "clan" stages (*anuloma-gotrabhū*).
For one who was a practitioner in a previous life, the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) are clear.
It is by these five reasons that they become clear.

Among these causes, however, the study of the scriptures (*pariyatti*), listening (*savana*), and thorough inquiry (*paripucchā*)—these three are exclusively powerful causes for the classification [of knowledge].
As for whether prior application (*pubbayoga*) is a powerful condition for realization (*adhigama*) but not for its classification: it is so; yet it is not in that same way.
For while the study of the scriptures, listening, and thorough inquiry may or may not have existed previously, by means of prior application, both formerly and now...

Furthermore, there is no so-called "analytical knowledge" (paṭisambhidā) without the investigation of mental formations (saṅkhārasammasana). These two, however, acting together, support and clarify analytical knowledge. Others have said:
"Prior application, great learning, the local dialect, and traditional lore;"
“Thorough inquiry, realization, reliance upon a teacher, and likewise the excellence of friends—these are the conditions for the analytical knowledges.
In this context, prior application is as previously described. “Great learning” refers to [mastery] in various scriptures and fields of craft.
And proficiency. "Local dialect" means skill in one hundred and one modes of expression, but specifically skill in the Māgadhī language.
"Scripture" means the mastery of even as little as the Chapter on Similes from the Buddha’s word.
"Inquiry" means asking for the determination of the meaning of even a single verse. "Realization" means the state of being a stream-enterer or a once-returner.
Or non-returning, or arahantship. "Dependence on a teacher" means dwelling in the presence of teachers who abound in learning and eloquence.
"Success in friends" means the acquisition of such friends as those very same ones.
In that regard, Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas [attain] the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) by depending upon both their prior application and their realization.
The disciples attain all these causes as well. There is no separate application of meditation on a subject (kammaṭṭhāna-bhāvanānuyoga) for the attainment of the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā);

rather, the attainment of the analytical knowledges occurs for those in training (sekkha) culminating in the deliverance of the fruit of training, and for those beyond training (asekkha) culminating in the deliverance of the fruit of non-training.
For the Tathāgatas, it is like the ten powers; for the Noble Ones, it occurs only through the noble fruits.
"The analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) succeed. The path to these four analytical knowledges is the "Path of Analytical Knowledge" (Paṭisambhidāmagga).
That very Path of Analytical Knowledge is the treatise (pakaraṇa), hence it is called the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-pakaraṇa*.
It is called a "treatise" (pakaraṇa) because various profound meanings, distinguished by manifold divisions, are therein "made manifest" (pakārena karīyante) or explained.
Thus, this treatise, the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, is rich in meaning and rich in phrasing; it is profound and possesses a profound meaning;
it elucidates the supramundane, is connected with emptiness, and is the means for accomplishing the specific fruits of practice while refuting the opposites of practice;
it is a mine of the supreme jewel of knowledge for practitioners and the cause of the excellence of the eloquence in Dhamma-talks for those who preach the Dhamma.
For the sake of providing consolation by showing the means of escape from suffering for those who fear *saṃsāra*, for the sake of destroying its opposites,
and for the sake of generating satisfaction in the hearts of the virtuous through the exposition of the meaning of many profound passages from the Suttantas,
the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, by means of the radiance of the great lamp of unimpeded omniscient knowledge in all respects, [proceeded].

By the Venerable Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma and a second Teacher to the Dhamma King, who— out of compassion for the world and possessing a heart moistened by the great love and affection renowned among all people—
desired that the Great Lamp of the True Dhamma, kindled for the purpose of dispelling the darkness of the defilements residing in the hearts of those to be trained,
should burn without ceasing for five thousand years through the sprinkling of the oil of the expansion of its intended meaning.
Having heard what was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council (Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti), it was compiled exactly as it had been heard.
This [work] belongs to the Suttanta Piṭaka among the three Piṭakas—namely, the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Suttanta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
Within the five Nikāyas—the Dīgha Nikāya, the Majjhima Nikāya, the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the Aṅguttara Nikāya, and the Khuddaka Nikāya—it is included in the Khuddaka Nikāya.
Among the Great Collections (Mahānikāya), it is included within the Minor Collection (Khuddakanikāya).
Within the nine limbs of the Teacher’s dispensation— Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla— it is comprised, as appropriate,
by the two limbs of Geyya and Veyyākaraṇa.
“I received eighty-two thousand [teachings] from the Buddha, two thousand from the bhikkhus,
and eighty-four thousand teachings that have been transmitted to me.
Thus it was declared by the Elder Dhammabhaṇḍāgārika, who was recognized as foremost in five respects.

Of the eighty-four thousand divisions of the Dhamma (dhammakkhandha) taken up by the Bhikkhu, it is comprised within two thousand divisions of the Dhamma, which include many hundreds of individual dhammakkhandhas.
It consists of three sections (vagga): the Mahāvagga, the Majjhima-vagga, and the Cūḷavagga.
Within each section, ten topics are grouped together, making thirty in total, beginning with the discourse on knowledge (ñāṇakathā) and ending with the discourse on the summary (mātikākathā).
Discourse. Thus, we shall provide a successive commentary on the meaning of the words of this treatise, the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, which has been established in many ways.
For this treatise, both by one who recites it and by one who explains it—whether according to the letter or the meaning—it should be recited and explained with care;
and likewise by one who learns it, it should be learned with care.
It should be learned and retained. Why is that? Because of the profundity of this treatise, for the benefit of the world and for its long endurance in the world.

In that regard, if it is asked why the discourse on knowledge (*ñāṇakathā*) is spoken first among the thirty discourses: it is because knowledge, by virtue of its capacity to purify the stains of practice, constitutes the beginning of practice. For it was said by the Blessed One:

“Therefore, bhikkhu, you should first purify the very foundation of wholesome states. And what is the foundation of wholesome states? It is virtue that is perfectly purified and view that is straight.
For by “straight view,” knowledge known as right view is meant. Thus, the discussion of knowledge was spoken at the beginning.
Furthermore, it has been said:
“In that regard, monks, right view comes first. And how, monks, does right view come first?
One understands right view as ‘right view’ and wrong view as ‘wrong view. That is one’s right view.
One understands right intention as ‘right intention’ and wrong intention as ‘wrong intention’...”
He understands wrong intention as "wrong intention. He understands right speech as "right speech," and he understands wrong speech as "wrong speech.
He understands right action as "right action," and he understands wrong action as "wrong action.
He understands right livelihood as "right livelihood," and he understands wrong livelihood as "wrong livelihood."
One understands right effort as "right effort," and one understands wrong effort as "wrong effort.
One understands right mindfulness as "right mindfulness," and one understands wrong mindfulness as "wrong mindfulness.
One understands right concentration as "right concentration," and one understands wrong concentration as "wrong concentration. This constitutes one's right view.

For once right view, which is the precursor, has been established, one will come to know even the state of wrong views in those who hold them; thus, the discourse on knowledge was first expounded in order to purify that knowledge known as right view.
"Furthermore, Udāyi, let alone the past, let alone the future; I shall teach you the Dhamma: when this exists, that comes to be;
with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this..."
And because it was stated that "this ceases," and because this refers specifically to knowledge—setting aside views concerning the past and the future—the discourse on knowledge was explained first.
"Enough, Subhadda; let this matter rest: 'Did they all, by their own claim, realize [the truth], or did none of them realize it?'"
"Or did some understand and others not? "Subhadda, I shall teach you the Dhamma;
listen well and attend closely, and I will speak.

Thus, having set aside the doctrines of the various wanderers, brahmins, and other teachers, the discourse on knowledge was spoken first because the Noble Eightfold Path was taught, and because within that Eightfold Path, knowledge—consisting of right view—is the primary factor.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four factors of stream-entry: association with superior persons, hearing the true Dhamma, careful attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
And: “Having conceived faith, one approaches; approaching, one pays respect; paying respect, one lends an ear;
lending an ear, one hears the Dhamma; having heard the Dhamma, one retains it; having retained the teachings, one examines their meaning with wisdom.”
“He investigates; as he investigates the meaning, his mind finds satisfaction in the Dhamma; through his finding satisfaction in the Dhamma, zeal arises;
being zealous, he exerts himself; exerting himself, he weighs it up; having weighed it up, he strives;
with resolute self, he realizes the ultimate truth by means of the body and penetrates and sees it with wisdom. And so it is said.
“Here a Tathāgata appears in the world... he teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning...
and so forth—beginning with the knowledge pertaining to the Sutta-piṭaka by way of such numerous Sutta passages, the discourse on knowledge has been explained from the outset in its proper sequence.
Furthermore, this discourse on knowledge is established in two ways: by way of summary (uddesa) and exposition (niddesa). In the summary: “Wisdom regarding the application of the ear... [and so on].
By way of the method beginning with "knowledge consisting in what is heard" (*sutamaye ñāṇa*), seventy-three knowledges have been presented as a matrix (*mātikā*).

In the *Niddesa*, by way of the method beginning with "How is wisdom regarding the application of the ear knowledge consisting in what is heard? The application of the ear that [considers]: 'These phenomena are to be directly known'—the wisdom that understands that is knowledge consisting in what is heard," those same seventy-three knowledges are explained in detail.
The Introduction to the Book is finished.
(1) The Great Chapter: 1.
Discourse on Knowledge.
Commentary on the Matrix (Mātikāvaṇṇanā) 1.
Regarding that, first, in the summary (uddesa): "Wisdom consisting of the application of the ear is knowledge consisting in what has been heard. Here, the word *sota* has many distinct meanings.
For it is seen in the following senses: the physical ear, consciousness, knowledge, and craving, and so forth.
On the Noble Path, and also in the continuity of consciousness (*cittasantati*).
For in such passages as “the ear-base (*sotāyatana*), the ear-element (*sotadhātu*), the ear-faculty (*sotindriya*)”, this word *sota* is seen to refer to the physical ear (*maṃsasota*).

In such passages as “having heard a sound with the ear,” it refers to ear-consciousness (*sotaviññāṇa*). In such passages as “with the divine ear-element,” it refers to the stream of knowledge (*ñāṇasota*). As for those streams...
"In the world" refers to those streams which have been proclaimed, fully proclaimed, declared, taught,
established, set forth, opened up, analyzed, made clear, and revealed by me— namely, the stream of craving, the stream of views,
the stream of defilements, the stream of misconduct, and the stream of ignorance— and so on, regarding these five things beginning with craving.
In such passages as, “The Blessed One saw a large log being carried away by the current of the river Ganges,” it refers to the stream of water.
In such passages as, “This, friend, is a designation for the Noble Eightfold Path, namely, ‘the stream’,” it refers to the Noble Path.
[And in the passage: “He understands a person’s stream of consciousness, uninterrupted on both sides, established here in this world... it refers to the stream of consciousness.
In such passages as "established in the other world," it refers to the continuity of consciousness (*cittasantati*). Here, however, it should be understood as the ear-organ (*maṃsasota*).
That by which—whether as a cause or as an instrument—one hears, attends to, and fixes upon [an object] is "ear-hearing" (*sotāvadhāna*).
What is that? It is "what is heard" (*suta*). And "what is heard" is as in such passages as: "He is one who has heard much, a bearer of what is heard, an accumulator of what is heard."
The collection of phenomena (dhammajāta) that has been cognized and determined by way of the ear-door is here called "attentive listening" (sotāvadhāna).
Wisdom that occurs in regard to this "listening," which is designated as attentive listening, is "wisdom in attentive listening" (sotāvadhāne paññā).

And "wisdom" (paññā) is so called in the sense of making known (paññāpana), which means making various objects clear; or else, it is so called by way of those [characteristics] such as impermanence and so forth.
Understanding is also called "wisdom" because it knows phenomena in their various modes.
Regarding the phrase "knowledge consisting in what is heard," here the word *suta* (heard) is both with and without a prefix:
"In going, in what is well-heard, in what is moistened, and in that which is accumulated through application."
And it is seen following the sense-door of the ear in such cases as "heard" (*suta*).

For instance, in phrases like "one who has set out with an army," the meaning is "going. In phrases like "of one who sees the Dhamma heard" (*sutadhammassa passato*), the meaning is "of one whose Dhamma is well-known" (*vissutadhammassa*).
In phrases like "of a lustful person toward a lustful person" (*avassutā avassutassa purisapuggalassa*), the meaning is "of one who is moistened" (*tintā tintassa*).

The meaning is as follows: in such passages as “the wise who are devoted to meditation” (*jhānapasutā dhīrā*), the meaning is “engaged in” (*anuyutta*). In such passages as “by you, merit has been accumulated in no small measure” (*tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappakaṃ*), the meaning is “accumulated” (*upacita*).
In such passages as “seen, heard, sensed, and cognized” (*diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ viññātaṃ*), the meaning is “sound” (*sadda*).

In such passages as “one is learned, a bearer of what is heard, a storehouse of what is heard” (*bahussuto hoti sutadharo sutasannicayo*), the meaning is “one who bears in mind what is cognized by following the door of the ear. But here, however—

The meaning is that it is cognized and determined by way of the ear-door. "Knowledge consisting in what has been heard" (sutamaye ñāṇaṃ) refers to that wisdom which, having taken as its object the True Dhamma—this which has been heard, cognized, and determined—arises for the very first time and subsequently continues in succession;
this is called "knowledge consisting in what has been heard. The meaning is "knowledge consisting in what has been heard" (sutamayaṃ ñāṇaṃ). Regarding "consisting in what has been heard" (sutamaye):
And this is a nominative singular form, just as in the expression “it should not be said thus.
In such passages as “as when the tops of forest thickets are in bloom,” and “there is no personal effort, there is no effort of another, there is no human effort,” it is the nominative singular;
it should be understood in the same way here as well. Therefore it was said: “the meaning is ‘knowledge consisting of what has been heard.’”
Alternatively, the collection of phenomena beginning with contact that is produced by what has been heard is "consisting of what is heard" (*sutamaya*).
The knowledge associated with that which occurs in relation to this collection of phenomena consisting of what is heard is "knowledge consisting of what is heard" (*sutamaye ñāṇaṃ*).

It is called "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) because it knows phenomena by way of their specific and general characteristics. That very same knowledge is, for the purpose of clarifying its intended meaning through a figurative expression, indifferently designated as "wisdom" (*paññā*).
It should be understood that after having spoken thus, he subsequently specified what was intended by saying, "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*).
Knowledge is characterized by the penetration of intrinsic nature, or it is characterized by unerring penetration, like the penetration of an arrow shot by a skilled archer;
its function is to illuminate the object, like a lamp; and its manifestation is non-delusion, like a guide in the forest. "Bhikkhus, one who is concentrated..."
From the statement, “The bhikkhu understands it as it really is,” it is the proximate cause (*padatthāna*) for concentration.

Regarding the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth, it should be understood that either the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) or the commonality (*sāmañña*) is called the characteristic; either the function (*kicca*) or the achievement (*sampatti*) is called the flavor (*rasa*);
either the mode of manifestation (*upaṭṭhānākāra*) or the fruit (*phala*) is called the manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*); and the immediate cause is called the proximate cause (*padatthāna*).
2. "Having heard, there is wisdom regarding restraint"—the Pātimokkha, mindfulness, knowledge, patience, and likewise energy:
these five qualities are proclaimed as "restraint."

“By means of this restraint of the Pātimokkha, he is endowed, well-endowed, arrived at, well-arrived at, possessed of, perfected in, and equipped with it”—thus restraint of the Pātimokkha is said to be "arrived at.
"Having seen a form with the eye, one does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
Because, if one dwells with the eye-faculty unguarded, covetousness and dejection..."

“Mindfulness-restraint is that which has been taught in such a manner as: ‘If evil, unwholesome states should flow in upon him, he practices for their restraint; he guards the eye-faculty; he achieves restraint over the eye-faculty.
“As for those streams in the world... (Ajita, said the Blessed One).
“Mindfulness is their prevention;
I call it the restraint of the streams.
By means of wisdom, these are closed off.”—Thus the restraint of knowledge has been presented. “And what, bhikkhus, are the taints that are to be abandoned by using? Here, bhikkhus,” [he said].
The restraint of using the requisites, which comes in the manner beginning with, "A bhikkhu uses his robe after reflecting wisely," is also included within the restraint of knowledge. [It is said:
"He is patient with cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things;
he is patient with abusive and offensive modes of speech that have arisen..."

"Being of a nature to endure bodily feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, bitter, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening"—thus is the restraint of patience (khantisaṃvara) described. "One does not tolerate a sensual thought that has arisen;
one abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end, and causes it to disappear"—according to this method and others like it, the restraint of energy (vīriyasaṃvara) is described.
“Here, the noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, maintains his life by right livelihood”—thus comes the restraint of purity of livelihood (*ājīvapārisuddhi-saṃvara*);

that too is included within the restraint of energy (*vīriya-saṃvara*). Among those seven restraints, the four restraints known as the restraint of the Pātimokkha, the restraint of the sense faculties, the restraint of purity of livelihood, and the restraint of using requisites (*paccaya-paṭisevana*) are intended here; and among these, specifically the restraint of the Pātimokkha. And all this restraint—
It is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*) because it restrains bodily misconduct and so forth, each according to its own category.

For one who, having heard the Dhamma taught in the knowledge consisting of what is heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*), restrains themselves and practices restraint, the wisdom associated with that state which occurs within that restraint is called "wisdom in restraint after hearing.
Alternatively, the word "having heard" (*sutvā*) may be understood in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).
There is also the meaning of "wisdom" (paññā) in the sense of restraint by means of what has been heard.
Regarding the phrase "knowledge consisting in virtue" (sīlamaye ñāṇaṃ): here, "virtue" (sīla) is so called in the sense of "steadying" (sīlana). What is this "steadying"?
It means either composure, in the sense of the non-distraction of bodily action and so forth through the power of good conduct; or it means upholding, [the state] of wholesome [states].
The meaning is that it is the state of being a support by way of being the foundation for phenomena. Indeed, those learned in the characteristics of words recognize only these two meanings here.

Others, however, explain *sīla* as follows: "in the sense of high service (*adhisevana*), in the sense of conduct (*ācāra*), in the sense of its habit (*tassīla*), in the sense of the head (*sira*), in the sense of coolness (*sītala*), and in the sense of auspiciousness (*siva*)."
The characteristic of that [volition] is its being manifest,
even when it is divided in many ways, just as visibility is the characteristic of visible form (rūpa),

even when it is divided in many ways. For just as the sense-sphere of visible form, though divided in many ways by distinctions such as blue, yellow, and so forth, has visibility as its characteristic.

Even though [visible form] is divided by distinctions such as blue and so forth, it does not transcend the state of being visible; likewise, even though virtue (sīla) is divided in many ways by distinctions such as volition (cetanā) and so forth, that very "virtuousness" (sīlana)— which is described as the settling of bodily actions and so on,
and as the foundation for wholesome states— is its characteristic, because it does not transcend the state of being a settling and a foundation, despite the divisions of volition and the rest.
Furthermore, regarding its characteristics: “The destruction of immorality,
The quality of blamelessness, and likewise The accomplishment of one’s duty—
by way of these meanings, It is called ‘the essence’.”

Therefore, this so-called virtue (sīla) should be understood as having the function of destroying immorality by way of its essential quality (rasa), and as having the flavor of blamelessness by way of its sense of accomplishment.
Its manifestation is purity; and it is described by the wise as having moral shame (hirī) and moral dread (ottappa) as its proximate cause.
That virtue has as its manifestation the purities described as "purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind";
it manifests as, that is, it comes to be apprehended as, the state of being pure.
Furthermore, moral shame (*hirī*) and moral dread (*ottappa*) are described as its proximate cause—that is, its immediate condition. For when moral shame and moral dread exist, virtue arises.

Knowledge associated with and conjoined with such virtue—namely, that which understands: "When there is non-restraint, it arises and persists; when there is no non-restraint, it neither arises nor persists"—is knowledge consisting in virtue (*sīlamaya-ñāṇa*).
Alternatively, virtue itself made manifest is "consisting in virtue" (*sīlamaya*); the knowledge conjoined with that which consists in virtue is [knowledge consisting in virtue].
This includes the contemplation of the danger in non-restraint and the contemplation of the benefit in restraint.

Furthermore, the reviewing of restraint and purity, and the reviewing of the defilement and cleansing of restraint, are included within knowledge consisting in virtue (*sīlamaya-ñāṇa*) alone. 3. "Wisdom in concentrating after having restrained":

this refers to one who, having restrained and established himself in virtue by means of the restraint of virtue described under knowledge consisting in virtue, concentrates and achieves one-pointedness of mind through access and absorption.
The wisdom associated with that concentration which is active during the process of concentrating is "wisdom consisting in the development of concentration.

Concentration (*samādhi*) is so called because it is placing [the mind] evenly and correctly; this is a synonym for concentration itself. Regarding the phrase "knowledge consisting in the development of concentration," here concentration is the one-pointedness of a wholesome consciousness. In what sense is it concentration?
Concentration (*samādhi*) is so called in the sense of concentrating (*samādhāna*). What is this "concentrating"?
It is the even and correct placing, or fixing, of the mind and mental factors upon a single object; this is what is meant.
Therefore, that state by whose power the mind and mental factors remain upon a single object—remaining even and correct, undistracted and unscattered—is what is called "concentrating."
It should be understood as follows:
"The characteristic of that concentration is non-distraction; its function is the destruction of distraction;
its manifestation is imperturbability; and its proximate cause is happiness."
It is called *bhāvanā* because it is cultivated (*bhāvīyati*) or increased (*vaḍḍhīyati*). Concentration itself is cultivation, thus "cultivation of concentration" (*samādhibhāvanā*);
or, the cultivation—that is, the increase—of concentration is "cultivation of concentration. By the expression "cultivation of concentration," he excludes other forms of cultivation.
As before, knowledge consisting in the cultivation of concentration occurs by way of access and absorption.
4. "Wisdom regarding the discernment of conditions" (*paccayapariggahe paññā*): here, that which goes toward the fruit by depending [on something] is a condition (*paccaya*).

"Depending" (*paṭicca*) means not without it; the meaning is "not excluding it. "Goes" (*eti*) means both arises and proceeds. Furthermore, the meaning of "condition" (*paccaya*) is the sense of being helpful.
Because those conditions are of many kinds, wisdom consists in the discernment and the defining of conditions.
Wisdom in the discernment of conditions.

Regarding the term "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*): first, the word *dhamma* is seen in such contexts as intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), wisdom (*paññā*), merit (*puñña*), designation (*paññatti*), offense (*āpatti*), scripture (*pariyatti*), insentience (*nissattatā*), modification (*vikāra*), quality (*guṇa*), condition (*paccaya*), and that which is produced by conditions (*paccayuppanna*).

For instance, in such passages as "wholesome phenomena (*kusalā dhammā*), unwholesome phenomena (*akusalā dhammā*), indeterminate phenomena (*abyākatā dhammā*)," it is used in the sense of intrinsic nature.
“In one who possesses these four qualities—the faithful seeker of a home:
truth, righteousness, fortitude, and generosity—he indeed does not grieve after passing away.
In such passages, it refers to wisdom (*paññā*).
In such passages as, “For neither the Dhamma nor the non-Dhamma have equal results;
the non-Dhamma leads to hell, while the Dhamma brings one to a happy destination,” it refers to merit (*puñña*).
In such passages as, “Dhammas as designations (*paññatti*), Dhammas as linguistic expressions (*nirutti*), Dhammas as designations (*adhivacana*),” it refers to a designation (*paññatti*).

In such passages as “offenses involving defeat (pārājika-dhammā)” and “offenses requiring formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa-dhammā),” it refers to an offense (*āpatti*). In such passages as “here a bhikkhu knows the Dhamma:

the discourses (sutta), mixed prose and verse (geyya), and expositions (veyyākaraṇa),” it refers to the scriptures (*pariyatti*). In such passages as “At that time, indeed, there are phenomena (dhammā).

He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena,” it refers to the state of being devoid of a sentient being (*nissattatā*). In such passages as “subject to birth, subject to aging, subject to death,” it refers to... [the nature of conditioned things].

In the sense of a modification, as in “the six Buddha-qualities” (*channaṃ buddhadhammānaṃ*); in the sense of a quality, as in “knowledge of the cause is the analytical knowledge of phenomena” (*hetumhi ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā*);
in the sense of a condition, as in “that element remains constant, the stability of phenomena, the fixed course of phenomena” (*ṭhitāva sā dhātu dhammaṭṭhitatā dhammaniyāmatā*);

and here too, it should be understood in the sense of that which has arisen through conditions. As for its meaning: they either "bear their own intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvaṃ dhārenti*) or they are "borne by conditions" (*paccayehi dhārīyanti*).

Alternatively, they are called *dhammas* as appropriate: because they bear their own fruit; or because they bear that which fulfills themselves by preventing one from falling into the states of misery (*apāya*);
or because they bear their respective characteristics; or because they are determined by the mind.
However, in this context, they are *dhammas* because they are borne by their own conditions; they are *dhammas* arisen from conditions.
"Dhamma-stability" (dhammaṭṭhiti) means that by means of this [conditionality], things stand, arise, and proceed;
it is a designation for conditioned phenomena (paccayadhamma). Knowledge regarding that stability of dhammas is "knowledge of the stability of dhammas" (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa).

For this [knowledge] belongs to one who, having begun the practice for the sake of seeing things as they truly are through the concentration described in the development of concentration, has analyzed name-and-form with a concentrated mind.
Knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) arises as a method for discerning the conditions of that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). If it is asked:
why is it called "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" rather than "knowledge in the defining of name-and-form"?

It is because by the very discernment of the conditions, the discernment of what has arisen from those conditions is established; for if that which has arisen from conditions is not discerned, the discernment of the conditions themselves remains incomplete.

It is not possible to do so. Therefore, it should be understood that by the very inclusion of the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*), the previously established knowledge of the discernment of mind-and-body (*nāmarūpavavatthānañāṇa*), which serves as its cause, is already stated.

If it is asked why this is not stated as "wisdom in the grasping of conditions after having concentrated [the mind]," as was done for the second and third knowledges, it is because serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) proceed in union (*yuganaddha*).
“Just as one who has attained concentration sees with insight, so too, while seeing with insight, one attains concentration;
then insight and serenity are equal in measure, yoked together, and proceed smoothly.
Thus it is said. Therefore, without relinquishing concentration, having yoked concentration and knowledge together, as long as—

It should be understood that it is stated as "wisdom in the discernment of conditions is knowledge of the stability of phenomena" specifically for the purpose of making known that the Noble Path must be exerted toward that end.
Regarding the phrase "wisdom in defining past, future, and present phenomena by way of synthesis," here [the reference is] to oneself.

"Past" (*atīta*) means those that have gone beyond or have transcended their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) or the moments of arising and so forth; "future" (*anāgata*) means those that have neither arrived nor reached either of those two;
"present" (*paccuppanna*) means those that, depending on various causes, have arisen, proceeded, and are occurring subsequent to the moment of arising and so forth.

Among the three types of the present—namely, the present as duration (*addhā*), the present as continuity (*santati*), and the present as moment (*khaṇa*)—it is the present as continuity that is intended here. Of these...

Wisdom (*paññā*) is the discernment, determination, and resolution regarding the defining characteristics of each of the five aggregates of past, future, and present phenomena, having condensed them and formed them into a heap by way of groups (*kalāpa*).
"Knowledge of comprehension" (*sammasane ñāṇaṃ*) is knowledge in the sense of grasping correctly, rubbing together, and examining; it is called "knowledge of comprehension of groups."

The meaning: for this knowledge of the establishment of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*), which follows immediately after the knowledge of the discernment of mind-and-body (*nāmarūpavavatthānañāṇa*) and consists in the grasping of the conditions for mind-and-body, when it is established, [one understands]:
"Whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all that form is impermanent..."
"By defining [it] as impermanent, this is one mode of comprehension; by defining it as suffering, this is one mode of comprehension;

by defining it as non-self, this is one mode of comprehension"—in accordance with this method, when one has applied the three characteristics to each individual aggregate previously defined, the knowledge of comprehension by groups (*kalāpasammasana-ñāṇa*) arises for one who is practicing insight into them as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
6. Wisdom in contemplating the change of presently arisen phenomena:
this is wisdom in seeing the change and seeing the dissolution of the five internal aggregates as they arise in a continuous stream.
Because the mind fixes itself upon dissolution alone—even while apprehending arising by noting that "these phenomena, having arisen, break up"—therefore, although it was not explicitly stated...

It should be understood that arising (udaya) is indeed already stated. Alternatively, because the seeing of arising is established by the seeing of present phenomena, arising is indeed already stated. For the arisen state of phenomena cannot be established without arising;
therefore, even though it is not explicitly said, "wisdom in the contemplation of the rise and fall of present phenomena," it is effectively already stated.
It should be understood that [this] occurs. And because it has been defined as "knowledge of contemplation of rise and fall," the seeing of the rise is already established;

thus, for one who has reached the culmination of the previously mentioned knowledge of comprehension (*sammasana-ñāṇa*), and having grasped the rise and fall that have become manifest through that very comprehension, begins the contemplation of rise and fall in order to delimit conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
The knowledge of contemplation of rise and fall arises. For that is called "contemplation of rise and fall" because it contemplates rise and fall.
7. "Reflecting upon the object": having reflected upon—that is, having known and seen—the object consisting of the aggregate of form and so forth from the perspective of its dissolution.
The wisdom regarding the contemplation of dissolution is the knowledge of insight; this [knowledge] has arisen by reflecting upon that object from the perspective of its dissolution.
The wisdom that consists in the contemplation of the dissolution of knowledge is what is called "knowledge of insight" (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).
"Insight" (*vipassanā*) means seeing in various ways (*vividhā passanā*). There is also the reading *ārammaṇa-paṭisaṅkhā*. Its meaning is as follows:
the reflection upon, the knowing, and the seeing of the object; thus, by the method already stated, "reflection on the object" (*ārammaṇa-paṭisaṅkhā*) is "wisdom in the contemplation of dissolution."

It is said, "knowledge in insight. However, since it is through the contemplation of dissolution alone that insight reaches its culmination, this specific [knowledge] is designated as "knowledge in insight.

Since the vision of knowledge of what is and is not the path arises for one who stands in the contemplation of rise and fall, once that [contemplation] is established, this [vision] is necessarily established as well.
It should be understood that without mentioning that [knowledge], the knowledge at the summit of insight is said to be precisely that which consists in the contemplation of dissolution.

When the rise and fall have been clearly seen through the contemplation of rise and fall, and when the formations—having been clearly delimited—are appearing very rapidly, and while knowledge is flowing keenly, mindfulness abandons the arising and becomes established in dissolution alone; for him, having arisen in this way...
When one sees that "formations indeed break up in this way," the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā-ñāṇa*) arises at this stage.

8. Wisdom as the appearance as terror (*bhayatupaṭṭhāne paññā*): The meaning is wisdom in the apprehension of the signs of arising, occurrence, accumulation, and rebirth-linking as being terrifying, due to their association with oppression and their state of being fearful. It is called "appearance as terror" (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna*) because they appear as terror.
The object is [the basis] for that appearance as terror. Alternatively, it is called "appearance as terror" (bhayatupaṭṭhāna) because wisdom appears as terror;
thus, it is wisdom that is referred to as "appearance as terror.
"Knowledge regarding danger" (ādīnave ñāṇaṃ) is simply a locative expression. "Both the wisdom regarding appearance as terror and the knowledge regarding danger..."

Since it has been said, "Disenchantment (*nibbidā*) and these [other] states are one in meaning, differing only in expression," even when spoken of as one, it is threefold according to its different stages,
such as the desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā*) and so forth. Therefore, it should be understood that although it is not explicitly mentioned,

it is effectively included because when the contemplation of fearfulness (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna*) and the contemplation of danger (*ādīnavānupassanā*) are established, the contemplation of disenchantment (*nibbidānupassanā*) is also established.
For one who practices, develops, and cultivates the contemplation of dissolution, which has the dissolution of all conditioned phenomena as its object,
those formations that differentiate within the three realms of existence, the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings—

just as for a timid man desiring to live in safety [the sight of] lions, tigers, leopards, hyenas, jackals, ogres, fierce bulls, and fierce dogs that have broken loose— [these formations appear as terrifying].

When these [formations] appear as a great terror—like a rutting fierce elephant, a fearsome venomous snake, a thunderbolt, a charnel ground, a battlefield, or a pit of glowing embers—the knowledge of the appearance of fear arises in one who sees:
"Past formations have ceased; present ones are ceasing;
and future ones likewise will cease. This is the knowledge of the appearance of fear in this context.
As he cultivates, develops, and repeatedly practices that knowledge of the appearance of fear,
he perceives no refuge, no shelter, no resort, and no protection in any state of existence, any womb, any destination,

any station, or any abode of beings. Among all formations— whether they have gone to any state of existence, womb, destination, station, or abode— he finds no aspiration for or clinging to even a single formation.
Or it does not exist: the three realms of existence (*bhava*) are like charcoal-pits filled with glowing embers; the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are like venomous snakes with terrible poison;
the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*) are like executioners with raised swords; the six internal bases (*ajjhattikāyatana*) are like an empty village;
the six external bases (*bāhirāyatana*) are like the village-destroying bandits; and the seven stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) and the nine abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*).
All conditioned phenomena appear as if set ablaze, fully ignited, and turned into flames by eleven fires;
they appear like boils, like diseases, like arrows, like calamities, and like afflictions— devoid of essence, devoid of flavor, and having become a great mass of danger—
even for a timid person who desires to live in comfort and perceives them as having a pleasant form.
It was like a forest thicket filled with tigers, like a cave containing leopards, like water infested with crocodiles and *rakkhasas*,
like enemies with raised swords, like food mixed with poison, like a road beset by thieves, like a house on fire, and like a battlefield where armies are arrayed for combat.
For just as that man, having encountered these things— the tiger-filled forest thicket and the rest— became afraid and agitated...

With his hair standing on end, he sees only danger on all sides; in the same way, when all conditioned phenomena have appeared as fearful to that practitioner through the contemplation of dissolution, he sees them as entirely sapless, devoid of gratification, and as nothing but danger.
As he contemplates in this manner, the knowledge of the contemplation of danger arises.

Thus, perceiving the danger in all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), he becomes disenchanted with, weary of, and finds no delight in the entire range of conditioned things—including all states of existence, wombs, destinies, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings—along with their various divisions.

Just as a golden royal swan, delighting in the foothills of Mount Cittakūṭa, finds no pleasure in the filthy cesspool at the gate of a village of outcasts, but delights only in the seven great lakes; so too does he find no delight in those conditioned things.
Just as he does not delight there, even so this king of swans among yogis does not delight in the conditioned state that is thoroughly seen as dangerous and subject to dissolution;
rather, because he is endowed with the joy of meditation through his delight in cultivation, he delights only in the seven contemplations.
And just as the lion, the king of beasts, does not delight even when cast into a golden cage, [let alone in a place] three thousand yojanas wide...
But he delights only in the Himālaya; even so, this lion of yogis does not delight even in the three types of happy states of existence, but delights only in the three contemplations (anupassanā).
And just as the all-white, seven-footed, powerful, sky-faring king of elephants, Chaddanta, does not delight in the midst of the city, but delights only in the Chaddanta Lake in the Himālaya;
Thus, this elephant among the best of yogis finds no delight in any conditioned state whatsoever;
rather, he delights only in the state of peace pointed out by such methods as "non-arising is security," and his mind becomes inclined toward it, slanting toward it, and leaning toward it.
At this point, his knowledge of contemplation of disenchantment has arisen.
9. Wisdom as the desire for deliverance, reflective contemplation, and composure is knowledge regarding equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*).

One who desires, wishes, or seeks to be delivered and to relinquish is "one desirous of deliverance" (*muñcitukāmo*); the state of one desirous of deliverance is "desire for deliverance" (*muñcitukamyatā*).

"Reflective contemplation" (*paṭisaṅkhā*) means examining or investigating; alternatively, it is the act of reflecting (*paṭisaṅkhānaṃ*). "Composure" (*santiṭṭhanā*) means remaining settled or maintaining equanimity (*ajjhupekkhati*).

*Saṇṭhiti* (stability) or *saṇṭhānā* (the act of stabilizing). Desirous-ness-for-deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā*), reflection (*paṭisaṅkhā*), and stability (*saṇṭhānā*) together constitute "desirous-ness-for-deliverance-reflection-stability.
Thus, in the preliminary stage, desirous-ness-for-deliverance is the wish to abandon arising and so forth by one who has become disenchanted through the knowledge of disenchantment.
Reflection occurs in the middle stage for the purpose of finding a means to deliverance.
Reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhā*). At the end, equanimity toward what has been released is "establishment" (*santiṭṭhanā*).
Thus, wisdom is threefold according to its different stages; it is knowledge regarding the equanimity toward formations.

However, for one who maintains that all three types of wisdom—namely those distinguished by their different stages called desire for deliverance, reflective contemplation, and establishment—constitute equanimity toward formations, [the term] "wisdom" [is used].

It should be understood that the plural form “in the equanimity towards formations” (*saṅkhārupekkhāsu*) is used, while the singular form “knowledge” (*ñāṇaṃ*) is used because there is unity despite the diversity of its states. And it has been said:

“That which is the desire for deliverance, that which is the contemplation of reflection, and that which is equanimity towards formations—these states have one meaning; only the phrasing is different. However, some [read] “in the equanimity towards formations”...
Some also say that the plural number is used because there are many equanimities towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) by way of both serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

Furthermore, "towards equanimities towards formations" should be understood as "expecting action. However, according to the distinction of stages, for one who becomes disenchanted and weary through that knowledge of disenchantment (*nibbidāñāṇa*) regarding all formations—whether they be included in the various categories of existence, birth, destiny, stations of consciousness, or abodes of beings—there arises...
The mind does not cling, does not adhere, and is not bound; it desires to be released from and to cast off all conditioned phenomena.

Or else, it is like a fish that has entered a net, a frog that has gone into the mouth of a snake, a wild cock that has been placed in a cage, a deer that has fallen under the power of a strong snare, a snake that has come into the hands of a snake-charmer, or one who has plunged into a great mire.

Just as an elephant, a king of serpents who has entered the mouth of a garuḷa, or the moon that has entered the mouth of Rāhu, or a man surrounded by enemies—such beings desire to be released from those very places and desire to escape;

even so, the mind of that meditator desires to be released from the entire range of conditioned phenomena and desires to escape from them. For when it is stated thus, it refers to "the desire for deliverance in one who desires deliverance."

The reading [“muñcitukamyatā”] is appropriate. And this being so, in such passages as “desire for deliverance from arising” (uppādaṃ muñcitukamyatā), it would have to be said “desire for deliverance from arising” (uppādā muccitukamyatā) and so forth;

therefore, the former meaning alone is more excellent. Then, for one who has lost all attachment to all conditioned phenomena and who desires to be delivered from everything that falls within the sphere of the conditioned, the knowledge of desire for deliverance (muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa) arises.
He thus [regards] everything included within the realms of existence, the modes of birth, the destinations, the stations of consciousness, and the abodes of beings...
Desiring to be liberated from conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) that are subject to differentiation, and for the purpose of accomplishing the means of liberation,

he again contemplates those same conditioned phenomena by applying the three characteristics through the knowledge of contemplation of reflection (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā-ñāṇa). For one who thus contemplates,
there arises the knowledge of reflection regarding the sign (nimitta) by way of impermanence, and the knowledge of reflection regarding occurrence by way of suffering.
Through the aspect of non-self, knowledge of reflection arises regarding both the sign and the occurrence.

Having seen that "all formations are empty" by means of the knowledge of contemplation of reflection, and having applied the three characteristics while comprehending formations, he abandons both fear and delight;
like a man who has cast off his wife upon seeing her faults, he [casts off] that wife.
He is indifferent toward volitional formations and remains neutral; he does not grasp at them as "I" or "mine.
For one who knows thus and sees thus, the mind recoils from, shrinks back from, and turns away from the three realms of existence, and it does not extend toward them.
Just as, for example, when a lotus leaf is slightly tilted, drops of water recoil from it, shrink back from it, and turn away from it.

They do not extend. Just as a cock’s feather or a strip of sinew thrown into a fire shrinks back, recoils, turns away, and does not extend, so too his mind toward the three realms of existence shrinks back, recoils, turns away, and does not extend;
equanimity becomes established. Thus, for him, there is the knowledge of equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*).

It has arisen. It should be understood that, together with this knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa*), the knowledge of conformity (*anulomañāṇa*)—which establishes the subsequent knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhuñāṇa*)—is indeed stated, even though it was not explicitly mentioned among the preceding and succeeding knowledges. For it was said by the Blessed One:
"Indeed, monks, that monk who regards any formation as permanent [cannot] possess the acceptance that is in conformity [with the truth]."
It is impossible that one who is not endowed with such [qualities] will be so endowed;
it is impossible that one who is not endowed with conformable patience will enter the certainty of rightness;
and it is impossible that one who does not enter the certainty of rightness will realize the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship.
“This possibility does not exist,” and so forth.
And it was said by the General of the Dhamma:
“In how many ways does one acquire conformable patience? In how many ways does one enter the certainty of rightness?”
"In forty ways one acquires conformity-patience (anulomika-khanti), and in forty ways one enters the certainty of rightness (sammattaniyāma)," and so forth.
And this was stated by the Blessed One in the *Paṭṭhāna*:
"Conformity is a condition for change-of-lineage by way of proximity-condition; conformity is a condition for purification by way of proximity-condition," and so forth.
For one who practices, develops, and cultivates that knowledge of equanimity towards formations,

resolute faith becomes stronger, energy is well-sustained, mindfulness is well-established, the mind is well-concentrated, and the knowledge of equanimity towards formations proceeds more keenly. Thinking,
"The path will now arise for him," he [directs his attention] toward formations with equanimity.
Having comprehended [the formations] as "impermanent," or as "suffering," or as "non-self," one enters the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).

Immediately after the life-continuum, mind-door adverting consciousness (*manodvārāvajjana*) arises, taking those same formations as its object—either as "impermanent," or as "suffering," or as "non-self"—in the very same manner as was done during equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*). Immediately following that, in the same way, it takes those formations as its object...
Having performed this, two, three, or four impulsion consciousnesses (*javana-citta*) arise. The knowledge associated with them is "conformity-knowledge" (*anuloma-ñāṇa*).

For that conforms to the function of truth of the preceding eight insight-knowledges, and it also conforms to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*) to be attained hereafter.
Just as a righteous king, at the place of legal judgment, [acts in accordance with the law].

Seated there, having heard the judgment of the eight chief judges, he abandons taking an improper course, remains impartial, and by expressing his approval with the words, "So be it," he accords with their judgment and with the ancient royal law.
In this context, conformity-knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa) is like the king; the eight kinds of insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) are like the eight chief judges.
The thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment are like the ancient kingly duties.

Just as a king, expressing his approval by saying "Let it be so," accords with both the legal judgments of the judges and the kingly law, so too does this [insight] accord with the eight kinds of insight-knowledge arising with reference to formations by way of impermanence and so forth, because it conforms to their true function. Furthermore, above...
And because it is the means for attaining the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*), it is therefore called "conformity knowledge" (*anuloma-ñāṇa*). 10.
Regarding "the wisdom of emergence and turning away from the external is lineage-knowledge" (*gotrabhu-ñāṇa*): here, "external" (*bahiddhā*) refers to the sign of formations (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*).
For that is said to be "external" in relation to the unwholesome aggregates within one’s own internal mental continuum. Therefore, "external"...

It emerges from the sign of formations; because it stands aloft having become detached, it is "emergence" (*vuṭṭhāna*). Because it turns away, turns back, and becomes averted, it is "turning away" (*vivaṭṭana*). It is both that emergence and that turning away, thus "emergence-turning-away" (*vuṭṭhānavivaṭṭana*). For this very reason it was said:

"The knowledge of change-of-lineage does not emerge from occurrence because it does not cut off its arising; but because its object is Nibbāna, it emerges from the sign—thus there is emergence in one respect."
It is called *gotrabhū* because it overcomes the lineage of worldlings (*puthujjanagotta*) and develops the lineage of the Noble Ones (*ariyagotta*).
For, at the conclusion of the cultivation of conformity-knowledge (*anuloma-ñāṇa*), this knowledge— whose mind is withdrawing from all conditioned phenomena like water from a lotus leaf—
takes as its object the signless (*animitta*) Nibbāna, thereby transcending the lineage of worldlings, the designation of worldlings, and the plane of worldlings.

Transcending the lineage of the noble ones, the designation of the noble ones, and the plane of the noble ones, it descends upon the object of Nibbāna; having become the first turning, the first application of attention, and the first act of coordination,

it arises as the summit of insight and its pinnacle, never to return again, establishing itself as a condition for the Path in six ways— by way of proximity, contiguity, repetition, decisive support, presence, and absence.
11. "Wisdom regarding emergence and turning away from both is knowledge of the path. Here, "from both" (*dubhato*) means from two sides or from the pair.
It is called "both" because it emerges and turns away from both the defilements by cutting them off, and from the aggregates that follow those defilements by making Nibbāna its object;
and it emerges and turns away from all external signs of conditioned phenomena. Thus it is "from both."
Wisdom regarding emergence and turning away. For this very reason it was said:
"The four kinds of path-knowledge emerge from the sign because their object is signless; they emerge from occurrence because they cut off its arising;
thus they are 'emergences from both sides. Knowledge of the path: it seeks or looks toward Nibbāna, or it is sought or investigated by those who desire Nibbāna.

It is called the "path" (*magga*) because it goes or proceeds while slaying the defilements; knowledge regarding that path is "knowledge of the path. The singular number is used by way of a generic class.

For that [knowledge], immediately following the change-of-lineage knowledge (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*), takes Nibbāna as its object, completely cuts off the defilements to be abandoned by itself without remainder, dries up the ocean of suffering of the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), and closes all doors to the states of misery.
Path-knowledge arises, closing off the sevenfold noble wealth, bringing about the manifestation of the sevenfold noble wealth, abandoning the eightfold wrong path,
pacifying all enmities and fears, leading to the status of being a legitimate son of the Perfectly Enlightened One,
and obtaining many hundreds of other benefits.
Just as a man wishing to stand on the far shore, having leaped over a trench,
might come back with speed and seize a rope or a staff tied to a tree on this side,
his body leaning toward the further bank after having crossed over.
But one who has reached the further shore, having abandoned that piercing, stands firm on the far shore.
So too the practitioner of yoga, having seen the danger in this hither shore consisting of self-identity,
desires to stand in the deathless further shore which is free from fear.
Contemplating rise and fall, one who has arrived with great speed should correctly grasp the "rope" called form, or the "staff" called the other aggregates.
Indeed, by means of the mind of adverting, according to the method previously described;
Having leaped over the anuloma [moments] and being inclined toward Nibbāna, one approaches that very seat.
Having abandoned that by means of the *gotrabhū* [state], yet failing to attain through repeated practice, one trembles;
having fallen short on the far shore of the conditioned, one then becomes established by means of path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*).
Just as one who wishes to see the moon, when the moon is covered by layers of clouds,
might see it once the thick, fine, and subtle clouds have been gradually dispersed by the wind; even so,
through the successive stages of the knowledge of conformity (anuloma-ñāṇa), one sees [the Truth].
When delusion, which obscures the truth, has been dispelled, the lineage-follower (gotrabhu) beholds the Deathless.
But the conformities do not behold the Deathless, just as winds cannot see the moon;
just as a man [cannot see the moon] because of clouds, the lineage-follower does not dispel darkness.
Just as a man standing at the rim of a whirling wheel, with the perception of something else [fixed],
might pierce a hundred wooden targets while looking at the flight of an arrow—
so too here, the knowledge of the path, without abandoning the perception given by the change-of-lineage (gotrabhu), [proceeds].
Occurring within Nibbāna, it shatters the mass of greed and the other [defilements].
It dries up the ocean of suffering in saṃsāra and closes the door to the miserable destinies;
it makes one a possessor of the noble treasures and causes one to abandon the wrong path.
It subdues the fears of rebirth, makes one an actual son of the Protector, and bestows hundreds of other benefits; this is called "knowledge of wisdom. 12.
Regarding "the knowledge of fruition is the wisdom of the subsiding of the application": here, "application" means intense application for the realization of the fruit.
The application for emerging from both [the lower and higher fetters] through the development of the path is the "application.
The subsiding of that application is its "termination," which is the subsiding of the application. What is that? It is the conclusion of the function of the four paths.

The wisdom regarding the fruit that arises based on that termination of the application—which serves as its cause—is "wisdom of the subsiding of the application. It is called "fruit" (*phala*) because it bears fruit and ripens.

In that fruit, there is the knowledge associated with it. For immediately after each respective path-knowledge, three, two, or one fruition-consciousnesses arise as its resultants, having Nibbāna as their object.
Precisely because they are immediate resultants of supramundane wholesome states, it is said: "They call this concentration immediate," and "One attains the immediate [fruit] slowly."

"...for the destruction of the taints," and so forth, is what was said. For one who has two moments of conformity (anuloma), there is the third as change-of-lineage (gotrabhu), the fourth as path-consciousness (maggacitta), and three moments of fruition-consciousness (phalacitta).

For one who has three moments of conformity, there is the fourth as change-of-lineage, the fifth as path-consciousness, and two moments of fruition-consciousness. For one who has four moments of conformity, there is the fifth...
The change-of-lineage consciousness, the sixth path-consciousness, and one fruition-consciousness—this is the fruition within the cognitive process of the path.
Furthermore, the fruition at a later time, which arises by way of meditative attainment, and that which arises for one emerging from cessation, are also included herein.
13. Wisdom in contemplating the eradication of the course: this refers to the respective defilements eradicated by each respective noble path.

Wisdom in subsequent reviewing. "Knowledge of liberation" (*vimuttiñāṇa*) means knowledge of liberation. "Liberation" (*vimutti*) refers to the mind that is liberated from and purified of defilements, or the state of being liberated. Knowledge of that liberation is "knowledge of liberation.
