One who reviews both the continuity of consciousness liberated from defilements and the state of being liberated from defilements [is said to possess] knowledge of liberation from defilements.

“‘He does not review without [reviewing]’—by this, the reviewing of abandoned defilements is stated. For it was said with reference to this very thing: ‘When liberated, the knowledge arises: “It is liberated.
However, it should be understood that even though the reviewing of remaining defilements was not explicitly mentioned, it is indeed stated by this very [phrase]. And it has been said:”
“When one thing has been stated, all those things that share the same characteristic as it are thereby stated;
thus is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (lakkhaṇa-hāra) described.

Alternatively, it should be understood that because an Arahant lacks the reviewing of remaining defilements, what is stated here is specifically the reviewing of the abandoned defilements as experienced by the four types of Noble Ones.

14. "At that time, wisdom is the vision regarding the phenomena that have arisen": at that time, during both the moment of the path and the moment of the fruit, wisdom is the seeing, the beholding, and the understanding of the phenomena of the path and its fruits—which have arisen, arrived, and been attained through acquisition and penetration—as well as the phenomena of the Four Truths.
"Knowledge in reviewing" refers to [wisdom] having turned back.
"Clear seeing, vision, and knowing" is knowledge (*ñāṇa*). By these two types of knowledge, the knowledges of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*) are expressed.
For in the case of a stream-enterer, at the conclusion of the path-moment of stream-entry, the mind descends into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
Then, having interrupted the life-continuum, mind-door adverting consciousness arises for the purpose of reviewing the path.
When that [consciousness] has ceased, there arise in succession seven javanas of path-reviewing.
Then, having descended into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), advertence and the other [mental states] arise by that same method for the purpose of reviewing the fruit and so forth.
Through the arising of these, he reviews the path, reviews the fruit, reviews the defilements abandoned, and [reviews] the remaining defilements...
He reviews [them]; he reviews Nibbāna. For he reviews the path, thinking, "By this very path indeed have I come";
then he reviews the fruit, thinking, "This benefit has been obtained by me";

then he reviews the defilements abandoned, thinking, "These specific defilements have been abandoned by me"; then [he reviews] the defilements remaining, thinking, "These specific defilements remain for me."
He reviews the defilements abandoned by the higher paths, and at the conclusion, he reviews the deathless Nibbāna, thinking: "This Dhamma has been attained by me as an object.
Thus, there are five kinds of reviewing for a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer.
And just as it is for the stream-enterer, so it is for the once-returner and the non-returner. However, for the Arahant, there is the reviewing of the remaining defilements.
There are only four reviews [regarding the future], thinking "there is no [further] name. Thus, there are nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge in total.
This is the maximum limit. For those in training (*sekkha*), the review of defilements already abandoned and those still remaining may or may not occur.
Indeed, because of the absence of that [review], the Sakyan Mahānāma asked the Blessed One: "What kind of Dhamma is mine..."
“Because it has not been abandoned within myself, at times even states of greed (lobhadhammā) persist, having seized hold of my mind,” and so forth.
Herein, this simile should be understood for the purpose of clarifying the eleven kinds of knowledge, beginning with the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa):
just as a man, thinking “I will catch fish,” takes a fish-net, casts it into water suitable for that purpose, and...
Having quickly lowered his hand, he perceived a black snake within the water as a fish;

seizing it firmly by the neck, he was delighted, thinking, "Oh, what a great fish I have caught! But upon lifting it up and looking at it, he recognized it as a snake by seeing the three auspicious marks (*sovatthika*).
Terrified, perceiving the danger, and becoming weary of having seized it, he desired to release it. Regarding the releasing:
Employing a stratagem, he withdrew his hand starting from the tip of his big toe, raised his arm, and whirled it two or three times above the snake’s head;
having thus weakened the serpent, he released it, saying, "Go away, you wicked snake!
Then, quickly climbing onto dry land and standing there, he was filled with joy, exclaiming, "Oh, how wonderful! I have been delivered from the mouth of a great snake!"
He should look back along the path he has come. In that regard,
just as that man might be satisfied after firmly seizing a black snake under the perception that it was a fish,

so too for this yogi who was formerly an ordinary worldling (*bālaputhujjana*), the five aggregates— which are terrifying by way of impermanence and so forth— are [seized] through the perception of permanence and so forth.
Just as one who, having firmly grasped something with the views and craving of "I" and "mine," feels satisfaction,

might then pull a snake out from its mouth and, seeing three auspicious knots, perceive it as a "snake"— so too, by discerning name-and-form together with its conditions, effecting a thorough analysis of what was previously perceived as solid,
and through the knowledges such as the comprehension of aggregates, one sees the three characteristics, beginning with impermanence, in the five aggregates.
The defining of it as “impermanent, suffering, and non-self” is like that [initial] fear; the knowledge of the appearance as terror is like the fear itself;
the knowledge of contemplation of danger is like seeing the peril in the snake; the knowledge of contemplation of disenchantment is like the revulsion at seizing the snake;
the knowledge of desire for deliverance is like the wish to let go of the snake; and the knowledge of contemplation of reflection is like employing the means for letting go.
Just as one might cause a snake to coil around, weaken it, turn it back, and render it incapable of biting, so too,
by applying the three characteristics, the knowledge of equanimity toward formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) and the knowledge of conformity (*anulomañāṇa*) cause formations to coil,
weaken them, and render them incapable of appearing again in the mode of permanence, pleasure, and self. The knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhuñāṇa*) is like the release of the snake.
The knowledge of the path and its fruits is like standing on dry land after releasing a snake;
the knowledge of reviewing the path and so forth is like looking back at the road one has traveled when joyful.
And regarding these fourteen kinds of knowledge, beginning with that consisting of what is heard, they follow the order of their arising and the order of the practice.

Because the order of exposition has been established, it should be understood that among the reflections, the reflection on the defilements comes first, followed by the reflections on the Path, the Fruit, and Nibbāna. [One] develops supramundane jhāna that is leading to liberation,
conducive to disintegration, for the abandoning of views, for the attenuation of sensual lust and ill will,
for the complete abandoning of sensual lust and ill will, and for the abandoning of lust for the fine-material realm, lust for the immaterial realm, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.

And because it is stated that the practice of the path is for the sake of abandoning [defilements] without remainder—emphasizing the abandonment of defilements themselves—it is logical that the reviewing of defilements occurs first, in accordance with the sequence of practice; however, the order mentioned in the Commentary has already been shown.
That order is fivefold: the order of arising, the order of abandoning, the order of practice, [the order of teaching, and the order of occurrence].
The sequence of stages is the sequence of the teaching:
"First there is the *kalala*; from the *kalala* comes the *abbuda*;
from the *abbuda* is born the *pesi*; from the *pesi* develops the *ghana*."
The sequence of arising is as follows: "Phenomena to be abandoned by vision, phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation," and so forth.

The sequence of abandoning is as follows: "Purification of virtue, purification of mind, purification of view, purification by overcoming doubt, purification by knowledge and vision of what is and what is not the path, purification by knowledge and vision of the way, and purification by knowledge and vision."

Such is the sequence of practice (*paṭipattikkamo*). “Dhammas pertaining to the sense sphere, dhammas pertaining to the fine-material sphere, dhammas pertaining to the immaterial sphere”—such is the sequence of planes (*bhūmikkamo*).

Or, “the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path,” or “the gradual discourse (*anupubbikathā*)…” [and so forth].
He spoke. That is to say: he gave a discourse on giving, a discourse on virtue, a discourse on heaven;
he explained the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the blessing of renunciation—such is the sequence of the teaching.
But here, the sequence of the teaching is according to both the order of the arising of the fourteen knowledges and the order of the practice, because it has been taught in that successive order.
Thus, three sequences should be understood.

15. Now, since the knowledge of the discernment of mind-and-body (*nāmarūpa-vavatthāna-ñāṇa*) was not previously stated in its specific form, there are five [knowledges] beginning with "wisdom in the discernment of the internal is knowledge of the diversity of bases," taught in order to show the fivefold classification of mind-and-body.
The knowledges have been indicated. For when the entirety of name-and-form has been stated, one will comprehend both that which is capable of being comprehended and that which is to be comprehended.
Indeed, supramundane name cannot be comprehended because it has not yet been attained, nor is it to be comprehended because it does not come within the scope of insight (*vipassanā*).
In that context, regarding "the definition of the internal": "occurring thus..."
It is "internal" (*ajjhattā*) because it occurs by making oneself the subject, with the intention such as, "We shall go to the apprehension of 'self'.

This term *ajjhatta*, moreover, is seen in four senses: in the sense of the internal field of activity (*gocarajjhatta*), in the sense of one's own internal [nature] (*niyakajjhatta*), in the sense of being internal to the internal (*ajjhattajjhatta*), and in the sense of the internal object (*visayajjhatta*). "Therefore, Ānanda, by that bhikkhu, in that very same..."

For in such passages as, "The mind should be established right within oneself on the sign of concentration; one who delights in the internal is concentrated," this [term *ajjhatta*] is seen in the sense of the "internal object" (*gocara-ajjhatta*).
In such passages as, "With internal confidence, or dwelling in the contemplation of phenomena among internal phenomena," it refers to the "individual internal" (*niyaka-ajjhatta*).
And in such passages as, "The six internal bases, internal phenomena," it refers to the "personal internal" (*saka-ajjhatta*).

Regarding *ajjhattajjhatte*: in such passages as, “Furthermore, Ānanda, this dwelling has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata, namely, that through non-attention to all signs, one enters and dwells in internal emptiness,” it refers to the *ajjhatta* (internal) of the object (*visaya*), meaning the place of mastery (*issariyaṭṭhāna*).
For the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) is indeed called the place of mastery for Buddhas. However, in this context, it refers to the *ajjhatta* of the internal (*ajjhattajjhatte*).

It should be seen. "In the determination of those internal [states]" means in the determination of the internal. "In the diversity of bases" (*vatthunānatteti*) means in the state of the variousness of bases;

the sense is "in various bases. Here, even the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), which serves as the condition for the impulsion mind-consciousness, is called a "base" because it is the place of its arising, just like the pentad beginning with the eye. Even the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*) must be understood as being dependent on that very [base].
“Externally” means: in those external objects relative to the six internal bases. “In the diversity of the objective field” means:

in the diversity of objects. 17. “In the determination of conduct” means: in the determination of modes of conduct by way of the conduct of consciousness, the conduct of ignorance, and the conduct of knowledge.
They also read it as “cariyāvavatthāne,” having shortened it. 18. “In the determination of four dhammas” means: by way of the fourteen tetrads, such as the sense-sphere plane and so forth.
In the discernment of four things. *Bhūmi* (ground) occurs in the sense of the earth, as in such passages as “that which is on the ground and that which is in the air.

In such passages as “Do not, dear one, resort to what is not the ground,” it occurs in the sense of a domain. In such passages as “in the happy ground, the sense-sphere realm,” it occurs in the sense of a place of arising.
Here, however, it occurs in the sense of a constituent part (*koṭṭhāsa*). Some also say it means a delimitation (*pariccheda*).

19. "In the discernment of nine sets of states" means: in the discernment of nine respective sets of states by way of the wholesome and so forth of the sense sphere, by way of having gladness as their root, and by way of having appropriate attention as their root.

And among these five kinds of knowledge, the first is stated first because "states internal to oneself are to be discerned," which refers to the knowledge of the diversity of the physical bases; thereafter, "their objects are to be discerned."

Immediately after that, knowledge of the diversity of the cognitive domain (*gocaranānatta*) was stated; following that, the next three knowledges were stated in accordance with the sequence of counting, by way of three, four, and nine [factors] respectively.
Now, since the knowledge of defining through the analysis of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) itself is the full understanding of the known (*ñātapariññā*), immediately after that—

There are three kinds of full understanding (*pariññā*): full understanding as investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*), and immediately following that, full understanding as abandoning (*pahānapariññā*). Along with these, there are the development (*bhāvanā*) and realization (*sacchikiriyā*).

Therefore, immediately after the knowledge of the diversity of phenomena (*dhammanānattañāṇa*), five knowledges beginning with the knowledge of the meaning of what has been known (*ñātaṭṭhe ñāṇa*) are listed.

For the three kinds of full understanding are: full understanding as the known (*ñātapariññā*), full understanding as investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*), and full understanding as abandoning (*pahānapariññā*). Among these, [the characteristic of being afflicted is] "having the characteristic of being afflicted..."

“Form, feeling has the characteristic of being felt”—wisdom that proceeds by way of discerning the individual characteristics of such and such phenomena is called *ñātapariññā* (full understanding through knowing).

Wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*) that takes characteristics as its object proceeds by applying the general characteristics to those respective phenomena in such a manner as: “Form is impermanent, suffering, and non-self; feeling is impermanent, suffering, and non-self,” and so forth.

This is called "full understanding by scrutinization" (*tīraṇapariññā*). Furthermore, the insight that has the characteristics [of impermanence, suffering, and non-self] as its object, which proceeds by way of abandoning the perception of permanence and so forth regarding those very same phenomena, is called "full understanding by abandoning" (*pahānapariññā*).

In this context, the stage for "full understanding by knowing" (*ñātapariññā*) begins from the delimitation of formations (*saṅkhārapariccheda*) up until the discernment of conditions (*paccayapariggaha*).
For within this interval, the primary function consists solely in the penetration of the individual characteristics of phenomena. From the comprehension by groups (*kalāpasammasana*)...

From the beginning up to the contemplation of rise and fall is the plane of full understanding by scrutinization; for within this interval, the contemplation of the general characteristics alone holds predominance.
Starting with the contemplation of dissolution, the subsequent stages constitute the plane of full understanding by abandoning.
For from that point onward, "contemplating as impermanent, one abandons the perception of permanence; contemplating as suffering, one abandons the perception of pleasure."
“Contemplating as non-self, one abandons the perception of self; becoming disenchanted, one abandons delight; becoming dispassionate, one abandons lust;
causing cessation, one abandons arising; relinquishing, one abandons grasping.
In this way, there is the predominance of the seven contemplations that accomplish the abandoning of the perception of permanence and so forth.
In this context, "wisdom of direct knowledge" (*abhiññāpaññā*) is the wisdom that knows phenomena by way of their intrinsic natures, such as their susceptibility to change (*ruppanādi*).
For, in the sense of being "excellent" (*sobhana*), it is called "direct knowledge" (*abhiññā*) because it is "an excellent knowing" by way of knowing the specific nature of various phenomena;
thus, through the prefix *abhi*, it is termed direct knowledge. "Knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) in the sense of "that which is known" (*ñāta*) is knowledge whose intrinsic nature is knowing.
21. Full-understanding wisdom (*pariññā-paññā*) is the wisdom of knowing.

For, in the sense of pervading, the word *pari*—by way of the common characteristics such as impermanence, or by way of accomplishing its own function—is taken to mean "pervasive knowing," and thus it is called full-understanding.
In the sense of scrutinizing, "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) refers to knowledge whose intrinsic nature is investigation, or whose intrinsic nature is comprehension (*sammasana*).

22. *Pahānapaññā* (wisdom of abandoning) is wisdom consisting in the abandoning of perceptions of permanence and so forth; or, it is "abandoning" (*pahāna*) because it abandons, or because one abandons by means of it. It is knowledge in the sense of relinquishment; that is, knowledge whose intrinsic nature is relinquishing. 23.

*Bhāvanāpaññā* (wisdom of development) is wisdom of increase. It is knowledge in the sense of a single function; that is, knowledge whose intrinsic nature is a single task, or knowledge whose intrinsic nature is a single flavor through the flavor of liberation.

24. *Sacchikiriyāpaññā* (wisdom of realization) is the wisdom that makes [the truth] directly manifest by way of penetration (*paṭivedha*) or by way of acquisition (*paṭilābha*). "Knowledge in the sense of touching" is knowledge whose intrinsic nature is to find [the truth] by way of both those [aspects].

25–28. Now, since the knowledges of abandoning (*pahāna*), development (*bhāvanā*), and realization (*sacchikiriyā*) are also associated with the Noble Paths and Fruits, immediately following that [section], the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidāñāṇa*) which are obtainable only by Noble Persons (*ariyapuggala*) are presented.

These have been enumerated. Among them, the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā-ñāṇa*) is enumerated first because its object, which arises as a condition, is as manifest and easy to understand as the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).
Following that is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā-ñāṇa*), because its object consists of the causal phenomena (*hetu-dhamma*) of that meaning.
Following that is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā-ñāṇa*), because its object consists of the linguistic expression of both of those.
Because it proceeds immediately after those three types of knowledge, the analytical knowledge of ingenuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa*) follows them;
they also recite it with a long vowel, as *pā*.

29–31. The three subsequent knowledges, beginning with the knowledge of dwelling in the [divine] abodes (*vihāraṭṭha*), belong exclusively to the Noble Ones (*ariya*), as they arise from the specific divisions of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).

And these were taught immediately after the knowledge of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). For the knowledge regarding the state of abiding (*vihāra*) is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*);

the knowledge regarding the state of attainment (*samāpatti*) is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*attha-paṭisambhidā*). Indeed, in the discourse on the analytical knowledges, it is stated that the knowledge regarding the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*) is the analytical knowledge of phenomena.
However, the knowledge regarding *nibbāna* is exclusively the analytical knowledge of meaning. In this context, "diversity of abiding" (*vihāranānatta*) refers to...
"In various abidings of insight" means by way of the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) and so forth.
"In the state of abiding" means in the essential nature of the abiding of insight. Furthermore, "abiding" refers specifically to insight together with its associated mental factors.

"In the diversity of attainments" means in the various fruition-attainments by way of the signless (*animitta*) and so forth. Furthermore, "attainment" refers to the states of consciousness and mental factors that constitute the supramundane fruit. "In the diversity of abidings and attainments" [means...]
This is stated by way of both [the path and the fruit].

32. Then, for one who accomplishes the knowledge of the meditative attainments (*vihārasamāpatti*), the capacity of the previously mentioned knowledge of the path (*maggañāṇa*)—defined as "wisdom in emerging from and turning away from both sides"—to eradicate the taints (*āsava*) and to bestow the immediate fruit is established through its causal basis.
Desiring to explain that same [knowledge] in another way by distinguishing it, he states: "Knowledge regarding the concentration of immediate succession (*ānantarika-samādhi*).
Therein, "due to its purity through non-distraction" (*avikkhepa-parisuddhattā*): that by which the mind is distracted is "distraction" (*vikkhepa*);

this is a name for restlessness (*uddhacca*). Non-distraction (*avikkhepa*) is the absence of distraction; this is a name for concentration (*samādhi*), which is the opposite of restlessness. Of that which is pure...

"Bhāva" means purity; "purity of non-distraction" (*avikkhepa-parisuddhatta*) refers to the purity of non-distraction. Therefore, the meaning is: "by way of the state of purity of concentration due to the purity of non-distraction.

This is indeed a statement of the cause for the cutting off of the taints (*āsava-samuccheda*) and for its yielding an immediate fruit. Regarding the term "cutting off of the taints," here the taints (*āsava*) are so called because they flow out (*āsavanti*).
It is said that they "flow" and "proceed" even from the eye... [and so on] ...up to the mind.

Alternatively, they are called *āsava* because they flow as far as the stage of the lineage (*gotrabhū*) in terms of phenomena (*dhamma*), and as far as the peak of existence (*bhavagga*) in terms of spatial scope (*okāsa*).

The meaning is that they proceed having taken these phenomena and this spatial scope within themselves; for this prefix *ā-* has the sense of "taking within. In the sense of being long-fermented, they are like liquor and such.
The *āsava*s are so called because they are like fermented liquors (*āsava*). For in the world, intoxicants such as wine that have been stored for a long time are called *āsava*.
And if they are *āsava* by virtue of being long-stored, then these [defilements] alone are worthy of being so designated. For this has been said:
"Bhikkhus, no prior limit of ignorance is known; before this, ignorance did not exist, and only afterwards did it come into being," and so forth.

They are called *āsava* because they flow (*savanti*) and pour forth the long-lasting suffering of *saṃsāra*. It is called "cutting off" (*samuccheda*) because by means of it [the defilements] are completely severed. "Wisdom" refers to the wisdom regarding the cutting off of the four *āsava*s, beginning with the *kāma-āsava*.

"Knowledge in the *ānantariya-samādhi*" refers to the path-concentration (magga-samādhi) which has received the name "uninterrupted" (*ānantariya*) because it unfailingly yields its fruit immediately following its own occurrence.
For when the path-concentration has arisen, there is nothing that can obstruct the arising of its fruit.
There is no obstacle whatsoever. As it is said:
"Suppose a person were practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, and it were the time for the world-age to be incinerated;
the world-age would not be incinerated until that person has realized the fruit of stream-entry."
“This person is called one who can remain for an eon (*ṭhitakappī*). Indeed, all persons possessing the path (*maggasamaṅgin*) are those who can remain for an eon.
This is the knowledge associated with that immediate concentration (*ānantarikasamādhi*).
Following this knowledge of the path, [the next section begins] because it arises only for noble ones (*ariya*) who have attained the fruit (*phala*) by means of this knowledge of the path.
The four knowledges beginning with the knowledge of dwelling without conflict (*araṇavihāra*) have been indicated.

Among these, the knowledge of dwelling without conflict is mentioned first because it occurs constantly and belongs exclusively to an Arahant. Immediately after that, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is mentioned;
for although this occurs in Non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and Arahants, it requires a great accumulation of requisites and is specifically designated as Nibbāna.
Knowledge has been taught; immediately after that, because it stands reaching as far as the time of final Nibbāna at a later time, the knowledge regarding final Nibbāna is taught as "long-term.

Immediately after that, because it stands reaching as far as the time of final Nibbāna immediately following the destruction of all defilements for one who has attained the "equal-headed" state, the knowledge regarding the equal-headed state is taught as "short-term. In this regard:

The word *ca* (and) in the phrase "the noble ones (*santo ca*)" should be connected with all three terms: the predominance of vision (*dassanādhipateyya*), the attainment of the noble abiding (*santo vihārādhigama*), and the inclination toward the sublime (*paṇītādhimuttatā*).
"Vision" (*dassana*) refers to the knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*). "Predominance" (*ādhipateyya*) means simply being predominant;
or, it is called "predominance" because it has come from being predominant. Thus, "vision-predominance" (*dassanādhipateyya*) means that which is both vision and predominant.
"Abiding" (*vihāra*) means that by which one abides; or, "it is through this that they abide," thus it is an abiding.

That which is reached and attained is an attainment (*adhigama*). An abiding that is itself an attainment is "abiding-attainment. And because it is free from the fever of the defilements, it is "peaceful" (*santa*).

And that is the wisdom of the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship. In the sense of being supreme and in the sense of being unsurpassed, it is "sublime" (*paṇīta*); it has reached the state of preeminence.
"Exalted" (*paṇīta*) means brought forth or refined. One who is intent upon the exalted, whose mind is expanded, and for whom that is supreme, is "intent upon the exalted" (*paṇītādhimutta*);

the state of being such is "intentness upon the exalted" (*paṇītādhimuttatā*). And that is precisely the wisdom of the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga-paññā*) which is intent upon the attainment of fruition (*phala-samāpatti*).

"In the dwelling without conflict" (*araṇa-vihāre*) means in the dwelling free from defilements (*nikkilesa-vihāre*). For greed and the other [defilements] are called "conflicts" (*raṇa*) because they cause sentient beings to clash, crush, and oppress them.
They are called *raṇas* because beings clash by means of them, or because they cry out and lament; thus, all three types of abiding (*vihāra*) have been mentioned.
It is "without conflict" (*araṇa*) because there is no conflict (*raṇa*) in it. It is an "abiding" (*vihāra*) because one carries away (*harati*) various adverse states by means of it.
In that conflict-free abiding, the first jhāna and so forth mentioned in the section on the detailed exposition are included precisely because of being inclined toward the sublime.

For it should be understood that the desire to attain the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) involves entering the first jhāna and so forth, emerging from them, and then practicing insight (*vipassanā*) into the states associated with those jhānas;

furthermore, the way of practice for non-affliction (*araṇa-paṭipadā*) taught by the Blessed One in the *Araṇavibhaṅga Sutta* is also included within this very category. Indeed, it was said there by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you the analysis of non-conflict... One should not devote oneself to the pleasure of sensual desires, which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial;
nor should one devote oneself to self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial.
Not approaching either of these two extremes, bhikkhus, is the middle way.”
This has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; it is conducive to the eye, conducive to knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, full enlightenment, and Nibbāna.
One should know what is elevating and one should know what is disparaging;

having known what is elevating and having known what is disparaging, one should neither elevate nor disparage, but should teach only the Dhamma. One should know the determination of happiness, the determination of happiness...
“Having understood this, one should devote oneself to internal happiness; one should not utter private speech; one should not speak of what has been exhausted in the presence [of others];
one should speak unhurriedly, not hurriedly; one should not adhere to local dialects; one should not override common usage.
This is the summary of the analysis of non-conflict (*araṇavibhaṅga*)... In that regard, monks, as for the pursuit of joy associated with the pleasure of the connection with sensual desires...”
Non-application is base... [as before] ...unconducive to welfare; this Dhamma is without suffering, without vexation, without despair, without fever, and is the right way of practice.

Therefore, this Dhamma is free from conflict... [as before] ....In this regard, monks, that which is non-application to the pursuit of self-mortification is suffering, ignoble, and unconducive to welfare.
This Dhamma is without suffering... [as before] ...therefore, this Dhamma is free from conflict.
It is without conflict. In this regard, monks, that middle way which has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata...
[this teaching is without suffering]... therefore this teaching is without conflict... In this regard, monks, that teaching of the Dhamma which involves neither exalting nor disparaging...
[this teaching is without suffering]... therefore this teaching is without conflict... In this regard, monks, [that which is]... [the same applies].
“Monks, that which is the happiness of renunciation, the happiness of seclusion, the happiness of peace, and the happiness of awakening—this Dhamma is without suffering...

[as before] ...therefore this Dhamma is without conflict... [as before] ...In this regard, monks, whatever private conversation there may be that is factual, true, and beneficial—this Dhamma is without suffering... [as before] ...therefore this Dhamma is without conflict... [as before] ...In this regard, monks...”
This speech which is face-to-face, true, factual, and beneficial—this Dhamma is free from suffering... [as before] ...therefore this Dhamma is free from conflict...
[as before] ...In that regard, monks, as for this speech spoken without haste—this Dhamma is free from suffering...
[as before] ...therefore this Dhamma is free from conflict... [as before] ...In that regard, monks, as for this local dialect...
"And non-adherence to designations, and not overstepping conventional designations—this Dhamma is without suffering... [as before] ...therefore this Dhamma is 'without conflict' (*araṇa*).
Therefore, monks, we shall know the Dhamma that leads to conflict and we shall know the Dhamma that is without conflict.
Having known the Dhamma that leads to conflict and having known the Dhamma that is without conflict, we shall practice the way that is without conflict. Thus, indeed, for you—
“Monks, you should train yourselves thus. And furthermore, monks, the clansman Subhūti has entered upon the practice of non-conflict.
In this context, the middle way is comprised of both the predominance of vision and the attainment of peaceful dwelling.
Non-indulgence in sensual pleasure and self-mortification is itself the middle way; for the insight of an arahant is preceded by the middle way.
The attainment of the fruit of Arahantship is the middle way of practice by way of the eightfold path.
It should be understood that the remaining [qualities] are included precisely because of being inclined toward the sublime.

Although all Arahants dwell in a state free from conflict (*araṇavihārin*), when other Arahants teach the Dhamma, they say of those who practice rightly, "They are practicing rightly," and of those who practice wrongly...
“Those who have entered upon the wrong way,” thus they teach the Dhamma by means of praise and disparagement based on individuals.
But the Elder Subhūti taught the Dhamma solely by means of the Dhamma itself, saying, “This is the wrong way; this is the right way.

For that very reason, the Blessed One praised him, saying, “Bhikkhus, among my disciples... and described him as one who has entered upon the practice of non-conflict (*araṇa-paṭipadā*). “This is the foremost, bhikkhus, of my...”
And he placed him in the foremost position among the disciples, the monks who dwell in freedom from conflict (*araṇavihārin*), saying, "That is Subhūti.

34. "By two powers" means by the power of serenity (*samatha*) and the power of insight (*vipassanā*). "Because of being endowed with" means because of being joined with or because of being perfected in them.
"And three" is a reversal of the grammatical case; it should be read as "of the three. "Of formations" refers to the verbal formation, the bodily formation, and the mental formation.
"By means of tranquility" (paṭippassaddhiyā) means for the sake of tranquility, for the sake of cessation; it is said to mean for the sake of non-occurrence.
"By sixteen" means by the eight [insight knowledges] beginning with the contemplation of impermanence, and the eight [supramundane states] consisting of the paths and fruits—thus by sixteen.

"By the courses of knowledge" (ñāṇacariyāhi) means by the occurrences of knowledge. "By nine" means by the nine consisting of the fine-material and immaterial-sphere jhānas together with their access concentrations. "Mastery" (vasibhāvatā).

"Wisdom" (*paññā*) means lightness; it is sovereignty (*issariya*) in moving according to one's pleasure, and mastery (*vasa*). One who possesses that is "masterful" (*vasī*); the state of being masterful is "mastery" (*vasibhāva*);
the very state of mastery is "mastery-ness" (*vasibhāvatā*), just as "repulsiveness" (*pāṭikulya*) is the same as "repulsiveness-ness" (*pāṭikulyatā*).
The meaning is that wisdom of such a kind is "wisdom by way of mastery. They also recite it with a long *si*-sound (*vasibhāvatāya*). Because of being endowed with [this].
The word "ca" (and) should be connected as follows: "with the knowledge of the practice of tranquility, with the knowledge of the practice of insight, and with the practices of concentration.

Regarding "knowledge of the attainment of cessation": this refers to the knowledge that has the attainment of cessation as its object for non-returners and arahants, just as in the expression, "the leopard is killed by the antelope skin.
Furthermore, the "attainment of cessation" is merely the absence of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
There is no phenomenon whatsoever; because it is a mere designation and a mere non-existence, it is called "cessation" (nirodha).
And because it is entered into by one who enters it, it is called "attainment" (samāpatti).

35. "Of one who is clearly comprehending" (sampajānassa): one who knows correctly in various ways is "clearly comprehending"; [the phrase refers to] "of that clearly comprehending one. "At the exhaustion of the occurrence" (pavattapariyādāne):
*Pavatta* means occurring; its meaning is "active manifestation. This refers to both the occurrence of the defilements (*kilesa-pavatta*) and the occurrence of the aggregates (*khandha-pavatta*).
The exhaustion, depletion, and non-occurrence of that occurrence is the "termination of occurrence" (*pavattapariyādāna*). Regarding that termination of occurrence:
"knowledge of final Nibbāna" refers to the arahant’s final Nibbāna—the non-occurrence of sensual desire and the other defilements—and the final Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-parinibbāna*).
It is the knowledge that arises in one who reviews both the parinibbāna of defilements and the parinibbāna of the aggregates.
36. "Of all phenomena" means of all phenomena belonging to the three planes. "Rightly and completely cuts off" means in the sense of a thorough cessation by way of the cutting off of the continuity.
"And non-manifestation in cessation" means because of not manifesting again once cessation has occurred. Again...
The meaning is "non-arising. The word "and" (*ca*) should be connected as follows: "the state of not being present in both right eradication and cessation.

Regarding the sense of "having a common head" (*samasīsa*), "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) refers to this: the thirty-seven factors beginning with renunciation (*nekkhamma*) are the "common" (*sama*); the thirteen factors beginning with craving (*taṇhā*) are the "heads" (*sīsā*).

They are "common" because they have stilled (*samita*) the opposing states; and they are "heads" because they are, respectively, the foremost and the culminating points. In a single posture (*iriyāpatha*)...

Or, because of a single illness, or by way of a homogeneous continuity (*sabhāga-santati*), or in respect of a single life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), one who possesses both the "equal" factors such as renunciation (*nekkhamma*) and so forth, and the "heads" such as faith (*saddhā*) and so forth, is called *samasīsi*. The meaning of *samasīsi* is *samasīsattha*.
In that sense of *samasīsattha*, it means the state of being *samasīsi*. [This applies] to a single posture (*iriyāpatha*), illness, or by way of a homogeneous continuity.
Or, having begun insight (vipassanā) while still living, one attains the four paths and fruits within that very same posture, illness, or similar life-span;
then, for an Arahant who attains final Nibbāna in that very moment, there is the state of being "one whose head is level" (samasīsī).
Thus, it is said that "knowledge regarding that state of being one whose head is level. And this is stated in the *Puggalapaññatti* and its commentary:

“And what kind of person is one who is ‘equal-headed’ (*samasīsī*)? That person for whom the exhaustion of the taints (*āsava*) and the exhaustion of life occur neither before nor after [each other]. This is called a person who is equal-headed.

In the exposition of the equal-headed person, “neither before nor after” means not earlier and not later; it means at one and the same time, simultaneously, by way of the present continuity (*santati*).
“Exhaustion” (*pariyādāna*) means complete consumption. “This” refers to this person who is named equal-headed.
It is said [that he is one who attains Parinibbāna]. Furthermore, this is threefold:

one whose attainment is simultaneous with his posture (*iriyāpatha-samasīsī*), one whose attainment is simultaneous with his illness (*roga-samasīsī*), and one whose attainment is simultaneous with his life-span (*jīvita-samasīsī*). Among these, one who, having begun insight while walking, attains Arahantship and attains Parinibbāna while still walking;
one who, having begun insight while standing, attains Arahantship and attains Parinibbāna while still standing; and one who, while sitting...
One who, having begun insight meditation (*vipassanā*) while sitting and attained *arahantship*, passes away (*parinibbāti*) while still sitting;

or one who, having begun insight meditation while lying down and attained *arahantship*, passes away while still lying down—this is called "one whose attainment of the goal coincides with the posture" (*iriyāpatha-samasīsī*).
Furthermore, one who, having fallen ill and begun insight meditation while still within that illness, attains *arahantship* and [passes away] by means of that very illness...
He attains final Nibbāna; this is called "the one whose head is simultaneous with the disease. Which is the one whose head is simultaneous with life? There are thirteen heads.
Among them, the path of Arahantship exhausts ignorance, which is the head of the defilements; the death-consciousness exhausts the life-faculty, which is the head of the process [of existence].
The consciousness that exhausts ignorance is not able to exhaust the life-faculty, whereas the [consciousness] that exhausts the life-faculty...
The mind is not able to exhaust ignorance. The mind that exhausts ignorance is one thing; the mind that exhausts the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is another.
One for whom these two "heads" reach exhaustion simultaneously is called "one whose head is level with life.

How does this become simultaneous? By way of equality of the occasion. For at whatever occasion the emergence of the path occurs—namely, at the stage of the stream-entry path (*sotāpattimagga*)—[the two heads are exhausted together].
There are five reviews: five on the path of once-returning, five on the path of non-returning, and four on the path of arahantship.
Having established himself in these nineteen knowledges of reviewing, he descends into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and attains final nibbāna.

It is precisely by this equality of the number of times that the completion of both ends is likewise equal. Therefore, this person is called "one whose end of life is equal to his end of the goal" (jīvitasamasīsī).
...is what is called [knowledge]. And it is this alone that is intended here.

37. Now, since the kinds of knowledge consisting of what is heard, what consists of virtue, and what consists of development are supports for the round of existence and are not called “effacement,” whereas these and other kinds of knowledge that support the supramundane are called “effacement,” therefore, by way of effacing the adverse states— [The text continues: ...in the manner of effacing the adverse states...
In order to show the knowledges that have already occurred, the knowledge in the sense of effacement is taught immediately after the knowledge in the sense of even-headedness.
Therein, "wisdom in the exhaustion of the diverse and manifold fires" refers to those things which— because they are unmixed with supramundane states—
are called "fires" in the sense of burning up the diverse and manifold lusts and so forth, as well as the various-natured states such as sensual desire and the rest.
Wisdom is the exhaustion and destruction of immorality and so forth; that is to say, wisdom regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment such as renunciation.
Alternatively, "fires" (tejā) refers to those that have become manifold and diverse; thus the meaning is:

wisdom is the exhaustion of these five fires which have become manifold and diverse, namely immorality and the rest. [This applies] to the manifold and diverse [fires] by means of the fires themselves.
We shall explain the summary in the section on exposition.
Regarding "knowledge in the sense of effacement": it is effacement (*sallekha*) because it effaces—that is, completely cuts off—adverse states;
knowledge in that which has the nature of effacement, consisting of thirty-seven factors such as renunciation and so forth. "Others will be harmful..."
It should be understood that even the forty-fourfold *sallekha* (effacement) spoken of by the Blessed One in the *Sallekhasutta*—beginning with the method, "We shall be non-violent in this regard;
thus effacement is to be practiced"—is indeed included within this [definition]. 38.

Now, in order to show the energy of right exertion (*sammappadhāna-vīriya*) to be performed by one established in effacement, [the text] immediately following that discusses the undertaking of energy (*vīriyārambha*).
Knowledge has been indicated. In that context, regarding the meaning of "exertion through a self that is unflagging and resolute":
one whose self (*atta*) is unflagging (*asallīna*)—that is, not slackened or shrunken due to indolence—is "one with an unflagging self. Here, "self" refers to the mind. As it is said:
"For water-carriers lead the water, and fletchers straighten the arrow-shaft;"
“Carpenters shape wood; the wise tame themselves. And so forth.
One who has sent forth, dispatched, or abandoned the self by means of this [practice] is called *pahitatto*. “Self” (*attā*) here refers to the personal existence (*attabhāva*).
As it is said: “But if a nun, having repeatedly struck herself, should weep,” and so on.
"One who is both unwearied and resolute" is *asallīnattapahitatto*. That which uplifts and supports co-nascent states (*sahajātadhamma*) is "exertion" (*paggaha*);
"the state of exertion" (*paggahaṭṭha*) means exertion itself is the purpose, or rather, it means the nature of exertion.
"The state of exertion of one who is unwearied and resolute" is *asallīnattapahitattapaggahaṭṭha*. In that state of exertion of one who is unwearied and resolute.
“Therefore, bhikkhus, you too should strive without turning back.
Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain, and let the flesh and blood dry up in the body;
yet as long as that which is to be attained by human strength, human energy, and human exertion has not been reached, there shall be no stopping of your effort.”
Because it has been stated [in this way], by the expression "unflagging and resolute," non-retrogression and non-turning-back in exertion are expressed.
By the expression "having the sense of exertion" (*paggahaṭṭha*), however, energy (*vīriya*) that is free from both sloth and agitation and proceeds with evenness is expressed.
Regarding "knowledge in the arousal of energy": heroism is energy, or the action of heroes, or [the application of] method, principle, and means.
Viriya is that which must be stirred up and set in motion. It has the characteristic of exertion; its function is to support co-nascent states;

it is manifested as non-collapse. According to the statement, "One who is moved by a sense of urgency strives with systematic application," its proximate cause is a sense of urgency (saṃvega), or else its proximate cause is the basis for the arousal of energy. When rightly undertaken, it is the foundation for all attainments.
It should be understood that it is the root. "Exertion consisting of energy" (*vīriyārambha*) means exertion characterized by energy.
By this, other forms of exertion are excluded. For this word *ārambha* occurs in many senses: in the sense of action, offense, activity, energy, and violence.
"Whatever suffering arises, all is conditioned by exertion."
“With the cessation of undertakings, there is no arising of suffering.
Here, indeed, karma is what has come down as “undertaking” (*ārambha*). In the passage, “He undertakes [an action] and then feels remorse,” it refers to an offense (*āpatti*).

In the passage, “Great sacrifices involving great undertakings do not bear great fruit,” it refers to activities such as the raising of a sacrificial post (*yūpa*). “Undertake [the effort]... [and so forth].

In the passage, “Exert yourselves, apply yourselves to the Buddha’s teaching,” it is energy (*vīriya*). In the passage, “They take up living beings for the sake of the ascetic Gotama,” it is violence (*hiṃsā*).
In the passage, “He abstains from injuring seeds and plants,” it is the disturbance consisting of cutting, breaking, and so forth.
But here, it is specifically energy that is intended. Therefore it was said: “consisting of energy.”
“Exertion is the exertion of energy. For energy is called “exertion” (ārambha) in the sense of beginning (ārabhana). Knowledge regarding that exertion of energy is [the factor].
Some also read “because of non-slackness and because of being urged forward” (*asallīnattā pahitattā*), meaning by way of the state of not being slack and the state of being urged forward;
however, the former reading alone is superior. But some [say] that it is the evenness of the enlightenment factors of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, and rapture...
They describe it as non-laxity, the evenness of the enlightenment factors of mindfulness, concentration, tranquility, and equanimity, and the state of being resolute;
they describe it as the sense of exertion, which is the evenness of the seven enlightenment factors. 39.
Now, having attained the path and its fruit accomplished through right effort, one should deliver a teaching on the Dhamma for the benefit of the world.
To demonstrate this, the knowledge of demonstrating the meaning (*atthasandassanañāṇa*) is listed immediately thereafter.

In that context, "the manifestation of various phenomena" (*nānādhammappakāsanatā*) means the manifestation, illumination, and teaching of various phenomena by way of all conditioned and unconditioned things. Furthermore, "manifestation" (*pakāsanatā*) is simply manifestation itself.
"Demonstrating the meaning" (*atthasandassane*) refers to the demonstration of various meanings to others. Both "phenomena" (*dhammā*) and "meanings" (*atthā*) are indeed those very things.

40. Now, in order to show the purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*)—which is the cause for that noble person who instructs others by means of a discourse on the Dhamma to teach the Dhamma according to its true nature—the knowledge of the purification of view is indicated immediately following that.
Therein, "the penetration of the unity and diversity of all phenomena" refers to the unification of all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena into a single category.

And the meaning of "penetration" (*paṭivedha*) is the realization of the diversity of sensual desire and so forth, and the unity of renunciation and so forth; that is, the wisdom of the path and the wisdom of the fruit.
The wisdom of the path is "penetration" because it penetrates by way of the realization of the truths at the moment of the realization of the truths;
the wisdom of the fruit is "penetration" because it has already been penetrated. Regarding the phrase "by way of a single inclusion": here, [it refers to...]
There are four kinds of inclusion: inclusion by birth, inclusion by kindred, inclusion by action, and inclusion by enumeration.
In this regard: "Let all khattiyas come; let all brahmins, all vessas, and all suddas come";
and: "Friend Visākha, whatever is right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these phenomena..."
“...are included within the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha). This is what is called a grouping by way of genus (*jātisaṅgaha*).
For here, all [factors] are grouped as one by way of genus, just as in the expression, “Let those of the same genus come. [It is like saying: “Let all the people of Kosala come;
let all the people of Magadha come; let all the people of Bhārukaccha come. And: “Friend Visākha, that which is right effort and that which is right mindfulness...”
“And whatever right concentration—these states are included in the aggregate of concentration. This is called inclusion by genus (*sañjātisaṅgaha*).
For here, all are included in one group by way of their place of birth, just as in the expression:
“Let those born and raised in one place come! [Likewise: “Let all elephant-riders come; let all horse-riders come.”
"Let all the charioteers come," and "Friend Visākha, that which is right view and that which is right intention—these states are included within the aggregate of wisdom.
This is called inclusion by action (*kiriyā-saṅgaha*). For indeed, they are all included together as a single group by virtue of performing their respective actions.
"Which sense-base, the eye-base, goes into the counting of the aggregates? The eye-base..."

It goes into the reckoning of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*). If the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) goes into the reckoning of the aggregate of form, then indeed, it must be said that the eye-base is included (*saṅgahita*) within the aggregate of form. This is what is called "inclusion by reckoning" (*gaṇanasaṅgaha*);
this is what is intended here. Among the twelve modes beginning with "the state of being thus" (*tathaṭṭha*), inclusion by each one individually is the delimitation by reckoning.
These are the unifications; the state of being unified is "unification" (*ekasaṅgahatā*).

"Knowledge of purification by vision" (*dassanavisuddhiñāṇa*) means that the knowledge of the path and fruit is "vision. Purification itself is vision, thus "purification by vision"; knowledge itself is purification by vision, thus "knowledge of purification by vision. It is called "purification by vision" because the knowledge of the path is purified by it.
The knowledge of fruition (*phala-ñāṇa*) is purification by vision (*dassana-visuddhi*) because of its purity.

41. Now, in order to show the two types of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) that accomplish purification by vision, the knowledge of acceptance (*khanti-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of pervasion (*pariyogāhaṇa-ñāṇa*) are listed immediately thereafter.
In this context, "wisdom" (*paññā*) is so called because of knowing; it arises from knowing the aggregate of form (*rūpa-kkhandha*) and the others as impermanent and so forth.

Wisdom (*paññā*). "Knowledge of patience" (*khantiñāṇa*): that which is known is simply endured, thus it is patience (*khanti*); patience itself as knowledge is "knowledge of patience. By this, he rejects the patience of mere endurance.
This is the knowledge of nascent insight (*taruṇavipassanāñāṇa*) occurring by way of the comprehension of the aggregates (*kalāpasammasana*), and so forth.
42. "Wisdom because of being touched": because it occurs through the contact of knowledge regarding the impermanence and other characteristics of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) and the rest.
Wisdom (*paññā*). "Knowledge of fathoming" means that it fathoms—that is, it penetrates—exactly what has been touched;

thus it is knowledge of fathoming. They also recite it with the *gā*-sound shortened [to *ga*]. This is the sharp insight-knowledge that occurs by way of the contemplation of dissolution and so forth.
Some, however, say: "The very same insight-knowledge is the knowledge of choice when it brings about faith, and the knowledge of fathoming when it brings about wisdom."
They say this. But if that were so, these two types of knowledge could not coexist in a single person;
and since they could not coexist, the sixty-seven types of knowledge common to disciples could not exist in a single disciple. Therefore, that [position] is untenable. 43.
Now, because both worldlings and those in training perceive the phenomena such as the aggregates, which are objects of insight, in their entirety...
They comprehend the whole, not just a portion; therefore, for them, dwelling in a specific place is not possible.

It is only for the Arahant that dwelling in a specific place according to his wish is possible. Having thus stated the knowledges that accomplish purification of vision, the knowledge of dwelling in a specific place—which is established through the purification of vision for the Arahant—is indicated immediately thereafter. In this context, "wisdom in the act of bringing together" (samodahane paññā) means:
It is the wisdom that synthesizes the dhamma of feeling, which is one part of the aggregates and so forth; it is the wisdom of compounding, the wisdom of making into a heap.
There is also a reading "wisdom in synthesis" (samodhāne paññā), which has the same meaning.
Regarding "knowledge in abiding by parts": abiding by way of a part, a portion, or a component of the aggregates and so forth is "abiding by parts" (padesavihāra).

Knowledge regarding that abiding in a portion (*padesavihāra*). In this context, "portion" (*padesa*) is manifold: it refers to the portion of the aggregates, the portions of the bases, the elements, the truths, the faculties, the modes of conditionality, the foundations of mindfulness, the jhānas, and the phenomena of mind and matter.
This [knowledge] is of such manifold kinds, yet it is simply feeling (*vedanā*). How so? It is a single part of the five aggregates by way of the aggregate of feeling;
it is a single part of the twelve bases by way of the base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*); and of the eighteen... [elements].
By way of feeling among the elements, it is a portion of the element of phenomena (dhammadhātu); by way of feeling among the four truths, it is a portion of the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca);
by way of the five feeling-faculties among the twenty-two faculties, it is a portion of the faculties;

by way of feeling conditioned by contact among the twelve factors of dependent origination, it is a portion of the mode of conditionality (paccayākāra); and by way of the contemplation of feelings among the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)...
Feeling is a portion of the foundations of mindfulness; it is a portion of the jhānas by way of the pleasure and equanimity of the four jhānas;
it is a portion of name-and-form by way of feeling among name-and-form; and it is a portion of all phenomena—such as the wholesome and so forth—by way of feeling among all phenomena.
Thus, feeling itself is the portion of the aggregates and so on; and dwelling in that portion consists in the reviewing of that very feeling.

44. Now, since ordinary persons (*puthujjana*) and those in training (*sekkha*) who are developing the knowledge consisting in the cultivation of concentration (*samādhibhāvanāmaya-ñāṇa*) and so forth,

having made those various states to be cultivated their dominant influence (*adhipati*) and their foremost, and having reflected upon the various states to be abandoned by way of their respective opposites as being of diverse natures and possessing manifold disadvantages as disadvantageous,
establish the mind through the power of each respective state to be cultivated—

They abandon those various contrary states. While abandoning them, at the time of insight (vipassanā), having seen all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) as empty, they later abandon them by means of complete eradication;
and while abandoning them in that way, they abandon them by penetrating the Truths through a single realization (ekābhisamaya).
In the manner already described, all Noble Ones (ariya) practice accordingly as appropriate; therefore, immediately after the knowledge of abiding in a particular state (padesavihārañāṇa)—
The six knowledges beginning with the knowledge of the turning away from perception have been taught in their proper order.

In this context, "wisdom by predominance" means wisdom that occurs by making renunciation and so forth predominant—that is, by making renunciation and so forth superior through the state of their predominance.
"Knowledge of the turning away from perception" means the turning away, the overturning, or the being turned away from perception.

"Turning away from perception" (*saññā-vivaṭṭo*) means that by whatever perception one makes those various states of development (*bhāvanādhamma*) predominant, through that perception acting as the cause or the instrument, there is knowledge in turning away from this or that—such as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and so forth.

Even though "turning away from this" is not explicitly stated, it is understood that one turns away from exactly that from which one turns away, just as in the case of the contemplation of turning away (*vivaṭṭanānupassanā*). That...

Furthermore, perception has the characteristic of perceiving; its function is to form a sign by perceiving again that "this is that very same thing," like carpenters and others with respect to timber and so forth;
its manifestation is the forming of an adherence according to the sign as it was grasped, like blind men who have seen an elephant;
or its manifestation is non-abiding for long, because its mode of existence does not penetrate deeply into the object, like a flash of lightning.

...as if [they were real], like the perception of "men" that arises in young deer toward grass-stalks and straw-figures, which have as their proximate cause the appearance of objects as they present themselves.

45. *Paññā nānatte* means wisdom that functions by seeing the danger in sensual desire and other such states—which are of a different nature—because one must develop [wisdom] regarding various natures (*nānāsabhāva*).
Furthermore, the locative case in *nānatte* is used in the sense of a sign (*nimitta*). Alternatively, *nānatta* refers to the abandoning of diversity (*nānattappahāna*).
The intention is that wisdom regarding renunciation and so forth is the sign for the abandoning of diversity and the cause for the abandoning of diversity.

"Knowledge regarding the turning away of the mind" refers to the knowledge regarding renunciation and so forth that effects the turning away of the mind from sensual desire and the like. Here, by "mind," volition is intended.
That volition is characterized by the state of being volitional, or it is characterized by directing toward; its function is exertion, and it is manifested as coordinating.
It is like the chief pupil, the master builder, and others who accomplish their own duties as well as those of others.
Furthermore, in matters such as urgent tasks and the recollection [of the Buddha], this wisdom is manifest through its quality of encouraging associated mental states.
46. Wisdom in resolution (*adhiṭṭhāne paññā*) is the wisdom that establishes the mind by means of renunciation (*nekkhamma*) and so forth. In the turning away of the mind (*cittavivaṭṭe*).

"Knowledge" (ñāṇa) refers to the knowledge that turns the mind away [from the cycle of existence] by means of abandoning sensual desire and the other [hindrances]. In this context, the mind has the characteristic of cognizing; its function is to precede [other mental states];
it is manifested as the sustaining [of continuity]; and its proximate cause is name-and-form.

"Wisdom regarding emptiness" (suññate paññā) is the wisdom of the contemplation of non-self, which occurs with respect to what is empty of self and of what belongs to a self. "Knowledge regarding the turning away from knowledge" (ñāṇavivaṭṭe ñāṇa): "turning away" (vivaṭṭa) means that knowledge itself turns away from dogmatic adherence; thus, it is the knowledge that constitutes the turning away from knowledge.

48. "Wisdom regarding relinquishment" (*vosagge paññā*): here, "relinquishment" (*vosagga*) means that which is relinquished; it is wisdom regarding renunciation (*nekkhamma*) and so forth, which is the relinquishing of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and the other [hindrances].

"Knowledge regarding turning away from liberation" (*vimokkhavivaṭṭe ñāṇaṃ*): one is liberated from sensual desire and the rest, thus it is "liberation" (*vimokkha*); liberation itself is the turning away (*vivaṭṭa*), hence "turning away from liberation"; that itself is knowledge.
49. "Wisdom regarding suchness" (*tathattha-paññā*) is wisdom that proceeds without confusion by way of its function toward the fourfold, non-erroneous intrinsic nature of each individual Truth.

"Knowledge regarding the turning away from the Truths" (*sacca-vivaṭṭe ñāṇaṃ*): because it turns away from the four Truths by way of emerging from both sides, it is called the "turning away from the Truths";
that itself is knowledge. That very same knowledge, according to the specific phenomenon it predominates over, is called the "turning away through perception" (*saññā-vivaṭṭo*).

It is stated in four ways as follows: "the turning away of the mind by way of the states to be abandoned" (*pahātabbadhammavasena cetovivaṭṭo*), "the turning away of the mind by way of establishing the mind" (*cittapatiṭṭhānavasena cittavivaṭṭo*), and "the turning away of liberation by way of abandoning opposition" (*paccanīkapahānavasena vimokkhavivaṭṭo*). The contemplation of non-self itself is called "knowledge in the turning away of knowledge" (*ñāṇavivaṭṭe ñāṇa*) by way of the aspect of emptiness (*suññatākāra*).
Path-knowledge itself was previously called "knowledge of the path" (*magge ñāṇa*) and "knowledge in the immediate concentration" (*ānantarikasamādhimhi ñāṇa*).
And it is stated in two ways; by way of the mode of turning away (*vivaṭṭanākāra*), it is called "knowledge of the turning away from the truths" (*saccavivaṭṭe ñāṇa*).

Now, following that knowledge of the turning away from the truths, six kinds of direct-knowledge (*abhiññā*) are listed in sequence according to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaye ñāṇa*).
Even among those, because its power is well-known in the world, it is called "the exceedingly wonderful."

First, the knowledge of the various supernormal powers (*iddhividhañāṇa*) was taught. Since the range of the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) is subtler than that of the divine ear (*dibbasotañāṇa*), which has a coarse range, the second, the divine ear knowledge, was taught;
and because its range is even subtler, the third, the knowledge of others' minds, was taught.

Among the three types of true knowledge (*vijjā*), the first, the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*), was taught because it dispels the darkness of the past that obscures previous existences.
It has been announced: the second, the knowledge of the divine eye, has been announced because it dispels both the present and the future;
the third, the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, has been announced because it utterly cuts off all darkness.

In that context, "the body as well" means the material body (*rūpakāya*); "the mind as well" means the foundational jhāna-consciousness (*pādakajjhānacitta*). "Establishing them together" refers to their being placed in unity with the preliminary consciousness and with the visible body.
Or, at the time of wishing to go with an invisible body, it is said that there is a mixing of both the body and the mind as appropriate.

Here, "body" (*kāya*) refers to the physical frame (*sarīra*). For the physical frame is called "body" because it is a collection of impurities, and because it is the source (*āya*) of the hundred diseases such as eye-diseases and the like, as well as of the foul things such as hair and so forth. And [there is] the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness.
Here, the word *ca* is employed in the sense of conjunction, having divided the single perception associated with the fourth jhāna into two types according to the diversity of its modes.
For in the fourth jhāna, equanimity is called "happiness" because it is peaceful;

the perception associated with that is "perception of happiness. That same [perception] is "light perception" because it is liberated from the hindrances as well as from the opposites such as applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth.
"By way of resolution" means by way of making it superior and establishing it; the intention is "by way of entering.

The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and by way of resolution" is to be connected [to the preceding]. Up to this point, the cause for each type of supernormal power (*iddhividha*) has been stated as appropriate.
"Wisdom in the sense of succeeding" means wisdom in the nature of succeeding. "Knowledge regarding the types of supernormal power" means that in the sense of succeeding, it is *iddhi*.
It is said [in the sense] of accomplishment and in the sense of acquisition. For that which is accomplished and acquired is called "successful" (*ijjhati*).
As it is said: "To one who desires sensual pleasures, this succeeds for him.
Likewise: "Renunciation succeeds, thus it is success (*iddhi*); it counteracts, thus it is a marvel (*pāṭihāriya*); the path to Arahatship succeeds, thus..."
“Success (*iddhi*) is called a ‘manifestation’ (*pāṭihāriya*) because it manifests. Another method: success is so called in the sense of succeeding;
this is a designation for the perfection of means. For the perfection of means succeeds because it brings forth the intended fruit.
As it is said: “This householder Citta is virtuous and of noble character; if he should make a resolve, he will become a king in a future time.”
"A wheel-turning monarch. For the mental aspiration of one possessed of virtue succeeds because of its purity.
Another method: beings succeed by means of this, thus it is "success" (*iddhi*); "they succeed" means they become successful, prosperous, and pre-eminent.
Success itself is the "mode of success" (*iddhividha*); the meaning is that it is a division of success or a classification of success. That mode of success—
"Knowledge" (ñāṇa) is what is meant.
51. "By way of the expansion of thought" (vitakkavipphāravasena): this refers to the time when one is performing the preliminary work for the purpose of producing the divine ear-element;

it means by way of the expansion of one's own thought, that is, by way of the momentum of thought regarding the signs of sounds. And here, "thought" (vitakka) is so called because it "thinks upon" (vitakketi).

Alternatively, *vitakka* is "thinking" (*vitakkana*); what is meant is "striking at. It has the characteristic of directing the mind onto an object, and its function is striking and repeatedly striking [the object]. For it is said that by means of it, the practitioner makes the object struck by thinking and repeatedly struck by thinking.
Its manifestation is the leading of the mind toward the object; however, by means of the corresponding attention (*tajjā-samannāhāra*),...

Because it arises without obstruction when the object is encompassed by the sense faculty, it is called "having the object that has come into the range as its proximate cause" (*āpāthagatavisayapadaṭṭhāna*).
"Of sound-objects of diverse and unitary nature" means of sound-objects that have various intrinsic natures and those that have a single intrinsic nature.

And here, sounds themselves are the "signs" (*nimittāni*) because they are the causes for the arising of applied thought (*vitakka*) and because they are the signs of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*). By way of the sound of a drum and so forth...
Whether they be many sounds that have become one mass, or sounds from various directions, or the sounds of various beings—these are "various sounds" (*nānattasaddā*).
Or they may be sounds from a single direction, or the sound of a single being, or individual sounds such as the sound of a drum—these are "unitary sounds" (*ekattasaddā*).
And here, "sound" (*saddo*) means that which is sounded (*sappati*); the meaning is that it is articulated. "Wisdom regarding thorough penetration" (*pariyogāhaṇe paññā*) is the wisdom of entry.

The meaning is "wisdom that understands. Regarding "knowledge of the purification of the ear-element": it is the "ear-element" (*sotadhātu*) in the sense of hearing and in the sense of being devoid of a living soul (*nijjīva*);
it is also called the "ear-element" because it performs the function of the ear-element. It is "purification" (*visuddhi*) because of its complete purity and freedom from defilements.
Thus, the ear-element itself as purification is "purification of the ear-element" (*sotadhātuvisuddhi*). [This is] the purification of the ear-element.
Such knowledge is the knowledge of the purification of the ear-element.
(52) "Of three kinds of consciousness" means of three kinds of consciousness by way of being accompanied by joy, accompanied by grief, and accompanied by equanimity.
"By way of expansion" (*vipphārattā*) means by way of its expansive nature; the meaning is "with speed. The ablative case (*nissakkavacana*) is used in the sense of a cause.

At the time of performing the preliminary work for the purpose of generating the knowledge of penetration of others' minds, [it is known] by means of the diffusion of the three types of consciousness of others.

"By way of the clarity of the faculties" means by way of the clarity of the six faculties, beginning with the eye; and here, the bases where the faculties are established are referred to as "faculties" by way of figurative designation (phalūpacāra), just as it is said: "Your faculties are indeed serene..."

“Friend, the faculties are purified; the complexion of the skin is bright and clear. Even when referring to the physical bases established by the faculties, it is the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) alone that is intended here.
Regarding the phrase “by way of clarity” (*pasādavasena*), it means by way of being undisturbed.

It should be understood that although one ought to say “by way of clarity and non-clarity” (*pasādappasādavasena*), the word for non-clarity (*appasāda*) has been elided. Alternatively, it refers to the apprehension of this [base] as non-clear.
Since it arises only by depending upon clarity (*pasāda*), it should be understood that by the very expression “by way of clarity,” even non-clarity is implied.

Wisdom that penetrates the diversity and unity of the movements of consciousness is the wisdom that, as the case may be, discerns the occurrence of the eighty-nine types of consciousness according to their various individual natures or their single common nature.
Herein, the movement of consciousness in one who is not concentrated is diverse; the movement of consciousness in one who is concentrated is unified. [This refers to] the mind with lust and so forth.
Or else, there is diversity in the case of minds such as those with lust, while a mind free from lust and so forth is unity.

Regarding "knowledge of penetration of minds" (*cetopariyañāṇa*): here, *pariya* means that which is encompassed; the meaning is that it delimits. The encompassing of the mind is "penetration of minds" (*cetopariya*); and since it is both that penetration of minds and knowledge, it is "knowledge of penetration of minds.
There is also the reading *vipphāratā*, the meaning of which is "by way of expansion."
53. "Of phenomena proceeding by way of conditions" means of those phenomena arisen from conditions that proceed by way of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
"By way of the diverse and uniform expansion of kamma": herein, unwholesome kamma is "diverse" (*nānatta*), while wholesome kamma is "uniform" (*ekatta*).
Alternatively, sense-sphere kamma is "diverse," while fine-material-sphere and immaterial-sphere kamma is "uniform. [This is] by way of the diverse and uniform expansion of kamma.
The connection is: "wisdom in the thorough penetration of phenomena as they proceed by way of conditions.
Regarding "knowledge of recollection of past lives" (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*): "past lives" (*pubbenivāsa*) refers to the aggregates (*khandhā*) in which one dwelt in former, past births.

"Dwelt" (*nivuttha*) means inhabited, experienced, having arisen and ceased within one's own continuum. Alternatively, the phenomena in which one dwelt in former, past births are themselves "past lives. "Dwelt" (*nivuttha*)... [means]...
They have been dwelt upon through dwelling in their range; they are cognized and delimited by one’s own consciousness, or else cognized by the consciousness of others.
These are found only in Buddhas, such as in the recollection of past existences (*chinnavaṭumakānussaraṇa*) and so forth.

"Recollection of past lives" (*pubbenivāsānussati*) refers to that mindfulness (*sati*) by which one recollects past lives; "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) refers to the knowledge associated with that mindfulness.

54. "By means of illumination" (*obhāsa*) means by means of the illumination of the *kasiṇa*—which is the object of the fourth jhāna—belonging to any one of the fire-*kasiṇa*, white-*kasiṇa*, or light-*kasiṇa*, when it has been extended for the purpose of seeing forms with the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*).

"Of the signs of various and single forms" (*nānattekatta-rūpa-nimittānaṃ*) refers to: the forms of various beings; or the forms of beings who have arisen in bodies of various kinds; or forms in various directions.
Or, "forms" refers to unmixed forms that are diverse; or the forms of a single being; or the forms of one who has been reborn with a single-body existence;

or forms in a single direction; or forms belonging to various directions that have become intermingled—these are "single forms. And here, "form" refers specifically to the sense-sphere of visible form (*vaṇṇāyatana*).
For it is called "form" (*rūpa*) because it "is formed" (*rūpayati*), as it undergoes transformation of color.
The meaning is that it makes manifest the state that has entered the heart. "Form itself" is the "sign of form.
Of those various and single signs of form, "wisdom in the sense of seeing" means wisdom whose intrinsic nature is seeing.

"Knowledge of the divine eye": it is called "divine" because it resembles the divine; for the divine eye is produced by the well-performed karma of devas, [being free] from bile, phlegm, blood, and so forth.
The divine eye of clarity (*pasādacakkhu*) is unobstructed; because it is free from defilements, it is capable of receiving objects even at a distance.
This eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*), which is produced by the power of the development of energy (*vīriyabhāvanābala*), is exactly like that.

It is called "divine" (*dibba*) because it resembles the divine; it is also "divine" because it is obtained through divine abiding (*dibbavihāra*) and because it is supported by divine abiding itself.

It is called "divine" (*dibba*) both because it possesses great radiance through its grasping of light, and because it possesses a vast range through its seeing of forms located beyond walls and other obstructions;

all of this should be understood according to the science of grammar (*saddasattha*). It is "vision" (*cakkhu*) in the sense of seeing, and it is "vision" as well because it performs the function of vision, as if it were an eye;
