thus, being both divine and vision, it is "divine vision" (*dibbacakkhu*). And being both divine vision and knowledge, it is "knowledge of divine vision" (*dibbacakkhuñāṇa*).
"By sixty-four modes" means by way of the sixty-four modes consisting of eight faculties for each of the eight paths and fruits.

"Of three faculties" refers to these three faculties: the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of knowing, and the faculty of one who has known. Wisdom is mastery; it is mastery by way of its state of mastery (*vasibhāvatā*).

Wisdom is said to be "active" because, although it is absent at the moment of the path of arahantship, its capacity to accomplish that goal is established through the causal efficacy of the mastery of the faculty of one who has already known (aññātāvindriya) by way of the eight aspects of the eight faculties present in the fruit of arahantship;

this is how it should be understood. "Knowledge of the destruction of the taints" refers to the knowledge of the path of arahantship which brings about the destruction of the taints that are to be abandoned by oneself.

56–59. Now, in connection with the knowledge of the path of arahantship—which is termed the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava*)—four kinds of knowledge are listed beginning with “wisdom regarding the meaning of full understanding,” in order to show that each of the four path-knowledges possesses a single simultaneous realization (*ekābhisamaya*).
Among these, the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) is the most easily understood because it is coarse and common to all sentient beings.
The first was stated; immediately after that, the truth of the origin (samudayasacca) was taught for the purpose of showing its cause.

Immediately after that, the truth of cessation (nirodhasacca) was taught for the purpose of making it known that with the cessation of the cause comes the cessation of the fruit. At the end, the truth of the path (maggasacca) was taught for the purpose of showing the means for attaining that [cessation].
Alternatively, the first was taught for the purpose of generating a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in beings who are attached to the gratification of the pleasure of existence.

He spoke of suffering; since that [suffering] does not come uncaused, nor arises from the creation of a Lord (Issaranimmāna) and so forth, but rather arises from this [cause], the Truth of Origination (samudayasacca) was taught immediately thereafter for the purpose of making this known.

Then, for those whose minds are agitated because they are overwhelmed by suffering accompanied by its cause, and who seek an escape from suffering, the Cessation (nirodha) was taught for the purpose of generating consolation through the vision of that escape. After that, the Path was taught for the purpose of attaining that cessation.
"The path that leads to the attainment of cessation. Now, the knowledges whose objects are those [truths] have been listed in that same sequence.
Therein, "in the sense of full understanding" refers to the fourfold nature of suffering to be fully understood, such as its meaning of oppression;
"in the sense of abandoning" refers to the fourfold nature of the origin to be abandoned, such as its meaning of accumulation; and "in the sense of realization" refers to cessation...

Regarding the fourfold nature of what is to be realized, beginning with the sense of escape; and regarding the fourfold nature of what is to be developed, beginning with the sense of departure of the path.
60–63. Now, either by way of reviewing the path already developed, or by way of hearsay regarding the path not yet developed—
Alternatively, in order to show the individual knowledges of the truths, four knowledges beginning with the knowledge of suffering (*dukkhe ñāṇa*) have been enumerated.
Therein, regarding the word "suffering" (*dukkhe*): here, the sound *du-* is seen to be used for that which is contemptible. For they call a contemptible son a "bad son" (*duputta*).
The sound *kha*, however, refers to the void. For the void sky is called "space" (*kha*). And this first Truth is contemptible.
It is "empty" because it is the locus of manifold calamities, being devoid of the state of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and selfhood imagined by foolish people.
Therefore, because it is contemptible and empty, it is called "suffering" (*dukkha*).
Regarding the term "the origin of suffering" (*dukkhasamudaya*): here, the word *saṃ-* signifies conjunction, as in such expressions as "coming together" (*samāgama*) or "united" (*sameta*).
It illuminates. The word *u* signifies arising, as in such expressions as "arisen" (*uppanna*) or "appeared" (*udita*). The word *aya*, however, signifies a cause.
Furthermore, this second truth is the cause for the arising of suffering when it is conjoined with the remaining conditions.
Thus, because it is the cause for the arising [of suffering] through its conjunction with suffering, it is called the "origin of suffering" (*dukkhasamudaya*).
Regarding the term *dukkhanirodha*: here, the prefix *ni-* signifies absence (*abhāva*), and the word *rodha* indicates confinement (*cāraka*).

Therefore, it is called "cessation of suffering" because there is an absence of the confinement of suffering—which is known as the prison of *saṃsāra*—due to the emptiness of all states of existence (*gati*) therein;

or alternatively, when that [cessation] is attained, there is an absence of the confinement of suffering within the prison of *saṃsāra* because it is the direct opposite of that [suffering]. Thus it is "the cessation of suffering."
It is so called because it is the condition for the non-arising and cessation of suffering; thus it is called "the cessation of suffering.

Regarding the phrase "the way leading to the cessation of suffering": herein, because this [way] goes toward that cessation of suffering by being directed toward it through the function of taking it as its object, and because it is the path for the attainment of the cessation of suffering, it is called the way leading to the cessation of suffering.

Therefore, it is called "the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. The four knowledges of the path themselves were previously described as "knowledge of the path" by way of illustrating the mode of emergence;
they were described as "knowledge of the immediately-resulting concentration" by way of illustrating the reason for its yielding immediate fruit;
and they were described as "knowledge of the turning away from the truths" by way of illustrating the mode of turning away. Precisely according to the sequence of the path—

In order to illuminate the arising of the knowledge of the path of arahantship and to show that this knowledge possesses the nature of direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā*), it is stated that "the knowledge of the destruction of the taints" (*āsavānaṃ khaye ñāṇa*) is precisely the knowledge of the path of arahantship.

Furthermore, in order to illustrate the single simultaneous realization (*ekābhisamaya*) of all four path-knowledges, the four knowledges beginning with "wisdom regarding the meaning of full understanding is knowledge of suffering" are stated. Again, with respect to each individual truth...
The four knowledges beginning with “knowledge of suffering” are enumerated by way of illustrating their arising individually;
thus, the distinction between the preceding and the following should be understood. 64–67.
Now, it is by the power of the Noble Path alone that the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidāñāṇa) are accomplished for all noble persons (ariyapuggala).
To demonstrate this, the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa*) beginning with "knowledge of the analytical knowledge of meaning" (*attha-paṭisambhide ñāṇa*) are again enumerated.
For these are the pure analytical knowledges (*suddhika-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa*) common to all noble persons (*ariya-puggala*), even in the absence of the differentiation of the analytical knowledges;
whereas those enumerated above are the analytical knowledges that have attained differentiation for those whose analytical knowledges are already distinguished (*pabhinnapaṭisambhida*).
"They are to be known" (veditabbāni)— this is the distinction regarding the expression "both meanings" for these [four analytical knowledges]. Or rather,

because the knowledge that has suffering as its object and cessation as its object is the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā), the knowledge that has origination as its object and the path as its object is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā),

the knowledge regarding the verbal expression of those [objects] is the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā), and the knowledge regarding those very knowledges is the analytical knowledge of knowledge (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).

The analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*); therefore, it should be understood that these pure analytical knowledges (*suddhika-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa*) are taught in order to demonstrate that specific distinction in meaning.
For this very reason, they were previously stated with the qualification of the word "variety" (*nānatta*), whereas here they are stated without such qualification.

68. Having thus enumerated, in order, the sixty-seven types of knowledge shared with the disciples, the six unique types of knowledge belonging exclusively to the Tathāgatas—beginning with the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties (*indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa*)—are now set forth in order to demonstrate those not shared with the disciples.
Among these, because the Tathāgatas, while surveying whether sentient beings are fit or unfit vessels for the teaching of the Dhamma, [proceed as follows...]

They survey with the Buddha-eye. The so-called "Buddha-eye" consists solely of the two types of knowledge: the knowledge of the degrees of maturity of the faculties (*indriya-paropariyatta*) and the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies (*āsaya-anusaya*). As it is said:

"The Blessed One, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, saw beings with little dust on their eyes and with much dust on their eyes, those with keen faculties and those with dull faculties," and so forth.
And while surveying the mental continua of beings, they first survey the maturity and immaturity of the faculties; and as for the maturity of the faculties—

Having known this, in order to teach the Dhamma in accordance with their dispositions and so forth, they next examine the dispositions (*āsaya*), underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), and temperaments (*carita*).

For that reason as well, the knowledge of the degrees of the faculties of others (*indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa*) was taught first, and immediately after that, the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies (*āsayānusaya-ñāṇa*).

Furthermore, when teaching the Dhamma, because they perform miracles for those who are to be disciplined by miracles, [the miracle-knowledge] follows immediately after the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies.

The knowledge regarding the Twin Miracle has been indicated. Immediately following that, for the purpose of illustrating the cause of these three knowledges, the knowledge of Great Compassion (mahākaruṇāñāṇa) is indicated.
Immediately following that, for the purpose of illustrating the state of purity of the knowledge of Great Compassion, the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa) is indicated.

Furthermore, for the purpose of illustrating that even for the Omniscient One, [knowledge] is dependent upon the mental advertence (āvajjana) toward all phenomena, [the knowledge of non-confusion is indicated].

It should be understood that the "unobstructed knowledge" (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*) is mentioned immediately thereafter for the purpose of illustrating the state of being unobstructed regarding omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of beings" (*indriyaparopariyattañāṇa*), the word "of beings" (*sattānaṃ*), which appears later, should be brought back here and joined as "knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of beings.
Although one might say *parāparāni* (the further and the near), [the compound is formed as follows:]...
By means of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), the letter *r* is inserted, and thus it is called *paropara*. The state of being *paropara* is *paropariya*;
*paropariya* itself is *paropariyattha*. The state of the five faculties—faith and the rest—of those beings who are to be trained is *indriyaparopariyattha*;
the knowledge of that state of the faculties is *indriyaparopariyatthañāṇa*. [This refers to] the faculties...
The meaning is "knowledge of the state of being supreme and unsurpassed. There is also a reading:

"knowledge of the state of being superior and more excellent" (*indriyavarovariyattañāṇa*). One should construe it thus: "superior and more excellent" (*varovariya*) refers to those things that are both superior (*vara*) and more excellent (*avariya*);

the state of these is "the state of being superior and more excellent" (*varovariyatta*). And "more excellent" (*avariya*) means not inferior (*na uttama*). Alternatively, "further and beyond" (*paropara*) refers to those things that are further (*para*) and beyond (*opara*); the state of these is "the state of being further and beyond" (*paropariyatta*).
It should be joined [to the preceding]. "Oparāni" is said to mean "orāni," which signifies "base" or "inferior," as in such passages as "paroparā yassa samecca dhammā.
There is also a reading using the locative case: "indriyaparopariyatte ñāṇaṃ" (knowledge regarding the high and low state of the faculties).

Regarding "knowledge of the inclinations and underlying tendencies of beings": here, beings are called *sattā* because they are attached (*visatta*) to the aggregates, beginning with form, through desire and lust. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Rādha, it is because of desire, lust, delight, and craving for form that one is attached there, bound there;

therefore one is called ‘a being. It is because of desire, lust, delight, and craving for feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness that one is attached there, bound there; therefore one is called ‘a being.’”

Grammarians, however, without investigating the meaning, maintain that this is "mere name. Even those who do investigate the meaning maintain that it is "sentient" (satta) by virtue of its connection with being;
[the phrase] "of those sentient beings" (tesaṃ sattānaṃ) refers to this.

It is called "abode" (āsaya) because they lie within it or depend upon it—namely, the continuum (santāna) which has been permeated by wrong view or right view, or by sensual desire and so forth, or by renunciation and so forth.
It is a designation (*adhivacana*). They are called *anusayas* because they lie latent (*anusenti*) and continue to flow along within the continuum of a being (*sattasantāne*);

this is a designation for lust for sensual pleasure (*kāmarāga*) and so forth when they have become firmly rooted. "Latent disposition" (*āsayānusaya*) is a compound consisting of both "disposition" (*āsaya*) and "latent tendency" (*anusaya*).

It should be understood as a singular form by virtue of both a collective inclusion (*jātiggahaṇa*) and a copulative compound (*dvandasamāsa*). Since temperaments (*carita*) and inclinations (*adhimutti*) are included within latent dispositions, therefore, in the summary list (*uddesa*)...

The knowledges regarding conduct and inclinations are included within the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies (*āsayānusaya-ñāṇa*), and thus it is called "the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies.
For the exposition was made with precisely the same intention as the summary.
70. Regarding "the knowledge of the Twin Miracle": here, the masses of fire, streams of water, and so forth, occur simultaneously, neither before nor after.
It is called a "pair" (*yamaka*) because it is manifested as a pair; it is a "wonder" (*pāṭihīra*) because it carries away the opposing states such as lack of faith;
thus, being both a pair and a wonder, it is the "Twin Wonder" (*yamakapāṭihīra*).
Regarding the phrase "knowledge of the attainment of Great Compassion": herein, when there is suffering in others, it causes the hearts of the virtuous to tremble.

*Karunā*: It is called *karuṇā* because it pities (*kināti*), or because it harms and destroys the suffering of others (*paradukkhaṃ hiṃsati vināseti*). Alternatively, it is called *karuṇā* because it is performed (*kirīyati*) by way of pervading those who are suffering.
Because it is great through its function of pervading and through its quality as a mental state (*kammaguṇa*), it is "great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*).

It is a "meditative attainment" (*samāpatti*) because those who possess great compassion enter into it; thus, it is the "great compassion attainment" (*mahākaruṇāsamāpatti*) because it is both great compassion and an attainment.
In that attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*), there is the knowledge associated with it.

72–73. Regarding the phrase "Omniscient Knowledge" (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) as "unobstructed knowledge" (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*): here, one who has known all—that is, everything categorized under the five paths of training—is "the Omniscient One" (*sabbaññū*).
The state of being omniscient is "omniscience" (*sabbaññutā*); that itself is the knowledge, which, though it should be called "knowledge of omniscience" (*sabbaññutāñāṇa*), [is referred to as such].

“Omniscient knowledge” (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) has been stated. For all phenomena (*dhamma*), classified as conditioned (*saṅkhata*) and unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*), and so forth, constitute only five objects of knowledge (*neyyapatha*):
formations (*saṅkhāra*), change (*vikāra*), characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), Nibbāna, and designations (*paññatti*).

Furthermore, there are five kinds of omniscient ones (*sabbaññu*): the gradual omniscient one, the instantaneous omniscient one, the constant omniscient one, the omniscient by power, and the omniscient by having known.

It may be so. Because it is impossible for all things to be known sequentially, there is no "sequential omniscience. Because there is no simultaneous grasping of all objects, there is no "simultaneous omniscience.

Because visual consciousness and the other types of consciousness arise only in relation to their respective objects, because they are incompatible with the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*), and because there is a lack of logical consistency, there is no "constant omniscience.
Finally, by way of elimination, it is "potency omniscience" because of the capacity to know all things.
Or it may be that, because all phenomena are known, there is "known omniscience. To claim that for one who is omniscient there is no knowing of everything is also untenable:
"There is nothing here that is unseen by him, nor anything unknown or not understood."
"Because it is said: 'The Tathāgata has directly known everything that is to be known;

by that he possesses the universal eye,' it is logical that he is indeed the supreme knower of all (sabbaññū) in terms of his realization. For this being so, his omniscience is established through his function, through his lack of confusion, through the proof of the cause, and through its dependence upon adverting the mind (āvajjana). Indeed, because it is dependent upon adverting the mind, there is [no simultaneous knowledge of all things]."
"The absence of an obstruction for this" is non-obstruction; that very thing is called "non-obstructive knowledge" (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*).
These are the seventy-three knowledges thus enumerated according to whether they are shared or unshared with disciples.
"Of these seventy-three knowledges" refers to these seventy-three knowledges mentioned from the beginning onwards.
In this context, the genitive case is used in the sense of "bringing forth" (*ubbāhana*). There is also a reading *tesattatīnaṃ*.
Where one would expect *tesattatiyā*, it should be understood as a plural form used for a singular. "Sixty-seven knowledges" refers to the sixty-seven knowledges starting from the beginning.

"Shared by disciples" (*sāvakasādhāraṇāni*): they are called "disciples" (*sāvaka*) because they are born into the noble lineage through hearing; they are so called because these [knowledges] are held in common (*samāna-dhāraṇa*) by them.
They are common; that is, they are shared by the Tathāgatas with their disciples, being common to disciples.
"Six knowledges" refers to the six knowledges mentioned at the end. "Not shared with disciples" means these are knowledges belonging exclusively to the Tathāgatas, not shared with disciples.
[From] the *Saddhammappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.
The commentary on the section on the enumeration of the matrix of the discourse on knowledge is finished.
1. Commentary on the exposition of the description of knowledge consisting of what is heard.
Commentary on the enumeration of the answers.

1. Now, in order to show the classifications of the phenomena (dhammas) comprised within the summary (uddesa) as it has been set forth, the section on exposition (niddesavāra) beginning with "How is wisdom regarding the application of the ear knowledge consisting in what is heard? is commenced.

Regarding this, as for what was stated—"Wisdom regarding the application of the ear is knowledge consisting in what is heard"—how is that so? This is a question arising from a desire to explain. For there are five kinds of questions.

— Inquiry for the purpose of revealing what has not been seen, inquiry for the purpose of correlating what has been seen, inquiry for the purpose of cutting through doubt, inquiry for the purpose of assent, and inquiry out of a desire to speak. This is their distinction:
What is inquiry for the purpose of revealing what has not been seen? It is when, by nature, a characteristic is unknown, unseen, unweighed, and unexamined.

When one asks a question for the sake of knowing, seeing, weighing, scrutinizing, clarifying, and bringing to clarity that which is unclarified and unmanifested, this is a question for the illumination of what has not been seen (*adiṭṭhajotanā-pucchā*). What is a question for the corroboration of what has been seen (*diṭṭhasaṃsandana-pucchā*)?
It is when the characteristic is already known by nature, having been seen, weighed, and scrutinized.
Having abandoned [wrong views] and having cultivated [right view], he asks a question for the sake of exchanging views with other wise people;
this is the question for the purpose of exchanging what has been seen.
What is the question for the purpose of cutting through doubt? He is by nature prone to uncertainty, prone to perplexity, and full of hesitation.
“Is it thus? Is it not thus? What indeed? How indeed? He asks this question for the purpose of cutting through doubt;
this is a question for the purpose of cutting through doubt.
What is a question for assent? The Blessed One asks a question with the assent of the bhikkhus: “What do you think of that?”
“Bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, venerable sir. “But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir. “But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “Certainly not, venerable sir. This is a question for assent.
What is a question asked out of a desire to speak? The Blessed One asks a question because of a desire for the bhikkhus to speak:
"Bhikkhus, there are these four foundations of mindfulness. Which four? This is a question asked out of a desire to speak.
Among those [three types of questions], this should be understood as the Elder’s question asked out of a desire to speak.
Now, regarding the inquiry into the desire to speak for the sake of a summary exposition: “These phenomena are to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*);
the application of the ear is this, and the wisdom that understands it is knowledge consisting in what is heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*)”—and so forth, there are sixteen summary expositions of answers.

Therein, in the phrase “these phenomena are to be directly known,” the words “to one who is teaching” are to be supplied as the remainder of the text. [The phrase] “these phenomena are to be directly known” [refers] to the Teacher, or to someone else...

Or, when a venerable fellow-celibate (sabrahmacārī) who is worthy of respect is teaching the Dhamma, "attending to what is heard" (sotāvadhāna) refers to the act of listening according to the method previously described.
The wisdom that understands that—namely, the understanding of what has been heard—is the wisdom that delimits the various modes [of expression];

this is the meaning of "knowledge consisting in what is heard" (sutamaye ñāṇa). "Understanding of that" (taṃpajānanā) is a genitive tatpuruṣa compound. "Understanding of that" (taṃ pajānanā)—[this is how it is analyzed].

Or, due to a shift in case endings, it is the accusative case. "To be directly known" (*abhiññeyya*) means they are to be understood in a beautiful manner through the realization of their specific characteristics (*sabhāva-lakkhaṇa*).

"To be fully understood" (*pariññeyya*) means they are to be understood pervasively through the realization of their general characteristics (*sāmañña-lakkhaṇa*) and through the fulfillment of their functions.
"To be developed" (*bhāvetabba*) means they are to be increased. "To be realized" (*sacchikātabba*) means they are to be made manifest to direct experience.
For realization is twofold: realization by acquisition and realization as an object.
Those that partake of decline (*hānabhāgiyā*) are so called because they partake of what is reckoned as decline—namely, falling away—due to the manifestation of opposing states.

Those that partake of stability (*ṭhitibhāgiyā*) are so called because they partake of what is reckoned as stability—namely, remaining steady—due to the stabilization of mindfulness in accordance with those [attainments]. Those that partake of distinction (*visesabhāgiyā*) are so called because they partake of distinction through the attainment of higher excellence.

They are "conducive to penetration" (*nibbedhabhāgiyā*). The Noble Path is called "penetration" (*nibbedha*) because it pierces and shatters the mass of greed, the mass of hatred, and the mass of delusion—things never before pierced or shattered.
They are "conducive to penetration" because they partake in that penetration by way of the active presence of perception and attention accompanied by disenchantment.
"All formations" (*sabbe saṅkhārā*) refers to all phenomena that possess conditions. For these are called "conditioned formations" (*saṅkhatasaṅkhārā*).

They are "formations" (*saṅkhārā*) because they are produced by coming together through conditions; and they are specifically described as "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*) because they have been made by those very conditions coming together.
According to the commentaries, the material and immaterial phenomena of the three planes produced by kamma are "formations that have been fully conditioned" (*abhisaṅkhatasaṅkhārā*).
These [formations] are included among the conditioned formations (*saṅkhata-saṅkhāra*) in such passages as “Impermanent indeed are all formations.

In such passages as “Bhikkhus, this person, being possessed of ignorance, performs a meritorious formation,” it is the formations conditioned by ignorance—namely, the wholesome and unwholesome volitions belonging to the three planes—that are called the “performing formations” (*abhisaṅkharaṇa-saṅkhāra*). As far as...

In such passages as, "The destination of volitional formation (abhisaṅkhāra); having gone that far, it stands as if struck by a pin," what is referred to is bodily and mental energy called *payogābhisaṅkhāra*.

[And it is said: "Friend Visākha, for a bhikkhu who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling (*saññāvedayitanirodha*), first the verbal formation (*vacīsaṅkhāra*) ceases, then the bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*), then..."

In such passages as "the mental formation," the terms refer to applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*). They are called verbal formations (*vacī-saṅkhāra*) because they form speech.

Inhalation and exhalation are called bodily formations (*kāya-saṅkhāra*) because they are formed by the body. Perception and feeling are called mental formations (*citta-saṅkhāra*) because they are formed by the mind.
However, in this context, conditioned formations (*saṅkhata-saṅkhāra*) are intended.
“Impermanent” is in the sense of non-existence after having been; “suffering” is in the sense of oppression. “All phenomena” is stated including even Nibbāna.

“Non-self” is in the sense of lack of mastery. In such passages as “This is the noble truth of suffering,” where one ought to say “the origin of suffering” and “the cessation of suffering,” the change of gender has been made by saying “the origin of suffering” and “the cessation of suffering.”
However, because the Noble Ones—beginning with the Buddhas—penetrate them, they are called "Noble Truths" (*ariyasaccāni*).
As it is said: "Monks, there are these four noble truths... [omission] ...These, monks, are the four noble truths.
The Noble Ones penetrate these; therefore they are called 'noble truths. They are also [called] "the truths of the Noble One."
The Noble Truths. As it is said: "In the world with its devas... including gods and humans, the Tathāgata is noble; therefore they are called 'Noble Truths'.
They are also called Noble Truths because the state of being noble is established through their full awakening. As it is said:
"Monks, it is because he has fully awakened to these four Noble Truths as they really are that the Tathāgata is an Arahant..."
“The Perfectly Enlightened One is called ‘Noble’ (ariya). Thus, they are called “Noble Truths” (ariyasaccāni) because they are truths belonging to the Noble Ones.
“Noble” means unerring; the meaning is that they are non-deceptive. As it has been said: “These four, monks, are the Noble Truths;
they are such, unerring, and not otherwise. Therefore, they are called ‘Noble Truths. What is the meaning of “truth” (sacca)?

Why is this? Because, when examined by the eye of wisdom, it is not like an illusion which is deceptive, nor like a mirage which is misleading, nor does it have an unfindable nature like the self imagined by the sectarians;

rather, it is indeed the objective domain of noble knowledge by way of its true, non-erroneous, and real state, characterized by affliction, origin, and the path of escape. This is the natural order of the world, just like the characteristic of fire.
And its state of being undistorted, unperverted, and real should be understood as its "truth-meaning" (*saccaṭṭha*).
As it is said in detail: "Bhikkhus, 'This is suffering'—this is real, this is not unreal, this is not otherwise. Furthermore:
Since suffering does not oppress [in the ultimate sense], and nothing other than suffering is oppressive;
By way of being a subverter, this is considered a truth;
without that [craving], suffering does not arise from anything else, nor does it arise from itself.
By way of being the cause of suffering, thus is "clinging" (visattikā) a truth.
There is no peace other than Nibbāna, nor is there anything peaceful that is not it;
because it is established by way of its state of peace, it is therefore considered the Truth.
There is no path of deliverance other than the Path, nor is that [Path] one that does not lead to deliverance.
Because it is the state of being "to-be-told" (taccha), it is thus considered "truth" (sacca). Thus,
the wise have declared that the meaning of truth, in all four [noble truths] such as suffering and the rest, consists in the state of being undistorted and unperverted, without distinction.
Furthermore, this word *sacca* (truth) is seen in various senses. For example: in such passages as "One should speak the truth and not be angry," it refers to verbal truth (*vācāsacca*).
In such passages as "Samaṇas and brāhmaṇas are established in truth," it refers to the truth of abstinence (*viratisacca*).

In such passages as "Why do they proclaim various truths, these experts in eloquent speech? it refers to the truth of views (*diṭṭhisacca*). And in the passage: "For there is but one truth, there is no second;... [it refers to the ultimate truth].
In such passages as "That in which people do not dispute, knowing it," [the term refers] to both Nibbāna and the Path, which are the ultimate truths (paramattha-sacca).

In such passages as "Of the four truths, how many are wholesome (kusala) and how many are unwholesome (akusala)," [it refers] to the noble truths (ariya-sacca). This [term] here also occurs in the sense of the noble truths.
[This concludes] the summary of the section on the exposition of the answers.
The commentary on the [first] section is finished.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Knowable (Abhiññeyya-niddesa).

Now, in order to show these phenomena, which were summarized in the enumeration of the questions, according to their classifications, [the text begins with]: "How are these phenomena to be directly known? and so forth.

The section of exposition has begun. Therein, among the five sections beginning with the exposition of what is to be directly known (*abhiññeyya-niddesa*), ten answers each—beginning with the "single" category and so forth—have been set forth according to the "ten-plus" method (*dasuttara-pariyāya*).

Among those, first, in the exposition of what is to be directly known, the phrase "all beings" refers to all states of existence (*bhava*), such as the sense-sphere existence (*kāma-bhava*) and so forth, the perception-sphere existence (*saññā-bhava*) and so forth, and the single-aggregate existence (*ekavokāra-bhava*) and so forth.
"All beings subsist by nutriment. Those whose stability (*ṭhiti*) is through nutriment are "subsisting by nutriment" (*āhāraṭṭhitika*).

Here, "stability" is intended in the sense of existence at its own moment. Thus, nutriment—the cause for the stability of all beings—is a single phenomenon that must be known with superior knowledge (*adhikena ñāṇena*).
For when the condition is directly known, those things arisen from the condition are also directly known; both are [then understood].
Because they are mutually dependent. By this, "full understanding through knowledge" (*ñātapariññā*) has been stated. But if this is so, does it not contradict what was said:
"The non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta* devas) are without root-cause (*ahetuka*), without nutriment (*anāhāra*), and without contact (*aphassaka*)"?

That does not contradict it; for their nutriment is meditative absorption (*jhāna*). Even so, [it is said]: "Bhikkhus, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have come to be..."
"Or for the assistance of those seeking rebirth. Which four? Edible food, whether gross or subtle;
second, contact; third, mental volition; fourth, consciousness"—this [statement] would be contradicted.
But this too is not contradicted. For in this sutta, by way of the primary sense (nippariyāya), only those phenomena characterized as nutriment are called "nutriments."
[It has been] stated [previously]. Here, however, nutriment is spoken of as a condition by way of a figurative expression (*pariyāya*). For a condition must be obtained for all conditioned phenomena;
and whatever fruit it produces, it is said to "bring" (*āharati*) that very thing. Therefore, it is called "nutriment" (*āhāra*). For this very reason, it was said:
"Bhikkhus, I say that even ignorance (*avijjā*) has a nutriment, not that it is without nutriment. And what, bhikkhus, is the nutriment of ignorance?"
"What is their nutriment? "It should be said: 'The five hindrances. Monks, I say that the five hindrances have a nutriment, not that they are without nutriment.
And what, monks, is the nutriment of the five hindrances? It should be said: 'Inappropriate attention,' and so forth.
This is what is intended here.
For when this nutriment of conditions (*paccayāhāra*) is taken, both the figurative nutriment (*pariyāyāhāra*) and the non-figurative nutriment (*nippariyāyāhāra*) are included.

Therein, the nutriment of conditions is found in the state of non-percipient beings (*asaññabhava*). For when a Buddha has not yet arisen, one may go forth in a sectarian order (*titthāyatana*), perform the preliminary work (*parikamma*) on the wind-kasiṇa, and having attained the fourth jhāna, emerge from it and think: "Alas, mind!..."
"Intellect is the mind; it is indeed excellent that there should be the very absence of mind.
For it is dependent upon the mind that suffering, with its conditions such as killing and imprisonment, arises; when the mind is absent, it would not exist.

Having thus developed conviction and preference, they pass away without falling away from their jhāna and are reborn in the non-percipient realm (*asañña-bhava*). Whatever posture was adopted by each while in the human world—
Having been produced with that posture, it remains for five hundred aeons.
For such a duration, it remains as if lying down, as if sitting, or as if standing. And for such beings, nutriment by way of conditions is obtained;
for whatever jhāna they have developed to produce that existence, that very jhāna becomes their condition, just as an arrow shot with the force of a bowstring [remains in flight].
As long as the momentum of the impulse exists, they continue; likewise, as long as the condition for meditation exists, they remain.
When that has ceased, they fall like an arrow whose momentum is exhausted.
As for those hell-beings who are said to "subsist on the fruit of non-arising and not on the fruit of merit," their—
What is their nutriment? Their nutriment is karma alone. Is it the case that there are five nutriments? It should not be said, "five" or "not five.
Is it not stated that "a condition is nutriment"? Therefore, that very karma by which they were reborn in hell is their nutriment, because it serves as the condition for their continued existence.
With reference to this, it was said: "They do not die [until that karma is exhausted]."
“...until that evil kamma is exhausted. Therefore, “subsisting on nutriment” means subsisting on conditions.
Furthermore, no dispute should be raised here regarding “taking edible food as an object,” for even the saliva produced in the mouth performs the function of nutriment for them.
For saliva is a condition for painful feeling when in hell, and for pleasant feeling when in heaven.

Thus, in the sensual existence (*kāmabhava*), there are four nutriments in the direct sense; in the fine-material and immaterial existences (*rūpārūpabhava*), excluding the non-percipient realm (*asaññabhava*), there are three;
and for the non-percipient beings as well as the rest, there is the nutriment of conditions. By means of this nutriment, all beings subsist on nutriment.

The phrase "all beings" is a teaching of the Dhamma expressed by way of the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*); the intended meaning is "all conditioned phenomena" (*saṅkhārā*). This is also [the view] of the Blessed One.
Indeed, the teaching is fourfold by way of both the Dhamma and individuals: teaching the Dhamma with reference to the Dhamma;
teaching individuals with reference to the Dhamma; teaching individuals with reference to individuals; and teaching the Dhamma with reference to individuals.
“Monks, I do not see even a single thing that, when developed in this way, becomes so wieldy as this...”
“Mind, monks. Mind, monks, when developed, becomes wieldy”—such is a teaching on the Dhamma based on the Dhamma.
“It is impossible, monks, it cannot happen, that a person possessed of right view should regard any conditioned phenomenon as permanent;
such a case is not found”—such is a teaching on persons based on the Dhamma. “One person...”
“Monks, when one appears in the world, he appears for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many,
out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans”— such is a teaching concerning persons based on a specific individual.
“Monks, through the manifestation of one person, there is the manifestation of the great eye”— such is a teaching concerning persons based on a specific individual.

There are two kinds of Dhamma-teachings: those based on the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhānā*) and those based on the phenomena themselves (*dhammādhiṭṭhānā*). Herein, it should be understood that this is a Dhamma-teaching based on the person.

Furthermore, because from the subsequent section up to the "Tens" only phenomena are taken up, it should be understood that by mentioning "beings" (*satta*), the phenomena are actually being referred to.

Alternatively, it should be understood that the mention of "beings" is made because the phenomena included within the continuity of a being must be examined according to their intrinsic nature through superior knowledge; [this applies] to the conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*).

Alternatively, it should be understood that because the mere designation "sentient being" arises based [on formations], the formations themselves are called "sentient beings" by way of metaphorical attribution (*phalopacāra*).
For there is no sentient being whatsoever existing as a conditionally established entity apart from formations;
yet, it is spoken of thus by way of conventional usage (*vohāra*). In this way, thorough knowledge by understanding (*ñātapariññā*) has been explained.

"Two elements" refers to the conditioned element and the unconditioned element. Therein, the five aggregates, produced by the coming together of numerous conditions, are the conditioned element; Nibbāna, which is not made by any conditions, is the unconditioned element.
"Three elements" refers to the sense-sphere element, the fine-material element, and the immaterial element. Therein, what is the sense-sphere element?
Taking the Avīci hell as its lower limit and including the Paranimmitavasavatti devas above, that which...

In this interval, whatever aggregates, elements, bases, forms, feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousness occur herein and are included herein—this is called the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*). In that regard, what is the fine-material element (*rūpadhātu*)?
Taking the Brahma-world as its lower limit and including the Akaniṭṭha devas at its upper limit, whatever occurs within this interval...

Herein, the states of mind and mental factors of one who has attained [a meditative absorption], or one who has been reborn [therein], or one who dwells in happiness in this very life—these are included therein;
this is called the form element (*rūpadhātu*). What, therein, is the formless element (*arūpadhātu*)?

Taking as its lower limit the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite space, and including within it the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception above, that which exists in this...

That which occurs within this interval, is included therein, and consists of the mental states and mental factors of one who has attained meditative absorption, or of one who has been reborn there, or of one dwelling in happiness in this very life—this is called the immaterial element (*arūpadhātu*). However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is said:

"As for the 'desire element' (*kāmadhātu*), the five aggregates of the existence of desire (*kāmabhava*) are found; as for the 'form element' (*rūpadhātu*), the five aggregates of the existence of form (*rūpabhava*) are found."

"The immaterial element (arūpadhātu) means that in the immaterial existence (arūpabhava), four aggregates (khandha) are found"—thus it is said. This is the application according to the *Dasuttara* method.

According to the *Saṅgīti* method, however: "Three wholesome elements (kusaladhātu)—the element of renunciation (nekkhammadhātu), the element of non-ill will (abyāpādadhātu), and the element of non-cruelty (avihiṃsādhātu).
Another three elements—the form element (rūpadhātu), the immaterial element (arūpadhātu), and the cessation element (nirodhadhātu). Another three elements..."
The elements spoken of as “the inferior element, the intermediate element, and the sublime element” are also applicable here.
Thought and applied thought associated with renunciation … [and so on] … right intention: this is called the element of renunciation. All wholesome states are the element of renunciation.
Thought and applied thought associated with non-ill will … [and so on] … right intention: this is the element of non-ill will.

That which is loving-kindness toward beings, the state of being loving-kind, the state of having been loving-kind, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness—this is called the element of non-ill will.
The thought, applied thought, and so forth, associated with non-cruelty, right intention—this is the element of non-cruelty.

That which is compassion toward beings, the state of being compassionate, the state of having been compassionate, the liberation of mind through compassion—this is called the element of non-cruelty. The form and formless elements.
It has already been stated. The element of cessation is *nibbāna*. The inferior element consists of the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness;

the middling element consists of the remaining phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence; and the superior element consists of the nine supramundane phenomena. Furthermore, all these are called "elements" (*dhātu*) in the sense of being devoid of a living soul (*nijjīva*).
The Four Noble Truths are as follows: the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.
The noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. A commentary on these will be given in the answers concerning the truths themselves.
"The five bases of liberation" refers to: hearing the teaching of the Dhamma as it is being delivered by others for one's own benefit;
teaching the Dhamma as one has heard it for the benefit of others; and the recitation of the Dhamma as one has heard it.

The mental reflection upon the Dhamma as it has been heard, and the object that is favorable [such as] the kasiṇas or the foul (asubha) and so forth—these are the five causes of liberation. As it is said:
"Here, monks, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to a monk, or some venerable fellow-celibate."
In whatever way, monks, the Teacher or another venerable fellow-practitioner teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu,
in that very way he becomes sensitive to the meaning and sensitive to the Dhamma in that teaching;
as he is sensitive to the meaning and sensitive to the Dhamma, gladness arises in him, and for one who is gladdened, rapture arises.
“Birth occurs; for one with a joyful mind, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one experiences happiness;
for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. This is the first basis of liberation.
Furthermore, monks, it may be that the Teacher does not teach the Dhamma to a monk, nor does anyone else...”
A venerable fellow practitioner of the holy life who, moreover, teaches the Dhamma in detail to others exactly as it has been heard and mastered.
In whatever way, monks, for a bhikkhu… [as before] …his mind becomes concentrated while he is happy.
This is the second basis for liberation.
“Furthermore, monks, it may be that neither does the Teacher teach the Dhamma to a monk,
nor does some other venerable fellow-celibate, nor does he himself teach the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard and mastered it;
rather, he recites the Dhamma in detail by way of rehearsal as he has heard and mastered it.
“In whatever way, monks, a bhikkhu’s mind becomes concentrated while he is happy... this is the third basis for liberation.
“Furthermore, monks, neither does the Teacher teach the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, nor does some other venerable fellow-celibate;
nor does he [the bhikkhu] himself explain in detail to others the Dhamma as he has heard it and mastered it.”
He does not teach the Dhamma as he has heard it and mastered it, nor does he recite it in detail as he has heard it and mastered it;
rather, he reflects upon the Dhamma as he has heard it and mastered it with his mind, ponders it, and examines it with his intellect.
In whatever way, monks, for a bhikkhu... [as before] ...his mind, being happy, becomes concentrated. This is the fourth basis for liberation.
“Furthermore, monks, it may be that neither does the Teacher teach the Dhamma to a bhikkhu,
nor does some other venerable companion in the holy life do so; nor does he teach the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard and mastered it,
nor does he recite it in detail as he has heard and mastered it.”
He reflects upon, examines, and contemplates with the mind the Dhamma as he has heard it and mastered it;
moreover, he has grasped a certain object of concentration well, attended to it well, retained it well, and penetrated it well with wisdom.
In whatever way, monks, that monk [applies] a certain object of concentration...
It is well-grasped, well-attended to, well-retained, and well-penetrated by wisdom;
thus, in regard to that Dhamma, he experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma. In one who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, gladness arises;
in one who is gladdened, rapture arises; in one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil.
"With a tranquil body, one feels pleasure; in one who feels pleasure, the mind becomes concentrated.
This is the fifth basis for liberation. Regarding "the six unsurpassables" (*cha anuttariyāni*): here, because there is nothing superior to them, they are "unsurpassable" (*anuttara*);

being unsurpassable, they are "unsurpassables" (*anuttariya*); the meaning is that they are the foremost. For this was said by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, there are these six unsurpassables. Which six? The unsurpassable sight, the unsurpassable hearing, the unsurpassable gain, the unsurpassable training, the unsurpassable service, and the unsurpassable recollection."
“And what, bhikkhus, is the unsurpassed sight? Here, bhikkhus, someone goes to see the elephant-treasure,
or goes to see the horse-treasure, or goes to see the gem-treasure,
or goes to see various high and low sights, or [goes to see] a recluse or a brahmin who holds wrong views and practices wrongly.”
One goes for the sake of seeing. There is such a thing as seeing, monks; I do not say that it does not exist.
Yet, monks, that seeing is inferior, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial;
it does not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, or Nibbāna.
...it leads [to that]. But, monks, whoever goes to see the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata with established faith,
established love, having gone to the one-sided conclusion, and being fully confident— this, monks, is the unsurpassed [condition] for the purification of beings,
for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, and for the cessation of pain and dejection.

For the attainment of the Dhamma, for the realization of Nibbāna, he goes to see either a Tathāgata or a disciple of a Tathāgata—one who is established in faith, established in love, having reached a single-minded resolve, and full of confidence.
This, monks, is called the unsurpassed excellence of seeing. Such is the unsurpassed excellence of seeing.
“And what is the unsurpassed hearing? Here, monks, someone goes to hear the sound of a drum;
he goes to hear the sound of a lute; he goes to hear the sound of singing;
or he goes to hear various sounds, such as those of a recluse or a brahmin who holds wrong views and practices wrongly.”
One goes to listen to the Dhamma. There is such listening, monks; I do not say that it does not exist. Yet, monks, that listening is inferior... [as before] ...it does not lead to Nibbāna.

But whoever, monks, goes to listen to the Dhamma of the Tathāgata or of a disciple of the Tathāgata, being established in faith and established in love... [as before] ...that listening is superior... [as before] ...it leads to Nibbāna. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall go to listen to the Dhamma of the Tathāgata or of a disciple of the Tathāgata, being established in faith and established in love. Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.
Having gone to one side, being full of confidence. This, monks, is the unsurpassed [condition] for the purification of beings through hearing...

up to ...for the realization of Nibbāna: namely, that one goes to hear the Dhamma from a Tathāgata or a disciple of a Tathāgata, with established faith, established affection, having gone to one side, and being full of confidence. This, monks, is called...
The unsurpassedness of hearing. Thus there is the unsurpassedness of seeing and the unsurpassedness of hearing.

And how does the unsurpassedness of gain come about? Here, monks, a certain person gains the gain of sons, gains the gain of a wife, gains the gain of wealth, or gains various kinds of gain. Or, among ascetics or brahmins...
Or he gains faith in one who holds wrong view and has entered upon a wrong path. "There is such gain, monks;
I say it is not non-existent," I declare. Yet, monks, that gain is inferior... [as before] ...it does not lead to Nibbāna.
But whoever, monks, gains faith in the Tathāgata or in a disciple of the Tathāgata, being established in that faith...
“With settled affection, having reached a state of certainty, and being fully confident—this, monks, is the unsurpassed thing for the purification of beings who have gained acquisitions...

[and so on] ...for the realization of Nibbāna, namely, that one gains faith in the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, possessing settled faith, settled affection, having reached certainty, and being fully confident. This is called...”
Monks, this is unsurpassed gain. Thus there is unsurpassed seeing, unsurpassed hearing, and unsurpassed gain.

And how is there unsurpassed training? Here, monks, a certain person trains in elephant-riding, trains in horsemanship, trains in chariot-driving, trains in archery, trains in swordsmanship, and various other [skills].
Or else one trains under a recluse or a brahmin who holds wrong view and practices wrongly.
"This training exists, monks; I say it is not non-existent," I declare. Yet this training, monks, is inferior...
[as before] ...it does not lead to Nibbāna. But as for that which, monks, has been proclaimed by the Tathāgata...

In this Dhamma and Vinaya, one trains in higher virtue, trains in higher mind, and trains in higher wisdom, with faith established, with love established, having reached a single-pointed conclusion, and being deeply convinced. This, monks, is the unsurpassed training for the purification of beings...
[and so on] ...for the realization of Nibbāna, namely, in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
He trains in higher virtue, he trains in higher mind, and he trains in higher wisdom;
he is established in faith, established in love, resolute, and full of confidence. This, monks, is called the unsurpassed training.
Thus there is the unsurpassed vision, the unsurpassed hearing, the unsurpassed gain, and the unsurpassed training.
“And how is there unsurpassed service? Here, monks, someone serves a kshatriya, or serves a brahmin, or serves a householder;
or he serves various [others], or he serves an ascetic or a brahmin who holds wrong views and practices wrongly. This, monks, is such a thing as exists.”
"I say that there is no such thing as service [that is not beneficial]. Yet, monks, this kind of service is inferior...

it does not lead to Nibbāna. But whoever, monks, serves the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, being established in faith, established in love, having gone to the one-sided conclusion, and being full of confidence—this, monks, is unsurpassed."

For the purification of beings who serve... [and so on] ...for the realization of Nibbāna, namely, when one serves the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata with established faith, established love, having gone to the conclusion, and being fully confident.
This, monks, is called the unsurpassed service. Thus: the unsurpassed seeing, the unsurpassed hearing, [the unsurpassed service].
The unsurpassed gain, the unsurpassed training, and the unsurpassed service.

“And how is there the unsurpassed recollection? Here, monks, someone recollects the acquisition of a son, recollects the acquisition of a wife, recollects the acquisition of wealth, or else recollects various high and low things.”
Or he recollects a recluse or a brahmin who holds wrong view and has practiced wrongly. Monks, this recollection exists;
I say it is not non-existent. Yet, monks, this recollection is inferior...
[as before] ...it does not lead to Nibbāna. But, monks, when one recollects the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata with established faith...
"One whose love is settled, who has gone to one side, and who is full of confidence. This, monks, is the unsurpassed thing among recollections for the purification of beings...

for the realization of Nibbāna, namely, that one recollects the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, with settled faith, settled love, having gone to one side, and being full of confidence. This is called..."
“...monks, the unsurpassed recollection. These, monks, are the six unsurpassed things. Regarding the phrase “seven bases of the state beyond training” (*satta niddasavatthūni*):
here, one who has no more ten years [of training] remaining is called *niddasa*.

The bases, that is, the causes, for the state of being *niddasa*—the state of being beyond training—are the “bases of the state beyond training. For one whose taints are destroyed, having attained final nibbāna at the age of ten, there is no further rebirth.
Furthermore, because he does not exist for ten years, he is called "without ten" (*niddasa*). Not only does he not exist for ten years, but he does not exist for nine years... [and so on] ...

nor even for a single moment. Not only is he one who has attained final nibbāna at the time of ten years, but one who has attained final nibbāna at the time of seven years is likewise without a being (*nissatta*), without ten years (*niddasa*), and without a moment (*nimuhutta*).
This is according to the system of the non-Buddhist sects (*titthiya-samaya*).

However, having attributed the conventional designation of "one whose taints are destroyed" (khīṇāsava) to one within the Dispensation, the Blessed One—showing the absence of such a person there [in the world] and their presence here [in the Dispensation]—stated the causes for such a nature as "the seven grounds for praise. As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, there are these seven grounds for praise. Which seven? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu..."
He has a keen desire for undertaking the training, and his affection for undertaking the training remains undiminished in the future.
He has a keen desire for settling in the Dhamma, and his affection for settling in the Dhamma remains undiminished in the future.

He has a keen desire for the removal of longing, and his affection for the removal of longing remains undiminished in the future. He has a keen desire for seclusion, and his affection for seclusion remains undiminished in the future.

He has not lost his affection for the arousal of energy; he has intense desire for the arousal of energy and will have undiminished affection for the arousal of energy in the future. He has intense desire for mindfulness and discernment;
he has intense desire for mindfulness and discernment and will have undiminished affection for mindfulness and discernment in the future. He has intense desire for the penetration of views;
he has intense desire for the penetration of views and will have undiminished affection for the penetration of views in the future. These, monks, are the seven grounds for commendation.”
The Elder likewise extracted the teaching in that same manner and said, "The seven bases of training.
Regarding the "eight bases of mastery" (*aṭṭha abhibhāyatanāni*): here, the "bases of mastery" are the meditative absorptions (*jhānāni*) because these absorptions master the bases;
the "bases" (*āyatanāni*) are the kasiṇa objects designated as "bases" in the sense of being their foundation. [He was] one whose excellence was in knowledge (*ñāṇuttariko*).
For a person of clear knowledge thinks, "What is there to be attained here as an object?
I have no burden in achieving one-pointedness of mind," and thus, having mastered those objects, he enters attainment;
the meaning is that he produces absorption right along with the arising of the sign. The jhānas produced in this way are called "bases of mastery" (*abhibhāyatana*).
“What are the eight? One percipient of forms internally sees forms externally as limited, beautiful or ugly; having mastered them, one perceives: ‘I know, I see. This is the first base of mastery.
One percipient of forms internally sees forms externally as immeasurable, beautiful or ugly; having mastered them, one perceives: ‘I know, I see. This is the second base of mastery.”
“Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally, limited, beautiful or ugly; having mastered them, one perceives: ‘I know, I see. This is the third base of mastery.
Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally, immeasurable, beautiful or ugly; having mastered them, one perceives: ‘I know, I see. This is the fourth base of mastery.”
“Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally—blue, blue-colored, blue in appearance, blue in luster.
Just as, for example, an *umā* flower is blue, blue-colored, blue in appearance, blue in luster;
or just as, for example, Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, is blue, blue-colored, [blue in appearance, blue in luster].”
Blue in appearance, blue in luster; even so, one who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally that are blue, blue-colored, blue in appearance, and blue in luster.
Having mastered them, he is percipient thus: "I know, I see. This is the fifth base of mastery.
“Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster.
Just as, for example, a *kaṇikāra* flower is yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster;
or just as, for example, a Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, is yellow, yellow in color, [yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster].”

yellow in appearance, yellow in luster—just so, one percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally that are yellow, yellow-colored, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster; having mastered them, he is percipient thus: "I know, I see.
This is the sixth base of mastery.
“Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally that are red,
red in color, red in appearance, and red in luster. Just as a *bandhujīvaka* flower is red, red in color, red in appearance,
and red in luster, or like a Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, [red, red in color, red in appearance, and red in luster].”

Red, red-colored, red-appearing, red-luminous; even so, one who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally that are red, red-colored, red-appearing, red-luminous, and having mastered them, he is percipient thus:
‘I know, I see. This is the seventh base of mastery.
“Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally that are white, white in color, white in appearance, and white in luster.
Just as, for example, the morning star is white, white in color, white in appearance, and white in luster;
or just like a Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, white, white in color, [white in appearance, and white in luster].”

white in appearance, white in luster—just so, one who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally that are white, white-colored, white in appearance, and white in luster; having mastered them, he is percipient thus: ‘I know, I see.
This is the eighth base of mastery. These are the eight bases of mastery.

The nine successive dwellings (*anupubbavihāra*): "Successive" (*anupubba*) means one after another; they are called "successive dwellings" because they are to be dwelt in and attained in succession. The meaning is: dwellings to be attained in regular order. "What are the nine?

Here, monks, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a monk enters and dwells in the first *jhāna*, which is accompanied by applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and possesses the rapture and happiness born of seclusion. [From] applied and sustained thought..."

With the subsiding of directed thought and evaluation, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without directed thought and evaluation, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration. And with the fading away of rapture, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending;
he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He who is equanimous..."
“mindful and dwelling in happiness,” he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.
With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, and the disappearance of perceptions of sensory reaction...
With the disappearance of perceptions of diversity and by not attending to perceptions of multiplicity, he enters and dwells in the base of infinite space, thinking, "Space is infinite.
By completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking, "Consciousness is infinite," he enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.
By completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, thinking, "There is nothing," he enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
"Having attained, he dwells; having completely transcended the base of nothingness, he attains and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he attains and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling.
Thus, these are the nine successive dwellings that have been described.

"The ten bases for wearing away" (*nijjaravatthūni*): they are called "wearings away" (*nijjarā*) because they wear away—that is, destroy—wrong view and so forth. "Bases" (*vatthūni*) means causes. Being both wearings away and bases, they are "bases for wearing away.
This is a designation for right view and the rest. "What are the ten? Monks, for one of right view, wrong view is worn away.
And those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong view are also worn away for him; [those] conditioned by right view..."
And many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development.
"Monks, for one of right intention, wrong intention is worn away.
And those many evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong intention are worn away for him; [and] conditioned by right intention..."
And many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development.
“Monks, for one of right speech, wrong speech is worn away.
And those many evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong speech are worn away in him; and conditioned by right speech, many [wholesome states arise].”
wholesome states reach fulfillment by development.
“Bhikkhus, for one of right action, wrong action is worn away.
And those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong action are worn away in him; and through the condition of right action, wholesome states come to fulfillment.”
And many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development.
"Monks, for one of right livelihood, wrong livelihood is worn away.
And those many evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong livelihood are worn away for him; and [those states] conditioned by right livelihood..."
“Many wholesome states reach fulfillment by development.
For one with right effort, monks, wrong effort is worn away.
And those many evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong effort are worn away for him; [and] conditioned by right effort...”
And many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development.
“Bhikkhus, for one who is rightly mindful, wrong mindfulness is worn away.
And those many evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong mindfulness are worn away for him; and conditioned by right mindfulness, many [wholesome states arise].”
wholesome states reach fulfillment through development.
“Monks, for one with right concentration, wrong concentration is worn away.
And those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong concentration are worn away for him; and those [states] conditioned by right concentration—”
And many wholesome states reach fulfillment through cultivation.
"Monks, for one who possesses right knowledge, wrong knowledge is worn away.
And those many evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong knowledge are worn away for him; and conditioned by right knowledge, many..."
Wholesome states reach fulfillment through development.
"Monks, for one who is rightly liberated, wrong liberation is worn away.
And those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong liberation are worn away for him; [those states] conditioned by right liberation..."
And many wholesome states reach full development through these ten bases for the wearing away [of defilements], as they have been stated.
3. It should be understood that the passage beginning with “All, monks, is to be directly known,” which was spoken by the Blessed One, has been brought forward and shown here.
As for the word *kiñca*—the particle *ca* is a mere expletive used to fill out the meter. There are thirty questions and answers concerning the eye and so forth.
In each of the six doors, five [consciousnesses] are set forth according to the sequence of the occurrence of the door and its object.
Therein, the eye is twofold: the fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*) and the wisdom-eye (*paññācakkhu*). Among these, the wisdom-eye is fivefold:
the Buddha-eye, the universal eye (*samantacakkhu*), the knowledge-eye (*ñāṇacakkhu*), the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), and the Dhamma-eye (*dhammacakkhu*). "I saw, indeed... [so it was said].
“Monks, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye”—this is what is called the *buddhacakkhu*.
“The all-seeing eye is said to be omniscient knowledge”—this is what is called the *samantacakkhu*. “The eye arose, knowledge arose”—this is what is called the *ñāṇacakkhu*.
“Monks, with the purified divine eye, I saw”—[this is what is called the *dibbacakkhu*].
This is called the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*). "The dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye arose"—this refers to the knowledge comprised by the three lower paths, which is called the Dhamma-eye.
The fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*) is also twofold: the eye as physical matter (*sasambhāracakkhu*) and the eye as sensitive materiality (*pasādacakkhu*). That which [is located] in the eye-socket...
It is established below by the bone of the eye-socket, above by the bone of the eyebrow, and demarcated on both sides by the eye-ridges and externally by the eyelashes;

it is a mass of flesh variegated with white and black circles, bound to the brain by a cord of sinews protruding from the middle of the eye-socket—this is called the "eye together with its constituent parts. As for that which...
But here, that which is dependent on this, bound to this—the sensitivity derived from the four great elements—this is what is called the "sensitivity-eye" (*pasādacakkhu*).

This is what is intended here. Now, this [sensitivity] is located in the center of the black circle (*kaṇhamaṇḍala*) surrounded by a white circle (*setamaṇḍala*) of that eye together with its material basis;
it is situated in the region of the visual field where the bodily configuration of those standing directly in front appears.
Like oil poured upon seven layers of cotton, it pervades the seven layers of the eye; in size, it is about the measure of a split green gram (*mugga*).
It remains there, fulfilling its function as the appropriate base and door for visual consciousness and the other [sensory consciousnesses].

It is called "eye" (*cakkhu*) because it sees (*cakkhati*); the meaning is that it experiences and discerns visible form (*rūpa*). They are called "visible forms" (*rūpā*) because they undergo transformation of color (*vaṇṇavikāra*).
The meaning is that they manifest the state of having entered the heart. Consciousness proceeding from the eye, or consciousness of the eye, is "eye-consciousness" (*cakkhuviññāṇa*).
It touches, thus it is "contact" (*phassa*). By embellishing the word with a prefix, it is called "impingement-contact" (*samphassa*).
Impingement-contact proceeding from the eye is "eye-impingement-contact" (*cakkhusamphassa*). "Conditioned by eye-impingement-contact" means conditioned by contact associated with eye-consciousness.
"Vedayitaṃ" means finding; thus, "feeling" (vedanā) is the meaning. That very thing which causes one to experience pleasure is "pleasure" (sukha);
the meaning is that it makes the one in whom it arises happy. Or, it is "pleasure" because it thoroughly consumes (suṭṭhu khādati) and digs away (khanati) physical and mental afflictions.
"Dukkha" means that which causes suffering; the meaning is that it makes the one in whom it arises miserable. Not-dukkha... [not-dukkha]... not-pleasure.
“Sukha” means neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*adukkhamasukha*). The letter *m* is used here for the sake of euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*).

Furthermore, that eye-contact is a condition in eight ways by way of being conascent, mutuality, support, resultant, nutriment, association, presence, and non-disappearance conditions for the feeling associated with itself; it is a condition in five ways—by way of proximity, contiguity, proximity-strong-dependence, absence, and non-disappearance—for the feeling associated with the [mental] reception (*sampaṭicchana*).
It is a condition by way of decisive support (upanissaya) for those states associated with investigation (santīraṇa) and so forth.

It "hears," thus it is the ear (sota). That [ear] exists within the ear-canal together with its constituent parts, in a location shaped like a finger-stall and covered with fine, dark hairs, performing the function of being the physical basis (vatthu) and the door (dvāra) for ear-consciousness and the rest, as appropriate. They "creep along," thus...
"Sounds" (*saddā*): the meaning is "that which are uttered. "Smelling" (*ghāyati*) is the nose (*ghāna*).

It stands within the nasal cavity along with its constituent parts, in a location shaped like a goat's hoof, establishing itself as the appropriate basis (*vatthu*) and door (*dvāra*) for nose-consciousness and the rest.

"Odors" (*gandhā*): the meaning is "that which make their own basis known. "The tongue" (*jivhā*): it is so called because it "invites life" (*jīvitaṃ avhāyati*), or else in the sense of "tasting" (*sāyana*).

The tongue: excluding the very tip, the root, and the sides of the tongue together with its constituent parts, it remains in the middle of the upper surface in a place shaped like the point of a split lotus petal, establishing itself as the appropriate basis and door for tongue-consciousness and the rest.
They are called *rasa* because beings relish them; the meaning is that they provide enjoyment. The body (*kāya*) is the coming-to-be (*āya*) of base, tainted phenomena. *Āya* means...

The place of arising. To whatever extent there is the occurrence of what is clung-to (*upādiṇṇa*) in this body, therein the bodily sensitivity (*kāyapasāda*) mostly remains, establishing itself as the respective basis (*vatthu*) and door (*dvāra*) for body-consciousness and the rest.

They are "touched" (*phusīyanti*), thus they are "tangibles" (*phoṭṭhabba*). It "measures" (*munāti*), thus it is "mind" (*mano*); the meaning is that it cognizes. They "bear their own characteristic" (*lakkhaṇaṃ dhārenti*), thus they are "mental phenomena" (*dhammā*).

"Mind" refers to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) together with the adverting consciousness (āvajjana). "Mental objects" refers to mental objects consisting of phenomena (dhammārammaṇa) divided into twelve types.
"Mind-consciousness" refers to the impulsion mind-consciousness (javana-manoviññāṇa). "Mind-contact" is the contact associated with that [consciousness].

It acts as a condition for the associated feeling by way of the remaining seven conditions, excluding the fruition-condition (vipāka-paccaya); for the immediately following [feeling], it acts by those same [seven] conditions; and for the others, it acts as a condition solely by way of decisive support (upanissaya).
The five questions beginning with "form" (*rūpa*) are explained by way of the aggregates (*khandha*). It is called "form" (*rūpa*) because it is broken (*ruppati*) or afflicted by cold and so forth.

It is called "feeling" (*vedanā*) because it feels (*vedayati*). It is called "perception" (*saññā*) because it perceives (*sañjānāti*). It is called "volitional formations" (*saṅkhārā*) because they construct (*saṅkharonti*). It is called "consciousness" (*viññāṇa*) because it cognizes (*vijānāti*).

The ten questions beginning with the eye and ending with mental investigation are explained by way of six sets; thus there are sixty questions by way of the aspect of the pleasant and the agreeable (*piyarūpa-sātarūpa*).

[These have been] explained. Feelings born of eye-contact and so forth are associated with their respective [mental states]. Perception of forms is "form-perception" (*rūpasaññā*). One intends, thus it is "volition" (*sañcetanā*);
the meaning is that one directs [the mind] toward an object. One thirsts, thus it is "craving" (*taṇhā*); the meaning is that one longs for.
One reasons, thus it is "applied thought" (*vitakka*); or, applied thought is the act of applying; what is meant is "investigation. By means of this, the mind [is directed] toward the object.
It is called *vicāra* because it investigates (*vicarati*), or *vicāra* is the act of investigating; what is meant is "moving along" (*anusañcaraṇa*). 4.
The six questions beginning with the earth element are explained in brief by way of the determination of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-vavatthāna*).

It is "earth" (*pathavī*) because it extends (*patthaṭattā*). It is "water" (*āpo*) because it flows (*appeti*), is flowed into (*āpīyati*), or causes to flow (*appāyati*). It is "fire" (*tejo*) because it heats (*tejayati*). It is "air" (*vāyo*) because it blows (*vāyati*).

Vāyo. It is called space (ākāsa) because it does not press against anything nor is pressed against; it cannot be ploughed, cut, or broken. In the sense of being devoid of a living being, it is an element (dhātu).
The ten answers beginning with the earth-kasiṇa are explained by way of the development of the kasiṇas. "Kasiṇa" is so called in the sense of all-pervading;
