thus it refers to the kasiṇa disk, the sign that appears therein, the consciousness with that as its object, and the jhāna itself. However, here—

Jhāna is intended here. At the beginning are the four jhānas having the four great primary elements (mahābhūta) as their kasiṇa objects; following those are the four [jhānas] having the color-kasiṇas as their objects.

"Space-kasiṇa" refers to the delimiting space and the jhāna having that as its object, as well as the space resulting from the removal of the kasiṇa and the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana) having that as its object.
"Consciousness-kasiṇa" refers to the consciousness of the base of infinite space and the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) having that as its object.
The thirty-two answers beginning with "hair" are set forth by way of the meditation subject of the thirty-two aspects.
Among these, when hair and so forth appear as repulsive, it is the meditation subject of foulness (asubha) by way of mindfulness occupied with the body;
when they appear by way of color, it is the meditation subject of the kasiṇas; and when they appear by way of elements, it is the meditation subject of the definition of the four elements.
The jhānas that have those [objects] as their referent—whether they appear as repulsive or by way of color—such as "hair" and so forth, should be understood as such.
For one who has established [the meditation] by way of elements, those body parts and the cultivation of the elements that have them as their referent should be understood.

Hair, bounded on both sides by the ear-lobes, in front by the edge of the forehead, and behind by the nape of the neck, enters into the skin enveloping the skull to the depth of a grain of rice; it is numbered in the many hundreds of thousands.

Except for the hair and so forth, which occupy their respective locations and the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, body hairs generally enter and remain within the skin of the body by a measure of a louse’s head in the ninety-nine thousand pores.
There are twenty nails situated on the upper surfaces of the tips of the fingers and toes.
There are generally thirty-two teeth situated in the two jawbones.
The skin is that which covers the entire body, situated beneath the outer layer of the skin and above the visible membranes.
The flesh consists of nine hundred pieces of flesh that remain smeared over more than three hundred bones.
The sinews consist of nine hundred sinews that remain binding the bones together throughout the entire body.
The bones: there are more than three hundred bones situated below the rest of the body and above the other bones.
The bone-marrow: this is the marrow found inside those respective bones.

The kidneys: these are two masses of flesh situated surrounding the heart-flesh, bound by a thick sinew that emerges from the throat, travels a short distance with a single root, and then divides into two.

The heart (*hadaya*) is the heart-flesh situated within the body between the two breasts; it is the internal support for consciousness, filled with about half a *pasata* of blood, and is the size of a basin that holds a *punnāga* seed.
The liver (*yakana*) is a pair of fleshy lobes situated within the space between the two breasts, resting against the right side.
The membrane (*kilomaka*) is the concealed membrane located throughout the entire body, covering the heart and lungs.
The flesh covering the skin is of two kinds: that which lies beneath the skin enveloping it, and that which is called the concealed *kilomaka* (pericardium).
The *pihaka* (spleen) is situated on the left side of the heart, resting against the upper side of the abdominal membrane; the *udarajivhāmaṃsa* (stomach lining) is likewise situated there.
The lungs (*papphāsa*) are a mass of flesh consisting of thirty-two lobes that cover and hang down over the heart and kidneys within the body, between the two breasts.
Because they are bound above at the throat and below at the passage of excrement, they occupy the interior of the body bounded by the throat and the rectum;
in a man they measure thirty-two cubits, and in a woman twenty-eight cubits, [occupying] twenty-one...
The intestinal lining is collapsed in its various places.
The intestinal ligament is the binding that holds the coils of the intestines together when they do not stick to one another; it is situated between twenty-one such intestinal coils.

The stomach contents have been crushed by the pestle-like teeth, turned over by the tongue and hands, and smeared with saliva and mucus; at that moment, their excellence of color, fragrance, taste, and so forth has vanished.
Resembling the vomit of a weaver’s donkey, it falls down, becomes enveloped by bile, phlegm, and wind, and is heated by the force of the digestive fire in the stomach;
swarming with hosts of worms, emitting layers upon layers of froth and bubbles, it reaches a state of extreme filth, foul stench, and loathsomeness,
remaining in the region known as the receptacle of undigested food (āmāśaya), situated above the navel and below the diaphragm, consisting of various kinds of things eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted.

Feces (*karīsa*) refers to the excrement situated at the end of the intestines, eight finger-breadths in height, between the navel and the base of the spinal column, within what is known as the receptacle of digested food (*pakkāsayasaṅkhāta*).

Bile (*pitta*) consists of both that which is situated between the heart, flesh, and lungs, supported by the liver tissue; that which is contained within the gall-bladder (*pittakosaka*), which resembles the pod of a large *kosātaki* gourd;
and that known as "bound bile" (*baddhapitta*). Furthermore, there is the bile located in the parts of the head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, and teeth where they are detached from the flesh.
Bile (*pitta*) is twofold: that which is called "unbound bile" (*abaddhapitta*), which remains pervading the rest of the body except for the stiff, dry skin; and [the other type].
Phlegm (*semha*) is the phlegm located on the surface of the stomach, measuring about one *pattha* full.
Pus (*pubba*) occurs when a part of the body is struck by stumps, thorns, weapons, flames, and so forth, or through the disturbance of the internal elements.
Or it is the transformation of blood that has ripened in boils, pustules, and the like.
There is also the blood that fills the lower part of the liver, which trickles down slightly from above the heart, kidneys, and lungs, remaining there moistening the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs;
this is known as "accumulated blood" (sannicitalohita), measuring about one *pattha*. Furthermore, there is [the blood] in the head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, and teeth...

Blood is twofold: that which is called circulating blood, which—excluding the place where the flesh is detached and the stiff, dry skin—remains pervading the entire appropriated body following the network of veins;

and that which consists of the sweat, which is the water element oozing from all the pores of the head hair and body hair when the body is heated by fire, the heat of the sun, changes in the seasons, and so forth.
Fat (*medo*) is a thin oil situated between the skin and the flesh throughout the body of a stout person; in a lean person, it is situated supported by the flesh of the calves and other such parts.
Tears (*assu*) are the water element that, having arisen from mental joy, grief, or an imbalance of nutriment and temperature, remains filling the eye sockets or flows out from them.

Grease (*vasā*) is melted oil produced by heat, which—due to an imbalance of fire-heat, sun-heat, or temperature—is mostly located in the palms of the hands, backs of the hands, soles of the feet, backs of the feet, nostrils, forehead, and tops of the shoulders.
Saliva is the water element mixed with froth that arises more abundantly when one sees such food, or remembers it, or places it in the mouth,
or feels weariness in the heart, or gives rise to disgust toward something;
having descended from both cheeks, it remains upon the tongue.
Snot is foul, impure, and slimy; it is that which, due to an incompatible diet or a seasonal change, arises from a disturbance of the elements, or which, when one is weeping,
flows down from the brain within the head, descends through the opening of the palate and the mouth, fills the nostrils, and remains there or trickles out.
Lasikā is a slimy secretion situated within the eighty-one joints, performing the function of lubricating those bone-joints.
Urine is the water element situated within the bladder, depending on food and temperature.
Brain matter is a mass of marrow consisting of four lumps, situated within the skull-bowl in dependence upon the four sutures.
The twelve answers beginning with the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) are explained by way of the twelve bases (āyatana).
It is called a "base" (āyatana) because it is the extending of arrival (āyānaṃ tananato), and because it leads (nayato) that which has arrived (āyatassa).

For, in the case of the eye, visible forms, and so forth, the mental states (citta) and mental concomitants (cetasika-dhammā)—namely, the various doors and objects—arrive, arise, and exert themselves through their respective functions such as experiencing.
It is said that they "exert. Furthermore, it is said that they "stretch out" or "expand" those phenomena which constitute their own source.
And it is said that they "lead on" or "cause to proceed" this exceedingly long suffering of saṃsāra, which has occurred throughout beginningless time, until it ceases.
Furthermore, *āyatana* (base) is so called in the sense of a place of residence, a source, a meeting place, a region of birth, and a cause.
For instance, in common usage, in expressions such as "the abode of Īśvara" (*issarāyatana*) or "the abode of Vāsudeva" (*vāsudevāyatana*), a place of residence is called an *āyatana*.

In expressions such as "a gold mine" (*suvaṇṇāyatana*) or "a silver mine" (*rajatāyatana*), it refers to a source. However, in the Teaching (*sāsana*), in the passage beginning "In delightful abodes... (*manorame āyatane*), [it refers to a place of birth].

In such passages as "The birds resort to it," it means a place of gathering (*samosaraṇaṭṭhāna*). In such passages as "The southern region is the abode (*āyatana*) of cattle," it means a place of origin (*sañjātidesa*).
In such passages as "He attains the capacity for realization in each respective case, whenever there is a suitable occasion (*sati sati-āyatane*)," it means a cause (*kāraṇa*).

Furthermore, in the case of the eye and so forth, those various states of mind and mental factors dwell [therein] because their existence is dependent upon them; thus, the eye and the rest [are called *āyatana*].

Their place of residence is [the body]; and because they are crowded within the eye and the other [faculties] due to having them as their support and having them as their object, the eye and the others are their mine;
and because they converge there through the bases, doors, and objects respectively, the eye and the others are their place of convergence;
and because they arise right there by virtue of having those [bases] as their support and object, the eye and the others are [their source].
There is no specific location for them, because they do not exist in the absence of the eye and so forth;
and since the eye and the rest are their cause, in the sense already stated, it is "the eye and that base," thus *cakkhāyatana*. The same applies to the remaining [bases].
The eighteen explanations beginning with the eye-element (*cakkhudhātu*) are demonstrated by way of the eighteen elements. Regarding the eye and the rest...
Each individual phenomenon (dhamma) brings about, holds together, or ordains its own arrangement; it is that by which, or in which, something is held—thus it is called a *dhātu*.

For mundane elements (*dhātuyo*), having been established as causal factors, bring about manifold kinds of suffering in saṃsāra, just as gold, silver, and other mineral ores produce gold, silver, and so forth.
And just as a burden is [carried] by those who carry the burden...
They are so called because beings are supported (*dhīyante*) by them; the meaning is that they are sustained. They are merely the instruments of suffering, since beings lack mastery over them.

By means of these [aggregates], which function as instruments, the suffering of saṃsāra is experienced by beings. Furthermore, that [suffering] is deposited (*dhīyati*) and placed within these very [aggregates];
this is the meaning. Moreover, just as for the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), what is called "self" does not exist by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), nor...
Thus they are these. Furthermore, they are called *dhātus* because they bear their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

And just as in the world various mineral constituents such as yellow orpiment and realgar are called *dhātus*, so too these are called *dhātus* because they are like those [minerals]. For they are diverse constituents to be known by wisdom.

Or alternatively, just as among the constituents that form the aggregate known as the body—such as lymph, blood, and so forth—which are demarcated by mutually dissimilar characteristics, [these are likewise distinct].

Regarding the designation "element" (*dhātu*): in the same way, this designation "element" should be understood to apply to the individual components of this personal existence (*attabhāva*) comprised of the five aggregates.
For these, beginning with the eye, are demarcated by their mutually distinct and dissimilar characteristics.
Furthermore, "element" is a synonym for that which is merely devoid of a living soul (*nijjīvamatta*). Thus, the Blessed One said in such passages as: "Monks, this person consists of six elements."
He taught the elements for the purpose of uprooting the perception of a living being (*jīva*). In the sense already stated, the eye is an element, thus it is the "eye-element" (*cakkhudhātu*);

the same applies to the rest. As for the "mind-element" (*manodhātu*), there are three mind-elements. As for the "dhamma-element" (*dhammadhātu*), it consists of the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations, the sixteen subtle forms, and Nibbāna.
As for the "mind-consciousness-element" (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), there are seventy-six mind-consciousness-elements.
The twenty-two answers beginning with the eye-faculty are demonstrated by way of the twenty-two faculties.
The eye itself exercises lordship in the characteristic of seeing, thus it is the eye-faculty (*cakkhundriya*).

The ear itself exercises lordship in the characteristic of hearing, thus it is the ear-faculty (*sotindriya*). The nose itself exercises lordship in the characteristic of smelling, thus it is the nose-faculty (*ghānindriya*).
The tongue exercises lordship in the characteristic of tasting, thus it is the tongue-faculty (*jivhindriya*).
The body exercises lordship in the characteristic of touching, thus it is the body-faculty (*kāyindriya*). It is called "mind" (*mano*) because it thinks; the meaning is that it cognizes.
However, the teachers of the Commentaries say: it thinks and knows the object, as if measuring with a scale or holding it with a great balance.
The mind (mano) exercises lordship (indaṭṭha) in the characteristic of cognizing; thus it is the mind-faculty (manindriya).
Life (jīvita) is so called because the phenomena co-arising with it live by means of it; that very same [life] exercises lordship in the characteristic of maintaining;

thus it is the life-faculty (jīvitindriya). That life-faculty is twofold: the material life-faculty (rūpajīvitindriya) and the immaterial life-faculty (arūpajīvitindriya). It is co-nascent with all matter born of kamma.

The life-faculty of form (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*) is the maintenance of co-nascent form; the life-faculty of the formless (*arūpa-jīvitindriya*) is the maintenance of co-nascent non-form that is co-nascent with all consciousness.

She is called a "woman" (*itthī*) because the womb (*gabbha*) is constricted (*thīyati*) and undergoes contraction within her. It is called a "faculty" (*indriya*) because it exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha*) over the female gender and so forth. Being the faculty of a woman exclusively, it is the "female faculty" (*itthindriya*). "Man" (*puṃ*) refers to hell;
one who is crushed (*risīyati*) or harmed in hell, which is designated as "man," is a "male" (*purisa*). [It is the faculty] over the male gender and so forth...
It exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha*), thus it is a faculty (*indriya*); specifically, that which is the faculty of a male alone is the masculinity faculty (*purisindriya*).
Among these two, each one is co-nascent with the kamma-born materiality of its respective individual.

Pleasure associated with wholesome-resultant body-consciousness exercises lordship in the sense of being characterized by bodily gratification; thus it is a faculty, and pleasure itself as a faculty is the pleasure faculty (*sukhindriya*).

Suffering associated with unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha*) over the characteristic of bodily unpleasantness; thus it is a faculty (*indriya*). Suffering itself as a faculty is the "suffering-faculty" (*dukkhindriya*).

One who possesses joy and mental happiness has a "beautiful mind" (*sumana*); the state of having such a mind is "mental happiness" (*somanassa*). It exercises lordship over the characteristic of mental pleasantness; thus it is a faculty. Mental happiness itself as a faculty is the "mental-happiness-faculty" (*somanassindriya*).
One who possesses mental grief has a "corrupted mind" (*dumana*), or else, because it is an inferior feeling, one has a "contemptible mind"; thus it is "dejected mind" (*dummana*).
The state of one who is dejected is *domanassa*; it is called a faculty (*indriya*) because it exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha*) over its characteristic of mental unpleasantness.

Thus, *domanassindriya* is the faculty of dejection itself. Equanimity (*upekkhā*) is so called because it looks upon the occurrence of the modes of pleasure and pain, remaining established in a neutral mode, and thus proceeds in that manner;
it is a faculty because it exercises lordship over its characteristic of neutrality. It is equanimity.
Such is the faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*).
It is called *saddhā* because one has faith by means of it, or because it itself has faith, or because its nature is simply that of faith.

It is a faculty in the sense of being a dominant influence (*adhipati*) due to its overcoming of lack of faith; or, it exercises the function of a lord (*indaṭṭha*) with respect to the characteristic of resolution (*adhimokkha*).
Faculty (*indriya*): faith itself as a faculty is the faith-faculty (*saddhindriya*).
Heroism is energy (*vīriya*); or, it is the action of heroes; or, it is that which should be set in motion or put forth according to method or principle—thus it is energy.
It is a faculty in the sense of being predominant because it overcomes laziness, or else it has the characteristic of exertion.
It exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha*), thus it is a faculty (*indriya*); energy itself as a faculty is the "energy-faculty" (*vīriyindriya*).
They remember by means of it, or it remembers itself, or its very nature is remembering; thus it is mindfulness (*sati*).

Because it overcomes forgetfulness, it is a faculty in the sense of being predominant (*adhipati*); or, because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of establishing (*upaṭṭhāna-lakkhaṇa*), it is a faculty; [this is] mindfulness (*sati*).
Thus, the faculty is the faculty of mindfulness (*satindriya*).
It is called "concentration" (*samādhi*) because it correctly places and fixes the mind upon the object;

it is a faculty in the sense of being predominant due to its overcoming of distraction, or it is a faculty because it exercises lordship over the characteristic of non-distraction. Concentration itself as a faculty is the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*).
Wisdom is that which understands the Noble Truths by way of the method beginning with “This is suffering. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated:
“Wisdom is so called because it makes known [things] as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. It is a faculty (*indriya*) in the sense of being predominant because it overcomes ignorance;
or, it is a faculty because it exercises the function of a lord (*indaṭṭha*) regarding the characteristic of seeing. Wisdom itself as a faculty is the "faculty of wisdom" (*paññindriya*).

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*) arises for one who has set out in practice with the thought, "In this beginningless cycle of saṃsāra, I shall come to know the Deathless State (*amata-pada*), or indeed the Dhamma of the Four Truths," because it occurs at that moment and because the function of the faculties is established. This is the name for the knowledge of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa*).
It does not transcend the limits of what was already known by that very path; rather, it pertains precisely to those same Dhammas of the Four Truths known through that path.
The faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*) is so called because it is a faculty that knows and because it arises in the sense of a faculty.
This is the name for knowledge in six states, beginning with the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*).

It is called the faculty of one who has fully known (*aññātāvindriya*) because it arises in an arahant whose taints are destroyed and who has completed the task of knowledge regarding the Four Noble Truths, and because it arises in the sense of a faculty.

And there is the faculty of one who has already known (aññātāvindriya). Or, for those who have completed their task regarding the four truths—those who stand having penetrated the four truths—it is the faculty of one who has already known (aññātāvindriya) by way of accomplishing the lordship (*indaṭṭha*) over internal phenomena. This is the name for the knowledge of the fruit of arahantship.

All these [faculties] are, as appropriate, so called in the sense of being a mark of a lord (*indaliṅga*), in the sense of being taught by a lord (*indadesita*), and in the sense of being seen by a lord (*indadiṭṭha*).

They are called *indriya* in the sense of being "authorized by the Lord" (*indasiṭṭha*) and in the sense of being "presided over by the Lord" (*indajuṭṭha*). For the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the "Lord" (*inda*) because of his state of supreme sovereignty;

and wholesome and unwholesome karma is [the "Lord"] among karmas because no one else possesses sovereignty over them. Therefore, in this context, the faculties produced by karma indicate wholesome and unwholesome karma, and they are authorized by that [karma];
thus, they are so called in the sense of being "marks of the Lord" (*indaliṅga*) and in the sense of being "authorized by the Lord" (*indasiṭṭha*).

And these are all faculties (*indriya*). Since all of them have been proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, as they truly are, and have been fully awakened to, they are called "faculties" in the sense of being taught by the Lord (*indadesita*) and in the sense of being seen by the Lord (*indiṭṭha*).

Furthermore, because some of them were cultivated by that same Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, through the cultivation of the range (*gocarasevanā*), and others through the cultivation of development (*bhāvanāsevanā*), they are also faculties in the sense of being mastered by the Lord (*indajuṭṭha*).
Moreover, these are called *indriyas* also in the sense of sovereignty (*issariyattha*), which is designated as predominance (*ādhipacca*).

For the predominance of the eye and the other [faculties] is established in the occurrence of eye-consciousness and so forth; for when that [faculty] is keen, [the consciousness] is keen, and when it is dull, it is dull.

The twelve answers beginning with "the realm of sensuality" (*kāmadhātu*) are demonstrated by way of the classification of existence (*bhava*). The realm associated with sensual desire (*kāma*), which is termed "sensual desire," is the realm of sensuality; or, the realm that is itself termed "sensual desire" is the realm of sensuality.
The element associated with form after abandoning sense-desire is the fine-material element (*rūpadhātu*); or, the element reckoned as form is the fine-material element.
The element associated with the immaterial after abandoning both sense-desire and form is the immaterial element (*arūpadhātu*); or, the element reckoned as immaterial is the immaterial element.
These same elements are further described by way of the cycle of existence (*bhava*). For that which comes into being (*bhavati*) is called "existence" (*bhava*). [This applies] to perception...

Existence associated with perception is "perceptual existence" (*saññā-bhava*); or, existence accompanied by perception is "perceptual existence"; or, because perception exists within this existence, it is "perceptual existence.

This consists of sense-sphere existence (*kāma-bhava*) excluding the non-perceptual realm, and form-sphere existence (*rūpa-bhava*) excluding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, as well as formless-sphere existence (*arūpa-bhava*). Non-perceptual existence (*asaññā-bhava*) is not perceptual existence; it is a portion of form-sphere existence.

Because of the absence of gross perception (*saññā*), it is "neither-perception" (*nevasaññā*); because of the presence of subtle perception, it is "not non-perception" (*nāsaññā*). Thus, it is "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññā*).

Existence associated with that is "existence of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññābhava*). Alternatively, because of the absence of gross perception and the presence of subtle perception in this existence, it is "existence of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññābhava*); this is a portion of the formless existence (*arūpabhava*).

Existence mixed with one aggregate of form is an existence with one constituent; thus it is "existence with one constituent" (*ekavokārabhava*), and that is precisely the non-percipient existence (*asaññabhava*).

Existence mixed with four immaterial aggregates is an existence with four constituents; thus it is "existence with four constituents" (*catuvokārabhava*), and that is precisely the immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*).

Existence mixed with five aggregates is an existence with five constituents; thus it is "existence with five constituents" (*pañcavokārabhava*), and that consists of both sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) and a portion of fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*).
6. The twelve answers beginning with the first jhāna are explained by way of the attainments of jhāna. Here, "jhāna" is intended merely as the divine abodes (brahmavihāra).
The first jhāna is associated with applied thought (vitakka), sustained thought (vicāra), rapture (pīti), happiness (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā).
The second jhāna is associated with rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind. [The third jhāna] is associated with happiness and one-pointedness of mind.
The third jhāna. The fourth jhāna is associated with equanimity and one-pointedness of mind.

It is called *mettā* because it gladdens (*medati*) or causes to rejoice; the meaning is that it is affectionate. Alternatively, it is *mettā* because it exists in friends, or because it is the activity of a friend.
It is "liberation" (*vimutti*) because it is freed from opposing states and because it is resolutely intent upon its object; thus, it is the liberation of the mind.
Liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*); loving-kindness itself is liberation of mind, thus it is "loving-kindness liberation of mind" (*mettā-cetovimutti*).
Compassion (*karuṇā*) has already had its meaning explained.
Those who possess it rejoice by means of it, or it itself rejoices, or it is simply the act of rejoicing; thus it is "appreciative joy" (*muditā*). "Free from enmity... [and so forth].
It is called *upekkhā* (equanimity) because one looks on with equanimity by abandoning activities such as "may they be" and so forth, and by attaining a state of neutrality.
The three divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) beginning with loving-kindness (*mettā*) are associated with the first three jhānas. The divine abode of equanimity is associated with the fourth jhāna.
It is "infinite" (*ananta*) because there is no end to its pervasiveness. "Infinite space" (*ākāsānanta*) refers to the space resulting from the removal of the kasiṇa.

Space itself is "infinite space" (*ākāsānañca*); that infinite space is the "base" (*āyatana*) in the sense of being a foundation for this jhāna together with its associated states, just as "the base of the gods" is for the gods;
thus it is the "base of infinite space" (*ākāsānañcāyatana*). The attainment of the base of infinite space is the "attainment of the base of infinite space" (*ākāsānañcāyatanasamāpatti*).
Furthermore, because there is no end to it due to its pervasive nature, it is "infinite" (*ananta*); that which has space as its object is [the base of infinite space].

Consciousness (*viññāṇa*). Since it is infinite, it is "infinite space" (*ānañca*); rather than saying "consciousness-infinite-space" (*viññāṇānañca*), it is called "consciousness-sphere" (*viññāṇañca*).

This is a conventional term (*ruḷhisadda*) used here. That consciousness-sphere is the "base" (*āyatana*) in the sense of being a foundation for this jhāna together with its associated states, just as "the base of the gods" (*devāyatanam*) refers to the gods;
thus it is the "base of infinite consciousness" (*viññāṇañcāyatana*). There is nothing whatsoever belonging to this, hence it is "nothingness" (*akiñcana*).
The meaning is that not even a mere fragment of it remains. The state of one who possesses nothing is *ākiñcañña* (nothingness).
This is a designation for the absence of consciousness pertaining to the base of infinite space. That is *ākiñcañña*.

In the sense of being a foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*), this is the "base" (*āyatana*) for the jhāna together with its associated states; thus, like "the base of the gods for the gods," it is called the *ākiñcaññāyatana* (base of nothingness).
Because of the absence of gross perception and the presence of subtle perception, this jhāna—along with its associated states—is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññā*).

And because it is both that "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" and included within the bases of the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the mental-object-base (*dhammāyatana*), it is called the "base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).
Alternatively, the perception that exists here does not perform the function of sharp perception.

Because it is incapable of performing [mental functions], it is "neither-perception" (*nevasaññā*); because it exists in a subtle state due to the presence of a residue of formations, it is "not non-perception" (*nāsaññā*);

thus it is "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññā*). And since this neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a "base" (*āyatana*) in the sense of being the foundation for the remaining phenomena, it is the "base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).
This is a designation for the attainment that has the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) as its object. Not...
In this context, it is only the perception that is of such a nature; however, the feeling is neither-feeling-nor-non-feeling. The consciousness is neither-consciousness-nor-non-consciousness.
The contact is neither-contact-nor-non-contact. This same method applies to the remaining associated mental states.
Yet, this teaching is presented under the heading of perception.
The twelve answers beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*) have been explained by way of the factors of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).

In the sense of being unfit to be fulfilled, bodily misconduct and so forth are called "unfindable" (*avindiya*), meaning they are not to be obtained. Ignorance is that which finds what is unfindable.
Conversely, bodily good conduct and so forth are called "findable" (*vindiya*); ignorance is that which does not find what is findable. [Regarding] the aggregates...

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is so called because it makes unknown the meaning of "clinging" in the case of the *rāsa* (mass), the meaning of "base" in the case of the *āyatanas*, the meaning of "emptiness" in the case of the *dhātus*, the meaning of "sovereignty" in the case of the *indriyas*, and the meaning of "suchness" in the case of the *saccas*.
Furthermore, it is ignorance because it makes unknown the fourfold fourfold meaning—namely, as affliction and so forth—of suffering and the rest.
It is ignorance because, in the beginningless *saṃsāra*, within all the modes of birth, destinies, existences, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings...

It is called ignorance (*avijjā*) because it causes beings to run about; it runs toward things such as "woman" and "man" which do not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), yet it does not run toward things that do exist, such as the aggregates (*khandha*).

Furthermore, ignorance is so called because it conceals the bases and objects of eye-consciousness and the rest, as well as the phenomena of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) and dependently originated (*paṭiccasamuppanna*) states.
It is called formations (*saṅkhāra*) because they form the conditioned (*saṅkhata*). It is called consciousness (*viññāṇa*) because it cognizes.

It bends toward [objects], thus it is "name" (*nāma*); or, it causes [the mind] to bend, thus it is "name. It is affected (*ruppati*), thus it is "form" (*rūpa*). It extends toward the future (*āye tanoti*) and leads what is extended, thus it is a "base" (*āyatana*).
It touches, thus it is "contact" (*phassa*). It experiences, thus it is "feeling" (*vedanā*). It agitates, thus it is "craving" (*taṇhā*). It grasps intensely, thus it is "clinging" (*upādāna*).

It comes into being, or it causes [existence] to develop, thus it is "becoming" (*bhava*). Being born is "birth" (*jāti*). Wearing away is "aging" (*jarā*). They die by means of this, thus it is "death" (*maraṇa*).
7. One hundred and eight [questions] beginning with "suffering" (dukkha) and eight [additional] questions are explained by way of their application to the Four Noble Truths.
For in such passages as "Suffering is to be directly known," there are twenty-four questions based on six tetrads;
and in the series beginning with "The eye is aging-and-death," and "The eye is to be directly known, the ear is to be directly known," and so forth, [the question of] birth—
These have been stated by connecting them with one hundred and ninety-five answers ending with the phrase "to be directly known.
There are one hundred and ninety-four tetrads; based on these tetrads, there are seven hundred and eighty answers.
In the tetrad beginning with "Old age and death are to be directly known," there are four answers; thus, all eight [tetrads] are accounted for.
And there are eight hundred questions and answers here. Furthermore, it should be understood that for each respective phenomenon, the predominant condition is "origination" (samudaya).
Nibbāna, which is empty of all conditioned formations (saṅkhāra), should be understood as "cessation" (nirodha).

This is said with reference to the absence of even the three supramundane faculties (lokuttarindriya), such as the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anaññātaññassāmītindriya) and the others, therein.
The cessation of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*) and so forth is thus appropriate.

Furthermore, in all instances, the "way leading to cessation" (*nirodhagāminī paṭipadā*) is exclusively the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). For when it is stated in this way, since the designation "path" can also apply to the fruits (*phala*), it is likewise appropriate for the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*) and the faculty of one who has known (*aññātāvindriya*).
Again, eight hundred and eight questions and answers have been set forth by way of the full understanding (*pariññā*) of suffering and the other truths, and their respective functions (*attha*).
Furthermore, one hundred and eight questions and answers are set forth by way of the meaning of the full understanding and penetration of suffering and the other truths.
Full understanding (*pariññā*) is "penetration" (*paṭivedha*) in the sense that it is to be penetrated; thus, it is "full-understanding-penetration.
The meaning of this full-understanding-penetration is "the meaning of full-understanding-penetration."

8. Furthermore, by joining those same two hundred and two items beginning with suffering and ending with aging-and-death with each of the seven sets of seven terms beginning with origin, one thousand six hundred and twenty questions are demonstrated according to the two hundred and eight groups of eight.
In this context, the condition that is predominant is "origin" (samudaya).
Its cessation is the cessation of the origin. Desire itself is lust; thus, "lustful desire" refers to the lustful desire for suffering due to the perception of pleasure in what is suffering.
Its cessation is the cessation of lustful desire. The pleasure and joy that arise dependent upon suffering is the gratification of suffering.
The impermanence of suffering, the quality of changeability of suffering, [is the danger of suffering].
The danger [is as follows]: the removal of desire and lust for suffering, the abandoning of desire and lust for suffering, is the escape from suffering.
Furthermore, because of the statement, "Whatever is existent, conditioned, and dependently arisen—its cessation is the escape," Nibbāna alone is the escape from suffering.
[It is characterized by] the cessation of suffering, the cessation of its origin, and the cessation of desire and lust.

It should be understood that Nibbāna alone is spoken of in these four instances by various synonymous expressions, by way of being the opposite of various conditioned phenomena. However, some say: "With the arising of nutriment there is the arising of suffering;

with the cessation of nutriment there is the cessation of suffering"—this is the cessation of the origin by way of its own inherent nature (*sarasavasena*); or else, it is by seeing the rise and fall [of things].
They say: "The cessation of origination together with insight is the path, the cessation of desire and lust.
But when this is said, since supramundane faculties do not involve insight, it would not be common to all; therefore, the method stated first should be adopted.
For among the supramundane faculties, because of the very absence of desire and lust, it is logical that there is the cessation of desire and lust.

Just as desire and lust for the body itself entails desire and lust for the parts of the body such as the hair and so forth, so too, by virtue of desire and lust for that which is subject to aging and death, desire and lust for aging and death themselves are already established. In this same way, the gratification and the danger should also be applied.
Furthermore, the two hundred and two sections beginning with suffering and ending with aging and death [should be analyzed] by means of the six [truths], beginning with the origin.
Having applied [the analysis] by way of six bases, according to two hundred and two sets of seven, one thousand four hundred and fourteen answers have been demonstrated. 9.
Now, the two hundred and one terms beginning with "form" and ending with "aging-and-death," by way of the seven contemplations—
Having thus applied [the analysis], first the seven contemplations beginning with the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) are explained.
Together with all those seven basic explanations of pure contemplation, they total one thousand four hundred and fourteen explanations.
The contemplation that [views things] as "impermanent" is the contemplation of impermanence; it is the antidote to the perception of permanence.
Contemplation as suffering is the contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*). It is the opposite of the perception of pleasure.

Contemplation as non-self is the contemplation of non-self (*anattānupassanā*). It is the opposite of the perception of self. Because of the fulfillment of these three contemplations, one becomes disenchanted; thus, it is "disenchantment" (*nibbidā*).
Since it is both disenchantment and a contemplation, it is "contemplation of disenchantment" (*nibbidānupassanā*). It is the opposite of delight (*nandi*). Of the four...
It is called "fading away" (*virāga*) because one fades away through the fulfillment of the contemplations; it is both fading away and a contemplation, thus it is the "contemplation of fading away.
It is the antidote to lust. It is called "cessation" (*nirodha*) because one brings lust to cessation through the fulfillment of the five contemplations;
it is both cessation and a contemplation, thus it is the "contemplation of cessation. It is the antidote to the origin [of suffering]. Through the six contemplations...

It is called "relinquishment" (*paṭinissagga*) because one relinquishes through its fulfillment. It is "contemplation of relinquishment" (*paṭinissaggānupassanā*) because it is both relinquishment and contemplation.

It is the opposite of grasping (*ādāna*). Although the supramundane faculties do not fall within the scope of insight (*vipassanā*), because of the statement, "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
all conditioned phenomena are suffering; all phenomena are non-self," they too possess the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
In that context, because of the absence of the perception of permanence, pleasure, and self, as well as delight and lust,
these [seven contemplations] are to be understood as being joined with those [three] as well— due to the contemplation of them as having cessation,

and due to the occurrence of relinquishment, renunciation, and leaping forward into renunciation. When things possessing aging and death are seen as impermanent and so forth, aging and death themselves are also [seen] as impermanent and so forth.
It is called "seen": one who becomes disenchanted with and detached from those possessed of aging and death becomes disenchanted and detached from aging and death;
when those possessed of aging and death are seen as subject to cessation, aging and death itself is called "seen" as subject to cessation;
and one who relinquishes those possessed of aging and death is indeed relinquishing aging and death itself.
It should be understood that the seven contemplations have been applied to aging and death.

10. Now, by way of the five objects—arising and so forth—which serve as the basis for the knowledge of danger (*ādīnavañāṇa*), fifteen answers concerning arising and its synonyms have been demonstrated; [likewise] for the knowledge of the state of peace (*santipadañāṇa*).
Fifteen answers beginning with "non-arising" (anuppāda) have been demonstrated by way of having as their object the opposites of those [states].
Furthermore, by joining those very same terms—arising, non-arising, and so forth—in pairs, thirty answers have been demonstrated.
Thus, in this method, there are sixty answers in total. Therein, "arising" (uppāda) refers to the condition of previous karma.
"Arising" here refers to rebirth. "Occurrence" refers to the process of that which has thus arisen. "The sign" refers to the sign of all formations (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*).
For to the practitioner, formations appear as if they possess a shape; therefore, they are called "the sign.
"Accumulation" refers to the kamma that serves as the cause for future rebirth-linking. For it is called "accumulation" in the sense of actively constructing (*abhisaṅkharaṇa*).
"Rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhi*) means arising in the future. For it is called "rebirth-linking" because it links one to another existence (*bhava*).
"Destiny" (*gati*) refers to the state of existence in which that rebirth-linking occurs; for it is called "destiny" because it is that which is to be gone to.

"Generation" (*nibbatti*) is the production of the aggregates (*khandha*). "Arising" (*upapatti*) is what is expressed by the phrase, "of one who has attained [meditative absorption] or of one who has been reborn."

The occurrence of fruition (*vipāka-pavatti*). "Birth" (*jāti*) means arising. It is the first manifestation of whichever aggregates appear for beings as they are being reborn in various places. "Aging" (*jarā*) means decaying. It is twofold:

the characteristic of the conditioned (*saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa*), which consists of the characteristic of change-while-standing (*ṭhitaññathatta*); and that which is recognized as brokenness and so forth, the state of antiquity of the aggregates included within a single existence throughout their continuity.

And that is what is intended here. "Disease" (*byādhi*) refers to an eightfold affliction arising from the disturbance of the elements (*dhātu*), conditioned by bile, phlegm, wind, their combination, seasonal changes, improper conduct, external assault, and the ripening of kamma.
It is called "disease" because it brings about various sufferings and consumes them; or else, it is called "disease" because it afflicts, torments, or causes trembling.
"Death" (*maraṇa*) is so called because beings die by means of it. It is twofold, being characterized by the mark of decay (*vaya*).

The characteristic of the conditioned (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*) and the interruption of the continuity of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) included within a single existence—this is what is intended here.
Sorrow (*soka*) is grieving; it is the burning of the mind in one who is afflicted by calamities concerning relatives, wealth, illness, virtue, or views.

Lamentation (*parideva*) is wailing; it is the verbal outburst of one who is afflicted by those very same calamities, such as the loss of relatives. Despair (*upāyāsa*) is intense exhaustion; [it is the exhaustion] of one who is afflicted by those very same calamities, such as the loss of relatives.

In one who is touched by it, there is indeed hatred intensified by extreme mental suffering. And herein, only the five beginning with arising (*uppāda*) are stated as the objective basis for the knowledge of danger (*ādīnavañāṇa*);
the rest are synonyms for them. For "origination" (*nibbatti*) is a synonym for arising;

"birth" (*jāti*) is a synonym for rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*); this pair, "destiny" (*gati*) and "reappearance" (*upapatti*), refers to the process of existence (*pavatta*); and "aging" (*jarā*) and so forth refer to the signs (*nimitta*).
However, by means of the terms "non-arising" and so forth, it is Nibbāna itself that is expressed.
Furthermore, by joining those same sixty terms—arising, non-arising, and so on—with the pair of terms "suffering" and "happiness," there are sixty answers;

by joining them with the pair of terms "fear" and "security," there are sixty answers; and by joining them with the pair of terms "with material gain" and "without material gain," there are sixty [answers].
By joining these with the terms "formations" (*saṅkhāra*) and "Nibbāna," sixty answers are demonstrated.
Therein, it is "suffering" (*dukkha*) because of its impermanence. It is "pleasure" (*sukha*) by way of being the opposite of suffering. That which is suffering is fear (*bhaya*).

It is "security" (*khema*) by way of being the opposite of fear. That which is fear is "carnal" (*sāmisa*) because it is not liberated from the bait of the round of existence (*vaṭṭāmisaloka-āmisehi*).
It is "unworldly" (*nirāmisa*) because it is the opposite of the worldly (*sāmisa*). That which is worldly is merely a conditioned formation (*saṅkhāra*).
It is *nibbāna* because it is peaceful due to being the opposite of formations; for formations are aflame, whereas *nibbāna* is peaceful.
Thus, with reference to its occurrence in various such modes—as the mode of suffering, the mode of fear, the mode of the worldly, and the mode of formations—it is described in those respective ways.
"It should be understood as 'said'.
11. The thirty-one answers beginning with "the sense of embracing" (pariggaha) are demonstrated by way of the moment of the Noble Path (ariyamagga).
For the states associated with the Noble Path are "embraced" (pariggaha) from the very beginning for the purpose of their arising; such is their intrinsic nature (sabhāva).

The sense of embracing (*pariggaha-ṭṭha*). The sense of being an attendant (*parivāra-ṭṭha*) by virtue of their mutual state of being attendants to one another. The sense of fulfillment (*paripūra-ṭṭha*) by virtue of the completion of development.
The sense of one-pointedness (*ekagga-ṭṭha*) with respect to the grasping of a single object through concentration (*samādhi*) of those very [factors].

The sense of non-distraction (*avikkhepa-ṭṭha*) with respect to the absence of distraction toward various objects. The sense of exertion (*paggaha-ṭṭha*) by virtue of energy (*vīriya*). By virtue of concentration...

The sense of non-diffusion is the state of not being scattered, like bath-powder by water. The sense of being untroubled is due to its being undisturbed through connection with concentration (*samādhi*).

The sense of immovability is due to its being unshakable. "By way of establishing in unity" means both by way of connection with concentration and by way of being firmly established upon a single object.
The sense of being established is the sense of being settled upon the object with an unwavering state.

It has the sense of an object by way of being the objective support for that [consciousness] which has Nibbāna as its object. It has the sense of a range by way of being the sphere of unimpeded movement therein.

It has the sense of abandoning in the case of Nibbāna by way of being the state of escape and relinquishment. It has the sense of relinquishing in the case of the Noble Path by way of the abandonment of the defilements.
It has the sense of emergence by way of emerging from both sides. It has the sense of turning away by way of turning back from signs and from the process [of existence].

The sense of turning back (*nivattanaṭṭha*). The sense of peace (*santaṭṭha*) because of being extinguished (*nibbutattā*). The sense of excellence (*paṇītaṭṭha*) because of being insatiable and supreme.

The sense of liberation (*vimuttaṭṭha*) because of being freed from defilements and because of being intent upon the object. The sense of being taintless (*anāsavaṭṭha*) because of being utterly pure by virtue of not being within the domain of the taints (*āsavā*).

The sense of crossing over (*taraṇaṭṭha*) by means of transcending the wilderness of defilements and the wilderness of saṃsāra. By the absence of the signs of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāranimitta*)...

The meaning of the signless (*animitta*). The meaning of the wishless (*appaṇihita*) by virtue of the absence of longing through craving. The meaning of emptiness (*suññata*) by virtue of the absence of a self-essence.
The meaning of single flavor (*ekarasa*) due to the single flavor of liberation, or due to the single flavor of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

The meaning of non-excess of one over the other between serenity and insight. The meaning of their yoke-mate union (*yuganaddha*). [This occurs] upon the emergence of the Noble Path from conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*).

The meaning of departure (*niyyāna-ṭṭha*). The meaning of cause (*hetu-ṭṭha*) by way of leading to Nibbāna. The meaning of seeing (*dassana-ṭṭha*) by way of making Nibbāna manifest. The meaning of predominance (*ādhipateyya-ṭṭha*) by way of its sovereign nature. 12.
The four answers beginning with “tranquility” (*samatha*) are explained by way of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

It is the meaning of contemplation (*anupassana-ṭṭha*) because of contemplating [the objects] one by one by way of impermanence (*anicca*) and so forth. By way of the single flavor (*ekarasa-bhāva*) of the pair of serenity and insight joined in yoke (*yuganaddha*),...
The meaning of non-transgression. The nine answers beginning with "training" (sikkhā) are explained by way of the beginning, middle, and end of the Noble Path.
It is called "training" because it is that which should be trained in; it is the "meaning of undertaking" because it is to be undertaken.

And because it is the basis for the occurrence of meditation upon the object taken up by way of a meditation subject once one is established in virtue, and because it is the range [of practice], it is the "meaning of domain."

The sense-sphere as an object. At the time of serenity or the time of insight, the sense of exertion—that is, the sense of uplifting—is the application of the factors of enlightenment consisting of investigation of phenomena, energy, and rapture, for the purpose of uplifting a mind that has become sluggish due to indolence.

The sense of restraint—that is, the sense of settling—is the application of the factors of enlightenment consisting of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, for the purpose of settling a mind that has become agitated due to restlessness.
"Of both purified" means of those purified from both sides, namely, from the side of the sluggish and the agitated.

The meaning is "having restrained the minds that are purified. It should be understood that the plural number is used with reference to the minds occurring in a continuous stream while remaining in a state of equipoise.
The sense of "looking on with equanimity" is the absence of active intervention in the processes of encouragement and discouragement.
The sense of "attaining distinction through development" is by way of a mind proceeding in equilibrium. By way of the manifestation of the Noble Path—
It has the sense of penetration into the higher [realms]. It has the sense of the clear realization of the truths by way of the penetration of the four truths accomplished through the Noble Path.
It has the sense of establishing in cessation by way of the attainment of fruition; for that [attainment] establishes the person possessing it in Nibbāna, which is termed "cessation."

The five answers beginning with the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) are stated by way of the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*). The meaning of "resolute confidence" (*adhimokkha*) is the sense of being resolved.
The meaning of "establishment" (*upaṭṭhāna*) is the sense of being established by approaching the object. The meaning of "seeing" (*dassana*) is the sense of observing the intrinsic nature.
The five answers beginning with the power of faith (*saddhābala*) are demonstrated by way of the meaning of "power" (*bala*). Faith itself, in the sense of being unshakable...
"Balanti" means the power of faith (*saddhābala*). "Assaddhiye" means by means of lack of faith (*assaddhiya*). And "lack of faith" (*assaddhiya*) is a mental state that is the opposite of faith.

"Akampiyaṭṭho" means the sense of being unshakable; the meaning is that it cannot be shaken. "Kosajje" means by means of sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*), which is designated as the state of indolence (*kusītabhāva*). "Pamāde" means by means of a mental state that is the opposite of mindfulness (*satipaṭipakkha*). "Uddhacce" means...
By restlessness, which is reckoned as non-quiescence. By ignorance means by delusion.

The seven answers beginning with the mindfulness enlightenment factor (*satisambojjhaṅga*) are explained by way of the meaning of "enlightenment factor" (*bojjhaṅga*). A factor of one who is awakening is an enlightenment factor (*bojjhaṅga*). An enlightenment factor that is praised and beautiful is a sublime enlightenment factor (*sambojjhaṅga*);
mindfulness itself as a sublime enlightenment factor is the mindfulness enlightenment factor (*satisambojjhaṅga*). One investigates the phenomena (*dhamma*).

Investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicaya*): this is a name for wisdom (*paññā*). Its meaning is "discernment" (*pavicaya*), which is the sense of investigation. Rapture (*pīti*): it raptures, thus it is rapture. Its meaning is "pervasion," which is the sense of spreading.
Tranquility (*passaddhi*): it is the act of calming; its meaning is "subsiding," which is the sense of being free from distress.

Equanimity (*upekkhā*): it views from a position of proximity; the meaning is that it views with impartiality, having become free from partiality. Here, it refers to equanimity as specific neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).
"Equanimity as a factor of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅgupekkhā*) is also its name. Its characteristic is "evenly bearing," hence its meaning is "reflective discernment.
The eight answers beginning with "right view" are explained by way of the Path.
It is right view because it sees rightly, or because they see rightly by means of it; it is "right view" because it is a praised or beautiful view. Of that right view.
One intends rightly, or they intend rightly by means of that; it is a praiseworthy or beautiful intention, thus it is *sammā-saṅkappa*.
The meaning of "placing upon" (*abhiropana*) is the meaning of placing the mind upon its object. There is also a reading: "the meaning of fixing firmly upon the object" (*ārammaṇābhiniropana*).
One speaks rightly, or they speak rightly by means of that; it is speech that is praiseworthy or beautiful, thus it is *sammā-vācā*. [This refers to] the abstention from wrong speech.
This is the name. "The sense of embracing" (*pariggahaṭṭha*) means the sense of embracing the fourfold restraint of speech.

It is "right action" (*sammākamma*) because it is performed rightly, or because they perform it rightly by means of it, or because it is praised and beautiful action; "right-action-path" (*sammākammanta*) is simply right action.
This is the name for the abstention from wrong-action-paths. "The sense of origination" (*samuṭṭhānaṭṭha*) means the sense of origination through the threefold restraint of body.
One lives rightly, or they live rightly by means of it; right livelihood is a praiseworthy or beautiful way of life. This is the name for the abstention from wrong livelihood.
"In the sense of purification" means in the sense of being completely pure. One exerts oneself rightly, or they exert themselves rightly by means of it;
right effort is a praiseworthy or beautiful exertion. One remembers rightly, or they remember rightly by means of it; [right mindfulness is] praiseworthy...

Right mindfulness (*sammāsati*) is so called because it is beautiful or because it is present. Right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*) is so called because one is rightly concentrated by means of it, or because it is a praised and beautiful concentration.
These ten explanations, beginning with the faculties (*indriya*), have been set forth collectively according to their successive order. The sense of predominance (*ādhipateyyaṭṭha*)...
The meaning of "sovereignty" (*adhipati*) is by way of exercising lordship (*indaṭṭha-karaṇa*). The meaning of "unshakability" (*akampiya*) is the sense of being impossible for opposites to shake.
The meaning of "outlet" (*niyyāna*) is the sense of emerging from both worldly and supramundane opposites.

The meaning of "cause" (*hetu*) is either that right view and so forth are the causes for the abandoning of wrong view and so forth, or that all [eight] factors beginning with right view are the causes for reaching Nibbāna.

Or it is so called because it is the cause (*hetu*) [of mindfulness]. It is "establishment" (*upaṭṭhāna*) because it establishes itself by leaping upon and plunging into the objects that are the foundations of mindfulness.
Thus, "foundation of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*) is simply mindfulness itself as establishment.

Furthermore, its fourfold division arises from its occurrence in relation to the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, by way of grasping the aspects of foulness, suffering, impermanence, and non-self, and by way of accomplishing the task of abandoning the perceptions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self.
These are found among various types of consciousness in the preliminary stage; however, at the moment of the Path, mindfulness alone receives four names.
Regarding the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*): it is called *padhāna* because one exerts by means of it; a beautiful exertion is a "right exertion" (*sammappadhāna*).
Alternatively, it is a "right exertion" because one exerts rightly by means of it; or else, it is both beautiful because it is free from the deformity of the defilements and an exertion.
It is called "right striving" (*sammappadhāna*) because it brings about a state of excellence by producing welfare and happiness, or because it effects a state of preeminence.

This is a designation for energy (*vīriya*). Furthermore, it functions in four ways by accomplishing the tasks of abandoning unwholesome states that have arisen, preventing the arising of those not yet arisen, producing wholesome states not yet arisen, and maintaining those already arisen.
There is a distinction. These [terms] are also found in various states of consciousness during the prior stage; however, at the moment of the Path (magga-khaṇa), a single energy receives four names.

"The sense of striving" (padahanaṭṭho) means the sense of exertion. There is also a reading "the sense of effort" (padhānaṭṭho), which has the same meaning. Regarding "bases of success" (iddhipādānaṃ):
here, in the case of desire, energy, consciousness, and investigation, each one succeeds, thus it is "success" (iddhi); it is accomplished.

The meaning is "it is accomplished. Or else, it is called *iddhi* because by means of it beings (*sattā*) succeed (*ijjhanti*), become successful (*iddhā*), prosperous (*vuddhā*), and reach the highest excellence (*ukkaṃsagatā*).

According to the first sense, *iddhipāda* is simply *iddhi* that is a foot (*pāda*); the meaning is "a portion of success" (*iddhikoṭṭhāsa*). According to the second sense, it is the foot of success, hence *iddhipāda*.
"Foot" (*pāda*) means a foundation (*patiṭṭhā*), the meaning being "the means for attainment" (*adhigamūpāya*). For by means of that, [one proceeds] higher and higher...
They reach and attain the supernormal power (iddhi) known as "distinction" (visesa); therefore, it is called "pāda.

These factors, beginning with zeal (chanda), are found in various states of consciousness during the preliminary stage by way of predominance; however, at the moment of the Path (magga-khaṇa), they are all found together.
The sense of "ijjhana" means the sense of accomplishment or the sense of establishment. "Of the truths" (saccānaṃ) refers to the four Noble Truths. The sense of "tatha" means...
The meaning of "according to its own nature" (*yathāsabhāvaṭṭho*). These eight answers are a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.

"Of the applications" (*payogānaṃ*) means of the four applications of the noble paths. "The meaning of subsidedness" (*paṭippassaddhaṭṭho*) refers to the meaning of subsidedness of the four noble fruits.
For the application of the path is subsided at the moment of the fruit because its task has been completed. [This is] due to the arising of the fruit from the applications of the path.
Or it is the state of subsidence. "The meaning of the realization of the fruits" means the act of making the noble fruits directly evident by way of reviewing them;
thus, the realization of the object has been stated, or else the realization of acquisition at the moment of the fruit.
The five answers beginning with "applied thought" (vitakka) are demonstrated by way of the jhāna factors. "Applied thought" (vitakka) is the act of applying the mind.
"They infer" is what is meant. "Investigation" (vicāra) means wandering about; "thorough wandering" is what is meant.

"The sense of close investigation" (upavicāraṭṭha) is the sense of continuous rubbing. "The sense of cohesion" (abhisandanaṭṭha) is the sense of moistening, which is the sense of one-pointedness of mind by way of concentration.
The fifteen answers beginning with "adverting" are demonstrated by way of miscellaneous topics. [These occur] in the five doors and the mind door.
The function of adverting belongs to the two types of consciousness that direct the stream of consciousness toward an object other than the life-continuum's (bhavaṅga) object.
The function of consciousness is cognizing. The function of wisdom is understanding. The function of perception is perceiving. The function of concentration is unification;

for in the second jhāna, concentration arises as one [undisturbed by] applied thought and sustained thought, and thus it is called "unified" (ekodi). It is from applied thought and sustained thought...
The meaning is that because it is not overcome [by hindrances], it arises as supreme and best; for even in the world, one who is best is called "one" (*eko*).
Alternatively, it is also appropriate to say that it arises "alone" (*eko*) in the sense of being without a companion, being devoid of applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*).
Or again, since all wholesome concentration is the antidote to the hindrances and so forth, or specifically to restlessness (*uddhacca*), it arises as supreme because it is not overcome by them.
"Or, being devoid of those [defilements], he arises alone"—thus it is appropriate to call him "solitary" (*ekodi*).

"The meaning of what is known by direct knowledge" (*abhiññāya ñātaṭṭho*) is the meaning of knowing the intrinsic nature through the full understanding of the known (*ñātapariññā*). "The meaning of investigating through full understanding" (*pariññāya tīraṇaṭṭho*) is the meaning of examining [the aggregates] as impermanent and so forth through the full understanding of investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*).
"The meaning of relinquishing through abandoning" (*pahānassa pariccāgaṭṭho*) is the meaning of abandoning the opposites through the full understanding of abandoning (*pahānapariññā*).
The sense of single flavor belongs to development proceeding evenly. The sense of touching is the sense of contacting and the sense of finding.

The sense of aggregates is by way of oppression, bearing a burden, and so forth. The sense of elements is by way of emptiness and so forth. The sense of bases is by way of their respective boundaries, spheres, and so forth.
The sense of the conditioned is by way of being produced through the coming together of conditions. The sense of the unconditioned is by way of the opposite of that.
14. Fifteen answers beginning with "the station of consciousness" (*cittatṭha*) are explained in connection with consciousness.
Regarding the term "station of consciousness": here, it is called *citta* because it "thinks" (*cinoti*) the object; the meaning is that it "cognizes.

Furthermore, that which is impulsion (*javana*) is also called *citta* because it "accumulates" its own continuity by way of the impulsion-process. That which is fruition (*vipāka*) [is so called] because of the karmic defilements...

It is called *citta* because it cognizes (*cināti*); it is also *citta* because everything, in its respective way, possesses the quality of being conscious (*cittatā*), and because it performs the function of consciousness (*cittakaraṇatā*);

furthermore, it is *citta* because it accumulates (*cinoti*) the suffering of *saṃsāra*, which is the condition for the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). Thus, the meaning of *citta* is "consciousness" in the sense of cognizing objects and so forth.
It is "immediate" (*anantara*) because there is no interval between its arising and the arising of its fruit; of that which is immediate...
The state is "immediacy" (*ānantariya*); the immediacy of consciousness is "consciousness-immediacy" (*cittānantariya*), which is the meaning of consciousness-immediacy.

The intention is that—excluding the death-consciousness of an Arahant—it is the capacity of any consciousness that has ceased immediately prior to give rise to a subsequent consciousness, and the capacity of the path-consciousness to give rise to its fruit immediately thereafter. Of consciousness...

The meaning of emergence (*vuṭṭhānaṭṭha*) is the meaning of emerging from the sign for the change-of-lineage consciousness, and the meaning of emerging from both the sign and the occurrence [of defilements] for the path-consciousness.
The meaning of turning away (*vivaṭṭanaṭṭha*) of the mind is the meaning of turning away toward Nibbāna for those two types of consciousness once they have emerged as previously described.
The meaning of cause (*hetuṭṭha*) of the mind is the meaning of cause for the nine causes that serve as the causal conditions for the mind. Of the mind...
The meaning of condition (*paccayaṭṭha*) refers to the meaning of the conditions for consciousness, such as the various bases, objects, and so forth.
The meaning of the basis (*vatthuṭṭha*) for consciousness refers to the meaning of the bases that serve as the foundation for consciousness, namely the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and heart-bases.
The meaning of the plane (*bhūmaṭṭha*) for consciousness refers to the sense-sphere plane and so forth, by way of the location where consciousness arises. [The meaning] of consciousness...

The sense of object (*ārammaṇattha*) means the sense of objects such as visible forms and so forth. The sense of range (*gocarāttha*) is in the sense of being the place where the mind ranges over an object that has been familiarized.
The sense of conduct (*cariyattha*) is by way of the mental behavior (*viññāṇacariyā*) described above; alternatively, the sense of conduct is the sense of the manifestation of application.

The sense of having gone (*gatāttha*) is in the sense of grasping objects whether distant or near, even though there is no actual physical movement of the mind. The sense of directing (*abhinīhārāttha*)...
The meaning of directing the mind is the leading forth of the mind for the purpose of attending to an object other than the one already grasped.
The meaning of the mind’s outlet is the meaning of the path-consciousness’s emergence from the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
The meaning of the mind’s escape is, according to the method stated in such passages as, “For one who has attained renunciation, the mind has escaped from sensual desire,” and so forth.
15. Forty-two answers beginning with "unity" (ekatta) are demonstrated in connection with unity.

"In unity" means in the unity of the object; the sense is "having a single object. By way of the first jhāna, it has the sense of launching forth. By way of the second jhāna, it has the sense of confidence.
By way of the third jhāna, it has the sense of composure. By way of the fourth jhāna, it has the sense of liberation.
The meaning of "seeing this as peaceful" is by way of reviewing. The five specific masteries over concentration are:

the state of being made a vehicle, the state of being made a foundation, the state of being established, the state of being cultivated, and the state of being familiarized. The "state of being made a vehicle" means it has been made like a suitable vehicle.

The "state of being made a foundation" means it has been made like a foundation in the sense of being a support. The "state of being established" means the state of being present. The "state of being cultivated" means [cultivated] on all sides.
The state of being well-undertaken (*susamāraddhaṭṭho*): this means the state of being properly undertaken (*suṭṭhu samāraddhaṭṭho*), that is, the state of being well-performed (*sukataṭṭho*).
Alternatively, the five terms may be applied in sequence according to the mastery of adverting, entering, resolving, emerging, and reviewing.

At the time when the development of the kasiṇa and other objects reaches its culmination, it is the state of the mind and mental factors being fully grasped, accompanied, and perfected. Because of their very being rightly concentrated, they [are established] upon a single object.
The sense of convergence is the sense of synthesis. The sense of resolution is the sense of establishing by way of overcoming the object through the attainment of power in those very [factors].
The sense of repetition is the sense of practicing with care from the beginning, whether in serenity or insight.
The sense of development is by way of increasing. The sense of cultivation is by way of doing again and again. Of that which has been cultivated...

The sense of "well-arisen" (*susamuggata*) is by way of having arisen properly. The sense of "well-liberated" (*suvimutta*) is by way of being well-freed from opposites and by way of being well-aimed at the object for one who has so arisen.

The four terms beginning with the sense of "awakening" (*bujjhana*) are stated by way of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*). [This refers to] the factors of enlightenment of the stream-entry path.

It is the sense of awakening. It is the sense of subsequent awakening for the factors of enlightenment of the once-return path. It is the sense of full awakening for the factors of enlightenment of the non-return path.
It is the sense of complete awakening for the factors of enlightenment of the arahant path. Alternatively, it is the sense of awakening for the factors of enlightenment of insight;
the sense of subsequent awakening for the factors of enlightenment of the path of seeing; and [the sense of full awakening] for the factors of enlightenment of the path of development.

The meaning of awakening. The meaning of fully awakening to the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). According to the method already stated, the four meanings beginning with "awakening" (bodhana) should be understood for the factors of enlightenment through their performing the awakening and so forth for each respective individual.
For the individual who has received the name "the Awakened One" (Bodhi) by way of the meaning of awakening to those very factors of enlightenment already mentioned—
They are called "factors of enlightenment" (bodhipakkhiyā) because they exist on the side of enlightenment.

For those very factors of enlightenment already mentioned, four meanings should be understood: the meaning of illumination (*jotana*) by way of insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*); the meaning of shining forth, further shining forth, counter-shining forth, and fully shining forth (*ujjotana-anujjotana-paṭijotana-sañjotana*) by way of the wisdom of the four paths in their respective order; or alternatively, the meaning of illumination and so forth by way of the wisdom of the four paths in their respective order.
The sense of illumination should be understood by way of the wisdom of the fruit (*phalapaññā*).
16. The eighteen answers beginning with the sense of inflaming (*patāpana*) are demonstrated by way of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).
For the Noble Path is called "inflaming" because when it arises in someone, it inflames, illuminates, and causes that person to shine; such is its sense of inflaming.
It has the sense of self-radiance through its exceedingly brilliant nature. It has the sense of scorching by means of the drying up of the defilements (*kilesa*).

It has the sense of being stainless because it takes stainless *nibbāna* as its object. It has the sense of being pure due to the absence of associated stains. It has the sense of being immaculate due to the absence of stains in the act of making [the object] its focus.
Alternatively, the path of stream-entry has the sense of being stainless; the paths of once-returning and non-returning have the sense of being pure.

The meaning of the path of arahantship is stainlessness (*nimmala*). Alternatively, the meaning of the disciple’s path is immaculate (*amala*); the meaning of the paccekabuddha’s path is pure (*vimala*);
and the meaning of the perfectly enlightened Buddha’s path is stainless (*nimmala*). It has the sense of evenness (*sama*) by virtue of the absence of the unevenness of the defilements.

It has the sense of a meeting point (*samaya*) in the sense of the abandoning of defilements, as in such passages as “through the right realization of conceit,” and so forth. [It is so called] with respect to what are reckoned as suppression, substitution by opposites, eradication, subsiding, and escape.

Among the five kinds of seclusion (*viveka*), because it is the seclusion of total eradication (*samuccheda-viveka*), it has the sense of being secluded (*vivekaṭṭha*) and the sense of absence (*vinābhāvaṭṭha*). Because one dwells in *nibbāna*, which is the seclusion of escape (*nissaraṇa-viveka*), it has the sense of dwelling in seclusion (*vivekacariyaṭṭha*).

Among the five kinds of fading away (*virāga*), because it is the fading away of total eradication (*samuccheda-virāga*), it has the sense of fading away (*virāgaṭṭha*) and the sense of becoming free from passion (*virajjanaṭṭha*).

Because one dwells in *nibbāna*, which is the fading away of escape (*nissaraṇa-virāga*), it has the sense of dwelling in fading away (*virāgacariyaṭṭha*). Among the five kinds of cessation (*nirodha*), because it is the cessation of total eradication (*samuccheda-nirodha*)...
The meaning of cessation (*nirodha*). The meaning of the practice of cessation (*nirodhacariyā*) because of proceeding toward Nibbāna, which is the cessation of suffering.

The meaning of relinquishment (*vosagga*) because of its nature as renunciation, leaping forward, and surrender. For the Noble Path is a relinquishment and surrender through the abandoning of defilements by means of their total eradication;

it is also a surrender through leaping forward toward Nibbāna by taking it as its object. Insight (*vipassanā*), however, [is a relinquishment] through the abandoning of defilements by way of "partial eradication" (*tadaṅgappahāna*).

The meaning of relinquishment (*vosagga*) is the relinquishing of what is to be abandoned. The meaning of leaping forward (*pakkhandana*) is the leaping forward into *nibbāna* by virtue of being inclined toward it.
That [meaning] is not intended here. The meaning of the practice of relinquishment (*vosaggacariya*) is because one proceeds by way of the state of relinquishment.

The meaning of liberation (*vimutta*) is because of liberation through complete cutting off (*samuccheda-vimutti*) among the five kinds of liberation. The meaning of the practice of liberation (*vimutticariya*) is because one proceeds within the liberation that is escape (*nissaraṇa-vimutti*).
In the four bases of psychic power (iddhipāda) known as desire, energy, mind, and investigation, ten [answers] are set forth for each individual base;
thus, by way of the four bases of psychic power, forty answers are demonstrated, beginning with "the meaning of desire" (chandaṭṭha).

The meaning of desire is the sense of wishing-to-do. At the time of commencing development, having made desire the primary factor, it has the sense of being the root. By way of providing a foundation for the co-nascent states...

The meaning of "foot" (*padaṭṭha*). Alternatively, the reading is *padaṭṭho*. Because they are the bases of success (*iddhipāda*), they have the sense of being preeminent through their sovereign nature.
