At the time of application, they have the sense of succeeding (*ijjhana*). Through association with faith, they have the sense of resolution (*adhimokkha*). Through association with energy, they have the sense of exertion (*paggaha*). Through association with mindfulness, they have the sense of establishment (*upaṭṭhāna*).

Through association with concentration, they have the sense of non-distraction (*avikkhepa*). Through association with wisdom, they have the sense of seeing (*dassana*). [And] the sense of exertion (*paggaha*).
The meaning of energy (*vīriya*): when taken as the head [of the path] at the time of beginning cultivation, it has the sense of being the root;

because of its own nature as energy, it has the sense of exertion (*paggaha*). The sense of mind (*citta*) consists of the sense of cognizing (*cintana*) and so forth; when taken as the head at the time of beginning cultivation, it has the sense of being the root.

The sense of investigation (*vīmaṃsā*) is the sense of examining (*upaparikkhana*); when taken as the head at the time of beginning cultivation, it has the sense of being the root; because of its own nature as investigation, it has the sense of seeing (*dassana*).

17. The sixteen explanations beginning with “the sense of oppression of suffering” are demonstrated by way of the true characteristics (*tathalakkhaṇa*) of the Truths. The sense of oppression is through the very seeing of suffering. The sense of the conditioned is through the seeing of the origin as the accumulation of suffering.

The sense of torment is through the seeing of the path, which is cool and removes the burning of all defilements. The sense of changelessness is through the seeing of cessation as having the nature of non-alteration.
The meaning of change; by the very seeing of the origin, the meaning of accumulation; by the seeing of suffering accumulated through the origin, the meaning of the source;

by the seeing of cessation, which is disjunction, the meaning of bondage; by the seeing of the path, which is the outlet, the meaning of impediment; by the seeing of cessation itself, the meaning of escape;
by the seeing of the origin, which is non-seclusion, the meaning of seclusion; and by the seeing of the path, which is the conditioned...
It has the sense of the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*). It has the sense of the deathless (*amata*) through the vision of suffering as something alien.

It has the sense of the outlet (*niyyāna*) precisely through the vision of the path. It has the sense of the cause (*hetu*) through the vision of the origin as that which is not the cause for the attainment of Nibbāna.

It has the sense of seeing (*dassana*) through the vision of cessation, which is so very difficult to see. And it has the sense of sovereignty (*ādhipateyya*), like a noble family, becoming manifest through the vision of suffering as being like the plight of a wretched person.
Thus, by means of the vision of each respective truth and the vision of the other truths, four characteristics have been stated for each truth.
The twelve answers, beginning with "the state of being such" (*tathaṭṭha*), are demonstrated by way of the twelve terms that encompass all phenomena.

"The state of being such" means the state of being according to its own intrinsic nature (*yathāsabhāva*). "The state of non-self" (*anattaṭṭha*) means the state of being devoid of a self. "The state of truth" (*saccaṭṭha*) means the state of non-deceptiveness.
The meaning of penetration (*paṭivedhaṭṭha*) is the meaning of that which is to be penetrated. The meaning of direct knowledge (*abhijānanaṭṭha*) is the meaning of that which is to be directly known.

The meaning of full understanding (*parijānanaṭṭha*) is the meaning of that which is to be fully understood by means of the full understanding consisting in knowing and scrutinizing. The meaning of the phenomenon (*dhammaṭṭha*) is the meaning of maintaining its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), and so forth.

The meaning of the element (*dhātuṭṭha*) is the meaning of emptiness (*suñña*), and so forth. The meaning of the known (*ñātaṭṭha*) is the meaning of that which is capable of being known. The meaning of realization (*sacchikiriyaṭṭha*) is the meaning of that which is to be realized.

“The sense of touching” (phassanaṭṭho) means the sense of what is to be touched by knowledge. “The sense of convergence” (abhisamayaṭṭho) means the sense of what is to be properly reached by the knowledge of review;

or it is the sense of what is to be acquired by knowledge. For even acquisition is called “convergence” (abhisamaya), as in such passages as “the wise man through the convergence of the goal” (atthābhisamayā dhīro).
18. The seven answers beginning with renunciation (nekkhamma) are demonstrated by way of access concentration (upacāra-jjhāna). Renunciation (nekkhamma): [etc.]
Non-greed is the antidote to sensual desire. Perception of light is the perception of the sign of light, which is the antidote to sloth and torpor.
Non-distraction is concentration, the antidote to restlessness. Discernment of phenomena is knowledge, the antidote to doubt.
Knowledge is knowledge, the antidote to ignorance. Gladness is the antidote to discontent.
*Rapture* (*pīti*). The eight responses beginning with the first jhāna are explained by way of the fine-material and immaterial attainments (*rūpārūpasamāpatti*).
Below that, immediately following the fine-material attainments, the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) are explained in connection with the fine-material jhānas.

The contemplations of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) and so forth are explained by way of the eighteen great insights (*mahāvipassanā*) occurring in the preliminary stage prior to the supramundane path (*lokuttaramagga*).
Below, however, only seven contemplations up to the stage of "joining with form" (*rūpa*) were mentioned; here, all of them are mentioned.

If it is asked why the "comprehension by groups" (*kalāpasammasana*) and the "contemplation of rise and fall" (*udayabbayānupassanā*) are not mentioned here: it is because, through those two, the contemplations of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) and so forth are accomplished;

thus, when these [seven] are mentioned, those two are also effectively mentioned. Or else, without the contemplations of impermanence and so forth, those two [comprehension by groups and contemplation of rise and fall] would not exist.
Because these two do not occur separately when these [other three] have been stated, both of them are already included when they are mentioned.

"Contemplation of destruction" (*khayānupassanā*) is the knowledge that sees the dissolution of the present aggregates of form and so forth, and the knowledge that sees the dissolution of the consciousness and mental factors that take those [aggregates] as their object immediately after seeing the dissolution of each respective aggregate.

"Contemplation of fall" (*vayānupassanā*) is the knowledge that, immediately after seeing the dissolution of the present aggregates, follows that very sequence to see the dissolution of past and future aggregates.

The knowledge of seeing dissolution (*bhaṅgadassanañāṇa*). "Contemplation of change" (*vipariṇāmānupassanā*) is the knowledge of seeing the change of all aggregates—past, future, and present—because of being intent upon that cessation known as dissolution;

it is the knowledge that sees the change of all things. "Contemplation of the signless" (*animittānupassanā*) is for one who, having thus seen the change of all conditioned phenomena, contemplates them as impermanent.

Contemplation of the signless (*animittānupassanā*) is so called because, by means of abandoning the sign of permanence through the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*), there is an absence of the sign of permanence.

Contemplation of the desireless (*appaṇihitānupassanā*) is so called because the contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*), which occurs immediately after the contemplation of impermanence, abandons the longing for pleasure;
thus, due to the absence of longing (*paṇidhi*), it is called the contemplation of the desireless.
"Contemplation of emptiness" (*suññatānupassanā*) is precisely the contemplation of non-self (*anattānupassanā*) that occurs immediately after the contemplation of suffering;
it is called "contemplation of emptiness" because, by way of abandoning the adherence to a self, it sees the emptiness of a self.

"Insight into phenomena through higher wisdom" (*adhipaññādhammavipassanā*) refers to the fact that for one who thus contemplates formations as impermanent and so forth, having repeatedly seen their dissolution, it is those very formations that break up.
Insight that proceeds by apprehending emptiness through the dissolution of formations— understanding that there is no other death for formations than their own breaking up—
is called "insight into phenomena as higher wisdom" (*adhipaññādhammavipassanā*), because it is both higher wisdom and insight into phenomena.
Knowledge and vision according to reality is the knowledge of the appearance of terror, which occurs by repeatedly seeing dissolution and thinking, "Formations are fearful."
Contemplation of danger (*ādīnavānupassanā*) is the knowledge that sees danger in all states of existence and so forth, which arises by way of the manifestation of fear (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna*).
Because of the statement, “The wisdom in the manifestation of fear, the knowledge of danger, and disenchantment (*nibbidā*):
these things are one in meaning, only the phrasing is different,” when the manifestation of fear and the contemplation of danger are mentioned, the contemplation of disenchantment is also included.
It is indeed mentioned here as well; however, it is not stated here because it was already stated by making it the fourth [insight] at the beginning.

"Contemplation of reflection" (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā*) is the knowledge consisting of the contemplation of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, known as the contemplation of reflection, which functions as the means for relinquishing that has arisen by way of the knowledge of the desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa*). "Both the desire for deliverance and the contemplation of reflection..."

Because of the statement, "Equanimity about formations and equanimity as a factor of liberation are identical in meaning, differing only in expression," when contemplation of reflection is mentioned, the knowledge of desire for deliverance and the knowledge of equanimity about formations are already included.
Contemplation of turning away is the knowledge of change-of-lineage that arises by way of conformity-knowledge; for the knowledge of change-of-lineage is accomplished through conformity-knowledge.
When the knowledge of the lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) is stated, the knowledge of conformity (anuloma-ñāṇa) is already stated as well.
For it is in this way that the sequence of the eighteen great insights (mahā-vipassanā), when being explained, accords with the Canon (pāḷi). Indeed, it is said in the *Indriyakathā*:

"In the prior stage, by means of the five faculties, the five faculties are transcended through the first jhāna; in the first jhāna, by means of the five faculties, the five faculties are transcended through the second jhāna."

By this method, the faculties are described in successive order up to the fruit of arahantship. Therefore, the eighteen great insights accord with the sequence stated in the Pāḷi. However, in the *Visuddhimagga* it is said:
“Contemplation of destruction is the knowledge of one who sees destruction in the sense of impermanence by resolving the compact mass;
contemplation of change is [the knowledge] by way of the sevenfold materiality and the sevenfold immateriality, etc., regarding each respective delimitation...”
It has been stated: “The vision of occurrence otherwise by transcending [the previous state]; or the vision of change through two modes—namely, aging and death—of what has arisen;
and ‘knowledge and vision according to reality’ is the discernment of mentality-materiality together with its conditions.

This appears to be in contradiction with that canonical text (pāḷi). It has also been stated: “Contemplation of turning away is both equanimity regarding formations and conformity. This too appears to be in contradiction with the canonical text. For in the *Cariyā-kathā* (Discourse on Conduct):
“The functional indeterminate advertence for the purpose of contemplating impermanence is a movement of consciousness; the contemplation of impermanence is a movement of knowledge...
[and so on] ...the functional indeterminate advertence for the purpose of contemplating reflection is a movement of consciousness; the contemplation of reflection is a movement of knowledge.
Thus, for whichever knowledge a separate advertence is obtained, for that [knowledge] there is a separate advertence.

It has been stated [thus]. However, regarding the contemplation of turning away (*vivaṭṭanānupassanā*), it is stated as "the cognitive process of the knowledge of turning away" (*vivaṭṭanānupassanā ñāṇacariyā*) without even mentioning the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*).

If the equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) and the knowledge of conformity (*anulomañāṇa*) were indeed called the contemplation of turning away, then—since the adverting consciousness would be possible for them—one would have mentioned the adverting consciousness for that purpose;
yet no such adverting consciousness is mentioned for that purpose. [This applies] to the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhuñāṇa*).
However, there is no separate adverting consciousness (āvajjana), because it arises within the very cognitive process of conformity-adverting (anuloma-āvajjana).

Therefore, since no adverting consciousness is mentioned for the purpose of the contemplation of turning away (vivaṭṭanānupassanā), it is appropriate that the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) itself is called "the contemplation of turning away. 19.
The eight answers beginning with the stream-entry path (sotāpatti-magga) are explained by way of the supramundane paths and fruits.
The entering into the stream is stream-entry (*sotāpatti*); the path itself that is stream-entry is the "path of stream-entry" (*sotāpattimagga*).

The fruit of stream-entry is the "fruit of stream-entry" (*sotāpattiphala*); it is called "attainment" (*samāpatti*) because it is attained; the attainment that is the very fruit of stream-entry is the "attainment of the fruit of stream-entry" (*sotāpattiphalasamāpatti*).
One who comes to this world only once more by way of rebirth-linking is a "once-returner" (*sakadāgāmī*); his path is the "path of the once-returner" (*sakadāgāmimagga*).
The fruit of the once-returner is the *sakadāgāmiphala*. One who does not return to the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) even by way of rebirth-linking is an *anāgāmī*;
his path is the *anāgāmimagga*. The fruit of the non-returner is the *anāgāmiphala*.

[He is so called] because he is far removed from defilements, because he has slain the enemies that are the defilements, because he has slain the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra, because he is devoid of shamelessness in committing evil deeds, and because of the conditions and so forth...

One who is worthy (arahant) is so called because he is worthy; the state of being worthy is "worthiness" (arahatta). What is that? It is the fruit of worthiness (arahattaphala). The path to worthiness is the "path to worthiness" (arahattamagga).
Worthiness itself as the fruit is the "fruit of worthiness" (arahattaphala).
The thirty-three [factors], beginning with "the faculty of faith in the sense of resolution" and ending with "the truths in the sense of suchness," are [as follows]:...
The answers have been demonstrated. They are identical to the thirty-three answers given previously, beginning with "The meaning of resolution is the faculty of faith.
The only difference is that there, the meanings were demonstrated by means of the phenomena (*dhamma*), whereas here, the phenomena are demonstrated by means of the meanings (*attha*).
Furthermore, regarding the four answers beginning with "Calm (*samatha*) is in the sense of non-distraction (*avikkhepa*")...
Below, the distinction between the four answers beginning with “The meaning of non-distraction is serenity” should be understood according to the method already stated.
The eight answers beginning with “In the sense of restraint” are explained by way of the states culminating in virtue and so forth, up to power.
“Purification of virtue” refers to the fourfold virtue, beginning with the well-purified restraint of the Pātimokkha, because it cleanses the stain of misconduct.
"Purification of mind" refers to the eight attainments (samāpatti) together with their preliminary stages. Here, concentration is spoken of under the heading of "mind";
it is called purification of mind because it purifies the defilements of the mind. "Purification of view" is the seeing of name-and-form according to their true nature;

it is called purification of view because it purifies the seven kinds of defilements consisting of wrong views. By way of its "freedness," [it is so called] through the function of overcoming those defilements.
In the sense of being liberated and in the sense of being intent upon the object. "Liberation" (vimokkha) refers here to liberation by way of its specific factor (tadaṅga-vimokkha).

"True knowledge" (vijjā) in the sense of penetration: the knowledge of recollection of past lives is true knowledge in the sense of penetrating former existences; the knowledge of the divine eye is true knowledge in the sense of penetrating the passing away and rebirth of beings;
and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints is true knowledge in the sense of penetrating the Truths.

"Knowledge" (*vijjā*). "In the sense of penetration" means in the sense of knowing. "Liberation" (*vimutti*) is in the sense of relinquishment; because one is liberated from whatever has been relinquished, it is the liberation of the fruit (*phala-vimutti*).

"Knowledge of destruction" (*khaye ñāṇa*) is in the sense of total eradication; it is knowledge regarding the Noble Path which brings about the destruction of the defilements, in the sense of cutting them off entirely.
"Knowledge of non-arising" (*anuppāde ñāṇa*) is in the sense of subsiding; this is because the application consisting of the function of the path has subsided.

Knowledge regarding the noble fruit that has arisen at the conclusion of the non-arising of those respective defilements to be abandoned by the path, which has itself not arisen through rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
The nine answers beginning with "Zeal in the sense of being the root" are explained according to the beginning, middle, and end of the noble path.
"Zeal in the sense of being the root": this refers to the zeal of wishing to act (*kattukamyatā-chanda*) toward wholesome states for the sake of practice.

And because it is the root by way of its production, it is in the sense of being a root. "Attention is in the sense of origination" means that wise attention originates all wholesome states; thus, it is in the sense of origination.

"Contact is in the sense of convergence" means that, specifically for craving, feeling is the primary cause; and when craving is abandoned, it is specifically through the full understanding of feeling.
It is abandoned; and for that feeling, contact alone is the primary cause. When that [contact] is fully understood, the feeling is fully understood.
Therefore, among the seven bases to be directly known, contact is mentioned first.

And because it is made known by way of its own cause, which is the concurrence of the triad, and because it is described as "manifesting as the concurrence of the triad," it is [said to be] so in the sense of its convergence.
It is to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*). Some, however, say that "the contact of knowledge is contact.

But because feeling, while exercising its own influence over the mind and mental factors, converges upon and enters into them—or rather, enters into the very continuum of consciousness—it is therefore said to be "to be directly known" in the sense of convergence. Some, however...
“They say: ‘All things that are to be fully understood converge upon feelings; when feelings are fully understood, every basis for craving is fully understood.
For what reason? Because all craving has feeling as its condition. Therefore, feelings are to be directly known in the sense of being the point of convergence.
This is because, like the central ridge-pole of a gabled house which binds together all the rafters, [feeling is the binding factor] of the mind and mental factors.”
Through its unifying function, concentration is the foremost and the chief among wholesome states; therefore, it is said that "concentration is the foremost in the sense of being the head.
The reading *pāmukhaṭṭhena* (in the sense of being the leader) is also found. Because for one developing serenity and insight, mindfulness is the dominant factor in the appearance of the object;
and when the object is established by mindfulness, all wholesome states accomplish their respective functions.
Therefore it is said: "Existence [is to be known] in the sense of predominance. "Wisdom in the sense of being superior to that":
noble-path wisdom is to be directly known in the sense of being superior and most excellent among those wholesome states.
Alternatively, it is "superior" (*taduttarā*) because it transcends and overcomes defilements or the cycle of saṃsāra; the meaning of that is "the sense of being superior to that" (*taduttaraṭṭho*).
By that sense of being superior to that. There is also a reading *tatuttaraṭṭhena*, which means "by the sense of being superior to that.

"Liberation in the sense of the core" means that the liberation of the fruit is the core because of its stability through non-decline; it is also the core because there is nothing else to be sought beyond it.
That liberation is to be directly known in the sense of being the core. It plunges into the deathless.
It is called *nibbāna* because there is no death (*mata*) characterized by passing away for it; thus it is the "Deathless" (*amata*).

Because it is the antidote to the poison of the defilements (*kilesa*), it is also the "Antidote" (*agada*). Because it has become the foundation for beings through its realization, it is the "Resting Place" (*ogadha*).

Because it is the pacification of the suffering of *saṃsāra*, it is "extinguished" (*nibbuta*); and because there is no craving (*taṇhā*) characterized as a "flood" (*vāna*) therein, it is *nibbāna*. It is the [goal] of the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
Because it is the ultimate state, it is to be directly known in the sense of being the final goal.
Thus, in this exposition of what is to be directly known, there are seven thousand seven hundred and forty answers.
Now, regarding those phenomena thus explained: "Whatever phenomena have been directly known, those very phenomena have been known."
He makes this the conclusion with the words “they are,” the intention being that they are known by facing toward them.
It is "knowledge" (ñāṇa) in the sense of knowing those aforementioned phenomena;

it is "wisdom" (paññā) in the sense of fully understanding (pajānana), that is, in the sense of knowing them in their various modes (pakārato). With the words "therefore it is said," the questions asked at the beginning are shown by way of conclusion.
For that reason, the meaning is as follows: “‘These states are to be directly known’—this is the application of the ear; the wisdom that understands that is knowledge consisting in what is heard.
Thus ends the commentary on the Exposition of What is to be Directly Known in the *Saddhammappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.
Commentary on the Exposition of What is to be Fully Understood (Pariññeyyaniddesa) 21.

Although three kinds of full understanding— full understanding as knowledge (*ñātapariññā*), full understanding as investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*), and full understanding as abandoning (*pahānapariññā*)—

are included under the term "full understanding" (*pariññā*) in this exposition, since "to be directly known" (*abhiññeyya*) was stated above in reference to full understanding as knowledge, [the subsequent category] is "to be abandoned" (*pahātabba*).
Because it is stated in the context of full understanding as abandonment (*pahānapariññā*), it is specifically full understanding as investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*) that is intended here.

"Contact accompanied by taints and conducive to clinging" refers to contact belonging to the three planes of existence, which serves as the condition for both the taints (*āsava*) and the clingings (*upādāna*). For that [contact] is "accompanied by taints" (*sāsava*) because it occurs together with the taints when they take self as their object; and it is so called because, having entered into the state of being an object, it connects one to clinging.

"Conducive to clinging" (*upādāniya*) means that which is beneficial to the clingings (*upādāna*). Because, when contact (*phassa*) is fully understood through the full understanding of investigation, the remaining immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) are also fully understood by way of contact, and material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) are fully understood by following from them, therefore only contact is mentioned.
In the same way, this should be applied accordingly to the remaining [bases] as well.
“Name” consists of the four immaterial aggregates and Nibbāna. “Form” consists of the four great elements and the twenty-four kinds of derived form based upon those four great elements.
The four aggregates are called “name” in the sense of bending;
for they bend toward their respective objects. Furthermore, everything is “name” in the sense of bending, for the four aggregates bend toward their objects.
They bend one another; Nibbāna bends blameless states within itself by way of being an object-predominance condition (*ārammaṇādhipatipaccayatā*).

Matter (*rūpa*) is so called in the sense of being disturbed (*ruppana*) by cold and so forth through the course of continuity (*santati*). "In the sense of being disturbed" means in the sense of being agitated.
For a class of phenomena that is susceptible to being struck by cold and so forth, by way of the transformation of continuity, is called matter. But here, "name" (*nāma*) refers only to the mundane.
What is intended [here] is that matter (*rūpa*) is exclusively mundane (*lokiya*).
"Three feelings" refers to pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;

these too are exclusively mundane. "Nutriments" (*āhāra*) means conditions (*paccaya*). For conditions are called "nutriments" because they bring about their own fruit. These are: physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*), nutriment of contact (*phassa-āhāra*), and so forth.
There are four [nutriments]: the nutriment of mental volition and the nutriment of consciousness. It is called "edible" (*kabaḷīkāra*) because it must be made into morsels;

it is called "nutriment" (*āhāra*) because it is to be swallowed. This is the name for the nutritive essence (*ojā*) which has rice, gruel, and so forth as its basis. For that [essence] is called "nutriment" because it brings in (*āharati*) the eight types of material form consisting of nutritive essence.
The sixfold contact, beginning with visual contact, is called "nutriment" because it brings in the three kinds of feeling.
"Volition of the mind, not of a being" means mental volition (*manosañcetanā*), just as one speaks of "one-pointedness of mind.

Alternatively, volition associated with the mind is mental volition, just as one speaks of a "chariot drawn by thoroughbreds. It refers to wholesome and unwholesome volition belonging to the three planes of existence.

For it brings about the three realms of existence; thus, it is a nutriment (*āhāra*). "Consciousness" (*viññāṇa*) refers to the nineteenfold rebirth-linking consciousness. For that [consciousness] is the name-and-form at the moment of rebirth-linking.

It is called "nutriment" (*āhāra*) because it nourishes (*āharati*). "Aggregates of clinging" (*upādānakkhandhā*) means aggregates that have clinging as their sphere; here, the middle term [of the compound] is to be understood as elided.
Alternatively, the aggregates produced from clinging are the "aggregates of clinging," just as one speaks of a "grass fire" or a "chaff fire.
Or, the aggregates subject to clinging are the "aggregates of clinging," just as one speaks of a "king's man. Or, the aggregates originating from clinging are the "aggregates of clinging."

Just as there is a flower-tree and a fruit-tree, so too there are four kinds of clinging (*upādāna*): clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*), clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*), clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*), and clinging to a doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*).
In terms of meaning, however, clinging is "grasping intensely" (*bhusam ādānam*).

There are five aggregates of clinging: the aggregate of form-clinging (*rūpupādānakkhandha*), the aggregate of feeling-clinging (*vedanupādānakkhandha*), the aggregate of perception-clinging (*saññupādānakkhandha*), the aggregate of mental formations-clinging (*saṅkhārupādānakkhandha*), and the aggregate of consciousness-clinging (*viññāṇupādānakkhandha*).
The six internal sense bases (*ajjhattikāni āyatanāni*) are: the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base.
The seven stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo*): what are the seven? For this was said by the Blessed One:

"There are, monks, beings who are diverse in body and diverse in perception, such as humans, some gods, and some beings in the states of deprivation (*vinipātikā*). This is the first station of consciousness."
“Bhikkhus, there are beings who are diverse in body and uniform in perception, such as the gods of the Brahma-order who have first reappeared there. This is the second station of consciousness.
“Bhikkhus, there are beings who are uniform in body and diverse in perception, such as the Ābhassara gods. This is the third station of consciousness.
“Bhikkhus, there are beings who are uniform in body and uniform in perception, such as the Subhakiṇha gods. This is the fourth station of consciousness.”

“Bhikkhus, there are beings who, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking ‘space is infinite,’ have reached the base of infinite space. This is the fifth station of consciousness.

“Bhikkhus, there are beings who, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking ‘consciousness is infinite,’ have reached the base of infinite consciousness. This is the sixth station of consciousness.”

“There are, monks, beings who, having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking ‘there is nothing,’ have reached the base of nothingness. This is the seventh station of consciousness. These, monks, are the seven stations of consciousness.
“Stations of consciousness” (*viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo*) means the bases for rebirth-consciousness; they are simply the aggregates accompanied by consciousness.
In this context, *seyyathāpi* is a particle used for the purpose of illustration. *Manussā* refers to humans among the countless humans in countless world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
There are not even two that are identical in terms of color, shape, and so forth.
Even those who are similar in color or shape are nonetheless different in their ways of looking forward, looking around, and so on; therefore, they are called "those of diverse bodies.
Furthermore, their rebirth-consciousness may be triple-rooted, double-rooted, or rootless; therefore, they are called "those of diverse perceptions. Some...
And "gods" refers to the gods of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). For among them, the bodies of some are blue, while those of others are yellow or other colors;
their perception (saññā), however, may be triple-rooted (tihetuka) or double-rooted (duhetuka), but it is never rootless (ahetuka).

And "certain beings in states of deprivation" (vinipātika) refers to those excluded from the four woeful states (apāya): the yakkhinī Punabbasu’s mother, Piyaṅkara’s mother, Phussamittā, and Dhammaguttā.

These and other such *peta*s are scattered throughout various realms. For their bodies are diverse, appearing with complexions ranging from white, black, mottled, and dark-brown, and varying in size from emaciated to stout and from short to tall.
Their perception is likewise diverse—being triple-rooted, double-rooted, or rootless—just as it is among humans.
However, unlike the gods, they do not possess great power; like wretched humans, they have little influence and find food and clothing difficult to obtain.
They dwell oppressed by suffering. Some are miserable during the dark fortnight and happy during the bright fortnight;

therefore, because they have fallen from a mass of happiness, they are called *vinipātika* (those fallen into ruin). However, among those here who possess three roots (*tihetuka*), there is also the realization of the Dhamma (*dhammābhisamaya*), as in the case of Piyaṅkaramātā and others.
The "Brahmakāyika" (Deities of the Brahma-body) are the Brahmapārisajja, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahmā deities.

They are all "first-born" in the sense that they are produced by the first jhāna. However, the Brahmapārisajja are produced by a limited degree [of the first jhāna], the Brahmapurohita by a middling degree, and their bodies are more expansive. The Mahābrahmā are produced by a refined degree, and their bodies—

It becomes much more expansive. Thus, due to the diversity of their bodies and the unity of their perception by way of the first jhāna, they are said to be "those with diverse bodies and unified perception.
And as it is for them, so it is for beings in the four states of misery.
For in the hells, the personal existence (attabhāva) of some is a quarter-league, of some half a league, and of some three-quarters of a league, such as that of Devadatta.
But they are born reaching up to one hundred *yojana*s in size. Among animals, some are small and some are large.
In the realm of the *petas* as well, some are sixty cubits tall, some eighty cubits, and some are handsome while others are ugly. The same applies to the black-clad *asuras*.
Furthermore, among them there are those called "long-backed *petas*" who even reach sixty *yojana*s; however, the perception (*saññā*) of all of them is the same.
It is exclusively the result of unwholesome kamma and is rootless (*ahetuka*). Thus, even those in the states of misery (*apāya*) are designated as "those with diverse bodies and unified perception.

As for the *Ābhassara* (Radiant) devas: because their radiance issues forth from their bodies and spreads out, falling as if in separate streams like sparks from a firebrand, they are called *Ābhassara*.
Among them, according to the fivefold method, the second and third jhānas are limited (*paritta*).
Having developed [the first jhāna] to a low degree, those who arise are called the Parittābhas; having developed it to a medium degree, those who arise are called the Appamāṇābhas;
and having developed it to a superior degree, those who arise are called the Ābhassarās. Here, however, all of them are included by way of the highest limit.
For the bodies of all of them are of one and the same radiance, while their perception is without applied thought and consists of sustained thought only.
And [the states] without applied thought and sustained thought are diverse.
"Subhakiṇha" means interspersed or scattered with beauty; the meaning is that they are a single mass through the beautiful radiance and color of their bodies.
For in their case, as in that of the Ābhassaras, the radiance does not go forth by breaking off in fragments. In the fourfold method, this refers to the third [jhāna].

In the fivefold system, by way of the fourth jhāna—whether limited, medium, or sublime—they are reborn as the Limited Beautiful, the Immeasurable Beautiful, and the Beautiful-Kiṇha devas respectively.
Thus, it should be understood that all of them possess a single-body form and perceive unity through the perception of the fourth jhāna.
The Vehapphala devas also belong to the fourth station of consciousness. The non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), however, do not [belong to this category] due to the absence of consciousness.
They do not fall within this classification; they belong among the abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*).
The Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*) stand on the side of evolution (*vivaṭṭa*); they are not present at all times.

Even for a hundred thousand aeons or an incalculable period (*asaṅkhyeya*), they do not arise when the world is empty of Buddhas; they appear only when Buddhas have arisen within the interval of sixteen thousand aeons.
They arise as if they were the military encampments of the Blessed One who sets the Wheel of Dhamma in motion;
therefore, they partake neither of the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) nor of the abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*). However, the Elder Mahāsīva said:
"But that abode of beings, Sāriputta, is not easily found which has not been inhabited by me during this long period of time, except for..."
By this sutta, "by the Suddhāvāsa devas," it is stated that the Suddhāvāsas also belong to the fourth station of consciousness and the fourth abode of beings;
since this is not contradicted by the sutta, it is accepted.

Just as with perception (saññā), the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is neither consciousness nor non-consciousness because of the subtlety of consciousness there; therefore, it is not mentioned among the stations of consciousness.
The eight worldly conditions (*loka-dhammā*) are: gain, loss, fame, disrepute, blame, praise, pleasure, and pain.
These are called "worldly conditions" because, while the world is in existence, they are subject to non-cessation due to the nature of the world.
There is no being whatsoever free from these; they occur even for the Buddhas. As it has been said:
“Monks, these eight worldly conditions revolve around the world, and the world revolves around these eight worldly conditions.
What are the eight? Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain.
These, monks, are the eight worldly conditions that revolve around the world, and the world revolves around these eight worldly conditions.”
In this context, "revolving around" means following after, not abandoning, or not turning back from the world—this is the meaning.
"Gain" (*lābha*) refers to robes and so forth for one who has gone forth, or wealth, grain, and so forth for a householder.

That very gain, when it is not obtained, is "non-gain" (*alābha*). If it were called "non-gain" simply because it is not gain, it would result in the loss of its actual meaning; thus, it must be fully understood (*pariññeyya*). "Fame" (*yasa*)...
Retinue. Fame and infamy are likewise unobtainable by that very person. "Censure" means speaking dispraise; "praise" means speaking praise.

"Happiness" refers to the bodily and mental [pleasure] of those in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*). "Suffering" refers to the bodily and mental [pain] of ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*), stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), and once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*);
for non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and arahants, it is only bodily.

The "nine abodes of beings" (*sattāvāsā*) are the dwellings of beings; the meaning is "places of residence. These, however, are simply the aggregates (*khandha*) manifested in such a way. Which nine? For this was said by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, there are these nine abodes of beings. Which nine?
There are, bhikkhus, beings who are diverse in body and diverse in perception, such as humans, some gods, and some in the states of misery (*vinipātika*). This is the first abode of beings."
“Bhikkhus, there are beings who are diverse in body and uniform in perception, such as the gods of Brahma’s company who were first reborn there. This is the second abode of beings.
“Bhikkhus, there are beings who are uniform in body and diverse in perception, such as the Ābhassara gods. This is the third abode of beings.
“Bhikkhus, there are beings who are uniform in body and uniform in perception, such as the Subhakiṇha gods. This is the fourth abode of beings.”
“Bhikkhus, there are beings who are non-percipient and devoid of experience, such as the non-percipient devas. This is the fifth abode of beings.

“Bhikkhus, there are beings who, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking ‘space is infinite,’ have reached the base of infinite space. This is the sixth abode of beings.”

“Monks, there are beings who, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, thinking ‘consciousness is infinite,’ have reached the base of infinite consciousness. This is the seventh abode of beings.
“Monks, there are beings who, having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking ‘there is nothing,’ have reached the base of nothingness. This is the eighth abode of beings.”

“Bhikkhus, there are beings who, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, have reached the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is the ninth abode of beings. These, bhikkhus, are the nine abodes of beings.

The ten bases (*dasāyatanāni*) are as follows: the eye-base, the form-base, the ear-base, the sound-base, the nose-base, the odor-base, the tongue-base, the taste-base, the body-base, and the tangible-object-base—thus there are ten. [The remaining two are] the mind-base and the mental-phenomena-base.

However, because they are mixed with supramundane states, they were not included. In these ten answers, the full understanding through scrutinization (*tīraṇapariññā*) is stated by way of insight (*vipassanā*).

But in such passages as, "Bhikkhus, everything is to be fully understood," there is the state of realization and development of the three beginning with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*), and the state of penetration of those very same [faculties] regarding cessation and the path.
Of the fifteen [meanings] such as the non-arising of the escape from suffering and so forth; of the thirty-one [meanings] such as the meaning of embracing;
of the three [meanings] such as the meaning of higher penetration; of the eight path-factors; of the two [meanings] such as "the meaning of the subsiding of efforts";
of the two [meanings] such as the meaning of emergence from the unconditioned; and of the [meanings] such as the meaning of awakening to the meaning of departure...

The full understanding through scrutiny (*tīraṇapariññā*) is said with reference to the acquisition of these phenomena: the three [knowledges], the three beginning with the state of discovery (*anubodha*), the three beginning with those conducive to discovery (*anubodhapakkhiya*), the four beginning with the state of illumination (*ujjotana*), the eighteen beginning with the state of inflaming (*patāpana*), the nine beginning with the contemplation of turning away (*vivaṭṭanānupassanā*), the knowledge of destruction (*khaye-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anuppāde-ñāṇa*), and the liberation through wisdom (*paññāvimutti*) and Nibbāna; as for the remaining ones...
It should be understood that the full understanding by scrutinization (*tīraṇapariññā*) is stated both by way of insight (*vipassanā*) and by way of acquisition (*paṭilābha*).
For when one exerts effort for the sake of acquiring various states (*dhammas*), those very states are acquired;
thus, because they are both fully understood and scrutinized, this is called "full understanding by scrutinization" in the sense of the completion of the task.
They are so called because when the task is completed, those states have been acquired.

However, some say that "full understanding through knowledge" (*ñātapariññā*) applies only to those things that do not enter into insight (*vipassanā*). This is not correct, because it has been stated in the context of what is to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*) that full understanding through knowledge applies [to all].
They are both fully understood and determined; thus, those very states that have been acquired are said to be "fully understood" and "determined."
"Name" (*nāma*) is the meaning. Thus, the meaning of "full understanding" (*pariññāta*) has been stated by way of the fulfillment of its function.

Now, in order to demonstrate that same meaning by applying it to each individual phenomenon (*dhamma*) through their attainment, and to conclude [the section], he says: "Renunciation" (*nekkhamma*), and so forth. All of that should be understood according to what was previously stated.
The commentary on the exposition of the objects of full understanding (*pariññeyya-niddesa*) is finished.
Commentary on the Exposition of What is to be Abandoned (Pahātabba-niddesa) 23.
Regarding the exposition of what is to be abandoned: "the conceit 'I am' (*asmimāna*)" refers to the conceit "I am" with respect to the five aggregates of clinging, beginning with form.
For when that is abandoned, one has attained Arahantship. Although lust for form and the other [defilements] still exist, the others are not mentioned; rather, only the conceit "I am" is specified.
It should be understood that speech is gross because it resembles [the nature of] views.

Ignorance (*avijjā*), according to the Suttanta method, is non-knowing regarding the four points beginning with suffering; according to the Abhidhamma method, it is non-knowing regarding eight points including the past and so forth. For this has been said:
"In this context, what is ignorance? It is non-knowing regarding suffering, non-knowing regarding the origin of suffering, non-knowing regarding the cessation of suffering..."

“Lack of knowledge regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering; lack of knowledge regarding the past; lack of knowledge regarding the future; lack of knowledge regarding both the past and the future;
and lack of knowledge regarding specific conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena.
Craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*) is the longing for states of existence such as sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) and so forth. As it has been said:

“In this context, what is craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*)? It is that which, regarding states of existence, is desire for existence, lust for existence, delight in existence, craving for existence, affection for existence, fever for existence, infatuation with existence, and clinging to existence.
There are three kinds of craving: craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*), craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*), and craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*).

Their definition is given in the Abhidhamma as follows: “In this context, what is craving for existence? Lust accompanied by the view of existence... [and so on] ...the intense passion of the mind; this is craving for existence.”
This is called craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*). In this context, what is craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*)? It is lust accompanied by the view of annihilationism...

[as before] ...the infatuation of the mind; this is called craving for non-existence. All remaining craving is craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*). In this context, what is craving for sense-pleasures?
It is lust associated with the realm of sense-pleasures... [as before] ...the infatuation of the mind; this is called craving for sense-pleasures. In this context, what is...
Craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*)? It is lust connected with the fine-material element and the immaterial element... [etc. ...In this context, what is craving for non-existence (*vibhava-taṇhā*)?
It is lust accompanied by the annihilationist view (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*)...

[etc. ...In the Commentary, however, it is said: "Lust regarding the five strands of sensual pleasure is craving for sense-pleasures (*kāma-taṇhā*); lust regarding the fine-material and immaterial realms of existence, accompanied by attachment to meditative absorption (*jhāna-nikanti*) and the eternalist view (*sassata-diṭṭhi*), is craving for existence."
“Lust for existence (*bhavataṇhā*) is the aspiration based on the view of becoming; lust accompanied by the annihilationist view (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) is lust for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*).

Thus it is said. This is the application according to the method of the *Dasuttara-sutta*. According to the method of the *Saṅgīti* and the method of the Abhidhamma, however, it is said: “There are another three kinds of craving:
craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*), craving for form (*rūpataṇhā*), and craving for the formless (*arūpataṇhā*). There are another three kinds of craving: craving for form...”

The cravings mentioned here as "craving for the formless" and "craving for cessation" are also applicable. Among them, five are associated with the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), the fine-material realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the immaterial realm (*arūpadhātu*);
the last is accompanied by the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*).

There are four floods (*oghā*): the flood of sensuality (*kāmogha*), the flood of existence (*bhavogha*), the flood of views (*diṭṭhogha*), and the flood of ignorance (*avijjogha*). Whoever possesses these remains within the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

They are called *oghā* (floods) because they carry away and cause one to sink. These are powerful defilements (*kilesa*). The flood regarding sense pleasures, which are designated as *kāma*, is the *kāma-ogha*;
this is a name for sensual craving (*kāmatanha*). The flood regarding existence, which is designated as *rūpa* and *arūpa*—being twofold both in terms of karma and rebirth—is the *bhava-ogha*;
this is a name for craving for existence (*bhavatanha*). View itself is the flood; thus, it is the *diṭṭhi-ogha*. [This refers to] such views as "the world is eternal," and so forth.
This is the name for view (*diṭṭhi*). Ignorance itself is the flood; thus it is "the flood of ignorance" (*avijjogha*), which is the name for lack of knowledge regarding suffering and so forth.

"The five hindrances" (*pañca nīvaraṇāni*) refers to the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*), the hindrance of ill will (*byāpāda-nīvaraṇa*), the hindrance of sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha-nīvaraṇa*), the hindrance of restlessness and remorse (*uddhacca-kukkucca-nīvaraṇa*), and the hindrance of doubt (*vicikicchā-nīvaraṇa*).
They are called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇāni*) because they hinder and envelop the mind. They are called "sensual pleasures" (*kāmā*) because they are desired.
The five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇā*). Desire for sensual pleasures is "sensual desire" (*kāmacchanda*). Or, it is called *kāma* because one desires (*kāmayati*);

it is the desire itself, not the desire for action (*kattukamyatā-chanda*) nor the desire for the Dhamma (*dhammacchanda*), hence it is "sensual desire. This is a name for craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*).

By means of this, the mind becomes corrupted and reaches a state of putrefaction; or, it causes harm to discipline, conduct, beauty, prosperity, welfare, and happiness. Thus it is "ill-will" (*byāpāda*).
Ill will (*vyāpāda*): this is a name for hatred (*dosa*). Lethargy (*thīna*) is the state of being lethargic; torpor (*middha*) is the state of being torpid;
the meaning is the lack of exertion and the loss of strength. Lethargy is the lack of exertion of the mind; torpor is the unwieldiness of mental factors (*cetasika*);

lethargy and torpor together are "lethargy-and-torpor" (*thinamiddha*). Restlessness (*uddhacca*) is the state of one who is restless; the meaning is non-tranquility. This is a name for distraction (*vikkhepa*).
*Nāmaṃ*: [This is] the name. *Kukataṃ* means what has been badly done; the state of having done badly is *kukkuccaṃ*; the meaning is "the state of reprehensible action.
This is a name for subsequent remorse (*pacchānutāpa*). *Vicikicchā*: from which healing (*cikicchā*) has departed, thus *vicikicchā*; the meaning is "one whose wisdom has departed.
Or, one who investigates the true nature (*sabhāva*) suffers and becomes weary by means of this, thus it is *vicikicchā*. This is a name for doubt regarding the Buddha and so forth.
This is the name. Sensual desire itself is the hindrance; thus it is "the hindrance of sensual desire. The same applies to the remaining [hindrances].
Alternatively, the reading is "six things" or "sixfold things. The six groups of craving are:

craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena (*dhamma*). Craving for forms is "craving for forms. That very [craving] is further divided into sensual craving and so forth.
Because they consist of many divisions, they are called "body" (*kāya*) in the sense of a collection (*rāsa*). The same applies to the remaining [aggregates].

The underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) of beings are: the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*), the underlying tendency of aversion (*paṭighānusaya*), the underlying tendency of conceit (*mānānusaya*), the underlying tendency of views (*diṭṭhānusaya*), the underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*), the underlying tendency of lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*), and the underlying tendency of ignorance (*avijjānusaya*).
They are called "underlying tendencies" because they lie latent in the sense of being unabandoned. Lust for sensual pleasures is "sensual lust" (*kāmarāga*).

Sensual desire itself is passion; thus, it is sensual-passion (*kāmarāga*). That which strikes against an object is resistance (*paṭigha*). View (*diṭṭhi*) is so called in the sense of seeing things as they are not.

That which conceives by way of "better" and so forth is conceit (*māna*). Passion for the realms of existence is passion-for-existence (*bhavarāga*). Sensual-passion that has become firmly established is the underlying tendency to sensual-passion (*kāmarāgānusaya*).
The same applies to the remaining [underlying tendencies].
The eight wrongnesses (*micchatta*) are: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration.
They are called "wrongnesses" because, even though they are desired with the thought, "May these bring me welfare and happiness," they do not exist in that way;
and because they function in a perverted manner, such as taking the beautiful and so forth in things that are actually foul and so forth, their intrinsic nature is wrong.
*Micchādiṭṭhi* (wrong view) is so called because one sees wrongly, or because one sees by means of this [view] wrongly. Alternatively, it is wrong view because it is a perverted view;
or it is wrong view because it is a view that is not according to reality (*ayāthāva*); or it is wrong view because it is a false view due to grasping [things] erroneously;
or it is wrong view because it is a view censured by the wise since it leads to non-selfhood. This also applies to wrong intention (*micchāsaṅkappa*) and the others.
The same method applies here. Wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) is the adherence to eternalism or annihilationism.

Wrong intention (*micchā-saṅkappa*) is the threefold thought, beginning with sensual desire-thought (*kāma-vitakka*). Wrong speech (*micchā-vācā*) is the fourfold volition, beginning with false speech (*musā-vāda*). Wrong action (*micchā-kammanta*) is the threefold volition, beginning with the taking of life (*pāṇātipāta*).

Wrong livelihood (*micchā-ājīva*) is the volition that gives rise to the practice of wrong livelihood. Wrong effort (*micchā-vāyāma*) is [the volition] associated with unwholesome consciousness (*akusala-citta*).
Energy. Wrong mindfulness is an unwholesome state of consciousness that stands as the opposite of right mindfulness.
Wrong concentration is unwholesome concentration. The nine rooted in craving: dependent on craving comes seeking; dependent on seeking comes gain; dependent on gain comes decision-making;
dependent on decision-making comes desire and lust; dependent on desire and lust comes attachment; dependent on attachment... [comes clinging].
Dependent on possession arises stinginess; dependent on stinginess arises guarding;
dependent on guarding arise the taking up of sticks and weapons, quarrels, strife, disputes, contention, slander, and false speech—many evil, unwholesome states come into being.
These are the nine states rooted in craving. Because craving is their root, they are called "craving-rooted."
Seeking and the others are exclusively unwholesome. "Dependent on craving" means relying upon craving.
"Seeking" is the seeking of objects such as forms; for that occurs when craving exists. "Gain" is the acquisition of objects such as forms; for that occurs when seeking exists.
"Decision," however, is fourfold by way of knowledge, craving, views, and thought. Among these, "decision regarding pleasure" [is explained as follows:]
“Having known the determination of pleasure, one should devote oneself to internal pleasure”—this is the determination by knowledge (*ñāṇa-vinicchaya*).

“Determination means two kinds of determination: determination by craving (*taṇhā-vinicchaya*) and determination by views (*diṭṭhi-vinicchaya*”). Thus, the eight hundred modes of the wandering of craving (*taṇhā-vicari-tāni*) that have come down [in the texts] are the determination by craving.
The sixty-two views are the determination by views. “Desire (*chando*)...”
"But, Lord of Devas, it has its origin in thought (*vitakka*). In this sutta, however, what is called "determination" (*vinicchaya*) refers specifically to thought itself.
For after obtaining gain, one determines—by means of thought alone—the desirable and undesirable, the beautiful and the ugly:
"This much will be for the sake of the object of visible form; this much for the sake of the objects of sound and so forth; this much..."
“‘This much will be mine; this much will belong to another; this much I shall enjoy;
this much I shall store away’—it is for this reason it is said: ‘In dependence on gain, there is discrimination.
‘Lustful desire’ (chandārāga) means that upon an object thus conceptualized by unwholesome thought, both weak lust and strong lust arise. Here, ‘desire’ (chanda) is a designation for weak lust.”

“Lust” (*rāga*) refers to strong passion. “Clinging” (*ajjhosāna*) is a strong determination in the form of “I” and “mine. “Possession” (*pariggaha*) is the act of grasping by way of craving and views.
“Avarice” (*macchariya*) is the inability to endure sharing with others.
For this very reason, the ancients explain its meaning thus: “May this wonder belong to me alone; may it not be a wonder for another.”
“Because it causes [the mind] to proceed, it is called stinginess. Guarding (*ārakkha*) means protecting thoroughly by means of locking doors, securing chests, and so forth.
It “makes something its basis,” thus it is a “basis” (*adhikaraṇa*); this is a name for a cause. “Guarding as a basis” (*ārakkhādhikaraṇa*) is a neuter abstract noun;
the meaning is “by reason of guarding. Taking up a staff, etc., refers to taking up a staff for the purpose of restraining others.
Taking up a staff is *daṇḍādāna*. Taking up a weapon, such as a single-edged blade, is *satthādāna*.

A quarrel may be either a physical quarrel or a verbal quarrel. The former instances of opposition are *viggaha* (conflict), while the latter instances are *vivāda* (dispute). "Tuvaṃtuvaṃ" refers to the use of the address "you, you" out of a lack of respect.
The ten wrong states (*micchatta*) are: wrong view... [and so on] ...wrong concentration, wrong knowledge, and wrong liberation. Among these:
"Wrong knowledge" (*micchāñāṇa*) is the delusion that arises in the form of reflecting, "I have done well," after having committed an evil deed by way of thinking up a means for such evil actions.
"Wrong liberation" (*micchāvimutti*) is the perception of being liberated while one is actually not liberated.

Now, in order to show the things to be abandoned through abandonment in its many varieties, the passage beginning with "two kinds of abandonment" (*dve pahānāni*) is commenced. Regarding these abandonments...
For when these various things to be abandoned have been clearly understood, they become easy to comprehend.

Among the five kinds of abandoning, two mundane abandonings and the abandoning by escape have been set aside; thus, the two supramundane abandonings, which require no further effort, were mentioned first.
It is "complete cutting off" (*samuccheda*) because by means of it the defilements are completely cut off; it is "abandoning" (*pahāna*) because by means of it the defilements are abandoned.
Abandoning (*pahāna*). Abandoning characterized as eradication, and not the other types of abandoning, is "abandoning by eradication" (*samucchedappahāna*).

It is "subsidence" (*paṭippassaddhi*) because of the subsiding of the defilements; it is "abandoning" because they have been abandoned. Abandoning characterized as subsidence is "abandoning by subsidence" (*paṭippassaddhippahāna*).
It transcends the world, thus it is "supramundane" (*lokuttara*). It goes to destruction, which is to say, *nibbāna*, thus...

"Leading to exhaustion" (*khayagāmī*): that path which leads to exhaustion is the "path leading to exhaustion. For one who develops that, the meaning is that the path is the abandonment by way of complete eradication (*samucchedappahāna*).
Likewise, at the moment of the fruit, the supramundane fruit itself is the abandonment by way of subsiding (*paṭippassaddhippahāna*).
In such passages as "This is the escape from sensual pleasures," the term "escape" (*nissaraṇa*) means that by means of this, one escapes from sensuality, from form, and from the conditioned.

It is "escape" (*nissaraṇa*) because it has escaped from those [sensual desires]. It is the "meditation on the foul" (*asubha-jjhāna*). It is "renunciation" (*nekkhamma*) because it has emerged from sensual desires; or it is the path of non-returning (*anāgāmi-magga*).

For the meditation on the foul is the escape from sensual desires by way of suppression; however, the path of non-returning, which is produced by taking that meditation as its basis, is the absolute escape from all sensual desires by way of their total eradication.
It is called "form" (*rūpa*) because it is affected (*ruppati*); that which is not form is "non-form" (*arūpa*).
The meaning is that it is the opposite of form (rūpa), just as enemies are the opposite of friends, or as non-greed (alobha) and so forth are the opposites of greed (lobha) and so forth.
Alternatively, it is "formless" (arūpa) because there is no form here; being formless, it is "formless-sphere" (āruppa). These are the formless jhānas.
They are called the escape from forms. Furthermore, even by means of the formless attainments, the path to arahantship [is reached], because it completely prevents future rebirth.
It is called the escape from forms. "Bhūta" means arisen. "Saṅkhata" means made by coming together through conditions.

"Paṭiccasamuppanna" means arisen properly and simultaneously in dependence upon those respective conditions. By the first [term], through its indication of having come into being, there is impermanence;
by the second, through its indication of the power of conditions even for that which is impermanent, there is dependence on others; by the third, even for that which is dependent on others...
By demonstrating that the conditions are devoid of activity while one is mindful, this "nature of things" (evam-dhammatā) is illustrated. "Cessation" (nirodha) means Nibbāna;
for it is by coming to Nibbāna that suffering ceases, and thus it is called "cessation.
Furthermore, because it has escaped from all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata), it is called the "escape" (nissaraṇa) from those conditioned things. However, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā):
“‘Its cessation is the escape’: here, the fruit of arahantship is intended by ‘cessation.
For when Nibbāna is seen through the fruit of arahantship, all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) no longer exist in the future;
thus, because it is the condition for the cessation known as arahantship, it is called ‘cessation’. So it has been said.
Regarding the phrases "for one who has attained renunciation" (*nekkhamma*) and so forth:

when the foulness-meditation (*asubha-jjhāna*) is the means of escape, sensual desires (*kāma*) are both abandoned and relinquished through abandonment by suppression (*vikkhambhana-pahāna*); when the non-returner path (*anāgāmi-magga*) is the means of escape, they are abandoned and relinquished through abandonment by eradication (*samuccheda-pahāna*).
Likewise, when the formless meditations (*arūpa-jjhāna*) or the arahant path (*arahatta-magga*) are the means of escape, the same applies to forms (*rūpa*).
[These terms] should be applied accordingly. For by the abandoning of desire and lust for forms (*rūpa*), there is the total eradication of forms.
And here, the grammatical gender has been altered [from masculine to neuter]. Because Nibbāna is the escape, through the abandoning of escape;

and because the fruit of Arhatship is the escape, through the abandoning of subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi*), formations (*saṅkhāra*) are both abandoned and relinquished. And because Nibbāna is the escape, by way of making it the object (*ārammaṇa*).
The attainment [of the fruit] is to be understood.

In the phrases "the truth of suffering" and so forth, "penetration by full understanding" and so forth are neuter nouns in the instrumental case. Penetration by means of full understanding is "penetration-by-full-understanding" (*pariññāpaṭivedha*).
That is penetration-by-full-understanding. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. "He abandons" means in such and such a manner.
The meaning should be understood as: while penetrating [the truth], one abandons the defilements that are to be abandoned.

Alternatively, even in the case of mundane and supramundane [states], the meaning is that one abandons them through the abandoning of desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*). "Abandons" (*pajahati*) is also a reading.
Just as a boat performs four functions simultaneously—neither before nor after—it abandons the near shore, cuts the current, carries the cargo, and [reaches] the far shore.
Just as a boat reaches the shore, even so path-knowledge (maggañāṇa) realizes the four truths simultaneously, neither before nor after:

it realizes suffering through the realization of full comprehension (pariññābhisamaya), it realizes the origin through the realization of abandonment (pahānābhisamaya), it realizes the path through the realization of development (bhāvanābhisamaya), and it realizes cessation through the realization of verification (sacchikiriyābhisamaya). What is meant by this?

Does it exist? Because it is stated that "having made cessation the object, one reaches, sees, and penetrates the four truths," it should be understood that the abandonments are spoken of as if they were distinct even though they occur in a single moment.
Among the five kinds of abandonment, [the first] is like the moss [removed] by a jar placed in water containing moss. By that [means], with each respective...
The suppression and distancing of adverse states such as the hindrances by means of mundane concentration is what is called "abandoning by suppression.

And it should be understood that when it is said, "one who develops the first jhāna abandons the hindrances," this refers specifically to the abandoning of the hindrances because that is what is manifest [at that stage]. For the hindrances [are indeed abandoned] even in the preliminary stage of jhāna.
Even subsequently, they do not suddenly overwhelm the mind; and when they have overwhelmed it, the jhāna falls away.
However, applied thought (vitakka) and the other factors continue to function as non-antidotes both before and after the second jhāna and so forth.
Therefore, the suppression of the hindrances is evident. As for that which [is seen] by means of a lamp lit during the night...

Just as darkness is dispelled by light, so too is each respective defilement to be abandoned abandoned by means of its specific counterpart, namely each factor of jhāna that constitutes a component of insight; this is called abandonment by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*).
And when it is said, "one who develops concentration partaking of penetration abandons the various types of views," the abandonment of those very views is intended here in a coarse sense.
It should be understood that it is so stated. For a "view-approach" (*diṭṭhigata*) is gross, whereas the perception of permanence and so forth are subtle.
In this context, "of view-approaches" (*diṭṭhigatānaṃ*) means that the view itself is the "view-approach," just as one speaks of "excrement-approach" (*gūthagata*) or "urine-approach" (*muttagata*).

Furthermore, it is called a "view-approach" because, since there is no place to go, it is merely the "gone" (*gata*) of the view; and also because it is included within the sixty-two views, it is the "gone among" (*gataṃ pi*) the views.
"Views" (diṭṭhigataṃ). By the plural, it refers to those various views. "Concentration partaking of penetration" (Nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ samādhiṃ) means concentration associated with insight (vipassanā).

Furthermore, that abandonment of the phenomena of the fetters (saṃyojana-dhamma) by means of noble path-knowledge (ariyamagga-ñāṇa), such that they do not arise again—just like a tree struck by a thunderbolt—is called "abandonment by eradication" (samucchedappahāna). Cessation (nirodho).
"Nibbāna" refers to Nibbāna, which is characterized as cessation.

Having thus shown the phenomena that are to be abandoned by way of their abandonment, he now says, "All, monks, is to be abandoned," and so forth, in order to show again the phenomena to be abandoned in their own essential nature.
Therein, the eye and the other [faculties] are [abandoned] through the abandonment of desire and lust.
[They] are to be abandoned. In such passages as "seeing form, one abandons," one who sees form as impermanent and so forth abandons the defilements that are to be abandoned.

In the two series beginning with "the eye... [and so on]... aging-and-death... [and so on]... Nibbāna, which plunges into the Deathless," the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*) is intended.
In the phrases "seeing... one abandons," it is this supramundane faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that one sees—that is, one looks toward.
"Looking forward and desiring, he abandons the defilements to be abandoned at the moments of insight"—this should be applied according to each respective state.
The commentary on the description of what is to be abandoned is finished.
The commentary on the description of what is to be developed.

25. In the exposition of what is to be developed (*bhāvetabba-niddesa*): "Mindfulness directed to the body" (*kāyagatāsati*) refers to the mindfulness associated with the appropriate form-jhāna (*rūpajjhāna*), as well as the attention (*manasikāra*) that defines—respectively—the breath (*ānāpāna*), the four postures (*iriyāpatha*), the minor postures, the thirty-two aspects (*dvattiṃsākāra*), the four elements (*catudhātu*), the nine cemetery contemplations (*sivathika*), and the repulsive (*paṭikūla*).

It is called "directed to the body" because it has gone to and proceeds within those bodies. "Accompanied by gratification" (*sātasahagatā*) means accompanied by what is reckoned as pleasant and sweet feeling (*vedayita*).

It has attained the state of arising together with pleasure (*sāta*). The word *sahagata* is seen in the Word of the Victor (*jinavacana*) in five senses: when mixed with that [state], in the object, in the support (*nissaya*), and in association (*saṃsaṭṭha*).
In the passage, “This craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust,” it is used in the sense of being that [state];
the meaning is “consisting of delight and lust. In the passage, “That investigation, monks, which is accompanied by indolence, associated with indolence,”...
Here, "intermingled" (*vokiṇṇa*) means intermingled with indolence (*kosajja*) arising from time to time.

In the phrase, "He is an attainer of attainments accompanied by the form realm or accompanied by the formless realm," it refers to the object; the meaning is "having the form or formless realms as their object.

In the phrase, "He develops the mindfulness factor of enlightenment accompanied by the perception of a skeleton," it refers to the support; [the meaning is] "having the perception of a skeleton as its support."
The meaning is: "having developed the perception of a skeleton, it is obtained.
In the phrase "this happiness is accompanied by, co-nascent with, and associated with this joy," the sense is "conjoined" (*saṃsaṭṭha*) or "mixed" (*sammissa*).
In this term as well, "conjoined" is intended; for it is said that what is conjoined with the pleasant is "accompanied by the pleasant. This [joy], excluding the fourth jhāna...

In the [first] three knowledges, it is accompanied by pleasure (*sāta*); and although it is also accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*), it is stated to be "accompanied by pleasure" because it occurs predominantly as such.
Alternatively, since the fourth jhāna is rooted in the preceding jhānas, it is stated to be "accompanied by equanimity" even though it is accompanied by pleasure.
Furthermore, because it is stated that there is pleasure when equanimity is present, the Blessed One has also stated that the fourth jhāna is "associated with pleasure."
"Tranquility and insight": it is called *samatha* because it calms (*sameti*) and destroys adverse states such as sensual desire;
this is a name for concentration (*samādhi*). It is called *vipassanā* because it sees phenomena through various aspects, such as impermanence and so forth;
this is a name for wisdom (*paññā*). Furthermore, these two are stated to be the "preliminary stages" in the *Dasuttara-sutta*, and in the *Saṅgīti-sutta*—

And [they are] mundane, supramundane, and mixed. "Three kinds of concentration" are: concentration with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitakka savicāra*), concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought only (*avitakka vicāramatta*), and concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought (*avitakka avicāra*). It is "with applied thought" (*savitakka*) by virtue of being accompanied by applied thought as it occurs;

it is "with sustained thought" (*savicāra*) by virtue of being accompanied by sustained thought. This consists of momentary concentration (*khaṇika-samādhi*), insight concentration (*vipassanā-samādhi*), access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*), and...
The concentration of the first jhāna. It is "without applied thought" (avitakka) because there is no applied thought (vitakka) in it.

It is "consisting of sustained thought only" (vicāramatta) because sustained thought (vicāra) is its sole measure, its limit, and its maximum; the meaning is that beyond sustained thought, it does not associate with applied thought.
This is the concentration of the second jhāna according to the fivefold method. That which is devoid of both is concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought (avitakka-avicāra).
Thus, in the fourfold method, the second jhāna and so forth; in the fivefold method, the third jhāna and so forth—these are form-sphere attainments (rūpāvacara-samādhi).
These three are exclusively mundane (lokiya). In the *Saṅgītipariyāya*, three other types of concentration are mentioned:
“emptiness concentration (suññato samādhi), signless concentration (animitto samādhi), and desireless concentration (appaṇihito samādhi). These are not intended here.

The four foundations of mindfulness are: the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body, the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of feelings, the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the mind, and the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of phenomena.

In the preliminary stage, for one who comprehends the body in fourteen ways, there is the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body; for one who comprehends feelings in nine ways, there is the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of feelings.
The foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of mind should be understood as occurring for one who comprehends the mind in its sixteen aspects;

the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of mental objects should be understood as occurring for one who comprehends mental objects in their five aspects. However, the supramundane is not intended here.
"Five-factored concentration" means that it possesses five factors; it refers to the concentration of the fourth jhāna.

The five factors are: pervasion by rapture (*pītipharaṇatā*), pervasion by pleasure (*sukhapharaṇatā*), pervasion by the mind (*cetopharaṇatā*), pervasion by light (*ālokapharaṇatā*), and the sign for reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇanimitta*).
Wisdom that arises while pervading rapture is called "pervasion by rapture" in two jhānas.
Wisdom that arises while pervading pleasure is called "pervasion by pleasure" in three jhānas. [Wisdom regarding] the minds of others...
Wisdom that arises pervading the mind is called "pervasion of the mind" (*cetopharaṇatā*).
Wisdom that arises pervading light is called "pervasion of light" (*ālokapharaṇatā*). Knowledge of reflection is called the "sign of reflection.
And this has also been said: "In two jhānas, wisdom is the pervasion of rapture; in three jhānas, wisdom is the pervasion of pleasure; [and] wisdom regarding the minds of others..."
The pervasion by joy is the sign of light; the wisdom of the divine eye is the pervasion by radiance;
and for one who has emerged from various meditative attainments, the knowledge of reviewing is the "sign of reviewing.
For that is called a "sign" because it grasps the mode of occurrence of one who has emerged from concentration. And therein, the pervasion by joy...
The pervasion by happiness is like the two feet; the pervasion by the mind and the pervasion by light are like the two hands;
the fourth jhāna serving as the basis for direct knowledge is like the torso; and the sign for review is like the head.
Thus, the Venerable Dhammasenāpati, the Elder Sāriputta, demonstrated the fivefold right concentration as being like a person endowed with all major and minor limbs.
The six bases of recollection (*cha anussatiṭṭhānāni*): they are called "recollections" (*anussatiyo*) because they arise again and again;

they are also called "recollections" because they are the appropriate mindfulness for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith, as they proceed precisely within the sphere of activity where one should proceed;
