and they are called "bases of recollection" because they are the foundation for joy and the other [factors] such as rapture. Which six? Recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma...

The recollection of the Saṅgha, the recollection of virtue, the recollection of generosity, and the recollection of the deities. "Factors of enlightenment" (bojjhaṅga) means limbs of enlightenment, or factors for enlightenment.

This is what is meant: that collection of states which, when arising at the moment of the supramundane path, [counteract] sluggishness, agitation, stagnation, exertion, devotion to sensual pleasure, devotion to self-mortification, adherence to annihilationism, adherence to eternalism, and so forth.

Because the noble disciple awakens by means of the harmony of qualities known as mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—which serve as the antidote to manifold calamities—he is called "Bodhi" (Awakening).
He "awakens" in the sense that he rises from the sleep of the continuity of defilements, or penetrates the Four Noble Truths, or realizes Nibbāna itself. Of that...

They are called "factors of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅgā*) because they are factors of the enlightenment (*bodhi*) which is defined as the harmony of states (*dhammasāmaggī*), just like the factors of absorption (*jhānaṅga*) or the factors of the path (*maggaṅga*).

Furthermore, since the noble disciple is called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) on account of awakening by means of this aforementioned harmony of states, these are also called "factors of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅgā*) because they are factors of that enlightenment, just like the factors of an army (*senaṅga*) or the factors of a chariot (*rathaṅga*). Thus say the teachers of the commentaries.

“The factors of a person who is awakening are ‘enlightenment-factors’ (bojjhaṅgā). Furthermore, the meaning of “enlightenment-factor” should be understood according to such methods as: “In what sense are they enlightenment-factors?
They lead to enlightenment; thus they are enlightenment-factors. As for “the noble eightfold path”:

it is called noble because it is remote from the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path, because it produces the state of a noble one, and because it brings about the attainment of the fruit of the noble ones.
And it is noble (*ariya*). It has eight factors, thus it is "eightfold" (*aṭṭhaṅgika*). Like a fourfold army or a fivefold musical ensemble, this consists of mere factors;

there is nothing apart from the factors. The factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) and the path factors (*maggaṅga*) are supramundane (*lokuttara*), yet they are also found in the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*) according to the *Dasuttara* method.
The nine factors of purification and striving (*pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅga*) are as follows: purification of virtue as a factor of purification and striving;

purification of mind as a factor of purification and striving; purification of view as a factor of purification and striving; purification by overcoming doubt as a factor of purification and striving;
purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path as a factor of purification and striving; and purification by knowledge and vision of the way.
The factor of striving for complete purity (*pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅga*): purification by knowledge and vision is a factor of striving for complete purity;

wisdom is a factor of striving for complete purity; liberation is a factor of striving for complete purity. "Pure virtue" (*sīlavisuddhi*) refers to the fourfold pure virtue capable of bringing about purification.
For it cleanses the stain of immorality. "Factor of striving for complete purity" (*pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅga*) means the primary [factor] for the state of being completely pure.
The supreme factor. Purity of mind (*cittavisuddhi*) refers to the eight masteries of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) which serve as the proximate cause for insight (*vipassanā*);

for these purify the stains of the mind, such as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*). Purity of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*) refers to the vision of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) together with their conditions; for that purifies the stain of the view of a self (*sattadiṭṭhi*).
Purity by overcoming doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi*) refers to the knowledge of the mode of conditions (*paccayākārañāṇa*); by means of this...
For one who sees that phenomena proceed by way of conditions throughout the three periods of time, one becomes purified by casting off the stain of the seven doubts regarding all three periods.

Regarding "purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path": at the moment of contemplating rise and fall, there arise ten imperfections of insight (*vipassanūpakkilesa*), namely: illumination-knowledge, rapture, tranquility, pleasure, resolution, exertion, establishment, equanimity, and longing.
It is not the path; rather, the knowledge of rise and fall that has entered the proper course is called "knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path.

For by means of this, one cleanses the impurity of what is not the path. This is "purification by knowledge and vision of the way," which consists of the knowledge of contemplation of rise and fall that has entered the proper course, the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution, the knowledge of contemplation of appearance as terror, the knowledge of contemplation of danger, and the knowledge of contemplation of disenchantment.

The knowledge of desire for deliverance, the knowledge of contemplation of reflection, the knowledge of equanimity towards formations, and the knowledge of conformity—these are the nine insights-knowledges.
For they cleanse the stains such as the perception of permanence. Purification by knowledge and vision is the wisdom of the four noble paths;
for it cleanses the stains of the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path through their total eradication.
"Wisdom" (paññā) refers to the wisdom of the fruit of arahantship. "Liberation" (vimutti) refers to the liberation of the fruit of arahantship.
"The ten kasiṇa bases" refers to: "One perceives the earth-kasiṇa above, below, and across, undivided and immeasurable;
one perceives the water-kasiṇa... [and so on] ...one perceives the fire-kasiṇa... [and so on] ...one perceives the air-kasiṇa... [and so on]."
"One person perceives the blue kasiṇa... one person perceives the yellow kasiṇa...
one person perceives the red kasiṇa... one person perceives the white kasiṇa... one person perceives the space kasiṇa...
one person perceives the consciousness kasiṇa above, below, across, non-dual and immeasurable"—thus ten are mentioned. For these, in the sense of completely pervading, [are called "totalities"].
The *kasiṇas* are "bases" (*āyatana*) in the sense of being fields for those states that have them as their object, or in the sense of being a foundation.
"Upward" means directed toward the upper surface of the sky. "Downward" means directed toward the lower surface of the earth. "Across" means delimited on all sides like a circular field.
For some extend the *kasiṇa* only upward, some downward, and some all around.
Or even a single person extends it in this way for various reasons, just as one desiring to see forms extends light. Therefore it is said:
"One perceives the earth-kasiṇa above, below, and across. However, the word "non-dual" (advaya) is stated for the purpose of showing that it does not become something else for that one person;
for just as for one who has entered water, there is only water in all directions.
It is not something else; even so, the earth-kasiṇa is simply the earth-kasiṇa, and there is no admixture with any other kasiṇa.
This principle applies everywhere. "Immeasurable" (appamāṇa) is said in reference to the immeasurability of its pervasion.
For when one pervades it with the mind, one pervades it in its entirety; one does not grasp a measure such as, "This is its beginning, this is its middle."

The space-kasiṇa consists of both the space revealed by the removal of the kasiṇa and the space as a delimited kasiṇa. The consciousness-kasiṇa is the consciousness occurring in the space revealed by the removal of the kasiṇa.

In this context, "above, below, and across" should be understood with respect to the space revealed by the removal of the kasiṇa by way of the kasiṇa itself, and with respect to the consciousness occurring therein by way of that space revealed by the removal of the kasiṇa;
it should also be understood by way of the delimited space-kasiṇa, because that too is subject to expansion.
26. Now, in order to show the classification of development (*bhāvanā*), he says, "Two kinds of development," and so forth.

Regarding the terms "mundane" (*lokiya*) and so on: the "world" (*loka*) is called the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) in the sense of breaking up and falling away. Those things are "mundane" because they are connected with the world by way of being included within it;
thus, the development of mundane phenomena is "mundane. Although it is spoken of by way of conventional usage as "the development of phenomena," [it refers to the cultivation of mundane states].
There is no separate cultivation (*bhāvanā*) apart from those [factors]; for it is those very phenomena, when being cultivated, that are called "cultivation.
"Crossed over" (*uttiṇṇa*) means "transcended" (*uttara*); because they are not included within the world due to their state of being supramundane, they are "supramundane" (*lokuttara*).

They "move within" form, which is reckoned as the form-existence (*rūpabhava*), thus they are "form-sphere" (*rūpāvacara*). Furthermore, the word "wholesome" (*kusala*) here refers to health, blamelessness, skillfulness, and pleasant ripening (*vipāka*).
It is seen [in the sense of] health, as in such passages as: “Is it well with you, sir?
Are you free from illness? And also: “But what, venerable sir, is wholesome bodily conduct? That bodily conduct which is blameless, Great King,” and:
“Furthermore, venerable sir, this is unsurpassed regarding wholesome states, namely, how the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma concerning wholesome states.”
In such cases as these, it refers to the blameless (*anavajja*). In passages such as, “What do you think, prince, are you skilled in the parts and components of a chariot?
and “The four types of women are skilled and trained in dance and song,” it refers to the clever (*cheke*).

In passages such as, “Because of undertaking wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*), this merit increases in this way,” and “Because of having performed and accumulated wholesome kamma,” [the term *kusala* refers to the wholesome].

And [the term] occurs in such contexts as "having a pleasant result" (*sukhavipāka*). Here, however, it applies to health, to blamelessness, and to having a pleasant result. As for the etymological meaning here:
they are called *kusala* because they crush (*salayanti*), shake (*calayanti*), tremble (*kampenti*), and destroy (*viddhaṃsenti*) base and evil states (*kucchite pāpake dhamme*);

or else, they are called *kusā* because they lie down or proceed in a base manner (*kucchitena ākārena sayanti pavattanti*); they cut away (*lunanti*) those things reckoned as unwholesome (*akusala*).
They are "wholesome" (*kusala*) because they cut away; or, *kusa* is so called because it cuts (*sāna*) and thins out what is vile (*kucchita*), namely, knowledge.
They are "wholesome" because they are to be taken up, grasped, and set in motion by that *kusa*.

Or, just as blades of *kusa* grass cut the area of the hand on both sides, so too do these [wholesome states] cut away the side of defilement on both sides, by way of both the arisen and the unarisen.
Therefore, they are "wholesome" (*kusala*) because they cut off [defilements] like *kuśa* grass. The cultivation of those wholesome states belonging to the fine-material sphere is [the subject].

They are "immaterial-sphere" (*arūpāvacara*) because they move within the immaterial realm, which is designated as the immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*). They are "included" (*pariyāpanna*) because they are comprised within and contained in the cycle of existence consisting of the three planes;
they are "not included" (*apariyāpanna*) because they are not included in that [cycle], being supramundane (*lokuttara*).

If it is asked why the development of wholesome states pertaining to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) is not mentioned, it is because in the Abhidhamma, "development" (*bhāvanā*) is intended specifically as that which has reached absorption (*appanā*). For it is said therein:

"In the spheres of work prescribed by yoga, or in the spheres of craft prescribed by yoga, or in the branches of science prescribed by yoga, [one contemplates] ownership of action, or conformity with truth, or form as impermanent, or feeling as impermanent, or perception..."

Whether it be "impermanent," or "formations are impermanent," or "consciousness is impermanent"—whatever such conformable acceptance, view, preference, gladness, perspective, or acceptance through contemplation of the Dhamma one acquires without having heard it from another, this is called wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmaya-paññā*).
Or, regarding the spheres of action prescribed for yoga... [and so on] ...acceptance through contemplation of the Dhamma.

"Having heard from another, one acquires it; this is called wisdom consisting in what is heard (sutamayā paññā). All wisdom of one who has attained meditative absorption is wisdom consisting in mental development (bhāvanāmayā paññā).

However, that development pertaining to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara-bhāvanā) is not called "development" [in this context] because it is interrupted by the moments of adverting (āvajjana) and the falling back into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga-pāta).

They should be understood. Since all merits are included within the three bases for performing meritorious deeds, it is established that access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) and insight concentration (*vipassanā-samādhi*) constitute merit consisting in development (*bhāvanāmaya-puñña*).
However, here they are subsumed under mundane development alone.

Regarding the threefold nature of the fine-material and immaterial realms, those that are inferior are "low" (*hīna*), meaning base. Those that exist between the low and the sublime are "middling" (*majjha*); *majjhima* is also a reading.
"Exalted" (*paṇītā*) means brought to a state of striving; the meaning is "supreme.

This inferiority, mediocrity, and excellence are to be understood by way of the exertion [of effort]. For that [concentration] in which, at the moment of exertion, desire, energy, mind, or investigation is inferior, it is called "inferior.
That in which those factors are mediocre is called "mediocre. That in which those factors are exalted—

That is called "exquisite" (paṇītā). Alternatively, that which is associated with weak faculties is called "inferior," that associated with middling faculties is "middling," and that associated with superior faculties is called "exquisite.

Because the state of being inferior or middling does not exist in the supramundane (apariyāpannā), it is described as being exclusively exquisite. For it is exquisite in the sense of being supreme and in the sense of being unsurpassed.
27. In the first tetrad on development (*bhāvanā*), "he develops" means that at one and the same moment, penetrating in such and such a way, he develops the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).
In the second tetrad on development, "development as seeking" (*esanā-bhāvanā*) refers to the development prior to absorption (*appanā*).

For it is called "seeking" because by means of it one seeks absorption. "Development as attainment" (*paṭilābha-bhāvanā*) is the development of absorption itself; for it is by means of that seeking [that absorption is attained].

It is called "acquisition" (*paṭilābha*) because it is acquired. "Cultivation of single flavor" (*ekarasa-bhāvanā*) refers to the cultivation at the time of the preliminary application for one who wishes to attain mastery over that acquisition.

For that [cultivation] is called "single flavor" because it is of a single flavor by virtue of the flavor of liberation, due to being liberated from those various defilements through their respective abandonings.
"Cultivation of repetition" (*āsevana-bhāvanā*) refers to [the practice] according to one's desire once mastery has been attained over the acquisition.

Cultivation occurs at the time of enjoyment; for it is that which is intensely practiced, and thus it is called "repetition" (*āsevanā*). Some, however, explain: "Cultivation as repetition is mastery;

cultivation of single flavor is all-pervading. Regarding the phrase "of those entering concentration" in the fourfold classification, this is a present-tense term used in proximity to a present state.
"Arising therein" means arising in that prior stage. "They become of a single flavor" means...
They have a common function in the production of absorption (*appanā*). "Of those who have attained concentration" means of those who have entered into absorption.
"Arisen therein" means arisen in that absorption. "They do not overstep one another" means that, due to their equal occurrence, they do not exceed one another.
In such passages as "he develops the faculty of faith in the sense of resolution," even within a single moment, each individual faculty performs its own respective function.
By virtue of their respective supports, the remaining faculties—which perform their own particular functions—also become of a single flavor through the flavor of liberation;

thus, in the sense of having a single flavor through the flavor of liberation, it is called "development" (*bhāvanā*). The same method applies to the powers, factors of enlightenment, and path-factors as well.
Furthermore, the change in gender (from feminine to neuter) has been made in the word *ekarasa*.
"A bhikkhu here" means a bhikkhu in this teaching; he is called a *bhikkhu* because he beholds (*ikkhati*) the danger (*bhaya*) in *saṃsāra*.

In expressions such as "at the time of the morning," the accusative case is used in the sense of absolute connection (*accantasamyoga*), yet in meaning it is simply the locative; the sense is "in the early part of the day.
"He cultivates" (*āsevati*) means he intensely practices the concentration that has reached mastery (*vasi*). "At the time of midday" refers to the middle of the day.
At midday. At the time of evening means at the evening portion of the day. Before the meal means at a time prior to the daytime meal. After the meal means at a time subsequent to the daytime meal.
In the first watch means in the first division of the night. In the dark [fortnight] means in the waning half of the moon.
In the bright [fortnight] means in the waxing half of the moon. In the first stage of life means in the first division of the lifespan.

The meaning is "in the first stage. For a person with a lifespan of one hundred years, there are thirty-three years and four months in each of the three stages. 28. Regarding the fourth tetrad on development (*bhāvanā*):
"In the sense of not overstepping the phenomena born therein" means, in that context, regarding renunciation (*nekkhamma*) and so forth.
By way of the non-transgression of one another among the paired qualities known as concentration and wisdom that have arisen through specific modes of development;

by way of the single function of the faculties, meaning that in that very state the faculties such as faith and the rest possess a single function through the flavor of liberation due to being freed from various defilements;
and by way of the exertion of energy directed toward that [state], meaning toward those [qualities] characterized by non-transgression and a single function.
By way of being the vehicle for appropriate energy. "In the sense of repetition" means the repetition that occurs at that time;
by way of being the repetition of that [repetition].
"Perception of form" refers to the fifteenfold perception of form, known as the fine-material-sphere jhāna, which functions as wholesome, resultant, or functional.
For even the fine-material-sphere jhāna is called "form" in such passages as, "Possessing form, he sees forms," and so on;
and the object of that jhāna is also called "form" in such passages as, "He sees external forms, beautiful and ugly.

Indeed, because it perceives forms by way of the characteristic of perception, the fine-material-sphere jhāna is called "perception of form" (*rūpasaññā*). As for "perception of resistance" (*paṭighasaññā*), it refers to wholesome resultant [consciousness].
Five [types of perception] are unwholesome-resultant, and five are wholesome-resultant; thus there are ten kinds of "perception of resistance" (*paṭighasaññā*).

For the perception associated with the two sets of fivefold consciousness is called "perception of resistance" because it arises through the impact (*paṭighāta*) of the bases, such as the eye, and the objects, such as visible forms.

It is also referred to simply as "perception of form," "perception of sound," "perception of odor," "perception of taste," and "perception of tangible object. This is precisely that same [perception].

“Name” (nāma). “Perception of diversity” (nānattasaññā) refers to the forty-fourfold perception of diversity, namely: eight wholesome perceptions of the sense sphere, twelve unwholesome perceptions, eleven wholesome-resultant perceptions of the sense sphere, two unwholesome-resultant perceptions, and eleven functional perceptions of the sense sphere.
For that [perception] exists in diversity—that is, in various natures—such as the distinctions of visible forms, sounds, and so forth.

“Perception occurring in relation to its object” is *nānatta-saññā* (perception of diversity). Alternatively, it is called *nānatta-saññā* because it consists of perceptions that are diverse in their divisions—forty-four in number—having different natures and being dissimilar to one another.
Although there is a plurality of perceptions, the singular number is used by way of referring to the genus (*jāti*).

“Perception of permanence” (*nicca-saññā*) means the perception [of something] as permanent; thus also for “perception of pleasure” (*sukha-saññā*) and “perception of self” (*atta-saññā*). “Delight” (*nandi*)...
"Accompanied by zest" refers to craving with zest. "Passion" refers to craving devoid of zest. "Origin" refers to the origin of passion.
Alternatively, because one sees only dissolution through the contemplation of dissolution, it is the arising of formations.

"Grasping" refers to the grasping of defilements by way of their production, or the grasping of conditioned objects due to a lack of aversion and insight. "Perception of density" refers to [the perception of continuity] by way of a continuous stream.
They conceive of perception. "Exertion" means making an effort for the sake of formations. "Perception of stability" means the perception that [things] are firm.
"Sign" means the sign of permanence. "Inclination" means the longing for pleasure.

"Adherence" means the adherence that "there is a self. "Adherence as grasping at the core" means the adherence that grasps at what is permanent, essential, and a core. "Adherence through delusion" means...

“Adherence through delusion” refers to the adherence [to views] such as “Did I exist in the past? and so forth, as well as the adherence [to the view] that “the world arises from a Supreme Lord” (Issara) and so forth.
“Adherence through attachment” refers to the adherence [to the idea] that “this is what one should cling to,” by means of failing to see its danger.
“Failure to reflect” refers to grasping by an improper means. “Adherence through bondage” refers to the manifestation of defilements such as the yoke of sensual desire (kāmayoga).
Regarding the term *diṭṭhekaṭṭhā*: they are called *diṭṭhekaṭṭhā* because they stand together with views (*diṭṭhi*) in one place.
Those are the *diṭṭhekaṭṭhā*. They defile, torment, and oppress, thus they are called *kilesā*. Those are the *kilese*. For "standing together" (*ekaṭṭha*) is twofold:

standing together by way of abandonment (*pahānekaṭṭha*) and standing together by way of co-arising (*sahajekaṭṭha*). Standing together by way of abandonment refers to [those factors] that are together with the sixty-three views, headed by the view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), as long as...
The meaning is that they are established in a single person by means of their abandonment through the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga).

This is what is intended here. For among the ten defilements (kilesa), only the defilement of views (diṭṭhi-kilesa) is mentioned here. However, among the remaining nine defilements—which lead to rebirth in the states of misery—namely greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, doubt, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing, these are included together with views.

Having become factors to be abandoned together, they are abandoned by the path of stream-entry; or rather, among the one thousand five hundred defilements headed by lust, hatred, and delusion, when view is being abandoned by the path of stream-entry, all defilements leading to the states of misery are abandoned by way of being factors to be abandoned together with that view.
Those [defilements] co-existent with view are abandoned together with view in a single moment of consciousness.

The meaning is "established. For when, by means of the stream-entry path (sotāpatti-magga), two types of view-associating spontaneous (asaṅkhārika) consciousness are abandoned, the defilements—namely greed, delusion, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness—which arise simultaneously with them, are abandoned by way of being co-existent and co-active.
When two types of view-associating prompted (sasaṅkhārika) consciousness are abandoned, the greed that arises simultaneously with them...
Delusion, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing—these defilements are abandoned by way of being co-existent and conjoined.
"Gross defilements" refers to gross forms of sensual lust and ill will. "Subtle defilements" refers to subtle forms of sensual lust and ill will.
"All defilements" refers to those remaining after they have been abandoned by the first three paths.
"He carries forth energy" means that the practitioner of yoga sets energy in motion.

The preceding terms—searching, attainment, single flavor, and cultivation—were stated for the purpose of showing the distinctions among the modes of development, [showing] that "development is of such a nature. Here, however, it is said:
"in the sense of the non-transgression of the states arisen therein; in the sense of the single flavor of the faculties; in the sense of carrying forth the energy directed toward them."
The statements beginning with "in the sense of repetition" are spoken for the purpose of showing the cause of development (bhāvanā), meaning: "Development occurs by means of this and that cause.
Previously, "repetition as development" was stated in terms of different moments; here, "development in the sense of repetition" is stated in terms of a single moment—this is the distinction.
In such passages as "one who sees form develops [the path]," form and so forth are to be seen in their respective modes.

The meaning is: "While contemplating, he develops the development that is to be developed. They are "of a single flavor" (ekarasa) by way of the flavor of liberation, or by way of the flavor of their function.
"Flavor of liberation" means the flavor of attainment. For it has been said: "The word 'flavor' (rasa) is used in the sense of the attainment of function.
The commentary on the exposition of what is to be developed is finished.
Commentary on the Description of What is to be Realized (Sacchikātabba-niddesa) 29.
In the description of what is to be realized, ten successive answers are given by way of the realization of attainment (*paṭilābha-sacchikiriyā*).
Therein, "unshakable deliverance of mind" (*akuppā cetovimutti*) refers to the deliverance that is the fruit of Arahantship. For that does not waver, does not shake, and does not decline.
It is unshakable; because the mind is liberated from all defilements, it is called "liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*). "True knowledge" (*vijjā*) refers to the three true knowledges.
"Liberation" (*vimutti*) is stated, according to the *Dasuttara* discourse, to be the fruit of arhatship; however, according to the *Saṅgīti* discourse, it is stated:
"Liberation is twofold: the liberation of the mind and Nibbāna. And herein, the eight attainments...

It is called "liberation" (*vimutti*) because it is thoroughly liberated from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth; it is called "liberation" because *nibbāna* is liberated from all conditioned things (*saṅkhata*).
The three knowledges (*tisso vijjā*) are: the knowledge of recollecting past lives is a knowledge; the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings is a knowledge;
the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava*) is a knowledge. It is a "knowledge" (*vijjā*) in the sense of piercing through darkness, and also in the sense of making things known.

Knowledge (*vijjā*). For the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*), when it arises, pierces the darkness that had been concealing past lives and makes those past lives known;
thus, it is "knowledge. The knowledge of passing away and rebirth (*cutūpapāte ñāṇa*) pierces the darkness that conceals death and rebirth and makes passing away and rebirth known;
thus, it is "knowledge. The knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavānaṃ khaye ñāṇa*) [pierces] the darkness that conceals the Four Noble Truths...
It pierces darkness and makes known the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths; thus it is "clear knowledge" (*vijjā*). The "four fruits of recluseship" (*sāmaññaphala*) are:
the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship.

One who pacifies (*sameti*) and destroys evil qualities is a "recluse" (*samaṇa*); the state of being a recluse is "recluseship" (*sāmañña*). This is the name for the four noble paths. Of recluseship...
The fruits are the fruits of asceticism.

The five aggregates of Dhamma are: the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
"Aggregates of Dhamma" means divisions of Dhamma, portions of Dhamma. This applies to the aggregate of virtue and the others as well.
The same method applies here. Worldly and supramundane virtue, concentration, and wisdom are themselves the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom.

The deliverances consisting in eradication, subsiding, and renunciation are themselves the aggregate of deliverance. The threefold reviewing of deliverance is itself the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of deliverance;
this is purely worldly. Knowledge in the sense of knowing and vision in the sense of seeing constitute "knowledge-and-vision" (ñāṇadassana) regarding the deliverances.

Knowledge and vision is called "knowledge and vision of liberation. However, the liberations consisting of suppression and through its factors are included within the aggregates of concentration and wisdom respectively.
These five aggregates of Dhamma are said to be "of the trainees" for trainees and "of the non-trainees" for non-trainees.
For among these, both the mundane and the liberation by way of escape are neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee. Even though they are [mundane], they belong to the trainees.

"These" refers to those in training (*sekkhā*); they are called "these" because they belong to those beyond training (*asekkhā*). Furthermore, in the passage, "He is endowed with the aggregate of liberation belonging to one in training," it should be understood that he is "endowed" by way of making the liberation of escape (*nissaraṇavimutti*) his object.

"The six direct knowledges" (*cha abhiññā*) means six superior knowledges. Which six? The knowledge of the modes of psychic power (*iddhividha*), the knowledge of the divine ear-element (*dibbasotadhātu*), [the knowledge of others' minds, the recollection of past lives, the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints].
The knowledge of recollecting past lives, the knowledge of penetration into others' minds, the knowledge of the divine eye, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints—these are the six.

Regarding "the seven powers of one whose taints are destroyed" (*khīṇāsavabala*): one whose taints are destroyed is a *khīṇāsava*; the powers of such a one are the powers of one whose taints are destroyed. Which are the seven? They were spoken by the Blessed One:
"Here, monks, for a monk whose taints are destroyed, all conditioned phenomena are seen as they really are with correct wisdom according to impermanence..."

They are well seen. Moreover, monks, that all conditioned phenomena are well seen as they really are with correct wisdom by a monk whose taints are destroyed—as impermanent—this too is a power of a monk whose taints are destroyed, by virtue of which power a monk whose taints are destroyed claims the destruction of the taints, saying: "My taints are destroyed."

“Furthermore, monks, for a monk whose taints are destroyed, sensual pleasures have been well seen as they really are with correct wisdom as being like a pit of glowing embers. That too, monks, is a power of a monk whose taints are destroyed...

[as before] ... “Furthermore, monks, for a monk whose taints are destroyed, the mind inclines toward seclusion, leans toward seclusion, tends toward seclusion, is established in seclusion, delights in renunciation, and has completely transcended all things that are the basis for the taints.”
...by means of phenomena. Monks, that too is a power of a monk whose taints are destroyed... [as before] ...This too is a power of a monk whose taints are destroyed...
"Furthermore, monks, for a monk whose taints are destroyed, the four foundations of mindfulness have been developed, well-developed.
The five faculties have been developed, well-developed. The seven factors of enlightenment have been developed..."
It is well-developed. The noble eightfold path has been developed, well-developed.
And, monks, that the noble eightfold path has been developed and well-developed by a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is a power of that bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed;
relying on this power, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed claims the destruction of the taints, saying: "The taints are destroyed in me."

Therein, the penetration of the truth of suffering is shown by the first power; the penetration of the truth of the origin by the second; the penetration of the truth of cessation by the third; and the penetration of the truth of the path by the [remaining] four.
As for the "eight liberations" (*vimokkha*): they are called liberations in the sense of being resolved upon an object and in the sense of being thoroughly released from opposing states.
"Which eight? Possessing form, one sees forms—this is the first liberation. Not perceiving form internally..."
One sees forms externally; this is the second liberation. Being intent upon the beautiful alone, this is the third liberation.

With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [perceiving] ‘space is infinite,’ one enters and dwells in the base of infinite space; this is the fourth [liberation].
the liberation. Completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," one enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness;

this is the fifth liberation. Completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing," one enters and dwells in the base of nothingness; this is the sixth liberation. Completely...
“Having completely transcended the base of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;

this is the seventh liberation. Having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling; this is the eighth liberation.”
The nine successive cessations are nine cessations in sequential order. Which nine?
For one who has attained the first jhāna, sensual perception has ceased; for one who has attained the second jhāna, applied and sustained thought have ceased;
for one who has attained the third jhāna, rapture has ceased; for one who has attained the fourth jhāna...
Inhalation and exhalation have ceased; for one who has attained the base of infinite space, perception of form has ceased;
for one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness, perception of the base of infinite space has ceased;
for one who has attained the base of nothingness, perception of the base of infinite consciousness has ceased; for one who has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception...
“The perception of the base of nothingness has ceased; for one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, both perception and feeling have ceased.

Regarding the “ten qualities of one beyond training” (*asekkha*): they are called *asekkha* because they do not train further, as there is no more training to be undertaken above them. Alternatively, in the three...
Those who train in the trainings are *sekkhā* (trainees). Those who have reached full growth among the trainees are *asekkhā* (those beyond training), namely the *arahants*.
These belong to those beyond training; thus they are called *asekkha* (belonging to those beyond training). "Which ten?

The right view of one beyond training, the right intention of one beyond training, the right speech of one beyond training, the right action of one beyond training, the right livelihood of one beyond training, the right effort of one beyond training, the right mindfulness of one beyond training, the right concentration of one beyond training, the right knowledge of one beyond training, and the right liberation of one beyond training."
“Right mindfulness, right concentration of one beyond training, right knowledge of one beyond training, and right liberation of one beyond training.

Right knowledge of one beyond training refers to all mundane wisdom (paññā) with the exception of the wisdom of the fruit of arahantship. Right liberation refers to the liberation of the fruit of arahantship.
However, it is stated in the Commentary:
“All these factors, beginning with ‘the right view of one beyond training,’ are indeed the states associated with the fruit.
Here, wisdom alone is spoken of in two places as ‘right view’ and ‘right knowledge. However, by the term ‘right liberation,’ the remaining states of the attainment of the fruit are included.”
In such passages as "All, monks, is to be realized," the realization of the object (*ārammaṇasacchikiriyā*) is to be understood.

In such passages as "One who sees form realizes," one who sees worldly forms and so forth in the manner they are to be seen realizes those very forms and so forth through the realization of the object;
or, seeing forms and so forth in the manner they are to be seen, by that cause one realizes Nibbāna, which is what is to be realized.
He realizes. For the scholars of phonology maintain that the word *passanto* (seeing) can also have the sense of a cause (*hetu*).

However, when one sees the supramundane faculties such as "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*) by way of reviewing, one realizes them precisely through the realization of their object.

As for the statement, "One realizes Nibbāna, which plunges into the Deathless, in the sense of the ultimate end," this refers [to the realization] among those things to be fully understood, abandoned, realized, and developed.
It is straightforward because it is to be realized. Whatever states are realized, those very states are touched;

thus, those realized through the realization of the object are touched by the contact with the object, and those realized through the realization of attainment are touched by the contact of attainment.
The commentary on the description of what is to be realized is finished.
Commentary on the Description of the Tetrad of Factors Conducive to Decline (Hānabhāgiya-cattukka-niddesa): 30.
Now, since the state of being conducive to decline and so forth belongs to each individual concentration through a distinction of its stages, therefore...
The tetrad pertaining to decline is explained from a single point of view. Therein, "one who has obtained the first jhāna" means one who possesses the first jhāna.
The accusative case is used here in the sense of the genitive (possessive). One is called "possessor" (*lābhī*) because they possess (*lābho*)—that is, have the realization of—that [jhāna].

Regarding the term "accompanied by sensual desire" (*kāmasahagatā*): here, the word *sahagata* is intended in the sense of "object" (*ārammaṇa*); thus, it means having the objects of sensual pleasure (*vatthukāma*) and the defilements of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*) as their objective support.
The meaning is as follows: "Perception and attention" refers to both the perception of the impulsion (*javana*) and the attention of the adverting consciousness (*tadāvajjana*);
it is also acceptable to take it as the attention associated with that perception. "Occur" means they arise. "Dhamma" refers to the dhamma of the first jhāna.

One falling away from the jhāna falls away for three reasons: either through the occurrence of defilements (*kilesa*), or through unwholesome activity (*asappāyakiriyā*), or through lack of application (*ananuyoga*).
One who falls away through the active manifestation of defilements (*kilesa-samudācāra*) falls away quickly;
one who falls away through engagement in unsuitable activity—by way of devotion to work, devotion to talk, devotion to sleep, and devotion to company—falls away slowly;
and one who falls away through lack of application, failing to attain [jhāna] frequently due to obstacles such as illness or lack of requisites, also falls away slowly. But here, however—
Showing only the primary cause, he speaks specifically of the manifestation of defilements (*kilesa-samudācāra*).
However, one who falls away from the second jhāna and so forth also falls away through the manifestation of a longing for the lower and lower jhānas. To what extent has one fallen away?
When one is no longer able to attain [the state], to that extent one has fallen away. "In accordance with that" (*tadanudhammā*) means following its course.
*Dhammo anudhammo* is a designation for the state of attachment that occurs by making *jhāna* predominant.
*Anudhamma* itself is *anudhammatā*; the state of being in accordance with that *jhāna* is *tadanudhammatā*. *Sati* means attachment.
*Santiṭṭhati* means it becomes established. Thus it is said: "The attachment, following along with that first *jhāna*, proceeds."
It exists. "Accompanied by non-thinking" (*avitakkasahagatā*) means having the second jhāna as its object; for since there is no thinking (*vitakka*) therein, it is called "non-thinking.

"Accompanied by disenchantment" (*nibbidāsahagatā*) means having insight (*vipassanā*) as its object; for that is called "disenchantment" because of the state of being disenchanted with conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), as it is said:
"Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate. "Conjoined with dispassion" (*virāgūpasaṃhitā*) means associated with the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).
Vipassanā. For when vipassanā has reached its culmination, it brings about emergence from the path.
Therefore, perception and attention having vipassanā as their object are said to be "conjoined with dispassion" (*virāgūpasaṃhitā*), for it is said: "By means of dispassion, one is liberated.

"Accompanied by applied thought" (*vitakkasahagatā*) means that, by way of applied thought, they have the first jhāna as their object. "Accompanied by equanimity and pleasure" (*upekkhāsukhasahagatā*) means by way of the equanimity of impartiality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).
And by way of pleasant feeling, it has the third jhāna as its object. "Accompanied by rapture and pleasure" means that, by way of rapture and pleasant feeling, it has the second jhāna as its object.
"Accompanied by neither-pain-nor-pleasure" means that, by way of the feeling of equanimity, it has the fourth jhāna as its object.
For that feeling is called "neither-pain-nor-pleasure" because it is neither painful nor pleasant; the letter *m* here is used for the sake of euphonic junction (*padasandhi*).

It has been said. "Accompanied by the material" means having the material jhāna as its object. Although the states conducive to decline, conducive to maintenance, and conducive to penetration exist for one established in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception itself is not specifically pointed out because it lacks the state of being conducive to distinction.
Furthermore, all this mundane concentration is conducive to decline for one who dwells in negligence and possesses dull faculties, whereas for one who dwells in diligence...
For one of dull faculties, it is "partaking of stability"; for one of craving-temperament with keen faculties, it is "partaking of distinction";
for one of view-temperament with keen faculties, it is said to be "partaking of penetration.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Tetrad Partaking of Decline is finished.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Triad of Characteristics (Lakkhaṇattikaniddesa) 31.
Now, since even each single mundane phenomenon is struck by the three characteristics, the triad of characteristics is explained together here.
In that context, "impermanent in the sense of destruction" means it is impermanent by way of perishing right there and then.
Some say it is "impermanent" because it is subject to decay, subject to passing away, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.

It is "suffering" in the sense of being fearful; for it is suffering due to its state of being accompanied by peril, since whatever is impermanent brings fear, as in the Sīhapotaka Sutta regarding the devas.
Some say it is "suffering" in the sense of the fear of birth, aging, sickness, and death. It is "non-self" (anattā).

“In the sense of being coreless”: it is non-self because of the absence of a self-essence (attasāra) such as is imagined—that is, a self that is a dweller, an agent, an experiencer, or one who has mastery over itself.
For whatever is impermanent and suffering cannot even maintain its own impermanence or the oppression of arising and passing away;
how much less can it possess the status of an agent and so forth? And it is said: “Bhikkhus, this form here...”
“If there were a self, this form would not lead to affliction,” and so forth. Some say: “It is non-self because it is devoid of the core of a self and the core of permanence.
The commentary on the exposition of the three characteristics is finished.
The commentary on the exposition of the truth of suffering.
The four noble truths are also presented together because the truths are interconnected by way of their true nature (*tathaṭṭha*).

In that context, "therein" (*tattha*) refers to within those four noble truths. "What is it? is a question arising from a desire to explain. "The noble truth of suffering" is the indication of the doctrine being asked about.
Regarding the statement "birth, too, is suffering" and so forth, many meanings for the word "birth" (*jāti*) have been proclaimed. As it has been said:
“Existence (bhava), family, class, virtue, designation, characteristic, birth, and connection—these are declared to be the meanings of ‘birth’ (jāti).
For thus, in such passages as “one birth, two births,” etc., its meaning is existence. Likewise, in “uncensured, unreviled,” etc., [it means] family.
In the phrase “by way of birth,” it refers to *kula* (clan). In the phrase “There is, Visākhā, a class of recluses called the Nigaṇṭhas,” it refers to *nikāya* (sect).
In the phrase “Sister, since I was born with the noble birth, I do not recall...,” it refers to *ariyasīla* (noble virtue).
In the phrase “The grass species called *tiriyā*, having grown up from the navel, stood touching the sky,” it refers to *paññatti* (conventional designation). “Birth [is determined] by two...”

In the phrase "included within the aggregates," this refers to the characteristic of the conditioned (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*). In the phrase "The Bodhisatta was just born, Ānanda," this refers to birth (*pasūti*).
In the phrases "With existence as condition, birth" and "Birth, too, is suffering," this refers to the aggregates of rebirth (*paṭisandhikhandhā*) by way of figurative expression (*pariyāyato*).
However, by way of the direct sense (*nippariyāyato*), it refers to whichever aggregates manifest for beings as they are being reborn here and there.
This is the first manifestation for each and every one of them.
But why is this birth suffering? Because it is the basis for many kinds of suffering. For there are many sufferings, namely:
the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkha*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*), the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*), and concealed suffering (*paṭicchannadukkha*).
There is suffering that is unmasked, suffering in a figurative sense, and suffering in a non-figurative sense.
Herein, bodily and mental painful feelings are called "the suffering of suffering" because they are suffering both by their intrinsic nature and by name.
Pleasant feeling is "the suffering of change" because it is a cause for the arising of suffering through transformation. And as for neutral feeling, and the remainder...
The formations belonging to the three planes are the suffering of formations because they are oppressed by arising and passing away.

Physical and mental affliction—such as earaches, toothaches, the fever born of lust, and the fever born of hatred—is "concealed suffering" because it is to be known only after inquiry and because the means [of its occurrence] are not manifest.
Affliction arising from the thirty-two tortures and so forth is [suffering that is] to be known even without inquiry and because the means [of its occurrence] are manifest.

Unconcealed suffering: with the exception of the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkha*), all else—birth and so forth as described in the analysis of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*)—is "suffering by way of metaphor" (*pariyāyadukkha*) because it serves as the basis for various forms of suffering.
However, the suffering of suffering is said to be "suffering in the literal sense" (*nippariyāyadukkha*).

In this context, "birth" is called suffering because it serves as the basis for that suffering pertaining to the states of woe—which was illustrated by the Blessed One through similes in such discourses as the *Bālapaṇḍita Sutta*—and for that suffering which arises even in the happy destinies within the human world, beginning with the descent into the womb.
Herein, this suffering beginning with the descent into the womb is as follows: for indeed—
A being being reborn in a mother’s womb is not reborn among blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, and the like; rather, it is reborn beneath the stomach and above the intestines,
in the midst of the abdominal membranes and the spinal vertebrae, in a place of extreme confinement, in thick darkness,
pervaded by winds of most foul odor permeated by the scent of various kinds of filth, and exceedingly loathsome.
It is born there like a worm in a place of rotting fish, putrid rice-gruel, a cesspool, and so forth.

Having been born there, for ten months it undergoes extreme suffering—being cooked as if by the heat produced within the mother’s womb like a packet of medicine being steamed, and being squeezed like a lump of dough, while deprived of the ability to contract or extend its limbs. This is...
Such is the suffering rooted in the descent into the womb.
Furthermore, when the mother suddenly stumbles, moves, sits, stands, or turns over, he is dragged, pulled about, shaken,
and tossed like a goat in the hands of a drunkard or a gambler, or like a young snake in the hands of a snake-charmer.
Through these efforts, he experiences intense suffering: when his mother drinks cold water, he experiences intense suffering as if he had been reborn in a cold hell;
when she swallows hot gruel, rice, and so forth, he experiences intense suffering as if surrounded by a shower of glowing coals;

and when she swallows salt, sour liquids, and the like, he experiences intense suffering as if subjected to punishments such as being smeared with caustic soda or beaten with whips. This is the suffering rooted in the maintenance of the womb.

Furthermore, that suffering which one experiences through cutting, tearing, and so forth in a place of arising pain— where even friends, ministers, relatives, and others cannot see one because the mother’s womb is obstructed—
is the suffering rooted in the failure of the womb. And that which occurs when the mother is giving birth, as the being is turned by the winds born of karma and led through the birth canal—
which is as terrifying as falling into hell— and through the extreme constriction of the vaginal opening, which is like the hole of a palm-wood pestle...
Suffering arises for the great being as he is dragged out like a hell-being and crushed by the mountains of the Saṅghāta hell.
This is the suffering rooted in birth.
Furthermore, when the newborn’s delicate body—resembling a fresh wound—is taken by the hand, bathed, washed, rubbed with cloth, and so forth, [suffering arises].
Suffering arises similar to being pierced by the point of a needle or split by the edge of a razor. This is the suffering rooted in emerging from the mother’s womb.

Beyond that, for one who continues in the course of existence, there is the practice of self-mortification and torment, such as through the observance of the naked ascetic (acelaka) vows, whereby one strikes oneself with one's own hand.
For one who does not eat due to anger, or who hangs oneself, there is suffering. This is suffering rooted in one's own initiative (*attupakkamamūlaka*).

However, that which arises for one experiencing slaughter, imprisonment, and so forth at the hands of others, is suffering rooted in the initiative of others (*parūpakkamamūlaka*). Thus, for all this suffering, birth (*jāti*) alone is the basis. Therefore, it is said:
“If a being were not born in the hells, then the unbearable heat of fire and such would not exist there.”
“Where could suffering find a footing?”— thus the Sage here declared that birth is suffering.
“Suffering among animals is manifold,
consisting of being struck by whips, goads, sticks, and the like.”
Whatever kind of birth there might be there,
even without that birth, it is suffering;
moreover, for the departed (petas), there is the suffering of hunger and thirst.
Because that manifold suffering arising from wind, heat,
and so forth does not exist for one who is unborn,
the Sage therefore called birth itself suffering.
“In the blinding darkness and the unbearable cold,
and whatever suffering there is among the Asuras in the intervals between worlds—
that would not exist for him there, nor would there be birth.”
This birth is suffering even from its very inception:
“Just as in a pit of excrement, so too within the mother’s womb does the being dwell for a long time; and when emerging from there, it is like being cast out.”
One encounters suffering that is most terrible;
yet even this does not exist without birth. Indeed, this birth itself is suffering.
What is the use of much speaking? Is it not the case that wherever one goes, [suffering follows]?
"There is indeed some suffering here at any time;
yet there is none when one is separated from birth.
Therefore, the Great Sage spoke of this first of all as 'suffering': birth."
"Old age, too, is suffering": here, old age is twofold: it is both the characteristic of the conditioned (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*), which is recognized as the state of being broken and so forth;

and the state of the aggregates (*khandha*) included within a single existence becoming worn out throughout the continuum (*santati*). It is this latter kind that is intended here. Furthermore, this [old age] is suffering both by way of its nature as the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*) and by way of being a basis for suffering.

For this consists of many conditions such as the loosening of limbs and members, the disfigurement of the sense faculties, the destruction of youth, the impairment of strength, the loss of mindfulness and intelligence, and being treated with contempt by others.
Bodily and mental suffering arises; aging is its basis. Therefore, this is said:
“From the loosening of the limbs, from the transformation of the faculties, from the destruction of youth, and from the impairment of strength.”
“Because of being separated from one’s own children and wife by hundreds and so forth,
and because of causing lack of confidence [in others], as well as for further falling into foolishness,
the mortal attains suffering— both physical and likewise mental.”
"All this has aging as its cause; therefore, aging is suffering.

Although the suffering of illness should have been mentioned immediately after the suffering of aging, it is understood that the suffering of illness is already included by the mention of "bodily suffering" (kāyika-dukkha); thus, it need not be stated separately.
Regarding the statement "death too is suffering," there too death is twofold: the characteristic of the conditioned (*saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa*), with reference to which—
It is said: "Old age and death are comprised within two aggregates.
That which is intended here is the severance of the continuity of the life-faculty included within a single existence, with reference to which it was said: "There is constant fear of death.
Death conditioned by birth is also known by the names: death by violence, natural death, death through the exhaustion of the life-span, and death through the exhaustion of merit.
Furthermore, the distinctions here should be understood as momentary death (*khaṇika-maraṇa*), conventional death (*sammuti-maraṇa*), and death by severance (*samuccheda-maraṇa*).
The dissolution of material and immaterial phenomena during the course of existence is called momentary death.

The expressions "Tissa has died" or "Phussa has died" refer, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramattha*), to the non-existence of a self (*satta*); whereas the expressions "the crop has died" or "the tree has died" refer to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).

The non-existence [of the aggregates] is called conventional death (*sammuti-maraṇa*). The passing away of one whose taints are exhausted without further rebirth is called death by eradication (*samuccheda-maraṇa*).
Apart from external conventional death, the other types—both conventional and death by eradication—are included precisely through the severance of the aforementioned bonds.
Furthermore, it is "suffering" because it is the basis for suffering. Therefore, this is said:
“For one who contemplates the signs of evil, such as wicked deeds;
for one who is unable to overcome the loss of beloved objects;
and for one who is dying—the mental suffering that arises is, without distinction, the same.”
“And whatever suffering arises from the body for all those whose vital points (*marmans*) are being pierced,
such as the severing of joints and ligaments— it is unbearable and incurable; since this is the nature of that suffering, [one should reflect upon it].”
“Death is the basis for this; therefore it is called ‘suffering. Regarding sorrow and the rest:

sorrow (*soka*) is the burning of the mind characterized by inward brooding in one who is struck by the loss of relatives and so forth. Suffering (*dukkha*), however, is [suffering] both as the suffering of pain itself and as the basis for suffering. Therefore, this is said:
“Sorrow strikes at the hearts of beings like a poisoned arrow.”
Like a flame, it burns again like chaff.
Because it brings about disease, as well as the breaking up through old age and death,
and because it brings various kinds of suffering, it is therefore called "suffering."

Lamentation (*parideva*) is the verbal outpouring of one who is struck by the loss of relatives and so forth. Suffering (*dukkha*), however, is so called because it is of the nature of the suffering of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāradukkha*) and because it is the basis of suffering. Thus it is said:

“When one, smitten by the dart of sorrow, laments, The suffering that arises from the parching of the throat, lips, and palate— Being difficult to endure—that very suffering increases even further. Therefore, the Blessed One called lamentation ‘suffering’.”

Dukkha is bodily suffering characterized by oppression of the body. It is called "suffering" both because it is the suffering of suffering itself and because it brings about mental suffering. Therefore, this is said:
"This bodily suffering oppresses the body, and it brings about even greater mental suffering;
since it produces these, it is specifically called 'dukkha'."
Mental grief (*domanassa*) is mental suffering characterized by the oppression of the mind.
It is "suffering" both because it is the suffering of suffering itself and because it brings about bodily suffering. For those possessed by mental suffering, they tear out their hair and weep;
they beat their breasts, wring their hands, and roll back and forth; they fall headlong, take up weapons, consume poison, [hang themselves] with ropes...
They hang themselves, they enter the fire—thus they experience various kinds of suffering. Therefore this is said:
“Since it oppresses the mind and brings about oppression of the body, ‘Suffering’ is called mental distress;
therefore those who are free from distress have so spoken.”
Despair (*upāyāsa*) is simply a state of corruption produced by excessive mental suffering in one who is afflicted by such things as the loss of relatives.

Some say it is "a single dhamma included within the aggregate of formations" (*saṅkhārakkhandha*). However, it is suffering because of the nature of the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*), because it burns the mind, and because it withers the body.
Therefore, this is said:
“Because it intensely burns the mind and withers the body,
the suffering that arises from despair is therefore called ‘suffering’. And here,
sorrow is like the cooking of food inside a vessel over a mild fire, whereas [despair] is like [the cooking] of what is being scorched by a fierce fire from the vessel.

Lamentation is to be seen as like the act of going outside; while despair is to be seen as like the cooking of what remains after one has gone outside—insufficient even to escape—until it is completely exhausted within the vessel itself.
Association with the unloved means being brought together with unloved beings and formations. However, it is suffering by virtue of being a basis for suffering. Therefore, this is said:
“Having seen the unpleasant, suffering first arises in the mind;
thereafter, it arises in the body through the application [of that mental state] here in this world.
Therefore, regarding the basis for both types of suffering, he [the Great Seer]—”
“It should be understood that ‘meeting with those who are unpleasant’ is said to be suffering.

What is called separation from the pleasant is the parting from beloved beings and conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*). It is suffering, however, by virtue of being a basis for suffering. Therefore, this is said:
“Due to separation from kinsmen, wealth, and so forth, people are pierced by the essence of grief as it strikes them.”
“From whatever cause it may be, this separation from what is dear is considered suffering.
Thus, even when one does not obtain what is desired among things that cannot be obtained, that very desire is said to be suffering.
Furthermore, the fact that one who desires an unobtainable thing through whatever means does not obtain it—that too [is suffering] regarding that unobtainable thing.
The meaning is that wishing is suffering. Furthermore, suffering arises from the basis of suffering.
Therefore, this is said: “For those who long for this or that, Because of not obtaining this or that, Whatever suffering consisting of distress Arises here for sentient beings.”
“For unattainable things, yearning is the cause;
therefore the Victor declared suffering to be the non-attainment of what is desired.
Regarding the phrase “in brief, the five aggregates of clinging,” the term “in brief” is stated with reference to the teaching itself.
Indeed, suffering cannot be condensed into "this many hundreds of sufferings" or "this many thousands of sufferings," but it can be taught [in such a way].
Therefore, summarizing the teaching by saying, "Suffering is nothing other than this: in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering," he spoke thus.
"Five" is the delimitation by number. "Aggregates of clinging" (upādānakkhandhā) [is as follows]:...
The aggregates are the domain of clinging.
Whatever suffering beginning with birth has been stated here by the Tathāgata,
and whatever has not been stated— all that would exist even without this [clinging].
Therefore, for this reason, these aggregates of clinging have been briefly described as "suffering" by the Great Sage, the teacher of the end of suffering.
For indeed, they are like fire to fuel, like weapons to a target, and like gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like to a herd of cattle.
Just as reapers [harass] a field, or village-robbers [harass] a village, so too birth and the other factors, afflicting the five aggregates of clinging in various ways,
arise within those very aggregates of clinging— just as grasses and creepers [grow] upon the earth, or flowers, fruits, and shoots [grow] upon trees. Furthermore,
among the aggregates of clinging, birth is suffering at the beginning, aging is suffering in the middle, and death is suffering at the end.
Death; the suffering of being consumed by the assault of death-bed agony; sorrow; lamentation, which is the suffering of wailing due to the inability to endure that [sorrow];
physical pain, which is the suffering of bodily affliction resulting from contact with undesirable tactile objects characterized as a disturbance of the elements;
and mental pain, which is the suffering of mental affliction arising from the production of aversion toward those [objects] by worldlings who are thus afflicted.

Grief (*domanassa*), despair (*upāyāsa*)—the suffering of not being able to shake off the dejection produced by the increase of sorrow and so forth—and the non-attainment of what is desired (*icchitālābha*)—the suffering of the frustration of one's wishes for those whose desires have been thwarted:
when the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandhā*) are examined in such various ways, they are indeed suffering.
Even if one were to point out each of these individually, it would be impossible to describe them in their entirety even in many eons (*kappa*).
The Elder spoke exactly as the Blessed One had stated— “In brief,
the five aggregates of clinging are suffering”— in order to show that all that [suffering] can be condensed within any of the five aggregates of clinging,
just as the taste of the waters of the entire ocean is contained within a single drop of water.
In the word-commentaries beginning with "Therein, what is birth?", the term "therein" (*tattha*) refers to birth and the other factors mentioned in the exposition of the truth of suffering.
"Of those various beings" (*yā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ*) is a collective designation for many beings in general.
For even if one were to speak for an entire day, saying, "the birth of Devadatta," "the birth of Somadatta," and so on, there would still be no end to beings.
They go; however, not every illustration of another's welfare is accomplished.
But by these two phrases, no being whatsoever remains uncomprised, and no illustration of another's welfare fails to be accomplished.
"In this or that" is a common designation for the many classes of beings according to their destinies and births. "In the class of beings" means in the group of beings, in the multitude of beings.

The meaning is "a collection of beings. "Birth" (*jāti*) is so called by way of the process of being born; this refers here to its specific intrinsic nature. "Arising" (*sañjāti*) is so called by way of the process of fully arising;
the prefix has been added to the word. "Descent" (*okkanti*) is so called by way of the process of descending.

Alternatively, it is "birth" in the sense of being born, which is stated by way of incomplete sense bases. It is "arising" in the sense of fully arising, which is stated by way of complete sense bases. It is "descent" in the sense of descending.

That [rebirth-linking] is spoken of by way of the egg-born and the womb-born; for they descend into the egg-shell and the membrane-womb respectively, and while descending, they take rebirth-linking as if entering. It is "arising" (abhinibbatti) in the sense of being produced;
that is spoken of by way of the moisture-born and the spontaneously born, for these arise having already become manifest. This, first of all, is the conventional explanation.
Now, "the manifestation of the aggregates" and "the acquisition of the sense bases" constitute discourse on the ultimate meaning (paramattha).
For it is only the aggregates that manifest in the ultimate sense, not sentient beings (*satta*).

And here, "of the aggregates" should be understood as referring to one aggregate in a one-aggregate existence (*ekavokāra-bhava*), to four aggregates in a four-aggregate existence (*catuvokāra-bhava*), and to all five aggregates in a five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokāra-bhava*).
"Manifestation" (pātubhāvo) means arising (uppatti). Regarding "of the bases" (āyatanānaṃ), the inclusion should be understood by way of the bases that arise here and there.
"Acquisition" (paṭilābho) is simply the manifestation within the continuity (santati); for it is precisely while they are manifesting that they are said to be "acquired.
"This is called birth" (ayaṃ vuccati jāti): this is what is designated as "birth."
In the explanation of aging (*jarā*), "aging" (*jarā*) is the designation of its individual essence (*sabhāvapaccatta*). "The state of decaying" (*jīraṇatā*) is the designation of its mode (*ākāra*).
The three beginning with "brokenness" (*khaṇḍicca*) are designations of function (*kicca*) regarding the lapse of time; the final two are designations of its natural state (*pakati*).

For by this term "aging," it is illuminated according to its essence; therefore, this is its individual essence. By "the state of decaying," it is [illuminated] according to its mode; therefore, this is its...

The description of the characteristics (*ākāraniddesa*). By the term "brokenness" (*khaṇḍicca*), it is indicated by way of its function of causing the teeth and nails to become broken when time has passed.
By the term "grayness" (*pālicca*), it is indicated by way of its function of causing the hair of the head and body to turn gray.

By the term "wrinkled skin" (*valittacatā*), it is indicated by way of its function of causing the skin to wrinkle after the flesh has withered. Thus, these three are descriptions of its functions when time has passed.
By means of observing these changes, manifest aging is demonstrated.

For just as the path traversed by water, wind, or fire is made evident by the breaking, crushing, or burning of grasses, trees, and so forth, yet that traversed path is not identical to the water and so on themselves;
even so, [aging is revealed] in the teeth and other parts through their brokenness and so forth due to old age.
A path already traveled is perceived even when one opens one's eyes; yet, aging is not merely the presence of brokenness and so forth. For aging is not something cognizable by the eye.
However, through these terms—"the decline of the life-span" and "the maturation of the faculties"—it becomes manifest specifically upon the passing of time.

It is explained as the natural state consisting of the exhaustion of the life-span and the maturation of the faculties such as sight; therefore, it should be understood that these two are descriptions of its natural state.
In this regard, because the life-span diminishes for one who has reached old age, aging is described by way of a metaphorical designation of the result as "the destroyer of the life-span.
And because during childhood the faculties are very clear and capable of grasping even their own subtle objects with ease—
The faculties, such as the eye and so forth, when they have reached old age, become overripe, disordered, and dulled;
even their coarse respective objects cannot be grasped by them. Therefore, "the ripening of the faculties" is spoken of only by way of a metaphorical designation for the fruit.
Furthermore, all this old age thus described is twofold: manifest and concealed. Among these, in the case of the teeth and so forth—
Because the state of being broken and so forth is visible in material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*), aging among them is called "manifest aging" (*pākaṭajarā*).
However, because no such transformation is seen in immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*), aging among them is called "concealed aging" (*paṭicchannajarā*).

In this regard, that which is seen as the state of being broken and so forth is simply the color of such things as teeth. Having seen that with the eye and reflected upon it by means of the mind-door, [one considers]: "These are teeth..."
One knows aging by seeing it "struck down by old age," just as one knows the presence of water below by observing cow-horns and the like tied up in a watery place.
Furthermore, this aging is twofold: with intervals (*savīci*) and without intervals (*avīci*).

In that regard, it is like the case of living beings among gems, gold, silver, coral, the moon, the sun, and so forth, or among flowers, fruits, and sprouts, [which are subject to the gradual decay] of ten-day periods and the like.

Furthermore, because it is difficult to discern specific changes in complexion and so forth from time to time—as in the case of those who are handless—this aging is called "uninterrupted aging" (*avīcijarā*);

the meaning is that it is continuous aging. On the other hand, because it is easy to discern specific changes in complexion and so forth from time to time in other cases as previously described, that aging is called "interrupted aging" (*savīcijarā*).
In this context, aging with intervals (*savīcijarā*) should be understood according to the categories of the appropriated (*upādiṇṇaka*) and the non-appropriated (*anupādiṇṇaka*).
For instance, in young children, what are called "milk-teeth" first emerge; these are not firm. When they fall out, teeth emerge again.
These are white at first, but when struck by the wind of aging, they become black. Hair, too, is first...

They are copper-colored, then black, then white; yet the skin remains reddish. As they grow and grow, the whiteness of the white parts and the blackness of the black parts become manifest. However, when struck by the wind of old age, it takes on wrinkles.
Just as all grain is white at the time of sowing and later turns blue, so too [the hair]—when struck by the wind of old age—[becomes white].
At the time of being struck, it becomes pale. It is also appropriate to illustrate this by means of a mango sprout.
In the description of death, "falling away" (*cuti*) is stated in the sense of the process of falling away. This is a general term for one, four, or five aggregates.

"The state of falling away" (*cavanatā*) is an indication of the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) by means of an abstract noun. "Dissolution" (*bhedo*) is an elucidation of the occurrence of the breakup of the aggregates at the moment of death.
"Disappearance" (*antaradhāna*) is a description of the absence of any state whatsoever for the broken aggregates of death, like a broken jar.
"Death" (*maccu maraṇa*) is death known as *maccu*, not momentary death.
"Time" (*kāla*) means the Ender; his "action" (*kiriyā*) is the "act of time" (*kālakiriyā*). By this much, conventional death is illustrated.

Now, in order to illustrate this according to the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), he says: "The breaking up of the aggregates," and so forth. For it is only the aggregates that break up in the ultimate sense;
no so-called "being" dies at all. However, when the aggregates are breaking up, one speaks conventionally of a "being dying," and when they have broken up, one speaks of "one who has died.

And here, the breaking up of the aggregates occurs by way of the four-constituent (*catuvokāra*) and five-constituent (*pañcavokāra*) [realms], and by way of the one-constituent (*ekavokāra*) [realm].
The laying down of the body, or the breaking up of the aggregates by way of the four planes of existence, should be understood as the laying down of the body according to the remaining two [planes].
Why? Because in both types of existence there occurs the laying down of the body, which is reckoned as the material body.
Or, because even among the Cātumahārājika devas and others the aggregates simply break up and nothing at all is laid down, therefore for them...
By means of this, there is the dissolution of the aggregates and the casting off of the physical body among humans and others.
And here, death is called "the casting off of the physical body" because it is the act of casting off the physical body.
By the phrase "the cutting off of the life-faculty," it is shown that what is called death occurs only for that which is bound by faculties, and not for that which is unbound by faculties.

This shows that what is called "death" does not exist [in an ultimate sense]. However, expressions such as "the crop is dead" or "the tree is dead" are merely conventional designations (*vohāramatta*);
in actual fact, such statements simply indicate the state of exhaustion and decay of the crops and so forth.
Furthermore, these things known as birth, aging, and death are like murderous enemies seeking an opportunity to strike these sentient beings.
They roam about. For example, when three enemies who are looking for an opportunity to strike against a man are roaming about, one might say:
"I will speak in praise of a certain forest and, having taken this man with me, I will go there; for me, there is nothing difficult about this.
A second one might say: "When you have gone after taking him, I will beat him and make him weak..."
“I shall do it; there is nothing difficult for me here. A third might say, “Now that you have beaten him until he is weak, let the cutting off of his head with a sharp sword be my burden.
Having spoken thus, they would act accordingly. In that case, the first enemy, having described the forest to him and taking him there—
The function of birth is to cast one out from the circle of dear friends and kinsmen and cause one to be reborn somewhere or other, like the passing of time;
