the function of aging is to fall upon the aggregates already produced and render them subject to others and destined for the bed of death, like striking a second person and weakening them;
the function of death is to cut off the head with a sharp sword.
It should be understood that its function is to bring about death by destroying life.
Furthermore, in this context, the suffering of birth should be regarded as like entering a great, perilous wilderness;
the suffering of aging as like being weak and deprived of food and drink therein; and the suffering of death as like a weak person whose capacity for maintaining the postures has been destroyed.
It should be regarded as being like bringing about ruin and calamity through wild beasts and the like.
In the exposition of sorrow (*soka*), "calamity" (*byasana*) means that which perishes; the meaning is that it casts away or destroys well-being and happiness.

"Calamity of relatives" (*ñātibyasana*) means the calamity of relatives; the meaning is the loss or destruction of relatives due to thieves, disease, fear, and so forth. By that calamity of relatives.
"Of one who is touched" means of one who is overwhelmed or overcome; the meaning is "of one who is possessed.
The same method applies to the others as well. However, this is the distinction: the misfortune of wealth is "wealth-misfortune" (*bhogabyasana*);

the meaning is the depletion or destruction of wealth through such causes as kings or thieves. Disease itself is the misfortune, "disease-misfortune" (*rogabyasana*); for disease causes health to perish and be destroyed.
*Byasana* means ruin. Ruin of virtue is *sīlabyasana*; this is a name for immorality (*dussīlya*).
A view that arises destroying right view is itself the ruin; thus it is *diṭṭhibyasana*.

Here, the first two are unconditioned (*anipphanna*), while the latter three are conditioned (*nipphanna*) and struck by the three characteristics. Furthermore, the first three are neither wholesome nor unwholesome.
The two calamities of virtue and view are unwholesome.
"By one or another" means by whichever among those already mentioned, or by whichever among those not yet mentioned, such as the calamity of friends or relatives.
"Of one who is possessed" means of one who is pursued [by them] and not liberated from them. "By one or another painful state" means...
By whatever cause sorrow and suffering arise. "Sorrow" (*soka*) is so called by way of the act of grieving; this is the specific individual essence of the sorrow that arises through those causes.
"Grieving" (*socanā*) is the mode of grieving. "The state of having grieved" (*socitatta*) is the condition of having grieved.
"Internal sorrow" (*antosoka*) is internal grief. The second term is augmented by a prefix; for it dries up the interior.
Because it arises as if drying up one’s inner being and as if parching it, it is called "inner grief" (*antosoka*) and "inner parching" (*antoparissoka*).
"The burning of the mind" (*cetaso parijjhāyanā*) refers to the manner in which the mind is consumed by fire. For when grief arises, it burns and consumes the mind like a flame;
it causes one to say, "My mind is scorched; nothing occurs to me. A pained mind is a dejected mind (*dummana*); its state is...
Mental distress (*domanassa*). In the sense of having entered [the heart], grief itself is a dart; thus it is "the dart of grief" (*sokasalla*). In the description of lamentation (*parideva*):
one laments, cries out, and weeps by repeatedly pointing to [objects] such as "my daughter," "my son";
thus it is "lamentation" (*ādeva*). One laments by repeatedly praising various qualities [of those objects]; thus it is "lamentation" (*parideva*).
The two subsequent pairs of terms are stated by way of describing the modes and the cultivation of the preceding two.
*Vācā* means speech. *Palāpa* is empty, meaningless speech. *Vippalāpa* is distorted speech that is empty and meaningless due to being half-spoken, spoken otherwise, and so forth.
*Lālappa* is speaking again and again. *Lālappanā* is the state of such repeated speaking. Of that which has been repeatedly spoken...

Existence is the state of constant lamentation. In the exposition of suffering (*dukkha*): it is "bodily" (*kāyika*) because it depends on the body; it is "unpleasant" (*asāta*) in the sense of being not sweet. By the term "bodily," mental unpleasantness is excluded;
by the term "unpleasant," bodily pleasure is excluded. That very thing causes one to suffer, thus it is "suffering" (*dukkha*), for that which arises [in one].
The meaning is that it makes one suffer. Or, "suffering" (*dukkha*) is so called because it is merely suffering. "Born of body-contact" means arisen from body-contact.
"Unpleasant painful feeling" means an unpleasant experience, not a pleasant one;
a painful experience, not a happy one. The following three terms are stated using the feminine gender: "unpleasant feeling," not pleasant; "painful," [not happy].

"Feeling is not pleasure"—this is precisely the meaning here. That which is bodily unpleasantness, painful feeling, that which is born of bodily contact, unpleasant and painful feeling—this is called "pain.

Such is the construction to be understood. In the description of mental grief (*domanassa*): one who is ill-minded is "dejected" (*dummana*); or, because it is an inferior feeling, one thinks [of it] as contemptible, thus it is "dejected" (*dummana*); the state of being dejected is "mental grief" (*domanassa*). Because it is dependent on the mind, it is "mental" (*cetasika*). "Born of mental contact" means arisen through contact with the mind.

In the exposition of *upāyāsa* (despair): it is called *āyāsa* in the sense of causing distress (*āyāsana*). This is a name for mental exhaustion that occurs in the mode of sinking and despondency. Intense *āyāsa* is *upāyāsa*. The state of being distressed is *āyāsitatta*; the state of being intensely distressed is *upāyāsitatta*. In the exposition of association with the unpleasant (*appiyasampayoga*):
"here" (*idha*) means in this world. "Of whom" (*yassa*) means of those who belong to him. "Unwanted" (*aniṭṭhā*) means not sought after.
Whether they have been sought or not sought, this is simply a name for objects that are disagreeable; they do not appeal to the mind.
They do not enter [the mind]—thus they are *akanta*. They are not dear to the mind, or they do not increase the mind—thus they are *amanāpā*.

“Forms,” and so forth, is the demonstration of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). They desire and seek what is disadvantageous—thus they are *anatthakāmā*. They desire and seek what is harmful—thus they are *ahitakāmā*.
They desire and seek discomfort and an unpleasant dwelling—thus they are *aphāsukāmā*. By these four...

They do not desire the security, fearlessness, and turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭa*) that comes through the yogas; rather, they desire and long for the very cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) which is fraught with fear.

Thus, they are "those who desire what is not the security from bondage" (*ayogakkhemakāmā*). Furthermore, because they do not desire the welfare (*attha*) consisting in the growth of faith and the other [faculties], and because they do desire the harm (*anattha*) consisting in the decline of those very same things, they are "those who desire what is harmful" (*anatthakāmā*). [This applies also] to the means (*upāya*) consisting of faith and the rest...
Because they do not desire what is beneficial and because they desire what is harmful—which serves as a means for the loss of faith and so forth—they are "those who desire harm" (*ahitakāmā*).
Because they do not desire a comfortable dwelling and because they desire an uncomfortable dwelling, they are "those who desire discomfort" (*aphāsukāmā*).
Because they do not desire anyone who is fearless and because they desire fear, they are "those who desire lack of security" (*ayogakkhemakāmā*); such is how the meaning should be understood here.
*Saṅgati* means meeting after having gone. *Samāgama* means meeting with those who have arrived. *Samodhāna* means being together in standing, sitting, and so forth.
*Missībhāva* means performing all tasks together. This is the application according to sentient beings (*satta*).

However, in terms of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), one should take whatever is applicable. Furthermore, that which is "association with the unpleasant" (*appiyasampayoga*) is, in its essential meaning, a single phenomenon (*dhamma*).
It does not exist [as a separate entity]; rather, it is called "suffering" because it serves as the basis for both kinds of suffering associated with the unpleasant.

The exposition on separation from the beloved should be understood by way of the opposite of what has been stated. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "mother" is spoken here to show those who desire one's welfare in their own form.
In that context: she cherishes (*mamāyati*) him, thus she is a mother (*mātā*); he cherishes him, thus he is a father (*pitā*); he shares (*bhajati*) [in common], thus he is a brother (*bhātā*).
Likewise for a sister. They are called *mittā* because they love (*mettāyanti*), or because they measure (*minanti*) by including [others] within all their secrets.
They are called *amaccā* because they are like those who are "at home" (*amā*) in the sense of being present together in what must be done and performed.

They are called *ñātī* because they know [one another], thinking, "This one is our own," or because they are known [as such]. They are called *sālohitā* because they are connected by blood. These are relatives on the father’s side and relatives on the mother’s side.
"Sālohitā" refers to relatives on the mother’s or father’s side, or relatives on the side of the mother-in-law or father-in-law.

In actual fact, this "separation from the beloved" is not a distinct category of phenomenon (dhamma) separate from others; it is merely called "suffering" because it serves as the basis for both kinds of suffering experienced by those separated from what is dear.
This is the explanation found in all the Commentaries. However, as for the Truths, they possess the characteristic of being "thus" (tatha).
It is appropriate to say that by the terms "conjoined" and "disjoined," only the objects of the unpleasant and the pleasant are specified.
In the exposition on the non-attainment of what is desired: "of things subject to birth" means of those whose nature is birth, whose character is birth.
"Desire arises" means craving arises. "Oh, would that! is an aspiration. "May we be" means may we become. But this is not [achieved] through mere desire.

"To be attained" means that which is desired—namely, the state of being subject to non-birth existing in virtuous ones who have abandoned the origin [of suffering], and the non-arrival of birth existing in those who have attained final Nibbāna—as expressed by the thought: "O, may we not be subject to birth, and may birth not come upon us!
Because this cannot be attained without the cultivation of the path even for one who desires it, and because it is attained even for one who does not desire it;

And because it is to be attained through cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it is not something to be attained by mere wish. "This too" (*idampi*) means this as well. The word *api* is used in reference to the remaining [factors] mentioned below.

In the exposition of the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*), *seyyathidaṃ* is a particle; its meaning is "if you ask, 'Which are they? "Form itself is the aggregate of clinging" is the "form-aggregate of clinging" (*rūpupādānakkhandha*). The same method applies to the others as well. The commentary on the exposition of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) is finished.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of Origin (Samudayasacca-niddesa) 34.
Regarding the phrase "that which is this craving" (*yāyaṃ taṇhā*) in the exposition of the truth of origin: it is this very craving (*taṇhā*). "Leading to renewed existence" (*ponobhavikā*):

renewed existence (*punobhava*) is the making of renewed existence; that which has the nature of producing renewed existence is "leading to renewed existence. Furthermore, it gives renewed existence, or [it leads] for the sake of renewed existence.

It leads on; it produces existence again and again, thus it is "leading to renewed existence" (*ponobhavikā*). Furthermore, this [craving] is both that which gives renewed existence and that which does not give it;

it is both that which conduces to renewed existence and that which does not so conduce; and even when rebirth-linking has been given, there is that which consists merely in the ripening of the substrate (*upadhivepakkamattā*).
Though it is of these three kinds, it receives the name "leading to renewed existence. It is also called *ponabbhavikā*.

The reading is as given; the meaning is the same. They are "accompanied by delight and lust" (*nandirāgasahagatā*) because they have gone together with the delight and lust known as *abhinandanā* (relishing).
What is meant is that, in terms of their actual meaning, they have reached a state of identity with delight and lust.
"Rejoicing here and there" means rejoicing wherever a personal existence (*attabhāva*) is produced, or else rejoicing in objects such as forms and so forth.
"Delighting here and there" means delighting in forms, delighting in sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena (*dhamma*).
There is also a reading "delighting in this and that," which means he takes pleasure in this and that. *Seyyathidaṃ* is a particle;
its meaning is "if it is asked, what is that? *Kāmataṇhā* is craving for sensual pleasures; this is a term for lust (*rāga*) directed toward the five strands of sensual pleasure.
It is a designation. "Craving for existence" (*bhavataṇhā*) is craving for existence.

This is a designation for lust accompanied by the eternalist view that arises through the longing for existence, as well as for lust for the fine-material and immaterial realms of existence and for attachment to meditative absorption (*jhāna*). "Craving for non-existence" (*vibhavataṇhā*) is craving for non-existence. This is a designation for lust accompanied by the annihilationist view.
Now, in order to show in detail the basis (*vatthu*) for that craving (*taṇhā*), he said: "But as for that... and so forth. Therein, "arises" (*uppajjati*) means it is born.
"Enters" (*nivisati*) means it establishes itself by way of recurring occurrence. The connection is: "Where does it arise when arising?
Where does it enter when entering? "That which in the world is lovely-form and pleasant-form" (*piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ*) refers to whatever in the world...

[It has] both a pleasing nature and a sweet nature. In the passages beginning with "The eye surveys the world," beings who are attached through possessiveness (*mamatta*) to the eye and so forth within the world—being established in prosperity—regard their own eye as having five translucent elements (*pañcapasāda*) that are perfectly clear, following the grasping of signs (*nimitta*) in mirrors and the like, just like a jeweled lion-lattice opened in a golden celestial mansion (*vimāna*). [They regard] the ear...
They imagine the body to be like a silver tube or a string of pearls;
they imagine the nose—which is conventionally designated as "high-nosed"—to be like a stalk of green bamboo set upright;
they imagine the tongue to be like a piece of red woolen cloth, soft, smooth, and yielding sweet flavor; and they imagine the body to be like a sal-tree trunk or a golden archway.
They conceive conceits; they conceive their own mind to be superior and unlike the minds of others. They conceive form to be like the color of a golden *kaṇikāra* flower and so forth;
sound to be like the gentle cooing of a intoxicated *karavīka* or a cuckoo, or like the resonance of a jeweled flute;
and regarding the objects of smell and so forth produced by the fourfold origination which they have themselves obtained, they conceive, "Whose else could such things belong?"—of them [this is said].
For those who conceive such notions, those eyes and so forth become both endearing and pleasant forms.
Consequently, craving that has not yet arisen arises therein, and that which has already arisen becomes firmly established through repeated occurrence.
Therefore, the Elder said: "The eye is a pleasant form, a delightful form in the world; it is here that this craving, when arising, arises," and so forth.
In this context, "arising" means that when it arises, it arises here.
The commentary on the description of the truth of the origin is finished.
The commentary on the description of the truth of cessation.

In the exposition of the truth of cessation, regarding the phrase "of that very craving": here, although one should say "of that very suffering," it is because suffering ceases only through the cessation of its origin and not otherwise. As it has been said:
"Just as a tree, though cut down, grows up again if its root remains unharmed and firm, even so, if the underlying tendency to craving is not uprooted, this suffering arises again and again."
Therefore, showing that cessation of suffering by way of the cessation of its origin, he spoke thus. For the Tathāgatas have a conduct like that of a lion;
when they bring suffering to cessation and demonstrate the cessation of suffering, they apply themselves to the cause, not to the fruit.
But the followers of other sects have a conduct like that of a dog; when they bring suffering to cessation and [demonstrate] the cessation of suffering...
Those who give [teachings] practice both through self-mortification and through the fruit of that very teaching, but not through its cause.

Because he lives like a lion, the Teacher, practicing through the cause, said: "He who... and so forth. The General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) also spoke according to the sequence stated by the Teacher.

In this context, "of that very craving" refers to that same craving which was previously described as "leading to renewed existence," analyzed by way of sensual craving and so forth, and explained above according to its arising and settling.

"The remainderless fading away and cessation": fading away (*virāga*) is said to be the Path, for it is stated, "Through fading away, one is liberated. Cessation by means of fading away is "fading-away-cessation" (*virāga-nirodha*).
Through the uprooting of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), there is no remainder; this is dispassion and cessation, the cessation through total dispassion.

Alternatively, "dispassion" (*virāga*) is said to mean abandoning; therefore, the construction here should be understood as: "the complete absence of dispassion" and "the complete absence of cessation.
In terms of meaning, however, all these terms—beginning with "cessation through total dispassion"—are synonyms for Nibbāna alone. In the ultimate sense...
Indeed, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering is called *nibbāna*.
Because, by resorting to it, craving is dispassioned and ceased without remainder, it is therefore called "the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving.

And because, by resorting to *nibbāna*, craving is abandoned, relinquished, released, and no longer clung to—even regarding the bases of attachment consisting of the strands of sensual pleasure—[it is so called].
And herein, not even a single *ālaya* (clinging) exists; therefore, Nibbāna is called "renunciation," "relinquishment," "liberation," and "non-clinging.
For Nibbāna is indeed one alone, yet its names are many, corresponding to the opposites of all conditioned things (*saṅkhata*).
They are as follows: the fading away without remainder, the cessation without remainder, renunciation, relinquishment, liberation, non-clinging, and the destruction of lust.
The destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion, the destruction of craving; non-arising, non-occurrence, the signless, the wishless, non-acquisition,
non-relinking, non-rebirth, non-going, the unborn, the unaging, the disease-free, the deathless, the sorrowless,
the lamentation-free, the despair-free, the undefiled, and so forth.
Now, although craving has been cut off by the Path and, having reached Nibbāna, has attained the state of non-occurrence, the Blessed One said, "But as for this...
and so forth, in order to show its absence precisely in those objects where its arising was previously demonstrated.
In this regard, it is just as if a man, seeing a bitter gourd creeper growing in a field, were to seek out its root starting from the tip and cut it there.
Having gradually withered away, it would reach a state of non-manifestation; then, one would say that the bitter gourd had ceased and been abandoned in that field.
In the same way, craving for the eye and so forth is like the bitter gourd in the field.
When its root is cut by the Noble Path, it reaches non-occurrence upon arriving at Nibbāna. Having thus gone, it no longer exists in those bases, as in the case of the field.

It is no longer discernible, like a bitter gourd. And just as if they were to bring thieves from the forest and execute them at the southern gate of a city, whereupon it would be said that the thieves in the forest were dead or had been killed;
even so, craving for the eye and the other [senses], which is like the thieves in the forest, has ceased upon reaching Nibbāna, which is like the southern gate.
They have ceased in Nibbāna. Having thus ceased, they are no longer perceived in those bases (vatthu), just as thieves are not seen in a forest.
Therefore, showing that their cessation occurs right there, he said: "The eye is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world;

it is herein that this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned," and so forth. Alternatively, because the basis for the arising of craving has been fully understood (pariññāta), [craving ceases] in that basis which has been fully understood.
Furthermore, because it does not arise again, it is said to cease right within the very basis for the arising of craving by way of non-arising cessation (*anuppāda-nirodha*).
Here, it is stated that "it is abandoned" by way of the opposite of arising, and "it ceases" by way of the opposite of subsiding.
The commentary on the description of the Truth of Cessation is finished.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of the Path:
In the exposition of the truth of the path, the phrase "this very [path]" is a restriction intended to exclude any other path.

It is called "noble" (ariya) because it is remote from the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path, because it brings about the state of a noble one, and because it brings about the attainment of the noble fruits. It is said to have "eight factors" (aṭṭhaṅga) because it possesses eight components.
It is eightfold. This [path], like a fourfold army or a fivefold musical ensemble, consists merely of its constituent parts;
there is nothing apart from the parts.
Now, demonstrating that the path consists merely of its parts and that there is nothing apart from the parts, he says: "Right view... pe ...right concentration," and so forth.
Therein, right view has the characteristic of right seeing; right intention has the characteristic of right directing onto [the object];
right speech has the characteristic of right embracing; right action has the characteristic of right originating;
right livelihood has the characteristic of right purification; right effort has the characteristic of right exertion; right mindfulness has the characteristic of right establishing.
Right mindfulness. Right concentration has the characteristic of right unification. Each of these [factors] has three functions. To wit:
first, right view abandons wrong view along with its own opposing defilements;
it takes cessation as its object; and it sees associated states by way of dispelling the delusion that obscures them.
...due to non-delusion. Right intention and the others likewise abandon wrong intention and so forth, and take Nibbāna as their object.
Specifically, however, in this context, right intention rightly directs the co-nascent states;
right speech rightly grasps them; right action rightly originates them; and right livelihood rightly [sustains them]...
He causes [the mind] to be purified; he exerts himself rightly; he establishes right mindfulness; he concentrates rightly.
Furthermore, this so-called right view, in its preliminary stage, has various moments and various objects, but at the time of the Path, it has a single moment and a single object.
By way of function, however, it receives four names, such as "knowledge regarding suffering" and so forth. This is also true for right intention and the others.
In the preliminary stage, they have various moments and various objects; at the time of the Path, they have a single moment and a single object.
Among them, right intention receives three names according to its function: "intention of renunciation," and so forth.
Right speech and the other three factors are both abstinences and volitions in the preliminary stage, but at the moment of the Path, they are abstinences only. Right effort and right mindfulness...
These two pairs also receive four names according to their function, by way of the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*) and the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
Right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*), however, is simply right concentration both in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the path.
Thus, among these eight factors, because they are of great assistance to the yogi practicing for the attainment of Nibbāna, [the Blessed One taught them].
Right view was taught first. For this is described as "the lamp of wisdom" and "the sword of wisdom.

Therefore, by means of this right view—which in its preliminary stage is termed insight-knowledge—the practitioner dispels the darkness of ignorance and slays the thieves of the defilements, thereby reaching Nibbāna in safety. That is why right view was taught first.
Right intention, however, is of great assistance to it; therefore, it is mentioned immediately after that.

For just as a money-changer, turning a coin over and over in his hand and examining it with his eye, knows "this one is counterfeit, this one is genuine," so too the practitioner of yoga, having reflected again and again with initial application (*vitakka*) during the preliminary stage, [discerns] by means of the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*).
Observing them, he knows: "These phenomena belong to the sense-sphere; these belong to the fine-material sphere, and so forth.

Or, just as a carpenter, having been given a large tree by a man who has turned it over and over again by grasping its end, brings it to his work after cutting it with an adze, so too does the practitioner of yoga, through wisdom, [bring] the phenomena given by thought after thinking upon them again and again.
Having delimited them by way of such a method as, "These states belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), these belong to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara)," one applies them to action (kamma).
Therefore, right intention (sammāsaṅkappa) is stated immediately after right view (sammādiṭṭhi).

And this [right intention], just as it is an aid to right view, is likewise an aid to right speech (sammāvācā). As it is said: "Householder, having first thought and reflected, one subsequently utters speech. Therefore, right speech is stated immediately after that.

However, because people first consult with speech, saying, "We shall do this and that," and then engage in worldly occupations, speech is thus an aid to bodily action; therefore, right action is mentioned immediately after right speech.

Furthermore, because the eightfold morality of livelihood is fulfilled only by one who abandons the fourfold misconduct of speech and the threefold misconduct of body and fulfills both types of good conduct, and not by anyone else, right livelihood is mentioned immediately after those two.
However, it is not proper for one who has thus purified their livelihood to remain complacent, thinking,
"My livelihood is pure," and to dwell in negligence; rather, to show that this energy must be exerted in all postures,
right effort is taught immediately thereafter.

Next, right mindfulness (*sammāsati*) is taught immediately after that in order to show that even for one who has initiated energy (*āraddhavīriya*), mindfulness must be well-established with respect to the four foundations,
such as the body and so forth. Furthermore, because when mindfulness is thus well-established,

one is able to settle the mind on a single object by investigating the courses of those phenomena that are either conducive or non-conducive to concentration (*samādhi*), right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*) follows immediately after right mindfulness.
It should be understood that it has been "stated.
In the exposition of right view, the meditation subject of the four truths is shown by the passage beginning with "knowledge of suffering.

Therein, the first two truths are the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), and the latter two are the cessation of the round (*vivaṭṭa*). Among these, the monk’s application of the meditation subject is directed toward the round.
There is [clinging] in the process of turning toward existence (*saṃvatta*), but there is no insistence on views in the process of turning away (*vivatta*).

For the practitioner (*yogāvacara*), having learned the first two truths—both briefly as "the five aggregates are suffering, craving is the origin" and in detail according to the method beginning with "Which are the five aggregates?
The aggregate of form," and so forth—from the presence of a teacher, repeatedly turns them over with his speech.

He performs the work [of practice] regarding them. However, regarding the other two truths, he performs the work by the mere hearing [of the teaching], thinking: "The truth of cessation is desirable, lovely, and pleasing; the truth of the path is desirable, lovely, and pleasing.

Performing his work in this way, he penetrates the four truths through a single penetration and realizes them through a single realization. He penetrates suffering through the penetration of full comprehension (*pariññā*).
One penetrates [the truth]; one penetrates the origin through the penetration of its abandonment. One penetrates cessation through the penetration of its realization;
one penetrates the path through the penetration of its cultivation. One realizes suffering through the clear comprehension of full understanding...
[and so on] ...one realizes the path through the clear comprehension of cultivation.
Thus, in the preliminary stage, there is for him penetration through learning, questioning, hearing, retention, reflection, and realization regarding two truths;

regarding the other two, there is only penetration through hearing. In the subsequent stage, there is penetration by way of function regarding three truths, and penetration as an object regarding cessation.
In this context, all knowledge of penetration is supramundane, whereas the knowledge of hearing, retention, and reflection is mundane and belongs to the sense-sphere.
However, reflective contemplation (*paccavekkhaṇā*) occurs for one who has attained the truths, whereas this [monk] is a beginner. Therefore, that is not mentioned here.

Furthermore, prior to his full comprehension, this monk lacks the application of attention, the coordination of mental factors, the act of attending, and reflective contemplation in the form of: "I fully understand suffering, I abandon its origin, I realize its cessation, and I develop the path."
It begins from the point of grasping. Later on, however, suffering is indeed fully understood... [and so on] ...the path is indeed developed.
Among these, two truths are profound because they are difficult to see; two are difficult to see because they are profound.
For the truth of suffering is manifest in its arising, as even when one encounters the striking of stumps, thorns, and the like, one exclaims, "Oh, what suffering!"
The truth of the origin is evident because it arises through such things as the desire to eat and the desire to consume;
however, from the perspective of penetrating its characteristic, both truths are profound. Thus, they are "profound" because they are difficult to see.
As for the application toward the other two [truths], it is like stretching out one's hand to grasp the peak of the world-system (Bhavagga) or stretching out one's foot to touch the Avīci hell.
It is like the joining of the tip of a hair split a hundredfold to another hair-tip; thus, they are difficult to see because of their profundity.

Because they are thus difficult to see, and because of the profundity within those four truths which are profound and difficult to see, this statement beginning with "knowledge regarding suffering" was spoken with reference to the arising of preliminary knowledge by way of learning and so forth. However, at the moment of penetration (paṭivedha):
That knowledge is indeed one.

However, others say that knowledge regarding the truths is fourfold: knowledge consisting in what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*), knowledge of discernment (*vavatthāna-ñāṇa*), knowledge of comprehension (*sammasana-ñāṇa*), and knowledge of realization (*abhisamaya-ñāṇa*).
In this regard, what is knowledge consisting in what has been heard? Briefly or in detail, the four [truths]...
Having heard the truths, one knows: "This is suffering, this is its origin, this is its cessation, this is the path.

This is knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*). What is knowledge of defining (*vavatthāna-ñāṇa*)? One examines the meaning of what has been heard according to the doctrine (*dhamma*) and according to the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*):
"These phenomena are included within this truth; this is the characteristic of this truth."
He makes a definitive conclusion. This is the knowledge of definition (*vavatthāna-ñāṇa*). What is the knowledge of comprehension (*sammasana-ñāṇa*)?

Having thus defined the four truths in their proper sequence, he then takes up suffering alone and comprehends it as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, up to the stage of the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*).
This is the knowledge of comprehension. What is the knowledge of penetration (*abhisamaya-ñāṇa*)? At the moment of the supramundane path (*lokuttara-magga*).
By means of a single knowledge, one realizes the four truths simultaneously— neither before nor after— realizing suffering through the realization of full understanding,
the origin through the realization of abandoning, cessation through the realization of witnessing, and the path through the realization of development.
This is the knowledge of realization (*abhisamaya-ñāṇa*).
In the exposition of right intention: "escaped from sensual desire" is the intention of renunciation; "escaped from ill will" is the intention of non-ill will;
"escaped from cruelty" is the intention of non-cruelty. Therein, the thought of renunciation arises, striking down and cutting off the thought of sensual desire;
the thought of non-ill will [strikes down] the thought of ill will; the thought of non-cruelty...
Of the thought of cruelty. Likewise, thoughts of renunciation, non-ill-will, and non-cruelty arise as opposites to thoughts of sensual desire, ill-will, and cruelty.
In that regard, for the purpose of striking down the footprint of a thought of sensual desire, the practitioner either contemplates that very thought of sensual desire or another [thought].

Or else, regarding some formation (saṅkhāra): at the moment of insight, the intention associated with insight arises, performing the striking down and the cutting off of sensual thought by way of "overcoming through substitution" (tadaṅgavasena);

having brought insight to its peak, it leads to the Path. Then, at the moment of the Path, the intention associated with the Path [arises] by way of total eradication (samucchedavasena) of sensual thought.

He arises [in insight] while performing the "striking of the word" (*padaghāta*) and the "cutting of the word" (*padaccheda*). For the purpose of striking the word of an ill-will thought (*byāpādavitakka*), he comprehends either that ill-will thought or another formation;
for the purpose of striking the word of a cruelty thought (*vihiṃsāvitakka*), he comprehends either that cruelty thought or another formation.
Then, at the moment of insight (*vipassanā-khaṇe*), everything should be applied in the same manner as previously described.

However, among the thirty-eight objects analyzed in the Canon for the three types of thoughts—sensuous thought (*kāmavitakka*) and the others—there is not even a single meditation subject that is not an antidote to them all.
Nevertheless, specifically, the first jhāna based on the foulness (*asubha*) subjects is the antidote to sensuous thought;

the third and fourth jhānas based on loving-kindness (*mettā*) are the antidotes to ill-will thought (*byāpādavitakka*); and [the third and fourth jhānas] based on compassion (*karuṇā*) are the antidotes to cruelty thought (*vihiṃsāvitakka*).

The threefold and fourfold jhānas. Therefore, for one who has performed the preliminary work on the foul and has entered jhāna, at the moment of attainment, the applied thought (vitakka) associated with that jhāna arises as an antidote to sensual thought by way of suppression.
For one who, having made jhāna the basis, establishes insight, at the moment of insight, [the applied thought] associated with insight [arises].
Aspiration arises as an antidote to sensual thought by way of its specific factor;
and for one who has intensified insight and reaches the path, at the moment of the path, aspiration associated with the path arises as an antidote to sensual thought by way of its total eradication.
It should be understood that when it has arisen in this way, it is called "aspiration for renunciation."

Furthermore, having performed the preliminary practice for loving-kindness (*mettā*) and having performed the preliminary practice for compassion (*karuṇā*), for one who has attained absorption (*jhāna*), everything should be construed in the same manner as previously explained.
Thus, that which has arisen is called "the intention of non-ill-will" (*abyāpāda-saṅkappa*) and is to be understood as "the intention of non-cruelty" (*avihiṃsā-saṅkappa*).
In this way, these intentions, beginning with renunciation (*nekkhamma-saṅkappa*), [are to be understood] by way of their arising through insight-absorption (*vipassanā-jhāna*).

In the preliminary stage, there is diversity; however, at the moment of the Path, by means of cutting off unwholesome intentions that have arisen in these three instances and establishing non-arising, a single wholesome intention arises, fulfilling the factor of the Path.
This is called right intention (*sammā-saṅkappa*).
In the exposition of right speech as well, because one abstains from false speech with one state of consciousness, and from malicious speech and so forth with another distinct state of consciousness,
these four abstinences are diverse in their prior stage; however, at the moment of the path,
they constitute a path-factor by way of preventing the occurrence of the fourfold unwholesome, immoral volition termed wrong speech through its severance.
When these three abstinences are fulfilled, that which is designated as right speech arises; this is called right speech (*sammāvācā*).

In the exposition of right action (*sammākammanta*) as well, because one abstains from killing living beings with one state of consciousness, from taking what is not given with another, and from sexual misconduct with another, these three abstinences are distinct in their preliminary stages; however, at the moment of the path, they are subsumed under what is designated as wrong action (*micchākammanta*).

By means of the non-arising of the threefold unwholesome and immoral volition through the method of establishing its non-occurrence, a single wholesome abstention termed right action (*sammākammanta*) arises, thereby fulfilling a factor of the Path. This is what is called right action.
In the description of right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*), "here" means in this Dispensation; "a noble disciple" (*ariyasāvaka*) means a disciple of the Noble One, the Buddha.
"Having abandoned wrong livelihood" means having abandoned an evil way of life. "By right livelihood" means by a wholesome livelihood praised by the Buddha.
"He makes his living" means he maintains the continuity of life.
Here too, because one desists from transgressions of the bodily door with one state of consciousness and from transgressions of the verbal door with another, therefore, in the preliminary stage—

It arises at various moments; however, at the moment of the Path (magga-khaṇa), through the cutting off of the unwholesome volition of wrong livelihood (*micchā-ājīva*)—which has arisen by way of the seven courses of action (*kamma-patha*) at the two doors—it arises as a single wholesome abstention termed right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*), fulfilling the factor of the Path (*maggaṅga*) by means of accomplishing non-arising. This is what is called right livelihood.
In the exposition of right effort (*sammāvāyāma*): "Here, a bhikkhu" refers to a bhikkhu practicing in this teaching.
"Of those that have not arisen" means of those not yet produced. "Evil" means base. "Unwholesome states" means states born of lack of skill.
"For their non-arising" means for the purpose of not producing them. "He generates desire" means he generates wholesome desire characterized by the wish to act.
"Produces" means he generates; "exerts" means he generates application and performs effort;
"arouses energy" means he exercises physical and mental energy; "strains the mind" means he uplifts the mind by means of that very co-nascent energy;
"strives" means he exerts the energy of striving. Furthermore, these four terms follow one another in sequence.
They should be applied through repeated practice, cultivation, frequent exercise, constancy, and performance.
"Of those that have arisen" refers to those that have reached a state where it cannot be said they are "unarisen. "For the abandoning" means for the purpose of relinquishing.
"Of wholesome states that have not arisen" refers to states produced by skill that have not yet come into being. "For the arising" means for the purpose of bringing them into existence.
"Of those arisen" means of those that have been produced. "For stability" means for the purpose of their remaining.

"For non-confusion" means for the purpose of not being lost. "For increase" means for repeated occurrence. "For abundance" means for a state of vastness. "For development" means for growth. "For fulfillment" means for the purpose of complete perfection.
Furthermore, these four right endeavors, termed right effort, are mundane during the preliminary stage, but at the moment of the Path—
They are supramundane. At the moment of the Path, however, this single energy receives four names by virtue of accomplishing its four functions.
Among these, the mundane types should be understood according to the method stated in the *Kassapa-saṃyutta*.
For it is said there: "Friends, there are these four right endeavors. Which four? Here, friends, a bhikkhu [thinks]: 'Unarisen unwholesome states...'"
He exerts himself with ardor, thinking: "Evil, unwholesome states, if they arise, would lead to my harm";
he exerts himself with ardor, thinking: "Evil, unwholesome states that have arisen in me, if not abandoned, would lead to my harm"; he exerts himself with ardor, thinking:
"Wholesome states that have not yet arisen in me, if they do not arise, would lead to my harm"; [he exerts himself with ardor, thinking: "Wholesome states that have arisen..."
"‘May my wholesome states, while ceasing, lead to my harm,’ thinking thus, he exerts himself with ardor.
In this context, “unarisen” means either unarisen by way of non-occurrence or unarisen by way of not having experienced the object;
for otherwise, in the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), there are no evil, unwholesome states that have not already arisen. Unarisen...
Furthermore, when they arise, only these [defilements] arise; when they are abandoned, only these are abandoned.

In this regard, for a certain person, the defilements do not manifest by virtue of one or another of the following: the duties (*vatta*), the bonds (*gantha*), the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), concentration (*samādhi*), insight (*vipassanā*), or the nine tasks (*navakamma*).
How so? For a certain person is perfected in the duties; there are eighty duties of the *Khandhaka*.

While one is performing the fourteen great duties—the duties regarding the shrine courtyard, the Bodhi-tree courtyard, the water pavilion, the Uposatha hall, those for visitors, and those for departing monks—the defilements find no opportunity.
However, at a later time, when he has abandoned these duties and wanders having broken his observances, the defilements arise through improper attention and the loss of mindfulness. Thus it is.
By way of non-occurrence, those [defilements] that have not yet arisen are said to arise.
A certain person is bound by the fetters; he takes up one Nikāya, two, three, four, or even five.
As he takes up the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Piṭakas according to its meaning, its text, its sequence, and its internal consistency, [the defilements do not arise].
While one is engaged in recitation, reflection, teaching, explaining, or proclaiming [the Dhamma], the defilements find no opportunity.
However, at a later time, when one has abandoned the work of study and wanders about indolently, they arise by way of improper attention and the neglect of mindfulness.
Thus, even in this way, those that have not yet arisen are said to "arise" by virtue of their non-occurrence.

But another person is a bearer of ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*); having undertaken and practicing the thirteen qualities of the ascetic practices, while he maintains those qualities of the ascetic practices, the defilements find no opportunity.
However, at a later time, having abandoned the ascetic practices and returning to abundance, they arise in him due to improper attention and the loss of mindfulness. Thus it is.
By way of non-occurrence, those [defilements] that have not yet arisen are said to arise.
A certain person has mastered the eight attainments;
while he dwells in the mastery of adverting and so forth regarding the first jhāna and the others, the defilements find no opportunity. Later, however, when his jhāna has been lost...
Or they arise for one who has abandoned jhāna or who dwells devoted to talk and such activities, due to unwise attention and the neglect of mindfulness.
In this way too, they are said to "arise" when previously unarisen by virtue of their non-occurrence.
Furthermore, a certain person is a practitioner of insight (vipassaka), [engaged] either in the seven contemplations or in the eighteen great insights.
While he dwells performing his work, the defilements find no opportunity in him as he so dwells.
However, at a later time, having abandoned the work of insight (vipassanā), as he dwells with an abundance of physical rigidity, they arise due to improper attention and the neglect of mindfulness.
In this way, even by way of non-occurrence, those that have not yet arisen are said to "arise."
A certain person is a builder; he constructs a Uposatha hall, a dining hall, and so forth.

While he is occupied with those requisites, the defilements find no opportunity. However, later on—whether the construction work is finished or abandoned—defilements arise due to improper attention and the abandonment of mindfulness.
In this way, even by virtue of non-occurrence, those that have not yet arisen are said to "arise."
But another, having come from the Brahma-world, is a pure being; because he has not practiced [defilements], the defilements find no opportunity.
However, at a later time, when he has acquired the habit of them, they arise through improper attention and the lapse of mindfulness.
Thus, even by way of non-occurrence, those that have not arisen are said to "arise. This, first of all, is by way of non-occurrence.
The state of not having arisen is to be understood.
How so by way of an object not previously experienced? Here, someone obtains an object—such as a pleasant one—that has never been experienced before;
then, due to improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) and the lapse of mindfulness (*sativossagga*) regarding that object, the defilements such as lust arise.
Thus, by way of objects not previously experienced, those that have not yet arisen are said to arise.

When there is the arising of such unwholesome states that have not yet arisen, one sees their disadvantage to oneself and develops the first right effort through application to the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) for the sake of their non-arising. However, when they have already arisen, [one sees] the disadvantage to oneself due to their failure to be abandoned.
Having seen [the danger] in those [unwholesome states], he develops the second right effort in the same way for their abandonment.
"Wholesome states that have not yet arisen" refers to both serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), as well as the Path (magga).
Having seen his own disadvantage in their non-arising, he develops the third right effort in the same way for the sake of their arising. Wholesome states that have already arisen...
"Dhammas" here refers specifically to serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). As for the path, once it has arisen and is ceasing, there is nothing that leads to harm;
for it ceases only after having provided the condition for the fruit.
Seeing their own potential harm in the cessation of those [two], namely serenity and insight, one applies the fourth right effort precisely for their maintenance.
He develops [it]. At the moment of the supramundane path, however, there is only a single energy.
It accomplishes the task of ensuring that those [defilements] which, if left unchecked, would arise—provided they have not yet arisen—do not arise;
and it accomplishes the task of abandoning those [defilements] that have already arisen. And here, "arisen" refers to fourfold arising.

There is arising that is present (*vattamānuppanna*), arising that has passed away after having been [previously] arisen (*bhūtāpagatuppanna*), arising that has made room [for future arising] (*okāsakatuppanna*), and arising that has attained its plane (*bhūmiladdhuppanna*).
Among these, all that is characterized by being possessed of arising, aging, and dissolution is called "arising that is present.

Wholesome and unwholesome [kamma] that have ceased after experiencing the flavor of the object is called "arising that has passed away after having been experienced" (*anubhūtāpagata*); and [that which] has ceased without having reached the triad of arising and so forth [is another type].

That which has arisen after having passed away from a formation, as well as other remaining formations that have arisen after passing away from what has occurred, is called "arisen after passing away.
As for the karma described in such passages as, "Whatever karmas were performed by him in the past," although it is past, it stands having set aside other results and made room for its own result;
and the result, although yet unarisen, [stands] because the opportunity was thus made.

When such an opportunity has been made, [the unwholesome state] is called "arisen by way of an opportunity made" because it arises exclusively when that opportunity is present. Unwholesome states that have not been eradicated in their respective planes are called "arisen by way of having reached the plane.
Herein, the distinction between the "plane" and "having reached the plane" should be understood: for "plane" refers to the object of insight meditation.
The five aggregates belonging to the three planes. "Acquired by the plane" refers to the class of defilements capable of arising within those aggregates.
Because it is indeed acquired by that plane, it is called "acquired by the plane. And this is not by way of the object;
for even all past and future aggregates, as well as those fully understood, are taken as objects by those whose taints are destroyed.
Defilements arise. And if that [defilement] were called "acquired by the plane," then because it could not be abandoned, no one would ever abandon the root of existence.
Rather, it should be understood as "acquired by the plane" by way of its basis (*vatthu*).
For wherever aggregates arise that have not been fully understood through insight, therefrom their very arising onwards, the root of the round of existence resides within them.
The arisen defilement underlies [the aggregates]. It should be understood as "having reached its soil" in the sense of being unabandoned.

Furthermore, in this context, whichever aggregates have defilements underlying them in the sense of being unabandoned, those very aggregates are the basis for those defilements, not the aggregates belonging to others. And regarding past aggregates, for those [defilements] that have underlain them without being abandoned—

The past aggregates alone are the basis for defilements, not the others. This same principle applies to the future aggregates and so forth. Likewise, among the sense-sphere aggregates, only the sense-sphere aggregates are the basis for those defilements whose underlying tendencies (anusaya) have not been abandoned, not the others. This same principle applies to the fine-material and immaterial spheres.
Furthermore, regarding the aggregates of whichever noble person—such as a stream-enterer and so on—the various types of defilements that are the root of the round of existence [persist] therein...

By whichever path [a defilement] has been abandoned, the aggregates associated with that [path] do not receive the designation "plane" (*bhūmi*) because they are merely the basis for those respective defilements rooted in the round of existence (*vaṭṭamūlaka*). Since an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) has not entirely abandoned the defilements rooted in the round,
whatever action he performs— whether wholesome or unwholesome— is conditioned solely by his karma and defilements.
The round (of saṃsāra) revolves; for each [being], that root of the round resides in the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) alone, not in feeling (*vedanā*) and the others.

Or rather, it should not be said that it resides in the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*) alone, and not in the aggregates of form and so forth. Why? Because it lies latent (*anusayita*) without distinction in all five aggregates.
How? Like the sap of the earth in a tree. For just as in a great tree, having its foundation in the surface of the earth, the sap of the earth—
Dependent upon the essence of water, and conditioned by it, the tree grows through its roots, trunk, branches, twigs, shoots, leaves, foliage, flowers, and fruits;
filling the sky and persisting as a lineage of trees through a succession of seeds until the end of the eon—
it remains rooted precisely in that initial essence of earth, not in the trunk and so forth, nor can it be said that it persists only in the fruit and not in the roots and so forth.
Why? Because it pervades all [parts] without distinction, beginning with the roots.

Just as, for example, if a certain person who has become disillusioned with the flowers, fruits, and so forth of that very tree were to strike it in the four directions with a poisonous thorn called *maṇḍūkakaṇṭaka*, then that tree, touched by the contact of that poison, would—due to the exhaustion of the essence of earth and the essence of water—come to possess the nature of scanty sap.
Just as that man would not be able to produce the continuity of the tree again once it had been destroyed,

even so the clansman who has become disillusioned with the arising of the aggregates undertakes the cultivation of the four paths within his own continuity, just as the man planted poisonous trees in the four directions.
Then, through the contact of that poison of the four paths, his continuity of aggregates is entirely freed from the defilements rooted in the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
Because it has been exhausted, all the various types of kamma— such as bodily action and so forth— which had previously entered into the mere nature of functional activity,
are unable to produce a continuity of existence in another life due to their inherent quality of not giving rise to renewed becoming in the future.
Consequently, through the cessation of the final consciousness, it attains final Nibbāna without fuel, like a fire whose fuel is spent, being now without any further grasping.
In this way, the distinction between the planes and that which has attained the plane should be understood.
Furthermore, there is another fourfold classification of what has arisen: arisen as manifestation, arisen as the grasping of an object, arisen as unobstructed, and arisen as unextirpated.
Among these, "arisen as manifestation" refers exclusively to what is currently occurring. As for the eye and so forth—
Even though a class of defilements does not arise in the preliminary stage when the object has come into range,
it is called "arisen by way of the object being grasped" because it will certainly arise later precisely due to that object having been grasped.

A class of defilements that has not been suppressed by either serenity (samatha) or insight (vipassanā), even if it has not yet entered the mental continuum, [is so called] because of its prevention of arising...

Due to the absence of a cause, it is called "arisen but not suppressed. However, even that which is suppressed by means of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) is called "arisen but not eradicated" because it has not been uprooted by the Noble Path and has not transcended the nature of arising.
And all three types—this arisen but not suppressed and not eradicated due to the non-appropriation of the object—are included within the category of "having attained the plane" (bhūmiladdha).
It should be understood that it "goes.

Thus, when these aforementioned varieties have arisen, that which is called "arisen" in the sense of being present, having occurred, having passed away, or having been made room for, cannot be abandoned by any knowledge of the path because it is not subject to the path. However, as for this...
That which is called "arisen" consists of objects acquired through the attainment of a stage (bhūmi), as well as those that are suppressed but not eradicated;
since that various mundane or supramundane knowledge arises by destroying the state of such things being arisen, therefore all of it must be abandoned.
Thus, with reference to those defilements which the Path abandons, it was said: "of those that have arisen," and so forth.
Now, how is there development for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen at the moment of the Path, and how is there stability for those that have already arisen?
It is precisely through the occurrence of the Path itself. For when the Path occurs, it is called "not yet arisen" because it has never arisen before.
Indeed, having come to a place where it has never been before, or having experienced an object never experienced before, [it is so designated].
People say: "We have come to a place not yet reached; we are experiencing an object never experienced before.
As long as it continues to proceed, this itself is called its "stationing" (*ṭhiti*); thus, it is also appropriate to say that one develops [the path] for the sake of stationing.
In this way, at the moment of the supramundane path, this single energy of the bhikkhu [functions] for the purpose of: "unarisen evil, unwholesome states..."
It receives four names beginning with “for the non-arising,” and so forth. This concludes the discussion on the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*) at the moment of the supramundane path.
Thus, in this context, the right exertions are demonstrated as being mixed—both mundane and supramundane.

In the description of right mindfulness (*sammāsati*), “the body” (*kāya*) refers to the material body (*rūpakāya*). For here, the material body consists of the limbs and members, as well as the phenomena such as head-hairs and so forth.
In the sense of a collection, "body" (kāya) is intended here as in the case of a "body of elephants" or a "body of chariots.

And just as it is in the sense of a collection, so too it is in the sense of the origin (āya) of things that are loathsome. For it is the origin of those things that are loathsome—those most repulsive things—that is called the "body.
"Origin" (āya) means a place of arising. Herein, this is the etymological analysis: they arise from there, thus it is an "origin" (āya). What arises? Loathsome things such as hair and so forth.
Thus, it is called "body" (*kāya*) because it is the coming together (*āya*) of things that are base.
"Contemplating the body" (*kāyānupassī*) means one whose nature is to contemplate the body, or one who is contemplating the body.

Although the word "body" has already been mentioned, the second mention of "contemplating the body" is for the purpose of demonstrating the defining of [the object] as unmixed, its resolution of the compact, and its analysis.

"It should be understood as 'what' (*katam*). By this, it is shown that there is a definition through non-confusion, by demonstrating the mode of contemplation of the body specifically upon the basis known as the "body"—neither contemplating feelings or states of mind within the body, but rather contemplating the body itself.

Likewise, one does not contemplate a single phenomenon apart from the limbs and members of the body, nor does one contemplate a woman or a man apart from the hair of the head, body hair, and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the body here— which is reckoned as a collection of primary elements (bhūta) and derived matter (upādāya)— one does not contemplate it as a single entity separate from those elements and derived matter; rather,

one contemplates it as a collection of limbs and members like one who inspects the parts of a chariot, or as a collection of head-hairs, body-hairs, and so forth like one who inspects the components of a city,
or like one who unravels an empty fist like separating the leaf-sheaths of a plantain trunk.

And because one contemplates the collection of primary and derived elements as if they were distinct, the resolution of the compact mass is demonstrated precisely through this mode of viewing the physical basis known as the "body" in its various aspects.

For herein, neither a body, nor a woman, nor a man, nor any other phenomenon whatsoever is perceived apart from the aforementioned collection; there is nothing but the mere collection of the phenomena already mentioned.
Nevertheless, beings form various kinds of wrong attachments. Therefore the ancients said:
"What one sees is not seen; what is seen, one does not see.
Not seeing, the deluded one is bound; being bound, he is not released."

It is stated that this is "for the purpose of demonstrating the resolution of the compact mass," and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the following meaning should also be understood here:
for one is a contemplator of the body (*kāyānupassī*) with respect to this very body, and not a contemplator of other phenomena. What is meant?
Just as people might contemplate water even in a mirage that is devoid of water, one does not [contemplate] this body as being anything other than impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul.

It is said that one does not contemplate this body as being permanent, pleasant, self, or beautiful; rather, one contemplates the body precisely as a collection of modes that are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul. Alternatively, it is as stated in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta:
"Here, monks, a monk, having gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree... he breathes in mindful... and so forth.

By way of method, the body has been described as beginning with inhalation and exhalation and ending with the state of powdered dust and bones; and that which is further mentioned in the subsequent discourse on the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) as:

"In this case, someone contemplates the earth-body as impermanent, the water-body, the fire-body, the air-body, the hair-of-the-head-body, the hair-of-the-body-body, the skin-body, the hide-body, the flesh-body, the blood-body, the sinew-body, and the bone-body."

The "body" is spoken of as "the body consisting of bones and marrow. Since one contemplates all of that within this very body, the meaning should also be understood as "one who contemplates the body in the body" (*kāye kāyānupassī*).
Alternatively, it is because there is no contemplation of anything to be grasped as "I" or "mine" in relation to the body.

Furthermore, because one contemplates that very collection of various phenomena beginning with head-hairs and body-hairs, the meaning should be understood as follows: "one who contemplates the body" (*kāyānupassī*) means one who contemplates the body as consisting of the collection of phenomena such as head-hairs and so forth.

Moreover, this refers to the entire set of modes—beginning with the characteristic of impermanence—that will be explained in sequence later on in the passage starting with, "In this body, one contemplates it as impermanent, not as permanent."

The meaning should also be understood as "contemplating the body" (*kāyassa anupassanato*) in the sense of "one who contemplates the body in the body" (*kāye kāyānupassī*). This, however, is the meaning common to all four foundations of mindfulness (*catusatipaṭṭhāna*). Regarding the phrase "one who contemplates the body in the body":
although the body has been described in many ways—beginning with the body of inhalation and exhalation—one is a contemplator of the body in each individual instance of that body.
"Dwells" (*viharati*) is an indication of being engaged in one of the dwellings among the four postures (*iriyāpatha*); it refers to the overcoming of the constraints of a single posture.
The meaning is that he carries and maintains himself without falling by interrupting [the flow of consciousness] through another posture.
"Ardent" (*ātāpī*) is an expression illustrating the conjunction with the energy (*vīriya*) that sustains the body;
for at that time, he is endowed with that energy which, because it burns away (*ātāpana*) the defilements within the three realms of existence, is called "ardor" (*ātāpa*). Therefore, he is "ardent."

It is said: "Possessed of clear comprehension" means endowed with the knowledge termed clear comprehension that encompasses the body. "Possessed of mindfulness" means endowed with the mindfulness that encompasses the body.

However, because one contemplates by means of wisdom after having encompassed the object by means of mindfulness—since there is no such thing as contemplation for one devoid of mindfulness—it was therefore said: "And mindfulness..."

“I call this, bhikkhus, beneficial in every respect. Therefore, by the words “he dwells contemplating the body in the body,” the meditation subject of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in body-contemplation has been stated.

Alternatively, because for one who is not ardent there is internal contraction which acts as an obstacle, and for one who is not clearly comprehending there is confusion regarding the adoption of skillful means and the avoidance of unskillful ones;
One who is muddle-minded is incapable of relinquishing what is not a proper means and grasping at what is a proper means; therefore, that meditation subject does not succeed for him.
Consequently, it should be understood that the words "ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful" are spoken in order to show those qualities by whose power that [meditation] succeeds.

Thus, having shown the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body and its associated factor, he now says, "having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world," in order to show its factor of abandoning.
Therein, "having removed" means having removed by way of abandonment through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgavinaya*) or by way of suppression (*vikkhambhanavinaya*).
"Regarding the world" refers to this very body which was previously grasped as "the world" in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating.
"Loka" means the world. The meaning is: "having abandoned covetousness and dejection regarding that world.
However, since covetousness and dejection are not abandoned in the body alone, but are indeed abandoned in regard to feeling and the other aggregates as well, it is stated in the *Vibhaṅga*:
"The five aggregates of clinging are the world. It is precisely because those phenomena are reckoned as the world that this [definition] is given by way of an extraction of their meaning.
It should be understood that it is so stated. As for what was said—“In this context, what is the world?
This very body is the world”—this alone is the meaning here. And “covetousness and grief” is stated as a compound;

however, in other readings of the *Saṃyutta* and *Aṅguttara Nikāyas*, they read them separately. Furthermore, it is called “covetousness” because by means of it one covets or longs for, or because it itself covets.
Or, it is called *abhijjhā* because it is merely the state of coveting. However, since sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is included here by the mention of *abhijjhā*,
and ill will (*byāpāda*) is included by the mention of *domanassa*,
it should be understood that the abandoning of the hindrances is stated by way of showing these two powerful factors comprised within the hindrances.

In particular, here, by the removal of covetousness (*abhijjhā*), there is the removal of attachment rooted in bodily excellence; by the removal of ill-will (*domanassa*), there is the removal of aversion rooted in bodily deficiency;
by the removal of covetousness, there is the removal of delight in the body; by the removal of ill-will, there is the removal of lack of delight in the cultivation of the body;
and by the removal of covetousness, [there is the removal] of the unreal qualities of beauty, pleasure, and so forth, in the body.
By the removal of dejection, the abandoning of the impure, unpleasant, and insubstantial nature of the primary elements within the body is stated.
By this, the practitioner’s power of yoga and his fitness for yoga are illuminated. For this is the power of yoga:
that he is free from attraction and aversion, endures both the unpleasant and the pleasant, and is devoid of the addition of what is unreal and the removal of what is real.
And he is one who is free from attachment and aversion, capable of enduring both the unpleasant and the pleasant;
being free from the false and not discarding the true, he is competent in yoga.
Another method: in the phrase “contemplating the body in the body,” the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) is stated by means of contemplation (*anupassanā*). “He dwells” (*viharati*)—

Herein, the maintenance of the body by one who practices a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) is by means of the aforementioned dwelling. Regarding the terms beginning with “ardent” (*ātāpī*): through ardor comes right effort;
through mindfulness and clear comprehension comes the universal meditation subject, or else the means for maintaining the meditation subject.

Alternatively, through mindfulness comes serenity (*samatha*) attained by way of the contemplation of the body, through clear comprehension comes insight (*vipassanā*), and through the removal of covetousness and displeasure—
It should be understood that this refers to the fruit of meditation (*bhāvanāphala*).

Furthermore, regarding the repeated mention of feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth in the passages beginning with "contemplating feelings in feelings," the purpose should be understood by applying it appropriately according to the method already explained in the section on contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*).
However, this is the specific meaning [of the present context]: regarding pleasant [feeling] and so forth...
In the *Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta*, it is taught that one contemplates each individual feeling among the many varieties of feelings as impermanent and so forth;
one contemplates each individual state of consciousness among the sixteenfold divisions of consciousness, such as those accompanied by lust and so forth, as impermanent and so forth;
and one contemplates each individual phenomenon among the remaining phenomena of the other planes, excluding the body, feelings, and consciousness, as impermanent and so forth.
Or, as stated by the method already explained, one is "a contemplator of phenomena such as the hindrances.

Herein, it should be understood that the singular form "in the body" (*kāye*) is used because the body is a single unit, while the singular form "in the mind" (*citte*) is used because no distinction is made in the nature of the mind when referring to it as a genus.
And just as feeling and the other aggregates are to be contemplated, so too, contemplating them in that way, one is "a contemplator of feelings in feelings," and [a contemplator] in the mind...
It should be understood as "contemplating the mind" and "contemplating phenomena among phenomena. How, first of all, should feeling be contemplated?

Feeling that is pleasant should be contemplated as suffering; feeling that is painful should be contemplated as a dart; and feeling that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant should be contemplated as impermanent. As it has been said:
“He who has seen pleasure as suffering, and has seen suffering as a dart,
and has seen the peaceful state that is neither-suffering-nor-pleasure as impermanent—
he indeed is a bhikkhu with right vision; he fully understands feelings.”
All these, indeed, should be contemplated as suffering. For this has been said: "Whatever is felt, all that I declare to be suffering.
And they should also be contemplated as both pleasure and pain. As it was said:
"A pleasant feeling is pleasant in its persistence and painful in its change; a painful feeling is painful in its persistence and pleasant in its change; a neither-painful-nor-pleasant..."
“Feeling is happiness when there is knowledge, and suffering when there is ignorance. Furthermore, it should also be contemplated by way of the seven contemplations on impermanence and so forth.

Regarding mental states (*cittadhamma*), first, consciousness (*citta*) should be contemplated by way of the seven contemplations on impermanence and so forth—distinguished by their various types such as object-condition, predominance-condition, conascence-condition, plane, kamma-result, and functional—and also by way of the sixteenfold distinctions such as being with lust and so forth. As for mental factors (*dhammā*):

It should be contemplated by way of specific and general characteristics, the dhamma of emptiness, the seven contemplations such as impermanence and so forth, and the peaceful and unpeaceful aspects, and so on. Now,
although for one who has abandoned covetousness and dejection regarding the world known as the body,

those same states are necessarily abandoned in the worlds of feeling and so forth as well, nevertheless, [this is stated] by way of different individuals and by way of the development of the foundations of mindfulness at various moments.
And this has been stated everywhere. Or rather, what is abandoned in one instance is abandoned in all others as well.
Therefore, it should be understood that it was stated in this way for the purpose of showing its abandonment therein.
Thus, these four foundations of mindfulness are found in various states of consciousness during the preliminary stage; for by means of one consciousness...
One contemplates the body with one [aspect], feeling with another, the mind with another, and mental objects with another.
However, at the moment of the supramundane path, they are obtained within a single consciousness alone.

For one who has arrived after first contemplating the body, the mindfulness associated with insight is called "contemplation of the body" (*kāyānupassanā*); a person endowed with that mindfulness is called "one who contemplates the body. [This applies to] insight...
For one who has exerted effort and attained the Noble Path, at the moment of the Path, mindfulness associated with that Path is called "contemplation of the body" (*kāyānupassanā*);
a person endowed with that mindfulness is called "one contemplating the body.

Having grasped feeling, having grasped the mind, and having grasped mental phenomena, the mindfulness associated with insight that has arrived is "contemplation of mental phenomena" (*dhammānupassanā*).
A person endowed with that mindfulness is called one who contemplates phenomena (*dhammānupassī*).
For one who has intensified insight and attained the Noble Path, the mindfulness associated with the Path at the moment of the Path is called contemplation of phenomena;
a person endowed with that mindfulness is called one who contemplates phenomena. Thus, for the time being, the teaching stands with respect to the person.
Furthermore, mindfulness that encompasses the body succeeds through the path by abandoning the perversion of perceiving the body as "beautiful"; thus it is called "contemplation of the body.
Mindfulness that encompasses feelings succeeds through the path by abandoning the perversion of perceiving feelings as "pleasant"; thus it is called "contemplation of feelings.
Mindfulness that encompasses the mind [succeeds through the path] by abandoning the perversion of perceiving the mind as "permanent"...

"It succeeds" refers to the mindfulness consisting in contemplation of mind (*cittānupassanā*). Mindfulness that grasps phenomena (*dhamma*) succeeds through the path by abandoning the perversion of regarding phenomena as "self";

this is called the mindfulness consisting in contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*). Thus, mindfulness associated with the supramundane path receives four names according to its accomplishment of the four functions.
Therefore it was said: "But at the moment of the supramundane path, they are obtained within a single consciousness alone."

In the description of right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*), the phrase "quite secluded from sensual desires" (*vivicceva kāmehi*) means having become secluded from, separated from, and departed from sensual desires.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the particle *eva* (quite) here has the sense of restriction (*niyama*).

And because it has the sense of restriction, it indicates that even though sensual desires are not actually present at the time of attaining and abiding in the first jhāna, they nonetheless constitute the opposite of that first jhāna.
It indicates his attainment precisely through the relinquishing of sensual desires. How so?
By making the restriction, "quite secluded from sensual desires," this is made known: surely sensual desires are the adversaries of this jhāna;
when they are present, this does not occur, just as the light of a lamp does not appear when there is darkness. And it is only through the relinquishing of them that his attainment occurs.
