It is like reaching the far shore by abandoning the near shore. Therefore, he establishes a restriction.
Herein, it might be asked: why was this stated only with the first term and not the second;
could one enter and dwell in jhāna even without being secluded from unwholesome states? This, however, should not be viewed in that way, because it is the escape from them.

For this [particle] was used in the preceding phrase. Indeed, because it transcends the sense-sphere (*kāmadhātu*) and because it is the antidote to sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), this jhāna is the very escape from sensual pleasures.
As it has been said: "This is the escape from sensual pleasures, namely, renunciation.
Furthermore, regarding the subsequent phrase, just as in the expression: "Right here, monks, is the ascetic; right here is the second ascetic," the word "only" (*eva*) is used.
Having brought this [point] forward, it is said that one should speak thus:

for it is not possible to enter and dwell in jhāna without being secluded from other unwholesome states termed hindrances. Therefore, this should be understood in both phrases as "quite secluded from sensual pleasures" and "quite secluded from unwholesome states. And although the word "secluded" (vivicca) occurs in both phrases—
By this general statement, the seclusion consisting in the factors [of the path], suppression, eradication, subsiding, and escape, as well as the seclusion of mind,
body, and acquisitions, are all included; nevertheless, in the preliminary stage, they should be understood as the seclusion of body, the seclusion of mind, and the seclusion by suppression,
whereas at the moment of the supramundane path, they are the seclusion of body, the seclusion of mind, the seclusion by eradication, the seclusion by subsiding, and the seclusion by escape.
By the phrase "by sensual pleasures" (kāmehi), all those sensual objects (vatthukāmā) that are described in the *Mahāniddesa* by way of the method beginning with, "What are sensual objects?
Agreeable forms," as well as those defilements of sensual desire (kilesakāmā) described in that same place and in the *Vibhaṅga* thus: "Desire is sensual pleasure; lust is sensual pleasure;
desire-and-lust is sensual pleasure; intention is sensual pleasure; passion is sensual pleasure; intention-and-passion is sensual pleasure"—all these are included.

It should be understood as "comprised" (*saṅgahitā*). For this being so, the meaning of "quite secluded from sensual pleasures" (*vivicceva kāmehi*) is appropriate as "secluded even from objective sensual pleasures" (*vatthukāmehi*);
by this, bodily seclusion (*kāyaviveka*) is expressed.
The meaning of "secluded from unwholesome states" (*vivicca akusalehi dhammehi*) is appropriate as "secluded from defilement-sensualities" (*kilesakāmehi*) or "secluded from all unwholesome states."
By this, seclusion of mind is expressed. Furthermore, by the first [phrase], because it speaks of seclusion from sensual objects (*vatthukāma*), the relinquishing of sensual pleasure is clarified;
by the second, because it speaks of seclusion from defilements (*kilesakāma*), the embracing of the happiness of renunciation (*nekkhammasukha*) is made manifest.
And thus, precisely through these expressions of seclusion from sensual objects and defilements, the abandonment of the basis for corruption is shown by the first.

By the second, the abandoning of defilement [is shown]. It should be understood that by the first, the relinquishing of the cause of greed is demonstrated, and by the second, that of the state of folly;
furthermore, by the first, purity of practice is clarified, and by the second, the nourishment of the underlying disposition (āsaya).
This, for now, is the method regarding the "sensual pleasures" mentioned here in the context of sensual objects (vatthukāma).

On the side of the defilement-objects of sensual pleasure (*kilesakāma*), however, what is intended by "sensual pleasure" (*kāma*) is simply sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), which has many divisions such as "zeal" (*chanda*) and "lust" (*rāga*).

Although this is included among the unwholesome states, it is mentioned separately in the *Vibhaṅga* in the passage beginning, "In that regard, what are sensual pleasures? Sensual desire is sensual pleasure," because it is the specific opposite of the factors of absorption (*jhānaṅga*) mentioned later; or else, because it is a defilement-object of sensual pleasure, it is placed in the preceding phrase.

It is stated [in the plural] because it is included within the unwholesome (*akusala*) in the second phrase. Furthermore, instead of saying "desire" (*kāma*)—which would imply a single variety—it is said "by desires" (*kāmehi*).

Moreover, although other phenomena (*dhammas*) also exist as unwholesome, they are not mentioned here; for in the *Vibhaṅga*, following the method beginning with "In this context, what are the unwholesome phenomena?
Sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*)," the subsequent sections demonstrate that these [five hindrances] function as the opposites and adversaries to the factors of absorption (*jhānaṅga*).
The hindrances themselves have been explained. For the hindrances are the opposites of the jhāna factors;
it is said that the jhāna factors themselves are their counteragents, their destroyers, and their annihilators. Thus it is stated in the *Peṭaka*:
“Concentration is the counteragent to sensual desire, rapture to ill will, applied thought to sloth and torpor, pleasure to restlessness and remorse, and sustained thought to doubt.”
Thus, here by the phrase “quite secluded from sensual desires,” the seclusion through suppression of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is stated;
by the phrase “secluded from unwholesome states,” that of all five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) is stated.

By taking what has not yet been mentioned, however, the first [phrase] refers to sensual desire, and the second to the remaining hindrances. Likewise, among the three unwholesome roots, the first [phrase] refers to...

By the first [verse], there is the abandoning of greed whose object consists of the various categories of the five strands of sensual pleasure; by the second, there is the abandoning of hatred and delusion whose objects consist of the various bases for resentment and so forth. Or else, regarding phenomena such as the floods (ogha) and so on:

by the first [verse], there is the abandoning of the flood of sensuality, the yoke of sensuality, the taint of sensuality, the clinging to sensuality, the bodily tie of covetousness, and the fetter of lust for sensuality; by the second, there is the abandoning of the remaining floods, yokes, taints, clingings, ties, and fetters. By the first...
By the first [term], the seclusion by suppression of craving and its associated states is stated; by the second, that of ignorance and its associated states.

Furthermore, it should be understood that by the first, the seclusion by suppression of the eight types of consciousness-arising associated with greed is stated, and by the second, that of the remaining four types of unwholesome consciousness-arising.

Having thus far shown the factor of abandoning for the first jhāna, the words "with applied thought (savitakka) and sustained thought (savicāra)," etc., are now stated in order to show the factors of association.
Therein, applied thought (vitakka) has the characteristic of directing the mind onto the object;
sustained thought (vicāra) has the characteristic of examining the object. And although these two are inseparable in some instances, by way of their relative grossness—
In the sense of being the forerunner, *vitakka* (initial application) is the mind’s first directed impact, like the initial strike of a gong;
in the sense of subtlety and its nature of sustained rubbing, *vicāra* (sustained application) is the continuous following-up, like the resonance of the gong.
Furthermore, *vitakka* is expansive at the time of its first arising, acting as a movement of the mind, like the flapping of the wings of a bird wishing to fly into the sky.
Investigation (vicāra) is the peaceful mode of activity of the mind, characterized by a lack of excessive agitation;
it is like the spreading of the wings of a bird that has flown up into the sky,
or like the circling above a lotus by a bee whose mind is following the fragrance as it falls toward the lotus.

In the commentary on the Dukanipāta, however, it is said: "Initial application (vitakka) occurs by way of directing the mind toward the object, like the movement of a great bird flying through the air which, having caught the wind with both wings, settles them;
sustained application (vicāra) occurs by way of continued mental contact, like the movement of that same bird as it flaps its wings to catch the wind."
It is said, “investigation. This is appropriate in terms of its continuous occurrence. However, that distinction between them becomes manifest in the first and second jhānas.

Furthermore, for one who holds a tarnished bronze vessel firmly with one hand while rubbing it with the other hand using a powder-and-oil ball, the hand that holds it firmly is like initial application (vitakka).

Investigation (vicāra) is like the hand that polishes [the clay]. Likewise, initial application (vitakka) is like the potter’s hand that presses down while spinning the wheel with a stroke of the stick to fashion a vessel; investigation is like the hand that moves it back and forth.
Likewise, sustained application (avitakka) is like a thorn fixed upright in the center of a circle being drawn.
Applied thought (*vitakka*) is like a thorn wandering outside, while sustained thought (*vicāra*) is like rubbing it; thus,

because it proceeds together with this applied thought and this sustained thought— just as a tree does with its flowers and fruits— this meditative absorption (*jhāna*) is called "with applied thought and with sustained thought" (*savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ*).

Regarding the term *vivekaja*: here, *viveka* means seclusion (*vivitti*), which signifies the disappearance of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). Alternatively, *viveka* means that which is secluded; thus, it refers to the mass of states associated with jhāna that are secluded from the hindrances.
Therefore, "born of seclusion" (*vivekaja*) means born from that seclusion, or arisen in that seclusion.
Regarding *pītisukha*: here, it is called *pīti* because it refreshes (*pīṇayati*); its characteristic is endearment (*sampiyāyana*). Furthermore, this [first jhāna] possesses minor *pīti*.
Rapture (pīti) is fivefold: momentary rapture, showering rapture, uplifting rapture, and pervading rapture.
Among these, minor rapture is only able to cause the hair on the body to stand on end.
Momentary rapture occurs from moment to moment like the flashing of lightning. Showering rapture descends upon the body like a wave upon the shore of the ocean.
Having descended, it breaks. *Ubbegā* rapture is powerful; having made the body rise upward, it reaches the point of making one leap into the air.

*Pharaṇā* rapture is exceedingly powerful. When it has arisen, it pervades the entire body, so that one becomes completely suffused like a filled bladder or like the interior of a mountain being flooded by a great torrent of water. And this—
The fivefold rapture, taking conception and reaching maturity, fulfills the two kinds of tranquility:

bodily tranquility and mental tranquility. Tranquility, taking conception and reaching maturity, fulfills both kinds of happiness: bodily and mental. Happiness, taking conception and reaching maturity...
As it proceeds, it fulfills three kinds of concentration: momentary concentration (khaṇika-samādhi), access concentration (upacāra-samādhi), and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi).

Among these, that joy which serves as the root for absorption concentration, which increases and becomes associated with concentration, and which is pervasive—this is the "joy" intended in this context.
Furthermore, it is called *sukha* because it "pleases" (*sukhayati*); the meaning is that it makes one who experiences it happy. Or, *sukha* is the act of pleasing;
or, it is called *sukha* because it thoroughly consumes (*suṭṭhu khādati*) and carves away (*khaṇati*) bodily and mental afflictions.

This is the name for the feeling of mental joy (*somanassa-vedanā*). Its characteristic is agreeableness (*sāta-lakkhaṇa*). And although there is sometimes an inseparable association between them, [mental joy] is the satisfaction arising from the acquisition of a desirable object.
Rapture (*pīti*) is the experiencing of the flavor once attained; bliss (*sukha*) is the relishing of that flavor. Where there is rapture, there is bliss;

but where there is bliss, there is not necessarily rapture. Rapture is included within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), while bliss is included within the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*).
Rapture is like seeing or hearing about water at the edge of a forest when one is exhausted by a desert journey; bliss is like entering the forest shade and partaking of the water.
It is like happiness. This should be understood as stated because of its manifest state at each respective moment.
Thus, because this rapture (*pīti*) and this happiness (*sukha*) belong to this jhāna, or because they exist in this jhāna, this jhāna is called "rapture-and-happiness" (*pītisukha*).

Alternatively, "rapture-and-happiness" (*pītisukha*) is a copulative compound (*dvanda*), like "Dharma-Vinaya" and so forth; it means rapture and happiness. [This is] rapture-and-happiness born of seclusion (*vivekaja*).

Or, it is "born of seclusion" because this jhāna possesses that joy and happiness born of seclusion; for just as the jhāna itself is born of seclusion, so too the joy and happiness herein are indeed born of seclusion.

Since he possesses that, it is therefore appropriate to form a compound by eliding the middle term (*alopa-samāsa*) and speak of it in a single phrase as "joy and happiness born of seclusion" (*vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ*).
"First": it is "first" because of its position in the numerical sequence; it is also "first" because it arises first. "Jhāna" is twofold:

jhāna as contemplation of the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) and jhāna as contemplation of characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*). Among these, the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) are designated as "contemplation of the object" because they contemplate objects such as the earth-kasiṇa and so forth.
However, insight (*vipassanā*), the path (*magga*), and the fruit (*phala*)...
This is called "contemplation of characteristics. In this context, insight is "contemplation of characteristics" because it closely contemplates the characteristics of impermanence and so forth;
the path is "contemplation of characteristics" because it succeeds through the path after the work has been done by insight;

and the fruit is "contemplation of characteristics" because it closely contemplates the characteristic of suchness, which is the truth of cessation. Among these, here [it refers to] the preliminary stage.
Contemplation of the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) is intended here; at the moment of the supramundane path, it is contemplation of the characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*).
Therefore, it should be understood as "jhāna" because of contemplating the object, because of contemplating the characteristics, and because of burning away the opposites.
"Having attained" (*upasampajja*) means having approached, which is to say, having reached; or it means having fully achieved, which is to say, having brought to completion.
"He dwells" means he conducts himself by means of a mode of deportment corresponding to that [jhāna];
having become possessed of the jhāna of the kind described, he brings about the maintenance of his personal existence (*attabhāva*).
"With the stilling of applied and sustained thought" (*vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā*): here, it refers to the stilling of these two, namely, applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
"By surmounting" means that at the moment of the second jhāna, [the factors] are no longer manifest; this is what is meant.
In this regard, although none of the factors of the first jhāna exist in the second jhāna, the contact and so forth in the first jhāna are indeed different from those here.
However, it is by the surmounting of each successive gross factor that the second jhāna and the others follow upon the first jhāna.
It should be understood that the phrase "with the stilling of applied and sustained thought" is stated for the purpose of showing the attainment [of the first jhāna].
"Internal" (ajjhatta) here refers to one's own internal state; therefore, the meaning is "arisen within oneself," or "produced in one's own mental continuum.
"Tranquillity" (sampasādana): faith is called tranquillity; because it is associated with tranquillity, the jhāna itself is also called tranquillity.

It is like a blue cloth because of its association with the color blue. Or, because that jhāna gladdens the mind (*cetas*) by being endowed with tranquility and by the subsiding of the agitation of applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*), it is therefore called "tranquillizing" (*sampasādana*).
And in this interpretation of the meaning, the connection between the words should be understood as "tranquillizing of the mind";
however, in the previous interpretation of the meaning, [the word] "of the mind" (*cetaso*)— [...is connected to the preceding term.]
It should be construed together with the term *ekodibhāvena*.

Herein, this is the construction of the meaning: it "rises as one" (*ekodi*); the meaning is that it rises having become pre-eminent and supreme because it is not overlaid by applied thought and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*).
For even what is supreme is called "one" (*eka*) in the world. Or, it is "one" because it is devoid of applied thought and sustained thought.

It is also appropriate to say that he becomes "without companion" (*asahāya*). Alternatively, it is called *udi* because it causes the associated mental states to arise (*udāyati*), meaning it makes them emerge.
Being both "one" (*eka*) in the sense of being supreme (*seṭṭha*) and *udi*, it is *ekodi*. This is a designation for concentration (*samādhi*).
Thus, because one develops and increases this *ekodi*, this second jhāna is "the state of oneness" (*ekodibhāva*). Furthermore, as for this *ekodi*:
It is of the mind, not of a being, nor of a soul. Therefore, this is called "the state of singleness of mind.
But is it not the case that this faith exists even in the first jhāna, and this concentration called "singleness" is present there too?
Why then is this alone described as "tranquillity of mind and singleness of mind"? It is said in reply: for that first jhāna...
Due to the agitation caused by applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*), it is not perfectly serene, like water disturbed by ripples and waves;

therefore, even though faith (*saddhā*) is present, it is not called "tranquillity" (*sampasādana*). And because of this lack of perfect serenity, concentration (*samādhi*) is also not clearly manifest here;
thus, it is not called "singleness" (*ekodibhāva*). However, in this jhāna, due to the absence of the hindrances of applied and sustained thought...
Faith is powerful when it has gained an opportunity, and through the acquisition of such powerful faith as its companion, concentration also becomes manifest;
therefore, it should be understood that this is stated in this very way.

It is "without applied thought and without sustained thought" because applied thought has been abandoned by means of cultivation; thus, there is no applied thought in this [state], or for this [state], hence it is "without applied thought."

By this same method, [the state] without investigation is established. Here it is asked: "Is not this meaning already established by the phrase 'with the subsiding of applied thought and sustained thought'?
Then why is it stated again as 'without applied thought, without sustained thought'? It is said in reply: This is indeed so;
this meaning is indeed established, yet this [phrase] does not illuminate that specific meaning. Have we not already said: "But of each successive gross factor..."?

Furthermore, it is said "with the stilling of applied and sustained thought" (*vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā*) in order to show that, through the surmounting of the [first] factor, there is the attainment of the second jhāna and those following the first jhāna.

Moreover, this serenity (*sampasādanaṃ*) arises from the stilling of applied and sustained thought, not from the turbidity of the defilements (*kilesakālussiya*). And as for applied and sustained thought...

Because of the subsiding [of applied and sustained thought] and the state of singleness, this statement indicates the causes for serenity (*sampasādana*) and singleness (*ekodibhāva*), unlike access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) which lacks the abandoning of hindrances, and unlike the first jhāna which lacks the manifestation of factors.

Likewise, because of the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, this is without applied and sustained thought (*avitakka-avicāra*), unlike the third and fourth jhānas which lack eye-consciousness and so forth.

And because it is "as if non-existent," this [term] illuminates the cause for the state of being without applied thought (*avitakka*) and sustained thought (*avicāra*). It does not merely illuminate the absence of applied and sustained thought;
rather, the expression "without applied thought, without sustained thought" (*avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ*) merely illuminates the mere absence of applied and sustained thought.
Therefore, even though the former has already been stated, it must nevertheless be stated again.
"Born of concentration" means born from the concentration of the first jhāna, or born from associated concentration; this is the meaning.

In this context, although the first jhāna itself is also born from associated concentration, nevertheless, this [specific] concentration alone deserves to be called "concentration," because it is exceedingly unshakable and perfectly serene due to its freedom from the agitation of applied and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra).
Therefore, for the purpose of praising this [jhāna], it is described as "born of concentration" (*samādhija*). "Rapture and happiness" (*pītisukha*) is exactly as previously explained.
It is called "the second" because of its position in the numerical sequence; it is also called "the second" because it arises as the second [stage].
"With the fading away of rapture" (*pītiyā ca virāgā*): "fading away" (*virāga*) means either a sense of disgust toward the aforementioned kind of rapture, or its transcendence.
But the word *ca* between the two has the sense of conjunction; it either conjoins "tranquillity" (*vūpasama*) or "the tranquillity of applied and sustained thought" (*vitakkavicāra-vūpasama*).
In that context, when it conjoins only "tranquillity," the construction should be understood as follows: "due to the fading away of rapture (*pīti-virāgā*), and furthermore, due to tranquillity.
And according to this construction, "fading away" (*virāga*) has the sense of disgust (*jigucchana*); therefore—
The meaning should be understood as "and by the overcoming of the loathing of rapture.

However, when one combines [the phrase] with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*), then the construction should be understood thus: "and through dispassion toward rapture, and furthermore, through the subsiding of applied and sustained thought.
In this construction, "dispassion" (*virāga*) has the sense of "overcoming"; therefore, regarding rapture...
And the meaning should be understood as: "by surmounting [the first jhāna] and by the subsiding of applied and sustained thought.

Granted, these applied and sustained thoughts have already subsided in the second jhāna itself; nevertheless, this is stated for the purpose of illustrating the path of this particular jhāna and for the purpose of praising it.
For when it is said, "by the subsiding of applied and sustained thought," this becomes evident.
“Surely the subsiding of applied and sustained thought is the path to this jhāna. And just as, in the case of the third noble path,
even though the five lower fetters such as personality-belief have not yet been abandoned,
their abandonment is spoken of as a way of praising that path— which inspires effort in those striving for its attainment— so too is it here.
In the same way, here, even though the thought-constructions and discursive evaluations (*vitakkavicāra*) have not yet subsided, the description of their subsiding constitutes a statement of praise.
Therefore, this meaning was stated as: "with the surmounting of rapture and with the subsiding of thought-constructions and discursive evaluations.

Regarding the phrase "and he dwells equanimous" (*upekkhako ca viharati*): here, it is called equanimity (*upekkhā*) because it looks on (*ikkhati*) from a position of evenness; it sees evenly, being impartial.

The meaning is: "having offered, he sees. Because one is endowed with that equanimity which is clear, vast, and firmly established, the possessor of the third jhāna is called "equanimous" (*upekkhaka*).
Furthermore, equanimity is tenfold: equanimity of the six factors, equanimity of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), equanimity of the enlightenment factor (*bojjhaṅga*), and equanimity of energy.
Equanimity regarding formations, equanimity regarding feelings, equanimity regarding insight, equanimity as specific neutrality, and equanimity of purification.
In this context, that which has come down in the passage: "Here, monks, when a monk whose taints are destroyed sees a form with the eye, he is neither glad nor sad;
he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending"—this refers to the sixfold equanimity of one whose taints are destroyed.
Equanimity that consists in the state of not abandoning one's naturally pure disposition when encountering the six types of desirable or undesirable objects at the sense doors—
this is called the equanimity of the six factors (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*). However,

the equanimity that consists in the attitude of neutrality toward beings, as it occurs in such passages as, "He dwells, having pervaded one direction with a mind accompanied by equanimity"— this is called the equanimity of the divine abode (*brahmavihārupekkhā*).

However, that equanimity which exists as the mode of neutrality among co-nascent states, as it occurs in the passage, “He develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity, which is based on seclusion,” is called equanimity-enlightenment-factor (*upekkhā-bojjhaṅga*).

On the other hand, that equanimity which is defined as energy that is neither too tense nor too lax, as it occurs in the passage, “From time to time he gives attention to the sign of equanimity,” is called energy-equanimity (*vīriyupekkhā*).

Furthermore, regarding the question, “How many kinds of equanimity toward formations arise by way of serenity (*samatha*), and how many kinds of equanimity toward formations arise by way of insight (*vipassanā*)?”...
"Do they arise? "Eight equanimities toward formations arise by way of serenity; ten equanimities toward formations arise by way of insight.

Equanimity that is neutral in the grasping of the reflective-stilling regarding the hindrances and so forth, as it has come down in such passages, is what is called "equanimity toward formations" (*saṅkhārupekkhā*).

However, that equanimity designated as "neither-painful-nor-pleasant" which occurs in such passages as, "At whatever time a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen accompanied by equanimity," is called feeling-equanimity (*vedanupekkhā*).

That equanimity which exists as a state of neutrality during investigation, occurring in such passages as, "He abandons what exists, what has come to be, and he attains equanimity," is called insight-equanimity (*vipassanupekkhā*).

But that equanimity which exists as a state of evenness toward co-nascent states, occurring among the "miscellaneous" factors beginning with desire (*chanda*), is called equanimity-as-a-neutral-fact (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).

Furthermore, that equanimity which arises in such passages as “and he dwells in equanimity,” producing a state of non-partisanship even toward that supreme bliss, is called *jhānupekkhā* (equanimity of absorption).

On the other hand, that equanimity which arises in such passages as “the fourth jhāna is purity of mindfulness and equanimity,” being purified of all opposing factors and remaining inactive even while those opposing factors are being stilled, is called *pārisuddhupekkhā* (equanimity of purification).

Among these, there is the sixfold equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*), the equanimity of the divine abodes (*brahmavihārupekkhā*), the equanimity of the enlightenment factor (*bojjhaṅgupekkhā*), and the equanimity of specific neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).

The equanimity of jhāna (*jhānupekkhā*), the equanimity of purification (*pārisuddhupekkhā*), and the equanimity of neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*) are identical in meaning; they are all simply the equanimity of neutrality.

However, this distinction arises from the difference in their respective states, just as there is a distinction among a single being according to whether he is a child, a youth, an elder, a general, or a king.
Therefore, where there is the sixfold equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*), there is no equanimity that is a factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅgupekkhā*) and so forth. Where...
Or rather, it should be understood that while there is equanimity as a factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅgupekkhā*), the sixfold equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*) and the others do not exist therein.
Just as these [two types] are identical in meaning, so too are equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) and equanimity of insight (*vipassanupekkhā*).
For they are simply wisdom (*paññā*), divided into two ways according to their function. Just as when a man sees a snake that has entered his house this evening...
Just as one who, having taken up a staff with a goat’s foot, while searching, sees that [object] lying in a granary of husks and,

looking at it to determine whether it is a snake or not, sees three svastikas and becomes free from doubt; then, in the investigation of whether "it is a snake" or "it is not a snake," there arises a state of equanimity—
exactly so is it for one who has begun insight (vipassanā), regarding the three characteristics by means of insight-knowledge.
When, upon seeing the formations, a state of equanimity arises through the investigation of their impermanence and so forth, this is insight-equanimity (*vipassanupekkhā*).
It is like that man who, having seized the snake firmly with the forked stick, seeks only the manner of releasing it, thinking:
"How might I release this snake without harming it or being bitten by it?"—while he is still in the act of holding it.

Just as there is neutrality toward a person who has seen three people set on fire, so too, for one who sees the three realms of existence as ablaze because of having seen the three characteristics, the neutrality regarding the grasping of formations is equanimity toward formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*).
Thus, when insight-equanimity (*vipassanupekkhā*) is established, equanimity toward formations is also necessarily established.
However, this [equanimity toward formations] is divided into two types by its function, which is termed neutrality in both investigation and grasping.

However, energy-equanimity (*vīriyupekkhā*) and feeling-equanimity (*vedanupekkhā*) are distinct from one another and from the remaining factors in terms of their essential meaning. And it has been said in this regard:
"Equanimity as neutrality, the factor of enlightenment, the sixfold limb, the jhāna-purity, Insight, formations, feeling, and energy."
“In detail there are ten kinds of equanimity;
six beginning with neutrality; two are wisdom; and then by means of two, these four come to be.
Thus, among these types of equanimity, it is *jhānupekkhā* (equanimity of absorption) that is intended here. Its characteristic is neutrality. Here it may be asked: “Is it not true that...”

"And since this, in terms of its meaning, is simply equanimity toward the middle (tatramajjhattupekkhā), and that exists even in the first and second jhānas, it would have to be said there too that 'he dwells equanimous';
why was it not stated there? [The answer is: "Because its function is not manifest there.

For its function is not manifest there because it is overwhelmed by applied thought (vitakka) and the other factors; but here, it is [not overwhelmed] by applied thought, sustained thought, and rapture."
Because they are unassailable, they have become manifest in their function as if with heads held high;

therefore, they are said [to be "spoken"]. Now, regarding the phrase "mindful and clearly comprehending": herein, one who remembers is "mindful" (*sato*); one who understands is "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāno*). Thus, both mindfulness and clear comprehension are stated by way of the person.
In that context, mindfulness has the characteristic of remembering; clear comprehension has the characteristic of non-delusion.

In this regard, although this mindfulness and clear comprehension exist even in the preceding jhānas—for one who is muddled in mindfulness and lacking clear comprehension does not achieve even access concentration, let alone absorption—nevertheless, because those jhānas are gross, the movement of the mind is easy, like that of a person on level ground;
thus, the function of mindfulness and clear comprehension is not prominent there. This is due to the abandoning of the gross factors.
However, because this jhāna is so subtle, the movement of the mind must be maintained by the functions of mindfulness and clear comprehension, as if on the edge of a razor;
therefore, it is stated right here [in the *Visuddhimagga*].
Furthermore, just as a calf accustomed to its mother, if removed from her and left unguarded, returns to her once again, so too does this bliss of the third jhāna.

Even if one has been removed from rapture (*pīti*), if one is not protected by the safeguard of mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*), one might again approach rapture and become associated with it.
Sentient beings are also infatuated with pleasure (*sukha*); and this pleasure is exceedingly sweet because there is no pleasure beyond it.
However, it is only through the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension that there is no infatuation with this pleasure here, and not otherwise.
It should be understood that this was stated right here in order to demonstrate this specific point as well.
Now, regarding the phrase "he experiences pleasure with the body":

although there is no mental application of experiencing pleasure for one possessing the third jhāna, nevertheless, because there is pleasure associated with his mental body (*nāmakāya*), or rather, that which is associated with the mental body—
Because his material body has been touched by an exceedingly sublime form arising from that [bliss], and because of being touched by that, he would experience bliss even after emerging from jhāna;
therefore, showing this meaning, it was said: "And experience bliss with the body."
Now, regarding that which the Noble Ones describe as "dwelling in happiness, mindful and equanimous": here,
for the sake of the third jhāna, by reason of the third jhāna, the Noble Ones— the Buddhas and others—
describe, teach, proclaim, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, expound, and praise the person who possesses the third jhāna.
The intention is: "How so? 'Equanimous, mindful, dwelling in happiness. Thus, the construction here should be understood as: "Having attained and dwelt in that third jhāna.
But why do they praise it in this way? Because it is worthy of praise. For this [jhāna], since it possesses an exceedingly sweet happiness...
Even when the third jhāna, which has reached the perfection of happiness, is attained, he remains equanimous;
he is not dragged away by attachment to that happiness. And because mindfulness is established so that rapture does not arise, he is mindful.
Furthermore, because he experiences with his mental body a happiness that is untainted and beloved by the noble ones, and frequented only by noble persons, he is worthy of praise.

Thus it is. Therefore, it should be understood that the Noble Ones, praising one who is worthy of praise by making manifest those qualities that constitute the grounds for such praise, praise him thus:
"He dwells in happiness, mindful and equanimous. "Third" means third in numerical sequence;
it is also called "third" because it arises as the third.
"By the abandoning of pleasure and by the abandoning of pain" means by the abandoning of bodily pleasure and bodily pain.
"Previously" means that this occurs previously, not at the moment of the fourth jhāna.
"With the disappearance of mental joy and mental grief" means that these two—mental pleasure and mental pain—also have their disappearance and abandoning previously.
Thus it has been said. But when does their abandonment occur? It occurs at the moment of access concentration for the four jhānas.

For mental joy (*somanassa*) is abandoned precisely at the moment of access to the fourth jhāna; while pain (*dukkha*), mental grief (*domanassa*), and physical pleasure (*sukha*) are abandoned at the moments of access to the first, second, and third jhānas respectively.
Thus, although not mentioned here in this sequence of abandonment, [they are explained] in the *Indriyavibhaṅga*.
However, the abandoning of pleasure, pain, joy, and grief—which are mentioned here as well according to the order of the faculties—should be understood [in this way].
But if these are abandoned at the very moment of the access concentration (*upacāra*) of each respective jhāna, then why [is it said]:
"And where, monks, does the arisen faculty of pain cease without remainder? Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded..."?
...having abandoned sensual desires... he enters and dwells in the first jhāna. Herein, the arisen faculty of pain ceases without remainder.
But where do the arisen faculties of grief, pleasure, and joy cease without remainder?
Here, monks, with the abandoning of pleasure... [he enters and dwells in] the fourth jhāna.
“He dwells [therein]. And herein, the arisen faculty of mental joy ceases without remainder. Is it thus that cessation is stated only in the jhānas?
Because it is a cessation of a superior degree (*atisayanirodha*). For their cessation of a superior degree occurs in the first jhāna and so forth, but not mere cessation.
However, at the moment of access (*upacāra*), there is mere cessation, but not a cessation of a superior degree. For instance, in the case of various objects of focus (*nānāvajjana*).

Even for one in whom the faculty of pain has ceased in the access concentration (*upacāra*) of the first jhāna, its arising may occur through contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like, or through the affliction of an uneven seat;
however, this does not happen within the attainment (*appanā*). Furthermore, even though it has ceased in access, it has not ceased thoroughly because it has not been struck down by its opposite.
But within the attainment, the entire body is suffused with bliss due to the pervasion of rapture (*pīti*).
It exists; and for one whose body has entered into bliss, the faculty of pain is thoroughly ceased because it has been destroyed by its opposite.

Furthermore, even though the faculty of grief was abandoned in the preliminary stage of the second jhāna through various acts of adverting, it arises when there is physical fatigue and mental affliction, which have thought and examination as their conditions; however, in the absence of thought and examination, [it does not arise].
It does not arise at all. However, where it does arise, that is in the presence of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).

Since applied thought and sustained thought have not yet been abandoned in the preliminary stage (*upacāra*) of the second jhāna, its arising might occur there; but it certainly does not occur in the second jhāna itself, because its conditions have been abandoned.

Likewise, in the preliminary stage of the third jhāna, although the faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*) has been abandoned, [it may still arise] for one whose body is touched by the sublime matter produced by rapture (*pīti*).
There might be its arising, but certainly not in the third jhāna; for in the third jhāna, the rapture that serves as the condition for pleasure has ceased entirely.

Likewise, there might be its arising in the access to the fourth jhāna, because the faculty of mental joy—which was abandoned there—is still near, and because one has not yet properly transcended it due to the absence of equanimity reached through absorption (appanā). But certainly not in the fourth jhāna itself.
And for this very reason, the term "without remainder" (*aparisesa*) is employed in various places in the passage: "Here the arisen faculty of pain ceases without remainder.
Here it may be asked: "If these feelings have already been abandoned in the access (*upacāra*) of each respective jhāna, why are they included here?

It is for the purpose of grasping the "pleasure. For that feeling which was described here as "neither-pain-nor-pleasure" (*adukkhamasukha*)— [...is what is meant by the inclusion of these feelings here.]
It is subtle, difficult to discern, and not possible to grasp easily;

therefore, just as a cowherd, for the sake of catching a rogue bull that cannot be caught by approaching it in any way whatsoever, gathers all the cows together in one pen and then, while driving them out one by one, says of the one that comes along in order: "This is it, catch him!"—so too [is this state].
He has them grasp it as well; in this very way, he collects all these [feelings] for the sake of easy grasping.

For when they have been collected in this manner and shown, it is possible to have them grasp it thus: "That which is neither pleasure nor pain, neither mental joy nor mental grief—this is the feeling that is neither-pain-nor-pleasure."
Furthermore, it should be understood that these [four bases of power] are also taught for the purpose of showing the conditions for the deliverance of mind that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.

For the abandoning of pleasure and pain, etc., are its conditions. As it is said: "There are, friends, four conditions for the attainment of the deliverance of mind that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Here, friends, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure... [as before] ...enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna."
“...having attained, he dwells. These, friends, are the four conditions for the attainment of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant liberation of mind.

Alternatively, it should be understood that just as the view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and so forth—though already abandoned elsewhere—are said to be abandoned there [in the third path] for the purpose of praising that path, so too these [fetters] are mentioned here for the purpose of praising this jhāna.
Alternatively, it should be understood that these [states] are mentioned here in order to show the extreme remoteness of lust and hatred by way of the destruction of their conditions.
For among these, pleasure is the condition for joy, joy for lust; pain is the condition for grief, and grief for hatred.
And by the destruction of pleasure and the rest, lust and hatred—along with their conditions—are destroyed and thus become extremely remote.
“Neither-painful-nor-pleasant” (adukkhamasukhaṃ): it is “not painful” because of the absence of pain; it is “not pleasant” because of the absence of pleasure.

By this, he indicates here a third type of feeling that is the opposite of both pain and pleasure, not merely the absence of pain and pleasure. This third feeling is called neither-painful-nor-pleasant, and it is also termed equanimity (upekkhā).
Its characteristic is the experience of what is contrary to both the desirable and the undesirable. “Purity of mindfulness due to equanimity” (upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ):...
The purity of mindfulness produced by equanimity. For in this jhāna, mindfulness is perfectly purified;
and that purity of mindfulness is brought about by equanimity, not by anything else. Therefore, it is called "purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
Furthermore, the equanimity by which there is purity of mindfulness here should be understood, in its actual meaning, as mental neutrality (*tatramajjhattatā*).

In this context, it is not only that mindfulness (*sati*) alone is purified, but rather all associated mental factors (*sampayutta-dhamma*) as well; however, the teaching is expressed by way of the heading "mindfulness.

In this regard, although this equanimity (*upekkhā*) is also present in the three lower jhānas, just as the sun’s radiance during the day overcomes [other lights] due to its gentle nature or because of its own beneficial influence, yet—despite being present during the day—it does not find a corresponding night.
Just as the crescent moon is impure and unpurified, so too this crescent moon of equanimity consisting in neutrality toward the object is—
though it exists— impure within the distinctions of the first jhāna and so forth, because it is overwhelmed by the heat of opposing states such as applied thought (*vitakka*),
and because it has not yet attained the corresponding feeling of equanimity and delight. And while that [moon] is impure, during the day, the impure crescent moon...

Even though mindfulness and the other factors arise simultaneously with it, they are not yet completely purified, like the light [of the moon]. Therefore, not even one of them is described as "purity of mindfulness through equanimity" (*upekkhā-sati-pārisuddhi*).

Here, however, because there is no overpowering by the fire of opposing states such as applied thought (*vitakka*), and because it has attained a corresponding delight in the feeling of equanimity, this crescent-moon-like line of equanimity toward the middle (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*) is exceedingly pure. Due to its purity—
Just as the radiance of a perfectly pure crescent moon is born together with it, so too mindfulness and the other factors are pure and bright.
Therefore, it should be understood that this alone is called "purity of mindfulness through equanimity. It is called "the fourth" because of its position in the numerical sequence;
it is also called "the fourth" because it arises as the fourth.
These four jhānas are different both in the pre-stage (pubbabhāga) and at the moment of the path (maggakkhaṇa). In the pre-stage they are different by way of attainment (samāpatti);
at the moment of the path, they are different by way of the various paths. For one person, the first path is associated with the first jhāna;

the second path and so forth may also be associated with the first jhāna, or they may be associated with any one of the others, such as the second jhāna and so on. For another person, the first path [is associated with the second jhāna and so forth].
One possesses a particular jhāna; those beginning with the second [path] also possess either a particular jhāna among the second and so forth, or they possess the first jhāna.
Thus, all four paths are either similar, dissimilar, or partially similar by way of jhāna.
However, this distinction arises through the restriction of the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*). For one who has attained the first jhāna, from the first jhāna...
For one who emerges from the second jhāna and practices insight, the path that arises is associated with the second jhāna; however, the path factors and enlightenment factors are complete therein.
For one who emerges from the third jhāna and practices insight, the path that arises—
In the third jhāna, there are seven path-factors and six enlightenment factors. This same method applies from the fourth jhāna up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

It is stated that in the immaterial realms, the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise, and these are exclusively supramundane, not mundane. How is this so? Even here, in the case of the first jhāna and the others, from which...

Having emerged [from that state] and attained the path of stream-entry, and having developed the formless attainments, the three paths arise for him there while he is still absorbed in the jhāna that had arisen in the formless realm.
Thus, it is the foundational jhāna itself that determines [the specific formless attainment].
Some elders, however, say that "the aggregates which have become the object of insight determine [it]. Others say, "The individual's inclination..."
Some say, "It is determined by the path. Others say, "Insight leading to emergence determines it.
Herein, this is the progressive account: for by the determination of insight, there is the path arisen in a dry-insight practitioner;
and also the path arisen in one who has attained meditative absorption (jhāna) without making jhāna the basis; and [the path] having made the first jhāna the basis.
Even the path generated after having comprehended miscellaneous formations is associated with the first jhāna;
in all such cases, there are seven factors of enlightenment, eight factors of the path, and five jhāna factors.
For their preliminary insight, whether accompanied by joy or accompanied by equanimity, attains the state of equanimity regarding formations at the time of emergence.
It is accompanied by joy alone.

In the system of the fivefold jhānas, when the second, third, and fourth jhānas are made the basis for the paths that have been produced, the jhāna in those paths respectively possesses four factors, three factors, and two factors; however, in all cases, there are seven path-factors.
In the fourth [jhāna], there are six enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga). This distinction arises both from the restriction of the foundational jhāna and from the restriction of insight (vipassanā).
For even though their preliminary insight may be accompanied by joy (somanassa) or accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā), the insight leading to emergence is necessarily accompanied by joy alone.

But in the path produced by taking the fifth jhāna as its basis, there are two jhāna factors—equanimity and one-pointedness of mind—and six or seven enlightenment factors and path factors respectively.
This distinction also arises from the dual restriction.
For according to this method, the preliminary insight is either accompanied by joy or accompanied by equanimity, while the insight leading to emergence is [accompanied by equanimity].
It is accompanied by equanimity alone. The same method applies to the paths produced after making the formless jhānas the basis.

However, here, according to the fourfold system, because there is no second jhāna consisting of only vicāra without vitakka, that must be excluded and the application made according to the remaining ones.
Thus, having emerged from the foundational jhāna and having comprehended whatever formations [are present],...
The attainment that has emerged in a location near where the path was generated makes itself conform to the nature of that [path], just as the color of the ground conforms to the color of a lizard.

However, according to the second Elder’s view, whichever attainment one emerges from and whichever dhammas of that attainment one comprehends before the path is generated, the path becomes similar to that specific attainment.
In this case as well, the rule regarding insight (*vipassanā*) should be understood in the manner already stated.

According to the third Theravāda, whichever jhāna one takes as the basis in accordance with one’s own inclination, and whichever jhāna factors one comprehends, the path that is produced becomes similar to that specific jhāna.
However, that [path] does not succeed through mere inclination alone, without either the basic jhāna or the jhāna that is being comprehended.
And here too, the rule regarding insight (vipassanā) should be understood according to the method already stated.
"This is called right concentration" refers to that one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*) found within these four jhānas.

This is called mundane right concentration in its prior stage, and supramundane right concentration in its subsequent stage. Thus, by way of the mundane and the supramundane, the General of the Dhamma teaches the Truth of the Path.
In that regard, on the mundane path, all the factors of the path (*maggaṅgāni*) are present in their respective appropriate manner toward the six objects of meditation.

They have various objects. However, for the noble disciple who has entered the supramundane path for the sake of penetrating the Four Truths, right view is the eye of wisdom with Nibbāna as its object that eradicates the underlying tendency of ignorance;
likewise, for one endowed with such a view, right intention is the mental application directed toward the state of Nibbāna that eradicates the three kinds of wrong intentions associated with it.

For one who thus sees and reflects, right speech (*sammāvācā*) is the abstention from wrong speech (*micchāvācā*), which eradicates the fourfold misconduct of speech associated with that [right view]. Likewise, for one who thus abstains, right action (*sammākammanto*) is the abstention from wrong action (*micchākammanta*), which cuts off the threefold misconduct of action associated with that [right view].
Furthermore, these very [abstinences] constitute the purification of those same vocal and physical actions.
Right livelihood is the very abstinence from wrong livelihood that cuts off hypocrisy and the like, associated with that [right concentration].

For one who is established upon this ground of virtue (sīla) comprised of right speech, right action, and right livelihood, there arises— associated with that same [concentration] and corresponding to it—

the factor that cuts off indolence and accomplishes the non-arising and abandonment of unwholesome states, as well as the arising and maintenance of wholesome states, whenever they have arisen or not yet arisen.

And the exertion of energy is right effort; for one who exerts himself in this way, right mindfulness is the non-forgetfulness of the mind that shakes off wrong mindfulness and accomplishes the contemplation of the body and so forth regarding the body and the other aggregates.
Thus, for one whose mind is well-guarded by supreme mindfulness, right concentration is the one-pointedness of mind associated with it that destroys wrong concentration.
This is the supramundane Noble Eightfold Path.
That which, together with the mundane path, is reckoned as "the practice leading to the cessation of suffering"— this very path,

because it is comprised of right view and intention under the category of *vijjā* (clear vision), and the remaining factors under the category of *caraṇa* (conduct), is indeed both *vijjā* and *caraṇa*.

And conduct (*caraṇa*). Likewise, because those two are comprised by the vehicle of insight (*vipassanā-yāna*) and the others by the vehicle of serenity (*samatha-yāna*), they constitute both serenity and insight. Furthermore, because those two are comprised by the aggregate of wisdom (*paññā-khandha*); the three immediately following them by the aggregate of virtue (*sīla-khandha*);
and the remaining three by the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-khandha*), as well as by the trainings in higher wisdom, higher virtue, and higher mind (*adhipaññā-adhisīla-adhicitta-sikkhā*).
It consists of both the three aggregates and the three trainings. Endowed with these, the noble disciple—
like a traveler possessed of eyes capable of seeing and feet capable of walking— becomes perfected in true knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇasampanna*),
and by means of the vehicle of insight (*vipassanā-yāna*) abandons devotion to sensual pleasure, and by means of the vehicle of serenity (*samatha-yāna*) abandons devotion to self-mortification.
Having avoided the two extremes and practiced the middle way,
he crushes the aggregate of delusion with the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of hatred with the aggregate of virtue, and the aggregate of greed with the aggregate of concentration; thus,

through the training in higher wisdom he attains perfection in wisdom, through the training in higher virtue he attains perfection in virtue, and through the training in higher mind he attains perfection in concentration.
Having attained the threefold success, he realizes the deathless Nibbāna.

Having entered the noble plane known as the fixed course of rightness—excellent in its beginning, middle, and end, and variegated with the thirty-seven gems of the factors of enlightenment—he has truly entered upon it.
The commentary on the exposition of the Truth of the Path is concluded.
Commentary on the Miscellaneous Truths:
Among the four truths, the truth of suffering has the characteristic of oppression; the truth of origin has the characteristic of being the source;

the truth of cessation has the characteristic of peace; and the truth of the path has the characteristic of leading out. Furthermore, they have the characteristics of occurrence and its producer, and of non-occurrence and its producer.
In this sequence, likewise, there are the characteristics of seeing the conditioned and the unconditioned through craving.
But why are exactly four noble truths stated—neither fewer nor more?
Because nothing else is possible and because none of these can be removed. For there is nothing else beyond these, nor can even one of these be omitted.
That which is to be removed arises. As it is said:
"Here, monks, a certain ascetic or brahmin might come and say: 'This is not the Noble Truth of Suffering;
there is another Noble Truth of Suffering. That which was taught by the ascetic Gotama—that is the Noble Truth of Suffering.'"
“...it is impossible that anyone could say, ‘Setting aside this other Noble Truth of Suffering, we shall proclaim another Noble Truth of Suffering’”—and so forth.
And as it was said:
“Bhikkhus, whatever ascetic or brahmin might say, ‘This is not the first [Noble Truth] of suffering;’”
“...the Noble Truth which has been taught by the ascetic Gotama;
it is impossible that I should reject this first Noble Truth of suffering and proclaim another suffering as the first Noble Truth,” and so forth.

Furthermore, when the Blessed One explained the process of occurrence (*pavatti*), he explained it with its cause; and when he explained the cessation (*nivatti*), he explained it with its means. Thus, regarding the occurrence, the cessation, and the causes of both—

In the ultimate sense, however, only four have been taught. Likewise, they are taught as four by way of the objects to be fully understood, the objects to be abandoned, the objects to be realized, and the objects to be developed;

and also by way of the basis of craving, craving itself, the cessation of craving, and the means for the cessation of craving; and furthermore, by way of the attachment, the delighting in attachment, the uprooting of attachment, and the means for the uprooting of attachment.
And here, the truth of suffering is stated first because it is easy to understand due to its grossness and because it is common to all beings.

Immediately after that, the truth of the origin is stated for the purpose of showing the cause of that very suffering. Following that, the truth of cessation is stated to make known that with the cessation of the cause comes the cessation of the fruit.
Finally, the truth of the path is stated to show the means for attaining that cessation. [This is for those] who are attached to the gratification of the pleasure of existence...
Or, for the purpose of generating a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) in beings, he first spoke of suffering.

He then spoke of its origin immediately thereafter, in order to make it known that this suffering does not come uncaused, nor does it arise from the creation of a Supreme Lord (*Issaranimmāna*) and so forth, but rather arises from this [cause].

Thereafter, for those whose minds are filled with urgency because they are overwhelmed by suffering accompanied by its cause, and who seek an escape from suffering, he spoke of the escape through the vision of that escape.
The cessation is for the purpose of producing relief; then, the path that leads to the attainment of cessation is for the purpose of reaching that cessation—this is their sequence.

Among these, however, the truth of suffering should be regarded as like a burden, the truth of origin as like the taking up of the burden, the truth of cessation as like the laying down of the burden, and the truth of the path as like the means for laying down the burden.
Or alternatively, the truth of suffering is like a disease, and the truth of origin is like the cause of the disease.

The truth of the origin is like the onset of a disease; the truth of cessation is like the subsiding of that disease; and the truth of the path is like the medicine. Alternatively, the truth of suffering is like a famine;
the truth of the origin is like a failure of rain; the truth of cessation is like an abundance of food;

and the truth of the path is like a timely rainfall. Furthermore, [they correspond] to the enemy, the root of enmity, the eradication of enmity, and the means for the eradication of enmity; or to the poisonous tree, the root of the tree, the cutting off of the root, and the means for its cutting off.

These should be understood through similes by way of fear, the root of fear, fearlessness, and the means for attaining that [fearlessness], as well as by way of the efforts that carry one from this shore across the great flood to the further shore.

Furthermore, all these truths should be understood as empty in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*) because of the absence of an experiencer, a doer, one who attains *nibbāna*, or one who goes [to a new existence]. Therefore, this is said:
“Indeed, there is only suffering, but no one who suffers; there is no agent, nor is there action.
There is extinction, but no person who has attained extinction; the path exists, but no traveler is found.
Alternatively:
The first two [truths] are empty of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and self; the state of "mine" is empty of those two alone.
The Path is devoid of permanence, pleasure, and self—such is emptiness regarding them.
Alternatively, the three [truths] are empty of cessation, and cessation is empty of the remaining three. Or else, here the cause is empty of its fruit, in the case of the Truth of Origin.
Because suffering does not exist [in the path], and because cessation exists in the path, the fruit is not pregnant with [a further fruit], unlike the *prakṛti* of those who propound *prakṛti*.
Furthermore, the fruit is empty of causes because there is no conjunction (*asamavāya*) between the origin of suffering and the cessation and the path;
the fruit of a cause is not conjoined with its cause, unlike the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth for those who propound conjunction (*samavāya*). Therefore, this is said:
“This cessation here is empty of that; by that very [cessation], even Nibbāna is empty.
The cause is empty of the fruit, and the fruit is empty of that cause.
Thus all the truths are mutually similar in terms of their non-falsity, their emptiness of self, and the difficulty of their penetration. As it has been said:
“What do you think, Ānanda, which would be more difficult to do or more difficult to accomplish:

for one to shoot an arrow from afar through a fine keyhole so that it passes through in continuous succession without missing, or for one to pierce the tip of a hair split sevenfold with the tip [of another hair]? This alone, Bhante, would be more difficult to do.”
“It is even more difficult to penetrate: namely, to pierce through the tip of a hair split seven times with the tip [of another hair].
Yet, Ānanda, those who penetrate this as it really is—‘This is suffering’ … pe … ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering’—penetrate what is even more difficult to penetrate.”

They are dissimilar because they are defined by their respective specific characteristics. Furthermore, the first two are similar in the sense of being difficult to fathom and profound, as well as being mundane and subject to taints;
yet they are dissimilar because of the distinction between fruit and cause, and because one is to be fully understood while the other is to be abandoned.
The latter two are also similar in that they are profound and difficult to fathom, as well as being supramundane and free from taints; yet they are dissimilar...
[The first and second truths differ] by way of the distinction between object and subject, and by way of being that which is to be realized and that which is to be developed.
Furthermore, the first and third [truths] are similar by way of being designated as results (*phala*), but dissimilar by way of being conditioned (*saṅkhata*) and unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*).

The second and fourth [truths] are also similar by way of being designated as causes (*hetu*), but dissimilar by way of being exclusively wholesome (*kusala*) and unwholesome (*akusala*). Moreover, the first and fourth [truths] are similar by way of being conditioned, but dissimilar...

By way of the mundane and the supramundane; and the second and third [categories] are similar because they consist of neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee states, yet dissimilar because one has an object and the other does not.
"Thus, by such modes and methods, the wise one..."
"One should understand the similarity and dissimilarity of the Noble Truths.
And herein, all suffering is of one kind by way of its state of occurrence; it is of two kinds by way of name-and-form;

it is of three kinds by way of the distinction between existence as rebirth in the sense-sphere, fine-material sphere, and immaterial sphere; it is of four kinds by way of the distinction between the four nutriments; and it is of five kinds by way of the distinction between the five aggregates of clinging.
Origination (*samudaya*) is also of one kind by way of its state as that which sets [existence] in motion; it is of two kinds by way of being associated with or dissociated from views;

it is of three kinds by way of the division into craving for sense-pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence; it is of four kinds by way of being abandoned by the four paths; it is of five kinds by way of the division into delighting in form and so forth;
it is of six kinds by way of the division into the six groups of craving. Cessation (*nirodha*) is also of one kind by way of its state as the unconditioned element; in a figurative sense...
Furthermore, it is twofold by way of being with or without residue; threefold by way of the subsiding of the three states of existence;
fourfold by way of being attainable through the four paths; fivefold by way of the subsiding of the five kinds of delight; and sixfold by way of the destruction of the six groups of craving.

The path, too, is singlefold by way of being something to be developed; it is twofold by way of the distinction between serenity and insight, or by way of the distinction between seeing and development.

It is threefold according to the division into the three aggregates (*khandha*). For this [Noble Eightfold Path], because it has a specific scope, is comprised by the three aggregates which are without specific scope, just as a city is comprised by a kingdom. As it was said:
"Friend Visākha, the three aggregates are not comprised by the Noble Eightfold Path; rather, by the three..."
Furthermore, friend Visākha, the Noble Eightfold Path is subsumed within the aggregates.
That which is right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these factors, friend Visākha, are subsumed within the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha).
That which is right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these factors are subsumed within the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha).
“Right view and right intention—these states are included in the aggregate of wisdom.
[The path] is fourfold by way of the stream-entry path and so forth.
Furthermore, all the truths are of one kind because they are non-false, or because they are to be directly known. They are twofold as mundane and supramundane.

Or [they are classified] by way of the conditioned and the unconditioned. They are threefold according to whether they are to be abandoned by seeing or by cultivation, or are not to be abandoned, or are neither to be abandoned nor not to be abandoned.
They are fourfold according to what is to be fully understood, what is to be abandoned, what is to be realized, and what is to be developed.
"Thus the wise one knows the method for the Noble Truths, which are so difficult to understand."
"One should know [them] according to their many divisions for the sake of welfare and happiness.
The commentary on the miscellaneous section on the Truths is finished.
Now, the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), having demonstrated the tetrad of truths at the end in the very order taught by the Blessed One, [said]: "That..."

Having demonstrated knowledge in the context of what has been heard by means of the fourfold set of truths through such passages as "knowledge in the sense of being known," he thus demonstrates everything previously stated, namely: "Wisdom regarding the application of the ear is knowledge in the context of what has been heard.
—From the *Saddhammappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.
The commentary on the exposition of knowledge consisting in what is heard is finished.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of Knowledge Consisting in Virtue 37.
In the exposition of knowledge consisting in virtue, "five" is the delimitation by number. "Virtues" (sīlāni) is the indication of the specific phenomena so delimited.

“Virtue of limited purification,” and so forth, is the exposition of the five types of virtue according to their specific characteristics. Regarding the terms “limited purification” (*pariyanta-pārisuddhi*) and the rest:
just as a cloth is called “blue” because it possesses the quality of blue color, so too, that which has a limit or boundary by way of enumeration is called “limited” (*pariyantā*).
[This refers to] the virtue of one who has received full ordination (*upasampanna*) in relation to the virtue of one who has not yet received full ordination (*anupasampanna*).
Alternatively, because it possesses an end (*avasāna*), it is "bounded" (*pariyanta*); that is, it has an end as its limit.
It should be understood that when one ought to say *sapariyantā*, the letter *sa* is elided, just as the vowel *u* is elided in the phrase *dakaṃ dakāsayā pavisanti*.
Purity (*pārisuddhi*) is the state of being completely pure; and since it is both bounded (*pariyantā*) and purity (*pārisuddhi*), it is "bounded purity" (*pariyantapārisuddhi*).
Virtue known as limited-purity is "limited-purity virtue. It is "unlimited" (*apariyanta*) because it is not limited by its opposite as previously described;
it is "unlimited" because there is no limit to it; and it is "unlimited" because its limit has been transcended.
Because it remains unbroken from the moment of its undertaking, even if it were broken, it is restored through the performance of atonement, and even by a mere arising of the thought...
Because it is free from defilement, it is pure like a gem of pure birth and like gold that has been well-purified and well-refined;

because it is the foundation for the Noble Path, it is complete in its lack of deficiency. Because wrong view has been abandoned and it is not grasped by the misapprehension of views, it is "unmisapprehended.
This is the fault in your virtue, such that no accuser could misapprehend it.
Or, they are "unclung-to" because they are impossible to cling to. At the moment of the fruit of arahantship, there is "subsidence" due to the subsiding of all distress.
"Of those who are not fully ordained": those who are fully endowed with the perfection of virtue by way of undertaking it without exception are "fully ordained" (*upasampannā*);
those who are not so ordained are "not fully ordained" (*anupasampannā*). Of them, the non-fully ordained.

Regarding the phrase *pariyantasikkhāpadānaṃ*: here, in the sense of that which is to be trained in, it is "training" (*sikkhā*); in the sense of a constituent part, they are "bases" (*padāni*), meaning "constituent parts of what is to be trained in.
Furthermore, because all wholesome states (*kusaladhammā*) are to be trained in by one established in virtue, they are "trainings";

and because virtues are the bases for those trainings in the sense of being their foundation, they are called "bases of training" (*sikkhāpadāni*) due to being the bases of the trainings; [these are] "limited" (*pariyantāni*).
Those for whom the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) have come to an end are those with limited training rules (*pariyanta-sikkhāpada*).
Of those with limited training rules, there are two kinds of limits: the limit of the training rules and the limit of time. What is the limit of the training rules?
It is the case of laymen (*upāsaka*) and laywomen (*upāsikā*) who, according to their undertaking, [observe] one, two, three, four, five, or eight [training rules].

Or there are ten training rules; for female trainees (*sikkhamānā*), male novices (*sāmaṇera*), and female novices (*sāmaṇerī*), there are ten training rules. This is the limit by way of training rules. What is the limit by way of time?
Lay followers (*upāsaka* and *upāsikā*), while giving a gift, undertake the precepts limited to the duration of the meal service;
having gone to a monastery, they undertake the precepts limited to the duration of their stay in the monastery; or [for one day] once or twice.
Or, having set a limit of three nights or more, they undertake the precepts. This is "limited by time.

Regarding these two types of limits, virtue undertaken by setting a limit on the training rules is extinguished either by transgression or by death; virtue undertaken by setting a limit on time is extinguished by the passing of that specific period of time.
Regarding the "infinite training rules":
"Nine thousand million,
eight hundred and fifty-six million."
“These disciplines and trainings were proclaimed by the Fully Enlightened One;
they are pointed out by way of enumeration as the training in the discipline of the Vinaya.
Thus, even though the training precepts (sikkhāpada) are limited in number, [one should undertake them] without exception for the sake of gain, fame, relatives, limbs, or life.
They are "boundless" (*apariyanta*) because they have no limit in terms of their extent, and because there is no defined boundary for the virtue that must be guarded above them.
Those who have boundless training rules (*sikkhāpada*) are "those of boundless training rules.
Alternatively, the meaning is "those whose training rules have the aged as their limit."
Regarding the phrase "of the virtuous worldlings" (puthujjanakalyāṇakānaṃ) and so forth:
"One is a worldling (puthujjana) because of various causes such as being born among many;
or because he is included within the multitude of worldlings; or because this person is manifold."
Even though he has not transcended the characteristics of the worldling as they have been described—
“Two kinds of worldlings were spoken of by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun:
the blind worldling and the noble worldling”— it is said:

Regarding the two types of worldlings mentioned: it refers to those "virtuous worldlings" (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*), who, by encountering wholesome qualities, have transcended the state of blind worldlings and are established in the state of virtuous worldlings; that is what is meant by "virtuous worldlings.
Alternatively, they are the "virtuous ones among worldlings," hence "virtuous worldlings."
Regarding the phrase "those engaged in wholesome states" (*kusaladhamme yuttānaṃ*): here, first of all, the word *kusala* is seen to apply to health, blamelessness, skill, and pleasant fruition.
Indeed, in such passages as, "Is it well with you, sir? Is there no ailment for you? it is seen to mean health.
And [in the passage], "But what, venerable sir, is wholesome bodily conduct? That bodily conduct which, O Great King, is blameless," it is seen to mean blamelessness.
“Furthermore, venerable sir, this is unsurpassed in the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*);
in such passages as these, it means “blameless. In passages such as “You are skilled (*kusala*) in the parts of a chariot;
the four women are skilled in dancing and singing,” it means “expert. “Monks, it is because of undertaking wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*),” etc.
In such passages as “Because of having performed and accumulated wholesome kamma,” it refers to a pleasant result (sukhavipāka).
Here, however, it applies to health, to the blameless, and to a pleasant result.
As for the etymological meaning here: they cause the base and evil states to waver, shake, tremble, and crumble.
They are wholesome (*kusala*). Or, they are called *kusa* because they lie down—that is, they proceed—in a contemptible manner;
those who cut or sever that *kusa* are "wholesome" (*kusala*). Alternatively, *kusa* is knowledge, because it thins out—that is, diminishes—the contemptible.

They are called "wholesome" because they are to be acquired, grasped, and set in motion by that *kusa*. Or, just as blades of *kusa* cut the area of the hand on both sides, so too do these [wholesome states].
They cut away the side of defilement belonging to both the arisen and the unarisen; therefore, they are "skillful" (*kusala*) because they cut like *kusā* grass.
Furthermore, they are skillful in the sense of health, in the sense of blamelessness, or in the sense of being produced by skill.

However, since it is specifically skill in insight (*vipassanā-kusala*) that is intended here, [the author] omits the rest and provides this definition for the sake of showing that specific type alone.

It should be understood that the term “*kusaladhamme*” is used in the singular. The meaning is: those who are devoted to the wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*) of insight (*vipassanā*) through constant application and thorough performance.
Regarding the phrase “those who fulfill [the training] up to the limit of the *sekkha*,” here the term *sekkha* refers both to those born into the three trainings (*sikkhā*) and to the seven...

They are called *sekkhā* because they belong to those in training (*sekkha*), or because they themselves are training; that is, the states consisting of the path and fruit of stream-entry, the path and fruit of once-returning, the path and fruit of non-returning, and the path of arahantship.
These states of training (*sekkhā dhammā*) are at its limit or end; or, these states of training are its limit or boundary—thus it is "ending with the states of training" (*sekkhapariyanto*).
The connection is: "in those states ending with the states of training. It means fullness, being complete.
