"Those who perform" (*paripūrakārino*) means those who bring to completion; or alternatively, they are "those who perform" because they possess the performance of completion (*paripūrakiriyā*).

Of them—of those who perform the completion of insight (*vipassanā*) regarding the factors of practice (*paṭipadādhamma*) that culminate in the stage of training (*sekkha*) and precede the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*).
"Without regard for body or life": here, "body" (*kāya*) refers to the physical frame (*sarīra*). For the physical frame...

It is called "body" (*kāya*) because it is a collection of impurities and because it is the source (*āya*) of loathsome things such as hair and so forth, as well as hundreds of diseases such as eye-diseases and so forth.
"Life" (*jīvita*) refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). For they live by means of it, thus it is called "life.

"Without regard" (*anapekkha*) means there is no looking toward these; the sense is that they are free from attachment. [The phrase] "of those who are without regard for that body and for life" [is thus explained].
Now, showing the reason for their lack of regard for those [objects], he said, "having renounced their lives.

For it is precisely by the renunciation of their own lives to the Blessed One or to the Teacher that they become indifferent toward their bodies even when they are suffering and toward their lives even when they are perishing.
"Of the seven trainees" (sekkhānaṃ) refers to those who have attained the path of stream-entry and so forth, who have received the name "trainees" (sekkhā) because they are training.
"Of the seven noble persons. "Disciples of the Tathāgata" means disciples of the Tathāgata.

For all eight noble persons are called "disciples" (sāvaka) because they have been born into the noble birth at the end of hearing [the Dhamma], and they listen attentively to the Blessed One’s teaching and instruction through the application of confirmed confidence.
Among them, he shows specifically those who stand in the fruit of arahantship by saying "those whose taints are destroyed" (khīṇāsava).
He said: the meaning is "those by whom all taints (*āsava*) have been completely destroyed through the knowledge of the path of Arahatship. Regarding "Paccekabuddhas":
one who has awakened to the Four Truths alone, without a teacher, depending upon various specific causes, is a *paccekabuddha*; [the phrase refers to] such *paccekabuddhas*. Regarding "Tathāgatas":
here, the Blessed One is a *tathāgata* for eight reasons—namely, he is a *tathāgata* because he has come in accordance with reality (*tathā-āgata*).
He is a Tathāgata because he has gone thus; he is a Tathāgata because he has come to the true characteristic; he is a Tathāgata because he has fully awakened to the true dhammas as they really are;

he is a Tathāgata by virtue of seeing things as they are; he is a Tathāgata by virtue of speaking things as they are; he is a Tathāgata by virtue of acting as he speaks; and he is a Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming.
How is it that the Blessed One is a “Tathāgata” because he has come in such a way?
It is because he has come just as the previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones came, having applied themselves with zeal for the welfare of the entire world. What is meant by this?

By the same aspiration through which the previous Blessed Ones came, our Blessed One has also come. Or alternatively, just as the previous Blessed Ones [came] by means of what is known as generosity, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, resolve, loving-kindness, and equanimity...
Having fulfilled the thirty perfections— namely, the ten perfections (*pāramī*), the ten secondary perfections (*upapāramī*), and the ten ultimate perfections (*paramatthapāramī*)—
and having practiced the five great renunciations, which consist of the sacrifice of his limbs, his eyes, his wealth, his kingdom, his sons, and his wife;
and having fulfilled his preliminary efforts, former conduct, teaching of the Dhamma, conduct for the benefit of others, and so forth, he reached the pinnacle of the practice of wisdom.

He has come; likewise, our Blessed One has also come. And just as previous Blessed Ones came having developed and cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path, so too has our Blessed One come—thus he is the Tathāgata.
“Just as the Buddhas beginning with Dīpaṅkara, those sages who have attained omniscience here, so too has this Sakyan Sage arrived; therefore, the Visionary One is called ‘Tathāgata.
How is he ‘Tathāgata’ because he has gone thus (*tathā-gata*)? It is because he has gone in the same way that the previous Blessed Ones went when they were first born. And how...
Did they go? Indeed, as soon as he was born, having established himself on the earth with level feet, he went seven steps toward the north.

As it is said: "Ānanda, as soon as he was born, the Bodhisatta, having established himself on the earth with level feet, goes seven steps toward the north, while a white parasol is held over him. All...
And he surveyed the quarters and uttered a lion’s roar: “I am the foremost in the world; I am the eldest in the world;
I am the best in the world. This is the final birth; there is now no further becoming.
And that going of his was real, not unreal, as a foretoken of many distinguished attainments. For...
As soon as he was born, he stood firm with both feet; this was the omen of his acquisition of the four bases of psychic power (*catur-ṛddhipāda*).

His facing toward the north was the omen of his state of being superior to the entire world. His taking seven steps was the omen of his acquisition of the seven jewels of the factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga-ratna*).
"The yak-tail whisks with golden handles are being waved [around him]"—this was the omen of his attainment of the sovereignty of a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*).
Furthermore, the waving of the yak-tail fan (cāmara) mentioned here is a precursor to the crushing of all rival teachers;
the holding of the white parasol is a precursor to the attainment of the supreme, stainless white parasol of liberation through the fruit of Arhatship;

the surveying of all directions is a precursor to the attainment of the unobstructed knowledge of omniscience; and the utterance of the voice of a bull (āsabhi-vācā) is a precursor to the irreversible turning of the sublime Wheel of Dhamma.
It was a foretoken. The Blessed One likewise proceeded in that manner.
And his proceeding was true and not false, insofar as it served as a foretoken for those very special attainments. Therefore the ancients said:
"Just as a newborn bull of the herd, Touches the earth with even feet;..."
Thus Gotama strode seven steps, and the Maruts held up a white parasol for him.
Having gone those seven steps, Gotama surveyed the quarters all around.
He uttered a voice endowed with eight factors, like a lion standing upon a mountain peak.
Thus he has come (tathā-āgata) as they [the Buddhas] have come; therefore he is the Tathāgata.
Or else, just as the previous Blessed Ones did, this Blessed One likewise, through renunciation, [abandoned] sensual desire...
pe... through the first jhāna, the hindrances... pe... through the contemplation of impermanence, the perception of permanence... pe... through the path of Arahantship, all defilements.
Having abandoned [them], he has gone; thus, he is a Tathāgata because he has gone in such a way.
How is he a Tathāgata because he has come to the true characteristic (*tathalakkhaṇa*)? The characteristic of hardness in the earth element is *tatha* (true), not false;
the characteristic of flowing in the water element, the characteristic of heat in the fire element, and the characteristic of motion in the air element...

The characteristic of distension belongs to the space element; the characteristic of non-obstruction belongs to the space element; the characteristic of cognizing belongs to the consciousness element.

The characteristic of being affected is that of form; the characteristic of being felt is that of feeling; the characteristic of perceiving is that of perception; the characteristic of volitional formation is that of mental formations; the characteristic of cognizing is that of consciousness.

Applied thought has the characteristic of directing the mind; sustained thought has the characteristic of examining; rapture has the characteristic of pervading; pleasure has the characteristic of gratification; one-pointedness of mind has the characteristic of non-distraction;

contact has the characteristic of touching. The faculty of faith has the characteristic of resolution; the faculty of energy has the characteristic of exertion; the faculty of mindfulness has the characteristic of establishing; the faculty of concentration has the characteristic of non-distraction; the faculty of wisdom has the characteristic of understanding.

The characteristic of the power of faith is unshakability by lack of faith; that of the power of energy is unshakability by laziness; that of the power of mindfulness is unshakability by forgetfulness; that of the power of concentration is unshakability by restlessness; and that of the power of wisdom is unshakability by ignorance.
The characteristic of the mindfulness enlightenment factor is establishing; that of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor is investigating;
that of the energy enlightenment factor is exerting; that of the rapture enlightenment factor is pervading; [and that of the tranquility enlightenment factor is] tranquility...

The characteristic of tranquility belongs to the enlightenment factor of concentration; the characteristic of non-distraction belongs to the enlightenment factor of equanimity; the characteristic of reflective discernment belongs to the enlightenment factor of equanimity.
Right view has the characteristic of seeing; right intention has the characteristic of directing onto; right speech has...
The characteristic of right action is non-grasping; the characteristic of right livelihood is purification; the characteristic of right effort is exertion;
the characteristic of right mindfulness is establishment; the characteristic of right concentration is non-distraction.
The characteristic of ignorance is unknowing; the characteristic of volitional formations is intention; the characteristic of consciousness is cognizing.
The characteristic of name-and-form is bending; the characteristic of form is being affected; the characteristic of the six sense bases is being a base;
the characteristic of contact is touching; the characteristic of feeling is being felt; the characteristic of craving is being a cause; the characteristic of clinging is grasping;
the characteristic of becoming is accumulating; the characteristic of birth is arising; the characteristic of aging is decaying.

Death has the characteristic of passing away; the elements have the characteristic of emptiness; the sense bases have the characteristic of being bases; the foundations of mindfulness have the characteristic of establishing;
the right efforts have the characteristic of exertion; the bases of psychic power have the characteristic of succeeding; the faculties have the characteristic of predominance.

The characteristic of the powers is unshakability; the characteristic of the factors of enlightenment is leading out; the characteristic of the path is being the cause. The characteristic of the truths is suchness;
the characteristic of serenity is non-distraction; the characteristic of insight is contemplation; the characteristic of serenity and insight is having a single flavor;

the characteristic of their union is non-transgression. The characteristic of purification of virtue is restraint; the characteristic of purification of mind is non-distraction; the characteristic of purification of view is seeing.
The characteristic of the knowledge of exhaustion is cutting off; the characteristic of the knowledge of non-arising is tranquility.
The characteristic of desire is the root; the characteristic of attention is origination; the characteristic of contact is convergence; the characteristic of feeling is meeting together;
the characteristic of concentration is preeminence; the characteristic of mindfulness is sovereignty.

The characteristic of being superior through wisdom, the characteristic of the core through liberation, and the characteristic of the ultimate consummation in Nibbāna—which plunges into the Deathless—are real and not unreal.
Because he has come by way of the course of knowledge, having reached and attained this characteristic of reality without missing it, he is the Tathāgata.
Thus, because he has come to the characteristic of reality, he is the Tathāgata.
How is he the Tathāgata because he has perfectly awakened to the true nature of things as they really are (*yāthāvato*)?
The "true nature of things" (*tathadhammā*) refers to the Four Noble Truths. As it is said: "Monks, these four are true, not false, and not otherwise.
What are the four? 'This is suffering,' monks—this is true, this is not false, this is not otherwise."
The full detail [is as follows]. And because the Blessed One has fully awakened to those [truths], he is called the "Tathāgata" due to having thus fully awakened.
For here, the word *gata* has the sense of "fully awakened.
Furthermore, the state of aging-and-death—which is produced and brought about with birth as its condition—is "thus" (*tatha*), not otherwise, not different... [and so on].

The meaning of the formations as having arisen and come about with ignorance as their condition is such, not otherwise, not different. Likewise, the meaning of the conditionality of formations for ignorance is such, not otherwise, not different...
[and so on] ...the meaning of the conditionality of aging-and-death for birth is such, not otherwise, not different.
The Blessed One has fully awakened to all that. Therefore, it is called "Tathāgata" because he has fully awakened to those things as they truly are.
The Tathāgata. Thus, because he has perfectly awakened to the true nature of phenomena (*tathadhamma*) as they really are, he is the Tathāgata.

How is he the Tathāgata by way of seeing things as they truly are? In the world with its devas... [as before] ...among gods and humans, whatever object of form (*rūpārammaṇa*) comes within the range of the eye-door for immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems, the Blessed One—

It exists; he knows and sees it in every aspect. By knowing and seeing thus, according to whether it is desirable or undesirable, or by way of the terms applicable to what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, [he understands]:
"What is that form which is the form-base (*rūpāyatana*)?
It is that form derived from the four great elements which possesses color and luster, is visible, and offers resistance—blue..."
When analyzed through numerous names—such as "Pītaka" and so forth—in thirteen sections and fifty-two methods, it remains exactly as it is;
there is nothing false. This same principle applies to sounds and other objects that come within the range of the ear-door and the other sense doors.
And this was said by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, whatever in the world with its devas... [and so on] ...among devas and humans..."
“Whatever has been seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or investigated by the mind—that I know, that I have directly known, that is understood by the Tathāgata;
yet the Tathāgata does not stand upon that. Thus, he is the Tathāgata because of his seeing things as they truly are.
In this context, the etymological derivation of the term *tathāgata* should be understood in the sense of “one who sees things as they truly are” (*tathadassī*).
In what sense is the Tathāgata one who speaks truthfully? From the night the Blessed One sat upon the invincible throne at the seat of enlightenment and,
having crushed the heads of the four Māras, fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,
until the night he attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue between the twin Sāla trees— in this interval spanning forty-five years— [he spoke only what was true].
Whether during the first enlightenment, the middle enlightenment, or the final enlightenment, whatever discourse (sutta), song (geyya), or...
[as above] ...analytical exposition (vedalla) was spoken by the Blessed One—all that is blameless and irreproachable in both meaning and phrasing;
it is neither deficient nor redundant, complete in every aspect, and subdues the intoxication of lust, as well as the intoxication of hatred and delusion. There is nothing [else like it].
In that regard, even a mere hair-tip of deviation is exactly as it is—just like everything being marked with a single seal, measured by a single scale, or weighed on a single balance. As it was said:
"Cunda, between the night the Tathāgata awakens to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and the night he passes away into the Nibbāna-element without remainder..."
“He attains final Nibbāna; whatever he speaks, utters, or explains in the interval between [his birth and his passing] is all exactly so and not otherwise.
Therefore, he is called ‘Tathāgata. Here, the word *gata* has the sense of “spoken. Thus, he is a Tathāgata because of speaking what is true.

Furthermore, *āgada* means "speaking"; it has the sense of "speech. Because his speaking (*āgada*) is "thus" (*tatha*), meaning unerring, by changing the letter *da* to *ta*, he is called the "Tathāgata. In this sense, the derivation of the word should be understood.
How is he the Tathāgata by virtue of acting accordingly? For the Blessed One’s body conforms to his speech, and his speech conforms to his body;
therefore, he is one who acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts. And for one such as this, just as his speech is...
The body, too, has thus gone forth; this is the meaning. And just as the body, so too speech has thus gone forth;
thus he is the Tathāgata. For this very reason it was said: "Monks, the Tathāgata acts as he speaks, and speaks as he acts.
Thus, acting as he speaks and speaking as he acts, he is therefore called the 'Tathāgata'. In this way, he is the Tathāgata by virtue of his acting accordingly.

In what sense is the Tathāgata so called in the sense of overcoming? Having made the peak of existence above and the Avīci hell below his limits, he overcomes all beings throughout immeasurable world-systems in the horizontal directions by means of virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
there is no equal or measure for him—he is incomparable, immeasurable, and unsurpassed.
He is the king of kings, the god beyond gods, the Sakka beyond Sakkas, the Brahmā beyond Brahmās. Therefore it was said: "Bhikkhus, in the world with its gods...
[and so on] ...in this world with its gods and humans, the Tathāgata is the conqueror, unconquered, all-seeing, and wielder of power.
Therefore he is called 'Tathāgata.'"

In this regard, the derivation of the word should be understood as follows: it is like an *agada* (antidote), hence it is called *agada*. But what is this? It is both the splendor of the teaching and the accumulation of merit.
For by means of that, this Greatly Powerful Physician overcomes all those of opposing doctrines and the world with its devas, just as one might overcome snakes with a divine antidote.
Thus, in the overcoming of the entire world, it is "true" (*tatha*)—that is, unerring—and consists of the splendor of the teaching.

And by changing the letter *da* to *ta* in the phrase "may he be a medicine consisting of merit," one should understand him as the *Tathāgata*. Thus, in the sense of overcoming, he is the *Tathāgata*.
Furthermore, he is the *Tathāgata* because he has gone (*gato*) to suchness (*tathāya*), and he is the *Tathāgata* because he has gone to what is real (*tathaṃ*).
"Gone" means understood, transcended, attained, and practiced. In this context, he has gone to and understood suchness by means of the full understanding through scrutiny of the entire world.
The Tathāgata is so called because he has gone (gato) to suchness (tathā), having transcended the origin of the world through the full understanding of its abandonment;
he is so called because he has gone to and attained suchness by realizing the cessation of the world;

he is so called because he has gone to and entered upon the true path leading to the cessation of the world. Therefore, as it was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, the world has been [truly] known by the Tathāgata..."
The Tathāgata has awakened to it and is detached from the world. Monks, the origin of the world has been awakened to by the Tathāgata;
the origin of the world has been abandoned by the Tathāgata. Monks, the cessation of the world has been awakened to by the Tathāgata;
the cessation of the world has been realized by the Tathāgata. Monks, the practice leading to the cessation of the world...
“The way leading to the cessation of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; that way leading to the cessation of the world has been developed by the Tathāgata.
Whatever, monks, in this world with its devas... has been explored by the mind, all that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.
Therefore he is called the ‘Tathāgata. This is how its meaning should also be understood. And this too is of the Tathāgata.
This is merely a brief introduction to the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s nature. In every respect, however, only a Tathāgata himself could describe the Tathāgata’s state of being a Tathāgata.
Since all Buddhas are exactly equal in their Tathāgata-qualities, he said "of the Tathāgatas" by way of including them all.

He said "of the Arahants" because they are far removed (*āraka*) from defilements, because they have slain (*hata*) the enemies and the spokes of the wheel of existence, and because they are worthy (*araha*) of requisites and so forth.

The Tathāgata is *arahaṃ* because he is secluded from the performance of evil. He is indeed *arahaṃ* because he stands far, very far away from all defilements, since the defilements along with their latent tendencies have been abandoned by means of the Path.
That from which one is separated is called *āraka*; it is that with which one lacks association.
The Lord is considered "Worthy" (Arahaṃ) because he is devoid of faults;

furthermore, since these enemies—the defilements—have been slain by him through the Path, he is "Worthy" also because of his having slain the enemies. For all enemies, comprised of lust and the rest, have been destroyed.
Because he has used the sword of wisdom [to cut it], he is therefore considered an *arhat*. Furthermore, as for this wheel of saṃsāra—
which has proceeded from beginningless time, which is yoked to the chariot of the three realms of existence by piercing it with the axle consisting of the origin of the taints (*āsava*),
and which has ignorance, becoming, craving, the hub consisting of merit and other formations, and the rim of aging and death— it is by means of this [sword] that...
Having established himself at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) upon the earth of virtue (sīlapathavī) with the feet of energy (vīriyapāda),
and having taken up the axe of knowledge (ñāṇapharasu)— which brings about the destruction of karma— with the hand of faith (saddhāhattha)— he is an Arahant because all spokes have been struck down.
Since the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra have been struck down by the sword of knowledge, he is therefore an Arahant.
Because of this, he is called "Arahant" by the Lord of the World.
Furthermore, because he is the foremost among those worthy of offerings, he is worthy of the requisites such as robes and so forth, as well as special forms of worship.
For this very reason, whenever a Tathāgata has appeared, no beings of great influence—whether gods or humans—perform their worship elsewhere. Thus, for example, Brahmā Sahampati...
He honored the Tathāgata with a jeweled necklace worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold, while other gods, humans, King Bimbisāra, King Kosala, and others did likewise according to their means.

Even after the Blessed One had attained final nibbāna, the Great King Aśoka, having disbursed ninety-six billion in wealth, established eighty-four thousand monasteries throughout the entire land of Jambudīpa; what need, then, to mention other specific acts of worship?
He is also "Arahant" because he is worthy of requisites and so forth.
Since this Lord of the World is worthy of special honor together with the requisites—
and since in the world things are called "worthy" (araha) when they accord with their purpose— therefore the Victor deserves this name.

Furthermore, just as in the world some fools who consider themselves wise commit evil deeds in secret out of fear of ill-repute, he never does so; thus, because he lacks secrecy in the commission of evil, he is an *arahaṃ*.
For there is no such thing as "secrecy" for one such as him regarding evil actions; because of this absence of secrecy, he is renowned as an *arahaṃ*.
Thus, in every respect:
Because he has kept far away from and destroyed the enemies that are the defilements,
that Sage has destroyed the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra and is worthy of offerings and the like.
“He does not commit evil deeds even in secret; therefore he is called an Arahant.
Furthermore, because all Buddhas are exactly equal in the quality of Arahantship, he says “of the Arahants” by way of including them all. Regarding “Sammāsambuddhānaṃ”:
he is a Sammāsambuddha because he has awakened (buddhattā) to all phenomena both correctly (sammā) and by himself (sāmaṃ). Likewise...

He is fully enlightened regarding all phenomena: he is enlightened as to what is to be directly known among the things to be directly known, as to what is to be fully understood among the things to be fully understood, as to what is to be abandoned among the things to be abandoned, as to what is to be realized among the things to be realized, and as to what is to be developed among the things to be developed. Therefore it was said:
“What is to be directly known has been directly known, what is to be developed has been developed, and what is to be abandoned has been abandoned by me; therefore, O brahmins, I am a Buddha.
Alternatively, the eye is the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*); the prior craving that originates it by being its root cause is the truth of origin (*samudayasacca*).

The non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation; the practice that leads to the full understanding of cessation is the truth of the path—thus has he perfectly and independently awakened to all phenomena by extracting each term one by one.
This same method applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
By this very method, [he understood] the six bases beginning with form, the six groups of consciousness beginning with eye-consciousness, and the six [types of contact] beginning with eye-contact.
The six types of contact, beginning with eye-contact; the six types of feeling, beginning with that born of eye-contact; the six types of perception, beginning with the perception of forms;

the six types of volition, beginning with volition regarding forms; the six groups of craving, beginning with craving for forms; the six types of applied thought, beginning with applied thought regarding forms; the six types of sustained thought, beginning with sustained thought regarding forms;
the five aggregates, beginning with the aggregate of form; the ten kasinas; the ten recollections; and by way of the perception of the bloated corpse, and so forth.
The ten perceptions; the thirty-two aspects beginning with head-hairs; the twelve bases; the eighteen elements; the nine existences beginning with sensual existence;
the four meditative absorptions beginning with the first; the four immeasurables beginning with the development of loving-kindness;
the four formless attainments; and the factors of dependent origination in reverse order beginning with aging-and-death, and in forward order beginning with ignorance.
And these [terms] are to be joined. Herein, this is the construction of the single phrases: aging-and-death is the truth of suffering; birth is the truth of the origin;
the escape from both is the truth of cessation; and the way leading to the realization of cessation is the truth of the path.
Thus, by extracting each phrase one by one, the Buddha has perfectly and independently awakened to and penetrated all phenomena. Or whatever else there is that is to be known—
By name, he is the "Perfectly Enlightened One" (Sammāsambuddha) because, through the knowledge pertaining to liberation, he has attained perfect enlightenment regarding all things.

However, its detailed analysis will be made clear further on. Furthermore, since all Buddhas are exactly equal even in their quality as Perfectly Enlightened Ones, he said "of the Perfectly Enlightened Ones" (sammāsambuddhānaṃ) by way of including them all.
38. Now, in order to show each of the two types of virtue—limited purity and unlimited purity—by dividing them each into five ways, he says:
"There is virtue that is limited; there is virtue that is unlimited," and so forth.
However, in the other three types of virtue, no such division exists. In this context, "limited by gain" means that which has its limit (pariyanta) through gain.
"Bhedo etassa" means "its limit is gain" (lābhapariyantaṃ). The same applies to the remaining terms. Here, "yasō" refers to one's retinue.
"Idha" means in this world. "Ekacco" means one person. "Lābhahetū" means gain itself is the cause; thus, it is said "because of the cause of gain.
This is the ablative case used in the sense of "cause. "Lābhapaccayā" and "lābhakāraṇā" are synonyms for that same term.
Indeed, it is called a "condition" (*paccaya*) because this fruit follows in dependence upon that very cause; and it is called a "cause" (*kāraṇa*) because it brings about the arising of the fruit.
"As undertaken" means whatever has been undertaken or adopted. "Transgresses" means he oversteps. "Of such a kind" means having such a nature;
the intention is that they are of the type already described. "Virtues" (*sīla*) refers either to the virtues of a householder or to the virtues of one who has gone forth.
Alternatively, those in which one [bone] at the beginning or end is broken are "fragmented," like a garment torn at the edges.
Those in which one [bone] in the middle is broken are "perforated," like a garment pierced through the center.
Those in which two or three are broken in succession are shaped like long cylinders and so forth, protruding from the back or the belly.
Like a cow that is brindled because its body has the color of one or another of the dissimilar colors— black, red, and so forth—
those [fetters] among which there are single broken [links] are like a speckled cow, variegated with drops of dissimilar colors here and there.
Or, without distinction, all [of them] are [bound] by the sevenfold union of sexual intercourse and by evil qualities such as anger and enmity.
Because they are impaired, they are broken, perforated, blotched, and mottled.

Since they do not bring about the state of freedom by releasing one from the slavery of craving, they are not "free. Because they are not praised by the wise, such as the Buddhas, they are not "praised by the wise.
Because they are grasped by craving and views, or because it is possible for someone to point out, "This is a fault in your precepts," they are [not] "unassailable."
They are "defiled. They do not lead to access concentration or absorption concentration, or alternatively, they do not lead to path concentration or fruition concentration;
thus, they are "not conducive to concentration" (*asamādhisaṃvattanikāni*). There is also a reading: "not conducive to concentration" (*na samādhisaṃvattanikāni*). However, some say:
"They are 'broken' because they have become a non-basis for wholesome states; they are likewise 'perforated.'"

They explain the meaning as follows: "They are 'variegated' (sabalāni) because they cause discolouration; they are likewise 'muddy' (kammāsāni). They are 'not free' (na bhujissāni) because they have fallen into the slavery of craving.
They are 'not praised by the wise' (na viññuppasatthāni) because they are censured by those who are skilled. They are 'misapprehended' (parāmaṭṭhāni) because they are grasped by craving.
They do not conduce to concentration (asamādhisaṃvattanikāni) because they become a basis for remorse. Thus they describe the meaning.
"Not bases for non-remorse" means that, because they bring about remorse, they do not serve as a foundation for non-remorse.
"Not bases for gladness" means that they do not become the basis for the weak rapture born of non-remorse, because they do not bring that about.
The same construction should be applied to the remaining terms as well. "Not bases for rapture" [refers] to the strong rapture born of weak rapture...
They are not the basis for serenity; that is, they are not the basis for the bodily and mental serenity born of powerful joy.

They are not the basis for happiness; that is, they are not the basis for the bodily and mental happiness born of serenity. They are not the basis for concentration; that is, they are not the basis for the concentration born of happiness.
They are not the basis for knowledge and vision of things as they truly are; that is, [they are not the basis for the knowledge and vision] born of concentration.
They are not the basis for the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are, which has concentration as its proximate cause.

In the phrases beginning with "not for utter disenchantment," one should apply the same method by taking only the negative particle *na* and joining it with the remaining terms in the sequence starting with "not for dispassion.
Alternatively, the reading in "not for dispassion" and so forth includes the negative particle *sa-* (i.e., *sana*). Therein, "for utter disenchantment" means for the sake of absolute disenchantment.
The connection is: “they do not lead to disenchantment with the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). The same should be applied to the remaining terms as well.
"For dispassion" means for the purpose of becoming dispassionate toward the round of existence. "For cessation" means for the purpose of the cessation of the round of existence.

"For peace" means for the purpose of pacifying the round of existence by way of its non-arising again once it has ceased. "For direct knowledge" means for the purpose of directly knowing the round of existence.
"For the sake of full enlightenment" means for the purpose of awakening from the cycle of existence by means of the departure from the sleep of the defilements (*kilesa*).

"For the sake of Nibbāna" means for the sake of the deathless Nibbāna. "For the transgression of the training rule as it was undertaken" means for the purpose of violating the training rule as it was undertaken.

Here, however, the accusative case has been used due to a shift in grammatical number (*vibhatti-vipallāsa*). "He does not even give rise to a thought" refers to the purity of the arising of the mind (*cittuppāda-suddhi*).
This was said for the purpose of showing the extreme purity of his virtue; however, virtue is not broken by a mere arising of thought.
"What will he transgress? means for what purpose would he commit a transgression? The meaning is that he will not commit a transgression at all.
Terms such as "unbroken" and so forth are to be understood according to the method of opposites explained below. Also, "not broken" means...
The reading: “For the sake of absolute disenchantment,” and so forth, should be applied in the manner beginning with “for the purpose of becoming utterly disenchanted with the round of existence.
Herein, however, “disenchantment” (*nibbidā*) refers to insight (*vipassanā*); “fading away” (*virāga*) refers to the path (*magga*); “cessation” (*nirodha*) and “peace” (*upasama*) refer to Nibbāna;

“direct knowledge” (*abhiññā*) and “enlightenment” (*sambodha*) refer to the path; and “Nibbāna” (*nibbāna*) refers to Nibbāna itself. In one instance it is insight, and in two instances [it is the path].

The path [is mentioned], while Nibbāna is stated in the three [remaining truths]; thus should this discourse on their respective positions be understood. However, by way of a figurative approach (*pariyāya*), all of these are indeed synonyms for both the path and for Nibbāna. 39.
Now, having shown the existing classifications by way of being limited or unlimited, [the text proceeds] again by way of the phenomena (*dhamma*) and by way of their classes (*jāti*).
In order to show the classification of virtue by way of its conditions and by way of its associated factors, he said, "What is virtue? and so forth.
In this context, that from which something arises is its "origin" (*samuṭṭhāna*); this is a name for a condition. That which has what as its origin is "of what origin" (*kiṃsamuṭṭhāna*).
That which has the coming together and the concurrence of how many states is "the concurrence of how many states" (*katidhammasamodhāna*).
Virtue as volition (*cetanā-sīla*) is the volition of one who refrains from killing living beings and so forth, or who fulfills the performance of duties.

Virtue as mental concomitant (*cetasika-sīla*) is the abstinence (*virati*) of one who refrains from killing living beings and so forth. Furthermore, virtue as volition is the volition of the seven courses of kamma of one who abandons killing living beings and so forth.
Virtue as mental concomitant is [the state] of one who, having abandoned covetousness for the world, is free from covetousness...
The phenomena of non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view are stated by way of such passages as, “he dwells with his mind...”.
Regarding the phrase “restraint is virtue,” restraint should be understood here as fivefold:

restraint of the Pātimokkha, restraint of mindfulness, restraint of knowledge, restraint of patience, and restraint of energy. Therein, [it is said]: “He is endowed, fully endowed, with this restraint of the Pātimokkha.”
This is restraint by the Pātimokkha. “He guards the faculty of the eye; he attains restraint over the faculty of the eye”—this is restraint by mindfulness.
“Those streams that exist in the world, O Ajita,” said the Blessed One, “mindfulness is their dam.
This is restraint by mindfulness.
“I call the restraint of the streams;
by means of wisdom they are closed.”—this is the restraint of knowledge (*ñāṇasaṃvara*). The practice of using requisites also falls within this very category.

Furthermore, that which is presented in the manner beginning with, “He is patient with cold and heat,” etc., is called the restraint of patience (*khantisaṃvara*). And as for this [which begins with], “When [an unwholesome thought] has arisen... [it is the restraint of mindfulness].
This is what is called "restraint through energy," as it comes in the manner beginning with: “He does not tolerate sensual thoughts,” and so forth.

Purity of livelihood is also included right here. Thus, this fivefold restraint, as well as the abstinence from the basis for success on the part of clansmen who fear evil—all this should be understood as "virtue as restraint" (saṃvara-sīla). Non-transgression...
"Virtue" (*sīla*) refers to the non-transgression of body and speech by one who has undertaken virtue. This, first of all, is the answer to the question, "What is virtue?
Regarding the answer to the question, "How many kinds of virtue are there?": namely, wholesome virtue, unwholesome virtue, and indeterminate virtue.

Herein, because in the world the natural disposition of various beings is called their "virtue"—referring to which it is said, "This person is of a pleasant character," and so forth—[it is included here].
They say, "This one has a habit of suffering, this one has a habit of quarreling, this one has a habit of ornamentation.

Therefore, in that figurative sense and by way of extracting the meaning, even unwholesome conduct is called "conduct" (sīla). However, because of the statement, "Having heard, [there is] wisdom regarding restraint," that is not the "conduct" intended here.

Since, however, the associated consciousness is the source (*samuṭṭhāna*) for virtue that is divided into types such as volition (*cetanā*), he therefore said: "Virtue originated by wholesome consciousness is wholesome virtue," and so forth.

"Virtue consisting in the convergence of restraint" (*saṃvarasamodhāna*) refers to the aggregates associated with restraint. For they are called "convergence of restraint" because they have come together and become mixed with restraint.
Virtue consisting in the convergence of non-transgression should be understood in the same way. In that state...
"Born volition" (*jātacetanā*) refers to the aggregates associated with volition that exist in the state of restraint and the state of non-transgression.

Since, in all three of these [types of] volition, the states associated with it are intended, one should understand that because mental factors are already included by way of the "convergence of volition," the virtue of the convergence of mental factors is not specified separately.
[This applies to] volition and so forth mentioned above.

These phenomena are called "virtue" (sīla). It should be understood that this triad was taught for the purpose of showing that it is not only those [three] alone that constitute virtue, but also the phenomena associated with them are virtue as well.

40. Now, since volition and mental factors are themselves the restraint and the non-transgression, and do not exist separately from them, therefore, regarding only the restraint and the non-transgression—

Applying [the analysis] in a common sequence up to the path of arahantship, he says: "Killing living beings is virtue in the sense of restraint; it is virtue in the sense of non-transgression," and so forth.

For abstention from killing living beings and the rest are called "virtue in the sense of restraint" and "in the sense of non-transgression" because they restrain their respective opposites and do not transgress them; thus, by way of restraining and by way of non-transgressing, they are virtue.
There is what is called virtue (*sīla*). In this context, "in the sense of restraint" regarding killing living beings means that virtue is so called because it closes off killing living beings.
What is that? It is abstention from killing living beings. And since that very [abstention] restrains one, one does not transgress it; thus, it is virtue in the sense of non-transgression.
In the same way, abstention from taking what is not given and so forth, as well as non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view, should be applied accordingly.

Regarding the ten unwholesome courses of action, beginning with "taking life" (*pāṇātipāta*): the taking away of life is *pāṇātipāta*. What is meant is the killing of a living being, the slaughter of a living being.
Herein, in conventional usage, "a living being" (*pāṇa*) refers to a sentient being; in the ultimate sense, it refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).

Now, regarding that living being, for one who perceives it as a living being, there arises—through the doors of body and speech—an action that originates from an effort intended to sever the life-faculty.
Killing is the volition of murder directed toward any particular door [of action].

It is less blameworthy in the case of animals and other beings who lack special qualities when the living being is small, and more blameworthy when the body is large. Why? Because of the greatness of the effort;
and even when the effort is equal, because of the greatness of the object. Among humans and others who possess qualities, it is less blameworthy when the living being lacks those qualities.

It is a grave offense when there is a great quality [in the victim]. However, it should be understood that when the qualities of the body are equal, the offense is slight if the defilements and the effort are mild, and grave if they are intense.
Its five constituent factors are: a living being, the perception of it as a living being, the intention to kill, the effort, and death by means thereof.
Taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*) means taking that which has not been given; it is spoken of as the seizing of another’s property, theft, or robbery.
In this context, "what is not given" refers to that which is possessed by another, such that if one were to exercise control over it as one pleases, one would be subject to punishment and reproach.
Regarding that which is possessed by another, for one who perceives it as being possessed by another, [the offense] is originated by the effort of taking it away.
Taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*) is the volition of theft proceeding through either the door of body or the door of speech.

That [offense] is less blameworthy when the property belonging to another is inferior, and more blameworthy when it is superior. Why? Because of the superiority of the object (*vatthu*). When the object is equal, it is more blameworthy in the case of property belonging to those who possess superior qualities; for, relative to each respective person of superior quality, [theft from] one of inferior quality [is less blameworthy].

In the case of one's own property, it is less blameworthy. It has five constituent factors: that which is possessed by another, the perception that it is possessed by another, the intention to steal, the preparatory effort, and the act of taking it away by that means.

Regarding "sensuous pleasures" (kāmesu), this refers to sexual conduct. "Wrong conduct" (micchācāra) is a reprehensible and base form of behavior. By way of its characteristic, however, wrong conduct in sensual pleasures is the volition of transgressing against a place where one should not go, proceeding through the door of the body with the aim of unrighteousness (asaddhamma).
In this context, "unapproachable places" (agamanīyaṭṭhāna) refers, first of all, to women protected by men:

those protected by their mother, protected by their father, protected by both parents, protected by their brother, protected by their sister, protected by their relatives, protected by their clan, protected by the Dhamma, those who have a protector, and those for whom there is legal punishment—these are the ten beginning with those protected by their mother;
as well as those bought with wealth, those living according to their own will, those living on their earnings, and those living on their clothes.

The ten types of women—namely, the woman with a water-lily bowl (*odapattakinī*), the woman with a head-cushion (*obhatacumbaṭā*), the female slave, the wife, the female laborer who is also a wife, the one captured under a banner (*dhajāhaṭā*), and the momentary wife (*muhuttikā*)—along with the twenty types beginning with those purchased for money, constitute the twenty women.

Among these women, other men [are forbidden] from approaching twelve types: the two protected by guardians (*sārakkha*) and punished by fines (*saparidaṇḍa*), and the ten beginning with those purchased for money; this is what is called an "unapproachable place" (*agamanīyaṭṭhāna*).
Furthermore, this sexual misconduct is less blameworthy when committed with one who lacks virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*) and in a place that is not forbidden;

it is more blameworthy when committed with one endowed with virtues such as moral discipline. Its four constituent factors are: the forbidden object, the intention to engage in it, the actual effort of engagement, and the acceptance of the act of proceeding along a path that is not the [proper] path.
*Musā* is a verbal or bodily effort that destroys one's welfare for one who has the intention of deceiving.
However, lying (*musāvāda*) is the volition that, with the purpose of deceiving, originates a bodily or verbal effort intended to deceive another. According to another method:
*Musā* is an unreal and untrue matter; *vāda* is the making known of that [matter] as real and true. As for its characteristic:
False speech is the volition that originates a communication of something as being thus, by one who wishes to make another understand a matter that is not thus as being thus.
It is slight in blame when the matter it destroys is slight, and grave in blame when the matter is great.
Furthermore, for householders, it is slight in blame when it proceeds in such a manner as "I have nothing" out of a desire not to give their own property; [but it is grave] for a witness...
When uttered for the purpose of destroying another's welfare, it is a grave offense (*mahāsāvajja*).

For those who have gone forth, if they obtain even a small amount of oil or ghee and, with a sense of humor, speak according to the manner of "filling" (exaggeration), saying, "Today in the village the oil flows like a river," it is a minor offense (*appasāvajja*);
however, for those who say things such as "I have seen what was not seen," it is a grave offense.
It has four constituent factors: an untrue matter, the intention to deceive, the corresponding effort, and another’s understanding of that meaning.

Or rather, by whatever speech one speaks those words, there is the manifestation of one’s own affection in the heart of the person to whom one speaks and the emptiness [of the other] regarding that person.
That which one performs is malicious speech (*pisuṇā vācā*).
But that speech by which one makes oneself and others harsh, or which is itself harsh—neither pleasant to the ear nor pleasant to the heart—is harsh speech (*pharusā vācā*).

That by which one prattles nonsense without purpose is idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*). The volition (*cetanā*) that serves as the root of these also receives the very names of malicious speech and so forth.
And that alone is intended here.
In this context, malicious speech (*pisuṇā vācā*) is the volition that originates the application of body and speech for the purpose of dividing others, or out of a desire for one's own favor.
It is less blameworthy when directed toward someone of little virtue, and more blameworthy when directed toward someone of great virtue.
It is a great offense. It has four constituent factors: another person who is to be divided;
either the intention to divide them with the thought, "In this way they will become estranged," or the desire for intimacy with the thought, "In this way I will become dear and trustworthy";

the corresponding effort; and the awareness that one's purpose has been achieved. However, as long as the others have not actually been divided, there is no breach of the course of action (*kammappatha*); it becomes such only when they are divided.
Harsh speech is an exclusively cruel volition that originates from bodily or vocal application intended to cut another’s vital parts.
However, even an application that cuts the vital parts does not constitute harsh speech if there is gentleness of mind.
For instance, parents sometimes say to their children, “May thieves cut you into pieces! and even [say] to them, “Even a lotus leaf...”
They do not wish for one who falls away from the higher training. And sometimes teachers and preceptors say to their dependents, "What are these shameless and unscrupulous ones?
Expel them! Yet they desire their success in the mastery of the scriptures and spiritual attainments.
And just as there is no harsh speech due to gentleness of mind, so too there is gentle speech due to gentleness of expression.
It does not exist. For one who wishes to kill, the words "Lay this person down comfortably" are not a harsh utterance;

rather, it is a harsh speech precisely because of the harshness of the mind. Depending on the qualities of the person toward whom it is directed, it is slightly blameworthy if that person has few virtues, and greatly blameworthy if they have great virtues.
It has three constituent factors: another person who may be reviled, a mind of anger, and the act of reviling itself.
Idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*) is unwholesome volition (*akusalacetanā*) that originates from bodily and vocal exertion and conveys what is meaningless.
It is slightly blameworthy when its habitual practice is weak, and greatly blameworthy when its habitual practice is great. It has two constituent factors:

the intent to engage in useless talk such as the *Mahābhārata* war or the abduction of Sītā, and the actual speaking of such talk. However, if others do not take up that talk, there is no breach of the path of action (*kammapatha*).
It occurs only when idle chatter has already been grasped by another.
"Coveting" (abhijjhā) means it proceeds by being directed toward another's goods and inclining toward them;
its characteristic is the coveting of another's goods, thinking, "O, may this be mine!"—just like the taking of what is not given.
[There are two types: those of slight blame and those of great blame. It has two constituent factors: another’s property and one’s own appropriation.
For even when greed arises with another’s property as its object, there is no breach of the path of action until one appropriates it for oneself, thinking, "O, may this be mine!"
Malice (*vyāpāda*) is so called because it seeks to destroy happiness. Its characteristic is mental corruption for the sake of another's ruin;
like harsh speech, it is slightly blameworthy yet greatly blameworthy. It has two constituent factors: another being and the thought of their destruction.
For even when anger arises toward another being, there is as yet no breach of the path of action (*kammappatha*) until one thinks, "Oh, if only this person..."
One does not contemplate its destruction with the thought, "It might be cut off or perish.
Because it lacks the apprehension of things as they truly are, one sees wrongly; thus, it is wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*).

Its characteristic is a distorted perception according to the method beginning with "there is no giving," and like frivolous speech (*samphappalāpa*), it is both slightly blameworthy and greatly blameworthy. Furthermore:
The indeterminate [wrong view] is of slight blame, while the determinate is of great blame. It has two constituent factors:
the perversion of the mode in which the object is grasped, and its appearing in accordance with that mode of grasping.
In this regard, the breach of the courses of kamma occurs only through the views of nihilism, causelessness, and non-action, and not through other views.

Furthermore, the exposition of these ten unwholesome courses of action (akusala-kammapatha) should be understood by way of five aspects: by way of their nature (dhammata), by way of their components (koṭṭhāsata), by way of their objects (ārammaṇata), by way of their feeling (vedanāta), and by way of their roots (mūlata).

In this regard, "by way of their nature": among these, the first seven are indeed volitional states (cetanā-dhamma), while the three beginning with covetousness (abhijjhā) are associated with volition.
"By way of their components": the first seven and wrong view—these eight are exclusively courses of action (kammapatha).
There are no roots [other than these]. Covetousness and ill will are both courses of action and roots. For when covetousness reaches the state of being a root, greed becomes an unwholesome root;
ill will, as hatred, becomes an unwholesome root. As for the object:
killing has the life-faculty as its object and thus has formations as its object; taking what is not given has sentient beings as its object.
Or it has formations as its object. Wrong conduct has formations as its object by way of tangible objects; some say it also has sentient beings as its object.
False speech has either sentient beings or formations as its object. So too with malicious speech. Harsh speech has only sentient beings as its object.
Frivolous chatter has either sentient beings or formations as its object, by way of what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized.

Likewise, covetousness (*abhijjhā*) is the same. Ill-will (*byāpāda*) has only sentient beings as its object. Wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) has only the mental formations (*saṅkhāra*) of the three planes as its object.
Regarding "it results in pain": killing living beings is painful to experience.
For even though kings, upon seeing a thief, may say with a smile, "Go, my men, kill him," their decisive volition (*sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā*) is nevertheless associated with suffering.
Taking what is not given (adinnādāna) is associated with three types of feeling. For one who, seeing another's property, seizes it with a joyful and delighted heart, there is pleasant feeling;
for one who seizes it while terrified and trembling, there is painful feeling; likewise for one reflecting upon the results of the ripening and outflow of that act.
However, for one who seizes it while remaining in a state of equanimity at the time of taking, there is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Sexual misconduct (micchācāra)...

By way of being neither-painful-nor-pleasant (*sukha-majjhatta*), it is associated with two feelings; however, in the consciousness that brings about a decision (*sanniṭṭhāpaka-citta*), there is no neutral feeling (*majjhata-vedanā*).

False speech (*musāvāda*) is associated with three feelings by the same method as explained for taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*); likewise for malicious speech (*pisuṇā vācā*). Harsh speech (*pharusā vācā*) is associated with painful feeling (*dukkha-vedanā*).
Frivolous chatter (*samphappalāpa*) is associated with three feelings; for when others are giving applause or waving cloths and the like, one is joyful and elated.
At the time of narrating events such as the abduction of Sītā or the Bhārata war, it is a pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*). However,
at the time of narrating for one who has first been given a fee but later returns and says, "Tell it from the beginning," and who is distressed,
thinking, "Shall I now tell it in its entirety, with its proper sequence and incidental details, or not?"— at that time of narration, it is a painful feeling (*dukkha-vedanā*).
When one speaks with equanimity, there is a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Covetousness has two feelings by way of pleasure and equanimity;
likewise for wrong view. Ill-will has a painful feeling. As for the roots:
killing living beings has two roots by way of hatred and delusion; taking what is not given has two roots by way of hatred and delusion.
Or, [adultery] occurs through greed and delusion; misconduct occurs through greed and delusion; false speech occurs through hatred and delusion or through greed and delusion.
Likewise for malicious speech and idle chatter. Harsh speech occurs through hatred and delusion;
covetousness has a single root, which is delusion; likewise for ill will. Wrong view has two roots: greed and delusion.
The Discussion of the Unwholesome Courses of Action is finished.
Now, the ten wholesome courses of action consist of the abstinences from killing living beings and so forth, together with non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view.

These are called the "wholesome courses of action" because by means of them one abstains from killing living beings and so forth, or because they themselves abstain, or because they are simply the act of abstaining.
Abstinence (*virati*). That abstinence associated with wholesome consciousness in one who refrains from killing living beings and so forth is, by way of its divisions, threefold:

abstinence through possession (*sampattavirati*), abstinence through undertaking (*samādānavirati*), and abstinence through eradication (*samucchedavirati*). Among these, for those who have not formally undertaken the training rules (*sikkhāpada*), it is [the first], having reflected upon their own birth, age, learning, and so forth, thinking:
"It is improper for us to commit such an evil deed."
The abstinence that arises in those who do not transgress the basis of attainment is called *sampattavirati*.

However, the abstinence that arises in those who have undertaken the training precepts—both at the time of undertaking the precepts and thereafter—in those who do not transgress the basis even at the cost of their own lives, is called *samādānavirati*.
Furthermore, the abstinence associated with the Noble Path is *samucchedavirati* (abstinence by eradication).
Indeed, from the moment of its arising, even the thought "we shall kill a living being" does not arise in noble persons (ariyapuggala).

Now, the exposition of these wholesome courses of action (kusalakammapatha) should be understood through five aspects—by way of their nature (dhammata), by way of their components (koṭṭhāsa), by way of their object (ārammaṇa), by way of feeling (vedanā), and by way of their roots (mūla)—just as was done for the unwholesome courses of action.

In that regard, "by way of their nature": among these, in the first seven, both volitions (cetanā) and abstinences (virati) are possible; at the end, however, the three are associated only with volition.
Regarding the "divisions": in their sequential order, there are only seven courses of action (kamma-patha), not roots; at the end, however, there are both three courses of action and roots.
For when non-covetousness reaches the state of a root, it becomes the wholesome root of non-greed (alobha); non-ill-will becomes the wholesome root of non-hatred (adosa);
and right view becomes the wholesome root of non-delusion (amoha).
Regarding the object (*ārammaṇato*): the objects of these [abstinences] are precisely the objects of killing and so forth.

For it is only by virtue of being something to be transgressed that there is such a thing as "abstinence" (*veramaṇī*). Just as the Noble Path, having Nibbāna as its object, abandons the defilements, so too these courses of action (*kamma-patha*), having the life-faculty and so forth as their objects, abandon the unwholesome conduct of killing and the rest.
Regarding "from feeling": all [feelings] are either pleasant feelings or neutral feelings. For once one has attained the wholesome, there is no such thing as painful feeling.
Regarding "from the roots": for one who abstains with a consciousness associated with knowledge, in successive order, they have three roots by way of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
For one who abstains with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge, they have two roots by way of non-greed and non-hatred. Non-covetousness...
For one who abstains with a consciousness associated with knowledge, it has two roots by way of non-hatred and non-delusion.
For one who abstains with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge, it has one root by way of non-hatred. Non-greed, however, does not have itself as its own root.
The same method applies to non-ill-will as well. Right view has two roots by way of non-greed and non-hatred.
The Discussion of the Wholesome Courses of Action is finished.
Having thus shown virtue by way of the ten wholesome courses of action, he now shows it by way of the thirty-seven factors culminating in the path to arahantship, beginning with renunciation:
through renunciation, virtue is the restraint of sensual desire.

He says, "Virtue (*sīla*) in the sense of non-transgression," and so forth. In this context, because one restrains sensual desire through renunciation (*nekkhamma*) and does not transgress it, the intention is that renunciation is virtue. Alternatively, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the direct object;
thus, "renunciation" is the meaning. This same method applies to the remaining terms. However, after showing renunciation and non-ill-will in the text, [it continues] below...
Because it follows the method already stated, the remainder has been abbreviated and only the path to Arahatship is shown at the end.

Having thus shown virtue by way of restraint and non-transgression, he now says, "The abandoning of killing living beings is virtue," and so forth, for the purpose of showing the divisions of those same two types of virtue. And here, the abandoning of killing living beings—
The construction should be made thus: virtue is the abstaining from the destruction of life; virtue is the volition that is the opposite of the destruction of life;
virtue is the restraint from the destruction of life; virtue is the non-transgression regarding the destruction of life.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as "abandoning" apart from the mere non-arising of the aforementioned factors, such as the destruction of life and so forth. For...

Furthermore, that respective abandoning is a "support" (*upadhāraṇa*) in the sense of providing a foundation for each respective wholesome state, and it is a "coalescence" (*samodhāna*) by way of not allowing their natures to become scattered;
therefore, it is called "virtue" (*sīla*) in the sense of "characterizing" (*sīlana*), which consists precisely of the aforementioned support and coalescence.
The other four states [of virtue] are [included] therein by way of abstinence from this or that [unwholesome action].

This is said with reference to the essential nature of the mind’s activity in one who, by way of restraint and by way of the volition associated with both, does not transgress this or that [precept], and by way of such non-transgression.
Alternatively, even abandonment (pahāna) exists as a real phenomenon (dhamma). How so? Because by means of it, the opposite of killing living beings and so forth is abandoned.
Or, it is "abandoning" (*pahāna*) because it abandons that which is its opposite. What is that? It is all wholesome aggregates (*khandha*).

However, other teachers say: "Even in the case of renunciation (*nekkhamma*) and so forth, there exists what is called 'abstinence' (*virati*), which is a factor included within the determinate (*niyata*) among all wholesome states," but they do not say this here. Thus, by means of these [factors] such as abandoning...
Having distinguished them by means of five terms, only the "infinite" (apariyanta) morality is mentioned among the two types of morality—the finite and the infinite.
For this very reason, such kinds of morality lead to non-remorse of the mind... [pe] ...it is said that one trains while realizing what is to be realized.
In that context, "they lead to non-remorse" refers to the statement: "Restraint has non-remorse as its purpose," and "they have non-remorse as their purpose."
Because of the statement, "Ānanda, wholesome virtues have non-regret as their benefit," they lead to non-regret.
Because of the statements, "Non-regret leads to gladness" and "Gladness arises for one who attends appropriately," they lead to gladness.
And because of the statements, "Gladness leads to rapture" and "Rapture arises for one who is glad," [they lead to rapture].
They lead to rapture because of the statement: "Rapture has the purpose of tranquility," and because of the statement: "The body of one whose mind is rapturous becomes tranquil.
They lead to tranquility because of the statement: "Tranquility has the purpose of pleasure," and because of the statement:
"One whose body is tranquil experiences pleasure. They lead to joy because mental pleasure is indeed joy.
It is said: "By repetition" (*āsevanāya*). Repetition means intense cultivation. Of what is there repetition?

Since pleasure (*sukha*) was mentioned immediately before the mention of mental joy (*somanassa*), pleasure is established. Furthermore, because of the statement, "The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated," concentration (*samādhi*) is established by that pleasure.
Thus, it is the repetition of that established concentration. Of that concentration...
"They lead to cultivation" means they lead to proficiency and strength.
"For development" means for the increase of that very concentration. "For frequent practice" means for the repeated performance of that very concentration.
By serving as the root cause for the occurrence of non-regret and so forth, and by providing the adornment of the faculties such as faith, they lead to adornment.
By accomplishing the equipment for concentration, beginning with non-remorse, they lead to requisites.
For here, as in such passages as, "And these requisites for life that must be acquired by one who has gone forth," the word *parikkhāra* has the sense of "equipment.
However, in such passages as, "The chariot has virtue as its equipment, meditation as its axle, and energy as its wheels," it has the sense of "ornament."
In such passages as, “It is well-furnished with the seven requisites of a city,” the meaning is that of *parivāra* (retinue or accompaniment).

However, here, because ornaments and retinues have been mentioned separately, it is said that the meaning is *sambhāra* (requisite or constituent). And the meaning of *sambhāra* is the meaning of *paccaya* (condition).

It is precisely by way of being the fundamental cause, through the accomplishment of states such as contact associated with concentration, that they lead to the retinue (*parivāra*) of concentration. Of concentration...
And because they bring about the state of being the proximate cause for insight (*vipassanā*) and the attainment of mastery over it, they accomplish its fulfillment;
thus, they lead to perfection.

Having thus shown concentration that is fulfilled in all its aspects by means of the support of virtue (*sīla*), [the text now says]: "When the mind is concentrated, one knows things as they truly are..."
Because of the statement, “He knows and sees; knowing and seeing as it really is, he becomes disenchanted; through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate;

through dispassion, he is liberated,” [the Blessed One] spoke the words beginning with “for the sake of utter disenchantment,” showing that the knowledge and vision of things as they really are, etc., have virtue as their root and concentration as their proximate cause.
For when disenchantment has been shown, its proximate cause—namely, [concentration]—is thereby indicated.
Knowledge and vision according to reality (*yathābhūtañāṇadassana*) has indeed been demonstrated. For if that is not established, disenchantment (*nibbidā*) is not established.

Those [terms] have their meaning already explained. Here, however, knowledge and vision according to reality consists in the discernment of mentality-materiality (*nāmarūpa*) together with its conditions.
Having thus shown the purpose of virtue, which culminates in the great Nibbāna of the Deathless, [the text now shows] the status of that virtue as the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*).

And wishing to show the training in higher mind and higher wisdom which have that [virtue] as their root, he said: "The restraint and purity of such virtues is 'higher virtue' (*adhicitta*)," and so forth.
In this context, "restraint-purity" (*saṃvarapārisuddhi*) means that the restraint itself is the purity.

The restraint and purity of such virtues—which are boundless and dependent on turning away from the round of existence—is "superior" (*adhika*) to other virtues because it is dependent on turning away from the round of existence.
"Virtue" (sīla) is called "higher virtue" (adhisīla). "The mind established in the purity of restraint":

the mind thus established in the purity of restraint through virtue does not fall into distraction because it brings about non-regret and so forth; the meaning is that it becomes established in concentration.
Non-distraction itself is purity; thus it is "purity of non-distraction. It is free from all defilements.
Concentration partaking of penetration is called "higher mind" (*adhicitta*) because it is superior to other forms of concentration.
For here, concentration is indicated by way of the term "mind. One "rightly sees the purity of restraint":

one rightly sees the completely pure restraint of virtue by means of both full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*) and full understanding through investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*); in the same way, [one rightly sees] that which is known as the purity of non-distraction.
One correctly sees pure concentration. For one who sees thus, the purity consisting in seeing is "purity of seeing" (*dassanapārisuddhi*).

That very [purity] is called "higher wisdom" (*adhipaññā*) because it is superior to the remaining types of wisdom. "That which is therein" means that which is among those [three]: restraint, non-distraction, and seeing.
"The state of restraint" (*saṃvaraṭṭho*) is the nature of restraint. In the same way, there are the states of non-distraction and seeing.
And they should be understood thus: the training in the higher virtue itself is the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*). The others should be understood in the same way.
Having thus shown the three trainings, he now said, "He trains by attending to these three trainings," etc., in order to show the sequence for their fulfillment.
Its meaning is this: even while attending to them in order to fulfill each one individually, he trains.
Indeed, even one who, having adverted [to the object], knows "this is such-and-such a training," is said to train; one who, having known it, sees it again and again, is said to train;
one who, having seen it, reviews it according to how it was seen, is said to train;

and one who, having reviewed it, makes the mind immovable and establishes it right there, is said to train—by means of the faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom associated with each respective training.

Even when performing one’s own respective duties, one is said to “train”; likewise, at the time of directly knowing what is to be known through direct knowledge (*abhiññeyya-abhijānanā*), while performing those various duties, one is also said to train in the three trainings (*tisso sikkhā*).
Furthermore, the phrases beginning with “the five precepts” have meanings already explained.
Regarding the passage beginning with “by means of the path of Arahantship, all defilements,” because Arahants lack excessive remorse and so forth, [they are free from them].

And those terms are indeed appropriate in the sense of being cultivated and so forth. However, phrases such as "for the sake of absolute disenchantment" and so on should be applied only to the moment of the path, just like the foundations of mindfulness and the right efforts.
As for the statement, "He correctly sees the purity of restraint; he correctly sees the purity of non-distraction," this—
The first two statements should be applied by way of insight (vipassanā) for the purpose of the attainment of the fruit (phala-samāpatti);
however, the second statement is also applicable by way of insight for the purpose of the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).

Regarding the five statements beginning with "he trains while adverting," although there is no further training left for an Arahant, it is said that "he trains" because he possesses the nature of the aggregates of virtue of one beyond training (asekha-sīla-kkhandha), and so forth.
This is how it should be understood. However, such statements as "one trains while resolving through faith" refer specifically to the moment of the path (*magga-khaṇa*).
Other statements concerning access concentration (*upacāra*), absorption (*appanā*), insight (*vipassanā*), and the path should also be applied accordingly as appropriate.
The commentary on the description of knowledge consisting in virtue (*sīlamaya-ñāṇa-niddesa*) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Exposition of Knowledge Consisting in the Development of Concentration 43.
In the exposition of knowledge consisting in the development of concentration, first of all, showing the classification of concentration starting from the singlefold up to the tenfold, he says:
"One kind of concentration," and so forth. Therein, "one-pointedness of mind" (*cittassa ekaggatā*) refers to the absence of distraction toward various objects.

That which has a single object (*ārammaṇa*) as its foremost and supreme [quality] is *ekagga*; the state of being *ekagga* is *ekaggatā*. Furthermore, that *ekaggatā* belongs to the mind (*citta*), not to a "being" (*satta*);
it is for the purpose of showing this that the word "of the mind" (*cittassa*) is stated.

Regarding the term "mundane" (*lokiya*): the world (*loka*) is called the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) in the sense of breaking up and falling apart; one who is connected to that world by way of being included within it is "mundane. "Supramundane" (*lokuttara*)...
"Crossed over" (*uttiṇṇo*) means "transcendent" (*uttaro*); because it is not included within the world by virtue of its state of being beyond the world, it is "supramundane" (*lokuttaro*).

In the *Tika*, that which is "with initial application" (*savitakko*) and "with sustained application" (*savicāro*) is "with initial and sustained application" (*savitakkasavicāro*). Likewise for "without initial and sustained application" (*avitakkavicāro*).

That which has "sustained application" (*vicāro*) alone as its measure (*mattā*) or standard (*pamāṇa*) among initial and sustained applications is "mere sustained application" (*vicāramatto*); it does not exceed beyond sustained application to enter into association with initial application.
The meaning is "it does not go. It is "without applied thought and with only sustained thought" (*avitakkavicāramatta*).

They recite [the text] by making a division even among the three [terms]. The meanings of the tetrads and pentads have already been stated. Regarding the hexad: because it arises again and again, mindfulness itself is "recollection" (*anussati*);
or, because it occurs precisely in the place where it ought to proceed, for a clansman who has gone forth through faith.
"Mindfulness that is appropriate" is also *anussati*. The mindfulness that has arisen with reference to the Buddha is "recollection of the Buddha" (*buddhānussati*).

This is a designation for mindfulness whose object is the qualities of the Buddha, such as those of an Arahant. Through this recollection of the Buddha, the one-pointedness of mind itself is "non-distraction" (*avikkhepa*), because it is the direct opposite of distraction, which is termed agitation (*uddhacca*). The mindfulness that has arisen with reference to the Dhamma...
Recollection of the Dhamma (*dhammānussati*). This is a designation for mindfulness having as its object the qualities of the Dhamma, such as its being well-expounded.

Recollection arisen with reference to the Saṅgha is recollection of the Saṅgha (*saṅghānussati*). This is a designation for mindfulness having as its object the qualities of the Saṅgha, such as its being well-practiced.

Recollection arisen with reference to virtue is recollection of virtue (*sīlānussati*). [This refers to mindfulness] having as its object the qualities of one’s own virtue, such as its being unbroken...

This is a designation for mindfulness. Mindfulness arisen with respect to generosity is "recollection of generosity" (*cāgānussati*). This is a designation for mindfulness that has as its object the qualities of one's own generosity, such as the state of having relinquished possessions.
Mindfulness arisen with respect to deities is "recollection of deities" (*devatānussati*).
This is a designation for mindfulness that has as its object one's own qualities, such as faith, having placed the deities in the position of witnesses.
