Skill in concentration (*samādhikusalatā*) regarding the sevenfold [set] is the proficiency in regard to concentration—which has many divisions, such as the singlefold and so on—in discerning:
"This kind of concentration is such-and-such; this kind of concentration is such-and-such. This is a designation for the wisdom that delimits concentration.
Skill in concentration is also proficiency in the method for the arising of concentration.
"Skill in the attainment of concentration" means proficiency in entering a concentration that has been produced; by this, mastery over entry is expressed.
"Skill in the persistence of concentration" means proficiency in maintaining a concentration that has been entered for as long as desired by way of its continuity;
by this, mastery over resolution is expressed. Alternatively, through the grasping of the sign...
For one who merely accomplishes those aspects, absorption itself succeeds, but it does not endure for long.

Long endurance, however, occurs because the states that are obstacles to concentration have been thoroughly purified. For a bhikkhu who has not properly suppressed sensual desire by reflecting on the danger of sense-desires and so forth, and whose bodily rigidity has not been well-allayed through bodily tranquility—
Having failed to properly dispel sloth and torpor by means of the application of energy and mental attention,
having failed to thoroughly eradicate restlessness and remorse by means of mental attention to the sign of serenity, and having failed to properly purify other factors that obstruct concentration,
he enters into jhāna; like a bee that has entered an unpurified hive, he is impure.

And like a king who has entered a park, he emerges very quickly. However, one who enters jhāna after having thoroughly purified the states that are obstacles to concentration is like a bee that has entered a well-cleansed hive, or like a king who has entered a perfectly pure park;
he remains within the attainment itself for the entire duration of the day.
It exists. Therefore the ancients said:
“Let one dispel desire for sense-pleasures and aversion, along with restlessness, sloth, and doubt as the fifth;
with a mind that brings joy through seclusion, one should delight there like a king who has reached the inner sanctum.”

Therefore, because it is said, “One who desires long endurance [of concentration] should enter jhāna after clearing away obstructive states,” it follows that by fulfilling that procedure, one becomes skilled in making concentration endure for a long time.

“Skill in emerging from concentration” means skill in emerging from concentration—whether it has been proceeding according to one’s preference in a continuous stream—at the very moment previously delimited for its conclusion.
This is as in the passage beginning, “The Dhamma which a person may know,” and so forth.
It should be understood that the genitive case is used here in the sense of an ablative (*nissakkattha*). By this, the state of being established in emergence (*vuṭṭhāna*) is expressed.
"Fitness and skillfulness in concentration" means that fitness is the state of not being ill and the state of being free from disease; for one who is ill is called "unfit.
It is also said in the *Vinaya*: "Venerable sir, I am not unfit. This is also found in the *Anaṅgaṇa Sutta* and the *Vaṭṭasutta*.

Skill in making concentration free from illness consists in being adept at producing a state of health in concentration through the absence of those evil, wishful states mentioned as opposed to the attainment of jhāna, and through the removal of the mental defilements such as covetousness;
that is to say, skill in the state of being free from the sickness of the defilements. Alternatively, "health" (kallatā) means...

Wieldiness is so called because it is a synonym for wieldiness of speech. For it is said: "That which is the unwieldiness and unwieldiness of the mind," and also, "the workable mind, the pliant mind, the unobstructed mind. Here, the word *kalla* has the meaning of being workable (*kammañña*).

Therefore, [one practices] in conformity with the kasiṇas, in reverse order of the kasiṇas, in both forward and reverse order of the kasiṇas, in conformity with the jhānas, and in reverse order of the jhānas.
By way of these fourteen modes— namely, by way of conformity with and reversal of the jhānas, by way of skipping jhānas, by way of skipping kasiṇas, by way of skipping both jhāna and kasiṇa,
by way of shifting factors, by way of shifting objects, by way of shifting both factors and objects, by way of defining the factors, and by way of defining the objects— or,
together with "by way of defining both factors and objects," by way of these fifteen modes.
By the taming of the mind, it is meant that there is skill in making concentration pliable.
"Skill in the range of concentration" means proficiency regarding those objects—the kasiṇas and so forth—which are the range of concentration;
it is the state of being adept with respect to those objects by means of performing adverting according to one's desire through the wish to attain this or that jhāna. By this—

Mastery over adverting is said to be by way of adverting to the kasiṇa. Alternatively, it is skillfulness regarding the objects of concentration by way of the pervasion of the kasiṇa in each respective direction and by way of the long endurance of the kasiṇa thus pervaded.
Skillfulness in directing concentration is the leading of lower and lower concentrations to the state of higher and higher concentrations by means of the method of unity (*ekattanaya*).
Skillfulness in directing and inclining [the mind] consists in this: access concentration (upacāra-jhāna), having attained mastery, directs itself toward the first jhāna or toward insight;
likewise, the first jhāna and so forth direct themselves toward the second jhāna and so forth, or toward insight;

the fourth jhāna directs itself toward the formless attainments, or toward the higher knowledges (abhiññā), or toward insight; and the base of infinite space and the others [direct themselves similarly].
"He directs [the mind] toward the base of infinite consciousness and so forth, or toward insight"—
this is skill in directing concentration here and there. Since skill is wisdom (*paññā*) and that is not concentration (*samādhi*),
it should be understood that sevenfold concentration is spoken of by way of the wisdom that guides concentration.
However, some teachers say: "Skill in concentration (*samādhikusalatā*) is skill regarding that mental attention by which the mind is not distracted.
Skill in attainment (*samāpattikusalatā*) is skill regarding that mental attention by which the factors of absorption (*jhānaṅga*) become manifest for one who is entering attainment.
Skill in maintenance (*ṭhitikusalatā*) is skill regarding that mental attention by which the concentrated mind, once entered, is not distracted."
Skill in that regard. Skill in emergence means: one knows the emergence from the hindrances in the first jhāna;
one knows the emergence from the factors in the [next] three jhānas; one knows the emergence from the object in the formless attainments;

one knows the emergence from distraction when there is an abundance of sense objects; and one knows the emergence by one's own will at the time of reaching the limit and at the time of performing the final task.

Skill in fitness: one knows that through the fitness of the mind, the fitness of the body, the fitness of food, the fitness of the lodging, and the fitness of the person, there is fitness for concentration. Skill in the resort:
one knows how to delimit the object, one knows how to pervade the directions, and one knows how to expand it. Skill in directing: ...
"By means of right attention here and there, one directs and inclines the mind;

when mastery over access has been attained, one directs it toward the first jhāna; likewise, one directs it toward the successive higher jhānas, the direct knowledges, the formless attainments, and insight.
Such is skill in directing the mind here and there. Thus they explain the meaning of these terms.

The *Aṭṭhaka* has already been explained. Regarding the *Navaka*: "belonging to the fine-material sphere" (*rūpāvacara*) means included among those states belonging to the fine-material sphere described by such passages as: "Which states belong to the fine-material sphere?
Taking the assembly of Brahmā’s ministers as the lower limit and including the Akaniṭṭha devas as the upper limit," and so forth.
Herein, this is the etymological meaning: form, consisting of the aggregate of form, moves within (*avacarati*) here; it does not...
"Kāma" refers to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*). For even the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) is called "form," as in such expressions as "the aggregate of form is form.
This [fine-material sphere] consists of the realms of the Brahma’s Retinue (*brahmapārisajja*), the Brahma’s Ministers (*brahmapurohita*), and the Great Brahmās (*mahābrahmā*);

the Limited Radiance (*parittābha*), Immeasurable Radiance (*appamāṇābha*), and Radiant (*ābhassara*); the Limited Beauty (*parittasubha*), Immeasurable Beauty (*appamāṇasubha*), and Shining Beauty (*subhakiṇha*); the Non-percipient Beings (*asaññasatta*) and the Vast Fruit (*vehapphala*); and the Aviha, Atappa, Sudassa, Sudassī, and Akaniṭṭha heavens.

The location is sixteenfold by way of its divisions. That location, which is designated as "of the fine-material sphere" (*rūpāvacara*), is called simply "form" (*rūpa*) by eliding the latter member of the compound.

It is "fine-material-sphere" (*rūpāvacara*) because it moves within that form. Alternatively, "form" refers to existence in the fine-material realm (*rūpabhava*); it is "fine-material-sphere" because it moves within that.
Although this concentration also moves within the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), it is nevertheless [designated thus] because it moves in the manner of one moving in battle.
An elephant who has received the name *saṅgāmāvacara* (a warrior) is called a *saṅgāmāvacara* even while wandering in the city;
likewise, creatures that move on land or in water are called "land-dwellers" or "water-dwellers" even when they are situated on neither land nor water.

In the same way, although this [consciousness] does not move elsewhere, it is called *rūpāvacara* (belonging to the form realm). Furthermore, it takes rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in the form known as the "form existence" (*rūpabhava*).

It is called "belonging to the fine-material sphere" (*rūpāvacara*) because it operates therein. "Inferior" (*hīna*) means base. That which exists in the middle of the inferior and the superior is "middling" (*majjha*).

There is also the reading *majjhima*, which has the same meaning. "Exalted" (*paṇīta*) means brought to a state of pre-eminence; the meaning is "superior. These, moreover, should be understood by way of their application (*āyūhana*).
For at the moment of application, if one's desire (*chanda*), energy (*vīriya*), consciousness (*citta*), or investigation (*vīmaṃsā*) is inferior...

Or, he whose [qualities] are inferior is called "inferior"; he whose qualities are middling is "middling"; he whose qualities are sublime is "sublime. Alternatively, one who has merely produced [them] is inferior;
one who has not fully cultivated them is middling; one who has fully cultivated them and attained mastery is sublime.
The formless-sphere [attainment] is to be understood according to the method explained for the fine-material sphere.

Regarding the passage beginning with "emptiness concentration" (*suññato samādhi*), when one is practicing insight according to the sequence of insight meditation—contemplating that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and non-self"—the emergence of the path occurs through the contemplation of non-self.

Because that insight proceeds as "empty" (*suññato*) regarding those conditioned phenomena which are devoid of a self, it is therefore called "emptiness. The noble-path concentration established by means of that [insight] is what is meant here.
It is called "emptiness concentration" (*suññato samādhi*); the meaning is "concentration occurring by way of emptiness. For it occurs in the mode of occurrence of insight (*vipassanā*).

Since that insight occurs as the opposite of the sign of permanence when the emergence of the path through the contemplation of impermanence has arisen, it is therefore called "signless" (*animittā*).
The noble-path concentration established by that [insight] is "signless concentration" (*animitto samādhi*).
It is called "the signless" (*animitta*); the meaning is that it is concentration devoid of the sign of permanence.

For it proceeds by way of the mode of occurrence of insight (*vipassanā*). When the emergence from the path through the contemplation of suffering has arisen, that insight is called "the desireless" (*appaṇihita*) because it proceeds as the opposite of longing;
therefore, the noble-path concentration established by that insight is "desireless concentration."
The meaning is "concentration devoid of aspiration. For it proceeds by way of the mode of occurrence of insight (*vipassanā*).
It should be understood that the three concentrations of fruition (*phala-samādhi*) are likewise included within these very three types of concentration.
However, because the supramundane (*lokuttara*) concentrations are sublime, their classification into inferior and so forth has not been mentioned.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the perception of the bloated corpse" (*uddhumātaka-saññā*) and so forth: it is called "bloated" (*uddhumāta*) because, like a bellows filled with air, it has become bloated by the process of putrefaction that arises in succession following the exhaustion of life. That which is bloated is itself the "bloated corpse" (*uddhumātaka*).
Alternatively, because it is loathsome, it is a "wretched bloating," hence "bloated corpse. This is a designation for such a carcass.
"Vinīla" means a discolored state; "vinīlaka" is simply that which is vinīla. Alternatively, it is called "vinīlaka" because it is loathsome (*kucchita*) due to its repulsiveness.

This is a designation for a corpse whose flesh has swollen up in places where it is red-colored, whose pus has accumulated in places where it is white-colored, and which is mostly blue-colored, appearing like a body wrapped in a blue cloth.
"Vipubbaka" refers to pus that is oozing out from fissured places;
it is "vipubbaka" because it is putrid, or because it is a loathsome, vile thing that has been putrid. This is a designation for such a corpse.
"Vicchiddaka" means that which is split open by being cut in two; it is "vichiddaka" because it is split, or because it is loathsome.
It is called *vicchiddaka* because it is cut apart (*vicchindati*) in a loathsome way; this is a designation for a corpse that has been severed in the middle.
It is called *vikkhāyita* because it has been devoured in various ways here and there by dogs, jackals, and the like;
although one should say *vikhāyita*, it is stated as *vikkhāyita*. *Vikkhāyitaka* is simply *vikkhāyita*, or it is called loathsome (*kucchita*) because of its repulsiveness.
"Devoured" (*vikkhāyita*) means "the devoured" (*vikkhāyitaka*). This is a designation for a corpse in such a state.
"Scattered" (*vikkhitta*) means scattered in various ways; that which is scattered is itself "the scattered" (*vikkhittaka*).
Alternatively, it is called "the scattered" because it is loathsome or vile due to being scattered here and there—such as one hand in one place, one foot in another, and the head in yet another.
This is a designation for a corpse. Because it is struck (hata) in the manner previously described and is scattered (vikkhittaka), it is called "the struck-and-scattered" (*hatavikkhittaka*).
This is a designation for a corpse that has been struck with a weapon upon its limbs and members in the shape of a crow’s foot and then scattered according to the method already stated.
It is called "bloody" (*lohitaka*) because blood is sprinkled (*kirati*), scattered, and trickles here and there. [It refers to] one smeared with trickling blood.
This is a designation for a skinless corpse. "Worms" (puḷava) refers to maggots; because it scatters worms, it is called "worm-infested" (puḷavaka).
This is a designation for a corpse filled with maggots. "Bone" (aṭṭhika) is simply bone;
or, because it is repulsive, it is a despicable bone, thus "bone" (aṭṭhika). This is a designation for both a skeleton and a single bone.
Furthermore, these names—beginning with the "swollen corpse" (uddhumātaka)—apply both to the signs that arise based on these [meditation subjects] and to the jhānas attained upon those signs.

Here, however, the perception (saññā) that arises by way of absorption (appanā), which grasps the aspect of repulsiveness within the sign of the swollen corpse, is called the "perception of the swollen corpse.
[The phrase] "by way of that perception of the swollen corpse" means by way of that perception of the swollen corpse. This applies to the remaining [subjects] as well.
The same method applies. "Fifty-five kinds of concentration" are stated by way of the singlefold and so forth.

Having thus shown the classification of concentration by way of the singlefold and so forth, now, desiring to show concentration by another method as well, he begins another exposition with the words "Moreover," and says "twenty-five," etc. Therein, regarding concentration...

The meaning of "establishment" (*samādhiṭṭha*) refers to the essential qualities (*sabhāva*) of concentration; those essential qualities by which it becomes concentration are its "meanings" (*attha*) in that context.
In the sense of being "grasped" (*pariggaha*), it is called concentration because it is grasped by the faculties such as faith;
therefore, concentration is characterized by the quality of being grasped. And those very faculties are mutually supportive of one another.
And they become fulfilled through the fulfillment of their cultivation. Therefore, concentration is so called in the sense of being a retinue and in the sense of being complete.

By way of that very concentration, it is in the sense of one-pointedness with regard to a single object, and in the sense of non-distraction with regard to the absence of distraction toward various objects;
and because it is to be attained only by the supramundane path through the great exertion of the power of energy, it belongs to the supramundane path alone.

Furthermore, because there is no wandering away due to the absence of decline, it should be understood that the meanings of "grasping" and "non-wandering" already taken up below are not included here.
Concentration (samādhi) is so called in the sense of being "unclouded" due to the absence of the turbidity of defilements; it is concentration in the sense of "immovability" due to its unshakability.
It is [concentration] because it is liberated from defilements either by suppression or by eradication, and because it is intent upon the object.
Concentration (*samādhi*) is so called in the sense of being liberated.

It is the state of the mind’s stability by way of the establishment of unity; that is, because through the very power of concentration the mind is firmly established upon a single object, it remains unshakable with respect to its object.
It seeks and searches among the eight pairs [of opposites], and it takes them up.

It should be understood that these three pairs—“does not take up,” “practices” and “does not practice”—are stated with reference to the degrees of weak, medium, and strong access concentration (upacāra) prior to the stage of absorption (appanā).
The pair “meditates” and “causes to meditate” should be understood as referring to access concentration within the context of the absorption process.
[The remaining pairs are: “because of being sought” and “because of not being sought,” “because of being taken up” and “because of not being taken up.”

It should be understood that these four pairs—“because of practicing” and “because of not practicing,” “because of having meditated” and “because of not having meditated”—are stated by way of absorption (*appanā*).

In this context, regarding such terms as “samādhi” (concentration), which means “it seeks what is even” (*samaṃ esati*), the word *sama* refers to absorption; for it indeed levels out (*sameti*) the adverse states.

It is *samā* because it causes [the mind] to settle; or, it is *samā* because it has become even (*samabhūtā*) due to the absence of opposing unevennesses. One seeks (*esati*) that evenness, searching for it by way of one's underlying intention (*ajjhāsayavasena*).
The word *iti* has the sense of a reason; thus, the meaning is "it is concentration (*samādhi*)" because one seeks what is even.

It does not seek the uneven (*visamaṃ nesati*), meaning it does not seek that which is called the unevenness consisting of the various opposites to the jhānas. For the preliminary-stage concentration (*pubbabhāgasamādhi*) has become pliant (*mudubhūta*).
Because it has become initial, it seeks what is even; this is called "seeking unevenness. Because it has become intermediate, due to its state of stability, it takes up what is even;
this is called "not taking up unevenness. Because it has become predominant, due to its proximity to the path of absorption (*appanā*), it proceeds evenly;
this is called "not proceeding unevenly. "It meditates evenly" (*samaṃ jhāyati*) is a neuter gerundive form; it means that having become even, it meditates.
The meaning is that one meditates (*jhāyati*) in an even manner.

For in the cognitive process of absorption (*appanāvīthi*), concentration proceeds in an even manner because it is peaceful due to the departure of opposing states, and because it remains in conformity with the peaceful state of absorption.
Furthermore, "meditates" (*jhāyati*) means "blazes forth" (*pajjalati*), as in: "These lamps blaze throughout the night in this circular hall. And: "Throughout the night..."
As in such passages as, “A lamp of oil burns; and here a lamp of oil would burn,” and so forth.

There is also a reading, “It arises evenly” (*samaṃ jāyati*), meaning it arises in an even manner. However, because of the pairing [of the two terms], the first reading alone is more excellent: “It meditates” (*jhāyati*) and “it causes to meditate” (*jhāpeti*).
“It causes to meditate” means it burns; for it burns by making the states opposed to concentration very distant.

[This is] the name. However, because it is established through the absorption (*appanā*) of seeking (*esanā*), non-seeking (*anesanā*), and so forth, absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*) is expressed by such terms as "because of being sought" (*esitattā*) and "because of not being sought" (*nesitattā*).
"Because of being ignited evenly" (*samaṃ jhātattā*) means because of being kindled evenly. There is also a reading: "because of being born evenly" (*samaṃ jātattā*).
Thus, by way of these eight pairs, there are sixteen; together with the nine preceding ones, these are the twenty-five bases of concentration for concentration.
"Both beneficial and pleasant, thus it is concentration": this, however, is stated for the purpose of establishing the benefit of concentration, which has been accomplished through twenty-five modes.
In that context, *sama* is the meaning of either the word *sama* or the word *saṃ*. For it is "even" (*sama*) because it is free from opposition, agitation, and unevenness.
*Hita* is the meaning of the prefix *ā-*, as it is "placed upon" (*āhita*) the object.
The intended meaning is that it is established by making [the mind] immovable. By both [of these], it is said to be "concentration" (*samādhi*), because it is both even (*sama*) and placed (*āhita*).

It is "blissful" (*sukha*) in the sense of being peaceful (*santa*). As it is said: "Venerable sir, this feeling which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant has been called 'peaceful' and 'sublime bliss' by the Blessed One," and: "But equanimity, because of its peacefulness, is spoken of as bliss."
And because it is so stated, by that word "peaceful" (*santa*) in its sense of being tranquil, concentration accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā-sahagata-samādhi*) is also included.
For all forms of concentration are spoken of here without restriction. And by that word "peaceful," the reason for its being established is stated;
the intended meaning should be understood as: "Because it is peaceful, therefore it is established upon a single object."
The commentary on the exposition of knowledge consisting in the development of concentration is finished.
4. Commentary on the Exposition of Knowledge of the Stability of Phenomena (Dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaniddesa) 45.

Regarding the exposition of the knowledge of the stability of phenomena, in such passages as "the arising and stability of ignorance and formations," etc., it is by means of this [knowledge] that they abide.
“Formations” means stability. What is that? It is ignorance. For it is the cause for the stability of formations by way of their arising and production; thus it is “stability as arising.
It is also the cause for the continued occurrence of those [formations] once they have arisen; thus it is “stability as occurrence.

Although the functional efficacy of a productive condition occurs only at the very moment of producing, nevertheless, because it is precisely those things produced by it that continue to occur, [ignorance acts as the cause] at their own respective moments.
There is indeed a cause for occurrence (*pavatti*); the meaning is that it is the cause for occurrence by way of continuity (*santati*).
Furthermore, *pavatta* is a neuter abstract noun (*bhāvavacana*); therefore, in meaning, *pavatta* and *pavatti* are one and the same.

However, because the word *pavatti* is more familiar, the meaning was stated by connecting it with that term. Since the word *ṭhiti* (stability) can also be formed as an abstract noun, it is not used here [in this specific sense].
The word "stability" (*ṭhiti*) refers to a state of being, and the word "stability" refers to a cause;
thus it is said that "the sign is stability. The meaning is "stability in the form of a sign," which is to say it is the cause.
It is not merely a sign, but rather, as if possessing activity in the production of formations, it exerts itself and strives; thus, [the author] shows its capacity as a condition.

It is said, “the stability of accumulation” (*āyūhana-ṭhiti*); the meaning is “stability consisting of accumulation. Because ignorance, while giving rise to volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), is said to “join them to arising”—that is, it connects them;
and while causing volitional formations to proceed, it is said to “bind them to occurrence”—that is, it fetters them.
Therefore, it is called “the stability of bondage” (*saññoga-ṭhiti*) and “the stability of obstruction” (*palibodha-ṭhiti*). It is that which constitutes bondage.

*Ṭhiti* means "stability," in the sense of being an obstacle. Because ignorance itself, while producing volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), is called the "origin" (*samudaya*) in the sense of being the root cause for both their arising and their continued occurrence;
thus, stability as that which constitutes the origin is "stability-as-origination" (*samudaya-ṭhiti*), meaning stability in the sense of being the root cause.
It is because ignorance itself is the productive condition for the arising of volitional formations, and for their continued occurrence...
Because it is a supporting condition (*upatthambhakapaccaya*), the station of the cause is called the "condition-station" (*paccayaṭṭhiti*);

the meaning is that it is a station consisting of a cause, a station consisting of a condition. For a productive condition is called a "cause," while a supporting condition is called a "condition. This should be applied similarly to the remaining cases as well.

However, in the case of "existence [is the condition] for birth" and "birth [is the condition] for aging-and-death," there is the station of arising (*uppādaṭṭhiti*), the station of binding (*saññogaṭṭhiti*), and the station of cause (*hetuṭṭhiti*).
It should be understood that the terms applied by way of arising are stated figuratively with reference to the aggregates (khandhas) that possess birth, aging, and death.
However, some explain the meaning here according to such a method as: "stability for the sake of arising is 'arising-stability' (uppādaṭṭhiti)," and so forth.
"Ignorance is the condition" is said with regard to the state of ignorance being a condition for volitional formations (saṅkhāras).
It has been said. Because ignorance, too, is produced by conditions, in order to show the discernment of its conditions as well, it was stated:
"Both these phenomena are dependently arisen; thus, wisdom consists in the discernment of conditions. This should be applied similarly to the remaining cases.

However, the statement that "birth is the condition" and "aging-and-death is dependently arisen" is made by way of a figurative expression (*pariyāya*). [The phrase] "the past time... also [is used in this manner].

"Past time" (*atikkantaṃ kālaṃ*) refers to time that has elapsed. "Future duration" (*anāgataṃ addhānaṃ*) refers to time not yet reached. In both cases, the accusative case is used in the sense of absolute connection (*accantasamyoga*). 46.

Now, immediately following the section on the nine modes, setting aside those nine modes and instead employing only the terms *hetu* (cause), *paṭicca* (dependent), and *paccaya* (condition), three sections are demonstrated beginning with:

"Ignorance is the cause; volitional formations are arisen from a cause," and so forth. In the section on the nine modes, [ignorance and formations] are treated by way of the producer (*janaka*) and the supporter (*upatthambhaka*).

The condition has been explained. Here, however, because the section on causes (*hetu-vāra*) and the section on conditions (*paccaya-vāra*) have been presented separately, "cause" (*hetu*) should be understood as the state of being a productive condition, and "condition" (*paccaya*) as the state of being a supporting condition; for each individual condition, such as ignorance (*avijjā*), both modes of functioning are possible.
In the section on dependence (*paṭicca-vāra*), it says "dependent on ignorance," because for its own arising, the formative forces (*saṅkhārā*) depend upon ignorance.
Ignorance (*avijjā*) is "dependent" (*paṭicca*) because it must be approached and gone toward by means of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).

By this, the capacity of ignorance to produce volitional formations is stated. Volitional formations are "dependently arisen" (*paṭiccasamuppanna*) because they have arisen equally, having been made to face—that is, directed toward—ignorance, proceeding in its direction without leaving it.
In the same way, the remaining [terms] should also be applied according to their respective grammatical gender.

"Dependent on ignorance" (*avijjā paṭicca*) is either a reading by way of emphasis, or else the meaning here should be construed by supplying the remainder of the text as "ignorance occurs dependent on its own condition.

The same applies to the remaining [factors]. And since, in all four of these sections, the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) must be demonstrated solely by way of the condition for the twelve factors of dependent origination, [the text specifies] ignorance and so forth...

The knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) is demonstrated by way of only eleven factors; however, it is not demonstrated by way of aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*), because that stands at the end [of the series].

Since aging-and-death is also a condition for sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, for one who examines them by taking aging-and-death as their condition, there is also [the knowledge] of that aging-and-death.
By means of this, the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) is indeed appropriate. 47.

Now, desiring to demonstrate the knowledge of the stability of phenomena by analyzing those same twelve factors of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppādaṅga*) according to twenty aspects, and by showing the four summaries, the three periods, and the three connections, he says:
"In the previous kamma-existence," and so forth. Therein, "in the previous kamma-existence" (*purimakammabhavasmiṃ*)...
"In the previous kamma-existence" means in the kamma-existence of a past birth. "Delusion is ignorance" (*moho avijjā*):

that delusion regarding suffering and so forth at that time, by which one, being deluded, performs kamma—that is ignorance. "Accumulation is volitional formations" (*āyūhanā saṅkhārā*): the preceding volitions of one performing that kamma;
for example, having generated the thought, "I shall give a gift," [and then] continuing for a month or even a year...

The volitions that arise while one is preparing the requisites for giving are called "preparatory volitions" (*purimacetanā*). However, the volition at the moment one places the offering into the hands of the recipients is called "existence" (*bhava*).

Alternatively, among the six impulsive moments (*javana*) consisting of a single cognitive object, the volitions are called "exertion" (*āyūhana*) and "formations" (*saṅkhāra*), while the volition in the seventh impulsion is "existence. Or, whatever volition constitutes existence, the factors associated with it—
The "accumulation" (āyūhanā) is what is called volitional formations (saṅkhārā).
"Attachment" (nikanti) is craving (taṇhā); that which is the longing and aspiration for the fruit of rebirth while one is performing karma is called craving.
"Approaching" (upagamana) is clinging (upādāna); that which serves as the condition for the existence of karma—namely, [the thought] "in this very..."
“Desires are fulfilled when actions are performed,” or “Having done this, I will enjoy desires in such-and-such a place,” or “The self is cut off,
it is well-cut off,” or “One becomes happy, free from fever,” or “One easily fulfills virtue and observances”—
this engagement, this approach, this firm grasping, is called clinging (*upādāna*). It is volition (*cetanā*).
"Becoming" (*bhava*) refers to volition (*cetanā*) spoken of at the conclusion of the process of accumulation;
it is that which occurred while the "kamma-becoming" of a previous birth was being performed. "Conditions here for rebirth-linking" means they serve as conditions for the present rebirth-linking.
Here, "rebirth-linking consciousness" (*viññāṇa*) is so called because it arises by way of linking to another existence within the present becoming.
That which is called "rebirth-linking" (paṭisandhi) is consciousness (viññāṇa). That which is called "descent" (okkanti) is name-and-form (nāmarūpa);

this refers to the descent of material and immaterial phenomena into the womb, as if they were arriving and entering. This is name-and-form. That which is the state of clarity is the sense-base (āyatana);
this is the sense-base. The singular number is used by way of including the genus. By this, the five sense-bases beginning with the eye are stated.
Regarding the statement, “Bhikkhus, this mind is luminous, but it is defiled by adventitious defilements,” it should be understood that here too,
because the mind-base (*manāyatana*) is of the nature of result (*vipāka*), and because it is clear due to the absence of the turbidity of defilements,
the mind-base is also expressed by the term “clarity” (*pasāda*). This is because the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅgacitta*) is intended there.
"Contacted contact" (phuṭṭho phasso) refers to that contact which has arisen having touched or contacted an object; this is contact.

"That which is felt is feeling" (vedayitaṃ vedanā) refers to the resultant feeling that has arisen together with either the rebirth-linking consciousness or with contact conditioned by the six sense bases;
this is feeling. Here, in this present existence of rebirth, it arises due to the condition of previously performed karma.
The meaning is: they proceed by way of the condition of karma performed in a past birth.

Here, because the sense bases (*āyatana*) have reached maturity, delusion and the other factors are shown at the time of performing the karma for one whose sense bases are matured. "In the future, at rebirth-linking" means at rebirth-linking in the future. "In the future, rebirth-linking is consciousness," and so forth, have meanings already stated.
But how are these twenty modes included within the twelve factors of dependent origination? [They are included] through ignorance...

"Formations" (*saṅkhārā*)—these two past causes are stated by way of their specific nature. However, because the ignorant person trembles with fear, and being fearful, clings, and because clinging is a condition for becoming (*bhava*), when those two [past factors] are grasped, craving (*taṇhā*), clinging (*upādāna*), and becoming are also necessarily included.
In the present, consciousness (*viññāṇa*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*), contact (*phassa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) are stated by way of their specific nature.
Craving, clinging, and becoming are stated as the present causes by way of their specific nature.

However, when "becoming" is included, its preceding factors or the formations associated with it are necessarily included; likewise, by the inclusion of craving and clinging, those factors associated with them are also included.
Furthermore, ignorance is necessarily included, for it is through being deluded by it that one performs kamma. In the future, there is birth, aging, and death.

Two [links] are stated by their own names; however, by the inclusion of birth (*jāti*) and aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*), the five beginning with consciousness (*viññāṇa*)—which have their results in the future—are indeed included.
For these very [five] have birth and aging-and-death as their [subsequent links]. Thus, twenty modes are grasped by means of the twelve factors.
"In the past, there are five causes; now, the pentad of results."
"Now, there are five causes and five future fruits"—this is the meaning stated by this verse.
"Itimeti" means "thus these. Or the reading is "iti ime.
"Catusaṅkhpe" means four groups. In the past, the five causal phenomena constitute one group of causes; in the present...
There are five resultant states, which constitute one summary of results; five causal states in the present, which constitute one summary of causes;
and five resultant states in the future, which constitute one summary of results.

"In three periods" means in three times. The past time is to be understood by way of the first pentad; the present time by way of the second and third pentads; and the future time by way of the fourth pentad.
"Tisandhi" means that which has three connections; thus, it is "tisandhi. Between the past cause and the present fruit there is one connection between cause and fruit;
between the present fruit and the future cause there is one connection between fruit and cause; and between the present cause and the future fruit there is one connection between cause and fruit.

According to how they appear in their specific form within the text of the *Paṭiccasamuppāda-pāḷi*, however, ignorance (*avijjā*) and volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) constitute one summary; consciousness (*viññāṇa*), mentality-and-materiality (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*), contact (*phassa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) constitute the second;
craving (*taṇhā*), clinging (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) constitute the third; and birth (*jāti*) and aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*) constitute the fourth.

Ignorance and volitional formations are two factors belonging to the past time; consciousness through becoming are eight factors belonging to the present time; and birth and aging-and-death [belong to the future].

There are two future times. Between formations (*saṅkhāra*) and consciousness (*viññāṇa*), there is one connection between cause and fruit; between feeling (*vedanā*) and craving (*taṇhā*), there is one connection between fruit and cause;
and between existence (*bhava*) and birth (*jāti*), there is one connection between cause and fruit.

"In twenty ways" means by way of twenty sections. The connection is that one knows dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*)—which consists of four summaries, three periods, and three connections—by means of these twenty ways.
"He knows" means he knows by means of the knowledge that initiates development (bhāvanārambhañāṇa) in accordance with what has been heard.

"He sees" means he sees by means of that very same knowledge, having made it clear as if seeing an emblic myrobalan fruit on the palm of the hand, just as something already known is seen with the eye.

"He fully understands" means he knows by means of that very same knowledge while practicing cultivation (āsevana) according to the limit of what has been seen; for here the syllable *ā* has the sense of a limit (*maryāda*). "He penetrates" means [he does so] through the fulfillment of development.

One who reaches the ultimate goal effects penetration by means of knowledge itself. One knows by way of specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*), sees by way of intrinsic nature (*sarasa*), understands by way of manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*), and penetrates by way of proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*).

In this context, "dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) should be understood as the phenomena that act as conditions; "dependently originated phenomena" (*paṭiccasamuppannā dhammā*) refers to those [phenomena] produced by them.
Phenomena produced by those conditions. If it is asked how this is to be known, it is by the word of the Blessed One.
For in the *Paṭiccasamuppāda-paṭiccasamuppanna-dhamma-desanā-sutta*, the Blessed One said:
"And what, monks, is dependent origination? With birth as condition, monks, there is aging and death; from arising..."
Whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this element remains fixed:
the stability of phenomena, the regularity of phenomena, specific conditionality. A Tathāgata awakens to this and realizes it;
having awakened to it and realized it, he declares it, teaches it, lays it out, establishes it, discloses it, analyzes it, clarifies it, saying: “Behold!”
And he said: "Bhikkhus, conditioned by birth is aging-and-death; conditioned by becoming is birth...
[and so on] ...conditioned by ignorance, bhikkhus, are volitional formations. Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this nature of things remains—this causal status, this causal sequence.

But the Tathāgata, having realized and directly known it, proclaims, teaches, establishes, discloses, analyzes, clarifies, and makes plain: 'Behold! Thus, bhikkhus, that which therein is suchness, non-falsity, and non-otherness..."
“Conditionality (idappaccayatā). This, monks, is called dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).
Thus, when teaching dependent origination through such synonyms as “suchness” (tathatā) and so forth, it is the very conditioned phenomena themselves that are called “dependent origination.
Therefore, dependent origination has the characteristic of being the condition for aging, death, and the rest; its function is the continuous succession of suffering.
It has the wrong path as its manifestation; this too, because it possesses conditions, has its own specific condition as its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*).
"Whether there is arising or non-arising" means whether there is arising or non-arising, that is, whether Tathāgatas have appeared or have not appeared.
"That element remains ever the same" means that the nature of the condition remains constant; it is never subject to birth, aging, or death.

The meaning is that it is not a condition. The stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitatā*), the fixed order of phenomena (*dhammaniyāmatā*), and specific conditionality (*idappaccayatā*) are simply the condition of birth.
For it is by means of the condition of birth that the phenomenon known as aging-and-death—which has arisen through conditions—persists because it is dependent upon it;
and the condition of birth alone determines the phenomenon of aging-and-death. Therefore, birth is called "the stability of phenomena" and "the fixed order of phenomena."
It is said: "This very birth is the condition for this aging-and-death" is *idappaccaya*; the state of being such a specific condition is *idappaccayatā*. "That" refers to that condition.
"He fully awakens to" means he fully awakens to it by means of knowledge. "He penetrates" means he arrives at [the truth] by means of knowledge.
"He declares" means he speaks of it. "He teaches" means he shows it. "He makes known" means he causes others to know it. "He establishes" means...
He places it at the opening of knowledge. "He opens up" means having opened it, he shows it. "He analyzes" means he shows it by way of its divisions.
"He makes plain" means he makes it manifest. "Iti kho" means "it is indeed thus. "Yā tatra" means that which [is taught] among those [formulas] such as "with birth as condition, aging-and-death.
Furthermore, this dependent origination [occurs] through those respective conditions, neither deficient nor redundant, for each respective phenomenon.
It is "suchness" (*tathatā*) because it occurs; it is "not-untrue" (*avitathatā*) because there is no absence of the arising of phenomena from those conditions once they have attained completeness;
it is "not-otherwise" (*anaññathatā*) because one phenomenon does not arise from the conditions for another phenomenon;

and it is "conditionality by this" (*idappaccayatā*) because of these aforementioned factors such as aging and death, either by way of their individual conditions or by way of the collection of conditions.

Thus it was said. Herein, this is the etymological analysis: the conditions for these [states] are "these-as-conditions" (*idappaccayā*); the state of being these-as-conditions is "this-conditionality" (*idappaccayatā*);
or else, the collection of these-as-conditions is "this-conditionality. Furthermore, the characteristic [of this term] should be understood from the science of grammar (*saddasattha*).
The commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) is finished.
5. Commentary on the Exposition of Knowledge of Comprehension (Sammasanañāṇaniddesa) 48.

In the exposition of the knowledge of comprehension, the phrase "whatever" (*yaṃ kiñci*) is an exhaustive inclusion without remainder. The term "form" (*rūpa*) is a restriction to prevent over-extension.
Thus, by these two words, the complete grasping of form is accomplished. Then, its classification according to the past and so forth is undertaken.

For that [past] is of various kinds, such as the past, the future, and so forth. This same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates as well. In this context, matter (*rūpa*) is called "past" in four ways:
by way of extent (*addhā*), continuity (*santati*), moment (*samaya*), and instant (*khaṇa*); likewise for the future and the present. Therein, first, by way of extent:
for a single person in a single existence, that which is prior to rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is past; that which is subsequent to death (*cuti*) is future.

The future is that which has not yet arisen; the present is that which exists between those two. By way of continuity, even though it proceeds in a sequence of prior and posterior, that which is produced by a homogeneous temperature or produced by a single nutriment is "present";
what was produced by a heterogeneous temperature or nutriment prior to that is "past," and what will be produced subsequently is "future.
That which is mind-born and produced by a single cognitive series, a single impulsion, or a single attainment is "present."
Prior to that, there is no distinction of past and so forth for what is originated by kamma, according to its own separate continuity;
rather, its state as past and so forth should be understood by way of its support for those [material phenomena] originated by temperature, nutriment, and consciousness.
By way of time, this refers to the continuity during times such as one muhutta, forenoon, afternoon, night, day, and so on.
That which is occurring at a particular time is called "present"; prior to that it is "past," and subsequent to it it is "future.
By way of moment, that which is comprised within the triad of moments beginning with arising is "present"; prior to that it is "future," and subsequent to that it is "past.

Furthermore, the past is that whose functions of cause and condition have already passed; the future is that whose function of cause has been completed but whose function of condition is not yet completed.
The present is that which has reached its own function; the future is that which has not yet reached the functions of both [present and past].

Alternatively, it is present at the moment of performing its own function, future prior to that, and past thereafter. In this context, the discussion of moments (*khaṇa*) and so forth is non-figurative (*nippariyāya*); the rest are figurative (*sapariyāya*).
"Internal" (*ajjhatta*)—among the five aggregates, what is intended here is the "internal by nature" (*niyakajjhatta*); therefore, it refers to one's own continuum (*santāna*).
Materiality that occurs as an individual (pāṭipuggalika) should be understood as internal.

However, materiality external to that—whether bound to the sense faculties or not bound to the sense faculties—is called external. "Gross" refers to the twelvefold materiality consisting of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, visible form, sound, odor, flavor, and tangible object, as well as earth, fire, and air;
it is gross because it is to be apprehended by way of impact. The remainder...

Furthermore, the sixteenfold materiality— consisting of the water element, the femininity faculty, the masculinity faculty, the life faculty, the heart-base, nutritive essence, the space element, bodily intimation, verbal intimation,
lightness of matter, malleability, wieldiness, integration, continuity, aging, and impermanence—
is subtle because it cannot be apprehended by means of impact. Or [it is classified as] inferior or superior.
Herein, the state of being inferior or superior is both figurative (pariyāyato) and literal (nippariyāyato).
In that regard, the form of the Sudassi deities is inferior to the form of the Akaniṭṭha deities, while that same [form] is superior to the form of the Sudassa deities.

In this manner, the state of being inferior or superior should be understood figuratively as far as the forms of beings in the hells. However, in the literal sense, wherever there is unwholesome kamma-result...
That which arises [as unwholesome result] is inferior; that wherein wholesome fruition occurs is sublime. Regarding the phrase "whether far or near":
herein, that which is subtle is "far" because its nature is difficult to penetrate; that which is gross is "near" because its nature is easy to penetrate.
He defines all form as impermanent: this is one mode of comprehension. He defines it as suffering: this is another mode of comprehension.
"Defining it as not-self is one kind of comprehension":

here, this bhikkhu, having delimited all form—referred to without restriction by the words "whatever form"—by means of eleven headings, namely the threefold division of the past and so forth together with the four dyads beginning with internal, he defines all that form as impermanent and comprehends it as "impermanent. How?
According to the method stated previously. For this has been said: “Material form—past, future, and present—is impermanent in the sense of destruction.
Therefore, that past material form is impermanent in the sense of destruction because it was destroyed in the very past and did not reach this existence;
and that future material form which will arise in the immediately succeeding existence is likewise [impermanent] right there.
"It will perish; it will not go to a further existence"—thus, in the sense of perishing, it is impermanent.
Whatever form is present, that perishes right here and does not go from here—thus, in the sense of perishing, it is impermanent.
Whatever internal form there is, that also perishes only internally and does not go to an external state—thus, in the sense of perishing, it is impermanent. Whatever...

One comprehends that whatever is external—whether gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all that is exhausted right here and does not go to a state of distance; thus it is "impermanent in the sense of exhaustion.
All of this constitutes a single mode of comprehension by way of the phrase "impermanent in the sense of exhaustion," yet in its detailed classification, it is elevenfold.
One comprehends all this as suffering in the sense of being fearful. "In the sense of being fearful" means in the sense of being accompanied by dread.
For whatever is impermanent brings fear, just as in the *Sīhupama Sutta* (The Simile of the Lion) regarding the devas.
Thus, this is one mode of comprehension by way of the phrase "suffering in the sense of being fearful"; however, in its detailed classification, it is elevenfold.
And just as it is suffering, so too he comprehends all that as non-self in the sense of being coreless.
"In the sense of being coreless" means by way of the absence of a self-core imagined to be "a self that dwells, acts, feels, and is its own master.
For whatever is impermanent and suffering cannot prevent even the self from being impermanent, or from being oppressed by arising and passing away.
How, then, could it have the status of an agent and so forth? Therefore he said:
“Bhikkhus, if this form were self, this form would not lead to affliction,” and so on. Thus, this is one mode of comprehension by way of the phrase “it is non-self in the sense of being coreless”;
however, when analyzed, it is elevenfold. This same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates. Thus, in each one...
By making eleven groups for each of the aggregates, there are fifty-five contemplations upon the five aggregates;
through the threefold contemplation— namely, fifty-five as impermanent, fifty-five as suffering, and fifty-five as non-self—
there are altogether one hundred and sixty-five contemplations.
However, some say: "By adding the phrases 'all form,' 'all feeling,' 'all perception,' 'all volitional formations,' and 'all consciousness'—
thus making twelve for each aggregate and sixty for the five aggregates— there are one hundred and eighty instances of comprehension by way of contemplation."

Regarding the division into past and so forth herein, the state of feeling as past, future, and present should be understood by way of the continuity (*santati*) and by way of the moment (*khaṇa*), and so on.

Therein, by way of continuity, those feelings included within a single cognitive process (*vīthi*), a single impulsive moment (*javana*), or a single attainment (*samāpatti*), and which arise in conjunction with a single type of object, are present;
those prior to that are past, and those subsequent are future. By way of the moment and so forth, those included within the three moments [of arising, presence, and dissolution] are present.
Feelings that have reached the past, future, and present, and are performing their own function, are "present"; those prior to that are "past," and those subsequent are "future.
The distinction between internal and external should be understood solely by way of one's own personal internal state (*niyakajjhatta*).
The state of being gross or subtle is as stated in such passages as: "Unwholesome feeling is gross; wholesome and indeterminate feelings are subtle."
It should be understood according to the method stated in the *Vibhaṅga*, by way of birth, intrinsic nature, person, mundane, and supramundane.

First, by way of birth: unwholesome feeling is gross compared to wholesome feeling because it is the cause of reprehensible activity, because its mode is the torment of the defilements, and because its course is unpacified;
furthermore, it is [gross] because it involves active effort, exertion, karmic result, the torment of the defilements, and blame.

Furthermore, they are gross compared to the resultant indeterminate (vipākābyākatā) because they possess fruition; and they are gross compared to the functional indeterminate (kiriyābyākatā) because they involve the feverish heat of the defilements, are accompanied by affliction, and are blameworthy.
Conversely, the wholesome and indeterminate feelings are subtle compared to the unwholesome feeling for the reasons already stated.
Both wholesome and unwholesome feelings, moreover, are characterized by activity, exertion, and fruition as appropriate.
The two kinds of the indeterminate are gross; conversely, both kinds of the indeterminate are subtle compared to those [other states].
Thus, first of all, grossness and subtlety should be understood by way of genus.
By way of intrinsic nature, however, painful feeling is gross because it is devoid of gratification, because it is expansive, because it causes agitation, and because it is terrifying.

By way of overcoming, the other two [feelings] are gross compared to the remaining two; however, the other two are subtle compared to suffering, respectively, by way of being pleasant, peaceful, refined, agreeable, and neutral.

Furthermore, both pleasure and pain are gross compared to neither-pain-nor-pleasure by way of their expansion, their capacity to cause agitation, their capacity to disturb, and their manifest nature; whereas that [neither-pain-nor-pleasure] is subtle compared to both of those by way of the reverse of what has been stated.
Subtle. Thus, grossness and subtlety should be understood by way of intrinsic nature.

By way of person, however, the feeling of one who has not attained meditative absorption is gross because it is distracted among various objects; conversely, the feeling of one who has attained absorption is subtle. Thus, grossness and subtlety should be understood by way of person.

By way of the mundane and the supramundane, however, feeling associated with the taints (*āsava*) is mundane; it is mundane because it is a cause for the arising of taints and because it is subject to the floods (*ogha*).
Coarse [states] are those bound by the yokes, bound by the fetters, bound by the hindrances, bound by clinging, subject to defilement, and shared with worldlings;

they are coarse in relation to the taintless. And the subtle are the taintless, being the opposite of the aforementioned. Thus should coarseness and subtlety be understood by way of the mundane and the supramundane.

In this context, the distinction [between types] must be avoided by way of birth (*jāti*) and so forth. For feeling associated with unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness, although it is subtle due to its being indeterminate (*abyākata*) by way of birth, it is nevertheless gross by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and other such factors.

Indeed, this has been said: "Indeterminate feeling is subtle; painful feeling is gross. Feeling of one who has attained meditative absorption is subtle; feeling of one who has not attained absorption is gross. Untainted (*anāsava*) feeling is subtle; tainted (*sāsava*) feeling is gross."
Just as painful feeling is, so too are pleasant feeling and the others. For these, by way of their genus (*jāti*), are gross;

yet by way of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and so forth, they are subtle. Therefore, the grossness and subtlety of feelings should be understood in such a way that there is no confusion regarding their genus and other factors.
For example, neutral feeling is subtle compared to wholesome and unwholesome feelings by way of its genus. In this regard, which...
Are they indeterminate? What is painful? What is pleasant? To whom who has attained meditative absorption? To whom who has not attained absorption? What is with taints? What is without taints?
Thus, the distinction according to intrinsic nature and so forth should not be misapprehended. This same method applies everywhere. Furthermore:
"But by taking this or that feeling as a reference, feelings are to be regarded as gross or subtle."
According to the verbal definition, among the unwholesome states and so forth, feeling accompanied by greed or accompanied by hatred is gross because it burns its support like a fire;
that which is accompanied by greed is subtle. Among those accompanied by hatred, that which is fixed is gross, while that which is unfixed is subtle.
Among the fixed, that which lasts for an eon is gross, while the other is subtle. Even among those lasting for an eon, that which is unprompted is gross, while the other is subtle.

[The latter] is subtle. However, that which is accompanied by greed and associated with wrong view is gross; the other is subtle. Furthermore, that which is fixed, lasting for an eon, and unprompted is gross;
the other is subtle. Generally speaking, unwholesome states with great fruition are gross, while those with little fruition are subtle.
Wholesome states, however, with little fruition are gross, while those with great fruition are subtle.

Furthermore, the wholesome states of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) are gross; those of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) are subtle; those of the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*) are subtler than those; and those of the supramundane (*lokuttara*) are subtler still.

Within the sense-sphere, those consisting of giving (*dānamaya*) are gross, while those consisting of virtue (*sīlamaya*) are subtle. Even among those consisting of virtue, those that are gross are subtler than those consisting of meditation (*bhāvanāmaya*).

Within those consisting of meditation, those with two roots (*duhetuka*) are gross, while those with three roots (*tihetuka*) are subtle. Even among those with three roots, those accompanied by volitional effort (*sasaṅkhārika*) are gross...

Coarse [states] are those that are unprompted, while subtle [states] are those that are prompted. Within the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), those associated with the first jhāna are coarse... pe ...while those associated with the fifth jhāna are indeed subtle.

Within the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*), those associated with the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*) are coarse... pe ...while those associated with the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) are indeed subtle.

Within the supramundane (*lokuttara*), those associated with the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*) are coarse... pe ...while those associated with the path of arhatship (*arahattamagga*) are [subtle].

Subtle. This same method applies to the resultant and functional feelings of each respective plane, as well as to the feelings described by way of being painful, etc., not attained, and with taints, etc.
Or else, by way of location: in hell, painful feeling is gross; in the animal realm, it is subtle...
[and so on] ...in the Paranimmitavasavatti deities, it is subtle. And just as with painful feeling, so too with pleasant feeling everywhere, according to what is appropriate.
They should be applied. Furthermore, by way of their basis (*vatthu*), any feeling with an inferior basis is gross, while that with a superior basis is subtle.
Within the division of inferior and superior, that which is gross should be understood as inferior, and that which is subtle as superior.
As for the terms "distant" and "near," unwholesome feeling is distant from wholesome and indeterminate feelings; unwholesome feeling...

[This] is analyzed in the Vibhaṅga by way of such passages as, “proximate to unwholesome feeling,” and so forth. Therefore, unwholesome feeling is distant from wholesome and indeterminate [feelings] because it is dissimilar, unassociated, and unlike; likewise, wholesome and indeterminate [feelings] are distant from the unwholesome.
This same method applies to all sections. However, unwholesome feeling is near [to other unwholesome feelings] because it is similar, associated, and like.
"And in the presence of the unwholesome"—this is the introductory heading for the detailed exposition on the classification of feeling into the past and so forth.

This should be understood in exactly the same way for perception and the other mental factors associated with each respective feeling. Furthermore, regarding those phenomena here—feeling and so on—which have been abbreviated by the formula "eye... [and so forth] ...aging-and-death":
Supramundane states have been mentioned; because they do not come within the scope of comprehension (*asammasanūpagattā*), they should not be included in this section.

However, they were stated merely to show that those states are comprised by various specific terms, and according to the method presented in the "Description of What is to be Directly Known" (*abhiññeyyaniddesa*).
Furthermore, among those states that do come within the scope of comprehension, whichever ones are clear to an individual and are easily grasped—

Among those [three periods], he should begin the contemplation (*sammasana*) with that [present period]. Although there is no separate contemplation by way of birth, aging, and death, it should be understood that when one contemplates those very things that possess birth, aging, and death, those [factors] are also contemplated;

thus, the contemplation is said to be performed by way of them as well, according to the method beginning with "he defines the past, future, and present as impermanent. This refers specifically to the triad of the past.
Since it is stated that comprehension is performed by way of the three periods of time, even though the internal and other divisions have not been specifically mentioned,
one must indeed perform the comprehension of impermanence and so forth by delimiting [the object] solely by way of the past triad.
Furthermore, because whatever is impermanent is necessarily characterized by the divisions of the conditioned and so forth, this is for the purpose of showing its synonyms.
Or, for the purpose of showing the occurrence of attention in various modes, he said: "Form—past, future, and present—is impermanent, conditioned," and so forth.
For that [form] is impermanent in the sense of having ceased after having been; it is impermanent by way of its impermanent termination or its possession of a beginning and an end.
It is conditioned because it is made by the coming together of conditions. It is equal (sama) by depending upon and relying on conditions.

Or, it is "dependently arisen" (paṭiccasamuppanna) because it has arisen together [with its conditions]. By this, he shows that even though things are produced by these conditions, the conditions themselves are devoid of agency (abyāpārataṃ).
"Subject to destruction" (khayadhammaṃ) means having the nature of decaying, having decay as its inherent character. "Subject to vanishing" (vayadhammaṃ) means having the nature of perishing.
This is not "subject to destruction" in the sense of a gradual fading away; rather, it simply has the inherent character of passing away. Of that which is abundant...
For even a state of becoming dull is called "decay" (vaya) in the world.

As for the phrase "subject to fading away" (virāgadhamma), this does not mean subject to decay by way of going anywhere; it simply means having the nature of transcending its own inherent essence. For it is said: "Fading away (virāga) means either disgust or transcendence.
As for the phrase "subject to cessation" (nirodhadhamma), this does not mean subject to returning again after transcending its own inherent essence; it simply means...

It should be understood that each subsequent term is stated by way of explaining the meaning of each preceding term, [showing] that its nature is to cease through non-returning cessation (*apunarāvatti-nirodha*).

Alternatively, it is "subject to destruction" (*khayadhamma*) by way of the dissolution of material form included within a single existence (*ekabhava*), and by way of the destruction of material form included within a single continuum (*ekasantati*).

One should also apply [the analysis] thus: "subject to vanishing" means subject to fading away by way of the momentary destruction of form; "subject to cessation" means subject to non-recurrence of all three [aggregates].
In such passages as "aging-and-death is impermanent," it is not aging-and-death itself that is impermanent, but rather the aggregates which possess the nature of impermanence.

Because it is subject to aging and death, what is born is called impermanent. This same method applies to the conditioned and so forth. In the intermediate series, the same method applies to birth as well regarding its impermanence and other characteristics.
The statement "with birth as condition, aging and death" and so forth is not stated by way of insight (vipassanā); it is merely [stated] for the sake of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).
It is stated figuratively that "knowledge of comprehension" (sammasanañāṇa) arises from defining [the aggregates] by way of each individual factor after having condensed them;

however, this knowledge of comprehension by groups (kalāpasammasanañāṇa) is not itself the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa). In the phrase "when there is no birth," a change of gender has been made;
it means "when there is no birth. In the phrase "when there are no formations," a change of number has been made; it means "when they do not exist."

"Regarding formations," this is what is meant. "With existence as condition, birth; if there were no [existence]," and so forth, should be applied according to the method beginning with: "With existence as condition, birth; if there were no existence, birth would not exist.
The commentary on the description of knowledge of comprehension is finished.
6. Commentary on the Exposition of Knowledge of Arising and Passing Away (Udayabbayañāṇa) 49.

Now, having reached the further shore by means of various methods of consolidating the development of the knowledge of comprehension (sammasanañāṇa) mentioned immediately prior, one who stands firm therein defines the formations seen as impermanent, etc., by way of their arising and passing away, and [views them] as impermanent, etc.
In the exposition of the knowledge of contemplation of rise and fall, which is taught for the purpose of insight (*vipassanā*), regarding the phrases "matter that has arisen" and so forth:

matter produced by its respective conditions in a continuous series is what is meant. Of that arisen matter, the characteristic of production—its arising, its new manifestation—is called "rise" (*udaya*);
the characteristic of change—its passing away, its dissolution—is called "fall" (*vaya*). This is the contemplation (*anupassanā*).
"Repeated observation" means the knowledge of contemplation of rise and fall (*udayabbaya-anupassanā-ñāṇa*). This same method applies to feeling (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates as well.

Since rise and fall must be discerned only in those things that possess birth, aging, and death, and because there is no rise and fall in birth, aging, and death themselves, the abbreviated formula (*peyyāla*) was made by omitting birth, aging, and death, beginning with "the eye that has arisen... and ending with "...existence that has arisen. He, thus...
Seeing the arising and passing away of the five aggregates, he knows thus:
"Prior to the arising of these aggregates, there was no heap or accumulation; even as they arise, there is no coming from a heap or from an accumulation;
even as they cease, there is no going to any direction or intermediate direction; and even when they have ceased..."
In a single location, there is no standing as a heap, a collection, or a hoard. Just as, when a lute is being played,
the sound that arises has no accumulation prior to its arising, nor does it come from an accumulation while it is arising,
nor is there any going toward the cardinal or intermediate directions as it ceases, nor does it remain anywhere once it has ceased.
"It does not remain stored; rather, depending on the lute, the plectrum, and the appropriate effort of the person, it comes into being where it was not, and having been, it passes away.
In this same way, all phenomena, both material and immaterial, come into being where they were not, and having been, they pass away.
Having thus shown the observation of arising and passing away in brief, he now shows it in detail regarding the five [aggregates].

Having asked about the counting by aggregate with such questions as, "When one sees the arising of the aggregates, how many characteristics does one see?", and having answered the counting by aggregate itself with such replies as,
"When one sees the arising of the five aggregates, one sees twenty-five characteristics," [the text continues] again with such questions as,
"When one sees the arising of the materiality aggregate, how many characteristics does one see? and so forth.
Having asked about the enumeration by way of classification, the answer was given after first stating that one who sees the arising of the aggregate of form sees five characteristics,

and so forth; then, having again asked about the analysis of the characteristics— specifically, "What five characteristics does one who sees the arising of the aggregate of form see?"— the answer was provided.

In this context, "with the arising of ignorance there is the arising of form" means that when ignorance—which was described as "delusion in a previous kamma-existence"—is present, there is the arising of form in this present existence.
"In the sense of the arising of conditions" means in the sense of the occurrence of the conditions. And here, ignorance, craving, and kamma are the causes for rebirth-linking in this life.
[This is] by way of past conditions. And when these three are taken, the clinging to formations is necessarily included as well.

Regarding "from the origination of nutriment," among the conditions for the process of existence (*pavatti*), edible nutriment (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*) is taken because it is the most powerful; and when that is taken, the temperature and consciousness that serve as causes for the process are also necessarily included.
"The characteristic of generation" refers to the materiality [of the aggregates] by way of the periods of time (*addhā*), continuity (*santati*), and moments (*khaṇa*).
Arising (uppāda) is called a "characteristic" precisely because it is a characteristic of the conditioned (saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa).
As for the "five characteristics," these five are ignorance (avijjā), craving (taṇhā), the nutriment of kamma (kammāhāra), and actualization (nibbatti).

For ignorance and the others are also "characteristics" in the sense that the arising of matter is characterized by them. Actualization, however, is itself a characteristic of the conditioned; it too is conditioned.
It is called a "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) because it is characterized by this.

Regarding the statement "with the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of form": when ignorance—which serves as the condition for future existence—is ceased in this present life through the knowledge of the path of Arahantship, the non-arising of future form due to the absence of its conditions is its cessation.
The meaning is "it comes to be. "By way of the cessation of conditions" means by way of the ceased state of the condition.
And here, "cessation" refers specifically to the cessation of ignorance, craving, and karma, which are the conditions for future rebirth-linking.

"With the cessation of nutriment, there is the cessation of form" means that in the absence of the edible nutriment, which is a condition for the process of existence, there is an absence of the material form produced by it.
The characteristic of change (*vipariṇāma-lakkhaṇa*) refers to the breaking up of material form (*rūpa*) by way of duration, continuity, and moment;
it is called a "characteristic" precisely because this breaking up is a conditioned characteristic (*saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa*). Here, "five characteristics" refers to five:

four consisting of the non-existence and cessation of ignorance, craving, and the nutriment of kamma, and one consisting of change. This same method applies to the sections on feeling and so forth. However, this is the distinction:

The observation of the arising and passing away of the formless aggregates is by way of the continuity of the life-span, not by way of the moment. Contact is the condition for the occurrence of the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations;
with the cessation of that [contact], there is the cessation of them. Name-and-form is the condition for the occurrence of the consciousness aggregate;
with the cessation of that [name-and-form], there is the cessation of it.

However, some say: “In the contemplation of rise and fall by way of conditions, without touching upon the classification into past and so forth, one grasps the mere state of arising—that it ‘arises through ignorance and the rest’—in terms of universal commonality, but not [the specific momentary] arising.
One grasps the mere state of non-arising—that it ‘ceases through the cessation of ignorance and the rest’—but not [specific] dissolution.
In the contemplation of rise and fall by way of moments, [one grasps] those of the present...”
“He grasps arising and passing away.
However, the practitioner of insight (vipassaka), while practicing insight, first attends to the rise and fall from the perspective of conditions;
then, at the time of insight, having set aside the four factors beginning with ignorance, he takes up only the aggregates that possess rise and fall, and [observes] their rise and fall.

Thus, for that practitioner of insight who sees in detail the rise and fall according to conditions and according to moments—seeing that "such is the rising of form and the rest, such is their passing away; thus do form and the rest arise, thus do they pass away"—his knowledge becomes even clearer:
"Indeed, these phenomena, having not been, come to be; having been, they vanish. This occurs through the distinctions of the truths, dependent origination, the method, and the characteristics.

They become clear. For when he sees the arising of the aggregates from the arising of ignorance and so forth, and the cessation of the aggregates from the cessation of ignorance and so forth, this is his vision of rise and fall in terms of conditions (*paccayato*).

But when, seeing the characteristics of production and the characteristics of change, he sees the rise and fall of the aggregates, this is his vision of rise and fall in terms of moments (*khaṇato*). Precisely at the moment of their arising...
For the characteristic of arising exists at the moment of generation, and the characteristic of change exists at the moment of dissolution.

Thus, for one who sees in this way the rise and fall in two ways—both from the perspective of conditions and from the perspective of moments—the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*) becomes evident through the vision of the rise from the perspective of conditions, because of the realization of the producer.
