Through the vision of the rise from the perspective of moments, the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) [becomes evident].
The truth of suffering becomes evident through the realization of the suffering inherent in birth.

Through the vision of passing away by way of conditions, the truth of cessation becomes evident, owing to the realization that what possesses conditions will not arise when those conditions do not arise. Through the vision of passing away by way of moments, the truth of suffering itself becomes evident, owing to the realization of the suffering of death.
And as for this vision of its arising and passing away, it is said: "This is the mundane path."
The truth of the path becomes clear there through the destruction of delusion.
And through the vision of its arising by way of conditions, the forward order of dependent origination becomes clear through the realization that "when this exists, that comes to be.
Through the vision of its passing away by way of conditions, the reverse order of dependent origination becomes clear.
It exists through the realization that "with the cessation of this, that ceases.

However, from the perspective of the moment, conditioned phenomena (*paṭiccasamuppanna-dhammā*) become evident through the vision of their arising and passing away, due to the realization of the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa*).
For those things which possess arising and passing away are conditioned, and they are dependently originated.

Through the vision of arising from the perspective of conditions, the method of unity (*ekattanaya*) becomes evident, because one understands the non-interruption of the continuum through the connection between cause and fruit.
Thereupon, one abandons the view of annihilation (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*) even more thoroughly.

Through the vision of arising from the perspective of moments, the method of diversity (*nānattanaya*) becomes evident, because one understands the arising of ever-new [states]. Thereupon, one abandons the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*) even more thoroughly.

He abandons [the view of self]. Through the vision of the arising and passing away of conditions, the method of non-agency becomes clear to him, because he realizes that phenomena are not subject to his control.

Then he abandons the view of self even more thoroughly. Furthermore, through the vision of arising by way of conditions alone, the method of the nature of things (*evam-dhammatā*) becomes clear, because he realizes that the fruit arises in accordance with its conditions. Then he [abandons it] even more thoroughly...
He abandons the view of non-action.

Through the vision of arising from the perspective of conditions, the characteristic of non-self becomes manifest, because of the realization that phenomena are devoid of agency and exist dependent upon conditions.

Through the vision of rise and fall from the perspective of moments, the characteristic of impermanence becomes manifest, because of the realization that what has come to be ceases to exist, and because of the realization of the seclusion of the past and future limits.
Furthermore, the characteristic of suffering becomes evident through the realization that [formations] are oppressed by rise and fall.
The characteristic of individual essence also becomes evident through the realization that they are delimited by rise and fall.

Within the characteristic of individual essence, the temporary nature of the characteristic of the formed also becomes evident, through the realization that there is no fall at the moment of rise, and no rise at the moment of fall.

When the method and characteristics of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) have thus become manifest to him, formations (*saṅkhārā*) appear as ever-new, such that he thinks: "In this way, indeed, these phenomena arise that have never arisen before; having arisen, they cease.
Not only are they ever-new, but like a dewdrop at sunrise or a bubble on water, they vanish as soon as they appear.

Furthermore, they appear as transient as a line of ants, a mustard seed on the point of an awl, or a flash of lightning; and they appear as essence-less and devoid of substance, like an illusion, a mirage, a dream, a water-wheel, a city of Gandharvas, a bubble, a plantain trunk, and so forth.
To this extent, by means of this mode—"only that which is subject to decay arises, and what has arisen passes into decay"—he has penetrated the fifty characteristics and stands firm.
The contemplation of rise and fall is the first knowledge of insight that has been attained; through its attainment, one comes to be reckoned as "one who has commenced insight.
For one established in this knowledge, ten imperfections of insight (vipassanūpakkilesa), beginning with illumination (obhāsa), arise.
Due to their arising, an unskilled practitioner, perceiving them as the knowledge of the path, [clings] to what is not the path.
If one grasps [them] thinking, "This is the path," one remains entangled in the tangle of the defilements.

However, the skilled practitioner, applying insight to those states, disentangles the tangle of the defilements and distinguishes between what is the path and what is not the path, thinking: "These states are not the path;
rather, the knowledge of insight that has entered the right course and is freed from defilements is the path. For him who does so...
The knowledge that stands having discerned both the path and the non-path is called purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path.

At this point, the determination of the four truths has been accomplished by him. How so? Because when there is a comprehension of mind-and-body (nāmarūpa), the comprehension of conditions becomes possible;
thus, it is stated by the very term "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa), which is synonymous with purification of view (diṭṭhivisuddhi).
By means of the determination of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-vavatthāpana*), the determination of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) is accomplished;

by means of the discernment of conditions (*paccayapariggahaṇa*), which is known as purification by overcoming doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇa-visuddhi*), the determination of the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*) is accomplished;

and by means of the contemplation of rise and fall (*udayabbayānupassanā*)—that is, by seeing rise and fall from the perspective of moments—the determination of the truth of suffering is accomplished, while by seeing rise from the perspective of conditions, the determination of the truth of origination is accomplished.

There is the definition [of the truth of suffering] through the observation of its passing away by way of conditions; there is the definition of the truth of cessation through the observation of its arising and passing away;

and because of the destruction of delusion regarding the thought "this path is mundane," there is made the definition of the truth of the path by the practitioner of insight correctly determining the right path within this purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path. Thus, by the mundane...
Thus, by means of that knowledge, the definition of the four truths has been accomplished.
The commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of arising and passing away is finished.
7. Commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution.

51. Thus, the practitioner established in the contemplation of rise and fall (udayabbayānupassanā), having identified through the discernment of what is and is not the path that the knowledge of the contemplation of rise and fall—now free from defilements and entered upon its proper course—is the "path," begins once again the contemplation of rise and fall in order to make that very path thoroughly clear by means of the observation of the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa). Through rise and fall...
He contemplates delimited formations as impermanent and so forth. Thus, his knowledge proceeds keenly;
formations appear swiftly. When knowledge proceeds keenly and formations appear swiftly, he transcends their arising and comes to rest in their dissolution alone.
Or, because of his inclination toward cessation, having abandoned arising—
One establishes mindfulness precisely upon dissolution. At this point, the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā-ñāṇa*) arises.
Now, regarding the exposition of that knowledge: "With a material object, consciousness arises and dissolves" means that consciousness with a material object arises and dissolves.
Alternatively, the meaning is: "Consciousness, in the state of having a material object, arises and dissolves."
“He reflects upon that object” means: having reflected upon—that is, having known—that visible-form object, he sees it as subject to destruction and subject to vanishing;

this is the meaning. “He contemplates the dissolution of that consciousness” means: with another consciousness, he contemplates the dissolution of that very consciousness by which that visible-form object was seen as subject to destruction and subject to vanishing; this is the meaning.
Therefore the ancients said: "One contemplates both the known and the knowing. Here, "mind" (citta) is intended as the mind together with its associated mental factors.
"Contemplates" (anupassati) means he sees again and again; the meaning is that he sees it repeatedly in various modes.
Thus he said: "How does he contemplate? He contemplates as impermanent," and so forth. In this context, since what is called "dissolution" (bhaṅga)...
It is the ultimate limit of impermanence; therefore, the practitioner who contemplates dissolution contemplates every form as impermanent, not as permanent.

Then, because what is impermanent is suffering, and because what is suffering is non-self, he contemplates that very same thing as suffering, not as pleasure. He contemplates it as non-self, not as self. For whatever is impermanent...
It is suffering and non-self; it should not be delighted in. That which should not be delighted in should not be lustfully attached to.

Therefore, by following this contemplation of dissolution, seeing that "it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self," he becomes disenchanted with the category of form that has been seen, rather than finding delight in it.
He becomes dispassionate, rather than lustful. Thus becoming dispassionate, first of all by means of the mundane [path]...
By means of knowledge he ceases lust; he does not cause it to arise, nor does he bring about its origination—this is the meaning.
Alternatively, he is so dispassionate toward the visible forms that he likewise ceases even the unseen by means of inferential knowledge (*anvaya-ñāṇa*);
he does not cause them to arise. He attends only to cessation, he sees only cessation, and not origination—this is the meaning.

Thus practicing in this way, one relinquishes; one does not grasp. What is meant by this? This contemplation of impermanence and so forth is both a relinquishment through abandonment and a relinquishment through leaping forward.
It is a relinquishment through abandonment because, by means of the "overcoming of factors" (*tadaṅga*), it completely casts off the defilements along with the formative activities of the aggregates.
And it is a relinquishment through leaping forward because, by seeing the fault in the conditioned, it leaps forward into Nibbāna—which is the opposite of that—by inclining toward it.
Thus it is said. Therefore, a bhikkhu endowed with that [insight] abandons the defilements and leaps into Nibbāna according to the method already described.
Nor does he take up defilements by way of rebirth, nor does he take up a conditioned object by way of seeing it as faultless.
For this reason it is said: "He relinquishes; he does not take up."
52. Now, in order to show by means of those knowledges which phenomena are abandoned, it is said: "Contemplating as impermanent, one abandons the perception of permanence," and so forth.
Therein, *nandi* is craving accompanied by rapture; *rāga* is the remaining types of craving;
*samudaya* is the arising of craving, or alternatively, the arising of whatever has become form (*rūpagata*). *Ādāna* is [craving] by way of its producing [rebirth].
It is the grasping of the defilements. The phrases "having feeling as its object," and so forth, should be understood according to the method already explained both here and below.

In the verses, however, "shifting the basis" means that after seeing the dissolution of each [object] among form and the rest, one again sees the dissolution of the very consciousness by which that dissolution was seen;
thus, it is a shifting from the previous basis to another basis by way of seeing the dissolution of that [consciousness]. By wisdom...
And "turning away" (*vivaṭṭanā*) is the abiding in the passing away after abandoning the arising.

"The power of adverting" (*āvajjanā-balañceva*) refers to the capacity to advert immediately thereafter for the purpose of seeing the dissolution of the mind that has dissolution as its object, after having seen the dissolution of each [factor] among form and so forth.
"Reflective insight" (*paṭisaṅkhā-vipassanā*) is this reflective contemplation of the object, known as the contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā*). By means of the sequence of the object...
"Both are defined as one" means that by following and pursuing an object seen directly, one defines both [the present and the future] as having the same single nature, thinking:
"Just as this is, so too the conditioned state broke up in the past, and it will break up in the future.
This has also been said by the ancients:
“With pure vision regarding what is presently existing, he leads [the mind] accordingly to the past and the future;
for all conditioned things are evaporating, like drops of dew when the sun has risen.
Thus, having established a single determination for both through their dissolution, one is intent upon cessation (*nirodha*). In this way...
The meaning is: being intent upon cessation, which is reckoned as dissolution; having respect for it, leaning toward it, inclining toward it, and tending toward it.
"Insight into the characteristic of fall" means that this is what is called insight into the characteristic of fall.
"And reflects on the object" means having known the preceding object, such as form and so forth. "And contemplates its dissolution" refers to that object.
Having seen the dissolution [of formations], he contemplates the dissolution of the consciousness that has that as its object. Regarding "the appearance as empty":

for one who thus contemplates dissolution, the appearance as empty succeeds, [realizing] that "only formations break up; their breaking up is death; there is nothing else whatsoever. Thus said the ancients:
“The aggregates cease, there is nothing else; the dissolution of the aggregates is called death.
He who is heedful sees their destruction, like piercing a gem with a diamond in the proper way.

Higher wisdom as insight (*adhipaññā-vipassanā*) consists of that which is reflection upon the object, that which is contemplation of dissolution, and that which is [contemplation] through emptiness (*suññatā*).
"Attendance"—this is what is meant by "higher wisdom insight.

"Skilled in the three contemplations" means a monk who is proficient in the three contemplations beginning with impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*). "And in the four insights" refers to the four insights beginning with disenchantment (*nibbidā*).
"Skill in the three modes of attendance" refers to this threefold [attendance] as destruction, as vanishing, and as emptiness (*khayato vayato suññato*).
"By skill in attendance. "He does not waver among various views" means he does not tremble amidst the various kinds of views such as eternalism and so forth.
Thus not wavering, his attention proceeds [with the thought]: "It is only that which has not ceased which ceases;
it is only that which is unbroken which breaks," just like a fragile vessel breaking, or like fine dust being scattered.
Just as when sesame seeds are being crushed, one sees only their breaking apart, having discarded the signs of their arising, stability, and occurrence; so too,
a man with good eyesight standing on the bank of a lotus pond or a river,
while heavy rain is falling, sees large water-bubbles arising upon the surface of the water.
Just as one might see bubbles arising and bursting very rapidly, even so he sees that all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā) are breaking up, breaking up.
It was with reference to such a practitioner that the Blessed One said:
"As one would see a bubble, as one would see a mirage..."
“The King of Death does not see one who thus contemplates the world.
For one who thus frequently sees that “all conditioned phenomena break up, they break up,” the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution, accompanied by eight benefits, reaches its full strength.
Therein, these are the eight benefits: the abandoning of the view of becoming;... [and so forth].

The relinquishing of attachment to life, constant application and exertion, purity of livelihood, the abandoning of zeal for gain, freedom from fear, the attainment of patience and gentleness, and the endurance of both the unpleasant and the pleasant. Regarding this, the ancients said:
"Having seen these eight supreme qualities, he reflects upon them there again and again."
“The sage is like one whose head and clothes are on fire; contemplating dissolution for the attainment of the Deathless.
The commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of contemplating dissolution is finished.
8. Commentary on the Exposition of the Knowledge of Disadvantage (Ādīnavañāṇa).
53. In the exposition of the knowledge of danger (ādīnava-ñāṇa): "Arising" (uppāda) is birth here through the condition of previous karma.
"Occurrence" (pavatta) is the process of that which has thus arisen. "Sign" (nimitta) is the sign of all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra-nimitta).

"Accumulation" (āyūhana) is the karma that serves as the cause for rebirth in the future. "Rebirth-linking" (paṭisandhi) is arising in the future. "Destiny" (gati) is the state of existence in which that rebirth-linking occurs. "Generation" (nibbatti) is—

The production of the aggregates. "Rebirth" (*upapatti*) refers to the occurrence of resultant consciousness as described in the phrase, "of one who has attained [jhāna] or of one who has been reborn.
"Birth" (*jāti*) is birth conditioned by existence (*bhava*), which serves as the condition for aging and the rest.
In the non-figurative sense, it is the first manifestation of whichever aggregates appear for beings being produced here and there.
Birth (*jāti*). Aging (*jarā*) is understood as the state of decay and so forth; it is the agedness of the continuum of aggregates included within a single existence.

Sorrow (*soka*) is the mental burning of one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives and other such misfortunes. Lamentation (*parideva*) is the verbal outpouring of one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives and other such misfortunes.
Despair (*upāyāsa*) is intense exhaustion; it is produced by the extreme mental suffering of one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives and other such misfortunes.
It is precisely this. And here, the five factors beginning with arising (*uppāda*) are stated as the objective bases for the knowledge of danger (*ādīnavañāṇa*);
the remaining terms are synonyms for them. For the pair "origination" (*nibbatti*) and "birth" (*jāti*) are synonyms for both arising and rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*);

the pair "destiny" (*gati*) and "reappearance" (*upapatti*) are synonyms for the process of existence (*pavatta*); and "aging" (*jarā*) and so forth are synonyms for the sign (*nimitta*). Therefore, he said:
“One sees arising and occurrence, and the sign as suffering;
accumulation and rebirth-linking—this is knowledge regarding danger.
And: “This knowledge of danger arises in five places.”

In all instances, the word *bhayanti* (it is fearful) should be analyzed as *bhayam iti* (it is fear). It is called "fear" (*bhaya*) because it is associated with affliction and possesses a state of dread. *Iti* is an indication of the cause for the manifestation of fear.

The passage beginning with "Non-arising is security; knowledge of the state of peace," etc., is stated for the purpose of showing the knowledge that is the antidote to the knowledge of danger (*ādīnava*).
Alternatively, for those whose hearts are agitated after seeing danger through the manifestation of fear, there is indeed fearlessness and security.
This was said for the purpose of producing confidence because it is free from defects;

or rather, it should be understood that this was said to show the benefits of the knowledge of danger (ādīnavañāṇa) established by way of the appearance as terror (bhayatupaṭṭhāna), since the mind of one for whom the arising and so forth [of formations] are well-established as fearsome becomes inclined toward their opposite. Non-arising (anuppāda).
"Non-arising," and so forth, refers to Nibbāna itself. "In the state of peace" (*santipade*) means in the portion that is peace; the meaning is "in Nibbāna.
For even knowledge that arises by taking up the mere name "state of peace" through hearsay is called "knowledge regarding the state of peace.
Both [terms]—arising as danger and non-arising as security—are combined by way of their opposites, as in the passage beginning, "Arising is fear, non-arising is security."
This was stated by taking "knowledge" (ñāṇa) as the subject. And herein, whatever is fear is necessarily suffering.

Whatever is suffering is indeed "with bait" (sāmisa), because it is not free from the bait of the round of existence (vaṭṭāmisā), the bait of the world (lokāmisā), and the bait of the defilements (kilesāmisā). And whatever is with bait is merely conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra-matta). Therefore, it is said:
"The wisdom that establishes [phenomena] as fearful—that arising is suffering—is knowledge of danger," and so forth. Even though this is so,

In this context, diversity should be understood by way of the diversity of modes (ākāra) and the mode of occurrence: as the mode of fear, the mode of suffering, the mode of the worldly (sāmisā), and the mode of formations (saṅkhārā).

Thus, without regard for the characteristics of arising and so forth—such as in the passages, "This refuge is not secure; this refuge is not supreme"—it is here considered solely with regard to its own characteristic, namely: "Arising is fear, suffering, the worldly, and formations."

It has been stated. Regarding the term "formations" (*saṅkhārā*), the plural number is used without regard for their oneness, as in such expressions as "unconditioned phenomena" (*appaccayā dhammā*) or "uncompounded phenomena" (*asaṅkhatā dhammā*).

Alternatively, it should be understood that the plural is used even for a part of many, because [the three characteristics] arising and so forth are parts of formations, just as in the expressions "the Eastern Pañcālas" or "the Southern Pañcālas. It is secure and blissful.
“Nirvāṇa is unworldly”: nirvāṇa itself is described in four ways by way of being the opposite of the aforementioned modes.

“He understands ten kinds of knowledge”: while understanding the knowledge of danger, he understands, penetrates, and realizes ten kinds of knowledge—five having arising and so forth as their basis, and five having non-arising and so forth as their basis. “Skill in two kinds of knowledge”...
"Through proficiency in these two kinds of knowledge, namely, the knowledge of danger and the knowledge of the state of peace.
"He does not waver among various views" means he does not tremble before views that occur by way of such things as the supreme Nibbāna in this very life.
The commentary on the description of the knowledge of danger is finished.
9. Explanation of the Description of Knowledge of Equanimity Towards Formations (Saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaniddesavaṇṇanā) 54.

In the description of the knowledge of equanimity towards formations, "arising" and so forth have meanings already explained. "Suffering," "fear," "the worldly," and "formations" are terms for the causes of the knowledge that relinquishes arising and so forth.
And thus, by way of its characteristic, it is equanimity towards formations.

Having thus shown [the term] by way of its phrasing, he now says "Equanimity regarding formations" (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) and so forth, in order to show it by way of its meaning: "He looks on with equanimity at those formations.

In this context, "he looks on with equanimity at formations" refers to that practitioner who has begun insight; because he has seen the three characteristics through the knowledge of insight, his activity regarding the investigation of characteristics has ceased.
Thus, as he views the three realms of existence as if they were ablaze, there is the grasping of formations.
The meaning is this: for one who is equanimous, that knowledge of insight observes those formations with distinction and observes them while being devoid of grasping;
thus it is called "equanimity regarding formations" (*saṅkhārupekkhā*).

Just as in the world, one who conquers with distinction is said to "conquer further" (*adhijayati*), and one who dwells free from food is said to "fast" (*upavasati*). Furthermore, [it observes] formations as impermanent and so forth...

Having practiced insight, one also practices insight into equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*)—which is established in a state of neutrality toward grasping—as being impermanent and so forth;
and because that very equanimity regarding formations exists as a mode of neutrality toward grasping, it is said: "both the formations and the equanimity," and so on.

55. Now, in order to show the different ways of directing the mind (*cittābhinīhāra*) through equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*), he says: "In how many ways," and so forth. Therein, "through equanimity towards formations" is a locative expression.

"Directing of the mind" means the intense carrying away (*bhusaṃ haraṇaṃ*) of another mind—distinct from that which has already attained equanimity towards formations—by making it face toward that equanimity towards formations. For in this context, the sense is "facing toward."
The word *abhi* has the sense of "intense" (*bhusa*), while *saddo* means "sound. Having answered the question "In how many ways?

by saying "In eight ways," and desiring to show those eight ways through the answer to the second question, he did not yet show them but instead posed the question: "In how many ways for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*)? and so forth. Regarding the term "of an ordinary person" (*puthujjanassa*) here—
Two kinds of worldlings were spoken of by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun:
the blind worldling and the beautiful worldling.

Therein, he who lacks study, inquiry, hearing, retention, reflection, and so forth regarding the aggregates, elements, bases, and so on, is the blind worldling. He who possesses these is the beautiful worldling. Furthermore, both of these—
A worldling (*puthujjana*) is so called because of causes such as the generation of various things;
or because this person is included among the multitude (*puthu*), thus he is a "worldling.
For he is a worldling by virtue of being the generator and so forth of various kinds of defilements and the like. As it has been said:
“They generate various defilements, thus they are *puthujjana*; they possess various, unbroken views of self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), thus they are *puthujjana*;
they look toward the faces of various teachers, thus they are *puthujjana*; they have not emerged from various states of existence (*gati*), thus they are *puthujjana*;
they perform various diverse volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*), thus they are *puthujjana*; they are swept away by various floods (*ogha*), thus they are *puthujjana*.”
They are called *puthujjana* because they are tormented by various individual fevers; they are called *puthujjana* because they are consumed by various individual burning pains;
they are called *puthujjana* because they are individually attached, greedy, infatuated, muddled, clinging, stuck, and entangled in the five strands of sensual pleasure;
they are called *puthujjana* because they are individually obstructed, covered, enveloped, and shut in by the five hindrances.

"Ordinary persons (puthujjana) are those who are covered and closed off. Alternatively, they are called *puthujjana* because they are included among the multitude (*puthu*)—those beyond the path of calculation, who have their backs turned toward the noble Dhamma and whose conduct consists of base qualities.

Or else, they are called *puthujjana* because they have come to be reckoned as a distinct class apart from the noble ones (*ariya*), being dissociated from those endowed with virtues such as morality and learning. Among them...
The "virtuous worldling" (kalyāṇaputhujjana) is intended here; for others, there is simply an absence of cultivation (bhāvanā).

Regarding the term "trainee" (sekha): here, there are seven trainees—those standing on the path of stream-entry, the fruit of stream-entry, the path of once-returning, the fruit of once-returning, the path of non-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the path of arahantship.
They are called "trainees" because they train in the three trainings (sikkhā). Among them, those established in the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, and non-returning are three [of these].
Here, it is the equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) belonging to the stage of the Path that is intended, because there is no further directing of the mind [toward higher stages].

"One who is free from lust" (*vītarāga*): here, one is "free from lust" because lust has departed through its complete eradication; this is a designation for the Arahant. In all three instances, the singular number is used by way of taking the genus.
"He delights in equanimity regarding formations": having acquired the perception of a comfortable dwelling in that abiding in equanimity.

"Delighting" means that, being oriented toward equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) due to a craving for a comfortable dwelling, one takes pleasure and generates a craving accompanied by rapture (*sappītika*).
"He sees clearly" (*vipassati*) means that he sees in various ways by way of impermanence and so forth:
a trainee (*sekkha*) for the sake of attaining the higher paths, and one free from passion (*vītarāga*) for the sake of a pleasant dwelling in this very life. "Having reflected" (*paṭisaṅkhāya*)...

Having investigated by way of impermanence and so forth; however, because noble ones such as stream-enterers and others are unable to attain their respective fruit-attainments (*phalasamāpatti*) without having practiced insight through the nine insight-knowledges beginning with the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbayañāṇa*),
it is therefore said that "having reflected, one attains the fruit-attainment."
Furthermore, in order to show the occurrence of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), this interrogation was posed regarding them:
What is the attainment of fruition? Who attains it? Who does not attain it? Why do they attain it? How does its attainment come about?
How does its maintenance occur? How does emergence from it occur? What is immediately prior to the fruition? And what is immediately after the fruition?
In this context, what is the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*)? It is the absorption (*appanā*) in the cessation of the noble fruit (*ariyaphala*).
Who attains it? And who does not attain it? All worldlings (*puthujjana*) do not attain it.
Why? Because they have not yet realized it. But all noble ones (*ariya*) attain it. Why? Because they have realized it. Furthermore, those of the higher [stages]...

They do not attain the lower [fruits] because they have become pacified through the attainment of the state of another person (a higher stage), and because the lower ones have not yet been reached by the upper one.
However, the definitive conclusion here is that all [noble persons] attain their own respective fruits.
Some, however, maintain that even stream-enterers and once-returners do not attain them, and that only the two higher [stages] attain them.
They say this, and their reason for it is: "For these [ten] are those who bring concentration to fulfillment.

But that is no reason at all, since even an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) enters into the mundane concentration (*lokīyasamādhi*) attained by himself. What is the point here of considering whether there is a reason or not?
Is it not stated right here in the Canon: "Which ten equanimities regarding formations arise by way of insight (*vipassanā*), and which..."?
In the answers to these questions—“Ten change-of-lineage states arise by way of insight”—it is stated separately for each:

“for the sake of attaining the fruit of stream-entry” and “for the sake of attaining the fruit of once-returning. Therefore, one must conclude that all noble ones (ariya) attain their respective fruits.
Why do they attain it? For the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life.

Just as kings enjoy the pleasures of sovereignty and deities enjoy divine bliss, so too do the Noble Ones, thinking, "We shall experience supramundane bliss," set a time limit and enter the attainment of fruition at whatever moment they desire.
How does its attainment come about, how its maintenance, and how its emergence? First of all, its attainment comes about in two ways:
by not attending to any object other than Nibbāna, and by attending to Nibbāna.
As it is said: "Friend, there are two conditions for the attainment of the signless deliverance of mind: non-attention to all signs and..."
“Non-attention and attention to the signless element. This, moreover, is the sequence for entering [this attainment]:

a noble disciple desiring the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), having gone to a secluded place and withdrawn into solitude, should practice insight into formations by way of their arising and passing away.
For him who has practiced insight in successive order, immediately after the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) which has formations as its object—
By means of the attainment of fruition, the mind enters into cessation.
And here, because of the inclination toward the attainment of fruition, even for one in training (sekha), only the fruition arises, not the path.

As for those who say, "A stream-enterer, having established insight with the thought, 'I shall attain the attainment of fruition,' becomes a once-returner; and a once-returner becomes a non-returner," they should be told: "In that case..."
“If there is a non-returner, he will become an arahant; an arahant, a paccekabuddha; and a paccekabuddha, a Buddha.
Therefore, one should not take it that this [statement] is rejected merely on the basis of the canonical text (pāḷi). Rather, this alone should be accepted:
even for one in training (sekkha), only the fruit (phala) arises, not the path (magga). And as for his fruit, if by him the first jhāna...

The path has been attained; it arises as belonging specifically to the first jhāna, or if it belongs to any one of the second jhānas and so forth, it arises as belonging specifically to that particular second jhāna and so forth—in this way, first of all, there is its attainment.

“Friend, there are three conditions for the persistence of the signless deliverance of mind: non-attention to all signs, [the presence of the perception of the base of infinite space, and the absence of applied and sustained thought].”
Furthermore, according to the statement, "There is attention to the signless element and prior volitional formation," its persistence occurs in three ways.
In this context, "prior volitional formation" refers to the determination of time before the attainment;
for because it has been delimited by the thought, "I shall emerge at such-and-such a time," it persists as long as that time has not yet arrived.
Thus there is a basis for it.
Furthermore, according to the statement: "Friends, there are two conditions for emerging from the signless deliverance of mind:
attention to all signs and non-attention to the signless element," its emergence occurs in two ways.
Therein, "all signs" refers to the signs of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Granted, one does not attend to all of these together at once; however, this is stated by way of including them all.
Therefore, for one who attends to whatever is the object of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), there is emergence from the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti).
In this way, its emergence (vuṭṭhāna) is to be understood.

What is immediate after the fruit, and what has the fruit as its immediate predecessor? First, for the fruit, either the fruit itself or the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is immediate. As for the fruit, there is that which is immediate after the path, there is that which is immediate after the fruit, and there is that which is immediate after change-of-lineage (gotrabhū).
“There is the immediate succession of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. In this context, within the sequence of the path, there is the immediate succession of the path;

the latter [moment] follows each preceding one as the immediate succession of the fruit; and in the attainments of fruition, each preceding moment of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*) is the immediate succession [of the subsequent attainment].
Here, "change-of-lineage" should be understood as "conformity" (*anuloma*). For it is said in the *Paṭṭhāna*: “For an Arahant, conformity is the immediate succession of the attainment of fruition.”

"It is a condition by way of proximity-condition (*anantarapaccaya*). The conformity (*anuloma*) of those in training (*sekkha*) is a condition for the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) by way of proximity-condition.
That fruition by which emergence from cessation occurs is "immediately after the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).
Therein, setting aside the fruition that arises within the course of the path (*maggavīthi*), all remaining fruition is by way of the attainment of fruition.
This is called "occurrence. Thus, by way of its arising either in the course of the path or in the attainment of fruition, it is said:
"The supreme fruit of recluseship is peaceful, with its distress calmed, beautiful with the deathless as its object, and free from the bait of the world."
This is the discussion here on the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).

"Having looked on with equanimity at that" means having looked on with equanimity at that equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) by means of another similar knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).
Regarding the phrases "by dwelling in emptiness," and so forth, they refer to one who wishes to dwell by means of the very dwelling of insight, without the attainment of fruition.

The dwelling in the threefold insight of one who, seeing the adherence to a self in an Arahant as fearful, is inclined toward emptiness (*suññatā*) and perceives the fall of formations through equanimity toward formations, is called the "dwelling in emptiness.

The dwelling in the threefold insight of one who, seeing the sign of formations as fearful, is inclined toward the signless (*animitta*) and perceives the fall of formations through equanimity toward formations, is called the "dwelling in the signless. [As for] the longing of craving...

The dwelling in the threefold insight of one who views [conditioned phenomena] as fearful, is inclined toward the wishless (*appaṇihita*), and perceives their passing away through equanimity regarding formations, is called the "wishless dwelling. For it is said further on:
"One who perceives insistence as fearful, because of being inclined toward emptiness (*suññatā*), sees the passing away again and again."
“The dwelling in emptiness: seeing the sign as fearful, because of being intent upon the signless, one sees the passing away [of formations] again and again;
this is the signless dwelling. Seeing aspiration as fearful, because of being intent upon the desireless, one sees the passing away [of formations] again and again; this is the desireless dwelling.”

Furthermore, because of the presence of the six kinds of equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*) and the presence of dwelling with the perception of the non-repulsive in the repulsive, the mind of the Arahant alone is subject to his will in every way;
therefore, it is said that this dwelling in insight (*vipassanāvihāra*) succeeds only for the Arahant.
Regarding the statement, "The one free from lust contemplates equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) through insight," there are three kinds of fear:

And it should be understood as "pure insight" (kevala-vipassanā) without falling into the threefold resolve (*adhimutti*). For if this were the case, there would be a distinction between what precedes and what follows.
Now, wishing to show the division of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) into unity and diversity by way of two or three types of persons, he said:
"How [is it] for the worldling and for the trainee," and so forth. In that context, the directing of the mind (*abhinīhāra*) is unity.
“Is one” (*hoti*) means he is a single entity; it should be understood as a term expressing the abstract state (*bhāva*) in its own sense (*sakatthe*).
Just as it is said that “this very condition” (*idappaccaya*) is “this-conditionality” (*idappaccayatā*), so too “one” (*eka*) is “oneness” (*ekatta*).

“Abhinīhāra” (directing) is either a nominative form used in the sense of a genitive, meaning “of the directing,” or it should be understood as a shift of case endings (*vibhattivipallāsa*), as in the expression “having swept that place” (*so deso sammajjitvā*). *Cittaṃ* (the mind).
"It becomes defiled" means that the mind is defiled by the defilement of greed known as attachment to insight; the sense is that it is heated and oppressed.
"It becomes an obstacle to development" means that there is an impairment of the development of insight already attained.
"It becomes an impediment to penetration" refers to the penetration of the truths which is to be attained through the development of insight.
There is an obstacle to obtaining [rebirth]. It becomes a condition for future rebirth-linking because the karma associated with equanimity toward formations is powerful;

thus, when a rebirth-linking in a happy destination is being given, the defilement of greed—consisting of excessive delight—is a condition for a future rebirth-linking in a happy destination of the sense-sphere.
This is because karma produces its result only when accompanied by defilements.
Therefore, kamma is the productive condition (*janaka-paccaya*), while the defilement is the supporting condition (*upatthambhaka-paccaya*).

"For the learner’s higher penetration" refers to the penetration of the Truths by way of the path of the once-returner and so forth. "It becomes a condition for future rebirth-linking" refers to the rebirth-linking in a fortunate realm of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-sugati*) being bestowed by the kamma of equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-kamma*) in the case of stream-enterers and once-returners among the learners who have not yet attained jhāna.

The defilement of delight (*abhinandanā-kilesa*) is a condition; however, for those who have attained the jhānas and for the non-returner (*anāgāmī*), it is not a condition because they obtain rebirth only in the Brahma-world.
It should be understood that this very same defilement is the condition for the rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) being given by the conformity (*anuloma*) and change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*) states.
"As impermanent" means as impermanent in the sense of having ceased after having been, due to its ultimate impermanence and its possession of a beginning and an end. "As suffering" means...
As suffering, in the sense of constant oppression—due to being oppressed by arising and passing away, and because it is the basis for suffering;
as not-self, in the sense of lack of mastery, because it exists dependent on conditions, and due to the absence of a master, an owner, a doer, or an experiencer;
as contemplation, in the sense of seeing [the object] repeatedly as impermanent and so forth. This is the diversity of the application of the mind.
It should be understood that "becomes" refers to the resolution (*abhinīhāra*), or that it becomes manifold, or that there is a state of manifoldness in the resolution.

"Wholesome" (*kusala*) is in the sense of health, in the sense of blamelessness, and in the sense of being produced through skill. "Indeterminate" (*abyākata*) means not defined by way of being wholesome or unwholesome.
"Well-known at certain times" means well-known at the time of insight (*vipassanā*). "Not well-known at certain times" means...
At the time of relishing, it was not well understood. "Completely well understood" means it is thoroughly understood because relishing has been abandoned.

Regarding the phrase "in the sense of being understood and in the sense of not being understood": here, for both the worldling and the trainee, even the state of being well understood is merely the state of being understood (as long as relishing remains);

but for one who is free from lust, even the state of being completely well understood is merely the state of being understood. For both of them, the state of not being well understood is indeed the state of not being understood.
"Unsatiated" means because that which is to be accomplished by insight has not been completed, due to the state of being non-absorbed. "Satiated" is the opposite of that.
"For the abandoning of the three fetters" means for the purpose of abandoning personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), and clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*).
Bodhisattvas in their final existence (*pacchimabhavika*) are also included herein. [Those who are] not in their final existence...
However, they establish [the practitioner] in equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) after having attained insight (*vipassanā*).
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of attaining the path of stream-entry," some read it without a compound (*asamāsetvā*), but the reading with the compound (*samāsetvā*) is more excellent.

The term "trainee" (*sekkha*) is stated generally for those who have abandoned three fetters—namely, the stream-enterer, the once-returner, and the non-returner—for even in the case of the once-returner and the non-returner, those [fetters] have indeed been abandoned.
"For the sake of attaining the higher" means for the sake of attaining the successive higher paths.

"For the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life" means for the sake of that happy dwelling which exists in the present visible state, in one's own personal existence. "In the sense of the attainment of dwelling" refers, for a trainee (sekha), to the sense of the attainment of fruition;
and for one free from passion (vītarāga), to the sense of the attainment of fruition as a dwelling in insight (vipassanā).
57. Now, in order to show the enumeration and definition of equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*), he says: "How many kinds of equanimity regarding formations? and so forth.
Therein, "by way of serenity" means by way of concentration; this is indeed the reading.
"Reflecting upon the hindrances" means having discerned the five hindrances as things to be abandoned. "Steadying" is due to being oriented toward the abandoning of the hindrances.
Even with regard to their abandoning, it is the establishment in equanimity by way of adopting a state of non-activity.
"In the equanimities toward formations" means: in the equanimities toward those formations known as the hindrances, by not performing any further effort regarding their abandonment.
This same method applies to applied thought, sustained thought, and so forth. Equanimity toward formations in serenity occurs in the stage immediately preceding the access to absorption (*appanā*).

This is the knowledge consisting of development attained through strength. In the four sections on the paths—beginning with "for the sake of attaining the path of stream-entry"—one or another of the paths of emptiness (*suññatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), or wishlessness (*appaṇihita*) is obtained.

However, in the four sections on the fruits—beginning with "for the sake of attaining the fruition attainment of stream-entry"—the fruition attainment of wishlessness (*appaṇihitā phalasamāpatti*) is to be understood. Why? Because [of the statement]: "For the sake of the attainment of the dwelling in emptiness..."
"...for the sake of attaining the dwelling in the signless" is stated because the other two fruition-attainments (*phalasamāpatti*) have been mentioned separately.

For the signless path arises by way of emerging from the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*); likewise, at the time of the fruition attainment, there is the signless fruition attainment.

The unconditioned path and fruition attainments arise by way of emerging from the contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*), and [the void fruition attainment] arises by way of emerging from the contemplation of non-self (*anattānupassanā*).
The attainments of emptiness, the path, and the fruit are to be understood according to the method of the Suttas.
Herein, in the four sections on the path, fifteen terms are stated: five root terms beginning with "arising" (uppāda) and ten synonymous terms beginning with "going" (gati).
However, in the six sections on the attainment of the fruits, only the five root terms are stated.
If one asks why that is: because when equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) is sharp, the path capable of abandoning the defilements can arise;
therefore, in order to demonstrate its sharpness, the root terms were stated together with their synonyms, making them firm.
Because the fruit is by nature peaceful due to its lack of exertion and because it is dependent upon the path, even though it is dull...
It should be understood that the root terms themselves were stated for the purpose of showing that equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) is a condition for the fruit. 58.
Now, having asked by way of birth, he says "How many kinds of equanimity towards formations are wholesome? and so forth, in order to answer according to what is obtainable.
Therein, "fifteen kinds of equanimity towards formations" refers to eight by way of serenity (*samatha*), and [three] by way of the four paths and three fruits.

By way of these [factors], there are fifteen types of beings. As for the eight equanimities toward formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) of an Arahant, their status as indeterminate (*abyākata*) is not explicitly stated because they are not suitable to be called "equanimity toward formations" in the technical sense;

this is due to the absence of the Arahant’s analytical reflection on the hindrances (*nīvaraṇapaṭisaṅkhā*), and because those formations are abandoned with ease, without the exertion required to abandon applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and so forth.
However, for the Arahant, when entering the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*)...

Since it is impossible to attain [the higher jhānas] without equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*), it is stated that the three types of equanimity towards formations are indeterminate (*abyākata*).
For an Arahant possesses three kinds of equanimity towards formations by way of the desireless (*appaṇihita*), the void (*suññatā*), and the signless (*animitta*).
Now, regarding the three verses spoken by way of commenting upon these equanimities towards formations, there is "reflecting" (*paṭisaṅkhā*) and "stopping" (*saṇṭhiti*).

"Wisdom" refers to equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*). "The eight ranges of the mind" means that the eight kinds of equanimity towards formations, spoken of by way of serenity (*samatha*), are the objects (*visaya*) of concentration;
the sense is that they are its "planes" (*bhūmi*). Just as in such passages as "Develop the mind and wisdom," concentration is indicated under the heading of "mind" (*citta*);
and just as in such passages as "Monks, wander in your own range, in your ancestral domain," the word "range" (*gocara*) [is used].

“Object” (visaya): For whatever is dependent upon something, that [latter] is called its object. “Two for the worldling” refers to [the attainments] by way of serenity (samatha) and by way of insight (vipassanā).
“Three for the trainee” (sekkha) refers to [the attainments] by way of serenity, insight, and meditative absorption (samāpatti).

“And three for one free from lust” refers to [the attainments] by way of the fruit-attainments of the wishless, the empty, and the signless. Although “three” (tisso) should have been said, the form “three” (tayo) is used as a change of gender (liṅgavipallāsa).
Or it should be construed as: "The three states of equanimity towards formations. By means of which the mind turns away:
by means of those states of equanimity towards formations, the mind departs from applied thought and sustained thought, or from arising and so forth.
For it is said that because equanimity towards formations exists even in one who is free from lust, the mind turns away from formations and leaps into Nibbāna. Eight [factors] of concentration...
“Conditions” means that, by way of serenity, they are stated as the eight conditions for absorption concentration because they bring about absorption.
“The ten spheres of knowledge” means that, by way of insight, they are stated as the planes for both path-knowledge and fruition-knowledge.
“Conditions for the three liberations” means they are the decisive-support conditions for the liberations of emptiness, the signless, and the desireless.

"He does not waver among various views" means that, without abandoning the contemplation of dissolution, one who practices insight into formations as impermanent and so forth does not tremble amidst the various kinds of views such as the eternalist view (*sassataditthi*).
The commentary on the description of the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa*) is finished.
10. Explanation of the Description of Knowledge of the Change-of-Lineage (Gotrabhū-ñāṇa-niddesa) 59.
In the description of the knowledge of the change-of-lineage, "is overcome" (*abhibhuyyati*) means it overcomes or transcends.

"The sign of formations external" (*bahiddhā saṅkhāra-nimittaṃ*) refers to the sign of formations that exists outside of the unwholesome aggregates occurring within one's own continuum. These are mundane formations (*lokika-saṅkhārā*).
They are called "signs" (*nimitta*) because they are the causes of the defilements, or because they appear in the form of signs. It is called "change-of-lineage" (*gotrabhū*) because it overcomes:
it is described as having the nature of change-of-lineage because it overcomes the lineage of the worldling (*puthujjana*). It is called "change-of-lineage" because it leaps forward:

it is described as having the nature of change-of-lineage because it develops the lineage of the Noble Ones (*ariya*). It is called "change-of-lineage" because it both overcomes and leaps forward; thus, both...

This is stated by way of abbreviation. Regarding the terms *vuṭṭhāti* (emerges) and *vivaṭṭati* (turns away from), they are used in the matrix [of the text] specifically for the purpose of overcoming the lineage (*gotra*) of the worldling (*puthujjana*), in accordance with the terms "emergence" and "turning away.

However, for those who are called "change-of-lineage" (*gotrabhū*) by way of serenity (*samatha*), they are so called because of their overcoming of the lineage of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth;
as in the passages beginning with, "for the sake of attaining the fruit of stream-entry," and so on.
In the six sections on the attainments (*samāpatti*), it is called "change-of-lineage" (*gotrabhū*) because it overcomes the lineage of arising and so forth;

in the three sections on the paths, such as "for the sake of attaining the path of once-returning," its meaning should be understood as the change-of-lineage because it overcomes the lineage of stream-enterers and so forth. Here, the meaning of "lineage" (*gotta*) is the meaning of "seed" (*bīja*).
For it is said in the *Vattanipakaraṇa*: "Lineage is said to be Nibbāna, [which is free] from all obstructions."

It is called *gotrabhū* because it protects (*guttattā*) that lineage (*gotta*); thus it is said: "The eight attainments are also a lineage because they protect the lineage from the obstructions to the lineage;
it is called *gotrabhū* because it enters into that lineage. Furthermore:

"The *gotrabhū* of the four paths has Nibbāna as its object, while the *gotrabhū* of the four attainments of fruition has conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) as its object, owing to the inclination toward the attainment of fruition."

They say this. For it is said in the *Visuddhimagga*: "For one whose insight has proceeded in regular succession, immediately after the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhu) which has formations as its object, the mind enters into cessation by way of the attainment of fruition.

Therefore, the inclusion here—taking the phrase "the sign of external formations" as the sixteenth in the sections on the Path, and taking it as the sixth in the sections on Attainment—is not [inconsistent].
It should be understood as "what. Otherwise, it would have to be understood by taking the root term itself.
However, others say: "That which is the first application of mind, the first attention, toward Nibbāna—this is called *gotrabhū*.
That does not apply here with reference to the fruit. In the passage, "The fifteen *gotrabhū* states are wholesome," because for the Arahant there is no longer any hindrance to be overcome...

It should be understood that the indeterminate nature of the *gotrabhū* states was not mentioned because they do not deserve the name *gotrabhū* in the sense of "overcoming," since initial application (*vitakka*), sustained application (*vicāra*), and so forth, are abandoned by means of pleasure itself.

However, when an Arahant enters the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), he is unable to enter it without overcoming the conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*); thus, "there are three *gotrabhū* phenomena... [is stated].
They are stated to be "indeterminate. However, some say: "Only the eight attainments that partake of penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya) are indicated here;
therefore, the eight attainments and the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) are wholesome. The same should be understood regarding equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā).

60. Regarding the phrase "with the carnal" (sāmisañca), etc.: among the "carnal" (sāmisa) aspects consisting of the bait of the round of existence (vaṭṭāmisā), the bait of the world (lokāmisā), and the bait of the defilements (kilesāmisā), it is "carnal" by way of the bait of the defilements because it is accompanied by attachment.

What is that? It is the eightfold knowledge of the change-of-lineage (gotrabhu) of serenity (samatha). Herein, "the bait of the round" (vaṭṭāmisam) refers specifically to the round of existence belonging to the three planes.
"The bait of the world" (lokāmisam) refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure. "The bait of defilement" (kilesāmisam) refers to the defilements themselves.

"The non-bait" (nirāmisam) refers to the tenfold knowledge of the change-of-lineage of insight (vipassanā), because it is free from attachment; for noble ones do not form an attachment toward the change-of-lineage. In the manuscript, it reads "sāmisañce."

They write it thus, but that is not more excellent. In the same way, one should understand what is "with wish" (paṇihita) and "wishless" (appaṇihita), what is "associated" (saññutta) and "dissociated" (visaññutta), and what is "emerged" (vuṭṭhita) and "not emerged" (avuṭṭhita).
For by means of the wish of craving, it is "with wish"; the meaning is that it is "longed for. By the absence of that, it is "wishless.
Precisely by the presence of the perception of craving, it is "associated"; by the absence of that, it is "dissociated. "Emerged" means...
It is precisely the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*) in insight that is called "emerged" (*vuṭṭhita*), because it cuts off attachment.

The other is "unemerged. Alternatively, it is "emerged" because of its emergence from external formations. For even the change-of-lineage associated with the fruit should be understood as "emerged from the signs of external formations," since it has become directed toward Nibbāna by virtue of its inclination toward Nibbāna. This applies also to the preceding sections on overcoming, emerging, and turning away.

It should be understood that the "fruit-noble lineage" (phala-gotrabhu) overcomes, emerges from, and turns away from [the lower realms] because it has become oriented toward Nibbāna by way of its underlying intention (ajjhāsaya).

Regarding the phrase "conditions for the three liberations": the serenity-noble lineage (samatha-gotrabhu) serves as a natural decisive support condition (pakatūpanissaya-paccaya) for the three supramundane liberations;
the insight-noble lineage (vipassanā-gotrabhu) serves as an immediate, contiguous, and decisive support condition (anantara-samanantara-ūpanissaya-paccaya).
"Whose wisdom is fully developed": whose preliminary wisdom (*pubbabhāga-paññā*) has been cultivated and perfected. "Skilled in emergence through turning away":
skilled and proficient in the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu-ñāṇa*), which is termed "turning away" by way of non-delusion;

or else, skilled in it by means of preliminary knowledge. "He does not waver amidst various views": he does not tremble before the various kinds of views that have been abandoned through their total eradication.
The commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of the lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) is finished.
11. Commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of the path (magga-ñāṇa). 61.
Regarding the exposition of the knowledge of the path, "he emerges from wrong view" means by way of complete eradication through the abandoning of the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya).

One emerges from wrong view by way of its sixty-two divisions. "From the defilements that follow it" means from the various kinds of defilements that arise through association with wrong view and through the decisive support (*upanissaya*) of wrong view, and which thus follow upon wrong view.
By this, the abandoning of those defilements associated with it is stated. For there are two kinds of association (*ekaṭṭha*): association by co-nascence (*sahaja-ekaṭṭha*)...

And "to be abandoned together" (*tadekaṭṭha*): those [defilements] which remain together with that view in a single consciousness or in a single person until its abandonment are "to be abandoned together.

For when that view is being abandoned, in the two types of non-reactive (*asaṅkhārika*) consciousness associated with that view, these defilements—greed, delusion, restlessness, lack of moral shame, and lack of moral dread—which are co-nascent with that view, [are also abandoned]. In the two...
Among the volitionally produced consciousnesses (*sasaṅkhārika-citta*), those defilements— greed, delusion, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness—
which are co-nascent with that view, are abandoned by way of being "abandoned together" (*sahajekaṭṭha*).

When the defilement of view itself is being abandoned, greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, doubt, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness— which reside in the same person as that [view] and lead to the states of misery (*apāya*)— are also abandoned.
"Non-fearfulness" (*anottappa*) refers to these defilements being abandoned by way of their being "abandoned together with [the path].

Regarding "by means of the aggregates": it is by means of the four formless aggregates that follow that view—both those that arise simultaneously (*sahaja*) and those that are "abandoned together with [the path"]—or alternatively, by means of the five aggregates including the material form originated by them, [all] conditioned by the defilements such as wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*).

"From future resultant aggregates that are to arise" means from those resultant aggregates yet to come. "And from all external signs" means from all signs of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*) existing outside of the aforementioned aggregates of defilements (*kilesa-khandha*).

"He emerges from wrong intention" means [from] the five types of consciousness associated with views—namely, the four associated with views and the one accompanied by doubt—which are to be abandoned by the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*), and which are unwholesome states of mind leading to the woeful states (*apāya*).
And one emerges from wrong intentions.
"One emerges from wrong speech" means one emerges from false speech, as well as from divisive, harsh, and idle chatter that lead to the states of misery.
"One emerges from wrong action" means one emerges from killing living beings, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct.
“He emerges from wrong livelihood” means he emerges from hypocrisy, flattery, hinting, belittling, and the pursuit of gain through gain;
or he emerges from the seven types of bodily and verbal actions rooted in livelihood.

The emergence from wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration should be understood in the same manner as that explained for the emergence from wrong intention. And regarding “wrong mindfulness,” it refers to [the absence] of mindfulness.
Arising in the mode of an antidote, it consists merely of an unwholesome state of consciousness.
In the three higher paths, the eight path-factors—such as "right view in the sense of seeing"—are obtained exactly as they are found in the first path of the first jhāna.
Therein, in the first path, right view is so called because it abandons wrong view.
Right intention and the others should also be understood in the sense of abandoning wrong intention and the rest.

This being so, since the sixty-two types of speculative views (*diṭṭhigata*) have already been abandoned by the first path alone, there would be no such thing as "view" to be abandoned by the three higher paths.
In that case, how can it be called "right view"? It is just as when there is an antidote (*agada*); whether or not there is poison, [the antidote remains].
Just as it is said regarding a medicine, so too, whether wrong view exists or not, this is indeed called right view.
If this were merely a matter of name, then it would follow that right view has no function in the three higher paths, and the path-factors would not be fulfilled.
Therefore, right view must perform its own function, and the path-factors must be brought to completion.
And here, right view should be illustrated as performing its own function according to the rule of what has been obtained.
For there is one type of conceit that is to be abandoned by the three higher paths; it stands in the place of [wrong] view, and right view abandons that conceit.
Indeed, in the path of stream-entry, right view abandons wrong view. But for the stream-enterer, that which is to be abandoned by the path of once-returning—
There is conceit; the abandoning of that conceit is right view. Within that same [state], there is intention co-arising with the seven unwholesome types of consciousness;

by means of those very consciousnesses, there is the movement of the vocal faculty, there is the movement of the bodily faculty, there is the enjoyment of requisites, there is co-arising effort, there is the state of non-remembrance, and there is co-arising one-pointedness of mind. These...

These are called wrong intention and the rest. On the path of the once-returner (sakadāgāmimagga), right intention and the rest should be understood as such by virtue of the abandoning of those [wrong states].

Thus, on the path of the once-returner, the eight factors perform their respective functions. For the once-returner, there exists conceit (māna) which is to be abandoned by the path of the non-returner (anāgāmimagga);
that stands in the place of views (diṭṭhi). The intentions and the rest that are co-nascent with his seven types of consciousness—
They exist. By their abandonment, the performance of the respective functions of the eight factors on the path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga) is to be understood.

For the non-returner, there exists conceit (māna), which is to be abandoned by the path of arahantship; this stands in the place of views (diṭṭhi). Furthermore, there are the five unwholesome types of consciousness (akusalacitta);

the volitions (saṅkappa) and other mental factors associated with them also exist. By their abandonment, [the performance of the functions of] the eight factors on the path of arahantship [is to be understood].
Its function as a duty-fulfiller should be understood.
"Gross" means it has become coarse by virtue of being a condition for transgression at the doors of body and speech.

"Fetters of sensual lust" refers to the fetter known as lust for sexual intercourse; for that indeed binds one to the realm of sense-desire (*kāmabhava*), and thus it is called a "fetter" (*saññojana*).
The fetters of repulsion (*paṭighasaññojana*) are the fetters of ill-will (*byāpādasaññojana*). For that [ill-will] strikes against the object; thus it is called "repulsion" (*paṭigha*).

These very same [fetters] persist in the continuum in the sense of being firmly established; thus they are called "latent tendencies" (*anusaya*). "Subsisting as minute" (*aṇusahagata*) means having become atomic, that is, having become subtle;
for here the word *sahagata* refers to their state of being so. Indeed, for a once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*), sensual lust and ill-will [are diminished] by two causes.
This is due to the rarity of their occurrence and the mildness of their obsession.
For in him, unlike an ordinary foolish person, defilements do not arise frequently; they arise only occasionally.
And when they do arise, they do not arise as they do in an ordinary foolish person—crushing, spreading, covering, and making one utterly blind—but rather by means of two paths.
Because they have been abandoned, they arise very faintly and in a subtle form; they are no longer capable of leading to transgression.

Thus, when they have become subtle, they are abandoned by the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*). "Attachment to the fine-material realm" (*rūparāga*) refers to desire and lust for existence in the fine-material realm (*rūpabhava*).

"Attachment to the immaterial realm" (*arūparāga*) refers to desire and lust for existence in the immaterial realm (*arūpabhava*). "Pride" (*māna*) has the characteristic of loftiness. "Restlessness" (*uddhacca*) has the characteristic of lack of tranquility. "Ignorance" (*avijjā*)...

...for the purpose of the mark of blindness. "Underlying tendency to lust for existence" (*bhavarāgānusaya*) refers to the underlying tendency to lust for existence that occurs by way of lust for the fine-material realm (*rūparāga*) and lust for the immaterial realm (*arūparāga*). 62.
Now, while providing a commentary on the knowledge of the path (*maggañāṇa*), he says:

"It burns what is unborn by means of what is born; therefore it is called *jhāna*. In this context, "by means of what is born" refers to each respective supramundane absorption (*lokuttarajjhāna*) manifested within one's own continuum.
The meaning is that a person endowed with that [path] burns, consumes, and utterly eradicates each respective defilement even before it has arisen;

for that reason, it is called "supramundane jhāna. Regarding "skillfulness in jhānas and liberations": by means of skillfulness through non-delusion regarding both the jhāna—consisting of applied thought (*vitakka*) and the rest associated with that noble path—and the noble path itself, which is termed "liberation," [one attains it] by the very first path.

When various views have been abandoned, one does not waver. Meditation (jhāna) is twofold: meditation that contemplates the object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and meditation that contemplates characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna).

Worldly first jhāna and so forth are called jhāna in the sense of contemplating objects such as the kasiṇas; insight is called jhāna in the sense of contemplating the specific and general characteristics of conditioned phenomena;
and the supramundane is [called jhāna] in the sense of contemplating the characteristic of suchness in Nibbāna.

Regarding *jhāna*: here, however, instead of referring to the meaning of "contemplation of characteristics" (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*) which is common even to the lineage-knowledge (*gotrabhu*), it is called *jhāna* in the sense of the uncommon "burning up of defilements" (*kilesajhāpana*).
Furthermore, the meaning of "liberation" (*vimokkha*) here is the sense of being thoroughly resolved upon Nibbāna as its object and the sense of being thoroughly liberated from defilements.

"And how he, having concentrated, sees with insight" (*samādahitvā yathā ce vipassati*): first, having performed the concentration of the mind by means of one of the concentrations—access, neighborhood, or momentary concentration—he subsequently sees with insight. The word "and" (*ce*) has a conjunctive sense;
it conjoins insight (*vipassanā*). "And if, while seeing with insight, he likewise concentrates": this so-called insight is indeed something that has become coarse.

Insipidity is absent, whereas serenity (samatha) is indeed smooth and possesses flavor. Therefore, while practicing insight (vipassanā), one should gladden the mind that has become coarse and likewise apply it with concentration.

The meaning is that while practicing insight, one should again enter into concentration and achieve the settling of the mind in exactly the same way as one did while practicing insight. Here, the word "and" (ce) includes the act of concentrating.
In both instances, the word "ca" (and) has been used to conform to the requirements of the verse composition; however, its meaning remains that of the particle "ca" itself.

Regarding the phrase "vipassanā ca samatho tadā ahu": since the manifestation of the Noble Path occurs when serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) exist in a state of union (*yuganaddha*), it follows that because they are capable of generating the Noble Path, whenever there is a conjunction of these two, then insight...
And when both serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) have arisen, the meaning is that they are called "true serenity-insight.
These two—serenity and insight—are "co-partnered" (*samānabhāga-yuganaddha*) at the time of facing the Noble Path and during the moment of the Path itself.

They are "co-partnered" because their parts or portions (*bhāga*) are equal (*samāna*), and they are "yoked together" (*yuganaddha*) like a pair of oxen, in the sense that they do not overstep one another.
"Of equal sweetness and equal strength" is the meaning. Its detailed exposition, however, will appear in the *Yuganaddha-kathā* (Discourse on the Coupling).
"The vision that 'formations are suffering, cessation is bliss'—wisdom that has emerged from both sides touches the deathless state.
This means that for one who has entered the path [seeing] "formations are suffering" and "cessation, Nibbāna, is bliss," there subsequently arises the vision of Nibbāna.
The knowledge of the noble path is called "wisdom that has emerged on both sides.

And it is this very wisdom that touches, meaning it attains through the contact of its object, the deathless state, Nibbāna. For Nibbāna is "deathless" (amata) because it is like the deathless in its quality of being insatiable;
it is also "deathless" in the sense that for it there is no death, no dying, no passing away. From the stage of the preliminary path onwards, with great effort...
It is called a "path" (*padam*) because one goes by means of it, or it is practiced.
"He knows the conduct of liberation" means he knows the occurrence of liberation by way of non-delusion, and he knows it by way of reflective contemplation.
"Liberation emerging from both sides; the four liberations emerging from both sides; of those emerging from both sides..."

"The four liberations in forward order and the four liberations as the subsiding of emergence from both sides"—this should be understood as the practice of liberation (vimokkhacariyā) mentioned in the subsequent discussion on liberation.
Their detailed exposition is given in that very same place.
"Skilled in their diversity and unity" means being proficient in the various aspects and the single aspect of those liberations, by way of the liberation of emergence from both sides.

For their unity should be understood as being due to the four noble paths; their diversity, either by way of the four noble paths themselves, or by way of the different modes of contemplation within each individual noble path; and their unity, by way of their nature as the noble path.

"Skill in two kinds of knowledge" means through skill in these two kinds of knowledge, namely that which is termed "seeing" and that which is termed "development. For "seeing" is the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*).
For that [path of seeing] is called "seeing" because it sees Nibbāna for the first time.
As for the change-of-lineage consciousness (*gotrabhu*), although it sees Nibbāna even earlier, it is like a man who has come to a king's presence on some business:
even though he sees the king from afar walking along the road mounted upon the neck of an elephant, when asked, "Have you seen the king? [he would say no].
Having seen [it], because the duty to be performed has not yet been accomplished, one says, "I do not see it.

In the same way, although Nibbāna has been seen, because the abandonment of defilements—which is what remains to be done—is still absent, it is not called "seeing. For that knowledge stands in the position of the path's adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*).
"Development" (*bhāvanā*) refers to the remaining three paths; for they function by way of development with respect to the very same phenomena already seen by the first path.
It arises, and one sees nothing that was not seen before; therefore it is called "development" (*bhāvanā*).

However, because the path of development had not yet been completed below [that point], it was not stated as "the two knowledges," but rather—referring to those who have attained the paths of stream-entry, once-returning, and non-returning—it was said to be "skillfulness in the jhānas and liberations.
But for one who has attained the path of Arahatship, [the path of] development...
It should be understood that because it has been brought to completion, it is stated as "skillfulness in two kinds of knowledge.
The commentary on the exposition of path-knowledge is finished.
12. Commentary on the Exposition of Fruition-Knowledge.
