63. In the exposition of the knowledge of fruition (*phalañāṇa*), the phrase "due to the subsiding of that application" means due to the subsiding of the application for emerging from both internally and externally.
For at its own moment, the path indeed performs the application for emerging from both sides by means of the abandoning of defilements;
however, at the moment of fruition, because the defilements have been abandoned, the path's application for emerging from both sides has subsided.
It is called "calmed. As for "it arises": it arises once or twice immediately after the path;
however, at the time of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), it arises many times. For one emerging from cessation (*nirodha*), it arises twice.
Indeed, all of that arises because the preparatory effort has subsided. It is called "fruit" (*phala*) in relation to the fruit of the path.

The neuter gender has been employed. In the case of the moment of the once-return path and so forth, the application regarding emergence should be understood by way of each individual path-factor alone.
The commentary on the description of the knowledge of fruition is finished.
13. Commentary on the Description of the Knowledge of Liberation.

64. In the exposition of the knowledge of liberation (*vimuttiñāṇa*): *Sakkāyadiṭṭhi* (personality-belief) means either a view (*diṭṭhi*) regarding the body (*kāya*), which is the pentad of aggregates (*khandha-pañcaka*), in the sense of its existing;
or, being itself existing, it is a view with respect to that body—thus it is *sakkāyadiṭṭhi*. *Vicikicchā* (doubt) means that by which medical treatment (*cikicchā*) has departed;

or, while investigating (*vicinanto*) its own nature, one suffers (*kicchati*) and is distressed by it—thus it is *vicikicchā*. *Sīlabbataparāmāsa* (clinging to rules and observances) [means] by virtue of moral conduct...
The adherence to the conviction that purification comes through vows or purification through rules and observances is the "clinging to rules and observances" (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*).
For this, having transcended intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), grasps at something external.

Although both [this view and the view of self-identity] are alike in being views, because the view of self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) is grasped by its very nature, without recourse to reasoning or the instruction of others, it is [distinguished] from the view of self-identity consisting of twenty bases which constitutes that very nature.
The view of a self-identity (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) is mentioned for the purpose of showing that by its abandonment alone, all views are abandoned.

However, it should be understood that the clinging to rules and observances (sīlabbataparāmāsa) is mentioned separately for the purpose of showing the falsity of the practice for those who have undertaken the practice thinking, "We are following the way to purification.
In order to show that the abandonment of all three occurs precisely through the abandonment of the underlying tendencies (anusaya), the underlying tendency of views (diṭṭhānusaya) [is mentioned].
It is said "the underlying tendency to doubt" (*vicikicchānusaya*), not because it is a separate defilement (*kilesa*).

They are called "defilements" (*kilesa*) because they defile (*kilesanti*), torment, and afflict. They are called "corruptions" (*upakkilesa*) because they are intense defilements in the sense of being firmly established.

"They are completely cut off" means they are completely cut off by the abandonment through cutting off (*samucchedappahāna*), that is, by cessation through non-arising. "Together with their obsessions" (*sapariyuṭṭhānehi*)...
They are called obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhānāni*) because they arise and emerge, completely enveloping the mind;
this is a designation for defilements that have reached the stage of active manifestation (*samudācāra*). "Together with obsessions" means *sapariyuṭṭhānāni*.

By those [defilements] together with obsessions, which are underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) and secondary corruptions (*upakkilesa*), the mind becomes liberated. This is because, through the continuity of the stream of being (*santati*), they have become incapable of arising again.
The mind that is occurring [in that state] is therefore called "liberated. Because it is thoroughly liberated, it is "well-liberated" (*suvimutta*).
"In the sense of knowing that liberation" means in the sense of cognizing that liberation.
The commentary on the Description of Knowledge of Liberation is finished.
14. Explanation of the Description of Knowledge of Reviewing (Paccavekkhaṇañāṇa-niddesa-vaṇṇanā).

65. In the description of the knowledge of reviewing, having first stated the path factors individually in the sense of cause at the very moment of the path, it further states that "awakening in the sense of awakening" (*bujjhanaṭṭhena bodhi*) refers to both those phenomena that constitute path factors and those that do not constitute path factors.
Because they constitute factors of the Noble One who has attained the name [of "Enlightened"], he showed the enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅga*) separately.

For the enlightenment factors of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, and concentration are indeed path-factors (*maggaṅga*), whereas the enlightenment factors of rapture, tranquility, and equanimity are not path-factors.

Furthermore, among those specified separately by way of the powers (*bala*) and the faculties (*indriya*), faith alone is not a path-factor. Moreover, these very phenomena arise only at the moment of the path.
Showing them by way of their grouping, he said, "In the sense of predominance," and so forth. Therein, in the sense of establishment, they are called *satipaṭṭhāna* (foundations of mindfulness).

Although mindfulness has only a single object—namely, *nibbāna*—it is called the four foundations of mindfulness according to its accomplishment of the function of abandoning the perceptions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self with respect to the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena.
Likewise, although energy has only a single object—namely, *nibbāna*—it is [divided] with respect to unwholesome states that have arisen and those that have not yet arisen...

The four right efforts (*sammappadhāna*) are so called by virtue of their function of abandoning [unwholesome states] that have arisen, preventing the arising of those not yet arisen, and accomplishing the arising and persistence of wholesome states that have not yet arisen.

They are called "truths" (*sacca*) in the sense of being suchness (*tathattha*), meaning they are non-deceptive regarding the nature of suffering and so forth; thus, there are the four noble truths (*ariyasacca*). These very same...
And herein, Nibbāna—which is mentioned separately as "Nibbāna plunged in the Deathless"—is fully present at that time in the sense of penetration;
the remaining factors, however, are fully present at that time in the sense of acquisition.

From the statement, "The Truths are fully present at that time in the sense of suchness," it is certain that one necessarily reviews the Four Truths at the conclusion of the Path and the Fruit. This is the conclusion.
One must go [to that state]. Furthermore, because of the statement, “What was to be done has been done;

there is nothing further for this state of being,” the reviewing reflection—“Suffering has been fully understood by me, its origin has been abandoned by me, its cessation has been realized by me, and the path has been developed by me”—is indeed stated. Such a reviewing reflection is also logical. And here, "origin" (samudaya) refers to...
It should be understood that each [defilement] is to be abandoned by its respective path.

Here, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that the two kinds of reflection on defilements, as well as the reflections on the path, fruition, and Nibbāna, are included here in their actual form by way of the reflection on the origin (*samudaya*) mentioned above.
Only the reflection on suffering (*dukkha*) was not mentioned. Although it was not mentioned, nevertheless, because of the existence of the text [it is to be understood].

And it must certainly be accepted because of its logical consistency. For when one who has entered the path for the sake of penetrating the Truths completes that penetration of the Truths, it is indeed logical to reflect upon the fact that "one's own task has been accomplished.

The statement beginning with "tranquility (samatha) in the sense of non-distraction" is said in order to show that the factors of tranquility and insight associated with the Path possess a single flavor and do not overstep one another in their respective functions. [In the sense of] restraint...
Purification of virtue consists precisely of right speech, right action, and right livelihood. Purification of mind in the sense of non-distraction consists precisely of right concentration.
Purification of view in the sense of seeing consists precisely of right view.

"In the sense of liberation" means in the sense of being liberated from the defilements to be abandoned by the path through their total eradication, or in the sense of resolute confidence in the object, which is Nibbāna. "Liberation" (vimokkha) [refers to this].
Liberation by eradication is the noble path itself. In the sense of penetration it is "true knowledge" (*vijjā*);
that is, true knowledge in the sense of penetrating the truths, which is right view itself. In the sense of relinquishment it is "liberation" (*vimutti*);

that is, liberation because of being freed from those defilements to be abandoned by the path through the act of abandoning them, which is the noble path itself. In the sense of eradication it is "knowledge of destruction"; that is, in the sense of cutting off the defilements.
Knowledge regarding the Noble Path that brings about the destruction of the defilements is precisely right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*).

Desire and the other factors should be understood according to the method explained above; however, here they are shown specifically at the moment of the Path (*magga-khaṇa*) in terms of the beginning, middle, and end of the Path.
Furthermore, "liberation" (*vimutti*) here refers exclusively to liberation by means of the Path (*magga-vimutti*). [In the sense of] "being thus" (*tathaṭṭhena*)...

It should be understood that although *nibbāna* was already included in the phrase "the truths," it is stated again here for the purpose of showing its status as the ultimate conclusion (*pariyosāna*).
The same principle applies at the moment of the fruit (*phala-kkhaṇa*). Here, however, the path is called the "path" in the sense of being the cause;

it is so designated precisely by way of being the path to the fruit. Regarding the "right efforts": at the moment of the path, they are the function of energy that accomplishes the four tasks; at the moment of the arising of the fruit, [they are the fruit itself].

It should be understood that [the term] is stated because of its established nature. Otherwise, at the moment of the fruit (phalakkhaṇa), the right exertions (sammappadhāna) themselves would not be found.
For it was said by the Elder, while enumerating the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) at the moment of the path (maggakkhaṇa):

"At the moment of the fruit, with the exception of the four right exertions, the remaining thirty-three factors are found. It is exactly so by virtue of the accomplishment of the function of penetration (paṭivedha-kicca) and so forth.
The factors beginning with truth (sacca) should also be understood according to their respective application. "Liberation" (vimokkha) refers to liberation as fruition (phala-vimokkha).
"Deliverance" (vimutti) refers to deliverance as fruition (phala-vimutti). Knowledge of non-arising in the sense of subsiding has already been explained.

"Having emerged" is said because there is no emergence in the interim; it is stated thus by way of the conclusion of the fruition. "These states have then come together" means that these aforementioned types of states [arise] at the moment of the path.
The connection should be understood by supplying the word “iti” (thus) as a textual ellipsis: “And at the moment of fruition, he reviews it as ‘arisen’.
The commentary on the description of reviewing knowledge is finished.
15. Commentary on the Description of Knowledge of the Diversity of Bases.
66. In the exposition of the knowledge of the diversity of bases (*vatthunānattañāṇaniddesa*), "he defines the eye as internal" means he establishes the eye as being internal.
Desiring to explain how he defines the eye, [the text] asks, "How does he define the eye as internal?
and then describes the manner of its definition by stating, "He defines the eye as arisen from ignorance," and so forth.
This is shown. In this context, ignorance and craving are past supporting causes; past karma is the producing cause;
and nutriment is the present supporting cause. By this, the temperature and consciousness that support the eye are indeed included.
"Derived from the four great elements" (*upādāya*) is a genitive used in the sense of an accusative; that is, having derived [the eye] from the four great elements.
"Are occurring" is the meaning. By this, its nature as the sensitive eye is shown, while its status as a physical aggregate (*sasambhāra*) is excluded.
"Arisen" refers to the present by way of the [four] periods of time or by way of the moment of continuity (*santati-khaṇa*). "Fully come forth" means arisen from its cause.
Up to this point, the determination of the eye prior to insight (*vipassanā*) has been shown. By the phrases beginning with "having not been, it has come to be," etc.,...
Contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*). Because it does not exist prior to its arising, it has come to be without having previously been;
because it will not exist after its passing away, it will not be after having been. "Having an end" (*antavanta*): that which has an end (*anta*) is "end-possessing" (*antavā*);

"end-possessing" is the same as "having an end," just as in the expressions "possessing mindfulness," "possessing gait," and "the sage who possesses fortitude. From that state of "having an end," because dissolution is evident.

The meaning [of the terms] is as follows: "Unstable" (*addhuva*) means it is not firm, because it falls away in all states and lacks the nature of stability. "Non-eternal" (*asassata*) means it is not permanent.
"Subject to change" (*vipariṇāmadhamma*) means its natural disposition is to undergo change in two ways: namely, through aging and through death.
"The eye is impermanent," and so forth, as well as "the eye is impermanence," and so forth, have already been explained. "Mind" (*mano*) here refers to the mind of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).

Because it is intended [in this sense], the statements beginning with "arisen from ignorance" and so forth are indeed appropriate. Regarding the phrase "arisen from nutriment," it should be understood here by way of the nutriment of contact associated [with consciousness] and the nutriment of mental volition.
Furthermore, "arisen" refers to the continuity of time and the continuity of the stages of existence.
The commentary on the description of the knowledge of the diversity of bases is concluded.
16. Explanation of the Description of Knowledge of the Diversity of Objects (Gocaranānattañāṇaniddesavaṇṇanā) 67.

In the description of the knowledge of the diversity of objects, "he defines form externally" means that he defines the phenomena of the form-base (rūpāyatana) which exist externally to the internal [self].
"Arising from ignorance," and so forth, refers to the fact that these are material phenomena born of kamma included within the personal existence (attabhāva).

It has been stated. For nutriment is also a supporting condition for matter born of kamma. However, because sound is produced by temperature and mind, the tetrad beginning with "arisen from ignorance" is not mentioned.
Because tangible objects are themselves the great primary elements, it is not said "derived from the four great primary elements.
And here, "mental phenomena" (dhammā) refers to the three immaterial aggregates associated with the mind-element (manodhātu) during the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
These include the subtle forms included within the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) that are produced by kamma, as well as all [other] forms and so forth.
Furthermore, whatever things arise from whichever cause, they should be understood as being produced by that specific cause.

Otherwise, even those phenomena such as forms included within one's own continuum would not be encompassed. This is because [the definition] includes even those forms and so forth that are not bound to the sense faculties.

They are included within insight; therefore, they should be understood as being comprised by the phrase "arisen from kamma. For these too are produced by the conditions of kamma and temperature common to all beings.
However, others say that "forms and so forth not bound to the faculties are not included within insight.
But regarding that— "When one sees with wisdom that 'all conditioned phenomena are impermanent'..."
“Then one becomes disenchanted with suffering; this is the path to purification.
This contradicts the initial portion of the Canon. And it is said in the *Visuddhimagga*: “Here, someone first fixes his attention on internal formations and then contemplates them with insight;
for the emergence of the Path does not occur merely by seeing pure internal [states].”

“...there is [the internal], and that which is to be seen externally must also be seen; therefore, one contemplates even the aggregates of another person and even non-clung-to formations as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
Therefore, the definition of the eyes and so forth belonging to others, as well as the definition of material phenomena not bound to the faculties and so forth, must certainly be accepted;
thus, there are no formations belonging to the three planes that are not suitable for insight (vipassanā).
The commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of the diversity of the resort is finished.
17. Commentary on the Exposition of the Knowledge of the Diversity of Conduct (Cariyānānattañāṇaniddesa) 68.

Regarding the phrase "conduct of consciousness" (*viññāṇacariyā*) and so forth in the exposition of the knowledge of the diversity of conduct: it is called "conduct" (*cariyā*) because it moves upon an object; thus, it is consciousness itself.

Conduct is the conduct of consciousness. Ignorance-conduct (*aññāṇacariyā*) means: proceeding by way of ignorance, or proceeding with ignorance, or proceeding regarding what is unknown, or the proceeding of ignorance.

Knowledge-conduct (*ñāṇacariyā*) means: knowledge itself as conduct, or conduct by way of knowledge, or proceeding with knowledge, or proceeding regarding what is known, or the proceeding of knowledge.
"For the purpose of seeing" means: occurring for the purpose of seeing forms.

Adverting functional-indeterminate (āvajjanakiriyābyākatā): It is called "adverting" (āvajjana) because it turns away from the continuum of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and directs or inclines the stream of consciousness toward a visible-form object.
It is called "functional" (kiriyā) because it is a mere activity devoid of karmic result (vipāka).

It is called "indeterminate" (abyākatā) because it is not defined as either wholesome or unwholesome. Regarding the sense of "seeing" (dassanaṭṭha): one sees by means of it, or it itself sees, or its nature is merely seeing.

"Seeing" (*dassana*) means that seeing itself is the purpose; thus, it has the sense of seeing (*dassanaṭṭha*). "Eye-consciousness" (*cakkhuviññāṇa*) refers to either wholesome resultant or unwholesome resultant consciousness.
"Because it has been seen" (*diṭṭhattā*): because there is no receiving of an object not yet seen, [it is said] because the visible-object base has been seen by eye-consciousness.
"The resultant mind-element is the application" (*abhiniropanā vipākamanodhātu*): it is "application" (*abhiniropanā*) because it mounts upon (*ati-ni-ropanā*) the very same object that was seen.
The receiving mind-element (*sampaṭicchana-manodhātu*) is the result of both [types of kamma]. "Because it has mounted upon" means because it has ascended to the visible-form object.

"Resultant mind-consciousness-element" refers to the resultant investigating mind-consciousness-element (*santīraṇa-manoviññāṇadhātu*). This same method applies to the ear-door and the others as well.

Although the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*) is not explicitly mentioned immediately after the investigating consciousness, it should be understood that it is included because it was stated by the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā.
"For the purpose of cognizing" means for the purpose of cognizing both mental objects (*dhammārammaṇa*) and objects such as visible forms (*rūpādi*).

"Functional-ineffective adverting" refers to the mind-door adverting consciousness (*manodvārāvajjana-citta*). "The purpose of cognizing" means that its sole purpose is the cognizing of the object immediately following it by way of the impulsion (*javana*);
there is no other purpose. This is because unwholesome impulsions and the impulsions of insight, the path, and the fruition have been treated separately below.

The subsequent impulsions (*javana*) might be understood here [as including all types]; however, because of the statement, “The movement of consciousness (*viññāṇacariyā*) is that which proceeds dissociated from wholesome kamma,” only the impulsion of the smile-producing consciousness (*hasituppāda-citta*) should be taken.

Since only rootless (*ahetuka*) states of consciousness are mentioned in regard to the six doors, there are two adverting consciousnesses, two fivefold sense-consciousnesses, two receiving consciousnesses, three investigating consciousnesses, and one...
The eighteen rootless consciousnesses (*ahetuka-citta*) alone should be understood as the "movements of consciousness" (*viññāṇacariyā*) in the sense of the arising of laughter.
Now, in order to show that the movements of consciousness consist merely in the knowing of objects, he says, "It moves without lust," and so forth;
for consciousness reaches different states when associated with lust and the like, or when associated with faith and the like, but not when these are absent.
It remains right here in its own abode. Therefore, by the terms "free from lust" (*nīrāga*) and so forth, he shows the mere functional activity of those aforementioned consciousnesses.
"Free from lust" means that there is no lust (*rāga*) in it; they also read it as *nirāgā*, shortening the vowel. Now, "lust" (*rāga*) is so called by way of being excited;

among the others, "hatred" (*dosa*) is by way of being malicious; "delusion" (*moha*) is by way of being bewildered; "conceit" (*māna*) is by way of conceiving; and [the last] is by way of perverted vision.

*Diṭṭhi* (view). *Uddhacca* is the state of being agitated or the state of being unpeaceful. *Vicikicchā* (doubt) has its meaning as already stated. They are called *anusaya* because they lie latent (*anusenti*).

Although one should say "without latent tendencies" (*niranusayā*), it is stated as "not latent tendencies" (*nānusayā*); the meaning is the same. Here, their absence should be understood as applying only to those who have reached the state of being free from obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
For the "conduct of consciousness" (*viññāṇacariyā*) is taught specifically for those whose latent tendencies have been abandoned. And that which is named "free from lust," etc., [is also included].
He said "dissociated from lust" and so forth in order to show another way of expressing that it is indeed dissociated from lust and the other [defilements].
Furthermore, he said "by wholesome kamma" and so forth to demonstrate its dissociation from others as well. Wholesome states alone are "blameless" because they lack the presence of lust and the rest.
They are "bright" because they are endowed with moral shame (*hiri*) and fear of wrongdoing (*ottappa*), which produce purity. Because they bring about happiness in their occurrence...
"Having a pleasant outcome" (*sukhudrayāni*) means that their arising (*udaya*) or origination is pleasant; or, because they have a pleasant result (*vipāka*), their arising or increase is pleasant.
The unwholesome (*akusala*) states should be understood by applying the opposite of what has been stated. "It moves among the cognized" (*viññāte carati*):
an object being made known by consciousness is called "the cognized" (*viññāta*); [it moves] among that cognized object. What is meant? Because of its association with the color blue...
Just as a cloth is called "blue" through its association with blue dye, so too consciousness is called "consciousness" (viññāṇa) because of its association with the act of cognizing.

It is said that it "moves within that consciousness," which is why it is called a "movement of consciousness" (viññāṇacariyā). The meaning is: such is the movement of consciousness; that is, for consciousness of the kind described, there is a movement of the kind described.
And the phrase "movement of consciousness" is spoken by way of conventional designation.
There is no mental behavior (cariyā) distinct from consciousness itself. This mind is naturally pure in the sense of being free from defilements;

thus, this aforementioned mind is pure by its very nature due to the absence of defilements such as greed. Therefore, it is said that "mental behavior" refers to the behavior of consciousness, meaning it is merely the act of cognizing.
The reading *nikilesaṭṭhena* (in the sense of being free from defilements) is also found.
"In agreeable things through the course of ignorance": they apply the mind to them and find confidence in them, or they nourish and increase the mind;
thus they are "agreeable" (*manāpa*), and being agreeable, they are "agreeable things" (*manāpiya*). In those agreeable things.
Whether they be desirable or undesirable, they are "agreeable" by way of being grasped. For it is not only in the desirable that lust arises, nor only in the undesirable that hatred arises.
"For the purpose of the impulsion of lust" means: it occurs as the impulsion of lust by way of a continuous stream (*santati*).
"Functional-ineffective advertence" refers to the mind-element (*manodhātu*), which is functional-ineffective advertence consisting in improper attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*) at the eye-door.
"Impulsions of lust" refers to the occurrence of lust for the most part seven times; it is lust itself occurring repeatedly. "Conduct of ignorance" means...
Because passion arises through ignorance, it is said that "passion has its course through ignorance. The same method applies to the others as well.

"In regard to an object that is not viewed with equanimity by both" means in regard to an object consisting of a visible-form stimulus (rūpārammaṇa) which is devoid of viewing with equanimity due to passion and hatred.
"For the sake of the impulsion of delusion" means for the sake of the impulsion of delusion by way of doubt and restlessness.
For the sake of speed. "Conduct of ignorance" means the conduct of ignorance itself, not that of anything else.
"Of bondage," and so forth, are terms expressing the intrinsic nature of pride and the rest. Therein, "of bondage" refers to that which stands having become bound by way of loftiness.
"Of misapprehension" refers to that which has grasped something beyond—having transcended the impermanent nature of form and so forth—and taken it to be permanent and so on.
“Seized”: [seized] by it. “One who has fallen into distraction” means one who has fallen into a state of being distracted toward a visible-form object (*rūpārammaṇa*).

“One who has reached non-conclusion” means one who has reached a state of lacking a definitive conclusion. “One who has become firm” means one who has attained strength. “In phenomena” (*dhammesu*) means either in the phenomena such as visible form (*rūpa*), or in those phenomena that have become objects of cognition. 70.
Since lust and the other [defilements] arise through ignorance, therefore, by way of association with lust and so forth, he qualifies ignorance as “with lust” (*sarāga*).

He says, "he courses," and so forth. Therein, "one with lust courses" should be understood as a course of conduct by way of the underlying tendencies of delusion, conceit, views, restlessness, and ignorance, and by way of the impulsion [of consciousness].

"One with hatred courses" is by way of the underlying tendencies of delusion, ignorance, and impulsion. "One with delusion courses" is by way of the underlying tendencies of lust, hatred, conceit, views, restlessness, and doubt, and by way of impulsion.
"One with conceit courses" is by way of the underlying tendencies of lust, delusion, sensual lust, lust for existence, and ignorance, and by way of impulsion. "One with views courses" is...

By way of the impulsions (javana) of latent tendencies for lust, delusion, sensual lust, and ignorance; and by way of the impulsions of the latent tendencies for delusion and ignorance, [it is said] "he conducts himself with restlessness" and "he conducts himself with doubt.

Regarding the phrase "he conducts himself with latent tendencies," here too, according to the method already stated, one should apply the state of having latent tendencies by taking each individual latent tendency as the root and including all other latent tendencies obtainable in that consciousness. "Associated with lust," and so forth.

It is merely a synonym for "with lust" (*sarāga*) and so forth. For that very same course of conduct receives the names "with lust" and so on because it proceeds together with lust and the other defilements by way of association (*sampayoga*).

It receives the names "associated with lust" (*rāgasampayutta*) and so on because it is conjoined with lust and the others through such modes as arising together, ceasing together, having the same basis, and having the same object.
And that very same [course of conduct] is called "dissociated" (*vippayutta*) because it is dissociated from wholesome and other types of kamma.
Because they are associated with unwholesome and other such kamma, he said "by wholesome kamma" and so forth in order to show that these too are modes of ignorance (*aññāṇacariyā*).
Therein, "unknown" refers to an object that has not been known according to its true nature, because delusion (*moha*) has the characteristic of ignorance. The rest has already been explained.

71. In the mode of knowledge (*ñāṇacariyā*), since the functional indeterminate (*kiriyābyākatā*) advertence (*āvajjanā*) serves as the immediate condition for the contemplation of turning away (*vivaṭṭanānupassanā*) and the others...
Since that [state] does not exist for them, the functional-ineffective (kiriyābyākata) adverting consciousness is not mentioned for their sake;

rather, only the contemplation of turning away (vivaṭṭanānupassanā) and so forth are stated. For adverting occurs only for the purpose of conformity-knowledge (anulomañāṇa), from which follow the contemplation of turning away, the path, and the fruit.
And here, by "attainment of the fruit" (phalasamāpatti), both the attainment arising immediately after the path and that arising at another time are intended.
In passages such as "she moves free from lust" (*nīrāgā carati*), the state of being "free from lust" and so forth should be understood by way of the opposites of lust and the other defilements;
however, in the context of the "conduct of consciousness" (*viññāṇacariyā*), it is in the sense of the mere absence of lust and the rest. "Known" (*ñāta*) means known according to its true nature.

By the phrases "another conduct of consciousness" and so forth, he shows the mutual non-mixture of the three types of conduct. For, by way of the mere function of consciousness, even rootless (*ahetuka*) states of consciousness [are included].

The conduct of consciousness (*viññāṇacariyā*) consists of the conduct of ignorance by way of the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness that possess the function of ignorance, and specifically the conduct of knowledge by way of insight, the path, and the fruit, which perform the function of knowledge. Thus, these [types of consciousness] are mutually unmixed;
and excluding insight, they include the wholesome and functional types of the sense-sphere accompanied by roots, as well as the resultant types of the sense-sphere accompanied by roots.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the wholesome and indeterminate states of the fine-material and immaterial spheres are excluded from the three modes of conduct (*cariyā*).

Because they are demonstrated as the mode of conduct of knowledge (*ñāṇacariyā*) belonging to the contemplation of turning away (*vivaṭṭanānupassanā*) which has Nibbāna as its object, the reviewing knowledges (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*) of both those in training (*sekkhā*) and those beyond training (*asekkhā*)—which consist in the reviewing of Nibbāna, the Path, and the Fruits—should be understood as being included within the mode of conduct of knowledge. These, too...
For they specifically perform the function of knowledge.
The commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of the diversity of conduct is finished.
18. Commentary on the Exposition of the Knowledge of the Diversity of Levels (Bhūminānattañāṇaniddesa).

72. In the exposition of the knowledge of the diversity of planes (*bhūminānattañāṇa*), "planes" (*bhūmi*) refers to divisions or sections. Regarding the term "belonging to the sense sphere" (*kāmāvacara*):

here, desire (*kāma*) is twofold—defilement-desire (*kilesakāma*) and object-desire (*vatthukāma*). Defilement-desire is sensual craving (*chandarāga*); object-desire is the round of existence in the three planes.
Defilement-desire is called "desire" because it desires; object-desire is called "desire" because it is desired. This twofold desire, by way of its occurrence...
The sphere in which one moves is called *kāmāvacara* (the sense-sphere), meaning "that in which desire (*kāma*) moves.
That sphere, moreover, is elevenfold by way of the four woeful states, the human world, and the six heavenly worlds.
For just as that region where men with weapons move about is designated as such even though other two-footed and four-footed beings are also present there;
Because they are particularly distinguished among those who range within it, it is called "the realm where weapons range" (*sasatthāvacara*).

Likewise, even though other realms such as the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) exist and beings range within them, this specific region is called "the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*) precisely because of the distinction of those [beings] who range there.
And just as the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*) is called "form" (*rūpa*), so too, by eliding the latter member of the compound, this is called simply "sense-desire" (*kāma*).
Each individual state (dhamma) that moves within this desire, which consists of eleven types of bases, is called "belonging to the sense-sphere" (kāmāvacara).
For although some states here also move within the realms of form and formlessness, just as an elephant who moves about in battle is named a "battle-mover" (saṅgāmāvacara),
and even when moving in the city is still called a "battle-mover," so too [these states are so termed].

Just as land-dwelling and water-dwelling creatures, even when situated on dry land or in water, are called "land-dwellers" and "water-dwellers" respectively, so too should it be understood that these [states], though they may range elsewhere, are indeed "belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*).
Alternatively, they are called *kāmāvacara* because sense-desire (*kāma*) ranges among these aforementioned types of phenomena by way of making them its object.
Granted, this [desire] also ranges among the phenomena belonging to the fine-material and immaterial spheres; however, [the term is used here specifically for those states].

It functions [therein]. However, this should be understood as being analogous to how, when it is said, "he speaks, thus he is a calf (*vaccha*)," or "he lies on the earth, thus he is a buffalo (*mahiṃsa*"), that name does not apply to every single one who speaks or lies on the earth. In the same way, this should be understood here:

having made all those phenomena into a single heap and with reference to the word "plane" (*bhūmi*) already mentioned, the feminine gender and number "belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacarā*) is used.

It is said. Regarding the terms "belonging to the fine-material sphere" (*rūpāvacara*) and so forth: material existence (*rūpabhava*) is "form" (*rūpa*); those that move within that form are "fine-material-sphere" (*rūpāvacara*).

Immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*) is "the formless" (*arūpa*); those that move within that formless are "immaterial-sphere" (*arūpāvacara*). Those included and contained within the cycle of existence consisting of the three planes are "included" (*pariyāpanna*);
those not included therein are "unincluded" (*apariyāpanna*).
In the descriptions of the planes such as the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), "below" means by way of the lower portion. Regarding "the Avīci hell":
it is called *avīci* because there is no interval (*vīci*), gap, or opening here between the flames, or between the beings, or between the sensations.

It is called *niraya* because there is no pleasure (*sukha*) reckoned as "good" (*aya*) here; it is also *niraya* in the sense of being devoid of delight (*nirati*). "Making that its limit" refers to that which is designated as Avīci.
"Making hell the limit. "Above" means by way of the upper portion.

"The gods who wield power over the creations of others" refers to those deities so designated because they exercise mastery over pleasures created by others. "Including within" means having placed inside.
"Whatever is within this interval" means whatever exists in this space; the change in gender and number (*liṅgavacanavipallāsa*) has been made [in the original]. "Having this as their range" means...
Because other beings also move about during that interval, since they may occasionally arise somewhere, the term "range" (*avacara*) was stated in order not to include them.
By this, it is meant those who move having plunged into one interval, because they arise everywhere and at all times;
and those who move in the lower region, below the Avīci hell, by way of the continued existence of the primary elements (*bhūta-upādāya*).
Their inclusion is thus accomplished. For they move having plunged [into the lower realms], and because they move in the lower regions, they are called "those who range there" (*avacara*).

However, by the term "included therein" (*pariyāpanna*), since these beings range there but also range elsewhere—and yet are not included elsewhere—their inclusion even while ranging elsewhere is thereby accomplished.

Now, demonstrating these phenomena included herein by way of their state as a collection, emptiness, and condition, [the Blessed One] spoke the words beginning with "aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
"Brahma-world" refers to the station of Brahmā, which is designated as the plane of the first jhāna. "Akaniṭṭha" means "not inferior" in the sense of being supreme.
"Of one who has attained" means of one who has entered into meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). By this...
Wholesome jhāna has been described. "Of one who has been reborn" means of one reborn in the Brahma-world by way of kamma-result;

by this, resultant jhāna is described. "Of one who dwells in happiness in the present life": dwelling in happiness in the very present, visible state of selfhood is "dwelling in happiness in the present life";
one who possesses that is "one who dwells in happiness in the present life," namely, the Arahant. [The phrase refers to] him, the one who dwells in happiness in the present life.
By this, the *kiriyajhāna* (functional absorption) is described. "Mental factors" (*cetasika*) means those existing in the mind; the meaning is "associated with consciousness.
"Those who have reached the sphere of infinite space" (*ākāsānañcāyatanūpaga*) means those who have entered into existence known as the sphere of infinite space.

The same method applies to the second term as well. "Paths" (*magga*) refers to the four noble paths. "Fruits of the paths" (*maggaphalāni*) refers to the four fruits of the noble paths. "The unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*).
And "the element" refers to the Nibbāna-element, which is unconditioned by causes.
Furthermore, "another four planes" should be understood according to each respective tetrad. The four foundations of mindfulness are:

the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body, the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of feelings, the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the mind, and the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of mental phenomena.
The meaning of this is as follows: it is called *paṭṭhāna* because it establishes (*patiṭṭhāti*); the meaning is that it stands near, plunges in, and leaps forward.

Mindfulness itself is the establishment; thus it is "establishment of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*). Alternatively, it is mindfulness in the sense of remembering (*saraṇa*), and it is an establishment in the sense of standing near (*upaṭṭhāna*);
thus it is "establishment of mindfulness" because it is both mindfulness and an establishment. There are many such mindful establishments by way of their objects.
The foundations of mindfulness. The four right efforts: the right effort for the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states;
the right effort for the abandoning of arisen unwholesome states; the right effort for the arising of unarisen wholesome states;
and the right effort for the maintenance of arisen wholesome states. It is called "effort" (*padhāna*) because by means of it they strive (*padahanti*) or exert themselves.
This is the name for energy (*vīriya*). "Right exertion" (*sammappadhāna*) means unerring exertion, causal exertion, strategic exertion, and systematic exertion.
Having divided this single energy into four according to its functions, it is called "right exertion.

The "four bases of psychic power" (*cattāro iddhipādā*) are: the base of psychic power consisting of desire (*chanda*), the base of psychic power consisting of consciousness (*citta*), the base of psychic power consisting of energy (*vīriya*), and the base of psychic power consisting of investigation (*vīmaṃsā*).

Its meaning has already been stated. Regarding "the four jhānas": the first jhāna possesses five factors by way of initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), rapture (pīti), happiness (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (citt’ekaggatā).
The second jhāna possesses three factors by way of rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind.

The third jhāna possesses two factors by way of happiness and one-pointedness of mind. The fourth jhāna possesses two factors by way of equanimity (upekkhā) and one-pointedness of mind. These are [the four jhānas].

Indeed, the factors are called "jhāna" in the sense of reflecting upon the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*). The four immeasurables (*appamaññā*) are loving-kindness (*mettā*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*). They are called "immeasurables" by virtue of their pervasiveness and boundlessness.

For these either pervade immeasurable beings by way of their object, or they pervade even a single being by way of a pervasive and complete suffusion; thus, they are so called by virtue of their pervasiveness and boundlessness.
They are called the "immeasurables" (appamaññā). The four formless attainments (arūpasamāpatti) are:

the attainment of the base of infinite space, the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness, the attainment of the base of nothingness, and the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. The four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) have already been explained.
The four modes of practice (paṭipadā) are: the painful mode of practice with slow direct knowledge, the painful mode of practice with quick direct knowledge, and the pleasant...

The four modes of progress (paṭipadā) spoken of are: the mode of progress that is difficult with slow direct knowledge, and the mode of progress that is pleasant with quick direct knowledge. The four objects (ārammaṇa) spoken of are:
the limited object with a limited range, the limited object with an immeasurable range, the immeasurable object with a limited range, and the immeasurable object with an immeasurable range.
These are stated because objects such as the kasiṇas and so forth cannot be definitively fixed [in their nature].
It should be understood that the meditative absorptions (jhānas) have been described as having objects (ārammaṇa). Regarding the four noble lineages (ariyavaṃsa):
"Noble ones" (ariya) refers to Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Tathāgata; the lineages, traditions, and successions of these noble ones are thus called "noble lineages.
What, then, are they? Contentment with robes, contentment with almsfood, contentment with lodgings, and delight in meditation.
These are the four. Contentment with requisites for the sick is already included when contentment with almsfood is mentioned;
for how could one who is content with almsfood be discontented with requisites for the sick?
"The four bases of sympathy" refers to the four means of winning over people: giving, kind speech, and so forth.
These four are: beneficence (*atthacariyā*) and impartiality (*samānattatā*). "Giving" (*dāna*) is giving according to what is appropriate.

"Pleasant speech" (*peyyavajja*) is agreeable speech according to what is appropriate. "Beneficence" (*atthacariyā*) is the act of increasing [another's] welfare by performing what ought to be done in various circumstances and by instructing on what should and should not be done.
"Impartiality" (*samānattatā*) means together with respect (*māna*); the meaning is that it is equal, measured, and reckoned.
"Equalizing oneself with another" (*samānatta*) means "one makes oneself equal to another"; the state of being so is "equalization" (*samānattatā*).
The meaning is: having reflected, "This person is inferior to me," "This person is equal to me," or "This person is superior to me," one acts toward them in a manner corresponding to that assessment.
Some also say: "The state of sharing the same pleasure and pain is equalization."

Regarding the phrase "the four wheels" (*cattāri cakkāni*): here, "wheel" (*cakka*) is fivefold—namely, the wooden wheel, the jewel wheel, the Dhamma wheel, the wheel of postures, and the wheel of prosperity.
Among these, the statement, "But that wheel which was finished by Your Majesty in six months less six days," refers to the wooden wheel.
The statement, "Having taken hold of the wheel as it turns," refers to the jewel wheel.
“‘The wheel set in motion by me’—this is the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*). ‘The four-wheeled [body] with nine gates’—this is the Wheel of Postures (*iriyāpathacakka*).
‘Monks, there are these four wheels; for gods and humans who possess them, the four-wheeled [chariot] rolls.
Which four? Dwelling in a suitable locality, relying on true persons, right self-direction, and [in the past...]”
"Having performed merit"—this is the wheel of success (*sampatticakka*). Here too, this very thing is intended.
In that regard, "dwelling in a suitable locality" means dwelling in a fitting place where the four assemblies are seen.
"Dependence on true persons" means relying upon, attending upon, and associating with true persons such as the Buddhas and others. "Right disposition of oneself" refers to one's own...
It is establishing [them] correctly. If one was previously possessed of lack of faith and so forth, it is the establishing of them in faith and so forth after abandoning those [unwholesome states].
"Merit performed in the past" means wholesome states accumulated previously; this alone is the measure here.
For whatever consciousness associated with knowledge has performed a wholesome deed, that very wholesome [consciousness] [establishes] that person.
He leads one to a suitable place, causes one to associate with true friends; such a person establishes himself rightly.
"The four factors of Dhamma" means four divisions of Dhamma. Which four?
Non-covetousness is a factor of Dhamma, non-ill will is a factor of Dhamma, right mindfulness is a factor of Dhamma, and right concentration is a factor of Dhamma. Non-covetousness...
The "Dhamma-footprint" (dhammapada) is either non-greed, attained by way of non-covetousness, or it is the jhānas, insight, the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna.
The "Dhamma-footprint" is non-ill will, which is non-anger, or it is the jhānas and so forth attained by way of loving-kindness (mettā).
The "Dhamma-footprint" is right mindfulness, which is well-established mindfulness, or it is the jhānas and so forth attained by way of mindfulness. Right concentration...
That which is called the *Dhammapada* refers either to the eight attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*) or the meditations (*jhāna*) and so forth attained by way of the heading of the eight attainments.

Alternatively, the meditations and so forth attained by way of the ten foul objects (*dasāsubha*) are the *Dhammapada* of non-covetousness; those attained by way of the four divine abodes (*catubrahmavihāra*) are the *Dhammapada* of non-ill will;

and those attained by way of the ten recollections (*dasānussati*), the perception of repulsiveness in food (*āhāre paṭikūlasaññā*), and so forth, are the *Dhammapada* of right mindfulness (*sammāsati*).
"Right concentration is the Dhamma-foot attained by means of the ten kasiṇas and mindfulness of breathing.
These four stages should each be applied according to their respective tetrads.
The commentary on the description of the knowledge of the diversity of planes is finished.
19. Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of the Diversity of Phenomena (Dhammanānattañāṇaniddesa) 73.

In the description of the knowledge of the diversity of phenomena, regarding the term "courses of action" (*kammapatha*): they are called "courses of action" because they are both actions (*kamma*) and paths (*patha*) leading to the states of deprivation.
These are the courses of action. The ten wholesome courses of action are: abstaining from killing, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from sexual misconduct.
"Abstention" refers to the three types of good conduct of body: abstaining from false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter—these are the four types of good conduct of speech;
non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view—these are the three types of good conduct of mind.
As for the ten unwholesome courses of action, they consist of the three types of misconduct of body: killing living beings, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct.
False speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter are the four courses of verbal misconduct;
covetousness, ill will, and wrong view are the three courses of mental misconduct.

Furthermore, only those wholesome and unwholesome states that produce rebirth-linking are called "courses of action" (*kammapatha*); the remainder, being manifold in their production of rebirth-linking, are not called "courses of action."
It should be understood that by the mention of gross wholesome and unwholesome [states], the remaining wholesome and unwholesome states are also included.
"Form" refers to twenty-eight kinds of form, distinguished as primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya*).

"Resultant" refers to twenty-three kinds of resultant, by way of the sixteen resultants of sense-sphere wholesome [kamma] and the seven resultants of unwholesome [kamma]. "Functional" refers to the three rootless functional [states] and the eight...

And by way of the eleven types of wholesome functional states (*kiriya*) accompanied by roots, there are eleven kinds of sense-sphere functional states. It is called "functional" (*kiriya*) because it is merely functional, being devoid of result (*vipāka*).
Up to this point, only the sense-sphere has been described by way of the indeterminate as result, the indeterminate as non-causally determined, and the indeterminate as functional.
"Of one established here" means of one established in this world; for, in the human world, the cultivation of meditative absorption (*jhāna-bhāvanā*) generally exists.
This was stated with reference to the human world; however, the jhānas are sometimes obtained even in the deva-world.
In the fine-material Brahma-world, they are obtained according to those who are reborn there, those who are reborn below that level, and those who are reborn above it.

But in the Pure Abodes and in the immaterial realm, there are none who are reborn below. Those in the fine-material and immaterial realms who have not developed the jhānas, when being reborn below, [fall back].
They are reborn only in the happy destinies of the sense-sphere realm, not in the miserable destinies.

"For one reborn there" refers to the four resultant jhānas occurring by way of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death for one reborn in the Brahma-world through the influence of kamma-result (vipāka).
Among the attainments of fine-material and immaterial-sphere jhānas, the functional-indeterminate (kiriya-abyākata) states are not mentioned. Although they are not mentioned, nevertheless—
It should be understood that because they function similarly to the wholesome states, when the wholesome states are mentioned, these [resultant states] are already included.

Just as in the *Paṭṭhāna* it is said, "When a wholesome or unwholesome [state] has ceased, its result arises as an object-condition," where the functional javana is included by the mention of the wholesome javana alone, so too should it be seen here.
"Fruits of recluseship" (*sāmaññaphalāni*) refers to the four fruits of recluseship.
By this, the supramundane resultant indeterminate is stated. "Nibbāna" refers to the Nibbāna indeterminate.
"Rooted in gladness" means those for which gladness is the root or the beginning; the sense is that they have gladness as their starting point.

For it is only when one is possessed of gladness that these states arise. Regarding the statement, "Gladness arises in one who attends to [the object] as impermanent," it is specifically in one who attends to it with wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) that this occurs.
Joy arises for one who attends to things methodically, not for one who attends to them unmethodically.

For one who attends unmethodically, there is no arising of even wholesome states, let alone insight. If it is asked why this is stated in its specific form, it is for the purpose of showing the powerful nature of joy.
For when joy is absent, there is dissatisfaction and weariness regarding secluded lodgings and sublime wholesome states.
[If] it arises [in this way], then meditation itself falters. But when there is gladness (*pāmojja*), because of the absence of discontent (*arati*), meditation reaches its fulfillment.
However, in order to show that wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) is of great benefit to meditation by virtue of being its root, he will state the next ninefold set above.
“From whatever [aspect] one contemplates the arising and passing away of the aggregates, one gains rapture and gladness; that is the deathless for one who understands.

According to this statement, gladness arises for the practitioner of insight (vipassaka) by way of insight (vipassanā) as its condition. Here, however, it arises by way of the condition of the comprehension of groups (kalāpasammasana).
Joy (pāmojja) is to be grasped. Joy is the state of one who is gladdened; it is a mild form of rapture (pīti).
The prefix *pa-* should be understood here in the sense of "beginning" or "initial. "Of one who is gladdened" (*pamuditassa*) means of one who is gladdened and satisfied by that joy.

There is also a reading *pamoditassa*, which has the same meaning. "Rapture" (*pīti*) refers to strong rapture. "With a mind possessed of rapture" (*pītimanassa*) means with a mind conjoined with rapture; the word *yutta* (conjoined) has been elided.
It should be understood as being like a chariot with horses. "The body" refers either to the mental body (*nāmakāya*) or to the physical body (*rūpakāya*).
"Becomes tranquil" means that agitation subsides. "With a tranquil body" means that the body is extinguished through the application of both types of tranquility.
"Experiences happiness" means one finds mental happiness, or [physical] happiness along with it. "Happy" refers to one who possesses happiness. "The mind becomes concentrated" means...

He fixes the mind evenly; it becomes one-pointed. The locative case in the phrase "when the mind is concentrated" (*samāhite citte*) is used in the sense of characterizing a state by means of that state.

For it is by way of the state of mental concentration that the knowledge of things as they truly are is characterized. "He understands as it really is" means he knows formations according to their true nature by means of the knowledge of arising and passing away, and so forth.
"He sees" means he makes that very same object clear, as if it were seen with the eye.

He sees with the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*). "He becomes disenchanted" means that through the application of the ninefold knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), he grows weary of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).

"Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate" means that, bringing that insight to its culmination, he becomes dispassionate toward conditioned phenomena through the application of path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*).
"Through dispassion, he is liberated" means that by means of the cause known as the path—dispassion—he attains liberation as the fruit through resolute confidence (*adhimokkha*) in *nibbāna*.
[He] is liberated. However, in some manuscripts, in this section, the method of the Truths (*saccanaya*) is written as:
"With a concentrated mind, one understands as it really is: 'This is suffering,'" and so forth; and that too, in some manuscripts, is written according to the method beginning with:
"One attends wisely (*yoniso manasikaroti*): 'This is suffering. In both instances, the difference lies merely in the phrasing (*byañjana*), not [in the meaning].

In terms of meaning: because it is stated that "one who becomes disenchanted becomes dispassionate" refers to the knowledge of the path (*maggañāṇa*), once the knowledge of the path is established, the task of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Four Noble Truths is necessarily accomplished as well.
Therefore, the application of the method of the Four Noble Truths stated in the previous section is not different in meaning from this section.
74. Now, since [the object] was stated without specifying the object by means of terms such as "impermanence," etc., he specifies the object as "form" (*rūpa*).
He says, "He attends to it as impermanent," and so forth. "Rooted in wise attention" means that wise attention is their root and foundation;
thus they are "rooted in wise attention. For indeed, apart from wise attention, the nine qualities beginning with gladness do not arise.
"With a concentrated mind" means by means of the mind acting as the cause. "He understands it as it really is" means...
One understands through wisdom. When it is said, "One attends to this as 'this is suffering' with wise attention," the prior awakening to the truths by way of hearsay is also included.
And "wise attention" means attention by way of the appropriate method.

"In dependence on the diversity of elements, there arises the diversity of contact": in dependence on the diversity of the eye-element and so forth, there arises the diversity of eye-contact and so forth.
The meaning is "it arises. "In dependence on the diversity of contact" means in dependence on the diversity of eye-contact and so forth.

"The diversity of feeling" means the diversity of feelings born of eye-contact and so forth. "The diversity of perception" means the diversity of perceptions of sensual desire and so forth. "The diversity of intention" means the diversity of intentions for sensual desire and so forth.
"The diversity of desire" [arises] because of that diversity of intention, such as desire for forms, desire for sounds, and so on.
In this way, diversity of desire arises. Regarding "diversity of fever": due to the diversity of desire, there arises the diversity of fever for forms, fever for sounds, and so forth;
thus, diversity of fever arises. Regarding "diversity of seeking": due to the diversity of fever, there arises the diversity of seeking for forms and so forth.
Regarding "diversity of gain": due to the diversity of seeking, there arises the diversity of obtaining forms and so forth.
The commentary on the exposition of the diversity of states (*dhammanānattañāṇa*) is finished.

20–24. Commentary on the Exposition of the Five Kinds of Knowledge (Ñāṇapañcakaniddesa). 75. Regarding the exposition of the five kinds of knowledge, because there exists a sequential connection among those five knowledges, they are treated from the very beginning.
The answers to the questions have been given. "They are well-known" means they are thoroughly known by way of knowing the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*).
"They are known" means they are called "known" because they are known by their own nature through the full understanding of what is known (*ñātapariññā*).
The connection is as follows: that knowledge by which those phenomena are known is "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) in the sense of being known, and it is "wisdom" (*paññā*) in the sense of understanding.

In this same manner, the remaining knowledges should also be applied. "They have been fully understood" means they have been known thoroughly by way of their general characteristics (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*).
"They have been scrutinized" means they have been investigated as impermanent and so forth, and are thus called "completed" by way of the full understanding through scrutiny (*tīraṇapariññā*).

"They have been abandoned" means that through the knowledge of the contemplation of impermanence and so forth, perceptions of permanence and the like are [abandoned] by means of the contemplation of dissolution.

From that point on, they are abandoned. "They are relinquished" means that by way of abandonment alone, they are indeed cast away. "They are developed" means they have been increased and thoroughly cultivated.
"They have a single flavor" means they have a single function through the performance of their own task and the abandoning of their opposites;
or else, by way of liberation from the adverse, they have a single flavor through the flavor of liberation. They are realized.
"They exist" means that the dhamma of the fruit is established through its acquisition and the dhamma of Nibbāna is established through its penetration;
thus they are directly realized. "They are touched" means that they are touched and experienced through both the contact of acquisition and the contact of penetration.

These five knowledges were previously described by way of knowledge consisting in what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*); here, they are described by way of the accomplishment of their respective functions.
The commentary on the exposition of the five kinds of knowledge is finished.
25–28. Commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of the analytical insights (paṭisambhidāñāṇa). 76.
In the exposition of the knowledge of the analytical insights, since it is not possible to state its function without first stating the phenomena (dhamma), therefore...
Without following the order of those [categories] already enumerated, the *dhammas* are first explained. The meanings of *dhamma* and so forth have already been stated.

Having spoken of those things included under the term *dhamma* by means of such phrases as "the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) is a *dhamma*," he speaks of "another *dhamma*, the faculty of faith," and so on, in order to show the meaning of the word *nānatta*.
For when it is said, "another *dhamma*," the diversity (*nānatta*) of the *dhammas* is indicated.
It has been shown. "Fully understood" means they have been understood through direct confrontation and thus become manifest;

by this, the meaning of the term *paṭisambhidā* is stated. By the phrases "the meaning is resolution" and so forth, he shows that the function of those qualities, such as faith and the rest, is indeed their "meaning," namely, resolving and so on.
"In order to point out" means in order to point it out to another who wishes to make [the truth] known to others. But for another...

It is indeed obtained even for one who merely hears the words. "Phrasing, etymological expression, and utterance" means the phrasing of a name (*nāma*), the etymological expression of a name, and the utterance of a name.
For a name is called "phrasing" (*byañjana*) because it makes the meaning manifest (*byañjayati*).

This is stated with its underlying reason, having been determined thus: "Monks, they are called 'formations' (*saṅkhārā*) because they construct the conditioned" (*saṅkhatam abhisaṅkharonti*). Thus, it is spoken of as being accompanied by a cause.
Regarding *nirutti*: that by which a meaning is expressed is called an "expression" (*abhilāpa*).
Furthermore, this name (*nāma*) is fourfold: the common name (*sāmañña-nāma*), the quality name (*guṇa-nāma*), the fame name (*kittima-nāma*), and the spontaneous name (*opapātika-nāma*).
Among these, the name of the king is "Mahāsammata" (Greatly Elect) because he was established by the great multitude after being chosen in the first eon.
This is a common name. With reference to this, it was said: “‘One approved by the great multitude,’ Vāseṭṭha—thus, ‘Mahāsammata, Mahāsammata’—is the first term that arose.

A name derived from qualities such as “a preacher of the Dhamma, a wearer of rag-robes, a bearer of the Vinaya, a bearer of the Tipiṭaka, faithful, and mindful” is a name based on qualities (*guṇanāma*). “The Blessed One, the Worthy One... [and so forth].
“Sammāsambuddha,” and so forth—these hundreds of names of the Tathāgata are indeed names based on his qualities. Thus it is said:
“The names of the Great Seer are incalculable according to his qualities;
even from a thousand names, his name is surpassed by his virtues.”

Furthermore, on the day of naming a newborn boy, after relatives have performed honors for those worthy of offerings and, standing nearby, having deliberated and reflected, give him a name such as "This one is named so-and-so," this is a conventional name (*kittimanāma*).
As for that which is a prior designation, it falls into a subsequent designation; the prior usage falls into a subsequent usage.
For example: in past aeons it was called "moon" (*canda*), and now too it is called "moon";
in the past it was called "sun," "ocean," "earth," and "mountain," and now too it is called "mountain. This is what is called a "conventional name" (*opapātika-nāma*).
These four kinds of names are all simply one kind of name; they are established merely by worldly convention and do not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*).

It is non-existent. Others, however, say: "Nāma is a sound that illuminates a meaning. The meaning of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) and the path-factors (maggaṅga) should be understood according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidāñāṇa) is finished.
29–31. Commentary on the Exposition of the Threefold Knowledge (Ñāṇattaya-niddesa) 78.

In the exposition of the threefold knowledge: "The sign" (*nimitta*) refers to the sign of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*). "Signless" (*animitta*) refers to Nibbāna, which is the opposite of the sign of conditioned phenomena.

"Because of being intent upon it" (*adhimuttattā*) means because the mind has been released by way of being inclined toward that [Nibbāna]. "Having repeatedly touched its passing away" (*phussa phussa vayaṃ*)...
"He sees" means that, having repeatedly touched the sign of formations with knowledge, he sees their dissolution by means of insight-knowledge itself.

By this, the contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā*) is established. That establishes the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*); because what is impermanent is suffering, it establishes the contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*);
and because what is suffering is non-self, it establishes the contemplation of non-self (*anattānupassanā*). Thus, in this context, there are these three contemplations.
They are thus described. "The signless abiding" (animittavihāra): because the sign has been seen as fear, that abiding in the threefold insight is called the signless abiding.
"Aspiration" (paṇidhi) means craving. "In the wishless" (appaṇihite) means in Nibbāna, which is the opposite of craving.
"Adherence" (abhinivesa) means adherence to a self. "In the void" (suññatāya) means in Nibbāna, which is devoid of a self. "Void" (suññato) means simply void.
"Emptiness. "Having looked on with equanimity at the occurrence" means having looked on with equanimity through equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) at the occurrence of fruition.

For beings generally delight in the occurrence of fruition designated as a happy destination (*sugati*). However, this person, desiring to enter the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), looks on with equanimity precisely after seeing that occurrence and all conditioned things (*saṅkhāra*) as impermanent and so forth. For it is thus...
One is able to attain the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) when [the object] is seen, and not otherwise. "Having adverted" means having adverted by means of adverting.

"Attains" means he enters into the attainment of fruition. It is called the signless attainment because it is entered upon after seeing the sign as fear. It is the attainment of the dwelling in the signless because it is by way of the dwelling in insight (vipassanā).
And by way of both the fruit and the attainment, it is called "both.
Now, in order to show the sign of formations (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*) by analyzing it, he says, "the sign of form," and so forth.

What needs to be said regarding the inclusion of aging and death has already been stated previously. He demonstrates this by concluding with what was already stated in such passages as, "another dwelling in the signless" (*animitta-vihāra*).

In brief, "knowledge of the state of abiding" (vihāraṭṭhe ñāṇaṃ) is the knowledge of the diversity of the insight-abidings for one who stands in the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa) prior to the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti).
"Knowledge of the state of attainment" (samāpattaṭṭhe ñāṇaṃ) is the knowledge of the diversity of the attainment of fruition.

"Knowledge of the state of both abiding and attainment" (vihārasamāpattaṭṭhe ñāṇaṃ) is the knowledge of the diversity of both those [abiding and attainment]. [This is said] of one who wishes to pass the time by means of the insight-abiding alone.

He maintains only the dwelling in insight; or, desiring to pass the time solely by means of the dwelling in the attainment of fruition, he strives through the sequence of insight and maintains only the dwelling in the attainment of fruition;
or, desiring to pass the time by both, he maintains both.
Thus it becomes threefold according to the individual's intention. The rest to be said here has already been stated in the commentary on the knowledge of equanimity towards formations.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Threefold Knowledge is finished.
32. Commentary on the Exposition of the Knowledge of Uninterrupted Concentration 80.

Regarding the phrase "by way of renunciation," etc., in the exposition of the knowledge of uninterrupted concentration, there are: knowledge of renunciation, non-ill will, perception of light, non-distraction, discernment of states, and gladness.

For one practicing dry-insight (sukkha-vipassaka), the seven factors associated with access concentration (upacāra-jjhāna) and acting as counteragents to their respective defilements are indeed associated with a single state of consciousness (ekacitta-sampayutta).
Concentration of mind (cittassa ekaggatā) is non-distraction (avikkhepa). The state of being one-pointed is "one-pointedness" (ekaggatā);
it is called "non-distraction" because the mind does not waver toward various objects. Thus, non-distraction is the concentration of mind characterized by one-pointedness.

The meaning [of the term] is as follows: "Concentration" (*samādhi*) means that by means of it, the mind is placed evenly (*samaṃ ādhīyati*) upon a single object; thus, "concentration" is the name for this—this is the meaning.

"By way of that concentration" means by way of access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*), because one whose mind is concentrated realizes things as they truly are; it is by way of the aforementioned type of concentration.
"Knowledge arises" means that path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*) arises in its proper sequence. "They are exhausted" means...

They are exhausted by way of complete eradication. "Thus" (*iti*) is the conclusion of the matter described in the manner stated. "First, serenity" (*samatha*) means that concentration (*samādhi*) occurs in the prior stage;
"subsequently, knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) means that knowledge occurs in the subsequent stage at the moment of the Path (*maggakkhaṇa*).

The "taint of sensual desire" (*kāmāsava*) is lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure. The "taint of existence" (*bhavāsava*) is the desire and lust for existence in the fine-material and immaterial realms, as well as attachment to meditative absorption (*jhāna-nikanti*).
Lust co-arising with the eternalist view is aspiration in the form of existence (*bhava*). The taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) refers to the sixty-two views.
The taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*) is non-knowing regarding the eight points beginning with suffering.

Having posed a question regarding the sphere by means of the word "ground" (*bhummavacana*), he shows the destruction of the taints by means of the path that effects the destruction of the taints—beginning with "by the stream-entry path"—and then [concludes] with "herein."
The relinquishing of the occasion has been performed; this is what is meant by "at the moment of the path. "Without remainder" (*anavaseso*) means that there is nothing remaining of it.

"Leading to the states of loss" (*apāyagamanīyo*): the four—namely, hell, the animal womb, the sphere of hungry ghosts, and the host of asuras—are called "losses" (*apāyā*) because they are devoid of what is reckoned as happiness;
one who possesses [the defilements] leading to these is called "leading to the states of loss," because he causes that person to go to those states of loss.
The discourse on the destruction of the taints (*āsava*) has been explained in the "Discourse on Emergence from Both Sides.

"By way of non-distraction" means by way of the concentration that serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the concentration currently occurring. In the phrases beginning with "by way of the earth-kasiṇa," the ten kasiṇas are mentioned by way of the absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*) that takes them as its object;
the recollections of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*) and so forth, as well as the recollection of death (*maraṇassati*), [are mentioned] by way of access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*).

The recollection of peace (*upasamānussati*) is stated by way of access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*); mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*) and mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) are stated by way of absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*);
and the ten kinds of foulness (*asubha*) are stated by way of the first jhāna.

Recollection arisen with reference to the Buddha is "recollection of the Buddha" (*buddhānussati*). It has as its object the qualities of the Buddha, beginning with: "Thus indeed is the Blessed One, the Worthy One... (*Itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ...*) and so forth.

This is a designation for mindfulness (*sati*), by way of that recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*). Likewise, the recollection arisen with reference to the Dhamma is the recollection of the Dhamma (*dhammānussati*);
this is a designation for mindfulness having as its object the qualities of the Dhamma, beginning with: "The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One.
The recollection arisen with reference to the Saṅgha is the recollection of the Saṅgha (*saṅghānussati*); [beginning with]: "The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples..."
This is a designation for mindfulness having the qualities of the Saṅgha—such as "the Saṅgha of disciples"—as its object. Mindfulness arisen with reference to virtue is *sīlānussati*.
This is a designation for mindfulness having the qualities of one’s own virtue, such as its being unbroken, as its object.
Mindfulness arisen with reference to generosity is *cāgānussati*. [This is a designation for mindfulness] having the qualities of one’s own generosity, such as being free-handed, as its object.
This is a designation for mindfulness (*sati*). Mindfulness arisen with reference to deities is "recollection of deities" (*devatānussati*);

this is a designation for mindfulness whose object is one's own qualities such as faith, having placed the deities in the position of witnesses. Mindfulness arisen with reference to inhalation and exhalation is "mindfulness of breathing" (*ānāpānassati*);
this is a designation for mindfulness whose object is the sign of inhalation and exhalation. With reference to death...

"Arisen mindfulness" refers to mindfulness of death (*maraṇassati*). This is a designation for mindfulness that has as its object death, defined as the cutting off of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) included within a single existence.

It is called "mindfulness directed to the body" (*kāyagatāsati*) because it is directed toward—that is, present and active in—the physical frame known as the "body," which is so designated because it is dependent upon and composed of the loathsome and repulsive things such as head-hairs and so forth;
or, it is mindfulness that has gone toward such a body. Although it should be called "mindfulness directed to the body" (*kāyagatasatī*), [the *i* is elided].
Without shortening it, it is called "mindfulness directed to the body" (*kāyagatāsati*). Likewise, here too, it is stated "by way of mindfulness directed to the body.
This is a designation for mindfulness that has the sign of repulsiveness as its object regarding the bodily parts beginning with the head-hairs.
Mindfulness arisen by taking tranquility as its object is "recollection of peace" (*upasamānussati*). This is a designation for mindfulness that has the pacification of all suffering as its object.
The ten foul subjects (*dasāsubhā*) have their meanings explained below.
