81. The phrases beginning with "by means of long inhalation" are stated specifically to show the different types of access and absorption concentration (*appanūpacāra-samādhi-bheda*).
"By means of long inhalation" means by means of the inhalation described as "long. "Breathing in long, I am breathing in long... [and so forth].
For it is said: "he understands. This same method applies to the remaining [phrases] as well.

"Experiencing the whole body" means experiencing the entire body of inhalation and exhalation. "Tranquilizing the bodily formation" means tranquilizing and pacifying the gross bodily formation consisting of inhalation and exhalation.
"Long or short, experiencing the whole body, tranquilizing the bodily formation."
By this very tetrad, absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*) is described. "Experiencing rapture" means making rapture manifest.
"Experiencing the mental formations" means making the mental formation known as perception and feeling manifest. "Gladdening the mind" means delighting the mind.
"Concentrating the mind" means placing the mind evenly upon the object. "Liberating the mind" means [liberating] the mind...

Liberating [the mind] from the hindrances and so forth; and the fourfold [formula]: "experiencing rapture, experiencing pleasure, experiencing the mental formations, and tranquilizing the mental formations"; and the fourfold [formula]:

"experiencing the mind, gladdening the mind, concentrating the mind, and liberating the mind"—[all] by way of absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*) and concentration associated with insight (*vipassanā-sampayutta-samādhi*).

And these have been stated. "Contemplating impermanence" is by way of the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*). "Contemplating dispassion" is by way of the contemplation of revulsion (*nibbidānupassanā*).
"Contemplating cessation" is by way of the contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā*). "Contemplating relinquishment" is by way of insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā*);

for that, by means of its specific factor (*tadaṅga*), relinquishes the defilements along with the formative activities of the aggregates (*khandhābhisaṅkhāra*). This is through seeing the fault in the conditioned.
And by inclining toward Nibbāna, which is the opposite of that, one leaps forward into it. This tetrad is stated specifically by way of concentration associated with insight.
Here, the phrases "by way of in-breath" and "by way of out-breath" are spoken merely by taking up the occurrence of the in-breath and out-breath, not by making them the actual object of meditation.
A detailed explanation of this will appear in the discussion on mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānakathā*).
The commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of the concentration of the immediate [result] is finished.
33. Commentary on the Exposition of the Knowledge of the Dwelling in Peace (Araṇavihārañāṇaniddesa) 82.

In the exposition of the knowledge of the dwelling in peace, the contemplations of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) and so forth have already been explained. "The dwelling in emptiness" (*suññato vihāro*) refers to the contemplation of non-self (*anattānupassanā*).
The attainment of the fruit of arahantship that occurs in the mode of emptiness for one who has emerged [from meditation] is the "signless abiding.
The attainment of the fruit of arahantship that occurs in the mode of the signless for one who has emerged through the contemplation of impermanence is the "signless abiding.

The attainment of the fruit of arahantship that occurs in the mode of the desireless for one who has emerged through the contemplation of suffering is the "desireless abiding. "Inclined toward emptiness" means...

In the case of emptiness, it is the state of being inclined toward the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) by means of the wisdom belonging to its preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga-paññā*). The same method applies to the other two as well.

By the terms "first jhāna" and so forth, the meditative attainments (*jhānasamāpatti*) that serve as the objects for insight (*vipassanā*) for one desiring to enter the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship are described. For it is only an Arahant who possesses the meditative attainments characterized by inclination toward the excellence of insight, fruition, and attainment.
Because all defilements have been abandoned, they are worthy of being called "dwelling in the conflict-free" (*araṇavihāra*).
One removes the hindrances by means of the first jhāna; thus, it is the "conflict-free dwelling.

The meaning is that one who possesses the first jhāna removes the hindrances by means of the first jhāna, and therefore that first jhāna is the conflict-free dwelling. This same principle applies to the remaining [jhānas] as well.

This is the method. It should be understood that although the Arahant is devoid of hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), it is said that "the first jhāna removes the hindrances" because the first jhāna is the antidote (*vipakkha*) to them.

If it is asked: "Having indicated the knowledge of the dwelling without conflict (*araṇavihāra-ñāṇa*) in three ways—by way of insight (*vipassanā*), fruition attainment (*phalasamāpatti*), and inclination toward the sublime (*paṇītādhimutti*)—why are only the jhāna attainments specified as the 'dwelling without conflict'? [The answer is: Because they are [included] by the very act of that indication.
This is because [the state of] dwelling without conflict (*araṇavihāra*) is established for the three [types of persons].

However, since the state of dwelling without conflict regarding the meditative attainments (*jhānasamāpatti*)—which serve as the basis for the insight (*vipassanā*) leading to the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*)—is not established unless it is explicitly stated, it should be understood that the passage beginning with "The first jhāna is a dwelling without conflict" was spoken in order to establish what was previously unestablished. For their state of being a dwelling without conflict is [demonstrated] by way of enumeration.
Although not yet established [as a specific term], it is considered established because it is mentioned in the *Niddesa*. Or else, according to the very method already applied to those [terms]:

"The contemplation of impermanence removes the perception of permanence, thus it is an abiding in non-conflict (*araṇavihāra*); the contemplation of suffering removes the perception of pleasure, thus it is an abiding in non-conflict;
the contemplation of non-self removes the perception of self, thus it is an abiding in non-conflict; the void abiding removes non-voidness, thus it is an abiding in non-conflict; the signless..."

It should be understood by applying the following: “The dwelling that removes the sign is the dwelling without conflict (araṇavihāra); the wishless dwelling that removes wishing is the dwelling without conflict;

the inclination toward emptiness that removes the inclination toward non-emptiness is the dwelling without conflict; the inclination toward the signless that removes the inclination toward signs is the dwelling without conflict;
and the inclination toward the wishless that removes the inclination toward wishes is the dwelling without conflict.”
The commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of dwelling in the conflict-free (araṇavihāra) is finished.
34. Commentary on the Exposition of the Knowledge of the Attainment of Cessation (nirodhasamāpattiñāṇaniddesa):

In the exposition of the knowledge of the attainment of cessation, "the power of serenity" (samathabala) refers to that which pacifies (sameti) the opposing states such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and so forth.
Tranquility (samatha) is itself power in the sense of being unshakable.

Because it has reached the state of fulfillment in concentration through the abandoning of sensual desire—the opponent of concentration—only in non-returners and arahants, their concentration alone is considered to have attained power;
thus it is called the "power of tranquility" (samathabala), and not that of others. There is also the reading "the power of concentration" (samādhibala).
"Insight power" (*vipassanā-bala*): It is called "insight" (*vipassanā*) because it sees phenomena in various modes, such as impermanence and so forth;
that very same [insight] is "power" in the sense of being unshakable. The knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) is the attainment of power by those two [calm and insight].
Therein, the power of calm (*samatha-bala*) is for the purpose of gradually pacifying the mental continuum and for the purpose of establishing it in cessation; the power of insight...
[This is] for the purpose of seeing the danger in the occurrence [of defilements] and for the purpose of seeing the benefit in their cessation.
Regarding the word "in the hindrances" (*nīvaraṇe*), it is a locative expression used in the sense of a cause; the meaning is "on account of the hindrances" or "with the hindrances as a condition.

Alternatively, it is a locative expression used in the sense of an instrument; the meaning is "by means of the hindrances. "Does not waver" refers to the person who possesses the meditative absorption (*jhāna*). Or else, "meditative absorption" (*jhāna*)...
Because the factors of jhāna are intended here, by means of the first jhāna, the concentration associated with it is unshakable by the hindrances.

This alone is the construction that should be understood here. "And by agitation" means in regard to both agitation—that is, in the arising of consciousness accompanied by agitation—and in regard to the state of being agitated.
Agitation is the state of being restless; its characteristic is lack of tranquility. "And by the defilements accompanied by agitation" [is said].

It does not waver, does not shake, and does not tremble—these are synonyms for one another—with respect to the defilements of delusion (*moha*), shamelessness (*ahirika*), and fearlessness of wrongdoing (*anottappa*), which are associated with restlessness (*uddhacca*) and have attained the state of arising together with it; and with respect to the aggregates (*khandha*), meaning the four aggregates associated with restlessness.
It does not waver in the face of restlessness; it does not shake the defilements associated with restlessness; [it does not tremble] the aggregates associated with restlessness.
"It does not waver" should be supplied [to the end of the sentence].

Since the power of insight (vipassanā-bala) is stated in connection with only the seven contemplations (anupassanā), it should be understood that the power of insight is perfected by means of those alone. "And of ignorance" refers to ignorance in all twelve types of unwholesome consciousness-arising.

"And of defilements accompanied by ignorance" refers, as appropriate, to the defilements associated with ignorance: greed, hatred, conceit, views, doubt, sloth, restlessness, lack of moral shame (ahirika), and lack of moral dread (anottappa).

“Verbal formations” (*vacīsaṅkhārā*) are applied thought and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*). According to the statement: “First, friend Visākha, one applies thought and sustains thought, and afterwards breaks forth into speech;
therefore, applied thought and sustained thought are verbal formations,” they are called verbal formations because they form—that is, they produce—speech.
“Bodily formations” (*kāyasaṅkhārā*) are inhalation and exhalation. “Inhalation and exhalation, friend Visākha, are bodily...”

Because of the statement, "These states are bound up with the body; therefore, in-breathing and out-breathing are bodily formations" (*kāyasaṅkhāra*), they are called bodily formations because they are formed by the body.
"The cessation of perception and feeling" (*saññāvedayitanirodha*) means the cessation of perception and feeling. "Mental formations" (*cittasaṅkhāra*) refers to perception and feeling.
Because of the statement, "These states are mental factors bound up with the mind; therefore, perception and feeling..."
Because of the statement “the mental formation,” they are called *cittasaṅkhārā* (mental formations) since they are formed by the mind.

84. It should be understood that among the modes of knowledge (*ñāṇacariyā*), by the inclusion of the contemplation of turning away (*vivaṭṭanānupassanā*) at the conclusion of the contemplations, or by the mention of the mode of conduct that constitutes its beginning, the other contemplations are also included when it is said “by the sixteen modes of knowledge. By the sixteen modes of knowledge...
And this is the maximum limit; however, for a non-returner (anāgāmī), it occurs even with all fourteen [powers], because his powers are complete, excluding only the path and fruit of Arahantship.

85. Regarding "by nine modes of concentration practice" (samādhicariyā): here, there are eight consisting of the first jhāna and so forth, and one consisting of access concentration (upacārajjhāna) applied everywhere for the sake of attaining the first jhāna and so on;
thus, there are nine modes of concentration practice. What is the distinction between these and the modes of power (balacariyā)?
For indeed, by the power of serenity (*samatha*), access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) is described through seven modes beginning with “by way of renunciation” (*nekkhamma-vasena*);
through the expansion of the formula, absorption and access concentration are described appropriately in seventy equal turns beginning with “by way of the first jhāna” (*paṭhama-jjhāna-vasena*);
and by the practice of concentration (*samādhi-carīya*), absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*) is described through eight modes beginning with “the first jhāna.”

It was stated [thus]. Since access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) was stated by way of eight modes beginning with "for the sake of attaining the first jhāna," it follows that in both instances only absorption and access concentration were spoken of.
Even so, they should be understood as "powers" (balāni) in the sense of being unshakable, and as "conducts" (cariyā) in the sense of mastery.
As for the power of insight (vipassanā-bala), the seven contemplations themselves are called the "power of insight."

Seven contemplations have been stated in terms of the course of knowledge (*ñāṇacariyā*), and nine others, beginning with the contemplation of turning away (*vivaṭṭanānupassanā*), have been stated specifically.

This is their distinction. Furthermore, the seven contemplations should be understood as "powers" (*balāni*) in the sense of being unshakable, and as "courses" (*cariyā*) in the sense of mastery (*vasībhāva*).
To explain the masteries mentioned in the passage, “Wisdom is mastery,” the term “mastery” is used here in the feminine gender as “five masteries.”

It has been said. "Mastery itself is mastery"—this is what is meant. Again, in order to explain those masteries by means of a teaching based on the person (puggalādhiṭṭhānā), he says, beginning with "mastery over adverting" (āvajjanavasī).
Mastery over adverting is "adverting-mastery"; one who possesses that is "one possessing mastery over adverting.
The same method applies to the remaining [masteries]. "The first jhāna wherever one wishes" means in whichever place one wishes, whether in a village...
Or in the forest; he adverts to this or that place. "At will" means whenever at any time—whether in the cold season or the hot season—he adverts to it.
Alternatively, whichever first jhāna he desires—whether having the earth-kasiṇa as its object or another object—that he adverts to.
This applies to those who have mastery over each individual kasiṇa-object jhāna.

Because it has been so stated, the former interpretation alone is more excellent. "As long as he wishes" means for as long a time as he desires—whether it be merely the snap of a finger or for seven days—for that long he adverts.
"By adverting" means by mind-door adverting. "Sluggishness" means the state of being subject to lack of control, or the state of being indolent.
"Enters" means he proceeds; the meaning is that he applies [the mind]. "He resolves" means...

Having made the internal attainment predominant, he remains [therein]. Regarding the phrase "the first jhāna" in the context of mastery over emergence (*vuṭṭhānavasī*), it is used in the accusative case with the sense of the ablative;
thus, the meaning is "from the first jhāna. "He reviews" means that having turned back from the impulsion-moments of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇa-javana*), he sees.
This is the commentary on the text in this instance.
This, however, is the explanation of the meaning: for one who has emerged from the first jhāna and adverts to the applied thought (*vitakka*), the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is interrupted;
immediately following the adverting consciousness, four or five impulsion moments (*javana*) arise having that very applied thought as their object.

Then two moments of the life-continuum follow. After that, there is again an adverting consciousness having sustained thought (*vicāra*) as its object, followed by impulsion moments in the same manner as described.
Thus, when one is able to direct the mind continuously toward the five factors of jhāna, then one’s mastery over adverting (āvajjanavasī) is indeed accomplished.
However, this mastery reached at its ultimate peak is obtained only by the Blessed One during the Twin Miracle itself;
beyond this, there is no such thing as a swifter mastery of adverting. For others, however, there are intervals of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

There is no counting [the number of attainments]. The Elder Mahāmoggallāna’s capacity to enter attainments swiftly, as in his subduing of Nanda and Upananda, is called mastery over entering (samāpajjana-vasī).
The capacity to maintain an attainment for the duration of a finger-snap or ten finger-snaps is called mastery over resolution (adhiṭṭhāna-vasī).
Likewise, the capacity to emerge from it quickly is mastery over emerging (vuṭṭhāna-vasī).

...so it is called. However, mastery in reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa-vasī) is said to be included within mastery in adverting (āvajjana-vasī), for the reviewing impulsions (javana) themselves follow immediately after the adverting consciousness in that context.
Thus, when mastery in adverting is established, mastery in reviewing is established;
and when mastery in resolving (adhiṭṭhāna-vasī) is established, mastery in emerging (vuṭṭhāna-vasī) is established. Even so, "this, however..."
Because it is said, "Mastery reaching the very peak is obtained only at the Blessed One’s Twin Miracle," there is no reviewing of the jhāna factors at the time of the miracle;
therefore, since the manifestation of various colors and so forth succeeds by way of various kasiṇas,
one who wishes to attain jhāna having that respective kasiṇa as its object should, according to their preference, quickly [enter] that kasiṇa in the manner described.
Mastery of adverting is the capacity for adverting; mastery of attainment is the capacity for entering and the capacity for absorption into that very jhāna within the cognitive process of adverting.
When it is explained in this way, the logic is not contradicted, and the sequence of the masteries is consistent with their proper order. However, regarding the reviewing of the jhāna factors:

Because it is stated that “only five impulsion moments reach the head [of the cognitive process],” when the seven impulsions are occurring according to the method already described, there is indeed mastery over the reviewing.
If it is argued that this being so, the statement “he adverts to the first jhāna” is not logical, [the answer is:
just as the jhāna that occurs with respect to the kasiṇa is called “the kasiṇa” by way of a metaphorical designation based on its cause, so too [is the jhāna] [designated] by way of its condition.
The term "kasiṇa" is spoken of as "jhāna" by way of a metaphorical designation for the fruit, as in such passages as "the arising of Buddhas is bliss.

For one who has remained for the duration previously delimited and has emerged, the act of entering jhāna again—just as when one who has woken from sleep falls back asleep—is indeed called "mastery over resolution" (adhiṭṭhāna-vasī).
However, for one who has emerged according to that same delimitation, there is mastery only over the emergence itself, not over the resolution.
Furthermore, there is also what is called "mastery over emergence"; this is the distinction between them.
However, for the purpose of analyzing the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), this inquiry is posed: What is the attainment of cessation?
Who attains it? Who does not attain it? Where do they attain it? Why do they attain it? And how is it attained?
There is the entering [into attainment], how is there the abiding, and how is there the emergence? For one who has emerged, what is the inclination of the mind?

What is the difference between one who is dead and one who has attained [cessation]? Is the attainment of cessation conditioned or unconditioned, mundane or supramundane, accomplished or unaccomplished?
In this context, what is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)? It is the non-occurrence of consciousness and mental factors by way of successive cessation.

Who attains it, and who does not? All worldlings (*puthujjana*), stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*), dry-insight practitioners (*sukkha-vipassaka*), non-returners (*anāgāmin*), and arahants do not attain it;
however, non-returners who have attained the eight meditative attainments do attain it.
And those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) also attain [this attainment].

Where do they attain it? In the five-aggregate existence (pañcavokārabhava). Why? Because of the presence of successive attainments (anupubbasamāpatti) there. However, in the four-aggregate existence (catuvokārabhava), the mere arising of the first jhāna and so forth does not even exist; therefore, it is impossible to attain it there. For what purpose do they attain it?

Having become weary of the diversity in the occurrence of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra), they attain it thinking: "In this very life, having become mindless, we shall dwell in happiness having reached cessation, which is Nibbāna."

And how does its attainment come about? For one who has performed the preliminary duties by striving through the means of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), and who brings the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) to cessation—in this way its attainment occurs.

For he who strives solely through the means of serenity remains after reaching the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. He who [strives] solely through the means of insight...

He exerts himself and, having attained the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), he remains therein. But he who, exerting himself by means of both [the fourth jhāna and the attainment of fruition], arrests perception at the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters that attainment; this is the summary here.
This, however, is the detailed account: here, a bhikkhu desiring to enter the attainment of cessation, having finished his meal duties and having well-washed his hands and feet...
In a secluded place, he sits on a well-prepared seat, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him.

Having attained the first jhāna and emerged from it, he contemplates the formations therein as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. This insight, moreover, is threefold: insight that grasps formations, [insight that examines formations, and insight that scrutinizes formations].
There are two kinds of insight: insight for the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti-vipassanā*) and insight for the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti-vipassanā*).
In this context, whether the insight that grasps formations (*saṅkhāra-pariggahaṇaka-vipassanā*) is weak or sharp, it certainly serves as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the Path.
Insight for the attainment of fruition must be sharp, being similar to the cultivation of the Path. However, insight for the attainment of cessation must be neither too weak nor too sharp.
Therefore, with insight that is neither too dull nor too sharp, he contemplates those formations with insight.
Then, having entered the second jhāna and emerged from it, he likewise contemplates the formations therein with insight. Then the third jhāna...
[and so on] ...then, having entered the base of infinite consciousness and emerged from it, he likewise contemplates the formations therein with insight. Then the base of nothingness.
Having entered [the attainment] and emerged from it, he performs the fourfold preliminary duty:
not disturbing what is bound separately, honoring the Saṅgha, summoning the Teacher, and delimiting the duration of the journey.
Therein, "not disturbing what is bound separately" refers to that which is not bound together with this bhikkhu, but is bound separately.

Having offered [the blessing], one should resolve that the bowl and robes, or the bed and chair, or the dwelling house, or whatever other kind of requisite is present, shall not be disordered and shall not be destroyed by fire, water, wind, thieves, rats, or the like.
Herein, this is the method for the resolution: "May this and this not be consumed by fire within these seven days."
"May it not be carried away by water; may it not be destroyed by wind; may it not be stolen by thieves; may it not be gnawed by rats and the like.
When one has made such a resolution, for those seven days no danger whatsoever befalls it; however, if no resolution is made, it is destroyed by fire and other such causes.
This is called "non-disturbance of what is not bound together. As for that which is bound together, such as the lower garment and the upper robe—
Whether it be a standing place or a sitting seat, there is no need for a separate formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) in that case; the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) itself protects it.

"Waiting upon the Saṅgha" means waiting for or looking toward the community of monks. The meaning is that as long as this monk has not arrived, the formal act of the Saṅgha (*saṅghakamma*) is not to be performed. Furthermore, in this context, "waiting" is not a preliminary duty for him.
The preliminary duty, however, is the adverting of the mind. Therefore, one should advert thus:

"If, while I am sitting having entered the attainment of cessation for seven days, the Saṅgha wishes to perform any formal act such as an act of seeking permission (apalokana-kamma), I shall emerge at the very moment no bhikkhu comes to summon me. Thus...
For one who has entered [attainment] at that time emerges immediately after having performed it.
However, for one who does not do so, the Saṅgha, having assembled and not seeing him, asks, "Where is such-and-such a bhikkhu?
When it is said, "He has entered cessation," they send a certain bhikkhu with the words, "Go and summon him in the name of the Saṅgha. Then, by that [messenger], he—
When a bhikkhu stands within earshot and merely says, "The Saṅgha, friend, is sending you back," that is itself the emergence.
For such is the weighty command of the Saṅgha. Therefore, having reflected on this, one should attain absorption in such a way that one emerges by oneself.
"Accosting the Teacher": here too, the preliminary duty for this [meditation] is precisely the adverting of the mind toward accosting the Teacher.

Therefore, that too should be adverted to in this way: "If, while I am sitting having entered the attainment of cessation for seven days, the Teacher should lay down a training rule regarding a matter that has arisen, or should teach the Dhamma by way of such an occasion."
"I shall rise at the very moment that no one comes to call me. Having made this resolve and sitting down, he indeed rises at that time.
However, as for one who does not do so, when the Teacher has assembled the Saṅgha and, not seeing him, asks, "Where is such-and-such a bhikkhu?
and it is said in reply, "He has entered the attainment of cessation," [the Teacher sends someone] to anyone...

He sends a bhikkhu, saying, "Go and summon him in my name. Then, as soon as that bhikkhu stands within hearing distance and says, "The Teacher summons the Venerable One," there is an emergence from the attainment. For such is the gravity of a summons by the Teacher;
therefore, having adverted to it, one should enter the attainment in such a way that one emerges automatically.
“Limitation of the duration” means the limitation of the life-span. For this reason, a bhikkhu must be skilled in the limitation of the duration;
he should enter the attainment only after having adverted [to his state], thinking: “Will my own life-formations continue for seven days, or will they not continue?
For if, without having adverted to the life-formations that are to cease within seven days, [he were to enter it]...
When he enters [the attainment], the attainment of cessation is unable to ward off death.
Because there is no death within the cessation of cessation, he emerges from the attainment midway; therefore, this must be entered after having adverted to it.
For the remainder, it is permissible not even to advert to it, but this one must indeed be adverted to—thus it is said. He, in this way, [the sphere of nothingness]...
Having entered [the attainment], emerged, and performed this preliminary duty, he enters the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Then, after passing over one or two mental moments, he becomes mindless and touches cessation.
But why do his mental states not proceed beyond two moments? Because it is the preliminary application for cessation. For this...
For a bhikkhu who has joined the two qualities of serenity and insight in yoke, the ascent to the eight attainments is the preliminary practice for successive cessation,
not the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; because it is the preliminary practice for cessation, no further consciousnesses proceed beyond those two.

What is the "occasion" (*ṭhāna*)? For one who has thus attained, there is an occasion by way of a limitation of time, and because of the absence of premature death due to the exhaustion of the life-span, or through the intervention of the Saṅgha, or the Teacher’s summons.
What is the "emergence" (*vuṭṭhāna*)? Emergence is twofold: for a non-returner, it is the attainment of the fruit of non-returning; for an arahant, it is the attainment of the fruit of arahantship.
When he has emerged, to what is his mind inclined? It is inclined toward Nibbāna. For this has been said: "In the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling..."
“Friend Visākha, when a bhikkhu has emerged [from jhāna], his mind tends toward seclusion, inclines toward seclusion, and leans toward seclusion.
What is the difference between one who is dead and one who has attained [jhāna]? This matter too is stated in the Sutta itself. As it is said:
“Friend, in the case of one who is dead and deceased, his bodily formations have ceased and subsided, as have his verbal formations...”
The formations of mind have ceased and subsided; life has been exhausted; heat has been quenched; the faculties have broken up.
As for this bhikkhu who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, his bodily formations have also ceased and subsided;
his verbal formations and mental formations have ceased and subsided; his life...
“The life-faculty is not exhausted, heat has not subsided, and the faculties are unimpaired.

However, regarding the question as to whether the attainment of cessation is conditioned (*saṅkhata*) and so forth, it cannot be said to be either “conditioned” or “unconditioned,” nor “mundane” (*lokiya*) or “supramundane” (*lokuttara*). Why?
Because it does not exist by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). Nevertheless, for one who enters [the attainment]...
Because one has entered [meditative attainment] by means of that [attainment], it is fitting to say that it is "accomplished" (nipphanna), not "unaccomplished.
Thus: "Such is this peaceful attainment, cultivated by the Noble Ones;
it is reckoned as Nibbāna even in this very life."
The commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of the attainment of cessation is finished.
35. Commentary on the Exposition of the Knowledge of Final Nibbāna: 86.
In the exposition of the knowledge of final Nibbāna, "here" means in this Dispensation. "Clearly comprehending" refers to clear comprehension of purpose (*sātthaka-sampajañña*).
He is fully aware by means of these four kinds of clear comprehension: clear comprehension of suitability, clear comprehension of domain, and clear comprehension of non-delusion.
"Arising" refers everywhere, as appropriate, to both the arising of the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) and the arising of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).
"Consuming" refers, in the case of those [states] mentioned by way of access and absorption, to their suppression; in the case of those mentioned by way of insight...
By way of its factors and by way of the path, it exhausts—that is, renders non-occurrence of—the [defilements] stated [to be abandoned] through their complete eradication.
For, by way of a summary, the second jhāna attainment, the great insight, and the path have been abbreviated.
Since the knowledge that occurs when one reviews this is called "knowledge of final Nibbāna," therefore there is suppression-Nibbāna and factor-Nibbāna.

"Parinibbāna by eradication" has also already been mentioned. By these [terms], the knowledge of reviewing the parinibbāna of the defilements (*kilesaparinibbāna*) is stated. Then, with the words "Or else... and so forth, he points out the knowledge of reviewing the parinibbāna of the aggregates (*khandhaparinibbāna*).

Regarding the phrase "in the element of Nibbāna without residue": for the element of Nibbāna is twofold—namely, that with residue (*saupādisesa*) and that without residue (*anupādisesa*). Therein, it is "taken up" (*upādīyate*)...
"It is grasped intensely as 'I' and 'mine,'" thus it is *upādi*; this is a designation for the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*).
That which remains, that which is left over, is *upādisesa*. That which exists together with this remainder is *saupādisesā*.
That wherein no remainder exists is *anupādisesā*. The state with remainder was mentioned first; this, however, is the state without remainder. By means of that state without remainder...
Regarding the element of Nibbāna: "the turning of the eye" means the activity of the eye, the manifestation of the eye. "Consumes" means it is exhausted, it is worn away.
This same method applies to the remaining [senses].
The commentary on the description of the knowledge of final Nibbāna is finished.
36. Explanation of the Exposition of Knowledge of the Eightfold Equal Headings (Samasīsaṭṭhañāṇaniddesa).
In the exposition of the knowledge of the eightfold equal headings, the inclusion of all phenomena is to be understood by means of ten groups, beginning with "the five aggregates.

For it is not possible [to include all phenomena] by means of each individual category alone; rather, apart from the groups of bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu), they are included by the remaining eight groups separately.

"Every phenomenon is included individually. However, since supramundane phenomena (*lokuttara-dhamma*) are not to be abandoned by the cutting off of their roots, therefore—even though they are included by the term "all phenomena"—supramundane phenomena are not to be taken here because they do not occur by way of abandonment through cutting off;
rather, only those phenomena belonging to the three planes (*tebhūmaka-dhamma*) which are to be abandoned by the cutting off of their roots are to be taken.

"He completely eradicates" means that, according to the circumstances, he completely eradicates by way of suppression, by way of its own constituent (tadaṅga), and by way of abandonment, while ceasing both the active obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna) and the underlying tendencies (anusaya).
Thus, complete eradication has been demonstrated through a teaching focused on the person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna).
"He ceases" means he ceases by way of non-arising cessation (anuppādanirodha). By this, the meaning of eradication is shown.
"Stated. "It does not stand again" means that when cessation has been effected in this way, each respective phenomenon does not stand up again;
it does not arise—this is the meaning. By this, the sense of cessation is stated. Thus, the state of non-standing is demonstrated by way of the nature of phenomena that do not stand again.

"Peaceful" (*santa*) means peaceful because of the pacification of sensual desire and the other [hindrances]. Those [factors] are the seven beginning with renunciation (*nekkhamma*), as well as the fine-material and immaterial jhānas.
There are eight [factors], eighteen great insights (*mahāvipassanā*), and four noble paths (*ariyamagga*), making thirty-seven in total.

Thirteen "heads" (*sīsa*) have been mentioned here by way of including all those that function as heads. However, in this context, only the eight heads beginning with faith (*saddhā*) are appropriate;
for an Arahant does not possess the five heads beginning with craving (*taṇhā*). The "head of impediments" (*palibodhasīsa*) refers to an obstruction.
*Palibodha* means an obstruction to the path to Nibbāna; this is the meaning. *Sīsa* means the chief, that is, the most prominent.

The *palibodha* itself is the "head" (*sīsa*), or else it is the "head" among all the *palibodhas* associated with it and so forth; thus it is called the "head-obstruction" (*palibodhasīsa*). This same method applies to the remaining terms.
In particular, however, *vinibandhana* refers to bondage within saṃsāra by way of being elevated or fixed [therein]. *Parāmāsa* means dogmatic adherence.
Distraction (*vikkhepa*) is the state of being scattered. Defilement (*kilesa*) is the act of defiling. Resolution (*adhimokkha*) is the act of resolving. Exertion (*paggaha*) is the act of striving.
Establishment (*upaṭṭhāna*) is the act of not forgetting. Non-distraction (*avikkhepa*) is the state of not being scattered. Seeing (*dassana*) is penetration according to the true nature of things.
Occurrence (*pavatta*) is the occurrence of the aggregates subject to clinging. Object-sphere (*gocara*) is the objective support. In all these twelve sections:

The meaning of striving (*padhāna*) is the meaning of the head (*sīsa*). "Liberation" (*vimokkha*) refers to the five kinds of liberation—liberation by suppression, liberation by its own nature, liberation by eradication, liberation by subsiding, and liberation by escape;
among these, liberation by escape is Nibbāna. "The head of formations" (*saṅkhārasīsa*) means the head, the limit, and the end of all conditioned formations (*saṅkhata-saṅkhāra*);
by this, parinibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-parinibbāna*) is expressed, by way of the mere absence of formations.

Or rather, it is said that there is only "extinction within the aggregates" (*khandha-parinibbāna*). One who has "equality as the head" (*samasīsī*) is so called because he possesses both the "equality"—namely renunciation and so forth—and the "head"—namely faith and so forth;
or alternatively, because he has these as his equality-and-head. Alternatively, among the thirteen "heads," the five beginning with craving are the truth of origination (*samudaya-sacca*);
the five beginning with faith are the truth of the path (*magga-sacca*); and the "head of occurrence," the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), is the truth of suffering (*dukkha-sacca*).

The "one who has the same head" (*samasīsī*) is so called because he possesses both the realization of these four Noble Truths— the head of the objective sphere (*gocarasīsa*), the head of formations (*saṅkhārasīsa*), and the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*)—
and Parinibbāna without residue (*anupādisesaparinibbāna*), whether within a single illness, a single posture (*iriyāpatha*), or a single homogeneous life-faculty (*sabhāgajīvitindriya*). Thus,
due to the existence of both the previously mentioned [realization] and these heads, he is called "one who has the same head."
The commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of the meaning of equanimity is finished.
37. Commentary on the Exposition of the Knowledge of the Meaning of Effacement (Sallekhaṭṭhañāṇaniddesa) 88.
In the exposition of the knowledge of the meaning of effacement, "lust is manifold" (*rāgo puthu*) means that lust is distinct; the sense is that it is unmixed with the supramundane states.

This same method applies to the remaining [defilements]. "Lust" (*rāga*) is so called in the sense of coloring; "hatred" (*dosa*) in the sense of being corrupt; "delusion" (*moha*) in the sense of deluding.

Having stated these three root-defilements as lust characterized by coloring, hatred characterized by corruption, and delusion characterized by deluding, he now speaks the passage beginning with "anger" (*kodha*) in order to show their classifications. Therein, "anger is characterized by being angry"—this is what is meant here.
The seven bases are intended here. Enmity (*upanāha*) has the characteristic of resentment; it is simply anger that has reached a state of firmness.

Slander (*makkha*) has the characteristic of smearing over the virtues of others; the meaning is "wiping away" the virtues of others. Hypocrisy (*paḷāsa*) has the characteristic of grasping with both hands;
the meaning is "seeing the virtues of others by way of grasping with both hands. Envy (*issā*) has the characteristic of being vexed by the success of others; it means "jealousy."
Meaning: Stinginess (*macchariya*) has the characteristic of concealing one’s own excellence; the meaning is: “May my excellence not belong to another.
Deceit (*māyā*) has the characteristic of hiding the evil committed by oneself; the meaning is: “It is like a trick (*māyā*) in the sense of concealment.

Crookedness (*sāṭheyya*) has the characteristic of proclaiming qualities that do not exist in oneself; the meaning is: “The state of being crooked (*saṭhabhāva*). [It] has the characteristic of inflation of the mind.

"Stiffness" (*thambho*) means the state of rigidity. "Aggression" (*sārambho*) is characterized by the desire for superiority. "Conceit" (*māno*) is characterized by loftiness. "Excessive conceit" (*atimāno*) is characterized by haughtiness.

"Intoxication" (*mado*) is characterized by the state of being intoxicated. "Heedlessness" (*pamādo*) is characterized by the mind’s relinquishment [of effort] toward the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Having thus shown these various defilements individually, [the text now treats] both those defilements already mentioned and others not yet mentioned by way of a comprehensive inclusion.

To demonstrate this, he said, "all defilements," and so forth. Therein, they are called *kilesas* (defilements) because they defile (*kilesanti*), afflict (*upatāpenti*), and obstruct (*vibādhenti*) beings in both the present life and future lives. They comprise both those included within the unwholesome courses of action (*akusala-kammapatha*) and those not so included.

They are called *duccaritā* (misconduct) because they are evil conduct (*duṭṭhu caritā*) or because they are the conduct of the corrupted (*duṭṭhā caritā*). These, moreover, are bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct.

They are of three kinds. They are called *abhisaṅkhārā* because they construct (*abhisaṅkharonti*) a result. These too are of three kinds: the meritorious formation (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*), the demeritorious formation (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*), and the imperturbable formation (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*).
They are called "leading to existence" (*bhavagāmina*) because they go toward existence by way of their result;

thus, "kamma leading to existence" means kamma that leads to existence. By this, although they possess the nature of formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*), those kamma that are not to be experienced (*avedanīya*) are excluded.
“Are” (honti) is the distinction here. Furthermore, in the terms “misconducts” (duccaritāni) and “kamma,” a change of grammatical gender has been made.

Regarding the phrase “diversity and unity” (nānattekatta): although the word for unity (ekatta) is absent from this summary (uddesa), because diversity and unity are mutually dependent, the summary was formulated as “diversity and unity” by one wishing to demonstrate unity as well.
When unity that effects the wearing away of diversity (nānattasallekhaka) is shown, it is the knowledge of wearing away (sallekhañāṇa).
"It will be shown with ease. "Diversity" (*nānatta*) means having various natures due to instability and agitation.
"Unity" (*ekatta*) means having a single nature due to stability and lack of agitation.
"The splendor of conduct" (*caraṇatejo*): it is called "conduct" (*caraṇa*) because by means of it they go toward the destination not yet reached—namely, Nibbāna. What is that? It is virtue (*sīla*).
That very [fire] is "fire" in the sense of burning away its opposites. "Virtue-fire" is the fire of concentration established upon virtue.
"Wisdom-fire" is the fire of insight established upon concentration. "Merit-fire" is the fire of skillful noble paths established upon insights.
"Dhamma-fire" is the fire of the Buddha’s word, which serves as the foundation for these four fires.
"Refined by the power of conduct" means made sharp by the power of virtue (*sīla*). "The power of immorality" refers to the power characterized as the state of being immoral;
for that too is called "power" because it heats the mental continuum. "Consumes" means exhausts.

"The power of non-virtue" is the power of distraction, which is the opposite of concentration (*samādhi*). "The power of poor wisdom" is the power of delusion, which is the opposite of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).

“Meritless fire” (*apuññateja*) refers to the power of unwholesome kamma that accompanies the defilements, which is abandoned through the elimination of the specific defilements targeted by each respective path.

For this not only exhausts demerit alone; according to the statement, “Bhikkhus, there is kamma that is neither black nor white, with neither-black-nor-white result, which leads to the exhaustion of kamma,” it likewise exhausts wholesome kamma as well. This is stated by way of being the opposite of “merit-fire” (*puññateja*).
"Demerit-force" (*apuññateja*) alone has been stated. "Unrighteousness-force" (*adhammateja*) refers to the force of the doctrines and speech of various non-Buddhist sectarians.

In the second interpretation of the meaning given in the commentary on this knowledge (*ñāṇa*), the nineteen types of misconduct beginning with lust (*rāga*) constitute the individual forces of immorality.
In the passage, "Volitional formations are kamma leading to existence," the unwholesome volitional formations and unwholesome kamma constitute the demerit-forces (*apuññateja*).

Mundane wholesome kamma-formations leading to the imperturbable (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*) are indeed on the side of demeritorious power (*apuññateja*), because they are exhausted by the very force of merit.

The fifteen different types beginning with sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) are powers of non-virtue; the eighteen different types beginning with the perception of permanence (*niccasaññā*) are powers of lack of wisdom (*duppaññateja*);
and the four different types to be abandoned by the four paths are powers of demerit (*apuññateja*). By means of the different type to be abandoned by the stream-entry path...
The fire of unrighteousness must be restrained.
In the *Niddesa*, wishing to demonstrate *sallekha* (effacement) by means of its opposite, *asallekha* (non-effacement), *sallekha* is explained preceded by *asallekha*.
This is because the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, such as renunciation (*nekkhamma*) and the rest, are themselves singlefold states that efface their respective opposites.
“Sallekha” is what has been stated. Knowledge regarding that thirty-seven-fold *sallekha*—beginning with renunciation—is "knowledge of the meaning of effacement.
The commentary on the exposition of knowledge of the meaning of effacement is finished.
38. Commentary on the Exposition of Knowledge of the Arousing of Energy (*Vīriyārambhañāṇaniddesavaṇṇanā*)

89. In the exposition of the knowledge of the arousal of energy (*vīriyārambhañāṇa*), "of those that have not arisen" means of those that have not been produced within a single individual existence (*attabhāva*) or with respect to a single object (*ārammaṇa*).
For in the beginningless round of existence (*saṃsāra*), there are no unwholesome states (*akusala*) that have not arisen;

however, there are wholesome states (*kusala*) that have not arisen. "Evil" means base. "Unwholesome states" means states produced by lack of skill (*akosalla*). "For the sake of their non-arising" means...
"Not for the sake of arising. "Of those that have arisen" means of those produced in this present existence. "For the sake of abandoning" means for the purpose of relinquishing.
"Of unarisen wholesome states" means of those states born of skillfulness that have not previously arisen in this present existence.
"For the sake of arising" means for the purpose of producing. "Of those that have arisen" means of those produced in this present existence.
"For stability" means for the purpose of remaining established. "For non-confusion" means for the purpose of non-destruction. "For increase" means for repeated occurrence.
"For expansion" means for a state of abundance. "For development" means for growth. "For fulfillment" means for the purpose of complete perfection.
Now, in order to distinguish sensuous desire (*kāmacchanda*) among unwholesome states and renunciation (*nekkhamma*) among wholesome states, [the text says] of that which has not yet arisen...
He says, "Of sensual desire," and so forth. Therein, "sensual desire" (*kāmacchanda*) is lust for sense pleasures, which is the opposite of concentration (*samādhi*).
"Renunciation" (*nekkhamma*) is the concentration of the first jhāna, or the first jhāna itself; alternatively, all wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*) are renunciation.
Now, having applied this by way of all defilements and the path of arahantship, which is the antidote to all defilements:

He said "of all unarisen defilements," etc., in order to show this. Therein, regarding the phrases "for the stability of the arisen path of Arahantship" and so forth, the construction should be understood as follows:
for the stability, etc., of the path of Arahantship that has arisen at the moment of its arising (uppādakkhaṇa), by way of the moments of its presence (ṭhitikkhaṇa) and dissolution (bhaṅgakkhaṇa).
In the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā* as well, it says: "And whatever its occurrence is, this very... [and so on].
It is said, "Stability (ṭhiti) means... However, some say that "the path prior to the path of Arahatship (arahattamagga) is to be understood.
The commentary on the description of the knowledge of the arousal of energy (vīriyārambhañāṇa) is finished.
39. Commentary on the description of the knowledge of the demonstration of meaning (atthasandassanañāṇa).
90. In the exposition of the knowledge of demonstrating the meaning (*atthasandassanañāṇa*), the terms "the five aggregates" and so forth have meanings already explained.

"He makes manifest" means he makes clear; the sense is that he brings about the seeing by the eye of knowledge for the listeners. By "various phenomena" (*nānādhammā*), all mundane and supramundane phenomena are meant.
If it is asked why only mundane phenomena are mentioned in the exposition of making manifest, it is because [they are made manifest] by way of impermanence and so forth.
Because they have been undertaken; and because they do not fall within the scope of reflective contemplation (*asammasanūpaga*), the supramundane states (*lokuttara*) are not mentioned here.

However, since they are included by way of the exposition of various phenomena (*nānādhammaniddesa*) and the exposition that demonstrates the meaning (*atthasandassananiddesa*), their manifestation is indeed a manifestation in the very manner in which they ought to be manifested.
"Abandoning" means causing the listener to abandon. "Demonstrating" means [showing] correctly to the listeners.
[The text] shows this. However, some read it according to the method beginning with, “Because sensual desire has been abandoned, he demonstrates the goal of renunciation,” and so forth.

It should be understood that this method was stated for the purpose of showing that when the listeners have accomplished the abandonment of faults and the acquisition of virtues in a straightforward manner, the Teacher’s knowledge of teaching reaches its ultimate perfection.
The commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of the demonstration of meaning is finished.
40. Commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of purification by vision. 91.
Regarding the exposition of the knowledge of purification by vision, "all phenomena are included in a single category" means all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.

All phenomena are comprised and delimited by a single [principle]. "In the sense of suchness" means in the sense of being real, that is, in the sense of existing by way of their own respective intrinsic natures.
"In the sense of non-self" means in the sense of being devoid of a self defined as an agent or an experiencer.
"In the sense of truth" means in the sense of being non-deceptive, that is, in the sense of the absence of any alteration in their own intrinsic nature. "In the sense of penetration" means...
In the sense of being penetrated by knowledge according to its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
Here, penetration should be understood as occurring through supramundane knowledge (*lokuttara-ñāṇa*) by way of non-delusion and by way of the object (*ārammaṇa*).

"In the sense of higher knowing" means in the sense that those various phenomena are to be known higher by way of their intrinsic nature, both through mundane knowledge by way of the object and through supramundane knowledge by way of non-delusion and the object.

“For all, monks, should be directly known,” so it was said. “In the sense of full understanding” means: in the sense of having to be known by delimiting, through mundane and supramundane knowledges in the manner already described, those phenomena that have been directly known as to their intrinsic nature (sabhāva) from the perspective of impermanence and so forth, and from the perspective of the outlet (niyyāna) and so forth.
“For all, monks, should be fully understood,” so it was said. “In the sense of phenomenon (dhamma)” means: in the sense of maintaining its own intrinsic nature (sabhāva-dhāraṇa), and so forth.
In the sense of being phenomena (*dhamma*). "In the sense of elements (*dhātu*)" means in the sense of being elements by way of being devoid of a living soul (*nijjīva*), and so forth.

"In the sense of being cognized (*ñāta*)" means in the sense of being capable of being known by mundane and supramundane types of knowledge. Just as it is said, "The seen, the heard, the sensed, and the cognized are form," by way of the meaning of being capable of being seen and so forth, so too here the sense of being capable of being known should be understood as "the sense of being cognized."
“In the sense of realization” means in the sense of making [the truth] directly evident as an object.

“In the sense of touching” means in the sense of repeatedly touching that object which has been made directly evident. “In the sense of convergence” means in the sense of being brought together by mundane knowledge.

For although it is said: “Wisdom regarding the state of suchness is knowledge of the turning away from the truths; wisdom of direct higher knowledge is knowledge of the state of what is known; wisdom of realization...”
In the passage, "Knowledge of the meaning of contact," only a single type of knowledge is mentioned.
And in the Commentary it is said: "It is seen in the sense of coincidence, moment, time, collection, cause, view, acquisition, abandoning, and penetration."

In the commentary on the verses (*gāthāvaṇṇanā*), the word *abhisamaya* is stated to have the meaning of "penetration" (*paṭivedha*). However, here its diversity should be understood according to the sense already mentioned. For it is in the *Aṭṭhakathā* itself that this "realization of the Dhamma" (*dhammābhisamaya*) is stated by way of mundane knowledge (*lokiya-ñāṇa*).
"Sensual desire is diversity" means that it is of diverse nature because of the presence of distraction and because of having various objects.

All defilements (*kilesa*) should be understood in the same way. "Renunciation is unity" means that it is of a single nature because of the presence of one-pointedness of mind and because of the absence of distraction toward various objects.

And "of one nature" is the meaning. In this way, all wholesome states are to be understood. Here, the diversity of unwholesome states such as ill-will (*vyāpāda*) and so forth—which have been abbreviated by means of a formulaic list (*peyyāla*)—is to be understood according to the meaning already stated.

However, the diversity of the lower factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) is to be understood in terms of their being grosser than each successive higher factor. This is because of the unity and diversity of those things comprised within a single category.

Penetration is accomplished through the penetration of the truths at the moment of the path; therefore, having extracted the term "penetration," he demonstrated the clear realization of the truths (*saccābhisamaya*).
Full understanding penetrates penetration; thus, one realizes it by means of the clear realization of full understanding. This same method applies to the remaining [terms].

For at the time of the realization of truth (saccābhisamaya), the knowledge of the path (maggañāṇa) performs four functions simultaneously: full understanding (pariññā), abandoning (pahāna), realizing (sacchikiriyā), and developing (bhāvanā).

Just as a boat performs four functions simultaneously—without priority or sequence—namely, it leaves the near shore, cuts across the stream, carries its cargo, and reaches the far shore; even so, [the knowledge of the path performs these four functions].
Path-knowledge, neither before nor after, realizes the four truths simultaneously: it realizes suffering through the realization of full understanding;
it realizes the origin through the realization of abandoning; it realizes the path through the realization of development;
and it realizes cessation through the realization of actualization. What is meant by this? Cessation is the object.
By performing its function, it reaches, sees, and penetrates all four truths.
Just as one abandons the near shore, so path-knowledge fully understands suffering (*dukkha*). Just as one cuts the stream, so it abandons the origin (*samudaya*).
Just as one carries goods, so it develops the path through its status as a co-nascent and other types of conditions. Just as...
It reaches the further shore; thus, it should be understood that the application of the simile is that one realizes cessation, which is like the further shore.
"Vision becomes purified" means that through the abandoning of the darkness of defilements to be abandoned by each respective path, the vision of knowledge attains a state of purity.
"Vision is purified" refers to the moment of arising of each respective fruit, at which time the knowledge of each respective path [is purified].
Because it has attained the accomplishment of its task, the knowledge and vision has reached the state of purification.
At the end, the knowledges of the path and fruit are mentioned because they are established by the wisdom that penetrates the diversity and unity of all phenomena through their synthesis into one.
The commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of purification of view is finished.
41–42. Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of Acceptance and the Knowledge of Penetration.

92–93. Regarding the descriptions of the knowledge of acceptance and the knowledge of penetration: "Form is known as impermanent" means it is known as impermanent through the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*).
"Form is known as suffering" means it is known as suffering through the contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*). Form...
"Known as not-self" means it is known as "not-self" through the contemplation of not-self (*anattānupassanā*).
"Whatever is known, that is approved" means whatever form (*rūpa*) is known as impermanent and so forth, that very form is approved—that is, accepted—as impermanent and so forth.
In some [commentaries], the phrases "form is known as impermanent" and "whatever is known, that is approved" are treated separately.
It is written in the manuscripts: “Feeling, perception, and mental formations are known as impermanent,” and so forth;
these should be applied by changing the gender and number. “Touches” means it touches or pervades by means of the touching of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).
“Grasps thoroughly” means it enters by means of insight-knowledge. There is also the reading *pariyogāhati*.
The commentary on the description of the knowledge of embracing through patience is finished.
43. Commentary on the description of the knowledge of dwelling in a portion. 94.
In the description of the knowledge of dwelling in a portion, the manner in which the portion indicated in the matrix (mātikā) is to be reviewed is as follows:
Demonstrating this, he said: "Feeling conditioned by wrong view," and so forth. Therein, "conditioned by wrong view" includes feeling associated with wrong view;
it also includes wholesome and unwholesome feelings, as well as resultant feelings, that have arisen by taking wrong view as their decisive support (upanissaya).
Among these, that which is associated with wrong view is exclusively unwholesome; however, [that which arises] by taking wrong view as its decisive support...
Both wholesome and unwholesome states arise. For those with wrong view, relying upon their view, give rice gruel, meals, and so forth on the observance days;
they establish a service for the blind, the lepers, and others; they build rest-houses at the four great crossroads;
they have lotus ponds excavated; they plant flower gardens and fruit orchards; and they construct bridges over rivers and difficult passages.
They make the uneven even; thus, wholesome feeling arises in them.
But relying on wrong view, they revile and abuse those with right view, subjecting them to killing, imprisonment, and the like, and having slaughtered living beings, they offer them to the deities;
thus, unwholesome feeling arises in them. As for resultant feeling, it belongs to those who have passed into another existence.

It exists. Furthermore, that wrong view acts as a condition for the feeling co-arising with it by way of the conditions of co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, and non-disappearance;

and a wrong view that has just ceased acts as a condition for the feeling associated with the presently arisen wrong view by way of the conditions of proximity, contiguity, decisive support, repetition, absence, and disappearance. [Regarding] wrong view...
For one who esteems and delights [in it], it is a condition for feeling accompanied by greed by way of object-predominance, object-strong-dependence, and object-nutriment conditions;
for one who makes wrong view merely an object for all unwholesome states, it is a condition for all unwholesome feelings;
and for one who reviews or contemplates wrong view, it is a condition for wholesome and indeterminate feelings by way of object condition.

It is a condition; it is a condition by way of decisive support for the wholesome and unwholesome feelings arising with wrong view as their condition, and for the resultant feelings in another existence.
Regarding "the condition of the subsiding of wrong view": the subsiding of wrong view is right view; therefore, that which [arises] by way of the condition of right view...
What was called "feeling" (vedayita) should be understood as being "conditioned by the subsiding of wrong view.
However, some say that "the subsiding of wrong view" refers to the moment of insight (vipassanā) and the moment of the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga).
Regarding the statement "feeling conditioned by right view," here too, feeling associated with right view is appropriate, as is right view itself.
Feeling—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or resultant—that has arisen by taking something as its decisive support (*upanissaya*) is also included here.

Among these, that which is associated with right view is exclusively wholesome. However, by relying on right view as a decisive support, people perform meritorious deeds such as making offerings to the Buddha, lighting lamps and garlands, listening extensively to the Dhamma, and establishing shrines at places where none existed before. Thus, for them...
Wholesome feeling arises. Relying on right view itself, they revile and abuse those with wrong view, exalt themselves, and disparage others;
thus, unwholesome feeling arises for them. However, resultant feeling occurs only for those who have passed to another existence.
Furthermore, that right view [is related] to the co-nascent [consciousness] and to that which has ceased immediately prior.
Present feeling is a condition for wrong view by the same conditions already stated;
mundane right view is a condition for feeling associated with reflection, associated with insight, and associated with delight, by way of object-condition;
it is also a condition for wrong view by way of decisive support-condition in the same manner as stated for wrong view; [and so is] the right view of the Path and Fruition.
It is a condition by way of the conditions of object, object-predominance, and object-strong-dependence for the feeling associated with reflection.
Regarding the phrase "feeling conditioned by the subsiding of right view," wrong view is what is called the "subsiding of right view";
therefore, that which was described as feeling conditioned by wrong view should be understood as "conditioned by the subsiding of right view."
The same method applies to such cases as "conditioned by wrong intention" and "conditioned by the subsiding of wrong intention.
For whenever it is said "conditioned by the subsiding of [something]," what is intended is that very feeling conditioned by the factor that is its opposite.
Regarding wrong knowledge and so forth, "wrong knowledge" refers to the devising of means for unwholesome actions; or alternatively, [it may refer to]...

Wrong knowledge (*micchāñāṇa*) is the knowledge of wrong reviewing. Right knowledge (*sammāñāṇa*) refers to all remaining wholesome and indeterminate knowledge, excluding insight-right-view (*vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi*) and supramundane right-view (*lokuttara-sammādiṭṭhi*).
Wrong liberation (*micchāvimutti*) is the state of being intent upon evil.
Alternatively, it is non-factual liberation, non-emancipating liberation, or the perception of being liberated while one is actually not liberated. Right liberation (*sammāvimutti*)...
[These are] the liberation through wholesome resolve and the liberation through the fruit. Right view and the other factors have already had their meanings explained above.

Regarding "joy conditioned by desire" and so forth: "desire" (chanda) here means greed; thus, joy conditioned by desire should be understood as feeling associated with the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed.
Joy conditioned by the subsiding of desire is simply the feeling of the first jhāna. Joy conditioned by applied thought (vitakka) is the feeling of the first jhāna.

The feeling of the second jhāna arises with the subsiding of applied thought as its condition. With perception as a condition, there are the feelings of the remaining six attainments, excluding the first jhāna.
The feeling of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception arises with the subsiding of perception as its condition.
In such passages as "desire is not yet subsided," the meaning is that desire, applied thought, and perception have not yet subsided.
"By that condition" (*tappaccayā*): that very non-subsidience of desire, applied thought, and perception is the condition; thus, "by that condition. The meaning is:

feeling arises by way of the condition of the non-subsidience of desire, applied thought, and perception. That [feeling] is feeling associated with the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed.
If desire has subsided but applied thought and perception have not subsided, then "by that condition" refers to the subsidence of desire.

The non-subsidience of applied thought and perception is itself the condition; that is "conditioned by that" (*tappaccaya*). Therefore, "conditioned by that" means: that very feeling of the first jhāna.
If desire and applied thought have subsided while perception has not subsided, then "conditioned by that" means:

the subsiding of desire and applied thought together with the non-subsidience of perception is itself the condition; that is "conditioned by that. Therefore, "conditioned by that" means: that very feeling of the second jhāna.
"If desire, applied thought, and perception have subsided": "conditioned by that" (*tappaccayā*) means that the very subsiding of desire, applied thought, and perception is the condition;
thus, it is "conditioned by that. That is simply the feeling of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

However, some say: "Desire" refers to the inclination toward the Dhamma (*dhammacchanda*) in the preliminary stage [with the thought], "I shall attain absorption," for one who has reached absorption...
"Thus desire is stilled; in the first jhāna there is applied thought (*vitakka*), but for one who has attained the second jhāna, applied thought is stilled.

In the seven attainments there is perception (*saññā*), but for one who has entered the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and for one who has entered cessation (*nirodha*), perception is stilled"—thus they describe it. But here, as for the attainment of cessation...
It is not appropriate. “For the attainment of what has not been attained” means for the sake of attaining the fruit of arahantship.
“There is life-force, there is energy. There is also the reading *āyāvantī*. In that case as well, it means “when that [path] has been reached”:
when the Noble Path—the cause for that fruit of arahantship—has been reached by means of the exertion of that energy. “And feeling conditioned by that” refers to the feeling of arahantship.
Feeling arises with the condition of its basis (*ṭhāna-paccaya*). By this, the supramundane feeling produced together with the four paths is included.
However, some explain it thus: "To 'possess' (*āyavanti*) means practice; 'not having arrived at that basis' means not having attained that plane.
The commentary on the description of the knowledge of dwelling in a particular portion is finished.
44–49. Commentary on the Exposition of the Sixfold Knowledge of Turning Away (Vivaṭṭañāṇa-chakka-niddesa) 95.

Regarding the exposition of the sixfold knowledge of turning away: "Wisdom through predominance of renunciation" (nekkhammādhipatattā paññā) means wisdom that occurs by making renunciation predominant, through the state of having renunciation as its overlord.
"One turns away from sensual desire by means of perception" means by means of the perception associated with wisdom that has renunciation as its overlord.
The meaning is that one turns away from, turns back from, and becomes averse to sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) because it has become a cause or an instrument [of suffering].
This same method applies to the remaining [fetters].
96. "Sensual desire is diversity" means that sensual desire is not of a single nature, due to the absence of peaceful conduct. Renunciation (*nekkhamma*)...

"Unity" (*ekatta*) means renunciation (*nekkhamma*), for it has a single nature due to its state of peaceful conduct. "He intends the unity of renunciation" means he brings about renunciation by seeing the danger in sensual desire.
"The mind turns away from sensual desire" means that at the moment of renunciation, the mind turns away from sensual desire after having seen its danger.
This same method applies to the remaining [hindrances].
97. "Abandoning sensual desire" means abandoning sensual desire by way of suppression at the moment of the occurrence of renunciation (*nekkhamma*).
"He resolves the mind through renunciation" means that by way of the renunciation already attained, he stands making that associated consciousness superior;
the meaning is that he causes it to stand, that is, he sets it in motion. This same method applies to the remaining [hindrances].
98. "The eye is empty of a self" means that the eye is empty of a self because of the absence of that self which is imagined by foolish people as an agent and an experiencer.
For when something is not present in a place, that place is said to be empty of it.

"Or empty of what belongs to a self" means that, precisely because of the absence of a self, there is also an absence of anything belonging to a self; thus, [the eye is empty] of what belongs to a self.

It is empty (*suñña*). Because the world can be grasped in two ways—as a self (*atta*) and as belonging to a self (*attaniya*)—the absence of self and the absence of what belongs to a self are stated for the purpose of negating both those modes of grasping.
It is empty of permanence because there is nothing whatsoever that remains after passing beyond dissolution.
It is empty of stability because there is nothing whatsoever that remains stable even at the moment of its occurrence.
It is empty of non-existence and of stability. Or, it is empty of eternalism because there is no existence of anything whatsoever at any time.

Or, it is empty of that which has the nature of being unchanging because there is no existence of anything whose intrinsic nature does not undergo the two-fold transformation of aging and dissolution. Alternatively, [it is empty] of permanence and of stability.
The meaning is that it is empty by way of permanence, by way of being subject to change, and by way of being devoid of an inherent nature. Or, the word "and" (*ca*) has a conjunctive sense.
"For one who knows and sees as it really is" means for one who knows according to its true nature through the knowledge of the contemplation of non-self, and who sees with the eye as it were.
"Knowledge turns away from the misapprehension of the eye" means [from the view] that "the eye is self," or...

Or, regarding the notion "mine" (*attaniya*), as it occurs through the adherence to views, knowledge turns away by means of abandoning that specific factor. This same method applies to the remaining [fetters].
99. "By renunciation one relinquishes sensual desire": a person who has attained renunciation abandons sensual desire, which is its opposite, by means of renunciation.
"Wisdom regarding relinquishment" refers to the wisdom associated with that renunciation, which constitutes the relinquishing of sensual desire.
Wisdom (*paññā*). This same method applies to the remaining [terms]. The meanings of "oppression" (*pīḷana*) and so forth have already been explained above.

"One who fully understands turns away" (*parijānanto vivaṭṭati*) is a teaching expressed in terms of the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*): the person possessing the path (*maggasamaṅgī*), by fully understanding the fourfold meaning of suffering through its functions, turns away by way of emergence from both sides. Even regarding the turning away of knowledge (*ñāṇavivaṭṭana*), it is said that "the one possessing knowledge turns away."

100. "Understanding of the state of suchness" (*tathaṭṭhe paññā*) means that for this very person, understanding is the turning away (*vivaṭṭanā*) from the state of suchness. This same method applies to the remaining [terms].

Now, in order to show the six kinds of knowledge of turning away (*vivaṭṭañāṇa*) according to their functions and diversity of aspects precisely at the moment of the Path, he sets forth the outline beginning with "turning away through perception" (*saññāvivaṭṭo*), and then, analyzing it by way of meaning, he says:
"One who perceives turns away," and so on. Therein, "one who perceives":
"Turning away through perception" (*saññā-vivaṭṭo*) means that because the yogi, having first perceived renunciation and so forth as predominant,
subsequently turns away from sensual desire and the like by means of knowledge associated with renunciation, therefore that knowledge is called "turning away through perception.
"Turning away while intending" (*ceto-vivaṭṭo*) means that because the yogi turns away [from defilements] while intending renunciation, unity, and so forth...

One turns away from sensual desire and so forth by means of the knowledge associated [with that consciousness]; therefore, the meaning is that this knowledge is called "turning away of the mind" (*cetovivaṭṭa*).

Because the practitioner, while discerning through the mental focus on renunciation and so forth, turns away from sensual desire and so forth by means of the knowledge associated with that [consciousness], therefore that knowledge is "turning away of consciousness" (*cittavivaṭṭa*).
"Name" means "meaning. Regarding "turning away by means of knowledge" (*ñāṇavivaṭṭa*):

because the yogi, while making the sixfold internal sense base known as empty through the knowledge of contemplation of non-self, turns away from adherence to views by means of that very knowledge, therefore that knowledge is called "turning away by means of knowledge"—this is the meaning. "Turning away while relinquishing" is "turning away by way of liberation" (*vimokkhavivaṭṭa*).

Because the yogi, relinquishing sensual desire and the other hindrances through renunciation and so forth, turns away from sensual desire and the rest by means of the knowledge associated with them, therefore that knowledge is called "turning away as liberation" (*vimokkhavivaṭṭo*); this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "it turns away from the state of suchness, thus it is turning away as the truths" (*tathaṭṭhe vivaṭṭatīti saccavivaṭṭo*):
because the yogi turns away from the fourfold state of suchness by way of emergence from both sides, therefore it is path-knowledge.

The meaning is "the turning away from the truths. Alternatively, the meaning is that path-knowledge itself turns away (vivaṭṭati) by way of emerging from both sides regarding the state of suchness; thus it is called "turning away from the truths" (*saccavivaṭṭa*).

Since [terms such as] "turning away from perception" and so forth are stated in the description of the knowledge of turning away from the truths, it refers specifically to the moment of the knowledge of turning away from the truths.
It should be understood that this was said with a specific intention (*sandhāya*). For indeed, at the very moment of the Path (*maggakkhaṇa*), all [the knowledges] are applicable.
