How so? In the "turning away through knowledge" (*ñāṇavivaṭṭa*), having excluded knowledge itself, the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) appears in its own essential form among the remaining [knowledges].

However, since the function of insight (*vipassanākicca*) is accomplished by the Path itself, the knowledge of the turning away through knowledge is also applicable at the moment of the Path by virtue of the accomplishment of the function of insight. It is precisely by means of Path-knowledge (*maggañāṇa*)...

Or, because [the fact that] "the eye is empty," and so forth, has already been penetrated by way of its function, it is indeed appropriate to speak of that knowledge at the moment of the path (*maggakkhaṇa*).

As for the application of the meaning here, it is according to the method of all combinations such as: "Where there is the turning away from perception (*saññāvivaṭṭa*) at the moment of the path, there is the turning away of the mind (*cetovivaṭṭa*);
where there is the turning away of the mind at the moment of the path, there is the turning away from perception. Thus it is in all such conjunctions.

The construction should be made. Alternatively, since the four noble paths are included within the turning away from perception (*saññā-vivaṭṭa*), the turning away from the truths (*sacca-vivaṭṭa*) is already implicitly included.
Furthermore, the turning away through knowledge (*ñāṇa-vivaṭṭa*) is established by way of its function through that very turning away from the truths.
And when the series (*peyyāla*) is expanded only for the turnings away from perception, mind, consciousness, and liberation:
“Because of its predominance in the contemplation of non-self, wisdom turns away from perception through its predominance;
thus, ‘wisdom is knowledge of the turning away of perception’”; and, “Adherence is diversity, while the contemplation of non-self is unity.

Since the mind turns away from adherence when one intends the unity of the contemplation of non-self, ‘wisdom is knowledge of the turning away of the mind in regard to diversity’”; and, “adherence...”

Because of the occurrence of the readings: "Wisdom in resolution is knowledge of the turning away of consciousness, as one resolves the mind by way of the contemplation of non-self while abandoning [the defilements]," and "Wisdom in relinquishment is knowledge of the turning away of liberation, as one relinquishes insistence through the contemplation of non-self," knowledge of the turning away of knowledge is also indeed included among them. Regarding the turning away of knowledge:

And for one who has emerged from the contemplation of non-self and attained the Noble Path, the turning away from the truths (*saccavivaṭṭa*) is obtained by way of its function, through the application [of the formula] beginning with, "The eye is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self.

Therefore, in each single turning away, the remaining five turnings away are obtained. Consequently, it is said: "Wherever there is the turning away from perception (*saññāvivaṭṭa*), there is the turning away of the mind (*cetovivaṭṭa*)," and so forth.
It should be understood that the cross-references have been stated.
The commentary on the exposition of the sixfold knowledge of turning away (*vivaṭṭa-ñāṇa*) is finished.
50. Commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*).
101. Regarding the exposition of the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (*iddhividhañāṇa*), "here a bhikkhu" means a bhikkhu in this dispensation.

"Endowed with concentration through desire and the volitional formations of striving" (*chandasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgata*): here, concentration caused by desire, or concentration in which desire predominates, is "concentration through desire";
this is a designation for the concentration obtained by making the desire to act the dominant factor. The volitional formations that constitute striving are "the volitional formations of striving."
This is a designation for the energy of right effort that accomplishes the four functions. The plural number is used because it accomplishes those four functions.
"Endowed" means possessed of both concentration of desire (*chanda-samādhi*) and the volitional formations of striving (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*).

"Base of psychic power" (*iddhipāda*): either in the sense of accomplishment (*nipphatti*), meaning in the sense of succeeding; or in the sense of succeeding, meaning by means of this, beings succeed, they become prosperous and grown.
The meaning is: by this method, they are called "supernormal powers" (*iddhi*) because they have reached the highest excellence;

and the "bases of supernormal power" (*iddhipāda*) are the remaining collection of mind and mental factors, which serve as the foundation in the sense of being the basis for the volitional formations of exertion associated with concentration through desire (*chandasamādhi-padhānasaṅkhāra*), which are themselves associated with wholesome states of consciousness such as access-concentration (*upacārajjhāna*).
For it is said in the *Suttantabhājanīya* of the *Iddhipādavibhaṅga*: "The 'base of supernormal power' is, for one who has become thus, the aggregate of feeling... [and so on]."

“the consciousness aggregate. And in the *Abhidhammabhājanīya*, it is stated: “The basis of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) is, for one who has become thus, contact, feeling... [and so on] ...exertion, non-distraction.

Therefore, regarding the phrase “the remaining collection of consciousness and mental factors,” it should be understood that each of the volitional formations consisting of desire, concentration, and exertion is treated as a single psychic power, and the term “the rest” is applied in conjunction with each pair. For in this way, there are four.
All aggregates and all phenomena such as contact and so forth are included herein. By this method, the meaning should be understood for the remaining [terms] as well.

For just as concentration attained by making desire the dominant factor is called "concentration of desire," likewise, concentration attained by making energy, mind, or investigation the dominant factor is called "concentration of investigation."

Thus, in each basis of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), there are three factors—namely, those beginning with desire (*chanda*), those beginning with energy (*viriya*), those beginning with consciousness (*citta*), and those beginning with investigation (*vīmaṃsā*)—which are both psychic powers and bases of psychic power;
however, the remaining four associated aggregates (*khandha*) are bases of psychic power alone.
Or rather, it is because these three sets of three factors succeed only in conjunction with the four associated aggregates.

Not without them; therefore, by that method, it should be understood that all four aggregates are called "success" (*iddhi*) in the sense of succeeding, and they are also called "feet" (*pāda*) in the sense of being a foundation.

Regarding the phrase "endowed with energy, concentration, and the volitional formation of striving" (*vīriya-samādhi-padahāna-saṅkhāra-samannāgata*): here, "energy" (*vīriya*) and "volitional formation of striving" (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*)...
And it is indeed one [factor]. If it is asked why it is stated in two ways: here, the first mention of *vīriya* (energy) is made by way of showing its status as the dominant factor (*adhipati*);
the term *padhāna-saṅkhāra* (determination of striving) is used for the purpose of showing that very same energy’s accomplishment of the four functions.
Because it is stated in this twofold manner, it is said here too that there are three factors each. However, some [commentators] say: "In the *Vibhaṅga*..."

Because it is said, “‘Success’ (iddhi) means the success, the achievement, the succeeding, the accomplishing of those various states,” they say that what is called “success” is unproduced (*anipphanna*), whereas the “basis of success” (*iddhipāda*) is produced (*nipphanna*).

However, here the conclusion is made that both the success and the basis of success are produced and characterized. By terms such as “success” and “achievement,” [it refers to] states by way of their mode of succeeding.
It should be understood that it is stated thus.
"Develops" means he cultivates. Just as in the *Suttantabhājanīya*, here too the development of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) is purely mundane (*lokiya*).

Therefore, one who desires to accomplish the various kinds of psychic power (*iddhividha*), while developing the mundane basis of psychic power among the eight [meditation subjects] such as the earth-kasiṇa, etc.,...
One who has attained the eight meditative attainments through intensive practice regarding the kasiṇas proceeds by way of: the kasiṇas in direct order; the kasiṇas in reverse order;
the kasiṇas in direct and reverse order; the jhānas in direct order; the jhānas in reverse order; the jhānas in direct and reverse order;
skipping jhānas; skipping kasiṇas; skipping both jhānas and kasiṇas; skipping factors; skipping objects; and skipping both factors and objects.

Having tamed the mind by means of these fourteen modes—namely, through the definition of the factors and the definition of the object—one repeatedly enters the jhānas by way of the predominance of desire, energy, consciousness, and investigation.

Some, however, maintain that there is also a definition of both the factors and the object. But for one who has fulfilled the prior causes and has attained mastery even over the fourfold jhānas in the kasiṇas...

Thinking, "It is fitting to do so," while developing concentration through each of the bases for psychic power (*iddhipāda*), he resolves upon the fourfold energy beginning with "for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states.
Having understood its decline and increase, he resolves upon the balance of energy.
Having thus cultivated his mind in the four bases for psychic power, he accomplishes the various kinds of psychic power (*iddhividha*).
Thus, regarding the passage beginning "In these four bases for psychic power," the word *so* refers to that bhikkhu who has developed the four bases for psychic power.

"He thoroughly develops the mind in the four bases for psychic power" means that by repeatedly making each one—desire and the others—the dominant factor (*adhipati*) and entering into meditative absorption (*jhāna-samāpatti*), he thoroughly develops the mind with respect to them;
the meaning is that he causes the latent tendencies (*vāsana*) of desire and the rest to be acquired. "He fully tames" means he makes it free from stubbornness (*nibbisevana*).
It makes [it so]. The preceding statement is the cause for the subsequent one: for a mind that has been cultivated becomes thoroughly tamed.
"It makes it pliant" means that it makes the tamed mind reach mastery (*vasi*). For a mind that functions under one's control is called "pliant.
"It makes it workable" means it makes it capable of action and fit for action; for a pliant mind is indeed workable.
It becomes like well-refined gold; here, however, it is capable of performing the work of the supernormal powers (*iddhividha*).

"That bhikkhu whose mind is cultivated" refers to that very person. The passage beginning with "he merges even the body into the mind" is stated to show the method of yoga for the purpose of accomplishing the movement of the mind at will during the exercise of supernormal power.
In this context, "he merges even the body into the mind" means his own physical body composed of the four elements (*karajakāya*).
He merges, enters, and mounts it upon the mind of the foundational jhāna; the meaning is that he makes the body follow after the mind.
Performing it in this way serves as an aid for traveling with an invisible body.
"He also merges the mind upon the body" means he merges and mounts the foundational jhāna-mind upon his own physical (karaña-) body; thus he makes the mind follow after the body.
The meaning is as follows. Acting in this way, the visible body becomes an aid for walking. There is also the reading *samādahati*, which means “he establishes.
“He directs the mind by means of the body” means that, having taken the mind of the foundational jhāna, he applies it to the physical body (*karaja-kāya*) and makes it conform to the body;
this is a synonym for the settling of the mind upon the body. By means of the mind...
“He transforms the body” means that, having taken up the physical body, he applies it to the mind of the access-concentration (*pādakajjhāna*) and makes it conform to the mind;
this is a synonym for the thorough integration of the body into the mind. “He resolves” means he resolves, “Let it be thus.
“Transformation” is stated for the purpose of explaining the meaning of “thorough integration,” and “resolution” is stated for the purpose of explaining the meaning of “transformation.”

It has been said. Since "he blends" (*samodahati*) is the root term, while "he transforms" (*pariṇāmeti*) and "he resolves" (*adhiṭṭhāti*) are the explanatory terms for its meaning, it was therefore stated by way of those two terms alone as "having transformed" and "having resolved," but not as "having blended.
"He dwells having entered upon the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness in the body" means the perception of pleasure co-nascent with the fourth jhāna, and...
By means of attaining the perception of lightness, he enters and dwells within the physical body made of the four elements.
Through that perception, even his physical body becomes as light as a tuft of cotton. "He" refers to that bhikkhu who has performed the prescribed practice.
The instrumental case in the phrase "with a mind thus developed" (*tathābhāvitena cittena*) expresses either a characteristic of the state attained or serves to indicate the cause.
"With a mind thus developed" means with that which has become the cause. "Purified" means purified by way of the purity of equanimity and mindfulness.
Precisely because it is purified, it is "bright"; the meaning is that it is luminous.

"For the sake of knowledge of the modes of supernormal power" means for the purpose of knowledge regarding the divisions of supernormal power or its various manifestations. "He directs his mind" means that the bhikkhu, by way of the aforementioned method...

When that mind, which serves as the basis for direct knowledge, has arisen, he directs the preliminary consciousness toward the attainment of the knowledge of the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*);
having withdrawn it from the kasiṇa object, he sends it forth toward the supernormal powers. "He inclines" means he makes his mind tend toward and lean toward the supernormal power to be attained.
"He" refers to that monk who has thus directed his mind. "In many ways" means of many kinds.

"Of various kinds" (*nānappakārakaṃ*). "The modes of supernormal power" (*iddhividhaṃ*) means a portion of supernormal power or a classification of supernormal power. "He experiences" (*paccanubhoti*) means he experiences directly;
the sense is that he touches, realizes, and attains it.
Now, in order to show its manifold nature, he says: "Having been one," and so forth. Therein, "having been one" (*ekopi hutvā*)...

"Having been one by nature before performing the miracle": wishing to walk back and forth, recite, or ask questions in the presence of many people, he becomes a hundred or even a thousand. But how does he become thus?
By fulfilling the qualities that serve as the ground, the soil, and the root of psychic power (*iddhi*), and [attaining] the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
Having entered and emerged from that attainment, if he desires to become a hundred, he performs the preliminary work (parikamma) by thinking, "May I be a hundred, may I be a hundred.
Then, having again entered the foundational jhāna and emerged, he makes the resolution (adhiṭṭhāti). Simultaneously with the mind of resolution, he becomes a hundred.
The same method applies to becoming a thousand and so forth. If it does not succeed in this way, he should perform the preliminary work again and for a second time...

Having entered [the attainment] and emerged, one should perform the resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*). For it is stated in the *Saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā*: "It is permissible to enter [the attainment] once or twice.
In that context, the foundational jhāna consciousness has the sign (*nimitta*) as its object, while the preliminary consciousnesses have either a hundredfold or a thousandfold object;
and these are by way of color alone, not by way of designation (*paṇṇatti*). The resolving consciousness (*adhiṭṭhānacitta*) also...

In the same way, whether the object is one or a thousand, immediately after the change-of-lineage (gotrabhu) consciousness, there arises only a single consciousness belonging to the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), just like that first absorption consciousness.
Among those many created forms, because they were created without being individually determined, they are identical to one another by the power of the possessor of psychic potency (iddhimat).
Whether in standing or sitting, or in speaking or remaining silent, [they all act in unison].
Whatever the possessor of psychic power (*iddhimā*) does, they all do that very same thing.

But if he wishes to make them various in appearance—some in the first stage of life, some in the middle stage, and some in the final stage; likewise, some with long hair, some half-shaved, some fully shaven;

some with mixed hair, some with half-red robes, some with yellow robes; [and performing] word-by-word recitation, preaching the Dhamma, eloquent exposition, asking questions, answering questions, dyeing robes, sewing robes, washing robes, and so forth—[they all do those things].

Or, if he wishes to perform other various kinds [of transformations], he should emerge from the basic jhāna, perform the preliminary work (parikamma) in the manner of saying, "Let so many bhikkhus be in their first stage of life," and so forth; then, having re-entered the attainment and emerged again, he should make his resolution (adhiṭṭhāna).
By means of the mind of resolution, they become exactly of the kind desired. This same method applies to "multiplying into many" as well.

...having sacrificed, he becomes one,” and so forth. However, this is the distinction: after this bhikkhu has thus manifested such a multiplicity, he might again think, “Having become one again, I shall walk back and forth, I shall recite my studies, I shall ask questions,” or [he might wonder], “This monastery has few bhikkhus;
if anyone should arrive, from where would these many identical bhikkhus come?”
Thinking, "They will surely know that this is the power of the Elder," or out of fewness of wishes,
one who desires "to be alone" should enter the basic jhāna, emerge, perform the preliminary work thinking "I am alone," re-enter the jhāna,
emerge, and then resolve, "I am alone. It is together with the resolving consciousness itself that—
He becomes one. However, by not acting in this way, he himself becomes one according to the time previously delimited.
"Manifestation" (*āvi-bhāva*) means making something manifest; "concealment" (*tiro-bhāva*) means making something hidden.
The connection with what precedes is: "he experiences manifestation; he experiences concealment. In this regard, this...
One possessing psychic power (*iddhimā*), desiring to make something manifest, turns darkness into light, or makes what is concealed visible, or brings what is out of range into range.

How so? For just as even that which is concealed or situated at a distance may be seen, one who wishes to make oneself or another thus visible emerges from the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*) and [thinks]: "This darkness..."

Having directed his mind with the thought, "Let there be light," or "Let this which is concealed become revealed," or "Let this which is not within range come within range," and having performed the preliminary work, he resolves in the manner already described. Simultaneously with the resolution, it becomes exactly as resolved.
Others standing at a distance see it, and he himself, wishing to see, sees it. [Likewise,] one who wishes to effect disappearance...
But it makes light into darkness, or what is uncovered into covered, or what is within range of vision into what is beyond range.

How so? For when one wishes to make oneself or another invisible—so that one is not seen even though one is uncovered or standing nearby—one emerges from the basic jhāna and thinks: "Let this place of light become dark."

Or, having directed his mind with the thought, “Let this which is uncovered become covered,” or “Let this which is within range become beyond range,” he performs the preliminary work and resolves in the manner already described. Simultaneously with the resolution, it becomes exactly as resolved.
Even those standing nearby do not see it; and he himself, wishing not to see it, does not see it. Furthermore, all of this...
The miracle of manifestation is called "becoming visible," while the miracle of non-manifestation is called "becoming invisible.

In that regard, within the miracle of manifestation, both the psychic power (*iddhi*) and the possessor of psychic power (*iddhimā*) are perceived; this should be illustrated by the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*).
Within the miracle of non-manifestation, only the psychic power is perceived, not the possessor of psychic power; this should be illustrated by the Mahaka Sutta and the Brahmanimantanika Sutta.
“Through a wall” (*tirokuṭṭa*) means another wall; it is said to be the other side of a wall. The same method applies to “through a fence” (*tiropākāra*) and “through a mountain” (*tiropabbata*).
A “wall” (*kuṭṭa*) is a house wall. A “fence” (*pākāra*) is the surrounding wall of houses, monasteries, villages, and so forth.

A “mountain” (*pabbata*) is either a mound of earth or a rocky mountain. “Without clinging” (*asajjamāno*) means not adhering. “Just as in space” (*seyyathāpi ākāse*) means just as if in space. Thus...

However, one who wishes to go should enter the space-kasina (ākāsakasiṇa), emerge, and having directed his attention toward a wall, a rampart, or a mountain, perform the preliminary exercise and resolve: "Let there be space. It becomes space itself.
For one wishing to descend below or ascend upwards, it becomes hollow; for one wishing to pass through by piercing, it becomes perforated. Therein, he...

He proceeds without attachment. However, if while that bhikkhu is proceeding after having made a resolution, a mountain or a tree should arise in his path, must he resolve again after entering the attainment? There is no fault.
For resolving again after entering the attainment is like a pupil receiving formal dependence (*nissaya*) from a preceptor. But by this bhikkhu...
Because it was resolved, "Let there be space," it indeed becomes space.
And by the power of that previous resolution, it is impossible for another mountain or tree made of the elements to arise in between.
However, when something has been created by another possessor of psychic power, the first creation is the stronger; the other must go either above or below it.
“They emerge and submerge in the earth”: here, “emerge” means rising up; “submerge” means sinking down; “emerging and submerging” is the compound of emergence and submergence.

One who wishes to do this should attain the water-kasina, then, having emerged, delimit the area, thinking, “Let there be water over this much space,” and perform the preliminary work (parikamma) in the manner already described.
It must be resolved upon. Simultaneously with the resolution, within the area thus delimited, the earth becomes water alone.
There he performs diving and surfacing as if in water. And it is not only diving and surfacing;
he does whatever he wishes—bathing, drinking, washing the face, rinsing vessels, and so forth. Not only that...

It becomes water itself; and regarding ghee, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth, whatever one desires, by adverting to it with the thought, "Let this and that be just this much," and performing the preliminary work and resolving, it becomes exactly as resolved.
When one draws it out and places it in a vessel, the ghee remains ghee, the oils remain oils, and the water remains water.
It is indeed water. There, one who wishes to moisten it does so; one who does not wish to moisten it does not.
And for that person alone, that earth becomes water, while for other people, it remains earth.

There, people walk on foot, they travel by means of vehicles and the like, and they even perform agricultural work and other tasks. However, if this [person] thinks, "May it be water for them as well," [they do so].

If one so desires, it certainly exists. However, once the delimited period has passed, setting aside that water which naturally remains in jars, ponds, and so forth, the remainder of the delimited space is earth alone.
Regarding the phrase "he walks even upon water that does not break": here, that water which sinks when stepped upon is what is meant by "breaking."

This is called the opposite of what is non-penetrable. However, one who wishes to go [through water] should enter the earth-kasiṇa attainment, emerge, delimit the area, thinking, "Let there be earth in this much space," perform the preliminary work, and then resolve in the manner already described.
Simultaneously with the resolution, in the delimited area, the water becomes earth itself. He...
There he goes as if on solid ground. Not only does he go, but whatever posture he desires, he adopts it.

Not only does he turn the earth itself into such, but regarding gems, gold, mountains, trees, and so forth, whatever he desires, he adverts to it and resolves upon it in the manner already described; and it becomes exactly as he has resolved.
That very water becomes earth for him alone, while for other people it remains only water. Fish, turtles, water-crows, and the like move about therein according to their pleasure.
If he wishes to turn that water into earth for other people as well, he does so;
however, upon the passing of the predetermined time limit, it becomes water once again.
"He travels cross-legged through the air" means that he goes through the sky by sitting with his thighs bound together on all sides.
"A winged bird" means a bird endowed with wings, not one whose wings are incomplete or whose wings have been clipped; for such a one is unable to travel through the air.
However, one who desires to travel through the air in this manner should enter into the earth-kasina attainment and then emerge.
If, while sitting, he wishes to go, he should delimit an area the size of a cross-legged seat, perform the preliminary work, and resolve it in the manner already described.
If, while lying down, he wishes to go, [he should delimit] an area the size of a bed;
if he wishes to go on foot, [he should delimit] an area the size of the path—thus, having delimited the appropriate area as the case may require, he should proceed in the manner already described.
One should resolve: “Let there be earth. With that resolution, it becomes earth itself.
Furthermore, a monk who wishes to travel through the air must also possess the divine eye. Why?

Because there may be mountains, trees, and so forth produced by seasonal conditions in the way, or because nagas, supaṇṇas, and others might create obstacles out of envy; [the divine eye is required] for the purpose of seeing these.
Having seen them, what should be done? One should enter the foundational jhāna, emerge from it, perform the preliminary work with the thought, "Let there be space," and then resolve upon it.
Furthermore, for the purpose of descending into a place, one who possesses this [power] must have attained the divine eye;
for if he were to descend into a non-designated spot, such as a bathing place or a village gate, it would cause distress to the great multitude.
It becomes manifest; therefore, having seen with the divine eye, one avoids what is unsuitable and descends into what is suitable.
Regarding the phrase "these moon and sun are so powerful and so majestic":

here, their power should be understood as arising from their movement forty-two thousand yojanas above [the earth], and their majesty as arising from their simultaneous illumination of the three continents. Thus, by way of their movement above and their pervasion with light—
"Of great psychic power" means possessing great majesty by virtue of that very same great psychic power. "Seizes" means grasps, or touches in one part.
"Wipes" means he wipes all around as if on the surface of a mirror.

This psychic power of his succeeds solely through the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*); there is no fixed rule here regarding the attainment of the kasiṇas. Now, if this...
If he wishes to go and touch it, he goes and touches it. But if, while remaining seated or lying down right here, he wishes to touch it, he resolves:
"Let it come within the reach of my hand. By the power of that resolve, it comes like a palm fruit released from its stalk and stands within the reach of his hand;
or else, he extends his hand and touches it. [The hand...]
But as for one who is increasing it, does what is clung-to increase or what is not clung-to?
It is by depending on what is clung-to that what is not clung-to increases. Having done this, he not only touches the moon and sun;
if he so desires, he makes a footstool and places his feet upon it, makes a chair and sits upon it, or makes a bed and lies down upon it.
Having made a back-rest of a wooden plank, he leans against it. As it is for one, so it is for another;

for even when many hundreds of thousands of monks do likewise, it succeeds for each and every one of them in exactly the same way. Even the movement of the moon and sun and their production of light occur in the same manner.
For just as when a thousand bowls are filled with water, the disk of the moon is seen in all those bowls.
The moon’s movement and its production of light are just as they naturally are; this miracle is comparable to that.

"He exercises mastery with his body even as far as the Brahma-world" means that, having made the Brahma-world the limit, he exercises mastery—that is, sovereign power—with his own body while performing various kinds of higher knowledge within that interval.
A detailed account of this will appear in the discussion on psychic power (*iddhi*).
The commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of the modes of psychic power is finished.
51. Commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of the purification of the divine ear-element (sotadhātuvisuddhiñāṇa). 103.
In the exposition of the knowledge of the purification of the divine ear-element, the passage beginning with “even sounds that are far away” refers to one who desires to produce the divine ear.
This was stated for the purpose of showing a method to a beginner monk.

In that context, "the sound-sign of sounds even at a distance" means the sound within the midst of distant sounds; for it is the sound itself that is called the "sound-sign" by virtue of its acting as a sign.
Although "at a distance" is said, it refers only to the range of the ordinary ear. "Gross" means coarse; "subtle" means minute.
"Of the very subtle" (*saṇhasaṇhānaṃ*) means more subtle than even the subtle; the meaning is "of those that are exceedingly subtle. By this, sounds that are supremely refined are described.

A beginner meditator who wishes to arouse this knowledge should attain the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), and having emerged from it, with a mind of preliminary concentration (*parikamma-samādhi*), he should first [direct his attention] toward a coarse [sound] at a distance within the range of the ordinary ear.

In the forest, one should direct the mind toward the sounds of lions and other such creatures. In the monastery, there is the sound of the gong, the sound of the drum, the sound of the conch, the sound of recitation by novices and junior monks as they study with all their might, the sound of those engaged in ordinary conversation saying, "What, venerable sir?
What, friend? and so forth, the sound of birds, the sound of the wind, the sound of footsteps, and the hissing sound of boiling water.
The sound of palm leaves drying in the heat, the sound of ants, termites, and so forth— in this way, starting from all that is gross,
one should attend to sounds in order of increasing subtlety. While doing so,
one should gradually take up the sign of sound in each of the ten directions, beginning with the east.

It should be brought to mind in the manner already described. And when bringing it to mind, one should set aside the ordinary ear and bring it to mind with a mind belonging to the door of the intellect (*manodvārika-citta*) regarding those sounds that are heard by the natural ear.
Those sounds become clear even to the ordinary mind, but they become especially clear to the mind of preliminary concentration (*parikamma-samādhi*). In this way, for him, the sign of sound—
Thinking, "Now the divine ear-element will arise," one takes one of those sounds as an object, and mind-door adverting consciousness arises;
when that has ceased, four or five impulsion moments flow.
Of these, the first three or four are of the sense-sphere, known respectively as the preliminary (parikamma), access (upacāra), conformity (anuloma), and change-of-lineage (gotrabhū).
The fourth or fifth absorption consciousness (appanā-citta) belongs to the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara).

Therein, the knowledge that arises together with that absorption consciousness is the divine ear element (dibba-sotadhātu). By one who stabilizes that [knowledge], it should be expanded after delimiting a space of about one finger’s breadth, thinking, “I hear sound within this range”;
then two fingers, four fingers, eight fingers, a span (vidatthi), a cubit (ratana), the interior of a room, the main hall, and so forth.

One should expand [the meditation] by repeatedly delimiting it according to the palace, the monastery grounds, the monastery itself, the village, the countryside, and so forth, up to the world-system (cakkavāḷa), or even beyond that.
Having thus attained supernormal power (abhiññā), when a sound enters the space touched by the object of the foundational jhāna,
this person hears it by means of the knowledge of supernormal power (abhiññā-ñāṇa) even without re-entering the foundational jhāna.

Hearing in this way, even if there is a single tumultuous uproar from the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, small drums, and so forth, reaching as far as the Brahma-world, he is indeed able to discern them individually with the intention of defining each one, thinking, "This is the sound of the conch; this is the sound of the kettledrum.
Having heard the meaningful sounds through the knowledge of direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*), he subsequently understands their meaning with a sense-sphere consciousness (*kāmāvacara-citta*).
The divine ear arises only for one who possesses a natural hearing, not for one who is deaf. They say that even later, when the natural hearing has perished, the divine ear does not perish.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the divine ear-element": it is called "divine" because it resembles the divine; for it is produced by the kamma of the good conduct of the devas.

The divine faculty of the ear element (*dibba-pasāda-sotadhātu*) is unobstructed by bile, phlegm, blood, and so forth; because it is free from such defilements, it is capable of receiving objects even at a distance.
Furthermore, this monk’s faculty of the ear element of knowledge (*ñāṇa-sotadhātu*), produced through the power of the development of energy (*vīriya-bhāvanā-bala*), is exactly like that;
thus, because it resembles the divine, it is called "divine. Moreover, it is called "divine" because it is obtained by means of the divine abodes (*dibba-vihāra*), and because of its own...

And it is "divine" (*dibba*) because it is based on a divine abiding (*dibbavihāra*). It is the "ear-element" (*sotadhātu*) in the sense of hearing and in the sense of being devoid of a living soul (*nijjīva*);

and because it performs the function of the ear-element, it is also called the "ear-element. "By that divine ear-element. "Purified" (*visuddhā*) means completely pure and free from defilements (*nirupakkilesā*).
"Surpassing the human" (*atikkantamānusikā*) means that by hearing sounds beyond the range of human beings, it surpasses what is human.
"Having transcended and passed beyond the fleshly ear-element" means having gone beyond it and remained [in that state]. "Hears both sounds" means he hears two kinds of sounds.
Which two? Divine and human; that is to say, the sounds of both gods and humans.
By this, the partial exhaustion [of the range] should be understood. "Those far and near" refers to those sounds which are far away, even in another world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
And whatever sounds are near—even including the sounds of minute organisms inhabiting his own body—he hears them; this is what is meant.
By this, it should be understood that there is a complete and exhaustive inclusion [of all sounds].
The commentary on the description of the knowledge of the purification of the ear-element is finished.
52. Commentary on the Exposition of the Knowledge of Penetrating Others' Minds (Cetopariyañāṇaniddesa) 104.
Regarding the statement "He understands thus" in the exposition of the knowledge of penetrating others' minds, this now indicates the method that is to be explained.
"This form is originated by the faculty of mental joy," and so forth, is the method to be practiced by a beginner meditator.
How so? By one who meditates and desires to arouse this knowledge, first the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*) must be developed.
For this [knowledge] succeeds by means of the divine eye; that is its preliminary work (*parikamma*).
Therefore, that bhikkhu, having increased the light, should, with the divine eye, observe the color of the blood existing in dependence upon the heart-matter (*hadaya-rūpa*) of another.
Having seen it again and again, the mind must be investigated.
For that blood, when wholesome joy is present, is red, the color of a banyan fruit; when unwholesome joy is present, that same [blood] is agitated;
when grief is present, it is black, the color of a rose-apple fruit, and agitated. When wholesome equanimity is present...
When it is clear, it has the color of sesame oil; when unwholesome equanimity is occurring, that very [blood] becomes turbid.

Therefore, having repeatedly observed the color of the blood in another's heart, he discerns: "This material form is originated by the faculty of joy; this material form is originated by the faculty of grief; this material form is originated by the faculty of equanimity."
One who seeks the mind must make the knowledge of penetration of minds firm.

For when that is made firm, one gradually understands all types of consciousness, such as those of the sense-sphere and so forth, by passing from one consciousness to another without seeing the physical heart.
This has also been said in the Commentary:
“Regarding the desire to know another’s mind in the immaterial realm (*ārūpa*), whose heart-matter (*hadayarūpa*) does he see, or whose alteration of the faculties (*indriyavikāra*) does he observe?
None at all. This is the domain of one possessing psychic power (*iddhimant*): namely, by directing his attention (*āvajjanto*) toward any [object], he knows the mind in its sixteenfold division.
However, this discussion is conducted from the perspective of one who has not yet achieved such mastery.”
"Of other beings" means of all beings excluding oneself. "Of other persons"—this has the same meaning as the former;
however, a difference in phrasing is made for the sake of those to be trained and as an elegance of teaching.

"Having encompassed their minds with his own mind, he understands them" means that, having delimited their minds with his own mind, he understands them in their various modes, such as being possessed of lust and so forth.
He knows. In the passage beginning with "sarāgaṃ vā" (with lust or), the word "vā" has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

Therein, the eightfold consciousness accompanied by greed is called "consciousness with lust" (*sarāga-citta*); the remaining wholesome and indeterminate consciousness of the four planes is called "consciousness free from lust" (*vītarāga*).
However, these four types of consciousness—the two types of unhappy consciousness, and the two types of consciousness consisting of doubt and restlessness—are, in this [context]...
They are not included in this dyad. However, some elders include even those [states] under the term "free from lust" (*vītarāga*).
As for the two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure (*domanassa*), these are called "consciousness with hatred" (*sadosa-citta*);

all wholesome and indeterminate consciousness belonging to the four planes is called "free from hatred" (*vītadosa*). The remaining ten unwholesome consciousnesses are not included in this dyad. Some...
However, the Elders include those [states] as well under the term "free from hatred" (*vītadosa*). Regarding the phrase "with delusion" (*samoha*) and "free from delusion" (*vītamoha*):
here, by way of having delusion as their sole root, only the two types associated with doubt and restlessness are "with delusion.

Since delusion occurs in all unwholesome states, it should be understood that all twelve kinds of unwholesome consciousness are "with delusion. The remainder—both wholesome and indeterminate—is "free from delusion."
That which is accompanied by sloth and torpor is contracted; that which is accompanied by restlessness is distracted. That which belongs to the fine-material and immaterial spheres is exalted;
the remainder is unexalted. All that pertains to the three planes is surpassable;

the supramundane is unsurpassable. That which has reached access or reached absorption is concentrated; that which has not reached either of those two is unconcentrated. That which has attained liberation through substitution of opposites, suppression, eradication, tranquillization, and escape—[is liberated].
And that which is liberated—this fivefold liberation, when not yet attained, should be understood as "unliberated.
Thus, a bhikkhu who has acquired the knowledge of penetration of minds understands the mind in its sixteenfold division.
However, worldlings do not know the path and fruition minds of the Noble Ones, nor do lower Noble Ones know the path and fruition minds of those higher than themselves.
They know; moreover, those in the higher realms know the minds of those in the lower realms.
The commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of penetration of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) is finished.
53. Commentary on the Exposition of the Knowledge of Recollection of Past Lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*).

105. In the exposition of the knowledge of recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*), the passage beginning with “he understands thus” is stated for the purpose of showing the method for generating that knowledge by one who desires to produce the knowledge of recollection of past lives through a mind cultivated in the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*).
For, in due order, having seen dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), [one sees] the present [constituents] known as consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling.
He sees the summary of the result; he sees its condition, which is the summary of causes consisting of karma and defilements in a previous existence;
he sees its condition, which is the summary of results in that same previous existence; and he sees its condition, which is the summary of causes in the third existence.
Thus, by seeing dependent origination, he sees the succession of births. In this way...
Attention directed toward dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) is of great benefit for the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
In this context, the statement, "When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises," is the summary formula for the exposition of dependent origination.
If it is asked why there is a twofold expression when the meaning is already established by either one of those two statements, it is because of the existence of a difference in meaning.
How so? "When this exists" means when this condition is present; this is a general statement applicable to all conditions.
"This comes to be" means this effect produced by conditions comes to be; this is a general statement applicable to all things produced by conditions.
By this entire statement, the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetukavāda*) is refuted. For those phenomena that arise from conditions...
They exist, not because of an absence of conditions; they are not what is called "causeless. "With the arising of this" means:
by reason of the arising of this condition. This is a statement indicating that all conditions possess the quality of arising.
"This arises" means: this conditionally arisen phenomenon arises. This is a statement indicating that all conditionally arisen phenomena arise from that [condition].
By this entire statement, the doctrine that [things] have an eternal cause is refuted. For those phenomena that possess arising are impermanent;
therefore, although these phenomena do indeed have causes, they have impermanence as their cause, and not such things as a Primordial Person (Puruṣa) or other causes accepted in the world as eternal.
The phrase "namely" (*yadidaṃ*) indicates the object to be demonstrated. Regarding the statement "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," that which [depends] upon...
It attains its fruit; that is the condition (*paccaya*). "Dependent" (*paṭicca*) means not without [it], that is, not rejecting it. "Attains" (*eti*) means both arises and proceeds.
Furthermore, the meaning of "condition" (*paccaya*) is the sense of being helpful. Ignorance (*avijjā*) is both itself and a condition, thus "ignorance-condition" (*avijjāpaccaya*).
Therefore, the construction is: "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) come to be. Thus is the word "come to be" (*sambhavanti*) [to be understood].
The same method of application should be made for the remaining terms as well. Among sorrow and the rest: *soka* is the act of grieving; *parideva* is lamentation;

it is called *dukkha* because one suffers (*dukkhati*), or alternatively, it is *dukkha* because it digs out (*khanati*) in two ways by way of arising and persistence; *domanassa* is the state of being dejected;
*upāyāsa* is intense distress. "Arise" means they are produced. "Thus" is an indication of the method already demonstrated. By that—

This shows that [the world] arises through causes such as ignorance alone, and not through the creation of a Lord (issaranimmāna) or other such factors. "Of this" refers to what has been stated above.
"Entire" means unmixed, or complete. "Of the mass of suffering" means of the aggregate of suffering, not of a sentient being, nor of pleasure, beauty, and so forth.
"Origin" means arising. "Occurs" means it comes into existence.

In this context, what is ignorance (*avijjā*)? It is lack of knowledge regarding suffering, lack of knowledge regarding the origin of suffering, lack of knowledge regarding the cessation of suffering, and lack of knowledge regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering;

lack of knowledge regarding the past, lack of knowledge regarding the future, lack of knowledge regarding both the past and the future, and lack of knowledge regarding specific conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena. What are volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*)? They are meritorious volitional formations...
The formation of demerit, the formation of the imperturbable, bodily formation, verbal formation, and mental formation.
The eight types of wholesome volition pertaining to the sense sphere and the five types of wholesome volition pertaining to the fine-material sphere constitute the formation of merit;

the twelve types of unwholesome volition constitute the formation of demerit; and the four types of wholesome volition pertaining to the immaterial sphere constitute the formation of the imperturbable.
Bodily volition is a bodily formation; verbal volition is a verbal formation; mental volition is a mental formation. Herein, one might ask:
"How is it to be known that these formations have ignorance as their condition? Because they exist when ignorance exists.

For he in whom the ignorance—known as lack of knowledge—regarding suffering and so forth has not been abandoned, [perceives] with respect to suffering first: ... [text continues] ... *Note: The provided source text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
And through ignorance regarding the past and so forth, one grasps the suffering of saṃsāra as pleasure and initiates the three kinds of formations that are the causes of that very suffering.
Through ignorance regarding the origin, one initiates the formations—though they are actually the conditions for craving and thus causes of suffering—while imagining them to be causes of pleasure.
But through ignorance regarding cessation and the path, [one initiates] specific states of existence which are not actually the cessation of suffering.
Perceiving [these] as the cessation of suffering, and perceiving the path to cessation even in sacrifices, self-mortification, and asceticism— which are not actually the path—
he aspires for the cessation of suffering and initiates the three kinds of formations by way of sacrifice,

self-mortification, and asceticism. Furthermore, because he has not abandoned ignorance regarding the Four Noble Truths, he especially [engages in these], despite their being permeated by numerous disadvantages such as birth, aging, sickness, and death.
Not knowing suffering— which is designated as the fruit of merit— to be suffering, one undertakes the volitional formation of merit,
consisting of the various activities of body, speech, and mind, for the sake of attaining it, just like one desiring a celestial nymph who leaps from a precipice.

Furthermore, even while failing to see that at the end of that fruit of merit— though it is considered happiness— there is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*) which produces great feverish distress, and its lack of true satisfaction, [one continues in this way].
Conditioned by that, he undertakes precisely the aforementioned kind of meritorious formation (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*), like a moth flying into the flame of a lamp,

or like one greedy for a drop of honey licking the edge of a blade smeared with honey. And, failing to see the danger in the pursuit of sensual pleasures and the like— which entail ripening results— he engages even through the three doors,
both due to his perception of them as pleasant and because he is overwhelmed by the defilements (*kilesa*).
Like a fool playing with excrement, or like one wishing to die eating poison,
he undertakes the formation of demerit. And even regarding the results of the formless realm, failing to understand the suffering inherent in the changeability of formations,

he undertakes the imperturbable formation— which is itself a mental formation— through the perversion of eternalism and so forth, like one who, being disoriented, sets out on a path toward a city of demons.

Thus, since the state of volitional formations exists only because of the existence of ignorance, and not because of its non-existence, it should be understood that "these volitional formations have ignorance as their condition.
Here it is asked: let us grant for now that "ignorance is a condition for volitional formations"; but is this ignorance itself a single entity?
Is ignorance the sole condition for volitional formations, or are there other conditions as well? What follows from this? If it were only one, it would result in the doctrine of a single cause.
If there are others as well, then the designation of a single cause—“with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise”—would be untenable. It is not untenable. Why? Because:
“One is not one here, nor is the many not many;
there is no fruit, yet there is purpose in illustrating the cause and fruit as one.
For the Blessed One, in some instances, teaches because of its predominance, in some because of its manifestness, and in some because of its uniqueness within the elegance of his teaching.
And he illuminates both cause and fruit as being one and the same, according to the needs of those to be trained.
Therefore, although other bases, objects, co-nascent factors, and so forth exist as causes for volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), it is ignorance (*avijjā*) that is emphasized here.

This is because of the statements: "In one who contemplates gratification, craving increases," and "With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of the taints (*āsava*). Thus, [ignorance is primary] even over other factors such as craving.

It should be understood that ignorance is explained as the cause of volitional formations because it is the primary cause among the causes of volitional formations, because it is evident from such statements as, "Bhikkhus, the ignorant person, immersed in ignorance,
performs even a meritorious volitional formation," and because it is the unique (asādhāraṇa) factor for volitional formations.
By this very same statement regarding the purpose of explaining each single cause and fruit, the purpose for explaining each single cause and fruit in all instances should be understood.

Here it is asked: Even if this is so, how is it logical for ignorance—which has exclusively undesirable results and is blameworthy—to be a condition for meritorious and imperturbable volitional formations?
For indeed, sugarcane does not arise from a nimba seed. How could it not be logical? For in the world it is said:
“Contrary and non-contrary, likewise similar and dissimilar;”
"The condition for phenomena is established, yet they are not themselves kamma-results.

Thus, this ignorance has exclusively undesirable results by way of its maturation (*vipāka*); and although it is blameworthy by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), it acts as a condition—whether contrary or non-contrary to the place, function, and nature of all these formative forces of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) and so forth—according to their respective suitability.
Furthermore, it should be understood that a condition exists by way of both similar and dissimilar conditions.
Moreover:
“In death and rebirth, in the cycle of existence, and in the characteristics of formations;”
"He who is deluded regarding dependently arisen phenomena constructs these three kinds of volitional formations;
therefore, ignorance is the condition for those three kinds."
“Just as a man born blind, having no guide,
Goes sometimes by the right path and sometimes by the wrong path; So the fool, wandering in saṃsāra, being without a guide, [goes sometimes by the right path and sometimes by the wrong path].”
At one time he performs merit, and at another time even demerit.
But when, having understood the Dhamma, he realizes the Truths, then,
through the subsiding of ignorance, he will wander as one who is at peace.
“With volitional formations as condition, consciousness” refers to the six classes of consciousness:

eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. Therein, eye-consciousness is twofold: wholesome resultant and unwholesome resultant.
Likewise for ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness. Mind-consciousness consists of the two resultant mind-elements (*vipākamanodhātu*).

There are twenty-two kinds: the three rootless mind-consciousness elements, the eight root-possessing resultant consciousnesses, the five fine-material-sphere [resultants], and the four immaterial-sphere [resultants]. Thus, there are thirty-two worldly resultant consciousnesses in total.
Herein, it might be asked: "How is it to be known that this aforementioned consciousness has formations as its condition?"
“Does it exist? Because there is no result in the absence of accumulated karma. For this is a result, and a result does not arise in the absence of accumulated karma.
If it were to arise [without such accumulation], the results of all beings would arise for everyone; yet they do not so arise.

Therefore, it should be understood that “this consciousness exists with volitional formations as its condition. Indeed, all of this occurs by way of both the process of existence (*pavatti*) and rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

It occurs in two ways. Among these, thirteen—namely, the two fivefold sensory consciousnesses, the two mind-elements, and the rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy—occur only during the course of existence (*pavatti*) within the five-aggregate realm.
The remaining nineteen occur, as appropriate, both during the course of existence and at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) across all three realms of existence.
“‘Having obtained conditions’—this is merely a phenomenon (dhamma) that enters into another existence;
it does not transmigrate from there, nor does it exist without a cause from there.
Thus, this mere phenomenon, whether material or immaterial, which arises having obtained conditions, is said to “enter into another existence.”
There is no being, no life-principle. For that [being], there is neither a transmigration here from a past existence, nor an appearance here without a cause from that [existence].
In this context, the former is called "death" (cuti) because of passing away, and the latter is called "rebirth-linking" (paṭisandhi) because of the linking to the beginning of another existence.

Here it is said: "But surely, if there is such manifestation without transmigration, then since the aggregates belonging to this human existence have ceased, and since the karma that is the condition for the fruit does not go there, that fruit would be something other than what it was, and would arise from something else.

Furthermore, if there is no experiencer, to whom would that fruit belong? Therefore, this formulation is not sound. To this, it is replied: [The following verse follows: "Though the aggregates cease here, and though the karma goes not there, The fruit arises from that very same cause; thus there is no fault. Just as a seed perishes here, yet the fruit appears elsewhere, So too, when the aggregates cease, the fruit arises from that cause. Thus it is said: "Though there is no transmigration of the aggregates, nor the passage of karma, nor the arrival of a soul, still, because the fruit arises from that very same cause, there is no fault.
Just as a seed perishes here, yet the fruit appears elsewhere, so too, when the aggregates cease, the fruit arises from that very cause. Therefore, this formulation is indeed sound.
“That fruit which exists in the continuum belongs neither to another nor from another;
the conditioning of seeds is what establishes this fact.
It is precisely through the arising of the fruit that the designation ‘experiencer’ is established.”
"Just as it is conventionally said that a tree bears fruit through the production of fruit.
Even if one were to say: "Even if this were so, these formations must either exist or not exist as conditions for the fruit.
If they exist, their result (vipāka) would have to occur at the very moment of their arising. Or, if they do not exist,"
"Once set in motion, they would constantly bring forth fruit both before and after. He should be told:
"These conditions are brought about by prior action, and they do not constantly bring forth fruit;
in this regard, examples such as a surety-bond and so forth should be understood."
"Conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form": here, "name" refers to the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations;
"form" refers to the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.

For those born from a non-fertilized womb and for those born from eggs, at the moment of rebirth-linking there are twenty types of form—the tenfold sense-base of the physical heart (vatthudasaka) and the tenfold body-base (kāyadasaka)—together with the three immaterial aggregates.
These twenty-three factors should be understood as "name-and-form" conditioned by consciousness.

When the tenfold materiality of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-dasaka*) is added, there are thirty-three. Among beings of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*), at the moment of rebirth-linking for those such as the deities of Brahma’s retinue (*brahmakāyika*), there are thirty-nine material phenomena—namely, the decads of eye, ear, and base, and the nonad of the life-faculty—and the three immaterial aggregates; thus, these total forty-two.

Mental phenomena conditioned by consciousness are name-and-form. Furthermore, in the sensual realm (*kāmabhava*), for the remaining types of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*) or moisture-born beings (*saṃsedaja*) whose sense bases are complete by nature, at the moment of rebirth-linking there are seventy material phenomena—namely, the decads of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and the sex-decad—and three immaterial aggregates;
these seventy-three factors are name-and-form conditioned by consciousness.

This is the maximum. However, by way of the minimum, for those deficient in various decads, the designation "name-and-form" conditioned by consciousness at rebirth-linking should be understood as being reduced accordingly.

For non-material beings, there are only the three non-material aggregates; for non-percipient beings, there is only the nonad of the life-faculty from the material side. This, then, is the method regarding rebirth-linking.
In this regard, it may be asked: "How is it to be known that the name-and-form of rebirth-linking has consciousness as its condition?

It is to be known from both scripture (sutta) and reasoning (yutti). For in the Suttas, the fact that feeling and the other mental factors have consciousness as their condition is established in many ways, such as the method beginning with the phrase, "states that follow upon consciousness. As for reasoning:
"For by means of the form born of mind, which is seen here, [the result] is accomplished;
even for form that is not seen, consciousness is the condition. Thus it is said:
"With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise. Here, however, form is necessarily the four primary elements.
The six bases consist of eleven factors: the life-faculty and the sixfold sense base—namely, the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base.

Herein, it may be asked: how is it to be known that "name-and-form is the condition for the sixfold sense base"? It is because they exist when name-and-form exists; for each respective sense base comes to be only when its corresponding name and form exist, and not otherwise.
“With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises”:
“In brief, there are only six kinds of contact, beginning with eye-contact;
in detail, they become thirty-two, just like consciousness.”
“With contact as condition, feeling arises”:
“Feeling is stated here by way of door, beginning with that born of eye-contact;
these six, when further divided, become thirty-two kinds of feeling here.”
"With feeling as condition, craving":
"Here, craving is shown as sixfold, divided into craving for forms and so on;
therein each one is considered to be threefold according to its mode of occurrence."
“The one who suffers yearns for happiness; the one who is happy desires even more.
But because equanimity is peaceful, it is described simply as ‘happiness.
Therefore, by way of craving as a condition, there come to be these three kinds of feeling.”
“With feeling as condition, craving arises”—thus it was said by the Great Seer.
“With craving as condition, clinging”: there are four kinds of clinging—clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to a doctrine of self.
“With clinging as condition, existence”: here, “existence” refers to kamma-existence (*kamma-bhava*). [There is also] rebirth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*).
But it is stated by way of the extraction of the terms. "With existence as condition, birth": this means the manifestation of the rebirth-linking aggregates with kamma-existence as condition.
Herein, one might ask: "How, then, is it to be known that existence is a condition for birth?

Because even when external conditions are equal, differences such as inferiority and superiority are observed. For among external conditions—such as the father, mother, semen, blood, food, and so forth—[there are variations].
Even among beings who are twins, a distinction such as inferiority or superiority is observed.
This is not without cause, because it does not exist at all times for all beings;

nor is it caused by anything other than kamma, because there is no other cause within the internal continuum of those beings produced thereby. Thus, it is caused solely by kamma. For kamma is [the cause] of beings...
It is the cause for the distinction between the inferior and the sublime, and so forth. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Kamma divides beings, that is to say, by way of the inferior and the sublime.
Regarding such statements as "with birth as condition, aging-and-death [arises]," because when birth is absent, there is no such thing as aging-and-death or states such as sorrow;
but when birth exists, there is aging-and-death, and for one who is touched by the state of suffering termed aging-and-death—
And because for the fool there arise states such as sorrow— either through connection with aging and death or through being touched by this or that painful phenomenon—
it should be understood that this birth is the condition for both aging and death, as well as for sorrow and the rest.
In the passage beginning "With a mind thus developed," the phrase "for the knowledge of recollecting past lives" means for the attainment of that specific knowledge.
"It is said" (*pattiyāti*) means it is stated. "In many ways" (*anekavihitam*) means manifold, of various kinds, or set forth in numerous modes;
this is the meaning. "Past lives" (*pubbenivāsam*) refers to the continuum of existence that has dwelt here and there, beginning from the immediately preceding past birth.
"He recollects" (*anussarati*) means [he does so] by way of the succession of aggregates and by way of death and rebirth-linking.
Or, having followed it back again and again, one recollects. Indeed, six types of persons recollect this past life:
the followers of other sects (*tīrthika*), ordinary disciples, great disciples, chief disciples, paccekabuddhas, and Buddhas.
Among them, the followers of other sects recollect only as far back as forty eons, and not beyond that. Why? Because their wisdom is weak. For they lack the discernment of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Wisdom is weak. Ordinary disciples, because their wisdom is powerful, can indeed recollect even a hundred or a thousand aeons.
The eighty great disciples recollect one hundred thousand aeons. The two chief disciples recollect one incalculable aeon and one hundred thousand aeons.
Private Buddhas recollect two incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand aeons; for such is the extent of their resolve. As for the Buddhas—
However, there is no fixed limit [to how far back they can recollect]. The members of other sects (titthiyā) remember only the succession of aggregates;

they are unable to recollect by way of death and rebirth-linking apart from that succession of aggregates. Just as the blind walk without letting go of their staff, so too they remember without letting go of the succession of aggregates.
Ordinary disciples (pakatisāvakā), however, recollect both by way of the succession of aggregates and [by way of death and rebirth-linking].
They also transmigrate by way of death and rebirth-linking; so too do the eighty great disciples. However, for the two chief disciples, there is no sequential succession of aggregates.
Having seen the death of one individual existence, they see the rebirth-linking;
then, having again seen the death of another, they see the rebirth-linking. In this way, they proceed by transmigration solely by way of death and rebirth-linking.

The same applies to the Paccekabuddhas. However, for the Buddhas, there is neither the function of following the sequence of aggregates nor the function of transferring by way of death and rebirth-linking.
For them, whatever place they desire—whether below or above—among many millions of eons, that very place becomes manifest. Therefore, having condensed even many millions of eons, whatever...
Desiring [to know], they proceed by leaping from place to place like a lion’s leap.
As they proceed in this way, their knowledge—remaining unattached amidst their intervening births—grasps only those places they desire to know.
However, among these six who recollect past lives, the insight into past lives of the non-Buddhist sectarians (tīrthikas) is like the light of a firefly.
Having been offered, it appears: for ordinary disciples like the light of a lamp; for great disciples like the light of a torch;
for chief disciples like the light of the medicinal star (the planet Venus); for paccekabuddhas like the light of the moon.
For Buddhas, it appears like the orb of the autumn sun adorned with a thousand rays. As for the recollection of past lives of those belonging to other sects—
It is like the blind man’s crawling along the edge of a staff; for ordinary disciples, it is like walking across a bridge of sticks; for great disciples, it is like walking across a bridge of logs;
for chief disciples, it is like walking across a bridge of carts; for paccekabuddhas, it is like traveling on a path for foot travel;
and for Buddhas, it is like traveling on a road for large carts. However, in this particular context, regarding the disciples—
The recollection of past lives is intended here. Therefore,
a beginner monk who wishes to recollect in this way should, after his meal, having returned from his almsround,
gone to a secluded place, and entered into seclusion, attain the four jhānas in succession, starting from the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā).
Having risen and reflected upon dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) in the manner described, one should bring to mind the very last sitting. Then,
one should reflect on the laying out of the seat, the entering of the lodging, the putting away of the bowl and robes, the time for eating,
the time of returning from the village, the time of wandering for alms in the village, the time of entering the village for alms, and the time of departing from the monastery.
The time for worshipping the Cetiya and the Bodhi tree, the time for washing the bowl, the time for receiving the bowl,
and from the receiving of the bowl up to the rinsing of the mouth— these duties performed at dawn, as well as the duties performed during the middle watch and the first watch,
should be recollected in reverse order throughout the entire day and night. However, this much is within the scope of even an ordinary mind.
It becomes clear; however, for the mind of preparatory concentration (*parikamma-samādhi*), it becomes exceedingly clear.
If, however, anything here does not become clear, one should again enter the foundational jhāna (*pādaka-jhāna*), emerge, and review [the object].
By this much, it becomes clear as if a lamp were lit. In this same way, by means of the reverse order alone, on the second day, and also on the third, fourth, and fifth days.
One should bring to mind what was done on the tenth day, the half-month, the month, or the year.

By this same method, as one brings to mind [the past] for ten years, twenty years, and so on until one's own rebirth-linking in this present existence, one must bring to mind the name-and-form that occurred at the moment of death in the previous existence. For a wise bhikkhu is indeed capable of this.
At the very first moment, having dispelled the rebirth-linking, it is able to take the name-and-form at the moment of death as its object.

However, because the name-and-form of the previous existence has ceased without remainder and something else has arisen here, that place is like a dense, blind darkness, very difficult to see for one of dull wisdom. Therefore, he thinks: "I am not able to [see] the rebirth-linking..."
One must not abandon the task with the thought, "I shall make name-and-form the object at the moment of death after opening [the door of concentration].
Rather, having repeatedly attained that same foundational jhāna and emerged from it again and again, one should advert to that state.
For by acting in this way, he is like a strong man cutting down a great tree for the sake of the rafters of a gabled house.
Just as one who, having failed to cut a great tree because his axe blade was blunted by the mere act of cutting branches and foliage,
would not give up the task but would go to a smithy, have the axe sharpened, and returning again cut it; and if it were blunted again,
he would likewise have it sharpened and cut it once more— cutting in this manner, he [would eventually succeed].
Just as a great tree would soon fall if one were to cut it again and again after it has already been cut, and continue cutting where it was not yet cut, so too,
if one emerges from the foundational jhāna and, instead of reviewing what was previously adverted to,
adverts only to the rebirth-linking [moment], one would soon break open that rebirth-linking and take the name-and-form at the moment of death as the object.

In this context, the knowledge that proceeds by taking as its object [the self] from the last sitting onwards until the moment of rebirth-linking is not called "knowledge of past lives" (*pubbenivāsāñāṇa*);
rather, it is called "knowledge of preparatory concentration" (*parikamma-samādhi-ñāṇa*). Some call it "knowledge of the past portion" (*atītamsañāṇa*);
this statement refers to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), because that knowledge of the past portion belongs to the fine-material sphere.

This is not logical. However, when that bhikkhu, having taken as his object the name-and-form (nāmarūpa) occurring at the moment of death beyond the moment of rebirth-linking, gives rise to mind-door adverting consciousness, and then—according to the method previously described—gives rise to the absorption consciousness (appanācitta), then the knowledge associated with that consciousness is called "knowledge of recollection of past lives" (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa). By means of that knowledge...
Through mindfulness associated [with that knowledge], one recollects past lives.
In this context, the phrase "namely" (*seyyathidaṃ*) is a particle used for the purpose of showing the specific manner in which [past lives] have been undertaken.
For that very reason, demonstrating the classification and divisions of those past lives thus undertaken, he said: "even one birth," and so forth. Therein, "even one birth" means:
Even a single series of aggregates (khandhasantāna) included within one existence, beginning with the root-linking (paṭisandhi) and ending with the final passing away (cuti), is [one birth].

This same method applies to "two births" and so forth. However, in expressions such as "many eons of dissolution" (saṃvaṭṭakappa), an eon that is contracting is a "dissolution eon," because at that time all beings gather together in the Brahma-world.
An eon that is expanding is an "evolution eon" (vivaṭṭakappa), because at that time [beings emerge] from the Brahma-world.
Because it causes beings to turn away [from existence]. In this context, by means of the contraction (*saṃvaṭṭa*), that which endures during the contraction is included, because it is rooted in that;
and by means of the expansion (*vivaṭṭa*), that which endures during the expansion is included. For it being thus: "Monks, there are these four incalculable periods of an eon (*kappa*). Which four?
When, monks, the eon contracts, it is not easy to calculate that. When...
"Monks, when a world-age is contracting... [as before]... when, monks, a world-age is expanding...
[as before]... when, monks, a world-age is expanding and remains so, it is not easy to calculate"—by these words, the four incalculable eons (*asaṅkheyya*) are encompassed.
In this regard, there are three kinds of destruction: destruction by fire, destruction by water, and destruction by wind. There are three limits of destruction:
the Ābhassara, the Subhakiṇha, and the Vehapphala realms.

When the world-system is destroyed by fire, everything below the Ābhassara realm is consumed by flames. When it is destroyed by water, everything below the Subhakiṇha realm is dissolved by the waters.
When it is convulsed by wind, everything below the Vehapphala realm is destroyed by the wind.
As for its extent, however, one entire Buddha-field is always destroyed. There are three kinds of Buddha-fields:

the field of birth (*jātikkhetta*), the field of authority (*āṇākkhetta*), and the field of range (*visayakkhetta*). Among these, the field of birth extends as far as ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
There is that which causes the Tathāgata to tremble at the moment of taking rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and so forth.

The field of his command (*āṇā-khetta*) extends as far as a hundred thousand times ten million world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), wherein the efficacy of these protective charms (*paritta*)—namely, the Ratana-paritta, Khandha-paritta, Dhajagga-paritta, Āṭānāṭiya-paritta, and Mora-paritta—prevails.
The field of his range (*visaya-khetta*) is infinite and immeasurable, as far as...
Or, it is said: "Whatever the Tathāgata desires, that he knows.
Thus, among these three Buddha-fields, one—the field of authority (*āṇā-khetta*)—perishes;
when that perishes, the field of birth (*jāti-khetta*) is already perished. Furthermore, they perish together, and they re-establish themselves together.
The destruction and the re-establishment of that world-system should be understood as follows:
At the time when the aeon is destroyed by fire, first of all a great cloud of aeon-destruction arises and pours down a single great rain over a hundred thousand million world-systems.
People, being delighted, bring out all their seeds and sow them. But when the crops have been grazed down by cattle to the mere extent of a cow’s footprint...
While beings are born there, it does not rain even a single drop as they bray like donkeys; at that time, the rain becomes utterly cut off.
Beings who depend on rain for their livelihood are gradually reborn in the Brahma-world, as are the deities who depend on flowers and fruits.
Thus, after a long period of time has passed, the water in various places comes to exhaustion.
Then, in due course, even fish and turtles die and are reborn in the Brahma-world, as are beings from the hells.
Regarding this, some say: "Beings from the hells perish upon the appearance of the seventh sun.
But since there is no rebirth in the Brahma-world without jhāna, how can those among these [beings] who are oppressed by famine or are incapable of attaining jhāna be reborn there?
