Regarding the phrase "they are reborn there": it is by virtue of having attained jhāna in the world of the gods.

For at that time, when it is known that "after the passing of one hundred thousand years, the emergence of the eon will occur," the sense-sphere deities called Lokabyūhas—having loosened their turbans, with disheveled hair, weeping faces, wiping away tears with their hands, dressed in red garments, and wearing extremely hideous attire—[appear].

Having offered the oblation, they wandered along the paths of men and proclaimed thus: "Venerable sirs, venerable sirs, after the passing of one hundred thousand years from now, the emergence of a new aeon will occur;
this world will be destroyed. Even the great ocean will dry up, and this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, will burn away and perish, all the way up to the Brahma-world."
“The destruction of the world will come to pass. Venerable sirs, cultivate loving-kindness; cultivate compassion... gladness... equanimity, venerable sirs.
Serve your mother; serve your father; be respectful toward the elders of the family.
Having heard their words, for the most part both humans and terrestrial deities were filled with a sense of spiritual urgency and became gentle-minded toward one another.
Having performed meritorious deeds such as loving-kindness (*mettā*), they are reborn in the world of the gods.
There, having partaken of divine ambrosial food and performed the preliminary work (*parikamma*) on the air-kasina, they attain meditative absorption (*jhāna*).

Others, however, are reborn in the world of the gods through karma to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparapariyavedanīya*). For one wandering in *saṃsāra* who is devoid of such karma to be experienced in a subsequent life...
There is no such being as a "soul" (satta). They too attain jhāna there in that very same way. Thus, by virtue of the jhāna attained in the world of the devas, all are reborn in the Brahma-world.
However, after the cessation of the rains, when a long period of time has passed, a second sun appears.
When that has appeared, neither the demarcation of night nor the demarcation of day is discerned. One sun rises and one sets;

the world is as if in a continuous succession of solar heat. And whereas in the natural sun there is a son of the devas named Sūriya, such a being does not exist in the case of the sun that destroys the aeon.
While that natural sun is in operation, clouds also appear in the sky.
Even the smoke crests move about. When the sun that destroys the eon is present, the sky becomes stainless like the surface of a mirror, free from smoke and clouds.
With the exception of the five great rivers, the water in all other small streams and such dries up.
Then, after a long period of time has passed, the third sun appears; with its appearance, even the great rivers dry up.
After the passing of a further long period of time, a fourth sun appears; with its appearance, these seven great lakes—
the sources of the great rivers in the Himalayas— namely, Sīhapapātaṇa, Haṃsapātaṇa, Kaṇṇamuṇḍaka,
Rathakāradaha, Anotattadaha, Chaddantadaha, and Kuṇāladaha— all dry up.

After that, with the passing of a long period of time, a fifth sun appears; through its appearance, gradually not even enough water to fill the impression made by a fingernail remains in the great ocean.
After another long period of time, a sixth sun appears;

through its appearance, the entire world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) becomes a single mass of smoke, its moisture completely consumed by smoke. Just as it is here, so it is for hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems.
After the passing of a further long period of time, a seventh sun appears;
through its appearance, the entire Cakkavāḷa, together with hundreds of thousands of millions of Cakkavāḷas, becomes a single mass of flame.
Even the peaks of Mount Sineru, measuring hundreds of yojanas and more, crumble away and vanish into the sky itself. That mass of fire rises up and seizes the realm of the Four Great Kings.
There, having incinerated the golden palaces, the jewel palaces, and the crystal palaces, it takes possession of the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
By this same method, it continues until it takes possession of the plane of the first jhāna. There, having incinerated those three as well, it reaches and remains fixed upon the Ābhassara realm.
As long as there exists even the slightest trace of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra), it does not go out; it is only through the total exhaustion of all conditioned phenomena that it ceases.
But it goes out, extinguished without leaving even so much as ashes, like the crest of a flame of ghee or oil being consumed.
Together with the lower space, the upper space becomes one vast darkness.
Then, after the lapse of a long period, a great cloud arises and first rains very fine, delicate rain.

Raining down gradually with torrents measuring from the size of a lotus stalk, a bone, a pestle, a palm-leaf, a tree trunk, and so forth, it fills all the burnt places throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) and then vanishes.
That water, driven by winds arising from below and across, becomes solidified into a mass, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. How, indeed, does such a vast mass of water [become so]?
If it is asked, "Does it make it solid?"—it does so by providing openings. For it provides openings here and there for that [wind].
Thus, being compressed and made solid by the wind, and being worn away, it gradually descends downward.
As each portion of water has descended, in the place of the Brahmā-world, Brahmā-worlds [are formed], and in the place above, the four sense-sphere deva-worlds.
And the worlds of the devas become manifest. However, when [the water] has descended to its former position on the earth, powerful winds arise.
These hold it back, rendering it motionless like water standing in a covered water-vessel.
As the sweet water is being exhausted, it brings forth a layer of "taste-earth" (rasa-pathavī) above; this is endowed with beautiful color.
It was endowed with fragrance and flavor, like a film upon the surface of water that has no sediment.

And at that time, beings who had previously been reborn in the Ābhassara Brahma-world fell away from there due to the exhaustion of their lifespan or the exhaustion of their merit and were reborn here.
They possessed self-luminosity and moved through the air. According to the method described in the Aggañña Sutta, they [partook of] that earth of flavor.
Having eaten, overcome by craving, they attempt to eat the food they have prepared.
Then their own radiance vanishes and darkness arises. Seeing the darkness, they are afraid.
Thereupon, to dispel their fear and produce courage in them, the solar disk appears, fifty yojanas in full extent.
It became manifest. Seeing it, they were thrilled and delighted, thinking, "We have obtained light!
They said, "He has arisen, dispelling the fear of us who were afraid and generating courage; therefore, let him be called Sūriya.
Thus they gave him the name Sūriya. Then, when the sun had made the day bright and had set, [they thought], "Even that light which we obtained..."
Thinking, "He too has been lost," they become afraid again, and it occurs to them, "It would be well indeed if we could obtain another light.
As if knowing their minds, the moon-disk, forty-nine yojanas in extent, becomes manifest.
Seeing it, they become even more exceedingly joyful and satisfied, thinking, "He has arisen as if knowing our desire."
"Therefore, let him be Canda"; thus they gave him the name Canda.
Thus, when the moon and sun had appeared, the lunar mansions and the forms of the stars appeared.
From that time forth, nights and days became discernible, and gradually months, fortnights, seasons, and years came into being. [Thus it was] with the moon and the sun.
However, on the very day they become manifest, Sineru, the Cakkavāḷa mountains, and the Himavanta mountains appear.
And these, moreover, appear simultaneously, neither before nor after, specifically on the full-moon day of the month of Phagguṇa. How so?
Just as when rice mixed with millet is being cooked, bubbles arise all at once—some parts becoming high and bulging, others low and hollow.
Some were level with the level; likewise, in places that were high, there were mountains; in low-lying places, there were oceans; and in places that were level, there were islands.
Then, as those beings consumed the savory earth (rasapathavī), gradually some became beautiful and others became ugly.
Thereupon, the beautiful ones looked down upon the ugly ones. Due to that pride on their part, that savory earth [disappeared].
The earth-crust disappears, and the *bhūmipappaṭaka* (earth-mat) appears.
Then, by that same process, that too disappears, and the *padālatā* (ground-vine) appears.

By that same process, that too disappears, and rice that ripens without cultivation appears—free from husks, without powder, pure, fragrant, and consisting of grains of rice. Thereupon, vessels appear for them. They [take] the rice...
Having placed it in a vessel, they set it upon a stone slab. A crest of flames rises up of its own accord and cooks it.
That rice becomes like jasmine or *jāti* flowers. It has no need for soup or condiments;
whatever flavor they desire to eat, that very flavor it becomes. For them, that [food] is coarse.
From that time on, for those taking food, urine and feces arise.
Then, in order for these to exit, openings of wounds break open. The male characteristic appears in the man, and the female characteristic appears in the woman.
There, indeed, the woman gazes excessively at the man, and the man gazes excessively at the woman. Due to their excessive gazing, [passion arises].
The fever of sensual desire arises. Consequently, they engage in sexual intercourse.
Because of their practice of unrighteous conduct, being censured and harassed by the wise, they build houses for the sake of concealing that unrighteousness.
While dwelling in those houses, they gradually follow the example of a certain person of a lazy nature.

As they began to take possession [of the grain], they stored it up. From that time on, even the husk and the chaff enveloped the rice grain, and the place where it had been harvested would not grow again.
They gathered together and lamented: "Alas, friends, evil states have appeared among beings!
For formerly we were mind-made," and so forth, to be expanded according to the method stated in the Aggañña Sutta.
Then they established boundaries.
Thereupon, a certain being took another’s portion that had not been given. After having rebuked him twice, on the third occasion they struck him with hands, clods, and sticks.
Thus, regarding the taking of what is not given, the censuring of such, the speaking of falsehoods, and the taking up of sticks...
When they had assembled, those beings who had appeared reflected:
"What if we were to appoint one being who would, for us, censure what should be censured, reprove what should be reproved, and banish what should be banished?
We, however, shall grant him a portion of the rice. When the beings had thus reached a decision, in this [place]—
For that entire eon, this very Blessed One, while still a bodhisatta, was at that time the most handsome, the most beautiful, and the most influential among those beings;
he was endowed with wisdom and capable of exercising restraint and encouragement.
They approached him, requested his consent, and consecrated him. Because he was consecrated by that great multitude, he is called Mahāsammata (“Greatly Consecrated”).
"He is the lord of the fields (khetta), thus he is a *khattiya*; he gladdens others through righteousness and equity, thus he is a *rājā*. Thus he became known by three names.
For whatever is a source of wonder in the world, the Bodhisatta alone is the first person therein.
Thus, with the Bodhisatta as the starting point, the circle of *khattiyas* was established, and subsequently the other castes, such as the *brāhmaṇas*, were also established.
Therein, from the great cloud that destroys the eon (*kappa*) until the cessation of the conflagration, this is called one incalculable period (*asaṅkheyya*) of the dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭa*).

From the cessation of the conflagration that destroys the eon until the great auspicious cloud that fills hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), this is called the second incalculable period of the duration of the dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*). From the great auspicious cloud until the manifestation of the moon and sun—

This third incalculable period is called the "evolution" (*vivaṭṭa*). From the appearance of the moon and sun until the great cloud that causes the destruction of the world-cycle returns, this fourth incalculable period is called the "duration of evolution" (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*). These four incalculable periods constitute one great aeon (*mahākappa*).
Thus, first of all, the destruction by fire and the re-establishment [of the world] should be understood.

But at the time when the world-system (*kappa*) is destroyed by water, it should be explained in detail according to the method previously stated, beginning with: "First of all, a great cloud that destroys the world-system arises. However, this is the distinction:
just as there was a second sun in that case, here a great cloud of caustic water that destroys the world-system arises. At first, it rains very fine rain.
In due course, it rains with great torrents, filling hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
The earth, mountains, and other things, wherever they are touched by the salt water, dissolve away. The water is held up on all sides by winds.
From the earth up to the plane of the second *jhāna*, the water takes hold; having caused even the three Brahma-worlds there to dissolve, it remains striking against the Subhakiṇha realm.
As long as there is even the slightest trace of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), it does not subside.
But when all conditioned phenomena have been overcome by that which follows the water, it suddenly subsides and vanishes.
Then, together with the lower space, the upper space becomes one, and there is great darkness; all else is as previously described.
However, in this context, the world first manifests starting from the Ābhassara Brahma-world.
Beings pass away from the Subhakiṇha realm and are reborn in the stations of the Ābhassaras and so forth.

Therein, from the great cloud that destroys the aeon until the cessation of the salt-water that destroys the aeon, this constitutes one incalculable. From the cessation of the water until the appearance of the great cloud of prosperity—
This is the second incalculable. From the great cloud of prosperity... [as before] ...these four incalculables constitute one great aeon (*mahākappa*).
Thus should the destruction by water and the re-establishment [of the world] be understood.
Furthermore, at the time when an aeon is destroyed by wind, first of all, the great cloud that destroys the aeon arises.
This should be elaborated in the same manner as previously stated. However, this is the distinction:
just as there was a second sun there, so here a wind arises for the purpose of destroying the world-age (*kappa*).
First it stirs up coarse dust, then fine dust, fine sand, coarse sand, gravel, stones, and so forth, up to stones the size of gabled houses.
It also uproots great trees standing on uneven ground. Having risen from the earth into the sky, they do not fall back down;
right there they are reduced to fragments and vanish.
Then, in due course, a wind arises from the great earth below, overturns the earth, turns its roots upward, and hurls it into the sky. [The earth] measuring a hundred yojanas—
Portions of the earth, measuring two, three, four, or five hundred yojanas, break apart and, tossed by the force of the wind, are reduced to dust and vanish into thin air.
Even the Cakkavāḷa mountain range and Mount Sineru are lifted up by the wind and hurled into the sky; they strike one another, are reduced to dust, and perish.

By this very means, destroying the terrestrial palaces and the celestial palaces, and having destroyed the six worlds of the sense-sphere devas, it destroys hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
Therein, the world-systems collide with world-systems, the Himalayas with Himalayas, and Mount Sinerus with Mount Sinerus;
having come together, they are reduced to dust and perish.
From the earth up to the plane of the third jhāna, the wind takes hold; having destroyed the three Brahma-worlds, it comes to rest, striking against the Vehapphala realm.
Thus, having destroyed everything comprised within conditioned phenomena, it itself perishes.
Together with the space below, the space above becomes one, a great darkness; all this is as previously described. However, here—
The world reappears beginning with the Subhakiṇha Brahma-world. Beings pass away from the Vehapphala realm and are reborn in the Subhakiṇha abode and other such places.
Therein, the period from the great cloud that destroys the aeon until the cessation of the wind that destroys the aeon constitutes one incalculable (*asaṅkheyya*).
From the cessation of the wind until the great cloud of prosperity, this is the second incalculable... [and so on].
These four incalculables constitute one great aeon (*mahākappa*). In this manner, both the destruction and the reformation [of the world] by wind should be understood.

For what reason does the world thus perish? It is due to the root of unwholesomeness (*akusalamūla*). Indeed, when the roots of unwholesomeness have become predominant, the world perishes in this way.
Furthermore, if passion (*rāga*) is more predominant, it perishes by fire; if hatred (*dosa*) is more predominant, it perishes by water.

It perishes. Some, however, say: "When hatred (*dosa*) is more predominant, it perishes by fire; when passion (*rāga*) is [more predominant], by water. When delusion (*moha*) is more predominant, it perishes by wind.
Even while perishing in this way, it is destroyed by fire for seven consecutive times, and on the eighth time, by water.
Again, for seven times by fire, and on the eighth time by water—in this manner, on every eighth [cycle].
During the period of destruction by water, after being destroyed seven times by water, it is again destroyed by fire for seven times.

By this point, sixty-three eons have passed. During this interval, the wind—having found its opportunity by warding off even the occasion for destruction by water that has arrived—destroys the world, disintegrating the Subhakiṇha realm whose lifespan is a full sixty-four eons.

Furthermore, a monk who recollects his past lives and possesses the memory of eons (kappa-anussaraṇaka) recollects within these eons many aeons of world-dissolution (saṃvaṭṭa-kappa), many aeons of world-evolution (vivaṭṭa-kappa), and many aeons of both dissolution and evolution (saṃvaṭṭa-vivaṭṭa-kappa).
The terms "aeon of dissolution" and "aeon of evolution" are stated by taking half of an eon; the term "aeon of both dissolution and evolution" is stated by taking the entire eon.
If it is asked, "How does he recollect? it is by way of the method beginning with, "I existed there. In that context, "I existed there" means:

in such-and-such a world-cycle, I existed in such-and-such a state of being, or in such-and-such a womb, or in such-and-such a destination, or in such-and-such a station of consciousness, or in such-and-such an abode of beings, or in such-and-such a class of beings.
"Of such a name" means Tissa or Phussa. "Of such a clan" means Kaccāna or Kassapa. This is his...

This was stated by way of recollecting one’s own name and clan in a past existence. However, if at that time one wishes to recollect one’s own excellence of physical appearance, or whether one’s livelihood was coarse or refined, or the abundance of pleasure and pain, or the state of having a short or long lifespan, one recollects that as well.
Therefore he said: "Of such appearance... [and so on] ...of such limit to the lifespan."
In this context: "of such beauty" means fair-skinned or dark-skinned. "Of such nutriment" means one whose nutriment consists of boiled rice and meat, or one who eats fallen fruit.
"Experiencing such pleasure and pain" means experiencing various kinds of bodily and mental pleasure and pain, distinguished as being with or without material substance, and so forth.
"With such a limit to his lifespan" means having a lifespan limited to such a duration, namely one hundred years.
Or with a lifespan reaching eighty-four hundred thousand eons.
"Having passed away from there, I arose elsewhere"— this means that having passed away from that state of existence, from that womb, from that destiny, from that station of consciousness,
from that abode of beings, or from that class of beings, I was again born in such-and-such a state of existence, in such a womb, in such a destiny, in such a station of consciousness.

I arose in a dwelling for beings or among a class of beings. "There too I was" means that in that very existence, womb, destiny, station of consciousness, or dwelling for beings, or among a class of beings, I existed once again. "With such a name," and so forth, is exactly as previously described.
Furthermore, "I was there" refers to the recollection of one who ascends step by step as far as one desires; this is [the first stage].
"Then passing away" (*tato cuto*) refers to the reviewing consciousness of one who is turning back [from death].

Therefore, it should be understood that the statement "reborn here" (*idhūpapanno*) was spoken with reference to his place of rebirth immediately following this present rebirth, as in "arose there" (*amutra udapādi*).

However, the passage beginning with "there he was known by such-and-such a name" (*tatrāpāsi*) refers to his name, clan, and so forth in that place of rebirth immediately following this present rebirth.
This was said for the purpose of recollection and vision. "Having passed away from there, I have reappeared here" means:

"Having passed away from that immediately preceding place of rebirth, I have been born here in such-and-such a clan of Kshatriyas or a clan of Brahmins. "Thus" (iti) means in this way. "With its modes and particulars" (sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ):
it is "with particulars" (sākāraṃ) by way of complexion and so forth, and "with particulars" (suddesaṃ) by way of name and clan. By name and clan...
For a being is designated by name and clan—as "Tissa," "Phussa," or "Kassapa"—and is recognized through its diversity by way of complexion and so forth—as "dark" or "fair.
Therefore, name and clan constitute the designation (uddesa), while the others are the modes (ākāra).
The commentary on the description of the knowledge of recollection of past lives is finished.
54. Commentary on the Exposition of the Knowledge of the Divine Eye (Dibbacakkhuñāṇaniddesa) 106.

Regarding the phrase "he attends to the perception of light" in the exposition of the knowledge of the divine eye: whether by day or by night, he attends to the light of the sun, fire, moon, or jewels as "light.
And because he directs his attention toward the perception of light while attending in this way, it is called "the perception of light" (*ālokasañña*).
"He attends to it" is what is said. "He resolves upon the perception of day": having thus attended to the perception of light, he establishes the perception that it is day.
"As by day, so by night": just as light was seen by day, in that very same way he attends to it by night. "As by night, so by day": just as light was seen by night, in that very same way...
One attends to it even by day. Thus, with a mind that is open, with a mind that is not shut off.
"Unenveloped" means not bound on all sides. "He develops a radiant mind" means he increases a mind accompanied by light.

By this, the mind that takes light as its object for the preliminary stage of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu) is described; it is specifically the fourth jhāna having the light-kasina (ālokakasiṇa) as its object.
Or it was said with this intention in mind. As he develops it in this way, his mind becomes luminous, free from the obstruction of darkness.

Therefore, a clansman who is a beginner and desires to arouse the divine eye should, following the guidance of this very text, bring the jhāna based on the kasiṇa object to a state where it is capable of being directed in all its aspects toward the fire kasiṇa.
Among these three kasiṇas—the white kasiṇa and the light kasiṇa—one or another should be made proximate; having made it the object of access concentration, it should be expanded and established.
The intention is that absorption (appanā) should not be induced therein.
For if one were to induce it, it would have the foundational jhāna as its support, not the preliminary work (parikamma). And among these three, only the light kasiṇa—
The former is superior, but the other two kasiṇas are mentioned as being in conformity with it.
Therefore, having taken the light-kasiṇa or one of the others as the object and having produced the four jhānas, one should again stand on the access stage itself and expand the kasiṇa.
One should perceive the visible form only within the area where the kasiṇa has been expanded and re-expanded. The visible form...
However, for one who does not perform the pervasion of light with that preparatory mind characterized by ill-will, the stage of the preparation passes away;
consequently, the light disappears, and when it has disappeared, even the range of visible forms is no longer seen.
Therefore, he must repeatedly enter the basic jhāna itself, emerge from it, and then pervade [the world] with light. Thus...
Gradually, the light becomes firmly established. Whatever extent of space one delimits, thinking, "Let there be light here," light remains right there.
Even if one sits for a whole day and looks, there is the seeing of forms.
In that regard, when [the object] has passed beyond the range of that bhikkhu’s physical eye—having gone inside the belly and being dependent on the heart-base—

When form—whether resting on the surface of the earth below, or situated beyond walls, mountains, or ramparts, or even beyond other world-systems—comes within the range of the eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*), it is as if it were being seen by the fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*); at that time, the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) has arisen.
And it is this [divine eye] alone that is capable of seeing form here, not the preliminary stages of consciousness (*pubbabhāgacitta*).

The sequence for the arising of the divine eye is as follows: having taken that aforementioned kind of visible form as its object, when the adverting consciousness at the mind-door has arisen and ceased, four or five impulsion consciousnesses arise taking that same visible form as their object;
this should be understood in the manner already explained. Furthermore, this knowledge is called both "knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings" and "divine-eye knowledge."
This is what is said. However, this constitutes an obstacle for the worldling (*puthujjana*).
For wherever he resolves, "Let there be light," that very place—even piercing through the earth, the ocean, and mountains—becomes uniformly illuminated.
Then, as he sees terrifying forms such as *yakkhas* and *rakkhasas* there, fear arises in him. By means of that, mental distraction occurs.
Having attained it, one becomes distracted from meditation. Therefore, one must be diligent in seeing forms.
"For the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings" means for the sake of knowing both the death and the rebirth of beings.
It is stated that this is for the purpose of the knowledge of the divine eye—that knowledge by which the death and rebirth of beings are known. By means of the divine...
"Cakkhunā" (by the eye) has the same meaning as previously stated. "Visuddhena" (purified):
it is purified because seeing the passing away and rebirth is the cause for the purification of view. For he who sees only the passing away and not the rebirth adopts the annihilationist view;
he who sees only the rebirth and not the passing away adopts the view of the spontaneous appearance of new beings. But he who [sees] both of these...
Because he transcends both of those types of views, his vision serves as the cause for purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*).
Both of these are seen by the sons of the Buddha. Therefore it was said: "It is 'purified' because seeing the passing away and rebirth is a cause for the purification of view.
By seeing forms beyond the human sphere after having transcended the human domain, it is "transcending the human" (*atikkantamānusaka*); [by seeing] the human, it is "human" (*mānusaka*).
Or, because it transcends the fleshly eye, it is "transcending the human.
With that divine eye, purified and transcending the human—“he sees beings” means he surveys beings just as humans do with the fleshly eye. “Passing away and being reborn” means...
Here, it is not possible to see [beings] at the moment of death or at the moment of rebirth with the divine eye;

rather, those who are near to death and will die now are "those passing away" (*cavamāna*). Those who have already taken rebirth-connection (*paṭisandhi*) or have just been reborn are intended by the term "those being reborn" (*upapajjamāna*).
He shows that one sees them in such states as passing away and being reborn. They are called "inferior" (*hīna*) because they are associated with the outflow of delusion (*moha-nissanda*).

"Despised" means being held in contempt, looked down upon, slighted, or disregarded on account of inferior birth, family, wealth, and so forth. "Exalted" (*paṇīta*) refers to that which is the opposite of those [inferior qualities], because it is associated with the outflow (*nissanda*) of non-delusion (*amoha*).
"Beautiful" (*suvaṇṇa*) refers to that which possesses a desirable, lovely, and pleasing color, because it is associated with the outflow of non-hatred (*adosa*).

"Ugly" (*dubbaṇṇa*) refers to that which possesses an undesirable, unlovely, and unpleasant color, because it is associated with the outflow of hatred (*dosa*); the meaning is also "unsightly" or "deformed. "Well-gone" (*sugata*)...

“In those who have gone to a good destination” means in those who have reached a happy state, or because they are endowed with the outflow of non-greed, in those who are wealthy and possess great riches.

“In those who have gone to a bad destination” means in those who have reached an unhappy state, or because they are endowed with the outflow of greed, in those who are destitute and lack food and drink. “According to their karma” means having arrived at whatever specific karma has been accumulated.

In this context, the function of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) was described by the preceding terms beginning with “passing away,” whereas by this present phrase, the function of the knowledge of rebirth according to karma (*yathākammūpagañāṇa*) is stated.
And this is the sequence for the arising of that knowledge:
here, a bhikkhu, having extended light toward the lower hells, sees beings in hell experiencing great suffering; that seeing is precisely the function of the divine eye.
He then attends to it thus: "Having performed what kind of kamma do these beings experience this suffering?"
Then, the thought "having done this," knowledge arises with that action as its object.
Likewise, having extended the light toward the higher deva-worlds, he sees beings in the Nandana Grove, Missaka Grove, Phārusaka Grove, and so forth, experiencing great prosperity;
that vision, too, is indeed the function of the divine eye. He reflects thus: "What now..."

“Indeed, having performed such-and-such kamma, these beings experience this success. Then, the knowledge arises for him that “having performed this very act,” identifying that specific kamma as its object.
This is what is called the knowledge of the way of kamma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa). There is no separate preliminary exercise for this.
Just as with this, so it is with the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa); for both of these have the divine eye as their foundation.
They succeed together with the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).

In phrases such as "These, indeed, are the venerable ones," the word *ime* (these) is a demonstrative term for those seen by the divine eye. *Vata* is a particle used in the sense of a conforming affirmation.
*Bhonto* means "venerable ones" (*bhavanto*). "Misconduct" (*duccarita*) refers to conduct that is wicked, or conduct that has become wicked due to being rotten with defilements (*kilesa*).
"Bodily misconduct" (*kāyaduccarita*) means misconduct committed by the body, or misconduct arising from the body;
the same method applies to the others as well. "Possessing" (*samannāgatā*) means being endowed with [those qualities].

"Revilers of the noble ones" (*ariyūpavādakā*) refers to those who, having no desire for the welfare of the noble ones—namely the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples, including even lay stream-enterers—speak against them through either some final charge or by disparaging their virtues.
Or they are revilers, abusers, and reproachers—this is what is meant. In this context, one who says, "These have no ascetic quality;
these are not true ascetics," reviles by means of the final ground (the ultimate offense).
One who says, "These have no jhāna, nor liberation, nor path, nor fruit," and so forth, should be understood as reviling by way of destroying their virtues. He...
Whether one reviles an Ariya knowingly or unknowingly, in either case it is indeed an insult to an Ariya. It is a grave offense, similar to an *ānantariya* crime;
it obstructs both rebirth in heaven and the attainment of the Path. However, it is remediable.
Therefore, whoever reviles an Ariya should go to them and, if he is senior to the venerable one, sit down in a squatting posture and say: "I [am guilty] toward the Venerable One..."
He should ask for forgiveness, saying: "I said this and that; please forgive me for that.
If he is junior, he should ask for forgiveness by prostrating, sitting in the kneeling position (ukkuṭika), and raising his joined palms, saying: "Venerable sir, I said this and that to you;
please forgive me for that. If he has gone away to another region, [the senior] should either go there himself or [send] a student (saddhivihārika) or someone else.

Or, having sent someone, he should ask for forgiveness. If it is not possible either to go there himself or to send someone, he should go into the presence of those monks who reside in that monastery;
if they are junior, he should sit in the *ukkuṭika* posture (on his heels), and if they are senior, he should proceed according to the method prescribed for elders, saying:
"Venerable sirs, I [am named so-and-so] regarding the Venerable [named so-and-so]..."

Having said, "I have said this and that; may that venerable one forgive me," he should ask for forgiveness. Even if the other person does not forgive him in his presence, this same procedure must be performed.
If the monk is traveling alone, and neither his place of residence nor his destination is known, he should go to a wise monk and say, "Venerable sir, I [have committed such-and-such]..."
One should say: "I spoke such-and-such to the Venerable One; as I recall that, remorse arises in me—what shall I do?
He will reply: "Do not worry; the Elder forgives you; let your mind be pacified.
Then, facing the direction where the Noble One has gone, one should raise one’s joined palms and say: "Forgive me. If...
He has attained final Nibbāna; having gone to the place where he attained final Nibbāna, and even as far as the charnel ground, one must ask for forgiveness.
When this is done, there is neither an obstruction to heaven nor an obstruction to the Path; it becomes just as it was before.
"Holders of wrong view" means those with perverted vision. "Those who have undertaken actions based on wrong view" means by way of wrong view.
Those who undertake various kinds of actions, and those who incite others to bodily actions and so forth rooted in wrong view. Here,
although slander of the Noble Ones is included by the mention of verbal misconduct, and wrong view is included by the mention of mental misconduct,
it should be understood that these two are mentioned again for the purpose of showing their status as being particularly blameworthy.
For reviling the Noble Ones is a very grave offense because it is similar to an immediate (ānantariya) deed. And this has been said:

"Sāriputta, just as a bhikkhu endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom might attain final knowledge in this very life, even so, Sāriputta, I say that this is the case for one who does not abandon that speech, who does not abandon that mind, and who does not abandon that view."
“Without relinquishing it, he is placed in hell just as he was carried there.
Indeed, there is nothing more blameworthy than wrong view. As it is said: “Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single thing that is so blameworthy as wrong view, bhikkhus; wrong view is supreme.”
“...O bhikkhus, these are the Vajjian practices.
“With the breaking up of the body” means with the relinquishing of the aggregates that have been clung to. “After death” means immediately thereafter, at the grasping of the rebirth-aggregates.
Alternatively, “with the breaking up of the body” means the cutting off of the life-faculty. “After death” means subsequent to the moment of the death-consciousness (*cuti-citta*).

"Apāya" and so forth—all these are synonyms for hell (*niraya*). Indeed, it is called "hell" (*niraya*) because it is devoid of "good fortune" (*aya*), which consists of merit that serves as the cause for heaven and liberation;
or else, it is an "apāya" because of the absence of the arrival (*āya*) of happiness. It is a "duggati" because it is the destination or refuge of suffering;
or else, it is a "duggati" because it is a destination produced by defiled (*duṭṭha*) karma due to an abundance of hatred. Therein, beings fall down helpless.
"Those who commit misdeeds" refers to the *vinipāta*. It is called *vinipāta* because those who are perishing fall into it with their limbs and members shattered.
It is called *niraya* because there is no "essence" (*āya*) here that is perceived as a gratification.
Alternatively, by the mention of the "woeful states" (*apāya*), he indicates the animal realm; for the animal realm is a woeful state because it is departed from the happy destinies (*sugati*).

There is no miserable destination (*duggati*) for those of great authority, such as the *nāgarāja*s and others, because of their existence [there]. By the mention of "miserable destination," the realm of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*) is intended;
for that is both a state of loss (*apāya*) and a miserable destination, since it is departed from the happy destinations (*sugati*) and has become a place of suffering.

However, it is not a "fall" (*vinipāta*), because it does not fall away in the manner of the asura hosts. By the mention of "fall," the asura host is intended; for that, in the sense already stated, is a fall.
It is called a "fall" (*vinipāta*) because it is a state of ruin, an evil destination, and because one has fallen away from all elevations.
By the mention of "hell," various types of hell such as Avīci and others are intended. "Reborn" (*upapanna*) means having approached; the intention is that they have been produced there.
The bright side (*sukkapaṅkha*) should be understood by reversing what has been stated.
However, this is the distinction: therein, by the inclusion of "a happy destination" (*sugati*), the human destination is also included;

by the inclusion of "heaven" (*sagga*), only the divine destination is meant. Therein, a "happy destination" (*sugati*) is a beautiful destination. "Heaven" (*sagga*) is that which is a supreme (*agga*) state through its objects such as forms and so forth.
All of that is called "the world" (*loka*) in the sense of crumbling and disintegrating; such is the etymological meaning. Thus [begins] the passage beginning with "with the divine eye."
This is the entire concluding statement. "Thus he sees with the divine eye"—this is the summary meaning here.
The commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of the divine eye is finished.
The miscellaneous section on the five knowledges.

Among these five knowledges, the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*) occurs with respect to seven kinds of objects by way of being limited, sublime, past, future, present, internal, and external.
The knowledge of the purification of the divine ear-element (*sotadhātu-visuddhi-ñāṇa*) occurs with respect to four kinds of objects by way of being limited, present, internal, and external.
The knowledge of penetration of minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*) [occurs] by way of being limited, sublime, immeasurable, pertaining to the path, past, future, present, and external.

It occurs with respect to eight kinds of objects. The knowledge of recollection of past lives occurs with respect to eight kinds of objects by way of limited, sublime, immeasurable, path, past, internal, external, and indeterminate objects.
The knowledge of the divine eye occurs with respect to limited, present, internal, and external objects.
Knowledge of the way beings fare according to their kamma occurs with respect to five kinds of objects: limited, sublime, past, internal, and external.
Knowledge of the future occurs with respect to eight kinds of objects: limited, sublime, immeasurable, the path, the future, internal, external, and the indeterminate.
Thus it proceeds with respect to these [eight] objects.
The Miscellaneous Section on the Five Knowledges is finished.
55. Commentary on the Exposition of the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints (Āsavakkhayañāṇa). 107.

In the exposition of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, the faculties such as "I shall come to know the unknown" (anaññātaññassāmītindriya) have their meanings already explained. How many bases (ṭhāna)?
The question "it goes" is asked for the purpose of determining the specific place of arising for each [consciousness]. "It goes to one place" means that it arises in one place;
for the place of the locus of arising is called "place" (*ṭhāna*) because they stand (*tiṭṭhati*) therein.
"Six places" refers to the six moments of the paths and fruits. Among the faculties, there are three beginning with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*).
It is stated that "the faculty of faith has resolution as its retinue," and so forth, for the purpose of showing that each one is indeed predominant.
Just as in such passages as "the meaning of the faculty of faith is resolution," where resolution and the rest are mentioned in terms of the specific functions of the faculty of faith and the others,
so too here, in the phrase "it has resolution as its retinue," the faculty of faith is [characterized] by the sense of resolution.
"It has its retinue" is what is meant. This same method applies to the remaining [faculties] as well. Furthermore, the term "retinue" (*parivāra*) is used here with a change of grammatical gender.
The "faculty of wisdom" (*paññindriya*) is mentioned separately for the purpose of showing its specific nature as understanding;
for even in the Abhidhamma, it is distinguished from the other faculties at the moment of the path and the moment of the fruit in order to demonstrate the specific function of wisdom.

And this single wisdom is analyzed eightfold. "The surrounding of moistening" means that it acts as a surrounding for the mind and mental factors through its function of lubricating them, just as water does for bath-powder.

This is stated specifically with reference to the path associated with joy (*somanassa*). However, in the case of the path associated with equanimity (*upekkhā*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*) should be understood in the place of the faculty of joy.

Furthermore, it should be understood as an accompaniment that does not excessively strengthen its associated factors. "Accompanied by the predominance of the evolving continuity" (*pavattasantatādhipateyyaparivāra*):
the evolving continuity is "evolving continuity" (*pavattasantati*), meaning the currently existing stream of existence. Predominance is the state of being dominant (*ādhipateyya*);
the predominance of the evolving continuity is "predominance of the evolving continuity. [This refers to] the presently functioning life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).

And because it serves as a condition for subsequent occurrence, it acts as the dominant factor for the continuity that proceeds by way of sequence; thus, it is the retinue of the "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" faculty (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*).
The statement "the states born at the moment of the stream-entry path," and so forth, is spoken for the purpose of praising all those factors associated with the path.
In this context, "born at the moment of the path" means they are precisely those arisen from the path, and not others. Furthermore, although [these factors] are indeed arisen from the path...
Material form does not receive the designation "wholesome" and so forth; therefore, excluding that, he says "mind-originated matter.
For all those states are "wholesome" (kusala) in the sense of flowing toward what is blameless, and so on.
When they proceed taking [Nibbāna] as their object, there are no taints (āsava) for them, thus they are "taintless" (anāsava). Cutting off the root of the round, they take Nibbāna as their object.
They are "leading out" (*niyyānika*) because, having been made [the path], they lead away from the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

They are "leading to dispersal" (*apacayagāmin*) because they proceed by taking as their object Nibbāna—which is termed "dispersal" because it is free from the accumulations known as wholesome and unwholesome—and thus they go toward dispersal;

alternatively, they are "leading to dispersal" because they go while dispersing and shattering the process of existence (*pavatta*). They are "not included in the world" (*loka-apariyāpanna*) because of their state of being beyond the world.
"Supreme" (*uttara*) means supramundane (*lokuttara*). "Having Nibbāna as their object" (*nibbānārammaṇa*) means that Nibbāna is the objective support for these [consciousnesses].

The statement beginning with "these eight faculties" is spoken for the purpose of illustrating the state of being an attendant (*parivāra*) as previously described, the state of being accompanied by that [wisdom], and the modes of occurrence mentioned at the outset.
In that context, "eight faculties" refers to [the faculties] together with the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) according to the method stated previously.
Together with eight. "Co-nascent attendants" means that among the eight, each one, together with the other seven which are co-nascent, becomes its co-nascent attendant.
Likewise, one is the attendant of another, and another is the attendant of yet another; thus they are mutual attendants.
In the same way, they are mutual support-attendants and associated-attendants. "Accompanied by" (sahagatā) means...
They have attained the state of simultaneous arising and so forth together with that faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown. "Co-nascent" means arisen together with that very same [faculty].
"Conjoined" means mixed together with that very same [faculty]. "Associated" means connected with that very same [faculty] equally through such modes as simultaneous arising and so forth.
"Those very" refers to those same eight dhammas of the faculties. "Of that" refers to the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown. "Aspects" refers to the constituent parts of its retinue.

At the moment of fruition, all phenomena that have arisen are indeterminate (*abyākata*); thus, because material form (*rūpa*) is also indeterminate, it is mentioned together with mind-originated matter (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa*).

Because the Path alone is wholesome (*kusala*), leading out (*niyyānika*), and conducive to dispersal (*apacayagāmin*), it is not described as "wholesome," "leading out," or "conducive to dispersal" at the moment of fruition.
The phrase beginning with "Thus" (*iti*) and so forth is the conclusion of the manner already stated.
In this context, "eight sets of eight" refers to eight sets of eight faculties (*indriya-aṭṭhaka*), each based on one of the eight paths and fruits.
"There are sixty-four" means there are sixty-four modes. The passage beginning with "the taints" (*āsava*) has already been explained in meaning below.

Here, rather than mentioning only the taints to be abandoned by the path of Arhatship, the mention of those to be abandoned by the remaining three paths is included because they share the common designation of "the destruction of the taints" (*āsavakkhaya*).

It should be understood that it is so stated. For it is the knowledge of the path to Arahantship itself that is called "knowledge of destruction" because it exhausts the taints without leaving any remainder.
And for this very reason, only an Arahant is called one whose taints are destroyed.
The commentary on the description of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints is finished.
56–63. Commentary on the Exposition of the Two Tetrads of Knowledge of the Truths (Saccañāṇacatukkadvayaniddesa).
108–9. In the exposition of the two tetrads of knowledge of the truths, the phrases "the meaning of oppression in regard to suffering," and so forth, have meanings already explained.

The passage beginning "The knowledge of one possessing the path is knowledge regarding suffering" is stated according to a single simultaneous realization (*ekābhisamaya*), as in the immediately preceding tetrad. For [knowledge] is of two kinds: ...

Knowledge of the truths (sacca-ñāṇa) is both mundane (lokiya) and supramundane (lokuttara). The mundane is twofold: knowledge of comprehension (anubodha-ñāṇa) and knowledge of review (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa).
Knowledge of comprehension occurs in the cessation and the path for a beginner by way of hearsay and so forth, and it occurs in suffering and its origin by way of taking them as objects.
Knowledge of review occurs in all four truths by way of taking them as objects once the truths have been penetrated.
Supramundane penetrative knowledge, taking cessation as its object, penetrates all four truths by way of its function.

As it has been said: "Bhikkhus, he who sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering, also sees the cessation of suffering, and also sees the practice leading to the cessation of suffering"—all this should be stated here as well. By this [statement], it is shown that...
This very point was stated in the *Vāra*. However, it was stated there in order to show that even supramundane knowledge receives such names as "knowledge of suffering" and so forth;
here, however, only mundane knowledge is intended. For this very reason, he said therein:
"What is knowledge of suffering? and so on.
In that context, "with reference to suffering" means having taken the truth of suffering as an object, or having made it the focal point—this is the meaning.
Regarding "wisdom" (*paññā*) and so forth: wisdom is so called in the sense of making known (*paññāpana*), which is defined as the act of making each respective object clear;

or alternatively, wisdom is so called because one knows phenomena (*dhammā*) through various modes such as impermanence and so on. This is its term for essential nature (*sabhāvapada*). The mode of understanding is "understanding" (*pajānanā*). [The terms] "impermanence" and so on...
"Vicaya" means investigating (*vicinati*). "Pavicaya" is a word expanded by means of a prefix; its meaning is "investigating in a particular manner.

Because it investigates the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths, it is called "dhammavicaya" (investigation of phenomena). It is the correct discernment of impermanence and so forth by way of their characteristics.
That very same discernment is described as "upalakkhaṇā" (noting) and "paccupalakkhaṇā" (repeated noting) due to the variety of prefixes. It is a profound discernment of characteristics.
The meaning is: it is a discernment (upalakkhaṇā) dependent upon those phenomena such as impermanence (anicca), etc.

Wisdom (paṇḍicca) is the state of being wise (paṇḍita). Skill (kosalla) is the state of being skilled (kusala). Ingenuity (nepuñña) is the state of being ingenious (nipuṇa). It is "discernment" (vebhabyā) by way of the analysis of impermanence and so forth.

It is "thought" (cintā) by way of reflecting upon impermanence and so forth; furthermore, it is called "thought" because that in which it arises causes one to think about impermanence and so forth. [Regarding] impermanence and so forth...
"It investigates" (*upaparikkhati*) is thus "investigation" (*upaparikkhā*). "Vast" (*bhūrī*) refers to the earth.
This [wisdom] is also called "vast" because it is subtle and extensive, like the earth. Alternatively, it is called "vast" because wisdom itself delights in vast objects.
It is "intelligence" (*medhā*) because it crushes and destroys defilements like a thunderbolt strikes a mountain; or else, it is intelligence in the sense of swift grasping and retention.
That in which [wisdom] arises leads one toward the practice for one's own benefit, toward the associated states, and toward the penetration of the characteristics of things as they truly are;
thus it is "the guide" (*pariṇāyikā*). It sees phenomena in various ways by way of impermanence and so forth; thus it is "insight" (*vipassanā*).

One who knows impermanence and so forth in their proper modes is "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāna*); the state of being such is "clear comprehension" (*sampajañña*). [This is like the case of] a horse that has gone astray onto a wrong path...

It is called a "goad" (*patoda*) because it prods the counterfeit consciousness—which is running off-course—into the right path for the purpose of placing it upon the path, just like a goad used to direct a horse.
It is called a "faculty" (*indriya*) because it exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha*) in its characteristic of seeing; thus, the faculty known as wisdom is the "wisdom-faculty" (*paññindriya*).
What is meant by this? It is not that the wisdom is the faculty *of* a person, as in the case of the "male-faculty" (*purisindriya*) and so forth; rather, it is the wisdom itself that is the faculty.
The faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*). However, it is said that wisdom itself is the faculty, thus "the faculty of wisdom.
It is the power of wisdom because it does not waver due to ignorance. Wisdom itself is the sword of wisdom (*paññāsattha*) in the sense of cutting through the defilements.

Wisdom itself is the palace of wisdom (*paññāpāsāda*) in the sense of being loftily elevated. Wisdom itself is the light of wisdom (*paññāāloka*) in the sense of illuminating. In the sense of radiating, [wisdom itself is the radiance].
Wisdom itself is the radiance; thus, "wisdom-radiance" (*paññā-obhāsa*). In the sense of illuminating, wisdom itself is the light; thus, "wisdom-light" (*paññā-pajjota*).
For when one possessed of wisdom sits cross-legged, the ten-thousandfold world-system becomes a single expanse of light, a single radiance, and a single illumination.
Therefore, this was said. Now, although this meaning is established even by a single word among these three terms, those which...
The Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, there are these four lights. Which four? The light of the moon, the light of the sun, the light of fire, and the light of wisdom.
These, bhikkhus, are the four lights. Of these four lights, bhikkhus, the foremost is this:
the light of wisdom. Likewise: “Bhikkhus, there are these four radiances... Bhikkhus, there are these four... [and so on].
Suttas have been taught according to the inclinations of beings. In this case as well, the Elder has given his teaching in accordance with that very principle.
For when the meaning is analyzed through many modes, it becomes well-analyzed; otherwise, one person understands it in one way and another in another way.
Furthermore, [the Dhamma] is so called in the sense of providing delight, in the sense of bestowing delight, and in the sense of generating delight.
In the sense of being highly esteemed, in the sense of its manifestation being rare, in the sense of being incomparable, and in the sense of being enjoyed by extraordinary beings, wisdom is a jewel;
thus it is the "jewel of wisdom" (*paññāratana*).

Non-delusion (*amoha*) is so called because beings are not deluded by it, or because it itself is not deluded regarding its object. The term "discernment of phenomena" (*dhammavicaya*) has already been explained.
But why is this stated again? It is for the purpose of showing that non-delusion (*amoha*) is the direct opposite of delusion (*moha*).
By this, he shows: "This non-delusion is not merely a state distinct from delusion;

rather, what is intended here is the specific state called non-delusion, which consists of the investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicaya*) and acts as the antidote to delusion. Right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) is the wholesome view that leads to liberation and accords with reality. In this regard:
"What is knowledge of the origin of suffering? Therein, what is knowledge of the cessation of suffering?
And therein, what is knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of suffering?"—these interrogative statements have been stated by way of summary.
The commentary on the exposition of the two tetrads of knowledge of the truths is finished.
64–67. Explanation of the Exposition of Pure Analytical Knowledge (Suddhika-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa-niddesa). 110.

In the exposition of pure analytical knowledge, because there is no differentiation among these knowledges, it is stated as "knowledge regarding meanings is the analytical knowledge of meaning" (*atthe ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā*) and so forth, without showing a differentiation as was done previously. This is even though there is a differentiation in wisdom (*paññā*).
Because there is a diversity [of aspects] based solely on the Dhamma of the Four Truths realized by oneself, it is said:

"Wisdom regarding the diversity of meanings is the knowledge of the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā)," and so forth. In that context, "diversity" (nānatta) refers to the manifold nature of the meaning and the other [factors].

"Determination" (vavatthāna) refers to the definitive discernment of the meaning and the others. "Observation" (sallakkhaṇa) refers to the correct seeing of the meaning and the others. "Discernment" (upalakkhaṇa) refers to the meaning and the others...
*Bhusaṃdassane*: in the thorough showing. *Pabhedeti*: in the various classifications of meaning and so forth. *Pabhāvaneti*:
in the production by means of making meaning and so forth manifest. *Jotaneti*: in the illuminating of meaning and so forth. *Virocaneti*: in the manifold illuminating of meaning and so forth.
*Pakāsaneti*: in the brightening of meaning and so forth. The phrase "in diversity" (*nānatte*) is stated as a general term, taking it as the root word. "In determination" (*vavatthāne*).

The application here should be made as follows: the terms "marking" (*sallakkhaṇe*) and "re-marking" (*upalakkhaṇe*) are stated with reference to the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*); "differentiation" (*pabhede*) and "manifestation" (*pabhāvane*) with reference to the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*);
and "illumination" (*jotane*), "radiance" (*virocane*), and "clarification" (*pakāsane*) with reference to the non-returner (*anāgāmī*) and the arahant (*arahat*).
Thus ends the commentary on the description of the knowledge of the pure analytical knowledges (*suddhika-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa-niddesa*).
Thus ends the first part of the *Saddhammappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Path of Discrimination (*Paṭisambhidāmagga-aṭṭhakathā*) in the Minor Collection (*Khuddakanikāya*),
Second Part.
68. Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of the Relative Superiority and Inferiority of Faculties (Indriyaparopariyattañāṇaniddesa). 111.
Regarding the phrase "of the Tathāgata" in the description of the knowledge of the relative superiority and inferiority of faculties:

although this expression does not appear explicitly in the summary list (*uddesa*), because it has been stated that "there are six knowledges not shared with disciples," it is indeed implied by the phrase "of the Tathāgata. Therefore...
The detailed exposition (*niddesa*) has been undertaken for that word of the Tathāgata which was established by way of its summary (*uddesa*). "He sees beings" means:
they are called "beings" (*sattā*) because they are attached and bound due to their desire and lust for form and so forth;

he sees those beings with the eye of the knowledge of the degrees of others' faculties (*indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa*), that is, he looks upon them. "With little dust in their eyes" means: those who have little dust, such as passion (*rāga*), in the eye consisting of wisdom (*paññāmaya*).

"Those with little dust in their eyes" (*apparajakkha*) means those who have little dust, such as passion (*rāga*), and so forth; thus they are *apparajakkha*. Regarding "those with much dust in their eyes" (*mahārajakkha*):

in the eye consisting of wisdom (*paññāmaya-akkhi*), those who have great dust, such as passion, and so forth, are *mahārajakkha*; or alternatively, those who have great dust, such as passion, and so forth, are *mahārajakkha*.

Regarding "those with sharp faculties" (*tikkhindriya*) and "those with dull faculties" (*mudindriya*): the faculties (*indriya*) are faith (*saddhā*) and the others, which are sharp [in the former case].

"Those with keen faculties" (*tikkhindriya*): those whose faculties, such as faith and the rest, are sharp are "those with keen faculties. "Those with dull faculties" (*mudindriya*): those whose faculties, such as faith and the rest, are weak are "those with dull faculties.

"Those of good disposition" (*svākāra*) and "those of bad disposition" (*dvākāra*): those whose dispositions (*ākāra*), parts, or components—namely faith and the rest—are beautiful are "those of good disposition";

those whose dispositions, parts, or components—namely faith and the rest—are contemptible or censurable are "those of bad disposition. "Those easy to instruct" (*suviññāpya*) and "those difficult to instruct" (*duviññāpya*): those who perceive the reason when it is explained...
Those who can be made to understand easily are "easy to instruct" (*suvijñāpayā*); those who are the opposite of that are "difficult to instruct" (*durvijñāpayā*).
Regarding the phrase "some who see the fear in the other world and in faults": some indeed perceive both the other world and faults such as lust (*rāga*) and so forth as fearsome;
however, since only the other world is mentioned in the commentary (*niddesa*) on this passage, it refers to the world of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth, as well as faults such as lust.
And those who are in the habit of seeing intense fear regarding the other world are "those who see the fear of wrongdoing in the other world.
This is how the meaning should be understood. "Some do not see the fear of wrongdoing in the other world" refers to those who are the opposite of that.

And "world" (*loka*) is so called in the sense of crumbling and disintegrating. And "wrongdoing" (*vajja*) is so called in the sense of being something to be avoided. Up to this point, the explanation of the summary has been completed.
Again, providing a further explanation of the exposition, he says: "Those with little dust in their eyes, those with much dust in their eyes," and so forth.
In this context, one who possesses faith—defined as conviction (*okappanā*)—regarding the Three Jewels is called "one endowed with faith" (*saddho*).

Such a person, being perfected in faith, has "little dust in their eyes" (*apparajakkho*) because of the smallness of the dust of lack of faith (*assaddhiya-raja*) and the remaining unwholesome dust rooted in that lack of faith. For him, there is none of this...
He has faith, thus he is "one possessed of faith" (*saddha*). Because the passion (*raja*) of the kind described is great in him, he is "one with great passion" (*mahārajakkha*).

He has aroused energy, thus he is "one who has aroused energy" (*āraddhavīriya*). Because the passion of indolence and the other unwholesome passions rooted in indolence are slight in him, he is "one with little passion" (*apparajakkha*).
Because he sinks in a base manner due to his inferior energy, he is "lazy" (*kusīda*); one who is lazy is simply *kusīta*.

Because the defilement (*raja*) of the aforementioned type is great, he is one "with great defilement" (*mahārajakkha*). One whose mindfulness (*sati*) stands having approached the object is "one with established mindfulness" (*upaṭṭhitassati*).
Because the defilement of forgetfulness (*muṭṭhassacca*) and the other unwholesome defilements rooted in forgetfulness are slight, he is one "with little defilement" (*apparajakkha*).
One whose mindfulness is lost or destroyed is "one with lost mindfulness" (*muṭṭhassati*). Of the aforementioned type...
Because his passion (rajas) is great, he is one of "great passion" (mahārajakkha).

One who is placed evenly or correctly upon the object by means of absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) or access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) is "composed" (samāhita); or, one whose mind is composed is "composed.

Because his restlessness-passion (uddhacca-rajas) and the other unwholesome passions rooted in restlessness are slight, he is one of "slight passion" (apparajakkha). One who is not composed is "uncomposed" (asamāhita).

Because the defilement (*raja*) of the aforementioned type is great, he is one "with great defilement" (*mahārajakkha*). Because he possesses the wisdom (*paññā*) that leads to arising and passing away, he is "wise" (*paññavā*).
Because his delusion-defilement (*moharaja*) and the other unwholesome defilements rooted in delusion are slight, he is "one with little defilement" (*apparajakkha*).
Because his wisdom is corrupted by being muddled with delusion, he is "dull-witted" (*duppañña*). Because the defilement of the aforementioned type is great...

One of great defilement. A person who is faithful with keen faculties means: one is "faithful" because of the frequent arising of powerful faith, and by that very faculty of faith, one has "keen faculties. An unfaithful person with dull faculties means:
one is "unfaithful" because of the frequent arising of lack of faith, and possesses a "dull faculty of faith" that arises only occasionally and is weak.

"One of dull faculties. This same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. "A person endowed with faith is one of beautiful appearance" means that by virtue of that very faith, they possess a beautiful appearance.
"A person devoid of faith is one of ugly appearance" means that by virtue of that very lack of faith, they possess an ugly appearance.

This same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. "Easy to instruct" means capable of being instructed with ease. "Difficult to instruct" means capable of being instructed only with difficulty. "One who sees the fear in the other world and in blame" means...
In this context, since faith and the other qualities become thoroughly purified only for one who is endowed with wisdom,

therefore one who is endowed with thoroughly purified faith and the rest becomes a seer of the peril in the next world and in blame through the wisdom associated with them— or rather, through the wisdom conditioned by that [faith] which is itself endowed with thoroughly purified faith and the rest.
For it is precisely for this reason that the four qualities beginning with faith are also described as "seeing the peril in the next world and in blame."
112. Now, in order to show the world (*loka*) and the fault (*vajja*) mentioned here in the phrase "one who sees the fear of blame in the next world," he says "the world," and so forth.
Here, the aggregates (*khandha*) themselves are the "world of aggregates" (*khandhaloka*) in the sense of breaking up and falling apart. The same method applies to the other two as well.

The "world of misfortune-existence" (*vipattibhavaloka*) is the world of the states of misery (*apāya*). For that is a "misfortune" (*vipatti*) because it is an undesirable fruit; it is called "existence" (*bhava*) because it comes to be.

"Becoming" (*bhava*) is itself misfortune; thus, "becoming as misfortune" (*vipattibhava*). "The world as becoming-misfortune" (*vipattibhavaloka*) refers to karma leading to the states of misery (*apāya*).
For that [karma] is the "source of arising" (*sambhava*) because the fruit arises from it. The source of misfortune is "misfortune-source" (*vipattisambhava*);
the world as the source of misfortune is "the world as misfortune-source" (*vipattisambhavaloka*). "The world as becoming-attainment" (*sampattibhavaloka*)...
The world of happy destinies (*sugatiloka*). For that is a "success" (*sampatti*) because it is a desirable fruit; it is "existence" (*bhava*) because it comes to be.
Success itself is existence, thus "existence as success" (*sampattibhava*); existence as success itself is the world, thus "the world of existence as success" (*sampattibhavaloka*).

The "world of the origin of success" (*sampattisambhavaloka*) refers to the karma leading to a happy destiny. For that is the "origin" (*sambhava*) because the fruit originates from it; it is the origin of success.

The arising of success (*sampattisambhava*); the world that is the arising of success is the "world of the arising of success" (*sampattisambhavaloka*). Phrases such as "one world" and so forth have meanings already explained below.
The neuter form "vajja" is used because it is not specified as "this" (*asu*) or "that. "Defilements" (*kilesa*) refers to lust and the rest. "Misconducts" (*duccarita*)...
"Killing living beings," and so forth. "Volitional formations" (*abhisaṅkhāra*) refers to meritorious volitional formations (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) and the rest.

"Kamma leading to existence" (*bhavagāmikamma*): they are called "leading to existence" because they go toward existence by way of giving their own result; thus, even among volitional formations, only those kammic acts that produce a result are mentioned.
"Thus" (*iti*) is an indicator of the manner already described. And in this world and that world: it means in the world of the aforementioned types.

"And in what is blameworthy. "Intense perception of fear" means a powerful perception of fear. "Intense" is stated as the meaning of the word *parasadda*; "perception of fear" is the meaning of the word *bhayasaññā*.
For both types of worldly offenses (*lokavajja*) are "fear" because they are bases for fear and are themselves fearful;
the perception that "this is fear" is the "perception of fear. "Is present" means it stands having approached and being dependent upon this or that [object].

It occurs. "Just as toward a murderer with sword raised" means that just as a sharp perception of fear arises toward an enemy who has drawn his blade to strike, even so a sharp perception of fear arises toward the world and toward faults.
"By these fifty modes" refers to each of the ten pentads, beginning with the "five with little dust in their eyes."
By way of five sets of five aspects, [he knows] through fifty modes. "These five faculties" refers to the five faculties beginning with the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*).
"He knows" means the Tathāgata understands through wisdom (*paññā*). "He sees" means he makes it as if seen by the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
"He fully knows" means he knows in every aspect through noble methods. "He penetrates" means he does so without leaving any part remaining.
"He shatters it with wisdom by way of seeing it without remainder.
The commentary on the description of the knowledge of the degrees of others' faculties is finished.
69. Commentary on the description of the knowledge of underlying tendencies (*āsaya-anusaya-ñāṇa*).
113. In the exposition of the knowledge of dispositions (*āsaya*) and underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), the description beginning with "herein, the Tathāgata" is set forth in five ways.
Among these, *āsaya* and *anusaya* have already been explained. *Carita* refers to wholesome or unwholesome karma performed in the past.

*Adhimutti* refers to the present mental inclination toward the wholesome or the unwholesome. *Bhabbābhabbe* means those who are capable and those who are incapable. Regarding the Noble Path (*ariyāya*)...
They are "capable" (*bhabba*) because they are born and will come into being through birth. The present tense is used here to denote that which is proximate to the present.

Alternatively, they are "capable" because they will exist or will be born; the meaning is that they have become fit vessels. Those who are suitable for the penetration of the Noble Path and are endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*) are "capable.
Their opposites, as previously stated, are "incapable" (*abhabba*).
“What is the disposition of beings? and so forth is a further explanation of the exposition. Therein, “eternal” means permanent. “The world” means the self (*attā*).
Here they imagine that only the body perishes, but the self remains the very same both here and in the hereafter.
For they imagine it to be the “world” because it is that which looks for itself (*sayaṃ eva āloketi*). “Non-eternal” means impermanent. [They hold that] the self [perishes] together with the body.

They conceive: "It perishes along with [the body]. Regarding "it is finite": having produced jhāna upon a limited kasiṇa, they conceive that the self is the consciousness which has that limited kasiṇa as its object, and thus it is finite.

Regarding "it is infinite": not being finite, having produced jhāna upon an immeasurable kasiṇa, they conceive that the self is the consciousness which has that immeasurable kasiṇa as its object, and thus it is infinite. "That is the soul, that is the body."
"The soul and the body are one and the same. Here, "soul" (*jīva*) refers to the self (*attā*); the neuter gender is used by way of a grammatical shift in gender.

"Body" (*sarīra*) refers to the pentad of aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*) in the sense of a mass. "The soul is one thing and the body another" means the soul is one thing and the pentad of aggregates is another.
"A Tathāgata exists after death" means that the aggregates perish right here, [and yet] the sentient being [continues] beyond death.
"He exists, he is found, he does not perish. And here they say that "Tathāgata" is a designation for a being (*sattādhivacana*).
However, some say, "The Tathāgata is an Arahant. These [latter] adopt this view because they see a fault in the position that "he does not exist. [They argue:
"If the Tathāgata does not exist after death, then the aggregates (*khandhā*) would perish right here, and the Tathāgata would [cease] with death."
"But it does not exist; it is cut off, it perishes. Having seen the fault in the position that "it exists," they grasp it thus.
"It both exists and does not exist": having seen the fault in grasping each of these individual positions, they grasp both positions.
"Neither exists nor does not exist": having seen that by grasping both positions one incurs the faults of both, [they think] "it exists..."
They take up the side of the Eel-Wriggler (*amarāvikkhepa*), saying: "It is not, nor is it both 'it is' and 'it is not'.
Herein, this is the method of the Commentary: By the ten modes beginning with "The world is eternal," only the various types of views are stated.
Therein, regarding the view "the world is eternal," having taken the pentad of aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*) as "the world," [one holds]: "This world is permanent, stable..."
The view that arises from the mode of grasping "it is eternal" when one takes [the world] as "lasting for all time.
The view that arises from the mode of grasping annihilationism when one takes that very same world as "it is cut off, it perishes," thinking "it is non-eternal.
The view that it is "finite" refers to one who has attained a limited kasiṇa and has entered into jhāna upon a kasiṇa the size of a thumb-joint or a saucer; [this occurs] within that attainment.

For one who apprehends the material and immaterial phenomena occurring [within] as "the world" and as "finite" by way of the boundary of the kasiṇa, there arises the view characterized by the mode of apprehension:
"The world is finite. That [view] is both an eternalist view and an annihilationist view.
However, for one who has attained mastery over a vast kasiṇa and has entered into jhāna upon that kasiṇa, regarding the material and immaterial phenomena occurring within that attainment—
The view that arises from the mode of grasping "the world is infinite" by one who takes it as "not finite" with reference to the limits of the kasiṇas is the view that "the world is infinite.
That [view] is both an eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi) and an annihilationist view (ucchedadiṭṭhi).

Because of the grasping of the body—which is subject to disintegration—as itself the "life-principle" (jīva) in the sense of "that life is that body," when the body is annihilated, the life-principle is also [annihilated].

The view that occurs in the mode of grasping at annihilation is [the thought]: "It is annihilated. In the second phrase, because a life-principle distinct from the body is grasped, the view that occurs in the mode of grasping at eternalism is [the thought]: "Even when the body is annihilated, the life-principle is not annihilated.
Regarding the statements "The Tathāgata exists" and so forth, for one who grasps: "A being named 'Tathāgata' exists; he exists after death," [this constitutes eternalism].
The first is the eternalist view (*sassatadṛṣṭi*). For one who grasps [the self] as "does not exist," the second is the annihilationist view (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

For one who grasps it as "both exists and does not exist," the third is the partial-eternalist view (*ekaccasassatadṛṣṭi*). For one who grasps it as "neither exists nor does not exist," the fourth is the eel-wriggling view (*amarāvikkhepadṛṣṭi*).

The word "thus" (*iti*) indicates the basis for these aforementioned types of views. Beings are either dependent upon the view of existence (*bhavadṛṣṭi*) or dependent upon the view of non-existence (*vibhavadṛṣṭi*).
"Becoming" (*bhava*) is called eternalism; the view arising by way of eternalism is the "view of becoming.
What is meant is: "becoming" is the view. "Non-becoming" (*vibhava*) is called annihilationism; the view arising by way of annihilationism is the "view of non-becoming.
What is meant is: "non-becoming" is the view. Thus, the tenfold view described above consists of the view of becoming and the view of non-becoming.
And thus it is twofold. Beings are dependent upon, reliant on, and attached to each of those two [extremes].
