Furthermore, in the phrase "without approaching either of these two extremes," the word *vā* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), as in expressions such as "from fire or from water or from the breaking of friendships.
And these two aforementioned positions, by way of eternalism and annihilationism—do not...
The meaning is: having approached, not clinging, and having abandoned. “Or conformity-acceptance” (*anulomikā khanti*) is merely a variant reading.

Regarding “in these conditionally arisen states of specific conditionality” (*idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppannesu*): the conditions for these [factors] such as aging-and-death are “specific conditions” (*idappaccayā*); the state of being those specific conditions is “specific conditionality” (*idappaccayatā*), or the collection of specific conditions is “specific conditionality.
The grammatical derivation (*lakkhaṇa*) here should be sought from the treatises on grammar (*saddasattha*). Those various conditions...

"Dependently arisen" (*paṭiccasamuppannā*) means those things that have arisen together and correctly in dependence. "In this conditionality" (*idappaccayatāya*) refers to that state of being a specific condition and to those phenomena that have arisen dependently.

"Conformable" (*anulomikā*) means conformable because they accord with supramundane phenomena (*lokuttaradhamma*). "Acceptance" (*khanti*) is knowledge (*ñāṇa*); for knowledge is called acceptance because it accepts [the truth].
"Is acquired" (*paṭiladdhā hoti*) means it has been attained by sentient beings. Regarding "this conditionality" (*idappaccayatāya*)...

Through patience toward things arisen by way of conditions, there is no adherence to annihilationism, because one sees that the non-cessation of the fruit follows from seeing the non-cessation of the conditions,
since the occurrence of conditionally arisen phenomena depends upon the completeness of their conditions. Through patience toward dependently arisen phenomena, there is no adherence to eternalism,
because one sees the arising of ever-new conditionally arisen phenomena whenever the completeness of conditions is present.

Thus, by not approaching either of these two extremes and by seeing dependent origination and dependently originated phenomena, the right view regarding the process [of existence] as being neither annihilation nor eternalism should be understood as "conformable acceptance" (*anulomikā khanti*).
For in this way, right view is stated as the antidote to both those views. Or, it is "knowledge according to reality" (*yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇaṃ*). According to reality...

It should be understood according to its true nature. In this context, even the knowledge occurring therein is called "knowledge of things as they really are" (yathābhūtañāṇa) by way of a metaphorical designation for its object.

However, what is intended here is the insight-knowledge (vipassanāñāṇa) culminating in equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā). Below, however, "the vision of knowledge of things as they really are" was stated to refer to the knowledge of the appearance as terror (bhayatūpaṭṭhānañāṇa).
Or, the connection is that knowledge of things as they really are is obtained by sentient beings.

Now, having shown the continuum of beings (sattasantāna) as permeated by wrong view through such [views] as "the world is eternal," and as permeated by right view through such [views] as "or rather these," he shows the continuum of beings as permeated by the remaining unwholesome states and the remaining wholesome states through such [phrases] as "only one who indulges in sensual pleasures.
Therein, the construction is: "The Tathāgata knows the person who is indeed indulging in sensual pleasures."

[These qualities] are to be practiced. "Serving" means serving by way of frequent practice. One for whom sensual desire (*kāma*) has become heavy due to having been cultivated previously is "one who is heavy with sensual desire" (*kāmagaruka*).
Likewise, one in whose underlying tendency (*āsaya*) or mental continuum (*santāna*) there is sensual desire is "one who has a tendency toward sensual desire" (*kāmāsayo*).

By way of that very continuum, one who is intent upon and attached to sensual pleasures is "one who is intent on sensual pleasure" (*kāmādhimutto*). The same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. Renunciation (*nekkhamma*) and the others have already had their meanings explained.

It should be understood that by the three beginning with sensual desire (*kāma*), the remaining unwholesome states are included; and by the three beginning with renunciation (*nekkhamma*), the remaining wholesome states are likewise included.
When it is said in three ways, "This is the underlying tendency (*āsaya*) of beings," it is the continuity (*santāna*) itself that is being shown.
Herein, this is the method of the Commentary: "Thus, those dependent on the view of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*)"—in this way, [it refers to] the eternalist view (*sassata-diṭṭhi*).

...or dependent upon [these two]. For here, the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*) is called the "view of existence" (*bhavadiṭṭhi*), and the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*) is called the "view of non-existence" (*vibhavadiṭṭhi*).

Since all views are subsumed under the views of eternalism and annihilationism, all these followers of speculative views (*diṭṭhigatika*) are dependent upon these very two views. And this has also been said: "Kaccāna, this person is dependent upon a duality..."
“The world for the most part [clings] to both existence and non-existence. Here, “existence” refers to eternalism (*sassata*), and “non-existence” refers to annihilationism (*uccheda*).
This, first of all, is the disposition (*āsaya*) of ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) who rely upon the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

Now, in order to show the disposition of pure beings who rely upon the turning away from the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*), it was said: “But by not approaching either of these two extremes,” and so forth. In that regard:
“Or these,” means these very ones. “Both extremes” refers to the two extremes known as eternalism and annihilationism.

“Without approaching” means without clinging. “Regarding phenomena that have arisen dependently through specific conditionality” means regarding both specific conditionality itself and the phenomena arisen dependently.
“Conformable acceptance” is insight-knowledge. “Knowledge in accordance with reality” is...

Knowledge of the path. This is what is meant: that insight which has been attained regarding both dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) and dependently arisen phenomena (*paṭiccasamuppannadhamma*), without falling into either of these two extremes of eternalism or annihilationism, as well as the further knowledge of the path beyond that—this is the disposition of beings.
This [is the disposition] of all those who are oriented toward the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) as well as those who are oriented toward its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*).
“This is the abode of beings; this is their dwelling place”—this is the common commentary of the teachers.
But the caviller says: “The so-called ‘path’ proceeds by destroying dwellings; yet you say that the path is a dwelling. He should be asked:
“Are you a reciter of the *Ariyavāsa* [Sutta], or not? If he says, “I am not,” [then...]
He should be told: "Because you are not a reciter, you do not know it. If he says, "I am a reciter," he should be told:
"Bring forth the sutta. If he brings it forth, that is well. If he does not bring it forth, he himself should bring it forth:
"Monks, there are these ten abodes of the noble ones, which the noble ones have dwelt in, do dwell in, or will dwell in. For this—
The Sutta illustrates the state of being a dwelling place for the Path; therefore, it is indeed well-spoken.
Furthermore, the Blessed One, knowing the dispositions of beings, knows even at the moment when these views and these knowledges of insight and the Path do not arise.
For this very reason, it was said: "He knows one who is actually indulging in sensual pleasures," and so forth.
In the exposition of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), in what sense are they called "underlying tendencies"? In the sense of lying latent (*anusayana*).
What is this so-called sense of lying latent? It is the sense of being unabandoned. For it is in the sense of being unabandoned that these lie latent within this or that individual continuum;
therefore, they are called "underlying tendencies. "They lie latent" means that they arise upon obtaining a corresponding cause. Furthermore—
It might be argued: "The meaning of 'latent tendency' (anusaya) is a state of being unabandoned; it is not logical to say that this [state] arises.
Therefore, latent tendencies do not arise. To this, the reply is as follows: It is not merely a state of being unabandoned that is called a latent tendency.

Rather, by way of its being unabandoned, the term refers to a defilement that has become firmly established. This is associated with consciousness, possesses an object, is accompanied by conditions in the sense of having a cause, and is exclusively unwholesome.
It exists in the past, the future, and the present; therefore, it is appropriate to say that it "arises. Herein, this is the proof:

in the very discussion on the realization (*abhisamaya*) here, having posed the question, "Does one abandon defilements in the present?", it is stated that "one abandons a latent tendency (*anusaya*) when it has become firmly established," because of the existence of the latent tendencies' state of being present.

In the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, within the word-commentary on delusion (*moha*), it is stated that delusion arises together with an unwholesome consciousness: “The underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusayo*), the obsession of ignorance (*avijjāpariyuṭṭhāna*), the yoke of ignorance (*avijjālaṅgī*), delusion, the root of the unwholesome—this, at that time, is delusion.

In the *Kathāvatthu*, it is said: “The underlying tendencies are indeterminate (*abyākata*); the underlying tendencies are rootless (*ahetuka*); the underlying tendencies are dissociated from consciousness (*cittavippayutta*).”
All [other] doctrines have been refuted. In the *Anusaya-yamaka*, within one of the seven great sections concerning the section on arising, it is stated:
“In whom the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) arises, in him the underlying tendency of aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) arises,” and so forth.
Therefore, as for what was said—that “they underlie (*anusenti*) means they arise upon obtaining a corresponding cause”—that is established by this scriptural authority (*tantippamāṇa*).
It should be understood as "appropriate. Furthermore, that which was stated—"associated with consciousness, having an object," and so forth—is also well-said.
For it must be concluded here that this so-called "latent tendency" (*anusaya*) is a fully established unwholesome dhamma associated with consciousness.
In such terms as "the latent tendency of sensual lust" (*kāmarāgānusaya*), sensual lust itself, insofar as it has not been abandoned, is the "latent tendency of sensual lust."

The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Herein, the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) is greed arising—either by way of co-nascence or by way of object—in consciousnesses accompanied by greed, and in the case of agreeable objects, it is greed arising solely by way of object toward the remaining sense-sphere phenomena.
And the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) is [hatred] arising—either by way of co-nascence or by way of object—in consciousnesses accompanied by displeasure.
In regard to unpleasant things and the remaining phenomena of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), hatred arises solely by way of the object (*ārammaṇa-vasena*).
The underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) arises by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta-vasena*) and by way of the object in consciousnesses associated with greed but dissociated from views;

and in regard to the remaining phenomena of the sense sphere—excluding those accompanied by painful feeling—as well as in phenomena of the fine-material and immaterial spheres, it arises solely by way of the object.

Pride (*māna*). The underlying tendency of views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) [arises] in the four types of consciousness associated with wrong views. The underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) [arises] in consciousness accompanied by doubt.

The underlying tendency of ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) [arises] in the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and by way of object (*ārammaṇa*). These three—view, doubt, and delusion—also arise in the remaining states of the three planes solely by way of object.
The underlying tendency of lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*) [arises] in the four types of consciousness dissociated from wrong views.

Even when arising, greed is not mentioned here by way of its co-nascence (*sahajāta*); rather, it is mentioned as arising with respect to objects (*ārammaṇa*) among the phenomena of the fine-material and immaterial spheres.
114. Now, in order to show the locus of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) for those aforementioned tendencies, he says: "That which one seeks," and so forth.
In this context, "that which is a lovely form in the world" refers to that which is of a lovely nature and a lovely essence in this world.
"A pleasant form" refers to that which is of a pleasant nature, the basis for gratification, and a desirable object.

"The underlying tendency of sensual lust underlies beings here" means that in regard to this desirable object, the underlying tendency of sensual lust underlies beings by way of its not having been abandoned. Thus: "a lovely form, a pleasant form."

And here, only the phenomena belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) are intended. Just as for one submerged in water there is only water below, above, and all around, even so, the arising of lust toward a desirable object is habitual and deeply ingrained in beings;
likewise is the arising of aversion toward an undesirable object. Thus, "in these two phenomena" means in these two types of phenomena consisting of desirable and undesirable objects.

"Overcome by ignorance" means that, being associated with sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and aversion (*paṭigha*), they are overcome by and followed by ignorance (*avijjā*) through the act of making it their object.

There is also a reading where a break is made [after "overcome"]. "Associated with that" means standing together with that ignorance by virtue of being co-existent (*sahaja*) and occupying the same position.
"Conceit, views, and doubt" refers to the ninefold conceit, the sixty-two kinds of views, and the eight-based doubt.

The construction is as follows: doubt (*vicikicchā*), the conceit associated with it (*tadekaṭṭho māno*), the view associated with it (*tadekaṭṭhā diṭṭhi*), and the doubt associated with it (*tadekaṭṭhā vicikicchā*).

They are "to be seen" (*daṭṭhabbā*); that is, they are to be observed and understood. Although there are three [categories], the plural number is used because they are treated as one. Furthermore, it should be understood that the underlying tendency to craving for existence (*bhavarāgānusayo*) is here included within the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusayo*).
In the exposition of formations (*caritaniddesa*), thirteen volitions are the formation of merit; twelve are the formation of demerit; and four are the formation of the imperturbable.
Among these, that which belongs to the sense sphere is of limited range (*parittabhūmaka*); the other is of great range (*mahābhūmaka*).
Alternatively, among these three, whichever has a slight ripening is to be understood as of limited range, and whichever has a great ripening is of great range.

115. In the explanation of "resoluteness" (*adhimutti*): "exist" (*santi*) means they are found. "Those of inferior resoluteness" (*hīnādhimuttikā*) means those whose underlying disposition (*ajjhāsaya*) is base.

"Those of sublime resoluteness" (*paṇītādhimuttikā*) means those whose underlying disposition is excellent. "They serve" (*seventi*) means they rely upon, they cling to. "They associate with" (*bhajanti*) means they approach.
"They attend upon" (*payirupāsanti*) means they approach again and again. For if the teachers and preceptors are not virtuous, then the resident pupils and co-residents...
Those who possess virtue do not even approach their own teachers and preceptors; they approach only those monks who are similar to themselves and worthy.
Even if their teachers and preceptors are worthy while others are unworthy, they still do not approach their teachers and preceptors;
they approach only those of inferior inclination who are similar to themselves. Such is this manner of approaching.
However, in order to show that this is not only the case now, but also in the past and the future, he said:

"In the past time as well," and so forth. Therein, "in the past time" (*atītampi addhānaṃ*) means in the past period; the accusative case is used in the sense of absolute connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).
The rest is of plain meaning. This, moreover, is simply the association with the immoral for those who are immoral, and the association with the virtuous for those who are virtuous.
What determines that association with the unwise is for those of poor wisdom, while association with the wise is for those possessed of wisdom?
It is determined by the element of inclination (*ajjhāsayadhātu*).

Regarding the demonstration of the capable and the incapable, the description of what is to be abandoned is given first, and the description of what is to be adopted is given afterwards; such is the order of the enumeration.

In reverse order, those who are incapable have been first pointed out. However, in the summary (uddesa), the word *bhabba* is placed first by virtue of the rule for prior placement (*pubbanipāta*) in a dvanda compound, as well as for words that are highly honored or contain short syllables.

"By the obstruction of karma" means by the fivefold karma of immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*). "Endowed with" means being possessed of. "By the obstruction of defilements" means by fixed wrong view (*niyata-micchādiṭṭhi*).
These two are called "obstructions" because they obstruct the paths to heaven. Actions such as violating a bhikkhunī are also included within the obstruction of karma (*kammāvaraṇa*).
By the "obstruction of fruition" (*vipākāvaraṇa*), one refers to rebirth without roots (*ahetuka-paṭisandhi*).

Since even those with two roots lack penetration of the Noble Path, it should be understood that rebirth with two roots is likewise an obstruction of fruition. "Lacking faith" refers to [lack of faith] in the Buddha and so forth.
"Devoid of faith" means lacking faith. "Lacking desire" means devoid of the wholesome desire that is the wish-to-act (*kattukamyatā*).
The humans of Uttarakuru have entered the state of being devoid of desire. "Lacking wisdom" means being deficient in the wisdom of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga-paññā*).
However, even one whose life-continuum wisdom is complete is still "lacking wisdom" if that life-continuum does not serve as a basis for the supramundane (*lokuttara*).

"Unable to enter into the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states" means they are unable to enter—that is, to penetrate—the Noble Path, which is designated as the "certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states.

For the Noble Path is "rightness" (*sammatta*) because it is perfectly true by its very nature; it is "certainty" (*niyāma*) because it yields its fruit immediately, or because it is itself immovable in its state.
They are unable to enter or penetrate that. Regarding the phrases "not by obstruction of karma," and so forth:
They should be understood by the very reverse of what has been stated.
The commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of underlying tendencies and latent dispositions is finished.
70. Commentary on the Exposition of the Knowledge of the Twin Miracle.

116. Regarding the explanation of the knowledge of the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihīrañāṇa*): it is said to be "not shared with disciples" because it was not mentioned in the explanation of the other uncommon knowledges due to the absence of space for such terminology;
however, it should be understood that it is mentioned here precisely because of the absence of such terminology [elsewhere].
"From the upper part of the body" means from above the navel of the physical frame. "A mass of fire proceeds" refers to the foundational jhāna having the fire-kasina as its object.
Having entered [the attainment] and emerged, he adverts thus: "Let a mass of flames issue from the upper part of my body.

Having performed the preliminary work, immediately after, when he resolves with the knowledge of direct higher power (abhiññā-ñāṇa) thus: "Let a mass of flames issue from the upper part of my body," then together with that resolution, a mass of flames issues from the upper part of his body.
For here, in the sense of a heap, it is called a "khandha" (aggregate). From the lower part of the body...

"From below the navel, a stream of water flows from the body": having entered the foundational jhāna with the water-kasiṇa as its object, and having emerged, one adverts thus, "Let a stream of water issue from the lower part of the body," and performs the preliminary work.

Immediately thereafter, when one resolves with direct knowledge (abhiññā-ñāṇa) thus, "Let a stream of water issue from the lower part of the body," then simultaneously with that resolution, from the lower part of the body—
A stream of water pours forth. It is said that in both cases [the fire and the water], they proceed without interruption.

Between the act of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and the act of adverting (*āvajjana*), two life-continuum consciousnesses (*bhavaṅga-citta*) occur. For this very reason, the masses of fire and streams of water proceed as pairs;
no interval is perceived between them. However, for others, there is no such delimitation by the life-continuum. "From the front part of the body" means...
*Abhimukhapassato*: from the front side. *Pacchimakāyato*: from the back side.
Phrases such as "from the right eye" or "from the left eye" are merely compound readings and nothing else. The reading "from the right nostril" or "from the left nostril" is excellent;

they also recite it with the short vowel (*nāsikāsotato*). Regarding "from the shoulder-peak" (*aṃsakūṭato*): here, it is called a "peak" (*kūṭo*) because it is like a peak in the sense of being elevated; it is simply the shoulder (*aṃso*).
*Kūṭa* means a shoulder-peak (*aṃsakūṭa*). *Aṅgulaṅgulehi* means from finger to finger. *Aṅgulantarikāhi* means from the spaces between the fingers.

In the phrases "from each single hair a mass of fire proceeds" and "from each single hair a stream of water proceeds," because all the hairs are exhausted by this repetitive expression (*āmeḍitavacana*), it is understood that from each and every hair alone there proceed both the mass of fire and the stream of water.

It is said that they proceed in pairs; that is, from every single pore of the skin a mass of fire proceeds, and from every single pore of the skin a stream of water proceeds—the same principle applies here as well. In some manuscripts, it is stated:
"From each individual hair a mass of fire proceeds; from every single pore of the skin a stream of water proceeds."
It is written: “A mass of fire issues from every pore; from each single hair, a stream of water issues forth.
This too is indeed appropriate. However, because it demonstrates the extreme subtlety of the miracle, the former reading alone is more excellent.
Now, what is the connection with the phrase “of the six colors”? It refers to the various parts of the body mentioned below by such terms as “from the upper part of the body,” and so forth.

It has been stated. By that [statement], it is meant that because a connection with the parts of the body occurs, and through the connection with the words and the context of the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihīra*), the rays—which are the six colors constituting the parts of the body—proceed as twins.
Furthermore, by way of the connection with the genitive case, a textual supplement of the word "rays" (*rasmiyo*) must certainly be supplied. Regarding the phrase "of the blue ones" (*nīlānaṃ*):
"Of the color of *umā* flowers" means of the color of *kaṇikāra* flowers. "Yellow" means of the color of *indagopaka* insects.
"White" means of the color of the morning star (*osadhitāraka*). "Madder-red" means of a pale red color.
"Radiant" means having a nature that shines, possessing a radiant color—even though a distinct "radiant color" does not exist apart from those already mentioned.
Among the five colors, whichever radiance is most brilliant is the most luminous.

For instance, when the Tathāgata performs the Twin Miracle, by the very power of the knowledge of the Twin Miracle, blue rays issue forth from the places where the hair and beard grow, as well as from the dark regions of the eyes;
through these rays, the vault of the sky appears as if strewn with powdered collyrium and covered with the petals of blue flax flowers and blue lotuses.
It is as if a fan with jeweled blades were being waved back and forth, or like a dark blue cloth being spread out.

From the yellow parts of the skin and the eyes, yellow rays stream forth; by means of these, the various directions shine as if being drenched with liquid gold, as if spread with a golden cloth, or as if strewn with specks of saffron powder and *kaṇikāra* flowers.
From the flesh and blood, and from the red parts of the eyes, rays of light emerge;

by means of these, the quarters of the sky shine as if colored with vermilion powder, as if being sprinkled with the juice of well-ripened lac, as if draped in red woolen cloth, and as if strewn with *jayasumana*, *pālibhaddaka*, and *bandhujīvaka* flowers. [From] the bones...
From his teeth and from the white parts of his eyes, white rays issued forth; by means of which the quarters of the world appeared as if surrounded by streams of milk being poured from silver jars,
as if covered by canopies of spread-out silver cloths, as if with silver fans waving about,
and as if strewn with flowers such as the *kunda*, *kumuda*, *sinduvāra*, *sumana*, and *mallikā*.
And they shine forth. From the palms of the hands, the soles of the feet, and other such slightly reddish areas, rays of madder-colored light issue forth;
by means of these, the various quarters of space shine as if encircled by a lattice of coral and as if strewn with red *kuravaka* flowers.
From the radiant areas such as the *ūrṇā* hair-tuft and the nails, bright rays of light issue forth. By means of these...
By means of this, the various quarters of space shine forth as if filled with clusters of medicinal herbs and stars, and as if filled with masses of lightning and the like.

The statement "the Blessed One walks back and forth," and so on, is spoken for the purpose of showing that "the performance of various postures by the Blessed One and his emanations occurs precisely through the Twin Miracle. For the postures of those emanations proceed only in pairs.

If there are many created beings, why is the singular form used in such expressions as “the created being”? It is for the purpose of showing that even among the created beings, each individual possesses various modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*).
For if it were stated in the plural, all the created beings would appear as if they simultaneously possessed only a single mode of deportment.
But when stated in the singular, it is shown that among the created beings, each one individually possesses various modes of deportment.
It is understood. Therefore, the singular number was employed. Even the Elder Cūḷapanthaka fashioned a thousand monks with various postures;
how much more, then, would the Blessed One not have created many emanations during the Twin Miracle?
Apart from the Elder Cūḷapanthaka, the other disciples were able to create various forms with various postures through a single act of attention (*ekāvajjana*).
It does not succeed. For when created by one possessing psychic power (*iddhimā*) without having fixed [the details], they become exactly like him.

Whether in standing, sitting, and so forth, or in speaking, remaining silent, and so forth, whatever the possessor of psychic power does, they do that very same thing. However, making them different or causing them to perform various actions—such as by resolving separately, "Let this many be like this;
let this many do such-and-such"—is achieved through an act of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*) after having adverted to each individually.
It succeeds. But for the Tathāgata, various kinds of emanations succeed through the mere resolution of a single advertence (*ekāvajjanādhiṭṭhāna*).

In the same way, this should be understood regarding the emanation of masses of fire and streams of water, as well as the emanation of various colors. In that context, "the Blessed One walks" means he walks either in the air or on the earth.
"An emanation" (*nimmita*) refers to a form of a Buddha created by supernormal power (*iddhi*). The phrases beginning with "or stands" and so forth are likewise explained.
"In the sky or on the earth. "He performs" means he does. This same method applies to [the phrases] "The Blessed One stands," and so forth.
The commentary on the description of the knowledge of the Twin Miracle is finished.
71. Commentary on the Description of the Knowledge of Great Compassion.
117. In the exposition of Great Compassion and Knowledge (*mahākaruṇāñāṇaniddesa*), "in many ways" refers to the eighty-nine modes that will now be described.
"Beholding" means looking with the eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*) and the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakkhu*). "Enters" means descends into or penetrates.

"Burning" means being set ablaze in the sense of being scorched due to its connection with affliction by way of the characteristic of suffering (*dukkhalakkhaṇa*). "Whatever is impermanent... [is suffering].

It should be understood that because it is stated as "suffering" (*dukkha*), it is first described as "ablaze" by way of the characteristic of suffering (*dukkha-lakkhaṇa*), owing both to the fact that all conditioned phenomena are oppressed by the characteristic of suffering and to the fact that [suffering] is the root of compassion.
Furthermore, its being ablaze with lust and so forth will be explained later. Alternatively, "ablaze" means ablaze precisely with lust and the other [defilements]. Later—
However, it should be understood that the phrase "there is no other extinguisher for him" is stated again by way of emphasizing the meaning.

Regarding "the world-dwelling": the five aggregates are the *loka* (world) in the sense of breaking up and falling apart; it is called *sannivāsa* (dwelling) because beings dwell therein by means of craving and views;
thus, the world itself is the dwelling, which is "world-dwelling. [It refers to] the suffering continuum of the aggregates.
Because the conventional designation "being" exists by depending [on the aggregates], and because it is joined with dwelling in the world, the multitude of beings is also the "dwelling in the world.
And that too consists precisely of the *khandhakas*. "Engaged" (*uyyutta*) means having applied oneself and exerted effort due to constant occupation with various duties;

the meaning is being diligent in perpetual tasks. Alternatively, "engaged" (*uyyutta*) means "joined in friction" (*ghaṭṭanayutta*). "Marching forth" (*payāta*) refers to those who dwell in the mountains (*pabbateyyā*).
Like a river with its unstable flow, he has begun to go toward death.
"Set upon a wrong path" means set upon a contemptible, false path. Later, however, this is stated with specific terms as "strayed onto a bypath.
"Is being led away" means that by way of aging, he is led toward and carried off to death; for aging is indeed described as "the destroyer of life."
“Unstable” (*addhuvo*) means not firm; it does not remain always the same. Because it is unstable, it is “led away”—this is a statement of the cause for the preceding [unstable state].
By this, the suffering of aging is described along with its cause. Having seen that suffering of aging, even wise people who are free from the loss caused by aging go forth into homelessness.
“Without refuge” (*atāṇo*) means devoid of one capable of protecting or guarding; it is said to be unprotected (*anārakkho*).
"Anabhissaro" means devoid of one who is capable of approaching, going to, and consoling through speech;
or it means "without a companion. Because he is without a protector (*anabhissaro*), therefore he is "without refuge" (*ataṇo*); this is a statement of the reason for the former.
By this, the suffering of separation from the beloved is stated along with its cause. Having seen that suffering of separation from the beloved, even those who are free from the loss of kinsmen—
The wise go forth. "Assaka" means being devoid of one's own belongings.
"Having abandoned everything that must be gone with" refers to all that is recognized as one's own belongings; having abandoned all that must be left behind by the world when departing.
Because everything must be abandoned when one goes, this is a statement of the reason for the former [term]. By this, the suffering of death is described along with its cause. Having seen that...
Even those free from the loss of enjoyments go forth as wise men. If it is asked:
how does this accord with what is stated elsewhere—that "human beings are the owners of their karma"—and here in the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta that "the world is ownerless"?
It is said to be "ownerless" with reference to what must be abandoned; however, karma is not something to be abandoned. Therefore, they are "owners of their karma."
It has been said. And in the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta itself, it is likewise stated: "But you shall go according to your karma. "Deficient" (ūna) means devoid of fullness.
"Unsatisfied" (atitta) means not contented even with ever-increasing aspiration; this is a statement of the cause for being deficient.
"A slave to craving" (taṇhādāsa) means having become a slave to craving because one is subject to its power; this refers to the state of being unsatisfied.
This is a statement of the cause. By this, the suffering of illness is described along with its cause, namely the pretext of the disease of desire.

Seeing that suffering of illness, even those wise ones who are free from the loss caused by illness go forth into homelessness. "Without protection" (*atāyano*) means one who has no protection even from children and so forth;
thus he is unprotected, or one for whom security cannot be obtained. "Without refuge" (*aleṇo*) means one who is unfit to be approached or relied upon, and [even for] those who have approached him...
And he does not perform the function of a shelter. "Without refuge" means that he is neither a protector from fear nor a destroyer of fear for those who depend on him.
"Becoming a non-refuge" means that he is without refuge precisely because of his own prior non-existence; the meaning is that he becomes a non-refuge at the very moment of his arising.
"Agitated" refers to the arising of restlessness among all unwholesome states, and to the abundance of the arising of unwholesome states within the continuum of sentient beings.

The world that possesses unwholesome states is "agitated" by that restlessness. "Untranquil" means it is untranquil due to its association with restlessness, which has the characteristic of non-tranquility;
it resembles a wandering deer. In the four instances beginning with "the world is led away," and in the five instances including "the world is agitated," the word "world" (loka) occurs;
in the remaining cases, it refers to the "dwelling of the world" (lokasannivāsa). In both cases, however, it is simply the world.
"Sasallā" means one who dwells together with the arrows of lust and so forth, which are designated as "arrows" (salla) because they cause affliction, pierce within, and are difficult to extract.
"Viddho" means that while deer and other animals are sometimes pierced by others, this world is constantly pierced by itself.

"Puthusallehi" refers to the seven arrows: the arrow of lust, the arrow of hatred, [the arrow of delusion, the arrow of views, the arrow of doubt, the arrow of conceit, and the arrow of craving for existence].
By the seven arrows mentioned—namely, the arrow of delusion, the arrow of conceit, the arrow of views, the arrow of defilements, and the arrow of misconduct.
"Of that" means of that worldly existence. "One who has extracted the arrows" refers to the person who has removed those arrows from the continuum of the seven [stages].
"Apart from me" means excluding me. Even those disciples of the Blessed One who extract the arrows...
Because they were extracted by the Blessed One’s very word, it is said that the Blessed One himself extracted them. "Enveloped in the darkness of ignorance" (*avijjandhakārāvaraṇo*):

ignorance itself acts like a blindfold by obscuring the vision of the true nature of things; thus it is the "darkness of ignorance. That very thing is an "obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*) because it prevents the comprehension of the true nature;

hence, he is "enveloped in the darkness of ignorance. "Cast into the cage of defilements" (*kilesapañjarapakkhitto*): the defilements themselves [are so called] in the sense that they obstruct progress toward the wholesome.
"Cage" means the cage of defilements (*kilesapañjara*). "Cast into the cage of defilements arising from ignorance" means thrown into it.

"One who shows light" means one whose nature is to show the light of wisdom (*paññāloka*), or alternatively, one who shows the light of wisdom. "Enveloped by ignorance" means having gone to or entered into ignorance.
It is not merely that there is an obstruction by ignorance; rather, [one is] as if entered into a thicket within the treasury of ignorance.
"Entered within" is the distinction from what precedes it. "Become like an egg," and so forth, are likewise distinctions. "Become like an egg" (*aṇḍabhūta*) means born or produced within an egg.

Just as certain beings produced within an egg are called "egg-born" (*aṇḍabhūta*), so too this world is called "egg-born" because it is produced within the shell of the egg of ignorance (*avijjā*). "Enveloped" means by that shell of the egg of ignorance.
"Covered all over" means bound and wrapped.

"Become like a tangled skein" means having become as disordered as a thread. Just as a poorly laid-out weaver’s thread, gnawed by mice, becomes entangled here and there—such that one cannot distinguish, "This is the tip, this is the root"—it is either a tip [of the thread] by means of a tip, or...
Just as it is difficult to bring back the root by means of the root itself, even so beings, having stumbled in the conditional mode (paccayākāra), become confused and utterly bewildered;
they are unable to make the conditional mode straight. In that regard, it might be possible to make it straight by relying on one's own personal effort (*paccatta-purisakāra*);
however, with the exception of the two types of Bodhisattas, no other being [can do so] for themselves.
By the very nature of things, there is no one capable of making the mode of conditions straight.
Just as when tangled thread is soaked in sour gruel and beaten with a shuttle, it becomes knotted and full of tangles here and there, so too this world,
stumbling over its conditions and unable to make them straight, [becomes entangled] by way of the sixty-two views.
He is born with a "family-knot" (kulagaṇṭhika), meaning he is tied by a knot. For whoever relies on views, none of them are able to make their conditions straight.
"Born with a family-knot" means he has become like a family-knot. A "family-knot" is said to be the shuttle-thread of a weaver.
Some say: "A 'kula' is a certain bird; its nest is the 'kulāvaka'. Just as...
Both of these are confused; it is difficult to bring the tip to the tip or the root to the root, and thus it should be applied according to the previous method.
"Become like *muñja* grass and *pabbaja* grass" means he has become like, or produced something similar to, *muñja* grass and *pabbaja* grass.
Just as when those two types of grass have been repeatedly pounded and made into a rope, and that rope has fallen somewhere after becoming worn out, one picks it up...
Regarding those blades of grass, it is difficult to align them so that the tip meets tip or the root meets root, thinking, "This is the tip; this is the root.
Even that might be possible to straighten by relying on individual personal effort;
however, apart from the two Bodhisattvas, no other being is capable of straightening the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*) through their own inherent nature.

There is none. Thus, this world, being unable to straighten out the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*), becomes knotted by way of the sixty-two types of views (*diṭṭhigata*) and does not transcend the states of loss, the miserable destinies, the fallen states, and *saṃsāra*.

In this context, "states of loss" (*apāya*) refers to hell, the animal realm, the sphere of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*), and the host of asuras. For all of these are characterized by the absence of prosperity.
They are called "states of loss" (apāya) because of the absence of gain. Likewise, they are "bad destinations" (duggati) because they are the destination of suffering.
They are "ruin" (vinipāta) because of falling away from the heights of happiness. Furthermore, it is said:
"The succession of the aggregates, and of the elements and sense-bases..."
“The continuous occurrence of these [processes] is called ‘saṃsāra.

One does not transcend, nor does one go beyond all of that; rather, taking up death and rebirth again and again—from death to rebirth, and from rebirth to death—one proceeds through the three realms of existence, the four modes of birth, and the five destinations.
In the seven stations of consciousness and the nine abodes of beings, it merely wanders about like a ship tossed by the wind in the great ocean, or like a mechanical ox.

"Stung by the poisonous sting of ignorance" means that ignorance itself is the "poison of ignorance" (*avijjāvisa*) because, by giving rise to unwholesome states, it destroys the life-force of the wholesome;

that very poison is the "poisonous sting of ignorance" (*avijjāvisadosa*) because it corrupts the continuity [of existence]. By means of that [sting], which consists of underlying tendencies, obsessions, and misconduct...

"Smeared and defiled" means smeared with the poison of the sting of ignorance (*avijjā*). "Become a mire of defilements" means that the very defilements rooted in ignorance and so forth are themselves the "mire" (*kalala*) in the sense of sinking or mud;
thus it is "defilement-mire. One who possesses this is "become a mire of defilements"—such is he.

"Entangled by the tangle of lust, hatred, and delusion" means that lust, hatred, and delusion—consisting of greed (*lobha*), aversion (*paṭigha*), and ignorance (*avijjā*)—are themselves [the tangle] regarding forms and so forth.

Because it arises again and again among objects by way of ascending and descending, it is called a "tangle" (*jaṭā*) in the sense of being entangled, like the network of branches of bamboo thickets and the like. He is "entangled" (*jaṭita*) by that tangle of lust, hatred, and delusion.

The meaning is that just as bamboos and the like are entwined by bamboo-entanglements and so forth, so too this world is entangled, bound, and interwoven by that tangle. "He disentangles the tangle" (*jaṭaṃ vijaṭeti*).

Having unraveled this triple-world (*tedhātuka*) which stands as a tangled skein—having unraveled it, cut it, and completely destroyed it—he is "clad in the cloak of craving" (*taṇhāsaṅghāṭapaṭimukka*).
Craving itself, because it proceeds without interruption and in the sense of being woven together, is called a "cloak" (*saṅghāṭa*); thus it is the "cloak of craving.
He is "clad in the cloak of craving" in the sense that he has entered into, is immersed in, and is contained within that cloak of craving.
"Enmeshed in the net of craving": craving itself is called a "net" (*jāla*) in the sense of binding together, according to the method explained previously;
thus it is the "net of craving. Enmeshed by that net of craving means covered on all sides and enveloped by it. "Carried away by the stream of craving":

craving itself is called a "stream" (*sota*) in the sense of dragging one along in *saṃsāra*; thus it is the "stream of craving. Carried away by that stream of craving means being dragged along by it.
"Bound by the fetter of craving": craving itself is called a "fetter" (*saṃyojana*) because it yokes and binds the world to the cycle of existence;
thus, it is the "fetter of craving. One is "bound" (*saññutta*) by that fetter of craving, meaning one is tied and constrained by it.

"Infused by the underlying tendency to craving": craving itself is called an "underlying tendency" (*anusaya*) in the sense of lying latent; thus, it is the "underlying tendency to craving. One is "infused" (*anusaṭa*) by that underlying tendency to craving, meaning one is followed by it and it has become firmly established.
"He is tormented by the torment of craving" means that craving itself is called "torment" because it torments the world both during its occurrence and at the time of its fruition;
he is tormented, that is, scorched, by that torment of craving.

"He is consumed by the fever of craving" means that craving itself, when it has become powerful, is a great fever in the sense of burning all around, both during its occurrence and at the time of its fruition.

The fever of craving (*taṇhā-pariḷāha*); by that fever of craving one is scorched, one is burned all over. The "assemblage of views" (*diṭṭhi-saṅghāṭa*) and the others should be applied according to this same method.
"Followed" (*anugata*) means entered into. "Pursued" (*anusaṭa*) means chased after. "Overcome" (*abhibhūta*) means oppressed. "Assailed" (*abbhāhata*) means struck down.
He is struck violently and directly. "Established in suffering" means established and adhering through the perversion of pleasure (*sukhavipallāsa*) toward the five aggregates of suffering.
"Entangled by craving" means overpowered by craving; for the eye, having been ensnared by the rope of craving, is caught upon the tusks of forms (*rūpa*).
"Uḍḍitaṃ" means that the ear and other sense-faculties have been bound by the rope of craving and fastened to the elephant-goads of sounds and so forth.

The world that possesses these [faculties] is likewise said to be "fastened. "Enclosed by the rampart of old age" means surrounded by old age, which acts as a rampart in the sense of being impossible to transcend.
"Encircled by the noose of death" means bound by death, which acts as a noose in the sense of being difficult to release.
"Bound by great bonds" means bound by great bonds because of their strength and difficulty to sever.
"By the bond of lust" (*rāgabandhana*): lust itself is the bond; it is called the "bond of lust" because it binds one and does not allow one to move out of *saṃsāra*.

[The phrase] "by that bond of lust" follows. The same method applies to the remaining [bonds] as well. "By the bond of defilements" (*kilesabandhana*) means by the bond of defilements other than those already mentioned. "By the bond of misconduct" (*duccaritabandhana*)...
In three ways. Furthermore, good conduct is both the cause for release from bondage and itself constitutes release from bondage.
Therefore, that [good conduct] should not be included here.
"One who releases his bondage" means one who releases his own bondage. There is also a reading, "one who releases from bondage," meaning from bondage.

The meaning is "he should release him. "One who has entered upon a great congestion" means one who has entered upon the thicket of lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, defilements, and misconduct—which is termed a "great congestion"—due to the oppression of unwholesome conduct. "One who shows the way" means one who shows the way to mundane and supramundane concentration and wisdom.
"Obstructed by a great impediment" means shut off by a great hindrance, or smeared with a great coating.
“Obstacle” (*palibodha*) refers specifically to the sevenfold [hindrances] such as lust (*rāga*) and so forth; some say it is the obstacle of craving (*taṇhā*) and views (*diṭṭhi*).

“One who has cut the obstacle” means one who has severed that obstacle. “In the great precipice” refers to the precipice of the five destinies (*pañcagati*), or the precipice of birth, aging, and death;

all of that is a “precipice” in the sense of being difficult to cross over. “Drawn out from the precipice” means rescued from that precipice. “Set out upon a great wilderness” (*mahākantārappaṭipanna*)...

He has entered upon the wilderness of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. That entire wilderness is a "wilderness" in the sense of being difficult to cross; he is one who carries others across that wilderness. Alternatively, the reading is "one who carries [others] out of the wilderness.
He has entered the great saṃsāra means he has entered the uninterrupted continuity of the aggregates (khandha-santāna). He is one who liberates from saṃsāra.
One who delivers from *saṃsāra*. Alternatively, the reading is "one who delivers from *saṃsāra*. "In the great wilderness" means in the wilderness of *saṃsāra*.

For *saṃsāra* itself is a "wilderness" (*vidugga*) in the sense of being difficult to traverse. "He wanders about" means he moves about, turning back repeatedly. "In the great mire" means in the great mud of sensual desire (*kāma*).
For sensual desire is a "mire" (*palipa*) in the sense of causing one to sink. "Mired" means stuck. There is also the reading "mired in the great mire."
"Smitten" (*abbhāhato*) means smitten by all calamities. "By the fire of lust" (*rāgaggi*): lust and the rest are themselves "fire" in the sense of burning;
[he is smitten] by that fire of lust. The same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. "Led away" (*unnīto*): led away after having been seized;

the meaning is that he has been seized by birth and led away toward the calamities of old age and so forth. Furthermore, the letter *ka* here should be understood as expressing compassion. "He is constantly struck down" (*haññati niccamatāṇo*).
Deprived of a protector, one is constantly oppressed. "One who has received a royal decree" means one who has been given an order by kings and others.
"A perpetrator" means a thief. "Bound by the fetters of the defilements" means bound by the fetters of the defilements such as lust and so forth.

"Standing at the place of execution" means having approached and stood at the spot where the knot of the law of death is tied. "Someone to release from bondage" means someone to release the bonds; "someone to release the bond" is also said.
*Pāṭho*: "Anātha" means one who has no protector (*nātha*), no lord; or, being oneself neither a protector nor a lord, one is *anātha*; or the meaning is "one without refuge.
"Paramakāpaṇṇappatto" means having reached a state of extreme wretchedness due to a lack of abundance in warding off old age and so forth.
"Tāyetā" means a protector. Alternatively, the reading "tāyitā" is better. "Dukkhābhitunno" means [overwhelmed] by the suffering of birth and so forth.
"Oppressed by many sufferings" means being intensely pierced and violently shaken. "Afflicted for a long time" means being tormented and struck by sufferings throughout a long duration.
"Lusting" means greedy with craving, or bound by the bodily tie of covetousness.
"Constantly thirsty" refers to thirst as the desire to drink or eat; that is indeed craving (taṇhā), and thus [afflicted] by the thirst of craving.
He is constantly thirsty.
"Blind" means he is one-eyed (*kāṇa*) due to the absence of wisdom (*paññā*), which is designated as "the eye" in the sense of seeing. For wisdom sees the true nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*).
Furthermore, that blindness did not arise later; rather, he is one who has been without eyes from the very beginning by his own nature.

This very term specifies his blindness. "One whose eyes are destroyed" (*hatanetta*): because of the absence of wisdom (*paññā*), which is designated as "eyes" in the sense of leading, he is one whose eyes have perished.
For it is said that "eyes" (*netta*) are so called because they lead the personal existence (*attabhāva*) toward what is even or uneven.
Wisdom leads one toward both good destinations (*sugati*) and bad destinations (*agati*). By showing that he lacks a leader precisely because his eyes are destroyed, [the text] demonstrates this.
"Without a leader," he said; the meaning is "one for whom no guide exists. What is meant is that no other leader is found for him.

"One who has strayed onto a wrong path": a wrong path is one that is perverted or uneven; one who has strayed into, entered, or set out upon that wrong path is "one who has strayed onto a wrong path"—that is, one who has set out upon wrong view, which is designated as a wrong path.
The meaning is as follows: "Añjasāparaddho" means one who has missed or strayed from the *añjasā*, that is, from the straight path, the Middle Way.
"Ānetā ariyapatham" means one who leads toward or establishes one in the Noble Eightfold Path (*ariya-aṭṭhaṅgika-magga*). "Mahoghapakkhando":

those things which exist [in him] are called "floods" (*ogha*) because they carry one away and cause one to sink into the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*); they are "great" compared to the ordinary floods.

The floods are the great floods. They are of four types: the flood of sensual desire (*kāmogha*), the flood of existence (*bhavogha*), the flood of views (*diṭṭhogha*), and the flood of ignorance (*avijjogha*).
One who plunges into these great floods is "one who has plunged into the great floods" (*mahoghapakkhando*); or, one who plunges into the great flood known as *saṃsāra*.
Now follows the method of single-increment. Therein, "by two types of views" refers to the views of eternalism and annihilationism. Therein—

“View itself is the state of view” (diṭṭhigata), just as one speaks of “feces-state” (gūthagata) or “urine-state” (muttagata). Alternatively, it is called “view-state” because there is no further going beyond the view;
it is merely the state of having gone into the view. Or again, this seeing has gone into views because it is included within the sixty-two views;
thus it is also called “view-state. For even among those sixty-two views, they are reduced to only two views: the eternalist view and the annihilationist view.
Therefore, summarizing all views, it is said: "by two types of views.

"Obsessed" (pariyuṭṭhita) means having reached obsession, having reached active manifestation; the meaning is that one has reached a state where the seizing of wholesome conduct is prevented from arising.
For this was said by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, obsessed by two types of views..."
“Some gods and humans lag behind; some overreach; but those with vision see clearly,” and so forth.
“By means of the three types of misconduct” means by the threefold bodily misconduct, the fourfold verbal misconduct, and the threefold mental misconduct.
“Mispracticed” (vippaṭipanna) means practiced in a distorted way; the meaning is that one has practiced wrongly. “Yoked to the bonds” means yoked to the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa).
They are called *yogas* because they yoke (*yojenti*), or they are *yogas* in the sense of affliction (*īti*). One who is "yoked by these four *yogas*" is bound and fettered by them.

"Yoked by the four *yogas*" means being yoked to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) by these four *yogas*—the *yoga* of sensual desire (*kāma-yoga*), the *yoga* of existence (*bhava-yoga*), the *yoga* of views (*diṭṭhi-yoga*), and the *yoga* of ignorance (*avijjā-yoga*)—just as a horse is yoked to a cart.
Attachment to the five strands of sensual pleasure is the *yoga* of sensual desire. Craving and attachment toward the realms of form and formlessness is the *yoga* of existence.

Attachment to meditative absorption (*jhāna-nikanti*) and the lust (*rāga*) co-arising with the eternalist view (*sassata-diṭṭhi*), which is a longing for existence, constitute the yoke of existence (*bhava-yoga*).

The sixty-two views constitute the yoke of views (*diṭṭhi-yoga*). Ignorance regarding the eight points constitutes the yoke of ignorance (*avijjā-yoga*). These same four, when they have become powerful, are the floods (*ogha*);
when they have become weak, they are the yokes (*yoga*).

"By four fetters": those in whom these are found are "fettered" (*gantha*) and "bound" (*ghaṭenti*) within the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) by way of death and rebirth-linking; thus they are called fetters.

They are of fourfold division: covetousness as a bodily fetter, ill will as a bodily fetter, adherence to rules and observances as a bodily fetter, and the dogmatic insistence that "this alone is the truth" as a bodily fetter. By means of this, one covets; itself...
It is called *abhijjhā* because one covets, or because it consists merely in coveting; it is simply greed (*lobha*).
It is a "fetter of the body" (*kāyagantha*) because it fetters the mental body (*nāmakāya*) and joins it to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) by way of death and rebirth-linking.

It is "ill-will" (*byāpāda*) because by means of it the mind becomes putrid, or because it destroys discipline, conduct, physical beauty, welfare, happiness, and so forth. [Regarding] "outside of this":

The adherence that [asserts] for recluses and brahmins that purification comes through virtue, purification through observances, or purification through both virtue and observances, is the adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*).
The dogmatic insistence that, having rejected even what was spoken by the Omniscient One, one clings to such views as "the world is eternal;
this alone is true, all else is false," is the dogmatic insistence on "this is the truth" (*idamsaccābhinivesa*). One is "bound" by these four fetters; the meaning is that one is tied down by them.
"By means of the four clingings": they are called *upādānas* because they take hold intensely, grasping with a firm grip. They are divided into four types:
clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*), clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*), clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*), and clinging to a doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*).

It is called clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*) because it takes hold of sense-pleasures, which are reckoned as the objective basis; alternatively, it is clinging to sense-pleasures because it is both sense-pleasure and clinging. It is clinging to views because it is both view and clinging.

It is the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*); it is also called the clinging to views because one clings to views. For in such cases as “The self and the world are eternal,” a subsequent view clings to a preceding view.
It is the clinging to virtue and observance (*sīlabbatupādāna*) because one clings to virtue and observance;

it is also called the clinging to virtue and observance because it is both virtue and observance and it is clinging. For [practices] such as the cow-virtue and cow-observance are thus considered purification.
The clingings are themselves [the views] due to their adherence. That by which they speak is "speech" (*vāda*); that by which they cling is "clinging" (*upādāna*).
What do they speak or what do they cling to? To a self. Or, clinging to one's own speech regarding a self is "clinging to the doctrine of self" (*attavādupādāna*);
or, that by which they cling to mere speech about a self as being a "self" is "clinging to the doctrine of self. Apart from these two views, all other views [are included].
The clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*). By means of those four types of clinging (*upādāna*). "Is clung to" (*upādīyati*) means it is grasped intensely.
Alternatively, the reading is *upādiyati*, meaning that the world intensely grasps various objects by means of the clingings.

"Mounted upon the five destinies" (*pañcagatisamāruḷha*): a "destiny" (*gati*) is so called because one goes to or approaches [it] due to the causes of good or evil deeds; it is that which shares a common locus.

The aggregates (*khandhā*). Hell, the animal realm, the sphere of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*), humans, and gods—these five destinies (*gati*) he has ascended intensely due to his state of transgression.
"By the five strands of sensual pleasure" means by the five constituent parts of objective desire, namely those consisting of visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangible objects.
"He is impassioned" means that, depending on improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), he is colored by them through the arising of lust.
The meaning is that it is made impassioned. Regarding "by the five hindrances": they are called *nīvaraṇā* because they obstruct and envelop the mind.
[This refers to] by the five hindrances known as sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
"Covered" means shut off from above.
"By six roots of dispute" means by six causes of dispute. As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, there are these six roots of dispute. Which six? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is prone to anger and resentment.
That bhikkhu who is prone to anger and resentment lacks respect for the Teacher..."
He dwells without respect and without deference toward the Teacher, and he does not fulfill the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, or the training.
Monks, that monk who dwells without respect and without deference toward the Teacher, and who does not fulfill the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, or the training, creates a dispute within the Saṅgha.
Such a dispute is for the harm of many people, for the unhappiness of many people, and for the detriment of the many.
"To the detriment, harm, and suffering of gods and humans.

Monks, if you should perceive such a root of dispute within yourselves or among others, you should strive, monks, for the abandonment of that very evil root of dispute. If you should perceive such a root of dispute within yourselves..."
Or externally. In that regard, monks, you should practice for the sake of the future non-outflow of that very same root of evil dispute.
In this way, there is the abandoning of that root of evil dispute; in this way, there is the future non-outflow of that root of evil dispute.
“Furthermore, monks, a monk is one who is contemptuous and insolent; he is envious and miserly; he is fraudulent and deceitful;
he has evil desires and wrong view; he is one who clings to his own views, holds them dogmatically, and is difficult to disabuse of them.
Monks, that monk who clings to his own views, holds them dogmatically, and is difficult to disabuse of them—”
“...even toward the Teacher... [and so on] ...there will be no further outflow for the future.

In this context, “one who is prone to anger” means one endowed with anger characterized by the act of being angry. “One who is resentful” means one endowed with resentment characterized by the non-relinquishing of enmity.
“To the detriment and suffering of gods and humans” refers to a dispute between two monks.
How does it lead to the harm and suffering of gods and humans?
As in the Kosambakakkhandhaka, when two monks have fallen into dispute, their pupils in that monastery dispute;
the community of nuns who receive their instruction disputes; and consequently, even their lay supporters dispute. Then, among the people...

The guardian deities are divided into two classes: the guardian deities of those who speak according to the Dhamma are themselves speakers of the Dhamma, while those of those who speak against the Dhamma are speakers against the Dhamma.
Consequently, the terrestrial deities who are friends of the guardian deities become divided.
Thus, in succession up to the Brahma-world, all gods and humans—with the exception of the noble disciples—are divided into these two classes.
[They] become so. However, those who speak what is contrary to the Dhamma (adhammavādī) are more numerous than those who speak according to the Dhamma (dhammavādī).
Consequently, setting aside the Dhamma as "all that which is accepted by the majority is true," they adopt what is contrary to the Dhamma in greater numbers.
Abiding with what is contrary to the Dhamma placed before them, they are reborn in the states of misery (apāya). Thus, the dispute between two monks leads to [the ruin] of gods and humans.
It leads to harm and suffering. "Internally" means within your own circle; "externally" means within the circles of others.
"Spiteful" means one possessed of malice characterized by the disparagement of others' virtues.
"Envious" means one possessed of envy characterized by grasping at opposition. "Jealous" means [one possessed of jealousy] characterized by envying the honor and so forth of others.
"Endowed with envy" means possessed of envy. "Miserly" means possessed of the five kinds of miserliness, beginning with the miserliness regarding one's dwelling.
"Crooked" means deceitful. "Guileful" means one who conceals the evil they have done. "Of evil desires" means an immoral person who desires unworthy honors.
"Of wrong view" means one who holds to the doctrine of non-existence, the doctrine of no-cause, or the doctrine of non-action. "One who clings to their own views" means...
He clings to his own view alone. "One who grasps with insistence" means one who holds firmly. "Difficult to release" means it is not possible to make him relinquish what he has grasped.
In the *Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga*, however, it says: "In that regard, what are the six roots of dispute?
Anger, contempt, envy, deceit, evil desire, and clinging to one's own views—these are the six roots of dispute."
Each single factor was stated by way of its specific exertion.

"By the six groups of craving" refers to the six types of craving stated as: craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena (*dhamma*).
In that context, each individual type of craving possesses multiple objects.

Because they arise repeatedly with respect to each individual object, they are manifold; therefore, by connecting them with the word "body" (*kāya*) in the sense of a collection, they are called "bodies of craving" (*taṇhākāyā*).
Even when "bodies of craving" is said, it is simply craving itself. "It lusts" means that it itself lusts after the object;
it becomes impassioned.
"By the six views" refers to those mentioned in the *Sabbāsava Sutta*. For it is said there:
"As he attends to things in this way by way of improper attention, one of six views arises in him.
Either the view 'I have a self' arises in him as true and certain, or the view 'I have no self' arises in him as true..."

Then a view arises firmly and truly: either the view arises firmly and truly that "I perceive self by means of self," or the view arises firmly and truly that "I perceive not-self by means of self," or the view arises firmly and truly that "I perceive self by means of not-self."
Or else he holds such a view as this: ‘This self of mine—which speaks and feels, and which experiences here and there the results of good and evil deeds—is indeed my self;
it is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain exactly so for all eternity.’”
Therein, the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*), thinking "I have a self," grasps the existence of a self at all times.
"Truly and really" means from the perspective of what has come to be (*bhūta*) and from the perspective of what is stable; it is said to mean with a state of firm conviction that "this is the truth.
The annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*), thinking "I have no self," grasps the non-existence of an existing being here and there. Now...
The first [view] is the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi) because it grasps that [the self] exists in all three times.

Grasping that only the present exists is the annihilationist view (ucchedadiṭṭhi). The last [view] is also an annihilationist view, like the proponents of the view who hold that "sacrifices end in ashes," because it grasps that [the self] does not exist in the past and future.
Grasping that [the self] exists only in the past is the eternalist view, like that of the proponent of fortuitous origination (adhiccasamuppannika).

"By means of self, one perceives self": having grasped the aggregates as "self" under the heading of the aggregate of perception (*saññā-khandha*), because one perceives the remaining aggregates through perception, the thought arises:
"By means of this self, I perceive this self. "By means of self, one perceives not-self":
having grasped the aggregate of perception alone as "self" and having grasped the other four [aggregates] as "not-self," because one perceives them through perception, it occurs thus.
"Taking the aggregate of perception as 'self' when it is actually 'not-self,' and taking the other four aggregates as 'self,' one perceives them through perception;
thus it occurs. All such views are indeed either eternalist or annihilationist views.
Furthermore, "the speaker," "the feeler," and so forth, are merely modes of dogmatic adherence to the eternalist view. In this context, "one who speaks" (*vada*) means a doer of verbal action.
It has been said: "He feels (vedayati), thus he is 'one to be felt' (vedeyya)"; it is meant that he knows and experiences. What does he feel?
He experiences the ripening of wholesome and unwholesome kamma here and there.

"Here and there" means in those various wombs, destinies, stations, abodes, and classes of beings, or in relation to objects. "Eternal" (nicca) means devoid of arising and passing away. "Stable" (dhuva) means firm.
It is the essence. "Eternal" means existing at all times. "Of an unchanging nature" means having a quality that does not abandon its own inherent state;
it does not undergo various transformations like a *kakaṇṭaka* (a type of thorny plant). "Equal to eternity":

by worldly convention, the moon, the sun, the ocean, the great earth, and the mountains are called "eternal. Equal to these eternal things is "equal to eternity. As long as these eternal things endure, [so too does it].
The view arises in one who grasps [the self] thinking, "It will remain exactly like that.
However, in the *Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga*, it is said: "In various places, for a long time, he experiences the result of wholesome and unwholesome kamma;
he was not born, nor has he not been born, nor will he not be born; he is permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change."
"Or else, a view arises in him as true and established"—thus the six views are stated with such distinctions.
Therein, "he was not unborn": that self, being subject to non-arising, is not called "born," meaning it is always already existing.
For that very reason, he did not exist in the past and will not exist in the future. For whatever is born, that existed; and whatever will be born, [that will exist].

Thus it is said, "he will be. Alternatively, because he has never not been born—that is, because he exists at all times—he has never not existed even in the past, nor will he ever not exist in the future. The latent tendencies (*anusaya*) have their meaning as already explained.
"By the seven fetters" refers to those mentioned in the *Sattaka-nipāta*. For it is said there:
“Bhikkhus, there are these seven fetters. Which seven?
The fetter of attachment, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of views, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of lust for existence, and the fetter of ignorance.
These, bhikkhus, are the seven fetters.”
Therein, the fetter of attachment (*anunayasaṃyojana*) is the fetter of sensual lust (*kāmarāgasaṃyojana*). All these are indeed "fetters" (*saṃyojana*) in the sense of being bonds.
"By the seven kinds of conceit" refers to those stated in the *Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga*. For it is said there:

"Conceit (*māna*), overweening conceit (*atimāna*), conceit beyond measure (*mānātimāna*), inferiority conceit (*omāna*), superiority conceit (*adhimāna*), the conceit 'I am' (*asmimāna*), and false conceit (*micchāmāna*)."
In this context, *māna* (conceit) is the inflation [of the mind] based on factors such as birth, without specifically referring to a person by way of superiority and so forth.
*Atimāna* (excessive conceit) is the inflation that exceeds [the truth] by thinking, "There is no one equal to me" on account of birth and so forth.

*Mānātimāna* (conceit-beyond-conceit) is the conceit arisen [thinking], "Previously this person was equal to me, but now I am superior and this person is inferior. *Ōmāna* (inferiority complex) is [the inflation] on account of birth and so forth...
The conceit "I am inferior" is simply the conceit that occurs by placing oneself below others.
"Overweening conceit" (adhimāna) is the conceit that thinks one has attained the Dhamma of the Four Truths when one has not yet attained it.

However, this overweening conceit arises in one whose virtue is purified, who is diligent in his meditation subject, who has defined name-and-form, who has dispelled doubt through the discernment of conditions, and [who contemplates] the three characteristics.

It arises in an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) who has begun insight meditation (*āraddhavipassaka*) and is contemplating the conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*) after having applied [the mind to them], but not in others.
"The conceit 'I am'" (*asmimāna*) refers to the conceit "I am" regarding the aggregates such as form;

it is said to be the conceit that arises in the manner of "I am form," and so forth. "False conceit" (*micchāmāna*) is the conceit that arises on account of a base sphere of action (*kammāyatana*), and so forth.

The world-phenomena (*lokadhammā*) have their meaning already explained. "It turns around" means that, due to the world-phenomena acting as causes, it turns violently toward the four [states] beginning with gain through attachment, and toward the four beginning with loss through aversion;

the meaning is that it abandons its natural state. The wrongnesses (*micchattā*) also have their meaning already explained. "It has gone out" means it has departed, it has plunged away; the meaning is that it has been overcome.
"By the eight faults of a man" refers to those stated together with similes in the *Aṭṭhaka-nipāta* and those stated without similes in the *Khuddakavatthu-vibhaṅga*.

For it is said there: "What are the eight faults of a man? Here, monks, they reprove a monk for an offense. Being reproved by the monks for an offense, that monk evades them out of sheer forgetfulness, saying, 'I do not remember, I do not remember.
This is the first fault of a man. Furthermore, monks reprove a monk for an offense. That monk, being reproved by the monks for an offense..."
He flares up at the very one who reproves him, saying: "What is the use of what you, a fool and an incompetent person, have to say?
Do you really think that you, too, should speak to me? This is the second fault of a person.
Furthermore, when monks reprove a monk for an offense, and that monk, being reproved by the monks for an offense...
He instead levels the charge against the accuser himself, saying, "You too have fallen into such-and-such an offense;
you should first make amends for yours. This is the third fault of a person.
Furthermore, when monks reprove a monk for an offense, that monk, being reproved by the monks for an offense...
He evades one matter with another, diverts the conversation to external topics, and displays anger, hatred, and resentment.
This is the fourth fault of a person.

Furthermore, when monks reprove a monk for an offense, that monk, being reproved by the monks for an offense in the midst of the Saṅgha, speaks while brandishing his arms. This is the fifth fault of a person.
“Furthermore, monks, monks reprove a monk for an offense.

While being reproved by the monks for an offense, that monk, disregarding the Saṅgha and disregarding the accuser, departs wherever he wishes while still possessed of the offense. This is the sixth fault of a person.
Furthermore, monks, monks reprove a monk for an offense. While being reproved by the monks for an offense...”
‘I have not committed an offense, nor am I free from offense,’ he remains silent and thereby harasses the Saṅgha. This is the seventh fault of a person.
“Furthermore, when monks reprove a monk for an offense, that monk, being reproved by the monks for an offense, says this:
‘Why, venerable sirs, are you so excessively preoccupied with me? Now I shall renounce the training.’”
‘I shall return to the lower life. Having renounced the training and returned to the lower life, he says:
‘Now, venerable sirs, you may be glad. This is the eighth fault of a person. These are the eight faults of a person.
In this context, “faults of a person” (purisadosā) means the defects of persons; they are called “faults” because they corrupt the mental continuum of a person. I do not recall...
“I do not remember”: by this he evades and releases [the charge] through lack of mindfulness, thinking, “I do not recall or perceive the place where this deed was committed.
He opposes the accuser himself means that he acts in opposition and stands as a counter-pledge.
“What indeed is yours? means: what is the use of what you, a fool and an incompetent person, have to say? You who...
It indicates: "You do not know the basis, nor the offense, nor the censure.
It overwhelms by saying: "Even you, being thus ignorant of anything, think you ought to speak. It attributes by saying: "You too indeed...
and so forth, thereby charging him with the same fault. "Confess" means: confess that which leads to confession; emerge from that which leads to emergence; then [you will be] in the state of purity.
"Once established, you will accuse another" is what this indicates. "He evades one matter with another" means that by means of another reason or statement, he conceals another reason or statement.
When told, "You have fallen into an offense," he says: "Who has fallen? What has been fallen into? In what has one fallen? How has one fallen? Whom are you speaking of? What are you saying?"
When asked, "Have you seen anything of this sort? he says, "I have not heard of it," and thus turns his ear away. How does he divert the conversation externally?
Being asked, "Have you fallen into such-and-such an offense? he replies, "We went to Pāṭaliputta.
When told again, "I am not asking about your going to Pāṭaliputta," he then says, "We went to Rājagaha. [Regarding] Rājagaha...
“Or go to the house of a brahmin; you have fallen into an offense.
How does one distract externally by saying such things as, “I obtained pork there”? *Kopa* is the state of being agitated; *dosa* is the state of being corrupted.
Both of these are names for anger (*kodha*). *Appaccaya* is the mode of dissatisfaction; it is a name for mental distress (*domanassa*). *Pātukaroti* means he manifests.
He shows; he makes manifest. "He speaks with arm-waving" means that having repeatedly waved his arms, he utters shameless words.
