"Without taking [it] to heart" means not grasping it with respect, but rather despising it; the meaning is that he is disrespectful. "He harasses" means he torments or oppresses.
"Excessively" means very strongly or beyond measure. "Engaged with me" means occupied with me.
"Having fallen away. "Having returned to the low life" means having returned for the sake of the low state of a householder; the meaning is, "having become a householder.
"Be glad" means be joyful in heart; he speaks with the intention: "Receive what you were to receive from me; dwell in the place where you were to dwell by me;
I have provided a comfortable dwelling for you. "He becomes corrupt" means he becomes wicked.
"By way of the nine grounds for malice (*āghātavatthu*)" means they are described solely according to their arising among sentient beings. As it is said:
"Monks, there are these nine grounds for malice. Which nine? One binds malice thinking, 'He has done me harm';
one binds malice thinking, 'He is doing me harm'; one binds malice thinking, 'He will do me harm'..."
“One binds a grudge, thinking: ‘He has done what is harmful to one who is dear and pleasing to me;

he is doing what is harmful; he will do what is harmful. One binds a grudge, thinking: ‘He has done what is beneficial to one who is not dear and not pleasing to me; he is doing what is beneficial; he will do what is beneficial.
These, monks, are the nine grounds for resentment.”
In this context, "bases for resentment" (*āghātavatthūni*) means causes for resentment. Here, "resentment" (*āghāta*) refers to anger;
and because that very anger serves as the basis for successive outbursts of anger, it is called a "basis for resentment. "One binds resentment" means one binds, performs, or generates anger.
[The bases are: "He has not acted for my benefit, he does not act, nor will he act; he has not acted for the benefit of what is dear and pleasing to me, he does not act..."
"He has not acted, does not act, and will not act for the harm of one who is disagreeable and unpleasant to me.
These other nine grounds for resentment mentioned in the *Niddesa* are also included within these same nine. "Resentful" (*āghātita*) means provoked.

Regarding "by the ninefold conceits" (*navavidhamānehi*): what are the ninefold conceits? The conceit "I am superior" in relation to one who is superior; the conceit "I am equal" in relation to one who is superior... [and so on].
The conceit "I am inferior" regarding one who is superior; the conceit "I am superior" regarding one who is equal; the conceit "I am equal" regarding one who is equal;
the conceit "I am inferior" regarding one who is equal; the conceit "I am superior" regarding one who is inferior; the conceit "I am equal" regarding one who is inferior;
and the conceit "I am inferior" regarding one who is inferior. These are the nine types of conceit.
In this context, however, the conceit "I am superior to one who is superior" arises both among kings and among those who have gone forth.
For a king forms this conceit, thinking, "Who is my equal in terms of kingdom, wealth, or vehicles?
and one who has gone forth likewise forms this conceit, thinking, "Who is my equal in terms of virtue, ascetic practices, and so forth?"

The conceit "I am equal to those who are superior" also arises among these very same people. For a king thinks, "What difference is there between me and other kings in terms of kingdom, wealth, or vehicles?

and thus he exercises this conceit; likewise, one who has gone forth thinks, "What difference is there between me and another monk in terms of virtue, ascetic practices, and so forth? and thus he exercises this conceit.
The conceit, "I am inferior to those who are better," also arises in these very persons.
For instance, a king whose kingdom, wealth, or vehicles and so forth are not abundant might harbor this conceit: "My title of 'king' is merely a source of conventional pleasure;
what is a 'king' anyway? Likewise, a renunciant who receives little gain or honor might think: "I am a preacher of the Dhamma..."
He conceives this pride, thinking: "It is a mere matter of words that I am 'learned,' a 'great elder'—what kind of Dhamma-preacher am I?
What kind of learned one am I? What kind of great elder am I, since I have no gain or honor?
Pride such as "I am superior to my equal" arises in ministers and others. For it may be a minister or a provincial official...
He conceives this pride, thinking: "What other royal official is equal to me in terms of enjoyments, vehicles, mounts, and so forth?
or "What distinction is there between me and others? or "I have the mere name 'minister,' yet I do not even have enough food and clothing;
what kind of minister am I? Thus he creates this pride.
Inferior persons give rise to conceit such as "I am superior" toward those who are their masters and so forth. For instance, a slave might think:
"As for my mother or my father, what other slave is there like me? Others became slaves because they were unable to support themselves and were born into slavery due to the condition of their wombs;
but I am superior because I have come down through a pure lineage," or because of his status as one descended from a pure lineage on both sides and being a slave of pure descent.

Or he conceives this conceit: "What difference is there between me and such-and-such a slave? Or: "I entered into slavery by way of my womb, but in terms of my mother and father's lineage, I have no status as a slave;
what am I, after all, a slave? Just as a slave does, so too do outcasts (pukkusa), caṇḍālas, and others likewise conceive this conceit. In this regard—

Furthermore, for one who is superior, the conceit arisen as "I am superior" is conceit that accords with reality (*yāthāvamāna*); the other two are conceits that do not accord with reality (*ayāthāvamāna*).
Likewise, for one who is equal, the conceit "I am equal," and for one who is inferior, the conceit "I am inferior," are conceits that accord with reality;

the other two are conceits that do not accord with reality. Among these, the conceits that accord with reality are to be abandoned by the path of Arahatship, while the conceits that do not accord with reality are to be abandoned by the path of Stream-entry.
It has already been stated that [these states] are rooted in craving (*taṇhāmūlaka*). "He is stained" (*rajjati*) means that he is not stained by lust (*rāga*) alone;

rather, since seeking and so forth—which are rooted in craving—also arise, the intended meaning is that he is stained, joined with, and bound by all unwholesome states (*akusaladhamma*) rooted in craving.

"By the ten bases of defilement": what are the ten bases of defilement? Greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, doubt, sloth, restlessness, lack of moral shame, and lack of moral dread—these are the ten bases of defilement.

In this context, they are called "bases of defilement" because they are themselves defilements; or else, they are "bases" because beings whose taints are not yet exhausted dwell there, being established upon greed and so forth.
Furthermore, they are "bases of defilement" because they are both defilements and the bases for beings who are established upon them. Since...
And herein, although the defilements arise by way of being immediate conditions (*anantarapaccaya*) and so forth, they are said to "dwell" [therein];
therefore, they are called "bases of defilement" (*kilesavatthu*). That by which one is greedy, or which itself is greedy, or which is merely the state of greed—that is greed (*lobha*).
That by which one is corrupted, or which itself is corrupted, or which is merely the state of corruption—that is hatred (*dosa*).
Delusion (*moha*) is so called because by it one is deluded, or one is oneself deluded, or it is merely the state of being deluded. "He conceives" (*maññati*) is pride (*māna*).
Views (*diṭṭhi*) and the rest have already been explained in their respective meanings. One who does not feel shame is shameless (*ahirika*); the state of that is shamelessness (*ahirika*).

One who does not feel dread of blame is reckless (*anottappī*); the state of that is recklessness (*anottappa*). Among these, shamelessness has the characteristic of lacking disgust toward bodily misconduct and the like.
Lack of moral dread (*anottappa*) has the characteristic of not being afraid of those very things [that cause fear]. It is "afflicted" (*kilissati*) in the sense that it is tormented and oppressed.
"By the ten bases for resentment" (*āghātavatthu*): this refers to the nine previously mentioned, together with the tenth stated as "or resentment arises toward what is inappropriate" (*aṭṭhāne*).
For resentment arises even toward what is inappropriate—such as a stump or a thorn—even without conceptualizing [the other nine], such as "He has done me harm," and so forth.
"By means of the ten unwholesome courses of action. What are the ten unwholesome courses of action?
Killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view.
These are the ten unwholesome courses of action. In this context, they are both unwholesome kamma and paths.
"Bad destinations" refers to the unwholesome courses of action. "Endowed with" means being possessed of them.
Regarding "by ten fetters," what are the ten fetters? They are:
the fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of views, the fetter of doubt, and the fetter of adherence to rules and observances.
The fetter of lust for existence, the fetter of envy, the fetter of avarice, and the fetter of ignorance—these are the ten fetters.
The wrongnesses have already been stated. Regarding "wrong view with ten bases": what is wrong view with ten bases? There is no giving... [and so forth].
"There is no sacrifice, there is no offering, there is no fruit or ripening of deeds well done or ill done;
there is no this world, there is no other world, there is no mother, there is no father, there are no beings spontaneously born;
there are in the world no recluses or brahmins who have fared rightly and practiced rightly, who have themselves realized this world and the other world."
Having realized them through direct knowledge, they declare them. This is wrong view with ten bases (*dasavatthukā micchādiṭṭhi*).
In this context, "with ten bases" means that it has ten bases. Regarding "there is no giving":
one knows that there is such a thing as giving—that it is possible to give something to someone—but [one holds] that there is no fruit or result of what has been given.
He grasps [this view]. He thinks, "There is no sacrifice (*yiṭṭha*)," for *yiṭṭha* refers to a great sacrifice;

he knows that it is possible to perform such a sacrifice, yet he grasps that there is no fruit or result (*vipāka*) from that sacrifice. He thinks, "There is no offering (*huta*)," for *huta* refers to acts of hospitality, invitations, and auspicious rites;
he knows that it is possible to perform them, yet he grasps that there is no fruit or result from them. Regarding the phrase "of well-done and ill-done deeds": here...
The ten courses of wholesome action are called "well-done deeds," and the ten courses of unwholesome action are called "ill-done deeds.
He recognizes their existence, yet he maintains that there is no fruit or result.

Thinking "this world does not exist," while standing in the world beyond, he maintains that this world does not exist. Thinking "the other world does not exist," while standing in this world, [he maintains that the other world does not exist].
He grasps at the notion that "it does not exist. He grasps at the non-existence of mother and father, even though he knows their actual existence;

he grasps at the idea that no fruit or result arises from the service rendered to them. He grasps at the notion that "there are no spontaneously born beings," meaning he grasps at the non-existence of beings who pass away and are reborn.
"Those who have fared rightly, those who have practiced rightly" refers to those who have entered upon the conformable practice—the righteous recluses and brahmins.

He holds that "there is no one in the world. He holds that "there is no omniscient Buddha capable of proclaiming [the truth] after having known this world... [and so on]... and the other world by means of his own preeminent knowledge.
Regarding "extreme views": it is called an extreme view because it grasps one side or one extreme, such as "the world is eternal," and so forth.

Alternatively, "extreme-grasping" (*antaggāha*) means grasping at an extreme; that which possesses such grasping is "extremist" (*antaggāhikā*). It is by means of that extremist [view]. That [view] has already been explained.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the eight hundred and one hundred proliferations of craving" (*taṇhāpapañca*): one hundred and eight is "eight hundred. It is called "proliferation" (*papañca*) because it causes one to proliferate in saṃsāra and makes one dwell there for a long time;
craving itself is the proliferation, hence "craving-proliferation. This is due to its repeated arising with respect to various objects.
And because craving is manifold, the plural form is used; thus, "of a hundred manifestations of craving" (*taṇhāpapañcasataṃ*) means [the same as] "of a hundred manifestations of craving.

Although one should have said "by a hundred manifestations of craving" (*taṇhāpapañcasatena*), the designation in the plural, "by a hundred manifestations of craving" (*taṇhāpapañcasatehi*), is made by way of a grammatical inversion (*vacanavipallāsa*).
The meaning should be understood as "by that hundred manifestations of craving known as the eight hundred."
It should be understood that, having set aside the eight non-expressible [cravings], only the seven are taken here.
However, in the *Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga*, they appear as "the eighteen modes of craving's wandering. As it is said:
"There are eighteen modes of craving's wandering based on the internal [person], and eighteen modes of craving's wandering based on the external [objects]."
“Having taken these up and having combined and condensed them together, there are thirty-six modes of craving’s wandering. Thus, the thirty-six modes of craving’s wandering in the past,
the thirty-six modes of craving’s wandering in the future, and the thirty-six modes of craving’s wandering in the present—
having taken these up and having combined and condensed them together— there are one hundred and eight modes of craving’s wandering.”
In this context, however, it is craving's own proliferations that are called "craving's wanderings. The meaning is: the manifestations of craving, the occurrences of craving.
"Depending on the internal" means depending on the fivefold aggregate of the internal. For here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.
Its detailed exposition should be understood according to the method already stated in its respective commentary (*Niddesa*). Furthermore, this other...

The method is as follows: there are three types of craving—craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*), craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*), and craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*)—which have visible forms as their object alone.
Likewise, with sounds and the other objects, there are eighteen types of craving for each of the six objects.
There are eighteen with internal objects and eighteen with external objects, making thirty-six. Those same [thirty-six] have past objects, and thirty-six have future objects.
Thirty-six with present objects and thirty-six with future objects—thus there are one hundred and eight modes of craving’s wandering (*taṇhāvicarita*).
"Proliferated" (*papañcita*) means proliferated or long-dwelled upon an object, or within *saṃsāra*.
Regarding the sixty-two views: "Which are the sixty-two types of views? In the *Brahmajāla* exposition..."

Were these spoken by the Blessed One? These are: the four eternalist views, the four partial-eternalist views, the four views on finitude and infinity, the four eel-wrigglers, the two fortuitous-originationists, the sixteen views on percipient beings, the eight views on non-percipient beings, the eight views on neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient beings, the seven annihilationist views, and the five views on Nibbāna in this very life. These are they.
"The sixty-two speculative views were spoken of by the Blessed One in the *Brahmajāla* exposition.
The detailed account here should be understood according to the method set forth in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.
"And I have crossed over" means that I have crossed over the four floods, or the ocean of saṃsāra. "Freed" means...
"Released from the bonds of lust and so forth. "Tamed" means free from worldly affectation and without agitation. "Peaceful" means become cool.
"Comforted" means having found relief through the vision of Nibbāna. "Parinibbuted" means parinibbuted by the parinibbāna of the defilements (*kilesa*).

"I am able" means I am capable. The particle *kho* is a fixed expression used for emphasis. Regarding the phrase "and [I am able] to cause others to attain parinibbāna," here the word *ca* following *pare* [functions as a conjunction].
It should also be connected with the phrases beginning with “and may he ferry others across.
The commentary on the description of the knowledge of great compassion is finished.
72–73. Commentary on the Description of Omniscient Knowledge.

119. In the exposition of the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), having asked, "What is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of omniscience?", the unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*) is explained together with that very [knowledge], because they share the same destination. For there is no unobstructed knowledge separate from the nature of phenomena (*dhamma*);
it is this single knowledge that is spoken of in two ways according to its different aspects, such as the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) and the power of faith (*saddhābala*).

Indeed, there is no obstruction whatsoever to this omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*); because it is impossible for any phenomenon (*dhamma*) or person (*puggala*) to create an obstruction, it is called "unobstructed" (*anāvaraṇa*). This is because all phenomena are dependent upon adverting (*āvajjana*).
Others, however, do not know even after they have adverted. Some, moreover, say: "Because it takes everything as its object, like mental consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*)."
It is the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). That very same knowledge is "unobstructed knowledge" (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*) because it is unimpeded regarding its objects, like Indra’s thunderbolt.
The knowledge of omniscience is the negation of gradual omniscience; unobstructed knowledge is the negation of instantaneous omniscience.
The Blessed One is called "omniscient" by virtue of having attained the knowledge of omniscience, yet he is not one who knows all things gradually.
"One is called 'omniscient' (sabbaññū) because of the attainment of unobstructed knowledge, yet one is not omniscient all at once.
In the phrase "he knows everything conditioned and unconditioned without remainder," "everything" (sabbam) refers to the complete inclusion of all phenomena by way of their classes;
"without remainder" (anavasesam) refers to the complete inclusion of every single phenomenon by way of all its aspects.
The demonstration of the twofold classification as "the conditioned" and "the unconditioned": for the conditioned is one division, and the unconditioned is the other division.
That which is made by coming together through conditions is "conditioned"; this refers to the pentad of aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*).
That which is not so conditioned is "unconditioned"; this refers to *nibbāna*. One knows the conditioned in its entirety through such aspects as impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
It knows the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) in its entirety through such aspects as emptiness (*suññatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*appaṇihita*).
It is "without remainder" (*anavasesa*) because there is no remainder of either the conditioned or the unconditioned left out. Both the conditioned and the unconditioned are included;

for although designation (*paññatti*) has many divisions, it belongs to the side of the unconditioned because it is not produced by conditions. Indeed, the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) encompasses all...
He knows the designations according to their manifold divisions. Alternatively, "all" refers to the inclusion of all phenomena (*dhamma*).

"Without remainder" refers to an inclusive, exhaustive inclusion. "Therein there is no obstruction" means that because the knowledge of omniscience is unattached to those [phenomena]—both conditioned and unconditioned, without exception—there is no obstruction therein;
thus, the meaning is that this very knowledge of omniscience is called "unobstructed knowledge."

120. Now, in order to show [the objects] according to the distinction of their various domains, he says "past," and so forth. Therein, "past, future, and present" is shown by way of the distinction of time;
"the eye and forms," and so forth, is by way of the distinction of base and object. "All that" thus refers to the exhaustive inclusion of those eyes and forms.
The same applies to the remaining [bases and objects]. "As far as" signifies exhaustive inclusion.

The passage beginning with "the meaning of impermanence" (*aniccaṭṭha*) is shown according to the classification of the general characteristics (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*). "The meaning of impermanence" (*aniccaṭṭha*) refers to the aspect of impermanence (*aniccākāra*);

or, it is the accusative case used in the sense of the reflexive pronoun (*paccattatthe*). This same method applies to similar instances. The passage beginning with "of form" (*rūpassa*) is shown according to the classification of the aggregates (*khandha*).

The sequence from "of the eye" (*cakkhussa*) up to "of aging-and-death" (*jarāmaraṇassa*) should be connected according to the method of the series (*peyyāla*) stated previously. In the passages beginning with "by direct knowledge" (*abhiññāya*), it is precisely the types of knowledge mentioned previously that are intended.

The "meaning of direct knowledge" (*abhiññaṭṭha*) is the nature of higher knowing (*abhijānana*). This same method applies to similar terms. The "meaning of aggregates" (*khandhaṭṭha*) for the aggregates, and so forth, should be understood according to the method already explained below.

The passage beginning with "wholesome states" (*kusale dhamme*) is a classification by way of the triad of the wholesome; that beginning with "states of the sense sphere" (*kāmāvacare dhamme*) is by way of the four planes.
In both instances, the plural reading "he knows all" (*sabbe jānāti*) is preferable.

However, because it fell under the category of the singular number, it was written in the singular in the manuscripts. "Of suffering," and so forth, refers to the differentiation of the objects of the fourteen Buddha-knowledges.

If one asks why the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) was not mentioned after stating the four knowledges beginning with the knowledge of the degrees of others' faculties (*indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa*), it is because what is being discussed here is [only] the knowledge of omniscience in terms of its specific object.

Indeed, when omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) is being discussed, that [specific] knowledge cannot be said [to be the object]; however, omniscient knowledge is certainly the objective domain of omniscient knowledge.

Furthermore, demonstrating the ground of omniscient knowledge according to the method stated in the *Kāḷakārāma-sutta* and other discourses, he said: "As far as the world with its devas," and so forth.
Therein, "with the devas" means *sadevakassa*; "with Māra" means *samārakassa*; "with Brahmā" means *sabrahmakassa*.
Of the world together with Brahmā; together with recluses and brahmins, including the assembly of recluses and brahmins; together with gods and humans, including the generation of gods and humans.
Because it is born (*pajāta*), it is called "the generation" (*pajā*); this is a synonym for the world of beings.

In that context, by the term "together with gods," the inclusion is of the five classes of sense-sphere gods; by the term "together with Māra," the inclusion is of the sixth class of sense-sphere gods.
By the phrase "together with Brahmā," there is the inclusion of the Brahmakāyika and other classes of deities belonging to the Brahmā realm;

by the phrase "together with recluses and brahmins," there is the inclusion of those recluses and brahmins who are adversaries and enemies of the Teaching, as well as those recluses and brahmins who have stilled evil and cast out evil;

by the word "generation" (pajā), there is the inclusion of the world of sentient beings; and by the phrase "together with gods and humans," there is the inclusion of conventional gods and the remainder of the human race.
It should be understood thus: here, by three terms the world of space (*okāsaloka*) is included, and by two terms the world of beings (*sattaloka*) is included according to their generation.

Another method: by the inclusion of "together with devas," the formless realm (*arūpāvacaraloka*) is included; by the inclusion of "together with Māras," the sixfold sense-sphere deva-world (*chakāmāvacaradevaloka*) is included;

by the inclusion of "together with Brahmas," the form-sphere Brahma-world (*rūpāvacarabrahmaloka*) is included; and by the inclusion of "with recluses and brahmins, etc.," the fourfold assembly (*catuparisā*) is included.
Either the world of humans together with the conventional gods (*sammutideva*), or the remaining world of beings.
Furthermore, by the term "together with the gods" (*sadevaka*), it establishes, by way of the highest limit, that the entire world possesses the quality of knowing what is seen and so forth.
Consequently, for those who might think: "Māra is of great power, the lord of the six sense-sphere realms, and a master of his own will; what [then] of him?"...
In order to dispel their doubt by saying, "He knows the seen and so forth," he said, "together with Māra.
However, for those who might think, "Brahmā is of great power; with one finger he radiates light throughout one thousand world-systems, with two...
[and so on]... with ten fingers he radiates light throughout ten thousand world-systems, and he possesses the unsurpassed bliss of meditative absorption (jhāna-samāpatti)," [the Buddha spoke thus].
[If one asks,] "Does he perceive it, and does he know their views and so forth as well?"—dispelling their doubt, he said, "of the world including the Brahmās.
Then, for those who might think, "There are many ascetics and brahmins who are adversaries of the Teaching;
does he know their views and so forth as well?"—dispelling their doubt, he said, "of the generation including the ascetics and brahmins. Thus, [he spoke] of those who are superior.

Having manifested the state of knowing what is seen and so forth, he then manifests the state of knowing what is seen and so forth regarding the rest of the world of beings—starting from conventional deities and the remaining humans—by way of the highest possible limit. This is the sequence of connection here.
However, the ancients have said: "Of the world together with its devas" means of the remainder of the world along with the devas; "together with Māra" means along with Māra.
"Of the rest of the world. "Together with Brahmā" means together with the Brahmās and the rest of the world.

Thus, having included all beings subject to the three realms of existence within three categories in three ways, he spoke again of "the generation with its recluses and brahmins, its devas and humans" in order to encompass them further by way of two categories.
In this manner, by means of these five phrases and through their respective modes, he has [described] precisely the threefold realm (*tedhātuka*).
"It is exhausted" means:
"Seen" refers to the sense-sphere of visible forms (*rūpāyatana*). "HearD" refers to the sense-sphere of sounds (*saddāyatana*).

"Sensed" refers to the sense-spheres of odors, tastes, and tangibles (*gandhāyatana*, *rasāyatana*, *phoṭṭhabbāyatana*), because they are to be grasped by reaching [them]. "Cognized" refers to the mental objects (*dhammārammaṇa*) such as pleasure, pain, and so forth. "Attained" refers to...
"Whether sought after or not sought after, the bowl. "Sought after" means that which has been sought, whether the bowl has been reached or not.
"Mentally traversed" means it has been mentally roamed over by the mind. By the phrase "he knows all," this is shown:
whatever form-object there is in the immeasurable world-systems of this world with its devas, such as "blue," "yellow," and so forth.

When something comes into the range of the eye-door, the omniscient knowledge of the Tathāgata knows all this: "At this very moment, having seen such-and-such a material object, this being has become glad, dejected, or neutral.
Likewise, throughout immeasurable world-systems, regarding this world with its devas, [he knows] the sound of drums...

The sound of a drum and so forth, as an object of sound, comes into the range of the ear-door; the scent of roots, the scent of bark, and so forth, as an object of odor, comes into the range of the nose-door;
the taste of roots, the taste of stems, and so forth, as an object of flavor, comes into the range of the tongue-door;
and that which is divided into the earth element, fire element, and air element—such as "hard" or "soft"—[comes into the range of the body-door].
When a tangible object as an objective field comes into the range of the body door, the Tathāgata’s omniscient knowledge knows all this:
"At this very moment, having touched such a tangible object, this being has become glad, dejected, or neutral.
Likewise, regarding this world with its devas throughout immeasurable world-systems...
When an object consisting of phenomena—distinguished as pleasure, pain, and so forth—enters the range of the mind-door, the Tathāgata’s omniscient knowledge knows all this:
"At this very moment, having cognized such an objective phenomenon, this being has become glad, dejected, or neutral.
Furthermore, having investigated this great multitude of people...
There is that which has not been attained; there is also that which has been attained after searching. There is that which has not been attained without searching;
there is also that which has been attained without searching. For the Tathāgata, through his omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), there is nothing whatsoever that is called "unattained.
121. Furthermore, by another method, for the purpose of establishing the state of omniscience, he recited the verse beginning with "na tassa" (not for him).

In this context, "there is nothing whatsoever unseen by him" means that for that Tathāgata, in this world of the three realms or in this present time, there is not even the slightest thing that is called "unseen" or does not exist.
The word *atthi* is a verb expressing the present tense. By this, [it refers to] that which belongs to the present time.
This shows that all phenomena (dhamma) are objects of knowledge. Here, the letter *da* is joined [to the preceding vowel] for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse composition.

In the phrase "and what is not yet known" (*atho aviññātaṃ*), *atho* is a particle used as a syntactical connector. "Not yet known" (*aviññātaṃ*) refers to some class of phenomena (*dhammajātaṃ*) that was unknown in the past.
The word "was not" (*nāhosi*) is to be supplied as a remainder of the text. When the indeclinable word *atthi* ("is") is understood, the remainder of the text [is thus completed].
It is indeed appropriate even without [the negative particle]. By this, he shows that all phenomena belonging to the past are objects of knowledge.
"That which is not to be known" means that there will be no class of phenomena belonging to the future that is not to be known, or none exists.
By this, he shows that all phenomena belonging to the future are objects of knowledge. Alternatively, here the vowel *a* is merely a grammatical marker for the action of knowing (*jānana*).

Regarding the phrase "He directly knew all that there is to be known": here, whatever category of phenomena (*dhammajāta*) there may be that is to be known—whether pertaining to the three times or timeless—that the Tathāgata directly knew;
he knew and penetrated it by means of his supreme knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
Here, because the word "there is" (*atthi*) includes both what pertains to the three times and what is timeless, the word "there is" [is used].

He should be seen as being truly immutable. The Tathāgata is "all-seeing" (*samantacakkhu*) because, by virtue of both time and space, his eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*) functions universally and without exception; thus he is all-seeing.
For the reasons stated above, it is said that the Tathāgata is all-seeing and omniscient. This verse is based on the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*).
Through this teaching, omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) has been established.
Furthermore, wishing to demonstrate omniscient knowledge by way of the range of the Buddha’s knowledges, he said: "Samantacakkhu— in what sense is it 'all-around eye'?
and so forth. In that regard, concerning the word *samantacakkhu* spoken in the verse, as for that which is the all-around eye:
In what sense does it have the meaning of "all-seeing eye" (*samantacakkhu*)? Its meaning is indeed expressed by such phrases as "to the extent of the meaning of suffering, of suffering.
For omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) is the all-seeing eye. As it is said: "The all-seeing eye is called omniscient knowledge.
When that state of omniscient knowledge is stated, the state of the all-seeing eye is likewise stated.
"Are" means they exist. "Buddha-knowledges" (buddhañāṇāni) means the knowledges belonging only to a Buddha.
For while the knowledge of suffering and so forth occur in every aspect only for the Blessed One, the Buddha, in others they occur only in a mere partial measure.
However, the phrase "shared with disciples" is said with reference to their existence even in a partial measure. "All is known" means all is known by means of knowledge. It is "understood" (aññāta).
The statement "there is no state of suffering" clarifies by way of negation the very meaning already stated.
"All has been seen" means not merely known, but rather made as if seen with the eye. "All has been understood" means not merely seen, but rather made manifest.
"All has been realized" means not merely understood, but rather through the attainment of knowledge regarding that [truth].
"Realized" (*paccakkhīkato*): "Touched in its entirety" (*sabbaṃ phassito*) means not only realized, but moreover touched again and again through its manifestation according to one's inclination.
Alternatively, it is "known" (*ñāto*) by way of its specific characteristic (*sabhāva-lakkhaṇa*); "seen" (*diṭṭho*) by way of its general characteristic (*sāmañña-lakkhaṇa*);

"understood" (*vidito*) by way of its function (*rasa*); "realized" (*sacchikato*) by way of its manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*); and "touched" (*phassito*) by way of its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*). Then...

Or it is "known" by way of the arising of knowledge; "seen" by way of the arising of the eye; "recognized" by way of the arising of wisdom (*paññā*); "realized" by way of the arising of true insight (*vijjā*);
and "touched" by way of the arising of light. And according to the method beginning with: "To whatever extent there is the state of suffering in suffering, all that has been seen;
there is no state of suffering not seen," and so forth, up to: "To whatever extent there is the world including its devas... [etc.]..."
The detailed explanation should be understood according to the method beginning with: "It was investigated by the mind; everything is known; there is nothing unknown.
The verse stated first is repeated here as a conclusion. For when the conclusion to that [subject] is made, the conclusion to the knowledge itself is also effectively made.
The commentary on the description of the knowledge of omniscience is finished.
The Explanation of the Discourse on Knowledge in the *Saddhammappakāsinī*, the Commentary on the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, is completed. 2.
The Discourse on Views.
1. Commentary on the Exposition of the View of Gratification (Assādadiṭṭhiniddesa) 122.
Now, following the discussion on knowledge, the sequential commentary on the discussion of views has arrived.
For this discussion of views serves to purify the stain of wrong view in one who has gained proficiency in knowledge through the preceding discussion on knowledge and who has attained right view.
It is easy [to attain], and right view becomes perfectly pure; thus, this discourse on knowledge was spoken immediately after the previous one.
In that context, the questions beginning with "What is view? are the inquiries. The response to those inquiries begins with "What is view? Adherence and misapprehension are view.
The detailed exposition of the answer follows the response, beginning with "How is adherence and misapprehension view? and so forth.
"All those views" refers to the "views-sutta correlation," beginning with "the view of gratification," and so forth;

thus there are these four chapters. Among them, in the Chapter on Questions (*Pucchāpariccheda*), first, "What is a view? is a question concerning phenomena (*dhamma-pucchā*) and a question concerning intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-pucchā*).

"How many bases for views (*diṭṭhi-ṭṭhāna*) are there? is a question concerning causes (*hetu-pucchā*) and a question concerning conditions (*paccaya-pucchā*); the meaning is: "How many are the causal factors for views?"
“How many obsessions by views?”: this is a question concerning manifestation and a question concerning modification.
For it is precisely the views that, by way of manifesting, arise as they envelop the mind; thus they are called “obsessions by views. “How many views?”:
this is a question concerning the enumeration of views and a question concerning their number. “How many dogmatic adherences to views?”: [this is] by way of the classification of their bases.

The question concerning the classification of views by way of the diversity of objects (*ārammaṇanānattavasena*). For it is precisely views that adhere to and misapprehend various bases as various objects;
thus they are called "misapprehensions by view" (*diṭṭhiparāmāsa*). "What is the uprooting of the basis for views?

is a question regarding the antidote to views and a question regarding the means of abandonment. For the aggregates and so forth, which are the causes of views, [are abandoned] through the uprooting of views.

Because their causes do not exist, those causes are said to have been eradicated. Therefore, it is called the "eradication of the bases of views" because by means of this, the bases of views are thoroughly and completely destroyed.
Now, regarding these six questions, there are six answers beginning with "What is the view? and so forth. In that context: "What is the view?"
The question to be answered is: "What is wrong view? The answer is: "Adherence through misapprehension is wrong view.
Now, it is called *abhinivesa* because it adheres to, establishes itself upon, and grasps firmly at a basis such as the impermanent by way of [perceiving it as] permanent and so forth.

It is called *parāmāsa* because, having transcended the actual mode [of being] such as impermanence, it reaches out to and grasps [the object] by way of [conceiving it as] permanent and so forth. Alternatively:

"Parāmāsa" means that which touches upon or grasps as "supreme" or "ultimate" that which is [actually] permanent and so forth; it is thus "adherence," and being both adherence and supreme, it is "adherence-supreme" (*abhinivesa-parāmāsa*).
By stating "such a kind is a view" (*diṭṭhi*), he explains the essential nature of a view in terms of its function.
"Three hundred" means three hundreds; a change in the wording has been made. "What is the eradication of the basis for views?"—this is the question.
The answer has been given that the path of stream-entry itself is the eradication of the basis for views, even without further extraction. 123.
Now follows the detailed exposition beginning with "How is it clinging and misapprehension? and so forth. Therein, "form" (*rūpa*) is the accusative case.

The connection is: "Form is clinging and misapprehension. And here, "form" refers both to the aggregate of form-clinging (*rūpupādānakkhandha*) and to the form of the meditation objects (*kasiṇa-rūpa*).
The adherence through insistence that “this is mine” is a view; the adherence through insistence that “I am this” is a view;
the adherence through insistence that “this is my self” is a view—these should be applied respectively. “This” (*etaṃ*) is a term of general reference.
For that very reason, in the passage “this feeling is mine, these formations are mine,” the neuter gender and the singular number are employed.
However, the masculine singular form is used here with reference to what is to be said [later]. "This is mine" is a view rooted in the conceiving of craving (*taṇhā-maññanā*).
"I am this" is a view rooted in the conceiving of conceit (*māna-maññanā*). "This is my self" is simply the conceiving of views (*diṭṭhi-maññanā*).

Some, however, say: "'This is mine' is the construction of 'mine-making' (*mamam-kāra*); 'I am this' is the construction of 'I-making' (*aham-kāra*); 'This is my self' is that which is constructed by both 'I-making' and 'mine-making'."

The adherence to a self (*attābhinivesa*) is thus, in due order, the settling based on craving as its root, the grasping by conceit; it is the adherence to a self settled upon by craving and grasped by conceit.

Furthermore, the adherence to a self is caused by not seeing the characteristic of suffering in formations (*saṅkhāra*), not seeing the characteristic of impermanence in formations, and not seeing the three characteristics in formations. [This occurs] regarding suffering...
For one who has fallen into the perversion of perceiving pleasure in the foul and beauty in the ugly; for one who has fallen into the perversion of perceiving permanence in the impermanent;

and for one who has fallen into the fourfold perversion and clings to a self—there is the conceptualization regarding past lives for the knowledge of recollecting past existences, the conceptualization regarding future acquisition for the knowledge of the divine eye, and the clinging to a self based on conceptualization regarding phenomena that have arisen through dependent origination with their conditions throughout the past and future limits.
Furthermore: "One pursues the past through delight; one longs for the future through delight; and regarding present phenomena, there is the adherence to a self due to being carried away [by them].
Also, there is the view caused by ignorance regarding the past; the view caused by ignorance regarding the future;
and the adherence to a self caused by ignorance regarding the past and the future, as well as regarding phenomena arisen through specific conditionality and dependent origination."
And they explain the meaning of these three statements as follows:
Herein, first, the views have the five aggregates as their basis.

Following that, there are the six internal and external sense bases, the body of consciousness, the body of contact, the body of feeling, the body of perception, the body of volition, the body of craving, the body of applied thought, the body of sustained thought, and the tenfold kasiṇa-element.

The views based on the thirty-two aspects have been stated. And regarding those thirty-two aspects, it should be understood that wherever a separate adherence is not logically possible, a separate adherence is treated as if it were made by way of adherence to the entire body.
Following that, the application was made by way of the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and the nineteen faculties. [Therein are] three faculties that are exclusively supramundane.

They are not included. For views do not have supramundane things as their basis. Furthermore, in all cases where mundane and supramundane phenomena are mixed, one should exclude the supramundane and take only the mundane. And matter not bound by the faculties (anindriyabaddha-rūpa) is certainly not to be included.

Then, [the mundane] is classified according to the three realms, according to the ninefold existence, according to the meditative absorptions (jhāna), the divine abodes (brahmavihāra), and the attainments (samāpatti), and according to the factors of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).
And the coordination has been made. The method of exemption regarding the separate mention of birth, aging, and death is exactly as previously stated.
All these factors, beginning with form and ending with aging and death, amount to one hundred and ninety-eight terms. 124.
Regarding the bases of views (*diṭṭhiṭṭhāna*), the aggregates (*khandha*) are also bases of views; thus, even for the embodiment-view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) consisting of twenty bases...
Because the five aggregates alone serve as the basis [for the notion of self], and because it has been said:

"Bhikkhus, whatever recluses or brahmins regard anything as self, they all regard it as the five aggregates of clinging, or one or another of them," the five aggregates of clinging are the cause of views. Ignorance, too, [is a cause].
“Basis for views” means that because views arise in those blinded by ignorance, [it is said]: “Venerable sir, as for this view:
‘Those who are not perfectly enlightened Buddhas are perfectly enlightened Buddhas,’ venerable sir, on what basis does this view appear?
Venerable Kaccāna, this is a great element, namely the element of ignorance (avijjādhātu). It arises, Kaccāna, dependent upon a base element.”
And because of the statement, "Low is perception, low is view," ignorance is the cause of views.
Contact (*phassa*) is also a basis for views, because views arise in one who is touched by that contact; as it is said:
"Those recluses and brahmins, bhikkhus, who are speculators about the past, who hold views regarding the past, and who assert various kinds of propositions concerning the past—that too..."

And because of the statement, "With contact as condition," contact is the cause of views. Perception (*saññā*) is also a basis for views because it is the cause for grasping things as they are not in their true nature by means of apprehending mere appearances.
Thus: "Those sixty-two [views] and those three, O one of vast wisdom, which are the seats of the recluses' doctrines..."
Because of the statement, “Having removed the resorts based on the perception of signs and sounds,

he has gone beyond the flood,” and because of the statement, “For conceptual proliferation (papañca-saṅkhā) has its source in perception (saññā-nidāna),” perception is the cause of views. Thought (vitakka) also is a basis for views, because views arise through the process of investigating modes—
“There are not indeed many various truths in the world, other than perceptions which are permanent.”

And from the statement: "Having fashioned for themselves various views, they have declared the two-fold dhamma of 'truth' and 'falsehood,'" it follows that *vitakka* (applied thought) is the cause of views.

Furthermore, since inappropriate attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*) is a basis for views, and because inappropriate attention is the unique cause of unwholesome states, [it is said]: "For one who attends inappropriately in this way, of the six..."
And because of the statement, "One or another view arises," improper attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*) is the cause of views.
Furthermore, a bad friend (*pāpamitta*) is also a ground for views; for since a view arises through following the example of a bad friend’s views, [the Buddha said]:
"Bhikkhus, considering external factors, I do not see even a single factor that leads to such great harm as this."
...it leads [to this]. And because of the statement, "Bhikkhus, it is just like this: bad friendship is the cause of views," one who has bad friends is the cause of views.
Furthermore, "the voice of another is a basis for views" means that views arise through hearing the poorly expounded Dhamma; thus:
"Bhikkhus, there are these two causes and two conditions for the arising of wrong view: the voice of another and improper attention..."
And because of the statement, “and attention,” the voice of another—consisting of discourse associated with wrong view from one who holds wrong view—is the cause of views.
Now, explaining the meaning of the term *diṭṭhiṭṭhāna* (basis of views), he says: “The aggregates are the cause; the aggregates are the condition,” and so forth.

The meaning is that the aggregates themselves, by way of clinging, are both the productive cause (*janakahetu*) and the supporting condition (*upatthambhakapaccaya*) for views. [He says this] in the sense of their being the source (*samuṭṭhāna*).
"Samuṭṭhāna" means that by which things arise or originate; the meaning is "cause. Thus, "in the sense of being a source" means in the sense of being the cause for views. 125.
Now, showing the classification of views according to their functions, he said: "What are the eighteen obsessions of views? and so forth.
In this context, "whatever view" is the common root term for the eighteen phrases that are about to be stated. The connection should be made with all of them as follows:
"Whatever is a view, that itself is a 'course of views' (diṭṭhigata); whatever is a view, that itself is a 'thicket of views' (diṭṭhigahana).
It is called a "view" (diṭṭhi) in the sense of seeing things as they are not; it is a "course of views" because it is a mode of seeing included within the sixty-two types of views.
*Diṭṭhigataṃ*. Its meaning has already been explained below. It is called *diṭṭhigata* because it goes exclusively toward two extremes.
That very same view is a "view-thicket" (*diṭṭhigahana*) in the sense of being difficult to cross over, just like grass-thickets, forest-thickets, and mountain-thickets.

It is a "view-wilderness" (*diṭṭhikantāra*) in the sense of being full of danger and peril, like a wilderness of robbers, a wilderness of wild beasts, a waterless wilderness, and a wilderness of famine.
In the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, it is mentioned by its full term as "the wilderness of views" (*diṭṭhikantāra*).

In the sense of piercing through and in the sense of being contrary, there is the "distortion of views" (*diṭṭhivisūka*). For when wrong seeing arises, it pierces through right seeing and is contrary to it.
In the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, it is mentioned as "pertaining to the distortion of views" (*diṭṭhivisūkāyika*). At times [it pertains] to eternalism...
Because it sometimes clings to annihilation, it is a "flickering of views" (*diṭṭhivipphandita*);
for one who has entered upon a wrong view (*diṭṭhigatika*) cannot remain established in a single position, sometimes recollecting eternalism and sometimes annihilation.

Because the view itself yokes one to what is harmful, it is the "fetter of views" (*diṭṭhisaññojana*). Because the view itself is difficult to remove in the sense of gnawing within and in the sense of being hard to extract...
And "the barb" refers to the barb of views (*diṭṭhisalla*). Views themselves, in the sense of being oppressive, are the "constriction of views" (*diṭṭhisambādha*).

Views themselves, in the sense of being an obstruction to liberation, are the "impediment of views" (*diṭṭhipalibodha*). Views themselves, in the sense of being difficult to release, are the "bond of views" (*diṭṭhibandhana*).
Views themselves, in the sense of being difficult to cross, are the "precipice of views" (*diṭṭhipapāta*). Views themselves...

In the sense of being firmly established, it is the underlying tendency (*anusaya*); thus, it is the underlying tendency of views (*diṭṭhānusaya*). Because view itself torments oneself, it is the torment of views (*diṭṭhisantāpa*).
Because view itself burns oneself, it is the fever of views (*diṭṭhipariḷāha*). Because view itself binds the mass of defilements, it is the fetter of views (*diṭṭhigantha*).
Because view itself grasps excessively, it is the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*). Because view itself [asserts things] by way of "this is truth," and so forth...

"It adheres" means adherence through views (*diṭṭhābhiniveso*). It is "clinging to views" (*diṭṭhiparāmāso*) because it grasps at this very view as supreme, or because it grasps at something other than that [view] as supreme.
126. Now, enumerating the sixteen views by way of groups, he says: "What are the sixteen views? and so forth.
Therein, a view regarding gratification, which consists of pleasure and joy, is the "gratification-view" (*assādadiṭṭhi*). A view that follows after a self is the "self-view" (*attānudiṭṭhi*).
The view of self (*attānudiṭṭhi*). A perverted view that occurs as "there is not" is wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*).
The view regarding the body, or the view that there is a body, is the embodiment-view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*). Here, "body" refers to the pentad of aggregates;

since this [view] has as its basis and support the "embodiment" (*sakkāya*)—which is designated as the pentad of aggregates—it is called "having the embodiment as its basis" (*sakkāyavatthukā*). The view that occurs as "eternal" is the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*).
The view that there is annihilation is the annihilationist view (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*). It is called "clinging to extremes" (*antaggāhikā*) because it grasps at extremes such as eternalism and so forth;

or, it is "clinging to extremes" because it possesses such clinging to extremes. The view that follows along with the past, which is reckoned as the prior end, is the view concerning the prior end (*pubbantānu-diṭṭhi*).

The view that follows along with the future, which is reckoned as the subsequent end, is the view concerning the subsequent end (*aparantānu-diṭṭhi*). It is called "fettering" (*saññojanikā*) because it binds one to what is disadvantageous.

The view that is bound, fixed, and produced by means of the conceit "I am" (*aham*)—which has arisen through the influence of the notion of "I" (*ahaṅkāra*) and serves as the root of views—is the "view bound by the conceit 'I am'.

Likewise, the view that is bound by means of the conceit "mine" (*mama*)—which has arisen through the influence of the notion of "mine" (*mamaṅkāra*)—is the "view bound by the conceit 'mine'. One's own speaking or declaring is "self-doctrine" (*attavāda*).
A view associated with that is a view connected with the doctrine of self (*attavāda*). Speaking and declaring "the self is the world" is the doctrine of the world (*lokavāda*);
a view associated with that is a view connected with the doctrine of the world. "Becoming" (*bhava*) is said to be eternalism;
a view arising by way of eternalism is the view of becoming (*bhavaditthi*). "Non-becoming" (*vibhava*) is said to be annihilationism; by way of annihilationism...
The view that arises is the view of non-existence (*vibhavadiṭṭhi*).
Now, desiring to demonstrate the three hundred types of adherence to views, [the author] asks, "What are the three hundred types of adherence to views?
and, without yet answering them, desires to answer them by means of the specific explanations for each individual adherence.
Having asked, by way of the method beginning with "In how many modes does there come to be misapprehension through the view of gratification?",
and having then answered that question regarding the enumeration of the modes of misapprehension for those sixteen views—
stating that "there comes to be misapprehension through the view of gratification in thirty-five modes"— he further answers those enumerations concerning the view of gratification as follows:
He said, "In what thirty-five modes is there misapprehension? and so forth. Therein, "dependent on form" means dependent on the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*).

"Pleasure and joy arise" means that, based on the excellence of form—thinking, "This body of mine is such"—there arises pleasure and joy associated with greed rooted in the household life. And "pleasure" is in the sense explained below.
And there is mental joy (*somanassa*). That very [joy] is the gratification (*assāda*) of form; thus it is the gratification based on form.
For that pleasure is "gratification" because it is relished and enjoyed by way of craving (*taṇhā*). "Adherence through misapprehension is view":
that gratification is adhered to as either eternal or subject to annihilation, or as making the self—which is either eternal or being annihilated—happy; this is adherence through misapprehension.

Therefore, although the view and the gratification are distinct, since that view does not exist without the gratification—even in the absence of the view’s own state of being the gratification—both are combined.
"Gratification-view" (assādadiṭṭhi) means a view that occurs with respect to gratification; this is what is meant.
Now, wishing to censure wrong view and the one of wrong view by correlating it with various suttas, [the author speaks of] the gratification-view...

He says, "wrong view," and so forth. Therein, "failure in view" (*diṭṭhivipatti*) means the failure of that view which is designated as wrong view—the destroyer of right view. "One failed in view" (*diṭṭhivipanna*) means one for whom right view has failed or been destroyed;
thus it is said, "one of failed view. Alternatively, one who has failed or been destroyed by wrong view is "one failed in view. Such a person is not to be associated with by approaching them.
"He should not be associated with in thought; he should not be attended upon by approaching and sitting down.
For what reason? This is a question regarding the reason why "that [acts such as] associating and so forth should not be done.
"Because his view is evil" is the answer regarding the reason. Since that person's view is evil, therefore one should not associate with him and so forth.
The meaning is "should be done. "Lust for views" (diṭṭhi-rāga) is the lust arising with respect to a view, thinking, "My view is beautiful.
"One stained by lust for views" (diṭṭhirāgaratta) is one who is stained like a cloth dyed by that color of lust for views.
"Not of great fruit" refers to the result of ripening (vipāka-phala). "Not of great benefit" refers to the outflowing result (nissanda-phala).
"Of a person" (*purisapuggalassa*) means of a person reckoned as a "man. According to worldly convention, the body is called "the city" (*puri*);

because he dwells (*seti*) or functions within that city, he is a "man" (*purisa*). "Hell" (*puṃ*) is what is meant; because he goes (*galati*) or descends into that hell, he is a "person" (*puggala*).
For the majority of beings, having passed away from a happy destination, are reborn only in an unhappy destination. Why is that?
As for "the cause," by what reason does that lack of great fruitfulness occur?
"For his view is evil" means that because this person's view is evil, it therefore does not bear great fruit; such is the meaning.
"Only two destinations" means that among the five destinations, there are only two: if the view fails, it is hell; if it succeeds, it is the animal realm.
And as for "whatever bodily action": this refers to bodily action such as wearing the full set of robes, application to the practice, saluting, rising to greet, and joining the palms in reverence.
And as for "whatever verbal action": this refers to verbal action such as mastering one's own doctrine, recitation, teaching, and encouraging others to practice.
And as for "whatever mental action": this refers to that which is associated with thoughts concerning this world and that which is associated with thoughts concerning the next world.

And mental action associated with reflection on what has been done and what has not been done. There are also bodily, verbal, and mental actions regarding the giving, bestowing, receiving, and consumption of grass, wood, grain, and seeds by one who holds the view of a living being.
"According to his view" means in accordance with whatever this view may be. "Fully undertaken" means complete.
"Adopted" means taken up.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is said: "This bodily action is threefold:
that which stands upon a particular view, that which arises simultaneously with a view, and that which is in conformity with a view. In this regard, for one who holds such a view as:

'There is no evil, nor is there any consequence of evil, for one who kills living beings, takes what is not given, or engages in sexual misconduct'—this [action] consisting of killing, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct..."
Bodily action; this is what is called bodily action established in accordance with one's view. Bodily action that arises simultaneously with this view and this perspective, such as:

"For one who kills living beings, takes what is not given, or engages in sexual misconduct, there is no evil resulting from that cause, nor is there any arrival of evil"—this is what is called bodily action co-arising with views (*diṭṭhisahajātakāyakamma*). That very same...
However, bodily action that is fully undertaken, adopted, grasped, and clung to in accordance with one's views is called "bodily action conformable to [wrong] view.

The same method applies to verbal and mental actions as well. In this context, for one who speaks falsehoods, speaks maliciously, speaks harshly, engages in idle chatter, is covetous, has a mind of ill will, or holds wrong view—there is no evil resulting from that cause; there is none.

The construction should be made as "the arrival of evil. And herein, the method described by way of wearing the marks [of a recluse], mastery of the scriptures, and concern for worldly affairs is commendable.
Among volition and the rest, volition that is co-nascent with views is called "volition. Aspiration that is co-nascent with views is called "aspiration.
The fixing of the mind by way of volition and aspiration is called "resolve. Furthermore, [it is] associated with those volitions and so forth.
The phenomena comprised within the aggregate of volitional formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), beginning with contact (*phassa*), are called "formations" (*saṅkhārā*).

By the terms "undesirable" (*aniṭṭha*) and so forth, suffering itself is expressed. For suffering is "undesirable" because it is not sought after by beings who desire happiness; it is "unpleasant" (*akanta*) because it is disagreeable;

it is "disagreeable" (*amanāpa*) because it does not increase the mind and does not spread through the mind; it is "non-beneficial" (*ahita*) because it is not auspicious for the future; and it is [suffering] because of its oppressive nature.
"It is suffering. "For what reason? means: for what cause does such a consequence occur?
Now, its cause is stated: "Because his view is evil. Since that person's view is evil—that is, base—therefore it results in such a consequence;
this is the meaning. "Planted in moist earth" means planted in ground saturated with water.
"Earth-essence and water-essence" refers to the excellence of the earth and the excellence of the water in their respective locations.
For it is not every portion of earth or every portion of water in the place where a seed is sown that causes the seed to bear fruit;
rather, only that specific part which touches the seed causes the seed to bear fruit. Therefore, for the nourishment of the seed—
That very location which serves as the condition should be understood as the "earth-essence" (*pathavī-rasa*) and the "water-essence" (*āpo-rasa*).
For the word *rasa* has the meaning of "perfection. As it is said: "The term *rasa* is spoken of in the sense of the perfection of function.

And in the world, when it is said, "The Gandhabba is *sura-sa* (of excellent essence)," the meaning understood is that the Gandhabba is well-perfected (*su-sampanna*). "It takes up" (*upādiyatīti*) means it grasps. For that location which is the condition...
When it encounters the appropriate conditions, that seed is said to "take up" them. "All" refers to all those varieties of sap. Regarding "for the sake of bitterness":

although that earth-sap and water-sap are themselves not bitter, by depending on a bitter seed, they lead to the state of bitterness in the fruits of trees such as the *nimba*. "For the sake of pungency" is a synonym for the former.
“Endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor, this mango was once so;

receiving such honor as that, why has the mango come to have bitter fruit?”—for here too, as in the cited passage, it should be understood that "bitter" (*kaṭuka*) is used in the sense of being unpleasant due to its lack of taste (*asātatā*). Because of its insipidity...
"For the sake of its lack of sweetness. There is also a reading "for the sake of its unsavoriness" (*asādu-ttāya*), which means "for the sake of its lack of savor" (*asādu-bhāvāya*).
For "savor" (*sādu*) is what is sweet. "Its seed" (*bījaṃ hissa*) means the seed of that [tree], such as the neem tree and so forth. "In this very way" (*evamevaṃ*) means exactly thus.
Since pleasant feeling is the supreme gratification, therefore the danger is shown by way of painful feeling with respect to wrong view. Again, by way of the eighteenfold division...
In order to show the danger of views (*diṭṭhi*), he said, "the gratification-view (*assādadiṭṭhi*) is a wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*)," and so forth; the meaning of that is exactly as stated.
By saying, "for one whose mind is obsessed by these eighteen modes, there is a fetter," he shows that the very bondage in *saṃsāra* is due to views.
Furthermore, since among the fetters (*saññojana*) there are both those that consist of views and those that do not, he [explains] that classification:

He said, "Showing that there are fetters," and so forth. Therein, because there is also a place where *kāmarāga-saṃyojana* (the fetter of sensual lust) is recorded as *anunaya-saṃyojana* (the fetter of attachment), it is therefore called *anunaya-saṃyojana*.

It should be understood that this was said with reference to greed (*lobha*) that occurs without having reached the state of *kāmarāga*. This same [principle] applies to the subsequent sections based on the remaining aggregates, bases, and so forth.
The meaning should be understood according to this method. Since gratification culminates in feeling, the teaching concludes with feeling;
perception and the other [aggregates] are not included here. "By these thirty-five modes" means by way of the objects of gratification arising in dependence upon these thirty-five bases:
namely, the five aggregates and the five sets of six, such as the internal sense bases.
[It is] by way of thirty-five aspects.
The commentary on the exposition of the view of gratification is finished.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of the View of Self.

130. Regarding the phrase "the uninstructed worldling (*assutavā puthujjana*) who holds the view of a self": one should understand "uninstructed" (*assutavā*) as being devoid of both scripture (*āgama*) and realization (*adhigama*).

For such a person lacks the scripture that negates the view of a self—due to being bereft of study, inquiry, and discernment concerning the aggregates (*khandha*), elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), truths (*sacca*), the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*), the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), and so forth—and because they have not attained what is to be attained through practice.
And there is no realization; because of the absence of both scripture (*āgama*) and realization (*adhigama*), he is to be known as "one who has not heard" (*assutavā*).

For "what has been heard" (*suta*) refers both to the scripture of the Buddha’s word and to realization—which, being the fruit of what has been heard, is designated by the name of its cause. One who possesses that which has been heard is "one who has heard" (*sutavā*); one who does not possess it is "one who has not heard" (*assutavā*).
And this person is a worldling (*puthujjana*) because of various causes such as being born among many (*puthu*).

Because he is included among ordinary people, or because this person is "many" (puthu), he is called a *puthujjana*. For he is a *puthujjana* due to causes such as generating (*janana*) various kinds of defilements and so forth. As it is said:
"They generate many defilements, thus they are *puthujjanas*; they possess many unbroken views of self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), thus they are *puthujjanas*."
They are "worldlings" (*puthujjana*) because they look up to various teachers; they are worldlings because they have not emerged from the various states of existence;
they are worldlings because they perform various volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*); they are worldlings because they are carried away by various floods (*ogha*);
they are worldlings because they are tormented by various fevers (*santāpa*); they are worldlings because they are consumed by various burning pains (*pariḷāha*).

“Ordinary persons (puthujjana) are so called because they are attached to, greedy for, infatuated with, obsessed by, stuck to, clung to, and entangled in the fivefold strands of sensual pleasure individually;
ordinary persons are so called because they are individually obstructed, covered, enveloped, shut in, concealed, and enclosed by the five hindrances.
Or else, they are “ordinary persons” because they are many, beyond the path of counting, and turned away from the noble Dhamma.
They are called *puthujjana* (worldlings) because they are included among those people who practice base qualities;

or alternatively, they are called *puthujjana* because this person is "separate" (*puthu*), having gone to a distinct reckoning and being dissociated from the Noble Ones who are endowed with virtues such as moral discipline and learning.
Thus, by these two terms—"the uninstructed worldling"—those who are...
“Two types of worldlings were spoken of by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun:
one is the blind worldling, and one is the worldling who is excellent.
Thus, two types of worldlings were spoken of; it should be understood that among them, the blind worldling is the one referred to here.

Regarding the passage beginning with "one who does not see the noble ones" (*ariyānaṃ adassāvī*): "Noble ones" (*ariyā*) refers to the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha. They are called "noble" because they are far removed from defilements (*ārakattā kilesehi*), because they do not proceed in what is not the right way (*anaye na iriyanato*), because they proceed in the right way (*aye ca iriyanato*), and because they are worthy of being sought after by the world together with its devas (*sadevakena ca lokena araṇīyato*).
Alternatively, in this context, "noble ones" refers specifically to the Buddhas. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, in the world with its devas... the Tathāgata is called 'noble'."
Regarding the term *sappurisā* (good persons): here, however, it should be understood that *paccekabuddhas* and *tathāgata-sāvakas* (disciples of the Tathāgata) are "good persons.

For they are "good persons" (*sappurisā*) because they are beautiful (*sobhana*) persons (*purisa*) due to their possession of supramundane qualities. Or rather, all of these are designated as such in both ways;
for Buddhas are both noble ones (*ariya*) and good persons, and so too are *paccekabuddhas* and the disciples of the Buddha. As it has been said:
“He who is grateful and mindful of what has been done, who is wise, a good friend, and firm in devotion;
who performs his duty with care for one who is suffering—such a person they call a true man.
For here, by the phrase “grateful and mindful of what has been done, who is wise,” the Paccekabuddha is meant; and by “a good friend, firm in devotion... [the noble disciple is meant].
"...and [he is] a disciple of the Buddha; he 'attentively performs the duties for one who is suffering,' thus he is a Perfectly Enlightened One.
Now, he who is by nature one who does not see those Noble Ones and does not act skillfully in seeing them should be understood as "one who has not seen the Noble Ones" (*ariyānaṃ adassāvī*).
And he is of two kinds: one who has not seen with the eye, and one who has not seen with wisdom. Among these, the one who has not seen with wisdom—

This is what is intended here. For even when seen by the noble ones with either the fleshly eye or the divine eye, they are as if not seen at all, because those eyes grasp only the mere color-form and not the domain of the noble state.
Even jackals, dogs, and the like see the noble ones with their eyes, yet they are not "seers" of the noble ones. Therefore, seeing with the eye is not true seeing.
Seeing is indeed seeing by means of knowledge. As it is said: "What is the use to you, Vakkali, of seeing this putrid body?

He who sees the Dhamma, Vakkali, sees me. Therefore, even one who sees with the eye, if he does not see with knowledge the characteristics of impermanence and so forth as seen by the Noble Ones, and does not attain the Dhamma attained by the Noble Ones—
Because he has not seen the qualities that make one noble and the state of being noble, he should be understood as "one who does not see the noble ones" (*ariyānaṃ adassāvī*).

"Unskilled in the noble Dhamma" means he is unproficient in the noble Dhamma distinguished by the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "undisciplined in the noble Dhamma," it is said here:
"Discipline (*vinaya*) is of two kinds; each of these is fivefold."
Because he lacks that, he is called "undisciplined" (*avinīta*).

For this discipline (*vinaya*) is twofold: the discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-vinaya*) and the discipline of abandonment (*pahāna-vinaya*). And within each of these two types of discipline, each individual discipline is further divided fivefold.
For the discipline of restraint consists of the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*), the restraint of mindfulness (*sati-saṃvara*), and the restraint of knowledge (*ñāṇa-saṃvara*).
Restraint is fivefold: restraint through patience, restraint through energy, and so forth. Discipline as abandonment is also fivefold:

abandonment by way of its own nature (*tadaṅgappahāna*), abandonment by suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*), abandonment by eradication (*samucchedappahāna*), abandonment by subsiding (*paṭippassaddhippahāna*), and abandonment by escape (*nissaraṇappahāna*).

Among these, "He is endowed with, fully endowed with this Pātimokkha restraint" refers to restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*). "He guards the faculty of the eye; he attains restraint over the faculty of the eye" refers to restraint of mindfulness (*satisaṃvara*).
“Whatever streams there are in the world, Ajita,” said the Blessed One,
“mindfulness is their obstruction;
I call the restraint of the streams wisdom, by which they are closed.”

This is the restraint of knowledge (*ñāṇasaṃvara*). “He is patient with cold and heat”—this is the restraint of patience (*khantisaṃvara*). “He does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire”—this is the restraint of energy (*vīriyasaṃvara*).

And all this restraint is called “restraint” (*saṃvara*) because it restrains—that is, controls—the respective bodily misconducts and so forth that ought to be restrained; and it is called “discipline” (*vinaya*) because of its disciplining nature.
Thus, first of all, it should be understood that the discipline of restraint (saṃvaravinaya) is fivefold. Likewise,
regarding the analytical knowledge of name-and-form (nāmarūpapariccheda) and other insights (vipassanāñāṇa),

there is the abandoning of their respective adverse states by means of those various insights— just as darkness is dispelled by the light of a lamp— for instance, through the discernment of name-and-form (nāmarūpavavatthāna).
By means of the comprehension of the person, [one abandons] the view of a self-identity; by the discernment of conditions, the views of no-cause and wrong-cause;

by the overcoming of doubt, the state of being wavering; by the contemplation of groups, the grasping of "I" and "mine"; by the determination of what is and is not the path, the perception of a path where there is no path;
by the vision of arising, the annihilationist view; by the vision of passing away, the eternalist view; and by the vision of danger, [the clinging to] that which is dangerous.

Through the perception of fearlessness, there is the abandoning of the perception of gratification by means of seeing danger; through the contemplation of disenchantment, there is the abandoning of the perception of delight;
through the knowledge of the desire for deliverance, there is the abandoning of the lack of desire for deliverance; through the knowledge of equanimity, there is the abandoning of non-equanimity;

through the knowledge of conformity, there is the abandoning of the contrary state toward the stability of phenomena and Nibbāna; and through the change-of-lineage, there is the abandoning of the grasping at the sign of formations.
This is called abandonment by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-pahāna*).

However, that abandonment of various states such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), which occurs through concentration— distinguished as access and absorption— by way of obstructing the process of existence,
like the removal of moss from the surface of water by striking it with a jar, is "abandonment by suppression" (*vikkhambhana-pahāna*).

That which is the absolute non-arising of the mass of defilements belonging to the side of origination— which, for one who possesses a particular noble path due to the cultivation of the four noble paths,
is abandoned within their own continuum according to the method stated as "for the abandoning of the various types of views," and so forth—
is called abandonment by cutting off (*samucchedappahāna*). Furthermore, that which is the subsiding of the defilements at the moment of the fruition (*phala-khaṇa*)—
This is called abandonment by subsiding. That which is Nibbāna—having abandoned all formations because it has escaped from all that is conditioned—is called abandonment by escape.

And since all this abandonment is abandonment in the sense of relinquishing (*cāga*) and discipline (*vinaya*) in the sense of leading away (*vinayana*), it is therefore called "abandonment-discipline" (*pahānavinaya*); or else, [it is so called] because of that [discipline] which possesses each respective abandonment.
Because this discipline arises from that [cessation], it is called "discipline as abandonment" (*pahāna-vinaya*). Thus, discipline as abandonment should also be understood to be fivefold.
In this way, this discipline is twofold in brief and tenfold in detail, because that which is to be abandoned has its restraint broken.
And because this [lack of training] does not exist for the uninstructed worldling due to its non-abandonment, it is therefore said of him, "he is untrained," owing to its absence.

This same method applies here as well to the phrases "one who has not seen true persons," "one who is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons," and "one who is untrained in the Dhamma of true persons.
