For there is no difference in meaning between these. As it has been said: "That very..."
Those who are noble are indeed those who are true persons; those who are true persons are indeed those who are noble.
Whatever is the Dhamma of the noble ones is indeed the Dhamma of the true persons; whatever is the Dhamma of the true persons is indeed the Dhamma of the noble ones.
Whatever are the trainings of the noble ones are indeed the trainings of the true persons; whatever are the trainings of the true persons are indeed the trainings of the noble ones.

"A noble one" or "a true person," "the Dhamma of the noble ones" or "the Dhamma of the true persons," "the discipline of the noble ones" or "the discipline of the true persons"—these are identical, one, of the same meaning, equal, of the same portion, of the same kind, and indeed the very same thing.
But why did the Elder ask, "In how many ways does misinterpretation occur through views concerning a self? and then...
Is it not by not omitting that [definition] that he points out the worldling (*puthujjana*) thus: "Here, the uninstructed worldling"?
It should be understood that he first points out the worldling in order to reveal that meaning through a teaching centered on the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*).
Having thus pointed out the worldling, he now states the enumeration of misapprehensions (*abhinivesuddesa*), beginning with: "He regards form as self," and so forth.
In this context, "one regards form as self" means that one regards the aggregate of form and the kasiṇa-form through the vision of wrong view as "self.
However, in its exposition (niddesa), because the subject matter concerns the five aggregates, the adherence to the aggregate of form is already evident;
therefore, it should be understood that the term "form" is used here in a general sense to refer specifically to the kasiṇa-form. "Possessing form" (rūpavantaṃ) ...
Or, having grasped the formless as "self," one regards that self as possessing form.
Or, having grasped the formless itself as "self," one regards form as being in that self.
Or, having grasped the formless itself as "self," one regards that self as being in form.
In this context, "one regards form as self" refers to pure form itself being called "self.
Furthermore, in these seven instances—regarding oneself as possessing form, form as being in oneself, oneself as being in form;
or regarding feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness as self—it is the formless (arūpa) that is called "self."

Whether it be "the self possesses feeling," or "feeling is in the self," or "the self is in feeling"—thus, by way of each of the three [factors] applied to the four aggregates, the self is described as a mixture of the material and immaterial in twelve instances.
These twenty views, moreover, are obstacles to the path, not obstacles to heaven; they are to be abandoned by the path of stream-entry.
Now, pointing that out, he says: "How is form? and so forth. Therein, "earth-kasiṇa" refers to the earth-disk;
it is called the earth-kasiṇa because it is produced in dependence upon the circle of earth and is reckoned as the counterpart-sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) due to its all-pervading nature.
"I" takes this referring specifically to oneself. "Self" means oneself. "Non-dual" means one and the same. "Of the oil-lamp" means...
"Of an oil-fed lamp": *jhāyato* means "while burning. The statement "that which is the flame, that is the color," and so forth, is said because there is no color apart from the flame.
And as for "both the view and the basis," the meaning is that when these two are taken together, it is called the "view of self based on form."
The water-kasiṇa and so forth are simply the kasiṇa-signs produced by depending on water and the other elements.

As for the limited-space kasiṇa, although it serves as the object for the fine-material jhāna, it should be understood that when it is called "space kasiṇa," it is not included because it is mixed with the space resulting from the removal of the kasiṇa, which is the object of the immaterial jhānas.
Furthermore, because this context concerns the fine-material realm, the consciousness kasiṇa should certainly not be included.
"Here, someone regards feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness as self"—this is stated by way of grasping the four aggregates together without having broken them apart.
For, being incapable of distinguishing between mind and mental factors individually, he groups them all together and grasps them as "self.
By this [statement], in the phrase "one who possesses form by means of this form," both the bodily form and the kasiṇa-form are included.
It is possible. "Endowed with shadow" means possessed of shadow, that is, not sparse. Regarding the word *tamenam*, here the suffix *-ena* is merely a particle;

alternatively, the meaning is *tam etam*. "Possessing shadow" means having existing shadow. Although form (*rūpa*) has not been grasped as "self," it is stated to be "based on form" because the view arises without letting go of form.

"He regards form in himself" means that because both the bodily form and the kasiṇa-form are dependent upon the mind, he regards that form within himself in that immaterial aggregate. "This is a fragrance" refers to the fragrance being smelled;
he speaks thus because fragrance is dependent upon the flower.
"He regards self in form" means that where form goes, there the mind goes.
Therefore, having grasped the mind as dependent on form, he regards that immaterial aggregate as the self in relation to that form.
Because form is gross, he calls it a "gross receptacle," like a basket.

132. Herein, in such passages as "feeling born of eye-contact," although there is no separate mention of each individual feeling, it should be understood that a separate application [of the term] is made because all feelings are included within the single mention of "feeling" (*vedanā*); for he [the practitioner] experiences them by way of feeling (*vedanā*).

Because it is gross, one grasps feeling alone as "self. When one regards perception, formations, consciousness, or form as self, one regards these immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma) and form together as a single unit and views them as "self.
For the worldling is like a madman; he grasps whatever appears to him in whatever manner it manifests.

133. In the passages beginning with "perception born of eye-contact," one grasps perception as "self" because perception is prominent due to its function of perceiving. The rest should be understood according to the method already explained for feeling. 134.

In the passages beginning with "volition born of eye-contact," among those phenomena included within the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), volition alone is specifically pointed out because it is predominant and prominent.
By means of that [mention of volition], the others are also effectively pointed out. He...
However, because it is manifest as a mental concomitant (cetasika), one grasps volition (cetanā) as "self. The rest is exactly as previously stated.

Regarding the terms "eye-consciousness" and so forth, because consciousness (citta) is manifest through the act of cognizing, one grasps consciousness as "self. The rest here also follows the same method already explained.
The commentary on the description of the view of self (attānudiṭṭhi) is concluded.
3. Explanation of the Description of Wrong View (Micchādiṭṭhiniddesavaṇṇanā) 136.

Wrong view has already had its meaning explained above. However, there is this other method: "There is no giving" is a denial of the fruit of giving because of holding an annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*).
"There is no sacrifice" (*natthi yiṭṭha*): here, "sacrifice" (*yiṭṭha*) refers to a minor offering. "There is no oblation" (*natthi huta*): [the same applies].
"A great sacrifice. He rejects the fruit for both [good and evil].
By rejecting the fruit of giving, he rejects the fruit of meritorious deeds such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth, on the grounds that "there is no fruit or result of well-done or ill-done actions.
By saying "there is no this world," he rejects the fruit of actions performed in the past. By saying "there is no other world," he [rejects the fruit] here...
"By the deed that has been done": this denies the fruit of actions performed toward one's mother and father, asserting "there is no mother, there is no father.
"There are no beings of spontaneous birth": this denies rebirth caused by karma. "In the world there are no recluses and brahmins... who proclaim [this world and the other world]":
this denies the practice for attaining direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) to perceive this world and the world beyond.
In this context, however, "there is no basis for what is given" means that there is no gift spoken of as "given";
the meaning is that it is the basis for that view. "One who speaks thus is wrong" means that such a doctrine, such a statement—that "there is nothing given"—is wrong, that is, perverted.
The commentary on the description of wrong view is finished.
4. Commentary on the Description of the View of a Real Entity (Sakkāyadiṭṭhi) 137.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the view of a real entity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) is simply the view of a self (*attānudiṭṭhi*); it is stated here for the purpose of showing alternative expressions found elsewhere.
The commentary on the description of the view of a real entity is finished.
5. Commentary on the Exposition of the View of Eternalism (Sassatadiṭṭhiniddesavaṇṇanā) 138.
“The view of eternalism based on the substrate of personality” (*sakkāyavatthukāya sassatadiṭṭhiyā*) is a *karmadhāraya* compound.

The connection should be made with the words “he regards” (*samanupassati*) at the end of the fifteen statements beginning with “the self as possessing form” (*rūpavantaṃ vā attānaṃ*), or that is the reading itself. Otherwise—

For it is not possible [to say] "he regards the self as possessing form. Thus, having shown only one instance—namely, "or he regards the self as possessing form"—the remaining fourteen are abbreviated.
The commentary on the exposition of the eternalist view is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Exposition of the Annihilationist View (Ucchedadiṭṭhiniddesa) 139.

Regarding the annihilationist view based on the five aggregates of personal existence (sakkāya), having thus shown only one instance—namely, "one regards form as self"—the remaining four are abbreviated.
The commentary on the exposition of the annihilationist view is concluded.
7. Explanation of the Description of Extremist Views (Antaggāhikā-diṭṭhi-niddesa) 140.

Regarding the extremist view (*antaggāhikā-diṭṭhi*), in the first section there is a question concerning the mode [of occurrence]. In the second, there is the grasping of the mode. In the third, there is the answering of the mode.
Therein, "the world" (*loka*) refers to the self (*attā*). That "end" (*anta*) refers to the two opposing extremes of eternalism (*sassata*) and annihilationism (*uccheda*).
In the grasping of eternalism, there is the extreme of eternalism; in the grasping of non-eternalism, there is the extreme of annihilationism.
"A limited space" means a small area, such as the size of a tray or the size of a bowl. "It pervades it as blue" means one takes the object as being blue.
"This world" is said with reference to the self (*attā*). "Enclosed on all sides" means having a boundary all around. "Perceiving a limit" means...
"One who perceives [the world] as finite": it should be understood that "finite" (*anta*) means that which has an end (*anto assa atthi*).

"That which it pervades" refers to the kasiṇa-form which it pervades. "That is both the basis and the world": that kasiṇa-form is both the objective support (*ārammaṇa*) and, in the sense of being something to be looked upon, the world (*loka*).
"That by which it pervades" refers to the mind by which it pervades; this is both the self (*attā*) and the world, in relation to the self.
The masculine form *kataṃ* refers to that mind; it is said that "the mind itself is the world in the sense of illuminating.
*Anto* means "inside. "It pervades by way of space" means that it pervades as light (*obhāsa*) by means of the light-kasina, the fire-kasina, or the white-kasina.
Since only the five bright kasinas—blue and so forth—are included here, [it does not include] the earth, water, or air kasinas.
"One should understand that there is no adherence to a self (*attābhinivesa*).
'A vast space' refers to a large area, such as the size of a threshing floor and so forth. 'Endless' (*anantava*) means having an endless increase.

'Unbounded' (*apariyanta*) means having an unbounded increase. 'Perceiving it as endless' means perceiving it as "endless. 'That which is the life-principle' (*taṃ jīvaṃ*) means that very life-principle."

A transposition of genders has been made. "The living soul" (*jīva*) is the self (*attā*) itself. The five [aggregates], beginning with form (*rūpa*), are the "body" (*sarīra*) in the sense of being a collection.

"The living soul is not the body": the living soul, which is designated as the self, is not the body, which is designated as form. This same method applies to feeling (*vedanā*) and the others. "Tathāgata" refers to a sentient being (*satta*).
"Some say 'arahant'. "After death" (*paraṃ maraṇā*): beyond death; the meaning is "in the other world" (*paraloka*).
"Form (rūpa) here is subject to death": by this, using his own visible aggregate as a representative head, he includes all five aggregates;
the meaning is that these are of a nature to perish right here in this world. The same method applies to the remaining aggregates.
"With the breaking up of the body" means after the dissolution of the body, which is comprised of the five aggregates. By this expression, [the phrase] "after death" is implied.

The meaning of this summary has been stated. Regarding the phrases "it exists" (*hoti*) and so forth: "exists" (*hoti*) is the root word. In all four instances, the particle *api* has the sense of conjunction.
"It remains" (*tiṭṭhati*) means it remains because of its permanence; the meaning is that it does not pass away.

Alternatively, it should be understood that the word "remains" (*tiṭṭhati*) is stated for the purpose of specifying the particular meaning of the word "exists" (*hoti*). "It arises" (*uppajjati*) refers to the manner of entering the egg-born and womb-born modes of birth.

The phrase "it arises" (uppajjati) means "it is produced"; the construction of the meaning should be understood as "it is produced by way of entry into the moisture-born (*saṃsedaja*) and spontaneously born (*opapātika*) modes of birth.
"It is cut off" (ucchijjati) means by way of the absence of continuity. "It perishes" (vinassati) means by way of dissolution.
"There is nothing after death" (na hoti paraṃ maraṇā) is the explanation of the meaning of the preceding terms; the sense is that it does not exist beyond the point of death (*cuti*).
"It both exists and does not exist" is the view of the partial-eternalists; the meaning is that it exists in one sense and does not exist in another sense.
What is stated is that it exists by way of its existence as a living being (*jīvabhāva*), but does not exist by way of the absence of its former life.
"Neither exists nor does not exist" is the view of the eel-wrigglers (*amarāvikkhepika*); [the meaning is] that it neither exists, nor is it the case that it does not exist.
The meaning is "it occurs. Out of fear of censure and fear of lying, and due to dullness and delusion, one merely performs a rejection of the method previously stated.
"By these fifty modes" means by way of the fifty modes consisting of the ten sets of five as already described.
The commentary on the exposition of extreme views is finished.
8. Commentary on the Exposition of Views Concerning the Past: 141.

Regarding the views concerning the past and the future, those who assert eternalism are called "eternalists" (*sassatavādā*). Alternatively, they are so called because they speak by means of this [view].
“Doctrine” (*vāda*) is a designation for a speculative view (*diṭṭhigata*). A doctrine that is eternal due to its connection with eternity is “eternalism”;
those who possess such an eternal doctrine are “eternalists” (*sassatavādā*). Likewise, a doctrine that [holds] some things are eternal is “partial-eternalism”;
those who possess this are “partial-eternalists” (*ekaccasassatikā*). Similarly, [those who hold that the world is] finite, infinite, both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite...

The doctrine that proceeds as "not finite" or "infinite" is *antānanta* (finite-infinite); those who hold such [views] are the *antānantikā* (those who maintain the finite-infinite view). "Does not die" is *amarā*. What is it?

It is both the view and the speech of one who follows a wrong path (*diṭṭhigatika*) that is devoid of limits, according to the method beginning with "It is thus for me, and it is not thus for me," and so forth.
*Vikkhepa* means various kinds of evasion; the evasion of the *amarā* view or the *amarā* speech is *amarāvikkhepa*.
They are called "eel-wrigglers" (*amarāvikkhepikā*) because they possess this [practice]. Another method: "Amarā" is a species of fish;
as it darts about in the water by way of surfacing and submerging, it cannot be caught. In the same way, this doctrine also darts hither and thither and does not come to a grasp;
thus it is called "eel-wriggling. They are called "eel-wrigglers" because they possess this.

"Arising by chance" (*adhiccasamuppanna*) means arising without a cause; the view that "the self and the world arise by chance" is *adhiccasamuppanna*, and those who possess this [view] are the *Adhiccasamuppannikas*.
The commentary on the description of the views concerning the past is concluded.
9. Explanation of the Description of the View of Eternalism (Aparantānudiṭṭhiniddesavaṇṇanā) 142.

“They assert that there is perception” means they are proponents of the view of perception (saññīvādā). “They assert that there is no perception” means they are proponents of the view of non-perception (asaññīvādā).

“They assert that there is neither perception nor non-perception” means they are proponents of the view of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā). Alternatively, a doctrine that proceeds by way of the term “one who has perception” is a “proponent of perception”; those [who hold such a doctrine] are [the proponents of perception].

"They say 'it exists'": these are the proponents of perception (*saññīvādā*); likewise, the proponents of non-perception (*asaññīvādā*) and the proponents of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā*).
"They speak of annihilation" means they are annihilationists (*ucchedavādā*). "The present life" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to the directly perceived phenomenon;

it is a designation for the individual existence (*attabhāva*) obtained here and there. "Nibbāna in the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammanibbāna*) means the subsiding of suffering within this very individual existence.
They speak thus regarding that goal; therefore, they are called "proponents of Nibbāna in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā*).

However, if this matter were to be explained in detail, the entire *Brahmajāla Sutta* together with its commentary would have to be recited. Since that would result in excessive prolixity, it has not been expanded upon here.
Those who desire to know the full meaning should consult that source.
The commentary on the exposition of the view of adherence to the extreme ends is finished.
10–12. Commentary on the Exposition of the Fettering View, etc. 143.

Since the fettering view is common to all views, its meaning—which is common to all views because it fetters one to all views—has been demonstrated. That [meaning] is identical to the obsession by views mentioned above.

144. Regarding "the adherence through misapprehension that 'I am the eye' among views bound by conceit": this is an adherence through misapprehension preceded by conceit. For a view is not associated with conceit.
It is for this very reason that it is called "bound by conceit" (*māna-vinibandha*); the meaning is that it is obstructed by conceit and rooted in conceit. 145.
Regarding "the adherence through misapprehension that 'the eye is mine'": here too the method is the same. However, in this case, [the term] "mine" (*mamā*)...
In the phrase "mine" (*mama*), the addition of the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*) should be understood.

In the phrase "I" (*aham*), because it is bound up with conceit (*māna*), even form and the other aggregates are internal; for one does not grasp external objects as "I" without the form of the kasiṇa.
However, because they are bound up with conceit, even external things can be [grasped] as "mine"; for one also grasps external things as "mine. But as for painful feeling...
Because it is not yet completed, it does not constitute a ground for conceit; therefore, the six feelings and their root-conditions, the six contacts, are not included here.
Furthermore, it should be understood that perception and the other factors are not included because they have been excluded in this context.
The commentary on the description of the fettering views, etc., is finished.
13. Commentary on the Exposition of Views Connected with the Theory of Self (Attavādapaṭisaṃyuttadiṭṭhiniddesavaṇṇanā) 146.
A view connected with the theory of self is precisely the view of a self (attānudiṭṭhi). It is stated again in this way because it is associated with the assertion of a "self.
The commentary on the exposition of views connected with the theory of self is finished.
14. Explanation of the Description of Views Concerning Worldly Discourse 147.
“The self and the world”: the meaning is that the very same self is both the self and the world in the sense of being that which perceives (*ālokana*).

“Eternal” is the view of the eternalists. “Non-eternal” is that of the annihilationists. “Both eternal and non-eternal” is that of the partial-eternalists. “Neither... [is the view of the neither-nor-eternalists].

"Is it eternal or non-eternal? refers to the Eel-Wrigglers (*amarāvikkhepika*). "Is it finite? refers to those who have attained the limited kasiṇas and to the rationalists (*takkika*), as well as the Nigaṇṭhas and Ājīvakas.
Alternatively, the annihilationists say: "A being is finite in the past by birth and finite in the future by death.
The proponents of fortuitous origination say: "A being is finite in the past by birth. "Is it infinite? refers to those who have attained the measureless kasiṇas.
The eternalists, however, say: "There is no past limit and no future limit; therefore, it is infinite.
The proponents of fortuitous origination say:

"It is infinite by way of the future limit. Those who hold that it is both finite and infinite refer to those who have expanded the kasiṇas horizontally, without expanding them upward or downward. Those who hold that it is neither finite nor infinite are the Eel-Wrigglers (Amarāvikkhepikas).
The commentary on the exposition of views associated with worldly talk is finished.
15–16. Commentary on the Exposition of Views Concerning Existence and Non-existence: 148.
Because there is no separate adherence apart from the aforementioned views, there is no separate exposition for the views concerning existence and non-existence.
Without posing a question to define each individual mode—namely "shrinkage" (*olīyana*) and "over-shooting" (*atidhāvana*)—by way of the very views already mentioned, some say:
"Adherence to shrinkage is the view of existence (*bhavaditthi*); adherence to over-shooting is the view of non-existence (*vibhavaditthi*).
In this context, the adherence to shrinkage is that which was stated as: "The mind does not leap forward when the Dhamma for the cessation of existence is being taught."
The meaning is that the adherence of eternalism is a contraction away from *nibbāna*. As for the adherence of over-exertion mentioned in the passage,

“But some, being terrified, ashamed, and disgusted by existence itself, delight in non-existence,” the meaning is that the adherence of annihilationism is an overstepping of the practice leading to cessation due to the perception of annihilation.
Now, in order to demonstrate how the views of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*) and non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*) are included among all views, he says:

"The view of gratification," and so forth. In this context, because those who hold the view of gratification rely on either eternalism or annihilationism and grasp at the notion that "there is no fault in sensual pleasures," therefore these thirty-five modes of the view of gratification may be views of existence, and they may also be views of non-existence.

...were stated. In this context, the meaning is that each of these views could be "views of existence" (*bhava-diṭṭhi*) by way of grasping at eternalism, or they could be "views of non-existence" (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*) by way of grasping at annihilationism. Regarding the view of self (*attānudiṭṭhi*):
one regards form as self, one regards feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as self; thus, among the five [aggregates]...

It is said that there are five views of non-existence (*vibhavadiṭṭhi*) because, since the self is not other than form and so forth, when those [aggregates] are annihilated, one grasps that "the self is annihilated.

Regarding the remaining fifteen positions, it is said that there are fifteen views of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*) because, since the self is other than form and so forth, even when those [aggregates] are annihilated, one grasps that "the self is eternal."
Regarding wrong view, because all such views of non-existence (*vibhavadiṭṭhi*) proceed by way of annihilationism, they are included among the views of "the world is finite" or "infinite.

Those who have attained jhāna with limited or immeasurable objects, having seen beings reborn elsewhere with the divine eye after passing away from the form realm, perceive the view of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*) not to apply and thus adopt the view of non-existence. Therefore:
In that regard, it was said: "There may be views of existence (bhava-diṭṭhi) and there may be views of non-existence (vibhava-diṭṭhi).
Here, in the phrase "both exists and does not exist," "exists" is a view of existence, and "does not exist" is a view of non-existence.
In the phrase "neither exists nor does not exist," "neither exists" is a view of non-existence, and "nor does not exist" is a view of existence. Therefore, the word "may be" (siyā) was used therein.
Those who hold views regarding the past, being some eternalists, proclaim both eternity and non-eternity;

therefore, that is both a view of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*) and a view of non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*). The four who hold views regarding the finite and infinite proclaim the self to be either finite or infinite;
therefore, that is similar to a view of the self (*attānudiṭṭhi*), being both a view of existence and a view of non-existence. The four...
The Eel-Wrigglers (*amarāvikkhepikā*) resort to verbal equivocation based on either the view of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*) or the view of non-existence (*vibhavadiṭṭhi*);
the rest, however, are views of existence alone. Therefore, with reference to those [Eel-Wrigglers], it is said: "it might be.

Regarding the views concerning the future (*aparantānudiṭṭhi*), seven annihilationist doctrines (*ucchedavāda*) are views of non-existence, while the remainder are views of existence. Therefore, with reference to those, it is said: "it might be."
It has been stated. Regarding the view that binds one by way of all views, it is said: "it may be.
Because of the grasping of the eye and so forth as "I" through the view bound by the conceit "I am," when those [faculties] perish, the self is destroyed;

therefore, it is said that all of them are views of non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*). Just like the views of self (*attānudiṭṭhi*), through the view bound by the conceit "mine" regarding the eye and so forth...
Because one thinks, "Even if they perish, the self will not perish due to its being other than them," all of these are called views of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*).

Since the views associated with worldly discourse are stated in the manner beginning with "The self and the world are eternal," the views of existence and non-existence (*bhava-vibhava-diṭṭhi*) are indeed evident.
Up to this point, [the views] beginning with the view of gratification and ending with the view of non-existence have been explained.
The sixteen views and the three hundred and sixty-three dogmatic attachments (*diṭṭhābhinivesa*) have been specified.

The view of self (*attānudiṭṭhi*), the embodiment-view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), and the view associated with the doctrine of self (*attavādapaṭisaññuttā diṭṭhi*) are in substance one, though spoken of in three ways by way of method.
Furthermore, all views that function as fetters (*saññojanikā diṭṭhi*) constitute views according to their various states.
Now, the passage beginning with “All those views are views of gratification” and so forth is a correlation of views by way of another method, as appropriate.

In this context, “all those views” refers to the views mentioned above without exception. They are “views of gratification” because they are colored by passion for views and because they rely on the gratification of craving;
they are “self-views” because they are accompanied by affection for a self; and they are “wrong views” because they are a distorted seeing.

Because they have the aggregates as their basis, these are views based on personality (*sakkāyadiṭṭhiyo*); because each extreme is grasped, they are views that grasp at extremes (*antaggāhikā diṭṭhiyo*);

because they fetter one to what is harmful, they are fettering views (*saññojanikā diṭṭhiyo*); and because they are associated with the doctrine of self, they are views associated with the doctrine of self (*attavādapaṭisaṃyuttā diṭṭhiyo*).
These seven views comprise all views; however, the remaining nine views do not comprise all views.

Now, summarizing all those views that have been explained in detail into just two types of views, and showing the twofold basis for the views of sentient beings, he spoke the verse beginning with "Existence and the view of existence" (*bhavañ ca diṭṭhinti*).

For all those views are either views of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*) or views of non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*). Regarding the phrase "existence and the view of existence, and non-existence and the view of non-existence":

However, the word *ca* (and) conjoins only the views, not the support (*nissaya*). For no single person relies upon both the view of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*) and the view of non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*).
As it is said: “Thus beings are either dependent on the view of existence or dependent on the view of non-existence.
“Rationalists” (*takkikā*) means those who speak by means of reasoning; for those proponents of views (*diṭṭhigatika*) lack the wisdom that penetrates the true nature of things (*sabhāva*).

They proceed merely by means of mere non-existence through reasoning. And even those who have attained meditative absorption (*jhāna*) or supernormal powers (*abhiññā*) yet still adopt views—they too are merely "reasoners" (*takkika*), because they grasp [their views] after having reasoned.
"Dependent" (*nissitāse*); the meaning is "they are dependent. This is either a single word, or the particle *se* is merely an expletive.
"There is no knowledge regarding their cessation"—this is a statement of the reason for their dependence on views.
Because they lack knowledge regarding the cessation of the view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), which is Nibbāna, the meaning is that these two views are dependent [upon it].
In the phrase “for there is no knowledge,” the particle *hi* is a marker used to indicate a reason. “Wherein this world has perverted perception”:
wherein, in regard to Nibbāna—which is bliss—this world, including the devas, possesses the perverted perception that it is “suffering”; in that [Nibbāna].
The connection is: "There is no elephant-knowledge regarding cessation. This sutta—beginning with "Suffering"—is taught because of the presence of perverted perception:
"Forms, sounds, tastes, smells, tangibles, and mental objects in their entirety;
those which are desirable, lovely, and pleasing, as far as they are called 'existent'."
“In the world with its devas, these are considered by you to be happiness;
but that wherein they cease is considered by them to be suffering.
The complete cessation of self-identity is seen as happiness by the Noble Ones.”
This is contrary to what is seen by the whole world:
"That which others call happiness, the Noble Ones call suffering;
that which others call suffering, the Noble Ones know as happiness."
“Behold the Dhamma, so difficult to understand, which the wise have here completely mastered;
for those who are shrouded there is darkness, a gloom for those who do not see.
But for the virtuous, it is opened up, like light for those who see.”
Even those dwelling nearby do not understand,

though they are skilled in the Dhamma: “This Dhamma is not easily awakened to by those who are overcome by the lust for existence, who follow the stream of existence, and who have entered the realm of Māra.”
“Who indeed, other than the Noble Ones, is able to awaken to that state,
having fully understood which state, they— free from taints— attain final Nibbāna? Now,
[the text] explains how all views fall into two categories and what Right View is for the uprooting of views.
Desiring to show this by means of a sutta, he cites the sutta beginning with "By two [things], O bhikkhus. In that context, "gods" (devā) refers even to the Brahmās.
"They shrink back" (olīyanti) means they contract. "They run too far" (atidhāvanti) means they go beyond. "Possessing vision" (cakkhumant) means possessing wisdom (paññā).

The word "and" (ca) has a distributive sense. "Delighting in existence" (bhavārāmā): for them, existence (bhava) is the delight (ārāma), their place of enjoyment; thus they are "delighting in existence."

"Delighting in existence" means being delighted by existence. "Rejoicing in existence" means being satisfied with existence. "While it is being taught" means while it is being taught by the Tathāgata or by a disciple of the Tathāgata.
"Does not leap forward" means it does not enter into the teaching of the Dhamma or into the cessation of existence.
"Does not become confident" means it does not attain confidence therein. "Does not settle down" means therein...
"It does not settle down; it does not resolve" means that it does not reach a state of density (solidification) therein. Up to this point, the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*) has been described.
"Being distressed" means undergoing suffering. "Being ashamed" means undergoing shame. "Being disgusted" means undergoing disgust.
"Rejoicing in non-existence" means they are satisfied by way of annihilationism (*uccheda*), desiring annihilation.
Or it means "meaning. *Kira* is a particle used in the sense of hearsay. *Bho* is a form of address. *Santam* means "extinguished" (*nibbūtam*).

*Paṇītam* is "excellent" because of the absence of suffering; or, it is "excellent" because it has been led to a state of preeminence (*padhāna-bhāvam*). *Yāthāvam* means "according to its true nature" (*yathāsabhāvam*).
By this much, the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*) has been stated.
"Here" means in this teaching. "The real" refers to suffering, which is produced from causes and consists of the five aggregates.
"He sees it as real" means he sees that this is real suffering. "For the sake of disenchantment" means for the purpose of insight (vipassanā).

"For the sake of dispassion" means for the purpose of the Noble Path. "For the sake of cessation" means for the purpose of Nibbāna. "One who has entered upon the way" means one who has undertaken the practice corresponding to those goals.

He is one who has entered upon the practice. "Seeing thus" means that they see by means of mundane knowledge in the preliminary stage, and by means of supramundane knowledge at the time of penetration.
Up to this point, right view has been explained.
Now, with two verses, he demonstrates the benefit of that right view. In that regard, [the verse begins: "Whoever [sees] the real as real..."

"Having seen" means having fully realized suffering through the clear comprehension of full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*). "And they transcend what has come to be" means having fully realized cessation through the clear comprehension of realization (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*).

"One is resolved upon it as it truly is" means that by way of the clear comprehension of the development of the path (*maggabhāvanābhisamaya*), one is resolved upon cessation according to its true nature, thinking:
"This is peaceful; this is sublime. "The complete exhaustion of craving for existence... [is the result].

The meaning is "by the abandoning of the origin. Furthermore, although there is no separate realization (abhisamaya) of the truths here, it should be understood that the expression "having seen"—which refers to a prior time—is stated by way of conventional usage together with the preliminary practice;
for one does not first see and subsequently resolve with conviction. The realization of the four truths occurs simultaneously.
Or, even when simultaneous, the words may be understood as preceding; thus there is no fault. "He indeed" (*sa ve*) means that Arahant certainly.

"One who has fully understood what has come to be" (*bhūtapariññāto*) means one who has fully understood suffering (*dukkha*). "Free from craving" (*vītataṇho*) means one whose craving has departed. Regarding "in becoming and non-becoming" (*bhavābhave*):
since the vowel *a* can have the sense of increase (*vuddhi*), "non-becoming" (*abhava*) refers to a great becoming (*mahābhava*), namely both small and great states of existence. He...

However, the state of being small or great is to be understood in relation to each respective basis (*upādāya*). Alternatively, "existence" (*bhava*) refers to eternalism (*sassata*), and "non-existence" (*abhava*) refers to annihilationism (*uccheda*).

One who is free from craving (*vītataṇha*) is so by virtue of the absence of attachment to views regarding both of these. "The non-becoming of what has come to be" (*bhūtassa vibhava*) is the total cutting off of the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
"He does not come to renewed existence" (*nāgacchati punabbhavaṃ*) describes the final *parinibbāna* of the *arahat*.
150. The passage beginning with “Three persons” is stated for the purpose of censuring those of wrong view and for the purpose of praising those of right view.
In this context, those whose views have reached a state of deformity are “those of failed view” (*vipannadiṭṭhī*);

those whose views have reached a state of excellence are “those of accomplished view” (*sampannadiṭṭhī*). As for “sectarians” (*titthiya*), a “ford” (*tittha*) is said to mean a view; they are so called because they have entered upon that [view].
One who stands firm (*titthati*) is a *titthiya*, or one who has a "standing place" (*titthaṃ yassa atthi*). This refers to one who has gone forth as a wanderer outside this [Buddhist] dispensation.

A "disciple of a *titthiya*" (*titthiyasāvaka*) is a householder who has entered into the following of their views. And "one who holds wrong view" (*micchādiṭṭhika*) is one who, without entering into either of those two states, holds some kind of wrong view whatsoever.
"Tathāgata" refers to the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha). The Solitary Buddha (Paccekabuddha) is also included herein.

"Disciple of the Tathāgata" refers to one who has attained the path (maggappatta) and one who has attained the fruit (phalappatta). "One who possesses right view" refers to one who possesses mundane right view, being distinct from both of those [the former two].
In the verses, "the angry one" is he who frequently becomes angry; "the resentful one" is one whose nature is to harbor resentment by increasing that very anger.
"Pāpamakkhī" means one who possesses base malice (*makkha*). "Māyāvī" means one who conceals the evil that has been committed. "Vasala" means one of low birth.

"Visuddha" means purified by the purification of knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*). "Suddhataṃ gata" means having attained the state of purity known as the path and its fruition (*magga-phala*).
"Medhāvī" means possessed of wisdom (*paññā*). By this verse, only one endowed with supramundane right view (*lokuttara-sammā-diṭṭhi*) is praised.
Abandoning the conventional designation of "persons" as "those of failed view" and "those of perfected view," he spoke while censuring and praising the Dhamma alone.
"This is mine" is a view based on the conceit of craving (*taṇhā-maññanā*). "I am this" is a view rooted in the conceit of pride (*māna-maññanā*).
"This is my self" is precisely the conceit of views (*diṭṭhi-maññanā*).

By means of the questions beginning with "What is the view that 'this is mine'?", the distinction, the enumeration, and the temporal inclusion of the three types of failed views are asked and then answered. In that context, "What is the view? means: among the many views, which one?
"Supported by which end? means: by which of the two periods of time—namely, the past (pubbanta) and the future (aparanta)—is it supported?

The meaning is "connected. Because one who misapprehends [the self] thinking "this is mine" misapprehends by referring to a past object, saying, "This was mine," "It was thus for me," or "That much was mine," therefore it is a view regarding the past (*pubbantānudiṭṭhi*).
And those views are supported by the past. Because one who misapprehends [the self] thinking "I am this" [misapprehends] "By this I..."
Or, thinking, "By virtue, or by observance, or by austerity, or by the holy life, I shall be purified," one misapprehends [the self] based on a future fruit;
therefore, this is a view regarding the future limit (*aparantānudiṭṭhi*). And those views are supported by the future limit.
Because one who misapprehends [the self], thinking "This is my self," takes up the continuity of appropriated aggregates (*upādinnasantati*) belonging to the past and the future, [thinking] "This..."
One misapprehends [them] as "this is my self," and one misapprehends them by way of the view of a personal entity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*);
therefore, there is the view of a personal entity. Furthermore, those views are supported by the past and the future.
Since the sixty-two views have the view of a personal entity as their foremost, and since the sixty-two views are eradicated precisely through the eradication of the view of a personal entity—
They proceed; therefore, it is said that there are sixty-two types of views (diṭṭhigata) with the view of a personal body (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) as their head.
The meaning is that there are sixty-two types of views by way of the view of a personal body, with the view of a personal body as their head—that is, through the door of the view of a personal body.

The reading *sakkāyadiṭṭhippamukhāni* is more excellent. They are called *sakkāyadiṭṭhippamukhāni* because the view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) is their head (*pamukha*), that is, their beginning (*ādi*). Which [are they]?
Which are they? The sixty-two views.
To the question "What is view? the answer is: the self-view with twenty bases, and the personality-view with twenty bases.
To the question "How many views are there? the answer is: the sixty-two types of views, headed by the personality-view.
The answer. Furthermore, that same *sakkāyadiṭṭhi* (personality-belief) is called *attānudiṭṭhi* (view of self) by virtue of the commonality of the expression “this is my self.
When that [personality-belief] is stated, the view associated with the doctrine of self (*attavādapaṭisaññuttā diṭṭhi*) is also necessarily stated.

151. The citation of the sutta beginning with “Whosoever, monks... is for the purpose of showing the classification of persons with perfected views, in connection with such persons who possess perfected views.
It has been said. "They have reached a conclusion therein" means they have reached a certainty that the Blessed One is the Perfectly Enlightened One by way of knowledge of the Path;
the meaning is that they are free from doubt. "Niṭṭhāgatā" is a compound word as a reading, but the meaning is the same.
"Those possessed of right view" means those who have attained the excellence of right view. Here, "conclusion" (niṭṭhā) refers to final Nibbāna in this realm of sense-desire. Here...
"Having abandoned, he reaches the end": having relinquished this existence of sense-desire (*kāmabhava*), he attains final nibbāna in the Brahma-world of the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsabrahmaloka*).

"One for whom seven births at most remain" (*sattakkhattuparama*): one for whom the arising of existence—the assumption of a personal identity—is limited to seven times, seven occasions; since he does not undergo an eighth existence beyond that, he is "one for whom seven births at most remain. [This refers to] such a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) for whom seven births at most remain.
"Kolaṃkola" means one who goes from family to family (*kulaṃ kulaṃ gacchatīti kolaṃkolo*).
From the moment of realizing the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*), there is no rebirth in a low family; the meaning is that one is reborn only in families of great wealth.
"Of that *kolaṃkola* stream-enterer. "Ekabīji" refers to what is called the "seed of the aggregates" (*khandhabīja*). For one who...
The stream-enterer has only one seed of the aggregates remaining and only one more taking up of a personal existence; he is called "one-seeded" (*ekabījī*).
Of that one-seeded stream-enterer, these names were given by the Blessed One according to the very names he had assigned to them.

For the Blessed One designated: "having gone this far, he is called 'seven-times-at-most' (*sattakkhattuparamo*); having gone this far, he is 'one who goes from family to family' (*kolaṅkolo*); having gone this far, he is 'one-seeded'."
Their names have been mentioned. For the Blessed One, having known that "this one will go to such-and-such a place; this one will go to such-and-such a place," took those respective names for them.
Indeed, a stream-enterer of dull wisdom who produces seven existences is called "one who has seven births at most" (sattakkhattuparama); one of medium wisdom who produces up to a sixth existence...
One who goes from family to family (*kolaṅkolo*) is so called because he possesses sharp wisdom; one who produces only a single existence is called "one-seeded" (*ekabījī*).

Furthermore, their status as having dull, medium, or sharp wisdom is determined by a previous cause. These three types of stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) are described here with respect to the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*);

however, in the fine-material and immaterial realms (*rūpārūpabhava*), they may take many rebirth-linkings (*paṭisandhi*). As for the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*), [the same applies] with respect to rebirth-linking.

One who comes to the existence of sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) only once is a "once-returner" (*sakadāgāmī*). Of that once-returner: "An arahant in this very life" means an arahant in this very personal existence (*attabhāva*).
*Araha* is also a reading [for *arahā*]. Here, the phrase "attains finality" is said with reference specifically to those wandering through the existence of sense-sphere existence.
However, noble ones (*ariya*) who have arisen in the fine-material or immaterial existences do not re-arise in the existence of sense-sphere existence; they attain final nibbāna right there.

"One who attains final nibbāna in the interval" (*antarāparinibbāyī*) is so called because he attains final nibbāna through the extinction of defilements precisely in the interval of the middle of his lifespan. He is of three types:

one who attains final nibbāna immediately upon rebirth, one who attains final nibbāna without reaching the middle of his lifespan, and one who attains final nibbāna having reached the middle of his lifespan.
[This refers to] such a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) who attains final nibbāna in the interval.

"One who attains final nibbāna upon landing" refers to a non-returner who attains final nibbāna through the extinction of defilements either after having passed the midpoint of their lifespan or by approaching the time of death.

"One who attains final nibbāna without exertion" refers to a non-returner whose nature it is to attain final nibbāna through the extinction of defilements without exertion—that is, without application, without performing excessive effort. "One who attains final nibbāna with exertion" refers to...

Of the non-returner whose nature it is to attain final nibbāna through the extinction of defilements—with volitional effort, with difficulty, and only by applying extreme exertion—there is the one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm.
He is called "one who goes upstream" (*uddhaṃsota*) because his stream of craving or his stream of the round of existence flows upward;
or else, because he must go upward to obtain [the goal], his stream of the Path flows upward.
"One who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm" means one who goes to the Akaniṭṭha realm by way of an upward stream.
This refers to a non-returner (anāgāmī) who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm. Furthermore, this non-returner is of four types:

he who, having cleared the four Brahmā-worlds starting from the Avihā realm and having gone to the Akaniṭṭha realm, attains final nibbāna—he is called an "upstream-goer bound for the Akaniṭṭha. He who...
Having purified the three lower Brahma-worlds and remaining in the Sudassī Brahma-world, one attains final Nibbāna;

this is called an "upstreamer" (uddhaṃsota) who does not go to Akaniṭṭha. One who goes from here directly to Akaniṭṭha and attains final Nibbāna is called an "upstreamer going to Akaniṭṭha" (akaniṭṭhagāmī).
One who, among the four lower Brahma-worlds, attains final Nibbāna right there in each respective place—
"This one is neither a 'stream-winner to the heights' nor a 'goer to the Akaniṭṭha realm. These five non-returners (anāgāmin) are spoken of with reference to the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa).

However, because they have not yet abandoned lust for the fine-material and immaterial realms, non-returners may, if they so desire, be reborn in other remaining fine-material and immaterial existences.
But those who have been reborn in the Pure Abodes are not reborn elsewhere. "Those with confirmed confidence" (aveccappasanna) refers to [the stream-enterers] by way of the Noble Path.
Having known and awakened, they are confident with unshakable faith. "Stream-enterers" means those who have entered the stream of the Noble Path.
By this, all individuals established in the noble fruits are included.
The commentary on the description of the views of existence and non-existence is finished.
The commentary on the Discourse on Views in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-aṭṭhakathā* of the *Saddhammappakāsinī* is finished. 3.
The Discourse on Mindfulness of Breathing (*Ānāpānassatikathā*).
1. Explanation of the Counting of the Rounds (Gaṇanāvāra-vaṇṇanā) 152.
Now, following the discussion on views, the commentary on the previously unstated subject matter of the discourse on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati) has arrived.
For this discourse on mindfulness of breathing serves to purify the stain of wrong view by one who has clearly understood the danger of views through the purification of that very stain.
For one whose mind is thoroughly purified, the development of concentration (*samādhi-bhāvanā*) becomes easy for the sake of realizing things as they truly are (*yathābhūtāvabodha*).

Furthermore, among all forms of concentration-development, because at the foot of the Bodhi tree all omniscient Bodhisattvas realized things as they truly are with their minds concentrated by means of this very concentration, this alone is the preeminent development of concentration;
thus it was explained immediately after the discussion on views (*diṭṭhi-kathā*). In that regard, there are sixteen bases (*vatthu*).
The enumeration of the number of knowledges begins with: "For one developing concentration through mindfulness of breathing, more than two hundred kinds of knowledge arise.

The detailed exposition of the number of knowledges begins with: "Eight knowledges regarding the obstacles," and so forth. The detailed exposition of all knowledges, from "Which are the eight knowledges regarding the obstacles?
up to the conclusion, "These are the twenty-one knowledges regarding the bliss of liberation," is as follows.

"Developing concentration through mindfulness of breathing with its sixteen bases," and so forth, is the conclusion. In this way, first, the determination of the textual basis (*pāḷivavatthāna*) should be understood.

Therein, regarding the section on counting, in the portion dealing with counting itself: "with sixteen bases" refers to the fourfold tetrad of body-contemplation (*kāyānupassanā*), namely: long [breath], short [breath], experiencing the whole body [of breath], and tranquilizing the bodily formation; and [the tetrads of] experiencing rapture and experiencing pleasure.
The tetrad of contemplation of feelings: "experiencing the mental formations and calming the mental formations"; the tetrad of contemplation of the mind:
"experiencing the mind, gladdening the mind, concentrating the mind, and liberating the mind";
and the tetrad of contemplation of phenomena: "contemplating impermanence, contemplating dispassion, contemplating cessation, and contemplating relinquishment."
It has sixteen bases (*vatthu*), foundations, and objects by way of these four tetrads; thus it is "having sixteen bases" (*soḷasavatthuka*).
Here, by way of abbreviation, the case ending has been elided. *Āna* is the internal wind that enters;
*apāna* is the wind that goes out. However, some state them in reverse order; for indeed, *apāna*...
That which has departed (*apeta*) is called *apāna*; however, in the *Niddesa*, disregarding the shortness of the letter *nā*, it is written as *āpāna*.
When there is mindfulness regarding that *ānāpāna*, it is *ānāpānassati*; this is a designation for the mindfulness that grasps inhalation and exhalation.
Concentration associated with *ānāpānassati*, or concentration in *ānāpānassati*, is *ānāpānassatisamādhi*.
“Cultivating” means cultivating that which partakes of penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*). “Exceeding” (*samadhika*) means they exist together with what is additional;
the meaning is “in excess. The letter *m* here serves as a euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*). Some, however, say “*saṃadhikānī*”;
if that were the case, it would follow that there are exactly two hundred knowledges in excess, which is not tenable. These...
For there are thus two hundred and twenty knowledges.
"Knowledges regarding obstacles" means knowledges that arise having made an obstacle their object. Likewise for "knowledges regarding aids" and "knowledges regarding defilements.
Regarding "knowledges regarding cleansing": it cleanses (*vodāyati*), and by means of it the mind becomes purified; thus it is "cleansing" (*vodāna*). What is that?

Knowledge (*ñāṇa*). Where it should have been said “knowledges of purification” (*vodāna-ñāṇāni*), it is stated as “knowledges in purification” (*vodāne ñāṇāni*), as in the case of “knowledge consisting in what is heard” (*suta-maye ñāṇaṃ*) and so forth.

One who acts with mindfulness and clear comprehension is an “act-with-mindfulness person” (*satokārī*); these are the knowledges of that act-with-mindfulness person. “Knowledges of disenchantment” (*nibbidā-ñāṇāni*) means knowledges that have become disenchantment.

“Knowledges in conformity with disenchantment” (*nibbidānuloma-ñāṇāni*) means knowledges that are favorable to disenchantment. They are also called “knowledges conforming to disenchantment” (*nibbidānulomi-ñāṇāni*).
The meaning of "conducive to disenchantment" (*nibbidānulomī*) is that they possess a reading (*pāṭha*) which is favorable to disenchantment.

"Knowledge of the subsiding of disenchantment" (*nibbidāpaṭippassaddhiñāṇāni*) refers to knowledges regarding the subsiding of disenchantment. "Knowledges in the bliss of liberation" (*vimuttisukhe ñāṇāni*) refers to knowledges associated with the bliss of liberation.
As for the question "Which eight? and so forth, it is because the obstacles and their aids form pairs of opposites and contraries; therefore, the knowledges [are presented] in relation to them.

These have been explained together. Sensual desire, renunciation, and so forth, have their meanings stated below. The word "upakāra" (benefit) is used in the neuter gender by way of a change in grammatical number (*liṅgavipallāsa*).
"All unwholesome states" refers to whatever unwholesome states remain after those already mentioned.
Likewise, "all wholesome states conducive to penetration" refers to those same wholesome states. And "obstacle" and "benefit" refer to each of those respectively.

The singular number is used by referring [to the preceding]. Here, having asked about both the knowledges regarding obstacles and the knowledges regarding aids, and having answered only their objects, he demonstrated those knowledges that have those as their objects by means of those very [objects].
The same method applies to the knowledges regarding defilements and so forth.
The commentary on the enumeration of the sections is finished.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of the Sixteen Knowledges: 153.
"By way of sixteen aspects" means by way of the sixteen divisions of knowledge stated according to both sides. "Appropriate" (uducitaṃ) [is explained as follows:]...
“Cittaṃ samuducitaṃ” means that on the level of access (upacāra-bhūmi), the mind has risen up and become refined;
it has rightly risen up and become refined, meaning it has been repeatedly cultivated higher and higher, rightly cultivated higher and higher. There is also the reading “udu-jitaṃ cittaṃ samudujitaṃ.

It is “udu-jitaṃ” because it has been conquered for the sake of higher states, or because it has been conquered by the knowledges that produce higher states. “Samudujitaṃ” [is explained as follows:]...
"Samā" means for the sake of higher states, or it is conquered by those knowledges that produce higher states. Here, "samā" is a negation of unevenness (*visamabhāva*).
In this reading, there are two prefixes, *u* and *du*. There is also a reading: "the mind is well-conquered" (*sammārūjitam*).
Here too, the meaning is simply "conquered. They say that "urū" and "arū" are merely particles (*nipāta*). (From the *Vīṇopama-aṭṭhakathā*)
The meaning stated as "conquered by that" (*tajjitaṃ*) and "well-conquered" (*sutajjitaṃ*) is not applicable here.

"It stands in unity" means that it first becomes established in unity within the access stage (*upacārabhūmi*) due to the absence of distraction toward various objects. Regarding the phrase "hindrances in the sense of obstructing the way out" (*niyyānāvaraṇaṭṭhena nīvaraṇā*):
here, even dissatisfaction (*arati*) and all unwholesome states are called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇā*) in the sense of being obstructions. Thus, "in the sense of obstructing the way out."
In the sense of blocking the path by which the ways of deliverance (*niyyāna*) arrive.

There is also a reading, "in the sense of obstructing the ways of deliverance," meaning in the sense of repelling the ways of deliverance. Renunciation (*nekkhamma*) is the deliverance of the noble ones;

because it is the cause for the Noble Path—which is termed the "deliverance" of the noble ones—standing in the place of the Path, it is called "the deliverance of the noble ones" by way of figurative designation (*phalūpacāra*). And by that...
By means of that which has become the cause, at the moment of the path (*magga-khaṇa*), the noble ones (*ariya*) go forth; they proceed. However, some say, "The 'going-forth' (*niyyāna*) is the path.

This is not tenable here, because it is the figurative usage (*upacāra*) that is intended, and because at the moment of the path there is neither the perception of light nor all wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*).
"Because of being shrouded" means because of being concealed. "He does not understand" is stated with reference to the person (*puggala*).
"Of one whose mind is purified" means while still on the level of access concentration (*upacāra-bhūmi*). "Momentary conjunction" (*khaṇika-samodhāna*):
because they arise in each and every moment of consciousness, these [defilements] possess moments; thus they are "momentary" (*khaṇika*).

The conjunction, meeting, and continuous succession of these momentary defilements is "momentary conjunction. Therefore, by way of momentary succession, the defilements that are arising—[are called] "from momentary conjunction."
It is said that they arise by way of a succession of moments, not by way of a single moment of consciousness.
The commentary on the exposition of the sixteen knowledges is finished.
3. Commentary on the Exposition of the Knowledge of Defilements.
The First Hexad. 154.

Regarding "the beginning, middle, and end of the breath" in the first hexad: for the wind entering inwardly, the tip of the nose or the sign of the mouth is the beginning, the heart is the middle, and the navel is the end. That [wind] has that as its beginning, middle, and end.
For the yogi who follows with mindfulness, as he follows the various positions [of the breath], the mind undergoes internal distraction.
That mind, having fallen into internal distraction, does not settle in unity; therefore, it is an obstacle to concentration.

"The beginning, middle, and end of the out-breath" means that for the air exiting outward, the navel is the beginning, the heart is the middle, and the tip of the nose or the sign at the mouth is the end.
Or rather, the limit is the external space. The construction here, however, should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

Regarding "the longing for an inhalation is the practice of craving": having observed that "this meditation subject depends on the breath of the nose," the very occurrence of craving is the longing (nikāmanā) consisting of a yearning for a grosser and grosser inhalation.
When there is such an occurrence of craving, [it leads to] unity.
Because it does not provide stability, it is an obstacle to concentration.

"Longing for out-breathing" (*passāsapaṭikaṅkhanā*) means attachment (*nikanti*), which is defined as the yearning for an out-breath preceded by an in-breath. The rest should be construed according to the method already stated.
"By one who is overwhelmed by the in-breath" means that when one makes the in-breath too long or too short, there is the presence of physical and mental fatigue rooted in that in-breath.
"Of one pierced and oppressed by that in-breath": this refers to one who, because of being oppressed by the in-breath, perceives gratification in the out-breath and longs for it;
thus, there is attachment (*rajjanā*) upon the attainment of that out-breath. The same method applies to what is rooted in the out-breath as well.
In the verses cited for the purpose of further illustrating the meaning already stated, "following after" means following along.
“Mindfulness” (*sati*) refers to the mindfulness that serves as the cause for internal and external distraction. “Distraction” (*vikkhepa*) is that by which the mind is distracted.
What is it? It is inhalation (*assāsa*). “Internal distraction” (*ajjhattavikkhepa*) is distraction within; the desire for that is the “desire for internal distraction. What is meant is:
the desire for inhalation, which causes internal distraction, due to improper attention (*asammāmanasikāra*). By this very [term],...
By this method, outward distraction and aspiration are to be understood. "By which" means by which defilements.

"Of one who is distracted" means of one being distracted, of one being made to fall into distraction. "And the mind is not liberated" means that the mind does not resolve upon the object of the inhalation and exhalation, nor is it liberated from opposing states. "The mind is not liberated through reliance on another" [means...]

The connection is: "and they exist. "Not understanding liberation" means that either he or another does not understand in this way both the liberation consisting in resolve toward the object (*ārammaṇādhimutti-vimokkha*) and the liberation consisting in freedom from the opposites (*paccanīka-vimutti-vimokkha*). "Those who rely on others" (*parapaccayikā*):

they deserve reliance on others, dependence on others, and faith in others; thus, while it should have been said "those who rely on others," it is stated as "those who trust in others" (*parapattiyā*), yet the meaning is the same.
The Second Sixfold Set. 155.
In the second sixfold set, "the sign" (nimitta) refers to the place where the in-breaths and out-breaths make contact.
For the in-breaths and out-breaths proceed by striking the nostril-aperture of one with a long nose, or the upper lip of one with a short nose. If this practitioner [perceives] that...
He adverts only to the sign; for him who is thus adverting to the sign, the mind wavers during the inhalation—it does not become established;
this is the meaning. Since concentration is absent because his mind is not established in that state, that wavering is an obstacle to concentration.
If he adverts only to the inhalation, his mind [wavers] by way of entering inwardly.
It brings about distraction; it does not become established in the sign; therefore, it wavers from the sign. In this same manner, the application should be made for the remaining [terms] as well.
Regarding the verses: "it is distracted" (*vikkhippati*) means it is being distracted, it is brought to a state of distraction.
This is the third group of six.
156. “The mind that pursues the past”: this refers to the mind that follows after the in-breath or out-breath once it has passed beyond the point of contact.
“Fallen into distraction”: this means either followed by distraction, or having itself fallen into—that is, entered into—distraction.
“The mind that hankers after the future”: this refers to [the mind] that has not yet reached the point of contact.
The mind that is longing for and awaiting either inhalation or exhalation.
"Agitated" means shaken by distraction due to a lack of stability in that [object]. "Lax" means contracted due to excessive laxity of energy and so forth.
"Overcome by indolence" means fallen into a state of sloth. "Over-exerted" means excessively stimulated by over-aroused energy and so forth.

"Overcome by agitation" means accompanied by distraction. "Inclined toward" means strongly inclined toward and attached to objects of gratification. "Averse" means repelled by objects that lack gratification;
or it means departed from them, or inclined away from them—the sense being that it has not departed from those [objects]. "Overcome by lust":
here, for one who is attending to the sign of the breath-in and breath-out, the joy and pleasure that arise—
Or else, passion (rāga) assails him regarding former occasions of laughing, talking, and playing. Regarding "assailed by ill-will" (byāpādānupatita):

here, either through the dejection (domanassa) that arises when the mind has become disinterested in attention, or through ill-will toward former objects of resentment (āghātavatthu), ill-will assails him.
"He does not concentrate on the verses" means he is not concentrated. "Higher mind" (adhicitta) is stated by way of the head-term "mind" (citta).
The superior concentration has been demonstrated.
Having thus demonstrated the eighteen secondary defilements by means of three sets of six, he now speaks the passage beginning with "the beginning,
middle, and end of the in-breath," etc., showing the disadvantage of those secondary defilements by establishing their nature as obstacles to concentration.
In this context, both the body and the mind are "agitated" (*sāraddha*);

that is, by way of the material phenomena produced by distraction, the physical body is agitated, and by way of the continuity of distraction, the mind is agitated with great turbulence and becomes restless.

Thereafter, they are "shaken" (*iñjita*) and "trembling" (*kampita*) to a lesser degree; thereafter, they are "quivering" (*phandita*) and "wavering" (*calita*) to an even lesser degree. This applies whether the agitation is strong or middling.
Even a slight agitation occurs; it cannot be said that there is no possibility of agitation. "Because of the mind’s wavering" means because of the mind’s state of being shaken.
In the verses, "uncultivated though complete" means that although it is complete, it has not been cultivated in such a way.
"Agitated" means shaken. "Quivering" means slightly shaken. Because they follow immediately after the hindrances mentioned below, [it says] "by these..."
Furthermore, the phrase "and from the hindrances" is used as a term indicating extreme proximity.
Here, however, in the conclusion, because the hindrances have been fully encompassed, the phrase "and from those hindrances" is used as a term indicating that which is turned away [from the speaker].
The commentary on the description of the knowledge of defilements is finished.
4. Commentary on the Exposition of Knowledge of Purification (Vodānañāṇaniddesavaṇṇanā) 158.
"Knowledges of purification" (*vodāne ñāṇāni*) means knowledges that are purified. "Avoiding that" should be connected as follows:
avoiding that mind which was previously described as chasing after the past and fallen into distraction. "He concentrates it in a single place" means...
He places and establishes [the mind] evenly at the place where the in-breaths and out-breaths touch.
“He resolves upon that very spot” means that when it is said “in one place,” he determines and makes his resolution right at the place where the in-breaths and out-breaths touch.

“Having exerted” means having exerted [the mind] through the cultivation of the investigation-of-phenomena, rapture, and equanimity factors of enlightenment. “Having restrained” means through the cultivation of the tranquility, concentration, and equanimity factors of enlightenment.

"Having restrained. Some say: "Having exerted by means of the faculty of mindfulness and the faculty of energy, and having restrained by means of the faculty of mindfulness and the faculty of concentration.

"Being clearly comprehending" refers to through the cultivation of the foul (*asubha-bhāvanā*) and so forth. "Again, being clearly comprehending" refers to through the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā-bhāvanā*) and so forth.
The connection is: "He abandons that lust by which he was assailed, and that ill-will (*byāpāda*) by which he was assailed. That...
Understanding "the mind is thus," one abandons lust through its opposite; or the meaning is that one abandons ill will.
"Purified" means free from defilements. "Bright" means luminous.
"It has attained unity" means that for one who has reached various specific stages, it has attained the corresponding unity.

“What are those unities?”—here he asks by grouping together the unified and the non-unified states that are applicable in this context. “Unity consisting in the presentation of the act of giving” (*dānūpasaggupaṭṭhānekatta*):
the “act of giving” (*dānūpasagga*) is the relinquishing (*vosajjana*) of what is called the basis for giving; it is the volition of renouncing the basis for giving.
The “presentation” (*upaṭṭhāna*) of that is its approaching and remaining as an object (*ārammaṇakaraṇavasena*). That itself is...
Unity (*ekatta*) means oneness; or rather, unity is the state of one-pointedness (*ekaggabhāva*), which is the unity of the arising of giving and relinquishing (*dāna-upasagga-paṭṭhāna-ekatta*).

The reading "unity of the arising of giving and relinquishing" (*dāna-vosagga-paṭṭhāna-ekatta*) is more excellent, and its meaning is the same. By this extraction of the term, the concentration of the recollection of generosity (*cāgānussati-samādhi*) is stated.

Although this is stated by way of extracting the specific term, it serves as the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for the other three kinds of unity as well; therefore, it is explained here.

They say so. For the great female lay follower Visākhā also said: "Venerable sir, monks who have spent the rains retreat in various directions will come to Sāvatthī to see the Blessed One. Having approached the Blessed One, they will ask:
'Venerable sir, a monk named so-and-so has passed away; what is his destination, what is his future state? To them the Blessed One [will reply]..."
He will give a prediction regarding the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or of arhatship.
I shall approach him and ask: "Venerable sir, has that noble one ever come to Sāvatthī before?
If they tell me, "That bhikkhu has indeed come to Sāvatthī before," I shall reach a conclusion there, free from doubt.

"Whether it was a rainy-season robe used by that venerable one, or food for newcomers, or food for those departing, or food for the sick, or food for those attending the sick, or medicine for the sick, or regular rice-gruel—recalling that, joy will arise in me;
in one who is joyful, rapture will arise; in one whose mind is rapturous, the body will become tranquil; and with a tranquil body..."

“I will experience pleasure; with a pleasant mind, my consciousness will become concentrated; that will be for me the development of the faculties, the development of the powers, and the development of the factors of enlightenment.

Alternatively, the first [case] is stated by way of access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) among the unities, the second by way of absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*), the third by way of insight (*vipassanā*), and the fourth by way of the path and fruit (*magga-phala*).
It should be understood thus: the sign of serenity is the "sign of serenity" (*samathanimitta*). Passing away, which is dissolution itself, is the "characteristic of passing away" (*vayalakkhaṇa*).
Cessation is Nibbāna. The rest should be applied to these three in the same manner as stated previously.

"Those intent on relinquishment" means those intent on giving. "Higher mind" (*adhicitta*) refers to the concentration that serves as the basis for insight (*vipassanāpādaka-samādhi*). "Those who possess insight" (*vipassakānaṃ*)...

For those noble persons—meaning the eight types of individuals—who are practicing insight into formations by means of the three contemplations starting from the contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā*).
The second and following three unities are applicable by way of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*) and by way of the remaining meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
"By four grounds" means by four reasons. It is "attained to unity" by way of concentration, insight, the path, and the fruit.

"The mind enters into the purification of the way (*paṭipadā-visuddhi*) and is nourished by equanimity (*upekkhā*), and is gladdened by knowledge (*ñāṇa*)," these are the summary statements (*uddesapada*).
"What is the beginning of the first jhāna? and so forth—these are the explanatory statements (*niddesapada*) preceded by questions from one desiring to elaborate upon those summary statements.
Therein, "entering into the purification of the way" means that the way itself [is so called] because it purifies the stains of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

Purity: it has leaped into and entered that purity of the way of practice (*paṭipadāvisuddhi*). "Strengthened by equanimity" (*upekkhānubrūhita*) means strengthened and increased by the equanimity of neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).
"And gladdened by knowledge" (*ñāṇena ca sampahaṃsita*) means gladdened, purified, and cleansed by purifying knowledge.
What is called "purity of the way of practice" is access concentration together with its requisites; [it consists in] the strengthening of equanimity.
Some explain it thus: "Establishment" (appanā) is the name for [the state of] absorption, and "gladdening" (sampahaṃsanā) is the name for reflection.

However, since it is said, "The mind that has attained unity both plunges into purification of the way (paṭipadā-visuddhi)," and so forth, therefore, within absorption itself, there is purification of the way by way of the process of arrival;
the intensification of equanimity by way of the function of equanimity as specific neutrality (tatramajjhattupekkhā); and of phenomena...
The encouragement should be understood as the accomplishment of the function of purifying knowledge by means of establishing the state of non-transgression and so forth.
How so? For in whichever turn absorption arises, the mind becomes purified from that mass of defilements known as the hindrances which are obstacles to that jhāna;
and because it is purified, having become free from obstructions—
One enters upon the middling sign of serenity (*majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ*). The so-called "middling sign of serenity" is simply access-concentration (*appanāsamādhi*) proceeding in equilibrium.
Immediately thereafter, however, the preceding consciousness, by way of transforming into a single continuity, approaches that state of suchness;
this is what is meant by "entering upon the middling sign of serenity. Because it has entered in this manner, through the approach to suchness—

Therein, it is said that "it leaps forward. Thus, first of all, the purification of the way (*paṭipadā-visuddhi*) should be understood as the arrival [of the mind] at the very moment of the arising of the first jhāna, which effects the state existing in the preceding consciousness.
Since there is nothing further to be purified once it has been thus purified, one who does not exert effort toward further purification possesses a purified mind.
"He looks on with equanimity" means this: because he has attained the state of serenity (*samatha*), one who is practicing for serenity does not exert further effort in its undertaking;
thus, he is said to "look on with equanimity" at the one practicing for serenity.

Furthermore, because he has already established himself in unity by abandoning contact with the defilements due to that very state of practicing for serenity, he does not exert further effort in establishing that unity again.
One contemplates the single state with equanimity. Thus, the intensification of equanimity should be understood by way of the function of equanimity as specific neutrality.
Furthermore, when equanimity has been thus intensified, the paired states consisting of concentration and wisdom—which have arisen therein—proceed without one surpassing the other;
and likewise the faculties such as faith and the rest, from which various defilements [have been removed].
Because they are liberated, they proceed having become of a single flavor through the flavor of liberation;

and since this [practitioner] exerts an energy that is appropriate for those states— which possess a single flavor in their non-transgression of that [liberation]— and since there is a cultivation occurring at that moment,
