all these modes [of practice] are such because, through wisdom, one has seen the respective dangers and benefits in both defilement and purification, and has accordingly [applied them].

It is said that because it has been gladdened, purified, and cleansed, it is accomplished; therefore, "gladdening" should be understood as the accomplishment of the function of the purifying knowledge by means of establishing the state of non-transgression regarding phenomena.
In this context, knowledge becomes manifest through equanimity, as it is said: "The mind thus well-exerted... [and so forth].
He looks on with equanimity; through the influence of equanimity and through the influence of wisdom, the faculty of wisdom becomes predominant.

Through the influence of equanimity, the mind is liberated from the various defilements; through the influence of liberation and through the influence of wisdom, the faculty of wisdom becomes predominant.
Because they are liberated, those states have a single flavor; in the sense of having a single flavor, there is development. Therefore, it is the function of knowledge.
It is said that "concluding with encouragement" refers to this.
Thus, the phrases "having thus reached the three stages," and so forth, are words of praise for that very consciousness.

In that context, "having thus reached the three stages" means by way of the method already described: through the launching into purification of the path, the development of equanimity, and the encouragement of knowledge.

It has attained a threefold state. "Endowed with applied thought" (*vitakkasampanna*) means it has reached a state of excellence through applied thought because it is free from the agitation of the defilements.

"Endowed with the steadiness of mind" (*cittassa adhiṭṭhānasampanna*) means it is complete and lacking nothing in its steadiness, which is defined as the uninterrupted occurrence of the mind upon that very object.
Just as the mastery of steadiness is called "steadiness," so too is the occurrence of the jhāna.
Likewise here too, "the steadying of the mind" (cittassa adhiṭṭhāna) is appropriately understood as one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā).

For by that [one-pointedness], the mind is steadied upon a single object and does not waver therein. However, because it is stated separately as "endowed with concentration" (samādhisampanna), it should be understood according to the method already explained.
Alternatively, since concentration itself is included within the jhāna, it means "endowed with the steadying of the mind."
This was stated by way of the five factors of jhāna. "Endowed with concentration" is stated by way of the five faculties because they are included among the faculties;
however, in the case of the second jhāna and those following, the words not found there are omitted, and it is stated as "endowed with rapture" and so forth according to what is actually present.

In the eighteen great insights, such as the contemplation of impermanence, applied thought (vitakka) and the other factors are indeed complete, because those [insights] belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).

And because absorption (*appanā*) is absent in these [preliminary stages], the purification of the way (*paṭipadā-visuddhi*) and the others should be applied by way of momentary concentration (*khaṇika-samādhi*).
Since thought (*vitakka*) and the other factors are obtained in the four paths by way of the first jhāna, thought and the rest are stated as being complete only insofar as they are actually obtained.
For in the paths belonging to the second jhāna and beyond, thought and the rest do not exist, just as they do not exist in those higher jhānas.
“They are fading away. To this extent, thirteen knowledges of purification have been explained in detail.

How so? There are six knowledges associated with concentrating in one place, resolving right there, abandoning laziness, abandoning restlessness, abandoning lust, and abandoning ill will; and those associated with the four unities.
Four kinds of knowledge, and three kinds of knowledge associated with the development of equanimity regarding purification of progress—
thus thirteen kinds of knowledge have been specified. Even so,
wishing to show their accomplishment by way of the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati), he [states] those...

Without yet concluding those knowledges, he first demonstrated the method for developing concentration through mindfulness of breathing—beginning with the words "the sign, inhalation, exhalation," and so forth—preceded by an exhortation;
then, at the end, he concluded those knowledges and demonstrated them. Therein, the "sign" has already been explained. Regarding the phrase *anārammaṇāmekacittassa*:
it means "without an object for a single consciousness. The letter *m* here serves as a euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*). It may also be read as *anārammaṇaṃ ekacittassa*.
"Reading" means that they do not become objects for a single state of consciousness. "Three things" refers to the three things beginning with the sign (*nimitta*).
"Development" refers to the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassatisamādhi*). "How?
is a question expressing the desire to explain the meaning of the verse of response spoken immediately after the verse of the challenge previously stated. "Na cime" means "and these [do not]."
*Na ca meti* is also a reading; the word-division (*padaccheda*) is the same. How is it that they are not unknown? How is it that the mind does not fall into distraction?
In this way, the word *kathaṃ* (how) is to be connected with the remaining five [questions].

And "exertion is evident" means that the energy which initiates the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassatisamādhibhāvanā*) is seen. For they exert themselves by means of that energy (*vīriya*).
"Exertion" (padhāna) is what is said. "And accomplishes the application" means that the yogi brings about the jhāna which suppresses the hindrances (nīvaraṇa).

For since jhāna is employed for the suppression of the hindrances, it is called "application. "He attains distinction" means that he obtains the path (magga) which effects the abandoning of the fetters (saṃyojana).
For the path is so called because it is the benefit (ānisaṃsa) of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).
It is called "distinction" (*visesa*). And because it is the primary element of the distinction, a conjunction was not made with the word "and" (*ca*).
Now, establishing that very meaning which was to be asked by means of a simile, he said: "Just as a tree," and so forth.

Its meaning is as follows: just as, for instance, when a tree has been hewn with an axe for the purpose of being split with a saw, at the time of splitting, [it is held] for the sake of remaining motionless—
It was placed on that same spot of ground after being made ready for use. "With a saw" means with a hand-saw.
"Having come" means having reached the side near oneself after touching the tree. "Having gone" means having reached the opposite side after touching the tree.
The word *vā* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). "They are not unknown" means [the parts] touched by the teeth of the saw on the tree [are known] by the person.
Because they have not reached the place where he is looking, and because there is no coming or going for them, all the saw-teeth are indeed known [by him].
"Exertion" (*padhāna*) is the effort of cutting the tree; "application" (*payoga*) is the act of cutting the tree. The statement "he attains distinction" has no [direct] simile.
"The sign of the basis" (*upanibandhanā-nimitta*) means that which serves as the sign for the mindfulness of the basis.

It is the tip of the nose or the sign of the mouth that serves as the cause. It is called "anchoring mindfulness" (*upanibandhanā sati*) because by means of it, the mind is anchored upon the object. "At the tip of the nose" refers to one with a long nose;
"at the sign of the mouth" refers to one with a short nose, [fixing it] on the upper lip. For the upper lip is called the "sign of the mouth" because it is the sign for mindfulness within the mouth.
"Come" means having come from the point of contact inward. "Gone" means having gone from the point of contact outward.
"Are not unknown" means that because there is no coming or going of the in-breaths and out-breaths until they reach the place of contact, all of them are indeed known.
"Becomes wieldy" means that by means of which energy both body and mind become wieldy, capable of the work of development.
It becomes fit for the task of meditation. This energy is called "exertion" (*padhāna*); thus, the cause is stated by means of its fruit.
"The defilements are abandoned" means that the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are abandoned by way of suppression.
"Thoughts are stilled" means that wavering thoughts which range over various objects come to rest. By means of which jhāna the defilements...
Thoughts are abandoned; discursive thoughts are stilled. This is called "the application" (*payoga*); the designation in the masculine gender is made with reference to this application.
"Fetters are abandoned" means that the fetters to be destroyed by each respective path are abandoned through abandonment by complete eradication (*samucchedappahāna*).
"Underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) come to an end" means that because those already abandoned are subject to non-arising again, their limit of arising or their limit of passing away has vanished.
"Or these are exhausted": they were not previously exhausted, but now they become exhausted; the meaning is that they perish.

He speaks of the exhaustion of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) in order to show that the abandoning of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) occurs through the abandoning of the underlying tendencies and not otherwise.
The meaning of "distinction" is this: the path by which the fetters are abandoned and the underlying tendencies are exhausted. In the fourth tetrad...
Since the Noble Path has also been demonstrated [previously], the Noble Path is mentioned here.

Because the absence of two objects for a single consciousness is established even without being explicitly stated, the conclusion is made without omitting that point: "Thus, these three states do not become the objects of a single consciousness."
160. Now, praising that practitioner of yoga who accomplishes success through meditation, [the author] spoke the verse beginning with "Ānāpānassati yassa" and then gave its exposition.

Therein, he for whom mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati) exists—just as it was taught by the Buddha—is one in whom it is complete, well-developed, and progressively cultivated. He illuminates this world. What?

Like what? Just as the moon, when released from clouds—just as the moon, once freed from clouds and the like, illuminates this world of space—so too does that practitioner illuminate this world of the aggregates and so forth; such is the connection of the verse.

Furthermore, it should be understood that in the explanation of the phrase "like the moon released from clouds," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) has been elided here, since mist and other such things are also mentioned therein.
In the Exposition of Verses (*Gāthāniddesa*), "neither out-breath nor in-breath" expresses that same meaning by way of negation for the sake of distinction.
"Establishment is mindfulness" means that mindfulness is the act of standing near—that is, approaching and remaining close to—precisely that in-breath due to its quality of non-forgetfulness;
the same applies to the out-breath. To this extent, the meaning has been stated: mindfulness regarding the in-breaths and out-breaths is "mindfulness of breathing" (*ānāpānassati*).
Now, wishing to point out the individual referred to by the words "for whom" (yassā) precisely by way of mindfulness (sati), it is said:
"It is established for him who inhales; it is established for him who exhales. The meaning is: for him who inhales, mindfulness stands having approached the inhalation;
for him who exhales, mindfulness stands having approached the exhalation. It is "complete" (paripuṇṇā) by way of the succession of jhāna, insight, and the path.

They are fulfilled by the attainment of the path of arahantship. Indeed, it is with reference to those very states of jhāna, insight, and the path that he said, "by way of being encompassed," and so forth.
For those states are "encompassments" (pariggaha) because they are being encompassed by this practitioner; thus, they are fulfilled by way of being encompassment.
In that context, they are fulfilled by way of being an "entourage" (parivāra), because all mind and mental factors are mutually attendant upon one another. By way of the fulfillment of development...
They are "fulfilled" in the sense of being complete. The phrases beginning with "the four developments" are stated by way of the meaning of the term "well-developed.
The four developments have already been explained above. "Made a vehicle" means made like a yoked vehicle.
"Made a basis" means made like a foundation in the sense of being a support. "Established" means present before one. "Cultivated" means [cultivated] all around.
"Citā" means accumulated. "Susamāraddhā" means well undertaken, well performed. "Yattha yattha ākaṅkhati" means if he so desires regarding whichever jhānas or whichever insights.
"Tattha tattha" means in those various jhānas and in those various insights.
"Vasippatta" means one who has attained mastery, that is, an abundance of power. "Balappatta" means one who has attained the power of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).
"Attained to intrepidity" means having attained a state of confidence and proficiency. "Those states" refers to the states of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
"Dependent on adverting" means dependent upon adverting; the meaning is that they enter into association with his mental continuum or with knowledge at the very moment of adverting.
"Dependent on desire" means dependent upon inclination; it means that at the very moment of inclining, [they arise] in the manner already described.
The meaning is that they go into association. Here, however, attention (*manasikāra*) is the arising of consciousness (*cittuppāda*) through adverting (*āvajjanā*).
It is stated as a synonym for "desiring" (*ākaṅkhanā*) for the purpose of explaining its meaning. By this it is said, "they have been made vehicles";
because they have been made thus, it is meant that they have been made like yoked vehicles.
"In whatever basis" means in each of the sixteen bases. "Well-established" (*svādhiṭṭhita*) means firmly established.
"Well-attended" (*sūpaṭṭhitā*) means properly attended.

These two factors are shown by being joined in both direct and reverse order because the mindfulness and the associated consciousness perform their respective functions together. Therefore it is said: "It has been made a basis. Thus...

What is meant is that they become firmly established precisely by way of their true nature (*bhūtattā*). "Whichever way the mind directs itself" means that, having withdrawn from its previous state of activity, one leads the mind toward whichever particular distinction of meditation (*bhāvanāvisesa*) it is directed toward.

"Mindfulness follows after that" means that mindfulness, becoming compliant with each of those very distinctions of meditation, turns back from its previous state of activity and proceeds accordingly.
And here, in the phrase “yena tenā,” the locative sense should be understood, as in such passages as “yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami.
Thus it is said, “anuṭṭhitā” (established); what is meant is that they are established by following each respective meditation through the very act of doing so.

Since mindfulness is the primary factor in mindfulness of breathing, it should be understood that in the terms “vatthukatā” (made the basis) and “anuṭṭhitā” (established), the connection is made with mindfulness.
However, because they are indeed fulfilled, cultivated, developed, and repeatedly practiced,
therefore the three meanings stated under the term "fulfilled" (paripuṇṇā) are also stated under the term "cultivated" (paricitā), and a fourth, specific meaning is also stated. Therein,
"grasping by means of mindfulness" means grasping that which is to be grasped by means of associated mindfulness or preliminary-stage mindfulness.
The yogī: he conquers evil, unwholesome states; that is, by way of complete eradication, he conquers and overcomes base defilements.
This is a teaching on the Dhamma expressed by way of the person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna). For when the states themselves are conquered, the person who possesses those states is also said to be conquered.
And those states, without abandoning mindfulness, have begun to be conquered at the very moment of their own occurrence and are thus "conquered."

They are spoken of just as one who has begun to eat is said to have "eaten. Furthermore, the grammatical characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) in this case should be understood from the science of grammar (*saddasattha*).
Even so, although it should be stated as "mastered" (*parijitā*), the letter *ja* is changed to the letter *ca*, and thus it is said "cultivated" (*paricitā*).

This is according to the characteristic of etymology (*niruttilakkhaṇa*), just as in the analysis of the meaning of "one who has gone well" (*sugata*), where the letter *da* is changed to the letter *ta* because he has gone rightly (*sammā gado assa*).

It should be understood here in the same way as it was explained previously. In this interpretation of the meaning, the word *paricitā* (cultivated) is an agentive derivation (*kattusādhana*), while the preceding three words are objective derivations (*kammasādhana*).
"The four well-commenced" means "the four things well-commenced"; thus, there is an elision of the word *attha* (thing/meaning).

It should be seen. It should be understood that here the meaning of the phrase "well undertaken" (*susamāraddhā*) is also expressed by the word "well undertaken," or else it refers to "states well undertaken.
It should be understood that they are said to be "four" by way of the division of their four meanings, not by way of a division of the phenomena themselves.
However, since only those states that are well developed are truly well undertaken and no others, therefore the three purposes of development are also [to be understood] here.

It has been stated. The sense of "repetition" (*āsevana*) is already included among the three that have been mentioned; therefore, instead of stating that, the sense of "the complete eradication of their opposites" has been stated.
For it is through the eradication of opposites that the beginning and end [of a task] are made known; thus, the sense of reaching the pinnacle of what has been well-commenced is expressed.
In this context, "of their opposites" refers to the opposites of those [states], namely, the jhānas, insight, and the path.

Of the defilements that have become adversaries—namely, sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and so forth associated with the perception of permanence (*niccasaññā*), as well as the view of a self-existent body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and so forth.

"Because they have been thoroughly eradicated" means because they have been properly uprooted and eliminated by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*), substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga*), and complete cutting off (*samuccheda*).
In manuscripts, however, it is written as "because they have been completely extirpated" (*susamugghātattā*); that is not correct.
161. Again, showing another alternative meaning for that same word, he said "well-purified" (*susama*), and so forth.

In this context, "arisen therein" means arisen in that particular excellence of cultivation which has reached its culmination. "Blameless" (*anavajja*) means free from the defects of the defilements because they do not become objects for those defilements.
"Wholesome" (*kusala*) means wholesome by way of their intrinsic nature. "Factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakkhiya*): in the sense of awakening, it is called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*).

They are called "factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakkhiya*) because they exist on the side (*pakkhe*) of the Noble One who has obtained the name [of "Buddha"]. For "existing on the side" means existing in a state of assistance.

And these are thirty-seven: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.

Phenomena (*dhammā*). "This is calm" (*samam*): at the moment of the Path, this collection of phenomena is called "calm" (*sama*) because it pacifies—that is, it utterly destroys—the defilements by means of their eradication.
"Cessation is Nibbāna": it is cessation (*nirodha*) because of the cessation of suffering;

it is Nibbāna because of the absence of craving, which is designated as "vāna. "This is perfectly calm" (*susamam*): this Nibbāna is perfectly calm because it is free from all conditioned disharmony (*visama*).

"Very even" (*susama*) means perfectly level. "Known" (*ñāta*) refers to that which is called the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya*); it is known through knowledge by way of non-delusion.
"The very even" (*susama*), which is Nibbāna, is known through knowledge by way of its being the object. That same pair is "seen" (*diṭṭha*) by that very eye, as it were.
"Understood" (*vidita*) refers to that same pair having been acquired by way of its arising within the mental continuum and by way of its being made the object.
It is realized and touched by wisdom as if it were already known. “Unflagging, unconfused, unagitated, one-pointed”:
this is the elucidation of the meaning of each preceding term. In that context, *āraddha* means established. *Asallīna* means uncontracted.
*Upaṭṭhitā* means standing having approached. *Asammuṭṭhā* means undestroyed. *Passaddho* means extinguished.
“Unrestless” means free from agitation. “Concentrated” means placed evenly. “One-pointed” means undistracted.
The phrase beginning with “the four well-undertaken” is the root meaning of the entire expression “well-undertaken.

However, “there is sameness,” etc., is an alternative meaning for the word “well,” while “known,” etc., is an alternative meaning for the word “undertaken. Herein, this is the coordination of the word-meanings:

When it should have been said as "equal, well-equal, and perfectly equal" (*samā ca susamā ca samasusamā*), the term "well-equal" (*susamā*) alone was stated by applying the grammatical rule of *ekadesasarūpekasesa* (retaining only one member of a group that shares a common form), just as "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) is used for "name, form, and name-and-form.

However, by treating it as independent of anything else—thinking "this is equal" and "this is well-equal"—the neuter gender was employed. Furthermore, since even what is already known is said to be "seen," [the word is used].
"Seen" (*diṭṭha*) and "undertaken" (*āraddha*) are one in meaning. However, "known," "realized," and "touched" are synonyms for "understood";
therefore, "known" is stated here as having the very same meaning as "undertaken.
The phrase "energy is undertaken, not slackened" expresses the straightforward meaning of the word "undertaken. "Established" (*upaṭṭhitā*)...

The words beginning with "being" (*satī*), however, are stated for the purpose of showing qualities that assist the associated energy (*sampayutta-viriya*), not for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the word "undertaken" (*āraddha*).
By the former sense, they are "well undertaken" (*susamāraddhā*); by this sense, they are "properly undertaken" (*susamā āraddhā*).
When the single remainder (*ekasesa*) is formed from these two meanings, they are called "well undertaken" (*susamāraddhā*). This is the meaning.
Having grasped [this], it is said: "Therefore it is called 'well undertaken'.
"Successive" (*anupubba*) means "in due order"; what is meant is that each preceding stage follows the one before it. "By way of long inhalation" means by way of the inhalation described as "long.
"Each preceding" refers to each preceding mindfulness. By this, the meaning of the term "successive" (*pubba*)—[is explained].
The meaning has been stated. "Successively, successively" means precisely that. By this, the meaning of the term *anu* (successive) has been stated.

By both [terms], the meaning of "cultivated both previously and successively" (*pubbañca anu ca paricitā*) has been stated. Since the sixteen bases are explained in detail further on, they are abbreviated here;
thus, only the final one, "contemplating relinquishment" (*paṭinissaggānupassī*), is shown. This is because for one whose development has reached its culmination...
All forms of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati) are also "repeatedly cultivated" because they are practiced again and again according to one's inclination.
Therefore it is said: "They are both mutually cultivated and repeatedly cultivated.

"According to the meaning" means according to their intrinsic nature. "For the purpose of self-taming" means, at the moment of the path of Arahatship, the purpose of making oneself free from defilements.
The meaning of “tranquility” (samatha) is the state of coolness. The meaning of “complete extinguishing” (parinibbāpana) is by means of the complete extinguishing of the defilements (*kilesa*).
The meaning of “direct knowledge” (*abhiññā*) is by way of all phenomena. The meanings of “full understanding” (*pariññā*) and so forth are by way of the functions of path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*).

The meaning of “clear realization of the truths” (*saccābhisamaya*) is by way of seeing the four truths as a single penetration. The meaning of “establishing in cessation” (*nirodha*) is by way of making it the object of focus (*ārammaṇa*).
Even though there was no Buddha before him, the word "Buddha" was used by one who wished to point out that specific Buddha who existed in the place where there had been no Buddha.
"Self-become" (*sayambhū*) means having become [enlightened] by oneself without instruction. "Without a teacher" (*anācariyako*) is an explanation of the meaning of the term "self-become.
For whoever penetrates the truths without a teacher is called "self-become. "In things previously unheard," and so forth.
This is the explanation of the meaning of the state of being without a teacher. "In things unheard before" means in things not heard from a teacher.
"By himself" (*sāmaṃ*) means by his own self. "Fully awakened" (*abhisambujjhi*) means he thoroughly and correctly penetrated them. And therein he attained omniscience regarding those truths;
that is, he reached the state of an omniscient one (*sabbaññubhāvaṃ*) with respect to those truths, just as those who penetrate the truths become omniscient.
It is stated thus because of his penetration of the truths (*sacca*). There is also a reading: "one who has attained omniscience" (*sabbaññutaṃ patto*).
And regarding "mastery over the powers": he attained sovereignty over the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
One who is such as this is called a Buddha. In that context, [his mind] is cultivated by the attainment of the unsurpassed liberation, characterized by knowledge unimpeded regarding all phenomena.

The Buddha is a specific kind of being designated (paṇṇatti) in dependence upon the continuity of the aggregates (khandhasantāna), or designated in dependence upon the realization of the truths (saccābhisambodhi), which is the foundation for omniscience (sabbaññutapadaṭṭhāna).
To this extent, the analysis of the Buddha has been made according to the meaning (atthato). 162.
Now, analyzing according to the phrasing (byañjanato), he says: "In what sense is one a Buddha? and so forth. Therein, just as...
In the world, one who has understood is called "understood"; likewise, because he has awakened to the truths, he is the Buddha.
Just as winds that wither leaves are called "leaf-withering," so too, because he awakens the generation of beings, he is the Buddha. He is the Buddha by virtue of omniscience;

this means he is the Buddha through the wisdom capable of awakening to all phenomena. He is the Buddha by virtue of all-seeingness; this means [he is so] through the eye of knowledge regarding all phenomena.

Because he has seen, he is called "Buddha. Because he is not to be led by others, he is called "Buddha"; because he has awakened by himself and does not need to be awakened by another, he is called "Buddha.
Because he has blossomed, he is called "Buddha"; because he has blossomed with various qualities, like a lotus in the sense of opening, he is called "Buddha.
He is called "Buddha" through these six modes of expression, beginning with "one whose taints are exhausted."
By the abandoning of those phenomena that cause the contraction of the mind, he is like a man awakened from the sleep of exhaustion;

because he is awakened from the exhaustion of the sleep of all defilements (*kilesa*), it is said that he is "Buddha. Since *saṅkhā* and *saṅkhāta* are identical in meaning, the word *saṅkhātena* means "by way of a portion.

Because of the absence of the stains of craving (*taṇhā*) and views (*diṭṭhi*), he is reckoned as being "unstained" (*nirupalepa*). [This refers to] all defilements together with their underlying tendencies (*savāsanā*).

Having distinguished [the Buddha] by means of the term "exclusive" (*ekanta*) due to his having abandoned [defilements], it is said: "one who is exclusively free from passion" (*ekantavītarāga*), and so forth.

"Exclusively free from defilement" (*ekantanikkilesa*) means one who is free from all defilements, including the remaining traces of lust, hatred, and delusion. Regarding the phrase "one who has gone the path traveled by only one" (*ekāyanamaggaṃ gata*):

because verbal roots meaning "to go" (*gamanattha*) also carry the sense of "to awaken" (*bujjhanattha*), those roots signifying awakening also signify going; therefore, [he is called] "Buddha" because he has gone the path traveled by only one.
"Because he has gone [to the goal], he is called a Buddha. And herein, regarding the "path traveled by only one":
"Path, road, way, track, the straight course, the journey, the vehicle;
boat, ford, bridge, raft, float, and crossing."
Among the many names for the path, it is spoken of by the name "way" (*ayana*). Therefore, the meaning is that the path is a single way, not a forked road.

Alternatively, it is called the "single-way path" (*ekāyana-magga*) because it is to be traversed (*ayitabba*) by one alone. "By one" means by a mind that has abandoned the company of crowds through seclusion.
"To be traversed" means to be practiced. Or else, it is a "way" (*ayana*) because one goes (*eti*) by means of it, away from saṃsāra.
The meaning is: "going to Nibbāna. *Ekāyana* means the way of some (*ekesaṃ ayano*). "Some" (*eke*) refers to the best;

and the Fully Enlightened Ones (*sammāsambuddhā*) are the best among all beings. Therefore, it is called the "way of one" (*ekāyanamagga*), meaning the path that serves as the way for the Fully Enlightened Ones.

Alternatively, it is called *ayana* because it goes (*ayatīti*); the meaning is that it proceeds or moves forward. It is the "way of one" (*ekasmiṃ ayano maggo*) that is the "way of one" (*ekāyanamaggo*).
It is said that the path proceeds only within the single teaching of the Buddha, and not elsewhere. Furthermore, it is "the sole way" (*ekāyana*) because it goes to one thing;
although it proceeds by various methods of cultivation during the preliminary stage, in the subsequent stage it goes only to the one *nibbāna*.
Therefore, the meaning of "the path that is the sole way" is "the path leading to the single *nibbāna*. One [who attains] the unsurpassed...

Regarding the statement "he is called a Buddha because he has awakened to perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*)," he is not called a Buddha because he was made so by others; rather, it is said that he is a Buddha because he himself has awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
Because he has destroyed non-intelligence (*abuddhi*) and attained intelligence (*buddhi*), he is a Buddha. *Buddhi*, *buddha*, and *bodha* are synonyms for this. In this regard, just as...

Just as a cloth is called "blue" or "red" due to its association with the qualities of blue or red, so too it was said to make known that he is called "Buddha" due to his association with the qualities of a Buddha.
Following that, the passage beginning with "‘Buddha’ is not a name" was spoken for the purpose of making it known that "this designation follows the meaning.
In this context, *mittā* means friends; *amaccā* means ministers; *ñātī* means paternal kinsmen; and *sālohitā* means maternal kinsmen.

"Ascetics" (*samaṇā*) are those who have gone forth into homelessness. "Brahmins" (*brāhmaṇā*) are those who address others as "venerable sir" (*bhovādino*), or those who have stilled evil and cast out evil.

"Devas" are [beings] such as Sakka and the Brahmās. "Pertaining to liberation" (*vimokkhantika*): liberation is the path to arahantship; the end of liberation (*vimokkhassa anto*) is the fruit of arahantship.
That which exists at that end of liberation is called "pertaining to liberation. For omniscience is accomplished by means of the path to arahantship.
It is established at the arising of the fruit of arahantship; therefore, omniscience occurs at the end of liberation.
That name, though called "indicative" (*nemittika*), is actually one that occurs at the end of liberation. Hence it is said: "This [name] of the Blessed Buddhas occurs at the end of liberation.
"At the root of the Bodhi tree, together with the attainment of omniscient knowledge" means, at the aforementioned moment, at the foot of the Great Bodhi tree.

Together with the attainment of omniscient knowledge. "Manifest designation" (*sacchikā paññatti*) refers to the designation arising from the realization of the fruit of arahantship or the realization of all phenomena.
That which is called "Buddha"—this designation "Buddha" is the elucidation of the Buddha by way of its phrasing (*byañjana*).
Regarding the line of the verse beginning with “*yathā buddhena desitā*,” the correlation based on the meaning explained in this word-commentary (*padabhājanīya*) is as follows:
both the mindfulnesses of breathing (*ānāpānassatiyo*) and the ten meanings of “as it is” (*yathatthā*) are “taught by the Buddha” (*yathā buddhena desitā*).
They are taught by whatever manner they were taught; thus, there is also the sense of manner conveyed by the word *yathā*.

It should be understood that the word "yathā" is stated by forming a single-remainder compound (*ekasesa*) through the method of identical remainder (*sarūpekasesa*) for both the word "yathā" [meaning "according to"] and the word "yathā" [meaning "nature"].
However, in the word-analysis (*padabhājanīya*), the singular form "desito" (taught) is used by way of applying it to each of the meanings of "yathā" individually.
Because it is stated, “Whether he be a householder or one gone forth,” it follows that in the first phrase as well, it is already implied: “of whichever householder or of whichever one gone forth.
The meaning of the world (*lokattha*) has already been explained. “He illuminates” (*pabhāseti*) means he makes his own knowledge manifest.

“Because of having fully awakened” (*abhisambuddhattā*) means because of the state of having penetrated [the truth] even by means of the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple. “He radiates” (*obhāseti*) refers to that which belongs to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
"The world": he illuminates the world consisting of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*). "He makes it radiant": he makes radiant the world consisting of the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*).
"Noble knowledge" (*ariyāñāṇa*) means the knowledge of the path to Arhatship. "Freed from mist" means freed from mist; "mist" (*mahikā*) is said to be frost.
There is also a reading: "freed from earth" (*mahiyā*). "Freed from smoke and dust" means freed from both smoke and dust. From the grasp of Rāhu...
"Completely liberated" (*vippamutto*) is said with the addition of two prefixes because Rāhu is a proximate defilement for the moon.
"Shines" (*bhāsate*) in the sense of being luminous; "glows" (*tapate*) in the sense of possessing brilliance; "radiates" (*virocate*) in the sense of being beautiful.
"In this very way" (*evamevaṃ*) means "just so. For even the moon, while itself shining, glowing, and radiating, illuminates this world of space.
And when a bhikkhu speaks with wisdom, glowing and shining, he illuminates this world of the aggregates and so forth with wisdom;
therefore, in both cases, instead of saying "he speaks" (*bhāseti*), it is said simply "he shines" (*bhāsate*). For when it is stated thus, the sense of a cause is also expressed.

If one asks: why is the simile of the moon used instead of taking the simile of the sun, which is much more brilliant? It is because [the moon] brings about the subsiding of the fever of all defilements.
It should be understood that these [qualities] are taken as being appropriate for a peaceful bhikkhu, comparable to the moon which is endowed with the quality of peace.

Thus, having encouraged the practitioner who has achieved success in the development of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*), he concludes by showing those knowledges, saying: "These are the thirteen knowledges of purification."
The commentary on the exposition of the knowledge of purification is finished.
5. Commentary on the Exposition of the Knowledge of Acting with Mindfulness (Satokāriñāṇaniddesa) 163.
In the exposition of the knowledge of acting with mindfulness, regarding the matrix (mātikā): "Here, a bhikkhu" means a bhikkhu in this dispensation (sāsana). For this...

Here, the word "here" (idha) indicates the teaching that serves as the support for the person who has produced the concentration of mindfulness of breathing in all its modes, and it negates the existence of such a state in any other teaching. For this has been said: "Right here, monks, is there a recluse... [and so on]...
empty are the doctrines of others of recluses other than these."

"Having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut"—this illustrates his selection of a dwelling suitable for the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassatisamādhi*).
For this bhikkhu’s mind, which for a long time has been dissipated among objects such as forms, does not wish to mount the object of concentration through mindfulness of breathing;
it runs only along the wrong path, like a chariot yoked to a wild bull. Therefore, just as...
Suppose a cowherd, wishing to tame a rogue calf that had grown fat by drinking all the milk from a deceitful cow,
were to remove it from the mother, drive it to a secluded spot, and bind it there with a rope to a large post he had driven into the ground;
then, that calf, after struggling here and there, being unable to escape, would sit down right next to that very post.

Or it might fall upon him; even so, this bhikkhu, desiring to tame the corrupted mind that has long been nourished by drinking the flavors of sense objects such as forms, should withdraw it from those objects like forms and lead it into the forest, the foot of a tree, or an empty hut, where he should bind it to the pillar of in-breathing and out-breathing with the rope of mindfulness. In this way, his mind—
Even though it flutters hither and thither, failing to find its former habitual object, it is unable to escape once the tether of mindfulness has been cut;
thus it settles down upon and lies down upon that very same object by way of access and absorption. Therefore the ancients said:
"Just as a man here might tie a calf to be tamed to a post, so too does one bind the mind to an object."
“One should thus bind one’s own mind firmly to the object by means of mindfulness.

In this way, that lodging becomes suitable for his meditation. Alternatively, because this [meditation on the body] is the preeminent among the various types of meditation subjects, it is the proximate cause for the distinguished attainments and the pleasant dwellings in this very life of all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha.
The meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing is not easy to develop without abandoning the vicinity of a village crowded with the sounds of men,
women, elephants, horses, and so forth, because sound is a thorn to jhāna. However, in a forest devoid of villages,
it is easy for a practitioner of yoga to take up this meditation subject, to produce the four jhānas of breathing, and to make that very attainment the basis for further progress.
Having comprehended mental formations (*saṅkhāra*), one attains the supreme fruit, which is Arahantship.
Therefore, pointing out a dwelling place suitable for him, the Blessed One said, "Whether gone to the forest," and so forth; likewise did the Elder.
For the Blessed One is like a master of site-selection (*vatthuvijjācariya*); just as a master of site-selection, having surveyed the ground for a city, [proceeds to build it].
Just as one who, having thoroughly investigated a site, points it out saying, "Build the city here," and when the city is completed in safety, receives great honor from the royal family;

even so, the practitioner of yoga, having thoroughly investigated a suitable lodging, points it out saying, "The meditation subject should be pursued here. Then, by one who is devoted to the meditation subject there—
When a yogī attains Arahatship through gradual practice, he receives great honor, thinking, "Truly, that Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One.

This bhikkhu, however, is said to be "like a leopard. For just as a great king of leopards, having hidden himself by relying on a thicket of grass, a forest thicket, or a mountain thicket in the wilderness, [preys upon] wild buffaloes, cattle-eared deer, wild boars, and so forth—

Just as a hunter seizes game by lying in wait, even so should it be understood that this bhikkhu, applying himself to his meditation subject in the forest and other such places, seizes the paths of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship, as well as the noble fruits, in their proper sequence. Thus said the ancients:
"Just as one called a leopard, Lying in wait, seizes game;..."
"In the same way, this son of the Buddha, devoted to practice and practicing insight,
enters the forest and grasps the supreme fruit. Thus,
showing him the forest dwelling as a ground suitable for the speed of his exertion, he said, "Whether gone to the forest," and so forth.
In this context, "gone to the forest" means one who has gone to any forest characterized by the solitude previously described.
"Gone to the foot of a tree" means one who has gone near a tree. "Gone to an empty place" means one who has gone to a vacant, secluded spot.

Furthermore, with the exception of the forest and the foot of a tree, it is also appropriate to say that one has "gone to an empty place" even when staying in any of the remaining seven types of lodgings.
For there are nine kinds of lodgings. As it is said: "He resorts to a secluded lodging:
the forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hill-cave, a charnel ground, a jungle-thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
Thus, having pointed out to him a lodging suitable for the three seasons, suitable for his temperament and conduct, and conducive to the development of mindfulness of breathing;
He said, “he sits,” indicating that he adopts a posture which is peaceful, free from sloth, and not conducive to restlessness.

Then, demonstrating the firmness of his sitting posture, the capacity for the continued flow of inhalation and exhalation, and the method for grasping the object of meditation, he said, “having folded his legs crosswise,” and so forth.
In this context, “crosswise” (*pallaṅka*) refers to a seat bound around the thighs on all sides. “Having folded” (*ābhujitvā*)—
Having bound [the body] and having set the body straight: having placed the upper part of the body upright, he aligns the eighteen vertebrae end-to-end.
For when one is seated in this way, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not bend.
Thus, those pains that would arise moment by moment due to their bending do not arise. Since they do not arise, [he remains undisturbed].
The mind becomes one-pointed, the meditation subject does not slip away, and it attains growth and expansion.
"Having established mindfulness facing the front" means having placed mindfulness directed toward the meditation subject.
"Mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out" means that the bhikkhu, having sat down in this way and having established mindfulness in this manner, [breathes in and out].
"Not abandoning mindfulness" means that being mindful, one breathes in mindfully and breathes out mindfully; what is meant is that one acts with mindfulness.
Now, in order to show the ways in which one acts with mindfulness, he said: "Breathing in long," and so forth.
Therein, "breathing in long" means causing a long inhalation to proceed; likewise for "short. As for that which...

Their length or shortness is to be understood by way of time. For sometimes humans breathe in and out long, like elephants, snakes, and so forth, due to the influence of time; sometimes they breathe in and out short, like dogs, rabbits, and so forth.
Otherwise, breaths that are broken up and fragmented are not called "long" or "short. Therefore, those [breaths] for a long duration...
It should be understood that when entering [the breath] it is long, and when exiting it is long; when entering and exiting for a short duration, it is short.
In this regard, by means of the nine modes mentioned above, this bhikkhu, while breathing in long and breathing out long, understands:
"I am breathing in long, I am breathing out long"; likewise with the short.
And for one who understands thus:
"The long and short inhalation, and likewise the exhalation—
these four colors proceed right at the tip of the bhikkhu's nose."
It should be understood that through one of these nine modes, the development of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body succeeds.

When it is said, "He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body'; he trains thus: 'I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body,'" this means that he makes known and makes clear the beginning, middle, and end of the entire body of in-breaths.
He trains thus: "I shall breathe in. Making known and making clear the beginning, middle, and end of the entire body of exhalation, he trains thus:
"I shall breathe out. Making it known and making it clear in this way, he breathes in and breathes out with a mind associated with knowledge.
Therefore, it is said: "He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in, I shall breathe out.'"
For one bhikkhu, when the body of inhalation or the body of exhalation has become scattered and dispersed, the beginning is manifest, but not the middle or the end.
He is able to discern the beginning alone, but he becomes weary regarding the middle and the end.
For another, the middle is manifest, but not the beginning or the end. He is able to discern the middle alone.
One tires at the beginning or at the end. For one person, the end is clear, but not the beginning or the middle;
he is able to grasp only the end, while tiring at the beginning and the middle. For another, everything is clear;
he is able to grasp all of it and does not tire anywhere. Showing that one should become like the latter, he said:
“Experiencing the whole body,” and so forth.
Therein, “he trains” means he strives and exerts himself in this way. Or, the restraint of one who has become thus is here the training in the higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*).
The concentration of one who has become thus is the training in the higher mind (*adhicitta-sikkhā*). The wisdom of one who has become thus is the training in the higher wisdom (*adhipaññā-sikkhā*).

These three trainings are practiced, cultivated, developed, and frequently repeated with respect to that object, by means of that mindfulness, and by means of that attention; this is how the meaning should be understood here.
In that regard, according to the previous method, one need only breathe in and breathe out, and nothing else need be done; but from this point onward, there is the arising of knowledge and so forth.
Yoga must be practiced. Therefore, having stated the text there in the present tense as "he understands: 'I am breathing in';

he understands: 'I am breathing out,'" the text should be understood as having been set forth hereafter in the future tense—beginning with "I shall breathe in while experiencing the whole body"—for the purpose of showing the manner (ākāra) of producing knowledge and so forth that is to be performed from this point forward.
“He trains thus: ‘Calming the bodily formation... ... [etc] ... “He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in, I shall breathe out, calming the bodily formation.

Herein, the grossness and subtlety, as well as the subsiding, should be understood as follows: Previously, when this bhikkhu had not yet comprehended [the breath], both his body and his mind were restless and gross.
While the restlessness and grossness of body and mind have not yet subsided, the in-breaths and out-breaths [are likewise gross].”
They become coarse and proceed with greater force; the nose is no longer sufficient, and one remains breathing in and out through the mouth.
But when both body and mind are fully mastered, they become calm and tranquil.
When these have become tranquil, the inhalations and exhalations proceed in a subtle manner, [and one perceives]: "There is..."

they have reached a state where one must investigate whether [the breath] exists or not. Just as when a man has run, or descended from a mountain, or lowered a heavy burden from his head and stands still, his inhalations and exhalations are coarse;
his nose is no longer sufficient, and he remains standing breathing in and out through his mouth. But when he has that fatigue...
Having amused himself, bathed, and drunk, he places a wet cloth against his heart and lies down in the cool shade;
then his inhalations and exhalations become so subtle that they reach a state where one must investigate whether they exist or not.
In this same way, the passage for the time when this bhikkhu has not yet discerned [the breath] should be explained in detail. For previously, at the time when he had not yet discerned it—
“There is no mental application consisting of directed attention and sustained application [when one thinks], ‘I am tranquilizing gross bodily formations’;

however, it exists at the time of having grasped them. Therefore, compared to the time when they have not been grasped, the bodily formation is subtle at the time when they have been grasped. Thus the ancients said:
‘When the body and mind are agitated, [the formation] proceeds excessively;’”
“When the body is not agitated, it proceeds subtly.

Thus, in the preliminary stage (*pariggahe*), it is gross; in the access concentration (*upacāra*) of the first jhāna, it is subtle. Even in that [access], it is gross; in the first jhāna itself, it is subtle.
In both the first jhāna and the access to the second jhāna, it is gross; in the second jhāna, it is subtle. In the second jhāna...
It is gross in the access to the third jhāna and subtle in the third jhāna;

it is gross in the third jhāna and subtle in the access to the fourth jhāna, and in the fourth jhāna it becomes extremely subtle, reaching a state of non-occurrence. This, first of all, is the opinion of the Dīgha-bhāṇakas and Saṃyutta-bhāṇakas.
However, the Majjhima-bhāṇakas maintain that it is "gross in the first jhāna and subtle in the access to the second jhāna," and so on, [extending] from each successive lower jhāna.
They maintain that even in the access (upacāra) to each successive jhāna, the mental state becomes increasingly subtle.

However, according to the opinion of all [teachers], the bodily formation (kāya-saṅkhāra) that occurs during the time when [the breath] is not yet grasped subsides at the time it is grasped; the bodily formation occurring during the time it is grasped subsides in the access to the first jhāna...
and so on... until the bodily formation occurring in the access to the fourth jhāna subsides in the fourth jhāna itself.
This, first of all, is the method regarding serenity (*samatha*).
In insight (*vipassanā*), however, when there is no yet-completed discernment, the bodily formation that has arisen is gross; it is subtle upon the discernment of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
That too is gross; it is subtle upon the discernment of derived form (*upādārūpa*). That too is gross; [it is subtle] upon the discernment of all material phenomena.
It is subtle. That too is gross; it is subtle when grasping the formless. That too is gross; it is subtle when grasping both the material and the immaterial.
That too is gross; it is subtle when grasping conditions. That too is gross; it is subtle when seeing conditioned name-and-form.
That too is gross; it is subtle in insight that has the characteristics as its object. That too is gross in weak insight.
With strong insight it is subtle. In this regard, the subsiding of each preceding stage by each succeeding one should be understood in the same manner as previously explained.
Thus, both the grossness and subtlety, as well as the subsiding, should be understood here.
This concludes the word-by-word commentary on the first tetrad taught by way of contemplation of the body.
Since, however, it is this very tetrad that is taught here as the meditation subject for a beginner,
whereas the other three tetrads are taught here as the contemplations of feelings, mind, and mental objects for one who has already attained jhāna,

therefore, having developed this meditation subject, one should, together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), [practice] insight based on the foundation of the four jhānas of mindfulness of breathing.
A clansman who is a beginner and desires to attain arahantship should perform all the necessary tasks, such as the purification of virtue, according to the method set forth in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Then, in the presence of a teacher endowed with the seven factors, he should learn the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) consisting of five stages.
These five stages are: learning, questioning, establishing, absorption, and the characteristic.
In this context, "acquisition" (uggaha) means the grasping of the meditation subject. "Interrogation" (paripucchā) means the questioning regarding the meditation subject.
"Establishment" (upaṭṭhāna) means the establishment of the meditation subject. "Absorption" (appanā) means the absorption of the meditation subject.

"Characteristic" (lakkhaṇa) means the characteristic of the meditation subject; what is meant is the discerning of the intrinsic nature of the meditation subject, thinking, "This meditation subject has such a characteristic."
One who learns the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) according to these five stages neither tires himself nor troubles his teacher.
Therefore, having had it recited in brief and having practiced the recitation for a long time, and thus having mastered the meditation subject according to these five stages,
one should avoid monasteries associated with the eighteen faults— whether in the presence of the teacher or elsewhere— and [dwell] in one endowed with the five factors.

While dwelling in a lodging, having severed minor impediments, having finished the meal and dispelled the drowsiness following the meal, one should, while sitting comfortably, gladden the mind by recollecting the virtues of the Triple Gem.

Then, without omitting even a single word from the teacher’s instruction, one should attend to this meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*). Herein, this is the method of attention:
“Counting, following, touching, fixing, observing;
turning away, purification, and reflection upon them.
Herein, counting is simply the act of counting. Following is pursuing [the breath]. Touching is the point where it is touched. Fixing is...
Absorption (*appanā*) is insight (*vipassanā*). Turning away (*vivaṭṭanā*) is the path (*magga*). Complete purification (*pārisuddhi*) is the fruit (*phala*).

And the reviewing of these is reflection (*paccavekkhaṇā*). In this regard, this son of good family who is a beginner should first attend to this meditation subject by means of counting. While counting, however, he should not go below five.
It should not be led beyond ten, nor should a break be shown in between.
For when one places it below five, the arising of consciousness wavers in the cramped space, like a herd of cattle confined in a narrow pen.
When one leads it beyond ten, the arising of consciousness remains dependent on counting. When one shows a break in between, [the thought] reaches its peak...
"Is this my meditation subject or not? Thus the mind wavers; therefore, having avoided these faults, one should count.
And while counting, one should first count by the slow method, like a grain-measurer.
For a grain-measurer, having filled the measure, says "one" and pours it out; then, while filling it again, seeing some chaff and discarding it—
He says, “one, one. This same method applies to “two, two,” and so forth.

In this very way, by means of this [method] as well, one should take whichever [breath] appears among the inhalations and exhalations, and starting from “one, one,” etc., count only after having observed each occurrence as it proceeds until “ten, ten.
As he counts in this manner, the breaths exiting and entering—
And the inhalations and exhalations become manifest.
Then, having abandoned that slow counting—the counting like a grain-measurer—he should count by means of quick counting, the "cowherd's counting.
For a clever cowherd, having taken pebbles and so forth in his lap, with a rope and staff in hand, early in the morning...
Having gone to the cow-pen and struck the cows on their backs, he sat upon the top of the threshold pillar and counted the cows as they reached the door,
throwing pebbles one by one for each, saying, "One, two. The herd of cattle, which had spent the three watches of the night suffering in the cramped space,
emerged in dense clusters, jostling against one another with great speed.
Having offered the oblation, he goes out. With great speed, he counts "three, four, five, ten.
As he counts in this manner according to the previous method, the inhalations and exhalations become manifest and move back and forth very rapidly again and again.
Then, knowing that they are moving back and forth repeatedly, he does not grasp them at the beginning or the end, but [grasps them] as they reach the door.

Having taken up the counting as soon as it reaches the door, one should count very rapidly: "One, two, three, four, five; one, two, three, four, five, six; one, two, three, four, five, six, seven... pe... eight, nine, ten.
For when the meditation subject is bound up with counting, the mind becomes one-pointed through the power of counting alone, by way of supporting the axle-pin.
It is like placing a boat in a violent current.
As he counts thus very rapidly, the meditation subject appears as if it were occurring without interruption.
Then, knowing that "it occurs without interruption," and without grasping at the wind inside or outside, he proceeds in the same manner as before.
It should be counted with great rapidity. For when one brings the mind in together with the air entering within, the interior seems as if struck by wind and filled with fat.
When one draws the mind out together with the air exiting outward, the mind becomes distracted toward external, manifold objects.
However, having established mindfulness at each point where [the air] touches, [one should proceed].

Only for one who develops it in this way does the development succeed. Therefore it was said: "Without apprehending the wind either internally or externally, one should count with increasing speed in the manner previously described.
But how long should this counting be practiced? Until mindfulness, independent of counting, becomes established upon the object of the in-breaths and out-breaths.
Counting is indeed for the purpose of establishing mindfulness upon the object of the breath-in and breath-out by cutting off discursive thoughts that have spread outward.
Having thus given attention through counting, one should give attention through continuous following (*anubandhanā*).

"Continuous following" means the uninterrupted tracking of the breath-in and breath-out by means of mindfulness after withdrawing from counting. And this is not by way of tracking their beginning, middle, and end.
The disadvantages of following [the breath] from its beginning, middle, and end have already been explained above.
Therefore, one who attends to it by way of following should not attend to it by way of its beginning, middle, and end;
rather, it should be attended to by way of touching and by way of fixing. By way of counting and following...
For there is no separate attention by way of touching and placing;
rather, while counting, one attends both by means of counting and by means of touching at each spot touched.
Then, withdrawing the counting right there and following those [spots] with mindfulness, and placing the mind through absorption, one attends "by way of following and touching."

"And he attends to it for the purpose of establishing [the mind]. This meaning should be understood through the similes of the cripple and the doorkeeper mentioned in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), as well as by the simile of the saw mentioned right here in the text (*pāḷi*).
Among these, this is the simile of the cripple: just as a cripple, having pushed the swing of his mother and son who are playing on a swing, [remains stationary].
Just as one sitting right there at the base of the swing’s pillar sees both ends and the middle of the swing’s plank as it comes and goes,
yet does not exert effort for the sake of seeing those two ends and the middle—
so too, a bhikkhu, standing at the base of the pillar of anchoring through mindfulness and swinging the swing of inhalation and exhalation, [sees them all].

Sitting right there at the sign with mindfulness, as he gradually follows with mindfulness the beginning, middle, and end of the in-breaths and out-breaths at the points where they touch those who are coming and going, he sees them after fixing the mind right there;
yet he does not become occupied in order to see them. This is the simile of the cripple.
This, however, is the simile of the gatekeeper: just as a gatekeeper does not investigate the men inside or outside the city, asking, "Who are you?

Where have you come from? Where are you going? What do you have in your hand?"—for these are not his burden—but investigates each person as soon as they arrive at the gate; even so it is with this bhikkhu.
The winds that have entered within and those that have gone outside are not a burden; only those that have reached the door are a burden—this is the simile of the gatekeeper.

As for the simile of the saw, it has already been explained here by way of the passage beginning, "The sign is the in-breath and out-breath. However, it should be understood that its purpose here is merely non-attention (amanasikāra) toward them according to their coming and going.
For someone who attends to this meditation subject, the sign arises without long delay, and the fixing known as absorption—
which is adorned with the remaining jhāna factors— is accomplished. However, for another person, from the very moment they begin attending by means of counting,
it is as if, when one with a rigid body sits on a bed or a chair, the bed or chair sinks down and creaks.

The bedspread takes a fold; however, when one sits with the body not agitated, the bed or chair neither sinks nor creaks, and the bedspread does not take a fold—the bed and chair become as if filled with cotton wool. Why?
Because the unagitated body is light. In the same way, from the time of attending to the breath by means of counting...
As one proceeds in this sequence, when bodily agitation has been stilled through the cessation of gross inhalation and exhalation, both body and mind become light;
the body becomes as if it has attained the state of leaping into the air.
When those gross inhalations and exhalations have ceased, the mind proceeds with the sign of the subtle inhalations and exhalations as its object.
When that too has ceased, another and yet another sign of the breath—inhalation and exhalation—more and more subtle than the previous one continues to occur.
This matter is to be understood by means of the simile of the heap of grain mentioned above.
For while other meditation subjects become clearer at each successive stage, this one does not; rather, it is as follows:
As he cultivates it further and further, it becomes subtle and does not even come into manifestation.
When it does not manifest in this way, that bhikkhu should not rise from his seat and depart, thinking, "I will ask my teacher," or "My meditation subject is now lost.
For if he goes about disturbing his posture, the meditation subject becomes ever more fresh.
Therefore, while remaining exactly as one is sitting, the subject must be brought forth from its source.
Herein, this is the method for bringing it forth: having recognized that the meditation subject does not appear, that bhikkhu should reflect thus:
"Where do these so-called in-breaths and out-breaths exist, and where do they not exist? Or in whom [do they exist]?"
“Does it exist, or for whom does it not exist? When he reflects in this way, having understood: “This does not exist within the mother’s womb;

it does not exist for those submerged in water; likewise, it does not exist for those who have become unconscious, for the dead, for those attained to the fourth jhāna, for those possessing existence in the fine-material or immaterial realms, and for those attained to cessation,” he should thus reproach himself by himself.

“Surely, O wise one, you are neither in the mother’s womb, nor submerged in water, nor unconscious, nor dead, nor entered into the fourth jhāna, nor possessed of existence in the fine-material or immaterial realms, nor have you attained the cessation of perception and feeling.
There are indeed in-breaths and out-breaths for you; it is only because of your dull wisdom that you are unable to discern them. Then, by way of his natural state, he [proceeded].

Having fixed the mind, attention should be applied. For these [breaths] occur by striking the nostril-aperture of one with a long nose, and the upper lip of one with a short nose. Therefore, he should fix the sign, thinking: "They strike this particular spot.
It was for this very reason that the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, I do not..."
“I say that the development of mindfulness of breathing belongs to one who is mindful and clearly comprehending.

For although any meditation subject whatsoever succeeds only for one who is mindful and clearly comprehending, this meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing becomes manifest even to one who is attending to something other than it;
yet this meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing is weighty, a weighty development, [practiced] by Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the sons of the Buddhas.
It is the domain of mental attention for great beings alone; it is neither trivial nor cultivated by inferior beings.
To whatever extent it is attended to, it becomes accordingly more peaceful and more subtle.
Therefore, in this matter, powerful mindfulness and wisdom are required.
For just as when sewing a smooth cloth, the needle must be fine and the needle-case even finer,
so too at the time of developing this meditation subject— which is like a smooth cloth— mindfulness,
which corresponds to the needle, and the wisdom associated with it, which corresponds to the needle-case, must both be powerful.
Furthermore, a bhikkhu endowed with those mindfulness and wisdom need not search for the in-breaths and out-breaths elsewhere than the place normally touched by them.
For it is as if a farmer, having ploughed his field and released his oxen to graze, were to sit down in the shade to rest;
then those oxen might suddenly bolt into the forest. Now, there is a clever farmer...
Furthermore, wishing to take them back and yoke them, he does not wander through the forest following their tracks.
Instead, taking his reins and goad, he goes directly to the bathing ford where they descend, and there he either sits or lies down.
Then, after those oxen have grazed for part of the day, they descend to the bathing ford, bathe, and drink.
Having seen them standing after they had stepped back, he would bind them with a rein, prick them with a goad, lead them back, yoke them again, and then perform his work.
In the same way, that bhikkhu should not seek those in-breaths and out-breaths anywhere other than the natural place where they touch.
Rather, taking the rein of mindfulness and the goad of wisdom, he should fix the mind upon the natural place where they touch.
Attention should be applied. For one who applies attention in this way, those [signs] will appear before long, like oxen at a watering place.

Then, having bound them with the rein of mindfulness and yoked them to that very spot, he should repeatedly devote himself to the meditation subject, prodding them with the goad of wisdom. As he devotes himself in this manner, before long—
The sign appears. However, this does not appear identically to everyone;
rather, some say that for certain individuals it appears like a tuft of cotton, a tuft of kapok, or a stream of air, producing a pleasant tactile sensation.
But this is the explanation in the commentaries: for some, indeed, it appears like the form of a star, or like a round gem.
To some it is like a pearl bead; to some it has a rough touch, like cotton-seed, or like a needle made of the heartwood of wood;
to some it is like a long silk thread, or like a garland of flowers, or like a column of smoke;
to some it is broad, like a spider's web, or like a mass of clouds, or like a lotus flower, or like a chariot wheel.
It appears like the moon’s disk, like the sun’s disk, and so forth;
and this is just as when many bhikkhus are sitting after having recited a sutta together, and one bhikkhu asks,
"In what way does this sutta appear to you?", and another replies, "To me it appeared like a great mountain river."
He said: Another [perceives it] as "like a single row of forest trees to me.

Another [perceives it] as "like a single tree with cool shade, full of branches, and heavy with fruit to me. For to them, that very same thread appears different due to the diversity of their perceptions.
In this way, even a single meditation subject appears different due to the diversity of perceptions; for this is born of perception.
Perception is the source, perception is the origin; therefore, it should be understood that because of the diversity of perception, the sign appears as diverse.
When the sign has appeared in this way, that bhikkhu should go to the presence of his teacher and report:
"Venerable sir, such and such a sign appears to me. Then the teacher should say: "Friend, this is the sign."
"Good man, attend to the meditation subject again and again," he should be told. Then he should fix the mind on the sign alone.
In this way, from this point forward, his development proceeds by way of fixing. For this was said by the ancients:
"Fixing the mind on the sign, Discerning its various aspects..."
“The wise man binds his own mind to the inhalation and exhalation.

From the moment the sign (nimitta) arises for him in this way, the hindrances are indeed suppressed, the defilements are stilled, and the mind is concentrated by access concentration (upacāra-samādhi). Then, he should not attend to that sign by way of its color.

It should not be reviewed by way of its characteristics; rather, it should be carefully guarded—just as a Cakkavatti’s embryo is protected by a Kṣatriya queen, or a rice and barley embryo by a farmer—by avoiding the seven unsuitable things, such as improper dwellings, and cultivating those same seven suitable things.
Then, having thus guarded it, by means of repeated attention...
Having brought about growth and increase, he should accomplish the tenfold skill in absorption and apply evenness of energy.
As he strives in this way, following the sequence described in the *Visuddhimagga*, the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise in that sign.
Now, when a bhikkhu has thus produced the fourfold and fivefold jhānas here, by means of the observation and turning away [of the jhāna],...
Desiring to attain complete purity by developing the meditation subject, he makes that same jhāna familiar and reaches mastery over it in five ways;
then, having defined name-and-form, he establishes insight. How so?
Having emerged from attainment, he sees that the origin of the in-breaths and out-breaths is the physical body born of karma and the mind. For just as, when a blacksmith’s bellows are blown...
Just as wind moves through a bellows being blown and through a person depending on the appropriate effort, even so,
inhalation and exhalation occur depending on the body and the mind. Thereupon, he defines inhalation and exhalation along with the body as form (*rūpa*),
and the mind along with its associated states (*dhammā*) as the formless (*arūpa*).
Having thus defined name-and-form, he searches for its condition;
and searching, having seen it, he dispels doubt regarding the occurrence of name-and-form throughout the three periods of time.

With his doubt dispelled, by means of the comprehension of groups, he applies the three characteristics—“impermanence, suffering, and non-self”—and, at the stage preceding the contemplation of rise and fall, when [the insight] has arisen...

Having abandoned the ten imperfections of insight beginning with illumination, and having defined the knowledge of contemplation of rise and fall as "the path" once it is freed from those imperfections,
one reaches the contemplation of dissolution after abandoning arising; then, through uninterrupted contemplation of dissolution,
becoming disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated toward all formations that appear as fearful, one proceeds in due order.
Having reached the four noble paths and being established in the fruit of arahantship, he reaches the culmination of the nineteenfold knowledge of reviewing;
thus he becomes the most worthy recipient of offerings in the world with its devas.
At this point, the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing—beginning with counting and ending with insight—is completed. This is [the exposition] in all its aspects.
Commentary on the First Tetrad.

As for the other three tetrads, since there is no separate method for the development of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā-naya), their meaning should be understood in this way according to the method of word-by-word commentary (anupada-vaṇṇanā).
"Experiencing rapture" (pīti-paṭisaṃvedī) means having rapture experienced.
He trains thus: "I shall breathe in and I shall breathe out making [the rapture] manifest. In this context, rapture is experienced in two ways:
by way of the object and by way of non-delusion. How is rapture experienced by way of the object?

One enters the two jhānas accompanied by rapture; at the moment of attainment, through the acquisition of the jhāna, rapture is experienced by way of the object because the object itself is experienced.

How is it through non-delusion? Having entered and emerged from two jhānas accompanied by rapture (*pīti*), one comprehends that rapture associated with the jhāna as subject to destruction and vanishing.
At the moment of insight (*vipassanā*), rapture is clearly understood through the penetration of its characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-paṭivedha*) due to non-delusion.
By this same method, the remaining terms should also be understood according to their meaning. This, however, is the point here:
The distinction is as follows: by way of the first three jhānas, there is a clear experience of pleasure (*sukha*).
By way of all four jhānas, there should be understood a clear experience of the mental formations (*cittasaṅkhāra*). "Mental formations" refers to the aggregates of feeling and perception.
"Calming the mental formations" means calming and ceasing each successive grosser mental formation.
The meaning: this should be understood in detail according to the method explained under the bodily formations (*kāyasaṅkhāra*).
Furthermore, here in the phrase concerning rapture (*pīti*), feeling is spoken of under the heading of rapture; in the phrase concerning pleasure (*sukha*), feeling is spoken of in its own form.

Regarding the two phrases concerning mental formations (*cittasaṅkhāra*), because of the statement: "Perception and feeling are mental factors; these phenomena are bound to the mind and are mental formations," [feeling] is associated with perception.
It should be understood that this tetrad was spoken by way of the method of contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā*).
In the third tetrad as well, the "clear comprehension of the mind" (*cittapaṭisaṃvidita*) should be understood by way of the four jhānas. "Gladdening the mind":
he trains himself, "I shall breathe in and I shall breathe out gladdening the mind, making it joyful, making it glad, and making it laugh."
In this regard, there is gladdening in two ways: by way of concentration and by way of insight. How by way of concentration?

He attains the two jhānas accompanied by rapture; at the moment of attainment, he gladdens and rejoices his mind with the rapture associated [with those states]. How by way of insight? Having attained the two jhānas accompanied by rapture...
Having emerged from that state, one contemplates the rapture associated with jhāna as subject to destruction and vanishing.
Thus, at the moment of insight, by making the rapture associated with jhāna the object, one gladdens and delights the mind.
One who practices in this way is said to "train thus: 'I shall breathe in and breathe out gladdening the mind.'"
"Concentrating the mind" means placing the mind evenly and establishing it evenly upon the object by means of the first jhāna and so forth;

or else, having entered and emerged from those jhānas, at the moment of insight when one contemplates the mind associated with the jhāna as subject to destruction and vanishing, momentary one-pointedness of mind arises through the penetration of characteristics. Thus...
By means of the momentary one-pointedness of mind that has arisen, he who places the mind evenly upon the object and establishes it evenly is said to "train himself, thinking:
'I shall breathe in and breathe out while concentrating the mind.
"Liberating the mind" means liberating and releasing the mind from the hindrances by means of the first jhāna, and [liberating it] by means of the second.
Liberating and releasing the mind from applied thought and sustained thought by means of the second jhāna, from rapture by means of the third, and from pleasure and pain by means of the fourth;
