or else, having entered and emerged from those jhānas, he contemplates the consciousness associated with the jhāna as subject to destruction and vanishing.
At the moment of insight, liberating and releasing the mind from the perception of permanence by means of the contemplation of impermanence, he—

While liberating and releasing the mind from the perception of pleasure through the contemplation of suffering, from the perception of self through the contemplation of non-self, from delight through the contemplation of disenchantment, from passion through the contemplation of dispassion, from origination through the contemplation of cessation, and from grasping through the contemplation of relinquishment, he breathes in and breathes out. Therefore, it is said: "Liberating..."

“He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in mindful of the mind; I shall breathe out mindful of the mind. Thus it should be understood that this tetrad was spoken by way of contemplation of the mind (*cittānupassanā*).

In the fourth tetrad, however, regarding the phrase “contemplating impermanence” (*aniccānupassī*), first impermanence (*anicca*) is to be understood, and impermanence-ness (*aniccatā*) is to be understood.
Contemplation of impermanence is to be understood, and one who contemplates impermanence is to be understood. In this context, "impermanent" refers to the five aggregates. Why?
Because they possess the nature of arising, passing away, and change. "Impermanence" is the very arising, passing away, and change of those same aggregates;

or it is their non-existence after having existed, meaning their dissolution through momentary breakup because those things that have been produced do not remain in that same state. "Contemplation of impermanence" is...
By way of its impermanence, there is the contemplation of "impermanence" regarding form and the other aggregates. One who contemplates impermanence is one endowed with that contemplation.
Therefore, it should be understood that one who breathes in and breathes out while being such as this trains thus: "I shall breathe in and breathe out contemplating impermanence."
Regarding the phrase "contemplating fading away" (*virāgānupassī*): here, there are two kinds of fading away—fading away as destruction (*khayavirāga*) and absolute fading away (*accantavirāga*).
In this context, fading away as destruction refers to the momentary dissolution of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*). Absolute fading away refers to Nibbāna.

Contemplation of fading away is both insight (*vipassanā*) and the Path (*magga*), which proceed by way of seeing both of these. Breathing in while being endowed with both of these types of contemplation...
And while breathing out, one should be understood as training thus: "I shall breathe in and breathe out contemplating fading away" (*virāgānupassī*).
The same method applies to the phrase "contemplating cessation" (*nirodhānupassī*).

Regarding "contemplating relinquishment" (*paṭinissaggānupassī*), there too there are two kinds of relinquishment: relinquishment as giving up (*pariccāga*) and relinquishment as leaping forward (*pakkhandana*).
The contemplation of relinquishment itself is "contemplation of relinquishment" (*paṭinissaggānupassanā*); this is a designation for insight and the path.
As for "insight": by way of its factor of substitution (*tadaṅgavasena*), it relinquishes defilements along with the formative activities of the aggregates;

and by seeing the fault in the conditioned, it leaps forward into Nibbāna—which is the opposite of that—by inclining toward it. Thus, it is both the relinquishment of abandoning and the relinquishment of leaping forward.

Thus it is said. The path abandons the defilements along with the formative activities of the aggregates by way of their total eradication, and it leaps forward into Nibbāna by making it its object; thus it is called both "the relinquishment of abandonment" and "the relinquishment of leaping forward.
Furthermore, because both of these are seen successively following each preceding knowledge, they are called "contemplations" (anupassanā).

Being endowed with both these kinds of contemplation of relinquishment, while breathing in and breathing out, he should be understood as training thus: "I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment; I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment.
And herein, "contemplating impermanence" is stated by way of nascent insight (*vipassanā*), whereas "contemplating fading away" is [stated] after that.
It should be understood that "contemplating cessation" is said by way of insight capable of becoming more powerful than the [preceding] insight capable of dispassion toward formations;
"contemplating relinquishment" is said by way of insight capable of ceasing the defilements, which is even more powerful than that, and which is extremely sharp, being proximate to the Path. Where...

However, the path is also obtained, and it is indeed undifferentiated. Thus, this tetrad is stated by way of pure insight (*vipassanā*), whereas the preceding three are by way of serenity and insight (*samatha-vipassanā*).
The commentary on the matrix of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati-mātikā*) is finished.
164. Now, in order to explain the matrix (mātikā) as it was set forth by dividing it in its proper sequence, the passage beginning with "herein" and "of this view" is commenced.
Therein, by means of these ten terms beginning with "of this view," the very teaching of the Omniscient Buddha—comprising the three trainings—is spoken of.
For that [teaching] is called a "view" (diṭṭhi) because it was seen (diṭṭha) by the Blessed Buddha; and by virtue of its being acceptable (khamana), [it is called an "acceptance"].

It is called *khanti* (patience/endurance) by way of being agreeable; *ruci* (liking) by way of approval; *ādāyo* (taking up) by way of grasping; *dhamma* (Dharma/phenomenon) in the sense of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*); *vinaya* (discipline) in the sense of that which is to be trained in;
*dhammavinaya* (Dharma-Vinaya) by both of these together; *pāvacana* (the word) by way of what has been spoken; *brahmacariya* (the holy life) in the sense of the best conduct;
and *satthusāsana* (the Teacher’s instruction) by way of the giving of guidance. Therefore, in such phrases as "of this view" (*imissā diṭṭhiyā*), etc., [it refers to] this...

The meaning should be understood as: "in this Buddha-view, in this Buddha-conviction, in this Buddha-liking, in this Buddha-guidance, in this Buddha-Dhamma, in this Buddha-Vinaya, in this Buddha-Dhamma-Vinaya, in this Buddha-word, in this Buddha-brahmacariya, in this Buddha-Teacher’s dispensation. Furthermore, this...

The entire teaching, known as the three trainings, is "view" (*diṭṭhi*) because it was seen by the Blessed One, because it is a condition for right view, and because it is preceded by right view. It is "patience" (*khanti*) by virtue of being acceptable to the Blessed One. It is "inclination" (*ruci*) by virtue of being pleasing to him.
It is "acceptance" (*ādāya*) by virtue of being grasped. It is "Dhamma" because it sustains its own agent from falling into the states of misery. That very same [teaching]...
It is called *vinaya* because it leads away from the side of defilement (*saṃkilesapakkha*). It is the *dhamma-vinaya* because it is both the *dhamma* and the *vinaya*;
or alternatively, it is the *dhamma-vinaya* because this is the leading away (*vinaya*) of unwholesome states by means of wholesome states. For this very reason it was said:
"And those qualities, Gotamī, that you may know lead to dispassion, not to passion... [and so on] ...absolutely, Gotamī."

"You should uphold this: 'This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction. It is "Dhamma-Vinaya" because it is through the Dhamma that there is discipline, not through punishments and the like. And this has also been said:
"Some discipline by means of punishment, And by means of goads and whips."
“The elephant tamed by the Great Seer is tamed without stick or sword.
Likewise: “For those who lead by the Dhamma, what envy can there be for one who understands? Or, the discipline for the sake of the Dhamma is *dhammavinaya*.
For this discipline is for the purpose of blameless states, not for the sake of existence or the bait of worldly enjoyment. Therefore the Blessed One said: “This is not...”
“...the holy life, bhikkhus, is lived for the sake of deceiving people,” and so on in detail. The Elder Puṇṇa also said:
“Friend, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the sake of final Nibbāna through non-clinging.

Or, it leads to purification, thus it is *vinaya*; the discipline according to the Dhamma is *dhammavinaya*. For [it leads away] from the phenomena of saṃsāra, that is, from the phenomena such as sorrow and so forth.
Or, it is called *dhamma-vinaya* because it leads to pure *nibbāna*, or because it is the discipline (*vinaya*) of the *dhamma* and not of other founders of sects (*titthakara*).

For the Blessed One is the embodiment of the *dhamma*, and this is his very discipline. Or, because only phenomena (*dhammas*)—which are to be directly known, fully understood, abandoned, developed, and realized—are the objects of this discipline, therefore it is a discipline regarding phenomena, and not regarding sentient beings or souls.

And thus it is the Dhamma-Vinaya. It is called *pavacana* (the spoken word) because it is the preeminent speech among other utterances due to its possession of both meaning and phrasing (*sāttha-sabyañjana*), and so forth;
that which is simply *pavacana* is *pāvacana*. It is *brahmacariya* (the holy life) by virtue of being a mode of conduct distinguished from all other modes of conduct.

It is the *satthusāsana* (the Teacher’s instruction) because it is the teaching of the Blessed One who has become the Teacher of gods and humans; or alternatively, it is *satthusāsana* because it is an instruction that has become [identical with] the Teacher.
“For, Ānanda, the Dhamma and the Vinaya that have been taught and laid down by me shall be your teacher after my passing away.
Thus it is said that the Dhamma and the Vinaya alone are the Teacher. In this way the meaning of these words should be understood.
Furthermore, because it is only in this very Dispensation that a bhikkhu who has produced the concentration of mindfulness of breathing in all its aspects exists, and not elsewhere—
Therefore, it should be understood that in various instances, this rule—that [the word] "of this" (*imissā*) and "in this" (*imasmiṃ*) [are used]—has been established.
This is the meaning of the commentary on the heading "here" (*idha*).

Furthermore, without explaining the etymological derivation of the word *bhikkhu* by means of the phrase "a virtuous worldling" (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*) and so forth, [it refers to] precisely the *bhikkhu* intended here.

This is explained as follows: therein, one is a "worldling" (*puthujjana*) because the defilements have not been eradicated, and "noble" (*kalyāṇa*) because of being engaged in the practice of virtue and so forth;
thus, he is a "noble worldling" (*puthujjanakalyāṇa*), and a "noble worldling" is the same as a "noble worldling" (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*).

One who trains in the higher virtue and so forth is a "trainee" (*sekkha*); this refers to a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner. The "unshakable" (*akuppa*) is the state of the fruit of arahantship, which cannot be moved.
“Horse” means one whose nature is unshakable; for he too develops this concentration.
In the description of the forest (*arañña*), first according to the Vinaya method, it is stated: “With the exception of the village and the vicinity of the village, the remainder is the forest.
According to the Sutta method, with reference to a forest-dwelling monk (*āraññaka bhikkhu*), it is said: “A forest dwelling (*senāsana*) is called...”

"...five hundred bow-lengths from the western boundary," so it is said. However, both the Vinaya and the Suttanta are called "teachings by way of a method" (pariyāyadesanā), whereas the Abhidhamma is a "teaching not by way of a method" (nippariyāyadesanā).
Therefore, in order to show the forest according to the Abhidhamma method, it is said:
"having gone out beyond the threshold-stone" (indakhīla); the meaning is, having gone out outside the threshold-stone. It is also said: "having gone out beyond the threshold-stone."
The reading implies that it is stated [to be] "outside" after having passed beyond the *indakhīla*. Here, *indakhīla* refers to the threshold of either a village or a city.

Since the foot of a tree (*rukkhamūla*) is well known, it was not mentioned in the description of the "foot of a tree," and thus he said "wherever," and so forth. Therein, "wherever" (*yattha*) means in whichever foot of a tree.
"Seat" (*āsana*) is so called because they sit (*āsanti*) upon it. "Arranged" (*paññatta*) means placed. "A bed" (*mañca*), and so forth...
These are the words concerning the classification of seats (*āsana*). For even a couch (*mañca*) is included here among the seats because it serves as a place for sitting.

It is one of the following types: with legs made of ivory, bound with cotton, with legs shaped like crabs, or with removable legs. A stool (*pīṭha*) is likewise one of those same types. A mattress (*bhisi*) is one of the following:
a woolen mattress, a cotton mattress, a linen mattress, a grass mattress, or a leaf mattress. A mat (*taṭṭikā*) is [made] from palm leaves and so forth.
"Built up" means constructed. "A piece of hide" refers to any piece of hide suitable for sitting upon. "Grass mats, etc. refers to those made by weaving grass and other materials together.
"Therein" means at that foot of a tree. By the words "walks about," and so forth, the suitability of the foot of the tree for the four postures is described.
By all the phrases beginning with "where," the dense shade and the seclusion from people of the foot of the tree are indicated.
It has been said. "By anyone" means by any group. Expanding upon that group, he says: "either by householders or by those gone forth. "Uncongested" means not crowded, not cramped.
A lodging for which there is a mountain thicket, a forest thicket, or a river thicket extending even a *gāvuta* or half a *yojana* on all sides, where no one [comes] at an improper time—
If one is able to approach it, this is called "unfrequented" even though it is nearby.
However, that which is half a *yojana* or a full *yojana* away is called "unfrequented" solely because of its distance.
"Vihāra" refers to any remaining dwelling except for a *aḍḍhayoga* and so forth. An *aḍḍhayoga* is a house with a gabled roof like a garuḍa (*supaṇṇa*). A "pāsāda" is...
A long palace (*dīghapāsāda*) is one constructed by taking two *kaṇṇikā* (corner-pavilions). A *hammiya* is indeed a gabled palace (*kūṭāgāra-pāsāda*) situated on an upper terrace in the open air.
Regarding "caves" (*guhā*), it is stated in the *Khandhaka-aṭṭhakathā* that there are brick caves, stone caves, wooden caves, and sand caves. However, in the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*, it is said:
"A monastery (*vihāra*) includes the surrounding path for circumambulation, as well as the night-quarters and day-quarters within it."
And having shown [this], the lodging has been prepared. "A cave" (*guhā*) refers to an earthen cave where it is necessary to have a lamp day and night.

The two—either a mountain cave or an earthen cave—are stated here as distinct options. In the *Mātikā*, the present tense was used for "he sits" (*nisīdati*) by way of a characteristic common to all times;
however, here, because the commencement of meditation exists for one who is already seated, [the past tense is used].
The word "seated" is used as a term denoting the conclusion in order to show the beginning and the end of the act of sitting.

However, because the body of one who sits with the body held straight becomes upright, he said "straight," etc., showing the intended meaning rather than paying attention to the mere literal expression.
In that context, "well-placed" means being upright because it has been placed straight.
"Steadfast" means not by oneself alone; this is the meaning. "The sense of embracing" (pariggahaṭṭha) means the sense of being embraced.
What is embraced? Deliverance (niyyāna). What is deliverance? Mindfulness of breathing itself is the deliverance that extends up to the path of Arahantship.

Therefore, it is called "the sense of deliverance" by taking the primary meaning of the word *mukha* (opening/face); that is, the sense of deliverance from the round of existence (*saṃsāra*). "The sense of establishment" (upaṭṭhānaṭṭha) is simply the sense of its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāvaṭṭha*).
The meaning expressed is: "having established mindfulness which has the escape encompassed by all these terms. Some, however, explain it thus:
"the sense of encompassing is the sense of encompassing by means of mindfulness; the sense of escape is the sense of the gateway for the entry and exit of the in-breaths and out-breaths.
What is meant is: "having established mindfulness that has the escape of the in-breaths and out-breaths encompassed."
165. "By way of thirty-two aspects" is said with reference to the complete inclusion, without remainder, of those [factors] that are obtained in their respective stages in due order.

"By way of long inhalation" means by way of the inhalation stated as "long" in the matrix (mātikā). The same applies to the remaining cases. "One-pointedness" (ekaggatā) is the state of being one-pointed.
"Non-distraction" (avikkhepa) is the absence of distraction; for it is precisely one-pointedness that [prevents] [the mind from wandering] among various objects.
It is called "non-distraction" because it prevents the mind from being distracted.

"Of one who understands" means of one who understands by way of non-delusion, or the meaning is "of one who finds"; or alternatively, it refers to one who understands by taking [the state] as an object, thinking, "Non-distraction has been attained by me.
"By that mindfulness" means by that established mindfulness. "By that knowledge" means by that knowledge which knows non-distraction.
Regarding the phrase "one who acts with mindfulness": here, only that mindfulness associated with knowledge is intended by the term "mindfulness" (*sati*), as it is said:
"He is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and circumspection. Therefore, by the word "mindful" (*sato*) alone, knowledge (*ñāṇa*) is also included.
166. "In what is reckoned as a long duration" means in time reckoned as long. For a long path is called a "duration" (*addhāna*). This too...
“Time” (*addhāna*) is called *addhāna* because of its long duration, like the path of time itself.

Although “inhaling” (*assasati*) and “exhaling” (*passasati*) have been stated separately as inhalation and exhalation, they are again stated together in a compound as “inhaling and exhaling” (*assasatipi passasatipi*) in order to show the uninterrupted progression of the meditation.
“Zeal arises” means for the sake of further increase through the growth of the meditation.
Zeal arises. It is said to be "more subtle" because of the presence of tranquility. "Gladness arises" means that joy is born through the fulfillment of development.

"The breaths of inhalation and exhalation turn away from the mind" means that when the counterpart sign arises based on the inhalations and exhalations, the mind withdraws from the natural inhalations and exhalations. "Equanimity becomes established" means:

When that counterpart sign is attained through access and absorption concentration, because there is no further need for effort in maintaining concentration, equanimity regarding the object (tatramajjhattupekkhā) is said to become established. Regarding the phrase "in nine ways":
here, from the commencement of the meditation onwards, prior to the arising of desire, there are three modes mentioned as "he breathes in and he breathes out"; from the arising of desire onwards...
There are three [stages] beginning with the arising of pure gladness (*pāmojja*), and three beginning from the arising of gladness itself; thus there are nine modes. "Body" (*kāya*):

even the in-breaths and out-breaths, though they are broken into minute particles, are called a "body" in the sense of being an aggregate. Even the sign (*nimitta*) that arises dependent upon the natural in-breath and natural out-breath receives the name "in-breath and out-breath.
"Establishment" (*upaṭṭhāna*) is mindfulness (*sati*); it so called because it stands having approached that object.

"Mindfulness is the foundation" means that "contemplation is knowledge. The meaning is that, by way of serenity (*samatha*), there is contemplation of the sign-body (*nimittakāya*), and by way of insight (*vipassanā*), there is contemplation of the name-body and form-body (*nāmakāya-rūpakāya*), which is knowledge. "The body is the foundation" means that mindfulness approaches and stands upon that body;
thus it is called the "foundation. "Not mindfulness" means that the body itself is not what is called mindfulness. "By that mindfulness" [refers to the aforementioned].
Regarding "the mindfulness just mentioned": "by that knowledge" means by the knowledge just mentioned.

"He contemplates that body" means he follows the body as it was described above, by way of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), and sees it either with knowledge associated with *jhāna* or with insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).
Although the terms "body" and so forth do not appear in the summary matrix (*mātikā*), this tetrad is stated specifically by way of contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*).
Now, with reference to the statement "the development of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body in the body," the explanation of the term "body" has been given.
"Contemplation of the body in the body" means the contemplation of each respective part within the manifold body;

or alternatively, it is said that there is contemplation of the body in the body, and not contemplation of other phenomena. [It is thus] in that which consists of the impermanent, the painful, the non-self, and the foul.
It is not the contemplation of the body as permanent, pleasant, self, or beautiful; rather, it is the contemplation of the body itself as impermanent, suffering, non-self, and unattractive.

Alternatively, it is said to be the contemplation of that very body alone, because there is no contemplation of anything to be grasped within the body—such as "I," "mine," "woman," or "man. Regarding feelings [in the subsequent section]:

The same method applies to the three [foundations] beginning with "contemplation of feelings" (vedanānupassanā). Mindfulness itself is the establishment; thus it is "the foundation of mindfulness" (satipaṭṭhāna).

The foundation of mindfulness associated with the contemplation of the body is "body-contemplation foundation of mindfulness" (kāyānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna); the cultivation of that is "the cultivation of the body-contemplation foundation of mindfulness" (kāyānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā).

167. That "body" (taṃ kāyaṃ) is specified by the word "body" (kāya) even though it was not previously specified, because the aggregate of name-and-form (nāmarūpa-kāya) is included therein by means of the term "body."

This was said by way of illustration. For the contemplations of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) and so forth are found only in the body of name-and-form (*nāmarūpakāya*), not in the body of signs (*nimittakāya*).

The terms "contemplation" (*anupassanā*) and "development" (*bhāvanā*) have already been explained. The passage beginning with "by means of long inhalation and exhalation," etc., was stated to show the benefits (*ānisaṃsa*) of developing mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*).
For its benefits are the fullness of mindfulness and the fullness of knowledge. In this regard:
"Understanding one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind" is said with reference to the one-pointedness of mind at the time of insight for one who has already attained jhāna.
"Feelings are known" means feelings are known by way of seeing their arising in a general sense.
"They appear known" means they appear known as destruction, as vanishing, and as empty. "They go to their passing away known" means [in a general sense]...
By the vision of their passing away, they are known to go to destruction; the meaning is that they break up.

The same method applies to perceptions (*saññā*) and applied thoughts (*vitakka*). When these three are mentioned, however, all remaining material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) are also included. If one asks why only these three were mentioned, it is because they are difficult to comprehend.
Among feelings (*vedanā*), pleasure and pain are indeed manifest, but equanimity (*upekkhā*) is subtle.

They are difficult to grasp and not clearly manifest. Even that [perception] becomes manifest to him; however, because perception grasps only the mere appearance, it does not grasp the thing according to its true nature (*yathāsabhāva*).
Furthermore, when associated with insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), which grasps both the specific and general characteristics of things, it becomes extremely unmanifest.
Even that [insight-knowledge] becomes manifest to him; for thought (*vitakka*) is distinct from knowledge because it merely resembles knowledge.
Having done so, it is difficult to grasp. For thought (vitakka) is a mere counterfeit of knowledge (ñāṇa). As it is said:
“Friend Visākha, both right view and right intention—these states are included within the aggregate of wisdom. And that thought of his becomes manifest;
thus, when these [two] are described as difficult to grasp, the remaining [factors] are already implied. Now, in the exposition of these terms:

Having asked, "How is feeling known as it arises?", and having answered that very question regarding the fact that the arising of feeling is known—without yet answering how feeling itself is known—he asks, "How is the arising of feeling known? and so forth.

The same method applies to the remaining cases as well. The phrases "from the origination of ignorance" and "from the cessation of ignorance," etc., have already been explained above. By this very [method]...

By this method, perception and thought should also be understood. However, in the section on thought (*vitakka*), instead of saying "from the arising of contact, from the cessation of contact," it says "from the arising of perception, from the cessation of perception" in place of contact.
If one asks why that is, it is because thought is rooted in perception; for it is said: "Dependent upon the diversity of perceptions, the diversity of intentions arises."

And in such passages as "attending to [feeling] as impermanent," etc., that very same state (dhamma) should be applied to each respective instance according to the method beginning with "attending to feeling as impermanent.

However, because feeling associated with insight (vipassanā) is incapable of performing the function of insight, it is of no assistance to insight; for that very reason, it is not included among the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma).
However, the function of perception associated with insight (vipassanā) is not clearly manifest; therefore, it is entirely of no assistance to insight.
On the other hand, without applied thought (vitakka), the very function of insight does not exist. For insight, when accompanied by applied thought, performs its own function. As it has been said:
"Wisdom, by its own nature, is unable to determine an object as impermanent, suffering, and non-self."
But when he strikes at the applied thought again and again before giving it up, he is able [to discern its nature]. How so?
Just as a money-changer, wishing to examine a coin on all sides while holding it in his hand, cannot turn it over merely by the surface of his eye;
rather, by turning it over and over with his fingers and joints, he is able to examine it from this side and that.
"In the same way, wisdom is not able by its own nature to determine an object as impermanent and so forth;

rather, it is only when struck and turned about, as it were, by initial application (vitakka)— which has the characteristic of directing and the function of striking and pounding— that wisdom is able to determine what has been handed over to it again and again."
Therefore, because feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saññā*) do not assist in insight (*vipassanā*), they are shown merely by way of their characteristics;
thus, the singular number is used in various places in the expression "of feeling and perception.
However, to show that there is as much variety in insight as there is in applied thought (*vitakka*), the plural number is used in various places in the expression "of applied thoughts."
It is appropriate to say, "What is it?

(168). Furthermore, the passage beginning with "By means of long inhalation and exhalation" is stated in order to show the perfection of the development of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*) and its fruit.
In that context, "he brings together" means he establishes the object; "he settles the object" means he fixes the object [of meditation].
Or it means "meaning" (*attha*). Even in the absence of the activity of blending together, it is said to "blend together" simply through the fulfillment of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

"Object" (*gocara*) refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) as the object during the moment of insight (*vipassanā*), and Nibbāna as the object during the moments of the Path (*magga*) and the Fruit (*phala*). "Equal" (*samattha*):
the meaning is simply "equal" (*sama*), or it is "equal in meaning" (*samassa attho*), thus "equal" (*samattha*). It is that which is equal. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.

"He brings the path together" means that at the very moment of the fruit of the path, the object is Nibbāna alone. "This person" refers specifically to the practitioner (yogāvacara) devoted to the cultivation of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati).
Regarding the phrase "in this object," here the term "body" includes the conditioned objects consisting of the aggregates of mind and matter;

subsequently, it refers to the path and to Nibbāna as its object. By the words "whatever of his," etc., [the author] clarifies the relationship between the terms "object" (ārammaṇa) and "range" (gocara).

"Identity" (ekatthatā) has been stated. "Of that" means of that person. "He understands" means that the person is understanding; thus it is said that the person understands by means of wisdom (*paññā*).

"The appearance of the object" refers to the appearance of the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) as the object at the moment of insight (*vipassanā*), and the appearance of Nibbāna as the object at the moments of the Path and the Fruit;
this appearance is mindfulness (*sati*). And here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object.
"Like the king’s attendance": non-distraction is concentration (*samādhi*). "Resolution" (*adhiṭṭhāna*) refers to the aforementioned formations as objects and Nibbāna as an object;
for the mind resolves upon that, thus it is called resolution. "Purification" (*vodāna*) is knowledge (*ñāṇa*);

for by means of it the mind is purified and cleansed, thus it is called purification. Concentration belonging to the side of sluggishness [is so called] because of its attainment of a state free from sluggishness.
It is "even" (sama) because it has become even; the knowledge associated with agitation is "even" because it has reached a state free from agitation due to having become even.
By this, the yoking together (yuganaddhatā) of serenity and insight at the moments of the path and fruit of insight is expressed.
Mindfulness, however, is "even" because it is universally beneficial and assists in the equilibrium of both; the object is [also] "even" because it is established upon that equilibrium.

The meaning of "even" (*samaṃ*). The meaning of "faultless" (*anavajjaṭṭha*) is the faultless nature of insight (*vipassanā*). The meaning of "stainless" (*niklesaṭṭha*) is the stainless nature of the path (*magga*).
Alternatively, the reading is *nikkilesaṭṭha*. The meaning of "purified" (*vodānaṭṭha*) is the thoroughly pure nature of the fruit (*phala*).
The meaning of "ultimate" (*paramaṭṭha*) is the supreme nature among all phenomena of Nibbāna. "Penetrates" (*paṭivijjhati*) means that one penetrates each respective nature without delusion.
And here, by the phrases "the appearance of the object" and so forth, right penetration is stated.

And since it is precisely here that the penetration of the state of cleansing is stated, those [other] states—the blameless state, the state free from defilement, and the ultimate state—which share the same characteristic as that [cleansing], are indeed stated by way of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics. As it has been said:
“When any states that have the same characteristic as the single state that has been stated are thereby stated as well,
that is the Mode of Conveying called ‘Characteristic.
Herein, the meaning of blamelessness and the meaning of freedom from defilement are the purpose of “evenness,” which is reckoned as non-distraction.
The meaning of "even" (*samattha*) is as follows: it is "even" in the sense of purification, referring to the purification of the path of insight;
it is "even" in the sense that the meaning of evenness—which is reckoned as the purification of the path—is the meaning of the fruit-purification;
furthermore, it is "even" in the sense that the ultimate meaning is indeed evenness, or because all evenness has Nibbāna as its purpose; such is that aforementioned kind.
Having formed a partial *sarūpa-ekasesa* compound of "the same" (*sama*) and "capable" (*samattha*), it is said that "one penetrates what is both the same and capable.

The factors of the faculties, powers, and enlightenment-factors (*indriya-bala-bojjhaṅga-dhammā*) are found at the moments of insight, the path, and the fruit; the path and the three purifications (*tisso ca visuddhiyo*) exist only at the moments of the path and the fruit;
and liberation (*vimokkho*), clear knowledge (*vijjā*), and the knowledge of destruction (*khaye ñāṇaṃ*) exist only at the moment of the path.
Liberation and the knowledge of non-arising occur only at the moment of the fruit; the remaining factors occur also at the moment of insight.
In the section on states (*dhammavāra*), with the exception of Nibbāna, the remaining states should be understood as they are appropriately combined with this object.
This, however, has been stated by way of the majority of cases. As for the meanings not explicitly mentioned here, they have already been explained below. Herein, according to each set of four:

Although the way to liberation has been shown [in general], the way to liberation is shown according to each individual factor because each part contained within the fourfold set serves as a necessary condition (*upanissaya*) for liberation.
For there is no liberation without each one of them.
The commentary on the description of long inhalation and exhalation is finished.
169. In the exposition of the "brief," "reckoned as short" means in a time reckoned as limited. The rest here should be understood according to the method already stated.

170. In the exposition of "experiencing the whole body," because feeling is gross among formless phenomena (arūpadhammā), feeling—which first experiences desirable and undesirable objects—is mentioned for the purpose of grasping [the nature of] pleasure. After that, it is said: "whatever one feels, that one perceives."
Thus, perception (*saññā*) grasps the aspect of the object of feeling; from that, by way of perception, arises volition (*cetanā*), which is formative;
from that, contact (*phassa*) arises, according to the statement: "Touched, one feels; touched, one perceives; touched, one wills";

from that, attention (*manasikāra*), which is the common characteristic of all [mental states]; and by means of volition and the others, the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) is described. Thus, in the three [aggregates]...
When the aggregates (khandhas) have been mentioned, the consciousness aggregate (viññāṇakkhandha), which is dependent upon them, is already included.

"And name" (nāmañca) refers to the kind of name already described. However, the phrase "and the body of name" (nāmakāyo ca) is stated in order to exclude Nibbāna—which is included under the term "name"—as well as supramundane states (lokuttara), which do not come within the scope of insight (vipassanā). For by the word "body" (kāya), Nibbāna is excluded.

Because Nibbāna is devoid of an aggregate. And as for those called "mental formations" (*cittasaṅkhārā*), even though they are spoken of thus: "Perception and feeling—these mental states are bound to the mind;
they are mental formations"—nevertheless, it is meant that these mental formations are here included within the mental body (*nāmakāya*) alone.
As for the "great elements" (*mahābhūtāni*): [they are so called] because of their great manifestation, because of the commonality of being great elements, and because of their great maintenance.
They are called *mahābhūtā* because they undergo great transformation (*mahāvikāra*) and because they are great entities (*mahantabhūta*). Furthermore, there are four: earth, water, fire, and air.
Regarding the term "derived matter" (*upādāyarūpa*) of the four great elements: the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative;

the meaning is "matter that proceeds by depending upon, relying upon, and not abandoning the four great elements. That [derived matter], moreover, consists of: the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue...

The body consists of twenty-four types: visible form, sound, odor, flavor, the female faculty, the male faculty, the life faculty, the heart-base, nutritive essence, bodily intimation, verbal intimation, the space element, lightness of matter, malleability of matter, wieldiness of matter, integration of matter, continuity of matter, aging of matter, and impermanence of matter;
as well as inhalation and exhalation, which are simply natural breath.
The counterpart sign that arises depending on the in-breath and out-breath receives that same name, just as in the case of the earth-kasiṇa and so forth.
And because it resembles material form, it also receives the name "form," as in such passages as "he sees external forms.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the sign and the anchoring": it is the sign for the anchoring of mindfulness; [it refers to] the in-breaths and out-breaths.
The place of contact. And as for those which are called "bodily formations" (*kāyasaṅkhāra*)—even though they are described thus: "In-breathing and out-breathing are bodily states;
being bound up with the body, they are bodily formations"—it is meant that these bodily formations are here included within the material body (*rūpakāya*) alone.

"Those bodies are clearly understood" means that at the moment of jhāna, the bodies consisting of the sign of the in-breath and out-breath are understood, and at the moment of insight (*vipassanā*), the remaining material and immaterial bodies are understood.
They are understood by way of their object; they are understood through non-delusion at the moment of the path.

The statement beginning with "by way of long inhalation and exhalation" was spoken with reference to the insight-path that arises for a yogi who has attained jhāna by means of inhalation and exhalation.

The phrases "understanding by adverting," etc., have meanings already explained in the discourse on virtue (*sīla*). Having brought those aforementioned modes of body within, it is said: "experiencing the whole body."

In such passages as "Experiencing the whole body [of breath] is the restraint of inhalation and exhalation," it is precisely the restraint (*saṃvara*) arising from the jhānas, vipassanā, and the path—produced by the aforementioned inhalation and exhalation experienced throughout the entire body—that constitutes purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*) in the sense of restraint.

Non-distraction itself is purification of mind (*cittavisuddhi*) in the sense of non-distraction. Wisdom itself is purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*) in the sense of seeing. Regarding the jhānas and vipassanā:
It should be understood that even in the absence of abstinence (*virati*), restraint (*saṃvara*) is merely the non-existence of evil.
171. In the explanation of "they tranquillize" and so forth, "bodily" (*kāyika*) means existing in the material body (*rūpakāya*).

"Connected with the body" (*kāyapaṭibaddha*) means bound to the body, dependent on the body; they exist when the body exists and do not exist when it does not. For this very reason, they are conditioned by the body (*kāyena saṅkharīyanti*).
Bodily formations. "Calming" means making them cool, making them settle. By the very word "calming," the calming of the gross [formations] is established.
"Stopping" means stopping them by not allowing the gross [formations] to arise.
"Quieting" means leading even the gross [formations] to a state of peace by way of transforming them into a single continuity. "Trains" means [he trains] by virtue of his specific task.
The connection is: "He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in'"; or alternatively, the meaning is that he trains in the three trainings (*tisro śikṣā*).
Now, in order to show the subsiding of the gross [state], he said "by such as these," and so forth. Therein, "such as these" (*yathārūpehi*) means "of such a kind.
"Bending" (*ānamanā*) is bending backward. "Bowing" (*vinamanā*) is bowing to both sides. "Sinking down" (*sannamanā*) is [bending] from all sides.
"Bowing" is bowing well. "Bending forward" is bowing toward the front. "Moving" is shaking. "Quivering" is slight movement.
"Trembling" is violent shaking. Whatever bodily formations there are by which there is the bowing...
[as before] ...the trembling of the body, they cause such bodily formations to be stilled; and as for that bowing... [as before] ...the trembling of the body.
And the connection should be made as "they cause that to become tranquil.
For when the bodily formations have become tranquil, the body's bending and so forth also become tranquil.
They cause tranquil even those bodily formations that are peaceful and subtle, such that through them there is no bending and so forth of the body. That which is [the absence] of the body's...

"Causing them to bend," and "calming what is present and subtle"—this should be understood according to their connection. "Present and subtle" is a neuter noun used adverbially (*bhāvanapuṃsakavacana*).
Regarding the phrase "it is said thus" (*iti kira*): here *iti* has the sense of "thus," and *kira* has the sense of "if.
Thus, it means: "If it is so, one trains: 'I shall breathe in and breathe out calming even the subtle in-breaths and out-breaths.'"

The exhortation has been undertaken by the exhorter. Alternatively, the particle *kira*—because it is the speech of the exhorter—is indeed appropriate in the sense of lack of faith, in the sense of intolerance, and in the sense of being out of sight;
thus, "I do not believe, I do not tolerate, it is not evident to me" is what is meant by the statement, "In this way, one trains in the subsiding of even subtle [defilements]."
"‘When this is so’: when there is such subsiding of the subtle [bodily formations]. ‘And there is no production of the perception of wind’ means:
of the perception of the wind of the in-breath and out-breath. ‘Perception’ (*upaladdhi*) means consciousness (*viññāṇa*).

There is no production—that is, no arising—of the meditative consciousness that has that wind of in-breath and out-breath as its object while it is being perceived; rather, there is cultivation of that object."

The meaning is that [it] does not exist. And "there is no manifestation of inhalation and exhalation" means that because even subtle inhalations and exhalations have been ceased through meditation (*bhāvanā*), there is no arising or occurrence of them;

this is the meaning. And "there is no manifestation of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*)" means that, precisely because of the absence of inhalation and exhalation, there is no manifestation of the consciousness associated with that meditation which has them as its object.
And because mindfulness does not proceed, there is consequently no cultivation of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati-samādhi) associated with it.
The word "na" here is a mere particle, as in expressions such as "the monk and not [others].
Thus, the wise neither enter that aforementioned attainment nor emerge from it.

The connection [is as follows]. Regarding the statement that provides the resolution for the position of the *codanā* (objection), the word "it is said" (*iti kira*) means exactly so. Here, the word *kira* should be understood in the sense of the particle *eva*.
"When this is so" (*evaṃ sante*) means precisely when there is such tranquility.
"In what manner? (*yathā kathaṃ viya*) means: in whatever way that aforementioned method exists, in that same way—how is it?—this is the simile.
He asks. Now, with the words "just as if," he shows that simile. "In a brass vessel" means in a container made of brass. "The sign" (*nimitta*) refers to the form of those sounds.
Furthermore, the word "sign" is used in the accusative case in the sense of the genitive; thus, the meaning is "of the sign. And the sign of the sound is not other than the sound itself.
"Because it was well-grasped" means because it was thoroughly mastered. It may also be read as "because it was well-held."
"Reading" means it has been well grasped. "Well attended to" means it has been well brought to mind.
"Well retained" means it has been well established in the mind. Regarding "the state of having a subtle sound-sign as its object":
because even subtle sounds have ceased at that time, there is no longer an ungrasped sound-sign; rather, a subtler sound-sign becomes the object.
Having made [the body] more subtle, the mind also proceeds with the sign of the sound as its object; or the meaning is that it does so by way of having the sign of the sound as a more subtle object.
In this same manner, the meaning should also be understood regarding absorption (*appanā*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "calming," the in-breaths and out-breaths spoken of as "calming the bodily formation" are what is meant by "body."
Regarding the phrase “tranquilizing the bodily formation,” the construction should be understood as follows: either that the inhalation and exhalation are the body.

Even when the bodily formation is being tranquilized through the purification of development, if the meditator attends to it with the thought, “I am tranquilizing the gross bodily formation,” it becomes extremely tranquilized by that effort.
Even though it does not manifest, it becomes subtle and easy to handle.

The eight knowledges of contemplation (*anupassanā-ñāṇa*) are as follows: regarding the four bases mentioned in the passage, "Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe in long; I shall breathe out long; calming the bodily formation, I shall breathe in long;
I shall breathe out long," there are four [knowledges] by way of inhalation and four by way of exhalation—thus making eight knowledges of contemplation.
And the eight foundations of mindfulness (*upaṭṭhānānussati*) are as follows: "By way of long inhalation, one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind... [and so on].

The eight foundations of mindfulness consist of four [foundations] according to the inhalation and four according to the exhalation, as stated in the passage beginning, “For one who understands, mindfulness is established,” regarding the four subjects. There is also a reading: “the eight foundations of mindfulness.
They are called the “four Suttanta subjects” because they were spoken by the Blessed One in the Ānāpānassati Sutta according to the first tetrad.
The four bases for the Suttanta.
The commentary on the exposition of the first tetrad is finished. 172.
In the exposition of the experience of rapture (*pīti*) within the second tetrad, regarding the phrase "rapture and gladness arise," here *pīti* means...
The root term is *mūlapada*. "Gladness" (*pāmojja*) is its explanatory term; the meaning is the state of being joyful.

Regarding the passage beginning with "that which is rapture is gladness," it is said that whatever receives such names as "rapture" (*pīti*) and "gladness" (*pāmojja*) is "rapture. In this context, "rapture" (*pītī*) is the term for its intrinsic nature.
Gladness (*pāmojja*) is the state of one who is joyful. The mode of gladdening is "gladdening" (*āmodanā*). The mode of rejoicing is "rejoicing" (*pamodanā*).

*Pamodanā*. Just as the mixing together of medicines, oils, hot water, or cold water is called "rejoicing" (*modanā*), so too this is "rejoicing" through the unification of mental states (*dhammā*). However, by embellishing the word with a prefix, it is stated as *āmodanā* and *pamodanā*.
It causes one to laugh, thus it is "laughter" (*hāsa*); it causes one to laugh loudly, thus it is "loud laughter" (*pahāsa*); these are terms for the modes of being joyful and exceedingly joyful.
It is a designation. "Vitti" means wealth; this is a name for riches. However, because it is a condition for joy (*somanassa*) and resembles wealth, it is called "vitti.
For just as joy arises in a wealthy person depending upon his wealth, so too does joy arise in one who possesses rapture (*pīti*) depending upon that rapture.
Therefore, it is called "vitti. For rapture is established in the nature of contentment.
This is the name. Furthermore, a person who possesses rapture (*pīti*) is called "elated" (*udagga*) because of the upliftedness and exaltedness of body and mind;
the state of being elated is "elation" (*odagya*). "Satisfaction of mind" (*attamanatā*) means having one's own mind [with oneself].

For the mind of one who is dissatisfied is not called "one's own mind" because it is the basis for suffering; however, the mind of one who is satisfied is called "one's own mind" because it is the basis for happiness.
Thus, *attamanatā* means self-satisfaction; the meaning is the state of being satisfied with oneself, or the state of one’s own mind.

Since that, however, is not the self-satisfaction of anyone else, but rather this state belonging to the mind itself—a mental factor (*cetasika dhamma*)—therefore it is called "self-satisfaction of the mind" (*attamanatā cittassa*).
The rest here and above should be understood by applying the method already explained below.

173. In the explanation of "experiencing pleasure" (*sukhapaṭisaṃvediniddesa*), the phrase "two kinds of pleasure" is stated for the purpose of showing the planes of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
For bodily pleasure is the plane of insight, while mental pleasure is the plane of both serenity and insight.
"Bodily" (*kāyika*) means "belonging to the body" (*kāye niyutta*); it is so called because it does not arise without the sensitive body (*pasādakāya*). "Mental" (*cetasika*) means...
It is called *cetasika* because it is bound to the mind by way of non-separation. Therein, by the term "bodily" (*kāyika*), mental pleasure is excluded;
by the term "pleasure" (*sukha*), bodily pain is excluded. Likewise, by the term "mental" (*cetasika*), bodily pleasure is excluded;
by the term "pleasure," mental pain is excluded. "Satisfying" (*sāta*) means sweet, very sweet. "Pleasure" (*sukha*) means simply pleasure, not...
"Suffering" (*dukkha*). "Born of body-contact" (*kāyasamphassaja*) means arisen from body-contact. "Pleasant, agreeable feeling" (*sātaṃ sukhaṃ vedayitaṃ*):
pleasant feeling, not unpleasant feeling; agreeable feeling, not disagreeable feeling. The three subsequent terms are stated using the feminine gender.
"Agreeable sensation" (*sātā vedanā*), not unpleasant; "pleasant sensation" (*sukhā vedanā*), not painful—this alone is the meaning here.

The exposition of mental pleasure (*cetasika-sukha*) should be applied according to the method of the opposites already stated. The change of gender in the phrase "those pleasures" (*te sukhā*) has been made;
what is meant is "those pleasures" (*tāni sukhāni*). The rest here in this tetrad is to be understood by the same method as was stated for the first tetrad above.
The four scriptural bases (*suttantika-vatthu*) are to be understood by way of the second tetrad.
The commentary on the second tetrad exposition is finished.
176. In the third tetrad exposition, "mind" (*citta*) is the root term; "consciousness" (*viññāṇa*) is the explanatory term.

The passage beginning with "that which is mind" and so forth should be applied according to the method already stated for rapture (*pīti*). Among those terms, such as "mind," it is called "mind" (*citta*) because of its variegated nature (*vicittatā*) regarding the object (*ārammaṇa*).

It is called *mano* because it knows by measuring (*minamānaṃ*). *Mānasaṃ* is simply *mano*. However, in the passage, "The snare that moves through the air, which wanders as the mental (*mānaso*)," the term *mānasa* refers to the associated mental states (*sampayuttaka-dhamma*). [As it is said:
"How indeed, Blessed One, can your disciple, delighting in your teaching..."
"A trainee whose mind has not yet attained its goal might die while listening to people"—here, "mind" (*mānasa*) is said to mean "arahantship.
But here, "mind" (*mānasa*) means simply "mind" (*mano*). This term has been expanded by way of its phonetic form (*byañjana*).
"Heart" (*hadaya*) means "consciousness" (*citta*). As in the passage: "I will either hurl your consciousness [from your body] or I will split your heart," where it refers to the chest (*uro*).
It is called "the heart" (*hadaya*). In the passage, "As if knowing heart with heart, he cleaves it," it refers to consciousness (*citta*).
In the passage, "The kidneys and the heart," it refers to the physical heart-organ (*hadayavatthu*). But here, it is consciousness itself that is called "the heart" in the sense of being internal.
That very same thing is "bright" (*paṇḍara*) in the sense of being purified. This is said with reference to the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). As it has been said: "This [mind] is luminous..."
“Monks, it is the mind, and it is defiled by adventitious defilements.

However, because it has emerged from that [state], even when unwholesome, it is described as “bright,” just as a river emerging from the Ganges is called the Ganges, and one emerging from the Godhāvarī is called the Godhāvarī.
For the mind, which has the characteristic of cognizing an object, is [inherently pure] despite its defilement.
Defilement does not exist; it is pure by its very nature. However, when there is association with defilements, it is called "defiled.
For this reason also, it is appropriate to call it "bright" (*paṇḍara*).
As for "mind" (*mano*) being the "mind-base" (*manāyatana*), here the mention of "mind" is for the purpose of showing that mind itself constitutes the base. Therefore, this...
He illuminates this: "It is not called the mind-base (manāyatana) because it is a base for the mind like a divine shrine (devāyatana);
rather, the mind itself is the base, thus it is the mind-base.

The meaning of "base" (āyatana) has already been explained above. It is called "mind" (mano) because it cognizes; the sense is that it discerns. Thus say the teachers of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathācariyā).
They say: it is called *mano* because it knows the object, like one measuring with a *nāḷi* or like one holding [the balance] on a great scale;

it is called *indriya* because it exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha*) over the characteristic of mentalizing (*manana*). Thus, the mind-faculty is the "mind-faculty" (*manindriya*). It is called *viññāṇa* because it cognizes.
Consciousness itself as an aggregate is the "consciousness-aggregate" (*viññāṇakkhandha*). It is called an "aggregate" (*khandha*) in its conventional sense.
For in the sense of a "heap" (rāsa), a single unit of consciousness is one part of the aggregate of consciousness.

Therefore, just as one who cuts a single part of a tree is said to "cut the tree," so too, even a single consciousness—which is but one part of the aggregate of consciousness—is called the "aggregate of consciousness" by way of conventional usage (ruḷhi).
Furthermore, the meaning of "aggregate" (khandha) is precisely the meaning of "heap."
It does not exist; even in the sense of a "portion," it is simply the sense of an "aggregate" (*khandha*). Therefore, the meaning is "the portion of consciousness" by way of being a portion.
"The corresponding mind-consciousness element" (*tajjā manoviññāṇadhātu*) means the mind-consciousness element that is suitable for those associated states, such as contact and so forth.
For in this term, the single state of consciousness is "mind" (*mano*) in the sense of measuring, and [it is "consciousness"] in the sense of cognizing.
Consciousness is called by three names—*viññāṇa*, *dhātu*, or *sattva*—in the sense of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) or in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being (*nissatta*).
"Exultation" (*abhippamoda*) is superior satisfaction.

In the exposition of concentration (*samādhi*), it is called "stability" (*ṭhiti*) because it stands upon the object by way of immovability; the following two terms [are explained] by way of prefixes.
It has increased (*vaḍḍhita*). Furthermore, it is "establishment" (*saṇṭhiti*) because it remains having gathered together the associated states upon the object.
It is "stability" (*avaṭṭhiti*) because it remains having plunged into and entered the object. For in the wholesome side, four factors plunge into the object:
faith, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. For that very reason, faith is called "conviction" (*okappanā*), and mindfulness is called "non-forgetfulness" (*apilāpanatā*).
Concentration is "stability," and wisdom is "penetration. On the unwholesome side, however, three factors penetrate the object:
craving, views, and ignorance; for that very reason, they are called "floods" (ogha).

It is "non-distraction" because it is the opposite of the distracted state of mind that occurs through restlessness and doubt; the meaning is "not wandering away. Precisely by way of restlessness and doubt...
The mind that wanders is said to be distracted; however, this [state] is not like that, thus it is non-distraction (*avikkhepa*).

It is by way of restlessness and doubt alone that the mind is called "distracted," being dragged hither and thither; this, however, is the state of a mind that is not dragged about, thus it is "non-distracted-mindedness" (*avisāhaṭamānasatā*).
“Tranquility” (*samatha*) is threefold: tranquility of mind, tranquility of legal issues, and tranquility of all conditioned formations.

Among these, one-pointedness of mind within the eight attainments is called “tranquility of mind. For, by means of that, the wavering of the mind and the agitation of the mind are stilled and pacified;
therefore, it is called “tranquility of mind. [The other types include] the sevenfold [methods], beginning with resolution in the presence (*sammukhā-vinaya*).
“Settling of legal issues” (adhikaraṇasamatha) means this: by resorting to it, various legal issues are settled and pacified; therefore, it is called “settling of legal issues.

However, because all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) are settled and pacified by resorting to Nibbāna, it is called “the settling of all conditioned phenomena. In this sense, it is the “settling of the mind” (cittasamatha).

This is what is intended. It exercises lordship over the characteristic of concentration, thus it is the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*). It is unshakable by restlessness, thus it is the power of concentration (*samādhibala*).
"Right concentration" (*sammāsamādhi*) refers to concentration according to reality, liberating concentration, and wholesome concentration.
By the phrases beginning with "liberating the mind from lust," liberation from the ten bases of defilement is stated. By the inclusion of "sloth" (*thina*) alone...
And here, by the mention of *middha* (drowsiness), and by the mention of *uddhacca* (restlessness) itself, the mention of *kukkucca* (worry) is also effected;

thus, in other readings, through the statement of liberation from the basis of the defilements by virtue of their association, the liberation from the hindrances by means of the first jhāna and so forth, as well as the liberation from the perception of permanence by means of the contemplation of impermanence and so forth, is already stated. How so?

"He contemplates that mind": here, in the series [of contemplations], the abandoning of the perception of permanence and so forth by means of the contemplation of impermanence and so forth has already been stated.
The four textual bases from the Suttas are to be understood according to the third tetrad.
The commentary on the exposition of the third tetrad is finished.
180. In the exposition of the fourth tetrad, because of the statement "that which is unspecified is neuter," since it is not specified as "this" or "that," the question "What is impermanent?
is posed using the neuter gender. "In the sense of arising and passing away" means by way of the meaning designated as arising and passing away;
that is to say, by way of the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of arising and passing away. And here, the five aggregates are the characteristic of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-lakkhaṇa*). Of the five...

The arising and passing away of the aggregates (*khandhā*) is their characteristic of change. By this, it is meant that they are impermanent (*anicca*) because of their non-existence after having existed.

For this very reason, although the *Aṭṭhakathā* states, "Impermanence by way of the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa*) is the arising, passing away, and alteration of those very [aggregates]," it further says, "or it is non-existence after having existed.
By this, it is stated that the mode of non-existence after having existed is the characteristic of impermanence.
[The text] says: "One who sees the arising and passing away of the five aggregates [sees] these characteristics by means of wisdom.
Having thus stated this as a formula (*peyyāla*), it continues: "Dhammas" refers to the aggregates of form and so forth, the dhammas as previously described.
In the description of "contemplating fading away," the phrase "seeing the danger in form" refers to [the stages] from the contemplation of dissolution onwards, as will be explained later.
Having seen the danger in the aggregate of form through its characteristics such as impermanence (*anicca*). "In the fading away of lust for form" (*rūpavirāge*) means in Nibbāna.
For it is by coming to Nibbāna that lust for form fades away; it ceases by attaining the state of non-rearising. Therefore, Nibbāna is called "the fading away of lust for form.
"One becomes filled with desire" means one possesses the desire for the Dhamma that has arisen through hearsay. "Resolved in faith" (*saddhādhimutto*)...
"He is resolved upon that very Nibbāna through faith and is certain. Regarding the phrase "his mind is well-established":

for this yogi, his mind is well-established and firmly grounded by way of the object upon the dissolution of form—known as destruction and fading away—and by way of tradition upon Nibbāna—known as absolute fading away from form. This is the connection [of the text].

It should be understood as follows: "Contemplating fading away in regard to form" (*rūpe virāgānupassī*) means that the fading away through the destruction of form is called "fading away in regard to form" by way of a locative expressing the natural state (*pakatibhummavacana*).
Alternatively, the absolute fading away of form is called "fading away in regard to form" by way of a locative expressing the sense of the sign (*nimittatthe bhummavacana*).

One who has the habit of contemplating both these kinds of fading away from the perspective of the object (*ārammaṇa*) and the underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*) is "one who contemplates fading away in regard to form."
Thus it was said. This same method applies to feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [aggregates]. The same method also applies to the exposition of the term "contemplating cessation" (*nirodhānupassī*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "In how many aspects," etc., this is the distinction here:

therein, by the very demonstration of the danger and the cessation of the factors of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) such as ignorance (*avijjā*), the danger and cessation of form (*rūpa*) and the rest are also demonstrated, because they do not transcend the factors of dependent origination.
And by this very specific expression, the distinguished nature of the contemplation of cessation (*nirodhānupassanā*) over and above the contemplation of fading away (*virāgānupassanā*) is stated.

In that context: "in the sense of impermanence" means in the sense of destruction, or in the sense of non-existence after having existed. "In the sense of suffering" means in the sense of fear, or in the sense of oppression.
"In the sense of non-self" means in the sense of being coreless, or in the sense of lack of mastery. "In the sense of burning" means...
In the sense of scorching the defilements (*kilesa*). "In the sense of transformation" means in the sense of transforming in two ways, by way of aging and dissolution.
"By the cessation of the source" means by the absence of the root condition. "Ceases" means it does not exist.
"By the cessation of the origin" means by the absence of the proximate condition. For the root condition is called the "source" just as unwholesome food is the source of a disease.

The proximate condition (*āsanna-paccaya*) is called the "origination" (*samudaya*) of disease, just as wind, bile, and phlegm are. For it is called "root-cause" (*nidāna*) because it definitively gives (*dadāti*) the fruit;
whereas it is called "origination" (*samudaya*) because the fruit arises thoroughly (*suṭṭhu udeti*) from it.
"By the cessation of birth" means by the absence of the arising of the root-condition. "By the cessation of the source" means by the absence of the arising of the proximate condition.
For it is appropriate to call birth "the source" (*pabhava*), because suffering originates from it.

"By the cessation of the cause" means by the absence of the productive condition (*janaka-paccaya*). "By the cessation of the condition" means by the absence of the supporting condition (*upatthambhaka-paccaya*).

For indeed, both the root condition and the proximate condition are likewise productive conditions and supporting conditions respectively. By these [means], at the moment of sharp insight (*tikkha-vipassanā*)—
"Cessation of its factors" refers to cessation by way of eradication at the moment of the path.

"By the arising of knowledge" means by the arising of either the knowledge of sharp insight or the knowledge of the path. "By the manifestation of cessation" means by the manifestation of the cessation that is destruction, which is directly perceived at the moment of insight;
and by the manifestation of what is termed cessation—namely, Nibbāna—which is [perceived] through hearsay; and by the direct perception [of it] at the moment of the path.

And by the manifestation of Nibbāna. By these [factors], the determination of object and subject is established, and the cessation consisting in the cutting off by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgasamucchedanirodha*) is stated.

182. In the exposition of the phrase "contemplating relinquishment" (*paṭinissaggānupassī*): "he relinquishes form," etc., means that through the vision of danger and through lack of concern, he relinquishes the aggregate of form.
"Relinquishment as relinquishment" means it is called relinquishment in the sense of relinquishing.
This has been stated. By this, the meaning of the word *paṭinissagga* (relinquishment) as "abandoning" is expressed; therefore, the sense is that one abandons the defilements.

And herein, insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā*) relinquishes the defilements by way of their specific factor-counteraction (*tadaṅgavasena*), while the path relinquishes them by way of their total eradication (*samucchedavasena*).
"The mind leaps into Nibbāna, the cessation of form"—this is because the insight leading to emergence is inclined toward that [Nibbāna].
It leaps forward; the path [leaps forward] by making [nibbāna] its object. "Relinquishment through leaping forward" means it is called relinquishment in the sense of leaping forward.
By this, the meaning of leaping forward is stated for the term "relinquishment";
therefore, the meaning is the casting of the mind into nibbāna. The four scriptural bases are according to the fourth tetrad.
These are to be understood. Regarding this tetrad, what is to be said concerning aging and death should be understood according to the method already stated below.

And in the case of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), the singular designation is made by way of the conventional expression of the unity of body and mind in the phrases "contemplation of the body in the body" and "contemplation of the mind in the mind.
[Likewise,] in the phrases "contemplation of feelings in feelings" and "contemplation of phenomena in phenomena," [the singular is used for] feelings and phenomena...
It should be understood that the presentation in the plural number is made by way of various modes of expression.
The commentary on the fourth tetrad is finished.
And the commentary on the presentation of the knowledge of acting with mindfulness is finished.
6. Explanation of the Description of the Six Groups of Knowledge (Ñāṇarāsichakkaniddesa) 183.

Now, regarding the description of the twenty-four kinds of knowledge taught under the six groups, first, in the description of the knowledge of concentration, there are twelve bases consisting of three tetrads beginning with body-contemplation (*kāyānupassanā*).
In each of these, one kind of knowledge arises by way of inhalation, and one kind by way of exhalation.
"One" and "two by two" refer to the concentrations; thus, there are twenty-four concentrations among the twelve bases.
At the moment of jhāna, there are knowledges associated with those [factors] by way of those twenty-four concentrations.
In the description of the seventy-two kinds of insight-knowledge, the phrase "long in-breaths" refers to the breath stated as "long. What is meant?

Does it exist? Having attained jhāna by means of long inhalation, at the moment of insight (vipassanā) with a concentrated mind, it is said that there is "insight" in the sense of contemplating as impermanent. This same method applies to what follows.
For each of those twelve bases, there are three insights by way of inhalation and three by way of exhalation; thus, there are six insights for each.

In the twelve bases, there are seventy-two contemplations (*anupassanā*). Those same seventy-two contemplations are, by way of the seventy-two kinds of insight (*vipassanā*), knowledges (*ñāṇa*). In the exposition of the knowledge of disenchantment (*nibbidā-ñāṇa*):
"Contemplating impermanence while breathing in"—that is, breathing in as one contemplating impermanence; the meaning is "proceeding as one contemplating impermanence.
Furthermore, this word "breathing in" (*assasa*) should be understood in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). [As it is said: "As it really is..."

"Knows and sees" means "knowledge of disenchantment" (*nibbidā-ñāṇa*). From the stage of the comprehension by groups (*kalāpa-sammasana*) up to the contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā*), one knows formations according to their true nature through the insight-knowledge that has arisen;
and just as something seen with the physical eye, one sees it with that very eye of knowledge.
Therefore, the meaning is "it is called knowledge of disenchantment"; what is meant is "knowledge of becoming disenchanted with formations. [The rest follows] above.

Since the knowledges such as "appearance as terror" (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna*) and those such as "desire for deliverance" (*muñcitukamyatā*) have been mentioned separately, it should be understood here that the insight-knowledges (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) exactly as previously stated are what constitute the knowledge of disenchantment (*nibbidā-ñāṇa*). In the exposition of the knowledge of conformity with disenchantment (*nibbidānuloma-ñāṇa*), regarding the passage:
"Breathing in contemplating impermanence, for one breathing in contemplating impermanence," the genitive case is used in the sense of agency (*sāmī-attha*).

This is the singular (paccatta) form. By the very expression "wisdom in the appearance as terror" (*bhayatupaṭṭhāne paññā*), the knowledges of the contemplation of danger (*ādīnavānupassanā-ñāṇa*) and the contemplation of disenchantment (*nibbidānupassanā-ñāṇa*) are also included, because these three share a single characteristic.

These three knowledges are called "conformity-knowledge in accordance with disenchantment" (*nibbidānuloma-ñāṇa*) because they conform to the preceding knowledges of disenchantment by way of being favorable to them.

In the exposition of the knowledge of the subsiding of disenchantment (*nibbidāpaṭippassaddhi-ñāṇa*), "contemplating impermanence while breathing" is exactly the same as the immediately preceding [section].

By the very expression "wisdom as reflective contemplation and composure" (*paṭisaṅkhā santiṭṭhanā paññā*), the knowledge of desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa*), the knowledge of reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā-ñāṇa*), and the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*) are stated, because these three share a single characteristic. By the expression "reflective contemplation and composure," the knowledge of conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of the path (*magga-ñāṇa*) are also [included].

They are grasped. For even the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*), because they have reached the peak of disenchantment (*nibbidā*), are called "knowledges of the subsiding of disenchantment" (*nibbidāpaṭippassaddhi-ñāṇa*) due to the abandonment of their function of generating disenchantment.

However, it is highly appropriate that the knowledge of the path (*magga-ñāṇa*) is called "knowledge of the subsiding of disenchantment" because it arises at the conclusion of the subsiding of disenchantment. Regarding the knowledges of conformity to disenchantment (*nibbidānuloma-ñāṇa*):

Without taking the knowledge of desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa*), which is the very beginning, the inclusion of the two final knowledges under the term "reflective settling" (*paṭisaṅkhā santiṭṭhanā*) is for the purpose of including them within the knowledge of the path (*magga-ñāṇa*).
For when "desire for deliverance" is mentioned, it includes the knowledge of conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*), not the knowledge of the path.
Indeed, the knowledge of the path is not called "desire for deliverance"; rather, it is called "settling" because it settles upon the accomplishment of its task.
It is so named. And in the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is also stated: "Contacting is absorption (*appanā*).
Since this knowledge of the path is an absorption in *nibbāna*, it is called "establishment" (*santiṭṭhanā*); thus, by the term "establishment," the knowledge of the path is also included.
Furthermore, since the knowledges of disenchantment and conformity are in actual fact simply knowledges of disenchantment, they too are subsumed under the knowledges of disenchantment.
Regarding the phrase "knowledge of disenchantment and knowledge of subsiding," only the mention of "disenchantment" (*nibbidā*) is made,
not the mention of "conformity with disenchantment" (*nibbidānuloma*). Furthermore, in each of these three sets of eight knowledges,
for each of the four bases stated by way of the tetrad of contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*), there are two knowledges each— one by way of inhalation and one by way of exhalation.
There are eight knowledges regarding the four bases.

In the exposition of the knowledge of the bliss of liberation, having shown "abandoning" by means of the phrase "because it has been abandoned," he says "because it has been eradicated" in order to show that this abandoning is an abandoning by eradication (*samucchedappahāna*).
"Knowledge of the bliss of liberation" refers to the knowledge associated with the bliss of liberation as fruition (*phala-vimutti*).
And there is the knowledge of reviewing that has as its object the bliss of liberation from the fruit.

The abandonment of the underlying tendencies is mentioned again for the purpose of showing that by the abandoning of the defilement which is the basis for the underlying tendencies, there is also the abandoning of the basis for the obsessions and misconduct.

With reference to the twenty-one kinds of knowledge regarding the fruit, the enumeration of knowledge is also made by way of the count of the abandoned defilements, as well as the reviewing knowledge.
By implication, the reckoning of the knowledge that reviews the fruit is accomplished through the reckoning of the reviewing of the defilements abandoned.
The commentary on the exposition of the six groups of knowledge is finished.
From the *Saddhammappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.
The commentary on the discourse on mindfulness of breathing is finished. 4.
Discourse on the Faculties.
1. Commentary on the Exposition of the First Sutta.
184. Now, following the discussion on mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*), the commentary on the previously unstated matter of the discussion on the faculties (*indriya*) has arrived.

For this discussion on the faculties is intended to show the method for purifying and so forth those faculties that are conducive to the development of mindfulness of breathing, since without those faculties conducive to the development of mindfulness of breathing, such development would not occur.
Since this was spoken immediately after the discourse on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati),

and since he wished to explain that discourse on the faculties (indriya-kathā) by first taking as his lead the Suttanta teaching whose intended meaning he had personally heard from the Blessed One’s own presence,
he first said, "Thus have I heard," and so forth, in order to elucidate its meaning.

In this context, *evaṃ* is a particle (*nipātapada*). *Me* and so forth are nouns (*nāmapada*). Regarding *viharati*, here *vi-* is a prefix (*upasaggapada*) and *harati* is a verb (*ākhyātapada*); by this method, the analysis of the words (*padavibhāga*) should first be understood.

As for the meaning (*atthato*), the word *evaṃ* is seen in the senses of comparison, instruction, censure, praise, manner of speaking, and inclusion, as well as in the sense of illustration (*nidassana*) and restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
Here, however, the word *evaṃ* is used in the sense of manner and illustration by a person of discernment.
It is used in the sense of "thus" and likewise in the sense of emphasis.
