Therein, by the word *evaṃ* in the sense of "manner," he illuminates this meaning:

[the teaching] which is skilled in various methods, originated from manifold inclinations, endowed with both meaning and phrasing, possessing diverse miracles, and profound in its penetration of the Dhamma, the meaning, the teaching, and realization—for all beings...
Who is capable of understanding in every way the word of that Blessed One as it comes within the range of hearing, according to each individual’s own language?
Nevertheless, having generated a desire to hear with all one's might, one should say: "Thus have I heard;
by me also it was heard in this manner."

In the sense of illustration, by liberating himself [from the charge] that "I am not self-become, nor have I realized this myself," he indicates the entire discourse now to be spoken with the words, "Thus have I heard; it was heard by me thus.

In the sense of emphasis, the Elder Sāriputta [shows his preeminence], for it was said: "Bhikkhus, among my disciples who are bhikkhus, Sāriputta is foremost in great wisdom," and, "Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single person other than..."
"He who thus correctly continues to turn the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by the Tathāgata—
just as this Sāriputta does, monks. For Sāriputta, monks, correctly continues to turn the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by the Tathāgata"—
in such a manner, [he reflects] upon his own state in accordance with the praise bestowed upon him by the Blessed One.
Demonstrating his power of retention, he generates in beings a desire to hear [the teaching], thinking: "Thus have I heard;
and that is neither deficient nor redundant in meaning or in phrasing; it should be seen exactly thus, and not otherwise.
The word *me* (by me) is seen in the senses of the instrumental, dative, and genitive cases. Here, however, it is appropriate in two meanings: "heard by me" and "my hearing."

The word *suta* (heard), when accompanied by prefixes (*sa-upasagga*) or without them (*an-upasagga*), is seen in the senses of what is well-known, what has been traversed, what is soiled, what is accumulated, application, and what is cognizable by the ear;
it is also used for that which is known by way of the ear-door. Here, however, its meaning is "that which was determined" (*upadhārita*) or "determination" (*upadhāraṇa*) by way of the ear-door.
Since the word *me* (by me) has the sense of *mayā* (by me), [the phrase] is: "Thus have I heard by way of the ear-door."
The term "upadhāritaṃ" (ascertained) is appropriate; for if the sense is "mine," it is appropriate as "thus have I heard"—that is, an ascertainment following the path of the ear-door.
Furthermore, by saying "Thus have I heard," one does not claim the state of having produced [the teaching] oneself, but rather clarifies the prior hearing:
"This was received directly by me from that Blessed One, who is confident in the four grounds of self-confidence and possesses the ten powers."

“This is the word of the Perfectly Enlightened One— the one who stands in the place of the bull, the roarer of the lion’s roar, the supreme among all beings, the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, the Sovereign of Dhamma, the Island of Dhamma, the Refuge of Dhamma, the Wheel-Turner of the sublime True Dhamma; herein,
no doubt or perplexity should be entertained regarding the meaning, the doctrine, the phrasing, or the syllables.”
In this Dhamma, it destroys lack of faith and gives rise to the perfection of faith. Therefore, this is said:
"It destroys lack of faith and increases faith in the Teaching;
Thus saying 'I have heard this,' the disciple of Gotama speaks."
"Ekanta" is a designation for a numerical limit. "Samaya" is a designation for a delimited [time]. "Ekaṃ samayaṃ" is an indication of an unspecified [time].
In this context, the word *samaya* is seen to be used in the senses of: a collection, a moment, time, a multitude, a cause, a view, acquisition, abandoning, and penetration.

But here, "time" (kāla) is the meaning. By this, he indicates a single occasion (*samaya*) among those periods that constitute the divisions of time, such as the year, the season, the month, the fortnight, the day and night, the morning, midday, evening, the first watch, the middle watch, the last watch, the hour, and so forth.
In that regard, although among these periods—such as the year and the rest—whatever discourse [was spoken] in whichever year...
Whether it was said [to have occurred] in a season, a month, a fortnight, during the portion of the night, or the portion of the day—all that is well-known and well-determined by the Elder’s wisdom.

For, if one were to say, "Thus have I heard: in such-and-such a year, in such-and-such a season, in such-and-such a month, in such-and-such a fortnight, during such-and-such a portion of the night, or such-and-such a portion of the day," it would not be easy to remember.
Or [if one were] to recite it oneself or cause it to be recited, there would be much that must be said; therefore, having condensed that meaning into a single phrase, he said, "At one time.

Or else, these are the occasions: the occasion of descent into the womb, the occasion of birth, the occasion of spiritual urgency, the occasion of the Great Renunciation, and the occasion of practicing austerities.

The time of victory over Māra, the time of full enlightenment, the time of dwelling in happiness in this very life, the time of teaching, the time of final nibbāna—such are the various times of the Blessed One, well-known among gods and humans, distinguished by many different occasions. Among those times, he indicates one specific time known as the "time of teaching.
Furthermore, this refers to the "time of the function of compassion" among the times for the functions of wisdom and compassion.
Among the occasions for practicing for one’s own welfare and for the welfare of others, it is the occasion for practicing for the welfare of others;
among the two duties for those who have assembled, it is the occasion for a discourse on the Dhamma; among the occasions for teaching and for practice, it is the occasion for teaching.
Referring to one such occasion among these, he said, "at one time."
However, since the sense of "constant conjunction" (*accantasamyoga*) is possible in the phrase "at one time," and because at whatever time the Blessed One taught this or another discourse,
he dwelt at that very time in a state of compassion,
the use of the instrumental case here is made for the purpose of indicating that meaning.
Regarding this, it is said:
"In view of various meanings, [the case endings] are stated as the locative and the instrumental;
except for the 'time' (samaya), which here is stated as the accusative."
The Ancients, however, explain: “At that time,” “by that time,” or “that time”—these are merely differences in expression;
in all cases, the meaning is simply the locative case. Therefore, even when it is said “at one time,” the meaning should be understood as “at one [particular] time.”

“Bhagavā” means venerable. For in the world they call one who is venerable “Bhagavā. And he is venerable to all beings because of his preeminence in all virtues; therefore he should be understood as “Bhagavā. It has also been said by the ancients:
“‘Bhagavā’ is the best of words; ‘Bhagavā’ is the supreme word.
He is venerable and worthy of reverence; for that reason he is called ‘Bhagavā.’”
Furthermore:
"He is fortunate (bhāgyavā), he has broken (bhaggavā), he is endowed with (yutto) the bhagas, and he has analyzed (vibhattavā) the bhagas;
he has enjoyed (bhattavā), he has cast out (vantagamana), and thus he is the Blessed One (bhagavā) regarding the states of existence (bhavesu)."

The detailed meaning of this word should be understood by means of this verse as well; and that has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga* in the exposition on the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati-niddesa*).

To this extent, here, by the word "thus" (*evam*), he indicates the excellence of the teaching; by "heard by me" (*me sutaṃ*), the excellence of the disciple; by "at one time" (*ekaṃ samayaṃ*), the excellence of the time; and by "the Blessed One" (*bhagavā*), the excellence of the teacher. Regarding "at Sāvatthī":
here, Sāvatthī is the city that served as the dwelling place of the sage Savattha, just as...
*Kākandī* and *Mākandī*—thus do the etymologists explain. However, the masters of the commentaries say:
"Whatever articles of enjoyment and use belong to humans, all of these are found here (*atthi*), thus it is Sāvatthī.
Furthermore, it is called Sāvatthī based on the statement "all is there" when asked, upon arriving with a caravan, what goods are available.
“Always all requisites are gathered together in Sāvatthī;
therefore, taking up everything, it is called ‘Sāvatthī.

In this context, the locative case in “in Sāvatthī” (sāvatthiyaṃ) expresses proximity. “Dwells” (viharati) refers, without distinction, to the postures, the divine abidings, the sublime abidings, and the noble abidings.
This is an illustration of one who possesses a particular abiding; here, however, it is an illustration of association with one of the various postures—standing, walking, sitting, or lying down.
Therefore, whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, the Blessed One is to be understood as "dwelling" (*viharati*).
For the Blessed One [removes] the obstruction of one posture by means of another posture.

Having severed [the continuity of existence], it carries on and causes to proceed the personal existence (attabhāva) without falling away; therefore, it is said, "he dwells" (*viharati*). Regarding the word "Jetavana":
herein, he who conquers his own adversaries is "Jeta"; or, it is "Jeta" because it was born when the King had conquered his adversaries;
or, out of a desire for auspiciousness, its name was made exactly so; it "vanayati" means...
*Vanaṃ* means that it causes sentient beings to feel devotion toward its own excellence; the meaning is that it arouses affection for itself.

Alternatively, *vanaṃ* means "it solicits" (*vanute*); the meaning is that, through the various fragrances of flowers and the songs of intoxicated cuckoos and other birds, and through the branches, twigs, shoots, and foliage of trees shaken by gentle breezes, it is as if it requests living beings, saying, "Come, enjoy me. *Jetassa vanaṃ* is *jetavanaṃ*. For that—
It was planted, nurtured, and protected by Prince Jeta, and he was its owner;
therefore, it is called Jetavana. In that Jetavana. Forests are of two kinds: those that are planted and those that grow of their own accord.
This [Jetavana] and places such as Veḷuvana are planted, while forests such as Andhavana and Mahāvana are self-grown.
"In the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika": that householder was named Sudatta after the name given by his parents.

However, because he provided alms-food (*piṇḍa*) at all times to those who were without protectors (*anātha*), owing to his success in all desires, his freedom from stinginess, and his possession of qualities such as compassion, he became known by the designation "Anāthapiṇḍika.
[The word *ārāma*] means "wherein living beings delight," or specifically, "wherein those who have gone forth delight."

An *ārāma* is so called because people come from here and there to delight and take pleasure in it, dwelling there without longing, due to its beauty of flowers, fruits, and so forth, and its possession of the five factors of a suitable dwelling—neither too far nor too near.
Alternatively, by means of such qualities, it draws those who have gone to various places back within itself and causes them to rejoice; thus it is an *ārāma*. It is that.
Indeed, after the householder Anāthapiṇḍika had purchased the land from Prince Jeta for eighteen crores of gold by covering it with a layer of gold coins,
and after having had dwellings constructed for eighteen crores of gold and completed the festival of the monastery for eighteen crores of gold,
he thus offered fifty-four crores of gold to the community headed by the Buddha.
It was dedicated to the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus; therefore, it is called "Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
In that park of Anāthapiṇḍika—here, the mention of "in Jeta’s Grove" is a reference to the former owner, while "in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park" is a reference to the latter owner.
What is the purpose of mentioning these two? It is so that those desiring merit may follow their example. For therein...
The eighteen crores of gold obtained from the sale of the land for the construction of the Dvāra-koṭṭhaka Palace, the trees worth many crores, and the gift of Jeta—all these belonged to Jettha;
while those belonging to Anāthapiṇḍika were fifty-four crores of gold.
Thus, by describing these two, the Venerable Sāriputta showed that those desiring merit perform meritorious deeds, and he [then] mentioned others who likewise desired merit.
He enjoins them to follow in the footsteps of those [who have attained].
Herein, it might be argued: if the Blessed One is dwelling in Sāvatthī, then it should not be said that he is "in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park";
and if he is dwelling there, then it should not be said that he is "in Sāvatthī. For...
"It would be possible for both to dwell together at one time. However, this should not be viewed in that way;

did we not say, "The locative case is used in the sense of proximity"? Therefore, just as herds of cattle grazing near the Ganges or the Yamunā are said to be "grazing on the Ganges" or "grazing on the Yamunā," so too here, in the vicinity of Sāvatthī—
Jetavana is the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika; when dwelling there, he is said to be "dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jetavana, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika.

The mention of Sāvatthī is for the purpose of indicating the village of his alms-round, while the remaining words are for the purpose of indicating a place of residence suitable for one who has gone forth.
In this regard, by the mention of Sāvatthī, the Venerable Sāriputta shows the Blessed One’s act of favoring householders;

by the mention of Jetavana and so forth, he shows his act of favoring those who have gone forth. Likewise, by the former, he shows the avoidance of devotion to self-mortification through the acceptance of the four requisites;
by the latter, he shows the means for avoiding devotion to sensual pleasure through the abandoning of sense-objects. Alternatively, by the former...
And by the former, application to the teaching of the Dhamma; by the latter, inclination toward seclusion. By the former, the approach through compassion;
by the latter, the withdrawal through wisdom. By the former, the inclination toward accomplishing the welfare and happiness of beings;
by the latter, freedom from attachment while performing the welfare and happiness of others. By the former, the cause for not abandoning righteous happiness.

The former [is for] dwelling in comfort; the latter is for the purpose of application to the superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*). By the former, there is the great benefit to human beings; by the latter, to the gods.
By the former, there is the state of being born in the world and having grown up in the world;
by the latter, there is the state of being unsullied by the world. By the former, it is said: "Bhikkhus, one person, arising in the world, arises for the welfare of many people..."
"By means of the welfare of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
From this statement, the first part elucidates the purpose for which the Blessed One appeared;
the latter part elucidates the kind of dwelling appropriate to that purpose, wherein he appeared. For the Blessed One first [appeared] in the Lumbinī grove...

The second [instance] is "at the seat of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*); because it arose in the forest itself for the arising of both the mundane and supramundane [qualities], he shows his dwelling in the forest itself—thus the construction of the meaning here should be understood by such a method.
In that context, "there" (*tatra*) is an indication of place and time; for when he dwells at whatever time, it is "at that time," and in whichever Jetavana.
He dwells there, and thus he indicates [his location] as "in the Jeta Grove. Or rather, he indicates the place and time that are appropriate for what is to be said.
For the Blessed One does not teach the Dhamma in an inappropriate place or at an inappropriate time. In this regard, the passage beginning with "It is not the right time, Bāhiya," serves as proof.

The particle *kho* is a mere filler (*padapūraṇa*), or it is a particle used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) or to indicate the beginning of a period of time (*ādikāla*). The term "Blessed One" (*bhagavā*) is an indication of his status as one revered by the world.

"Bhikkhu" is a term for a person engaged in listening to discourse. Furthermore, in this context, the etymological meaning should be understood according to such methods as: "He is a bhikkhu because he begs (bhikkhati)," or "He is a bhikkhu because he has entered upon the practice of begging.

"Āmantesi" means he addressed, spoke to, or called out; this is the sense here. However, elsewhere it also signifies making known or summoning. "Bhikkhave" is an illustration of the manner of addressing.
By means of that speech— accomplished through his possession of qualities such as the habit of begging,
the nature of begging, and excellence in the practice of begging— he reveals the mode of livelihood practiced by those of inferior and superior status,

thereby effecting a restraint against the states of arrogance and dejection. And by the address “O Bhikkhus,” preceded by a glance from eyes gentle with the expansion of compassion, he brings them face-to-face before him.
By means of that very statement which illuminates his desire to speak, he generates in them a desire to hear.
And by that same address, he enjoins them to listen and attend with care; for the success of the Dispensation depends upon careful listening and attention. If it is asked:

"Since other gods and humans were present, why did he address only the bhikkhus?"—it is because they are the eldest, the most excellent, those who are constantly near him, and the most suitable recipients [of the teaching].
For the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma is common to all assemblies. And among these assemblies, the monks are the eldest because they were the first to arise;
they are the best because, starting from the state of homelessness, they followed the Teacher’s conduct and received the entire Dispensation;

they are the closest because, among those seated there, they are in the immediate presence of the Teacher; and they are always in close attendance because they move within the Teacher’s personal vicinity.
And they alone are the fit vessels for the teaching of the Dhamma, because of their existence in practice exactly as instructed.
Herein, it might be asked: "For what purpose did the Blessed One, while teaching the Dhamma, first address the bhikkhus rather than teaching the Dhamma directly?
It was for the sake of arousing mindfulness. For in the assembly, the bhikkhus might have been thinking of other things or have distracted minds.
There may also be those who are seated reflecting on the Dhamma or attending to their meditation subject;
if the Dhamma is taught without addressing them, they might fail to discern, "What is the source of this teaching? What is its condition? For what occasion of significance was it taught?
and thus they would fall into distraction or grasp it incorrectly. Therefore, for their sake...
For the purpose of generating mindfulness, the Blessed One first addresses them and afterwards teaches the Dhamma.
"Bhadante" is a term of respect, or it is the giving of a reply to the Teacher.
Furthermore, in this context, when the Blessed One says "Bhikkhus," he addresses those bhikkhus; when they say "Bhadante," they address the Blessed One in return.
Thus the Blessed One addressed them, saying, "O monks," and they replied to him, "Venerable Sir.
He caused them to give the response, "O monks," and they gave the response, "Venerable Sir. "Those monks" refers to those whom the Blessed One addressed.
"They responded to the Blessed One" means they heard the Blessed One's address in return; having turned toward him, they listened.
They accepted; the meaning is that they received [it]. "The Blessed One said this" means the Blessed One spoke this entire discourse which is now to be recited.

And up to this point, [the Blessed One described] that lotus pond whose waters were bright with lotuses and water-lilies, pure, and sweet-tasting, for the sake of easy descent—[a pond] possessing the grace of steps fashioned from spotless stone slabs, and whose white ground was strewn with sand resembling scattered nets of pearls.

It was like a landing-place; it was like a staircase for the easy ascent of that excellent palace—which possessed a towering height as if wishing to touch the path of the stars and was surrounded by a railing of variegated walls beautifully divided—shining with a mass of light from clusters of gems entwined with golden creepers upon smooth, soft wooden planks made of ivory;
and it resounded with the sweet voices of the household folk, mingled with chatter and laughter, accompanied by the clinking sounds of golden bracelets, anklets, and other ornaments.

Just as a great gate with well-constructed, wide door-panels, brilliantly illuminated by the radiance of gold, silver, gems, pearls, coral, and other jewels, serves to facilitate the easy entry into a magnificent mansion adorned with noble majesty and wealth;
so too, for the sake of easy comprehension of this Sutta— which is endowed with both meaning and phrasing and which reveals the profound nature of the Buddhas’ knowledge of teaching—
is there the Nidāna, adorned with the factors of time, place, teacher, and assembly.
The explanation of the meaning of what was spoken is completed.
In the Sutta, "five" is the delimitation by number. "These faculties" is the indication of the specific phenomena delimited. The meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*) has been stated above.
185. Now, having shown this Sutta, [the following is] the method for the cultivation of purification regarding the faculties mentioned in this Sutta.
Desiring to show both the cultivated mind (*bhāvitatta*) and its subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi*), he said, "These five faculties," and so forth.
In this context, "they become purified" means they reach purification. "In one who lacks faith" refers to one devoid of faith in the Three Jewels.

"In one who has faith" refers to one endowed with faith in the Three Jewels. "Of one who serves" means of one serving with the mind. "Of one who frequents" means of one approaching. "Of one who attends upon" means...
"To one sitting respectfully": in a discourse that inspires confidence, meaning a discourse connected with the qualities of the Triple Gem that generates faith.
"Lax" (*kusīta*): they are called lax because they sink down in a contemptible manner; those who are lax are simply "the lax ones. "In regard to right effort" (*sammappadhāna*):
in a discourse connected with the energy that accomplishes the four functions. "Forgetful" (*muṭṭhassati*): in regard to one whose mindfulness is lost.

"In the *Satipaṭṭhāna* [suttas]" means in those discourses whose subject matter is the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). "In the *Jhānavimokkha* [suttas]" means in those discourses whose subject matter is the fourth jhāna, the eight liberations (*vimokkha*), and the threefold liberation.
"Those of dull wisdom" (*duppañña*) means those devoid of wisdom; or alternatively, they are called "of dull wisdom" because their wisdom is corrupted due to the absence of true wisdom.
"The profound course of knowledge" refers to those discourses associated with the four truths, dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), and so forth.
Or in a discourse similar to the *Ñāṇakathā*. Regarding the "sections of the Suttanta" (*suttantakkhandha*), this refers to divisions within the Suttantas.

In the passage beginning with "lack of faith" (*assaddhiya*), "lack of faith" means the state of being without faith. One who sees the danger in lack of faith abandons lack of faith while developing the faculty of faith;
one who sees the benefit in the faculty of faith develops the faculty of faith while abandoning lack of faith. This same method applies [to the other faculties].
Regarding the terms: *kosajja* means the state of indolence; *pamāda* means the lapse of mindfulness; *uddhacca* means the state of agitation, which is to say distraction.
"Because they have been abandoned" means because they have been abandoned through the fulfillment of jhāna by way of absorption (*appanā*).

"Because they have been well-abandoned" means because they have been thoroughly abandoned through the fulfillment of insight (*vipassanā*) by way of that which leads to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī*). "It has been developed, well-developed" [is said].

It should be applied according to the sequence already stated. For it is appropriate to say "well-abandoned" because [the hindrances] have been abandoned by means of their opposites through insight (vipassanā).
And for that very reason, it is called "well-developed," but not so by means of meditative absorption (jhāna).

Since the accomplishment of development occurs through the abandoning of what is to be abandoned, and the accomplishment of the abandoning of what is to be abandoned occurs through the accomplishment of development, therefore—
This has been explained by means of a pair (yamaka).

186. In the section on subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi*), the phrases "they are developed and well-developed" indicate that there is a state of being well-developed for those very things already developed;
and "they have subsided and are well-subsided" indicates that there is a state of being well-subsided for those very things already subsided.

...have been stated. At the moment of the fruit (phala), the state of being cultivated and the state of subsidedness (paṭippassaddhatā) should be understood by way of the accomplishment of the function of the path.

"Purifications by eradication" (samuccheda-visuddhiyo) are precisely the purifications of the path. "Purifications by subsiding" (paṭippassaddhi-visuddhiyo) are precisely the purifications of the fruit.
Now, in order to demonstrate those faculties (indriya) as they have been described by applying them to the types of persons who perform [the practice], [it asks]: "Of how many..."

He says, "Of persons," and so forth. Therein, "Buddha by hearing" means that through hearing a discourse on the Dhamma from the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), one has awakened to the Four Truths;
the meaning is "having known. This is a statement of the cause for the state of having developed faculties (*bhāvitindriya*).

For it is because the Path is "awakened to" (*buddha*) by way of the clear realization through cultivation (*bhāvanābhisamaya*) that one possesses developed faculties at the moment of the Fruit (*phala*). [This applies] to all eight noble ones of the Tathāgata.
Having distinguished him from other disciples, he said "one whose taints are destroyed" (khīṇāsava) specifically to show that he alone stands at the stage of the fruit of arahantship.

For it is he alone who is called "one whose faculties are developed" (bhāvitindriya) due to the accomplishment of all duties; however, the others as well are, in a figurative sense, indeed "those whose faculties are developed" due to the accomplishment of the respective duties of their own paths.
And for this very reason, during the four moments of fruition, it is said: "The five faculties are both developed and well-developed."

And so it is said. However, because the cultivation of the faculties for the sake of the higher paths still exists for them, they are not, in the ultimate sense, those who have cultivated the faculties.

"By himself in the sense of having come to be" means that, without a teacher, he is the Blessed One (Bhagavā) in the sense of having come to be (bhūtaṭṭhena) and in the sense of being born (jātaṭṭhena) through noble birth.
For he too, by virtue of the perfection of his development, is self-become (sayambhū) at the moment of the fruit.

Thus, he is one whose faculties are developed in the sense of being truly become. "In the sense of being immeasurable" means in the sense of being impossible to measure due to his possession of infinite qualities.
At the moment of fruition, the Blessed One is immeasurable because of the perfection of his development; for that very reason, he is one whose faculties are developed.
The commentary on the exposition of the first sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Second Sutta Exposition (Dutiyasuttantaniddesavaṇṇanā) 187.
Having again set forth another sutta, desiring to demonstrate the classification of the faculties (*indriyavidhāna*), he shows the sutta beginning with "Bhikkhus, these five...
and so forth. In that context, the phrase "whosoever" (*ye hi keci*) is an exhaustive inclusion; the particle *hi* is used merely to fill out the metrical line.
This is a particle. "Whether recluses or brahmins" is stated according to worldly convention. "Originate" means by way of conditions.
"Cease" means the passing away of what has arisen, or the non-arising of what has not yet arisen.

"Gratification" means the benefit. "Disadvantage" means the fault. "Escape" means the departure. "As it really is" means according to its true nature. "Among recluses" means among those who have stilled evil.

“Recognized as recluses”: they are not recognized by me as recluses. When “recognized” (*sammatā*) is spoken of in reference to the present tense, according to the rules of grammar, the word “me” (*me*) here functions solely as a genitive case. “Among brahmins” (*brāhmaṇesu*): among those who have banished evil.
“The goal of recluseship” (*sāmaññattha*): the purpose of the state of being a recluse. “The goal of brahminhood” (*brahmaññattha*): the purpose of the state of being a brahmin. By both [of these]...
Only the fruit of arahantship is mentioned. Alternatively, "the goal of recluseship" refers to the three lower fruits;
"the goal of the holy life" refers to the fruit of arahantship. For "recluseship and the holy life" is indeed the Noble Path itself.
"In this very life" means in the very manifest personal existence. "Having realized by one's own direct knowledge" means having made it manifest for oneself through superior wisdom.
“Upasampajja” means having reached or having accomplished. 188.
In the exposition of the Sutta, after first asking for the enumeration of the classifications of the arising of the faculties and so forth, that enumeration of classifications is then answered.
Therein, “one hundred and eighty” (*asītisata*) means one hundred and eighty. By the wise, it is called “one hundred and eighty.”
The construction is "by the modes already stated.

Again, in the description of enumeration that is preceded by a question regarding the classification and number [of factors], the phrase "for the purpose of resolve" means for the purpose of resolving, that is, for the purpose of conviction.
"The origin of adverting" refers to the origin of the mind-door adverting consciousness. Of the faculty of faith...

"Arising" (*samudaya*) is a condition for the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*). The preliminary adverting consciousness with the thought "I shall arouse faith" is the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for the faculty of faith.

The adverting consciousness for the impulsion of the faculty of faith is the proximity condition (*anantara-paccaya*) for the first impulsion, and it is the decisive support condition for the second impulsion and those following.
"By way of resolve" (*adhimokkha-vasena*) means by way of resolve associated with desire (*chanda*).

The "arising of desire" (*chanda-samudaya*) is the arising of that specific factor (*dhammacchanda*) which is associated with resolution (*adhimokkha*), is a mundane state (*yevāpanaka*), and has arisen conditioned by the preliminary advertence (*pubbabhāga-āvajjana*).

Furthermore, it acts as a condition for the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) by way of being co-nascent (*sahajāta*), mutual (*aññamañña*), support (*nissaya*), associated (*sampayutta*), present (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*);

and at the time when desire is predominant, it also acts as a predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*). That same [desire] acts as a condition for the second [factor] by way of proximity (*anantara*), immediate-proximity (*samanantara*), contiguity-support (*anantarūpanissaya*), repetition (*āsevana*), absence (*natthi*), and disappearance (*vigata*).
It is a condition. In this same manner, the application [of the analysis] should also be made for attention (*manasikāra*).
However, here "attention" refers specifically to the occasional attention characterized by recollection; it does not possess the status of a dominant condition (*adhipatipaccayatā*).
It should be understood that among the associated states, only these two are mentioned because they are powerful conditions. "By way of the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*)"—
By means of the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*), which has reached the state of a faculty through the growth of its cultivation.
"Establishment in unity" (*ekattupaṭṭhāna*) means that by way of remaining immovably upon a single object, it becomes a powerful basis for the successive arising of the faculty of faith.
Just as it was explained for the faculty of faith, so too should the remaining faculties be understood. Thus, for each individual faculty, there are four [conditions].
Regarding "arising": there are twenty arisings of the five faculties. Furthermore, by joining five faculties to each of the four arisings, twenty arisings are stated.
They say that the first twenty should be understood according to various paths, while the second twenty should be understood according to a single path. Thus...
There are forty modes. The "descent of the goal" (atthaṅgama) should also be understood by this same method. That descent of the goal, however, is:
the descent as non-attainment for one not devoted to the development of the faculties; the descent as loss of what was attained for one who has fallen away from the development of the faculties;
and the descent as subsiding for one who has reached the fruit. As for "the non-manifestation of unity":
Non-appearance in solitude.
189. Commentary on the Description of Gratification:
Regarding the phrase "non-appearance of lack of faith" in the description of gratification, it refers to one who avoids persons lacking faith and [approaches] those possessing faith...
For one who associates with such persons, who reviews the discourses that inspire confidence, and who repeatedly applies wise attention to them, lack of faith does not arise.
Regarding the phrase "the non-arising of the fever of lack of faith":
here, when a talk on faith is being delivered to one who lacks faith, suffering and mental distress arise; this is the "fever of lack of faith."

"Confidence in the practice of resolution" means that for one who has attained mastery through either the basis of faith or through meditation, there is a state of fearlessness in the operation of faith.
"The attainment of a peaceful abiding" refers to the acquisition of either serenity (*samatha*) or insight (*vipassanā*).
Regarding "bliss and joy," the term "joy" (*somanassa*) is used here in order to show that it is mental bliss.
Physical pleasure is indeed obtained by one whose body is touched by the refined matter produced by the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*).
Because pleasure and joy are the primary gratification (*assāda*), it is stated specifically that "this is the gratification of the faculty of faith.
By this same method, the gratifications of the remaining faculties should also be understood by applying the same principle.
Kha. Commentary on the Exposition of Disadvantages (Ādīnavaniddesa) 190.

Regarding the phrase "in the sense of impermanence" in the exposition of disadvantages: it means in the sense of the impermanence of the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*). What is meant is that this state of impermanence is the disadvantage of the faculty of faith.
The same method applies to the other two as well. These are the meaning of origin, the meaning of passing away, the gratification, and the disadvantage.
It should be understood that these refer specifically to the mundane faculties (*lokiya-indriyānaṃ*). Commentary on the Exposition of Escape (Nissaraṇaniddesa-vaṇṇanā) 191:
In the exposition of escape, regarding the phrases "in the sense of resolution" (*adhimokkhaṭṭhena*) and so forth, five [aspects] are to be applied to each individual faculty.
Twenty-five modes of emergence for the five faculties have been demonstrated by way of the paths and fruits.

Therein, "the acquisition of a more excellent faculty of faith" means by way of the acquisition of a faculty of faith that is more excellent at the moment of the path than the faculty of faith that was active at the moment of insight. [It is] from the previously mentioned faculty of faith...
"It has escaped" means that at the moment of the path, the faculty of faith has emerged from the faculty of faith that occurred during the preceding stage of insight (vipassanā).
In this same manner, the faculty of faith at the moment of the fruit should be applied in both cases, as should the remaining faculties. 192.
"By the five faculties in the prior stage" refers to the five faculties in the access to the first jhāna, by way of the eight attainments beginning with the first jhāna.
There are eight modes of escape; eighteen modes of escape by way of the eighteen great insights beginning with the contemplation of impermanence;

and eight supramundane modes of escape by way of the path of stream-entry and so forth. Thus, thirty-four modes of escape have been demonstrated according to the jhāna attainments, the great insights, the paths, and the fruits, through the successive surmounting of each preceding state.
[The passage continues with] "In renunciation, the five faculties," and so on.
However, thirty-seven modes of escape have been demonstrated by way of their opposites through the abandoning of those opposites.

Among them, the seven modes of escape beginning with renunciation (*nekkhamma*) are stated by way of the access stages (*upacāra-bhūmi*); however, their fruits (*phala*) are not stated because there is no abandoning of opposites in the case of the fruits.
193. "By those associated with views" (*diṭṭhekaṭṭhehi*): because they abide together with wrong view in a single person up to the path of stream-entry, they are called "associated with views.

"By those associated with views" means by those [defilements]. "By the gross" (*oḷārikehi*) means by the coarse sensual lust and ill will. "By those that have become subtle" (*aṇusahagatehi*) means by the very same sensual lust and ill will when they have become subtle.
"By all defilements" (*sabbakilesehi*) refers to sensual lust for the form realm and so forth; for when those [specific ones] are abandoned, all defilements are [abandoned].
They have been abandoned; therefore, it is said, "from all defilements. Furthermore, the words whose meaning has not been stated here are exactly as their meanings were explained below.

For all those whose taints are destroyed, the five faculties exist in various places—in those aforementioned instances such as "in the sense of resolution" and so forth—the five faculties [exist] for Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples in each respective place.

For those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), these [states] have escaped from this or that [defilement] accordingly. In this section, they are stated according to the method previously explained, specifically by way of those whose taints are destroyed.
But how do these modes of escape (*nissaraṇa*) become one hundred and eighty? It is said: they are stated by way of the paths and fruits.
There are twenty-five [deliverances] stated by way of transcending; thirty-four stated by way of the opposites; and thirty-seven stated by way of the antidotes.

Thus, in the first section, there are ninety-six deliverances in total. These same ones, when twelve are removed in the second section by way of those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), amount to eighty-four. Thus, the previous ninety-six and these eighty-four—
There are one hundred and eighty. Which, then, are the twelve to be excluded for those whose taints are destroyed?
Among those stated by way of transcendence, the eight deliverances stated by way of the paths and fruits;
and among those stated by way of opposites, the four stated by way of the paths—these twelve are to be excluded. Why are those stated by way of the fruit of arahantship to be excluded?

Why? Because among the twenty-five modes of escape mentioned first, they are obtained only by way of the paths and fruits. Thus, the modes of escape are stated only by way of the fruit of Arahantship.

However, since those in higher and higher fruition-attainments do not enter the lower and lower fruition-attainments, the three lower fruits are not obtained at all below that point. [This applies to] jhāna-attainments, insight, renunciation, and so forth.
And these are obtained by way of functional activity (*kiriyā*). Furthermore, because their opposites have already been subsided, even these five faculties are indeed escaped from their opposites.
The commentary on the exposition of the second sutta is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Exposition of the Third Discourse 194.
Having set aside another discourse, desiring to explain the classification of the faculties (*indriya-vidhāna*), he said: "Bhikkhus, these five... and so forth.

Therein, regarding the phrase "in the factors of stream-entry" (*sotāpatti-aṅgesu*): here, the "stream" (*sota*) is the Noble Eightfold Path; the "entry into the stream" (*sotassa āpatti*) is the thorough [attainment].

Attainment is stream-entry (*sotāpatti*); the factors and requisites for stream-entry are the "factors of stream-entry" (*sotāpatti-aṅgāni*). These are the factors for the acquisition of the preliminary stage leading to the state of a stream-enterer.
Associating with noble persons is a factor of stream-entry; hearing the true Dhamma is a factor of stream-entry; appropriate attention is a factor of stream-entry;
practice in accordance with the Dhamma is a factor of stream-entry—these are the four.

The factors of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-aṅga*). The remaining ones have already been explained above. And this has been stated for the purpose of showing the preeminence of these faculties within their own respective domains.

For example, when four sons of wealthy merchants, together with a king’s son as the fifth, descend to the street thinking, "We shall enjoy the festival," at the time when they have gone to the house of one of the sons of the wealthy merchants, the other four sit in silence.
Just as a master of the house manages the household, saying, "Give hard food and soft food to these;

give perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and so forth to these," when the second, third, and fourth have gone to the house, the other four sit in silence, while the master of the house himself says, "Give hard food and soft food to these; give perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and so forth to these."
Just as one manages affairs within a household, and then, at the very last, when the king has gone to his own palace— even though the king is the master everywhere—
yet at that time he manages affairs only within his own palace, saying, "Give hard food and soft food to these people; give perfumes, garlands, ornaments,
and so forth to these people," even so it is with the faculties, of which faith is the fifth.
Just as when those friends enter the street together, even though they arise with a single object,
the other four remain silent in the house while the master of the house alone deliberates; so too, having reached the factors of stream-entry,
the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*), characterized by resolution, becomes the eldest and the forerunner, while the others follow in its wake.

They are as follows. Just as in the second man’s house the other four sit in silence while the master of the house alone deliberates, so too, having reached the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*), the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*)—characterized by exertion—is the chief and the forerunner, while the remaining [faculties] follow in its wake.
Just as in the third man’s house the other four sit in silence while the master of the house alone...
When one reflects thus, having reached the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), the faculty of mindfulness (*satindriya*) alone—characterized by establishing—is the chief and the precursor;

the others follow in its wake. Just as in the fourth house the other four sit in silence while the master of the house alone reflects, so too, having reached the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*) alone—characterized by non-distraction—is the chief.
The eldest is the leader, and the others follow in its wake. But when they have all finally reached the king’s palace,
just as the other four sit in silence while the king alone deliberates, so too, once the Noble Truths have been reached, the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya)—
characterized by understanding— is the eldest and the leader, while the others follow in its wake.

Ka. Commentary on the Exposition of the Enumeration of Categories (Pabhedagaṇananiddesavaṇṇanā) 195. Regarding the exposition of the enumeration of categories preceded by the inquiry into the enumeration of categories of the Sutta:

"In association with good persons" (sappurisasaṃsevā) means in the proper service of excellent persons. "In the sense of having resolution as the dominant factor" (adhimokkhādhipateyyaṭṭhena) means by way of that which is termed resolution.
The meaning is: in the sense of being predominant among the remaining faculties, and in the sense of being the precursor to the remaining faculties.

Regarding "listening to the true Dhamma" (*saddhammasavana*): the Dhamma of the noble ones (*sata*), or the beautiful Dhamma, is the "true Dhamma" (*saddhamma*); it is in the listening to that true Dhamma. Regarding "appropriate attention" (*yonisomanasikāra*):
it is attention by means of the proper method. Regarding "practice in accordance with the Dhamma" (*dhammānudhammapaṭipatti*): here, it follows the nine supramundane states (*lokuttaradhamma*).
"Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma; "dhammānudhamma" refers to the practice and undertaking of the Dhamma-in-accordance-with-Dhamma, which is comprised of virtue, concentration, and wisdom.
This same method applies to the right efforts and so forth as well.
(Section on Conduct: Explanation)
196. In the section on conduct (*cariyāvāra*) as well, the meaning should be understood according to this same method.

The only difference is that the first section was stated by way of the time of the arising of the faculties, whereas the section on conduct was stated by way of the time of the cultivation of those [faculties] once arisen and by way of the time of their fulfillment.
For "conduct" (*cariyā*), "nature" (*pakati*), and "predominance" (*ussanna*) are one and the same in meaning.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Modes of Conduct and Abiding (Cāravihāra-niddesa-vaṇṇanā) 197.

Now, desiring to demonstrate the classification of the faculties by means of another method—the exposition of the modes of conduct and abiding—in connection with the [preceding] discussion of conduct, he first sets forth the summary beginning with "Conduct and abiding," and then provides its detailed explanation. Therein:

First, regarding the summary: the connection of the summary should be understood as follows—that the wise fellow-celibates, observing his conduct and behavior, would have confidence in him regarding profound matters, thinking, "Surely this venerable one has attained [the goal] or will attain it";
thus, the conduct and behavior of one endowed with the faculties are understood and penetrated by wise fellow-celibates.
In the exposition of the summary (uddesaniddesa), "conduct" (*cariyā*) is simply "course" (*cāra*). For "course" and "conduct" are one in meaning.
Therefore, in the exposition of the term "course," it is stated as "conduct. "Conduct of the postures" (*iriyāpathacariyā*) means the conduct, that is, the proceeding, of the postures.
The same method applies to the remaining [terms]. However, "conduct of the sense bases" (*āyatanacariyā*) is the conduct of mindfulness and clear comprehension regarding the sense bases.

“*Patti*” means fruits; for since they are reached (*pāpuṇiyanti*), they are called “*patti*. Worldly aims (*lokattha*) are the benefits pertaining to this life and the life to come for the world of sentient beings; this is the distinction.
Now, showing the ground (*bhūmi*) for those types of conduct, he said: “in the four postures,” and so forth. “In the foundations of mindfulness” (*satipaṭṭhānesu*).

Regarding the foundations of mindfulness as objects: even when the foundations of mindfulness themselves are being discussed, they are spoken of as if they were distinct from mindfulness by way of conventional designation (*vohāra*).

"In the noble truths" is said by way of the individual discernment of each truth through mundane knowledge prior to the path. "In the noble paths and fruits" is also said merely by way of conventional designation.

"Partially" (*padesa*) means in one part of the conduct for the welfare of the world (*lokatthacariyā*). For it is only Buddhas who practice the conduct for the welfare of the world in its entirety (*nippadesato*).
Again, showing those very same conducts by way of the individuals who perform them, he says "those endowed with aspiration" (*paṇidhisampannānaṃ*), and so forth.
In that context, "endowed with aspiration" means they are perfected in the guarding of their postures because of the composure of their postures; they possess unshakable postures.
They are endowed with a peaceful deportment befitting the state of a bhikkhu. Regarding the phrase "guardians of the doors of the sense faculties" (*indriyesu guttadvārānaṃ*):

among the six sense faculties, such as the eye and so forth, each faculty functions toward its own respective object; because they have thus guarded their individual doors, they are called "guardians of the doors.
Of these guardians of the doors: here, "doors" refers specifically to the eye and the other faculties by way of being the doors for the arising [of consciousness].
"To those who dwell in diligence" means to those whose practice consists in dwelling with diligence regarding virtue and the other perfections.
"To those devoted to higher consciousness" means to those devoted to concentration, which is termed "higher consciousness" because it serves as the foundation for insight (vipassanā).

"To those endowed with wisdom" means to those endowed with the knowledge that proceeds from the discernment of name-and-form up to the stage of the lineage (gotrabhu). "To those who have entered upon the right path" means...
"At the moment of the four paths" means at the moment of attaining the four fruits.
"Resolving" means performing resolution (*adhimokkha*). "Proceeding by means of faith" means occurring through the influence of faith.
"Exerting" means striving with the energy of the four right efforts (*sammappadhāna*). "Establishing" means establishing the object of focus through mindfulness (*sati*).
"Practicing non-distraction" means not being distracted by way of concentration (*samādhi*). "Understanding" means knowing clearly through the wisdom that understands the Four Noble Truths.
"Discerning" means discerning the object by means of the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana-viññāṇa*) which precedes the impulsion (*javana*) associated with the sense faculties.
"By the movement of consciousness" means by way of the movement of the adverting consciousness. "For one who has thus practiced" means...

"For one practicing the conduct of the faculties for the sake of the co-nascent forest": "wholesome states bring about [their own] arrival" means that wholesome states proceeding by way of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) bring about an intense arrival; the meaning is that they proceed.
"By the conduct of the bases" means by the intense conduct of basing, the conduct of exerting, and the conduct of proceeding of wholesome states; this is what is meant.
"He attains distinction" means he attains distinction by way of suppression, its constituent factor, eradication, and subsidence.
The terms "practice of seeing" (*dassanacariyā*) and so forth have already been explained.

In passages such as "he dwells with faith," one should understand it as the dwelling in the postures (*iriyāpatha*) of one who possesses faith and the other [faculties]. "One who has awakened after" (*anubuddha*)...
"By means of inferential cognition" (*anumānabuddhiyā*). "Penetrated" (*paṭividdha*) means by means of direct perceptual cognition (*paccakkhabuddhiyā*).

Since when the states of resolution (*adhimokkha*) and so forth have been understood (*anubuddha*) and penetrated (*paṭividdha*), their range (*cāra*) and abiding (*vihāra*) are also understood and penetrated, therefore both the understanding and penetration of the states of resolution and so forth have been demonstrated.
In the passage beginning "Thus practicing with faith," the word *evaṃ* indicates the aforementioned manner, thereby explaining the meaning of the term *yathā*.
Regarding the words *viññū* and so forth: they are called *viññū* (wise) because they know according to the true nature (*yathāsabhāvaṃ*) of things.

They are called *vibhāvī* because they make manifest—that is, they clarify—the known true nature. It is called *medhā* because it crushes or destroys defilements like a thunderbolt striking a mountain; [it is also] swift...

Alternatively, *medhā* is so called in the sense of grasping and retaining; those who possess this *medhā* are *medhāvī*. They are *paṇḍitā* because they move, proceed, and function by way of knowledge (*ñāṇagati*).
They are *buddhisampannā* because they are endowed with the perfection of intelligence (*buddhi*).

They are *sabrahmacārino* because they practice together with the supreme path of conduct that leads to the Brahmā (the Noble Ones). The fourfold formal act (*kamma*) consists of the act of obtaining permission (*apalokanakamma*), and so forth.

An action is "one" by virtue of being performed as a single unit. Likewise, the fivefold recitation of the Pātimokkha is a "single recitation. Those who possess the same training are "those of equal training" (*samasikkhā*);
the state of being those of equal training is "equality of training" (*samasikkhatā*). They also read it as *samasikkhātā*.
Those for whom there is one action, one recitation, and equality of training—these are called "fellow practitioners of the holy life" (*sabrahmacārī*). "Meditative absorptions" (*jhānāni*)...
In the phrase "jhānā," a change of gender has been made. "Vimokkhā" refers to either the three or the eight liberations.

"Samādhī" refers to the three concentrations: with applied thought and sustained thought, without applied thought and with sustained thought only, and without applied thought and without sustained thought. "Samāpattiyo" refers to the emptiness, signless, and wishless attainments.
"Abhiññāyo" refers to the six direct knowledges.
"One-sided" (*ekaṃsa*) means a single part or portion, not a second; the statement of such a one-sided matter is "one-sided speech" (*ekaṃsavacana*).
The same method of application should be made for the remaining terms as well. Specifically, however: it lies or proceeds equally or all around, thus it is "doubt" (*saṃsayo*);
there is no doubt here, thus it is "without doubt" (*nissaṃsayo*). Having been indecisive regarding one thing alone, one then wavers regarding the other as well.

Doubt (*kaṅkhā*); one for whom there is no doubt here is "free from doubt" (*nikaṅkho*). Duality of being is "divisiveness" (*dvejjha*); one for whom there is no divisiveness here is "undivided" (*advejjho*).
It causes one to waver or tremble in two ways, thus it is "wavering" (*dveḷhaka*); one for whom there is no wavering here is "unwavering" (*adveḷhako*).
A statement made with necessity and certainty is a "definitive statement" (*niyogavacana*). They also read it as *niyyogavacana*. Of that which is infallible and uncontradicted...
The speech concerning a matter that leads to liberation is "unerring speech" (*apaṇṇaka-vacana*). "Decisive speech" (*avatthāpana-vacana*) means speech of certainty.
For all of this is a synonym for the absence of doubt. It is "affectionate speech" (*piya-vacana*) because it speaks of a matter that is dear;
thus, it is indeed affectionate. Likewise for "respectful speech. Together with reverence—that is, with a sense of respect—it is "reverential" (*sagārava*). "Reliance" (*patissayana*)...
*Patissayo* means relying on another after making them one's teacher; the meaning is "not looking for support elsewhere.

Alternatively, *patissavo* is derived from *patissavana*, meaning the hearing of another’s words due to living in a humble manner. In both cases, this is a name for the state of regarding another as superior.
*Sagāravaṃ* means "conducting oneself with reverence. *Sappatissayaṃ* means conducting oneself with reliance (*patissaya*) or with hearing (*patissava*).
Or, where it should have been said “*sappatissavan*,” the *ya*-sound or the *va*-sound has been elided, and thus it is stated as “*sappatissan*.

An elevated or distinguished expression is an “*adhivacana*” (designation). That which is both respectful (*sagārava*) and deferential (*sappatissa*) is “respectful-deferential” (*sagāravasappatissa*).
The term “respectful-deferential designation” (*sagāravasappatissādhivacana*) [is used] because of the variety of synonymous alternatives in both instances.
"It is said: 'Again and again this' refers specifically to the jhānas and so forth, whether they have been attained or will be attained.
The commentary on the exposition of the third discourse is concluded.
4. Commentary on the Exposition of the Fourth Discourse.
198. Having again set aside the very first sutta, he demonstrates the faculties (indriya) by another method.
Therein, "In how many ways and in what sense are they to be regarded? means: in how many ways are they to be regarded?
By asking "in what sense are they to be regarded," he asks both regarding the manner of being regarded and the meaning of being regarded. "In six ways, they are to be regarded in that sense."
They are to be seen in six aspects; thus they are to be seen in the sense of being designated by those six aspects.

"In the sense of predominance" means in the sense of being a dominant factor (*adhipati*). "In the sense of purifying the beginning" means in the sense of purifying virtue (*sīla*), which is the beginning of wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*).
"In the sense of abundance" means in the sense of strength. For that which has an abundant measure (*mattā*) or quantity (*pamāṇa*) is strong.

"Adhimatta" is said [to mean] "predominance. In the sense of a foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*) means in the sense of a support (*patiṭṭhāna*). In the sense of exhaustion (*pariyādāna*) means in the sense of wearing away (*khepana*).
In the sense of one who establishes (*patiṭṭhāpaka*) means in the sense of establishing (*patiṭṭhāpana*). [End of] the commentary on the exposition of the sense of predominance (*ādhipateyya*).

199. In the exposition of the sense of predominance (*ādhipateyya*), the statement "abandoning lack of faith," and so forth, is a description of the abandonment of the respective opposites for each individual faculty.
It is stated for the purpose of establishing the state of predominance in accomplishing its own specific task of abandoning its opposite, even within a single moment.
The remaining four faculties are mentioned as being associated with that [faith]. Alternatively, they may be taken one by one across different moments.

It should also be understood that it is stated [in some instances] by making a particular faculty the leader—that is, making that specific faculty the most preeminent as the antidote to its respective opposite—and making the remaining faculties subordinate to it.
However, the passage beginning with "Abandoning sensual desire" (*kāmacchanda*) and so forth is stated by way of a single moment (*ekakkhaṇa*).
[End of] the commentary on the section describing the purification of the bases, such as the eye and so forth.
200. In the exposition of the state of purification of the beginning (*ādivisodhanaṭṭha*):

"Purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*) in the sense of restraint from lack of faith" means that it is called purification of virtue because it purifies the stains of virtue by way of abstention, which has the sense of warding off lack of faith.

"Purification of the beginning of the faculty of faith" means the purification of virtue, which is the beginning of the faculty of faith by way of its decisive support (*upanissaya*). By this very [statement]...
By this method, the remaining faculties, which are rooted in the restraint of sensual desire and so forth, should also be understood.
201. Commentary on the Description of the Sense of Excess:
Regarding the statement, "In one who possesses faith, zeal arises for the cultivation of the faculty of faith," it refers to the faithful person.

Having heard a Dhamma discourse connected with faith, or having seen the benefit in the development of the faculty of faith, a desire for the Dhamma (*dhammacchanda*) arises in one skilled in the faculty of faith.
"Joy arises" means that because desire has been generated, a weak form of rapture (*pīti*) arises.
"Rapture arises" means that because of being gladdened, a powerful form of rapture arises. "Tranquility arises" means...
Through being gladdened by rapture (*pīti*), tranquility of body and mind arises. "Pleasure arises" means that because body and mind are tranquil, mental pleasure (*cetasika-sukha*) arises.
"An illumination arises" means that because one is suffused with pleasure, the illumination of knowledge (*ñāṇobhāsa*) arises.

"A sense of urgency arises" means that because the danger of conditioned phenomena has been understood through the illumination of knowledge, a sense of urgency regarding the occurrence of conditioned phenomena arises.
"It arises. "Having stirred the mind, he concentrates it" means that having produced a sense of urgency (*saṃvega*), he brings the mind to concentration by means of that very urgency.
"He exerts it well" means that, having freed it from the states of sluggishness and agitation, he exerts it properly.
"He looks on with equanimity well" refers to the application of the balance of energy once the energy has already begun to proceed evenly.
Not performing any active effort, one is said to "carefully look on with equanimity" by way of the equanimity of neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).
"By way of equanimity" means by way of the equanimity of neutrality, which has the characteristic of being even-handed.

"By various defilements" means by defilements of diverse natures that are the opposites of insight (*vipassanā*). "By way of liberation" means starting from the contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā*).
By way of liberation from various defilements (*nānattakilesa*). "Because of being liberated" means because they are liberated from various defilements.

"Those states" refers to the states beginning with desire (*chanda*). "They become of one flavor" means they become of one flavor by way of the flavor of liberation. "By way of development" means by way of development that results in a single flavor.
"They turn away toward what is more refined than that" means, for that reason, [they turn away] from the object of insight (*vipassanā-ārammaṇa*).

By means of the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*), which is known as the contemplation of turning away (*vivaṭṭanānupassanā*) and has the more sublime Nibbāna as its object, the states beginning with desire turn back;
the meaning is that they depart from having conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) as their object and proceed with Nibbāna as their object.
"By way of turning away" means by way of turning away from the object of conditioned phenomena at the moment of change-of-lineage. Because it has turned away...

"Then he relinquishes": because the person possessing the Path has turned away by means of the "emergence from both sides" at the very moment of the Path's arising, for that reason he relinquishes both the defilements and the aggregates. "Because they have been relinquished, they cease from there":
because the defilements and the aggregates have been relinquished at the very moment of the Path's arising, for that reason the defilements...
And the aggregates cease by way of non-arising and cessation. The word "vosajjitatta" (the state of being relinquished) is used in the sense of a past participle (*bhūtavacana*) to express certainty.
Furthermore, because the cessation of the aggregates necessarily occurs when there is the cessation of the defilements, the cessation of the aggregates is mentioned.

"By way of cessation" means by way of the cessation as previously described. Desiring to show two types of relinquishment at the very moment of the arising of that Path, [he speaks] by way of cessation.

He states, "Two kinds of relinquishment," and so forth. Both of these have already been explained in meaning below. In the passages beginning with "Desire arises for the abandoning of lack of faith," the meaning should be understood in detail according to this same method.
This same method applies to the sections rooted in the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*) and the others as well.
By this very method, the detailed exposition of the bases of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) should also be understood. However, here—
"He resolves" (*adhiṭṭhāti*) is the specific term; "he establishes" (*patiṭṭhāti*) is the meaning.
(Gha-ṅa) Commentary on the Exposition of the Sense of Consummation and the Sense of Establishing (202–203).
In the exposition of the sense of consummation, "consummates" (*pariyādiyati*) means he exhausts. In the exposition of the sense of establishing, [the one who is] faithful...

“He establishes the faculty of faith in resolution” means that one endowed with faith, resolving that “all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and non-self,” establishes the faculty of faith in resolution.

By this specific individual, the distinction in the development of the faculties is demonstrated. [The phrase] “In the case of one who has faith, it establishes the faculty of faith in resolution” [is explained as follows].
In a person endowed with faith, the faculty of faith establishes that very faith; likewise, resolving in such a way, it establishes one in resolution.
By this specific development of the faculties, the distinction between individuals is demonstrated.
Thus, exerting the mind, one establishes it in exertion; establishing mindfulness, one establishes it in its presence.

"Concentrating the mind, he establishes it in non-distraction; seeing [things] as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, he establishes it in vision"—this application should be understood for the remaining cases as well.
A "practitioner of yoga" (*yogāvacara*) is so called because he moves about (*avacarati*) in the yoga of serenity (*samatha*) or the yoga of insight (*vipassanā*).
He "moves about" means that having entered [into them], he practices.
The commentary on the exposition of the fourth sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Coordination of the Faculties (Indriyasamodhānavaṇṇanā) 204.
Now, desiring to show the coordination of the faculties for one who is developing concentration and for one who is developing insight:
First, in order to explain the various types of skill in establishing [the mind], he said, "An ordinary person develops concentration," and so forth.
Therein, "an ordinary person develops concentration" means developing concentration that partakes of penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).

However, for one in training (*sekkha*) and for one free from lust (*vītarāga*), supramundane (*lokuttara*) concentration is also obtained. "Because it has been adverted to" refers to the sign (*nimitta*) of the kasiṇa and so forth.
"Because of having brought it to mind" means that, having performed the preliminary work (*parikamma*) on the kasiṇa or other objects, one has produced the sign (*nimitta*) therein.

"Skilled in the appearance of the object" means skilled in the appearance of that very sign which has been produced. "Skilled in the appearance of the sign of calm" means [skilled] in the sign for the calming of the mind by way of the cultivation of the enlightenment factors of tranquility (*passaddhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*), when the mind has become agitated due to over-exerted energy and so forth.

Skilled in establishing [the mind]. "Skilled in establishing the sign of exertion" means being skilled in establishing the sign of mental exertion by means of the cultivation of the enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, and rapture, when the mind has become sluggish due to excessive laxity of energy and so forth.
"Skilled in establishing non-distraction" refers to the concentration associated with a mind that is neither agitated nor sluggish.

Skilled in establishing [the sign]. "Skilled in the establishment of the illumination" means that when the mind is devoid of interest due to weakness in the application of wisdom, one arouses a sense of urgency (*saṃvega*) by reflecting upon the eight bases of urgency, and thus becomes skilled in the establishment of the illumination of knowledge (*ñāṇobhāsa*). The eight bases of urgency are: the four consisting of birth, aging, sickness, and death;
the suffering of the states of deprivation as the fifth; the suffering rooted in the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) in the past; and the suffering rooted in the round of existence in the future.
Suffering in the present is suffering rooted in the search for nutriment.

One skilled in establishing gladdening is one who, when the mind is devoid of relish due to the non-attainment of the bliss of tranquility, becomes skilled in establishing gladdening by inspiring confidence in the mind through recollecting the virtues of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. One skilled in establishing equanimity is [one so skilled] when [the mind] is free from faults such as restlessness.
He is skilled in the establishment of equanimity by means of bringing about the absence of activity regarding the suppression, exertion, and so forth, of the mind.

A "learner" (*sekha*) is one who trains in the three trainings; thus he is a learner. He is "skilled in the establishment of unity" because, through the abandoning of personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and the rest, he is skilled in the establishment of unity such as renunciation and so forth.
"Free from lust" (*vītarāga*) means one who is free from lust because he has abandoned lust entirely; he is an Arahant whose taints (*āsava*) are destroyed.

"Skilled in the manifestation of knowledge" (*ñāṇūpaṭṭhānakusala*) means that, being devoid of delusion regarding phenomena, the Arahant is skilled in the manifestation of non-deluded knowledge in each respective instance.

"Skilled in the manifestation of liberation" (*vimuttūpaṭṭhānakusala*) means skilled in the manifestation of the liberation that is the fruit of Arahantship. For by "liberation," it is intended the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship, since it is liberated from all defilements.

205. Regarding the presence and non-presence [of signs] in the development of insight (*vipassanā-bhāvanā*), such as "impermanence" and so forth, and "permanence" and so forth, these should be understood in the same manner as explained in the discourse on virtue (*sīla-kathā*). According to the text, however:

"One skilled in the presence of accumulation, skilled in the presence of change, skilled in the presence of the signless (*animitta*), skilled in the non-presence of signs, skilled in the presence of the desireless (*appaṇihita*), and skilled in the non-presence of desire..."
In the phrase “skilled in the non-appearance of misapprehension,” the compound word should be analyzed using the genitive case (*sāmivacana*).
In the remaining cases, however, the reading uses the ablative case (*nissakkavacana*).

Furthermore, regarding the term “skilled in the appearance of emptiness” (*suññatūpaṭṭhānakusalo*), it should be understood either as “skilled in appearing as empty” (*suññato upaṭṭhānakusalo*) or “skilled in appearing through emptiness” (*suññatāya upaṭṭhānakusalo*).

Or rather, the word-division should be made thus: "Because these eight great insights—namely, contemplation of disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, relinquishment, higher wisdom, insight into phenomena, knowledge and vision of things as they truly are, reflective contemplation, and contemplation of turning away—are distinguished by their own specific intrinsic natures, not by their objects; therefore, of these eight, [as] 'as impermanent'..."
Statements such as "he is skilled in establishing [the mind]" do not apply to statements like "he is skilled in establishing through revulsion," and so forth.
Therefore, these eight [factors] have not been included here. However, the contemplation of danger is implicitly included by the meaning of the paired statement:
"He is skilled in establishing emptiness; he is skilled in not establishing misapprehension. Thus, [it is included] by way of danger.

“He is skilled in establishing [the mind], and he is skilled in not establishing through attachment and insistence”—this is already included [in the previous definition] and thus is not stated separately.
Thus, among the eighteen great insights (*mahāvipassanā*), one should understand that these nine—including the preceding eight and this contemplation of danger (*ādīnavānupassanā*)—are not combined;
rather, only the other nine are combined. One who is “skilled in the establishment of knowledge” is a trainee (*sekkha*).

Because of the absence of the defilements of insight (vipassanūpakkilesa), he is skilled in the manifestation of knowledge through the cultivation of insight; however, because of the presence of attachment to concentration (samādhi), he is not described as "skilled in the manifestation of knowledge" in the context of the cultivation of concentration. He is "skilled in the manifestation of disjunction":
that is, disjunction from the bond of sensual desire (kāmayoga), disjunction from the bond of existence (bhavayoga), and disjunction from the bond of views (diṭṭhiyoga).
He is skilled in the manifestation of the fourfold disjunction as it is stated: "the disjunction from the bond of ignorance.
He is skilled in the non-manifestation of the fourfold bond as it is stated by way of the bond of sensual desire, the bond of existence, the bond of views, and the bond of ignorance.
He is skilled in the manifestation of cessation as it is stated: "Furthermore, monks, for a monk whose taints are destroyed..."

"The mind is inclined toward Nibbāna, sloping toward Nibbāna, leaning toward Nibbāna; it is established in seclusion, delights in renunciation, and has completely become free from all things that are the basis for the taints.

By virtue of the power of one whose taints are exhausted—as stated above—because his mind is thus inclined toward Nibbāna, only one whose taints are exhausted is skilled in the manifestation of Nibbāna, which is termed cessation.

Regarding the phrase "by way of skill in the appearance of the object" and so forth: here, *kusala* means knowledge (*ñāṇa*). For knowledge is called *kusala* because it is associated with a person who is skilled (*kusala-puggala*), just as phenomena are called "wise" (*paṇḍita-dhammā*) because they are associated with a wise person. Therefore, the meaning is "by way of proficiency. 207.

Now, the passage beginning with "by sixty-four modes" and so forth, although already stated in the Discussion on Knowledge (*Ñāṇakathā*), has been brought here in connection with the Discussion on the Faculties (*Indriyakathā*). That should be understood according to the method explained below. 208.
Again, wishing to explain the classification of the faculties in connection with the Universal Eye (*Samantacakkhu*), [the author] says: "There is nothing here that has not been seen by him."
He says, "Something," and so forth. Therein, "all-seeing eye" refers to the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).

By the passage beginning with "by way of the faculty of wisdom," he shows the inseparability of the five faculties. Through the five tetrads rooted in each single faculty, beginning with "one who has faith exerts," he shows that at the time of the application of the inclinations toward the five faculties, or at the moment of the Path (*magga-khaṇa*), they possess a single flavor (*ekarasa-bhāva*).
And it demonstrates their state of mutual conditionality (*aññamaññapaccayabhāva*).

By means of the five tetrads beginning with "because of being believed in, it is exerted," which are rooted in each single faculty, it demonstrates that at the time of the production or at the time of the fruition of the five faculties, they possess a single flavor (*ekarasa*) and a state of mutual conditionality.
Furthermore, wishing to explain the classification of the faculties in connection with the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakkhu*), [the author says:]...

He said, "That which is called the Buddha-eye," and so forth. Therein, "the Buddha-eye" refers to the knowledge of the higher and lower degrees of the faculties (*indriya-paropariyatta-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of inclinations and latent tendencies (*āsaya-anusaya-ñāṇa*).
"Buddha-knowledge" is also these same two; the remainder has already had its meaning explained below.
The commentary on the combination of the faculties is finished.
The explanation of the Discourse on the Faculties in the *Saddhammappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, is completed. 5.
The Discourse on Liberation (*Vimokkhakathā*).
1. Commentary on the Exposition of the Liberations (Vimokkhuddesavaṇṇanā) 209.
Now, following the discussion on the faculties (indriya), the commentary on the previously unexplained portion of the discussion on the liberations (vimokkha) has arrived.
For this discussion on the liberations follows the discussion on the faculties because liberation exists for one who is devoted to the development of the faculties.
It was explained. And while explaining it, he did so by first presenting the discourse on the Sutta as heard in the presence of the Blessed One.
Regarding that, first of all, in the case of the "emptiness liberation" (*suññato vimokkho*) and so forth within the Sutta:

the Noble Path that proceeds by taking Nibbāna as its object in the mode of emptiness is the "emptiness liberation. For it is called "emptiness" because it has arisen from the element of emptiness (*suññatā-dhātu*).
