It is called "liberation" (*vimokkha*) because it is liberated from defilements (*kilesa*). In this same manner, it should be understood that when one proceeds by taking Nibbāna as the object in its signless aspect (*animitta-ākāra*), it is the "signless" liberation;
and when one proceeds by taking Nibbāna as the object in its desireless aspect (*appaṇihita-ākāra*), it is the "desireless" liberation.
For one person, from the very beginning, comprehends formations as impermanent. However, it is not by the mere comprehension of them as impermanent alone—
Emergence occurs from the path; it must indeed be comprehended both as suffering and as non-self, therefore he comprehends it both as suffering and as non-self.

For one practicing in this way, if emergence from the path occurs at the time of comprehending as impermanent, this is called "having resolved upon the impermanent, emerging by way of the impermanent. But if for him [it occurs] through suffering or non-self...
At the time of comprehension, there is emergence by way of the path; this is called "emerging after having resolved upon [the object] as impermanent, emerging as suffering, and emerging as non-self.
This same method applies to the emergences after having resolved upon it as suffering or as non-self.
And here, whether one has resolved upon it as impermanent, or as suffering, or as non-self—at the time of emergence, if the emergence is by way of impermanence—
If there is emergence through the pleasant, all three persons abound in resolve, acquire the faculty of faith,
are liberated by way of the signless liberation, are followers by faith at the moment of the first path, and are liberated by faith in seven instances. But if there is emergence through the painful,
all three persons abound in tranquility, [acquire] the faculty of concentration...
They attain [the fruit]; they are liberated by means of the wishless liberation; they become body-witnesses in every respect.
However, for one whose basis here is formless jhāna, he is "liberated in both ways" regarding the highest fruit.
Then, their emergence occurs by way of non-self; all three persons abound in feeling and attain the faculty of wisdom.
They are liberated by means of the emptiness liberation; at the moment of the first path, they are followers by Dhamma (dhammānusārino);
in six respects, they have attained vision (diṭṭhippattā); and at the fruit of the highest stage, they are liberated by wisdom (paññāvimuttā).
Furthermore, the "path" receives its name for five reasons: either from its own essence, or from its opposite, or from its qualities.
Either by its object, or by its approach. For if equanimity towards formations emerges after having comprehended formations as impermanent, one is liberated by the signless liberation.
If it emerges after having comprehended them as suffering, one is liberated by the desireless liberation.
If it emerges after having comprehended them as non-self, one is liberated by the void liberation. This is by way of its own nature.

It is called "name" (nāma). However, because it has arrived by means of the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) after effecting the resolution of the compactness of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) and abandoning the signs of permanence, stability, and eternity, it is "signless" (*animitta*).

Because it has arrived by means of the contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*) after abandoning the perception of pleasure and drying up aspiration and longing, it is "desireless" (*appaṇihita*).

Because it has arrived by means of the contemplation of non-self (*anattānupassanā*) after abandoning the perception of a self, a being, or a person, and [viewing] conditioned phenomena as empty (*suññato*), it is so named.
"Because it is seen as empty" is its name from the perspective of its opposite. However, "empty" (suññato) is because it is empty of lust and so forth;
"signless" (animitto) is because of the absence of the sign of form and so forth, or specifically the absence of the sign of lust and so forth;
and "wishless" (appaṇihito) is because of the absence of the wish for lust and so forth—this is its name according to its own qualities. This very Nibbāna is empty, signless, and wishless.
Because it takes as its object that which is empty, signless, and desireless, it is called "empty," "signless," and "desireless.
This is its name according to its object (*ārammaṇato*). As for its arrival (*āgamana*), it is twofold: arrival by way of insight (*vipassanā*) and arrival by way of the path (*magga*).

Among these, arrival by way of insight is found in the path, while arrival by way of the path is found in the fruit. For the contemplation of non-self is called "emptiness" (*suññatā*); thus, through emptiness-insight...
The path is emptiness; the fruit of the path of emptiness is emptiness. Contemplation of impermanence is called "signless"; the path of signless insight is the signless.
However, this name is not found in the Abhidhamma method; it is found in the Sutta method.
For therein, the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa), having made signless Nibbāna its object, is given the name "signless."
They say that after making the offering, one stands at the place where one must arrive oneself and gives the name to the path; therefore, the path is called "signless" (*animitta*).

It is indeed appropriate that the fruit is signless because it is reached by means of the path. The contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*) is called "desireless" (*appaṇihita*) because it arrives having dried up longing for conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*);
the path of desireless insight (*appaṇihitavipassanā*) is desireless, and [the fruit] of the desireless path...
"The fruit is the signless"—thus insight gives its own name to the path, and the path [gives its name] to the fruit;
this is what is called a "name by way of lineage" (*āgamanato nāma*). In this way, equanimity regarding formations determines the specific liberation.
Having thus pointed out the three liberations based on the great foundations as taught by the Blessed One, by means of their very exposition, others too...

Desiring to demonstrate the liberations (*vimokkha*), he said, "Furthermore, there are sixty-eight liberations," and so forth. In this context, "furthermore" (*api ca*) indicates another method of exposition.
How is it that they become sixty-eight? Is it not the case that they are seventy-five? True; according to the literal expression, they are seventy-five.
However, since the Blessed One, setting aside the three liberations taught by him, demonstrated other liberations, these [sixty-eight] are included within those.

And these three are not to be counted: the three liberations beginning with internal liberation (ajjhattavimokkha) are not to be counted because they are already included within the detailed exposition itself;

the "liberation that is directed" (paṇihito vimokkho) and the "liberation that is undirected" (appaṇihito vimokkho)—here, the liberation that is undirected is not to be counted because it shares the same name as the one previously mentioned. Thus, when these seven have been excluded...
The remaining sixty-eight are liberations. If this is so, why are the three beginning with the void liberation (suññatavimokkha) mentioned again?

It is for the purpose of providing a detailed exposition (niddesa) after having grouped them together in the summary (uddesa). Furthermore, the three beginning with emergence from the internal (ajjhattavuṭṭhāna) were mentioned according to their basic category without further sub-classification; however, the "wishless" (appaṇihita) is mentioned again by way of being the opposite of the "fixed" liberation (paṇihitavimokkha).
It should be understood that "the liberation has been taught.
Regarding the terms *ajjhattavuṭṭhāna* and so forth: it emerges from within, thus it is "emerging from within" (*ajjhattavuṭṭhāna*). They conform, thus they are "conformable" (*anuloma*).
The subsiding and disappearance of the emergences from within is "subsidence of the emergences from within" (*ajjhattavuṭṭhānapaṭippassaddhi*). "Possessing form" (*rūpī*)...
The material jhāna produced with respect to internal [objects] such as head-hairs is "matter" (*rūpa*); because he possesses that matter, he is "possessed of matter" (*rūpī*).

"He sees forms" means that he sees external forms, such as the blue *kasiṇa*, with the eye of jhāna. By this, the attainment of jhāna regarding the *kasiṇas* based on both internal and external objects is shown.
"Perceiving no matter internally" (*ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī*) means not perceiving matter internally; [not perceiving] one's own...

The meaning is: one who has not yet produced fine-material-sphere jhāna regarding [objects such as] hair and so forth. By this, it is shown that the jhāna is attained externally after having performed the preliminary work externally.
"Intent only on the beautiful" means intent upon the object precisely as "beautiful.

In that regard, although there is no mental application (*ābhoga*) of "beautiful" within the absorption itself, that which takes sentient beings as its object in an aspect that is not repulsive— [...]* (Note: The provided text fragment ends here)
He dwells shattering [the object]; because he is intent upon "the beautiful" alone, the summary is thus formulated.

It is a "temporary liberation" (samaya-vimokkha) because the liberation by suppression exists only at the very moment it is applied. That same [liberation] is called "occasional" (sāmayika) because it is restricted to the moment of application by virtue of performing its own specific function.
There is also a reading *sāmāyiko*. It is so called because it is capable of being disturbed or broken.
It is subject to change (*kuppa*). It is "worldly" (*lokika*) because it is connected to the world (*loka*) since it does not transcend it; *lokiya* is also a reading for this.

It is "supramundane" (*lokuttara*) because it transcends the world, or because it has already crossed over it. It is "with taints" (*sāsava*) because it is accompanied by taints (*āsava*) by way of being an object.

It is "without taints" (*anāsava*) because there are no taints here, either by way of being an object or by way of association. It is "with material sustenance" (*sāmisa*) because it is accompanied by material food (*āmisa*), which is designated as form (*rūpa*).
"More unworldly than even the unworldly" means that because of the total abandonment of both the material and the immaterial, it is more unworldly than the unworldly.
"Directed" means directed or longed for by way of craving. "Bound" means bound by the fetters through the act of making them an object.
"The liberation of unity" means a liberation of a single nature because it is not overrun by defilements. "Perception-liberation" refers to insight-knowledge itself.

It is "liberation by perception" (*saññā-vimokkha*) because of being liberated from perverted perception. That same knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) is "liberation by knowledge" (*ñāṇa-vimokkha*) in the sense of being liberated from delusion;

thus it is knowledge itself as liberation. "The liberation that may become cool" (*sītisiyā-vimokkha*) is the liberation that proceeds with the thought, "May this very knowledge of insight become cool.
There is also the reading *sītisikā-vimokkho*, which means "the liberation that causes coolness."

They explain its meaning as follows: "Jhāna-liberation" means that jhāna itself—distinguished by the divisions of access and absorption, and by the divisions of the mundane and the supramundane—is liberation.
"The mind’s liberation through non-clinging" means the liberation of the mind by not clinging, that is, by not making a grasping.
The rest should be understood according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the description of the liberations (*vimokkhuddesavaṇṇanā*) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of the Liberations (*Vimokkhaniddesavaṇṇanā*) 210.
Regarding the exposition of the summary beginning with "What is [the first liberation]?", the phrase "he reflects thus" means he investigates in this way: "This is empty."
This pentad of aggregates is empty. Empty of what? Empty of a self or of what belongs to a self (*attaniya*).

In this context, "of a self" means it is empty of that self imagined by foolish people, because such a self does not exist. "Of what belongs to a self" means it is empty of anything belonging to that imagined self.
Precisely because of the non-existence of a self, there is the non-existence of what belongs to a self.
That which is called "belonging to a self" (attaniya) would have to be either permanent or pleasant; neither of these two exists.

By the negation of permanence, the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) is expressed; by the negation of pleasure, the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā) is expressed. The statement, "This is empty of a self," expresses precisely the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā).
"He" refers to that bhikkhu who is thus practicing insight (vipassanā) through these three contemplations.
“He does not form an adherence” means that by way of the contemplation of non-self, he does not form an adherence to a self.
“He does not form a sign” means that by way of the contemplation of impermanence, he does not form a sign of permanence.
“He does not form an aspiration” means that by way of the contemplation of suffering, he does not form an aspiration. These three liberations occur, in a figurative sense, at the moment of insight.
They can also be obtained by way of their factors; however, in the direct sense, they are attained by way of complete eradication only at the moment of the path.
The four jhānas are the "internal emergence liberation" because they emerge internally from the hindrances and so forth.
The four formless attainments are the "external emergence liberation" because they emerge externally from their objects; for the object, too, is like an external sense-base.
Here, "externally" is what is stated. These two are liberations by suppression (*vikkhambhana-vimokkha*); however, liberation by eradication (*samuccheda-vimokkha*) is the emergence from both sides.

The internal emergence is stated explicitly through such phrases as "he emerges from the hindrances. Since the transcendence of the kasiṇa objects and so forth is evident through such phrases as "from the perception of form," that is not mentioned;
rather, it is the transcendence of the perception of form and so forth as taught in the Suttantas [that is intended].
...is said. "Sakkāyadiṭṭhi-vicikicchā-sīlabbataparāmāsa" is a compound word; the analysis is: "sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā, vicikicchāya, sīlabbataparāmāso.
Or this very reading [may be taken as such]. 211.
By the phrases beginning with "vitakko ca," the access stages of the jhānas and the attainments are stated. By the phrases beginning with "aniccānupassanā,"...
The insight preceding the four paths has been explained. "Acquisition" (*paṭilābha*) means that the acquisition is pervaded and extended by the attainment of the fivefold mastery;
for when mastery is attained, all application toward the jhānas and all application toward the attainments (*samāpatti*) become tranquilized.
Therefore, this acquisition is called the "liberation through tranquilization" (*paṭippassaddhivimokkha*). It is a result (*vipāka*).
However, it is direct that there is a subsiding of both the jhāna and the attainment. Some, however, say:

"Because of the subsiding of the preparatory effort, there is the acquisition of the jhāna and the attainment; therefore, the acquisition of the jhāna and attainment is called 'liberation through subsiding' (paṭippassaddhivimokkha)."
212. *Ajjhattaṃ* means occurring with reference to oneself (*attānaṃ*). *Paccattaṃ* means occurring in dependence upon oneself.
By both terms, he illuminates precisely that which is one's own internal (*niyakajjhatta*). *Nīlanimittaṃ* means simply blue.
*Paṭilabhati nīlasaññaṃ* means he acquires the perception "this is blue" regarding that blue sign. *Suggahitaṃ karoti* means [he makes it well-grasped] on the preparatory stage (*parikammabhūmi*).
He makes it well-acquired. "He reflects upon what has been well-reflected upon" means that having made it well-reflected upon on the plane of access (upacāra-bhūmi), he reflects further.
"He establishes what has been well-established" means that he decides with certainty what has been well-decided on the plane of absorption (appanā-bhūmi).

There is also a reading: "he defines" (vavatthāpeti). For one performing the preliminary work (parikamma) on the internal blue [kasina], [one must avoid] the hair, the bile, or the pupil of the eye...
Or he does so. "An external blue sign" refers to any one of the blue kasiṇas, such as a blue flower, a blue cloth, or the blue element.
"Directs the mind" means he leads the mind [toward it]. The same method applies to yellow and the other colors as well.
"Cultivates" means he practices that very perception from the beginning. "Develops" means he increases it. "Practices repeatedly" means he does it again and again. "Form" refers to the blue sign.
"Form. "Perceiving form": perception of that form is "form-perception"; one who possesses that is "one perceiving form.
When performing yellow preparatory work internally upon the signs of yellow and so forth, one does it in the fat, or in the skin, or in the yellow parts of the eyes.
When performing red preparatory work, one does it in the flesh, or in the blood, or in the tongue, or on the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet.
Or he applies it to the red parts of the eyes. While performing the whitening treatment, he applies it to the bones, teeth, nails, or the white parts of the eyes.
"Internally formless" means that there is no sign of form internally.
"Accompanied by loving-kindness" means endowed with loving-kindness by way of the first, second, or third jhāna. "With the mind":
"With the mind": "One direction" is said by way of pervading the beings included in one direction, taking as a basis a single being first apprehended in one direction.
"Having pervaded" means having touched and made it the object. "Dwells" means he maintains the dwelling in the postures established upon the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
"Likewise the second" means just as he dwells having pervaded any one direction among the east and so forth, [he does the same for the others].
The meaning is: "in the same way, immediately after that, the second, the third, and the fourth.
Thus, by this very method, it is said that [he looks] "above," which means toward the upper direction. "Below" and "across"—the lower direction and the intermediate directions—are exactly the same.

In this context, "below" (*adho*) means downward; "across" (*tiriyam*) means the intermediate directions. In this manner, in all directions, like a horse's circle (*assamaṇḍalika*), he is like a horse.

“He directs his mind imbued with loving-kindness and he surveys it back and forth. Up to this point, the directed pervasion of loving-kindness has been shown by encompassing each direction individually.
However, the passage beginning with “in all places” is stated for the purpose of showing the non-directed pervasion.
Therein, “in all places” means everywhere. “In all respects” means among all the various categories of friends, enemies, neutrals, and so forth—whether inferior, middling, or superior.
“By means of selfhood” means not making a distinction such as “this is another being,” but rather by means of equality with oneself; this is what is meant.
Alternatively, “by means of all-selfhood” means by means of the entire state of consciousness, which is to say, without wavering even slightly outwardly.

“Possessing all” (*sabbāvanta*) means possessing all beings; the meaning is “associated with all beings. There is also a reading *sabbavanta*. “The world” (*loka*) refers to the world of beings (*sattaloka*).
Because of the demonstration of such modes of expression as "vast" (*vipula*) and so forth, the phrase "accompanied by loving-kindness" (*mettāsahagatena*) is stated here once again.

Alternatively, since neither the word "thus" (*tathā*) nor the word "in this way" (*iti*) is used here—as they were in the case of the specific pervasion—therefore it is stated again as "with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness.
Or else, this is stated by way of conclusion. Regarding the term "vast" (*vipula*) here:
Its vastness is to be understood by way of its pervasiveness. As for its being "exalted" (*mahaggata*), this is by way of its plane:

for it has attained greatness through its capacity to suppress the defilements, through its abundant fruit, and through its long duration; or else, it is "exalted" because it has been entered upon and practiced by those who are great, possessing sublime zeal, energy, mind, and wisdom.
It is "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*) by way of its proficiency and by way of having immeasurable beings as its object.

It is "free from enmity" (*avera*) through the abandoning of its adversary, ill will (*vyāpāda*). It is "free from affliction" (*abyāpajja*)—meaning it is without suffering—due to the abandoning of mental distress (*domanassa*).
"They appear without being repulsive" means they appear to the bhikkhu’s mind as things that are not repulsive.

The remaining cases should also be applied in the same manner according to the method already stated, by way of compassion (*karuṇā*), appreciative joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*). [In the case of compassion,] it is through the abandoning of its adversary, cruelty (*vihesā*).
It is "free from enmity" through the abandoning of the adversary that is aversion by means of sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
"Accompanied by equanimity" means being endowed with equanimity by way of the fourth jhāna. It is "free from enmity" through the abandoning of the adversary that is lust;

it is "free from ill-will" because of the abandoning of the joy based on worldly attachment. For all unwholesome states are [considered] such because of their connection with the fever of the defilements (*kilesa-pariḷāha*).
"Accompanied by ill will" (*sabyāpajja*)—this is the distinction between these two.
"In all ways" (*sabbaso*) means in every manner, or of all [perceptions], without remainder; this is the meaning.

"Of perceptions of form" (*rūpasaññānaṃ*) refers both to the fine-material-sphere jhānas—which are spoken of under the heading of "perception"—and to their objects. For even the fine-material-sphere jhāna is called "form."
In such passages as “one possessing form sees forms,” and “he sees external forms, beautiful or ugly,” it refers to the object.
Therefore, here “perception of form” (*rūpasaññā*) is a designation for the fine-material-sphere jhāna described by way of its perception;
that is, it is called “form-perception” because form is its perception, meaning that form is its name. Thus, [it refers] to the various types beginning with the earth-kasiṇa.
It should be understood that this is a designation for that which has those as its object. "By surmounting" means by way of fading away and cessation.

What is meant? In every respect, [there is the surmounting] of these fifteen perceptions of form—termed jhānas—which exist by way of wholesome, resultant, and functional states, and of these nine perceptions of form termed objects, which exist by way of the earth-kasiṇa and so forth.

Or, through the fading away and cessation of all [perceptions] without remainder, and by means of the cause for fading away and the cause for cessation, he enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
For it is not possible to enter and dwell in this without having completely transcended the perception of form.
Since these attainments are to be reached by the transcendence of the object, they are not [attained] in only one [moment].
Just as the first jhāna and the others [are defined] by their object. Furthermore, for one who is not dispassionate toward an object, there is no transcending of perception;
therefore, it should be understood that this commentary on the meaning has also been made by way of the transcending of the object.
"The subsiding of perceptions of resistance" means: through the resistance of the bases, such as the eye, and of the objects, such as visible forms.
"Arisen perceptions of resistance": this is a designation for perceptions of form (*rūpasaññā*) and so forth.

By the subsiding, abandoning, and non-arising—that is, by bringing about the non-occurrence—of all ten perceptions of resistance, namely the five wholesome-resultant and the five unwholesome-resultant ones; this is what is meant. Granted that these [perceptions] persist even for one who has attained the first jhāna and so on...
They do not exist, for at that time the mind does not proceed by way of the five doors; nevertheless, although they have been abandoned elsewhere,

these [fetters] are mentioned here by way of praise for this jhāna, in order to generate enthusiasm for it— just as with pleasure and pain in the fourth jhāna, or as with the view of a self-identity and so forth in the third path.

This is how it should be understood. Alternatively, although those [hindrances] do not exist for one who has attained the fine-material-sphere absorption, they do not exist there because they have been abandoned.
For the development of the fine-material sphere does not lead to dispassion toward the material; rather, their occurrence is dependent upon the material itself.
This development, however, leads to dispassion toward the material; therefore, it can be said that they are abandoned here.
It is appropriate. Not only is it appropriate to say so, but it is also appropriate to maintain this as an absolute certainty.
For it was precisely because those [hindrances] had not been abandoned prior to this that the Blessed One stated, "For one who has attained the first jhāna, sound is a thorn.
And here, it is precisely because they have been abandoned that the imperturbability (*āneñjatā*) and the peaceful liberation (*santavimokkhatā*) of the formless attainments are stated.
"Non-attention to perceptions of diversity" refers to perceptions that occur with respect to a diverse range of objects, or to diverse perceptions themselves.
This is because these [perceptions] occur with respect to a diverse range of objects— such as the distinctions of forms, sounds, and so forth—
and because they consist of the eight wholesome perceptions of the sense sphere, the twelve unwholesome perceptions, and the eleven wholesome-resultant perceptions of the sense sphere.
There are two types of unwholesome-resultant perceptions and eleven types of sense-sphere functional perceptions;
thus, these forty-four perceptions are diverse, of different natures, and mutually dissimilar. Therefore, they are called "diverse perceptions.
By not attending to, not directing the mind toward, and not generating in the mind all those diverse perceptions—since one does not direct the mind toward them—one [attains this state].
And because one does not produce them, does not attend to them, and does not review them—this is what is meant by "therefore.

Furthermore, since even in the existence produced by this jhāna the aforementioned perception of form and perception of resistance do not exist, let alone at the time of entering and abiding in this jhāna within that very existence, it is therefore said: "by surmounting them" and "by their disappearance."

In both cases, it is simply non-existence that is stated. Regarding the "perceptions of diversity," however, it should be understood that what is meant by "non-attention" to them is because these twenty-seven perceptions—namely, the eight wholesome perceptions of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), the nine functional (*kiriyā*) perceptions, and the ten unwholesome perceptions—exist in the existence produced by this jhāna;
therefore, there is no attention paid to them. For even therein, this jhāna...
While dwelling having attained [the base of infinite space], he dwells precisely by way of non-attention toward those [perceptions]. However, one who attends to them has not attained it.
And here, in brief, by the phrase “with the surmounting of perceptions of form,” the abandoning of all phenomena belonging to the fine-material sphere is stated.
By the phrase “with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity,” all...
It should be understood that the abandoning of the mind and mental factors of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and their non-attention have been stated.
Regarding the phrase "boundless space" (*ananto ākāso*): because it is a mere designation (*paññatti-matta*), neither its arising-limit nor its passing-away-limit is discerned; thus it is "boundless.
It is also "boundless" by way of its infinite pervasion; for that yogi does not pervade it by way of a single part, but rather by way of its entirety.
It pervades. "Space" refers to the space remaining after the removal of the kasiṇa. The base of infinite space and so forth have their meanings as already stated.

"Having attained and dwells" means that having reached and accomplished that state, one dwells in a posture corresponding to it. That very state is called "attainment" (samāpatti) because it is to be entered into.
"Having completely transcended the base of infinite space": according to the method explained previously, both the jhāna and its object are the "base of infinite space."
For the object as well—being infinite space—is called the "base of infinite space" (*ākāsānañcāyatana*) because it is the object of the first immaterial jhāna;
thus, in the sense of being a foundation, it is a base (*āyatana*), just as the gods' realm is a base for the gods.
Likewise, infinite space is so called because it is the cause of the arising of that jhāna, just as in such expressions as "Kamboja is the base of horses."
It is also called the "base of infinite space" (ākāsānañcāyatana) in the sense that it has arisen as a sphere (āyatana) like space.

Thus, because this base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) is to be entered upon and dwelt in only after having transcended both this jhāna and its object by means of non-occurrence and non-attention, therefore, combining both together, it is said: "having completely transcended the base of infinite space."

This should be understood as what was said. "Infinite consciousness" means that one attends to that very consciousness which has proceeded by pervading [space] with the thought "infinite space" as "infinite consciousness.
Or, it is infinite by virtue of the act of attention; for he, attending to that consciousness which has space as its object without exception, attends to it as infinite.

"Having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*). Here too, according to the method explained previously, both the jhāna and the object are the "base of infinite consciousness.

For the object, according to the method explained previously, is "infinite consciousness" (*viññāṇañca*) because it is the object of the second immaterial jhāna, and it is a "base" (*āyatana*) in the sense of being a support;
thus it is the "base of infinite consciousness. Likewise, [the jhāna] is infinite consciousness...

Because it is the cause for the arising of that very jhāna, it is also called a "base" (*āyatana*) in the sense of being the place of its arising; thus it is the "base of infinite consciousness" (*viññāṇañcāyatana*).

Since this base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) is to be entered and dwelt in only after one has transcended both this jhāna and its object by means of non-occurrence and non-attention, therefore both of these together— [The text continues: ...are combined into one.
It should be understood that this was said [in the sutta] as: "having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness.
"There is nothing" means "it is not, it is not," "empty, empty," "secluded, secluded"—this is what is meant by one who attends to it in such a way.
Regarding the phrase "having completely transcended the base of nothingness," here too, according to the method already explained, the jhāna itself is the base of nothingness.

The object as well. For the object too—namely, nothingness—is called the "base of nothingness" (ākiñcaññāyatana) because it is both nothingness and a base in the sense of being the foundation for the third immaterial jhāna, according to the method explained previously.
Likewise, it is also called the "base of nothingness" because that same nothingness is both nothingness and a base in the sense of being the source of origin for that very jhāna.
Since this base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is to be entered upon and dwelt in only after one has transcended both this jhāna and its object by means of non-occurrence and non-attention,
it should be understood that these two are combined together when it is said: "having completely transcended the base of nothingness."
The discussion on the cessation of perception and feeling has already been explained above.

The seven liberations, beginning with “one possessing form sees forms,” are called *vimokkha* (liberations) in the sense of being well-liberated from opposing states and in the sense of being well-released through delighting in the object;
however, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) [is so called] because of the mind and mental factors...

In the sense of being liberated, it is liberation (*vimokkha*). Because one is liberated at the time of attaining the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) but not liberated at the time of emerging from it, it is "liberation by occasion" (*samaya-vimokkha*).

Because they are absolutely liberated by way of liberation through eradication, the Noble Paths (*ariya-magga*) [are absolute liberation]; because they are absolutely liberated by way of liberation through subsiding, the fruits of recluseship (*sāmañña-phala*) [are absolute liberation];
and because it is absolutely liberated by way of liberation as escape, Nibbāna [is absolute liberation].
It is liberation not dependent on occasion (*asamayavimokkha*). Likewise, there are liberations that are occasional and those that are non-occasional.
It is "shakable" (*kuppa*) because one falls away from it through negligence; likewise, it is "unshakable" (*akuppa*) because one does not fall away from it.

It is "mundane" (*lokiya*) because it leads toward the world. It is "supramundane" (*lokuttara*) because the Noble Paths transcend the world, as do the fruits of recluseship and Nibbāna, which are beyond the world.
"Crossed over" means supramundane. Just as flies do not alight upon a glowing iron ball, the taints (*āsava*) do not cling to the supramundane Dhamma because it is intensely hot;
thus, it is "taintless" (*anāsava*). "Associated with the form realm" refers to the form-sphere jhānas. "Associated with the formless realm" refers to the formless attainments (*arūpasamāpatti*).
That which is clung to or directed by craving is "with desire" (*sapaṇihita*); that which is not clung to is "desireless" (*appaṇihita*). [This applies to] the paths and fruits.
It is the "liberation of unity" because it has a single object and a single goal; Nibbāna is the "liberation of unity" because it is without a second;
and it is the "liberation of diversity" because of the diversity of objects and the diversity of results.
214. *Siyā* means "it might be"; the meaning is that it "might be ten" and it "might be one. And as for "*siyā*":

This is a statement of a rule, not a statement of a question. "By way of the bases" means that there are ten [knowledges] by way of the ten bases, such as the perception of permanence and so forth. "By way of method" means that there is one [knowledge] by way of the method of liberation. Regarding "how could it be":
he asks how that which is prescribed as "it might be" (siyā) or "what might it be" (yaṃ vā siyā) could be. "Knowledge of the contemplation of impermanence" is a compound word.

Alternatively, the reading is *aniccānupassanāñāṇaṃ* (knowledge of the contemplation of impermanence); the same applies to the remaining [terms]. "By perception of permanence" means by perception occurring as permanence;
the meaning is "by perception occurring as 'permanent'. This method applies here too in the phrases "by perception of pleasure," "of self," and "of signs.
And "by a sign" means by the sign of permanence. "By perception of delight" means by perception occurring by way of delight.

“Of perception” means of perception associated with delight. This same method applies here as well in the phrases “from lust,” “from origination,” “from grasping,” “from longing,” and “from misapprehension, of perception.

For the three contemplations of destruction, fall, and change are specific types of contemplation of dissolution that serve as powerful conditions for strengthening the three contemplations of impermanence and so forth;
indeed, it is through the seeing of dissolution that the contemplation of impermanence [becomes firm].

It becomes powerful. When the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) has become powerful, the contemplations of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*) and non-self (*anattānupassanā*)—according to the principle that "what is impermanent is suffering, and what is suffering is non-self"—also become powerful.

Therefore, when the contemplation of impermanence and the others are mentioned, those three are also effectively mentioned. And because the contemplation of emptiness (*suññatānupassanā*) [arises] from the perception of adherence...

By the very statement “he is liberated,” it is already stated that he is liberated from perception through its attachment to the essential, its attachment to misapprehension, its attachment to the underlying tendency, and its attachment to bondage;
and by the mere absence of such attachments, it is already stated that he is liberated from perception without further deliberation.
Therefore, the five contemplations beginning with higher wisdom and insight into phenomena have not been mentioned.

They should be understood thus. In this way, among the eighteen great insights (*mahāvipassanā*), it should be understood that these eight contemplations (*anupassanā*) have not been mentioned; rather, only ten contemplations have been stated.

"Contemplation of impermanence as knowledge in accordance with reality" means that the contemplation of impermanence itself is knowledge in accordance with reality. Both terms are in the nominative case. "Knowledge in accordance with reality" expresses the meaning of "knowledge.
The same applies to the remaining [contemplations]. [The phrase] "from delusion, ignorance" [is explained as follows].
They are deluded and ignorant. "Is liberated" (*muccati*) is stated as having the meaning of liberation (*vimokkha*).

216. Regarding the phrase "the knowledge of the supreme state of coolness through the contemplation of impermanence": it is "supreme" (*anuttara*) in the sense of being unsurpassed because it exists only within this very Teaching (*sāsana*), or it is "supreme" because it is a condition for the unsurpassed [Nibbāna]. "Knowledge of the state of coolness" (*sītibhāvañāṇa*) means that the state of coolness itself is the knowledge.

That is the unsurpassed knowledge of coolness known as the contemplation of impermanence. In the passage, “Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with six qualities is capable of realizing the unsurpassed state of coolness,” the term “unsurpassed state of coolness” refers to Nibbāna;
however, here it refers to insight (vipassanā). [It is so called] because of the fever, burning, and distress of [viewing things] as permanent.
Regarding the phrase "he is liberated": here too, it is the very defilements that have arisen which are called "suffering" (*saṃtāpa*) in the sense of tormenting both in this world and the next;
they are called "fever" (*pariḷāha*) in the sense of burning; and they are called "distress" (*daratha*) in the sense of heat. 217.

*Jhāna* is so called because one meditates (*jhāyati*) on renunciation (*nekkhamma*), and so forth—the meanings of these terms have been explained below. Furthermore, in this context, renunciation and the others refer exclusively to the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) that partake of penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).
218. “Liberation of the mind through non-clinging (*anupādā cittassa vimokkho*)”: here, this refers specifically to insight (*vipassanā*).

However, in the passage, “This is the purpose of discussion, this is the purpose of consultation, namely, liberation of the mind through non-clinging,” it is Nibbāna that is the liberation of the mind through non-clinging.
“By how many clingings? means by how many types of clinging. “Which one clinging? means from which one type of clinging.
"From this one kind of clinging" means from one or another kind of clinging. "This" refers either to the preceding knowledge.
Regarding the liberations from clinging, because one first sees the arising and passing away of formations again and again, one contemplates with the contemplation of impermanence;
subsequently, seeing only the dissolution of formations, one contemplates with the contemplation of the signless. This is precisely a specific distinction of the contemplation of impermanence.
For this is the contemplation of the signless. Through the seeing of the arising and passing away of formations, and through the seeing of their dissolution, the absence of a self becomes manifest.
By that means, there comes about the abandoning of clinging to views and clinging to the doctrine of self.
And precisely through the abandoning of views, because the view that "the self is purified by rules and observances" is absent, there comes about the abandoning of clinging to rules and observances.

And because one sees the non-existence of a self directly through the contemplation of non-self, and because the contemplation of emptiness is indeed a specific mode of the contemplation of non-self, these four kinds of knowledge are liberated from the three types of clinging, beginning with clinging to views.

However, it is only the four [contemplations] beginning with the contemplation of suffering that are the direct opposites of craving, whereas the contemplations of impermanence and so forth— [Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated. The translation above reflects the complete logical structure of the preceding sentence.]
The liberation from the four kinds of clinging to sense-desires has not yet been stated.

This is because, first, for one who contemplates suffering by seeing "formations are suffering," and subsequently, for one who contemplates the wishless by seeing "formations are suffering," the aspiration for formations is abandoned.
For the contemplation of the wishless is indeed a specific mode of the contemplation of suffering. And because, regarding formations...
For one who becomes disenchanted through the contemplation of disenchantment and becomes dispassionate through the contemplation of dispassion, the aspiration for conditioned phenomena is abandoned;
therefore, these four knowledges are liberated from clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*).
Since one brings about the cessation of defilements through the contemplation of cessation and relinquishes defilements through the contemplation of relinquishment, therefore these two knowledges...

"They are liberated from the four kinds of clinging"—thus, by way of the diversity of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and the diversity of their modes (*ākāra*), sixty-eight liberations have been demonstrated.

Now, having shown the "gateways" (*mukha*) of the three liberations mentioned at the beginning, and desiring to show the specific faculties (*indriya-viśeṣa*) and the specific individuals (*puggala-viśeṣa*) preceded by those gateways to liberation, he said:
"There are, however, these three," and so forth. In this context, "gateways to liberation" means:
The gateways to the three liberations lead to the departure from the world; that is, they lead to the departure and emergence from the world of the three realms.
"By way of regarding all formations as limited and circumscribed" means by way of regarding all formations as limited and circumscribed through their arising and passing away.

The phrase "it is the departure from the world" (*lokaniyyānaṃ*) is a remainder of the text. For the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*), having delimited that conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) do not exist prior to their arising, and investigating their course, one sees that they do not go beyond their passing away; rather, they vanish right here.
Thus, it contemplates them as being circumscribed and limited. For all conditioned phenomena are delimited by the prior limit [of arising].

By age, it is delimited by the future limit. And by "the mind’s leaping forward into the signless element" (*animittāya dhātuyā cittasampakkhandanatāya*), there is an escape from the world through the inclination toward Nibbāna even at the moment of insight (*vipassanā*), because [phenomena] appear in the mode of the signless, and through the entry of the mind into the Nibbāna-element, which is termed "signless.
By "the stirring of the mind" (*manosamuttejanatāya*) means by the agitation of the mind. By the contemplation of suffering...
For the mind is indeed found within formations (*saṅkhāra*). And by the phrase "in the desireless element" (*appaṇihitāya dhātuyā*):

because at the moment of insight (*vipassanā*) it appears in the aspect of being desireless due to its inclination toward Nibbāna, it refers to the element of Nibbāna, which is designated as "desireless.

Regarding the term "all phenomena" (*sabbadhamma*): although Nibbāna is not included within the scope of insight, because the intrinsic nature of non-self (*anatta-sabhāva*) is present in it, the term "all phenomena" is used instead of saying "all formations."

It has been said. "By way of viewing as other" means: because it is dependent on conditions, being neither master nor subject to one's own will, one views it as non-self, thinking, "I am not, this is not mine. And "by way of the element of emptiness" means:

because even at the moment of insight (vipassanā) it appears in the mode of emptiness due to its inclination toward Nibbāna, it is by way of the element of Nibbāna, which is designated as emptiness. Thus...
These three statements are spoken by way of the contemplations of impermanence, suffering, and non-self. For that very reason, immediately following them, it is said:
"He brings it to mind as impermanent," and so forth. In this context, "as exhaustion" means as something that wastes away; "as terror" means as something fearful;
"as voidness" means as being devoid of self.

"Abounding in resolve" (*adhimokkhabahula*): For one who has practiced with faith through the contemplation of impermanence, thinking "formations break up by way of momentary dissolution," the mind becomes abundant in faith because of the direct perception of momentary dissolution, [thinking] "Truly, the Blessed One speaks the truth.
Alternatively, it refers to the impermanence of presently arisen partial formations.
Having seen this, by resolving that "all conditioned phenomena, past, future, and present, are thus impermanent," the mind becomes abundant in resolve (*adhimokkha*).

It is "abundant in tranquility" (*passaddhi-bahula*) because, through the abandonment of the aspiration for mental agitation caused by the contemplation of suffering, the mind becomes abundant in tranquility due to the absence of mental distress.
Alternatively, it is so called because the contemplation of suffering generates a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
For one who is stirred by a sense of urgency and strives with systematic application, the mind becomes abundant in tranquility due to the absence of distraction.

"Abundant in wisdom" means that for one who perceives the profound characteristic of non-self—which was not seen by outsiders—the mind becomes abundant in knowledge through the contemplation of non-self.
Alternatively, it refers to the mind of one who is joyful, thinking, "The characteristic of non-self, which has not been seen by the world including the devas, has now been seen."
The mind becomes abundant in contentment.

"One who is abundant in resolve acquires the faculty of faith" means that when resolve occurs abundantly during the preliminary stage, it becomes what is called the faculty of faith through the completion of its cultivation; he is said to acquire that. Abundant in tranquility...
“He acquires the faculty of concentration”: in the prior stage, for one who abounds in tranquility, because of the statement, “One whose body is tranquil feels happiness;
the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated,” the faculty of concentration arises through the condition of tranquility upon the fulfillment of cultivation;
that is what is meant by his “acquiring” it. “One who abounds in knowledge acquires the faculty of wisdom.”
In the preliminary stage, when knowledge (veda) is frequently occurring, it becomes what is called the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) for the sake of the fulfillment of development;
he is said to acquire that.
It is "dominant" (ādhipateyya) because, although desire and the other factors are also dominant, it is dominant by way of accomplishing its own specific function.
He becomes one who exerts himself. "For development" (*bhāvanāya*) is a locative expression, or it means for the sake of developing further and further.

"They follow that" means they are followers of that, they conform to that. "They are co-nascent conditions" means that, as they arise, they act as supportive factors by way of arising together, like a lamp for illumination.
"They are mutual conditions" means [they act] through the state of mutually producing and supporting one another.

They are supportive of one another like a tripod, providing mutual stabilization. They are related by way of dependence (*nissaya-paccaya*), meaning they are supportive through the modes of reliance and support, just as the earth and canvas are for trees and paintings respectively.

They are related by way of association (*sampayutta-paccaya*), meaning they are supportive through the state of association characterized by having a common basis (*ekavatthuka*), a common object (*ekārammaṇa*), a common arising (*ekuppāda*), and a common cessation (*ekanirodha*).
220. At the time of penetration (*paṭivedhakāla*), that is, at the moment of the Path (*maggakkhaṇa*) when the Truths are being penetrated, the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) is predominant.

This means that at the moment of the Path, having made Nibbāna its object, the faculty of wisdom alone is the chief by virtue of performing the function of seeing the Truths and the function of abandoning the defilements (*kilesa*).
"For the sake of penetration" (*paṭivedhāya*) means for the purpose of penetrating the Truths. "Of one flavor" (*ekarasa*)...
"By means of the flavor of liberation. "In the sense of seeing" means in the sense of seeing the truths.

The statement, "one who penetrates thus also develops [the path], and one who develops also penetrates," is said for the purpose of showing that at the moment of the path (*maggakkhaṇa*), both development and penetration exist simultaneously.

The word "also" (*api*) is employed in the phrase "even at the time of penetration" because even at the moment of insight (*vipassanākkhaṇa*), the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) alone holds sovereignty through the contemplation of non-self (*anattā*).

221. "When one attends to [the formations] as impermanent, which faculty becomes predominant? and so forth—this was stated in order to show the distinction between individuals based on the distinction of their faculties.

In this context, "predominant" (*adhimatta*) means superior. Therein, the predominance of the faculty of faith, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom should be understood through equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*). Although it is stated here without qualification as "one liberated by faith" (*saddhāvimutta*), [it refers to those who have reached that state].

Because it was stated above with specific qualification, excluding the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*), it is said that one is "liberated by faith" (*saddhāvimutta*) in the remaining seven instances.
One is "liberated by faith" due to the predominance of the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*);
it is also implied that one is not "liberated by faith" in every case merely because of the predominance of the faculty of faith. At the moment of the path of stream-entry, [the faculty of faith...]

They say that because of the predominance of faith alone, even when the faculties of concentration and wisdom are predominant among the remaining ones, he is still called "one liberated by faith" (saddhāvimutta).

He is a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhī) means that he is a body-witness in all eight instances. He is "one who has attained vision" (diṭṭhippatto) should be understood in the same manner as described for one liberated by faith.

"One who is liberated while believing" means "liberated through faith" (*saddhā-vimutta*); this is said because, due to the predominance of the faculty of faith, one is liberated at the moment of the fruit in all four stages while having believed at the moment of the stream-entry path.

He will now explain the state of being liberated through faith during the moments of the three higher paths. However, at the moment of the stream-entry path, one is a follower by faith (*saddhānusārī*). Subsequently...

He will say: "Because he has touched it, he has realized it, he is a body-witness (kāyasakkhī). When there is dry-insight (sukkha-vipassaka), because of having touched the contact of access-concentration (upacāra-jjhāna);
and when there is attainment of fine-material and immaterial jhānas, because of having touched the contact of fine-material and immaterial jhānas, he has realized Nibbāna—thus he is a body-witness.
What is meant is that he is a witness (sakkhī) to both the aforementioned types of jhāna-contact and to Nibbāna by means of the mental body (nāmakāya).

"Attained through vision" (*diṭṭhippatto*) means that because Nibbāna was first seen at the moment of the stream-entry path (*sotāpattimagga*) by means of the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) associated with it, one subsequently attains Nibbāna by way of the fruit of stream-entry and so forth;
thus, "one attained through vision" means one who has attained Nibbāna by means of the vision consisting of the faculty of wisdom. At the moment of the stream-entry path...
However, he will later explain the state of being a follower of the Dhamma (*dhammānusāritta*).

"One who is liberated while believing" means one liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutta*); because the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) is predominant, one is liberated while believing during the moments of the paths of once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship—thus, one is "liberated by faith.
Here, even while in the process of being liberated, one is called "liberated" by way of speaking of what has already occurred in anticipation. "The contact of jhāna" (*jhānaphassa*)...
The contact of jhāna is threefold. The terms “contact of jhāna” and so forth, as well as “suffering formations” and so forth, are stated by way of qualifying the two [terms] mentioned previously.
“It is known,” etc., have meanings already explained above.
And herein, a person who has attained jhāna, having emerged from the contemplation of suffering that is conducive to the faculty of concentration, [attains] the paths and fruits.
The intention of the teachers (*ācariya*) is that [one] "attains.
"Siyā" means "they might be," "they would be"—this is the sense. "Siyā" is precisely a term of injunction (*vidhi*).

"Three persons" refers to the three persons mentioned by way of the fixed sequence of insight (*vipassanā-niyama*) and the fixed sequence of faculties (*indriya-niyama*). "By way of the basis" means by way of the basis for each respective faculty among the three contemplations (*anupassanā*).
"By way of turn" means by that very method. What is shown by this section?

It shows that, while the predominance of each respective faculty was stated above according to the majority of cases for each individual contemplation, sometimes even when all three contemplations are present, the predominance belongs to only one faculty.
Alternatively, [it refers to] at the moment of preliminary insight (*pubbabhāga-vipassanā*).
Because all three contemplations (anupassanā) are present, one considers the predominance of the respective faculties within those preliminary stages of insight (pubbabhāga-vipassanā);
thus, at the moments of the path and fruit, the names "liberated by faith" (saddhā-vimutta) and so forth arise.

For when it is stated in this way, the determination of persons according to the predominance of faculties—both regarding the insight leading to emergence mentioned below and that which follows above—is established.
He becomes both well-composed and indeed motionless. In the subsequent section, "siyā" means "might be another," thus the sense is "it might be so.
Here, the restriction is exactly as stated previously.
Now, in order to show the distinction between individuals by way of the paths and fruits, [the text says]: "for one who attends to [the object] as impermanent... and so forth.

He says, “He attains the path of stream-entry,” and so forth. In that context, one who recollects and follows faith, or who recollects and follows Nibbāna by means of faith, is a *saddhānusārī* (faith-follower). “Realized” (*sacchikata*) means made manifest through direct experience (*paccakkhakata*).
“Arahatship” (*arahatta*) refers to the fruit of arahantship. One who recollects the Dhamma characterized as wisdom, or who [recollects] Nibbāna by means of that Dhamma—
"He recollects" means he is a follower of the Dhamma (*dhammānusārī*).
Furthermore, wishing to describe the distinction between individuals by way of the excellence of the three faculties through other methods, [the Blessed One] said, "Whoever...
and so forth. In that context, "have been developed" (*bhāvitā vā*) means they developed them in the past; "are developing" (*bhāventi vā*) means they are developing them in the present.
"Will come to be" means in the future. "Have attained," and so forth, is stated for the purpose of explaining the meaning of each preceding term individually.

"Have touched" means they have touched by means of the contact of knowledge (*ñāṇa*). "Have reached mastery" means they have reached the state of sovereignty (*issarabhāva*). "Have reached perfection" means they have reached the state of completion (*vosāna*).
"Have reached fearlessness" means they have reached the state of confidence (*visāradabhāva*). In all instances, [the terms] such as "liberated through faith" (*saddhāvimutta*) and so on [apply].

The foundations of mindfulness and so forth occur at the very moments previously mentioned; the eight liberations, such as "one possessing form sees forms," are attained only upon reaching the path of analytical knowledge (*paṭisambhidā*);
and the three trainings—the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom—are trainings that are realized only upon reaching the path.

“Fully understanding suffering,” and so forth, refer specifically to the moment of the path (*magga-khaṇa*). “He penetrates by means of the penetration of full understanding” means he penetrates by way of the penetration of full understanding;
or, that which is to be penetrated by full understanding is the “penetration of full understanding. The same applies to the remaining terms.

Having distinguished them by means of “all phenomena” and so on, the “penetration of direct knowledge” (*abhiññā-paṭivedha*) and others are stated. However, the “penetration of realization” (*sacchikiriyā-paṭivedha*) occurs only at the moment of the path.
It should be understood as being established through the knowledge of reviewing Nibbāna. Thus, five noble persons (ariyapuggala) are defined here;
however, these two—the one liberated both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta) and the one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta)—are not defined. But elsewhere it is said:
"Furthermore, he who, attending to [the object] as suffering, possesses much tranquility and acquires the faculty of concentration, in all cases..."
"He becomes a body-witness (kāyasakkhī); moreover, having attained formless jhāna and reached the highest fruit, he becomes one liberated both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutto).
But he who, attending to [the aggregates] as non-self, possesses abundant feeling and acquires the faculty of wisdom, is a follower by Dhamma (dhammānusārī) at the moment of the stream-entry path;
he is one who has attained vision (diṭṭhippatto) in six respects; and at the highest fruit, he is one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutto). Thus it is said.
These are included here among those who have attained realization through bodily witness (*kāyasakkhī*) and those who have attained it through vision (*diṭṭhippatto*).

In terms of meaning, however, one who is liberated by both parts—namely, by means of formless jhāna and the noble path—is called "liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutto*). One who is liberated while understanding is called "liberated by wisdom" (*paññāvimutto*).
Up to this point, the distinctions between individuals according to their faculties have been explained.
223–226. Now, wishing to show the specific distinction of liberation preceded by liberation itself, as well as the specific type of person [who attains it], he says:
"He attends to [the object] as impermanent," and so forth. In this context, "two liberations" refers to the wishless (*appaṇihita*) and emptiness (*suññata*) liberations.

For the path, having acquired the name "signless liberation" (*animittavimokkha*) by way of approaching the contemplation of impermanence, [is the means for the abandoning] of the longings of lust, hatred, and delusion.
Because it is devoid of [craving] and because those very aspirations are absent, Nibbāna—having obtained the name "wishless" (appaṇihita)—takes that as its object;
thus, by way of its object, it also receives the name "wishless liberation" (appaṇihitavimokkha).

Likewise, because it is empty of greed, hatred, and delusion, and because it is empty of those very things such as greed, Nibbāna—having obtained the name "emptiness" (suññata)—is taken as its object.

Because it acts upon its object, it also receives the name "emptiness liberation" (*suññatavimokkha*). Therefore, those two liberations are called "consequent to the signless liberation" (*animittavimokkhanvaya*).
It should be understood that even though they are not other than the signless path, they function as co-nascent and other conditions by way of each of the eight path-factors of the signless path.
Furthermore, the "two liberations" refers to the emptiness and signless liberations.
Indeed, because it proceeds by way of contemplation of suffering, the path receives the name "the desireless liberation.

Furthermore, because of the absence of the signs of form and so forth, the signs of lust and so forth, and the signs of permanence and so forth—and because of the absence of those very signs even in their positive qualities—it takes Nibbāna, known as the "signless," as its object;
thus, it is also called the "signless liberation" from the perspective of its object.
He attains it. The remainder should be construed according to the method already stated. Furthermore, "two liberations" refers to the signless (animitta) and the desireless (appaṇihita) liberations.
The application here follows the same method as previously stated.
Regarding the time of penetration, it is stated according to the sequence of the faculties. However, setting aside the moment of the Path (magga-khaṇa), at the moment of insight (vipassanā-khaṇa)—

There is no such thing as a "liberation" (vimokkha) [independent of the path]. However, the liberation of the path (maggavimokkha), which was mentioned first, has been shown by distinguishing it with the expression "at the time of penetration.

Furthermore, the two sections beginning with "And this person who is liberated through faith," and the section beginning with "One who attends to [the object] as impermanent attains the stream-entry path," have been stated in brief by way of liberation.

However, it should be understood in detail by applying [the following]. For whatever section beginning with "Those who [attain] renunciation" is stated, it should be understood in the same manner already described.
Up to this point, the specific types of persons regarding the liberations have been demonstrated. 227.
Furthermore, desiring to demonstrate the gateways to liberation and the liberations themselves in their manifold aspects, he says: "One who attends to [the object] as impermanent," and so forth.
In this context, "as it really is" means according to its true nature (*yathāsabhāvena*). "He knows" means he knows by means of knowledge (*ñāṇa*).

"He sees" means he sees by that same knowledge, as if with an eye. "By following after that" means by following along with that; the meaning is: by following what has been seen through direct knowledge (*paccakkha-ñāṇa*).
"Doubt is abandoned" means that through the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*), doubt regarding permanence is abandoned, and by the others...

The doubt regarding other things. "The sign" means that, by analyzing the compactness of continuity (*santatighana*), one knows the sign of formations (*saṅkhāranimitta*)—which has become the object—as it truly is, because the perception of permanence has been abandoned. Therefore, it is called "right seeing.
By that knowledge of things as they truly are, that wisdom is called "right seeing. Regarding "occurrence": having dispelled the perception of pleasure in the mode of what is actually suffering...

By the abandoning of the perception of pleasure— that is, by the abandonment of craving known as *paṇidhi*— he knows, in accordance with reality, even that occurrence of fruition which is considered pleasant.

And as for "the sign and the occurrence," because the perception of self has been abandoned in both ways— through the application of attention to various elements (*nānādhātumanasikāra*) and through the analytical separation of the compact mass (*samūhaghanavinibbhoga*)— he knows, in accordance with reality, both the sign of formations (*saṅkhāranimitta*) and the occurrence of fruition.
He knows. And that which is called "knowledge as it really is" (yathābhūtañāṇa) is precisely what has just been stated; it is nothing else.
"It appears as a terror" means that by seeing the absence of permanence, pleasure, and self, each respective [aggregate] appears as a terror in its proper order.

And as for "the wisdom that consists in the appearance as a terror," etc., this refers to the knowledge of contemplation of rise and fall, the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution, and the knowledge of the appearance as a terror.

Among the nine insight-knowledges comprised within the purification by knowledge and vision of the way— namely, the knowledge of contemplation of danger, the knowledge of contemplation of dispassion, the knowledge of desire for deliverance,
the knowledge of contemplation of reflection, the knowledge of equanimity towards formations, and the knowledge of conformity— these [latter two] are one in meaning,
though distinguished by their different stages in connection with the establishment of fearfulness.
Three kinds of knowledge have been mentioned, not the others.

Furthermore, in order to show that the contemplation of emptiness is identical with the contemplation of non-self—which stands at the end of the three contemplations and is immediately contiguous with it—the text says:
"That which is the contemplation of non-self and that which is the contemplation of emptiness," and so forth.
For these two types of knowledge are identical in meaning, though they are distinguished by their different states;
and just as these are, so too the contemplation of impermanence and the contemplation of the signless are one and the same knowledge in meaning,
while the contemplation of suffering and the contemplation of the desireless are one and the same knowledge in meaning— they are distinguished solely by their different states.

Since it has been stated that the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā) and the contemplation of emptiness (suññatānupassanā) are identical, their identity is effectively stated because these two pairs of knowledges possess the same characteristic.
Regarding the phrase "the knowledge of reflection on the sign arises":
having understood by way of the characteristic of impermanence that "the sign of formations is unstable and temporary," knowledge arises.

Granted that knowledge does not arise subsequently after having first known [the object], yet it is spoken of in this way by way of conventional usage, as in such passages as: "Dependent on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises.

Furthermore, those learned in the science of grammar accept this grammatical construction even when referring to simultaneous events, as in such expressions as: "Darkness vanishes upon reaching the sun."
Alternatively, it should be understood that this was stated by taking the preceding and the following as one according to the method of unity (*ekattanaya*).

By this same method, the meaning should also be understood for the other two pairs of terms. The fact that the three knowledges beginning with the desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā*) have a single function is exactly as explained in the method given below.
"Mind emerges from the sign": by seeing the fault in the sign of formations, the mind does not adhere to it; thus, it is said that "mind emerges from the sign of formations.
"Mind enters the signless": by being inclined toward Nibbāna—which is known as the signless and is the opposite of the sign of formations—the mind penetrates it.
The meaning in the case of the other two contemplations should also be understood according to this method.
By the phrase "in cessation, the element of Nibbāna," both of the first two contemplations mentioned here are already included. "In cessation" (*nirodhe*) is also a reading.
"Wisdom in emerging externally and turning away" refers to the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*) by virtue of its connection with emerging.
"States that are change-of-lineage" refers to the knowledge of change-of-lineage itself; otherwise, their identity would not be tenable. "The unconditioned..."
Or it should be understood that the plural number is used as in such passages as “dhammā, appaccayā dhammā,” or by way of the four paths.

Since liberation (*vimokkha*) is the path, and the path emerges from both sides, therefore, in connection with that, it is said: “the wisdom that effects emergence from both sides and turning away (*vivaṭṭana*),” and so forth.
228. Furthermore, wishing to show the method of the single moment for the various moments of liberations, he says: “In how many ways...? and so on.
In this context, "in the sense of predominance" means in the sense of being foremost. "In the sense of foundation" means in the sense of a basis.
"In the sense of directing" means in the sense of leading out from the path of insight. "In the sense of outlet" means in the sense of approaching Nibbāna.
"He attends to it as impermanent" refers precisely to the moment of insight leading to emergence. "The signless liberation" refers precisely to the moment of the Path.
This same method applies to the remaining cases. "He resolves with the mind" means he stands having made the mind predominant; the intention is that he establishes the mind [in concentration].
"He directs the mind" means he leads the mind out from the path of insight (*vipassanā-vīthi*). "It leads to cessation, to Nibbāna" means it approaches Nibbāna, which is termed cessation.
Thus, by way of the diversity of these modes, the fourfold diversity of the moments [of consciousness] has been shown.

"In the sense of convergence through simultaneity" means in the sense of coming together in one place. "In the sense of attainment" means in the sense of finding. "In the sense of acquisition" means in the sense of reaching.
"In the sense of penetration" means in the sense of penetrating by means of knowledge. "In the sense of realization" means in the sense of making manifest before the eyes.
"In the sense of touching" means in the sense of touching by means of the contact of knowledge. "In the sense of clear comprehension" (abhisamaya) means...
In the sense of coming face-to-face. Here, "in the sense of convergence" (*samodhāna*) is the root term, while the others are synonyms for attainment (*adhigama*).
For this very reason, a single answer has been given for all of them. It is "liberated from signs" (*nimittā muccati*); that is, it is liberated from the sign of permanence.
By this, the meaning of liberation (*vimokkha*) is stated. "From which it is liberated" means from which sign it is liberated. "Therein it does not long" (*na paṇidahati*)...
One does not form an aspiration for that sign. "Wherein one does not direct [the mind]" means that sign for which one does not direct it.
"Empty of that" means empty of that sign. "By which it is empty" means by which sign it is empty.
By the phrase "signless because of that sign," the meaning of the signless (animitta) is stated.
“Released from aspiration” means released from aspiration (*paṇidhi*). The reading “aspiration is released” has the sense of an ablative (*nissakka*).
By this, the meaning of liberation (*vimokkha*) is stated. “In which he does not aspire” means in which suffering he does not aspire.
“Empty of that” means empty of that suffering. “By which it is empty” means empty of that sign of suffering (*dukkhanimitta*). “By which sign” means...
"By which sign of suffering": herein, by the phrase "he does not aspire," the meaning of the wishless (*appaṇihita*) is stated;
by the phrase "he is liberated from adherence," the meaning of liberation (*vimokkha*) is stated. "By which it is empty": it is empty of that sign of adherence.
"By which sign": by which sign of adherence. "It is empty of that wherein he does not aspire": in that [object] wherein he does not aspire, it is empty.
One does not aspire toward the sign of misapprehension; therefore, it is empty of that sign of misapprehension. By this, the meaning of emptiness is stated.
(229) Furthermore, desiring to demonstrate the eight liberations and so forth, he says: "There is liberation," and so on.

In this context, "misapprehension as permanent" and so forth should be understood according to the method explained under the "liberation through perception. "From all misapprehensions" refers to those of the aforementioned types.
By means of these [three] clingings. Thus, by way of liberation from clinging, they are called the "emptiness liberation" (*suññatavimokkha*);

by way of liberation from the signs of permanence and so forth, they are the "signless liberation" (*animittavimokkha*); and by way of liberation from the aspirations such as "permanent," they are the "desireless liberation" (*appaṇihitavimokkha*). And here, in all cases, it should be understood that the ablative sense is intended in the phrase "aspiration is liberated from. Alternatively, the reading is "liberated from aspiration" (*paṇidhiyā muccati*).

And here the proof is the phrase, “He is freed from all resolves. Thus, these three contemplations are called “liberations” in a figurative sense, both because they constitute liberation by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgavimokkha*) and because they are conditions for liberation by eradication (*samucchedavimokkha*).

In this context, although the preceding discussion concerned liberation through insight (*vipassanāvimokkha*), since the present discourse concerns liberation by the path (*maggavimokkha*), the term “arisen” is used.
It means that they have arisen in that path and liberation. "Blameless wholesome states" means wholesome states free from the blemish of lust and so forth.
Alternatively, there is a reading with a break [after *anavajjakusalā*]. "Dhammas conducive to enlightenment" refers to:
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
“The path” refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhammā*).
“This is the gateway” means that this aforementioned class of phenomena is called a “gateway” because it serves as the entrance for entering *nibbāna* by way of its object.

“Of those phenomena” means of those factors of enlightenment. “This is the gateway to liberation” [refers to] *nibbāna* among the liberations consisting of suppression, substitution of opposites, eradication, tranquillization, and renunciation.

It is an escape and a liberation; and because it is said, “Bhikkhus, whatever states there are, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared the foremost of those states,” it is a door in the sense of being supreme.
Thus, by way of a *kammadhāraya* compound—“it is both liberation and a door”—this is precisely the meaning of *vimokkhamukha*.
It has been stated. Regarding the phrase "and liberation," a change of gender has been made here. The three unwholesome roots are greed, hatred, and delusion.

The three types of misconduct are bodily, verbal, and mental misconduct. "All unwholesome states" refers to those associated with the unwholesome roots and associated with misconduct—both those that are associated and those that are dissociated—excluding the states such as sorrow that are to be cultivated.
All unwholesome states (*akusala-dhamma*). The wholesome roots (*kusalamūla*) and good conduct (*sucarita*) are to be understood by way of the opposites of what has been stated.

"All wholesome states" refers, according to the method already described, to all wholesome states—both associated (*sampayutta*) and dissociated (*asampayutta*)—which serve as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for liberation (*vimokkha*).
The discourse on turning away (*vivaṭṭa-kathā*) was explained above. However, here, in connection with liberation and turning away (*vimokkha-vivaṭṭa*), [the following applies]:

The remaining terms regarding turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) have also been explained. "Cultivation" (*āsevanā*) means practicing from the beginning. "Development" (*bhāvanā*) means the further increase of that very same practice.

"Repeated exercise" (*bahulīkamman*) means performing that very same practice again and again until mastery is attained. However, in the case of the Path, cultivation and the other terms should be understood by way of accomplishing its function in a single moment.
Furthermore, terms such as "acquisition" (*paṭilābha*) or "fruition" (*vipāka*) have meanings already explained below.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Liberations is finished.
The commentary on the Discussion of the Liberations in the *Saddhammappakāsinī*,
the sub-commentary to the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, is finished.
