6. Discourse on Destiny (Gatikathā). Commentary on the Discourse on Destiny (Gatikathā-vaṇṇanā): 231.
Now, by way of demonstrating the perfection of causes that serve as the basis for the arising of that liberation, the discourse on destiny is explained.

Commentary on what has not been stated before: For even in one who has a double-rooted rebirth-linking, since it is said, "There is no jhāna for one without wisdom," even jhāna does not arise, much less liberation.

In that context, "by success in destination" means by success in the destination consisting of humans and devas among the five destinations reckoned as hell, the animal womb, the sphere of afflicted spirits, humans, and devas. By this, the first three failures of destination are excluded.
He rejects it. "Accomplishment in destiny" (*gatisampatti*) means accomplishment within a [favorable] destiny; what is meant is a "good destiny" (*sugati*).

And by "destiny," the aggregates (*khandhā*) together with their common locus are intended. Among the five destinies, the realm of the *asuras* is included by the very mention of the sphere of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*).

"Devas" refers to the six classes of sense-sphere devas and the *brahmās*. By the mention of "devas," the *asuras* are also comprised. "Associated with knowledge" (*ñāṇasampayutta*) means at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) associated with knowledge.
Indeed, even a single moment should be understood as being spoken of by that same conventional expression through its association with wisdom (*ñāṇa*).

"Of how many roots? means: of how many among the roots of non-greed (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adosa*), and non-delusion (*amoha*). "Rebirth" (*upapatti*) means the act of arising; the sense is "origination.
However, since those born into pure families may also possess three roots, the first question was asked with reference to them. Since...
Furthermore, because they are for the most part born into three great *sāla*-families (*mahāsālakula*) that possess great merit, there are three questions according to those three families.
However, the reading [of the text] is abbreviated. They are called "great *sāla*" (*mahāsāla*) because they have a great *sālā* (house);

the meaning is that they have large dwellings and great wealth. Alternatively, although they should be called "great essence" (*mahāsāra*) because they have a great essence (*sāra*), the letter *ra* was changed to the letter *la*, resulting in "great *sāla*" (*mahāsāla*).
It has been said. "Khattiyamahāsālā" means great householders among the khattiyas, or great householders who are khattiyas.

The same method applies to the remaining [classes] as well. In that context, a khattiya in whose house there is a hundred million pieces of wealth stored in a treasure-house at the very least, and twenty ambraṇa measures of kahāpaṇas go out for daily expenditure, is a khattiyamahāsāla.

...is so called. That brahmin in whose house there is eighty crores of wealth stored away as a hoard at the very least, and ten ambuṇas of kahāpaṇas come out for daily expenditure—this one is called a "brahmin mahāsāla.
That householder in whose house there is forty crores of wealth stored away as a hoard at the very least, and five ambuṇas of kahāpaṇas...
They go out to their business during the day; such a person is called a "wealthy householder.
Because those in the fine-material and immaterial realms possess exclusively triple-rooted consciousness, the term "associated with knowledge" (*ñāṇasampayutta*) is not mentioned [in that context].

However, because among humans there exist those with double-rooted and rootless consciousness, and because among the gods of the sense-sphere there also exist those with double-rooted consciousness, [the qualification is necessary].

Regarding the knowledges, it is stated as "associated with knowledge. In this context, the gods of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) are called *devas* because they sport in the delight of the five strands of sensual pleasure and shine with the radiance of their bodies;
the brahmās of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) are called *devas* because they sport in the delight of meditative absorption (jhāna) and shine with the radiance of their bodies;
and the brahmās of the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara) are called *devas* because they sport in the delight of meditative absorption and shine with the radiance of their knowledge (*ñāṇa*).

232. Regarding the phrase "at the moment of impulsion of wholesome kamma": this refers to the seven occasions of impulsion within the cognitive process (*javana-vīthi*), during which the wholesome sense-sphere kamma of the three roots—which produces a rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) with three roots in this present life from a past birth—arises repeatedly.

"At the time of occurrence" is the meaning. The three roots that are wholesome are: non-greed as a wholesome root, non-hatred as a wholesome root, and non-delusion as a wholesome root. In that [context]...
"At the moment when volition has arisen" means: at that very moment mentioned, by means of the wholesome volition that has arisen. "They are co-nascence conditions" means:
while arising, they are supportive by way of simultaneous production. "Therefore it is said" means: it is said precisely because of that state of being a co-nascence condition.
"Volitional formations have wholesome roots as their condition" is stated according to the method of the mode of conditions within a single moment of consciousness.
By the plural term "formations" (*saṅkhārā*), it should be understood that all mental factors included within the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) are taken there.
By the word "also" (*api*), it is further stated that wholesome roots are also conditioned by formations.
At the moment of attachment (*nikanti-khaṇe*), [this refers to] either the kamma that has manifested itself to give its own result, or [the mind associated with] such manifested kamma.
At the moment of attachment arising toward a kamma-sign or a destination-sign that has been presented.
"Attachment" (*nikanti*) means longing or aspiration. For one whose death is imminent, because the mind is agitated by delusion (*moha*), attachment arises even toward the flames of the Avīci hell;
how much more so toward other signs? "Two roots" refers to greed as an unwholesome root and delusion as an unwholesome root.

However, craving for existence (*bhavanikanti*) arises in all individuals immediately upon emerging from the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) stream that occurs after the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), taking as its object the continuity of one's own aggregates (*khandhasantāna*). This very [craving] is what is referred to in such passages as:
"Is it the case that for whomsoever unwholesome states have not arisen in a certain place, wholesome states have also not arisen there? Yes, they have. And so forth.
This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). "At the moment of the volition born at that time" refers to unwholesome volition (*akusalacetanā*).
"At the moment of rebirth-linking" means at the moment of rebirth-linking grasped by that kamma.

"Three roots" refers to non-greed as an indeterminate root (*abyākatahetu*), non-hatred as an indeterminate root, and non-delusion as an indeterminate root. "At the moment of the volition born at that time" refers to resultant indeterminate volition (*vipākābyākatacetana*).

Regarding the statement "with name-and-form as condition, consciousness [arises]": here, at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the three roots of kamma-result (*vipāka-hetu*) and the remaining mental factors (*cetasika*) constitute "name" (*nāma*), while the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) constitutes "form" (*rūpa*). From that condition of name-and-form, rebirth-linking consciousness proceeds.

Regarding the statement "with consciousness as condition, name-and-form [arises]": here too, "name" is of the same kind already mentioned; however, "form" here refers to the rebirth-linking of a human being accompanied by roots.
Because they are intended [here], for those born from a womb there are thirty material phenomena consisting of the ten bases, the ten bodies, and the ten existences;
for moisture-born and spontaneously born beings with fully developed sense bases, there are seventy material phenomena consisting of the ten eyes, the ten ears, the ten noses, and the ten tongues.
That aforementioned name-and-form, at the moment of rebirth-linking—
It proceeds conditioned by rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "the five aggregates": here, at the moment of rebirth-linking, the material phenomena obtained through the rebirth-linking consciousness constitute the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*);

the co-nascent feeling constitutes the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*); perception constitutes the aggregate of perception (*saññākkhandha*); and the remaining mental factors constitute the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
The rebirth-linking consciousness is the aggregate of consciousness. Regarding "they are co-nascence conditions":
the four immaterial aggregates are co-nascence conditions for one another; within the aggregate of material form, the four great elements are co-nascence conditions for one another;
the immaterial aggregates and the heart-base (hadaya-rūpa) are co-nascence conditions for one another; and the great elements [are likewise].

They are related to derived material phenomena as co-nascent conditions (*sahajāta-paccaya*). They are related as mutuality conditions (*aññamañña-paccaya*) means they are mutually supportive by way of arising and supporting one another;
the four immaterial aggregates (*arūpa-khandha*) are related as mutuality conditions, and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are related as mutuality conditions.
They are related as support conditions (*nissaya-paccaya*) by way of being a foundation and by way of being a basis.

They are benefactors; and the four immaterial aggregates (arūpino khandhā) are mutual support conditions (nissayapaccaya) for one another, and thus they should be explained in detail as if they were co-nascent (sahajāta).

They are dissociation conditions (vippayuttapaccaya): they are benefactors by way of their state of dissociation, through not falling into the condition of having a common physical basis (ekavatthuka) and so forth.
The immaterial aggregates are dissociation conditions for the materiality of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi-rūpa), and the heart-base (hadayarūpa) [is likewise].
It is the dissociation condition for the immaterial aggregates. Here, the phrase "the five aggregates" is stated according to what is available.
Regarding "the four great elements," three conditions have already been mentioned previously.
"The three formations of vitality" refers to life-span, heat, and consciousness. "Life-span" consists of both the material life-faculty and the immaterial life-faculty. "Heat" is the fire element.

"Consciousness" (viññāṇa) refers to rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa). These are called "life-formations" (jīvitasaṅkhāra) because they form and sustain the life-formation successively as they proceed.

They function as conascent conditions (sahajāta-paccaya): the immaterial life-faculty (arūpa-jīvitindriya) and rebirth-linking consciousness are mutual conascent conditions for the associated aggregates and for the heart-base (hadayarūpa);
likewise, the fire element (tejodhātu) is [a mutual condition] for the three primary elements (mahābhūta).
It is a mutual and co-nascent condition (*aññamañña-sahajāta-paccaya*); it is indeed a co-nascent condition for derived matter (*upādārūpa*).
It should be understood that the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*) is, in a figurative sense, a co-nascent condition for the co-nascent material phenomena.

Regarding the pair "they are mutual conditions" and "they are support conditions," the immaterial life-faculty and the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*) [are conditions] for the associated aggregates.

They are related by way of mutual condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*). They are related by way of mutual support condition (*aññamañña-nissaya-paccaya*); this should be understood by applying the same method as previously stated.

Regarding "they are related by way of dissociation condition (*vippayutta-paccaya*)," the immaterial life-faculty (*arūpa-jīvitindriya*) and the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*) are dissociation conditions for the material phenomena of rebirth-linking.
However, the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*), in its capacity as a mutual support and dissociation condition...
That is not tenable. Therefore, it is said that "there are three formations of life" according to how they are obtained.
Name and form should be applied to the four conditions in the same manner already stated.
As for the "fourteen phenomena," they are the five aggregates, the four great elements, the three formations of life, and name and form; thus, by way of enumeration, there are fourteen phenomena.
The manner in which these and others function as co-nascent and other types of conditions is exactly as previously described.

They are "associated conditions" because they provide assistance through the state of association, characterized by having a common physical basis, a common object, a common arising, and a common cessation.
"The five faculties" refers to the faculty of faith and the rest. "And mentality" here refers to the three aggregates beginning with feeling. "And consciousness" refers to...
Rebirth-consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*). Again, "fourteen states" refers to the four aggregates, the five faculties, the three roots, and both mentality (*nāma*) and consciousness;
thus, by way of enumeration, there are fourteen states. "Twenty-eight states" means the previous fourteen and these [other] fourteen, making twenty-eight.
Here, because material form (*rūpa*) is also included, it constitutes the associated condition (*sampayutta-paccaya*).
Having removed [the others], the dissociation condition (vippayuttapaccaya) was stated.

Thus, having shown the various specific types of conditions for each respective conditioned phenomenon existing at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), and having concluded the discussion on the roots (hetu) first mentioned, he now demonstrates [them] by saying: "Of these eight..."

He said, "Rebirth occurs through causes and conditions. Thus, there are eight causes: three wholesome causes at the moment of karmic accumulation, two unwholesome causes at the moment of longing [for rebirth], and three indeterminate causes at the moment of rebirth-linking.

Among these, the three wholesome causes and the two unwholesome causes serve here as decisive-support conditions (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for the occurrence [of existence] at the moment of rebirth-linking.
There are three indeterminate causes which, as appropriate, act as conditions by way of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) and the conascence-condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*).
This same method applies to the remaining sections as well.
However, because of the absence of matter in the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*), it is stated that name is a condition for consciousness, and consciousness is also a condition for name.
The fourteenfold [consciousness] mixed with form is also excluded. Because that is excluded, the section stating "twenty-eight factors" is not obtained.

Now, having shown the triple-rooted rebirth-linking that serves as the condition for liberation, and wishing to show the distinction of double-rooted rebirth-linking through that same connection, he says:
"In the attainment of a fortunate destination, dissociated from knowledge," and so forth. This refers to wholesome kamma.

"At the moment of impulsion" means, in the same manner as described above, at the moment of impulsion of the two-root wholesome kamma that produces rebirth-linking here in this present life from a past birth.

"Two roots" refers to the wholesome root of non-greed and the wholesome root of non-hatred, because [this consciousness] is dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇa*). The two indeterminate roots are likewise non-greed and non-hatred.
"Four faculties" refers to the four beginning with the faculty of faith (saddhindriya), excluding the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya).

"Twelve factors" means twelve because both the faculty of wisdom and the root of non-delusion (amoha) have been abandoned. "Twenty-six" occurs because only those two [the faculty of wisdom and the root of non-delusion] have been abandoned.
"Of six roots" refers to the two wholesome roots, the two unwholesome roots, and the two...

"Of the ripening causes"—thus [it refers] to the six causes. However, those pertaining to the fine-material and immaterial spheres are not included here because they are exclusively associated with three roots.
The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated in the first section.

Since in this section it is stated that for a rebirth-linking with two roots there is only karma with two roots, it follows that a rebirth-linking with two roots does not occur through karma with three roots.

Therefore, that which is stated in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā* according to the opinion of the Elder Tipiṭaka Mahādhammarakkhita—namely, "Rebirth-linking by means of a three-rooted kamma is itself three-rooted;
it is not two-rooted or rootless. Rebirth-linking by means of a two-rooted kamma is two-rooted or rootless;
it is not three-rooted"—is consistent with this canonical text (*pāḷi*). However, as for that [opinion] of the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga...
In the discourses of the Elder Mahādatta, a resident of Moravāpi, it is stated: "Rebirth-linking by means of a three-rooted kamma may be three-rooted or two-rooted, but it is never rootless.
Rebirth-linking by means of a two-rooted kamma may be two-rooted or rootless, but it is never three-rooted.
This appears to be in contradiction with the present canonical text, because this discussion concerns the specific subject of the roots (hetu).
"Rebirth-linking without a cause has not been mentioned.
The commentary on the Discussion of Destinies is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of Kamma.
Commentary on the Discussion of Kamma (Kammakathāvaṇṇanā) 234.

Now follows the explanation of the previously unstated points in the discussion of kamma, which was spoken by the Teacher while demonstrating the kamma that serves as the condition for that perfection of causes.
In this context, regarding such statements as "there was kamma, there was the result of kamma," [this refers to] what was performed in past existences.
Having taken as an example the ripened result (*vipāka*) of karma that occurred in past existences alone, it is said: "There was karma; there was the result of that karma.

Furthermore, regarding that same past karma—whether to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*) or to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*)—if its result has not ripened due to a deficiency in conditions within those very past existences, and regarding one who has attained final Nibbāna (*parinibbuta*) in the past, whether that karma was to be experienced in the present life, upon rebirth, or in a subsequent life (*aparapariyāyavedanīya*), [it is likewise said].
Taking as an example a past action whose result has not yet matured, it is said: "The action existed, but the result of the action did not exist.
Taking as an example the result of that very same past action which has not yet matured but is maturing due to the presence of conditions in the present existence, it is said:
"The action existed and the result of the action exists. [And taking as an example] that very same past action whose time for maturation has already passed...
And for one attaining final Nibbāna in the present existence, having taken up the result that has not yet matured, it is said:

"There was karma, but there is no result of karma. Having taken up the result that is to mature through the fulfillment of conditions in a future existence—belonging to past karma that is subject to ripening but whose result has not yet matured—it is said: "There will be karma."

It is said, "the result of kamma. Having taken as "result" the unripened result of past kamma whose time for ripening has passed and that which is to be attained through parinibbāna in a future existence—[thinking] "there was kamma, but there will be no [further] kamma-result"—it is said, "the result of kamma.
Thus, past kamma is shown in six ways by way of past, present, and future results, as well as non-results.

Having taken as the result that which ripens right here for karma performed in the present existence that is to be experienced in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*), it is said: "there is karma, there is the result of karma.

Furthermore, [it is said] regarding that same present karma which does not ripen here due to a deficiency of conditions, and that which does not ripen here for one who attains final nibbāna in this very life.

Having taken the ripening (*vipāka*) of present karma—both that to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*) and that to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparapariyāyavedanīya*)—it is said: "There is karma; there will be the ripening of karma.
Having taken the ripening that is to be ripened in a future existence from that very same present karma—both that to be experienced upon rebirth and... [the rest of the sentence continues].

Taking as an example the result that is not to ripen in a future existence due to a deficiency of conditions, and the result of karma to be experienced in a subsequent life—which is to be fully extinguished (parinibbāyitabba) in a future existence and thus not to ripen—it is said: "There is karma, but there will be no ripening of that karma.
In this way, present karma is shown in four ways by way of present and future ripening and non-ripening.

It is said that "there will be action" and "there will be the ripening of the fruit of action" by taking into account the fruit that is to ripen in a future existence for the action to be performed in a future existence. Furthermore,
this is stated by taking into account the fruit that would not ripen in a future existence due to a deficiency in conditions for that very same future action,
as well as the fruit that would not ripen for one who is to attain final nibbāna in a future existence.
It is said: "There will be karma; there will not be the ripening of karma. Thus, future karma is shown in two ways: by way of future ripening and non-ripening.
Taking all that together, karma is shown as being of twelve kinds.
Standing on this point, three sets of fourfold karmas are brought forward and explained; for when these are stated, the following meaning [is established].

"It will become more manifest. For karma is fourfold: karma to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*), karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*), karma to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparapariyāyavedanīya*), and defunct karma (*ahosikamma*).

Among these, the first impulsion volition—whether wholesome or unwholesome—within the seven consciousnesses of a single impulsion-process is called "karma to be experienced in the present life. That [karma] is in this very...

It yields its result within one's own personal existence (*attabhāva*). However, when it is unable to do so, it becomes what is called "lapsed karma" (*ahosikamma*) by way of this triad: "The karma existed, but the result of the karma did not exist; the result of the karma will not exist; there is no result of the karma.

On the other hand, the seventh impulsion volition that accomplishes the purpose is called "karma to be experienced upon rebirth" (*upapajjavedanīyakamma*). That [volition] [yields its result] in the immediately following...
It gives its result within that very lifetime. If it is unable to do so, it becomes what is called "ineffective karma" (*ahosikamma*) according to the method already described.
Between these two, however, the five impulsion volitions are called "karma to be experienced in a subsequent state.
When they obtain an opportunity in the future, they then give their result. As long as the process of saṃsāra continues, there is no such thing as ineffective karma.

Furthermore, there is another fourfold classification of kamma: that which is heavy (*garuka*), that which is habitual (*bahula*), that which is proximate (*āsanna*), and then the kamma of what has been stored up (*kaṭattā*).
Among these, whether it be wholesome or unwholesome, that which is heavy among the heavy and the not-heavy—such as the kamma of matricide and so forth, or sublime kamma—that alone ripens first.
Likewise, among the habitual and the non-habitual, that which is habitual...
Whether it be good conduct or misconduct, that very same thing ripens first. That which is called "proximate" refers to either an action performed or an action recollected at the time of death.
For one is reborn according to that very action which one is able to recollect or perform when death is near.
Apart from these three, however, there is that which has been habitually practiced again and again, or that which was performed [in this life].
There is such a thing as kamma. In its absence, that [kamma] draws forth rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
Alternatively, there is another fourfold classification of kamma: productive (janaka), supportive (upatthambhaka), obstructive (upapīḷaka), and destructive (upaghātaka).
Among these, the "productive" is both wholesome and unwholesome; it produces resultant form and non-form (rūpārūpa-vipāka) both at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence (pavatta).
It produces [the rebirth-linking]. However, it is not able to produce a supporting [kamma];

rather, once the rebirth-linking has been produced by another kamma and the resultant [consciousness] has arisen, it supports the pleasure and pain that arise therein and causes them to persist for a duration.
An obstructing [kamma], on the other hand, oppresses the pleasure and pain arising from the resultant produced by the rebirth-linking given by another kamma.
It obstructs; it does not allow the course [of other karma] to proceed.
However, an obstructive karma—whether wholesome or unwholesome—having destroyed another weak karma and warded off its fruition, makes room for its own fruition.
When the opportunity has thus been made by that karma, that fruition is said to have arisen.

Thus, among these twelve types of kamma, both the intervals between kamma and the intervals between results become manifest in their true nature only to the Buddhas through their knowledge of the result of kamma;
this is not shared by disciples. However, a practitioner of insight (vipassaka) should understand the intervals between kamma and the intervals between results at least in part.
Therefore, this distinction of kamma has been explained here by way of a mere introduction.

235. Having thus stated the first section by way of pure action (*suddhika-kamma*), that same action is divided into two and ten further sections are stated by way of ten methods, according to the pairs of wholesome (*kusala*), unwholesome (*akusala*), and so forth.

Therein, "wholesome" is in the sense of health, and "unwholesome" is in the sense of ill-health; this dyad is stated by way of birth. Unwholesome [action] alone, through its association with defilements such as lust and so on—

It is blameworthy; it is wholesome because of the absence of that [blame], and thus blameless. The unwholesome is "dark" because of its impurity, or because it is a cause for rebirth in a dark lineage;
the wholesome is "bright" because of its purity, or because it is a cause for rebirth in a bright lineage.

The wholesome has a happy outcome because it increases happiness; the unwholesome has a painful outcome because it increases suffering. The wholesome has a pleasant result because it possesses a pleasant fruit.
Because it yields a fruit of suffering, the unwholesome is called "having a painful result" (*dukkha-vipāka*); in this way, their various distinctions are to be understood.
The commentary on the Discussion of Kamma is finished. 8.
The Discussion of Perversions (*vipallāsa*).
Commentary on the Discourse on the Perversions (Vipallāsakathāvaṇṇanā) 236.
Now follows the commentary on the new subject matter of the discourse on the perversions—which was spoken preceded by a sutta—in order to show the perversions that serve as conditions for that karma.
First, regarding the sutta: "Perversions of perception" means the state of being perverted in perception.
"Perverted state" means a perverted perception (*saññā*). The same principle applies to the other two [perverted views] as well.
When unwholesome perception, devoid of wrong view (*diṭṭhi*), is strong while the function of consciousness (*citta*) is weak, there is perversion of perception (*saññā-vipallāsa*).

When unwholesome consciousness, devoid of wrong view, is strong while its own function is strong, there is perversion of consciousness (*citta-vipallāsa*). In a consciousness associated with wrong view, there is perversion of view (*diṭṭhi-vipallāsa*).
Therefore, the perversion of perception (*saññā-vipallāsa*) is the weakest; the perversion of consciousness (*citta-vipallāsa*) is stronger than that;

and the perversion of view (*diṭṭhi-vipallāsa*) is the strongest of all. For perception is like a child who has not yet developed intelligence seeing a coin, because it merely grasps the mode of appearance of the object.
Consciousness is like a villager seeing a coin, because it also penetrates its characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*).
Because it brings [the object] to completion. Because one grasps and misapprehends by means of views, just as a blacksmith grasps iron with a large pair of tongs.
Regarding "perception-inversion (saññā-vipallāsa) as permanence in the impermanent": perception that arises having apprehended an impermanent basis as "this is permanent" is perception-inversion.
The meaning in all the following passages should be understood according to this method. It is not perception-inversion; it is not mind-inversion (citta-vipallāsa).
"Not a perversion of view" means that because there is an absence of the twelve types of perverted grasping regarding the four bases, it is described as a "grasping according to reality.
In the verses, "in what is non-self, [perceiving] self" means those who possess such a perception (saññī) regarding what is non-self.
"Struck by wrong view" means they are not only perceivers, but are also struck by wrong view arising just as their perception arises. "With deranged minds" (khittacittā).
They are possessed of a mind that has been cast off and distracted, arising just like perceptions and views.
"With perverted perception" (*visaṃñino*) is merely a way of teaching; the meaning is "those with perverted perception, mind, and view.
Alternatively, because view is preceded by perception, first the perversion of perception was stated by the four preceding terms; thereafter, "struck by wrong view" refers to the perversion of view.

"Deranged in mind" (*khittacitta*) refers to a perversion of the mind (*cittavipallāsa*). "Senseless" (*visaṇṇī*) means being devoid of natural perception due to the three types of perverted grasping, having fallen into delusion—just as it is said in the passage:
"He was stupefied by the force of the poison; he became senseless.

Those who are "yoked to Māra" (*mārassa yogayutta*) are those persons, those beings, who are indeed joined to the bond of Māra. "Not finding rest from the bonds" (*ayogakkhemino*) refers to [those bound] by the four bonds (*yoga*).
Not having attained the security of Nibbāna by means of these [paths], beings wander in *saṃsāra*; it is those very persons who transmigrate through *saṃsāra*.
Why? Because they go toward birth and death; therefore, the meaning is that they "transmigrate. "Buddhas" refers to those who have awakened to the Four Noble Truths, the Omniscient Ones.
The plural number is used in the sense of being common to the three times. "In the world" means in the world of space (*okāsaloka*). "Light-makers" (*pabhaṅkara*)...
They create the light of wisdom for the world. "Proclaiming this Dhamma" means they illuminate the Dhamma that abandons the perversions.
"Leading to the subsiding of suffering" means leading toward Nibbāna, which is the cessation of suffering.
"Having heard from them" means having heard the Dhamma from those Buddhas. "The wise" refers to those who are capable and possess wisdom. "Recovered their own minds" means...
Having regained their own minds, free from perversion—*paṭiladdhū* being the word-division—or alternatively, *paṭilabhiṃsu paṭialaddhuṃ* being the word-division.
"They saw as impermanent" means they saw precisely by way of impermanence. "In what is not-self, [they saw] 'not-self'" means they saw non-selfhood as "not-self.
Or alternatively, in the basis that is not-self, there is no self.

They have seen. "Having undertaken right view" means having grasped right vision. "They have transcended all suffering" means they have completely passed beyond the suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*). In response to the question regarding what is abandoned and what is not abandoned:
for one "endowed with vision," that is, for a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), the perception arises that there is happiness in what is suffering.
"Consciousness arises": because the turbidity of delusion has not been abandoned, there arises a mere perception or a mere consciousness;
this arises even in a non-returner, so what need be said for a stream-enterer? These two [perceptions] are abandoned only by an arahant.
The perception "the beautiful in the foul" arises. "Consciousness arises": this arises even in a once-returner, so what need be said...

Regarding the stream-enterer (sotāpanna): "These two are abandoned by the non-returner (anāgāmī)," so it is stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). Therefore, it should be understood that this pair was spoken with reference to the stream-enterer and the once-returner (sakadāgāmin).

Since the non-returner has abandoned sensual lust (kāmarāga), it should be understood that the perversions of perception and mind regarding "the beautiful in the ugly" are also said to be abandoned. [This is explained] by the phrases beginning with "in two bases," etc.

By means of these words, he demonstrates [the distinction] between what has been abandoned and what has not been abandoned. Therein, regarding the two objects—“the impermanent as permanent” and “the non-self as self”—the six perversions have been abandoned.
Regarding the two objects—“suffering as pleasure” and “the foul as beautiful”—the two perversions of view have been abandoned. In some manuscripts, the word “two” is written first.
“Afterwards, six. Regarding the phrase “in four bases”: this is stated by taking four [pairs] together. “Eight”: two in each of two [bases], thus eight. “Four”:
in each of the two bases of suffering and the unattractive, there are two each of the perversions of perception and mind;
thus, four. In some manuscripts, even in places where it is written “six in two,” it is likewise written as such.
The commentary on the Discourse on Perversions is finished.
9. The Discourse on the Path.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Path.

237. Now follows the commentary on the previously unstated meaning of the discourse on the Path, which was spoken by one who intends to show the Noble Path that effects the abandonment of those three perversions.

In this context, "Path" (magga): in what sense is it called a "path"? The meaning is: in what sense does that which is called "the Path" in the Buddha’s teaching receive the name "Path"? Regarding the phrases "for the abandoning of wrong view," and so forth: [The text continues with the detailed explanation of the four paths.]
Among the ten methods, each first [method] is stated by way of being the direct opposite of its respective path-factor.

“It is both the path and the cause”: it is a path in the sense of being the practice for performing its respective function, and it is a cause in the sense of being that which brings about [the goal].
Thus, the sense of practice and the sense of bringing about are stated for the path. This is as in such passages as, “This is the path; this is the practice,” and so forth.
For the path is the practice; in such passages as “the meaning of the path is the sense of outlet and the sense of cause,” it is the cause that brings about attainment.
Thus, by means of two pairs of terms, the answer to the question “In what sense is it the ‘path’? has been given.
“For the support of co-nascent states” means: for the sake of supporting the immaterial (arūpa) states co-nascent with itself, by way of being their co-nascence, mutuality, support, and so forth.

"For the sake of providing support": for the purpose of maintaining [the path]. "For the exhaustion of the defilements": for the elimination of those remaining defilements that are to be abandoned by each respective path.
"For the purification of penetration and so forth": here, because of the statement, "And what is the beginning of wholesome states?
Virtue that is well-purified and a view that is straight," both virtue and view constitute the beginning of the penetration of the Truths.
And it is purified at the moment of the initial path. Therefore, it is said: "for the purification of penetration and so forth.
"For the resolution of the mind" means for the establishment of the associated mind in its own function. "For the cleansing of the mind" means for the state of complete purity of the mind.
"For the attainment of distinction" means for the acquisition of a distinction from the mundane. "For further penetration" means...

For the purpose of penetrating what lies beyond the mundane. "For the realization of the truths" means for the single penetration of the four truths by way of accomplishing their respective functions.
"For establishing [the mind] in cessation" means for the purpose of establishing either the mind or the person in *nibbāna*.
Having combined the eight path-factors together at the moment of the once-returning path and so forth...
The abandoning of the specific defilements to be eliminated by each respective path has been stated. The reason for stating it in this way has already been explained above.
Since, even by means of the successive higher paths, there is a thorough purification of the beginning and a thorough clarity of the mind, those terms as well have been stated.
From the words "the path of seeing" onwards, up to the conclusion, the meaning of "path" has been stated in terms of the characteristic of that Dhamma.

All those terms have their meanings already explained in the exposition of what is to be directly known (*abhiññeyya-niddesa*). Thus, herein the mundane and supramundane path has been described according to its occurrence.
Furthermore, the eightfold path is described as "the path" in the sense of being the cause (*hetu-ṭṭhena*);

because it is the path in the primary sense (*nippariyāya*), it is not stated again as "the path. And [the terms] beginning with "the faculties" (*indriyāni*) are [described] in the sense of predominance (*ādhipateyya-ṭṭhena*), and so forth for the faculties and the rest.
These are stated by way of their function, not by way of being factors of the path. And here, "truths" refers to the knowledges of the truths.
All those states are the path in the sense of being the way leading to Nibbāna.

However, it should be understood that Nibbāna, mentioned at the end, is called the "path" because it is sought and pursued as the path by true persons who, being overwhelmed by the suffering of saṃsāra, desire the escape from suffering.
The commentary on the Discussion of the Path is finished.
10. The Discussion of the Drink in the Pavilion. Commentary on the Discussion of the Drink in the Pavilion.

238. Now follows the commentary on the previously unstated meaning of the "discourse on the cream" (*maṇḍapeyya-kathā*), which was spoken by the Blessed One preceded by a portion of his own words in order to demonstrate that this path is like the cream of ghee.

In this context, "the cream of ghee" (*maṇḍapeyya*) refers to how, just as well-prepared, stainless, and clarified ghee is called the "cream of ghee" (*sappimaṇḍa*), so too [this path] is a "cream" (*maṇḍa*) in the sense of being perfectly clarified, and a "beverage" (*peyya*) in the sense of being something to be drunk.

“Drinkable” (peyya): for that which, having been drunk, causes one to fall unconscious in the middle of the street and renders even one’s own robes and so forth ownerless—that should not be drunk, even if it is clear.
But this holy life of the Dispensation (sāsanabrahmacariya) of mine, being comprised within the three trainings, is “clear” because it is perfected, stainless, and serene;
and it is “drinkable” because it brings about beauty and welfare. Thus, it is called “the drink of clarity” (maṇḍapeyya).
It illuminates. That which has the "drink of essence" (*maṇḍapeyya*) therein is called the "drink of essence. What is that? It is the holy life (*brahmacariya*) of the Dispensation.
Why is the threefold training called the "holy life"? Nibbāna is called "sublime" (*brahma*) in the sense of being supreme;

because the threefold training proceeds for the sake of Nibbāna—that is, for the sake of the sublime—it is called the "holy life" (*brahmacariya*), as it is a practice for the sake of the sublime. Thus, it is the "holy life of the Dispensation."
"The Teacher himself is present"—this is the statement of the reason here.
Because the Teacher is present, therefore you should exert effort and drink this medicinal decoction (*maṇḍa*).

For regarding an external medicinal decoction, there is a suspicion among those drinking it in the absence of the physician that they may not know the proper measure, or its absorption and excretion. [But] in the case of the physician...
But because they know that the physician is present before them, they drink without hesitation. In the same way, he enjoins them to drink from the "pavilion of the Dhamma," saying:

"The Teacher, our Master of the Dhamma, is present; therefore, exert yourselves and drink! He is called the "Teacher" (*satthā*) because he instructs according to what is appropriate through the goals pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal (*paramattha*).
Furthermore, the definition of the term is given here according to the *Niddesa* method, beginning with: "The Blessed One is the Teacher, the Caravan-Leader."
The meaning should be understood as follows: "present" (*sammukhībhūta*) means that which has become manifest to the face (*sandissamāna-mukha*).

In the description of *maṇḍapeyya*, "threefold state" (*tidhatta*) refers to the condition of being threefold (*tidhā-bhāva*). "Threefold-essence" (*tidhattamaṇḍa*) means essence by way of the threefold state;

the sense is "essence in a threefold manner. The phrase "when the Teacher is present" (*satthari sammukhībhūte*) is for the purpose of showing the completeness of all aspects of the threefold essence.
It has been stated. However, even when the Teacher has attained final Nibbāna, the threefold excellence (maṇḍatta) continues to exist in part.
For this very reason, it should be understood that in its exposition (niddesa), instead of saying "when the Teacher is present," it says, "What is the excellence of the teaching?

and so forth. The "excellence of the teaching" (desanāmaṇḍa) is the teaching of the Dhamma itself as the excellence. The "excellence of the recipient" (paṭiggahamaṇḍa) is the recipient of the teaching itself as the excellence. The "excellence of the holy life" (brahmacariyamaṇḍa) is the holy life of the Path itself as the excellence.
*Ācikkhanā* (explaining) is the speaking by way of names, [indicating] that "these are the names" of the Truths (*sacca*) and so forth which are to be taught. *Desanā* (teaching) is showing.
*Paññāpanā* (making known) is causing to know, or placing [them] within the gateway of knowledge; for one who sets out a seat is said to "make the seat known.
*Paṭṭhapanā* (establishing) is making known, meaning setting in motion, or placing within the gateway of knowledge. *Vivaraṇā* (unveiling)...
*Vivaṭakaraṇaṃ* means making manifest; the meaning is "showing after having opened. *Vibhajanā* is the act of analysis; the meaning is "showing by way of division.
*Uttānīkammaṃ* is the act of making clear. Alternatively, *ācikkhanā* (explaining) is the root term for the six terms beginning with "teaching" (*desanā*).
The six terms beginning with "teaching" are stated for the purpose of explaining its meaning. In that regard:
"Teaching" (*desanā*) refers, by way of those who understand through a brief summary (*ugghaṭitaññū*), to the teaching first given by way of a mere enumeration.
For those who understand through a brief summary penetrate what is stated concisely and what is stated first.

"Proclamation" (*paññāpanā*) refers, by way of those who understand through elaboration (*vipañcitaññū*), to the subsequent detailed exposition of that which was first stated in brief, through gladdening their minds and sharpening their intelligence.
*Paññāpanā* (making known): this is the making known by means of a more detailed statement through a further exposition (*paṭiniddesa*) of that very exposition (*niddesa*) already indicated.
*Vivaraṇā* (unveiling): this is the unveiling by repeating what has already been indicated. *Vibhajanā* (analyzing):

this is the analyzing by means of making a division of what has already been stated repeatedly. *Uttānīkammaṃ* (clarifying): this is the clarification of what has been unveiled by means of a more detailed statement.
And the clarification is by means of an illustrative statement regarding what has been analyzed. This teaching serves for the penetration even of those who are to be led (neyya).
"Some others included among the 'and others'" refers to those fallen into the lower realms, such as Piyaṅkaramātā and so forth.
"Those who understand" refers to those who understand the supramundane Dhamma by way of penetration. For these—beginning with the bhikkhus—receive the teaching of the Dhamma by way of penetration.

"Acceptance. The phrases "this very [path]" and so forth have meanings already explained in the description of the first knowledge. Because it flows together with Nibbāna, the Noble Path is called "the holy life" (*brahmacariya*), as it is a practice for the sake of the sublime (*brahma*). 239.
Now, by means of the terms "the essence of resolve" and so forth, [the text explains] the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and path-factors that exist at that moment of the Path.
Having applied [the term] to the "maṇḍapeyya" (the drink of the cream), he demonstrates it. Therein, "adhimokkha-maṇḍa" means the cream known as resolve (*adhimokkha*).
"Kasaṭa" means turbid, being devoid of clarity. "Chaḍḍetvā" means having abandoned by way of complete eradication. Regarding the phrase "he drinks the maṇḍa-cream of the faculty of faith":
although the maṇḍa-cream of resolve is not distinct from the faculty of faith itself, it is called "maṇḍapeyya."
Although it is not different [from the mind], it is spoken of by way of conventional usage as if it were something else;
just as in the world, although the body of a young *nisada* fish is not different from the young *nisada* fish itself, one still says "the body of the young *nisada* fish";

and just as in the Canon, in such passages as "the state of touching" (*phusitatta*), a state that is not different from the phenomenon (*dhamma*) is spoken of as if it were different; and just as in the Commentary, [it is said]: "having the characteristic of touching."
In such passages as "contact" (*phassa*), although the characteristic is not other than the phenomenon itself, it is spoken of as if it were distinct;

thus it should be understood. Here, "he drinks" means that the person possessing those [qualities] is meant. By taking it that "the person possessing them drinks that cream," it is stated that because that cream is to be drunk by that person, it is called "cream-drink" (*maṇḍapeyya*). "Cream-drink" (*maṇḍapeyyo*).
And when it should have been said “*maṇḍapeyyan*,” the change of gender has been made. The meaning of the remaining [terms] should also be understood by this method.
However, regarding those not mentioned before: *pariḷāha* (fever) is the burning of the defilements, which is the opposite of *pīti* (rapture), characterized by refreshment.

*Duṭṭhulla* (coarseness) is a state of grossness or unreality due to the defilements, which is the opposite of tranquility (*upasama*). *Appaṭisaṅkhā* (lack of reflection) is the opposite of reflective discernment (*paṭisaṅkhāna*).
The state of not being driven by the defilements (kilesa). 240.
Furthermore, desiring to demonstrate the method for making it palatable (maṇḍapeyya) by another way, he said, "There is the 'maṇḍa,'" and so forth.
Therein, "therein" refers to that faculty of faith (saddhindriya). Regarding "the essence of the meaning" (attharasa) and so on, it is the resolving (adhimuccana) of the faculty of faith.
The goal (*attha*) is the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*), which is the phenomenon (*dhamma*); that very same thing, because it is liberated from various defilements, is liberation (*vimutti*).

The attainment of that goal is the flavor of the goal (*attharasa*). The attainment of that phenomenon is the flavor of the phenomenon (*dhammarasa*). The attainment of that liberation is the flavor of liberation (*vimuttirasa*).
Alternatively, the delight in the acquisition of the goal is the flavor of the goal; the delight in the acquisition of the phenomenon is the flavor of the phenomenon.
The delight in the attainment of liberation is the essence of liberation. "Delight" refers to the joy (*pīti*) associated with that [liberation] or having it as its object.
In this manner, the meaning should be understood for the remaining terms as well. In this context, the meaning expressed is *maṇḍapeyya*, which means "the drink of the cream.
Thus, according to the sequence of the factors conducive to enlightenment beginning with the faculties—namely, the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and path-factors—

Having shown the "essence of the assembly" (maṇḍapeyya), he then, showing the "essence of the holy life" (brahmacariyamaṇḍa) standing at the end, took the Path as the precursor because of its preeminence and showed the path-factors, factors of enlightenment, powers, and faculties in reverse order.
In the sense of being predominant, the faculties are the "essence," and so forth; these essences are both mundane and supramundane as appropriate. That [which was] below...
It should be understood according to the method already stated. Regarding the statement, "In the sense of being suchness, the truths are the 'essence' (maṇḍa)":

here, because suffering and its origin lack the quality of being an essence, it should be understood that the knowledges of the truths are called "truths" (*sacca*) just as they are in the *Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta*.
—From the *Saddhammappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.
The commentary on the Maṇḍapeyya-kathā is finished.
The commentary on the Mahāvagga is also finished.
(2) The Yuganaddha-vagga.
1. The Discourse on the Coupling (Yuganaddha-kathā). Commentary on the Discourse on the Coupling:
Now, this [discourse] preceded by the Sutta was spoken by one who, in demonstrating the quality of the coupling of the Noble Path—the quality of being worthy of offerings—[proceeds as follows].
The commentary on the previously unstated matter regarding the discourse on the Coupling (Yuganaddha).

Since the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) passed away in the very year of the Dhamma-King’s Parinibbāna while the Dhamma-King was still living, this Sutta— taught by the Keeper of the Dhamma-Treasury (Ānanda) while the Dhamma-King was still alive—
he heard in the presence of that very person and thus said, "Thus have I heard," and so forth.
This should be understood. In this context, "Venerable" (*āyasmā*) is a term of affection, a term of respect, and a term expressing reverence and deference;
its meaning is "possessor of life" (*āyu-mant*). "Ānanda" is the name of that elder. For even as he was being born, he brought great joy (*ānanda*) and intense satisfaction to his family;
therefore, it should be understood that his name was made "Ānanda. "In Kosambī" refers to the city of that name.
In various places within that city, such as its parks and lotus ponds, *kosamba* trees grew in abundance;
therefore, it came to be known by the name Kosambī. According to some, it was so called because it was established not far from the hermitage of the seer Kusamba.
Regarding the Ghositārāma: it is a park built by the merchant Ghosita. For in Kosambī there were three merchants, among whom was the merchant Ghosita.
The merchant Kukkuṭa and the merchant Pāvārika—these three, having heard that "a Buddha has arisen in the world," had five hundred carts each loaded with provisions for almsgiving.
They went to Sāvatthī, pitched their camp near the Jeta Grove, approached the Teacher, paid homage, exchanged greetings, and sat down. Then they listened to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma.
Having heard this, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).

He then invited the Teacher and, having given a great almsgiving for half a month to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, he prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet and requested permission from the Blessed One to go to his own country.
To him, the Blessed One said: "Householders, Tathāgatas indeed delight in empty dwellings."
When this was said, knowing that "the Blessed One has granted us his promise," they were exceedingly joyful. Having paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, they departed;
along the way, having had monasteries built for the Blessed One's residence every *yojana*, they eventually reached Kosambī.
In their respective ārāmas, they made great sacrifices of wealth and had monasteries constructed for the Blessed One.
Therein, the monastery built by the merchant Ghosita was called Ghosita’s Monastery; that built by the merchant Kukkuṭa was called Kukkuṭa’s Monastery;
and that built by the merchant Pāvārika in the mango grove was called Pāvārika’s Mango Grove. It is with reference to this that it is said:
“in the monastery built by the merchant Ghosita.”
Regarding the phrase "Āvuso bhikkhave": here, when the Blessed Buddhas address their disciples, they address them as "Bhikkhave.
However, the disciples, thinking "May we not be like the Buddhas," first say "Āvuso" and then say "Bhikkhave.
When addressed by the Buddhas, the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus gives the reply "Bhadante"; when addressed by the disciples, they reply "Āvuso."
"Whoever" (*yo hi koci*) is an indefinite expression; by this, all such monks are included. "In my presence" (*mama santike*) means near me.
"One who has attained Arahantship" (*arahattappatta*): this is a past participle used in the neuter gender to denote an abstract state, meaning one who has personally attained Arahantship.
Alternatively, the word division is *arahattaṃ pattaṃ*, which means "Arahantship attained by oneself. [The compound] *arahattappattaṃ*.
Or, there is an alternative reading: *attānaṃ* (oneself). "By means of four paths" refers to the four paths of practice mentioned below, not the Noble Paths (*ariyamagga*).

Because it is stated separately as "by means of four paths," for some Arahants, the path is preceded by agitation regarding the Dhamma (*dhammuddhacca*), for one [Arahant] it is preceded by serenity (*samatha*), and for another it is preceded by insight (*vipassanā*).
It should be understood that for one person, there are four paths of practice, each preceded by the "yoke" (yuganaddha).
Or, by "one or another of these": the meaning is that he declares one who has attained Arahantship by means of one or another of these four paths of practice.
For in the case of a dry-insight (sukkhavipassaka) Arahant, the path of stream-entry is preceded by agitation regarding phenomena (dhammuddhacca-pubbaṅgama).
For one who has reached the remaining three paths by means of pure insight alone, the attainment of Arahantship is preceded by the "frenzy for the Dhamma" (*dhammuddhacca*).
Whether or not one has reached the "grasp of the frenzy for the Dhamma," the attainment of Arahantship by an Arahant who has reached the four paths by way of each of the three modes of practice—
those preceded by serenity (*samatha*), etc.— is preceded by each of those respective other paths.
Therefore he said: "by one or another of these.
"He develops insight preceded by serenity" means that having made serenity the precursor and the forerunner, he develops insight;
the meaning is that having first produced concentration, he subsequently develops insight. "The path arises" means...
The first supramundane path arises. In such passages as "he cultivates that path," there is no such thing as repetition and so forth for a path that lasts for only a single moment of consciousness;
however, when one gives rise to the second path and those that follow, it is said of that very same path: "he repeats, develops, and cultivates it.
Thus, the fetters are abandoned and the underlying tendencies are eliminated, up until the path of Arahantship.

By means of gradual practice, all fetters are abandoned and underlying tendencies are brought to an end. "Underlying tendencies are brought to an end" means that they have reached their limit through non-arising once again.
"And furthermore" (*puna caparam*) means another further reason. "He develops serenity preceded by insight" (*vipassanāpubbaṅgamaṃ samathaṃ bhāveti*) means insight...
The meaning is that one develops serenity (samatha) by making it the precursor and the forerunner; having first generated insight (vipassanā), one subsequently develops concentration (samādhi).
"One develops them in conjunction" means one develops them after having joined them together.
Herein, it is not possible to enter absorption with that very same mind and then comprehend mental formations (saṅkhāra) with that very same [mind]. This...
To the extent that he enters into attainments, to that extent he contemplates formations; to the extent that he contemplates formations, to that extent he enters into attainments.
How so? He enters the first jhāna, and having emerged from it, he contemplates formations.
Having contemplated formations, he enters the second jhāna, and having emerged from it...
He comprehends formations. Having comprehended formations, he enters the third jhāna... [and so on] ...up to the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
emerging from that, he comprehends formations. In this way, it is said that he develops serenity and insight in conjunction.
Regarding the phrase "the mind is seized by agitation over states" (*dhammuddhacca-viggahita*), this refers to the fact that for meditators of dull wisdom, this serves as a basis for defilement.

Among the ten states known as the imperfections of insight (*vipassanupakkilesa*), such as illumination (*obhāsa*) and so forth, agitation (*uddhacca*)—which is reckoned as distraction—is the arising of a state of consciousness accompanied by restlessness due to wavering.

A mind that is "struck by the agitation of states" (*dhammuddhaccaviggahita*) is a mind that is seized, deformed, and brought into conflict by that agitation of states; or rather, [it is so called] because of that agitation of states.

The mind becomes conflicted due to the arising of craving, conceit, and views rooted in that [distraction]. Alternatively, the reading is *dhammuddhaccaviggahitamānasaṃ* (a mind conflicted by agitation regarding phenomena).

By the phrase "There comes a time, friend," he shows the moment when, having warded off that agitation regarding phenomena through the discernment of what is the path and what is not the path, one has once again entered the course of insight (*vipassanā*). "That mind which... refers to that in which...
At that time, the mind that has entered and proceeded along that path of insight (vipassanā-vīthi) "abides only internally.
This means that having descended from the path of insight, at that moment it abides and is established upon the object designated as the internal range (gocara-ajjhatta).
It "sits down" (sannisīdati) in the sense that it settles properly right there by way of its occurrence. It "becomes unified" (ekodi hoti) in the sense of being one-pointed (ekagga).
It exists. "It is concentrated" means it is properly placed; it becomes well-established.
This is the commentary on the Sutta.
1. Commentary on the Exposition of the Sutta.
2. Regarding the explanatory discourse on that sutta: "the states arisen therein" refers to the mental and mental-concomitant states (citta-cetasika-dhammā) arisen in that concentration.
By the phrase "in the sense of contemplating as impermanent," etc., he shows the divisions of insight (vipassanā).
"Right view is the path" means the path consisting of right view; for among the eight path factors, each one indeed is the path.
It is said: "He cultivates" means by way of the stream-entry path (*sotāpatti-magga*). "He develops" means by the arising of the once-returning path (*sakadāgāmi-magga*).

"He practices repeatedly" means by the arising of the non-returning and arahant paths (*anāgāmi-arahatta-magga*). Although there is a distinction between these three stages, the answer is given as identical because [the functions of] adverting and so forth are common to all of them.

3. The contemplations of the relinquishment of the perception of light and so forth, as well as non-distraction and the rest, have been abbreviated because they were already explained in the exposition of the knowledge of immediate concentration—namely, the jhānas, attainments, kasiṇas, recollections, foulness, and the long inhalations and so forth.
And therein, the phrase "by way of non-distraction" should be understood by way of the preliminary stage of non-distraction.
Regarding the passage beginning with "contemplating impermanence by way of inhalation," etc.:

In the fourfold set described by way of pure insight (suddhavipassanā), however, at the stage of nascent insight, strong insight preceded by concentration associated with insight should be understood. 4.
In the section on insight-precedence, first, without determining the object by means of "impermanence" and so forth, there is insight.
[The terms] were stated; subsequently, they were stated by defining the object through such phrases as "form is impermanent.
In that context, "of those born" means of those mental states (citta) and mental factors (cetasika) born of that insight (vipassanā).

Regarding the phrase "having Nibbāna as their object": here, "relinquishment" (vosagga) is Nibbāna. For Nibbāna is called "relinquishment" because it is the relinquishing of the conditioned and because it is a state of letting go. And insight—

The states associated with that [consciousness] have Nibbāna as their object because they are established in Nibbāna through the influence of the underlying disposition (*ajjhāsaya*) directed toward Nibbāna.
For even a "support" (*patiṭṭhā*) is called an "object" (*ārammaṇa*) insofar as it is taken as a support; thus, by virtue of being established in Nibbāna, they have Nibbāna as their object.
Indeed, elsewhere in the Canon too, a "support" is spoken of as an "object. As it is said:

“Just as, friend, if a man were to approach a reed-thicket or a grass-thicket, dry and withered for three years, from the eastern direction with a burning grass-torch, the fire would find an entry point; the fire would find a foothold,” and so forth.
Therefore, because the phenomena born therein have relinquishment as their object, they have Nibbāna as their foundation.
The non-distraction—comprising both access and absorption—that is produced by that [insight] acting as its cause and is defined as one-pointedness of mind, is called "concentration.
Thus, the concentration partaking of penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya-samādhi*), which arises subsequent to insight, is indicated.
For this very reason, it is said: "First comes insight, afterwards serenity."

5. In the exposition of the yoke-pair (yuganaddha), since the sequence of the yoke-pair explained below in the commentary on the Suttanta is already clear through the method of the first two expositions,
but the sequence of the yoke-pair at the moment of the path (maggakkhaṇa) is not clear, [the author], without mentioning the practice of the yoke-pair as being non-universal in the prior stage,
shows only that practice of the yoke-pair which is obtained with absolute certainty at the moment of the path.

He said, "In sixteen aspects," and so forth. Therein, among the seventeen aspects beginning with "in the sense of an object" (*ārammaṇaṭṭhena*), the term "yoked together" (*yuganaddha*) mentioned at the end is excluded because it is identical in meaning to the root term; thus, by way of the remaining [sixteen], it is stated as "in sixteen.
"In the sense of an object" means in the sense of an objective support (*ālambana*); that is, by way of the object. The same applies to the others. "In the sense of a range" (*gocaraṭṭhena*).
Even when there is an object (*ārammaṇa*), it is by way of the sense of being supported. "By way of abandoning" (*pahāna*) means by way of relinquishing.
"By way of giving up" (*pariccāga*) means by way of giving up even while there is abandoning, through not taking it up again. "By way of emergence" (*vuṭṭhāna*) means by way of rising up.
"By way of turning away" (*vivaṭṭana*) means by way of turning back through non-returning even while there is emerging. "By way of peace" (*santa*) means...
In the sense of being extinguished (*nibbuta*). "In the sense of being sublime" (*paṇīta*) means, even while being extinguished, in the sense of being supreme or in the sense of being insatiable.

"In the sense of being liberated" (*vimutta*) means in the sense of being free from bondage. "In the sense of being taintless" (*anāsava*) means, even while there is liberation from bondage, in the sense of being devoid of taints that might otherwise arise by taking [the state] as an object.
"In the sense of crossing over" (*taraṇa*) means in the sense of floating across without sinking, or in the sense of transcending.

"In the sense of the signless" means in the sense of being devoid of the signs of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*). "In the sense of the wishless" means in the sense of being devoid of longing (*paṇidhi*).
"In the sense of emptiness" means in the sense of being devoid of dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*). "In the sense of having a single flavor" means in the sense of having a single function.
"In the sense of non-excess" means in the sense of not overstepping one another. "In the sense of the yoke-joined" means in the sense of being a pair.
"Abandoning restlessness" and "abandoning ignorance" are stated according to the abandonment of their respective opposites by that practitioner.
And here, "cessation" (nirodha) refers specifically to Nibbāna. They do not overstep one another:
if serenity (samatha) were to overstep insight (vipassanā), then because serenity belongs to the side of dullness, the mind would lead to indolence. If insight...
If serenity should overreach insight, because insight would then be on the side of agitation, the mind would tend toward restlessness.
Therefore, when serenity does not overreach insight, it does not fall into sloth;
and when insight does not overreach serenity, it does not fall into restlessness. Serenity proceeding evenly [protects] insight from falling into restlessness.
Vipassanā, as it proceeds evenly, protects calm (samatha) from falling into indolence.

Thus, these two have a single function through their function of not overstepping one another; being equal as they proceed, and not overstepping each other, they bring about the accomplishment of the goal.
Their state of being yoked together occurs at the moment of the Path, while at the moment of the insight leading to emergence—
It exists precisely because of the state of being yoked together (yuganaddha).

Since [the terms] "abandoning," "relinquishing," "emerging," and "turning away" are stated by way of the functions of the Path, the defilements and aggregates associated with restlessness and the defilements and aggregates associated with ignorance are specified in order to demonstrate the entire function of the Path.
Because the others are not stated in that manner, they are presented merely as the factors that serve as counteragents.
Restlessness and ignorance alone are indicated. "Turning away" means for one who is turning back.
"Concentration is liberated from the taint of sensual desire" is said because concentration is the direct opposite of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*).
"Through the fading away of lust": that which possesses the fading away—the surmounting—of lust is "fading away of lust"; "from the fading away of lust" is an ablative expression.
Or: "Likewise, through the fading away of ignorance" refers to the liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*), which is concentration associated with the Path;

"liberation by wisdom" (*paññāvimutti*) refers to wisdom associated with the Path. "Crossing over" (*tarato*) means for one who is crossing. "By all aspirations" (*sabbapaṇidhīhi*) means by aspirations of greed, hatred, and delusion, or by all yearnings.
Having thus answered in fourteen ways, [the Blessed One] did not further analyze the sense of having a single flavor (*ekarasa-ṭṭha*) and the sense of non-transgression (*anativattana-ṭṭha*).

He said, "By these sixteen aspects. Why? Because at the conclusion of each of those fourteen aspects, it is specified that "they have a single flavor, they are yoked together, and they do not overstep one another";
thus, those two aspects are also included as specified. Therefore, he said "by sixteen. However, the meaning of being "yoked together" was not even mentioned in the summary (uddesa).
2. Commentary on the Section on Over-excitement Regarding Phenomena (Dhammuddhacca-vāra-niddesa) 6.
In the section on over-excitement regarding phenomena, concerning the statement "a light arises for one who attends to [the object] as impermanent":

this refers to one who stands firm in the contemplation of rise and fall (*udayabbayānupassanā*) and who, through three modes of contemplation, repeatedly contemplates formations (*saṅkhāra*) while practicing insight. As he thus contemplates again and again, within his insights (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), a light arises.

When the mind has become purified through the abandoning of defilements by means of that very factor as it reaches maturity, then at the moment of mental attention (manasikāra) to [the object] as impermanent, suffering, or non-self, a natural radiance arises through the power of insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa).
Thus, first of all, the radiance for one who attends to [the object] as impermanent has been explained. An unskilled practitioner of insight [might then] [misinterpret] that radiance...
When such a radiance arises, he thinks, "Indeed, never before has such a radiance arisen for me; surely I have attained the path, surely I have attained the fruit.
Thus, taking what is not the path to be the path and what is not the fruit to be the fruit, his course of insight (vipassanāvīthi) is interrupted. He [misconstrues] his own course of insight...
Having abandoned [the object], he either falls into distraction, or he sits while conceiving that very radiance through craving, views, and conceit.
Now, this radiance arises for some bhikkhu illuminating only the place where he is sitting cross-legged; for some, it illuminates the interior of the room;
for some, even the exterior of the room; for some, the entire monastery; and for some, a quarter-league or half a league.
[The light] extended for one *yojana*, two *yojanas*... [and so on]... for some, it created a single expanse of light from the surface of the earth up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma-world.
But for the Blessed One, it arose illuminating the ten-thousandfold world-system.
Indeed, this radiance arises illuminating each respective place even within darkness possessed of the four factors.
"Light is a phenomenon": one adverts to light; this means one attends to that various light as either the phenomenon of the path (*maggadhamma*) or the phenomenon of the fruit (*phaladhamma*).

"From that, distraction is restlessness": the meaning is that the distraction which arises from that light, or from the act of adverting, is called restlessness (*uddhacca*). "With a mind agitated by that restlessness."

With his mind opposed by that restlessness as it thus arises— or rather, with his mind opposed to the arising of defilements rooted in that restlessness because that restlessness serves as their cause—
the practitioner of insight, having entered the path of insight, does not, due to being established in distraction or in those defilements rooted therein,
perceive things as they truly are in terms of impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
“He does not understand. Thus the word *iti* should be construed as: “Therefore it is said that his mind is seized by agitation regarding phenomena (*dhammuddhacca-viggahita-mānaso*).
There comes a time when even for a yogi whose mind is defiled by gratification, if investigation arises, he understands thus:
“Insight has conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) as its object; the paths and fruits have Nibbāna as their object.”
“Furthermore, these states of mind have formations as their object; therefore, this illumination is not the path.

Only the contemplation of rise and fall is the mundane path to Nibbāna. Having thus distinguished the path from the non-path and avoided that distraction, he stands firm in the contemplation of rise and fall and clearly discerns formations as impermanent, suffering, and non-self through insight.
For one who investigates in this way, that time arrives. However, not seeing [the truth] in this manner, one becomes overweeningly conceited, thinking, "I have attained the path and its fruit.
"That mind" refers to that very mind of insight (vipassanā-citta). "Internally indeed" means precisely within the internal domain of the object of the contemplation of impermanence.
"Knowledge arises" refers to that same practitioner as he weighs material and immaterial phenomena.
As he investigates, there arises the knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa)—sharp, heroic, and exceedingly clear, with unimpeded momentum like the released thunderbolt of Indra.

"Rapture arises": at that very moment, this fivefold rapture associated with insight—namely, minor rapture (khuddikā), momentary rapture (khaṇikā), showering rapture (okkantikā), uplifting rapture (ubbegā), and pervading rapture (pharaṇā)—fills his entire body.
It arises filling [the body]. "Tranquility arises" means that at that time, there is no distress, no heaviness, no rigidity, no unwieldiness, no sickness, and no crookedness in his body and mind.
Rather, his body and mind are tranquil, light, pliant, wieldy, dexterous, and perfectly clear.

They become truly straight. At that time, with his body and mind assisted by these qualities beginning with serenity (*passaddhi*), he experiences a delight called "superhuman" (*amānusī*). With reference to this, it was said:
"For the bhikkhu who has entered an empty hut, whose mind is peaceful..."
“Supernatural delight arises for one who clearly sees the Dhamma with right insight.
Insofar as one contemplates the arising and passing away of the aggregates, one gains rapture and joy; that is the deathless for one who understands.”
Thus, while he is accomplishing this superhuman delight, there arises bodily and mental tranquility (passaddhi) associated with insight and accompanied by lightness and the other [qualities].
"Pleasure (sukha) arises": at that very time, pleasure associated with insight arises, flooding his entire body. "Resolution (adhimokkha) arises": at that very time...
Faith associated with insight arises as an extraordinary clarity of mind and mental factors.
"Exertion arises" means that at that very time, energy associated with insight arises—neither lax nor over-exerted, but well-exerted.
"Establishment arises" means that at that very time, mindfulness is well-established and firmly grounded.
Mindfulness associated with insight arises, firmly planted and immovable like the king of mountains.
Whatever object he adverts to, attends to, brings to mind, or reviews,
that very object appears to his mindfulness as if the other world appeared to the divine eye, having entered into it and leaped upon it.
"Equanimity" refers both to equanimity of insight (*vipassanupekkhā*) and to equanimity of adverting (*āvajjanupekkhā*).
At that time, equanimity of insight—which is a state of neutrality toward all conditioned phenomena—arises powerfully, as does equanimity of adverting at the mind-door.
For him, as he adverts to this or that object, it is like a loose thunderbolt or a red-hot iron arrow leaping into a leaf-cup.
And it flows with sharpness like a sword. For thus it is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Regarding "equanimity of insight" (*vipassanupekkhā*), the teachers say: "It is the equanimity of indifference (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*) associated with insight.

For if "insight-knowledge" (*vipassanāñāṇa*) were taken [as the meaning], there would be the fault of tautology, since the arising of insight-knowledge has already been mentioned in the phrase "knowledge arises. And in the commentary on the third jhāna...
“It has been said: ‘Equanimity regarding formations and equanimity of insight are identical in meaning;

they are both simply wisdom (paññā), distinguished into two types by way of function. Therefore, there is no fault of tautology when equanimity as specific neutrality associated with insight is mentioned, and it accords with the description of the third jhāna. And because [it is included] among the five faculties...”
“Knowledge, resolve, exertion, and establishment”—by these, the faculties of wisdom, faith, energy, and mindfulness are indicated;
however, the faculty of concentration remains unindicated. Moreover, the faculty of concentration must indeed be indicated by way of its union with the others.
Therefore, concentration that has proceeded evenly [with the other factors] further effects the relinquishing of effort regarding the act of concentrating.
It should be understood that this is what is meant by the term “equanimity.

“Attachment arises”: thus, as one forms an attachment to insight adorned with such phenomena as the aura-light, a subtle and peaceful form of attachment arises, which cannot even be identified as a defilement (*kilesa*). And just as it is with the aura-light...
Thus, when any one of these has arisen, the practitioner of yoga thinks: "Indeed, never before has such knowledge arisen in me;
never before have such joy, tranquility, happiness, resolution, exertion, establishment, equanimity, and inclination arisen.
Surely I have attained the path; surely I have attained the fruit. In this way, he regards what is not the path as the "path."
