He takes what is fruitless as "fruit. For one who takes what is not the path as "the path" and what is fruitless as "fruit," the course of insight (vipassanā-vīthi) is interrupted.
Having abandoned his own original meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), he sits taking pleasure only in that which is attractive.
And here, luminosity and the other [hindrances] are called "defilements" (upakkilesa) by virtue of being the basis for defilement, not because they are unwholesome (akusala).
But *nikanti* (attachment) is both a defilement and the basis for defilement. By way of their bases alone, these are ten;

however, by way of the modes of grasping, they become thirty. How so? For one who grasps [the illumination] thinking, "An illumination has arisen for me," there is the grasping of views (*diṭṭhiggāha*).

For one who grasps it thinking, "Oh, what a pleasing illumination has arisen," there is the grasping of conceit (*mānaggāha*). For one who relishes the illumination, there is the grasping of craving (*taṇhāggāha*).

Thus, regarding illumination (*obhāsa*), there are three modes of grasping by way of view, conceit, and craving. Likewise for the remaining [objects]. Thus, by way of these modes of grasping, there are thirty defilements (*upakkilesa*).

The meaning should be understood in this same manner for the sections on "contemplating as painful" and "contemplating as non-self. For here, the arising of each individual defilement of insight occurs by way of each individual contemplation (*anupassanā*).

It should be understood that this applies not to one person alone, but to all three types of contemplation (*anupassanā*). Having thus shown the defilements by way of insight (*vipassanā*) without differentiation, he now speaks of "attending to form as impermanent" and so forth, in order to show them again by way of differentiation.
In that context, "old age and death appear as impermanent" means:
The appearance of aging and death as impermanent.

7. Because, due to the thirty previously mentioned defilements, an unskilled and incompetent practitioner wavers regarding the aura and so forth, and regards each of these—the aura and so on—as "this is mine, this am I, this is my self."
Therefore, in order to demonstrate that meaning, he spoke the pair of verses beginning with "In the radiance and in knowledge.
Therein, "it wavers" means it trembles and shakes in various ways due to the diverse defilements upon such objects as the radiance.
"By which the mind trembles" means by which [states of] tranquility and bliss the mind trembles and shakes in many ways due to the diverse defilements. Therefore...
The connection should be understood as: "the practitioner wavers both from tranquility and from bliss.
Regarding the phrase "and from the adverting of equanimity": it wavers from the adverting that is termed equanimity; the meaning is that it wavers from the equanimity of adverting.
In the *Visuddhimagga*, however, it is stated as "and from the adverting of equanimity" (*upekkhāvajjanāyañca*). And "from equanimity" refers to the type of equanimity described above.

The meaning is that it wavers due to equanimity (*upekkhā*) and it wavers due to attachment (*nikanti*). And here, because two kinds of equanimity have been pointed out, the meaning has been stated in both ways in the previous passage where it was said, "equanimity arises.

Furthermore, since only a single advertence-equanimity (*āvajjanupekkhā*) exists in each of the contemplations such as the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*), each contemplation is indeed singular: "impermanence, impermanence," and so forth.
It is said that "suffering, suffering" and "non-self, non-self" are cultivated again and again.
For when a skillful, wise, competent, and intelligent practitioner of yoga (yogāvacara) perceives the arising of illumination and so forth, he thinks: "This illumination has arisen for me;
however, it is impermanent, conditioned, dependently originated, subject to destruction, and subject to vanishing."
Or he delimits and examines it with wisdom, thinking: "It is subject to fading away; it is subject to cessation.
Alternatively, it occurs to him: "If light were self, it would be right to grasp it as 'self. But this is non-self and yet is grasped as 'self.
Therefore, seeing that it is non-self in the sense of being not subject to one's mastery, he eradicates the [wrong] view."
If light were permanent, it would be appropriate to grasp it as "permanent. However, this [light] is impermanent, yet it is grasped as "permanent.
Therefore, seeing it as impermanent in the sense of its non-existence after having existed, one eradicates conceit (*māna*).
If light were pleasant, it would be appropriate to grasp it as "pleasant. However, this [light] is painful, yet it is grasped as "pleasant. Therefore, this...
Seeing it as suffering in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away, he exhausts attachment. And just as with the radiance (*obhāsa*), so it is with the rest.
Having thus investigated, he regards the radiance as: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
He regards knowledge... [and so on] ...regards attachment as: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Thus.
Observing thus, he does not waver or tremble regarding the light and the other signs.
Therefore, in order to demonstrate that meaning, he spoke this verse beginning with "These ten points. In this context, "the ten points" refers to the light and so forth.

"Whose wisdom is fully cultivated" means whose wisdom—freed from defilements—is repeatedly touched by, and thoroughly developed through, these points. One who is skilled in the agitation regarding phenomena...

"He becomes skilled" means that the practitioner who has cultivated the ten stages through wisdom becomes expert by means of penetrating the true nature of the aforementioned "restlessness regarding phenomena" (*dhammuddhacca*).
"And he does not fall into delusion" means that precisely because of his skill regarding restlessness regarding phenomena,
he does not fall into delusion by way of the eradication of craving, conceit, and views.
Now, demonstrating once again by another method the very procedure explained previously, he recites the verse beginning with "He is both distracted and defiled.
In this context, a practitioner of dull wisdom encounters both distraction regarding the [meditative] illuminations and the arising of the remaining defilements.
One of middling wisdom encounters only distraction, but not the arising of the remaining defilements; such a person is conceited.
There is. One of sharp wisdom, even after falling into distraction, abandons that overestimation (*adhimāna*) and initiates insight (*vipassanā*).
One of extremely sharp wisdom does not fall into distraction, nor does there arise any remaining defilements (*kilesa*).

"And he is distracted" means that among those [three], the one of dull wisdom falls into the distraction known as agitation regarding phenomena (*dhammuddhacca*). "And he is defiled" means by the defilements of craving, conceit, and views (*taṇhā-māna-diṭṭhi-kilesa*).

"It is defiled" means it is afflicted and oppressed. "The cultivation of the mind falls away" means that for one of dull wisdom, the cultivation of the mind through insight falls away from its very place among the defilements because it has been struck down by their opposites; the meaning is that it collapses.
"It is distracted but not defiled" means that one of medium wisdom is distracted by distraction, but is not [defiled] by the defilements.

"It is defiled": because that one of medium wisdom is conceited, insight fails due to the absence of an undertaking of insight; the meaning is that it does not proceed. "It is distracted but not defiled":
even one of sharp wisdom is distracted by distraction, yet he is not defiled by the defilements. "Insight does not fail": for that one of sharp wisdom...

Even though there is distraction, by abandoning that distraction of overweening pride (*adhimāna-vikkhepa*), because of the presence of the commencement of insight (*vipassanā*), the cultivation of insight does not decline;

the meaning is that it proceeds. "The mind is not distracted and is not defiled" means that for one of exceedingly sharp wisdom, the mind is not distracted by distraction, nor is it defiled by defilements. "There is no falling away from the cultivation of the mind."
His development of the mind through insight (vipassanā-cittabhāvanā) does not fall away; the meaning is that it remains in its proper place due to the absence of the defilements of distraction.

Regarding the phrase "by these four bases," etc., by means of these four bases just mentioned—which function as causes or instruments—the mind, which is agitated by both contraction and distraction, [is established] in the ten bases beginning with illumination.

The commentary on the meaning should be understood according to the connection: "The fourth skilled practitioner of great wisdom, being free from the arising of distraction and defilements, knows in various ways that 'the minds of the other three practitioners of dull wisdom and so forth become thus and thus.
And here, "in brief" refers to the manner in which distraction and defilements arise.

The state of sluggishness of the mind is to be understood. As for "distraction": based on the sense of distraction mentioned in two places—namely, "it is distracted, it is not defiled"—the state of agitation of the mind is to be understood.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Coupling is finished.
2. Discourse on Truth (Saccakathā). Commentary on the Discourse on Truth: 8.
Now, by way of the Noble Path possessing the quality of the "yoke-pair" (yuganaddha), [the Buddha] explained the meaning of truth and the specific excellence of the penetration of truth.

This is a commentary on the previously unstated meaning of the discourse on the Truths, which was delivered with the Suttanta preceding it and which demonstrates the method for discerning the characteristics of the Truths and so forth.
Regarding that, first, in the Suttanta: "tathāni" means "true" (*tacchāni*) by way of their intrinsic nature (*yathāsabhāvavasena*).

For the various classes of phenomena (*dhammajātāni*), being just as they are in their intrinsic nature, are "Truths" (*sacca*) in the sense of truth (*saccaṭṭhena*). The meaning of "truth" (*saccaṭṭha*) is [explained] in the commentary on the description of the first knowledge (*paṭhamañāṇaniddesa*).
It has been said: "Not otherwise" means they are not devoid of the nature as it was stated; for truths do not become non-truths.
"Not different" means they are devoid of any other nature; for what is not a truth does not become a truth.
"This is suffering, monks, this is suchness"—monks, that which is called "this is suffering" is so because of its being according to its own nature.
It is thus (*tathaṃ*). For suffering itself is indeed suffering (*dukkhaṃ*). It is not otherwise (*avitathaṃ*) because there is no deviation from its stated nature;

for suffering does not become what is called "non-suffering. It is not different (*anaññathaṃ*) because it is devoid of any other nature; for suffering does not possess the nature of the origin (*samudaya*) and so forth.
This same method applies to the origin and the other [truths] as well.

1. Commentary on the Exposition of the First Sutta "In the sense of suchness" (*tathaṭṭhena*) means in the sense of its intrinsic nature (*yathāsabhāva*). The meanings of "affliction" (*pīḷana*) and so forth have already been explained in the discourse on knowledge (*ñāṇakathā*).

9. "To be penetrated by a single penetration" (*ekappaṭivedhāni*): there is a penetration by means of a single path-knowledge; or, those which have a penetration [of all truths] simultaneously are "to be penetrated by a single penetration."
“In the sense of non-self” means that all four truths are non-self because they are devoid of a self. For this is said in the *Visuddhimagga*:

“In the ultimate sense, all truths indeed should be understood as empty because of the absence of an experiencer, a doer, one who attains Nibbāna, or one who goes [to a new existence]. Therefore, this is said:
‘There is only suffering, but no one who suffers; there is no doer, but only action exists.’”
“There is extinction, yet no person who has extinguished; there is the path, yet no traveler is found.
Alternatively:
“The first two [truths] are empty of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and self; the state of non-self is empty of even the mere measure of those two.”
"Devoid of a self that is permanent and blissful—this is emptiness regarding them.
"In the sense of truth" means in the sense of non-deceptiveness. "In the sense of penetration" means in the sense of what is to be penetrated at the moment of the path.
"Comprehended under one [heading]" means they are subsumed under each single meaning, such as the sense of "suchness," and have thus come to be counted as one.
The meaning is as follows: "That which is comprised by one is unity" means that because it is comprised by a single [factor], therefore it is "unity.
Although there is a plurality of truths, the singular number is used with reference to their unity.
"One penetrates unity with a single knowledge" means that, having previously established the specific and general characteristics of the four truths while remaining firm, at the moment of the Path—
By means of a single knowledge of the path, one penetrates the unity of the respective suchness and so forth. How?
When the unity of the suchness and so forth of the truth of cessation is penetrated, the unity of the suchness and so forth of the remaining truths is likewise penetrated.
Just as, in the prior stage, having defined the diversity and unity of the five aggregates as they are established, [one penetrates them].

For one established [in the path], at the time of emerging from the path—whether emerging by way of impermanence, suffering, or non-self—even when one aggregate is seen as impermanent and so forth, the remaining aggregates are also seen as impermanent and so forth; it should be understood in this way.

Regarding the phrase "the meaning of suffering is the meaning of suffering, the meaning of suchness": the fourfold meaning of the truth of suffering, beginning with its sense of oppression, is [its] essential nature (*sabhāva*) in the sense of being its intrinsic nature.

Such is the meaning of "thusness" (*tathattha*). This same method applies to the remaining Truths as well. That very fourfold meaning is the meaning of "not-self" (*anattattha*) because of the absence of a self;

it is the meaning of "truth" (*saccattha*) because it is non-deceptive regarding its stated intrinsic nature; and it should be understood that it is called the meaning of "penetration" (*paṭivedhattha*) because it is to be penetrated at the moment of the Path.
10. That which begins with "whatever is impermanent," etc., is presented preceded by the general characteristics (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*). Therein, "whatever is impermanent,"...
That is suffering. That which is suffering is impermanent; thus, the origin and the path are included.
For those three truths are indeed impermanent, and because they are impermanent, they are suffering. That which is impermanent and suffering is non-self;
thus, those same three are included. And that which is impermanent, suffering, and non-self—along with those three, the truth of cessation is also included.
It is included. For all four [truths] are indeed non-self. "That is thus" means that this tetrad of truths is of the nature of reality (*sabhāvabhūta*).
"That is truth" means that very same tetrad of truths is non-deceptive regarding its own specific nature.

Regarding the phrases beginning with "by nine modes," because of the statement, "Bhikkhus, everything is to be directly known," it is so in the sense of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*); and in the sense of the full understanding of suffering (*dukkha-pariññā*).

In the sense of abandoning the origin, in the sense of developing the path, and in the sense of realizing cessation—here, because full understanding through knowledge exists in all four truths, it is included in the sense of full understanding; because abandoning occurs through the vision of the four truths, it is included in the sense of abandoning;
because development of the four truths exists, it is included in the sense of development; and because the realization of the four truths exists...

It should be understood that this is explained in the sense of realization (*sacchikiriya*). In the phrases "in nine ways in the sense of suchness" (*tathaṭṭha*) and so forth, the construction should be made according to the method stated previously.

Regarding "in twelve ways" and so forth, the meanings of "suchness" (*tathaṭṭha*) and the rest have already been explained in the discussion on knowledge (*ñāṇakathā*); their exposition should also be understood according to the same method stated there.

12. Regarding the question, "How many characteristics do the truths have? and so forth, he says there are two characteristics by dividing the six characteristics to be discussed above into two categories: the conditioned (*saṅkhata*) and the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*). Therein, the characteristic of the conditioned and the characteristic of the unconditioned are as follows:
"Monks, there are these three characteristics of the conditioned for the conditioned: arising is discerned, passing away is discerned, [and changeability is discerned]."
“Change while standing is discerned. “Bhikkhus, there are these three unconditioned characteristics of the unconditioned:
arising is not discerned, passing away is not discerned, and change while standing is not discerned. Thus it is said;
this refers both to the conditioned characteristic of the conditioned as "conditioned" and to the unconditioned characteristic of the unconditioned as "unconditioned."

But the conditioned is not the characteristic, nor is the characteristic the conditioned. It is not possible to make known the conditioned without the characteristic, nor the characteristic without the conditioned. However, it is by means of the characteristic that the conditioned becomes manifest.
Furthermore, showing those same two characteristics in detail, he said: "six characteristics. Of the conditioned...
"Of the truths" means of the truths of suffering, origin, and the path; for these are conditioned (*saṅkhata*) because they are produced by coming together through conditions.
"Arising" is birth. "Is manifested" means it is known. "Dissolution" is destruction.

"Alteration of that which has endured" is aging—the state of being otherwise in those things that have reached a state of endurance. Because the three conditioned truths are produced, their arising, dissolution, and alteration are mentioned.
Furthermore, because arising, aging, and dissolution are not themselves produced [as conditioned phenomena], "arising, passing away, and change" cannot be predicated of them.
It should not be said that "arising, passing away, and change are not discerned because they depend on the conditioned";
rather, it should be said that they are "conditioned" because they are transformations of the conditioned. [This applies to] the arising, aging, and dissolution of suffering and its origin.
They say that those factors included within the truths are "included in the truth," whereas the arising, aging, and dissolution of the Truth of the Path are not included in the truth.

In this regard, at the moment of the arising of conditioned phenomena, both the conditioned phenomenon itself and the characteristic of arising are discerned; even that moment reckoned as time is discerned.
When arising has passed, both the conditioned phenomenon itself and the characteristic of aging [are discerned]; even that moment reckoned as time...

"It is discerned; at the moment of dissolution, the conditioned, aging, and the characteristic of dissolution—which is reckoned as time—its very moment, are also discerned," so it is said in the *Khandhaka-vagga-ṭīkā*.
"Of the unconditioned truth" means of the truth of cessation (*nirodha-sacca*).

For that is "unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*) because it is not produced by the coming together of conditions, but is itself spontaneously accomplished. "Of that which is established" means because of its permanence.
It is "stationary" (*ṭhita*), not because it has reached a state of stability. Again, showing those same two characteristics in detail, he says there are "twelve characteristics.

Regarding the questions such as "Of the four truths, how many are wholesome (*kusala*)?", [the answer is] "indeterminate" (*abyākata*). Among the four types of indeterminate—resultant indeterminate (*vipākābyākata*), functional indeterminate (*kiriyābyākata*), material indeterminate (*rūpābyākata*), and Nibbāna indeterminate (*nibbānābyākata*)—it is the Nibbāna indeterminate.
For all four [truths] are indeed devoid of the characteristic of being wholesome or unwholesome.

They are "indeterminate" (abyākata) because they are not explained [as either wholesome or unwholesome]. They might be wholesome by way of the wholesome states of the sense-sphere, fine-material sphere, and immaterial sphere.
They might be unwholesome by way of the remaining unwholesome states, excluding craving.
They might be indeterminate by way of the resultant and functional states of the sense-sphere, fine-material sphere, and immaterial sphere, as well as by way of material phenomena. They might...

In such passages as "the three truths," they are included, meaning they are counted. "By way of basis" means by way of the bases consisting of the unwholesome, the wholesome, the indeterminate, and suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
That which is the truth of suffering, excluding craving, is the remainder of the unwholesome. In the sense of being unwholesome, two truths are included within one truth;
that is, these two—the truths of suffering and origin—are included within one truth in the sense of being unwholesome.
The meaning is that they are subsumed; thus, there is what is called the unwholesome truth (*akusalasacca*). One truth is subsumed by two truths:

one unwholesome truth is subsumed by the two truths of suffering (*dukkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*). That which is the wholesome truth of suffering refers to the wholesome states belonging to the three planes (*tebhūmaka*). These two—suffering and the path truths—are subsumed by one truth in the sense of being wholesome.
There is what is called the wholesome truth (*kusalasacca*). One wholesome truth is comprised by two truths:

the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) and the truth of the path (*maggasacca*). That which is the indeterminate (*abyākata*) truth of suffering consists of the resultant and functional states of the three planes, as well as matter (*rūpa*).

These two truths—the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodhasacca*) and the path—are comprised by one truth in the sense of being indeterminate; thus, there is one indeterminate truth. This is one indeterminate truth.

It is comprised by two truths of the cessation of suffering. Three truths are comprised by one truth: the truths of origination, the path, and cessation are comprised by the single truth of suffering, which consists of the unwholesome, the wholesome, and the indeterminate. One truth is comprised by three truths:
the single truth of suffering is comprised by the truths of origination, the path, and cessation, which are respectively unwholesome, wholesome, and indeterminate.

It is included. However, some explain it thus: "The truths of suffering and its origin are included by the truth of origin in the sense of being unwholesome (akusala), but not in the sense of vision (dassana).
The truths of suffering and the path are included by the truth of the path in the sense of being wholesome (kusala), but not in the sense of vision.
The truths of the cessation of suffering are included by the truth of cessation in the sense of being indeterminate (abyākata), but not in the sense of the unconditioned (asaṅkhata)."
2. Commentary on the Second Discourse (Dutiyasuttantapāḷivaṇṇanā) 13.

Furthermore, desiring to demonstrate the penetration of the truths (*saccappaṭivedha*) by means of the meaning of another discourse, he brought forward and showed the following discourse beginning with "Formerly, monks...
(*pubbe me, bhikkhave*). Therein, "Formerly, monks, before my full enlightenment" (*pubbe me, bhikkhave, sambodhā*)...
"Monks, before my full enlightenment, before my attainment of omniscient knowledge. 'Of one who was not yet fully enlightened' means one who had not yet penetrated all phenomena.
'While being a bodhisatta' means while existing as a bodhisatta. 'This occurred to him' means that while seated at the seat of enlightenment, this reflection arose.
'Gratification' (assāda) means that which is gratified; thus it is called gratification. 'Disadvantage' (ādīnava) means fault."
*Nibbāna* (Emergence) means going away or departure. *Sukha* (Happiness): it is called *sukha* because it makes one happy (*sukhayati*);
the meaning is that it makes whatever arises in one happy. *Somanassa* (Joy): because of its association with rapture and joy, the mind is beautiful (*sobhana-manas*), thus it is *sumanas*;

the state of being *sumanas* is *somanassa*. It is simply happiness distinguished by its association with rapture. *Anicca* (Impermanent) means not lasting. *Dukkha* (Suffering) [is so called] because it is the basis for suffering.

And it is suffering because of the suffering inherent in formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*). "Subject to change" means that, being helpless, its very nature is to undergo transformation through aging and dissolution;
by this, its lack of selfhood (*anattabhāva*) is expressed. "The removal of desire and lust" (*chandārāgavinaya*) is the restraint of lust characterized as desire, not the lust for beauty.
"The abandoning of desire and lust" (*chandārāgappahāna*) is the relinquishing of that very same desire and lust.
Regarding the passage beginning with "As long as," etc.: "As long as I had not fully understood these five aggregates of clinging...

[as before] ...had not penetrated them with higher knowledge, so long did I not claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, nor did I profess to have realized the unsurpassed state of omniscience"—this is the connection [of the text].
*Attha*: meaning. *Kīvañca*: a mere particle. *Yato*: because, or when. *Atha*: immediately thereafter.
"And knowledge and vision arose in me" means that through the performance of the function of seeing, the reviewing-knowledge designated as "vision" arose in me.
"Unshakable" means incapable of being disturbed or moved. "Liberation" refers to the liberation of the fruit of Arhatship (*arahattaphala-vimutti*).
By this very reviewing of the fruit, the reviewing of the path and Nibbāna is also implicitly stated.
"This is the last birth" means this is the final occurrence of the aggregates. "There is no more renewed existence" means there is no further arising now.
By this, the reviewing of the abandoned defilements is expressed; for an Arahant has no reviewing of remaining defilements.
3. Commentary on the Second Exposition of the Discourses 14.

Regarding the sequence for applying the knowledge of penetration into the Truths: in the preliminary stage, having understood that "this is the gratification of form associated with craving," which is called the penetration of abandoning;
and at the moment of the Path, [that which is] termed the abandoning of the origin...
The penetration of the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*). "The truth of the origin" refers to the knowledge of the penetration of the truth of the origin.

For even knowledge that has the noble truths as its object is called "truth" (*sacca*), as in such passages as: "Whatever wholesome states there are, all of them are included within the four noble truths.
This [knowledge] is the penetration of full understanding (*pariññā*) regarding the danger (*ādīnava*) of form; in the prior stage, it is [the knowledge]: "This..."
Having known, "This is the danger of form," at the moment of the Path, there is the penetration of the Truth of Suffering, which is defined as the full understanding of suffering (*dukkhapariññā*).
"The Truth of Suffering" refers to the knowledge of the penetration of the Truth of Suffering. "This is the escape from form" is the penetration by means of realization;
having known, "This is the escape from form," in the preliminary stage, at the moment of the Path, there is what is defined as the realization of cessation (*nirodhasacchikiriyā*).

The penetration of the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*). "The truth of cessation" refers to the knowledge of the penetration of the truth of cessation which has the truth of cessation as its object.

The construction is: "that view and that intention which proceed by way of penetration regarding these three points"—namely, these three aforementioned [points], namely origin, suffering, and cessation. "Penetration through development" (*bhāvanā-paṭivedha*) refers to this cultivation of the path (*maggabhāvanā*).
The penetration of the truth of the path. "Truth of the path" refers to the knowledge of the penetration of the truth of the path. 15.
Again, by another method, showing both the truths and the penetration of the truths, he said: "In how many aspects is it called 'truth'? and so forth.
Therein, because all omniscient Bodhisattvas, seated at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimanda*), [realize] aging, death, and so forth...
Seeking "What indeed is it? they search for the truth of origination—birth and so forth—which is the cause of the truth of suffering;
and while thus searching, they discern and comprehend that birth and so forth are the condition for the truth of suffering, namely aging-and-death and so forth.
Therefore, both that seeking and that comprehension are called "truth" because of the seeking and the comprehension of the truths.
It is said: "In the sense of seeking and in the sense of embracing. And this method applies even to the Paccekabuddhas in their embracing of requisites;
however, for the disciples, it applies in their embracing of requisites by way of hearsay.
"In the sense of penetration" means that at the moment of the Path, there is a single penetration of those things which were previously sought and embraced.
In the passage beginning with "What is the cause" (*kiṃnidāna*), all terms such as "cause" (*nidāna*) and the rest are synonyms for "reason.
For a reason is called "cause" (*nidāna*) because it brings forth (*nideti*) the fruit, as if it were saying, "Come, take this!

It is called "origination" (*samudaya*), "birth" (*jāti*), and "source" (*pabhava*) because the fruit arises (*samudeti*), is born (*jāyati*), and originates (*pabhavati*) from it. Now, in this context:
The meaning: "What is its source? thus it is *kiṃnidānaṃ*. "What is its origin?
thus it is *kiṃsamudayaṃ*. "What is its birth? thus it is *kiṃjātikaṃ*. "What is its provenance? thus it is *kiṃpabhavaṃ*.
However, since its birth is, in the sense already stated, both its source, its origin, its birth, and its provenance, he therefore said: "with birth as its source," and so forth. "Aging-and-death."
The truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*). "The origin of aging-and-death" refers to the truth of origin (*samudayasacca*), which is its condition.

"The cessation of aging-and-death" refers to the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*). "The way leading to the cessation of aging-and-death" refers to the truth of the path (*maggasacca*). In this same manner, the meaning should be understood for all instances. 16.
"Understanding of cessation" means the understanding of cessation by taking it as an object. Birth may be the truth of suffering.

It may be the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*). In the sense of being manifested through the condition of existence (*bhava*), it is the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*); in the sense of being the condition for aging and death, it is the truth of origination.

This same method applies to the remaining [truths] as well. Furthermore, ignorance (*avijjā*) may be the truth of suffering in the sense that the origination of the taints (*āsava*) is the origination of ignorance.
The commentary on the Discourse on Truth is finished.
3. The Discourse on the Factors of Enlightenment (Bojjhaṅga-kathā). Commentary on the Discourse on the Factors of Enlightenment.

17. Now follows the commentary on the previously unstated meaning of the discourse on the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), which was delivered with a Sutta as its introduction by one who wishes to show the specific excellence of the factors of enlightenment established through the penetration of the Truths.
Regarding that, first in the Sutta: "Factors of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅgā*) means the limbs (*aṅgā*) of enlightenment (*bodhi*), or the limbs of one who is enlightened (*bodhis-sa*).
What is meant? It is this collection of states (*dhamma-sāmaggī*) by which, at the moment of the supramundane path, [the mind becomes enlightened].

It is called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) because the noble disciple awakens by means of this harmony of factors— consisting of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—
which serves as the antidote to numerous calamities such as the occurrence of lethargy and agitation, the accumulation [of defilements], devotion to sensual pleasure and self-mortification,
and the adherence to annihilationism and eternalism; for he awakens from the sleep of the continuity of defilements.
It emerges [from the attainment], or it penetrates the four noble truths, or it realizes Nibbāna itself—this is what is meant.
As it is said: "Having developed the seven factors of enlightenment, he fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.

These are called *bojjhaṅgas* because they are the factors (*aṅga*) of that enlightenment (*bodhi*), which is defined as the harmony of these states, just like the factors of jhāna, the factors of the path, and so forth.
Because one awakens by means of this aforementioned harmony of the Dhamma, the noble disciple is called "awakening" (*bodhi*);

and because they are factors of that awakening, they are called "factors of awakening" (*bojjhaṅga*), just as there are factors of an army or factors of a chariot. Therefore, the teachers of the commentaries said: "They are factors of the person who is awakening;
thus, they are 'factors of awakening'. The meaning of the mindfulness factor of awakening and the others has been stated in the *Niddesa* on the "To-be-known-by-super-knowledge" (*abhiññeyya*).
In the exposition of the meaning of the enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅga*), "they conduce to enlightenment" means they conduce to the act of awakening. For what purpose is this awakening?
It is for the purpose of awakening to Nibbāna through the reviewing of it once the task has been accomplished by means of the Path and its Fruit;

or rather, it is for the purpose of awakening from the sleep of the defilements by means of the Path, and for the purpose of the state of being awakened by means of the Fruit. This also applies to powerful insight (*vipassanā*).
The factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) lead to enlightenment. Therefore, this is the common meaning of the factors of enlightenment pertaining to insight, the path, and the fruit.

For in all three instances, they lead to enlightenment, that is, to the penetration of Nibbāna. By this it is meant that they are "factors of enlightenment" (bojjhaṅga) because they are limbs of enlightenment (bodhi).
This refers to the factors of enlightenment as described in the five tetrads beginning with "they awaken, thus they are factors of enlightenment."

The source of their arising has been stated in the *Abhiññeyyaniddesa*. Furthermore, the designation as "agent" (*kattuniddesa*) is for the purpose of showing that the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) possess the capacity to perform their own respective functions, in the sense that they "awaken.

The designation as "state" (*bhāvaniddesa*) is for the purpose of showing the absence of an agent even when there is the capacity to perform one's own function, in the sense of "awakening. They "cause to awaken" those who are awakening through the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment.

Because they are the instigators for yogis, this is an exposition of the factors as causes of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*). "In the sense of awakening" is an exposition of their nature by way of being the instigators and causes, according to the method already stated first.
What is meant is that these are the limbs (*aṅga*) of enlightenment (*bodhi*), hence "factors of enlightenment.

"In the sense of being on the side of enlightenment" means that because they exist on the side of the yogi—who has received the name "enlightenment" in the sense of awakening—they are so called. This is an exposition of their state of being beneficial to the yogi.

"Factors of enlightenment" (bojjhaṅga) means that these are the factors for enlightenment (bodhi). Regarding the set of six beginning with "in the sense of attaining enlightenment": "In the sense of attaining enlightenment" means, for the practitioner, in the sense of reaching enlightenment by means of wisdom (buddhi).
"In the sense of planting" means in the sense of establishing [the seed of enlightenment] in sentient beings.
"In the sense of bringing to completion" means in the sense of bringing to final consummation what has been established. These are the insight-factors of enlightenment (vipassanā-bojjhaṅga).
They say that the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) pertaining to the path and its fruits are distinguished by the three prefixes (*upasagga*)—*pati*, *abhi*, and *saṃ*.

It should be understood that for all these factors designated by the term "dhamma," they are called "factors of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅga*) because they are limbs (*aṅga*) of enlightenment (*bodhi*).
[End of] the commentary on the ten groups beginning with the root-group.

18. Regarding "in the sense of being a root," and so forth: in the tenfold set beginning with "the root-root," "in the sense of being a root" means that among insight and the other [factors], each preceding enlightenment factor (bojjhaṅga) is the root for each subsequent enlightenment factor and for their co-nascent phenomena, both in terms of mutual relationship and as a root.
"In the sense of the practice of the root": practice or occurrence while having become the root is "root-practice. It is in that sense of the practice of the root.

The meaning is: "by way of being the root" in the sense of proceeding [from it]. "By way of the inclusion of the roots": those very factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are "inclusions" because they are grasped for the purpose of being produced from the very beginning; the roots themselves are the inclusions, thus "inclusion of the roots. By that sense of the inclusion of the roots.
Those very same [factors] are "by way of retinue" in the sense of being a retinue through their mutual association. By way of the fulfillment of development...
In the sense of fulfillment. In the sense of ripening by way of reaching the ultimate goal.

Those very same roots, because they are divided into sixfold distinctions, are called "analytical knowledges" (*paṭisambhidā*); thus, they are the "root analytical knowledges. In that sense of root analytical knowledge.
"In the sense of leading to the root analytical knowledges" means that for the practitioner devoted to the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment, those root analytical knowledges—
In the sense of "removing evil. In the sense of mastery over that very same root analytical knowledge (*mūlapaṭisambhidā*) by that yogi.
It should be understood that in other such designations of persons as well, they are called "factors of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅga*) because they are limbs of enlightenment.

Even in the case of those who have attained mastery over the root analytical knowledge—in such expressions of completion as these—it should be understood that they are "fruition-enlightenment factors" (*phalabojjhaṅga*). There is also a reading: "of those who have attained mastery."
The Root-of-Roots Decade is finished.
In the remaining nine decades, beginning with the Root-of-Cause, the meaning of the common terms should be understood by this same method.
However, regarding the uncommon [terms], the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) mentioned above are the causes (hetu), because they produce the states (dhamma) mentioned above.

They are called "conditions" because they act as supports. They are called "purification" because they have become, respectively, purification by substitution of opposites, purification by cutting off, purification by tranquillization, and purification by transcendence.
They are called "blameless" because they are devoid of fault. They are called "renunciation" because of the statement: "All wholesome states are renunciation.
They are called "deliverance" because they are liberated from defilements by way of deliverance through substitution of opposites and so forth.
The enlightenment factors of the path and the fruits are "taintless" (*anāsava*) because they are devoid of taints that have become objects [of consciousness].
All three types of enlightenment factors are "secluded" (*viveka*) because they are empty of defilements by way of secludedness through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-viveka*) and so forth.

The enlightenment factors of insight and the path are "relinquishment" (*vosagga*) because of their nature as relinquishing and because of their nature as leaping forward into relinquishing. The enlightenment factors of the fruit are "relinquishment" because of their nature as leaping forward into relinquishing.

19. The nine decads beginning with "understanding the meaning of the root" (mūlaṭṭhaṃ bujjhantī) should be understood according to the method already stated, as they are demonstrated by way of individual terms.
However, the phrase "of those who have attained mastery" (vasībhāvappattānaṃ) has not been applied here because it is not in the present tense.
The meanings of "the sense of embracing" (pariggahaṭṭha) and so forth are those explained in the *Abhiññeyya-niddesa*.

20. Again, the Elder, having recited the Sutta he himself had taught and wishing to show the method of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) by way of its exposition, stated the introductory setting beginning with "At one time" and then recited the Sutta.

Because it was a Sutta taught by himself, the phrase "Thus have I heard" was not used here. Furthermore, the words "The Venerable Sāriputta" were included here for the purpose of indicating the excellence of the teacher.
This is said by treating oneself as another. For such expressions are employed in the world and in the texts.

"In the morning time" (*pubbaṇhasamayaṃ*) means throughout the entire morning time; the accusative case is used here in the sense of continuous connection. The same method applies to the other two [phrases] as well. "If it occurs to me:
'This is the mindfulness factor of enlightenment' (*satisambojjhaṅgo iti ce me hotī*)" means: if it occurs to me thus, "This is the mindfulness factor of enlightenment. "Immeasurable" (*appamāṇo*).
"It occurs to me thus: 'It is immeasurable'"; "It occurs to me thus: 'It is well undertaken'"; "It occurs to me thus: 'It is perfectly fulfilled'.
"Abiding" means abiding by way of occurring with Nibbāna as its object. "Falls away" means it departs from having Nibbāna as its object.
The same method applies to the remaining factors of enlightenment as well.
"Of the royal minister" means of the king’s chief counselor, or one endowed with a great measure of wealth—that is, the extent of his possessions.
"Various colors" means dyed in various hues; the genitive case is used here in the sense of completion, meaning "with various colors. "A chest of cloth" means a casket for garments.
"A pair of cloths" means a set of two pieces of clothing. "To wear" means to cover oneself. In this sutta, [the intention] of the Elder...

The factors of fruition-enlightenment (phala-bojjhaṅga) have been explained. For when the Elder enters the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) having made the enlightenment factor of mindfulness (sati-sambojjhaṅga) the head, then the others follow along with it.
When he takes any one among the investigation of phenomena (dhamma-vicaya) and the rest, then the remaining ones also follow along with it.
Thus, demonstrating his mastery over the attainment of fruition, the Elder [uttered] this:
"He preached the Suttanta.
Regarding the commentary on the exposition of the Suttanta (21):

If it is asked, "How does it become the enlightenment factor of mindfulness? [the answer is: "It is the enlightenment factor" means that, taking the enlightenment factor of mindfulness as the primary [factor], it is called an enlightenment factor.

When one enters the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), even though other factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are present, if it is said, "In this way, this is the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (satisambojjhaṅga)," then what is the meaning of how that becomes the mindfulness factor of enlightenment?
"To the extent that cessation (nirodha) stands before one" means for as long a time as cessation stands before one; for as long a time as Nibbāna stands before one as an object (ārammaṇa).
The meaning is as follows: "To whatever extent there is a flame" means by whatever measure there is a blaze.

If it is asked, "How does it become immeasurable?"—the sense is: even though the mindfulness enlightenment factor exists, how does this mindfulness enlightenment factor become immeasurable for one who has thus proceeded? "Bound by measure" refers to the defilements and the obsessions.
Furthermore, the formations leading to renewed existence are called "bound by measure" (*pamāṇabaddha*).

According to the statement, "Lust makes a measure, hatred makes a measure, delusion makes a measure," lust and the others are called "measure" because they establish a limit for whoever arises in them, such that one can say, "This person is of this much [extent].
Those defilements and so forth which are bound to, tied to, and dependent upon that measure are called "bound by measure."

They exist. "Defilements" (kilesā) refers to those that have become underlying tendencies (anusaya); "obsessions" (pariyuṭṭhāna) refers to defilements that have reached the stage of active manifestation.
"Formations leading to renewed existence" (saṅkhārā ponobhavikā): "renewed existence" (punabbhava) is the making of existence again and again;

those whose nature is this renewed existence are "leading to renewed existence" (ponobhavika). Formations consist of wholesome and unwholesome kamma. "Immeasurable" (appamāṇo) refers to the aforementioned kind of measure.

It is immeasurable by way of non-existence. Because even the paths and fruits are immeasurable, it is stated as "in the sense of being unshakable" and "in the sense of being unconditioned" in order to distinguish it from them.
It is unshakable because of the absence of dissolution; it is unconditioned because of the absence of conditions.
For that which is both unshakable and unconditioned is utterly devoid of measure.
If it is asked, "In what way is it well-undertaken?", it should be connected according to the method stated immediately following [the section on] the enlightenment factor (*bojjhaṅga*).
"Uneven" (*visama*) means both because they themselves are uneven and because they are the cause for an uneven state; thus they are "uneven.

"A state that is even" (*samadhamma*) means a state that is equal in the sense of being peaceful and in the sense of being sublime. It is "peaceful" (*santa*) due to the absence of measure. As it is said: "To whatever extent, monks, there are conditioned phenomena..."
Because of the statement, “Whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (virāga) is declared the foremost of those phenomena,” it is sublime in the sense of being the supreme among all phenomena.

When it is said, “well-balanced in that state,” it means well-commenced in that which is perfectly even (*susame āraddho susamāraddho*). The phrase “because of having been adverted to” is said with reference to the time when the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) occurs;
it means because the mind-door adverting consciousness has arisen toward Nibbāna, which is characterized by non-arising and so forth.

This has been stated. "It persists" means it continues to proceed. The meanings of "arising" and so forth have already been explained below. This same method applies to the sections concerning the roots of the remaining factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*).
The commentary on the discussion of the factors of enlightenment is finished.
4. Discussion on Loving-kindness (*Mettā*)

Commentary on the Discourse on Loving-kindness (Mettākathāvaṇṇanā) 22. Now follows the commentary on the previously unstated subject of the discourse on loving-kindness, which follows the sequence of the discourse on the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) and is preceded by the Suttanta.
Therein, regarding the Suttanta first: "cultivated" (*āsevitāya*) means cultivated with diligence (*ādarena*).
"Bhāvitāya" means developed. "Bahulīkatāya" means practiced repeatedly. "Yānīkatāya" means made like a vehicle.
"Vatthukatāya" means made like a foundation in the sense of being a basis. "Anuṭṭhitāya" means established.
"Paricitāya" means gathered around or accumulated on all sides. "Susamāraddhāya" means well undertaken, well performed.
"Advantages" (*ānisaṃsa*) means qualities. "To be expected" (*pāṭikaṅkha*) means to be anticipated or desired.
"He sleeps happily" means that unlike other people who sleep in pain, tossing and turning and scratching themselves, he does not sleep in such a manner but sleeps happily;
even when entering sleep, he is as if one who has attained meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). "He awakens happily" means that unlike others who awaken yawning...
Yawning and tossing about, they wake up with suffering; but he, not waking in such a way, wakes up happily and without agitation, like a lotus flower opening.
"He does not see an evil dream" means that even when seeing a dream, he sees only an auspicious one—like one who is worshipping a cetiya, making an offering, or listening to the Dhamma.

And it is as if he were [being pursued]. However, he does not see such an evil dream as others do when they see themselves surrounded by thieves, oppressed by wild beasts, or falling over a precipice.
He becomes dear to people: like a pearl necklace fastened upon the chest or a garland bound upon the head, he becomes dear and pleasing to people.
"He is dear to non-human beings" means that just as he is dear to human beings, so too is he dear to non-human beings.
"Deities protect him" means that deities protect him just as parents protect a child.
"Neither fire, nor poison, nor weapons affect him" means that neither fire, nor poison, nor weapons affect—that is, do not enter—the body of one who dwells in loving-kindness.

It is said that it does not disturb his body. "The mind quickly becomes concentrated" means that for one who dwells in loving-kindness, the mind becomes concentrated very swiftly; there is no sluggishness in him.
"The complexion of the face brightens" means that his face has a serene complexion, like a ripe palm fruit released from its binding. "He dies unconfused."
For one who dwells in loving-kindness, there is no such thing as a death in delusion; he passes away as if falling asleep without confusion.

"Failing to penetrate further" means that being unable to attain Arahantship beyond the meditative attainment of loving-kindness, upon passing away from here, he goes to the Brahma-world like one waking from sleep; this is the meaning of "he is reborn in the Brahma-world."

In the exposition of loving-kindness (*mettā*), "pervasion without limit" (*anodhiso pharaṇā*) means that *odhi* is a boundary or limit; *anodhi* is the absence of a limit. From that, "without limit" (*anodhiso*) or "limitlessly" (*anodhito*) is the meaning;

what is intended is "touching [the object] without restriction. "With limit" (*odhiso*) is by way of a partial extent. "Pervasion of the directions" (*disāpharaṇā*) is pervading within the directions. "All" (*sabbā*) is a term used to include everything without exception.
The meaning of the word "beings" (*sattā*) is explained in the commentary on the matrix for the discourse on knowledge (*ñāṇakathāmātikā*).

This term is used [for those free from passion] by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhīsadda*), just as the term "palmyra fan" (*tālavaṇṭa*) is applied even to a specific type of fan made of split bamboo.
"Averā" means free from enmity (*vera*). "Abyāpajjā" means free from ill will (*byāpāda*). "Anīghā" means free from suffering (*dukkha*).
There is also a reading "anigghā. "Sukhī attānaṃ pariharantu" means: being happy, may they maintain their own self-being (*attabhāva*).
“Without enmity” (*averā*) shows the absence of enmity both within one’s own continuum in relation to others, and within the continua of others in relation to oneself.

In the phrases beginning with “without ill will” (*abyāpajjā*), from the absence of enmity follows the absence of ill will rooted therein. From the absence of ill will follows the absence of suffering rooted therein, as indicated by “without distress” (*anīghā*).
“May they maintain themselves in happiness” indicates the maintenance of the personal existence (*attabhāva*) in happiness due to the absence of suffering.

"Shown": thus should the connection of the words here be understood. And among these four phrases, beginning with "May they be free from enmity," one pervades with loving-kindness according to whichever one is most manifest. Regarding the terms "beings" (*pāṇā*) and so forth:

they are "beings" (*pāṇā*) because of their breathing; the meaning is that their existence depends upon inhalation and exhalation. They are "creatures" (*bhūtā*) because of their having come to be (*bhūta*).
The meaning is "reborn. *Puṃ* refers to hell; they go (*galanti*) into that *puṃ*, thus they are called *puggalā*.
The term *attabhāva* refers to the body, or specifically to the five aggregates (*khandha-pañcaka*), because it exists merely as a designation based upon them.
Those who are included, delimited, and contained within that *attabhāva* are said to be "included within the *attabhāva*" (*attabhāvapariyāpannā*). And just as [the term] "beings" (*satta*)—
In this way, the remaining terms should also be understood by applying them through conventional usage; all of these are synonyms for "all beings.

While there are indeed other synonyms for "all beings" such as "all creatures" (*sabbe jantū*) and "all living things" (*sabbe jīvā*), these five alone are taken here for the sake of clarity when it is said: "The liberation of mind through loving-kindness is an undirected pervasion in five ways."
However, for those who would maintain that there is not only a difference in the mere wording of "beings," "living things," and so forth,
but also a difference in their meaning, the practice of radiating [loving-kindness] without limitation would be contradicted. Therefore, without grasping the meaning in that way,
one radiates loving-kindness without limitation by means of any one of these five aspects.
However, in the case of limited pervasion (*odhiso pharaṇa*), it is stated by way of gender as "women" and "men"; by way of noble and ordinary persons as "noble ones" and "non-noble ones";

and by way of rebirth as "devas," "humans," and "those in the states of misery. In the case of universal pervasion (*anodhiso pharaṇa*), because one pervades all directions without making a distinction between directions according to the method beginning with "all beings," it is called "unlimited pervasion. [In this case,] in all directions, [one pervades] "all women," and so forth.
There is directed pervasion by way of method and limited pervasion.

However, since these three kinds of pervasion with loving-kindness are described in terms of a consciousness that has reached absorption (*appanā*), therefore absorption should be understood in the three sections.
First, in the case of non-directed pervasion: "May all beings be free from enmity" is one; "may they be free from affliction..."
One [says] "May they be free from enmity," another "May they be free from affliction," and another "May they maintain themselves in happiness.
For these four are also spoken of by way of bringing about welfare; for loving-kindness has the characteristic of bringing about welfare.
Thus, with respect to the five aspects beginning with "beings," there are twenty attainments (appanā) by way of the four attainments for each aspect, specifically...
In the case of the "all-pervading" (pharaṇa) meditation, there are twenty-eight attainments (appanā) by way of four for each of the seven modes, such as "all women.

In the "directional pervasion" (disāpharaṇa), however, following the method of "all beings in the eastern direction," etc., there are two hundred [attainments] by taking twenty for each individual direction. Then, following the method of "all women in the eastern direction," etc.,...
By applying this method of twenty-eight for each direction, there are two hundred and eighty, which makes four hundred and eighty attainments (*appanā*).
Thus, all those mentioned here amount to five hundred and twenty-eight attainments.

And just as the pervasion (*pharaṇā*) by means of the threefold method was stated for loving-kindness (*mettā*), it should be understood that the same is stated for compassion (*karuṇā*), gladness (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*).
1. Explanation of the Chapter on the Faculties (Indriyavāra) 23.
Now, in order to show the manner of bringing forth loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the cultivation of the faculties and so forth, he said:
"Having avoided the affliction of all beings," and so on. In this context, "affliction" (*pīḷana*) refers to internal bodily affliction; "injury" (*upaghāta*) refers to external [affliction].
*Śarīropaghātam*: physical injury. *Santāpanti*: mental distress, whether by such means or otherwise. *Pariyādānaṃ*: the natural exhaustion of life and other factors. *Vihesanti*:
harming from the side of others, i.e., the destruction of life. *Vajjetvā*: having removed each of these—oppression and so forth—by one's own mind alone.
These five terms, beginning with oppression, are presented by way of avoiding their opposites in the practice of bringing forth loving-kindness (*mettā*).
The phrases beginning with "without oppression" (*apīḷanāya*) and so forth are stated by way of the extension of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
"Without oppression" means in a manner free from oppression; the connection is: "he extends loving-kindness toward all beings. The same applies to the remaining [phrases].

"May they not be hostile, may they not suffer, may they not experience suffering"—these three are also statements that negate the opposites of the extension of loving-kindness. Regarding the word "may not" (*mā*), it means "may they not be."
The meaning is as follows: "Free from enmity, happy, with happy hearts"—these three are expressions concerning the application of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
It should be understood that the pair "unafflicted and free from distress" is included within the expression "happy.
"With happy hearts" is a demonstration of the constant occurrence of that very happiness. Furthermore, "with happy hearts" means "may they maintain themselves in happiness."

And they are one in meaning. Alternatively, by the words "without oppression" (*apīḷanāya*) and so forth, the expressions for non-affliction (*abyāpajja*) and fearlessness (*anīgha*) are included. "By eight modes" means by these eight modes:
the five modes of bringing about loving-kindness beginning with "without oppression," and the three modes of bringing about loving-kindness beginning with "may they be free from enmity.
"He loves" (*mettāyati*) means he feels affection. "He intends that state" (*taṃ dhammaṃ cetayati*) means he intends that bringing about of welfare.
It means that one intends, aims, and sets [the mind] in motion.
"One is liberated from all obsessions of ill will" means one is liberated by way of suppression from all occurrences of ill will, which constitute the opposites of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
Loving-kindness, the mind, and liberation—these are simply the single state of loving-kindness described in three ways.
The three terms "secure," "safe," and "blissful" are stated as a concise summary of the modes previously mentioned.
The five faculties, described by way of the formula beginning with "one resolves with faith," are indeed associated with loving-kindness (*mettā*).

Regarding the six sections beginning with "cultivation" (*āsevanā*): in these, "cultivation" (*āsevanā*) refers to that by which loving-kindness is cultivated; likewise, "development" (*bhāvanā*) is the frequent practice.
*Alaṅkāra* means adornment. *Svālaṅkatā* means well-adorned, embellished. *Parikkhāra* means requisites. *Suparikkhatā* means well-provided with.

*Parivāra* [is so called] in the sense of protection. Furthermore, the twenty-eight terms beginning with "cultivation" (*āsevana*) are stated for the purpose of praising loving-kindness (*mettā*). Among these, *pāripūrī* means the state of being fulfilled. *Sahagatā*...
“Accompanied by loving-kindness”: likewise for “co-nascent,” and so forth. “Entry-points” (*pakkhandanā*) means entering into loving-kindness;
or, that through which one enters into loving-kindness are the entry-points. Likewise for “sinking,” and so forth.

“The touching of this as peaceful” means that this loving-kindness is touched as being peaceful by these [mental factors]; the neuter gender is used here, as in such expressions as “this is the foremost” (*etadaggaṃ*).
"Well-established" means well-settled. "Well-raised up" means well-elevated.
"Well-liberated" means well-freed from their respective opposing factors. "Producing" means, having become associated with loving-kindness (*mettā*), they produce loving-kindness.
"Illuminating" means they make it manifest. "Causing to shine forth" means they cause it to radiate.
2–4. Explanation of the Triplets on the Powers, etc. (24–27).

The Powers should be understood in the same manner as explained in the section on the Faculties (*indriya*). The sections on the Factors of Enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) and the Factors of the Path (*maggaṅga*) are stated by way of a formal enumeration (*pariyāya*), not according to their specific characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*).
In the section on the Factors of the Path, Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood are included by way of the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*) of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
These are stated by way of access concentration (*upacāra*), not by way of absorption (*appanā*); for these do not coexist with loving-kindness (*mettā*).
The meaning of the remaining seven sections beginning with "all breathing things" should be understood in the same manner as that explained for the first section.
As for the method of developing loving-kindness, it should be taken from the *Visuddhimagga*.
The commentary on the Discourse on Loving-kindness is finished.
5. The Discourse on Dispassion;
Commentary on the Discourse on Dispassion.

28. Now follows the commentary on the previously unstated meaning of the discourse on dispassion (*virāga*), which was spoken immediately after the discourse on loving-kindness (*mettā*)—the latter concluding with the purpose of the path—and which has dispassion as its precursor to the path.

In this regard, first of all, one who wishes to demonstrate the meaning of the two Sutta passages stated thus: "Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated" (*Mahāva 23*).
"Dispassion is the path, liberation is the fruit"—this is the summary established. Therein, wishing first to demonstrate the meaning of the words, he said: "How is dispassion the path? and so forth.
In that context, "it discolours" (virajjati) means it becomes dispassionate (virattā). The remaining terms have meanings already explained in the exposition of path-knowledge.
As for "dispassion" (virāga): since right view discolours [the defilements], therefore its name is "dispassion"—this is the meaning. It...
And because it is fading away (*virāga*), its object is fading away... [as before] ...it is established in fading away; therefore, it is called "fading away.

In this way, the connection of the five expressions beginning with "having fading away as its object" should be understood. Therein, "having fading away as its object" means having Nibbāna as its object.
"Having fading away as its domain" means having Nibbāna as its sphere. "Arisen in fading away" means arisen in Nibbāna. "Established in fading away" refers to the mode of its occurrence.
"Established in Nibbāna": established in Nibbāna by way of non-returning. "And Nibbāna is dispassion (*virāga*)":
Nibbāna is called dispassion because it is the cause of dispassion. "Arising with Nibbāna as its object":
arisen with Nibbāna as its object, or arisen by way of having Nibbāna as its object. All those phenomena, beginning with contact, that are associated with the Path—

They are called "dispassion" (virāga) because they become dispassionate in the sense of being free from passion. "Conascent" means the seven path-factors beginning with right view that are conascent with right view.
"They go toward dispassion" means that the path goes by making Nibbāna—dispassion—as its object;
thus, because it has dispassion as its object, it is called "dispassion," and in the sense of "seeking," it is called the "path."
The meaning is "it occurs. Each individual path-factor (maggaṅga) receives the name "path" (magga).

Thus, when the path-nature of each factor is stated, the path-nature of right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) is also already stated. For this very reason, it is said "by means of this path," referring to the inclusion of the eight path-factors.
And by the phrase "and the Buddhas," the Pacceka-buddhas are also included; for they too—these two... [text continues]
Because it is said, "Monks, there are two Buddhas: the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Paccekabuddha," they are indeed Buddhas.
*Agataṃ* means that which has never been gone to (*agatapubba*) in the beginningless (*anamatagga*) cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). *Disā*:

it is called *disā* because it is seen (*dissati*), pointed out (*apadissati*), and aimed at (*abhisandahīyati*) by means of the entire practice; or else, it is so called because it is seen as the supreme happiness by all Buddhas.
It is called *disā* because it is pointed out (*apadissati*) or spoken of; or else, it is called *disā* because all suffering is seen, relinquished, and cast off by means of it.

That is the direction. What is meant by "the eightfold path"? It is said that this collection of eight factors is called a "path" (*magga*) in the sense of going, because by means of it one goes to Nibbāna. [This is] for the sake of the many recluses and brahmins...
"Of the doctrines of others" means of the various [teachings] of other ascetics and brahmins who hold views different from this one.
"Foremost" means distinguished among those remaining paths. "Best" means most worthy of praise compared to the remaining paths. "Liberation" (mokkha) means "good for the mouth" (*mukhe sādhu*);
the meaning is that this alone is good as facing toward the [goal], compared to the remaining paths. "Supreme" means having transcended the remaining paths by far.
He is honored by the rest of the world through various modes of service. The word *iti* is a particle used in the sense of a reason.
Therefore, the intention is that it was said by the Blessed One: "Of paths, the Eightfold is the best. For it was indeed said by the Blessed One:
"Of paths, the Eightfold is the best; Of truths, the Four are supreme."
“Dispassion is the best of states, and the Visionary is the best of bipeds.

Having omitted that [line] here, it is stated: “The Eightfold Path is the best of paths. In the remaining sections as well, the meaning should be understood according to this method and the method explained below.
Regarding “dispassion as vision,” etc.: dispassion in the sense of vision is “dispassion as vision. From the standpoint of the faculties, [this refers to] the power.
It should be understood that because of its preeminence, power (*bala*) is mentioned here before the faculties (*indriya*).

The passage beginning with "the faculties in the sense of predominance" is an exposition of the meaning of the faculties and so forth, not of dispassion (*virāga*). "The truths in the sense of suchness" should be understood as the knowledge of the truths (*sacca-ñāṇa*).
"Purification of virtue" refers to right speech, right action, and right livelihood. "Purification of mind" refers to right concentration. "Purification of view" refers to...

"Right view and right intention. "In the sense of being liberated" means in the sense of being freed from the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path. "True knowledge" (*vijjā*) is right view. "Liberation" (*vimutti*) is liberation by eradication. Nibbāna, which plunges into the deathless, is the "path" in the sense of being the ultimate goal;
it is called the "path" because it is sought after through the reviewing of the path and its fruit.

All the states mentioned in this exposition of fading away (*virāga*) occur only at the moment of the path (*magga*). In the exposition of deliverance (*vimutti*), they occur at the moment of the fruit (*phala*). Therefore, zeal and attention are also associated with the path and the fruit. 29.
The meaning in the exposition of deliverance should be understood in the same manner as stated in the exposition of fading away.

Here, however, the fruit is "deliverance" because it is deliverance through subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi-vimutti*); Nibbāna is "deliverance" because it is deliverance through escape (*nissaraṇa-vimutti*). [The states] that arise together...
Passages such as “the seven factors” are not mentioned here because they are not found in this context.
It is stated only that it is “liberation in the sense of relinquishment” because it is itself liberated from its own fruit. The rest is exactly according to the method already explained.
The commentary on the discussion of dispassion (*virāga*) is finished.
6. Discourse on the Analytical Knowledges (Paṭisambhidākathā) 1. Explanation of the Section on the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakkapavattanavāra-vaṇṇanā) 30.
Now, by way of demonstrating the various divisions of the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) accomplished through the path characterized as dispassion (virāga), that which has been spoken...
A commentary on the previously unstated meaning of the *Paṭisambhidā-kathā*, preceded by the *Dhammacakkappavattana-sutta*.
First, regarding the *Suttanta*: "At Bārāṇasī" means that there is a river named Bārāṇasā; the city situated not far from that Bārāṇasā is Bārāṇasī.
[The Buddha was] in that Bārāṇasī. "In the Deer Park at Isipatana" refers to the place so named because it was a landing and departure point for sages (*isi*).
In the monastery known as Migadāya (the Deer Park), because it was the place where the gift of safety to the deer had been bestowed.
For it is there that all the Buddhas who have arisen fall [like rain], meaning they sit down for the purpose of setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.

Having emerged from the attainment of cessation after seven days had passed since leaving the Nandamūlaka mountain slope, and having performed the duty of washing his face at Lake Anotatta, he traveled through the air.

It is called "Isipatana" because seers (isī) come here and descend by way of gathering together as *paccekabuddhas*, they assemble for the purpose of the Uposatha and for non-Uposatha occasions, and they fly back from there toward Gandhamādana;
thus, it is called "Isipatana" by way of the descending and flying up of these seers.
There is also the reading "Isipadana. Regarding the term "Pañcavaggiya":
“Koṇḍañña, Bhaddiya, Vappa, Mahānāma, and Assaji—these five great elders are called the ‘group of five’ (pañcavagga).
A group consisting of these five monks mentioned thus is the “group of five. That which exists within that group of five, because it is included therein, [is called pañcavaggiya].
"To the group-of-five [monks], to those five monks. "He addressed the monks" means:
from the time he made his resolution at the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs) in due order until reaching his final existence;
and in that final existence, having gone forth, reached the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), and sat there upon the invincible throne (aparājita-pallaṅka), having shattered the army of Māra—
Having recollected his former existences during the first watch of the night, having purified the divine eye during the middle watch,
and having attained omniscience at the conclusion of the final watch— causing the ten-thousandfold world system to resound and tremble— he spent seven days at the seat of enlightenment.
Then, at the request of Mahābrahmā, he surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye and, out of compassion for the world, [prepared to teach the Dhamma].
Having gone to Bārāṇasī and persuaded the group of five monks, desiring to set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, he addressed them:
"These two, monks, are the extremes. "These two, monks, are the two divisions.
Now, by the utterance of these words, the sound of that utterance reached down as far as the Avīci hell and up as far as the peak of existence, spreading throughout the ten-thousandfold world system.
At that very moment, eighteen koṭis of Brahmās assembled.
While the sun was setting in the western quarter, the full moon, conjoined with the constellation Uttarāsāḷha, rose in the eastern quarter.
At that time, the Blessed One, beginning the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, said: "These two..."
“Monks, these are the extremes,” he said, beginning with those words.
Therein, “by one who has gone forth” means by one who has gone forth after cutting off the household fetter and sensual desires.

“Should not be cultivated” means they should not be frequented. Because they are specifically suitable vessels for the practice of those who have gone forth, [the Buddha said]: “By one who has gone forth...”

"It should not be pursued," it is said. And as for this "devotion to the pleasure of sensual desires among sensual pleasures": this refers to devotion to the defiled pleasure of sensual desires (*kilesakāmasukha*), or to that which is the basis for defiled sensual pleasure, directed toward objective sensual objects (*vatthukāma*).
"Inferior" means base. "Vulgar" means belonging to village-dwellers.
"Common to the worldlings" means practiced by worldlings (*puthujjana*), that is, by blind and foolish people. "Unnoble" means...
It is not noble. Or else, it does not belong to the pure, supreme Noble Ones (*ariya*).

"Associated with what is harmful" means not associated with what is beneficial; the meaning is that it is not dependent on a cause that brings about happiness. "Devotion to self-mortification" means devotion to one's own mortification;
the meaning is causing suffering to oneself. "Suffering" refers to [practices] such as lying on a bed of thorns, which lead to the destruction of oneself.
It brings suffering. Because ascetics regard it as "the highest austerity," it is not called "inferior" here in order to protect their minds;
because it is the nature (dhamma) of those who have gone forth, it is not called "vulgar"; and because it is not shared with householders, it is not called "worldly.
However, in that context, some who merely claim to have gone forth—adhering to the doctrine of Nibbāna in this very life—[say]: "Since..."
"Friends, this self is provided with and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure and enjoys them;
to this extent, friends, this self has attained Nibbāna in the present life.

Because he grasped it thus, and for the sake of protecting their minds, and because that undertaking of the Dhamma was pleasant in the present, it was not said to be "suffering. This is the pursuit of sensual pleasure.
The pursuit of sensual pleasure should not be cultivated because it is defiled by craving and views in the present, because it results in suffering in the future for those devoted to it,
and because those so devoted are bound by the fetters of craving and views; likewise, the pursuit of self-mortification should not be cultivated because it is defiled by views in the present,
because it results in suffering in the future for those devoted to it, and because those so devoted are bound by the fetter of views.
"These, indeed" means "these are those. "Without approaching" means not having approached.
"Middle" means they exist in the middle because of the absence of defiled pleasure and pain; that very [path] is the "way" (*paṭipadā*) because one proceeds toward Nibbāna by means of it.

"Fully awakened to" means penetrated. Regarding the phrases beginning with "making the eye": it makes the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*), thus it is "making the eye. It is "making knowledge" (*ñāṇa-karaṇī*).

This is a synonym for that very thing. "For the sake of peace" means for the sake of the pacification of the defilements (*kilesa*). "For direct knowledge" means for the purpose of directly knowing the Four Truths.
"For full enlightenment" means for the purpose of fully awakening to those very same truths. "For Nibbāna" means for the purpose of the realization of Nibbāna.
Alternatively, it is "eye-making" because it produces the knowledge of the path of seeing; it is "knowledge-making" because it produces the knowledge of the path of cultivation.
For the subsiding of all defilements; for the direct knowledge of all phenomena; for the realization of the fruit of Arahantship;
and for the extinction (nibbāna) of both defilements and the aggregates. The discourse on the Truths has been stated in the exposition of what is to be directly known.
Thus, having proclaimed the Truths, the Blessed One [described] the sequence of his own penetration for those who had placed great trust in him.

Having heard this, by instilling great respect for practice and standing firm in that practice, he perceived the penetration of truth and showed the sequence of his own realization with the words, "Bhikkhus, 'This is the Noble Truth of Suffering'—thus it was, etc.
In that context, *ananussutesu* means "not heard from others"; the sense is: not heard by following after another. The meaning of *cakkhu*, etc., is as follows: [text continues]

It will be made manifest later. "This is the noble truth of suffering, this is the origin of suffering, this is the cessation of suffering, this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering"—this is the penetration through vision of the four truths on the stage of training (*sekhabhūmi*).
"To be fully understood, to be abandoned, to be realized, and to be developed"—[this is the penetration] of the four truths...
