Penetration by development occurs on the plane of the trainee (sekha-bhūmi) itself. The reviewing of the four truths—namely, "it has been fully understood," "it has been abandoned," "it has been realized," and "it has been developed"—occurs on the plane of the non-trainee (asekha-bhūmi).
"Three turnings" refers to the three turnings consisting of the knowledge of the truth, the knowledge of the task, and the knowledge of what has been done.

It has three turnings, thus it is "three-turning" (*tiparivaṭṭa*). For herein, the knowledge of things as they truly are regarding the four truths—namely, "This is suffering, this is the origin of suffering, this is the cessation of suffering, this is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering"—is called "knowledge of the truths" (*saccañāṇa*).
Regarding those very same [truths], [the knowledge that] "it is to be fully understood, it is to be abandoned, it is to be realized..."
"Should be developed": the knowledge that recognizes what must be done in this way is called "knowledge of duty" (*kicca-ñāṇa*). "Fully understood, abandoned, realized, and developed":
the knowledge that recognizes the state of having completed that duty in this way is called "knowledge of what has been done" (*kata-ñāṇa*).
"Twelve aspects" means twelve aspects by way of three aspects for each of those very truths.
"Assa" means twelvefold. "Knowledge and vision" (ñāṇadassana) refers to the vision characterized as knowledge that has arisen by way of these twelve aspects consisting of the three turnings.
"Attamanā" means with a mind that is one's own (sakamana). For because beings desire happiness and are averse to suffering, their minds are associated with rapture and joy;
thus they are called "with a mind that is one's own," or "with a mind delighted by rapture and joy," or "with a mind seized [by joy]," or "with a mind pervaded [by joy]."
Or it means "the meaning. *Abhinandunti* means they rejoiced, having become intent upon [it]. *Veyyākaraṇe* refers to the Suttanta;
for the Suttanta, being devoid of verses (*niggāthaka*), is called a *veyyākaraṇa* simply because it explains the meaning. *Bhaññamāne* means while being spoken;
the present tense is used here to indicate proximity to the present, meaning "when it has been spoken. *Virajaṃ* means free from the dust of passion and so forth.

"Stainless" (*vītamaḷaṃ*) means free from the stains of lust and so forth. For lust and the like are called "dust" (*rajo*) in the sense of overwhelming, and "stain" (*maḷa*) in the sense of defiling.
"The eye of Dhamma" (*dhammacakkhu*) refers in some instances to the knowledge of the first path, in some to the first three path-knowledges, and in some even to the fourth path-knowledge;
however, here it refers specifically to the knowledge of the first path. "Whatever has the nature of arising," [is subject to cessation].
The meaning is that the *dhammacakkhu* (the eye of the Dhamma) arose for him as he proceeded thus by way of insight (*vipassanā*), [realizing]: "All that is subject to cessation.
Regarding the term *dhammacakka*: it refers both to the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of teaching (*desanā-ñāṇa*).

For the Blessed One, while seated on the seat of enlightenment (*bodhipallaṅka*), possessed the twelvefold knowledge of penetration regarding the Four Truths; and likewise, while seated at Isipatana, he possessed the twelvefold [knowledge] of teaching.

The knowledge that sets in motion the teaching through the proclamation of the Truth is also called the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*). For both of these are indeed the knowledge set in motion by the One of Ten Powers.
By the Blessed One, in proclaiming this through this teaching, the Wheel of Dhamma is said to have been set in motion.
Now, as for this Wheel of Dhamma, it [was turned] until the Elder Aññāta-Koṇḍañña, together with eighteen koṭis of Brahmās...
As long as one has not yet been established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), the Blessed One is said to be "setting it in motion";
but once one is established, it is said to have been "set in motion. With reference to this, it is said: "And when the Wheel of Dhamma had been set in motion by the Blessed One.

"The earth-dwelling deities" (*bhummā devā*) refers to the deities who dwell upon the earth. "They raised a cry" means that they simultaneously gave their approval with the exclamation "Well done! (*sādhukāra*).
Saying "This is so, Blessed One," and so forth, they raised a great sound of acclaim. "Irrefutable" means that it is impossible to state a contrary view, such as "this is not so.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the gods and Brahmās who had assembled there all gave their approval with a single voice;
however, those who had not come to the assembly, such as the earth-dwelling deities and others, [gave their approval] individually.
It should be understood that upon hearing the sound, they gave their approval. Among them, the earth-deities (*bhummadeva*) are those born upon mountains, trees, and so forth;
although they are included within the realm of the Four Great Kings (*cātumahārājika*), they are mentioned here separately.
They are called "those belonging to the Four Great Kings" because these deities have the four great kings—namely Dhatarattha, Virūḷhaka, Virūpakkha, and Kuvera—as their lords.
They are situated in the center of Sineru. Among them, some are mountain-dwelling and some are space-dwelling; their succession extends as far as the Cakkavāḷa mountain range.

The Khiḍḍāpadosika, Manopadosika, Sītavalāhaka, Uṇhavalāhaka, the divine son Candima, and the divine son Suriya—all these also belong to the realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika). [The Thirty-three]...

They are called the Thirty-three (Tāvatiṃsa) because people were born there. Furthermore, it is also said that "Tāvatiṃsa" is simply the name of those deities. Among them, some dwell on mountains and some dwell in the sky;
their lineage extends as far as the Cakkavāḷa mountain range, and the same is true for the Yāma and other deities.
For even within a single divine world, there is no lineage of deities that does not reach the Cakkavāḷa mountain range.
There is none. They are called *Yāma* because they have gone to and arrived at divine bliss (*dibba-sukha*). They are called *Tusita* because they are contented and delighted.
They are called *Nimmānarati* because, when they desire to enjoy more than the naturally provided objects, they create and create whatever enjoyments they wish for and then delight in them.
They are called *Paranimmitavasavatti* because, having known the inclinations of others' minds, they exercise mastery over the enjoyments created by others. [In] the Brahma-world...
"Appointed for the Brahma-vessel" means belonging to the Brahma-group (*brahmakāyika*). All five-aggregate (*pañcavokāra*) Brahmas are included.

By specifying the word "at that moment" (*tena khaṇena*), it is stated as "at that instant" (*tena muhuttena*). This means by an instant reckoned as a "moment," not by an ultimate moment (*paramattha-khaṇa*).
"As far as the Brahma-world" means including the Brahma-world within the limit. "Sound."
The sound of "Well done! [arose]. "Ten-thousandfold" means encompassing ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*). "It shook" means it shook intensely as it rose upward.
"It trembled" means it trembled intensely as it rose upward and descended downward. "It quaked" means it quaked intensely as it moved toward the four directions.
And when the Bodhisatta was descending into his mother’s womb for the sake of attaining full enlightenment...
Then, as he was departing from there, the great earth trembled through the power of his merit; at the time of his full enlightenment, through the power of his penetrative knowledge;
at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, through the power of his knowledge of teaching, the earth trembled through the majesty of the deities as if wishing to give a cry of "Well done!";
and at the relinquishing of the life-force during the Great Parinibbāna, it trembled because it could not endure the agitation of the mind caused by compassion.
The earth trembled as if by the supernatural power (*devatānubhāva*) of the deities. "Immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*) means the measure of a Buddha.
"Exalted" (*uḷāra*): in such passages as "they were eating exalted, exalted hard foods," it is said that what is sweet is exalted;
in such passages as "his mind does not incline toward exalted clothing and enjoyments," it is said that what is refined is exalted. "Truly, you are exalted... [and so forth].
In such passages as "Vacchāyana praises the ascetic Gotama with praise," it is said to be "supreme" or "exalted.
But here, it is said to be "vast" and "exalted. "Radiance" refers to the radiance produced by the power of the knowledge of the teaching and the power of the deities.
"In the world" refers specifically to the ten-thousandfold world-system (*cakkavāḷa*). "Surpassing even the divine majesty of the gods" refers to the gods...
This is his majesty: the radiance of his robes extends for twelve *yojanas*, as does that of his body, his ornaments, and his celestial mansion (*vimāna*).
The meaning is that it surpasses even the divine majesty of the gods. "Utterance" (*udāna*) refers to an exclamation consisting of joy and knowledge.
"He uttered" (*udānesi*) means he made this utterance. The sound of the utterance of this [first] exclamation was: "O Koṇḍañña, you have indeed understood! (*Aññāsi vata, bho Koṇḍañño*).
It remained pervading the ten-thousandfold world system. *Aññāsikoṇḍañño* means "Koṇḍañña who knows thoroughly.

In the exposition of the eye and so forth, regarding the phrases "in the sense of seeing" and so on: the single knowledge (*ñāṇa*) is called the "eye" because it performs the function of seeing toward the knowable object as previously described;
it is called "knowledge" because it performs the function of knowing; and it is [called "wisdom"] because it performs the function of knowing in various modes.

It is wisdom (*paññā*). It is true knowledge (*vijjā*) by way of effecting penetration without remainder. It is called light (*āloka*) by way of performing the function of illuminating in every respect; such is the meaning.
In the passages beginning with "the eye is a phenomenon" (*dhamma*), it is one and the same knowledge that is described in five ways according to its diversity of functions.

They are "objects" (*ārammaṇa*) in the sense of providing support. They are "spheres" (*gocara*) in the sense of being a domain. In the phrases beginning with "in the sense of seeing," the function of knowledge is fivefold.
Thus it was said. Following this method, by taking five [factors] in each of the three sections, there are fifteen phenomena (*dhamma*) and fifteen meanings (*attha*).

In the two sets of fifteen, there are thirty expressions (*nirutti*); thus, based on the fifteen phenomena, the fifteen meanings, and the thirty expressions, sixty kinds of knowledge (*ñāṇa*) are to be understood.
This same method applies to the remaining Noble Truths as well. In the four...

In each of the Noble Truths, by way of fifteen phenomena and fifteen meanings, there are sixty phenomena and sixty meanings. Within those sixty phenomena and sixty meanings, there are two hundred modes of expression (*nirutti*);
"two hundred" means one hundred and twenty. Within the sixty phenomena and sixty meanings, there are one hundred and twenty...
"Niruttīsū" means thus: forty-two hundred knowledges. 2–3.
Commentary on the Section on the Foundations of Mindfulness, etc.:

In the *Paṭisambhidā-niddesa*, both the meaning and the enumeration should be understood by this same method, beginning with the Sutta on the Foundations of Mindfulness and beginning with the Sutta on the Bases of Psychic Power.
4–8. Explanation of the Seven Bodhisatta Sections (33–37).

Regarding the seven Bodhisattas, in each of their respective discourses, there are ten factors: five, such as the eye and so forth, in the context of origination, and five in the context of cessation;
and five, such as the state of seeing and so forth, in the context of origination, and five in the context of cessation.

By way of these meanings, there are twenty modes of expression (*nirutti*) and forty kinds of knowledge (*ñāṇa*). When the seven [sets] are combined together, the stated enumeration is indeed easy to understand.

In the exposition of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā-niddesa*) given by way of the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*), within each of the five expressions—“known, seen, understood, realized, and touched with wisdom”—based on each single root, [the same applies].
There are twenty-five phenomena and twenty-five meanings by way of the five beginning with the eye and the five beginning with seeing;
the linguistic expressions (nirutti) are double that number, and the knowledges (ñāṇa) and the objects of knowledge (ñeyya) are double that again.

When these five are taken together as stated in the section [of the text], and when five sets of twenty-five are made five times over, there are one hundred and twenty-five phenomena and one hundred and twenty-five meanings.
There are eight meanings (*attha*), twice as many linguistic expressions (*nirutti*), and twice as many types of knowledge (*ñāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*ñeyya*).

Here, "two hundred and fifty" refers to two hundred and fifty. This same method applies to the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth. By this very method, the enumeration of phenomena (*dhamma*) and the rest in the sections on the Truths (*sacca*) and the Analytical Knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) should be understood.
9. Explanation of the Section on the Buddha’s Qualities (Buddhadhammavāra) 38.
In the section on the Buddha’s qualities, "one hundred and fifty" refers to one hundred and fifty-six;

the grammatical expressions (*nirutti*) are double that number, and the types of knowledge (*ñāṇa*) are double that number. "In the context of the analytical knowledges" (*paṭisambhidādhikaraṇe*) means in the section concerning the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
"Eight hundred and fifty dhammas": there are sixty among the four truths first mentioned;
sixty among the four foundations of mindfulness; sixty among the four right efforts; seventy among the seven declarations concerning the Bodhisatta;

one hundred and twenty-five among the five beginning with the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*); one hundred and twenty-five among the five beginning with the aggregates (*khandha*); and again, [sixty] among the four noble truths.
There are one hundred [qualities] in the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), and one hundred and fifty in the six qualities of a Buddha;
thus, there are one hundred and fifty dhammas. Likewise, there are exactly that many meanings (*attha*).

Similarly, there are one hundred and twenty expressions (*nirutti*) in the three places beginning with the Truths (*sacca*), one hundred and forty expressions in the seven types of exposition (*veyyākaraṇa*), and [so on] in the eight direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) and so forth.

Regarding the "meaning of the aggregates" (*khandhaṭṭha*) and so forth, there are two hundred and fifty etymological explanations (*nirutti*) each; regarding the Noble Truths (*ariyasacca*) and the Analytical Knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), there are two hundred each;
and regarding the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadhamma*), there are three hundred. Thus, there are one thousand seven hundred etymological explanations in total.
In the same way, in the three locations beginning with the Truths, there are two hundred and forty...
There are two hundred knowledges; regarding the seven types of exposition, there are two hundred and eighty knowledges;

regarding the eight direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) and so forth, and the eight bases of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth, there are five hundred knowledges each; regarding the truths (*sacca*) and the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), there are four hundred knowledges each;
and regarding the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadhamma*), there are six hundred knowledges. Thus, there are three thousand four hundred knowledges in total.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Analytical Knowledges is finished. 7.
The Exposition of the Wheel of Dhamma.
1. Commentary on the Section on the Truths.

39. Furthermore, this is a commentary on the previously unstated meaning of the discourse on the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, which was spoken with the *Dhammacakkappavattana-sutta* as its precursor.
Therein, "having suffering as their basis" (*dukkhavatthukā*) means that suffering is the basis for these [noble truths] by way of a single simultaneous realization (*ekābhisamaya*).
Having specified that very suffering, he said, "having truth as their basis," and so forth. Therein, "truth" (*sacca*) is the object (*ārammaṇa*).

They have the truths as their object (*saccārammaṇā*) because these [truths] are their support. They have the truths as their range and domain (*saccagocarā*) because the truths are their sphere of activity.

They are "comprised within the truths" (*saccasaṅgahitā*) because they are included within the truth of the path. They are "encompassed by the truths" (*saccapariyāpannā*) because they are dependent upon the truth of the path. They are "fully arrived at the truths" (*sacce samudāgatā*) because they have arisen in relation to the truth of suffering through the full understanding of suffering.
Likewise, they are established and firmly grounded right there.
40. Now, wishing to demonstrate the Wheel of Dhamma mentioned in the phrase "and when the Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion by the Blessed One," he says:
"The Wheel of Dhamma," and so forth. Therein, the Wheel of Dhamma is twofold: the Wheel of Dhamma of penetration (*paṭivedha-dhammacakka*) and the Wheel of Dhamma of teaching (*desanā-dhammacakka*).
The Wheel of Dhamma of penetration [was turned] at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhipallaṅka*); the Wheel of Dhamma of teaching [was turned] at Isipatana. And he sets the Dhamma in motion.
"Cakkañca" refers to the Wheel of Dhamma of penetration; "and he sets in motion the wheel and the Dhamma" refers to the Wheel of Dhamma of teaching.

How so? For while seated at the seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka), at the moment of the Path, the Blessed One sets in motion the Dhamma distinguished by the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path-factors, and so forth;
and that very same Dhamma is a weapon-wheel because it proceeds for the purpose of slaying the enemy of the defilements.
And he set the wheel in motion. It is precisely while setting the Dhamma in motion that the Blessed One is said to "set the wheel in motion.

By this, it is stated through a *kammadhāraya* compound that the Dhamma itself is the wheel. Seated at Isipatana, at the moment of teaching the Dhamma, the Blessed One also sets in motion the wheel of the teaching, which is like a weapon-wheel because it proceeds to strike down the enemy of the defilements within the mental continuums of those to be trained.

He sets it in motion; he also sets in motion the Wheel of Dhamma—which is distinguished by the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, factors of the path, and so forth—within the mental continuum of those to be trained.
By this, the compound *dhammacakka* is stated as a *dvanda* (copulative) compound, meaning both "Dhamma" and "Wheel.
However, since there can be no "setting in motion" in the absence of one who sets it in motion, the word "sets in motion" (*pavatteti*) is used in all instances in the sense of causing to proceed.

However, it should be understood that the word "wheel" (*cakra*) is what is being stated. It should be understood that expressions such as "the Wheel of Dhamma" (*dhammacakka*) are spoken with reference specifically to the Wheel of Dhamma as a teaching, in the sense that "it sets in motion by means of the Dhamma.

In this context, "it sets in motion by means of the Dhamma" means that because it proceeds according to the true nature of things (*yathāsabhāva*), it is a wheel that proceeds by means of the Dhamma; thus, it is called the "Wheel of Dhamma."

This is what is meant. "He sets it in motion through the practice of the Dhamma" means that the wheel which functions for the sake of the Dhamma within the mental continuum of those to be trained is called the "Dhamma-wheel.
By the phrases "established in the Dhamma," and so forth, the Blessed One’s state of being the Dhamma and his lordship over the Dhamma are expressed.
As it is said: "Friends, that Blessed One knows what should be known and sees what should be seen; he has become the eye..."
“The Tathāgata is become wisdom, become Dhamma, become Brahmā; he is the speaker, the proclaimer, the guide to the goal, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of Dhamma.
Therefore, because it is the wheel of the Dhamma for them, it is called the “Dhammacakka. “Established” means established by way of being an object.
“Firmly established” means established by way of immovability. “Attained mastery” means attained lordship. “Attained perfection” means...
"Attained to the ultimate" (*koṭippatto*). "Attained to fearlessness" (*vesārajjappatto*) means having attained a state of confidence.

By the words beginning with "establishing [others] in the Dhamma," which are spoken with reference to the mental continuum of those to be trained, it is meant that he possesses the wheel for the sake of the Dhamma by virtue of his mastery over the Dhamma.
By the words beginning with "honoring the Dhamma," it is meant that he possesses the wheel for the sake of the Dhamma; for he who honors the Dhamma through acts such as reverence—
He sets it in motion; he sets the meaning of the Dhamma in motion.
"Honoring the Dhamma" means performing that Dhamma in such a way that it becomes well-performed. "Revering the Dhamma" means honoring it through the arising of respect for it.
"Loving the Dhamma" means dwelling having made the Dhamma dear and worthy of cultivation. The Dhamma...
"Paying homage" means performing worship by means of the worship of teaching and practice, referring back to that [Dharma].
"Honoring the Dharma" means acting with humility toward that very Dharma through acts of respect and reverence.

"The Dharma-bannered, the Dharma-ensign" means that because he proceeds having placed that Dharma before him like a banner and raised it up like an ensign, he is "the Dharma-bannered, the Dharma-ensign."
And the meaning is "having sacrificed. "Having the Dhamma as its overlord" means having come from the sovereignty of the Dhamma;
and by performing all activities solely through the power of the Dhamma of meditation, one becomes one who has the Dhamma as overlord.

Furthermore, that Wheel of the Dhamma is "irreversible," which is said because it proceeds unimpeded due to the impossibility of anyone turning it back. Therefore, that Dhamma, in the sense of proceeding...
The word "wheel" (*cakkam*) is what is meant.

The faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) is the Dhamma; "it sets that Dhamma in motion" means that by producing the faculty of faith associated with the Path within the mental continuum of those to be trained, it sets that faculty of faith—the Dhamma—in motion.
This same method applies to the remaining [faculties] as well. "Truths" (*saccā*) refers to the knowledges of the truths.
Insight (vipassanā) and clear knowledge (vijjā) are simply the knowledge of the path. "Knowledge of non-arising" is the knowledge of the fruit of Arahantship.
That too is indeed set in motion within the mental continuum of those to be trained; and when one penetrates Nibbāna, it is said to be "set in motion.

In the sections on the origin and so forth, the specific terms "having the origin as its basis," "having cessation as its basis," and "having the path as its basis" have been shown, after which they were abbreviated. Here too, what has been stated should be understood in the same manner as previously explained.
2–3. Explanation of the Sections on the Foundations of Mindfulness, etc. 41–42.

The sections preceded by the Foundations of Mindfulness and the Bases for Spiritual Power are also stated by way of the moment of the Path. These too have been abbreviated by showing specific terms here and there.
The explanation of the Discourse on the Wheel of Dhamma is concluded.
8. Discourse on the Supramundane (Lokuttara-kathā). Commentary on the Discourse on the Supramundane: 43.
Now follows the discourse on the supramundane, which was spoken immediately after the discourse on the Wheel of Dhamma concerning the supramundane states.
A commentary on what has not been previously stated: therein, the meaning of the term *lokuttara* (supramundane) will be clarified in the section of the detailed exposition (*niddesa*).

The thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*), beginning with the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), are associated, as appropriate, with the paths and fruits.

They are called "conducive to enlightenment" (*bodhipakkhiya*) because they exist on the side (*pakkhe*) of the Noble One who has received the name "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) in the sense of "awakening" (*bujjhana*).
[The word] *nāma* [is used]. It is called "foundation" (*upaṭṭhāna*) because it stands (*bhavatta*) on the side (*pakkhe*), that is, because it remains in the state of being helpful.
It is a "foundation of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*) because mindfulness itself is the foundation, in the sense that it establishes and enters into those objects.

Furthermore, with regard to the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, it accomplishes its function of abandoning the perceptions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self by way of grasping the aspects of foulness, suffering, impermanence, and non-self.

And when it has proceeded, it becomes fourfold; therefore, it is called the "four foundations of mindfulness" (*cattāro satipaṭṭhānā*). It is called "exertion" (*padhāna*) because one exerts by means of it.
"Right exertion" (*sammappadhāna*) is either a beautiful exertion, or that by which they exert rightly.
Or else, it is a beautiful exertion because it is free from the unsightly occurrence of the defilements, and it is an exertion in the sense of producing welfare and happiness.
It is called "right endeavor" (*sammappadhāna*) because it brings about the state of excellence and because it effects the state of preeminence; this is a designation for energy (*vīriya*).

Since it accomplishes the task of abandoning unwholesome states that have arisen and preventing those not yet arisen from arising, as well as the task of producing wholesome states not yet arisen and maintaining those already arisen, it is fourfold. Therefore, there are four right endeavors.

It is so called. By way of derivation from its accomplishment (*nipphatti*), it is "success" (*iddhi*) in the sense of succeeding; or by this alternative method, it is success because through it beings succeed, become prosperous, and reach the pinnacle.

It is a "basis of success" (*iddhipāda*) because it is the foot of that success—meaning it is the preceding factor for the associated [consciousness] and the causal factor in the prior stage for that which has become the fruit.
It is categorized according to zeal (*chanda*), energy (*vīriya*), consciousness (*citta*), and investigation (*vīmaṃsā*).
It is of four kinds; therefore, it is called the "four bases of psychic power" (*iddhipāda*).

It is called a "faculty" (*indriya*) in the sense of sovereignty known as "overcoming," because it overcomes lack of faith, laziness, negligence, distraction, and delusion. It is called "power" (*bala*) in the sense of being unshakable, because it cannot be overcome by lack of faith and the other hindrances.
Both of these are fivefold, according to the factors of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Therefore, they are called the five faculties and the five powers.

Furthermore, because they serve as factors for a being who is awakening, the seven states beginning with mindfulness are the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga); and in the sense of leading to liberation, the eight factors beginning with right view are the factors of the path (maggaṅga).
Hence it is said: "The seven factors of enlightenment and the noble eightfold path."

Thus, these thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment, while occurring during mundane insight in the preliminary stage, constitute the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the body for one who comprehends the body in fourteen ways;
the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of feelings for one who comprehends feelings in nine ways;
and [the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of mind] for one who comprehends the mind in sixteen ways.
The foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of mind, and the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of mental objects for one who comprehends mental objects in five ways.

Thus, having seen an unwholesome state that has arisen in another—which had not previously arisen in this [one's own] personal existence—one reflects: "I shall not practice in the same way as he practiced so that this arose in him; thus it will not arise in me. Regarding that...
The first right effort is at the time of striving for non-arising;
the second is at the time of striving to abandon unwholesome states that have reached manifestation within oneself;
the third is for one striving to arouse either jhāna or insight that has never before arisen in this present existence; [and the fourth is] so that what has arisen does not decline.
For one who arouses [the mind] again and again, there is the fourth right effort. When producing the wholesome by making zeal the primary factor, it is the basis of psychic power consisting of zeal;
when producing the wholesome by making energy, consciousness, or investigation the primary factor, it is the basis of psychic power consisting of investigation.
At the time of refraining from wrong speech, it is right speech; at the time of refraining from wrong action and wrong livelihood, it is right livelihood.
Thus they are found in various types of consciousness. However, at the moment of the four paths, they are found in a single consciousness;
at the moment of the fruits, with the exception of the four right efforts, the remaining thirty-three are found.

Thus, among these qualities found in a single consciousness, mindfulness alone—which has Nibbāna as its object—is called "the four" by way of accomplishing the task of abandoning perceptions of beauty and so forth regarding the body and other objects.

It is called "the foundations of mindfulness. And likewise, the single energy itself is called "the four right endeavors" by virtue of its accomplishment of the respective tasks of preventing the arising of the unarisen and so forth.
In the remaining [factors], there is no decrease or increase.
Furthermore, regarding them—
Nine are of one kind, one is single; then two, four, and five kinds;
eight kinds and nine kinds as well—thus they become sixfold.
"Nine are of one kind" refers to: desire, consciousness, rapture, tranquility, equanimity, intention, speech, action, and livelihood.
These nine are of one kind by way of the bases of psychic power beginning with zeal; they do not belong to any other category.
"One is twofold" means that faith is established in two ways by way of the faculties and the powers. "Then four and five" means that another one is established in four ways and another in five ways.
In that context, concentration alone is [established] by way of the faculties, the powers, the enlightenment factors, and the path factors.
It is established in four ways; and by way of the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) and the category of wisdom (*paññā*), it is fivefold.

"In eight ways and nine ways" means that another one is established in eight ways and another one in nine ways. Mindfulness (*sati*) is established in eight ways by way of the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), and the path factors (*maggaṅga*).
[It is also established] by way of the four right efforts (*sammappadhāna*), the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path factors.
Energy is ninefold. Thus:
"These factors conducive to enlightenment are fourteen in total when undivided;
they are sevenfold according to their sections, and thirty-seven according to their detailed classification."
Because they accomplish their respective functions and because they are stated in their own forms,
all of them arise whenever the Noble Path arises.
Having thus shown the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment associated with the path and its fruit, [the author] further [discusses] them in relation to the paths and fruits.
Having condensed them, he said: "The four noble paths and the four fruits of recluseship. The state of being a recluse is *sāmañña*; this is the name for the four noble paths.

The fruits of these recluseships are the *sāmaññaphalāni*. Nibbāna, however, is entirely unmixed with anything else. Thus, in detail, there are thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the four paths, the four fruits, and Nibbāna.
It should be understood that, by way of their specific modes, there are forty-six supramundane states;
then, in brief, nine supramundane states consisting of the four paths, the four fruits, and Nibbāna; and even more briefly, three supramundane states consisting of the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna.
When the supramundane nature of the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, as well as the paths and fruits, has been stated, [it follows] for those associated with them...

It has already been stated that contact (phassa) and the other factors are likewise supramundane (lokuttara). However, they are mentioned specifically as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so forth by virtue of their being the primary factors.
Furthermore, in the Abhidhamma, in the exposition of supramundane states, it is indeed stated that contact and the other factors associated with the Path and Fruition are supramundane.
"They cross over the world" means they transcend the world. All such expressions here refer to the present tense; these four...
This was said with reference to the Noble Path. For the stream-entry path crosses over the world of the lower realms;
the once-return path crosses over one portion of the sense-sphere world; the non-return path crosses over the sense-sphere world;
and the path of arahantship crosses over the form and formless-sphere worlds. "Crossing over the worlds" means emerging from the worlds. And "from the world" means from the world.
And that same word in the ablative case is shown here as being qualified. "Transcending the world" (*lokaṃ samatikkamanti*) has the same meaning as stated previously;
there it was stated without regard for the sense of the prefix (*upasagga*), whereas here it is stated together with the sense of the prefix.
"Having transcended the world" (*lokaṃ samatikkantā*) means having properly transcended the world as previously described. All such expressions here refer to the past tense.
This was said with reference to the fruits of liberation (*phala-nibbāna*).

For the fruits beginning with stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*) exist having transcended the world as previously described, while Nibbāna itself always exists having transcended the entire world. "Exceeding the world" (*lokena atirekā*) means being superior to the world.
This was said with reference to all supramundane phenomena (*lokuttara-dhamma*). "They escape" (*nissaranti*) means they go forth. "Escaped" (*nissaṭā*).
They have gone forth. The eighteen statements beginning with “they do not stand in the world” apply even to those who are transcendent over the entire world.
“They do not stand” is said because they are not included within the world. “They do not smear themselves in the world”:

although they exist within the continuity of the aggregates (*khandha-santāna*), the meaning is that they do not smear themselves therein. “They are not smeared by the world”: for those who have not yet attained penetration, by any state of mind...
The meaning is that for those who have attained penetration, even with an unwholesome mind that is only slightly heedless, they are not smeared.

"Unsmeared" (*asaṃlitta*) and "unstained" (*anupalitta*) are distinguished by the addition of prefixes. "Completely liberated" (*vippamutta*) is a distinction of that very state of being unsmeared expressed through different terminology. For whoever is unsmeared by whatever [defilement] or in whatever [place], [they are so called].
They are liberated from that there. The three phrases beginning with "liberated from the world" (*lokā vippamuttā*) are stated in the ablative sense (*nissakkavasena*).

"Free from attachment" (*visaṃyuttā*) is a qualification of the state of being liberated. For whoever is liberated from something, by means of something, or from something, they are said to be "free from attachment" (*visaṃyutta*) to that thing, by that means, or from that source.
"The worlds are purified" (*loka sujjhanti*) means that the worlds are purified by washing away the defilements of the world.

"Are purified" (*visujjhanti*) means that very same [action] is distinguished by the prefix (*upasagga*). "Are emerging" (*vuṭṭhahanti*) means they have arisen. "Are turning away" (*vivaṭṭanti*) means they are turning back.
"Do not cling" (*na sajjanti*) means they do not adhere. "Are not seized" (*na gayhanti*) means they are not grasped. "Are not bound" (*na bajjhanti*) means they are not oppressed.
"Cut off completely" (*samucchindanti*) means they bring about non-occurrence. And "because the world has been cut off" (*yathā ca lokaṃ samucchinnattā*)...

In the same way, the passage beginning with “The worlds, because of their purity,” and so forth, has already been explained. “They cause to subside” means they bring about cessation. The four terms beginning with “non-paths” (apathā) apply to all supramundane states (*lokuttara*).
“Non-paths” (*apathā*) means not being paths. “Non-destinations” (*agati*) means having no foothold. “Non-domains” (*avisaya*) means not being dependent [on them].

“Not shared” (*asādhāraṇa*) means not common [to the mundane]. “Vomit up” (*vamanti*) means they eject [them]. “Do not vomit back” (*na paccāvamanti*) is according to the method of the opposite of what was stated.
The meaning is that they do not eat again what has been spoken and vomited. By this, the state of the vomited being well-vomited is expressed.
This same method applies to the three following pairs as well. "Visīnenti" means they scatter or disperse; the meaning is that they do not bind.
"Na ussīnenti" means they do not scatter or disperse. The reading with the short vowel—"visinenti" and "na ussinenti"—is more elegant.
"Vidhūpentī" means they extinguish. "Na saṃdhūpentī" means they do not kindle.
"Standing having transcended and overcome the world" means that all supramundane states (lokuttara-dhammā) stand having rightly transcended and overcome the world; thus they are "supramundane.
By all these aforementioned modes, the state of being superior to the world belongs to the supramundane.
And the state of superiority has been stated.
The commentary on the discussion of the supramundane is finished. 9.
Discussion of the Powers (Bala).
Commentary on the Discourse on the Powers (Balakathāvaṇṇanā) 44.

Now follows the commentary on the previously unexpounded subject matter of the Discourse on the Powers, which was spoken immediately after the Discourse on the Supramundane and is preceded by the Suttanta.
Therein, at the outset, the five powers are shown by way of the Suttanta.
Desiring then to show other powers as well, he said, "Furthermore, there are sixty-eight powers," and so forth.

All of these are called "powers" (bala) in the sense of being unshakable by their respective opposites. Regarding "the power of moral shame" (hiribala) and so on: one feels shame (*hirīyati*) because of evil through this, thus it is *hirī*; this is a name for modesty (*lajjā*).
One trembles (*ottappati*) because of evil through this, thus it is *ottappa*; this is a name for dread of wrongdoing (*ubbega*).
Moral shame (*hirī*) originates from within; moral dread (*ottappa*) originates from without. Moral shame has oneself as its governing principle; moral dread has the world as its governing principle.
Moral shame is established in the nature of modesty; moral dread is established in the nature of fear. Moral shame has the characteristic of being deferential;
moral dread has the characteristic of seeing danger and fearing faults. That very same moral shame does not waver because of the absence of shame (*ahirika*).
The power of moral shame (*hiribala*). That same [power] does not waver due to a lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), thus it is the power of moral dread (*ottappabala*).
It does not waver due to a lack of reflective discernment (*appaṭisaṅkhāna*), thus it is the power of reflective discernment (*paṭisaṅkhānabala*); this is a name for the wisdom that investigates.

The power that arises in one who develops the seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) under the heading of energy (*vīriya*) is the power of cultivation (*bhāvanābala*). This [refers to] the four aggregates (*khandha*) proceeding in such a manner.
Name. Pure virtue and so forth are the power of blamelessness (*anavajjabala*). The four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*) are the power of sympathy (*saṅgahabala*);

there is also a reading that says "the power in sympathy" (*saṅgahe balaṃ*). Enduring hardships is the power of patience (*khantibala*). Satisfying others with a discourse on the Dhamma is the power of exposition (*paññattibala*).
Causing another to attain the meaning one has mastered oneself is the power of self-dedication (*nijjhattibala*). Regarding wholesome states...
Abundance is the power of sovereignty. Establishment in wholesome states according to one’s inclination is the power of determination.
The meaning of the powers of moral shame (*hiribala*) and so forth has been stated by taking the specific application of the phrasing in the summary headings (*mātikāpadesu*).
The "power of serenity" and the "power of insight" refer specifically to serenity and insight that have attained the status of powers.
In the exposition of the *mātikā*, it is stated that "it does not waver in the face of lack of faith" is the meaning of the power of faith (*saddhābala*) as the root-power;
having thus stated this, he demonstrates that very same power by distinguishing it through nine further modes.

For whatever dhamma is unshakable and has attained strength supports its co-nascent factors, exhausts the defilements that are its opposites, and constitutes the virtue (*sīla*) that is the beginning of penetration.
It purifies view; it establishes the mind upon its object; by making the mind luminous, it cleanses it;
by bringing mastery over it, it causes one to attain distinction; by leading further beyond that, it causes one to achieve higher penetration;
having gradually led one to the Noble Path, it causes the realization of the Truths; and through the attainment of the fruit, it establishes one in cessation (nirodha).
Therefore, the sense of power is distinguished in nine ways. This same method applies to the four powers beginning with energy (*vīriya-bala*).
"He feels shame regarding sensual desire" means that the yogi associated with renunciation feels shame because of renunciation, out of regard for sensual desire.

The same method applies to moral dread (*ottappa*) as well. By these [terms], feeling shame and moral dread regarding all unwholesome states have already been explained. The same applies to "ill-will" (*byāpāda*) and so forth.
The meaning should be understood by this same method. "Reflects" means he examines [it] for its danger by way of non-delusion.
"Develops" means he increases it. "Faults" refers to the faults of lust and so forth. "Grasps" means he binds.
"Tolerates" means it is acceptable and pleasing to that practitioner. "Makes known" means he satisfies. "Causes to contemplate" means he causes him to reflect. "Brings under control" means...
Having become master over the mind, one causes the mind to proceed by bringing it under one's own control. "Resolves" means "establishes.

All such things as the power of development (bhāvanā-bala) and so forth are themselves simply the factors of renunciation (nekkhamma) and the rest. It should be understood that although these were stated differently in the commentary on the Matika, they are not repeated here because their meaning is already clear from the phrasing itself.
Having demonstrated in detail the power of serenity (samatha-bala) and the power of insight (vipassanā-bala)...

At the end, the statements "it does not waver from the defilements accompanied by restlessness and the aggregates," and so forth, as well as "it does not waver from the defilements accompanied by ignorance and the aggregates," and so forth, are stated for the purpose of showing the characteristics of the powers of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

Regarding the powers of the trainee (*sekha*) and the non-trainee (*asekha*), it is called a "power of the trainee" because the person who is a trainee trains in right view; thus, "he trains in right view."
The learner (*sekha*) possesses that right view as his strength; thus, the meaning is "the strength of a learner" (*sekhabala*).

In this context, it is called the "strength of one beyond training" (*asekhabala*) because he has already trained. That is to say, because the person beyond training (*asekhapuggala*) has completed his training in that right view and no longer trains therein, he is "one beyond training" (*asekha*);
that very same right view is his strength, hence it is the "strength of one beyond training. This same method applies to right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*) and the others as well.

“Right knowledge” (*sammāñāṇa*) is reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*). For even though it is mundane, it is called the “power of the trainee” (*sekhabala*) when it occurs in a trainee, and the “power of the one beyond training” (*asekhabala*) when it occurs in one beyond training.

“Right liberation” (*sammāvimutti*) refers to the remaining states associated with the fruit, excluding the eight path factors. However, some say that it refers to all liberations other than supramundane liberation.
They say, “right liberation. His status as one in training (sekkha) and one beyond training (asekkha) is exactly as described by the method already stated.

Among the powers of one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), all are powers of knowledge (ñāṇabala). The genitive case in the phrase “of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed” is used in the sense of the instrumental; the meaning is “by a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed.
“As impermanent” means as impermanent in the mode of non-existence after having existed. “As it really is” (yathābhūtaṃ):
"According to their true nature. "By means of wisdom" means by means of the path-wisdom accompanied by insight (*vipassanā*).
They are well-seen as impermanent, as suffering, and as non-self because they are rooted in that [wisdom]. "Yam" is a neuter noun in the instrumental case;
or its meaning is "by which reason. "Having approached" means depending upon. "Admits" means accepts or makes a formal acknowledgment. "Like a pit of glowing embers."
In the sense of great torment, it is compared to a pit of glowing embers. "Sensual pleasures" (*kāmā*) refers both to sensual objects (*vatthukāmā*) and to defilements (*kilesakāmā*).

"Inclined toward seclusion" (*vivekaninna*) means inclined toward Nibbāna, which is designated as the seclusion from the substrata (*upadhiviveka*), by way of the attainment of the fruit. For there are three kinds of seclusion:
seclusion of body, seclusion of mind, and seclusion from the substrata. And seclusion of body belongs to those who dwell in solitude and delight in renunciation.

There is seclusion of mind for those devoted to higher consciousness; and there is seclusion from acquisitions for persons free from acquisitions who have reached the cessation of formations, or that which inclines toward Nibbāna, which is reckoned as the seclusion of escape. For there are five kinds of seclusion:

seclusion by suppression, seclusion by substitution of opposites, seclusion by cutting off, seclusion by tranquillization, and seclusion by escape. "Inclining toward seclusion" means inclined toward seclusion.
"Inclined toward seclusion" (*vivekapona*) means bent toward seclusion. "Leaning toward seclusion" (*vivekapabbhāra*) means having seclusion as its primary burden.
Both of these are synonyms for the former. "Withdrawn from seclusion" (*vivekaṭṭha*) means abandoned by defilements, or become distant from them.

"Delighting in renunciation" (*nekkhammābhirata*) means delighting in *nibbāna*, or delighting in the life of going forth. "Brought to an end" (*byantībhūta*) means that which has reached the state of being gone; it does not adhere even in part.
"Completely liberated" means dissociated. "In every way" (*sabbaso*) means in all respects.

"By means of states that are the basis for the taints" (*āsavaṭṭhāniyehi dhammehi*) means by means of defiled states that serve as the causes for the taints through the mode of bondage; this is the meaning. Alternatively, "become exhausted" (*byantībhūtaṃ*) means having become free from craving;
the meaning is "without thirst. From what? "From states that are the basis for the taints in every way," that is, from all states belonging to the three realms.
The meaning: Here, by means of the ten powers of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), the mundane and supramundane path of the one whose taints are destroyed is explained.
“All conditioned phenomena are impermanent” is the power of full comprehension of suffering; “Sensual pleasures are like a pit of glowing coals” is the power of abandoning the origin [of suffering];
“The mind inclines toward seclusion” is the power of realizing cessation; and “the four foundations of mindfulness,” etc., [are the power of developing the path].
They also speak of the sevenfold power of the development of the path. The ten powers of supernormal success (iddhi) will be explained in the discourse on supernormal success.
In the description of the powers of the Tathāgata, "powers of the Tathāgata" means powers belonging exclusively to the Tathāgata and not shared by others.
Or alternatively, just as the powers of previous Buddhas arrived through the perfection of their accumulated merit, they are thus called "powers that have come [to him]."
The meaning. In this context, the power of a Tathāgata is twofold: physical power and the power of knowledge. Of these, the physical power is to be understood according to the lineage of elephants.
For it has been said by the ancients:
“The black one from Avaka, the one from the Ganges, the white, and the tawny-brown;”
“Gandhamāṅgala, Hema, and the ten Uposatha and Chaddanta breeds.
These are the ten elephant breeds. Therein, “Kālāvaka” should be understood as the ordinary elephant breed.
The bodily strength of ten men is equal to the strength of one Kālāvaka elephant. [The strength] of ten Kālāvakas...
The strength of one [ordinary elephant] is equal to the strength of one *gaṅgeyya* elephant; the strength of ten *gaṅgeyyas* is equal to that of one *paṇḍara*;
the strength of ten *paṇḍaras* is equal to that of one *tamba*; the strength of ten *tambas* is equal to that of one *piṅgala*;
the strength of ten *piṅgalas* is equal to that of one *gandhahatthin*; the strength of ten *gandhahatthis*—
The strength of one auspicious elephant is equal to that of ten auspicious elephants; the strength of ten auspicious elephants is equal to that of one Hemavata elephant;
the strength of ten Hemavata elephants is equal to that of one Uposatha elephant; the strength of ten Uposatha elephants is equal to that of one Chaddanta elephant;
the strength of ten Chaddanta elephants is equal to the power of a Tathāgata. It is also called the Nārāyaṇa-compound strength.
This is what is called [the strength of the Tathāgata]. By the calculation of ordinary elephants, this constitutes the strength of a thousand crores of elephants;
by the calculation of men, it is the strength of ten thousand crores of men. This, first of all, is the bodily strength of the Tathāgata.
As for his power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*), the knowledge of the ten powers (*dasabala-ñāṇa*) has already been mentioned here and elsewhere in the Canon, as well as in the *Majjhima Nikāya*.

The knowledge of the four grounds of self-confidence, the unshakable knowledge regarding the eight assemblies, the knowledge that delimits the four modes of birth, the knowledge that delimits the five destinations, the seventy-three knowledges mentioned in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, and the seventy-seven knowledges—thus there are many thousands of other such knowledges as well.

This is what is called the power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*). Here too, it is specifically this power of knowledge that is intended. For knowledge is called "power" in the sense of being unshakable and in the sense of providing support.
"As a ground, as a ground" means as a cause, as a cause. For a cause is called a "ground" because the fruit stands upon it;
since it arises and proceeds in dependence upon that [cause], it is therefore called a ground.
The Blessed One [taught] that whichever phenomena are the causes and conditions for the arising of whichever phenomena, those are the respective grounds. Whichever phenomena...

Knowing that which is not the cause or condition for the arising of phenomena as "not the proper occasion," one understands, as it truly is, what is a possible occasion as a possible occasion and what is an impossible occasion as an impossible occasion.
The phrase "by whatever" refers to the knowledge by which [one knows this]. The phrase "this too" means that this knowledge of the possible and the impossible is called a power of the Tathāgata.
In the same way, the application [of the meaning] should be understood for the remaining sections as well.
"Āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ" means the pre-eminent position, the supreme position; or alternatively, "āsabhā" refers to the former Buddhas, and the meaning is "the position of those.
Furthermore, an *usabha* is the leader of a hundred cows, while a *vasabha* is the leader of a thousand cows;
or an *usabha* is the leader of a hundred bulls (*vaja*), while a *vasabha* is the leader of a thousand bulls; it is the best of all cattle, capable of enduring all hardships, white, and beautiful.
The bearer of a great burden, who is not to be terrified even by the sound of a hundred thunderbolts, is the *nisabha*; here, he is intended as the *usabha*. This is indeed a synonym for him.
"Belonging to the bull" (*usabhassa idaṃ*) is *āsabhaṃ*. "Standing" (*ṭhānaṃ*) means standing firm after pressing down upon the earth with all four feet.
And this [standing] is like that of the bull; thus it is called *āsabhaṃ*, just as the one designated as the *nisabha* is.
Just as a bull endowed with the strength of a bull stands firmly on a steady footing after pressing down upon the earth with its four feet,
so too the Tathāgata, endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, presses down upon the earth of the eight assemblies with the four feet of self-confidence;
he stands on a steady footing, unshakable by any adversary or enemy in the world including the devas.
He stands; and while standing thus, he claims, approaches, and does not renounce that bull-like state (*āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ*), attributing it to himself.
Therefore it is said: "He claims the bull-like state.

Regarding the phrase "in assemblies" (*parisāsu*): this refers to the assemblies of khattiyas, brahmins, householders, recluses, and those belonging to the realms of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three Gods, Māra, and Brahmā.
In the eight assemblies, he "roars the lion’s roar" (sīhanādaṃ nadati); that is, he roars the supreme roar, the fearless roar, or he roars a roar similar to that of a lion.

This meaning should be illustrated by the *Sīhanāda Sutta*. Or, just as a lion is called a "lion" (sīha) because of his endurance (*sahana*) and his slaying (*hanana*), so too the Tathāgata is [called a lion] because of his endurance of worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*) and his slaying of the doctrines of others (*parappavāda*).
It is called a "lion. The roar of the lion spoken thus is the "lion's roar.

In this regard, just as a lion, endowed with lion-like strength, confident in every respect and free from timidity, lets out a lion’s roar, so too the Tathāgata-lion, endowed with the powers of a Tathāgata, confident among the eight assemblies and free from timidity, [utters his roar] beginning with "Such is form," and so forth.
By means of this method, he roars the lion’s roar, endowed with the various graces of teaching. Therefore it is said: “He roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies.
Regarding the phrase “he sets in motion the Brahma-wheel”: here, *brahma* means supreme, most excellent, and pure.
As for the word *cakra*, it refers to prosperity, a characteristic mark, a wheel of a chariot, and a mode of deportment.
The term *dāna* is seen in the sense of giving, as well as in the context of the "jewel-wheel" (*ratana-cakka*) and so forth;
here, however, it is understood as the "Wheel of Dhamma" (*dhamma-cakka*), which one should analyze in two ways.
For in such passages as, "Monks, there are these four wheels, possessed of which gods and humans... this [term]...
It is seen in the sense of prosperity: in the passage, “Wheels have appeared on the soles of his feet,” it refers to a mark (lakkhaṇa).
In the passage, “Like the wheel of one who draws [a cart],” it refers to a part of a chariot (rathaṅga). In the passage, “Four-wheeled, nine-gated,” it refers to the modes of deportment (iriyāpatha).
In the passage, “Give, enjoy, and do not be negligent; set the wheel in motion, O Lord of Kosala,” it refers to giving (dāna). [And] the divine wheel-treasure (dibbaṃ cakkaratanaṃ) ...
In the phrase “he appeared,” it refers to the wheel of jewels (*ratanacakkra*). In the phrase “the wheel set in motion by me,” it refers to the wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakkra*).

In the phrase “the wheel revolves upon the head of the man struck by desire,” it refers to the chest-wheel (*uracakkra*). In the phrase “even with a wheel whose edge is like a razor,” it refers to the wheel as a weapon (*paharaṇacakkra*).
In the phrase “a thunderbolt-wheel (*asanivicakkra*),” it refers to the circle of the thunderbolt (*asanimaṇḍala*). However, here it is understood as the wheel of Dhamma.

Furthermore, this Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*) is twofold: the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of teaching (*desanā-ñāṇa*). Therein, the knowledge of penetration is developed through wisdom (*paññā*) and brings about the noble fruit for oneself;
the knowledge of teaching is developed through compassion (*karuṇā*) and brings about the noble fruit for disciples.
Therein, the knowledge of penetration is twofold: that which is arising and that which has arisen. For, from the time of the Great Departure...
Up until the arising of the path of Arahatship, it is called "arising"; at the moment of the fruition, it is called "arisen.
Or, from the Tusita heaven until the path of Arahatship arises at the seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka), it is called "arising"; at the moment of the fruition, it is called "arisen.
Or, starting from the time of the Ten-Powered One Dīpaṅkara until the path of Arahatship arises, it is called "arising"; at the moment of the fruition...
It is called "arisen. The knowledge of teaching (*desanāñāṇa*) is also twofold: that which is occurring while it is in process, and that which has occurred at the moment of fruition.

For that [knowledge] is said to be "occurring" from the time of the Elder Aññā-Koṇḍañña’s path to arahantship until the moment of the fruit; it is said to have "occurred" at the moment of the fruit itself.

Of these, the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedhañāṇa*) is supramundane (*lokuttara*), while the knowledge of teaching is mundane (*lokiya*). Yet both of these are not shared by others; they belong to the Buddhas alone.
It is direct knowledge (*orasañāṇa*). Therefore it is said: "He turns the Brahma-wheel.

Regarding "of the undertakings of action" (*kamma-samādānānaṃ*): this refers to wholesome and unwholesome actions performed after having undertaken them; or rather, "action" itself is what is meant by "undertaking of action.
"By way of place and cause" means by way of both condition (*paccaya*) and cause (*hetu*). In that context, destiny, the basis, time, and effort [are the conditions] for the result.
The basis. Karma is the cause.
"Leading everywhere" means leading to all destinations, both those that are good destinations and those that are bad destinations. "The way" means the path.
"He understands it as it really is" means that even among many people killing a single living being, the volition of this [particular person] leads to hell.
"By this method—'He will be born in the animal realm'—he knows, without error, the true nature of the practices comprised of wholesome and unwholesome volitions even within a single instance.
'Many elements' (*anekadhātu*) means having many elements by way of the eye-element and so forth, or the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth. 'Diverse elements' (*nānādhātu*)..."

Because those very elements (dhātu) have diverse characteristics, it is the "element of various kinds. "The world" (loka) refers to the world of aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu).
"He understands it as it really is" means he penetrates the specific nature (sabhāva) of each respective element without error.
"Various inclinations" (nānādhimuttikata) refers to the state of having diverse inclinations through such inclinations as inferior, superior, and so forth.
"Of other beings" (parasattānaṃ) means of superior beings. "Of other persons" (parapuggalānaṃ) means of those others who are inferior beings. Or else, these two phrases have the same meaning;
they were spoken by the Blessed One in two ways for the sake of those to be trained. Here too, it is stated according to the method spoken by the Blessed One.
"The penetration of the faculties of others" (indriyaparopariyattaṃ) means the higher state and the lower state of the faculties such as faith and the rest.
The meaning is "increase and decrease.
Regarding "the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments": this refers to the four jhānas beginning with the first; the eight liberations beginning with "one possessing form sees forms";
the three concentrations beginning with "with applied thought and sustained thought" (savitakka-savicāra); and the attainments of the first jhāna and so forth.
Of the nine successive attainments. *Saṃkileso* is a state conducive to decline.
*Vodānaṃ* is a state conducive to distinction. *Vuṭṭhānaṃ* is the cause by which one emerges from the jhānas and so forth;
that cause is described as "both purification is emergence, and emerging from this or that concentration is also emergence," referring thus to the mastery of jhāna.

And there are the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). For each lower jhāna that has been mastered serves as the proximate cause (padatthāna) for each higher one;

therefore, it is said that "purification (vodāna) is also emergence (vuṭṭhāna). However, emergence from all jhānas occurs by means of the life-continuum, and emergence from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) occurs by means of the attainment of fruition. It is with reference to this that [it was stated].
It is said: “Emerging from this or that concentration is also emergence.
The knowledge of past lives, the divine eye, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints have already been explained above.
In that context, “the destruction of the taints” means the destruction of all defilements by means of the path of arahantship. “Taintless” means free from the taints.
Regarding the phrase "liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom": here, by the word "mind" (ceto), the concentration associated with the fruit of Arahantship is meant;

and by the word "wisdom" (paññā), the wisdom associated with that same state is meant. In this context, it should be understood that concentration is called "liberation of mind" because it is liberated from lust, and wisdom is called "liberation by wisdom" because it is liberated from ignorance. For this was said by the Blessed One: "For him who... [and so forth].
“Monks, whatever concentration there is, that is his faculty of concentration. Whatever wisdom there is, monks, that is his faculty of wisdom.
Thus, monks, through the fading away of lust comes liberation of mind; through the fading away of ignorance comes liberation by wisdom.

Furthermore, it should be understood here that the power of serenity (samatha) is liberation of mind, and the power of insight (vipassanā) is liberation by wisdom. “In this very life” (diṭṭheva dhamme).

"In this very life" means in this very personal existence (*attabhāva*). "Having realized by direct higher knowledge" (*sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā*) means having made it personally manifest through superior wisdom;
the meaning is that one has known it independently of others. "Attaining" (*upasampajja*) means having reached or having accomplished it.
Furthermore, the detailed exposition of these ten knowledges of the Ten Powers (*dasabalañāṇa*) should be understood according to the method set forth in the Abhidhamma.
In this regard, there is the argument of an opponent: "The knowledge of the ten powers (*dasabalañāṇa*) is not a separate kind of knowledge;

it is merely a classification of the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). That should not be viewed in such a way. For the knowledge of the ten powers is indeed one thing, and the knowledge of omniscience is another.
The knowledge of the ten powers knows only its own respective functions, whereas the knowledge of omniscience knows those as well as what remains beyond them.

He knows. For among the ten powers of knowledge (*dasabalañāṇa*), the first knows precisely what is a cause and what is not a cause; the second, precisely the diversity of kamma and the diversity of its results (*vipāka*);

the third, precisely the delimitation of kamma; the fourth, precisely the cause for the diversity of elements (*dhātu*); the fifth, precisely the underlying tendencies and inclinations (*ajjhāsaya-adhimutti*) of beings;
the sixth, precisely the sharpness or dullness of the faculties (*indriya*); and the seventh, [precisely] by means of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and so forth...

Together with these, it understands the first [category], which is defilement and so forth; the eighth, which is the continuity of the aggregates in previous existences; the ninth, which is the death and rebirth-linking of beings;

and the tenth, which is the analysis of the Truths. However, the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa) understands both what is to be known by these and what lies beyond them. Yet, it does not perform all the functions of these [other knowledges]. For that—
Having become jhāna, it cannot enter [attainment]; having become psychic power (iddhi), it cannot perform transformations; having become the Path, it cannot exhaust the defilements (kilesa).

Furthermore, the opponent should be asked thus: "Is this so-called knowledge of the Ten Powers (dasabalañāṇa) with applied thought and sustained thought (savitakka-savicāra), or without applied thought and with only sustained thought (avitakka-vicāramatta)?"
“Without applied thought and without sustained thought, pertaining to the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere; mundane and supramundane. Knowing this, he will say:

“In succession, seven knowledges are with applied thought and sustained thought. He will say: “The two following those are without applied thought and without sustained thought. “The knowledge of the destruction of the taints may be with applied thought and sustained thought, may be without applied thought and with sustained thought alone, or may be...”

He will say, "without initial application and without sustained application. Likewise, he will say, "in sequence: seven belonging to the sense-sphere, two following those belonging to the fine-material sphere, and finally one supramundane.
Furthermore, he will say, "the knowledge of omniscience, however, possesses both initial application and sustained application, belongs only to the sense-sphere, and is mundane only."

Having thus understood the commentary on the previously unstated matter herein, one should now consider that the Tathāgata, by means of his knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭhāna-ñāṇa*),

first perceives the absence of the veil of defilements— which constitutes the possibility and impossibility for trainable beings to attain or fail to attain the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*)—
both because he sees the position of mundane right view and because he sees the absence of the position of fixed wrong view.
Then, by means of the knowledge of the ripening of kamma, he sees their absence of obstruction due to kamma-result, because he perceives a rebirth-linking with three roots.
By means of the knowledge of the way leading everywhere, he sees their absence of obstruction due to kamma, because he perceives the absence of any immediately effective (ānantarika) kamma.

Thus, for those who are unobstructed, he discerns their specific temperament by means of the knowledge of the many elements and the diversity of elements, for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma in accordance with it.
He sees [their dispositions] by seeing the diversity of their elements (*dhātu*).

Then, by means of the knowledge of their diverse inclinations (*nānādhimuttikatāñāṇa*), he sees their inclination even without relying on formal application, for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma according to that inclination.

Then, having thus seen their inclinations, in order to teach the Dhamma according to their capacity and strength, he perceives the degree of their faculties (*indriyaparopariyatta*) by means of the knowledge of the degrees of the faculties (*indriyaparopariyattañāṇa*).
He sees them because he perceives the sharpness or dullness of their faculties, such as faith and the rest.

Furthermore, even though he has thus fully understood the higher and lower states of their faculties, if they are far away, he then approaches them quickly through a specific supernormal power (*iddhi*), owing to his mastery over the jhānas and other meditative attainments via the knowledge of jhāna and so forth.
Having approached them, he discerns their previous births through the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa*) and by the power of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
Seeing the specific state of the mind at present by means of the knowable psychic power of reading others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*),

and because he is free from delusion regarding the path leading to the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*) through the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of the destruction of the taints. Therefore,
it should be understood that these ten powers (*bala*) are stated according to this sequence.
45. Now, wishing to demonstrate all the powers by way of their characteristics, he formulated a question in the manner beginning with "In what sense is it the power of faith?

and provided an answer in the manner beginning with "In the sense of being unshakable by lack of faith. Therein, the passage beginning with "It feels shame" (*hiriyati*) is a teaching expressed in terms of the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*).
Regarding the powers of development (*bhāvanābala*) and so forth, ending with the power of resolve (*adhiṭṭhānabala*), the word "therein" (*tattha*)—and so on—is used.
It should be understood that the words “by that” (*tena*) and “that” (*tam*) refer specifically to renunciation (*nekkhamma*) and so forth.
“By that the mind becomes one-pointed” (*tena cittaṃ ekaggam*) means that by means of that concentration (*samādhi*), the mind becomes one-pointed.

“Arisen therein” (*tattha jāto*) means arisen in that serenity (*samatha*) by way of association, or arisen having that [serenity] as its object for insight (*vipassanā*). “He trains therein” (*tattha sikkhati*)...
In this context, "the power of the trainee" (sekhabala) means that the trainee trains by means of it; thus, it is the power of the trainee. Regarding "because of having trained therein":
because the one beyond training (asekha) has trained therein, it is the power of the one beyond training (asekhabala).

"By which the taints are destroyed": by that mundane and supramundane knowledge the taints (āsava) are destroyed; that knowledge is the power of the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsavabala). For even by mundane knowledge, it is said that the taints are destroyed.

Because in the absence of insight (vipassanā), there is an absence of the supramundane path (lokuttara-magga). Thus, "the power of one whose taints are destroyed" (khīṇāsavabala) means the power belonging to one whose taints are destroyed.
"It succeeds for him" means it is the power of success (iddhibala); for that possessor of success, because it succeeds, success itself is the power—hence "power of success.
"In the sense of being immeasurable": because disciples know what is possible and impossible (ṭhānāṭhāna) and so forth only partially, whereas [the Buddha's] knowledge is in every aspect.

It is said, "he understands it as it really is" with reference to this. Although the phrase "he understands it as it really is" is not explicitly stated in the context of the three types of clear knowledge (*tisso vijjā*), because it is stated elsewhere, it is effectively stated for them as well.

"Elsewhere" refers to the remaining seven powers of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*), in the Abhidhamma, and in all ten powers (*bala*). However, the knowledge of the degrees of the faculties of others (*indriyaparopariyattañāṇa*) is [stated] in every respect.
It is indeed not shared with disciples. Therefore, even the ten powers are not shared with disciples.

In the sense of being preeminent and in the sense of being incomparable, they are immeasurable; for that very reason, it is said that "the power of a Tathāgata" is so called in the sense of being immeasurable.
The commentary on the discussion of the powers is finished.
10. Discourse on Emptiness (Suññakathā). Commentary on the Discourse on Emptiness: 46.
Now, immediately following the discourse on the powers (*bala*), which concludes with the supramundane powers, is the discourse on supramundane emptiness (*suññatā*).

A commentary on the meaning of the previously unexplained discourse concerning emptiness (*suññatā*), preceded by the Suttanta. First, regarding the Suttanta: *atha* is a particle used for the purpose of introducing a statement.
By this, the introduction of the words beginning with *āyasmā* (Venerable) is effected. *Khu* is a particle used for the purpose of completing the metrical line (*padapūraṇa*).
*Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami* is an instrumental case used in the sense of a locative; therefore, it means "wherever the Blessed One was, there [he approached]."

"Approached" (*upasaṅkami*)—this is how the meaning should be understood here. Or rather, by whatever reason the Blessed One is to be approached by gods and humans, by that very same reason he "approached"—this is how the meaning should be understood here. And for what reason is the Blessed One to be approached?
With the intention of attaining various distinguished qualities, and with the intention of enjoying sweet fruit.
Like a great tree that is constantly bearing fruit through its hosts of birds, for that reason he "approached" (*upasaṅkami*); such is the meaning to be understood here.
"Approached" (*upasaṅkami*) means that he "went" (*gato*). "Having approached" (*upasaṅkamitvā*) indicates the completion of the act of approaching.
Alternatively, it also means that having gone in this manner, he went to a place even closer than before, which is reckoned as the vicinity of the Blessed One.
"Having paid homage" means having worshipped by prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground.

Now, desiring to ask about the purpose for which he had come to attend upon the Supreme Person in the world, he placed his hands joined in reverential salutation—resplendent with the ten nails pressed together—at his head and sat down to one side.
The term "to one side" (*ekamantaṃ*) is a neuter singular adverbial expression, as seen in such phrases as "the moon and sun move unevenly."
Thus, the meaning here should be understood as: "he sat down" in such a way that he was seated to one side.
Alternatively, this accusative case is used in the sense of a locative. "He sat down" means he took his seat.
For wise gods and humans, having approached one who stands in a position of honor, sit to one side out of skill in the etiquette of seating; and this [person] likewise...
A certain elder among them sat down to one side.
But how does one sit down to one side? By avoiding the six faults of sitting. Namely:
too far away, too near, upwind, on high ground, directly in front, or directly behind. [Too far away...]
If one sits down wishing to speak, one must speak in a loud voice. If one sits too close, one causes physical contact.
If one sits upwind, one is troubled by the odor of the body. If one sits on high ground, one displays a lack of respect.
If one sits directly in front, if one wishes to look at [the teacher], one must press eye to eye.
It must be seen. If one sits too far back and wishes to see, it must be seen by stretching out the neck.
Therefore, he also sat down, avoiding these six faults of sitting. Thus it is said: "He sat to one side. He said this:
"Etadavoca" means he spoke this.
“‘The world is empty, the world is empty,’ venerable sir, it is said”: the meaning is that those various bhikkhus who have entered upon this teaching say, “The world is empty, the world is empty.
Because there are many such utterances here and there, the repetition (*āmeḍita*) is employed for the purpose of including them all.
For when it is stated in this way, all those utterances [are encompassed].
They are included. "To what extent" (*kittāvatā*) means by what measure. *Nu* is a particle used in the sense of doubt.

"Empty of self or of what belongs to self" (*suññaṃ attena vā attaniyena vā*) means empty of the self imagined by the world—namely, as an agent, an experiencer, or one who is independent—as well as empty of the requisites belonging to that self, precisely because of the absence of a self. All mundane things, such as the eye and so forth...
The category of phenomena (dhammajāta) is called the "world" (loka) in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating.
And because herein there is no self (atta) and nothing belonging to a self (attaniya), it is therefore said that "the world is empty" (suñño loko); this is the meaning.
