Furthermore, even supramundane (lokuttara) phenomena are indeed empty of self and what belongs to a self; however, in accordance with the question asked, only mundane (lokiya) phenomena were mentioned. And as for the term "empty," it refers to phenomena.

When it is said "it does not exist," it is not the non-existence of the house or the jar that is being stated; rather, the absence of the essence of self or what belongs to a self within that phenomenon is what is stated.
And when it is said in the world, "the house is empty" or "the jar is empty," it is not the non-existence of the house or the jar that is stated;
rather, the absence of something else within that house or jar is what is stated. And by the Blessed One, [when he said] "thus..."
"For whatever is not there, one perceives that as empty of it; but whatever remains there, one understands that which is present as 'this is here.
This is precisely the meaning stated. Likewise, this same meaning is found in the *Ñāyagrantha* and the *Śabdagrantha*.
Thus, in this sutta, only the characteristic of non-self (*anattalakkhaṇa*) is taught.

47. In the *Suttantaniddesa*, twenty-five matrix headings (*mātikāpada*) beginning with "emptiness of emptiness" (*suññasuñña*) are first set forth in connection with emptiness, and then their exposition (*niddesa*) is given. Regarding that, first, in the matrix:

emptiness is designated as "emptiness" (*suñña*) and is not qualified by any other subordinate term; thus it is "emptiness of emptiness. Furthermore, because it is not specified as "this" or "that," it is simply emptiness itself.
The neuter gender has been used by taking [the collective sense] into account. The same applies to the remaining terms.

It is "emptiness of formations" (*saṅkhāra-suñña*) because the formation itself is empty of the remaining formations. "Change-emptiness" (*vipariṇāma-suñña*) means that transformation (*pariṇāma*) is disfigured by way of aging and dissolution; it is empty of that transformation.
"Ultimate emptiness" (*agga-suñña*) means that it is both supreme (*agga*) and empty of self or what belongs to a self, or empty of all formations.
The characteristic itself is empty of the remaining characteristics; thus it is "emptiness of characteristics" (*lakkhaṇasuñña*). It is empty by way of suppression through renunciation and so forth;
thus it is "emptiness by suppression" (*vikkhambhanasuñña*). This same method applies to the four types beginning with "emptiness by substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅgasuñña*).
It is empty internally of self and what belongs to self, etc.; thus it is "internal emptiness" (*ajjhattasuñña*). And it is empty externally of self and what belongs to self, etc.; thus...
"Empty externally. Both of these are empty of self and what belongs to a self, etc.; thus it is "empty of both. That which has a similar portion is "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*);
that which is homogeneous and empty of self and what belongs to a self, etc., is "homogeneously empty" (*sabhāgasuñña*), meaning "similarly empty.
That from which the homogeneous has departed is "dissimilar" (*visabhāga*); that which is dissimilar and empty of self and what belongs to a self, etc., is "dissimilarly empty" (*visabhāgasuñña*).
The meaning is "emptiness of the dissimilar. In some manuscripts, "emptiness of the similar," "emptiness of the dissimilar," and "emptiness of the escape" are written after [the previous section].
Emptiness of search (*esanā-suñña*) is the emptiness of the search for renunciation and so forth from sensual desire and so forth.

The same method applies to the three beginning with emptiness of grasping (*pariggaha-suñña*). And because it is established upon a single object, there is no distraction toward various objects; thus, there is unity (*ekatta*).
That which is empty of diversity is the "emptiness of unity. That which is the opposite of that—diversity itself being empty of unity—is the "emptiness of diversity.

The desire for renunciation and so forth being empty of sensual desire and so forth is the "emptiness of resolve" (*khantisuñña*). The same method applies to the "emptiness of determination" (*adhiṭṭhānasuñña*) and the "emptiness of penetration" (*pariyogāhanasuñña*);
there is also a reading as *pariyogahanasuñña*. "Of one who is clearly comprehending" (*sampajānassa*) means by means of clear comprehension (*sampajañña*).
Of the Arahant who possesses [these qualities] and is attaining final Nibbāna. "The exhaustion of the process" means final Nibbāna through non-clinging (*anupādā-parinibbāna*).
"Of all emptinesses" means of all that is empty. "Ultimate emptiness" is the emptiness that constitutes the supreme state because of the absence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*). 48.
In the exposition of the matrix (*mātikā-niddesa*), "or by way of the permanent" refers to anything permanent that exists having transcended dissolution.

It is empty of permanence because of the absence of anything permanent. Or, it is empty of stability because even at the time of its existence, there is nothing stable due to its dependence on conditions for its continued occurrence.
Or, it is empty of eternity because of the absence of anything that exists uninterruptedly at all times.
Or, it is empty of that which has the nature of non-change, meaning anything whose intrinsic nature is not subject to alteration through aging or dissolution.
It is empty because of the non-existence of anything [permanent] and because of its nature of being subject to change.

Although emptiness of self (*attasuññatā*) alone was taught in the Suttanta, here, in order to demonstrate both emptiness of permanence (*niccasuññatā*) and emptiness of pleasure (*sukhasuññatā*), the phrases "by the permanent" and so forth are also stated.

For since that which is impermanent is suffering due to its association with oppression, when emptiness of permanence is stated, emptiness of pleasure is also effectively stated. [This applies to] form and the other aggregates.

In this context, it should be understood that the six objects, the six consciousnesses beginning with eye-consciousness, the six contacts beginning with eye-contact, and the six feelings beginning with feeling born of eye-contact are abbreviated.

Regarding the terms "meritorious volitional formation" (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) and so forth: it "purifies" (*punāti*) its own agent, fulfills his underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*), and is itself worthy of honor (*pujja*).

It is "merit" (*puñña*) because it produces existence (*bhava*). It is "volitional formation" (*abhisaṅkhāra*) because it constructs (*abhisaṅkharoti*) kamma-result (*vipāka*) and the matter produced by past deeds (*kaṭattā-rūpa*);

thus, merit as volitional formation is "meritorious volitional formation" (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*). Non-merit (*apuñña*) is the opposite of merit; non-merit as volitional formation is "non-meritorious volitional formation" (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*). It is "unshakable" (*aneñja*) because it is not shaken (*na iñjaṃ*);
it is "unshakable volitional formation" (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*) because it constructs unshakable existence (*aneñja-bhava*). [This concludes] meritorious volitional formation.
There are thirteen types of volition: the eight wholesome sense-sphere volitions that occur by way of generosity, virtue, and meditation;

the five wholesome fine-material-sphere volitions that occur solely by way of meditation; the twelve unwholesome volitions that constitute the formation of demerit and occur by way of killing living beings and so forth;
and the four [fine-material-sphere volitions] that constitute the imperturbable formation and occur solely by way of meditation.
"Volition pertaining to the formless realm": thus these three formations together constitute twenty-nine types of volition.
Regarding "bodily formation" (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) and so forth: it is called a bodily formation because it proceeds from the body, or because it is a formation of the body.

The same method applies to the verbal formation and the mental formation. This triad is for the purpose of showing how the meritorious formations and the rest proceed by way of the doors at the moment of accumulating kamma.

It has been stated: the twenty-one types of volition—namely, the eight wholesome sense-sphere volitions, the twelve unwholesome volitions, and the volition of direct knowledge—that arise from the body door having originated bodily intimation, are called "bodily formation" (kāyasaṅkhāra).
Those same [volitions], when they arise from the speech door having originated verbal intimation, are called "verbal formation" (vacīsaṅkhāra). At the mind door...
Furthermore, all twenty-nine types of volition that have arisen are called "mental formations" (*cittasaṅkhāra*). Regarding the phrases "past formations," and so forth:
all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhatadhammā*) that have reached their own moment and ceased are "past formations";
those that have not yet reached their own moment are "future formations"; and those that have reached their own moment are "present formations."
Having shown the present within the emptiness of change, the present phenomena were first displayed so that their respective changes could be easily explained.
Therein, "form born" refers to present form. "Empty of its own-nature" (*sabhāvena suñña*):
here, "own-nature" (*sabhāva*) means its own being; the meaning is its own arising. Alternatively, "own-nature" is the being of what exists.
The meaning is that its arising is from itself alone. Because it exists in dependence on conditions, there is no existence of its own accord (sayameva) without conditions;

or, there is no existence from itself (attato) in this [dhamma]. Thus, it is "empty by way of intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvena suññaṃ*); what is meant is that it is empty of existence by way of itself, or empty of existence from itself.
Alternatively, *sabhāva* means the state of one's own (*sakassa bhāvo*). For among the many [elements] such as the earth-element (*pathavīdhātu*) and so forth—
Among material and immaterial phenomena, each individual phenomenon is called "its own" (*saka*) in relation to others. Furthermore, "state" (*bhāva*) is a synonym for "phenomenon" (*dhamma*).
Since there is no other phenomenon designated as a "state" belonging to a single phenomenon, it is therefore empty of another state of its own;
the meaning is that its own [nature] is empty of another state. By this, the fact that a single phenomenon has a single intrinsic nature is stated.
It exists. Alternatively, "empty by its own nature" means it is empty precisely because its nature is emptiness. What is meant?
It is meant that it is empty solely through the emptiness of emptiness (*suññasuññatā*), and not empty through other figurative modes of emptiness (*pariyāyasuññatā*).
However, if some were to say, "Own-nature (*sabhāva*) is one's own being; it is empty of that own-nature," what would be meant?
What is it that exists? "Bhāva" (existence) is a phenomenon (*dhamma*); when that is qualified by its own term in relation to another, it is called "intrinsic nature" (*sabhāva*).
Since no phenomenon whatsoever exists [independently], the statement "arisen form is empty of intrinsic nature" expresses the non-existence of form.
This being the case, it contradicts the expression "arisen form," for that which is devoid of arising cannot be called "arisen."
It exists. For Nibbāna is devoid of arising; it is not called "born. And birth, aging, and death—being devoid of arising—are not called "born.

Therefore, in this context, instead of stating, "Born birth is empty of its own intrinsic nature (sabhāva); born aging-and-death is empty of its own intrinsic nature," existence (bhava) alone is taken as the final term and thus explained. If [this were so] even for that which is devoid of arising...
The expression “born” would be appropriate [only if it were something produced]; one would have to say, “birth is born,” or “aging-and-death is born.

Since the expression “born” is not used for birth and aging-and-death—which are devoid of arising—therefore, the statement that they are “empty of intrinsic nature and non-existent” contradicts the expression “born,” because that which is non-existent lacks arising.
Furthermore, the statement that what is non-existent is "empty" contradicts the worldly expression mentioned above, as well as the word of the Blessed One and the explanations in the *Ñāyasaṅgaha*;
it also contradicts numerous logical arguments. Therefore, that statement should be discarded like refuse.
"Bhikkhus, whatever is agreed upon by the wise in the world as existing..."
I too say that it exists. And what, monks, is considered non-existent in the world by the wise, which I also say does not exist?
And what, monks, is considered existent in the world by the wise, which I also say exists?
Form, monks, which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is what is considered existent in the world by the wise.
One must reach the conclusion here that phenomena exist only at their own moment, based on numerous authorities of the Buddha’s word such as “I too say that it exists,” and on many logical arguments.
"Past form" (*vigataṃ rūpaṃ*) is form that has arisen and reached dissolution, having ceased; and "altered form" (*vipariṇataṃ*).
"And empty" means that it has reached an unsightly transformation due to aging and dissolution;

and because transformation exists only for what is presently occurring, while there is no transformation for what is past, it is "empty" of that transformation—this is the meaning. The same method applies to the phrases "born feeling," and so forth.
However, as for birth, aging, and death, because they are unconditioned (*anipphanna*) and thus not perceivable by way of their own intrinsic nature (*sakabhāva*), [they are treated] here...

That is not tenable; therefore, having set aside the two methods beginning with "birth is born" and "ageing-and-death are born," it is established by making the method beginning with "existence" (bhava) the conclusion.
*Agga* means existing at the summit (*agge*). *Seṭṭha* means exceedingly praiseworthy. *Visiṭṭha* means preeminent. *Viseṭṭha* is also used.
The reading [is as follows]. Nibbāna is praised in three ways; it is called a "state" (*pada*) because it is to be entered upon by means of the right practice. "Yadidaṃ" means "that which is this.

This indicates the Nibbāna that is about to be described. Because, by coming to Nibbāna, there is the subsiding (*samatha*) of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), [it is the state] of the acquisitions (*upadhi*)—namely, those consisting of the aggregates (*khandha*), the defilements (*kilesa*), the volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*), and the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).

There is relinquishment; there is the destruction, fading away, and cessation of cravings. Therefore, it is called the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, fading away, and cessation.
Thus, "Nibbāna" is concluded by way of its essential characteristic (*sabhāva-lakkhaṇa*). For regarding characteristics, it is said:
"Monks, these three are the characteristics of a fool, the signs of a fool, the attributes of a fool."
“What three? Here, monks, a fool is one who thinks ill-thought thoughts, speaks ill-spoken words, and performs ill-done deeds.
These, monks, are the three characteristics of a fool, the marks of a fool, the attributes of a fool,” so it was said.
The characteristic of a fool is threefold, being recognized by the wise as a fool. “These three... [and so forth].
“Monks, there are these three characteristics of a wise person, marks of a wise person, and deeds of a wise person.
What are the three? Here, monks, a wise person is one who thinks well-thought thoughts, speaks well-spoken words, and performs well-done deeds.
These, monks, are the three characteristics of a wise person, marks of a wise person, and deeds of a wise person.”
It has been said. The characteristic of a wise person is threefold, according to how it is observed by the wise as "a wise person is wise":

"Bhikkhus, there are these three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned. Which three? Arising is discerned, passing away is discerned, and the alteration of that which stands is discerned. These, bhikkhus, are the three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned. [End of quotation]
It is said, “the characteristics of the conditioned. Since arising itself is the characteristic of the conditioned, it is called a "characteristic of the conditioned" (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*).

The meaning should be understood in the same way for the other two as well. By this, the absence of the remaining two at the moment of arising, the absence of the remaining two at the moment of presence, and the absence of the remaining two at the moment of dissolution is demonstrated. Furthermore, regarding that which is here [stated] by way of a formulaic summary (*peyyālamukha*) concerning birth and...

The characteristic of arising and so forth for aging-and-death has been stated; however, that contradicts both the statement that excludes birth, aging, and death due to the emptiness of transformation (*vipariṇāma-suññatā*), and the method of speaking only up to the end of existence (*bhava-pariyosāna*), as well as the occasion when the arising and so forth of arising and so forth are not mentioned.
Nevertheless, it should be understood that because it falls within the stream of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-sota*), it was written down as having fallen into that stream.

And just as it is stated in the *Abhidhamma*, in the section on inclusion (*saṅgaha*), that although the jhāna factors are found in the rootless resultant mind-element and mind-consciousness-element, they are not mentioned because they have fallen into the stream of the fivefold sense-consciousness; so too here, one should understand their state of having fallen into the stream.
Or alternatively, the arising and so forth of formations that possess birth, aging, and death are [collectively] called "birth, aging, and death."
It should be understood that this is stated by treating them as if they were [the same], as in the passage beginning "as impermanent" (*aniccato*).

By means of renunciation (*nekkhamma*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is both suppressed and empty; thus, sensual desire is empty of renunciation because of its suppression by renunciation and because of the absence of that very thing called suppression—namely, renunciation—therein.
And so should the application be made for the remaining [factors] as well.

Here, in the case of abandonment by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-pahāna*) and abandonment by eradication (*samuccheda-pahāna*), that which is abandoned by way of substitution of opposites and by way of eradication is also rendered distant; thus, suppression (*vikkhambhana*) is spoken of in the sense of this "rendering distant.

Through renunciation (*nekkhamma*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is empty by way of substitution of opposites; thus, sensual desire abandoned by means of renunciation is [rendered distant] by that which is termed renunciation.
It is empty of that factor. Alternatively, whatever sensual desire there may be is empty of renunciation because of its absence therein;
this same application should be made for the remaining factors as well.

And here, by the mere absence of each respective factor in its corresponding place, there is "emptiness as a factor" (tadaṅga-suññatā) by way of access concentration, absorption concentration, and insight.

[The insight knowledges] have been demonstrated. However, because there is no statement indicating their abandonment, insight is demonstrated as ending with the contemplation of turning away (*vivaṭṭanānupassanā*), and the four paths are not demonstrated.

In such passages as "By renunciation, sensual desire is both cut off and void," the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated regarding suppression (*vikkhambhana*). This is by way of partial suppression (*tadaṅga-vikkhambhana*).
Furthermore, because they no longer manifest even though they have been abandoned, they are called "completely cut off" (*samucchinna*); it is in this sense that "cutting off" is spoken of.

Alternatively, it should be understood that it is also spoken of by way of the renunciation (*nekkhamma*) and other factors associated with the path, through their performance of the specific function of cutting off each respective defilement.
Regarding subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi*), emergence (*nissaraṇa*), and emptiness (*suñña*), the meaning should be understood here according to the same method as has been stated.
In this context, however, it is stated by taking up the mere subsiding and the mere escape regarding the abandonings through substitution of opposites, suppression, and eradication.
Among these five voids, renunciation and the rest are themselves expressed by the names of suppression, substitution of opposites, eradication, subsiding, and escape.
"Internal" means that which has become internal. "External" means that which has become external. "Void in both ways" means void in both respects.
For even in the case of *paccatta* and so forth, the expression *to iti* indeed occurs.
The six internal bases (*ajjhattikāyatana*) and so forth are "similar" (*sabhāga*) by virtue of being the state of the six internal bases and so forth; they are "dissimilar" (*visabhāga*) to others.

And here, in such expressions as "the groups of consciousness" (*viññāṇakāya*), it is the consciousnesses themselves that are expressed by the word "group" (*kāya*). In [terms such as] "seeking renunciation" (*nekkhammesanā*) and so forth...
Renunciation and the rest are called "seeking" (*esanā*) because they are sought after by the wise who desire them.
Alternatively, it is said that even the seeking of renunciation and the rest in the prior stage is empty of sensual desire and so forth, let alone renunciation and the rest themselves.

Among the categories beginning with "embracing" (*pariggaha*), renunciation and the rest are what were sought in the prior stage and are embraced in the subsequent stage; thus they are called "embraced. They have been embraced.

They are called "acquisition" (*paṭilābha*) because they are acquired by way of attainment; and they are called "penetration" (*paṭivedha*) because, having been acquired, they are penetrated by way of knowledge.

Having asked about both the emptiness of unity and the emptiness of diversity at once, the conclusion was made once and for all after answering the question regarding the emptiness of unity, even though the emptiness of diversity had not yet been answered. Why was it not answered?

Why? It should be understood that the application [of the terms] here was not explained because it can be understood through the very method already stated. However, the application here is as follows:
renunciation is unity, sensual desire is diversity; sensual desire is diversity, and renunciation is empty of that.
In this same way, the application should be understood for the remaining cases as well.
Among patience (*khanti*) and the other [perfections], renunciation (*nekkhamma*) and the rest are called "patience" because they are endured and because they are approved;

they are called "determination" (*adhiṭṭhāna*) because one enters and remains within what has been approved; and they are called "thorough penetration" (*pariyogāhana*) because one cultivates them exactly as approved once one has entered and remained therein.
Here, the description of ultimate emptiness beginning with "possessing full awareness" (*sampajāno*) has already been explained in the description of the knowledge of final Nibbāna.

And among all these [types of] emptiness, the emptiness of formations (*saṅkhāra-suñña*), the emptiness of change (*vipariṇāma-suñña*), and the emptiness of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-suñña*) are for the purpose of showing that the phenomena already mentioned are not mutually mixed.

However, where the emptiness of unwholesome factors by means of wholesome factors is stated, it is for the purpose of showing the danger (*ādīnava*) in the unwholesome. But where [the emptiness] of wholesome factors by means of unwholesome factors...
Emptiness (suññatā) has been taught for the purpose of showing the benefits of the wholesome.

Where emptiness is taught by way of the absence of self and what belongs to self, it is for the purpose of generating disenchantment with all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra). It should be understood that the supreme emptiness and the ultimate emptiness have been taught for the purpose of generating enthusiasm for Nibbāna.
Among those, the "supreme void" (*aggasuñña*) and the "ultimate void" (*paramatthasuñña*)—these two voids are in fact one and the same Nibbāna;
they are stated as two by way of the supreme and ultimate sense, and by way of being with remainder (*saupādisesa*) and without remainder (*anupādisesa*).

These two are similar in their voidness of self and what belongs to self, and in their voidness of formations (*saṅkhāra*). [They are also] the voidness of the void, the voidness internally, the voidness externally, and the voidness of both.
These six kinds of emptiness—emptiness of the similar and emptiness of the dissimilar—are themselves simply the "emptiness of emptiness.
Furthermore, they are spoken of as sixfold according to the distinctions of internal and so forth. And these six are similar in their emptiness of self and what belongs to self.

They are the emptiness characterized by the transformation of formations, the emptiness of suppression, of its factors, of eradication, of subsiding, and of escape; and the emptiness of search, of embracing, of acquisition, and of penetration.
The seventeen voids— namely, the voidness of unity, diversity, and emptiness, as well as the voidness of patience, resolution, and penetration—
are stated individually according to the non-existence of their respective phenomena, which do not exist within the self. However,
the voidness characterized by the transformation of formations is common to all, insofar as each is unmixed with the others.
The five beginning with suppression are similar by virtue of being empty of the side of the wholesome;

the four beginning with seeking, and the three beginning with patience, are similar by virtue of being empty of the side of the unwholesome; those empty of unity and diversity are similar by virtue of being mutual opposites.
All phenomena, in brief, are of three kinds, two kinds, and likewise one kind.
Those who know the meaning of emptiness explain it thus here in the Dispensation:
How so? First of all, all mundane phenomena (*lokiya-dhamma*) are empty of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and self, because they are devoid of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and self.

The phenomena of the Path and its Fruits (*magga-phala-dhamma*) are empty of permanence and pleasure, because they are devoid of permanence and pleasure. Precisely because of their impermanence, they are [empty] of pleasure.
They are empty. Because they are free from taints (*āsava*), they are not empty of beauty. The phenomenon of Nibbāna is empty of self because of the very absence of a self.
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*), whether mundane or supramundane, are empty of a being (*satta*) because of the absence of any such being.
The unconditioned phenomenon of Nibbāna is empty of formations (*saṅkhāra*) because of the absence even of those formations. And all phenomena, both conditioned and unconditioned, are...
Because of the non-existence of a person designated as "self," there is "emptiness of self.
This concludes the commentary on the Discourse on Emptiness from the *Saddhammappakāsinī*,
the commentary on the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.
The commentary on the Yuganaddhavagga is finished.
Also finished is the commentary on the previously unexplained portions of the Majjhima-vagga.
(3) The Paññāvagga.
1. The Discourse on Great Wisdom (Mahāpaññākathā). Commentary on the Discourse on Great Wisdom:
Now, following the discourse on emptiness—which specifically serves as the foundation for wisdom—the discourse on wisdom is explained.

The commentary on what has not been previously established. Therein, first of all, seven kinds of wisdom based on each one of the seven contemplations (*anupassanā*) are demonstrated by means of questions;
furthermore, three kinds of wisdom based on the seven contemplations and based on each successive [contemplation] are demonstrated without posing questions.
Thus, the completion of ten kinds of wisdom is demonstrated from the beginning. Therein—
First, as for the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*):

because it impels toward suffering—as in "what is impermanent is suffering"—and toward non-self—as in "what is suffering is non-self"—with respect to the formations seen as impermanent, therefore, when developed and cultivated, it fulfills the wisdom of impulsion (*javanapaññā*).
For it is called "impulsion" (*javanā*) because it impels toward its own objects; and that which is both impulsion and wisdom is "wisdom of impulsion."
Swift wisdom (*javanapaññā*). Contemplation of suffering, having become powerful by being supported by the faculty of concentration, pierces and breaks through aspiration;
therefore, it fulfills penetrative wisdom (*nibbedhikapaññā*). For that [wisdom] penetrates, thus it is "penetrative" (*nibbedhikā*);

and since it is both penetrative and wisdom, it is "penetrative wisdom. Contemplation of non-self, through the attainment of growth by means of the vision of emptiness (*suññatā*), [fulfills penetrative wisdom].
Because it has reached greatness, it fulfills great wisdom (*mahāpaññā*). For that wisdom is called "great wisdom" because it is both great—having reached growth—and wisdom.

Since the contemplation of disenchantment (*nibbidānupassanā*) is capable of causing disenchantment with all conditioned phenomena due to its state of having attained strength through prior cultivation by the three preceding contemplations, it is sharp; therefore, it is "sharp wisdom" (*tikkhapaññā*).

It fulfills [wisdom]. Contemplation of fading away (*virāgānupassanā*) also fulfills vast wisdom because, having reached the power of cultivation even prior to the three preceding contemplations, it becomes extensive by being capable of fading away from all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
Contemplation of cessation (*nirodhānupassanā*) also [fulfills wisdom] because, having reached the power of cultivation even prior to the three preceding contemplations...
Because it exists in a more advanced stage, it is profound in that it is capable of seeing the cessation of all conditioned phenomena by way of their characteristic of decay;

therefore, it fulfills profound wisdom. For cessation is profound because it provides no foothold for those of superficial wisdom, and the wisdom that has gained a footing in that profundity is likewise profound. Furthermore, as for the contemplation of relinquishment:

Because it is a more advanced stage than even the three preceding contemplations which have already attained the power of cultivation (āsevanābala), it becomes capable of relinquishing all conditioned phenomena by way of the characteristic of decay (vaya-lakkhaṇa) and thus becomes "without peer" (asāmanta).

The meaning is that, because it has reached the limit of growth, it is far removed from the six kinds of wisdom. Therefore, by virtue of being itself without peer, it fulfills the "wisdom without peer."
For it is called "unrivalled wisdom" (*asāmantapaññā*) because it is far removed from, or not in the vicinity of, the lower types of wisdom.
"Fulfilling cleverness" means fulfilling the state of being a wise person.

Because, having fully developed the seven aforementioned types of wisdom, one who has attained the characteristics of a wise person [proceeds] by means of the knowledges of equanimity towards formations, conformity, and change-of-lineage—which are comprised within the insight leading to emergence and reaching the peak.
Having become wise, he is endowed with wisdom; therefore it is said, "fulfilling wisdom.
"The eight kinds of wisdom" refers to all eight types of wisdom together with that wisdom designated as "cleverness" (*paṇḍicca*).
"Fulfilling broad wisdom" means that, being endowed with that cleverness, that wise person, immediately after the knowledge of the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*), [attains] Nibbāna.

By taking that as its object, one attains the wisdom of the path and fruition—known as "wide wisdom"—because it has become distinct and separate from the mundane due to the attainment of the supramundane state.
Therefore, it is said: "The eight kinds of wisdom fulfill wide wisdom.

Regarding the passage beginning "These nine kinds of wisdom," etc., [it refers to] the utilization of sublime supramundane states by a noble person who has successively attained the path and fruition.

Because the continuum of consciousness is refined and because the continuum of consciousness proceeds in a state of elation, there occurs first the reviewing of the Path for one who has emerged from the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) immediately after the fruit;
then, for one who has descended back into the life-continuum and emerged from it, there occurs the reviewing of the Fruit.
By this same method, there occurs the reviewing of the defilements abandoned and the reviewing of the remaining defilements.

Regarding the "reviewing of Nibbāna," five types of reviewing take place. Among those reviews, the reviewing of the Path and the reviewing of the Fruit constitute the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*). How so?

By following the text of the Abhidhamma: "Whatever is produced by conditions, Nibbāna, the meaning of what is spoken, resultant [kamma], and functional [kamma]—these five things are 'meaning' (*attha*)."

This is stated in its commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). Because Nibbāna is an "object" (*attha*), the knowledge of the path and fruit which has that as its object is the "analytical knowledge of the object" (*atthapaṭisambhidā*), according to the statement: "Knowledge regarding objects is the analytical knowledge of the object.

The reviewing knowledge of that path and fruit knowledge—which constitutes the analytical knowledge of the object—is the "analytical knowledge of perspicuity" (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*), according to the statement: "Knowledge regarding knowledges is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity."

There is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*). This is reflective wisdom; it is called "wisdom of laughter" because it occurs in the form of laughter within a mental continuum that is proceeding with a joyful mode.
Therefore, it is said that the nine types of wisdom fulfill the wisdom of laughter, and that the wisdom of laughter is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity.
Furthermore, all forms of wisdom, in the sense of making things known—defined as the act of making various objects manifest—[are included therein].
*Paññā*: it is wisdom because it knows phenomena (*dhamma*) in this or that manner; thus it is *paññā*.
"Of him" means of that noble person (*ariyapuggala*) described in the aforementioned manner. The genitive case is used here in the sense of the instrumental.
"By way of the determination of meaning" means by way of the defining of the fivefold meaning as previously stated. And this has also been said in the *Samaṇakaraṇīyakathā*.

“Nibbāna is the fruit of the cause; as for the meaning of the word, it is [also] fruition and functional [consciousness]. Thus, among the fivefold classification of meanings, knowledge is that which has entered into the first division.
It is “attained” (adhigatā) means it is acquired (paṭiladdhā). That very [knowledge] is realized through the realization of acquisition.
It is touched by wisdom through the very contact of acquisition. From the “definition of phenomena” (dhammavavatthānato): “Whatever produces a fruit...”

"By way of defining the five things stated in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka according to the text as 'the cause, the noble path, what has been spoken, the wholesome, and the unwholesome'— and this is also said in the *Samaṇakaraṇīyakathā*:
'The cause, the noble path, speech, the wholesome, and the unwholesome— these are the fivefold divisions of things, falling under the second division.'"
"Knowledge. By way of determining the etymological definitions: this means by way of establishing the appropriate etymological definitions for each respective meaning and phenomenon.
By way of determining the inspired eloquence: this means by way of establishing the three kinds of analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidāñāṇa) known as inspired eloquence.
"Tassimā" is a concluding statement.

2. Having thus shown the distinction between the contemplations (*anupassanā*) by way of their all-inclusive nature, [the author] now says, "Contemplation of impermanence in form," etc., in order to show them by way of the classification of their bases (*vatthu*).

That has already been explained in meaning above. Furthermore, desiring to show the impulsive wisdom (*javanapaññā*) regarding form and so forth by way of the past, future, and present, [he speaks] both by way of form and so forth alone, and by way of past, future, and present form and so forth.
And having made the question the "tail," he gave the answer by means of that very question-tail. In this regard, among all the answers based on the past,

future, and present roots, the wisdom already indicated in the answers concerning pure matter and so forth is indicated as "wisdom of impulsions" (javanapaññā) by way of impulsion within those [answers] regarding the past and so on.
3. Furthermore, desiring to show the various classifications of wisdom preceded by numerous Suttantas, he first recited the Suttanta.
Therein, "association with good persons" (*sappurisa-saṃsevo*) means the cultivation of good persons of the type described above.

"Hearing the true Dhamma" (*saddhamma-savanaṃ*) means hearing the words of the true Dhamma that elucidate the practice of virtue and so forth in the presence of those good persons. "Careful attention" (*yoniso-manasikāro*)...
Attention by way of means consists in the investigation of the meaning of the teachings that have been heard.
"Practice in accordance with the Dhamma" (dhammānudhammapaṭipatti) is the undertaking of the practice of virtue and so forth that follows upon the supramundane Dhamma.
"For the acquisition of wisdom, for the increase of wisdom, for the expansion of wisdom, for the abundance of wisdom"—these four are expressions of development (bhāva) by way of wisdom.
The remaining twelve [terms] are expressions for the types of persons (*puggala*). 1.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Sixteen Kinds of Wisdom (Paññā). 4.

In the Sutta-exposition, regarding "the six kinds of direct-knowledge wisdom" (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*): these are the knowledge of supernormal powers (*iddhividha*), the divine ear (*dibbasota*), penetration of the minds of others (*cetopariya*), recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsa*), the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), and the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*).

"Of the knowledges of destruction": this refers to the knowledges common to disciples that have been specified in the *Ñāṇakathā* (Discourse on Knowledge) as "the seventy-seven knowledges. Regarding the phrase "of the seventy-seven knowledges," it refers to the passage:
"Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the seventy-seven bases of knowledge; listen to it and attend to it well... [and so forth].
"Attend, monks, I shall speak. What, monks, are the seventy-seven bases of knowledge? The knowledge that 'with birth as condition there is aging-and-death';
the knowledge that 'in the absence of birth, there is no aging-and-death. Regarding the past time, the knowledge that 'with birth as condition there was aging-and-death';
the knowledge that 'in the absence of birth, there was no aging-and-death. Regarding the future time..."
The knowledge that "with birth as condition, there is aging-and-death"; the knowledge that "in the absence of birth, there is no aging-and-death.
Furthermore, the knowledge that even this knowledge of the stability of phenomena is subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.

The knowledge that "with existence as condition, there is birth" … [and so on] … the knowledge that "with clinging as condition, there is existence" … the knowledge that "with craving as condition, there is clinging."

Knowledge that "craving has feeling as its condition" … knowledge that "feeling has contact as its condition" … knowledge that "contact has the six sense bases as its condition" … knowledge that "the six sense bases have name-and-form as their condition" … knowledge that "name-and-form has consciousness as its condition" … knowledge that "consciousness has volitional formations as its condition" … knowledge that "volitional formations have ignorance as their condition"; [and] when there is no ignorance...
There is the knowledge: "There are no volitional formations. There is the knowledge: "In the past, too, with ignorance as condition there were volitional formations";

there is the knowledge: "If there were no ignorance, there would be no volitional formations. There is the knowledge: "In the future, too, with ignorance as condition there will be volitional formations";
there is the knowledge: "If there were no ignorance, there would be no volitional formations. And that knowledge of the stability of phenomena is itself subject to destruction.
“...the knowledge that it is subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation. These, monks, are called the seventy-seven bases of knowledge.
Thus were the seventy-seven knowledges spoken of by the Blessed One in the Nidāna Vagga. By means of this [formula]:
“Knowledge of aging-and-death, knowledge of the origin of aging-and-death, knowledge of the cessation of aging-and-death, knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of aging-and-death.”
However, the forty-four bases of knowledge (*ñāṇavatthu*), which are stated by taking four from each of the eleven factors according to the method [of the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*], are not included here.
In both cases, they are called "bases of knowledge" (*ñāṇavatthu*) because knowledge itself is the basis for welfare and happiness.
Regarding the terms beginning with "gain" (*lābha*), "acquisition" (*paṭilābha*) is said by distinguishing it through a prefix. Furthermore, by way of explaining its meaning:

It is said, "attainment" (*sampatti*). "Touching" (*phassanā*) means contacting by way of realization. "Direct realization" (*sacchikiriyā*) means direct realization as acquisition. "Full attainment" (*upasampadā*) means bringing to completion.
And regarding "the seven trainees" (*sekkhā*):
they are designated as "trainees" because they train in the three trainings; these refer to those such as one standing on the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*), and so forth.

Of the seven. And of the "virtuous worldling" (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*): that is, of the worldling who is designated as "virtuous" (*kalyāṇa*) in the sense of being excellent because he is engaged in the practice leading to Nibbāna.
"Increasing the increased" (*vaḍḍhitavaḍḍhanā*): that by which there is an increase of what has already been increased.
This refers specifically to the growth of wisdom (*paññāvuddhi*) by means of all eight kinds of wisdom mentioned above, and particularly by means of the wisdom of the Arahant. Likewise...

"For the expansion of wisdom. In such passages as "he grasps great meanings," the noble disciple who has attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) grasps meanings and so forth by taking them as objects. All great wisdom belongs exclusively to noble disciples.
And the objects of that wisdom are exactly as explained below.
In the phrases beginning with "in various and diverse aggregates," the word *nānā* (various) is a synonym for the word *puthu* (diverse). Regarding the expression "knowledge proceeds":
because knowledge proceeds toward those aggregates and so forth that have been described in such a way, that knowledge is called "vast wisdom" (*puthupaññā*).
This is the meaning. In the phrase "in various dependent originations," it refers to the multiplicity of conditions by virtue of the phenomena that have arisen dependently.

It has been said: "In the non-apprehension of various kinds of emptiness" (*nānāsuññatamanupalabbhesu*). "Apprehension" (*upalabbho*) means the act of apprehending; that is, grasping. "Non-apprehension" (*anupalabbho*) is the absence of apprehension.

Because there is a multiplicity of such non-apprehensions, they are expressed in the plural as "non-apprehensions. Alternatively, because of the twenty-five types of emptiness, there is the non-apprehension of a self or anything belonging to a self within those various kinds of emptiness;
thus it is "the non-apprehension of various kinds of emptiness. [The phrase refers] to those. Thus: "In the non-apprehension of various kinds of emptiness."
In such expressions as “neither-painful-nor-pleasant,” the letter *m* is used by way of euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*).
These five types of wisdom are shared with ordinary persons (*puthujjana*), whereas the wisdom regarding various meanings and so forth belongs to the Noble Ones (*ariya*) alone.

Regarding the phrase “states shared with ordinary persons,” this refers to mundane states (*lokika-dhamma*). By this final method of explanation, because it has as its object the *nibbāna* which is distinct from the mundane, [it is called "wisdom of the distinction"].
"Extensive wisdom" (puthupaññā) means that which is broad and manifold; this is what is meant by the term "extensive wisdom.
It should be understood according to the method of "vast wisdom" (vipulapaññā) and "great wisdom" (mahāpaññā).

This is because of the greatness of the qualities in one who comprehends the aforementioned phenomena, the greatness of the wisdom that comprehends those phenomena, and the inherent greatness of those phenomena themselves.
The loftiness of the states and the vastness of the wisdom should be understood.
Profound wisdom is to be understood by way of extensive wisdom. Those states and that wisdom are profound because they are unattainable and because they provide no foothold for ordinary people.
"Of which person" refers specifically to the noble person (*ariyapuggala*). "Anyone else" refers to the worldling (*puthujjana*). "To master" means to reach or attain.
"Unattainable" (*anabhisambhavanīya*) means impossible to reach. "By others" (*aññehi*) refers specifically to worldlings (*puthujjana*).
"Of the eighth person" (*aṭṭhamakassa*) refers to one who stands on the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*), being counted as the eighth starting from the stage of the fruit of arahantship.
"Far" (*dūra*) means separated. "Very far" (*vidūra*) means especially separated. "Extremely far" (*suvidūra*) means thoroughly and especially separated.

"Not in the vicinity" means not in close proximity. "Not in the neighborhood" means not in the surrounding area. These two expressions, joined with the negations, serve to define the state of being far removed.
"Depending on" means in reliance upon. "Of a stream-enterer" means of one who stands at the fruit of stream-entry.
By this very [statement], it is expressed that the wisdom of each respective path is distant from the wisdom of each respective fruit. "A paccekabuddha" [is as follows].
[The first term] is qualified by a prefix, whereas the other two have come down [in the texts] in their pure form.

Having stated such things as, "The wisdom of a Paccekabuddha and of the world with its devas is far from the wisdom of a Tathāgata," he says, beginning with "skilled in the classification of wisdom," desiring to demonstrate that very state of being distant in many ways. Therein:

"Skilled in the classification of wisdom" means one who is expert in the infinite varieties of wisdom. "One whose knowledge is manifold" means one whose knowledge has attained infinite classifications.

By this, he shows that even while being skilled in the classification of wisdom, those various wisdoms possess infinite divisions. "One who has attained the analytical knowledges" (paṭisambhidā) means one who has acquired the supreme knowledge of the four analytical insights (catu-paṭisambhidā).
"One who has reached the four grounds of self-confidence" (vesārajja) refers to the four states characterized by fearlessness.
He has attained the knowledges. As it is said:

"Regarding these things that you claim to have fully awakened to as a Perfectly Enlightened One, there might indeed be some ascetic or brahmin, or a deva, or Māra, or Brahmā, or anyone else in the world who could rightfully challenge me, saying: 'These things have not been fully awakened to by you.'"
“Bhikkhus, I do not see any ground for this. Not seeing such a ground, bhikkhus, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, having attained intrepidity.

For one who claims, ‘My taints are destroyed,’ to say, ‘These taints are not yet fully destroyed,’ or that those things which have been declared by me to be obstructive are not sufficient to obstruct one who indulges in them—[I see no basis for this].”
‘It will be an obstacle,’ or ‘The purpose for which the Dhamma has been taught by you does not lead one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering’—
in this regard, monks, I do not see any ground on which any ascetic or brahmin, or any god, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world, could rightfully reproach me.
“Not perceiving even this sign, monks, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, having attained intrepidity.

“He who possesses the power of the Ten Powers”: those who have these ten powers are the “Ten-Powered Ones” (*dasabala*); the powers of the Ten-Powered Ones are the “powers of the Ten-Powered Ones” (*dasabalabala*); he who maintains those powers of the Ten-Powered Ones is the “possessor of the power of the Ten-Powered Ones,” which means he is the possessor of the power of the knowledge of the Ten-Powered One.
By these three terms, a mere glimpse of the classification of those things to be known (*neyya*), which possess infinite divisions, has been shown.

By virtue of his application of wisdom (*paññāyogavasena*), he is a "bull among men" (*purisāsabha*) in the sense of being highly auspicious and esteemed. He is a "lion among men" (*purisasīha*) in the sense of being fearless. He is an "elephant among men" (*purisanāga*) in the sense of greatness.
He is a "thoroughbred among men" (*purisājañña*) in the sense of understanding. He is a "stallion among men" (*purisadhorayha*) in the sense of bearing the yoke of the world's duties.

Now, desiring to show the specific qualities such as majesty (*teja*) obtained from infinite knowledge, and demonstrating that those qualities like majesty have their root in infinite knowledge, he said "infinite knowledge" and then spoke the words beginning with "infinite majesty.
In this context, "infinite knowledge" refers to knowledge that is devoid of limits both in terms of its enumeration and its power.
"Infinite majesty" [is so called] because it dispels the darkness of delusion within the mental continuums of those to be trained.
Infinite knowledge and splendor. Infinite fame means that through the very qualities of his wisdom, the sound of his infinite renown has spread throughout the three worlds.
Prosperous means enriched by the abundance of the wealth of wisdom.

Of great wealth means that even as the wealth of wisdom increases, he possesses a great wealth of wisdom due to its vast power; thus he is "of great wealth" (*mahaddhana*). There is also a reading *mahādhano*. Possessing wealth means possessing the praiseworthy wealth of wisdom.
He is "wealthy" (dhanavā) because he possesses the wealth of wisdom that is ever-conjoined, and because he possesses the wealth of wisdom that is pre-eminent.
For grammarians accept this term in these three senses.

Having thus shown the accomplishment of the Blessed One’s personal perfection through the quality of wisdom, [the text] further shows the accomplishment of his perfection for the welfare of the world through that same quality of wisdom.

He spoke the words beginning with “leading,” and so forth. In this context, he is a leader who leads those to be trained from the place of fear known as *saṃsāra* to the place of safety known as *nibbāna*.
At the very time of leading them there, he is a trainer who trains those to be trained by means of the discipline of restraint and the discipline of abandonment.

At the very time of teaching the Dhamma, he is an attractor who attracts them by cutting through their doubts. Having cut through their doubts, he is an elucidator who elucidates the meaning that ought to be made known.
He is the one who causes others to contemplate by means of determining those things thus proclaimed; he is the one who observes the purpose of the practice regarding the meaning thus contemplated;
and he is the one who inspires confidence in those practicing thus by means of the fruit of that practice.

In the phrase "for he is the Blessed One," the particle *hi* is a fixed expression used to indicate the reason for the meaning just stated. He is the one who brings about the arising of the path not yet arisen.
He is the one who, for the benefit of the world, produced within his own continuum at the foot of the Bodhi tree the Noble Path—

which had never previously arisen in his own continuum and which serves as the cause for the sixfold uncommon knowledge. He is the one who "generates the unarisen Path," meaning that by turning the Wheel of Dhamma,

he generated within the continua of those to be trained the Noble Path— which had never previously arisen in their continua and which serves as the cause for the disciple’s perfection-knowledge (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*).
From that time until the present day, he is the one who generates [the Path] within the mental continuums of those to be trained.
For since the Noble Path is generated even within the mental continuums of those disciples to be trained solely by means of the Blessed One’s spoken word, the Blessed One is called "the generator.
He is "the proclaimer of the unproclaimed Path" for those Bodhisattas who, endowed with the eight qualities, have made the resolution for Buddhahood.
Having given the prophecy for the state of Buddhahood regarding the path of the perfections (pāramitā) never before taught,
he was the one who proclaimed the Noble Path that must arise at the foot of the Bodhi tree simply by means of the prophecy itself, saying, "He will become a Buddha.
This same principle applies even to the prophecy concerning a Pacceka-bodhisatta.
"Knower of the path" (*maggaññū*) means one who knows the Noble Path generated by oneself through the process of reviewing it.

"Discerner of the path" (*maggavidū*) means one who is skilled in the Noble Path that ought to be generated within the mental continuum of those to be trained. "Expert in the path" (*maggakovida*) means one who is discerning regarding the path to be taught to Bodhisattvas.

Alternatively, he is a knower of the path of practice for Perfect Enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*), a discerner of the path of practice for Private Enlightenment (*paccekabodhi*), and an expert in the path of practice for Disciple Enlightenment (*sāvakabodhi*).

Alternatively, according to the statement, "By this path they have crossed in the past, they will cross, and they are crossing the flood," the application of the meaning should be understood in due order:

by way of the paths of the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the past, future, and present; by way of the paths of emptiness (*suññatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*appaṇihita*);
and by way of the paths of persons who are to be enlightened through a condensed teaching (*ugghaṭitaññū*), through an expanded teaching (*vipañcitaññū*), and through being led (*neyya*).

They practice. And those who follow the path means: having become followers of the path traversed by the Blessed One. Here, the particle *ca* is a grammatical particle used in the sense of a reason; by this, the reason for attaining the qualities such as the arising of the path in the Blessed One is stated. The particle *pana* is a grammatical particle used in the sense of "done"; by this, the performance of making the path by the Blessed One is stated. "Endowed with [them] afterwards" means: * **The Path:** This is the Noble Eightfold Path, beginning with Right View and ending with Right Concentration. It is called "the path" (*magga*) because it leads to the destruction of suffering. * **The Factors of the Path:** These are the eight qualities beginning with Right View. They are called "factors" (*aṅga*) because they are the constituent parts of the path. * **The Fruit of the Path:** This refers to the four fruits of asceticism (*sāmaññaphala*), beginning with the fruit of Stream-entry and ending with Arhatship.

It is called "fruit" (*phala*) because it is the result produced by the path. * **Nibbāna:** This is the cessation of suffering, the unconditioned state. It is called "Nibbāna" because it is the extinguishing of the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion. Regarding the phrase "endowed with afterwards": this indicates that after the Blessed One had first realized these qualities himself, others subsequently became endowed with them by following his path. Thus, the sequence is established: first the Blessed One's realization, followed by the attainment of others.
She was endowed with the qualities of virtue and so forth that followed after the Blessed One had first departed.

Thus, because all of the Blessed One’s qualities— virtue and the rest— had come about by depending solely upon the path to arahantship, the Elder spoke of his quality by depending specifically on that path to arahantship, saying, "He is the arouser of the unarisen path," and so forth.
"He knows what should be known" means he knows that which is to be known;

by virtue of his omniscience, whatever there is that can be known by wisdom, all of that—which constitutes the path of the knowable—he knows through wisdom. "He sees what should be seen" means he sees that which is to be seen;
by virtue of his universal vision, making that very same path of the knowable appear as if seen with the eye, he perceives it with the eye of wisdom.
The meaning is "he sees. Or rather, just as someone who grasps things erroneously does not know even though he knows, and does not see even though he sees, so it is not with the Blessed One.
The Blessed One, however, grasping according to the true nature of things, knows as one who knows and sees as one who sees.
And thus, in the sense of being the guide for vision, he has become the eye; in the sense of being that which is known, and so forth...

He is "become knowledge" (*ñāṇabhūta*). Alternatively, he is "become Dhamma" (*dhammabhūta*) because he has set forth the Dhamma of the scriptures in the sense of being of an unerring nature, or because he has uttered the Dhamma consisting of the teachings after having reflected upon it with his heart. He is "become Brahma" (*brahmabhūta*) in the sense of being supreme.

Or else, he is "become an eye" (*cakkhubhūta*) because he is like an eye; "become knowledge" (*ñāṇabhūta*) because he is like knowledge; and "become Dhamma" (*dhammabhūta*) because he is like the Dhamma.

"Become as Brahmā" (*brahmabhūta*) means he has become like Brahmā. He is the "Speaker" (*vattā*) because he speaks the Dhamma or because he practices it. He is the "Proclaimer" (*pavattā*) because he proclaims it through various modes of speaking or practice.
He is the "Guide to the Meaning" (*atthassa ninnetā*) because he leads others by repeatedly extracting and bringing forth the meaning.

He is the one who causes the attainment of the Deathless (*amata*) because he teaches the practice for its realization, or because through his teaching of the Dhamma that reveals the Deathless, he brings about the attainment of the Deathless.

He is the giver of the Deathless. Because he has brought forth the supramundane Dhamma, and because he gives the supramundane Dhamma at will according to the needs of those to be trained, he is the Lord of the Dhamma;
thus he is the Master of the Dhamma. The meaning of the term *Tathāgata* has been explained above.
Now, wishing to demonstrate omniscience by distinguishing it through the specific qualities described in the passage beginning with "knowing, he knows," [the text] discusses omniscience...

He said, “There is nothing that remains to be accomplished,” and so forth. For such a Blessed One, because all delusion along with its latent tendencies has been destroyed regarding all phenomena by means of the knowledge of the path to arahantship—which is produced by the power of the merit of his perfections—there is nothing that has not been realized.
Because all phenomena have been known through non-delusion, there is nothing that is not known. And likewise, regarding all phenomena...

Because it has been seen with the eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*) just as with the physical eye, there is nothing that is unseen. Because it has been reached by knowledge, there is nothing that is unknown.
Because it has been realized through the realization of non-delusion, there is nothing that is unrealized.
Because it has been touched by the wisdom of non-delusion, there is nothing that is untouched by wisdom. "Present" refers to either the present time or present phenomena.
"Dependent upon" (*upādāya*) means having taken up, the sense being "having included within. By the very word "dependent upon," even *nibbāna*, which is timeless, is indeed included.
And the expressions "past," etc., are connected either with the expression "does not exist," etc., or with the expression "all," etc.
"All phenomena" (*sabbe dhammā*) is a comprehensive inclusion of all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena. "In every aspect" (*sabbākārena*) refers to [the nature] among all phenomena...
The complete exhaustion of all aspects, such as the aspect of impermanence and so forth, of each individual phenomenon. "Facing toward knowledge" (*ñāṇamukha*) means facing toward knowledge.

"Come into the range of vision" (*āpāthaṃ āgacchanti*) means they enter into the field of approach. The word "to be known" (*jānitabba*) is stated for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the word "to be led" (*neyya*).

In the phrases beginning with "or one's own welfare" (*attattho vā*), the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of conjunction. "One's own welfare" (*attattha*) is the welfare of oneself. "The welfare of others" (*parattha*) is [the welfare] of others.
The welfare of the three worlds. "Welfare in both" means the welfare of both oneself and others at once.

"Belonging to the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammika*) refers to welfare that is connected to or has its purpose in the present life. "Belonging to the future life" (*samparāyika*) refers to that which is connected to or has its purpose in the future life.
Regarding the terms "clear" (*uttāna*) and so forth, it is said that they are easy to establish by way of conventional usage.

It is "upturned" (uttāna). Having transcended conventional usage (*vohāra*), it is to be described as "profound" (*gambhīra*) because it is established upon suffering and is associated with emptiness (*suññatā*).

It is "hidden" (*gūḷha*) because it is supramundane (*lokuttara*) and utterly concealed. It is "concealed" (*paṭicchanna*) because its characteristics such as impermanence are covered over by density and so forth.

It is "to be inferred" (*neyya*) because it must be led to its intended meaning without grasping it according to the literal expression, being expressible only through non-common parlance. Through common parlance...
It is to be called "concluded" because its intended meaning has been brought to completion by the mere statement.
It is "blameless" because its purpose—perfectly purified virtue, concentration, and insight—is free from fault by way of the removal of defilements through their respective factors of abandonment.

It is "stainless" because it is the purpose of the Noble Path due to the total eradication of the defilements. It is "pure" because it is the purpose of the Noble Fruit due to the subsiding of the defilements. It is the supreme state among all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.

Nibbāna is the ultimate reality (*paramattha*). "It revolves" means that because it does not exist outside the domain of the Buddha’s knowledge, it exists by pervading, encompassing, embracing, or specifically revolving within the Buddha’s knowledge.
By the phrases "all bodily action," etc., he demonstrates that the Blessed One consists of knowledge (*ñāṇamaya*). "It revolves in accordance with knowledge" refers to knowledge.
"It revolves" means that it is not devoid of knowledge. "Unobstructed" indicates its state of being free from hindrances.
Furthermore, desiring to establish omniscience by means of a simile, he says "as much as," and so forth. In this context, "that which is to be known" is the *neyya* (the knowable);

"having the limit of the knowable" (*neyyapariyantika*) means that for him there exists a boundary or end to what is to be known. However, for those who are not omniscient, there is indeed such a limit to the knowable.

There is none. This same method applies even to the "limit of knowledge" (ñāṇapariyantika). By means of this pair (yamaka), he shows the meaning already stated in the first pair, but with a distinction;
by means of the third pair, he shows it as determined through negation. And herein, the "knowable" (neyya) is called the "path of knowledge" (ñeyyapatha) because it is the range of knowledge.
"Standing as mutual limits" means having exhausted both the knowable and knowledge from their very position.
They are characterized by abiding within the limits of one another. "Dependent on adverting" means dependent on mind-door adverting;

the meaning is that it knows immediately after adverting. "Dependent on desire" means dependent on inclination; the meaning is that it knows by means of impulsion-knowledge immediately after adverting.
The other two phrases are for the purpose of explaining the meaning of these two phrases respectively.
These have been stated. Phrases such as "The Buddha knows the disposition" and so forth are described in the *Ñāṇakathā* (Discourse on Knowledge).

In the *Mahāniddesa*, however, it appears as "the Blessed One knows the disposition. In that context, where it appears as "of the Buddha, the Blessed One," it is here in some instances written as "of the Buddha."
"Antamasa" means by way of the upper limit. Regarding "timi, timiṅgala": here, *timi* is a species of fish;
*timiṅgala* is a species of fish with a body even larger than that, capable of swallowing a *timi*;
and *timitimiṅgala* is a species of fish with a body five hundred *yojanas* long, capable of swallowing even a *timiṅgala*. In this context, the singular number is used to denote the genus.
It should be understood that "katam" means "which. Regarding the phrase "Garula, the son of Venateyya":
here, "Garula" is a name based on his birth, while "Venateyya" is based on his lineage (*gotta*). "In one place" means in a certain location.

It should be understood that the expression "equal to Sāriputta" is stated by taking the Elder Dhammasenāpati as the standard for all Buddhas; for the remaining disciples are indeed equal to the Elder Dhammasenāpati in wisdom.
There is none. As it was said: “Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus of great wisdom, namely Sāriputta.
And in the Commentary it is said:
“Setting aside the Lord of the World, whatever other living beings there may be...”
“...they do not equal even a sixteenth part of Sāriputta’s wisdom.

Regarding “having pervaded”: the Buddha’s knowledge stands having reached the wisdom of all gods and humans, having pervaded—that is, having spread throughout—their wisdom from its very basis. Regarding “having surpassed”: the Buddha’s knowledge [surpasses] the wisdom of all gods and humans.
Having transcended them, it stands having rubbed against and broken through all that is knowable (neyya), even though it is not within their domain.
In the *Mahāniddesa*, however, the reading is "having overcome" (*abhibhavitvā*), which also has the meaning of "having crushed. By the words "those who...

and so forth, he shows the means of direct perception for standing [in that state] after thus pervading and thoroughly rubbing against [the knowable]. In that context, "wise" (*paṇḍita*) means endowed with wisdom (*paṇḍicca*). "Clever" (*nipuṇa*)...
They possess subtle and refined intelligence, capable of penetrating subtle differences in meaning.
"Having mastered the doctrines of others" means both having understood the doctrines of others and having cultivated the practice of debate with them.

"Like hair-splitting archers" means they are like archers who can pierce a single hair; as it is said, "they move about, as it were, piercing through the positions of views with the vehicle of wisdom," just as a hair-splitter [pierces] even the finest hairs.
The meaning is that they proceed as if shattering the views of others with their own course of wisdom (*paññā*).

Alternatively, just as in the expressions "gone to excrement" (*gūthagata*) or "gone to urine" (*muttagata*), so too "courses of wisdom" (*paññāgatāni*) refers to wisdom itself, and "courses of views" (*diṭṭhigatāni*) refers to the views themselves.
"Having formulated a question" means having composed an inquiry consisting of two lines, three lines, or four lines. Of them...
Because the questions were so numerous, they were stated twice for the purpose of including them all. The phrase "obscure and hidden types of meanings" (*pāṭhaseso*) is an ellipsis.

Having seen their discipline in that manner, they asked the question because it was intended by the Blessed One thus: "Let him ask the question he himself has formulated. However, [the Blessed One] did not grant even the opportunity for others to ask.
The Blessed One teaches the Dhamma to those who approach him. As it has been said:
“They formulate a question, thinking: ‘Having approached the ascetic Gotama, we will ask him this question;
if the ascetic Gotama, being asked thus, answers thus, then we shall refute his argument in such a way.’”
‘If he is questioned in this way, he will answer thus, and we shall then refute his argument in this manner.
They approached the ascetic Gotama, and the ascetic Gotama instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the ascetic Gotama with a discourse on the Dhamma, they...
"Being thus encouraged and cheered, they do not even ask the ascetic Gotama a question, so how could they ever refute his doctrine?
On the contrary, it is only the disciples of the ascetic Gotama who succeed.
If one asks why they do not ask a question, it is said that while the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma in the midst of the assembly, he [overwhelmed] the assembly...
He examines their underlying intention. Then he sees: "These wise ones have come having made this question hidden, secret, and like the core of a palm fruit.
Even before being asked by them, he thinks: "In the asking of a question there are so many faults; in the answering, so many;
regarding the meaning, the phrases, and the syllables, there are so many [details]. One asking these questions should ask thus; one answering should answer thus..."
“...should answer. Having thus made the questions the very core of his girdle, he brings them forward and demonstrates them by inserting them into the midst of his discourse on the Dhamma.
Those wise men become delighted, thinking: “It is indeed better for us that we did not ask these questions.
Even if we had asked them, the ascetic Gotama would have cast us out, leaving us without a foothold. Moreover—
When the Buddhas teach the Dhamma, they pervade the assembly with loving-kindness (*mettā*).

Through this pervasion of loving-kindness, the minds of the great multitude find confidence in the One Possessed of the Ten Powers. Indeed, the Buddhas have attained the perfection of form; they are endowed with vision, possess sweet voices, soft tongues, and well-polished lips and teeth.
As if sprinkling the heart with the Deathless (*amata*), they discourse on the Dhamma. In that regard:
As their hearts were filled with confidence through the pervasion of loving-kindness, it occurred to them:
"We shall not be able to take up an opposing position against the Blessed One, who speaks such words that are free from duplicity, not in vain, and leading to liberation.
Thus, because of their own state of confidence, they did not ask a question.
"Expounded and answered": by the recitation of the questions asked—namely, "Ask thus"—those questions have indeed been expounded by the Blessed One;
and just as they were to be answered, they have indeed been answered. "With the reasons demonstrated":
by answering with a cause, making it so that "it is thus because of this reason, because of this cause."
Those questions are indeed of a kind already indicated by the Blessed One.

And they "become cast into the presence of the Blessed One" means that those wise kṣatriyas and others, through the Blessed One’s very answering of their questions, become "cast near" or "cast at his feet";
the meaning is that they become disciples or lay followers, or rather, they attain the excellence of discipleship.

"Attains the excellence of a lay follower (*upāsaka*)"—this is what is meant. "Then" (*atha*) refers to the sense of immediate succession; the meaning is: immediately after those aforementioned excellences.
"Therein" (*tattha*) means in that place or in that context. "He outshines" (*atirocati*) means he shines forth and is made manifest exceedingly.
"By this wisdom" (*yadidaṃ paññāya*) means: by that very wisdom which belongs to the Blessed One, the Blessed One alone outshines [all others]; such is the meaning.
The word *iti* is used in the sense of a reason; thus, the meaning is: "for this reason, he is one whose wisdom is supreme and peerless.
6. "He overcomes lust" means "one of vast wisdom" (*bhūripañño*). That specific path-wisdom overcomes, masters, and crushes the lust that is to be abandoned by itself;
thus, it is "vast wisdom. For the word *bhūrī* has the sense of being pervasive (*phuṭa*) and clear (*visada*). And that which is pervasive is...
It overcomes its opposite; it is not untouched by it. Therefore, the meaning of "overcoming" is stated for "vast wisdom" (*bhūripaññā*). As for "having overcome":
that respective wisdom of the fruit has overcome—that is, crushed—that particular lust; thus it is "vast wisdom. Alternatively, the reading is "overcomes" (*abhibhavatā*).
The same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. Among lust and the others, however, lust has the characteristic of being impassioned. Hatred has the characteristic of hating.
Hatred has the characteristic of hating. Delusion has the characteristic of being deluded. Anger has the characteristic of being angry. Resentment has the characteristic of persisting in anger.
Anger occurs at an earlier time; resentment occurs at a later time. Slander has the characteristic of smearing over the virtues of others.
Contempt has the characteristic of grasping with both hands. Envy has the characteristic of being vexed by the success of others. Avarice has the characteristic of concealing one's own success.
Deceit (*māyā*) has the characteristic of concealing the evil one has committed oneself. Crookedness (*sāṭheyya*) has the characteristic of displaying qualities that do not exist in oneself.
Rigidity (*thambha*) has the characteristic of the mind being puffed up. Aggression (*sārambha*) has the characteristic of seeking preeminence in action.

Conceit (*māna*) has the characteristic of loftiness. Overweening pride (*atimāna*) has the characteristic of excessive loftiness. Intoxication (*mada*) has the characteristic of being intoxicated. [Regarding] the five...
Heedlessness (pamāda) has the characteristic of the relinquishing of the mind toward the strands of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa).

Regarding the phrase "the enemy is lust (rāga), and wisdom is the crushing of that enemy," etc., what is meant? Defilements such as lust, having arisen in the continuum of consciousness, are the "arisen enemies" (bhū-ari);
by means of euphonic combination (padasandhi), the letter *a* is elided, and it is thus called "vast" (bhūrī). Of that vast [wisdom]...
It should be understood that although it ought to be called *maddanī paññā bhūrimaddanipaññā*, the word *maddanī* has been elided and it is stated as “*bhūripaññā*.
The word division (*padaccheda*) should be made as either “*taṃ ariṃ maddanī*” (crushing that enemy) or “*tesaṃ arīnaṃ maddanī*” (crushing those enemies).
“Equal to the earth” (*pathavīsamāya*) means equal to the earth in the sense of being extensive and vast. “Because of its extensiveness” (*vitthatāya*) refers to the object to be known.
"Spread out" means not existing in only one place. "Vast" (*vipulā*) means having become extensive. In the *Mahāniddesa*, however, it is stated as "vast and expanded.
"Endowed with" refers to the person. The word "iti" has the sense of a reason;
for this reason, because the person is endowed with abundant wisdom (*bhūripaññā*), that wisdom of his is called "abundant wisdom"—this is the meaning of the term.

The meaning is "she delights. Regarding the term *bhūripaññapaññā*, although it should have been stated as such, one instance of the word *paññā* has been elided, and thus it is said to be "*bhūripaññā*.
Alternatively, it is "*bhūripaññā*" because it is wisdom that is vast (*bhūri*). The phrase "moreover" (*apica*) is stated for the purpose of showing another method of explanation.
"*Paññāyametaṃ*" means "this [is] of wisdom. "*Adhivacanaṃ*" means a superior designation. "*Bhūrī*" refers to the vast object.

It is called *bhūri* because it delights (*ramati*). It is called *medhā* because it "cleanses" (*medhati*) or destroys defilements (*kilesa*), just as a thunderbolt (*asani*) strikes a mountain crag;

or else, *medhā* is so called in the sense of quick grasping and retention. It is called *pariṇāyikā* because, when it arises in a being, it leads that being toward the practice of what is beneficial and toward the penetration of the characteristics of things as they truly are, along with the associated mental states; thus, it is a guide. These and others...
These are statements concerning the synonyms for wisdom (*paññā*).
"Abundance of wisdom" (*paññābāhulla*): one who has much wisdom is "wisdom-abundant" (*paññābahulo*); the state of being such is "abundance of wisdom.

And that [state] is simply wisdom as it occurs in abundance. Regarding the phrases "here, a certain person," etc., this refers either to a "good worldling" (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*) or to a noble one (*ariya*).
One for whom wisdom is heavy is "one who values wisdom" (*paññāgaruka*). One whose conduct and activity consist of wisdom is "one whose temperament is wisdom" (*paññācarita*).
