One whose inclination is wisdom is "one whose disposition is wisdom" (*paññāsayo*). One who is intent upon wisdom is "one resolved on wisdom" (*paññādhimutta*). One for whom wisdom itself has become a banner is "one whose banner is wisdom" (*paññādhaja*).
One for whom wisdom itself has become a crest is "one whose crest is wisdom" (*paññāketu*). Wisdom itself as the sovereign ruler is "wisdom-sovereignty" (*paññādhipati*).

It is "dominated by wisdom" because it has come about through the predominance of wisdom (*paññādhipati*). It is "abounding in investigation" because it possesses an abundance of the discernment of the specific nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*).
It is "abounding in thorough investigation" because it possesses an abundance of the discernment of the specific nature of phenomena in its various aspects.
It is "abounding in penetration" because it possesses an abundance of *okkhāyana*—that is, the plunging into phenomena with wisdom, their becoming manifest, and their being made clear.
Abounding in clear vision (*okkhāyana*). "Clear vision" (*sampekkhā*) is the correct beholding of each respective phenomenon through wisdom;

the movement or proceeding by means of that clear vision is "clear-visioning" (*sampekkhāyana*); one whose nature or disposition is such clear-visioning is "one whose nature is clear-visioning" (*sampekkhāyanadhammo*).
He dwells having made each phenomenon manifest and evident, thus he is "one who dwells in manifestation" (*vibhūtavihārī*), or alternatively, his dwelling is manifest.

"He has it" means he dwells in its manifestation (*vibhūta-vihārī*). That wisdom is his "conduct" (*carita*); when it is heavy (*garuka*), frequent (*bahula*), and so on for him, he is "one whose conduct is that," "one for whom that is heavy," or "one who is abundant in that.
He is inclined toward, slanted toward, leaning toward, and intent upon that wisdom; thus he is "inclined to that," "slanted to that," "leaning to that," and "intent on that.
That wisdom is the dominant influence (*adhipati*); what comes from that is "dominated by that" (*tad-adhipateyya*). [The terms] such as "heavy with wisdom" and so forth follow this pattern.
In passages such as, “He knows that this person is one who values sensual pleasures while actually indulging in them,” these qualities are described from the perspective of previous births.
Expressions such as “one whose conduct is consistent with that” (*taccarito*) are described in reference to this present birth.
Swift wisdom (*sīghapaññā*), quick wisdom (*lahupaññā*), laughing wisdom (*hāsapaññā*), and fleet wisdom (*javanapaññā*) are a mixture of both mundane and supramundane. In the sense of being rapid...
It is "swift wisdom" (*sīghapaññā*) because it is rapid. It is "light wisdom" (*lahupaññā*) in the sense of being buoyant. It is "laughing wisdom" (*hāsapaññā*) in the sense of being full of joy.

It is "impetuous wisdom" (*javanapaññā*) in the sense of impetuosity toward both the formations that lead to insight and toward the unconditioned (*visaṅkhāra*). It is stated twice—"swift, swift"—for the purpose of including many factors such as virtue and so forth.
"Virtues" (*sīlāni*) refers to the morality of restraint by the Pātimokkha, which are established by way of what is to be practiced and what is to be avoided.

"Restraint of the sense faculties" (indriyasaṃvara) means the warding off and blocking of the six sense faculties, beginning with the eye, by means of the door-bolt of mindfulness so that they do not allow passion or aversion to enter.
"Moderation in eating" (bhojane mattaññutā) means knowing the proper measure in food by way of reflective consideration before consuming it.
"Devotion to wakefulness" (jāgariyānuyoga) refers to [the practice] during the three periods of the day and during the first and last periods of the night.

One who is awake, does not sleep, and performs the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) is called "awake" (*jāgara*). The state of being awake, or the activity of one who is awake, is "wakefulness" (*jāgariya*).
The application to wakefulness is "application to wakefulness" (*jāgariyānuyoga*). That is "application to wakefulness.

"The aggregate of virtue" (*sīlakkhandha*) refers to the aggregate of virtue of one in training (*sekkha*) or one beyond training (*asekkha*). The other aggregates should be understood in the same way. "The aggregate of wisdom" (*paññākkhandha*)...

"Path-wisdom" refers to the wisdom of those in training (*sekha*) and those beyond training (*asekha*), as well as mundane wisdom. "The aggregate of liberation" refers to the liberation of the fruit (*phala-vimutti*). "The aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation" refers to the knowledge of review (*paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa*).
"Abounding in laughter" is the root phrase. "Abounding in joy" is the explanatory phrase, referring to the feeling of mental pleasure (*somanassa-vedanā*) associated with that very rapture (*pīti*).
"Abounding in gladness" refers to the aspect of gladness produced by rapture that is not excessively strong. "Abounding in delight" refers to strong rapture.
By way of the state of being joyful. 7.

"Whatever form," etc., has the meaning explained in the description of knowledge of comprehension (*sammasana-ñāṇa*). "Having weighed" means having weighed by way of comprehension of groups (*kalāpa-sammasana*).

"Having scrutinized" means having scrutinized by way of the contemplation of rise and fall (*udayabbaya-anupassanā*). "Having analyzed" means by way of the contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅga-anupassanā*), and so forth.
"Having made manifest. "Having made clear" means having made it evident by way of equanimity toward formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) and conformity (*anuloma*).

"Sharp wisdom" refers exclusively to the supramundane (*lokuttara*). "Arisen" means that although [defilements] have been abandoned through suppression or as a factor of its destruction by way of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), because they have not been eradicated by the Noble Path and have not transcended the nature of arising, they are called "arisen without being eradicated" (*asamūhatuppanna*).
That is what is intended here. "Does not tolerate" means he does not allow it to take root in the mental continuum. "Abandons" means he abandons by way of complete eradication.
"Dispels" means he casts it out. "Brings to an end" means he makes it reach its limit of disappearance.
"Causes it to go to non-existence" means he causes it to go to non-existence following the sequence of insight (vipassanā), having reached the Noble Path, by way of eradication alone.
The meaning is "he causes to go. In this context, thought associated with sensual desire is *kāma-vitakka*.
Thought associated with the death of others, such as "May these beings die," is *byāpāda-vitakka*.
Thought associated with the harming of others, such as "May these beings be harmed," is *vihiṃsā-vitakka*. "Evil" means base. "Unwholesome states" means states produced by lack of skill (*akosalla*).
"Penetrating wisdom" (*Nibbedhikapaññā*) is precisely the path-wisdom that has arisen in a person who abounds in disenchantment (*nibbidā*).

"Abounding in upliftment" (*ubbegabahula*) means abounding in fear by way of the dread of knowledge (*ñāṇabhaya*). "Abounding in terror" (*uttāsabahula*) means abounding in intense fear. This is an exposition of the meaning of the former [term].

"Abounding in weariness" (*ukkaṇṭhanabahula*) means abounding in weariness due to being directed toward the unconditioned (*visaṅkhāra*) beyond conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*). "Abounding in dissatisfaction" (*anabhiratibahula*)...
It indicates the absence of delight by way of weariness alone. Now, he explains that same meaning with two statements.
Therein, "outward-facing" means facing toward Nibbāna, which is external to conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*). "Does not delight" means does not find pleasure.
"Never before pierced through" means never before reached its end by bringing it to a conclusion throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). "Never before split open" means...
This is the explanation of its meaning: the sense is that it has been crushed by the very act of making an end. "The mass of greed" (*lobhakkhandha*) means a heap of greed or a portion of greed.
One who is "endowed with these sixteen kinds of wisdom" is stated here as the highest limit, referring specifically to an Arahant.

However, since it is stated further on that "one [of them] has attained the analytical knowledges of a trainee" (*sekkhapaṭisambhidappatta*), it follows that stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners are also included.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of Distinct Individuals (Puggalavisesaniddesavaṇṇanā) 8.
By means of the passage beginning with "Two individuals," etc., [the author] shows the sequence of distinct individuals who have attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).

Therein, "prior application" (pubbayoga) refers to the application of merit that served as the cause for attaining the analytical knowledges in previous births. "By that" means by that cause of prior application.
The same applies to the remaining terms as well. "It becomes excessive" (*atireko hoti*) means it becomes redundant; or, because it is associated with excess, it is called "excessive.

"It becomes superior" (*adhiko hoti*) means it becomes foremost. "It becomes distinguished" (*viseso hoti*) means it becomes special; or, because it is associated with distinction, it is a "distinction.
"Knowledge is split open" (*ñāṇaṃ pabhijjati*) means it reaches the differentiation of the knowledge of the analytical insights (*paṭisambhidāñāṇa*).
"Learned" (*bahussuta*) means by way of the Buddha’s word. "Abounding in teaching" (*desanābahula*) means by way of the teaching of the Dhamma.

"Dependent on a superior person" (*garūpanissita*) means dependent on a superior person who is preeminent in wisdom. "Abounding in dwelling" (*vihārabahula*) means abounding in the dwelling of insight (*vipassanā*), or abounding in the dwelling of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).

"Abounding in reflection" (*paccavekkhaṇābahula*) means that when there is the dwelling of insight, one is abundant in the reflection upon insight; when there is the dwelling of the attainment of fruition—

One who frequently reviews the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*). "One who has attained the analytical knowledges of a trainee" (*sekha-paṭisambhidāppatta*) means having become a trainee (*sekha*) and attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).

Likewise for "one who has attained the analytical knowledges of one beyond training" (*asekha-paṭisambhidāppatta*). Regarding "one who has attained the perfection of a disciple" (*sāvakapāramippatta*):

here, for the Great Disciple who is the foremost among those of great wisdom, the reaching of the further shore (*pāra*) regarding the sixty-seven types of knowledge of disciples is *pāramī*; the perfection of a disciple is "disciple-perfection" (*sāvakapāramī*), and that—
"Attained the perfection of a disciple" means one who has reached the perfection of a disciple (*sāvakapāramippatta*). Alternatively, the reading is *sāvakapāramitāppatta*.

He is the supreme great disciple, the protector and fulfiller of the sixty-seven kinds of disciple-knowledge. This activity of knowledge consisting of sixty-seven divisions belongs to that supreme one;
it is his state or his function, thus it is "perfection" (*pāramī*). The perfection of that disciple is "disciple-perfection" (*sāvakapāramī*).

"He has attained that" means he has attained the perfection of a disciple (*sāvakapāramippatta*). "One who has attained the perfection of a disciple" refers to any disciple whatsoever, such as the Elder Mahāmoggallāna and others.
Because there is no other disciple superior to one who has attained the perfection of a disciple, he says "a single Paccekabuddha.

Furthermore, by the phrases "skilled in the distinctions of wisdom" and so forth, he demonstrates the very meaning already stated as a conclusion. This concludes the discussion on knowledge (*ñāṇakathā*).
Generally, many kinds of knowledge have been demonstrated. However, in the discourse on wisdom (*paññā*), generally even a single type of wisdom is spoken of by dividing it into various modes;
this is the distinction. The commentary on the discourse on great wisdom (*mahāpaññā*) is finished.
2. Discourse on Supernormal Power (Iddhikathā) Commentary on the Discourse on Supernormal Power (Iddhikathāvaṇṇanā): 9.

Now follows the explanation of the previously unstated meaning of the discourse on supernormal power, which was spoken by one who, immediately after the discourse on wisdom, demonstrated the power of wisdom.
Therein, regarding the questions first: "What is success? (*iddhi*) is a question concerning its intrinsic nature. "How many kinds of success?

is a question concerning its classification. "How many planes? is a question concerning its requisites. "How many bases? is a question concerning its foundation. "How many steps? is a question concerning its proximate cause.
"How many roots? is a question concerning its primary cause. Regarding the answers: "Success" (*iddhi*) is so called in the sense of succeeding (*ijjhana*), that is, in the sense of accomplishment.
The meaning is: "in the sense of acquisition. For that which is accomplished and acquired is called "successful" (*ijjhati*).
As it is said: "If this succeeds for one who desires sensual pleasures... and "Renunciation is successful, thus it is success (*iddhi*);
it counteracts [the defilements], thus it is a marvel (*pāṭihāriya*)," and so forth. Another method: it is success in the sense of being successful; this refers to the perfection of means.
It is a designation. For the perfection of skillful means succeeds because it brings forth the intended fruit. As it was said:

"This householder Citta is virtuous and of wholesome character; if he should make a mental aspiration, 'In a future time may I be a wheel-turning monarch,' then the mental aspiration of one who is virtuous will succeed because of its purity. Another method [of explanation] is by means of this...
"Successes" (*iddhi*) means that beings succeed (*ijjhanti*). "Succeed" means they become successful, prosperous, and reach the pinnacle; this is what is meant. 10.

Among the ten kinds of success, it is called "success by resolution" (*adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi*) because it is accomplished through the power of resolution. It is called "success by transformation" (*vikubbanā-iddhi*) because it proceeds by way of the alteration and casting off of one's natural form.
[It is called "success by mind-made body"] because of the production of another mind-made body within the interior of one's own body.

The success produced by the mind is so called because it proceeds from the mind. The success of the "expansion of knowledge" is a specific excellence produced by the power of knowledge, whether prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneous with the arising of that knowledge.
The success of the "expansion of concentration" is a specific excellence produced by the power of serenity, whether prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneous with the concentration.
The success of the Noble Ones arises only for those Noble Ones who have attained mastery over their minds; therefore, it is called "Noble success."

The distinction born of the ripening of kamma is success born of the ripening of kamma (*kammavipākajā iddhi*). The distinction born of merit performed in the past is success belonging to one possessed of merit (*puññavato iddhi*).
The distinction born of clear knowledge (*vijjā*) is success consisting of clear knowledge (*vijjāmayā iddhi*).

The accomplishment of this or that kamma through this or that right application is success in the sense of accomplishment through the condition of right application in each respective case (*sammāpayogapaccayā ijjhanaṭṭhena iddhi*).

Although it is stated without qualification that "there are four planes of success (*iddhi*)," these planes belong specifically to the success of resolve, transformation, and the mind-made body according to how they are obtained, and not to the others.

"The plane born of seclusion" (*vivekajā bhūmi*) means a plane born from seclusion or in seclusion. "The plane of rapture and pleasure" (*pītisukhabhūmi*) means a plane associated with rapture and pleasure.
"The plane of equanimity and pleasure" (*upekkhāsukhabhūmi*) refers to [the plane associated] with the equanimity of onlooking-equipoise (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).
And the stage associated with pleasure is the stage associated with pleasant feeling. "The stage of neither-pain-nor-pleasure" is the stage associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Among these, the first and second jhānas are characterized by the pervasion of rapture; the [next] three jhānas are characterized by the pervasion of pleasure;
and the fourth jhāna is characterized by the pervasion of the mind. And here, because the first three jhānas involve the pervasion of rapture and the pervasion of pleasure...
Having entered upon the perception of bliss and the perception of lightness, and having become light, soft, and wieldy in body, one attains supernormal power (*iddhi*);
therefore, by this method, because they lead to the attainment of supernormal power, they should be understood as the "stages of equipment" (*sambhāra-bhūmi*).

The fourth jhāna, however, is the very "natural stage" for the attainment of supernormal power. "For the attainment of supernormal power" means by way of its manifestation within one's own mental continuum.
"For the sake of obtaining the *iddhis*. Regarding "for the sake of attaining the *iddhis*":

either it means for the sake of regaining those *iddhis* already lost by means of the exertion of energy (*vīriyārambha*), or the word has been expanded by means of a prefix (*upasagga*). "For the sake of the transformation of *iddhis*" means for the state of performing various kinds of transformations through *iddhi*. "For the sake of the radiance of *iddhis*":
one who emits (*savati*), produces (*janeti*), or sets in motion (*pavatteti*) various distinctions (*visesa*) is called a *visavī*; thus, it is a manifold emission (*vividhaṃ savanaṃ*).

One who possesses poison (*visa*) is a *visavī*; the state of being such is *visavitā*. The meaning is: for that *visavitā*, that is, for the manifestation of various specific qualities through that supernormal power (*iddhi*).

"For mastery over supernormal power" (*iddhivasībhāvāya*) means for sovereignty over supernormal power. "For confidence in supernormal power" (*iddhivesārajjāya*) means for proficiency in supernormal power. The bases of supernormal power (*iddhipādā*) have their meanings explained in the discourse on knowledge (*ñāṇakathā*).

“If a bhikkhu, depending on desire” means: if a bhikkhu, depending on desire and making desire the dominant factor, “obtains concentration,” that is, he acquires and produces concentration. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. In this context, there are eight factors:
desire, energy, consciousness, and investigation are four factors, and the four concentrations associated with them are the other four factors. Thus, there are eight factors.

However, since the desire to produce supernormal power (*iddhi*), when conjoined with concentration, leads to the attainment of such power—and likewise for energy and the other factors—it should be understood that these eight steps were taught.
This is because the Blessed One, showing the method of practice to be performed by a yogi desiring to produce direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), said: "He..."

“When the mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from defilements, become supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability (*āneñjappatta*)”—thus the imperturbability of the mind is stated.
The Elder, demonstrating that in sixteen ways, spoke the words beginning with “sixteen roots.
In this context, *anonataṃ* means not bent down by way of indolence; the sense is that it is not sluggish. *Anunnataṃ* means [not raised up] by way of restlessness.
"Not ascended upwards" means not uplifted; "not bent forward" means not bent forward by way of greed (*lobha*), that is, not clinging;
it is said that such [bending] does not exist here, where bending forward means being inclined through desire.
"By passion" means by greed having conditioned phenomena as its object. "Not bent away" means not bent away by way of hatred (*dosa*), that is, not struck.
“Bowed” (*nataṃ*) and “bending” (*natī*) are one in meaning. “Free from bowing” (*apagatanataṃ*) means it is not bent; what is meant is that it is not like that.
“Independent” (*anissitaṃ*) means that because it has been seen as non-self, it does not depend on anything as “self” or “belonging to self” through the influence of views.
“Unbound” (*appaṭibaddhaṃ*) means it is not bound by the hope for a reciprocal favor. “In desire and lust” (*chandarāge*) refers to [desire] based on the entity of a sentient being.
"By greed. "Completely freed" means completely freed from sensual lust by way of liberation through suppression (*vikkhambhana-vimutti*).
Alternatively, it is completely freed from sensual lust by way of the fivefold liberation. Or alternatively, it is completely freed from each respective opposite by way of the fivefold liberation.

This [refers] to the knowledge of the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti-ñāṇa*), because of the arising of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) even for worldlings (*puthujjana*), trainees (*sekha*), and non-trainees (*asekha*).
“By means of the sixteen modes of knowledge” is stated according to the maximum limit as described by the aforementioned method;
however, it should be understood according to what is actually attained. “Free from lust for sensual pleasures” means free from the lust for sexual intercourse.

“Dissociated” means dissociated from the remaining defilements by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*), or dissociated by way of eradication (*samuccheda*) according to the maximum method. “With the barriers removed” means [dissociated] from the remaining defilements.

It has been made free from the boundary of defilements by way of suppressing the boundary of those [defilements], or it has been made free from the boundary of defilements by way of abandoning the boundary of those [defilements] through each respective path.
"By the boundary of defilements" means by that boundary of defilements which has been abandoned through each respective [path].
And here, a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*) should be understood. "Attained to unity" means attained to a single object. "By various defilements" means...
By means of defilements occurring with various objects. This was stated with reference to the object;

however, the phrase beginning with "not bent" (*anonata*) refers specifically to the defilements. "Attained to illumination" (*obhāsagata*) means having reached the illumination of wisdom by way of the clear functioning of wisdom.
"In the darkness of ignorance" (*avijjandhakāre*) refers to powerful ignorance. And the four planes and the sixteen roots of psychic power (*iddhi*).

These are stated by way of the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*); the four bases (*pāda*) and eight steps (*pada*) are stated both by way of the preliminary stage and by way of association (*sampayoga*).

Having thus shown the states that serve as the ground, the bases, the steps, and the roots of supernormal power (*iddhi*), he now, in order to show those supernormal powers themselves, says: "What is the supernormal power of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi*)? and so forth.
Therein, the meaning of the summary terms (*uddesapada*) is [to be found] in the exposition of the knowledge of the various kinds of supernormal power (*iddhividhañāṇa-niddesa*).
This has already been stated. “A bhikkhu here” means a bhikkhu in this dispensation (*sāsana*).
By this, it is shown that there is no one elsewhere who performs the various modes of supernormal power (*iddhividha*) in every way. The explanation of these two terms has already been given above.

And for that very reason, one who is endowed with the qualities that serve as the ground, the footings, and the roots of supernormal power—namely, the fourteen [qualities] described in the *Visuddhimagga*—[is qualified].
The state of having a mind thoroughly tamed by fifteen modes is stated,

as well as the state of the mind being made soft and wieldy through the attainment of each dominant influence such as desire (*chanda*), and through mastery over the processes beginning with adverting the mind (*āvajjana*).

A bhikkhu endowed with powerful past application (*pubbayoga*)— having attained the special qualities of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and so forth precisely through the attainment of Arahatship via that past application— [proceeds] by means of the earth-kasiṇa and other [meditative objects].
Having stated that he "is endowed with the [necessary] qualities," this too has already been explained.

Regarding the phrase "he adverts to many": having entered the fourth jhāna as a basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā) with the earth-kasiṇa as its object, and having emerged from it, if he wishes to become a hundred, he adverts by way of performing the preliminary work (parikamma), thinking, "May I be a hundred, may I be a hundred."
"Having adverted, he resolves by means of knowledge": having thus performed the preliminary work (*parikamma*), he resolves by means of the knowledge of direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*).
Here, the re-entry into the basic jhāna after performing the preliminary work is not mentioned. Although it is not mentioned, nevertheless, in the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is stated:
"He adverts" is said by way of the preliminary work itself; "having adverted, he resolves by means of knowledge" [is said next].

This was stated by way of direct-knowledge knowledge (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*); therefore, one adverts to "I am many," and then enters attainment at the conclusion of those preliminary consciousnesses (*parikamma-citta*).

Having emerged from attainment, one again adverts, "May I be many," and thereafter, immediately after three or four preceding access-consciousnesses (*pubbhāga-citta*), there is the resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) by way of the finalizing consciousness that has arisen.

It must be understood exactly as it has been stated: "The meaning here should be seen thus: he resolves by means of that single knowledge of direct higher power (abhiññā-ñāṇa) which has already been acquired.
Just as when it is said, "Having eaten, he lies down," the meaning is not that he lies down immediately after eating without having drunk water or washed his hands;
for even though other duties exist in the interval, [the statement does not imply their omission].
"Just as it is said, 'having been, he lies down,' so too should it be understood here. For even the initial attainment of the foundational jhāna is not explicitly mentioned in the text.
However, by means of that very knowledge of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-ñāṇa*), there is a hundred [of them] together;
the same method applies to a thousand and even a hundred thousand. If this does not succeed, one should perform the preliminary work again, attain it for a second time, and...
Having emerged, one must resolve. For it is said in the *Saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā*: "It is permissible to enter [the attainment] once or twice.
In that context, the foundational jhāna-consciousness has the sign as its object;

the preliminary consciousnesses have either a hundredfold or a thousandfold object, and these are by way of color, not by way of a conceptual designation (*paṇṇatti*). The resolving consciousness also...

In the same way, whether it has a hundred objects or a thousand objects, immediately after the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) consciousness, there arises only one consciousness belonging to the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), just like the absorption consciousness mentioned previously.

This is for the purpose of demonstrating bodily witness (kāyasakkhi) regarding the state of being manifold, as when the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka, though being one, became many, saying: "Having been one, he becomes many."
This has been said. However, it should be understood that the present tense is used here because the Elder was of a disposition to act accordingly and because he was still living at that time.
The same method applies to the section beginning with "he becomes one.
In this regard, there is this story: those two brothers, it is said, received the name "Panthakas" (Road-born) because they were born on a road.
Among them, the eldest, Mahāpanthaka, having gone forth, attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Having become an Arahat, he ordained Cūḷapanthaka and said:
"Just as a fragrant red lotus, blooming at dawn, remains full of its scent;”
“Behold Aṅgīrasa shining forth, blazing like the sun in the sky”—with these words he gave him this verse.
He was unable to master it within four months. Then the Elder said to him, “You are incapable in this Dispensation;
depart from here. At that time, the Elder was the distributor of meals.
Jīvaka Komārabhacca, taking many garlands, perfumes, and ointments, went to his own mango grove;

there he honored the Teacher, listened to the Dhamma, and after paying homage to the One of Ten Powers, he approached the Elder and said, "Venerable sir, tomorrow please accept almsfood at our residence, bringing with you five hundred bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. The Elder replied, "Except for..."
“I accept Cūḷapanthaka for the sake of the rest,” he said. Upon hearing this, Cūḷapanthaka became even more overcome with grief;
the following day at dawn, he left the monastery and stood weeping at the gateway of the vihāra, full of longing for the Teaching.
The Blessed One, perceiving his underlying potential (*upanissaya*), approached him and asked, “Why are you weeping? He [related] that occurrence.
The Blessed One said, "One who is unable to perform recitation is not called incapable in my teaching;

do not grieve, Panthaka. Having touched his head with his hand, which was like the surface of a painted wheel, and having taken him by the arm, he entered the monastery, seated him at the entrance of the Perfumed Chamber, and [offered] that which was perfectly pure, fashioned through supernormal power.
Having said, "Panthaka, sit down while rubbing this piece of rag with your hand, thinking, 'This is a dust-remover,
a dust-remover,'" and having given him that piece of rag, he— surrounded by the community of monks—
went at the announced time to Jīvaka’s house, sat down on the prepared seat, and [Jīvaka] gave him that piece of rag as he was rubbing it in that manner.
Having become soiled, it gradually turned black in color. Regaining his composure, he thought, "This piece of cloth is pure;
there is no fault here. This fault exists only in dependence upon this physical body. Having thus regained his perception, he applied his knowledge to the five aggregates and developed insight.
Then the Blessed One, emitting a radiance, sat before him.
Appearing as if manifesting his form, he spoke these verses of illumination:
“Lust is not called ‘dust,’ nor is it called ‘grime’; this is a designation for lust: ‘dust.
Having utterly abandoned this dust, O monks, they dwell in the teaching of him who is free from dust.”
“Hatred... [and so on] ...in the Teaching.
‘Delusion is called dust, not grit; this is a designation for delusion: “dust.
Having completely abandoned this dust, monks, they dwell in the Teaching of one who is free from dust.’”
“For the one of lofty mind, who is diligent, the sage training in the paths of sagehood—sorrows do not come to such a one, who is peaceful and always mindful.

At the conclusion of this verse, the elder attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). He was a master of the meditative attainments of the mind-made body (manomaya-jhāna).
Having sacrificed, he was able to become one after being many, and many after being one.
By means of the path of arahantship itself, the three Piṭakas and the six higher knowledges (abhiññā) came to him.
Jīvaka also offered water for the guest-offering to the One of Ten Powers. The Teacher covered his bowl with his hand.
When asked, "What is it, venerable sir? he replied, "Jīvaka, there is a certain bhikkhu in the monastery.
He then dispatched a man, saying, "Go, take the noble one and return quickly.
Before that man had even arrived, the Elder Cūḷapanthaka, desiring to make his brother aware of the distinction he had attained, manifested a thousand bhikkhus, each of whom was unlike the other.
Furthermore, he performed the duties of a novice, such as the distribution of robes for that single monk, in a manner unlike anyone else.
A man went to the monastery, saw many monks there, and upon returning, said to Jīvaka, "Venerable sir, there are many monks in the monastery;
I do not see the noble one who was to be summoned. Jīvaka asked the Teacher about him, and having stated his name, [he sent him back] again.
He sent him. Having gone there, he asked, "Venerable sir, which one is named Cūḷapanthaka? "I am Cūḷapanthaka! I am Cūḷapanthaka!
he replied, speaking with a thousand mouths all at once. He went back again and said, "It seems they are all Cūḷapanthakas;
I do not know which one I am to summon. Because he had penetrated the Truths, Jīvaka [knew], "He possesses supernormal power..."
He understood from the manner [of address] that they were monks. The Blessed One said: "Go;
when you see the first one, take him by the corner of his robe and say, 'The Teacher summons you,' and then bring him back. He went and did exactly as instructed.
At that very moment, all the created forms vanished. The Elder, having dismissed him and completed his bodily needs such as washing his face, etc., [proceeded].

Having arrived first, he sat down on the prepared seat. At that moment, the Teacher, having received the water for the guest-offering and finished his meal, had the Elder Cūḷapanthaka deliver a discourse on the Dhamma as a thanksgiving for the meal.
The Elder delivered a discourse on the Dhamma of such magnitude as the Long and Middle Collections (Dīgha and Majjhima Nikāyas).

Other bhikkhus, having manifested a mind-made body through resolution, manifest three or four [bodies], creating many that are exactly alike and performing only a single kind of action. But the Elder Cūḷapanthaka created a thousand bhikkhus with a single act of attention;
he did not make even two people alike, nor did he perform a single kind of action.
While performing an action, he is thus called the foremost among those who manifest a mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*).
However, many others created by the possessor of psychic power (*iddhimā*) without such specific determination are merely similar to him.

In standing, sitting, and so forth, as well as in speaking or remaining silent, whatever the possessor of psychic power does, they do that very same thing. But if he wishes to make them of various colors, [they become so].

Some are in the first stage of life, some in the middle stage, and some in the final stage; likewise, there are those with long hair, those with half-shaven heads, those with shaven heads, and those with mixed hair;

those with half-yellow robes, and those with pale yellow robes; and others who desire to perform various tasks such as reciting the words of the Dhamma, delivering Dhamma discourses, engaging in debates, asking questions, answering questions, dyeing robes, sewing robes, washing robes, and so forth—having emerged from the foundational jhāna, he [should visualize] "this many..."

Having performed the preliminary exercise (parikamma) in the manner beginning with “May the bhikkhus be in their first stage of life,” and having again attained [jhāna] and emerged from it, one should make the resolution (adhiṭṭhātabba).
By means of the mind of resolution, they become exactly in whatever form is desired.
This same method applies to such cases as “having been many, may I become one,” and so forth.
This, however, is the distinction: one who is many by nature remains many even during the interval while he has manifested [himself].

And having manifested such multiplicity, this bhikkhu may think, "Having become one again, I will walk up and down, I will recite my studies, I will ask questions," or [he may think], "This monastery has few bhikkhus; if anyone..."
“They will come and think, ‘Where have all these identical monks come from? Surely this is the power of the Elder,’ and thus they will know me.

Out of fewness of desires, or wishing to be alone midway, one should enter the basic jhāna, emerge, perform the preliminary work with the thought “May I be alone,” re-enter the jhāna, emerge, and resolve: “May I be alone.”
Together with the mind of resolution (*adhiṭṭhānacitta*), he becomes alone. However, for one who does not act in this way, he becomes alone by virtue of the time limit as previously determined.

11. Because it is stated that after placing the word "manifestation" (*āvi-bhāva*), it "is not covered by anyone," the meaning of the word "manifestation" is expressed by the phrase "not covered by anyone" as being the state of being evident.
By the word "is" (*hoti*), the remainder of the reading "he makes" (*karoti*) is expressed.
It exists. For when it becomes manifest, its manifestation has been effected. "Uncovered by anything" means not covered by anything whatsoever, such as a wall, and thus being devoid of obstruction.
"Unconcealed" means not covered from above. That very thing is "unveiled" because it is uncovered;
it is "manifest" because it is unconcealed. It "effects concealment," that is, it effects a state of being obstructed. It is indeed covered.
It is covered by that obstruction; it is indeed concealed, being shut off by that very concealment.
"By the attainment of the space-kasiṇa" means by the attainment of the fourth jhāna produced upon the space-kasiṇa of delimitation.
"An obtainer" (lābhī) means one who has the obtaining (lābha); thus he is an obtainer. "Unenclosed" means in a place not enclosed on all sides by anything whatsoever.

Here, because it is specifically the space-kasina that has been described, it should be understood that only the jhāna developed therein serves as the condition for the production of space, and no other.
In the subsequent cases of the water-kasina and so forth, too, only the jhāna having that as its object should be understood, and not any other.
[The phrases] "he adverts to earth," "he adverts to water," and "he adverts to space" refer to natural earth, water, and space.
He adverts. "In the sky" indicates that this space is far removed from the earth.

12. Regarding the wiping away of the moon and sun, since it is stated without distinction as "one possessing psychic power who has attained mastery over the mind," it should be understood that there is no fixed rule here regarding the attainment of the *kasiṇa*. Whether sitting or lying down...
Whether sitting or lying down—by these two, the other two postures are also already implied.
"Let it be within arm's reach" means let it be near the hand. There is also a reading, "let it be at the side of the hand. This is stated with reference to one who wishes to do so.
But this person, having gone there and even having extended his hand, touches it. "Touches" means he slightly makes contact with it.
"Grasping" means touching firmly. "Rubbing" means touching all around. "A form that has come into range" refers specifically to a form situated within reach of the hand.
"He resolves that what is distant be near": having emerged from the foundational jhāna, he adverts to a distant realm, such as a world of the devas or the Brahma-world, thinking, "Let it be near.
Having so adverted and performed the preliminary work, he enters the attainment once more; then, having emerged—
He resolves with knowledge, “Let it be near,” and it becomes near. This same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.

However, having explained how one who wishes to go to the Brahma-world makes the distant near, [the author] says “even though near,” etc., showing a specific excellence achieved through this supernormal power (*iddhi*), even for that which does not assist in going to the Brahma-world.
In that context, it is not only the making of the small great and the making of the great small, but...
In cases such as “the non-sweet as sweet,” whatever one desires, all that succeeds for one possessing psychic power (*iddhimant*).
Another method: “He resolves even what is distant to be near” means he resolves the Brahma-world, though it is distant, to be near to the human world.
“He resolves even what is near to be distant” means he resolves the human world, though it is near, to be distant in the Brahma-world. Even what is much...
“He resolves that ‘much’ becomes ‘little’: if many Brahmās have gathered together, because of their great personal size (attabhāva), they leave the range of sight and the range of hearing;
[the Buddha] then contracts both the range of sight and the range of hearing into one, and resolves that even what is much becomes little.
He resolves that ‘little’ becomes ‘much’: if he wishes to go with a large retinue...”
Because of his singleness, he resolves upon himself as being many and goes with a great retinue;
this is how the meaning should be understood here. This being so, that fourfold assistance is conducive to going to the Brahma-world.
"With the divine eye he sees the form of that Brahmā" means that, standing here, having extended his light, he [sees] him...
Desiring to see the form of that Brahmā, he sees the form of that Brahmā with the divine eye.
Standing right here, he hears the sound of that Brahmā speaking with the divine ear-element.
He understands the mind of that Brahmā through the knowledge of penetration of minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*). "By being seen" means by being beheld with the eye. By way of the body...
"He transforms the mind" means he transforms the mind by means of the material body. Taking the mind of the foundational jhāna, he applies it to the body;
he makes it conform to the body, moving slowly. For the movement of the body is slow.
"He resolves" is a synonym for that same term; the meaning is "he determines. "Having entered upon the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness" means:

Having descended into, entered into, touched, and attained the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness that are co-nascent with the supernormal power-consciousness (iddhicitta) which has the foundational jhāna as its object.
Now, the so-called "perception of pleasure" is a perception associated with equanimity (upekkhā).

For equanimity is called "peaceful pleasure," and that very perception, because it is liberated from the hindrances as well as from opposing factors such as applied thought (vitakka), etc., [is termed the perception of pleasure].
It should also be understood as a "light perception. For one who has entered that state, even the body born of karma becomes as light as a tuft of cotton.
With such a body, which is visible and as light as a tuft of cotton tossed by the wind, he goes to the Brahma-world.
And while going thus, if he so desires, he creates a path in the sky by means of the earth-kasiṇa.
He goes on foot. If he so desires, by means of the earth-kasiṇa alone, he creates a lotus at every step and goes on foot, placing his foot upon each lotus.

If he so desires, by means of the air-kasiṇa, having resolved upon the wind, he goes with the wind like a tuft of cotton-wool. Moreover, the mere desire to go is the measure here; provided there is mindfulness...
Indeed, through the very desire to go, one whose mind has been thus resolved proceeds while being impelled by the force of that resolve,
like an arrow seen flying when impelled by the force of its string.

"One transforms the body by means of the mind" means that, having taken up the body composed of karma (*karajakāya*), one mounts it upon the mind of the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhānacitta*), such that it follows the lead of the mind.
It effects swift movement. For the movement of consciousness is indeed swift.

"Having entered upon the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness" means the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness that are co-nascent with the supernormal power-consciousness (*iddhicitta*) which has the physical body as its object. The rest should be understood according to the method already stated.
However, this is merely the movement of consciousness. Thus, moving with an invisible body, he...
When it was asked, "Does that mind of resolution go at the moment of its arising, or at the moment of its presence, or at the moment of its dissolution?
the Elder replied, "It goes during all three moments. Furthermore, when it was asked, "Does it go itself, or does it send forth a created being (nimmita)?
he said, "It acts according to its wish. However, in this instance, only its own going is intended.
"Mind-made" (*manomaya*) means made by mind because it is fashioned by the act of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*). "With all limbs and minor parts" means possessing all major and minor limbs.
"With unimpaired faculties" is said here with reference to the shape of the eye, ear, and so forth; however, in the case of the created form, there is no sensitivity (*pasāda*).
If that possessor of psychic power (*iddhimā*) walks, the created being also walks there—and so on; all of this applies to what is created by a disciple.
This was said with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*). However, as for those created by the Buddha (*buddhanimmita*), they perform whatever the Blessed One does;
furthermore, by the power of the Blessed One’s mind, they can even perform other things. "Smokes and blazes" refers to the fire-kasina (*tejokasiṇa*).

"Speaks the Dhamma," and so forth—these three [actions] are stated without specific restriction. "Stands together" means standing having come together. "Converses" means speaking having come together.
"He enters into conversation" means he engages in discussion by way of giving and receiving successive replies to one another.
And herein, that which this possessor of psychic power (iddhimā), while remaining right here, sees a form with the divine eye, hears a sound with the divine ear-element,
and understands the mind with the knowledge of penetration of others' minds— that too [is included], as is his [interaction] with that Brahmā while remaining right here.
He stands together with him, converses with him, enters into discussion with him;

furthermore, there is his resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*) such as "he resolves that even what is far away is near," and also the fact that he goes to the Brahma-world by means of a body that is either visible or invisible—up to this point, he does not exercise mastery over the body.
But as for [the passage] beginning, "In the presence of that Brahmā, he manifests a material form (*rūpiṃ abhinimmināti")... [and so forth]."
One enters upon the procedure as stated by way of method; to this extent, one is said to "exercise mastery over the body.

The remainder, however, is stated for the purpose of showing the preliminary stage to the exercise of mastery over the body. This, then, is supernormal power consisting of resolve (*adhiṭṭhānā iddhi*).

13. In the description of supernormal power consisting of transformation (*vikubbaniddhi*), the mention of a disciple of the Blessed One Sikhī is for the purpose of showing a person who is a "body-witness" (*kāyasakkhī*) regarding the supernormal power of transformation.

This has been stated. Demonstrating that as well, he first showed the supernormal power of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāniddhi*)—an event of extreme wonder and marvel—in which, while standing in the Brahma-world, he made himself heard by his voice throughout a thousandfold world-system (*sahassilokadhātu*).
Now, to further illustrate this matter, the following is said: for from this eon, thirty-one eons ago...

The Blessed One Sikhī, having passed away from the Tusita heaven in his immediately preceding birth, was reborn in the city of Aruṇavatī in the womb of the chief queen named Pabhāvati, the consort of King Aruṇavata.

Having reached the full maturity of wisdom, he made the Great Renunciation, penetrated the knowledge of omniscience at the seat of enlightenment, and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma. [He then returned] to Aruṇavatī...
While dwelling there, one day, having attended to his bodily needs early in the morning, he set out surrounded by a great community of monks with the intention, "I shall enter Aruṇavatī for alms.
Having departed, he stood near the gatehouse of the monastery and addressed his chief disciple named Abhibhū: "It is still too early, monk, to enter Aruṇavatī for alms."
“Let us go to a certain Brahmā world,” he said. As it is recorded:
“Then, monks, the Blessed One Sikhi, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, addressed the monk Abhibhū:
‘Come, brahmin, let us go to a certain Brahmā world, for it is now time for our meal.’”
"It will be so, Bhante. "Very well, Bhante," the bhikkhu Abhibhū replied to the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Then, bhikkhus, the Blessed One Sikhī and the bhikkhu Abhibhū went to a certain brahmā-world.
There, having seen the Perfectly Enlightened One, Mahābrahmā was delighted; he went out to meet him, prepared a Brahmā’s seat, and offered it to him.
They also prepared a suitable seat for the Elder. The Blessed One sat down on the seat that had been prepared, and the Elder sat down on his own assigned seat.
Mahābrahmā, too, paid homage to the One of Ten Powers and stood to one side.
He sat down. Therefore it was said: "Then, monks, the Blessed One Sikhi, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, addressed the monk Abhibhū:
'May a discourse on the Dhamma occur to you, brahmin, concerning Brahmā, the assembly of Brahmā, and the retinue of Brahmā.
'So be it, Bhante,' the monk Abhibhū replied to the Blessed One Sikhi."
Having assented to the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, he delivered a discourse on the Dhamma to Brahmā, the assembly of Brahmā, and the retinue of Brahmā.

While he was delivering that discourse on the Dhamma there, the Brahmās complained, saying, "It has been a long time since we have had the opportunity to receive the Teacher’s visit to the Brahma-world;
yet this bhikkhu, setting aside the Teacher himself..."
“...began a discourse on the Dhamma. The Teacher, perceiving their dissatisfaction, said this to the bhikkhu Abhibhū:
“Brahmā, the assembly of Brahmā, and the retinue of Brahmā are indeed complaining, O Brahmin.
Therefore, Brahmin, stir them even more with a sense of spiritual urgency. Having received the Teacher’s word, the Elder—
Having performed various kinds of miraculous transformations, he made himself heard throughout a thousandfold world-system with his voice, saying:
“Exert yourselves! Strive! Apply yourselves to the Buddha’s teaching!
Shake off the army of Death, as an elephant shakes down a reed-hut!”
“He who, in this Dhamma and Discipline, shall dwell with diligence,
having abandoned the wandering-on of birth, will make an end of suffering.”—
Thus he spoke these two verses.
But what did the Elder do to make himself heard by his voice throughout a thousandfold world-system?

First, having attained the blue kasiṇa absorption and emerged from it, he pervaded the entire darkness within a thousand world-systems with his knowledge of supernormal power (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*). Then, when beings wondered, "What is this darkness?
and their attention was aroused, he attained the light kasiṇa absorption, emerged from it, and displayed light.
To those who were wondering, “What light is this? he revealed himself.
And throughout a thousand world-systems, gods and humans stood with palms joined, paying homage to the Elder alone.
The Elder, thinking, “Let the great multitude hear me as I teach the Dhamma,” recited these verses. All of them sat down in the midst of the assembled company that had gathered.
They heard a sound as if he were teaching the Dhamma; the meaning also became clear to them.
With reference to that making known, it is said: "He made himself known by his voice. With reference to the various kinds of supernormal transformations performed by him, it is further said:
"And again, while being seen," and so forth. In this context, "he taught the Dhamma" refers to the manner previously described.

It should be understood that he taught the Dhamma while displaying his supernormal transformations (*iddhivikubbana*), and then made himself understood by means of his voice while reciting two verses in the sequence previously described.

Furthermore, in the phrases "even with the visible body" (*dissamānena pi kāyena*) and so forth, the instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic of a particular state; the meaning is: "having become a body of such a kind."
Now, having shown that instance, and wishing to demonstrate the method for another possessor of psychic power (*iddhimant*) to perform the miracle of transformation (*vikubbaniddhi*), he said:

"He, having abandoned his natural form," and so forth. Therein, "he" refers to that bhikkhu possessing psychic power whose mind has been made pliant and workable by the method described below. If he desires to perform the miracle of transformation, [he abandons] his own natural form and natural shape.

Or he displays the form of a young boy. How so? Having emerged from the fourth jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā) with the earth-kasiṇa as its object, he adverts to the form of a young boy to be created, thinking, "May I become such a young boy.
After completing the preliminary work, he enters the attainment once more, and upon emerging, he resolves by means of direct knowledge, thinking, "May I be such a young boy."
"By means of resolution, one becomes a youth. In the *Visuddhimagga*, in the description of the *kasiṇas*, it is stated:

"By means of the earth-*kasiṇa*, having been one, one becomes many... such things as these succeed. By this statement, the foundational jhāna here is appropriately taken as having the earth-*kasiṇa* as its object.
Furthermore, in the same work, in the description of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), regarding the supernormal power of transformation (*vikubbaṇiddhi*) among the earth-*kasiṇas* and so forth:

It is said, “having emerged from the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā) with a particular object,” and in that same context it is further stated, “one’s own form as a youth should be adverted to.
This [latter statement] seems not to apply to the manifestation (nimmāna) of a nāga or other such forms. The same principle applies to the manifestation of the form of a nāga and so forth.
In this regard, “the form of a nāga” means the shape of a snake; “the form of a supaṇṇa” means the shape of a garuḷa; “the form of Indra” means...
The form of Sakka; "the appearance of a deva" means the form of other devas. Furthermore, the appearance of the ocean is accomplished by means of the water-kasiṇa.
"An army" means a foot-soldier force. "Various military arrays" refers to a multitude of troops of many kinds, such as elephants and so forth.
In the *Visuddhimagga*, however, the passage beginning with "he even displays an elephant" is explained here by way of displaying elephants and so forth externally as well.
It has been said: "In that regard, one should not resolve, 'May I become an elephant,' but rather resolve, 'Let there be an elephant.

The same method applies to horses and so forth. However, this contradicts both the root phrase used, "having discarded his natural form," and the nature of the power of transformation (*vikubbaniddhi*).
For according to the sequence stated in the Canon, by means of resolution one [becomes] another without having discarded one's natural form.

The supernormal power of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāniddhi*) is the seeing [of oneself] otherwise by means of resolution after having abandoned one's natural appearance. The supernormal power of transformation (*vikubbaniddhi*) is the seeing of oneself otherwise by means of resolution after having abandoned one's natural appearance.

14. In the exposition of the knowledge of the supernormal power of the mind-made body (*manomayiddhiñāṇa*), regarding such passages as "he creates another body from this body," a bhikkhu possessing supernormal powers who wishes to exercise the supernormal power of the mind-made body emerges from the foundational jhāna that has the space-kasiṇa as its object, and [regards] his own material body...
Having directed his attention thus far, he resolves according to the method already described, "Let it become hollow," and it becomes hollow.
Then, having directed his attention to another body within that [hollow] by means of the earth-kasiṇa and performed the preliminary work, he resolves according to the method already described;
another body comes to be within it. He draws that out from the mouth and places it outside.
Now, illustrating that meaning by means of similes, he said "seyyathāpi" and so forth. Therein, "from muñja grass" means from the muñja-grass plant.
"He would draw out a reed" means he would pull out a shoot. "From its sheath" means from the sheath; the sense is "from the old skin-casing.
And therein, "he would extract it" should be understood as an extraction by means of the mind alone, for this is indeed called a snake.
Standing among his own kind, or leaning against a gap between logs or between trees, with a strength characterized by the effort of stripping the body from its skin,
he casts off his own cloak by himself for these four reasons, loathing the old skin as if it were devouring his body.

And here, these similes are stated for the purpose of showing that just as the *īsikā* grass and so forth are similar to the *muñja* grass and so forth, so too this mind-made (*manomaya*) form is similar in every respect to that produced by one possessing psychic power (*iddhimant*).

In the passage, “With a mind-made body, he approached by means of psychic power,” the body produced by the supernormal knowledge of the mind is called the “mind-made body. [In the phrase] “a certain... [the text continues].
Regarding the phrase “he arises with a mind-made body”: here, a body produced by means of jhāna is called a “mind-made body” because it is made by that mind.
However, in this context, a body produced by means of direct knowledge (abhiññā) is called a “mind-made body” because it is made by that mind.
This being so, a mind-made body is one produced by the supernormal power of resolution (adhiṭṭhāniddhi) and the supernormal power of transformation (vikubbaniddhi).

[Question: Is it so? [Answer: Indeed it is. However, because these have been described here specifically by distinguishing them individually as "the supernormal power of resolve" (*adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi*) and "the supernormal power of transformation" (*vikubbanā-iddhi*), it should be understood that the creation [of forms] from within is what is called "the mind-made supernormal power" (*manomaya-iddhi*). 15.

Regarding the description of the supernormal power of the expansion of knowledge (*ñāṇavipphāriddhi*): it is "of the expansion of knowledge" because it possesses the expansion, which is to say, the momentum, of knowledge. Furthermore, in this context, it should be understood that while the supernormal power is shown specifically by way of the seven contemplations (*satta-anupassanā*), the remaining powers up to the path of arahantship are abbreviated.
Regarding the passage beginning "the elder Bākula’s supernormal power through the expansion of knowledge," the Elder Bākula was so named because he grew up in two families;
he was an elder who had performed meritorious service under previous Buddhas and was endowed with the perfection of merit.
For, while experiencing great prosperity as he transmigrated through the realms of gods and humans, even before our Ten-Powered One (the Buddha) was born...
He was reborn in a merchant family in Kosambī. At the time of his birth, for the sake of auspiciousness, he was taken to the Yamunā River with a great retinue;

while a nurse, accompanied by her attendants, was bathing him, making him dive in and out of the water as a play, a large fish approached with its mouth wide open, thinking, "This is my food. The nurse abandoned the child and fled.
The great fish swallowed him. The meritorious being, as if entering his own bedchamber and lying down, did not experience any suffering at all.

Through the power of the boy’s spiritual energy, the fish—as if swallowing a red-hot plowshare—was scorched and traveled thirty *yojanas* with great speed until it entered the net of a fisherman living in Bārāṇasī. By the power of the boy’s energy, he...

As soon as he was pulled from the net, he appeared as if dead. The fishermen took him whole and, wandering through the city crying out, "We give him for a thousand pieces," they went to the door of a wealthy merchant who possessed eighty million coins and was childless.
They gave him to the merchant’s wife for a single kahāpaṇa. She herself placed him upon a wooden board behind her.
Tearing open the belly of the fish, she saw a golden-colored boy.
Crying out, “I have found a son within the belly of a fish!,” she took the boy and approached her husband.
The merchant immediately had the drums beaten and, taking the boy, brought him into the presence of the king and reported the matter. The king said, “This boy is meritorious; raise him.”
He said: "Another merchant family, having heard that news, went there and disputed [with the first], saying, 'The child is ours,' in order to take the boy.
Both families went to the royal court. The King said, 'It is not possible to make either of you childless;
let him be the heir to both. From then on, both families attained the highest degree of wealth and glory."
He was born. Because he was raised by two families, they gave him the name "Bākulakumāra.
When he reached the age of discretion, they had three palaces built for him in each of the two cities and provided him with theatrical performances.
He resided in each city for four months. While he was staying there in one of the cities for four months, on board his ships...
Having had a pavilion constructed, they placed him there along with his dancers;
while he was enjoying great prosperity, they led him halfway to the other city over the course of two months.

The dancers residing in that other city also thought, "He will have arrived halfway in two months," and so they went out to meet him in the same manner, and in those two months [they reached] their own...
They lead him to their own city. The other actors, having turned back in the middle, go to their own city.
Having stayed there for four months, he returns again to the other city by that same method.
Thus, while experiencing such prosperity, eighty years were fulfilled for him.
At that time, our Bodhisatta, having attained omniscience and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma, reached Kosambī while traveling on his gradual journey.
[According to] the Majjhimabhāṇakas, it was Bārāṇasī.
The merchant Bākula, having heard that "the Ten-Powered One has arrived," took many perfumes and garlands and went into the presence of the Teacher to hear a discourse on the Dhamma.

Having heard this, he gained faith and went forth. Being an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) for only seven days, on the eighth dawn, together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), he attained *arahantship*.

Then, women who were well-acquainted with him in two cities came from their own homes, stayed right there, and sent robes after having had them made. For one fortnight, the Elder [was provided] by those dwelling in Kosambī...

He used robes sent to him; for one half-month, those from the residents of Bārāṇasī were brought according to this very same rule—whatever was the finest in each of the two cities was brought specifically for the Elder.
Even after he had gone forth, eighty years passed for him in comfort. In both places, not even the slightest affliction, let alone a major one, ever arose for him, even for a mere moment.
Thus, at the end of his life, having preached the Bākula Sutta, he attained final Nibbāna.
In this way, the state of being healthy while in the womb of a fish was due to the power of the knowledge of Arahatship to be attained by the Venerable Bākula in that final existence;
it is therefore called "success through the expansion of knowledge" (*ñāṇavipphārā iddhi*). It is [also] the analytical knowledge (*paṭisambhidāñāṇa*) attained as the fruit of well-performed deeds.
They even say it was through his majestic power (*ānubhāva*).
Elder Saṅkicca, who had performed meritorious deeds in the past, was reborn in the womb of the daughter of a wealthy family in Sāvatthī, who was the attendant of the Elder Dhammasenāpati.
When he had entered her womb, she was afflicted at that very moment by a certain illness.
She passed away; when her body was being cremated, they burned all the flesh except for the flesh of the fetus.
Then, having removed the fetal flesh from the funeral pyre, they pierced it in two or three places with stakes. The tip of a stake touched the corner of the infant’s eye.
Having thus pierced the fetal flesh, they threw it onto a heap of charcoal and [burned it] with the very coals.
Having covered [the pyre], they departed. The flesh of the womb burned away, but on the top of the embers there was a boy resembling a golden image, lying as if upon the interior of a lotus.

For a being in his final existence, there is no passing away from life until he has attained *arahantship*, even if he were to be crushed by Mount Sineru. On the following day, they arrived, thinking, "We shall extinguish the funeral pyre."
Seeing the boy lying thus, they were struck with a sense of wonder and amazement; taking the boy with them, they went to the city and questioned the fortune-tellers.
The fortune-tellers said, "If this boy lives as a householder, his kinsmen will remain in poverty for seven generations.
But if he goes forth into homelessness, [he will be surrounded] by five hundred ascetics."
“He will wander about surrounded [by a retinue],” they said. His grandmother raised that boy.
When he had grown up, his relatives also raised him, thinking, “We shall have him ordained in the presence of our noble master. When he was seven years old, [they told him]:
“While you were dwelling in your mother’s womb, she passed away; even when her body was being cremated, you did not burn. To the boys—
Having heard this, he thought, "I have indeed been delivered from such dangers; what is the use of the household life for me? I shall go forth.
He informed his relatives, who said, "Very well, dear one," and led him into the presence of the Elder Dhammasenāpati. They handed him over, saying, "Venerable sir, please ordain him.
The Elder gave him the meditation subject of the five aggregates (the *tacapañcaka*) and ordained him. At the very moment of the shaving of his hair...

He attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Having reached full age and received the higher ordination (upasampadā), he traveled about at the age of ten with a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus.
In this manner, the fact that the Elder Saṅkicca remained free from disease while on the wooden pyre is called the "success (iddhi) consisting in the expansion of knowledge."
The Elder Bhūtapāla was also one who had fulfilled his past causes. His father was a poor man in Rājagaha.
Taking that boy with him, he went by cart into the forest for the sake of firewood; having made a load of wood, he reached the vicinity of the city gate in the evening.
Then his oxen broke the yoke and entered the city. He, having seated his little son at the foot of the cart—
Following after the oxen, he entered the city itself. Before he had even departed, the gate was closed.

The boy lay down beneath the cart and fell asleep for the entire night. Rājagaha was already naturally infested with non-human beings (*amanussa*), and this particular location was near a charnel ground (*susāna*).
Yet, no *yakkha* [could harm] that one who was in his final existence (*pacchimabhavika*).
He was unable to cause any misfortune for the boy. At a later time, having gone forth and attained arahantship, he became known as the Elder Bhūtapāla.

Thus, even in a place frequented by fierce yakkhas, the Venerable Bhūtapāla’s state of health was due to what is called the supernormal power (*iddhi*) arising from the expansion of his knowledge (*ñāṇavipphārā*), according to the method already described.

16. In the exposition of the supernormal power of the expansion of concentration (*samādhivipphāriddhi*), regarding the passage beginning "the venerable Sāriputta’s supernormal power of the expansion of concentration," it is said that while the venerable Sāriputta was dwelling with the Elder Mahāmoggallāna at Kapotakandara,
on a moonlit night, as he sat in the open air with his hair recently shorn, a certain wicked *yakkha* together with a companion *yakkha*— [...continued...]

Even though he was being restrained, he struck him on the head. Although the sound of his shouting was like that of a thundercloud, at the moment of the blow, the Elder had entered into meditative absorption (samāpatti) and remained seated. Consequently, the blow caused him no affliction whatsoever.
This was the elder’s supernormal power (iddhi) resulting from the expansion of concentration (samādhivipphārā). As it is said:
Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna were dwelling at Kapotakandara.
At that time, on a moonlit night, the Venerable Sāriputta’s hair had been freshly shorn.
He was sitting in the open air, having attained a certain state of concentration.
Now at that time, two yakkha friends were traveling from the northern direction toward the southern direction on some business.
Those yakkhas saw the Venerable Sāriputta during the bright night.
Seeing him sitting in the open air with his hair freshly shorn, one yakkha said this to the second yakkha:
“It occurs to me, friend, to strike this ascetic on the head. When this was said, that yakkha replied to the other yakkha:
“Enough, friend; do not assault the ascetic. That ascetic, friend, is sublime.”
“...of great psychic power and great majesty.
A second time... and a third time, that yakkha said this to the other yakkha:
“It occurs to me, friend, to give a blow to the head of this ascetic. And a third time, that yakkha [said] to that yakkha...
He said this: “Enough, friend; do not revile the ascetic. That ascetic, friend, is sublime, possessed of great power and great majesty.
But that yakkha, disregarding the other yakkha, struck the venerable Sāriputta on the head.
Such was the force of that blow that it would have killed a nāga seven or seven-and-a-half cubits in height.
He might cast him down, or split apart a great mountain peak; yet that *yakkha*, crying out, "I am burning!
I am burning!", fell right there into the Great Hell.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, with his purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, saw this.
Seeing that blow being dealt by the yakkha to the head of the Venerable Sāriputta, he approached the Venerable Sāriputta and said to him: “I hope you are bearing up, friend Sāriputta;
I hope you are getting by; I hope you have no great pain? “I am bearing up, friend Moggallāna; I am getting by.”
"It is bearable for me, friend Moggallāna, yet my head is slightly pained.
"It is wonderful, friend Sāriputta! It is marvelous, friend Sāriputta! How great is the psychic power and majesty of the Venerable Sāriputta!
For here, friend Sāriputta, a certain yakkha struck you on the head, and yet it was only that slight [pain]."
The blow was struck; yet with that blow one might have felled a nāga seven or seven-and-a-half cubits high, or shattered a great mountain peak. And yet the Venerable Sāriputta spoke thus:
“It is bearable for me, friend Moggallāna; it is tolerable for me, friend Moggallāna; however, my head is slightly painful.”
“It is wonderful, friend Moggallāna! It is marvelous, friend Moggallāna!
How great is the psychic power and majesty of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, that he can even see a *yakkha*, whereas we at present cannot even see a dust-demon (*paṃsupisāca*)!”
With his purified divine ear-element, which surpasses that of humans, the Blessed One heard this conversation between those two great beings.
Then the Blessed One, having understood the significance of this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation:
“Whose mind is like a rock, steady and unshakable;”
“Detached from things that cause passion, he does not become angry at things that cause anger;
for one whose mind is thus developed, from where shall suffering come?
And here, by the words spoken by the Blessed One, “From where shall suffering come to him,” it is shown that no one [is harmed] by that blow.

The commentarial statement, "There was an affliction," is highly appropriate. Therefore, by the words "Moreover, my head is slightly painful," it is not that there is a painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*);
rather, it is said to be "painful" with reference to the head's lack of functional capacity (*akammaññabhāva*).
For even in the world, one who can be maintained without difficulty is said to have a pleasant nature (*sukhasīla*), whereas one who can be maintained only with difficulty...
"He is called one whose virtue is difficult to maintain. This too should be understood as being due to the period immediately after emerging from attainment (*samāpatti*);

for during the time he was absorbed in attainment, even that would not have occurred. It was not said [earlier] because of his inability to see even a "dust-demon" (*paṃsupisācaka*) at that time, but rather because of his lack of engagement with the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*). The Elder...

It is said that, out of compassion for future generations—fearing they might perceive worldly psychic power (*iddhi*) as the essence—he generally did not employ such powers. As stated in the *Theragāthā*:
"Neither for the sake of recollecting past lives, nor for the divine eye..."
“Regarding the supernormal power of reading the minds of others, regarding death and rebirth, and regarding the purification of the divine ear-element—I have no aspiration for these.

Thus the Elder himself stated his lack of longing for the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*). Furthermore, the Elder had attained mastery in sixty-seven of the perfections of knowledge pertaining to disciples (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*).

Furthermore, regarding the Elder Sañjīva, the second chief disciple of the Blessed One Kakusandha, who had attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), the cowherds and others, perceiving him as "dead," gathered grass, wood, and other materials and set them on fire.
Not even a single thread of the Elder’s robe was consumed by the flames.
This was because it had been produced through the power of serenity (samatha) proceeding by way of the successive attainments (anupubbasamāpatti).
Supernormal power through the expansion of concentration. As it is said:
"At that time, O Evil One, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had arisen in the world.
Now, O Evil One, for the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, there was the Vidhura-sañjīva [rebirth]..."

There was a pair of disciples, a supreme and auspicious pair. But as for all the disciples of the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, O Evil One—among them, there was none who was even equal to the Venerable Vidhura in this regard, namely, in the teaching of the Dhamma.
It is by this method, O Evil One, that the Venerable Vidhura is called "Vidhura."
a designation arose. But, Evil One, the Venerable Sañjīva, whether he has gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, enters the cessation of perception and feeling with ease.
"Formerly, Evil One, the Venerable Sañjīva [entered] the cessation of perception and feeling at the foot of a certain tree."

He was seated, having attained the cessation of perception and feeling. Then, Evil One, cowherds, shepherds, farmers, and travelers saw the Venerable Sañjīva seated at the foot of a certain tree, having attained the cessation of perception and feeling.
Upon seeing him, they thought: “It is wonderful, indeed! It is marvelous, indeed! This ascetic is sitting there...”
“He has passed away; come, let us cremate him.
Then, Evil One, those cowherds, shepherds, farmers, and travelers gathered grass, wood, and cow dung, piled it upon the body of the Venerable Sañjīva, set fire to it, and departed. Then, Evil One...
"Evil One, at the end of that night, the Venerable Sañjīva emerged from that meditative attainment,
shook out his robes, dressed for the morning, and taking his bowl and outer robe, entered the village for alms.
Evil One, those cowherds, shepherds, farmers, and travelers saw the Venerable Sañjīva [entering] for alms."
Seeing him walking about, they thought: “It is wonderful indeed, sir! It is marvelous indeed, sir!
This ascetic died while sitting, yet he has come back to life! It was by this means, Evil One, that the venerable Sañjīva acquired the designation “Sañjīva” (the Revived).
The Elder Khāṇu-koṇḍañña, however, was naturally abundant in meditative attainments (*samāpatti*). One night, he sat in a certain forest having entered into an attainment.

Five hundred thieves, having stolen goods and while on their way, thought, "Now there is no one following behind us," and desiring to rest, they were unloading their goods when [the Elder] said, "This is a stump."
Thinking thus, they placed all their belongings on top of the Elder.
As they were departing after having rested, at the moment they reached for the first item they had set down, the Elder emerged by means of the time-limit.
Seeing the Elder’s movement, they cried out in fear. The Elder said, “Do not be afraid, lay followers; I am a bhikkhu.”
Having come and paid homage, they went forth out of faith directed toward the Elder and, together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), attained Arahantship.
From that time on, the Elder was known as the Elder Khāṇu-koṇḍañña.

This absence of affliction in that venerable one, who was overwhelmed by five hundred bundles [of goods], was a supernormal power (*iddhi*) resulting from the expansion of concentration (*samādhi-vipphārā*).
The laywoman Uttarā, however, was the daughter of the very wealthy merchant Puṇṇa in Rājagaha;

while still a young girl, she attained the fruit of stream-entry together with her parents. When she reached marriageable age, she was given in marriage by the merchant of Rājagaha to his son, who held wrong views, despite the great reluctance of the family.
She [went] for the purpose of seeing the Buddha, hearing the Dhamma, and [paying homage to] the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
