Being distressed because she could find no opportunity to give alms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and hear the Dhamma, she summoned a courtesan named Sirimā to that very city.
Having given her fifteen thousand kahāpaṇas—which she had brought from her father’s house solely for the purpose of securing an opportunity—she said:
"Take these kahāpaṇas and [arrange for] this son of a merchant for half a month..."

Having entrusted her husband with the task of looking after the household, she herself resolved upon the precepts of the Uposatha, thinking with a joyful heart, "For these half-months, I shall obtain the opportunity to see the Buddha and perform other such duties.
Until the Pavāraṇā ceremony, she invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha and gave a great almsgiving for half a month;
after the meal, she provided various kinds of hard and soft foods in the kitchen.

She caused her consciousness to depart. Her husband, standing at the window with Sirimā while looking outside on the thought, "Tomorrow is the invitation ceremony," saw her wandering about in that state—drenched in sweat, covered in ashes, and smeared with charcoal and soot—and laughed, saying, "This fool performs what is called 'wholesome' action without enjoying her own prosperity.
Uttara, too, looked at her and [said], "For the sake of the future world..."
“The fool does no wholesome deed,” she said, laughing.
Having seen the conduct of both women, Sirimā—thinking, “I am the mistress of the house”—was overcome with jealousy;
becoming angry at Uttarā, she descended from the palace, intending to cause her suffering. Uttarā, perceiving this, sat down upon a seat.

She suffused him with a mind of loving-kindness. Descending from the palace, Sirimā entered the kitchen, took a bowlful of boiling clarified butter from the place where cakes were being fried, and poured it over his head.
It flowed away like cool water upon a lotus leaf. The female slaves struck Sirimā with their hands and feet and threw her to the ground.
Uttarā, having emerged from the meditation on loving-kindness, dismissed the female slaves. Sirimā asked Uttarā for forgiveness.
Uttarā said, "Forgive me tomorrow in the presence of the Teacher," and when she requested her assistance with the physical chores, she instructed her on how to prepare the side dishes.
Having prepared them, she [invited] the Teacher together with the Saṅgha and her own retinue of five hundred courtesans.

Having served the meal, she said, "Be my companions in seeking forgiveness," and on the following day, together with those courtesans, at the conclusion of the Teacher’s meal, she paid homage to the Teacher and said, "Blessed One, I have offended against Uttarā; may Uttarā forgive me.
The Teacher said, "Forgive her, Uttarā. When she replied, "I forgive you, Blessed One," the Teacher said, "By non-anger..."

He taught the Dhamma beginning with, “Conquer anger,” and so forth. Even before the Teacher had finished his discourse, Uttarā brought her husband and her parents-in-law into the presence of the Teacher.
At the conclusion of the teaching, those three people and all the courtesans were established in the fruit of stream-entry.
Thus, the Upāsikā Uttarā’s freedom from the affliction caused by the boiling ghee was a supernatural power (iddhi) resulting from the expansion of concentration (samādhivipphārā).
The laywoman named Sāmāvatī was the chief queen of King Udena in Kosambī.
For that king had three chief queens, each accompanied by five hundred female attendants. Among them, Sāmāvatī was the daughter of the merchant Bhaddiya in the city of Bhaddiya.
When her father passed away, she increased her retinue of five hundred women in the household of Ghosita the merchant in Kosambī, who was her father’s friend.
Seeing that he had reached maturity, the king, having conceived affection for him, brought him with his retinue to his own home and gave him the place of consecration.
King Caṇḍapajjota had a chief queen named Vāsuladattā.
There was also the daughter of the brahmin Māgaṇḍiya, who, having served as an attendant at the feet of the Blessed One, was being given away by her father.
“Having seen lust, aversion, and passion, there was no desire even for sexual intercourse;
why indeed would one wish to touch with one’s feet this thing filled with urine and excrement?
Having heard this verse spoken by the Blessed One, she harbored resentment toward the Blessed One. At the conclusion of the teaching of the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta, her parents...
Having attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), they went forth and reached arahantship.
Māgaṇḍiya, her younger paternal uncle, took her to Kosambī and gave her to the king; she became the king’s chief queen.
Now, there were three guild-leaders in the world—the guild-leader Ghosita, the guild-leader Kukkuṭa, and the guild-leader Pāvārika—who [heard] of the appearance of the Tathāgata.

Having heard this, he went into the presence of the Teacher at Jetavana; having heard the Dhamma and attained the fruit of stream-entry, he gave a great almsgiving for half a month to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Having requested the Teacher to go to Kosambī, he went to Kosambī and had three monasteries built—Ghosita’s Monastery, Kukkuṭa’s Monastery, and Pāvārika’s Monastery—by means of three individuals.
In due course, as the Teacher arrived there, they accommodated him in turn, one day at each monastery,
and each of them gave a great almsgiving to the Blessed One and his Saṅgha. Then one day, their attendant, a florist named Sumana,
having requested the Teacher from the merchant, had him sit in his own house to eat with the Saṅgha.
At that moment, a female slave named Khujjuttarā, who was an attendant of Sāmāvatī, took eight kahāpaṇas and went to his house.
He said, "Be an assistant in serving food for the Teacher together with the Saṅgha.
She did so, and having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma at the conclusion of the meal, she became a stream-enterer. On another occasion, four...
Because she was incapable of taking what was not given—since she would not take even a single kahāpaṇa for herself—she took flowers worth eight kahāpaṇas and presented them to Sāmāvatī.
When asked by her the reason for the large quantity of flowers, she was unable to speak falsely and told the truth as it was.
When asked, "Why did you not take [flowers] today?", she replied, "[I heard] the Dhamma of the Sammasambuddha..."
“Having heard the Deathless, I have realized it,” she said. “Mother Uttare, please explain that Dhamma to us as well.
She replied, “In that case, bathe me, give me a pair of clean garments, and having seated me on a high seat, let all of you sit on low seats.
They all did exactly so. She was a noble female disciple who had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) of one still in training (sekha).
Having dressed in one robe and arranged the other as an upper garment, she took a fan and taught them the Dhamma.
Sāmāvatī and the five hundred women attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
They all paid homage to Khujjuttarā, saying, "Mother, from this day forward, without performing our domestic duties, you shall stand in the place of a mother and a teacher to us."
"Having stood there and heard the Dhamma taught by the Teacher, please tell it to us," they said.

Acting accordingly, she later became a bearer of the Three Piṭakas (Tipiṭakadhara) and, being appointed by the Teacher to the foremost position among learned female lay disciples (upāsikā), she attained that preeminent rank.
The women of Sāmāvatī’s retinue longed for a vision of the Buddha; [they waited] in the street where the One of Ten Powers was walking.
As they were following along, the windows proving insufficient, they broke through the walls to gaze upon the Teacher and offered him salutations and worship.
When Māgaṇḍiyā went there and saw those breaches, she asked for the reason;
having learned that the Teacher had arrived, she became resentful toward the Blessed One and, growing angry even with them, said: "O Great King, Sāmāvatī and her companions have gone outside..."
“There is a conspiracy; having broken through the wall, they are watching for the ascetic Gotama, and in a few days they will kill him,” she said to the king.
Although the king saw the breaches, he did not believe her words and had upper window-vents constructed.
Again, wishing to break them up, Māgaṇḍiyā had the king bring eight live cocks.
“Great King,” she said, “in order to test them, have these cocks killed and send them with the message: ‘Cook them for my sake.
The king sent them accordingly. When they replied, “We do not commit the taking of life,” he spoke again, saying, “Cook them and send them to that ascetic Gotama.
When the king had sent them thus, Māgandiyā [took] the eight dead cocks...
Having spoken thus, she sent [the message]. Sāmāvatī cooked [the food] and sent it to the One of Ten Powers. Māgaṇḍiyā was unable to incite the king’s anger even by that means.
For the king, among his three chief queens, would stay for seven days at each of their residences in turn.
When the king went to his own quarters, he would take with him the lute called *hatthikanta*. At the time when the king was going to Sāmāvatī’s palace, Māgaṇḍiyā...
Having had the fang washed with an antidote and placed inside a bamboo tube, he had a young black snake brought and put inside the lute, covering the opening with a cluster of flowers.
When the king arrived there, [the queen], acting as if she were moving back and forth, removed the flower cluster from the opening of the lute. The snake emerged and hissed.
Having formed a hood, she lay down upon the surface of the bed. She cried out in a loud voice, "Shame on this snake!

When the king saw the snake, he became angry. Sāmāvatī, perceiving the king's anger, gave a signal to the five hundred women, saying, "Today, you must pervade the king with the meditation of universal loving-kindness.
She herself did likewise. Then the king [took up] his thousand-fold-strength bow...

Having taken his bow, he struck it with his hand, placed Sāmāvatī at the front, and having had all those women stand in a row, he fastened a poison-tipped arrow to his bow, drew the string, and stood there. He was unable to either shoot the arrow or lower it;
sweat broke out from his limbs, his body trembled, and saliva fell from his mouth.
He did not see the arrow that was to be grasped. Then Sāmāvatī said to him, “Are you weary, Great King?
“Yes, Queen, I am weary; be my support. “Very well, Great King, place the point of the arrow upon the ground.
The king did so. She then made this resolve: “May the arrow be released from the king’s hand.”
At that moment, the arrow was released. The king immediately submerged himself in the water, and with wet clothes and wet hair, he fell at Sāmāvatī’s feet and said:
“Forgive me, O Queen—for I am bewildered, I am deluded;
all the directions are confused to me.”
“Sāmāvatī, protect me! May you become my refuge,” he said. Sāmāvatī replied:
“Do not go to me for refuge; go instead to that one to whom I have gone for refuge.”
"Go for refuge to that Buddha, and you too shall be my refuge," she said.
The king replied, "In that case, I go for refuge to him and to the Teacher; and I grant you a boon.
She said, "Let the boon be accepted, Great King. The king approached the Teacher, went for refuge, and invited him [to a meal].
Having given a great almsgiving for seven days to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, he said, “Choose a boon, Sāmāvatī.
She replied, “Very well, Great King, grant me this boon: let the Teacher come here together with five hundred bhikkhus;
I shall listen to the Dhamma. The king, having paid homage to the Teacher, said, “Venerable Sir, together with five hundred bhikkhus...”
“Come here regularly,” she said, “together with Sāmāvatī, saying, ‘We shall hear the Dhamma.
The Teacher said, “Great King, it is not fitting for Buddhas to go to one place regularly; the great multitude will also look forward to it.
“In that case, venerable sir, please command the monks. The Teacher commanded the Elder Ānanda. The Elder [sent] five...
Taking hundreds of bhikkhus, he went regularly to the royal palace. Those women, headed by the queen, also listened to the Dhamma after feeding the Elder.
And the Teacher placed Sāmāvatī in the foremost position among female lay disciples who dwell in loving-kindness.
Thus, the king’s inability to discharge his arrow was due to the supernormal power of the lay disciple Sāmāvatī’s concentration.

Regarding "supernormal power" (*iddhi*): here, one is called a "lay follower" (*upāsikā*) because she honors the Three Jewels through unwavering confidence (*aveccappasāda*), or through confident trust (*okappanapasāda*), or by going for refuge to the Three Jewels. 17.

In the description of noble supernormal power (*ariyiddhi-niddesa*), "noble supernormal power" refers to that which occurs only for noble ones (*ariya*) who have reached mastery over the mind and whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
"It is called noble supernormal power. Here, "a bhikkhu" refers to a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed within this teaching.
"Regarding an undesirable object" means regarding an object—whether a sentient being or a conditioned formation—that is by its very nature unpleasant.

"He pervades it with loving-kindness" means that if it is a sentient being, he pervades them through the cultivation of loving-kindness. Or, "he resolves it by way of the elements" means [if it is] a conditioned formation.
Whatever exists, he applies attention to the elements, thinking, "It is merely elements. It is also appropriate to apply the application of elements to sentient beings.
Or, he pervades with the foul: if it is a sentient being, he pervades them with the meditation on the foul.
Or, he applies it as impermanent: if it is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṅkhāra*), he applies attention to it as "impermanent. "Both of those" means both of these. "One who is equanimous" means...

“He is equanimous through the equanimity of the sixfold base” means he is equanimous by way of the equanimity associated with the six sense bases. “Mindful” means because he has attained the fullness of mindfulness. “Clearly comprehending” means because he acts with clear comprehension through wisdom.
“Having seen a form with the eye” means having seen a form with the visual consciousness capable of seeing forms—which is conventionally designated as the “eye” in the sense of being its instrument.
However, the Ancients have said: “The eye does not see the form, because it is devoid of consciousness;”

"The mind does not see because it lacks the faculty of sight; rather, it sees by means of consciousness which has the sensitive matter (pasāda) as its basis when there is a collision between the door and the object.
However, this is a figurative expression involving the instrument, such as in the phrases 'he pierces with a bow' and so forth. Therefore, the meaning here is:
'having seen the visible form with eye-consciousness. Alternatively, [it means] "by means of the eye acting as the instrument."
"Having seen a form" is the meaning. "Neither glad" is a negation of the joy based on attachment to the household life, not of the feeling of joy that is a functional state (*kiriyabhūtā*).

"Neither sad" is a negation of all forms of dejection. "He dwells in equanimity" refers to what is called "sixfold equanimity" (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*), because it occurs at the six sense-doors in a manner that does not abandon one's naturally pure state even when confronted with desirable or undesirable objects.

One dwells equanimous by means of that equanimity which has acquired the name "equanimity as neutrality" (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*). The same method applies to the passages beginning with "having heard a sound with the ear.

18. In the exposition of the supernormal power of the tongue born of kamma-vipāka: "of all winged creatures" means the movement through the air of all those belonging to the class of winged beings, even without [the attainment of] jhāna or direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
Likewise, there is the movement through the air and the acts of seeing, etc., of all deities. Of some...
"Of humans" refers to the humans of the first eon.

"Of some who have fallen into the states of misery" refers to those such as Piyaṅkaramātā, Punabbasumātā, Phussamittā, Dhammaguttā, and others, who are called "fallen into the states of misery" because they have fallen away from a happy existence;
it also refers to other *petas*, *nāgas*, and *supaṇṇas*. Their supernormal power (*iddhi*), consisting of traveling through the air and so forth, is born of the ripening of kamma.
In the exposition of the supernormal power of one possessing merit: "A king" (*rājā*) is so called because he delights others through righteousness (*dhamma*).

"One who turns the wheel" (*cakkavattī*) is one who sets the wheel of gems (*ratana-cakka*) in motion. "He goes through the air" (*vehāsaṃ gacchati*): the accusative case is used in the sense of absolute connection (*accanta-saṃyoga*).

"Consisting of four divisions" (*caturaṅginīya*): it possesses the four divisions known as elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. "Army" (*senā*) refers merely to the collection of those [divisions]. "At the very least" (*antamaso*)...
"At the very least. "Horse-keepers" means those who protect horses. "Cowherds" means those who protect cattle. "Having taken up" means without giving them away.
Thus, their traveling through the air is the supernormal power (*iddhi*) of one possessing merit;

the meaning is that it is the supernormal power of the householder Jotika, who possesses merit. Regarding the phrase "the supernormal power of the householder Jotika": Jotika was one who had previously performed services for the *paccekabuddhas*.

In the city of Rājagaha there was a merchant. It is said that on the day of his birth, all weapons throughout the entire city burst into flame, and even all the ornaments worn upon the bodies of the people emitted light as if they were ablaze, so that the city became a single mass of radiance.
Therefore, on the day of his naming ceremony, because the whole city had become one with light (*ekajotibhūta*), they gave him the name Jotika.

Then, when he had reached maturity and the ground was being cleared for the purpose of building a house, Sakka, the king of the devas, arrived; having split open the earth over an area of sixteen karīsas,
he caused a seven-storied palace made of the seven precious gems to arise,
and surrounding the palace, he constructed seven walls made of the seven precious gems, provided with seven gate-towers.
He caused [them] to arise; he caused sixty-four wish-fulfilling trees (*kapparukkha*) to arise along the perimeter of the wall;
at the four corners of the palace, he caused four treasure-pots to arise, measuring one *yojana*, three *gāvutas*, two *gāvutas*, and one *gāvuta* respectively.
At the four corners of the palace, four sugarcanes made of gold arose, as large as the trunks of young palm trees.

Their bowls were made of jewels and their rims were made of gold. At each of the seven gate-towers, seven yakkhas—each surrounded by a retinue of one, two, three, four, five, six, and seven thousand yakkhas respectively—took up their guard.
When King Bimbisāra heard of the arising of the palaces and other structures, he sent the umbrella of a chief merchant. He was the merchant Jotika.

Having become renowned throughout the entire Jambudīpa, he lived in that palace enjoying great prosperity together with his wife, who had been brought from Uttarakuru by deities and seated in the inner chamber; she arrived bringing one measure of rice and three fire-stones.
With that single measure of rice, their food was sufficient for the rest of their lives.
If they wish to fill even a hundred carts with rice, it remains there as a mere stalk of rice.
At the time of cooking the meal, they place the rice in a pot and set it upon those stones;
the stones ignite at that very moment and go out as soon as the meal is cooked. By that very sign, [they know] of the meal...
They knew when the food was cooked. The same principle applied even at the time of cooking soups and other dishes.
Thus, their food was cooked by means of fire-stones, and they lived by the light of jewels. They were not aware of the radiance of either a fire or a lamp.
It became renowned throughout the whole of Jambudīpa that Jotika possessed such prosperity. Great crowds of people went out in vehicles and other conveyances to see him.
He arrived. The merchant Jotika had meals prepared for those who came from *uttarakuru* rice;

he gave orders, saying, "Let them take clothes and ornaments from the wish-fulfilling trees," and he gave orders, saying, "Let them open the mouth of the treasure-jar one *gāvuta* deep and take as much as is needed for their livelihood.
As all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa were taking wealth and departing, the treasure-jar—
"There was not even a finger’s breadth less [of the cloth]"—this is the supernatural power (*iddhi*) of that merit-possessor.

Regarding "the supernatural power of the merit-possessor Jaṭila the householder": Jaṭila was a merchant in Takkasilā who had performed meritorious services at the relic-stupa of the Blessed One Kassapa.
It is said that his mother was a beautiful daughter of a merchant in Bārāṇasī.
She came into being. When she was fifteen or sixteen years old, they had her reside on the upper floor of a seven-storied palace for her protection.
One day, while she was looking out through an open window, a *vidyādhara* traveling through the air saw her;
moved by affection, he entered through the window and engaged in intimacy with her.
She conceived a child by him. Then, when a female slave saw her, she asked, "Madam, what is this?
She replied, "Let it be; do not tell anyone," and remained silent out of fear. When the tenth month arrived, she gave birth to a son.
Having had a new vessel brought, she laid the infant down in it, covered the vessel, and placed garlands of flowers on top.
Setting her aside, he commanded a maidservant, saying, "Carry this on your head, go, and cast it into the Ganges;
and when asked, 'What is this?', you should say, 'It is an offering for my mistress. She did exactly as she was told.
Furthermore, two women who were bathing in the lower reaches of the Ganges saw that vessel being carried along by the water, and one of them said, "This vessel is mine."

One said, "Whatever is inside this belongs to me," and when the vessel was brought, she took it, placed it on dry land, opened it, and seeing the boy, said, "The boy is mine alone, because you said, 'The vessel is mine.
The other said, "Because you said, 'Whatever is inside the vessel belongs to me,' the boy is mine. Thus they disputed.
Having gone to the court of justice, when the ministers were unable to reach a decision, they went into the presence of the king.
Having heard their words, the king said, "You take the boy; you take the bowl.
Now, she who had received the boy was the attendant of the Elder Mahākaccāyana. She thought, "I shall have this boy ordained in the presence of the Elder."
He was possessed [of such qualities]. On the day he was born, because the impurities of the womb had not been washed away, his hair remained matted;
therefore, they gave him the name Jaṭila (the Matted-hair One).
When he was walking about on foot, the Elder entered that house for alms. The laywoman, having seated the Elder, [served him].
She gave him food. When the Elder saw the boy, he asked, "Lay sister, have you obtained a son? "Yes, venerable sir;

I shall cause him to go forth in your presence and support him," she said. The Elder replied, "Very well," and taking him with him as they went, he looked to see whether this boy possessed the merit to enjoy the prosperity of a householder, and perceived that he was one of great merit.

Thinking, "This being will experience great prosperity, yet he is still so young, and his wisdom has not yet reached maturity," he took the child and went to the house of a lay supporter in Takkasilā.
After the elder had paid homage and stood there, the man saw the boy and asked, "Venerable sir, have you found a child? "Yes, lay follower."
“Let this youth go forth first; let him remain in your presence for a while. He replied, “Very well, venerable sir,” and having placed him in the position of a son, he looked after him.
Now, for twelve years, his household goods had been accumulating in the house.
When he went to another village, he brought all those goods to the market, and having explained the price of each item, he said:
Having said, "Take this and that amount of wealth and give it to me," he departed.
On that day, the deities presiding over the city ensured that even those who needed only a little cumin or pepper were directed toward his very shop.
Thus, he sold the vast stock of merchandise accumulated over twelve years in a single day.
The householder returned and, seeing nothing at all in the shop, said, "My dear son, you have lost all your merchandise.
"I have not lost it, father; everything has been sold according to the manner you instructed.

Here is the capital for so-and-so, and here is the capital for so-and-so," he replied, handing over the entire capital to him. The householder, being inspired with confidence, thought, "This man is priceless."
“Capable of living anywhere,” he said, and having given his daughter—who had reached marriageable age—to him, he commanded his men, “Build a house for him.
When the house was finished, he said, “Go now; dwell in your own home.
Then, at the moment of entering the house, as soon as he had stepped upon the threshold with one foot, at the rear part of the house—

At the site of the ground, a golden mountain eighty cubits high rose up. Having heard that a golden mountain had indeed risen by bursting through the earth in the house of the matted-hair ascetic (jaṭila), the king sent him the parasol of a chief merchant.
Thus he became known as the Jaṭila-seṭṭhi; this was the supernatural power (iddhi) of that meritorious man.

Regarding "the supernatural power of the meritorious merchant Meṇḍaka": Meṇḍaka was a merchant in the city of Bhaddiya in the kingdom of Magadha who had performed services for the Blessed One Vipassi.

It is said that in the area of his western house, measuring eight karīsas, golden rams the size of elephants, horses, and bulls broke through the earth, striking one another back and forth on their backs.

They arose, and balls of five-colored thread were placed in their mouths. When there was a need for ghee, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth, or for clothing, coverings, silver, gold, and so forth, they would remove the ball from their mouths.
From the mouth of even a single ball, there was enough ghee, oil, honey, molasses, clothing, coverings, silver, and gold to satisfy all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa.
He went forth. From that time on, he became known as Meṇḍaka Seṭṭhi; this was the supernatural power (*iddhi*) of that merit-possessor.

Regarding "the supernatural power of the merit-possessor Ghoṣita the householder": Ghoṣita was a merchant in Kosambī in the kingdom of Sakka who had performed meritorious service for a Paccekabuddha named Ghoṣita.
It is said that after passing away from the world of the gods, he [was reborn] in Kosambī as the son of a courtesan of the city...
He was conceived in the womb. On the day he was born, she laid him upon her bed and cast him away on a heap of refuse.
Crows and dogs sat surrounding the boy. A certain man, seeing him, conceived the idea that it was his own son and took him home, thinking, "I have found a son.
At that time, the merchant of Kosambī saw the chaplain and asked, "What is it, teacher?"

Having asked, "Today, have you examined the lunar days, the astrological divisions, the constellations, and so forth? and being told, "Yes, Great Merchant," he asked, "What will happen to the country?
He replied, "The boy born in this city today will become the chief merchant.
At that time, the merchant's wife was heavily pregnant; therefore, he sent him home quickly, saying, "Go!"

“Find out whether she has given birth or not. Having heard that she had not yet given birth, he went home, summoned a maidservant named Kāḷī, gave her a thousand pieces of money, and said, “Go, investigate this city today, and having found the child born today, bring him back.
While searching, she went to that house, and knowing that the child was born on that very day, she took the thousand pieces of money—

Having given it and brought it back, he showed it to the merchant. The merchant thought, "If a daughter is born to me, I will have her live with him and make him the master of the merchant’s estate; if a son is born, I will have him killed.
Having thus reflected, he raised the child in his own house.
Then, after a few days had passed, his wife gave birth to a son. The merchant thought, "If this boy does not exist, my [other] son will obtain the position of treasurer.
It is fitting that I kill him right now. He addressed Kālī, saying, "Go, girl;
at the time when the cattle are leaving the pen, lay this child across the middle of the gate. The cows will trample and kill him."
"Having ascertained whether he has been beaten or not, come back," she said. She went and, as soon as the gatekeeper had opened the gate, she laid him down in that manner.
Although the bull, the leader of the herd, would normally go out last of all at other times, on that day he went out first of all;
he stood placing the boy between his four legs.
Hundreds of cows emerged, rubbing their flanks against the bull’s two sides.
The cowherd, thinking, "This bull used to come out last of all, but today he has come out first and stands motionless in the middle of the gate;
what could this be? went over and saw a boy lying beneath him, and [was overcome with] paternal affection.
Having received it, [the merchant] thought, "I have gained a son," and took it home.
Kāḷī went and, when questioned by the merchant, reported the matter;
being told, "Go, give him this thousand [pieces of money] again and bring it back," she brought it back and gave it to him. Then the merchant said to her: "Mother Kāḷī, regarding this..."
"Five hundred carts leave this city at dawn to go on trade.
Take her and lay her down in the path of the wheels; either the oxen will trample her, or the wheel will crush her.
Once you have learned what has happened to her, you may return. She went and laid her down in the path of the wheels. The chief of the carters was in front.
It happened that when his oxen reached that place, they dropped their yokes; even though he repeatedly re-yoked them and drove them, they would not move forward.
While he was thus struggling with them, dawn broke. Thinking, "What have the oxen done?
and looking down the road, he saw the boy and thought, "Alas, what a heavy burden of work!"
With a joyful heart, thinking, "I have obtained a son," he led her home.
Kāḷī also went there, and when questioned by the merchant, she explained what had happened. Told, "Go, give another thousand and bring him back," she did accordingly.
Then the merchant said to her: "Now, having led him to the raw charnel ground..."
“Make him lie down in the middle of the road; there he will die, bitten by dogs or struck by a non-human being.
Once you have ascertained whether he is dead or alive, you may return. She led him there, made him lie down, and stood aside.
Neither the dogs nor any non-human being were able to approach him. Then a certain goat-herd...
Leading the goats toward their grazing ground, he went along the edge of the charnel ground. One goat, while eating leaves, entered the thicket;
seeing a child there, she knelt down and gave the child her teat.
Even when the goat-herd called out "He! He!", she did not come out. Thinking, "I will strike her with my staff and drive her out," he entered the thicket.
Having entered and stood on his knees, he saw a woman nursing a child;
having conceived a motherly affection for the child, thinking, "I have found a son," he took him and departed.
When Kāḷī returned and was questioned by the merchant, she explained what had happened and said, "Go; give him another thousand [pieces of gold]."
When she was told, "Give it to him and bring him back," she did exactly so. Then the merchant said to her:
"Mother, take this man, climb the Corapapāta mountain, and throw him over the precipice. As he strikes against the interior of the mountain, he will break into pieces and fall to the ground;
once you have ascertained whether he is dead or alive, you may return. She took him accordingly and reached the summit of the mountain.
Standing there, he threw it. Now, near that mountain cleft, a great bamboo thicket had grown following the contour of the mountain;
its summit was covered by a dense cluster of *jiñjuka* trees. As the boy fell, he landed upon it as if upon a leather bag.
On that very day, the head reed-worker’s bamboo-tax payment was due. He, together with his son—
Having gone there, she began to cut down that bamboo thicket. When it moved, the boy made a sound.
Thinking, "That is the sound of the boy," she climbed up one side, saw him, and with a joyful heart, thinking, "I have found my son," she took him and departed.
When Kāḷī returned and was questioned by the merchant, she explained what had happened and said, "Go; give him another thousand [pieces of money]."
Having been told, "Give it and bring it back," she did exactly so.
While the merchant was occupied with this and that task, the boy grew up. Because of his loud cries, he was given the name Ghosita.
He caused a sensation like a thorn in the merchant's eye; he could not even look straight ahead.
Then, contemplating a means for his death, he went to his own potter and asked him, "When will you coat the kiln?
When the potter replied, "Tomorrow," he said, "In that case, take this thousand pieces of money and do a job for me.
"What is it, Master? "I have a son of low birth; I shall send him to you."
“Then, having inserted him into the womb, you should cut him into pieces with a sharp axe, place him in a jar, and put it into the pit.
This thousand [pieces of gold] is like a pledge for your truth; as for what else is appropriate for you to do hereafter, we shall do that later.
The potter accepted this, saying, “Very well.”
On the following day, the merchant summoned Ghosita and sent him off, saying, “Yesterday I commanded a potter to perform a certain task;
come, my dear, go to him and say: ‘Please complete the work that was commanded for me by my father yesterday.
He replied, “Very well,” and went there. As he was departing, the other [the potter] heard from the merchant’s...
Seeing his son playing ball with other boys, he called him over and asked, "Where are you going?
Having received his father's message, the boy replied, "I am going to the potter's;
these boys have won many stakes from me, so give them back to me by winning them back. [The father said,] "I am afraid of my father."
"Do not fear, brother; I shall carry that message for you. "Many have defeated me; until I return, mark my stake for me," he said.
It is said that Ghosita was skilled at playing with marbles, and so he bound him with these words.
He too replied to him, "In that case, go and tell the potter: 'Yesterday, it seems, my father gave me a certain task.'"
"Produce it," he urged. He went to the potter's presence and spoke accordingly.
Then the potter killed him according to the method instructed by the merchant and threw him into the pit. Ghosita, too, having spent part of the day in play, returned home at the time of evening.
When asked, "Why, dear, have you not gone? he explained both the reason for his own failure to go and the reason why his younger brother had gone.
He announced it. The merchant, crying out "Woe! Woe!
with a great cry, his entire body as if filled with boiling blood, raised his arms and went weeping into the potter's presence, exclaiming, "O potter, do not destroy it! Do not destroy it!
Seeing him approaching in that manner, the potter said, "Master, do not make a noise; the work is finished."
He said: "Overwhelmed by a grief as vast as a mountain, he experienced no small measure of dejection.
Nevertheless, the merchant was unable to look him straight in the face. Thinking, 'How can I have him killed?
and seeing a stratagem—'I will send him to my official in charge of a hundred villages and have him executed'—he thought, 'This man..."
“Kill this son born of a low-caste woman and throw him into the cesspool; when this has been done, I shall know what must be done for my maternal uncle.
Having written this letter for him, he said, “Dear Ghosita, there is an official in our village of a hundred households;
take this letter and give it to him,” and he tied the letter to the hem of his garment. But as for the script...
He did not know. For since his childhood, the merchant had been trying to kill him and was unable to do so;
how then could he teach him the art of writing? As he was departing, having tied his own death-warrant to the hem of his garment, he said:
"I have no provisions for the journey, dear father. [The other replied: "There is no need for provisions for the journey; at such-and-such a village along the way..."
“I have a merchant friend named Nāma; having taken your morning meal at his house, proceed on.
Saying “Very well,” he paid homage to his father and set out. Upon reaching that village, he asked for the merchant’s house, went there, and saw the merchant’s wife.
When she asked, “From where have you come? he replied, “From within the city. She asked, “Whose son are you?”
“Is he your best friend, mother? “Yes, mother. “And what is his name? “He is Ghosita, mother.
At the mere sight of him, maternal affection for a son arose within her. Now, the merchant had a daughter about fifteen or sixteen years old, beautiful and graceful;
having given her only a single maidservant to attend to her needs, she lived on the seventh floor of a seven-storied mansion.
They were residing in the inner chamber on the upper floor of the palace. At that moment, the merchant’s daughter sent the slave-girl to the market.
When the merchant’s wife saw her, she asked, "Where are you going?
Upon being told, "By the mistress's command," she replied, "Come here first; let that errand wait. Spread out a seat for my son and bring some water."
“Wash your feet, anoint them with oil, spread out the bed, and give it to me; afterwards you may go on your errand,” she said.
She did exactly so.
Then, when she returned late, the merchant’s daughter rebuked her. Thereupon she said to her, “Do not be angry with me; the merchant’s son—”
“Ghosita has arrived; having done this and that for him, I have come here after going there.

As soon as the merchant’s daughter heard the name “Ghosita, the merchant’s son,” love arose within her through the power of their former association, piercing through her skin and other layers until it reached and rested upon the very marrow of her bones.
Then she asked him, “Where is he, mother? “He is lying on his bed, fast asleep. “Is there...”
"Is there anything in his hand? "There is a letter in the envelope.

Thinking, "What could this letter be?", while he was sleeping and his parents were unaware because they were preoccupied with other matters, she descended, went to him, opened the letter, took it, entered her own room, closed the door, and [went to] the window.
Having opened it and read that letter with skill in the art of deciphering scripts, he thought: "Alas!
This fool wanders about with his own death-warrant tied to his garment; had I not seen it, there would be no life left for him.
Tearing up and destroying that letter, he wrote another letter at the word of the merchant: "This is my son..."
"Let Ghosita, having had gifts brought from a hundred villages, perform an auspicious ceremony together with the daughter of this chief merchant of the district;

then, having built a two-storied house in the center of his own village, let him provide it with well-arranged protection by means of a surrounding wall and guards of men, saying: 'This and that was done by me.'"
"Send a message back. Once this has been done, I shall know what is appropriate for my uncle to do.
Having written this, he folded the letter and tied it with a cloth right there.
After sleeping for part of the day, he rose, ate, and departed; on the following day at dawn, he went to that village.
Having gone there, he saw the village official performing his duties. Upon seeing him, [the official] asked, "What is it, dear sir?
When [the man] replied, "My father has sent a letter for you," he took the letter, read it, and with a joyful heart said, "See, sirs!
My master, having conceived affection for me, wishes to perform an auspicious ceremony for my eldest son. [He then went] to my presence...
Having sent word, he commanded the householders, "Quickly bring wood and other materials.

Having had a house built in the middle of the village according to the description given, and having had gifts brought from a hundred villages, he brought home the daughter of the provincial merchant, performed the auspicious ceremonies, and sent a message to the merchant: "This and that have been done by me."
Upon hearing this, the merchant thought, "What I do is not right; what I do not do is right," and great dejection arose within him.
That grief, joining with his sorrow for his son, produced a burning sensation in his belly and brought on dysentery.
The merchant’s daughter also thought, "If anyone comes from the presence of the merchant, he must not speak to me [without my knowledge]."
"Do not speak of this to the merchant’s son first," he commanded.
The merchant, thinking, "I will no longer make my wicked son the master of my wealth," said to an official:
"Uncle, I am longing to see my son; send a footman and write a letter, and then send for my son."
“Summon him. Saying “Very well,” he gave a letter and dispatched a man.
During the time of the merchant’s severe illness, the merchant’s daughter went with Ghoṣita-kumāra. The merchant passed away.

When his father had died, the king bestowed upon him the wealth enjoyed by his father and granted him the position of merchant with a full hundred [pieces of gold]. Thus, he became known as the merchant Ghoṣita.

Established in great prosperity, upon hearing the words of the merchant’s daughter Kāḷī, he realized from the very beginning that his life was not destined to end in death at seven specific locations;
consequently, he began giving alms by disbursing one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] every day.
Thus, his freedom from illness in those seven locations was the supernatural power (*iddhi*) of a meritorious person. In this context, "house" (*gaha*) refers to a dwelling.

*Gaha* means "house"; *gahapati* means "householder. This is a name for one who is a lord (*adhipati*) in a family like that of a great sal tree (*mahāsāla*). In some manuscripts, Meṇḍaka is written after Ghosita.
Regarding the phrase "the power of merit of the five greatly meritorious ones," the meaning here is that the "power of merit" should be understood as belonging to the five greatly meritorious ones.
The five greatly meritorious ones are: the merchant Meṇḍaka, his wife Candapadumā, and his son the merchant Dhanañjaya.
The daughter-in-law Sumanadevī, and the one named Puṇṇa—these five persons had performed meritorious deeds for the Paccekabuddhas.
Among them, the merchant Meṇḍaka, having had one hundred and thirty-five granaries cleaned, bathed his head and sat at the door looking up;
from the sky, a stream of red rice fell and filled all the granaries. His wife...
Having taken a single stalk of rice and had a meal cooked, and having had soup prepared in a single vessel for the curry,
she— adorned with all her ornaments— sat upon a seat prepared at the gateway and caused it to be proclaimed,
"Let all who need food come! Having summoned them, she took a golden spoon and [served] the vessels brought by those who arrived one after another.
Having filled it, she gives it; even though she gives for an entire day, only the space occupied by a single ladleful taken once is perceived.
Her son, having bathed his head and taken a bag of a thousand [coins], causes a proclamation to be made: "Let those who need kahāpaṇas come!
To each person as they arrive, he fills their vessels and gives them. In the bag, there are exactly a thousand kahāpaṇas.
He had a daughter-in-law who, adorned with all her ornaments, took a basket of rice sufficient for four *doṇas* and sat upon a seat.
She caused it to be proclaimed, "Let those who need seed-rice come forward," and as each person arrived, she filled their vessels and gave them to them;
yet the basket remained exactly as full as before. His slave, likewise adorned with all his ornaments, [held] a golden yoke...
Having yoked oxen with golden straps, taken up a golden plow-handle, and given scented ointments for the five fingers of the oxen, he fastened golden bags upon their horns;
then, going to the field, he drove them, saying, "Three this way, three that way, one in the middle," and so seven furrows were split open as they went.
As for the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, regarding food, seed-corn, gold, silver, and so forth—
They took as much as they desired from the merchant’s house itself.

Subsequently, when the Blessed One arrived in the city of Bhaddiya, through the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, both the five Great Fortunate Ones and Visākhā, the daughter of the merchant Dhanañjaya, attained the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). This, then, was the power of the merit of those five Great Fortunate Ones.
In brief, however, "success belonging to one who possesses merit" (*puññavato iddhi*) refers to the specific accomplishment that arises when the equipment of merit has reached full maturity.

Regarding the description of success based on knowledge (*vijjāmayiddhi*): they are called "knowledge-bearers" (*vijjādharā*) because they maintain a spell (*vijjā*), such as the *Gandhārī* spell, which is accomplished through ritual application, or one accomplished by mere aspiration, or any other such spell. "Having recited the spell" means having recited the spell according to its prescribed ritual application.
Having turned it over with the mouth. The remainder has the meaning already stated.
In the exposition of the "success through right application" (*sammāpayogiddhi*), because there is no other distinction [to be made] after asking merely for the mode of success, the question "How?
(*kathaṃ*) was asked by one who, without asking "Which?", asks merely for the manner; likewise, the conclusion is "Thus" (*evaṃ*).
It has been said. And here, the textual passage (pāḷi) that follows is similar to the preceding one, insofar as it illustrates right application (*sammāpayoga*) in the sense of practice itself.

However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), it is stated that it includes any kind of arrangement such as forming military arrays like a wagon-formation (*sakaṭabyūha*), any craft-work, any medical practice, the study of the three Vedas, and the study of the three Piṭakas.

Even down to such acts as ploughing and sowing, having performed various deeds and produced specific results, that which arises in various places through the condition of right application is called "success" (iddhi) in the sense of succeeding; thus it is handed down.
The commentary on the discussion of success is finished.
3. Discourse on Clear Comprehension (Abhisamayakathā) Commentary on the Discourse on Clear Comprehension:
Now, following the discourse on psychic power, there is the discourse on clear comprehension, which was spoken by one who intends to show clear comprehension—the supreme form of psychic power.
The commentary on what has not been stated before: therein, *abhisamaya* means the coming together face-to-face (*abhimukha*) with the Truths;
the meaning is "penetration" (*paṭivedha*). When it is asked, "By what does one realize?"—what is meant [by this]?

In such passages from the Suttas as, "Monks, the realization of the Dhamma is of such great benefit," that which is called "realization" (*abhisamaya*), while that realization is occurring, the person who realizes is...
"By what phenomenon does one realize the truths? It means that one approaches them face-to-face and penetrates them.
This, first of all, is the questioner's inquiry. "One realizes them by means of the mind (cittena)"—this response is given because there is no realization apart from the mind.
"If it is so," and so forth, is a further objection. "If" (hañci) has the sense of "if" (yadi). Because it was stated, "by means of the mind," [the objection follows].

"Therefore, one who lacks knowledge realizes [the truth]," he said. "One who lacks knowledge does not realize" is a negation because realization occurs through the mind alone; thus, it is absent in one lacking knowledge. "One realizes by means of knowledge" is the affirmation.
Again, the objection beginning with "But if... arises because of the statement "by means of knowledge," suggesting that one who lacks knowledge is without mind.
"One who is without mind does not realize" is a negation because realization is absent in one who is without mind.

"By means of the mind" and so forth is the admission (*paṭiññā*). Again, "If indeed" and so forth is the challenge (*codanā*) by way of what is common to all knowledge of the mind. This same method applies to the remaining challenges and responses as well.

However, further on, regarding "by means of the mind that has the ownership of action as its object and by means of knowledge," this refers to the mind and knowledge occurring through the principle of the ownership of action—that is, "beings have action as their own.
Regarding "by means of the mind and knowledge conforming to the truths," this refers to the penetration of the truths.
Because of its conformity, it is [accompanied] by the consciousness associated with insight—which is termed "conformable to truth"—and by the knowledge of insight.
How? This is a question arising from the desire to explain how the realization (abhisamaya) occurs.
"Predominance over arising" means that since there is no arising of mental factors in the absence of the arising of consciousness, for consciousness is indeed what grasps the object.
How could the mental factors (cetasika) arising together with that [consciousness] arise if the object were not grasped?

Even in the Abhidhamma, mental factors are analyzed only by way of the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda); therefore, the meaning is "the consciousness that serves as the dominant condition (adhipati) for the arising of path-knowledge.
"Of knowledge" means of path-knowledge. "Cause and condition" means both the producer (janaka) and the supporter (upatthambhaka). "Associated with that" means...
It is associated with that knowledge. "Having cessation as its domain" means having Nibbāna as its object.
"Having vision as its predominant factor" means that because the other [factors] lack the function of seeing, it is the predominant factor in the vision of Nibbāna.
"Of the mind" refers to the mind associated with the Path. "Associated with that" means associated with that mind.
Since this too is a figurative way of speaking— wherein the realization (*abhisamaya*) consists not only of the consciousnesses associated with the knowledges of the mind,
but rather all mental states (*citta-cetasika*) associated with the path are called "realization" by virtue of their accomplishing the task of realizing the Truths—
he, wishing to show this figurative usage as well, asked, "Is the realization only this much? and having rejected that statement with "No," [he continued].
He said, "At the moment of the supramundane path," and so forth. "The clear realization of seeing" (*dassanābhisamaya*) means a clear realization that consists of seeing.

This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. "Truths" (*sacca*) refers to the knowledges of the truths. Path-knowledge itself is "insight" (*vipassanā*) in the sense of contemplating *nibbāna*.

"Liberation" (*vimokkha*) refers to the liberation of the path. "True knowledge" (*vijjā*) is simply path-knowledge. "Deliverance" (*vimutti*) is deliverance by eradication. "*Nibbāna* is clearly realized."
"Abhisamaya" [is so called because] the remaining [factors] realize through these; thus they are "abhisamayas.
Furthermore, in order to show the analysis of abhisamaya by way of the paths and fruits, he said, beginning with "What now," and so forth.

However, at the moment of the fruit (phalakkhaṇa), since the knowledge of destruction (khaye ñāṇa) is not obtained in the sense of total eradication, it is therefore [obtained] in the sense of subsiding (paṭippassaddha).
"Knowledge of non-arising" has been stated. The remainder, however, should be understood according to its respective context.
Now, since the realization (*abhisamaya*) occurs when there is the abandoning of defilements (*kilesappahāna*), and the abandoning of defilements occurs when there is realization, he said "yvāyaṃ...
and so forth, wishing to show the abandoning of defilements preceded by an exhortation. In that passage, "yvāyaṃ" means this noble person (*ariyapuggala*) who stands upon the path.

These four statements beginning with "thus" here are the questions of the challenger. Furthermore, "he abandons past defilements" is the response given for the purpose of providing an opportunity for the challenge. "Exhausted" means exhausted by way of dissolution.
"Cessated" means ceased through non-arising again and again by way of the continuity [of the stream]. "Departed" means gone away from the present moment.
"Vigameti" means he causes it to depart. "Atthaṅgataṃ" means gone to non-existence. "Atthaṅgameti" means he causes it to go to non-existence.
In that context, having pointed out the fault, it is rejected by the statement: "one does not abandon past defilements. Regarding the censure of the future:
"ajātaṃ" (unborn) means not yet reached birth; "anibbattaṃ" (unproduced) means not yet reached its own nature; "anuppannaṃ" (unrisen) means from the point of arising onwards.
It is not one who has entered the path. "Not manifest" means it is not manifest to the mind by way of its present state.
The view that for one abandoning the past and future, effort is fruitless because of the non-existence of what is to be abandoned, is rejected as being both [untenable].
One who is "infatuated" abandons lust; that is, one infatuated with a presently occurring lust abandons that very same lust. This applies even to the defilements that are currently occurring.
The same method applies here. “Firmly established” means having reached a state of stability.
“Black and white” means that unwholesome and wholesome states proceed in union, equally; such is the meaning of what is asserted.
“Defiling” means that when they are thus associated with defilements, the cultivation of the path becomes bound up with defilement; such is the meaning of what is asserted. Thus...
For one who abandons [defilements] in the present, since there exists that which is to be abandoned along with effort, the cultivation of the path would be defiled and effort would be fruitless.
This is because it is impossible for present defilements to be dissociated from the mind.
"Not so" (*na hi*) is a negation of the statement as it was stated in four ways. "It is" (*atthi*) is an admission. How so?
The question is asked for the purpose of showing an illustration of the state of existence (*atthibhāva*).
The meaning is: "In what manner does it exist? In what way does it exist? What is it like that exists? The phrase *seyyathāpi* means "just as if.

The inclusion of the word "young" (*taruṇa*) regarding the tree is for the purpose of indicating its capacity to bear fruit. The term "one whose fruit has not yet arisen" (*ajātaphala*) refers to a time prior to the actual production of fruit, even though the capacity to produce fruit already exists.
*Tamenaṃ taṃ rukkhaṃ*: *enaṃ* is merely a particle; or the meaning is "that very one. *Mūlaṃ chindeyya*:
he would cut it from the root. *Ajātaphalāni*: fruits that have not yet been produced. *Evamevaṃ*: in this very way.

By the four terms—arising (*uppāda*), occurrence (*pavatta*), sign (*nimitta*), and accumulation (*āyūhana*)—only the continuity of the present aggregates (*khandhasantāna*) is expressed. For in whichever continuity of aggregates...

Whatever path-knowledge arises, by that very path-knowledge the continuum of the aggregates (khandha-santāna) becomes seedless with respect to those defilements (kilesa) that are to be abandoned by that path.
Because it has become seedless, due to that condition, those respective defilements, having not yet arisen, do not arise at all.
"Having seen the danger" means having seen the danger from the perspective of impermanence and so forth. By the four terms beginning with "non-arising" (anuppāda), Nibbāna itself is expressed.
"The mind leaps forward" means that the consciousness associated with the Path leaps forward.

"With the cessation of the cause, there is the cessation of suffering" means that with the cessation through non-arising of the continuum which serves as the seed for the defilements, there is the cessation through non-arising of the defilements that serve as the causes for future suffering consisting of the aggregates.
Thus, it is through the cessation through non-arising of the defilements that are the causes of suffering.
There is the non-arising and cessation of suffering. Thus, because the method for abandoning the defilements exists, he said, "there is the development of the path," and so forth.
However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is asked: "What is illustrated by this? It illustrates the abandoning of those defilements that have already arisen on the plane.
But what kind of [defilements] have arisen on the plane? Are they past, future, or present? Only those that have arisen on the plane [are meant]."

Having said "the names," the detailed exposition on the abandoning of the defilements already mentioned should be understood according to the method stated in the commentary on the description of the Truth of the Path within the discourse on knowledge consisting in what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*);
however, in this context, only those defilements that are to be abandoned by the knowledge of the path (*magga-ñāṇa*) are intended.
The commentary on the discourse on clear realization (*abhisamaya*) is finished.
4. Discourse on Discrimination (Vivekakathā). Commentary on the Discourse on Discrimination: 22.
Now, immediately following the discourse on clear realization (*abhisamaya*), which concludes with abandonment, [the author] speaks while demonstrating the mode of abandoning.

A commentary on the previously unstated meaning of the discourse on seclusion that precedes the Suttanta. Therein, in the Suttanta first of all, "whosoever" (*ye keci*) is an exhaustive inclusion of all without remainder.

"Strength-making" (*balakaraṇīyā*) means those things to be performed by the strength of the thighs and the strength of the arms. "Labor" (*kammantā*) refers to tasks such as running, leaping, mowing, and sowing.

"Are being done" (*karīyanti*) means they are performed by those who possess strength. "Depending upon virtue" (*sīlaṃ nissāya*) means depending upon the virtue of the fourfold purification (*catupārisuddhisīla*).
"Having done. Regarding "develops": because there is no development for one whose virtue is broken, what is intended here is the mundane and supramundane development of the path (*maggabhāvanā*).

"Dependent on seclusion" means dependent on the seclusion that is the factor of substitution (*tadaṅgaviveka*), the seclusion that is eradication (*samucchedaviveka*), and the seclusion that is escape (*nissaraṇaviveka*). "Seclusion" (*viveka*) means state of being secluded.
For this yogi engaged in the development of the noble path, at the moment of insight (*vipassanā*), by way of function—

At that time, he develops [concentration] based on seclusion from the limbs [of jhāna], based on seclusion as an escape through his underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*), based on seclusion as abandonment through its function at the moment of the Path, and based on seclusion as an escape through its object.

This same method applies to those based on dispassion (*virāga*) and so forth. For seclusion itself is "dispassion" in the sense of fading away, "cessation" in the sense of stopping, and "relinquishment" in the sense of letting go. Alternatively, [the terms may be explained as follows: *Note: The text provided appears to be a commentary on the stages of concentration development, specifically focusing on the distinctions between different types of seclusion (*viveka*) and their corresponding terms such as dispassion (*virāga*), cessation (*nirodha*), and relinquishment (*vosagga*). The translation reflects the technical Abhidhammic context.*

It is seclusion (*viveka*) because of being secluded from defilements; it is fading away (*virāga*) because of being dispassionate toward defilements; it is cessation (*nirodha*) because of the ceasing of defilements;
and it is relinquishment (*vosagga*) because of the abandoning and letting go of defilements, and because of the letting go of that which is centered on Nibbāna.
Furthermore, relinquishment is twofold: relinquishment as abandonment and relinquishment as leaping forward. Therein, relinquishment as abandonment is...

The abandoning of defilements occurs by way of partial eradication (*tadaṅga*) at the moment of insight (*vipassanā*), and by way of total severance (*samuccheda*) at the moment of the Path (*magga*).
"Leaping forward and relinquishment" refers to leaping forward into Nibbāna through being inclined toward it at the moment of insight, and through making it the object at the moment of the Path.
Both of these are appropriate within this method of explaining the meaning that is mixed with both the mundane and the supramundane. For thus it is:
Each individual factor among right view and the others abandons the defilements and leaps toward Nibbāna in the manner already described.

By this entire expression, "leading to relinquishment" (*vosaggapariṇāmī*), it is meant that it has been directed toward, transformed into, ripened for, and matured in the sense of relinquishment. This [person] too is devoted to the cultivation of the Noble Path.

A bhikkhu develops each individual factor, such as right view and the rest, in such a way that it ripens for the purpose of relinquishing the defilements through renunciation and for the purpose of leaping forward toward Nibbāna through renunciation;
and he develops it in the manner in which it becomes fully matured.
23. "Seed-plant and herb-plant": herein, there is the root-seed, the stem-seed, the joint-seed, the node-seed, and the seed-seed.

The seed is fivefold; "seed-group" (bījagāma) means a collection of seeds. That same [collection], however, from the moment the fully developed green sprout appears, is called the "being-group" (bhūtagāma);
the meaning is a collection of beings (*bhūta*)—that is, of produced things whose roots and green sprouts have come into being.
Since this occurs starting from the time of the green sprout when there is possession by deities, it belongs to those beings reckoned as deities.
They say that even a "village" is a "living village. "Growth" (*vuddhi*) is by way of sprouts and so forth; "increase" (*virūḷhi*) is by way of trunks and so forth;
"expansion" (*vepulla*) is by way of flowers and so forth. Regarding phenomena (*dhamma*), however, "growth" is by way of the arising of a phenomenon not previously arisen;
"increase" is by way of the accomplishment of performing its own function; "expansion" is by way of the fulfillment of its function—the meaning being a state of abundance.
*Vipulattanti pi pāṭho*: "The reading is also *vipulatta*. Alternatively, they apply these three terms to virtue (*sīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*paññā*) as well.

**Commentary on the Description of the Factors of the Path (24)** In the description of the Sutta, the term "right view" (*sammādiṭṭhiyā*) is used in the genitive case. [It refers] to jhāna, insight, the path, the fruit, and nibbāna.

And in the case of the mundane consciousness associated with renunciation, there is right view which—whether by way of association or by way of object—is unified with right view through its common characteristic. "Seclusion by suppression" means seclusion by way of suppressing or by way of distancing.
Of what? Of the hindrances. "He develops the first jhāna," and so forth.
The first jhāna alone is mentioned by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*). When that is mentioned, the remaining jhānas are also effectively mentioned.

Since right view exists within the jhānas as well, there is what is called the "seclusion of right view. "Seclusion by factor" (*tadaṅgaviveka*) means seclusion by means of each respective factor of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "of speculative views" (*diṭṭhigatānaṃ*): because the seclusion from views is difficult to achieve and is the primary task, it is emphasized.
And only seclusion from views has been mentioned. When that is stated, seclusion from the perception of permanence and so forth is also implicitly stated.

"Concentration partaking of penetration" refers to concentration associated with insight (*vipassanā*). "Seclusion by eradication" is seclusion through the complete eradication of the defilements (*kilesa*).
"The supramundane path leading to destruction" refers to the supramundane path leading to *nibbāna*, which is termed destruction. "Seclusion by subsiding" is...
Seclusion by means of the subsiding of the defilements. "Seclusion as an escape" refers to seclusion from formations, which consists in escaping from all that is conditioned.
"He becomes one in whom desire has arisen" means that in the prior stage, desire for the Dhamma has arisen.
"Resolved with faith" means that even in the prior stage, he is resolved through faith. "And his mind is well-established" [means] even in the prior stage...
And his mind, that of the practitioner, becomes well-attended and well-established.
Thus, these three factors—zeal, faith, and mind—are called "supports" because they serve as the decisive support for those who have attained seclusion in the prior stage.
Some, however, say: "His mind being well-attended refers to concentration. This same method applies to dispassion and the other [qualities] as well.
In the section on cessation (*nirodha*), however, by showing a synonym for the word "cessation" other than that term itself, it is called "the deathless element" (*amata-dhātu*).
In the remaining cases, both "cessation" (*nirodha*) and "Nirvana" (*nibbāna*) refer to Nirvana alone. Regarding the "twelve supports" (*nissaya*):
there are twelve supports by taking three each from among the four—seclusion (*viveka*), and so forth—for desire (*chanda*), faith (*saddhā*), and mind (*citta*).
25. The application of the meaning for right intention, effort, mindfulness, and concentration should also be understood by this same method.

However, because right speech, action, and livelihood are absent during the moments of jhāna and insight (vipassanā), it should be understood that these are spoken of as being dependent on jhāna and insight by way of the abstinences occurring in the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga) and the subsequent stage (parabhāga) of jhāna and insight. [Regarding] the hindrances...

It should be understood that for those who have abandoned views, the seclusion, fading away, cessation, and relinquishment of such occurring abstentions are themselves called "seclusion" and so forth. As it is said in the Aṭṭhaka-nipāta:
"Therefore, monk, you should develop this concentration with applied thought and sustained thought;
you should develop it without applied thought and with sustained thought only; you should develop it without applied thought and without sustained thought."
“You should develop it with zest, you should develop it without zest, you should develop it accompanied by rapture, and you should develop it accompanied by equanimity.

Thus, loving-kindness and the rest, as well as the contemplations of the body and so forth, are described as consisting of fourfold and fivefold jhānas by way of concentration rooted in one’s own internal states;
in the same way, it should be understood that here too the abstinences are described by way of their prior and subsequent stages. This is merely a shadow of the literal phrasing.

Having grasped [the meaning], one must not misrepresent the Blessed One. For the word of the Buddha is profound; it should be grasped according to its intended meaning (adhippāya) by attending upon a teacher.
In the sections on the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), the powers (bala), and the faculties (indriya) as well, the meaning should be understood by this same method.
The commentary on the Discourse on Discrimination is finished.
5. The Discourse on Conduct (Cariyākathā):
Commentary on the Discourse on Conduct.
28–29. Now, following the discussion on seclusion (*viveka*), in order to show the means for realizing Nibbāna— which is the ultimate seclusion known as the seclusion of escape (*nissaraṇa-viveka*)—
and likewise to show how one who has realized cessation (*nirodha*) performs deeds for the welfare and happiness of the world,
the discourse on temperament (*cariyā*), although already indicated in the discourse on the faculties (*indriya*), is presented once again.
It has been explained. The commentary on its meaning has already been given in the discussion on the faculties (*indriya*).
The commentary on the discussion of conduct (*cariyā*) is finished.
6. The Discussion on Marvels (*pāṭihāriya*).
Commentary on the Discourse on the Miracles (Pāṭihāriyakathāvaṇṇanā):

30. Now follows the commentary on the new subject matter of the Discourse on the Miracles, which was spoken by the Buddha—preceded by a Sutta—to demonstrate the miracle that concludes the instruction for the welfare of the world, immediately following the discourse on the conduct [of the Bodhisatta] that concludes his career for the welfare of the world.
In that regard, first concerning the Sutta: "Marvels" (*pāṭihāriyāni*) are so called because they ward off opposition (*paccanīka-paṭiharaṇa*).

"The marvel of psychic power" (*iddhipāṭihāriya*): it is "psychic power" (*iddhi*) by way of succeeding (*ijjhanavasena*), and it is a "marvel" (*pāṭihāriya*) by way of warding off; thus, psychic power itself as a marvel is the "marvel of psychic power.

As for the other two, "reading of minds" (*ādesanā*) is so called by way of pointing out (*ādissanavasena*), and "instruction" (*anusāsanī*) is so called by way of teaching (*anusāsanavasena*). The rest is according to the method already stated.
*Idha* means in this world. *Ekacco* means a certain person. The exposition of the miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*) has already been explained above.
*Ādisati nimittena* means he speaks by means of a sign—either a sign of coming, a sign of going, or a sign of standing still.
*Evampi te mano* means "in this way too your mind is"—whether it be joyful or sorrowful, or associated with sensual thoughts and so forth.

Or. The word *api* has the sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍana*). "In this way too, your mind"—this is a description of the various modes even within each single type of consciousness, beginning with that which is accompanied by joy.
"In this way indeed is your mind" means: "Your mind proceeds while contemplating this and that object.
"And even though he points out much"—that is, something other than the mind, such as "this and this."
He speaks much, saying, "It was so," "it is so," or "it will be so. And it is exactly thus, not otherwise;
everything, however it was spoken, becomes exactly so and does not become otherwise.
"But he does not predict by means of a sign" means that even though he knows the sign, he does not speak solely on the basis of the sign alone.
Furthermore, "also" (*api ca*) indicates another method of exposition. "Of humans" (*manussānaṃ*) refers to those humans who know the minds [of others].

"Of non-humans" (*amanussānaṃ*) refers to *yakkhas*, *pisācas*, and so forth, whether they possess supernormal knowledge (*sāvita*) or do not (*assāvita*). "Of deities" (*devatānaṃ*) refers to those such as the Cātumahārājika gods.
"Having heard the sound" (*saddaṃ sutvā*) means having heard the sound of others speaking after knowing their minds. "Again" (*pana*) is a particle used to introduce a new beginning.

"Vitakkayato" means for one who is thinking this or that by means of applied thought (*vitakka*). "Vicārayato" means for one who is examining by means of sustained thought (*vicāra*) associated with applied thought.

"Hearing the sound of the diffusion of applied thought" means hearing the sound of the clamor arising from those who are sleeping, intoxicated, or otherwise negligent due to the force of their applied thought;
it refers to the sound that arises for one who is thinking, by way of that [sound].
“Is your mind thus? and so forth, he says.

The phrase “concentration without initial application and sustained application” (avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhiṃ) is spoken by way of demonstrating the capacity to know even a peaceful mind that is free from the agitation of initial and sustained application;
as for knowing other types of consciousness, there is simply nothing further to be said. “Having encompassed the mind with his own mind” (cetasā ceto paricca).

"He understands" means one who has attained the knowledge of penetration into others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*). "Sir" refers to the Venerable One. "Mental formations have been directed" means that the mental formations—the volitions of the mind—have been established.
"He will direct a thought named so-and-so" means he understands that he will direct or set in motion a wholesome or other type of thought.
And in understanding, he knows by way of the approach, he knows by way of the preliminary stage, and [he knows] the mind within the attainment.
He knows by looking. "He knows by the approach" means that even at the time of the preliminary work for the *kasiṇa*, he knows:
"In whatever manner this person has begun the meditation on the *kasiṇa*, he will produce either the first jhāna, or the second and subsequent jhānas, or the eight attainments.
"He knows by the prior stage" means that as soon as insight (*vipassanā*) has been commenced, he knows thus: "In whatever manner this person..."
He knows: "One who has initiated insight will produce either the path of stream-entry... or the path of arhatship.
Having observed the mind within meditative absorption, he knows by way of the manner in which this person's mental formations have been established:
"Immediately after this particular state of consciousness, this person will direct such-and-such an initial application of thought (vitakka); having emerged from this [absorption],..."
He knows: "For this person there will be either concentration partaking of decline, or partaking of stability, or partaking of distinction, or partaking of penetration;

or he will arouse the direct knowledges. And "even though he speaks much" means that because the knowledge of others' minds takes only the mind and mental factors as its object, he speaks much only by way of the sixteenfold classification beginning with "with lust," and not by way of anything else.
It should be understood. "It is just so" means that this is absolutely just so; for what has been known by way of the knowledge of penetration into others' minds can never be otherwise.
"Think thus" means: think by setting forth thoughts of renunciation and so forth. "Do not think thus."
"Do not think thoughts of sensual desire and so forth; attend thus"—that is, attend precisely to the perception of impermanence, or to one of the others such as the perception of suffering.
"Do not attend thus"—do not attend by way of [perceiving things] as permanent and so forth.
"Abandon this"—abandon this lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure and so forth. This...
"Attain and dwell"—this means: having reached and accomplished precisely that supramundane state (lokuttaradhamma) distinguished by the four paths and fruits, dwell therein.
Now, specifically demonstrating another method regarding the miracle of psychic power (iddhipāṭihāriya), [the Buddha says]: "Renunciation succeeds."

He says, "supernormal power" (*iddhi*), and so forth. Therein, "it overcomes sensual desire" (*kāmacchandaṃ paṭiharati*) means that, being capable, it carries away—that is, abandons—the sensual desire that is its own opposite; thus, that very renunciation (*nekkhamma*) is called a "miracle.
"Those who are endowed with that renunciation" refers to those persons who possess that renunciation which overcomes sensual desire.
They are endowed with it by way of attainment. "With purified minds" means their minds are purified due to the absence of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*).
"With untroubled intentions" means their intentions for renunciation (*nekkhamma-saṅkappa*) are not agitated by intentions for sensual pleasure.

Thus, "the miracle of direct address" (*ādesanā-pāṭihāriya*) means that such an address is performed by one skilled in the minds of others, or by another, or by the Perfectly Enlightened One himself, or by the disciples of the Buddha.

Alternatively, the term *ādesanā-pāṭihāriya* (the miracle of direct address) should be understood by supplying the word *ādesanā* [to the compound] as "direct address" (*ādesana*) and "miracle" (*pāṭihāriya*).
"It should be cultivated in this way" means it should be practiced from the beginning in this manner and in that manner. The same method applies to the remaining three [bases of accomplishment].
"Mindfulness in accordance with that should be established" means mindfulness that is conducive to that renunciation (*nekkhamma*) should be established.

It should be firmly established. Thus, regarding the "miracle of instruction" (*anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya*), the construction should be made here in the same manner as in the construction for the "miracle of mind-reading" (*ādesanā-pāṭihāriya*).
This same method applies to non-ill-will (*abyāpāda*) and the other [immeasurables] as well.

However, the text has been written by abbreviating the jhānas and so forth, and showing only the path to Arahantship at the end. In that regard, for all four paths, the phrase beginning with "thus it should be cultivated" (*evaṃ āsevitabbo*) and so on [is to be understood].
It should be understood that this is stated by way of the preliminary stage, because the path consists of a single moment of consciousness.

For when the practice of repetition and so forth is performed for the sake of producing the path—by means of the mundane path known as "insight leading to emergence," which constitutes the preliminary stage of the path—it should be understood that the path arising through that [insight] is likewise said to have been practiced, developed, and cultivated. (The teachers who maintain the doctrine of universal applicability).
