However, they say that "each individual path consists of sixteen moments. But the establishment of mindfulness in accordance with the Dhamma (tadanudhammatā-sati-upaṭṭhāpana) is indeed appropriate in the preliminary stage.

32. The phrases "supernormal power succeeds again" (*puna nekkhammaṃ ijjhati*), "it is success" (*iddhi*), and so forth, are stated for the purpose of showing that the compound *iddhipāṭihāriya* is a *kammadhāraya* (descriptive determinative) compound.

For when, among the three types of wonders mentioned in the Suttanta, the status of being a compound is stated only for the wonder of supernormal power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*), it implies that the same applies to the other two as well.

"Is it not already stated?"—in this context, it should be understood that the summarized meaning of the miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*), which serves as the foundation, has indeed been stated.
The commentary on the discussion of miracles is finished. 7.
Discussion on Being Equal in Height (*Samasīsaka-kathā*).

Commentary on the Discourse on the Equal-Headedness (Samasīsakathāvaṇṇanā) 33. Now, following the discourse on the miracles, the discourse on equal-headedness— which constitutes the first miracle and is included within the miracle of psychic power— is presented here as well,
for the purpose of illustrating how the state of being "equal-headed" is itself a miracle of psychic power, even though it was already demonstrated in the discourse on knowledge.
It has been spoken again in connection with the miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*). The commentary on its meaning has already been given there.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Equal Head is finished. 8.
The Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
Commentary on the Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhānakathāvaṇṇanā) 34. Now follows the exposition of the new subject matter in the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness—

which was spoken after the "Equal-Headed" discourse (*samasīsaka-kathā*)— preceded by a sutta, and which demonstrates the seven specific contemplations that accomplish the miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*) described by [the author] himself.
In this context, regarding the Sutta first: "four" is a delimitation by number; by that, it indicates the delimitation of the foundations of mindfulness as being neither less than nor more than that.
"These" is the pointing out of what is to be pointed out. "O monks" is an address to the persons who receive the Dhamma. "Foundations of mindfulness":
there are three foundations of mindfulness, which are also the objects of mindfulness; [it refers to] the Teacher’s [teaching] toward disciples who have practiced in three ways.

There is also the sense of "having transcended aversion and attachment. For in such passages as, "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the arising and the passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness," the objective domain of mindfulness is called "foundation of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*). Its meaning is as follows:

it is a foundation (*paṭṭhāna*) because mindfulness is established (*patiṭṭhāti*) therein. What is it that is established? Mindfulness. The foundation of mindfulness is thus the establishment of mindfulness.

Regarding the statement, “The three foundations of mindfulness which the Noble One cultivates, cultivating which the Noble One is worthy to instruct a group,” here the Teacher’s transcendence of aversion and attachment toward disciples who have practiced in three ways is called “foundation of mindfulness.
Its meaning is as follows: it is a “foundation” (paṭṭhāna) because it is to be established; that is, it is to be set in motion. By what is it to be established?

“By means of mindfulness. In the phrase “the establishment of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) is the establishing (*paṭṭhāna*) by means of mindfulness,” it is simply mindfulness that is called “establishment of mindfulness. However, in such passages as “The four establishments of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment,” it is mindfulness itself that is called “establishment of mindfulness.

Its meaning is as follows: it is established (*patiṭṭhāti*), thus it is an “establishment” (*paṭṭhāna*); it stands near (*upaṭṭhāti*), meaning it proceeds by plunging into and leaping forward [toward its object]. It is mindfulness itself.
*Paṭṭhāna* means *satipaṭṭhāna*. Alternatively, it is *sati* in the sense of remembering (*saraṇa*), and *upaṭṭhāna* in the sense of being established (*upaṭṭhāna*).
Thus, because it is both *sati* and that which is *upaṭṭhāna*, it is called *satipaṭṭhāna*. This is what is intended here. If this is so, why is the plural form *satipaṭṭhānā* used?
Because of the multiplicity of mindfulness. For there are many such mindful states due to the diversity of their objects.
"What are the four? is a question asked with the desire to explain. "Here" means in this teaching. "Bhikkhu": he is called a *bhikkhu* because he beholds (*ikkhati*) the fear (*bhaya*) in *saṃsāra*.

As for the commentary on the meaning of the remaining terms, it has already been stated here in the commentary on the description of the Truth of the Path within the discourse on knowledge consisting of what is heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*).
But why did the Blessed One teach exactly four foundations of mindfulness, neither fewer nor more? Because it was for the benefit of those to be trained (*veneyya*).

For among those of craving-temperament (*taṇhācarita*), view-temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*), serenity-vehicle (*samathayānika*), and insight-vehicle (*vipassanāyānika*), who proceed in two pairs according to their dullness and sharpness, the path of purification for the one of dull craving-temperament is the foundation of mindfulness of body-contemplation (*kāyānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna*) which is gross;

for the sharp one, it is the foundation of mindfulness of feeling-contemplation (*vedanānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna*) which is subtle. For the one of dull view-temperament as well, it is that which has not reached too much differentiation.

For one whose vehicle is serenity (*samathayānika*) and who is dull-witted, the first foundation of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), which has the sign as its object that is easily attained, is the path to purification;
for one who is sharp-witted, the second [foundation], because it does not settle upon a coarse object, is the path. For one whose vehicle is insight (*vipassanāyānika*) as well—
For one of dull faculty, the third has an object that is not excessively analyzed; for one of sharp faculty, the fourth has an object that is excessively analyzed.
Thus, exactly four are taught, neither fewer nor more.

Or alternatively, they are for the purpose of abandoning the perversions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self. For the body is indeed impure, and therein beings are perverted by the perversion of beauty.
Beings. For the purpose of abandoning that perversion by means of seeing the nature of foulness therein, the first foundation of mindfulness was taught for them.

Furthermore, although feelings and so forth are grasped as "pleasure," "permanent," and "self," feeling is actually suffering, the mind is impermanent, and mental phenomena are non-self; and beings are perverted regarding these by way of the perversions of pleasure, permanence, and self.
By showing the state of suffering and so forth regarding those [objects], the remaining three [foundations of mindfulness] were taught for the purpose of abandoning those distortions (*vipallāsa*).
Thus, they were taught as four precisely for the purpose of abandoning the distortions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self.

Furthermore, it should be understood that they were taught as four not only for the purpose of abandoning the distortions, but also for the purpose of abandoning the four floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), taints (*āsava*), ties (*gantha*), and clingings (*upādāna*), as well as for the purpose of fully understanding the four kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*).
35. (Ka) In the exposition of the Suttanta, "the earth-body" (*pathavīkāya*) refers to the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*) within this physical body.

However, because there are many instances of the earth element throughout the entire body, the term "body" (*kāya*) is used in the sense of a collection (*samūha*) in order to include all instances of the earth element.
The same principle applies to the water-body (*āpokāya*) and the others as well. Because there are also many hairs and so forth, the term "hair-body" (*kesakāya*) and so on is employed.
However, it should be understood that the kidneys and so forth are not included because, being limited in scope, they do not warrant inclusion under the term "body.
(Kha) Regarding the phrases "pleasant feeling" and so on: "pleasant feeling" refers to either bodily or mental pleasant feeling;
likewise for "painful feeling. "Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling," however, refers exclusively to the mental feeling of equanimity (*upekkhā*).
"Sensual pleasant feeling" refers to the six types of joyful feelings based on the household life. "Spiritual pleasant feeling" refers to the six types of joyful feelings based on renunciation.
"Sensual painful feeling" refers to the six types of sorrowful feelings based on the household life.
"Spiritual painful feeling" refers to the six types of sorrowful feelings based on renunciation. "Sensual neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling..."

"Feeling" refers to the six kinds of feeling based on worldly equanimity (*upekkhā*). "Spiritual feeling that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant" refers to the six kinds of feeling based on renunciation (*nekkhamma*).
(Ga) "The mind with lust," and so forth, have their meanings explained in the discussion on knowledge (*ñāṇakathā*).
(Gha) "The remaining phenomena" refers to those phenomena belonging to the three planes (*tebhūmaka*) other than those [already mentioned] regarding the body, feeling, and mind. In all cases...
"By that knowledge" means by that sevenfold knowledge of contemplation (*anupassanā-ñāṇa*).
Furthermore, those meanings not stated here and there in between have already been explained in their respective places below.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness (*Satipaṭṭhāna-kathā*) is finished.
9. Discourse on Insight (Vipassanākathā). Commentary on the Discourse on Insight: 36.
Now, immediately following the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness connected with insight, [the author discusses] the classification of insight.
This is a commentary on a previously unstated point regarding the discourse on insight preceded by the discourses spoken by the Buddha.

Therein, in the discourse (*suttanta*), the term "that" (*so*)—being a pronoun—includes everyone, whether it refers to "he" (*yo*) or "she" (*sā*). The word "vatā" is a particle used in the sense of emphasis.
"Any formation whatsoever" (*kañci saṅkhāraṃ*) means even the slightest formation. Regarding the phrase "conformable acceptance" (*anulomikāya khantiyā*): here...
Insight-knowledge itself conforms to the supramundane path, thus it is "conformable" (*anulomika*); with reference to that very conformability, these [knowledges] are called "conformable.
All conditioned phenomena are "endured" (*khamanti*)—that is, accepted—as impermanent, suffering, and non-self; hence they are "acceptance" (*khanti*).
This acceptance is threefold: weak, medium, and sharp. It begins with the comprehension by groups (*kalāpasammasana*) and ends with the knowledge of rise and fall (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*).

Gentle and conformable patience. The middle, conformable patience consists of the knowledge of equanimity toward formations, beginning with the contemplation of dissolution and ending with that knowledge.
Sharp, conformable patience is the knowledge of conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*). "Endowed" means possessed.

"This state is not possible" means that this aforementioned state or cause does not exist. Regarding "the certainty of rightness" (*sammatta-niyāma*), here [it refers to] that which brings about welfare and happiness...

It is "rightness" (*sammatta*) because it is rightly so for one who aspires thus, "May it be mine," because it arises exactly in that way, and because there is the occurrence of non-erroneous [perception] such as "the foul" in regard to the foul and so forth.
It is "certainty" (*niyāma*) because it constitutes the fixed course (*niyāma*) for the arising of Arahantship by yielding its immediate fruit;
the meaning is "decision. Being both rightness and certainty, it is "rightness-certainty" (*sammattaniyāma*). What is that? The supramundane path.
In particular, however, it is the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). For, because one becomes fixed by way of that path, it is said: "one is fixed with enlightenment as one's destination.
The meaning is that it is impossible for such a person to enter—that is, to penetrate—that rightness-of-orientation (sammatta-niyāma).

But since the state of lineage (gotrabhū) stands in the place of the preliminary adverting (āvajjana) for the path, setting that aside, the entry into rightness-of-orientation occurs immediately after the conformity-patience (anulomika-khanti).

It should be understood that it is "said. Alternatively, since among the eighteen great insights (*mahāvipassanā*), change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu*) is the contemplation of turning away (*vivaṭṭanānupassanā*), it is included within conformity-acceptance (*anulomikakhanti*) itself.
The meaning in all four discourses (*suttanta*) should be understood according to this same method.
By way of these—conformity-acceptance, rightness-of-nature (*sammatta*), the fixed course of rightness (*niyāma*), and the four noble fruits (*ariyaphala*)—there are six factors.
In the Chapter on Sixes (Chakkanipāta), four discourses (suttanta) are taught. For there are indeed four discourses by way of the two sides:

the dark side and the bright side. Regarding the exposition of the discourses that begins with the question "In how many ways," one who has begun insight meditation by means of the comprehension of aggregates (kalāpasammasana)—having discerned both name-and-form and the conditions for name-and-form in such passages as "the five aggregates are impermanent"—[proceeds].
The practitioner of yoga sees each individual aggregate among the five aggregates as impermanent by way of its impermanence and finitude, and by way of its having a beginning and an end;
as suffering by way of its oppression by arising and passing away, and by way of its being a basis for suffering;

as a disease by way of its dependence on conditions, and by way of its being the root of disease; and [as a boil] by way of its association with the sting of suffering, its oozing of the filth of defilements, and its arising, aging, and dissolution.
As a boil (*gaṇḍa*) because of its being swollen, ripened, and burst; as a dart (*salla*) because of its producing pain, its piercing within, and its being difficult to extract;
as misfortune (*agha*) because of its being censurable, its bringing about non-prosperity, and its being a basis for calamity;

as affliction (*ābādha*) because of its producing a state of lack of mastery and its being the proximate cause of disease; and as "other" (*para*) because of its being uncontrollable and not subject to one's will, [and] because of sickness, aging, and death.
It is "disintegrating" (*paloka*) because of its state of breaking down and crumbling away; it is "an affliction" (*īti*) because it brings about manifold calamities;
it is "a disaster" (*upaddava*) because it brings about vast, unknown misfortunes and serves as the basis for all calamities;
it is "a danger" (*bhaya*) because it is the source of all fears and because it is the opposite of the supreme consolation known as the subsiding of suffering. By many...
It is "an affliction" (upasagga) because it is like an external calamity due to being pursued by misfortunes, being beset by faults, and being unfit for endurance;
it is "fickle" (cala) because of its instability caused by disease, old age, death, and the worldly conditions such as greed;

it is "perishable" (pabhaṅgu) because of its inherent nature to fall into dissolution through both external assault and internal spontaneity; and it is [devoid of] stability because it falls into every possible state.
Because it is non-existent and impermanent; because it does not provide refuge and offers no security, it is without shelter;

because it is unworthy of being relied upon and fails to perform the function of a refuge even for those who rely on it, it is without a haven; because it lacks the quality of being a support that removes fear for those who depend on it, it is without a resort;
and because it is empty of the qualities of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and self as they are imagined, it is void. Precisely because of this emptiness...

It is "void" (*tuccha*) because it is empty or because it is insignificant; for even that which is insignificant in the world is called "void. It is "empty" (*suñña*) because it is devoid of a master, an inhabitant, an experiencer, a doer, or a controller.

It is "non-self" (*anattā*) because it itself lacks the state of being a master and so forth. It is "disadvantageous" (*ādīnava*) because of the suffering inherent in its occurrence and because of the peril of suffering.
Alternatively, it is "disadvantageous" (*ādīnava*) because it "goes toward" (*vāti*) or proceeds toward misfortune (*ādi*); this is a term for a wretched person.
It is "from the disadvantage" because of the similarity in their nature as disadvantages, such as the aggregates being merely miserable.

It is "of a nature to change" because it is subject to transformation in two ways: through aging and through death. It is "insubstantial" because of its weakness and its susceptibility to being broken like soft wood-pith.
It is "the root of misfortune" because it is the cause of misfortune. It is "murderous" because it betrays trust, like a treacherous friend with a smiling face.

It is "from non-existence" because it is free from becoming and has arisen from the absence of becoming. It is "with taints" because it is the basis for the taints (*āsava*). It is "conditioned" because it is constructed by causes and conditions.
It is "the bait of Māra" because it serves as the material sustenance for the Māra of death and the Māra of defilements.

It is "subject to birth, aging, sickness, and death" because its nature is birth, aging, sickness, and death. It is "subject to sorrow, lamentation, despair, and anguish" because it is the cause of sorrow, lamentation, despair, and anguish.
He sees them as defiled phenomena because they possess the nature of objects for the defilements of craving, views, and misconduct.
And in all these instances, the word "sees" (*passati*) should be understood as an ellipsis.

38. Regarding the phrase "in the five aggregates," although this refers to a collection, the commentary on the meaning is given according to each individual aggregate in the description of the knowledge of comprehension by groups (*kalāpasammasana-ñāṇa*).
It should be understood that [the term "five aggregates"] is used because the contemplations are enumerated individually according to each aggregate at the beginning and at the end;
and because words that function for a whole can also function for its parts.
Alternatively, it is stated as "five aggregates" by way of summarizing the individual contemplations that have occurred separately into one.

It should be understood that either the simultaneous comprehension of the five aggregates is appropriate— given the presence of the commentarial statement, "He emerges from the five aggregates all at once"—

or else [the process occurs] by way of the knowledge of the state of peace (*santipada-ñāṇa*) at the time of insight, according to the method described in the exposition of the knowledge of danger (*ādīnava-ñāṇa*), such as: "One sees the cessation of the five aggregates as permanent Nibbāna."

One who perceives Nibbāna as permanent enters the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*). One enters it at the moment of the Path (*magga-khaṇa*), whereas at the moment of the Fruit (*phala-khaṇa*) one is said to have already entered.
This same method applies to all expressions concerning the entry into certainty. "Health" (*ārogya*) means that which has become health;

"thornless" (*visalla*) means devoid of the thorn. This same method applies to such terms as these. "Freedom from affliction" (*anābādha*) means devoid of affliction, that which is the opposite of affliction.
Or [the particle] *vā*. This method applies to such cases as well. "Not dependent on another" (*aparappaccaya*) means being devoid of any other condition.

Some read it by combining the two terms *upassaggato* and *anupassagga*. "Supreme emptiness" (*paramasuñña*) is so called because it is empty of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) and because it is the highest.

"The ultimate goal" (*paramattha*) is the supreme object because it is the pinnacle of both the conditioned and the unconditioned. [This is stated] by way of a change in grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*).
This is in the neuter gender. Because of the emptiness and selflessness of *nibbāna*, the reverse method of explanation is not stated for these two [terms].
"Untainted" (*anāsava*) means free from the taints (*āsava*). "Unworldly" (*nirāmisa*) means free from worldly material things (*āmisa*).

"Unborn" (*ajāta*) means unarisen because it is devoid of birth. "Deathless" (*amata*) means free from death because of the absence of dissolution; for even "death" is called "the dead" (*mata*) by way of the neuter gender expression.

39. Thus, when these forty contemplations have been explained in their successive order as distinguished by various modes, [the author], grouping them into only three contemplations by way of their inclusion within their intrinsic natures, says:
"As impermanence" (*aniccato*), meaning "contemplation of impermanence" (*aniccānupassanā*), and so forth.
Among those, the application should be made to impermanence, suffering, and non-self (*anattatā*) according to what is appropriate for each. At the end, however, these are enumerated individually.
...shown. Among the enumerations, in accordance with the sequence of counting, the contemplation of non-self (*anattānupassanā*) is counted first.

Therein, "twenty-five" refers to twenty-five contemplations of non-self across the five aggregates, by taking five for each aggregate according to the formula: "as alien, as hollow, as vain, as empty, and as non-self. "Fifty" refers to [fifty] by way of "as impermanent, as disintegrating..."
“Because it is moving, perishable, unstable, subject to change, coreless, disintegrating, conditioned, and subject to death”— thus,
by taking ten aspects for each aggregate, there are fifty contemplations of impermanence across the five aggregates.
As for the phrase “one hundred and twenty-five,” the remaining [contemplations], beginning with “as suffering, as a disease,” and so forth, consist of twenty-five for each aggregate.
Having performed the contemplation of suffering in the five aggregates as two hundred and fifty, one should understand the connection thus:

"those which are proclaimed regarding suffering" refers to those contemplations of the fivefold aggregate of suffering that are proclaimed by way of enumeration, and they are precisely two hundred and fifty.
Furthermore, in this context, "yāni" (which) should be understood as a change in grammatical gender.
The commentary on the Discourse on Insight (Vipassanākathā) is finished.
10. Commentary on the Discourse on the Schedule (Mātikākathā).

40. Now, immediately after the discourse on insight (*vipassanā*), the Great Elder, desiring to praise through various methods and diverse aspects the phenomena of serenity (*samatha*), insight (*vipassanā*), the path (*magga*), and Nibbāna as set forth throughout the entire *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, first set forth nineteen matrix headings (*mātikā*) beginning with "free from hunger" (*nicchāto*).
He then delivered what is known as the "Commentary on the Matrix" (*Mātikākathā*) by way of explaining those headings. This is the commentary on their previously unstated meaning.
First, regarding the *mātikā*: "unfaded" (*nicchāta*) means unshrivelled (*amilāta*). For all defilements (*kilesa*) are shrivelled because they are associated with affliction.
Even lust (*rāga*), when it proceeds uninterruptedly, burns the body; how much more so other defilements? Furthermore, in the passage, “Bhikkhus, there are these three fires:

the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion,” only the three primary defilements are mentioned as the leaders of the defilements; however, those associated with them are also included.
They indeed burn away. Thus, due to the absence of the defilements of hunger (*chātaka-kilesa*), one is "free from hunger" (*nicchāta*).
Who is this? In connection with liberation (*vimokkha*), it should be understood as "liberation. It is called *mokkha* because one is released (*muccati*);

the meaning is that it is *vimokkha* because one is fully released (*vimuccati*). This is one heading (*mātikāpada*). "Knowledge and liberation" (*vijjā-vimutti*) means knowledge itself is liberation; this is one heading. "Meditative absorption and liberation" (*jhāna-vimokkha*) means meditative absorption itself...
Liberation (*vimokkho*). This is one matrix heading (*mātikāpada*). The remaining ones are each single [terms]; thus, there are nineteen matrix headings in total. 41.

"By means of renunciation (*nekkhamma*), one is free from hunger regarding sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*)," means that because the yogi has departed from sensual desire by means of renunciation, he is free from defilement (*nikkileso*) regarding sensual desire.
The liberation obtained through that renunciation is also "free from hunger" and "free from defilement. The same applies to the remaining [terms].
"By means of renunciation (*nekkhamma*), one is liberated from sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*); thus it is called 'liberation' (*vimokkha*).

The meaning is that because the yogi is liberated from sensual desire by means of renunciation, that renunciation is "liberation. The same applies to the remaining [terms]. "It exists" (*vijjati*) means "clear knowledge" (*vijjā*).

The meaning is that it is called "clear knowledge" because it exists, is present, and is found as an intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). Alternatively, it is so called because it is sought by yogis who have entered the path for the purpose of knowing the intrinsic nature.
The meaning is that it is called "knowledge" (*vijjā*) because one experiences and knows its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
Alternatively, the meaning is that it is called "knowledge" because it is experienced and attained by yogis who have entered the path for the sake of attaining distinction.

Alternatively, the meaning is that it is called "knowledge" because one finds and attains the ground that is to be found by oneself. Alternatively, because it is the cause for seeing the intrinsic nature, the intrinsic nature is known.
The meaning is: "it makes known," thus it is called *vijjā* (clear vision). "While making known, one is liberated; while being liberated, one makes known.

Thus, the aforementioned phenomenon (*dhamma*), existing in the sense stated, is liberated from that which was stated; and while being liberated from that which was stated, it exists in the sense stated—this is the meaning of "liberation through clear vision" (*vijjāvimutti*).
"In the sense of restraint regarding sensual desire" means that renunciation is called "purity of virtue" (sīlavisuddhi) in the sense of warding off sensual desire;
this is the meaning. Because it is the cause of non-distraction, that same [renunciation] is "purity of mind" (cittavisuddhi) in the sense of non-distraction.

Because it is the cause of seeing, it is "purity of view" (diṭṭhivisuddhi) in the sense of seeing. The same method applies to the remaining [purifications] as well. "It calms" means by means of renunciation and so forth.
The meaning is that the state of renunciation and so forth is called "tranquility" (passaddhi) because the practitioner causes sensual desire and the rest to subside.

"Because they have been abandoned" means because they have been abandoned by this or that specific abandonment. "Knowledge in the sense of having known" means that renunciation and so forth are called "knowledge" in the sense of having known by way of the reviewing of jhāna, by way of insight (vipassanā), and by way of the reviewing of the path.
"Seeing" (*dassana*) is so called because of having seen (*diṭṭhattā*); here too, the method is the same. "He is purified" (*visujjhati*) refers to the practitioner (*yogī*);

purification consists of renunciation (*nekkhamma*) and so forth. In the exposition of renunciation: renunciation is an escape (*nissaraṇa*) because, through non-greed, it has escaped from sensual lust; thus it is "renunciation" (*nekkhamma*) because it has gone out from that.
When it is said, "This is the escape from forms, namely renunciation," [it refers to] a specific distinction of the formless (*āruppa*).
This is called "formless" (*ārūppa*) precisely in the same sequence as the textual passage stated elsewhere, for the purpose of showing the distinction that is not otherwise visible.
And that formlessness is called "renunciation" (*nekkhamma*) because it has emerged from form; this is stated by way of the specific context.
"Becoming" (*bhūta*) is an indication of its association with arising. "Conditioned" (*saṅkhata*) shows the particularity of the power of conditions. "Dependently arisen" (*paṭiccasamuppanna*)...
Even when conditions are assembled, this demonstrates the inactive nature of those conditions.
"Cessation is its renunciation" means that because it has emerged from that conditioned state, Nibbāna is called the renunciation of that conditioned state.
The mention of both the formless (āruppa) and cessation (nirodha) is made according to the sequence stated elsewhere in the text: "The renunciation of sensual desire is renunciation."
If it were stated [again], it would be redundant. Furthermore, since its renunciation (*nekkhamma*) is already established by the word "renunciation" itself, that [word] was not mentioned;

rather, only the remaining forms of renunciation were stated. That is straightforward. In the exposition of "escape" (*nissaraṇa*) as well, the meaning should be understood according to this same method.
However, herein, the elements conducive to escape (*nissaraṇīyā dhātuyo*) are explicitly stated as "renunciation. As for "seclusion" (*paviveka*):
The state of seclusion consists precisely of renunciation (*nekkhamma*) and the rest. One who relinquishes is a "yogi" (*yogī*); renunciation and the rest are the "relinquishing" (*vosagga*).

When a yogi brings about renunciation, he is said to "conduct himself by means of renunciation. That renunciation, moreover, is a "practice" (*cariyā*). This same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well.
What ought to be said regarding the exposition of the jhānas and liberations has already been stated in the discussion on liberation (*vimokkhakathā*). Only there...

It was stated that "jhāna-vimokkha" means "he knows," but here, the teaching is presented by way of a person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), namely, "he knows" and "he meditates" (jhāyati); this is the distinction.

Furthermore, in the exposition on life devoted to development (bhāvanādhiṭṭhānajīvitaniddesa), the teaching is likewise presented by way of a person; however, from the perspective of the dhamma itself—
"Bhāvanā" (development) means precisely renunciation and the rest. "Adhiṭṭhāna" (resolution) means the mind itself established by way of renunciation and the rest.
"Jīvita" (livelihood) means the right livelihood of one whose mind is established by way of renunciation and the rest. What is this so-called "right livelihood"?
It is the abstention from wrong livelihood and the effort in seeking requisites through the Dhamma and in accordance with justice. Therein, "justice" (samaṃ) [is as follows:]...
"He lives rightly" (*sammaṃ jīvati*) means he lives with evenness; it is either a neuter abstract noun or it is said that he lives by means of evenness.
"Not unevenly" (*no visamaṃ*) establishes a restriction by way of negating the very meaning already stated as "he lives rightly.
"Rightly" (*sammā*) is an indication of the manner. "Not wrongly" (*no micchā*) is its specific determination. "He lives purified" (*visuddhaṃ jīvati*)...
He lives a life purified by natural purity. "It is not defiled" is a restriction referring specifically to that [life].
With the words "Whatever it may be," etc., he shows the benefit of the three kinds of excellence already mentioned. In this context, "whatever it may be" means whichever one it is.
"An assembly of khattiyas" is a gathering of khattiyas; for they sit down (sīdanti) on all sides there, having no prior understanding.
"Assembly" (parisā) is what is meant. The same method applies to the other three [classes of assemblies].
Because they alone possess both the excellence of lineage and the excellence of knowledge—namely, the khattiyas and so forth—only those four are mentioned, and not the assembly of the *suddas*.

"Confident" (*visārada*) means endowed with the threefold perfection, free from timidity; the meaning is "fearless. "Not cowed" (*amaṅkubhūta*) means not shrinking back, not having become devoid of luster.
"Taṃ kissa hetū" means: "By what cause, by what reason, does that confidence exist?"—this is the meaning. Now, "tathā hi" is the statement of the reason for that.
Since he is thus endowed with the threefold perfection, therefore [the Blessed One] concluded by showing the cause of the state of confidence, saying: "he is confident."
The explanation of the Discourse on the Matrix in the *Saddhammappakāsinī*,
the commentary on the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, is completed.
The explanation of the Chapter on Wisdom is completed.
The commentary on the Cūḷavagga is completed. And with this,
the commentary on the meaning of the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*— which comprises three sections and is adorned with thirty discourses— is finished.
The Concluding Discourse:
The Mahāvagga, the Majjhima, and the Cūḷavagga by name—
these three chapters have been recited here according to their measure and sequence.
In each chapter, ten discourses have been proclaimed;
these summary verses (uddānagāthā) follow them in their proper order for all of them:
Knowledge, View, Mindfulness of Breathing, the Faculties, and Liberation as the fifth.
Destiny, action, perversion, the path, and the circle—these are the ten.
The yoke-and-fetter, the truths, the factors of enlightenment, loving-kindness, and dispassion as the fifth;
The analytical knowledges, the wheel of Dhamma, the supramundane, the powers, and emptiness.
Wisdom, supernormal power, clear realization, seclusion, and conduct as the fifth;
the miracle, the "equal-headed" state, mindfulness, and insight are the matrix.
This [work] belongs to those who have heard the Sugata, by one who has become their sovereign and who delights in the welfare of beings.
This commentary on the meaning of the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, which was spoken by the Elder endowed with steadfast virtues,
has been undertaken by me based upon the method of the ancient commentaries as well as logical reasoning, and it has now reached its conclusion.
That Uttaramantī, endowed with the virtues of wisdom and possessed of faith,
caused a monastic cell (pariveṇa) of manifold noble qualities to be built within the Mahāvihāra.
While the Elder Mahābhidhāna was residing there, this [work] was brought to completion.
In the third year after the passing of King Moggallāna,
the elders— who were lamps of the Theravāda— completed this commentary, which generates welfare for the world, in accordance with the proper occasion.
May all beings, conforming to the Dhamma and accomplishing their own welfare and the welfare of others,
reach their goal just as they desire. By those skilled in calculation,
[this has been done] here for the commentary that elucidates the True Dhamma.
The recitation sections (bhāṇavāra) have been calculated as fifty-eight;
they should be understood thus. When counted according to the *anuṭṭhubha* meter and its metrical composition, however, the verses number fourteen thousand and five hundred.
Out of reverence, for the sake of the long endurance of the Dispensation and for the welfare of the world,
I have composed this work; whatever abundant and no small merit has been acquired by me through this,
may the world, by that merit, [partake] of the elixir of the True Dhamma of the One Possessed of Ten Powers.
"Having enjoyed the stainless [Dhamma], may they attain happiness through happiness itself.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* treatise, titled *Saddhammappakāsinī*.
